lawyer:
Muhammad Ohiullah, Advocate ----- For the Petitioner. 
lsrat Jahan, DAG ----- For the Respondents.
parties:
Pacific Ocean Lines  ----- Petitioner
Vs.
Government of Bangladesh & others   ----- Respondents
full_judgment:
Shahidul Karim J : By this Rule the respondents were called upon to show cause as to why the order as contained in নথি নং ৫ম (১)১২/কাস/আপীল/চট্ট 2030/2544 dated 15-7-2010 (Annexure- G) issued by respondent No. 2 on behalf of respondent No. 1 directing the petitioner to deposit 50% of the penalty amount in cash in the appeal pending before respondent No.' I arising out of Adjudication Order No. 15 dated 4-1-2010 passed by Respondent: No. 5 should not be declared to have been passed without lawful authority and is of no legal effect and as to why the aforesaid appeal should be not heard and disposed of accepting the bank Guarantee already furnished by the petitioner for the entire penalty amount before respondent No.1 and/or pass such other or further order or orders as to this Court may seem fit and proper.

2. Facts relevant, for the purpose of disposal of the Rule are, In brief, that the petitioner is a proprietorship firm and is engaged in the business of a shipping agent and do all kinds of acts, things and deeds relating thereto. The petitioner is also the shipping agent of the vessel MT Pujawatt' which arrived at Chittagong port on 21-5-2008 with a cargo of 11,500 metric tons of Crude Degummed Soyabean Oil (CDSO). Upon arrival of the said vessel at the outer anchorage of the Chittagong port, an ullage survey was carried out by a qualified Government surveyor in presence of all including the customs officer on duty on board the vessel and a quantity of 11,478.119 metric tons of CDSO was ascertained on board the vessel prior to discharging of the cargo therefrom. Thereupon, the entire quantity of the said Crude Degummed Soyabean Oil (CDSO) was discharged by the vessel in full in to the shore tanks at the port of Chittagong and there remained no cargo of CDSO on board the vessel. ' On completion of the discharge of the entire quantity of CDSO into the shore tanks, the tanks of the vessel were inspected and checked by all the parties concerned including the customs officer on duty on board the vessel and a Dry. Tank Certificate certifying as to the dryness and emptiness of the tanks was issued. Subsequently, the Respondent No.4 issued a letter of call dated 19-11-2008. to the petitioner relating to a short- landed quantity of 31.080 metric tons of CDSO from the vessel when the petitioner submitted its explanations by giving its comments on the alleged shortage of CDSO. Thereafter; the Adjudication Officer i.e. the Respondent No.4 however most illegally and without considering the explanations of the petitioner arbitrarily imposed a penalty of Taka 8,15,667 for the alleged short-landed quantity of 31.080 metric tons of CDSO. Against the aforesaid order the petitioner preferred an appeal under section 193 of the Customs Act, 1969 together with an application praying for dispensation of the deposit or the. penalty amount before the hearing of the appeal. The Respondent No.3 however vide its letters dated 20-6-2010 and 6-7-2010 called upon the petitioner to deposit the entire amount of Taka 8,15,667 within 10 days. But due to financial hardship, the petitioner submitted a Bank Guarantee covering the entire penalty amount in favour of the Respondent No. 1. Thereafter, the Respondent No.2 vide letter dated 15-7-2010 most illegally and arbitrarily directed the petitioner to deposit the penalty amount by way of 50% in cash and 50% in Rank Guarantee, failing which the appeal would be rejected.

3. Feeling aggrieved by and dissatisfied with the above action of the respondents, the petitioner finding no other efficacious remedy moved this Court and obtained the present Rule.

4. Mr Muhammad Ohidullah, learned Advocate appearing on behalf of the petitioner submits that since financial hardship was asserted and a bank guarantee was submitted by the petitioner covering the entire penalty amount, the respondents ought to have accepted the same in exercise of the discretion vested upon them by the 2nd proviso of section 194 of the Customs Act, 1969. But inspite of doing that, the respondents No.2 most illegally and arbitrarily directed the petitioner to deposit the penalty amount by way of 50% in cash and 50% in Bank guarantee and made the same a condition precedent of acceptance of the appeal ignoring the fact that the petitioner is a mere agent of the vessel in question who does not hold any fund from the principal as well as the very fact of his financial hardship" Referring to the case of Rainbow shipping Lines vs Collector of Cus toms, 53 DLR 408,. Seabon Shipping Ltd. vs Commissioner of Customs, 6 BLC 516, Sentrans Maritime (Bd) limited vs The Commissioner of Customs, 6 MLR 2001,249 and Ocean Trade Ltd. vs The Commissioner of Customs, Excise and VAT, 11 BLT 2003, 438 Mr Ohidullah lastly submits that in a number cases similar issue of filing appeal before the commissioner of customs on furnishing. 100% Bank. Guarantee of the penalty amount was raised and settled by this Court and since the petitioner standing -on the same footing, his case can be dealt with in the like manner.

5. Ms Israt Jahan, learned Deputy Attorney- General opposes the Rule.

6. We have heard the learned Advocate for the petitioner as well as the learned Deputy Attorney-General and perused the writ petitioner along with the annexures and also considered the facts and circumstances of the case.

7. Admittedly, the petitioner firm is the shipping agent of the vessel in question, namely, MT PUJAWATT which was penalized by the custom authority for alleged of short-landed of 31,080 metric tons of CDSO. Materials on record clearly show that the petitioner preferred an appeal against the above adjudication order to the Respondent No. 1 along with an application praying for dispensation of the deposit of the penalty amount before the hearing of the appeal. Subsequently, the petitioner furnished' a bank guarantee for Taka 8,15,667 issued by Hongkong and Shanghai Banking Corporation Limited, Dhaka being No. GTEDAK. 105434 dated 31-5- 2010 covering the entire penalty amount in favour of respondent No. 1 together with an application for acceptance of the same. It Appears further from annexure-C that in Para 11 of the Memo of Appeal the petitioner disclosed that as the agent of the ship in question they did not hold any fund from its foreign principal as well as they had been subjected to manifold miseries for which making deposit of entire penalty amount in cash is not possible on its part. But in-spite of that, as it appears for annexure-G, the respondent No.2 directed the petitioner to deposit 50% of the penalty amount in cash and 50% by way of Bank Guarantee within next 10 (ten) days from 15-7- 2010, failing which the appeal preferred by the petitioner would be rejected considering the same to be incomplete. Annexure-G does not show any consideration of any hardship as to deposit. of 50% penalty in cash, instead without exercising the discretion the respondent No.2 has arbitrarily issued the said annexure which is not sustainable in law.

8. In this context it would be profitable for refer to section 194 of the Customs Act which reads as under:

"194. Deposit, Pending appeal, of duty demanded or penalty levied-(1) Any person desirous of appealing under section 193 or section 196A against any decision or order relating to any duty demanded in respect of goods which have ceased to be under the control of customs authorities or to any penalty levied under this Act shall, at the time of filing his appeal or if he is so permitted by. the appellate authority at any later stage before the consideration of the appeal, deposit with the appropriate officer fifty percent of the duty demanded or fifty percent of the penalty imposed, or both, as the case may be:

Provided that such person may, instead of depositing the amount of the penalty as aforesaid deposit only fifty percent thereof and furnish a guarantee from a scheduled bank for the due payment of the balance:

Provided further that where, in any particular case, the appellate authority is of the opinion that the deposit of duty demanded or penalty imposed will cause undue hardship to the appellant, it may dispense with such deposit, either unconditionally or subject to such conditions as it may deem fit to impose. (2) ……………	"

<u>9. From a plain reading of the aforesaid provisions of law it appears manifestly that 2nd proviso of section 194 of the said Act has given discretion upon the appellate authority to dispense with the deposit of the penalty amount either conditionally or unconditionally on the ground of undue hardship of the appellant. Since financial hardship was asserted on behalf of the petitioner claiming that they did not hold any fund from its principal and as 100% Bank guarantee was submitted for the entire penalty amount, the respondent No. 2 could have exercised his discretion by accepting the said Bank guarantee. Refusing to exercise such discretion by the respondent No.2 has 'rendered his action unjust and not sustainable in law. It reveals further from the materials on record that the matter in issue in the instant case has already been settled by this Division on a number of occasions.</u>

10. In the case of Rainbow Shipping Lines vs Collector of Customs, 53 DLR 408, it was observed as follows:

"It appears from annexures that the petitioner has stated the hardship in paying the 50% penalty in cash and also furnished Bank guarantee for the entire amount being No. GT02/2000/0014 dated 25-1-2000 covering the entire penalty amount of Taka 24,67,496,000. from ANZ Grind lays Bank Limited. The said' impugned order does not show any consideration of any hardship as to . deposit of 50% penalty; instead without exercising the discretion the respondent No: 1 has arbitrarily issued the, impugned order which is not sustainable in law. In view of the fact that legal complication would 'arise, in transmitting 50% of the penalty in foreign exchange until disposal of the appeal finally and there would be 'obvious restriction by the Bangladesh Bank pending the final decision in appeal and the time that would be consumed in transmitting the amount for preparing in appeal and that the penalty is secured by 100% Bank guarantee from' ANZ Grindlays Bank.. Chittagong, ends of justice would be best served if the petitioner is allowed to prosecute the appeal directing acceptance of Bank guarantee for the, 100% of the penalty amount which is already on record in the Appeal. In view of the above we direct the respondent No. 1 to proceed with the hearing of the appear accepting the Bank guarantee, which is for the 100% of the penalty amount and in that view of the matter set aside that impugned order dated 1-6-2000. directing to deposit in cash as has been issued without any lawful. authority. The Rule is accordingly made absolute without any order as to.

11. Similar view was also taken in the case of Seacom Shipping Ltd vs Commissioner of Customs, 6 BLC 516 wherein it was held as under:

"The petitioner has furnished a Bank Guarantee for 100% of the penalty along with the memo of appeal before the respondent and prayed for accepting the same together with assertions in the body of the memo about undue hardship. The petitioner though in' clear terms has not made out a case of undue hardship for exercising discretion by the respondent but by furnishing Bank Guarantee for 100% of the penalty has prayed for accepting the same. The petitioner as 'well in paragraph 9 of this writ petition has asserted that the petitioner is in financial hardship: and as they do not hold the funds from their principal, the 'petitioner prayed before the respondent No. 1 along with a. bank guarantee for Taka 856,882, issued by, Standard Chartered Bank; . Dhaka, Bangladesh being No,864/CC, 9900003 dated  5-1-1999 covering the entire penalty amount in favour of the respondent No.1 and prayed for stay of the deposit of 50% of the penalty amount in cash before-hearing of the appeal.

In view of the' fact' that the petitioner represented the foreign vessel and' that there would be positive; inconvenience in transmitting foreign exchange at 50%· of deposit prior to filing, the- appeal and considering the foreign exchange "restriction ,of the Bangladesh Bank for the cash amount pending final decision in the, appeal together with the ground asserting hardship' and the assertions made in the application and that the penalty amount is' secured by a 100% Bank guarantee furnished by Standard Chartered Bank, Dhaka, ends of Justice would 'be best served if the Petitioner is allowed to prefer the appeal with l 00% Bank guarantee instead of  50.% deposit in cash.

In view of the above; the respondent No. I .is directed to admit the appeal with the . Bank guarantee for the entire amount of fine filed before .him· instead. of . 50% Bank Guarantee and 50% in cash, setting aside the . impugned order in the circumstances to have been issued without  any law authority.

In the result, this' Rule, is made absolute without any order as to costs.

12. In the case of 'Sentrdns Maritime (Bd) Limited vs The Commissioner df Customs, 6 MLR' 2001, 251 wherein it was held as follows:

In view of the fact ·that the petitioner  represented the .foreign vessel and that there - would be positive inconvenience in transmitting-foreign exchange at 50% of  deposit prior to filing the., Appeal and considering the foreign exchange restriction  of the Bangladesh Bank for the· case amount pending final decision in the appeal together with the ground. asserting hardship and the assertions made in the application and that the penalty amount is secured by a 100% Bank Guarantee furnished by Agrani Bank, Chittagong, ends - of justice would he best served if the petitioner is allowed to prefer the appeal with-l00% Bank guarantee instead of  50% deposit in cash."

13. In the case of Ocean Trade Ltd vs The Commissioner- of Customs, Excise and VAT, 11 BLT 2003, 440 this Court on the self-same issue observed as follows:

"The petitioner has taken a ground of hardship and also has furnished a bank guarantee for the full amount. The Commissioner of Customs being an appellate authority by exercising his statutory discretionary power could have accepted the appeal. In view of the facts and circumstances the impugned order is liable to be set aside and struck' down. The Commissioner of appeal is directed to admit the appeal and dispose of the same - within 3 months from date of receipt of this order upon famishing bank guarantee by the appellant for the entire amount instead of 50% bank guarantee and 50% in cash."

14. We don't find any plausible ground to deviate ourselves from the decisions arrived at by their lordships in the cited cases, rather we are in full agreement with the same since the facts and circumstances of the aforesaid cases are similar with that of the instant one in our hard.

15. In the premises aforesaid, we find substance in the Rule.

16. Accordingly, The Rule is made absolute. Respondent No.1 is directed to admit the appeal with the 100% Bank guarantee of the entire penalty amount instead of 50% Bank guarantee and 50% in cash and in that view of the matter, the impugned order dated 15-7-2010 is hereby set-aside adjudging the same to be unjust and without any lawful authority.

However, there would be no order as to costs.

End.

case_source: (From Judgment and order dated 29th July, 1993 passed by the High Court Division, Dhaka in Writ Petition No. 688 of 1989)
full_judgment: Muhammad Habibur Rahman CJ: I have gone through the judgments proposed to be delivered by my learned brother ATM Afzal J and by my learned brother Latifur Rahman J. I agree with the judgment of my learned brother ATM Afzal J. ATM Afzal J: These two appeals by leave involve mainly consideration of a common question of law, namely application of section 5 of the Abandoned Buildings (Supplementary Provisions) Ordinance 1985 (Ordinance No. LIV of 1985), briefly, the Ordinance Accordingly they are taken up together for disposal although the facts of the two cases are different and they arise out of two different proceedings. 3. Civil Appeal No. 80 of 1993 is from judgment and order dated 29 July, 1993 passed by a Division Bench of the High Court Division discharging the Rule in Writ Petition No. 688 of 1989. Appellant filed the said writ petition calling upon the respondents to show cause as to why the enlistment of house No. 9/1, Block 'F', Joint Quarters Mohammadpur Housing Estate, Dhaka in the 'Ka' list of the Bangladesh Gazette Extraordinary published on September 23, 1986 and further why the judgment and order dated 23.5.1989 passed by the Court of Settlement in Case No. 668 of 1988 should not be declared to have been made/passed without lawful authority, etc. 4. The case of the appellant, briefly, is that the disputed house was originally allotted by the Government to one Md. Zahooruddin under memo dated 12.6.1962 followed by a proper deed of conveyance dated 16.1.1963 leasing out the land to him for a period of 99 years and transferring to him by hire purchase the house built thereon on payment of cost of the house. Md. Zahooruddin paid the entire cost of construction and the possession of the disputed property was handed over to him on 29.1.1963. While in possession he entered into an agreement on 19.1.1971 with the appellant for sale of the said property at a consideration of Taka 12,000.00 of which he received Taka 11,500.00 and upon which he delivered all the documents and papers to the appellant with an assurance to execute and register a proper deed of conveyance after completing all formalities but subsequently he avoided to perform his part of the contract which compelled the appellant to file Title Suit No. 249 of 1984 in the First Court of Munsif, Dhaka (now Assistant Judge) for specific performance of contract impleading the Government as defendant No. 2. 5. The Government contested the suit by filing a written statement contending that the suit property is an abandoned property and claiming possession thereof. The suit was ultimately transferred to the Additional Court of Munsif. Dhaka and was renumbered as Title Suit No. 14 of 1986. The suit was decreed ex parte against the original owner by judgment and decree dated 26.7.1986. The appellant obtained delivery of possession through Court on 5.2.1989 and since then he has been living in the disputed house with the members of his family. Respondent-Government filed appeal against the ex parte decree in the Court of the District Judge, Dhaka being Title Appeal No. 176 of 1986 which was once dismissed for default on 30.8.1987. At the time of hearing of this appeal the learned Advocate for the appellant informed the Court that the said appeal has been revived and is pending for hearing in the First Court of Subordinate Judge, Dhaka. 6. The appellant learnt to his utter surprise that the list published by the Government under section 5 of the Ordinance included the disputed building as being an abandoned property. The appellant filed an application under section 7 of the said Ordinance which was registered as Case No. 668 of 1988 in the Court of Settlement. The Government did not file any written statement but contended mainly at the hearing of the matter that the original lessee was absent, his whereabouts were not known and he left the suit property uncared for and, therefore, the same became abandoned property by operation of President's Order No. 16 of 1972 and vested in the Government. 7. The Court of Settlement by its judgment and order dated 23.5.1989 dismissed the case holding, inter alia, that the appellant has not acquired any right or interest in the disputed property. Appellant then moved the High Court Division and obtained a Rule Nisi in the writ petition mentioned above which has after hearing been discharged by the impugned judgment and order. 8. Respondent Nos. 1 and 2 contested the writ petition by filing an affidavit-in-opposition. They denied the allegations made by the appellant in his writ petition and asserted that Md. Zahooruddin had left Bangladesh during the war of liberation and after liberation his whereabout was not known and the case property vested in the Government as abandoned property under President's Order No. 16 of 1972 and the same had been under the absolute control, management and supervision of the Government through different allottees. The appellant filed the suit for specific performance of contract after long 13 years upon suppression of all material facts and obtained an ex parte decree and then a sale deed through Court on 11.12.1988 which are void ab initio and hit by articles 6, 14, 20 and 24 of President's Order No. 16 of 1972. The last allottee of the Government was Abdul Majid who was illegally evicted on 5.2.1989 by the appellant through Court. 9. Civil Appeal No. 49 of 1994 is from order dated 15 May, 1994 passed by a Division Bench of the High Court Division in Writ Petition No. 810 of 1944 rejecting the same summarily. The appellant filed the said writ petition calling upon the respondents to show cause as to why the inclusion of the building. Holding No. B/36, Block 'E' Zakir Hossain Road, Mohammadpur, Dhaka in the 'Ka' list of the Bangladesh Gazette Extraordinary published on 23rd September, 1986 under the aforesaid Ordinance No. 54 of 1985 and judgment dated 8.2.1994 passed by the First Court of Settlement in Case No. 378 of 1989 followed by the letter of respondent No. 4 dated 8.5.1994 shall not be declared to have been made/ passed without lawful authority, etc. 10. The appellant's case, briefly, is that the aforesaid holding was allotted by the then Government to one Zafar Ali in the year 1960 and on payment of full premium a lease deed was executed and registered for a period of 99 years. Zafar Ali died on 13.9.1970 leaving a son Ramjan Ali and a daughter Roksana who entered into an agreement with the appellant on 17.2.1972 for sale of the disputed property for Taka 10,000.00 out of which the appellant paid Taka 3,000.00 on the date of execution of the agreement. Subsequently she paid Taka 1,500.00 on 29.12.1974 and Taka 3,000.00 on 11.9.1977 upon obtaining valid receipts. Upon the refusal of the vendors to execute and register a sale deed the appellant instituted Title Suit No. 588 of 1982 in the First Court of Munsif, Dhaka for specific performance of contract and obtained an ex parte decree on 10.4.1982. The Government was party thereto and received notice of the suit. She obtained a deed through Court on 19.6.1982 and possession of the case property on 28.8.1982 in Title Execution Case No. 12 of 1982. 11. On 31.10.1982 the Deputy Commissioner, Housing and Settlement issued a notice upon the appellant to show cause why she should not be evicted from the case property. The appellant filed Title Suit No.332 of 1982 for declaration of title against the Secretary Ministry of Public Works and others. The suit was decreed ex parte although notices were duly served upon the defendants. The Government-defendants filed Miscellaneous Case No. 153 of 1986 under Order IX rule 13 CPC but the said Miscellaneous case was dismissed for default. 12. During the pendency of Title Suit No. 332 of 1982 the Deputy Commissioner. Housing and Settlement again issued a Memo dated 28.11.1982 directing the appellant to surrender the suit property to the Abandoned Property Cell. The appellant's attorney moved the said Abandoned Property Cell unsuccessfully and the appellant was constrained to file on 2.1.1983 Title Suit No. 1 of 1983 through her constituted attorney Sardar Nisar Ahmed praying for permanent injunction against the Secretary Ministry of Public Works and others. On 1.2.1983 temporary injunction was granted ex parte but on 2.2.1983 the appellant was evicted in violation of the order of temporary injunction. The appellant filed Miscellaneous Case No. 10 of 1983 for restoration of possession under section 144 CPC. The Government-defendants contested and the application was allowed on contest on 7.8.1983 and the appellant obtained possession through the process of the Court on 22.8.1983. On 16.4.1985 Title Suit No. 1 of 1983 was decreed ex parte. 13. Having learnt that the disputed property was included in the 'Ka' list as an abandoned property under Ordinance No. 54 of 1985 the appellant filed an application under section 7 thereof which was registered as Case No. 378 of 1989 in the First Court of Settlement. 14. The Government did not file any written statement in the Court of Settlement but the Ministry's file on the case property was made available to the Court of Settlement. 15. The Court of Settlement held that the basis of the appellant's claim remained vague and not proved at all, that there is no paper and document to prove that Ramjan Ali and Roksana are the son and daughter of Zafar Ali nor is there any document to prove the alleged agreement between them and the appellant on the basis of which the ex parte decree was obtained in Title Suit No. 588 of 1981, that no reliance could be placed on the succession certificate in the circumstances of the case, that there is no proof that Zafar Ali died on 13.9.1970, that there is no explanation why the appellant filed Title Suit No. 588 of 1981 after 9 years, that the series of suits in quick succession were mere contrivances to cover the alleged transfer in the appellant's favour with a false shade of genuineness, that the appellant herself or her husband did not file the suits and cases but one Sardar Nasir Ahmed claiming himself to be an attorney of the appellant filed those suits, that there was no power of attorney in support of this story and as such the enlistment of the case property in the 'Ka' list was upheld by judgment and order dated 8.2.1994. 16. The High Court Division in the impugned order reiterated the findings of the Court of Settlement and held that it did not find any unimpeachable document to show that the appellant had acquired the case property legally from the heirs of original allottee Zafar Ali. 17. In Civil Appeal No. 80 of 1993 leave was granted to consider the submission whether in view of the decree passed in the suit for specific performance of contract, Title Suit No. 14 of 1986, and the appeal taken by the Government from the said decree, Title Appeal No. 176 of 1986, which is pending in the Court of the District Judge, Dhaka wherein the question of the disputed building being an abandoned property is sub judice, the inclusion of the same in the 'Ka' list is barred under Proviso (b) of section 5 of the Ordinance. In the other appeal, Civil Appeal No. 49 of 1994, although the leave was granted to consider somewhat different points Syed Ishtiaq Ahmed, learned Counsel for the appellant, mainly argued on the same ground as above, that is, whether the inclusion of the disputed building in the 'Ka' list (in this case) is barred under Proviso (a) of section 5 of the Ordinance in view of the ex parte decree passed in Title Suit No. 588 of 1981. 18. Mr. MI Farooqui, learned Counsel appearing for the appellant in Civil Appeal No. 80 of 1993 drew our attention to certain facts of the case in order to invoke ultimately the bar of inclusion under section 5 of the Ordinance. He first of all pointed out that in the suit for specific performance of contract filed by the appellant the Government asserted in its written statement that the disputed building is an abandoned property and has been under the management, control and supervision of the Government through its allottees. The trial Court in its judgment considered the question of maintainability of the suit and found that during the pendency of the suit the suit property could not be included in the list of abandoned property. The suit was decreed and the Government took an appeal from the said decree. In the Memo of Appeal it has been asserted that the issue as to the maintainability of the suit has been wrongly decided by the trial Court. It has further been asserted that it ought to have been held that the suit was barred under President's Order No. 16 of 1972 and the Ordinance. Mr. Farooqui submits that the question of the disputed building being an abandoned property or not was very much in issue in the suit and the same is now the main ground of the appeal filed by the Government. 19. Mr. Farooqui then draws our attention to President's Order No. 142 of 1972 and points out that the Government is a necessary party under Article 6 of the said Order in a suit for specific performance of any contract relating to the transfer of immoveable property or for declaration of title to, or assertion of ownership of any such property. This provision was made, he submits, to afford an opportunity to the Government to raise objection if the suit was in respect of a property which had vested in the Government under any law like President's Order No. 16 of 1972. The issue of abandoned property having been raised in the suit which is now a subject matter of the appeal by the Government, there is a positive bar, according to Mr. Farooqui for inclusion of the disputed building in the list under Proviso (b) of section 5 of the Ordinance. 20. In the case of Mr. Ahmed the difference on fact is that the appellant got an ex parte decree in the suit for specific performance of contract. The Government-defendant filed a miscellaneous case under Order 9 rule 13 CPC for restoration of the suit but the miscellaneous case was dismissed for default. Mr. Ahmed also submitted that the Government was made a party in the suit as required under President's Order No. 142 of 1972 and, as such, it got an opportunity to raise the question of the property being an abandoned property. The purpose of enacting President's Order No. 142 of 1972, Mr. Ahmed argued, was to ensure that nobody can steal a march in respect of any property which had vested in the Government behind its back. The Government allowed itself as a result, to be bound by a decree passed in such suit. A decree having been passed in the suit and possession having already been taken in execution of the said decree, Mr. Ahmed submits that bar of inclusion under Proviso (a) is attracted in the facts of this case. 21. At this stage section 5 of the Ordinance may be quoted for ready reference: "5. Publication of list of buildings—(1) The Government shall after the "Commencement of this Ordinance and before the 30th day of September, 1988, publish from time to time in the official Gazette". (Subs. by Act 12 of 1988) (a) lists of buildings the possession of which have been taken as abandoned property under the President's Order. (b) "Lists of buildings in respect of which notices" (Subs. by Act 12/85) for surrendering or taking possession as abandoned property under the said Order have been issued : Provided that no such list shall include any building in respect of which— (a) any decree or order has been passed, at any time before the publication of the list in the official Gazette, by any Court declaring the building not to be an abandoned property or not to have vested in the Government under the President's Order or declaring the possession by the Government of the building as an abandoned property under that Order to be illegal or invalid or directing the Government or any officer or authority subordinate to it to return, restore or transfer the building to any person, or (b) a suit appeal, application or other legal proceeding is pending before any Court immediately before the date of publication of the list in the official Gazette, in which the vesting in, or possession of, the Government of the building as abandoned property under the President's Order has been called in question in any manner whatsoever or any prayer has been made for return, restoration or transfer of the building by the Government or by any officer or authority subordinate to it to any person. (2) The lists published under sub-section (1) shall be conclusive evidence of the fact that the buildings included therein are abandoned property and have vested in the Government as such." 22. The question for consideration is whether the decree obtained in the suit for specific performance of contract answers the description as in Proviso (a). The other question will be whether the Government appeal Title Appeal No. 176 of 1986 which is pending for hearing is one which is covered by Proviso (b). 23. Both the learned Counsels have argued that a suit for specific performance of contract in respect of a building the possession of which has been taken by Government as abandoned property or in respect of which notice for taking possession has been issued by the Government has been barred under section 6 of the Ordinance. The bar is prospective. They also pointed out section 11 of the Ordinance which provides for an extended period of limitation for setting aside an ex parte decree obtained at any time before commencement of the Ordinance. Mr. Ahmed particularly referred to the proviso to section 11 which says that the aforesaid provision shall not apply where the order or decree of the Court has been duly executed. In his case, the decree has been executed long ago in 1982. Reference to all these provisions were made to support the contention that a suit for specific performance of contract although not specifically mentioned in Provisos (a) and (b) the same is to be held included impliedly therein when the Government is made a party (under President's Order No. 142 of 1972). 24. Mr. Ahmed explained at great length the implication of a decree, even though ex parte, in a suit for specific performance of contract after making the Government a party. The decree has a sanctity which is inviolable. Even the Legislature cannot set aside a decree although the effect of a decree may be nullified by the legislature by appropriate legislation. In a subsequent suit the bar of res judicata may be pleaded on the basis of an ex parte decree. In a decree for specific performance of contract delivery of possession of the disputed property is implied and can be enforced. Mr. Ahmed referred to some decisions to support the aforesaid propositions which are respectively, Mofizur Rahman vs. Government of Bangladesh 34 DLR (AD) 321. Amir Khan vs Controller of Estate Duty 13 DLR (SC) 105. Maksud Ali vs. Eskandar Ali 28 DLR (AD) 99 25. The learned Additional Attorney-General who appeared as amicus curiae in Civil Appeal No. 49 of 1994 and generally made submission only on points of law has not disputed the correctness of the propositions of law raised by Mr. Ahmed with regard to an ex parte decree under consideration. The learned Additional Attorney-General has, however, submitted that notwithstanding the fact that Government has been made a party in the suit for specific performance of contract the decree passed in that suit is not one which is contemplated under Proviso (a) and as such the bar of inclusion is not attracted. 26. It will be seen that in Proviso (a) no particular kind of suit has been mentioned. The reference is to any 'decree' or order which has been passed by any Court at any time before the publication of the list in the official Gazette. The list shall not include any building if the decree or order is found declaring (1) the building not to be an abandoned property or (2) not to have vested in the Government under the President's Order (President's Order 16 of 1972) or (3) the possession by the Government of the building as an abandoned property under that Order to be illegal or invalid or directing (4) the Government or any officer or authority subordinate to it to return, restore or transfer the building to any person. The decree obtained by the appellants in the suit for specific performance of contract does not come under any of the clauses. There is no declaration in the decree that the building is not an abandoned property or that it has not vested in the Government under President's Order No.16 of 1972. There is no declaration that the possession of the Government is illegal nor there is any direction upon the Government to return the building to anybody. Although the Government has been made a party as required under President's Order No. 142 of 1972 it will be seen that no relief has been prayed for against the Government. The decree does not require the Government to do anything. It is possible that in a particular case as in the case of Mr. Farooqui the Government may have appeared and raised objection on the ground of the suit property being an abandoned property and that objection may not have succeeded but that fact cannot render the decree as one as contemplated in Proviso (a). A 'decree' by definition means the formal expression of an adjudication which, so far as regards the Court expressing it, conclusively determines the rights of the parties with regard to all or any of the matters in controversy in the suit and may be either preliminary or final. The decree in the suit for specific performance of contract will show that it has only decided the controversy between the vendor and the vendee and directed the vendor to execute the necessary document in favour of the vendee. I have, therefore, no hesitation to hold that such a decree is not the one which is mentioned in Proviso (a) and, as such, the existence of such a decree cannot be pleaded as a bar for inclusion of the building in the list. 27. As for the appeal in Mr. Farooqui's case we find upon examination of the terms of Proviso (b) that the same is not covered by the said terms. A suit or appeal to be covered by Proviso (b) must be one "in which the vesting in, or possession of, the Government of the building as abandoned property under the President's Order has been called in question in any manner whatsoever or any prayer has been made for return, restoration or transfer of the building by the Government or by any officer or authority subordinate to it to any person." 28. In the appeal by the Government it has not questioned the vesting or possession of the property as abandoned property; it cannot because it is the case of the Government that it has vested as an abandoned property. The calling in question must be by one who claims that it is not an abandoned property. The Government being in possession cannot ask for restoration to itself. I have therefore no doubt in my mind that the pendency of the appeal by the Government will be no bar for including the disputed building in the Gazette in the case of Mr. Farooqui. 29. The views expressed above as to a decree in a suit for specific performance of contract as in the present cases is in line with our view already expressed in rejecting CPLA No. 290 of 1990 which is reported in 46 DLR (AD) 9 and which has been noticed in the impugned judgment of the High Court Division. The High Court Division has also relied on our decision in CPLA No.6 of 1991. 30. Neither of the Counsels has argued, I think advisedly, that because there has been a decree for specific performance of contract in favour of the appellants, the buildings can no longer be treated as abandoned property under President's Order No. 16 of 1972. If a property has vested in the Government as abandoned property under President's Order No. 16 of 1972, it shall be exempt from all legal processes, etc. (vide Article 14 of President's Order No. 16 of 1972). The transfer under the decree shall also be null and void (Article 6). Section 5(2) of the Ordinance provides that the publication of the lists under sub-section (1) shall be conclusive evidence of the fact that the buildings included therein are abandoned property and have vested in the Government as such. Therefore as soon as the lists are published one has to start accepting the buildings included therein as abandoned property. In that case, a decree as referred to above is of no avail. All the endeavor of the learned Counsel has therefore been to bring the decree within the ambit of Proviso (a) so as to invoke the bar of inclusion in the list. They admit that the language used in the section apparently does not take in a decree as under consideration. Mr. Farooqui therefore argued that the section should not be construed literally but the intention underlying the section must be gathered. Where the Government has an opportunity in a suit made possible by law to raise the question of a property being abandoned, the decree in such suit, even if it be a suit for specific performance of contract, is impliedly in eluded in Proviso (a). That is the underlying implication of the proviso, Mr. Farooqui submits. To support his submission, he referred to Lord Denning in Seaford Court Estates Ltd. vs. Asher [1949] 2 K B 481 as quoted in his book 'The Discipline of Law'. The relevant passage reads: "A judge, believing himself to be fettered by the supposed rule that he must look to the language and nothing else, laments that the draftsmen have not provided for this or that, or have been guilty of some or other ambiguity. It would certainly save the judges trouble if Acts of Parliament were drafted with divine prescience and perfect clarity. In the absence of it, when a defect appears a judge cannot simply fold his hands and blame the draftsman. He must set to work on the constructive task of finding the intention of Parliament, and he must do this not only from the language of the statute, but also from a consideration of the social conditions which gave rise to it, and of the mischief which it was passed to remedy, and then he must supplement the written word so as to give 'force and life' to the intention of the legislature. That was clearly laid down by the resolution of the judges in Heydon's case, and it is the safest guide today. Good practical advice on the subject was given about the same time by Plowden ................Put into homely metaphor it is this: A judge should ask himself the question: If the makers of the Act had themselves come across this ruck in the texture of it, how would they have straightened it out? He must then do as they would have done. A judge must not alter the material of which it is woven, but he can and should iron out the creases." 31. Mr. Ishtiaq Ahmed has supplemented the submission of Mr. Farooqui by trying to give 'force and life' to the intention of the law-maker by emphasising on the impact of a civil Court decree passed in a suit wherein by prescription the Government is made a party. I have already considered the submissions and recorded my opinion. I do not think that there is any scope to contend that a decree of the kind referred to above is included in Proviso (a) even by implication. In the case of the pending Government appeal, the object is to get the decree for specific performance of contract set aside and not to call in question the vesting of the building under President's Order No. 16 of 1972 or not to pray for return of the same by the Government (which will be absurd on the face of it, if it were). So, proviso (b) is not at all attracted. 32. Mr. Ishtiaq Ahmed obtained leave on another ground, that is, the High Court Division failed to consider that in the absence of any written statement the Court of Settlement could not have come to a conclusion on facts by a mere perusal of the government’s file without showing the file to the appellant and giving her an opportunity to controvert those allegations on which the Court of Settlement relied upon and further that there has been a failure of fair trial in the Court of Settlement which arrived at its conclusion in violation of the principles of natural justice. 33. Upon a reference to the writ petition we find nothing in the ill-drafted and ill-conceived grounds taken there that any question of denial of fair trial has been raised. As for filing of a written statement by the Government it may be observed that section 10 of the Ordinance provides that except as provided therein the provisions of the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908 shall not apply to a Court of Settlement. In a proceeding under section 7 the entire onus is on the person claiming any right or interest in a building included in the list to show that the building is not an abandoned property and has not vested in the Government under President's Order No. 16 of 1972 or that his right or interest in the building has not been affected by the provisions of that Order. The fact that a building is included in the list is proof of its being an abandoned property {section 5(2)} and the Government has nothing to prove or deny. It is for the aggrieved person to establish his claim by whatever evidence he chooses to produce. The denial of a fair trial will only arise if a proper opportunity is not afforded to the person for producing his evidence or any evidence sought to be adduced by him is unreasonably shut out or he is not given a reasonable opportunity of being heard. A Court of Settlement under section 10(5) is obliged to make such enquiry as it may deem necessary and give reasonable opportunity to the parties concerned of being heard and to produce evidence, both oral and documentary, if any. 34. In the instant case (Civil Appeal No. 49 of 1994) it appears that the appellants mainly produced the certified copies of decrees and orders in various suits and few municipal receipts and one receipt showing payment of electricity bill. It has been indicated above that the decrees and orders as produced by the appellant do not help her unless she can prove the genuineness of the agreement upon which she relics. Mr. Ahmed at one stage argued that the point of inquiry should have been whether the agreement dated 17.2.1972 was genuine rather than whether the property was abandoned because even if it was so, it was subject to the agreement as President's Order No. 16 of 1972 came into force after the agreement. There is some force in his submission but then he has not been able to point out what evidence the appellant had adduced to prove the agreement but was not considered by the Court of Settlement. The case of the appellant has been disbelieved by the Court of Settlement upon going through the evidence on record and referring to the facts and circumstances of the case, I do not think therefore that there is any valid ground for complaining about a fair trial. 35. Yet another ground upon which leave was obtained is that the High Court Division did not consider that the case property was not in possession of the Government when it was listed in the 'Ka' list and thus the provision of section 5(a) of the Ordinance has been contravened. Admittedly the appellant was not in possession of the building for more than 10 years since her alleged agreement dated 17.2.1972 until she obtained possession on 28.8.1982 after the ex parte decree. There appears to be no evidence that either the appellant's vendors or anybody on their behalf were possessing the building during those 10 years. In the High Court Division the Government got no opportunity to explain whether possession was taken over by it as the writ petition was summarily rejected. But from the appellant's own statement it appears that the authority evicted the occupants of the suit property on 2.2.1983 but on their application for restoration of possession the Court allowed the same on 7.8.1983 and the appellant got back possession on 22.8.1983. Thus it is admitted that the possession of the building was taken over by the Government after the appellant went into possession following ex parte decree in the first suit. 'Ka' list is to include "buildings the possession of which have been taken as abandoned property". According to the appellant herself the authority took over possession after issuing notice to surrender although a suit was pending at that time and possession was taken allegedly in violation of an order of temporary injunction. In the circumstances of the case it cannot be said that the building was included in the 'Ka' list illegally. In the result, therefore, both the appeals are dismissed without any order as to costs. Mustafa Kamal J: I have gone through the judgments proposed to be delivered by my learned brother ATM Afzal, J and by my learned brother Latifur Rahman J. I agree with the judgment of my learned brother ATM Afzal J. Latifur Rahman J: After reading the judgment of my learned brother ATM Afzal J. I could not persuade myself to agree with the same. Hence I am writing out a separate judgment giving my reasons thereof. 39. I do not find any reason to re-state the facts of the cases as ATM Afzal J has very meticulously dealt with the same. 40. Civil Appeal Nos. 80 of 1993 and 49 of 1994 are heard together and are disposed of by this common judgment as the question of law involved in these two appeals are the same. Civil Appeal No. 80 of 1993 relates to listing of House No. 9/1, Block "E". Joint Quarter Mohammadpur and Civil Appeal No. 49 of 1994 relates to listing of Holding No. V/6, Block "E", Jakir Hossain Road, Mohammadpur respectively in "Ka" list of abandoned properties under Section 5 of Ordinance No. 54 of 1985 published in extraordinary Gazette. 41. The main question to be decided in these two appeals is, when in a suit for specific performance of contract Government is a necessary party (under President's Order 142 of 72), does such a suit come within the mischief of proviso (a) and (b) of section 5(1) of Ordinance 54 of 1985. 42. In Civil Appeal No. 49 of 1993, leave was granted to consider whether the learned Judges of the High Court Division acted wrongly in not considering this material aspect of the case that the lower appellate Court is in seisin of the appeal preferred by the Government defendant from the decree in the suit for specific performance of contract, in which possession by the Government of the building as abandoned property under President's Order No.16 of 1972 has been called in question and the trial Court dealt with the matter and came to a decision on the question rightly or wrongly, which is the subject matter of appeal. In such circumstances the suit squarely comes within the proviso (b) of section 5 of Ordinance 54 of 1985 and therefore during pendency of this suit the inclusion of the appellant's property in 'Ka' schedule was unwarranted by law. 43. In Civil Appeal No. 49 of 1994, leave was granted to consider whether the High Court Division erred in law in holding that the inclusion of the case property in the "Ka" list was ex facie illegal as the appellant first obtained possession on 28.8.82 and again after eviction by the Government on 2.2.83 got possession through the process of court in Title Suit No. 1 of 1983 and Ordinance No. 54 of 1985 was promulgated on 26.11.85 and the suit property was not in possession of the Government cannot be listed in the "Ka'' list and further to consider whether the High Court Division failed to consider that in the absence of any written objection the Court of Settlement could come to a conclusion on the facts by mere perusal of the Government file without showing the file to the petitioner and giving her an opportunity to controvert those allegations which the Court of Settlement relied upon and consequently there has been a failure of fair trial and a violation of the mandatory provision of sub-section (5) of section 10 of the Ordinance. 44. Apart from the leave granting orders, both the learned Advocates for the appellants argued on various provisions of President's Order 142 of 1972 and on the relevant provisions of Ordinance 54 of 1985. In view of the arguments of the learned Advocates we thought it proper to summon Additional Attorney-General as Amicus Curiae to assist us in correctly exposing the law on the topic. Mr. Abdul Wadud Bhuiya, the learned Additional Attorney-General appeared before us and made his submissions on law. 45. Mr. MI Farooqui, learned Advocate appearing for the appellant in Civil Appeal No. 49 of 1993, submits, first that under President's Order 142 of 1972 the Government is a necessary and proper party in a suit for specific performance of contract and the Government having appeared and contested the suit up to the appellate stage asserting that the property is an abandoned property, the listing of the same under Ordinance No. 54 of 1985 is in violation of the provisos (a) and (b) of section 5(1) of Ordinance No.54 of 1985 as the decree has been passed by the civil court and the same issue is still pending in appeal before the appellate Court of civil jurisdiction. 46. Mr. MI Farooqui, next submits that section 6 of the Ordinance only bars suits for specific performance of contract, declaration of title and direction to the Government to restore possession in respect of abandoned property and these three types of suits are prospectively barred in respect of abandoned property, but there being no embargo on filing such suits in the past, provisos(a) and (b) of section 5(1) of Ordinance 54 of 1985 clearly contemplates all kinds of suits including a suit for specific performance of contract where the abandoned character/vesting/possession of the Govt. can be called in question in any manner whatsoever. 47. The learned Advocate further submits that the use of the terms as suit, appeal, application or other legal proceedings as mentioned in proviso (b) of section 5(1) of the Ordinance connote a variety of legal proceedings and a suit for specific performance of contract is such a suit in view of President's Order 142 of 1972. 48. Lastly, he submits that a decree of a civil Court binds all parties before it and the Court of Settlement as a quasi-judicial tribunal could not sit over the judgment and decree of a civil Court and held that the same is void and illegal and, as such, the Court of Settlement acted in excess of its jurisdiction and contrary to the mandate of section 5 of the Ordinance and the learned Judges of the High Court Division acted illegally in not exercising the writ jurisdiction which is in the nature of certiorari. 49. Mr. Syed Ishtiaq Ahmed, learned Advocate appearing in Civil Appeal No. 49 of 1994, very strenuously argues before us about the legislative purpose of President's Order 142 of 1972 and submits that in a suit for specific performance of contract the Government being a necessary party, the Government ought to have raised the plea that the property is an abandoned property in respect of which no suit for specific performance of contract is maintainable and the Government having not raised that issue and a finality having reached the same can only be set aside by a competent civil Court and the Court of Settlement illegally assumed jurisdiction to sit over the decree of a civil Court. 50. He further submits that the final list of the abandoned buildings having been published under the Ordinance, the Court of Settlement has exclusive jurisdiction to decide the abandoned character of the building and that can be done by making enquiry as contemplated in sub-section 5 of section 10 of the Ordinance and the Court of Settlement totally failed to exercise that jurisdiction vested in it by law. 51. In view of the arguments of the parties and points raised in these appeals I will dispose of all the points herein below. 52. Normally in a suit for specific performance-of contract the real contest is between the vendor and the purchaser and in such a suit the primary question is whether the agreement is genuine and on the basis of the agreement the purchaser is entitled to specifically enforce his contract against the vendor to perform his part of the contract. But the promulgation of Bangladesh Transfer of Immoveable Property (Temporary Provision) Order, 1972 (President's Order 142, of 1972), briefly, the Order, restricting transfer of immovable property by agreement of sale has introduced a new dimension in a suit for specific performance of contract so far Government is concerned. Why a third party has been introduced by this order in such a suit? I will answer this question herein below. 53. Under President's Order 142 of 1972, Government is made a necessary party in a suit for specific performance of contract. Under the Order not only the Government is a necessary party in a suit for specific performance of contract, but without impleading the Government as a party no one can file such a suit or such a suit can be proceeded with. After the liberation of the country the Bangladesh Abandoned Property (Control, Management and Disposal) Order, 1972 (President's Order No.16 of 1972) was promulgated on the 26th February, 1972. Section 2 of President's Order 16/72, defines "abandoned property". President's Order 142 of 1972 was promulgated on 28.11.72 and in this President's Order certain provisions are made and I will elaborately deal with those provisions as an argument has been made before us from the Bar that this President's Order 142 of 1972 was promulgated to restrict the transfer of abandoned property which by operation of law has vested in the Government and the abandoned property cannot be the subject matter of private transfer between two private individuals as in the meanwhile by operation of law the same vested in the Government and in respect of such property all legal process shall be exempted and the Government shall not be divested or dispossessed of such property, It is not for nothing that this President's Order 142 of 1972 was promulgated. Every enactment has a purpose and meaning for which it is enacted and governs the field. The preamble of President's Order 142 of 1972 says that, "whereas it is expedient to make provisions for restricting the transfer of immovable property in Bangladesh in public interest". So the preamble clearly says that a restriction is imposed on transfer of immovable property by private individuals. Article 2 defines 'transfer' which also includes any agreement for such transfer. Article 3 says that no transfer of any immovable property by way of any contract or agreement made after the commencement of this Order shall be deemed to be valid and legal unless the provisions of this Order have been complied with. Article 4 speaks that an affidavit is to be filed along with the document for registration that the property proposed to be transferred is not an abandoned property within President's Order 16 of 1972. Article 6 says that in a suit for specific performance of contract relating to the transfer of any immovable property the Government' is a necessary party and no one can file such a suit without impleading the Government as a party or such a suit will proceed in the absence of the Government, Article 7 reads as follows: "A transfer of immovable property in contravention of the provision of this Order shall be null and void and the property so transferred shall stand forfeited to the Government." So not only in a suit for specific performance of contract, Government is a necessary party but even a transfer of immovable property in contravention of the provision of this Order shall be null and void and the property so transferred stands forfeited to the Government An analysis of sections 3, 4 arid 6 of President's Order 142 of 1972, clearly shows that a transfer of an immovable property by way of an agreement is not valid and legal unless the provisions of this Order have been complied with. The Government is not only a party in a suit for specific performance of contract but no document of transfer shall be registered without an affidavit to the effect that the properly is not an abandoned property under President's Order 16 of 1972. Thus two restrictions are imposed on transferring of the property, before passing of the decree and also before registration of the document by which right, title, interest and possession is transferred to the purchaser. In a decree for specific performance of contract for sale of a property, the delivery of possession of the property was an implied term of the contract and also an implied term of the decree for specific performance of contract. Reference may be made to the case of Moksud Ali vs. Ishkender Ali 28 DLR (AD) 99. 54. I have very elaborately dealt with the relevant provisions of this Order above to show the importance and purpose of the Order, and by merely raising the issue of abandoned character of the property by the Government, the appellants would be non-suited as no decree for specific performance of contract could be passed in respect of an abandoned property. Specific performance is the discretion of the court and it has a complete power to refuse it if the contract is opposed to a statute or an attempt to evade a statute like President's Order 16 of 1972. In both the suits for specific performance of contracts, the Government including all the relevant functionaries of the Government were added as parties by the purchasers-appellants. In these suits, Government was made a party and in spite of due service of summons on the Government, Government did not appear to contest the suit in Civil Appeal No. 49 of 1994 and the suit was decreed ex parte. In Civil Appeal No. 80 of 1993, Government filed written statement in the trial Court and asserted that the suit building is an abandoned property, but did not ultimately contest the suit. In these decrees along with the vendor, the Government was also a party and it is needless to say that a decree whether contested or ex parte binds all the parties in a suit and the decision conclusively determines the rights of the parties in the suit. In the presence of the Government the purchasers filed the suit for specific performance of contract and as per the relevant provisions of President's Order 142 of 1972 as discussed above the Government could have raised an objection that the property by operation of law vested in the Government as an abandoned property. There is also nothing on record to show that this ex parte decree which binds the Government was attempted to be set aside at any point of time in Civil Appeal No. 49 of 1994 and thereby the Government accepted the decree that the transaction between the vendor and purchaser was a transaction of private individuals where the abandoned character of the property was not involved. Thus, though the suit was for specific performance of contract, but due to promulgation of President's Order 142 of 1972, the Government is authorized to raise the plea of abandoned character of the property and same having not been raised in defence by the Government the Government impliedly accepted that the property is not an abandoned property so far as the decree of the civil Court stands. It is needless to say that a decree of a civil Court has a solemn sanctity of its own and the same can be set aside only as provided under the existing law. Hence, the question comes up, whether in the face of the existence of a decree the Tribunal could sit over the decree as an appellate Court. The primary question that is to be decided here is, first, whether can the court of settlement sit over the decree of a civil Court by saying it is fraudulent and illegal. Secondly, apart from the decree, whether the Ordinance gives jurisdiction to the Court of Settlement to independently decide the question of abandoned character of the property. My answer to the first question is in the negative. My answer to the second question is, that the Court of Settlement could decide the abandoned character of the property for which the Court of Settlement was, in fact, established under the Ordinance provided the property is an "abandoned property" as defined in section 2 of President's Order No. 16 of 1972. 55. I will discuss the relevant provisions of Ordinance No. 54 of 1985 herein below: The Abandoned Building (Supplementary Provisions) Ordinance, 1985 (Ordinance No LIV of 1985), briefly, the Ordinance, provides a supplementary provision relating to abandoned buildings. This Ordinance makes a final list of ail abandoned buildings and the same has been notified in the official Gazette. This Ordinance gives a last opportunity to an aggrieved person to challenge before the Court of Settlement the inclusion of any building as an abandoned building. 56. Section 2(c) of this Ordinance speaks of President's Order 16 of 1972 which means that a property will be an "abandoned property" as per definition of Article 2 of President's Order 16 of 1972. Hence, the Court of Settlement is required to make an investigation as to whether the property is an abandoned property as published in the official Gazette as per section 2 of President's Order 16 of 1972. 57. I will quote section 5 as the same is indeed very important for our purpose. "Publication of lists of buildings-(1) The Government shall after the "Commencement of this Ordinance and before the 30th day of September, 1988, published, from time to time in the official Gazette". (Subs by Act 12 of 1988) (a) lists of buildings the possession of which have been taken as abandoned property under the President's Order. (b) "Lists of buildings in respect of which notices" (Subs. by Act 12/88) for surrendering or taking possession as abandoned property under the said order have been issued: Provided that no such list shall include any building in respect of which- (a) any decree or order has been passed, at any time before the publication of the list in the official Gazette, by any court declaring the building not to be an abandoned property or not to have vested in the Government under the President's Order or declaring the possession by the Government of the building as an abandoned property under that Order to be illegal or invalid or directing the Government or any officer or authority subordinate to it to return, restore or transfer the building to any person, or (b) a suit, appeal, application or other legal proceeding is pending before any court immediately before the date of publication of the list in the official Gazette, in which the vesting in, or possession of the Government of the building as abandoned property under the President's Order has been called in question in any manner whatsoever or any prayer has been made for return, restoration or transfer of the building by the Government or by any officer or authority subordinate to it to any person. (2) The lists published under sub-section (1) shall be conclusive evidence of the fact that the buildings included therein are abandoned property and have vested in the Government as such." 58. I want to mention that provisos (a) and (b) of section 5 of the Ordinance take into note of the decree or order of a civil Court which has been passed at any time before publication of the list in the official Gazette, by any court declaring the building not to be an abandoned property. Even proviso (b) speaks of a pending suit, appeal, application or other legal proceeding before any court immediately before the dale of publication of the list in the official Gazette in which the abandoned character/ vesting/possession has been called in question in any manner whatsoever or even a prayer for return, restoration or transfer of the building to an aggrieved person is pending for adjudication. So I find that these two provisions of section 5 very much refer the decree of a civil Court and the pendency of a legal proceeding in which abandoned character of the property, vesting, possession and return of the property is in question. 59. Section 5(I)(b) speaks of a suit, appeal, application or other legal proceeding and a suit may also include a suit for specific performance of contract as before promulgation of this Ordinance such a suit was never barred. 60. From provisos (a) and (b) of section 5 of the Ordinance, it is abundantly clear that the decree or order passed in any suit, appeal, application or other legal proceeding whether final or pending has been protected from the mischief of the Ordinance to avoid any conflicting decision between the decree of a civil Court and the order of a Court of Settlement. The Ordinance itself has taken into consideration earlier decree/order of a civil Court and pendency of a case before the civil Court relating to abandoned property. This being the intent of the Ordinance, the listing of the houses as abandoned houses in "Ka" list is contrary to provisos (a) and (b) of section 5 of the Ordinance. In Mr. Farooqui's appeal, in the suit for specific performance of contract, Government was a party and Government raised an issue that the property is not an abandoned property and the same was negatived by the trial Court. 61. The issue was discussed and decided by the trial Court in the following manner: "Issue 1: This point has to be discussed after the settlement of the point whether the suit property is an abandoned property or not. On perusal of the Gazette Notification of 1986, it appears that the suit property was listed as an abandoned property. But in section 5(1) of the Abandoned Buildings (Supplementary Provisions) Ordinance, 1985 it is clearly mentioned that no such list shall include any building in respect of which a suit, appeal, application or other legal proceeding is pending before any court, immediately before the date of publication of the list in the official Gazette in which the vesting in or possession of the Government of the building as abandoned property under the President's Order has been called in question in any manner whatsoever or any prayer has been made for return, restoration or transfer of the building to the Government or any officer or authority subordinate to it to any person. From perusal of the record it appears that the instant suit has been filed on 21.4.84. So, during the pendency of the suit, the suit property has been included in the list of abandoned property. As per section 5(b) of the Abandoned Buildings (Supplementary Provisions) Ordinance, 1985 such inclusion is illegal and invalid. Therefore, this issue is decided in favour of the plaintiff. 62. Against that order, an appeal is pending before the appellate Court of civil jurisdiction wherein the Government has specifically raised the issue that the property is not an abandoned property. Three grounds in the memo of appeal before the appellate Court is quoted below which clearly show that the abandoned character is in issue in the pending appeal. Grounds as follows: "(a) For that the learned Munsif, Additional Court decided the issue No.1 in favour of the respondent. (Plaintiff) without considering the contents of Ordinance LIV of 1985 Abandoned Buildings (Supplementary Provisions) Or4in-ance, 1985 with a judicial mind and wrongly and arbitrarily held that inclusion of the suit property in the list of abandoned property is illegal and invalid an as such, the aforesaid judgment and the decree are liable to be set aside. (b) For that the learned Court below ought to have held that the suit was barred under section 6 of Ordinance LIV of 1985 and articles 23 and 24 of President's Order 16 of 1972 and hold that the learned Court had no jurisdiction to entertain and try the instant suit. (c) For that the learned court quoted on a wrong notion of law in respect of the law and rules i.e. President's Order 16 of 1972 and subsequent Ordinance thereof under which abandoned properties are controlled and managed and fell in error in decreeing the suit." 63. A reference to section 6 of the Ordinance shows that after the promulgation of Ordinance No. 54 of 1985, suits of following nature are barred "(i) Suit for specific performance of contract in respect of a building the possession of which has been taken by the Government as an abandoned property or in respect of which a notice has been issued for taking possession of the house as an abandoned property; (ii) Suit for declaration that the building is not an abandoned property or the right and interest of any person has not been affected by the provisions of President's Order 16 of 1972; (iii) Suit for a direction to the Government to restore, return or transfer any building the possession of which has been taken by the Government as an Abandoned Property. It is clear that bar with respect to the suits of above nature were imposed after the promulgation of this Ordinance. Before that there was no such bar of filing of a suit for specific performance of contract making Government a party under President's Order 142 of 1972. Suits as specified in section 6 are prospectively barred. As if no suit in respect of abandoned property will lie after the publication of this Ordinance. This Ordinance gives a finality to all abandoned properties and the investigation will be only under the Ordinance. 64. A Court of Settlement as per section 9 of the Ordinance consists of Chairman and two other members. A Chairman shall be a person, who is or has been, or is qualified to be a judge or additional judge of the Supreme Court and amongst the two members one shall be a person who is or has been judicial officer not below the rank of Additional District Judge and the other person not below the rank of Deputy Secretary to the Government. 65. Sub-section 5 of section 10 speaks as to how a Court of Settlement shall determine and decide a case filed before it. Sub-Section 5 of section 10 reads as follows: "A Court of Settlement shall, after such enquiry as it may deem necessary and after giving reasonable opportunity to the parties concerned of being heard and also adducing evidence, both oral and documentary, if any, make such decision on the prayer of the application as it deems fit." 66. In section 11 of the Ordinance period of limitation has been extended for setting aside the ex parte decree after the commencement of this Ordinance. But the proviso of this section speaks that nothing in the section shall apply. (I) Where the decree or order of the court has lien duly executed. Thus in these cases where the decree of the civil Court has been duly executed the same are not to be disturbed. Thus reading section 5 and section 11 it is clear that the listing is contrary to the Ordinance. When a Court of Settlement consists of such persons and when sub-section (5) of section 10 of the Ordinance gives power of investigation a reasonable opportunity must be given to the party not only of being heard but also of adducing evidence both oral and documentary. 67. Hence, I will see whether reasonable opportunities were given to the parties to prove their cases. A finality has been given to a decision of the, Court of Settlement and the decision of the Court of Settlement is binding on all the parties. In such scheme of Ordinance one can legitimately make a grievance that an opportunity of fair trial must be given while disposing of the case by the Court of Settlement. There is also nothing on record more particularly from the judgment of the Court of Settlement that there was any hearing in the matter and that any opportunity was provided to the parties to adduce any evidence. The judgment of the Court of Settlement only speaks about the two agreements on the basis of which the decrees were passed by the civil Court. The Government ought to have filed a written objection challenging the assertions of the appellant and the documents. Then the appellant would: have got an opportunity to adduce evidence in rebuttal or the Government could have adduced oral or documentary evidence to dislodge the statement of the appellant. From a perusal of the judgment I do not find that anything in rebuttal was adduced by the Government challenging the contents in the petition before the Court of Settlement. Mr. Syed Ishtiaq Ahmed submits that the procedure that has been followed in the case is that, the Government file was only produced and the Court of Settlement considered the Government file and passed the impugned Judgment. I have no hesitation at all in accepting such submission of the learned Advocate as because I do not find anything in the judgment itself from where a conclusion can be drawn that the Court of Settlement independently decided the question of abandoned character of the property, other than commenting on the civil Court's decrees. It will not be out of place to mention that in the Government file there cannot be anything to show that the property is an abandoned property, but then how the Court of Settlement held without any contrary evidence in rebuttal that the building is an abandoned building. Prior to listing of the houses under Ordinance No. 54 of 1985, the houses were never treated as an abandoned property. The material findings of the Court of Settlement is referred herein below to show that the Court of Settlement really acted on pure surmise and conjecture with total disregard of its duty imposed on it under the Ordinance. 68. The Court of Settlement found that no written objection was filed by the Government but the Ministry's file was made available to the court. The Court of Settlement found that in Title Suit No. 5 of 1981 an ex parte decree was passed on the basis of an agreement between the appellant and the vendor and held as follows: "The certified copy of the order-sheet in the suit shows that the court passed the ex parte decree upon perusal of the plaint, document and deposition and it does not appear that the alleged agreement or bainapatra was produced and exhibited before the court." 69. Could there be a decree for specific performance of contract without the agreement? The mention of document in the order of the Civil Court is indicative of the agreement itself. 70. It is true that the Court of Settlement is not a civil Court but it notified the Government to file written objection; and a date was fixed for that purpose, but no written objection was filed. This shows that as a practice the Court of Settlement is asking for a written objection for proper disposal of the matter in accordance with law. Ordinarily an opportunity of making written objection against the petition will meet the requirement of natural justice, but that too has not been followed. The order-sheets of the cases were not filed by the parties, but that does not alter the position as the judgment is bereft of any tangible material, other than surmises, conjectures and comments on civil Court's decrees. The listing of the houses in "Ka" list are conclusive evidence that the houses are abandoned properties, but the Court of Settlement has been given a wide power to decide that question after thorough enquiry. There is nothing on record to show that any opportunity was given to any party to produce evidence or that the appellants chose not to avail of any opportunity of hearing. It will not be improper to say that the matter was decided on the basis of verbal submissions of the Advocates. In the circumstances, I have no hesitation in holding that sub-section (5) of section 10 has been totally ignored in deciding these two cases. 71. The Court of Settlement is a quasi-judicial tribunal set up under the Ordinance and it has full legal authority to determine the question regarding the abandoned character of the building affecting the rights of the parties. The Ordinance imposed a duty on it to act judicially and the Court of Settlement acted in violation of the principles of natural justice and norms of fair trial and failed to act in accordance with the jurisdiction vested in it by law. The Court of Settlement is not a court of civil jurisdiction, but it has to perform judicial function as per section 10 of the Ordinance and, therefore, discharges the functions of a court.
