The primary meaning of judicial function is the function of a court and this primary meaning has been widened to include quasi-judicial body like the Court of Settlement as it discharges judicial functions in the sense, without being a court. Sub-section (5) of section 10 of the Ordinance enjoins upon the Court of Settlement to act exclusively upon evidence and by giving reasonable opportunities to the parties. Certainly this Court of Settlement has got some of the trappings of a court but not all of them. Therefore, the Court of Settlement has a duty to follow the judicial approach in determining the question of fact involved in these cases. But unfortunately there was no judicial approach in the judgments. Judicial function contemplates hearing of evidence between the appellant and its adversary. Under Ordinance LIV of 1985, the Court of Settlement was duty bound to give a judicial approach to the whole controversy in issue between the parties. But unfortunately, the Court of Settlement on no evidence whatsoever erroneously decided the matter. 72. A duty having been cast on the Court of Settlement to dispose of a case in accordance with the direction of law and the same having not been done, the High Court Division in exercise of its writ jurisdiction which is in the nature of certiorari could very well set aside the judgment. 73. Mr. Farooqui argued with reference to proviso (b) of Section 5 of the Ordinance and contended that the question whether the property is an abandoned property or not is very much an issue both in the suit and in the pending appeal and as such the same cannot be listed under the Ordinance. To my mind, "called in question in any manner whatsoever" means a 'dispute' with regard to the abandoned character of a property which may be raised by any party as mentioned in proviso (b) of Section 5 of the Ordinance. The argument of Mr. Farooqui appears to be of substance. 74. Mr. Syed Ishtiaq Ahmed argued that listing of the property in "Ka" list under section 5(1) of the Ordinance is illegal as the possession of the property has not been taken as an abandoned property. The Ordinance came in 1985, but admittedly the appellant was in possession of the property in 1982 and again in 1983. So strictly speaking, possession being with the appellant the listing of the same in "Ka" list is contrary to section 5(1) of the Ordinance. Hence I hold that suit for specific performance of contract where the Government is a party under President's Order 142 of 1972, is a suit which is contemplated in provisions (a) and (b) of section 5 of the Ordinance and, as such, the listing is illegal and in violation of the proviso. Apart from the listing, the Ordinance gives a jurisdiction to the Court of Settlement to decide the question of abandoned character independently on evidence. This enquiry having not been done at all, the judgment of the Court of Settlement is no judgment in the eye of law. The Court of Settlement illegally sat over the judgments and decrees of the civil Court to pronounce its judgment. 75. Before parting with the case, I must very frankly say that in some leave petitions I held that a suit for specific performance of contract does not come under the provisos (a) and (b) of section 5(1) of the Ordinance. But after hearing the learned Advocates of the parties on President's Order 142 of 1972 and Ordinance 54 of 1985, I am constrained to take a different view in the matter after reviewing my own opinion. For the foregoing reasons, the appeals are allowed. End.

caseno: First Appeal No. 384 of 2011 with Civil Rule No. 553(F) of 2013
lawyer:
Ruhul Amin Tuhin, Advocate ----- For the Appellants. 
Abdul Wadud Bhuyan, with Md Ishaque Miah, Advocates ----- For the Respondents.
parties:
Hamidur Rahman and others ------ Petitioner
Vs.
Abdul Hashim and ors. ------ Opposite Parties
full_judgment:
Shahidul Karim J : This appeal is directed against the judgment and decree dated 23-8-2011 (decree signed on 29-8-2011) passed by the learned Joint District Judge, 1st Court, Brahmanbaria in Title Suit No. 17 of 1985 decreeing the suit.

2. The predecessor of respondent No. 1(a), namely, Abdul Hashim (since deceased) as plaintiff filed the original suit being Title Suit No. 17 of 1985 against the predecessor of defendant-appellants, namely, Abdul Mannan and others on the averments that he purchased the suit land from defendant Nos. 2 & 3 in the year 1964. That he had no prior knowledge about the contract of sale alleged to have been entered into between Abdul Mannan and defendant Nos. 2 & 3. After 3 (three) years into his purchase of the suit land, Title Suit No.01 of 1967 was filed by said Abdul Mannan for specific performance of contract with regard to the self-same land wherefrom he came to know about the alleged contract of sale. In the said suit the plaintiff was impleaded as defendant and he contested the same by filing written statement. But, eventually, the suit was decreed against which the present plaintiff took an appeal being Appeal No.156 of 1968 in the Court of District Judge, Comilla which was allowed and the decree passed by the trial court was knocked down. Feeling aggrieved thereby, the plaintiff of Title Suit No.01 of 1967 preferred a second appeal being Appeal No. 198 of 1970 before the then High Court, Dhaka which was ultimately allowed. Thereupon, the present plaintiff filed a civil petition for leave to appeal before the Appellate Division of the Supreme Court of Bangladesh being No. 231 of 1984 which was eventually dismissed. Thereafter, against the aforesaid order of dismissal a review petition was moved which was also ended up in the negative. However, while disposing of the aforesaid second appeal as well as the civil petition for leave to appeal, the relevant courts observed that the plaintiff is entitled to get compensation. The plaintiff has been possessing the suit land since his purchase in 1964 and during these years he made a considerable improvement on the suit land by erecting different structures as well as by doing several development activities. In the aforesaid backdrop, the plaintiff is entitled to get Taka 6,08,189 as compensation and hence the suit. It is to be noted further that during pendency of the suit an Advocate Commissioner was appointed on the prayer of the plaintiff party to assess the value of different structures standing on the suit land as well as the improvement cost employed thereon, who however submitted a report on 8-2-1989 wherein the value was shown as more than Taka 43 lacs and accordingly, the plaint was amended whereby the claim of compensation was raised to the tune of Taka 43 lacs and odd.

3. Defendant No.1(Zha) contested the suit by filing written statement denying all the material allegations made in the plaint and contended, inter-alia, that the suit is not maintainable in its present form and manner; the suit is barred by limitation; and it is not entertainable as per provision of section 51 of the Transfer of Property Act (hereinafter referred to as the Act). The further case of defendant No.1 (Zha) is that the suit land along with other land measuring 5.81 acres originally belonged to Gongabasi Debi and others which was put on auction for non-payment of rent in certificate case No.55921of 1960-61 whereupon defendant No.2 Ismail and defendant No.3 Abdul Ahad purchased the said land on 3-7-1961 and got sale certificate thereof as well as delivery of possession on 19-2-1963 through court. While the aforesaid auction purchasers were owning and possessing the said land, they proposed to sell 4.81 acres of land to the father of the defendant, namely, Abdul Mannan and accordingly, a talk of sale was held on 9 Magh 1369 BS wherein the price of the land was settled at Taka 5000 in presence of defendant No. 4 and others. In that meeting it was further agreed that the father of the defendant would pay Taka 601 as earnest money to defendant Nos.2 & 3 whereupon they in return would execute a bainapatra in favour of the former and would also hand over possession and subsequently upon receiving income tax clearance certificate and nationality certificate they would execute and register a sale deed on receiving the balance consideration money amounting to Taka 4399. Thereupon, in terms of the above contract on 10th Magh 1369 BS the defendant Nos. 2 & 3 executed a bainapatra in the name of the father of the answering defendant, Abdul Mannan upon receiving Taka 601 as earnest money in presence of the witnesses. Subsequently, on different occasions the father of the defendant Abdul Mannan paid Taka 4000 to defendant Nos. 2 & 3 who acknowledged the same by issuing receipt thereof. But, eventually, the defendant Nos. 2 & 3 did not execute and register a sale deed in favour of Abdul Mannan whereupon he was rather compelled to institute a suit being Title Suit No.01 of 1967 for specific performance of contract in the court of the then Sub-Ordinate Judge, 2nd Court, Comilla which was ultimately decreed on contest. Against the said decree, an appeal being Appeal No. 156 of 1968 was filed which was, however, allowed. Thereupon, the father of the defendant, Abdul Mannan took a 2nd appeal in the then High Court, Dhaka being appeal No. 198 of 1970 which was allowed on contest and the decision of the trial court was restored. The said verdict of the High Court was also upheld by the Appellate Division in civil petition for leave to appeal No. 231 of 1984 preferred by the present plaintiff and defendant Nos. 4 & 5 and subsequently, their review petition was also rejected by the highest court of the country. The present plaintiff and defendant Nos. 4 & 5 had full knowledge about the contract of sale of the father of the defendant. But, in spite of that, they created some fake and spurious deeds with respect to the self-same land. In the aforementioned suit and appeal it was also decided by the relevant courts that the present plaintiff and defendant Nos. 4 & 5 were not bonafide purchasers of the suit land without notice, rather they were well conversant with the bainanama of the father of the defendant. The plaintiff did not make any improvement on the suit land and all the works he had done therein were for his own use and occupation and therefore, he is not entitled to get any improvement costs and, as such, the suit is liable to be dismissed with costs.

4. Upon the aforesaid pleadings, the learned judge of the trial court framed the following issues:

1. Whether the suit is maintainable in its present form and manner?

2. Whether the suit is barred by limitation?

3. Is the suit bad for defect of parties?

4. Whether the plaintiff has any right, title and possession in the suit land?

5. Is the plaintiff entitled to get decree as prayed for?

6. What other reliefs the plaintiff is entitled to get?

5. In support of his claim the plaintiff adduced 3 (three) witnesses and also submitted some documents which were duly marked as Exhibits. On the other hand, the defendant examined one witness to prove his case but did not produce any documentary evidence.

6. Upon a consideration of the facts, circumstances and evidences on record the learned Joint District Judge decreed the suit by the impugned judgment and decree dated 23-8-2011 holding that as per observations made by the Higher Courts in Civil Revision No.905 of 1986 and Leave Petition No.137 of 1985 the plaintiff is entitled to get compensation and also that admittedly the plaintiff has been possessing the suit land for about 40/50 years wherein he

constructed building, excavated ponds as well as made plantation of different types of trees for which he is entitled to receive compensation to the tune of Taka 43,79,155 as reflected in the advocate commissioner's report which was accepted without any objection from the side of the defendant.

7. Feeling aggrieved thereby, the defendant along with other heirs of late Abdul Mannan preferred the instant appeal.

8. Mr Ruhul Amin Tuhin, learned advocate appearing for the defendant-appellant at the outset has taken us through the pleadings of the parties, impugned judgment, evidences and other connected materials available on record and then submits strenuously that the learned judge of the trial committed patent illegality in decreeing the suit inasmuch as no observation was made either by the High Court or by the Appellate Division in Civil Revision No.905 of 1986 as well as Leave Petition No.137 of 1985 respectively regarding the status of the plaintiff so far the matter of his being bonafide purchaser without notice of the earlier contract is concerned. He further submits that the suit in question was filed by the plaintiff-respondent No.1 under section 51 of the Act under which a person having a defective title if evicted from the land in dispute can maintain a suit for compensation. But since the plaintiff- respondent has admittedly been possessing the suit land and as he is yet to be evicted therefrom, his claim for compensation is not tenable in law being premature in nature. Moreover, the plaintiff has miserably failed to prove the very fact that he is a bonafide purchaser without notice of the contract of sale of defendant's predecessor Abdul Mannan by adducing any cogent evidence which is a precondition for maintaining a suit under section 51 of the Act. Rather, in Title Suit No.01 of 1967 as well as connected 2nd appeal No.198 of 1970 it was decided that the plaintiff was not a bonafide purchaser of the suit land and he was well aware of the contract of sale of Abdul Mannan and, as such, he is not entitled to get any compensation. But the trial court utterly failed to appreciate this aspect of the case and on a misconstruction of both the intent and purport of section 51 of the Act as well as the tenor of the judgment passed by the superior courts of the country in civil revision No.905 of 1986 and civil petition No.137 of 1985 most illegally decreed the suit, the learned Advocate further added. Finally, Mr Tuhin submits that the impugned judgment and decree is bad in law and facts inasmuch as the plaintiff has hopelessly failed to prove that he. was a bonafide purchaser of the suit land without notice of the earlier contract of sale by adducing any sort of convincing evidence and also that he has not actually been, evicted from the suit land rather he is yet to be evicted and, as such, the impugned judgment and decree is liable to be knocked down being devoid of any substance.

9. As against this, Mr Abdul Wadud Bhuiyan, learned Advocate representing the plaintiff-respondent supports the impugned judgment and decree which, according to him is just, proper and legal. He submits that the trial court below on proper appreciation of both facts and law rightly and lawfully decreed the suit by the impugned judgment which does not warrant any interference by this court as it is based on evidence on record as well as supported by the uncontroverted report of the advocate commissioner. He further submits that the suit is not a premature one as because plaintiff, being a bonafide holder of the land in question under registered sale deeds, is entitled to get back the improvement costs. According to him, the words "evicted therefrom" as occurring in section 51 of the Act includes a person who is about to be evicted and since there is no other option for the petitioner to retain the land in dispute rather, he is about to be evicted therefrom, his claim of compensation under section 51 of the Act is well maintainable.

10. We have given our anxious consideration to the submissions advanced by the learned advocates of both the sides, perused the plaint as well as written statement, evidences and other connected materials on record including the impugned judgment and decree dated 23-8-2011 and also considered the relevant law bearing on the subject extensively.

11. It is indisputable that the predecessor of the defendant-appellants, namely, Abdul Mannan got a decree for specific performance of contract with regard to the suit land including other land which was upheld by the highest courts of the country. Admittedly, the plaintiff of the instant suit Abdul Hashim (since deceased) was made party in the aforesaid suit along with other defendants and their contention so far their purchase of the suit land without notice of the earlier contract of sale of said Abdul Mannan was turned down by the High Court as well as by the Appellate Division in 2nd appeal No. 198 of 1970 and civil petition for leave to appeal No. 23 I of 1984 respectively. Thereafter, the said Abdul Hashim instituted the instant suit claiming compensation for the various improvement works alleged to have been carried out by him on the suit land. This claim of the plaintiff was resisted by the defendant 1(Zha) by filing written statement wherein it has been categorically asserted that the plaintiff along with other defendants of Title Suit No.01 of 1967 had prior knowledge about the contract of sale of the predecessor of the defendant and he is not a bonafide purchaser of the suit land without notice of the earlier contract. Furthermore, the defendant did not make any improvement on the suit land, as such, and his claim of compensation under section 51 of the Act is untenable in law. With a view to appreciate the issue involved in the case, we feel it expedient to have a glimpse at section 51 of the Act which reads as under:

"51. Improvements made by bona fide holders under defective titles—When the transferee of immovable property makes any improvement on the property, believing in good faith that he is absolutely entitled (hereto, and he is subsequently evicted therefrom by any person having a better title, the transferee has a right to require the person causing the eviction either to have the value of the improvement estimated and paid or secured to the transferee, or to sell his interest in the property to the transferee at the then marked value thereof, irrespective of the value of such improvement. The amount to be paid or secured in respect of such improvement shall be the estimated value thereof at the time of the eviction. When, under the circumstances afore-said, the transferee has planted or sown on the property crops which are growing when he is evicted therefrom, he is entitled to such crops and to free ingress and egress to gather and carry them."

12. On a careful analysis of the aforesaid provision of law it is apparent that a person who has been evicted can claim compensation under section-51, provided he is (1) a transferee, (2) he has made the improvement, (3) he has made such improvement believing in good faith that he was absolutely entitled, and (4) he was evicted. The above various capacities or qualifications are to be filled or fulfilled by the person who sought compensation under the above section. Let us now examine how far the plaintiff of the instant suit has been able to satisfy or fulfill the above conditions which are considered to be pre requisites for getting a favourable order under section-51 of the Act.

13. On a reference to Exhibits-1 to 5 it reveals that the plaintiff-respondent and defendant Nos.4 & 5 purchased the suit land in between the years 1963 to 1966 through 5 sale deeds from defendant Nos. 2 & 3 namely, Md Ismail Mia and his son Abdul Ahad. Therefore, the plaintiff-respondent Abdul Hashim can be regarded as a transferee so far the land covered by Exhibits-3 to 5 is concerned. But that alone would not entitle him to get any compensation under section 51 of the Act. In this case at our hand the paramount question that calls for our determination is, whether the plaintiff was a bonafide purchaser of the land in question for value without notice of the earlier contract of sale thereof between respondent-defendant No.1 Abdul Mannan on one hand and defendant Nos.2 & 3 on the other hand as well as whether the plaintiff did the alleged improvement works in good faith believing him to be the real owner.

14. Upon scanning through the evidences on record it appears palpably that in fact no satisfactory as well as cogent evidence has been adduced by the plaintiff party to prove the aforesaid aspects of the case. It is undeniable that the plaintiff herein as well as defendant Nos.4 & 5 was made party in suit Title Suit No.01 of 1967 filed by the aforesaid Abdul Mannan for specific performance of contract wherein by filing written statement they raised the plea of bonafide purchaser of the land in question without notice of the earlier contract of sale. It appears that while deciding Title Suit No.01 of 1967 an issue being issue No. 3 was framed touching the status of the plaintiff herein so far his claim of being bonafide purchaser without notice of the earlier contract with respect to the land in dispute is concerned in the following words: (3) Are the 2nd party-defendants bonafide purchasers for value and without notice of contract of sale?

15. Admittedly as well as it reveals from the materials on record that such plea of the plaintiff was negatived by the trial court with a clear finding that the plaintiff and defendants Nos.4 & 5 (who were termed as 2nd party defendants in Title Suit No. 1 of 1967) had full knowledge about the contract of sale of plaintiff Abdul Mannan (defendant No. 1 of the instant suit) with regard to the suit land. It is true that the aforesaid finding of the trial court was nullified by the learned District Judge while disposing the connected appeal being Title Appeal No.156 of 1968. But ultimately the decision of the learned District Judge, Comilla was, however, reversed and that of the trial judge was restored by this Court while dealing with the connected 2nd Appeal being No. 198 of 1970. It appears further that against the verdict of this court civil petition for leave to appeal being No.231 of 1984 was moved before the Appellate Division which was also dismissed and the above observation of this court was maintained. To have a better view of the issue, we feel it necessary to quote the relevant portion of the judgment passed by my lord Mr Justice ATM Afzal in 2nd Appeal No. 198 of 1970, which reads as under: "Now coming to the issue No.3 it must be pointed out at the outset that the District Judge has totally failed to make a systematic and correct approach in the matter as was done by the Subordinate Judge, In view of the allegation and counter-allegation of collusion between the plaintiff and the 1st party-defendants on the one hand and between the 1st party defendants and the 2nd party-defendants on the other, it was absolutely necessary for the District Judge to assess the stand and evidence of the 1st party-defendants in the matter which he, at all, did not do upon a consideration of all the relevant aspects of the case. Be that as it may, while considering whether defendants No. 3 and 4 had knowledge of the disputed contract before purchasing the suit lands he failed to notice that besides the plaintiff the defendants No.1 and 2, who were the sellers, themselves admitted in their written statement that defendant No. 3 was present at the time of settlement of the contract. PW 2, Bidhu Bhusan Das, of course, did not support the plaintiff's case as to the presence of defendant No.3, Abdul Gafur for which he was cross-examined by the plaintiff. But then there was the evidence of PW 3 Abdul Malek. There were some suggestions of enmity given to this witness from the side of the defendants No. 3 & 4 but the witness denied the said suggestions. Therefore, the trial court found him to be an independent witness but the District Judge seemed to have been impressed by the suggestions given to the witness which were denied. Obviously, this was not a correct approach in assessing the evidence. Furthermore, neither the plaintiff (PW 1) nor PW 3 were put any straight question in cross-examination by defendants No. 3 & 4 denying the presence of Gafur at the settlement of the contract. The District Judge made no endeavor to assess the role and character of PW 2 Bidhu Bhusan Das in view of his relationship with both the 1st party-defendants and the plaintiff. The Subordinate Judge made a shrewd assessment of his evidence and gave him the importance that was due to him. The District Judge was nowhere near the way, in which the evidence was sifted, analysed and assessed by the trial Court. Then with regard to the knowledge of the defendant No. 5, the evidence has come from a person no other than the vendor himself i.e. defendant No. 1 (DW 1). In this case also the District Judge made a mistake by holding that the defendant No.5 if at all was informed about that, even if it was executed by the defendant No.1, it was definitely a malafide one and could not but be termed as collusive. Evidently, this was nobody's case that exhibit-2 was collusive. The 1st party-defendants alleged the same to be forged. But upon a meticulous consideration, the Subordinate Judge found exhibit-2 to be a genuine receipt. Now the District Judge out of the blue found that it was a collusive receipt. Indeed, he was not at all called upon to decide on the receipt, inasmuch as, the point at issue whether the appellants were bonafide purchasers for valuable consideration without notice did not involve the consideration of the receipt which was between the 1st party-defendants and the plaintiff. The impugned judgment has been so loosely written that it becomes difficult to keep track with what the discussion was aiming at. On the balance and for the reasons stated above, I am satisfied that it was not at all a proper judgment of reversal and the same is liable to be set aside. "

16. Furthermore, while deciding Civil Petition for Leave to Appeal No.231 of 1984, the highest court of the country has observed as follows:

"Mr MH Khondker appearing for the defendants 3 to 5 attempted to argue that they were bonafide purchasers for value without notice of the plaintiff's contract. This argument does not appeal to us inasmuch as the finding of fact by the trial court was affirmed by the High Court Division in Second Appeal after due assessment of the plaintiffs evidence which is unassailable. Mr Khondker took exception to certain casual observations made in the judgment of the High Court Division which, however, could not make any difference in evaluating the evidence that the defendants had prior knowledge of the contract of the plaintiff. In this view of the matter, there is no hesitation to say that the High Court Division rightly restored the judgment and decree of the trial court which decreed the suit for Specific Performance of Contract. In the result therefore this petition is dismissed."

17. It is also an admitted position that the plaintiff of the instant suit moved a review petition being No.01 of 1985 before the Appellate Division and the said review petition was also turned down.

18. The essence of our above discussion is that the plaintiff-respondent was not a bonafide purchaser without notice of the contract of sale of the predecessor of the contesting defendant-appellants, namely, Abdul Mannan, rather he was well aware of the said contract of sale. Furthermore, since the issue of bonafide purchase without notice has already been settled between the parties by the highest court of the country, the same cannot be reopened in any subsequent suit between the same parties as the verdict of the highest court of the country is biding upon them.

19. It further appears that admittedly a lengthy as well as tedious legal battle with respect to the land in question has been fought between the parties the starting point of which dates back to 1967 and the same is still continuing. It is on record that the predecessor of the defendant-appellants, Abdul Mannan instituted the suit for specific performance of contract in 1967 which was decreed on contest against the plaintiff of the instant suit and others on 20-9-1968. From the above decision of the court concerned several legal proceedings were originated up to the Appellate Division of the country wherein the claim of the said Abdul Mannan was eventually sustained and that of the contesting defendants of that suit was nullified. In the said legal proceedings it was further decided that Abdul Mannan purchased the structures standing on the land in question from its original owner by paying money. Now the plaintiff herein has filed the instant suit in 1985 claiming compensation for the improvement works alleged to have been done by him on the suit land which, in view of the explicit provision of section 51 of the Act, appears to be wholly untenable inasmuch as he did not do it in good faith believing him the real owner. Rather, in the facts and circumstances of the case it is apparent that the plaintiff was well aware of the fact that he is not the real owner of the land in question as he knew it very well from the very beginning about the contract of sale of the predecessor of the defendant-appellants as observed by the highest court of the country regarding which we have noticed earlier. In the alternative it can be said that the alleged improvement on the land in question was made by the plaintiff for his own use and occupation taking the risk on his shoulder.

<u>20. It transpires from the record that at the time of filing of the instant suit on 3-3-1985 the amount of improvement cost was shown as Taka 6,08,189.50 which was ultimately raised to Taka 43,79,155 by way of amendment of plaint done on the basis of a report dated 8-2-1998 filed by the Advocate Commissioner whereby the value was enhanced keeping congruity with the then market price 'of the alleged improvement works. On a perusal of the impugned judgment it reveals that the learned judge of the trial court decreed the suit and directed the contesting defendant-appellant to pay the above amount of Taka 43,79,155 to the plaintiff. The aforesaid decision of the court below is totally unfounded in law as because as per section 51 of the Act a bonafide transferee can maintain a suit for compensation if he is evicted from the land in dispute and that too for the estimated value of the improvement works done at the time of such eviction. But in the instance case we found that the plaintiff has hopelessly failed to fulfill the above two criteria inasmuch as he is not a bonafide transferee rather he had full knowledge about the earlier contract of sale (which issue has already been settled by the highest court) and he has not been evicted either from the land in dispute as admittedly the land in question is still under his possession. There is no legal scope for a person intended to be evicted from a piece of land to claim compensation under section 51 of the Act. Only the person actually evicted can maintain a suit under the above provision of law and that too for the period till eviction is made. Moreover, there is no right to compensation for improvements made pendent lite with full knowledge of the risk in doing so and, as such, the claim of compensation of the plaintiff for the improvement works alleged to have been done during pendency of the suit is altogether unacceptable.</u>

21. It appears that while delivering the impugned judgment the learned Joint District Judge opined that as per observations of the higher courts made in Civil Revision No.905 of 1986 and Leave Petition No.137 of 1985 (Exhibits-6 & 7) the plaintiff is entitled to receive compensation. This finding of the trial court is palpably wrong and perfunctory in nature as nowhere in their judgments this Court as well as the Appellate Division made any such observations. Therefore, we are unable to go along with the above findings of the trial court and, as such, the same is liable to be scrapped. Furthermore, on a query by us, the learned Advocate for the plaintiff-respondent also finds it difficult to support the aforesaid findings of the trial court.

<u>22. During making submissions, Mr Wadud Bhuiyan, learned Advocate for the plaintiff-respondent tried his best to impress upon the court by saying that since the plaintiff-respondent is a bonafide holder of the land in dispute under defective title and as admittedly he did a lot of improvement works thereon as such he is entitled to get compensation for the above improvement costs which has been duly reflected in the unassailed report of the advocate commissioner, though he is yet to be evicted from the suit land. But on the face of the evidence record and in view of the facts and circumstances of the case we are unable to see eye to eye with the above view expressed by Mr Bhuiyan inasmuch as we have already noticed that the plaintiff had full knowledge about the contract of sale of the defendant-appellants predecessor, namely, Abdul Mannan and that the alleged improvement works were done by the plaintiff for the purpose of his own use and comfort and that too during the pendency of the earlier suit as well as the instant one between the parties taking the risk on his shoulder. Therefore, under no circumstances the plaintiff can be regarded as a bonafide holder of the suit land. On top of that, the plaintiff is still in possession of the suit land and he is yet to be evicted. Keeping in view the language used is section 51 of the Act, we have no hesitation but to hold that a person intended to be evicted from a land cannot maintain a suit for the alleged improvement costs under the section, rather his right to sue would accrue only after actual eviction is made.</u>

23. It appears that the aforesaid aspects of the case have altogether escaped the notice of the learned trial judge who, being goaded by some unfounded observations as well as without construing the true intent of section 51 of the Act, most illegally decreed the suit in favour of the plaintiff by the impugned judgment dated 23-8-2011 which, as it appears, has failed to withstand the test of legal scrutiny and therefore, the same is liable to be knocked-down.

24. In the light of our aforementioned observations and the decisions made thereunder, we are impelled to hold that the appeal merits consideration and therefore, it must succeed.

25. Accordingly, the appeal is allowed on contest without any order as to costs. The judgment and decree impugned against herein is set aside and the original suit being Title Suit No. 17 of 1985 is dismissed on contest.

26. Since the appeal is allowed, the connected Rule being Civil Rule No.553 (F) of 2013 is accordingly disposed of.

Send down the lower Court's record along with a copy of the judgment forthwith.

End.

Monoruddin (Md) ----- Plaintiff-Appellant-Petitioner
Vs
Md. Salauddin Sarkar and others ----- Defendant-Respondent-Opposite-Parties
full_judgment:
This Rule was issued calling upon the opposite party Nos. 1-4 to show cause as to why the impugned judgment and decree dated 26-7-2011 and 1-8-2011 respectively passed by the Joint District Judge, 2nd Court, Gazipur in Other Class Appeal No. 140 of 2008 disallowing the appeal and affirming the judgment and decree dated 21- 10-2008 and 28-10-2008 respectively passed by the Assistant Judge, 4fh Court, Gazipur in Title Suit No. 249 of 2006 dismissing the suit should not be set aside and/or such other or further order or orders passed as to this Court may seem fit and proper.

2. The fact of the case lies in a very short compass. The petitioner as plaintiff filed title Suit No. 249 of 2006 in the Court of 4th Assistant Judge, Gazipur, for a decree of permanent injunction against the defendant opposite parties, stating, inter alia, that the suit lands originally belonged to Hazmat Ali and accordingly, recorded in his name in CS Khatian No. 124. Hazmat Ali sold out 0.90 sataks of land out of 1.11 acres in CS plot No. 359 and 0.06 acres in CS plot No. 360 totalling 0.96 acres to his son Mohammad Ali by a registered deed No. 7083 dated 7-10-1942. Mohammad Ali sold 0.171/2sataks out of 0.90 sataks from plot No. 359 to Bhaira Lal Ruhidash. The said Bhaira Lal Ruhidash again sold out the said 0.171/2sataks to Ayeb Ali and others vide registered deed No. 13892 dated 6-12-1948. Then Ayeb Ali and others sold the. Saido.17 and 1/2 sataks land to the plaintiff Md Monoruddin vide registered deed No. 4808 dated 11-4-1970. Mohammad Ali again sold 0.12 sataks of land out of 0.72 and 1/2 sataks to one Mokles Uddin Mia vide registered deed No. 8642 dated 17-4-1961, 0.17 and 1/2sataks to the plaintiff Mdonoruddin by registered deed No. 138 dated 2-1-1,967 and 0.17 and 1/2sataks to Lal Mia vide registered deed No. 3087 dated 6-2-1961. So, after the transfers aforesaid Mohammad Ali had 25 and1/2sataks of land in plot No. 359 under CS khatian No. 124. Hazmat Ali died leaving behind 2 (two) sons namely, Mohammad Ali and Ohad Ali and 3 (three) daughters, Moziran Nessa, Asia Khatun and Alemon Nessa. From remaining 21 sataks land in plot No. 359 each son got 0.06 sataks and each daughter got 0.03 sataks. Among the aforesaid sons and daughters of Hazmat Ali, .Ohad Ali and Moziran Nessa sold 0.06 + 0.03 = 0.09 sataks land to the plaintiff vide registered deed No. 5788 dated 22-5-1967 and another two daughters Asia Khatun and AlemonNessa sold their 0.03 + 0.03 = 0.06 sataks land to the plaintiff vide registered deed No. 9219 dated 8-9-1969. Moklesuddin sold 0.12 sataks land in plot No. 359 to the plaintiff vide registered deed No. 3385 dated 1.6-3-1970 and deed No. 8642 dated 17-4-196L After the transfers Mohammad Ali had 25 and 1/2sataks in plot No. 159 and 0.06 sataks in plot No. 360 and accordingly for the said quantum of land RS record has been prepared in his name. He died leaving' behind son Shahajuddin and daughter Tara Banu. Thereafter, Tara Banu sold 0.09 sataksvide registered deed No. 6187 dated 6-6-1967 and 0.09 sataks vide deed No. 7322 dated 24-7-1967 to the plaintiff but handed over possession of 0.121/2sataks land. Shahajuddin sold 0.25 sataks land to the plaintiff vide registered deed No. 2067 dated 19-2-1970. Accordingly, the plaintiff has become owner of 0.99 and 1/2sataks land covered by plot Nos. 359 and 360 by purchase: The plaintiff sold 0.58 sataks land out of 0.991/2sataks to the different persons and he has been owning and possessing 0.41 and 1/2sataks land. The defendant has mutated his name in the khatian by filing Mutation Case No. 7005/1999-2000 and 5005/2001-2002 on the basis of a fabricated deed No. 22684 dated 11- 12- 2001 alleged tohave been executed by one Alauddin who had no title in the suit property. The Plaintiff upon receipt of information about the same prayed for cancellation of the alleged mutation cases before the Assistant Commissioner (Land), Gazipur, by filing a Miscellaneous Case No.4 7 of 2002. The Assistant Commissioner (Land), advised the plaintiff to go to civil court for prop relief. Thereafter, the plaintiff filed Title Suit No. 259 of 2003 which was renumbered as Title Suit No.7 of 2005 but for some mistake in the plaint, he has withdrawn the said suit for filing a fresh suit. The defendant threatened the plaintiff with dispossession and tried to take over possession of the suit land on 2- 9-2005 at 9-00 am. Hence, the instant suit for permanent injunction.

3. The opposite party No.1 as defendant contested the suit by filing written, statement denying all the material allegations made in the plaint contending, inter alia, that the land in CS khatian No. 124 originally belonged to Hazmat Ali. He died leaving behind only son Mohammad AIL Mohammad Ali died leaving behind son Alauddin and daughter Tara Banu. Mohammad Ali has/had no son named Shahajuddin. The said Alauddin and Tara Banu while owning and' possessing the land they sold 0.60 sataks to the defendant No. 1 vide registered deed No. 22683 dated 11-12-2001 and on the same date they sold 0.06 sataks land vide registered Deed No. 22864 totaling 0.66 sataks to the defendant No. 1 and handed over possession of the same. Mohammad Ali never sold his land in his life time to anybody. Alauddin sold a portion of the suit plots to the defendant No.1 by registered deed and exchanged 0,06sataks with the defendant No.1. The defendant' No.1 after purchase got his name mutated vide case No. 5005/2001-2002 and paid rent upto 1411 BS and possessing the suit land, as such, the suit is liable to be dismissed.

4. The plaintiff examined 4 (four) witnesses and defendant examined none to-prove his case.

5. The trial court upon contested hearing dismissed the suit by its judgment and decree dated 21-10-2008. Against the judgment of the trial court, the plaintiff-petitioner preferred Other Class Appeal No. 140 of 2008 before the District Judge, Gazipur and the said appeal was heard by the Joint District Judge, 2nd Court; Gazipur on transfer, who upon contested hearing disallowed the appeal affirming the judgment and decree of the trial court. At this stage, the plaintiff-appellant-petitioner moved this Court by filing this revisional application under section 115(1) of the Code of Civil Procedure and obtained the present Rule and order of status-quo. During pendency of this revision the petitioner died and his heirs have been substituted.

6. Mr Md Mahbub Ali, senior Advocate, with, Mr Sk Habib-ul-Alam, the learned Advocates appearing for the petitioners submit that the petitioner successfully proved the case before the trial court by adducing sufficient evidences both oral and documentary relating to the suit property and even by amending the plaint in appeal but both the courts below upon misconception of law as well as misreading Of the evidences on record most illegally dismissed the suit as well as the appeal. He further submits that the defendants though filed a written statement denying the case of the plaintiff but at the time Of hearing did not adduce any evidence even produced a single paper before the trial court in support of his claim and, as such, the defendant-opposite party has no case before the court in accordance with law. It is also argued that the petitioner categorically stated his case in the plaint as well as' at the time of recording deposition and produced witnesses in support of their possession in the suit property but both the courts below upon misconstruction of the evidences adduced before the trial court most illegally dismissed the suit 'of the plaintiff as well as the appeal on the finding that the plaintiff could not prove their possession and title in the suit property by producing sufficient evidences both, oral and documentary and, as such, the judgments and decree of the' courts  below is liable to be set-aside

7. Mr Md Mozaminel Hossain, the learned Advocate appearing for the opposite party Nos.1 and 2 submits that the suit was filed by the plaintiff seeking a decree against the defendant. The cardinal principal of law is that the plaintiff is to prove his case by adducing and producing sufficient evidences before the trial court and he cannot depend upon the weakness of the defence; But in the instant case the petitioner as plaintiff could not prove, his case by filing sufficient documents in support of his alleged title and also failed to prove his exclusive, possession in the suit land and, as such, both the courts below rightly dismissed the suit as well as the appeal and by refusing the prayer of the petitioner, both-the courts below have not committed any error of law, resulting in an error in the decision occasioning failure of justice.

8. Heard the learned Advocate for the parties, gone through the application, judgments of both the courts below and the evidences lying in the lower court records.

9. Admittedly the property in question covered by two CS plot Nos. 359 arid 360 under CS Khatian No. 124 measuring 1.17acres originally belonged to one Hazmat Ali, who by areglistered deed dated 7-10-1942 transferred 90 sataks of land from Plot Nos: 359 (part) and 360 (full) to his son Mohammad Aliand thesaid Mohammad Ali by different kabalas of different dates transferred total quantum of landmeasuring  64 and 1/2   sataksout of his purchased 0.90 sataks land. The remaining 21 sataks of plot No. 359 left by Hazmat Ali were inherited by his son Mohammad Ali and Ohad Ali, three daughters namely, Mojiran Nessa, Asia Khatun and Alemon Nessa; The petitioner claimed that he purchased the suit land from Mohammad Ali, his brother, sisters and his :son Shahajuddin and daughter Tara Banu on differentdates by different kabala stotalling 0.99 and 1/2sataks. Out of the purchased land the petitioner transferred 0.58 sataks of land to different persons who have been possessing the same with specific boundary.

10. The opposite parties claimed that Hazmat Ali had only son named Mohammad Ali He had no other heirs named Ohad Ali, Mojiran Nessa, Asia Khatun and Alemon Nessa. Mohammad Ali died leaving son Alauddin and daughter Tara Banu.: The opposite party claimed that they got 0.06 sataks of land from Plot No. 359 by way of exchange with the son and daughter Mohammd Ali and after exchange they got their names mutated in the khatian and possessing the same on payment of regular rents to the Government. On the other hand, the petitioners claimed that Mohammad Ali died leaving son Shahajuddin and Tara Banu who got 0.37 nad 1/2 sataks of land by inheritance and sold the same to the petitioner in the year 1967 and by purchase the petitioners have been possessing the suit land with specific boundary. The petitioner in support of his claim adduced 4 witnesses including the petitioner's son.

11. It appears from the examination-in-chief that PW 1 chronologically stated the case of the petitioner with reference, to the deeds of transfer. PWs 2, 3 and 4 deposed in respect of possession of the petitioner. The plaintiff-petitioner to prove his title in the property produced some documents which were duly exhibited as Exhibits-2-8. In cross-examination by the defendant opposite parties, PWs told that Hazmat Ali had two sons and three daughters and Mohammad Ali died leaving son Shahujuddin and daughter Tara Banu and denied the suggestion that Hazmat Ali had only son Mohammad Ali.

12. I have gone through the judgment of the trial court. It appears that the trial court chronologically stated the case of the plaintiff and considered the exhibits filed by the petitioner and also considered the written statement filed by the opposite parties as defendant but the trial court in its judgment observed that though the defendant- opposite parties filed written statement and cross- examined the PWs giving suggestions but did not adduce any evidence both oral and documentary and observed that the defendants claim has no basis at all. The trial court upon consideration of the evidences and the documents filed by the petitioner came to a finding that:

বাদীপক্ষ দাবী করে যে বিভিন্ন দলিল মূলে ক্রয়সূত্রে এবং ১/২ শতাংশ সম্পতিতে মালিক দখলদার থাকা কালে ৫৮ শতাংশ জমি বিভিন্ন লোকের বরাবর হস্তান্তর করে দখল বুঝিয়ে দিয়ে বাকী ৪১ এবং ১/২ শতাংশ জমির ভোগ দখলকার আছেন। বাদীর দাখিলী প্রর্দশনী চিহিূত  দলিল সূত্রে বাদীর ৪০ শতাংশ জমিতে মালিক থাকা প্রমানিত হলে ও দাবীকৃত বাকী জমির মালিকানা বিষয়ে উপযুক্ত প্রমাণ দাখিল হয়নি। তাছাড়া বাদী তার মালিকানাধীন কোন দাগ বা খতিয়ানের কতটুকু জমি, কি সুত্রে কার বরাবর হস্থান্তর করেছে তার বণর্না বাদীর আর্জিতে উল্লেখ করেনি।

বাদী ৩১৪ নং RS খতিয়ান ভূক্ত ৪৯৫ দাগে ৬০ শতাংশ জমির কাতে ৩৫ এবং ১/২ শতাংশ এবং ৪৯৬ দাগের ৬ শতাংশ একুনে ৪১ এবং ১/২ শতাংশ জমিতে চিরস্থায়ী নিষেধাজ্ঞার প্রার্থনা করেছেন বাদীর দাখিলী প্রদ: ৫ চিহিত RS ৩১৪ নং খতিয়ানের সই মুহরি নকল পর্যালোচনায় দেখা যায় যে ৪৯৫ দাগে রেকর্ডভূক্ত মোট জমির পরিমান ৬০ শতাংশ, এরকাতে ৩৫ এবং ১/২ শতাংশ হচ্ছে নালিশী জমি বাদীর দাবীকৃত জমি দাগের অংশ বিশেষ হলে ও আর্জিত দাগের মোট জমিতে উক্ত আংশিক জমির অবস্থান নকশা যোগে প্রদর্শন করা হয়নি। তাছাড়া দাবীকৃত ৪৯৫ ও ৪৯৬ দাগের জমির অবস্থান সম্পর্কে কোন বর্ণনা সাক্ষ্য সূত্রে পাওয়া যায়না। ফলে নালিশি জমি অস্পষ্ট বিবেচিত হয়। (৯নং পৃষ্ঠা) অস্পষ্ট জমি বাবদ নিষেধাজ্ঞার আদেশ অকার্যকর হবার সম্ভাবনা আছে।

বাদী নালিশী জমিতে তার দখলের প্রমাণ স্বরুপ দাখিলী প্রর্দশনী ৭(ক) চিহ্নিত খাজনার দাখিলা পর্যালোচনায় দেখা যায় উহা একটি ৪৯৩ বি খতিয়ানভূক্ত ৩৫৯,৩৬০ ও ৪২৬ নং দাগভূক্ত জমির খাজনার দাখিলা যা নালিশী জমিভূক্ত নয়। বাদীর মৌখিক সাক্ষ্য সূত্রে দখলের প্রমাণ জেরায় ভিন্নরূপ প্রমাণিত হয়না।”

13. The aforesaid findings of the trial court established that the plaintiff apparently could able to prove title over the property by some documents but the plaintiff could not prove exclusive possession in the suit land and the schedule to the plaint is vague and indefinite and, as such, no decree of permanent injunction can be passed on a vague schedule.

14. With the above findings the suit was dismissed.

15. The appellate court also in its judgment concurrently found that the schedule to the plaint is vague and indefinite but found title of the plain- tiff only in 0.15 sataks of land in place of 40 sataks found by the trial court, Both the courts below concurrently observed that though the plaintiff in the plaint categorically given a chain of documents of title since 1942 but those documents have not been as marked exhibits in due process of law for which both the courts below came to a finding that the plaintiff could not properly prove his title in the suit property, In a suit for permanent injunction the paramount consideration is possession of the plaintiff in the suit land but both the courts below instead of giving emphasis on that point most erroneously put stress mainly on the title of the plaintiff. The appellate court found title of the plaintiff in 0.15 decimals of land only whereas the trial court found title in 0.40 decimals of land. The appellate court failed to assign any reason why it disagreed with the findings of the trial court on that finding.

16. From a perusal of the plaint, evidences on record both oral and documentary as contained in the lower court records this Court finds that the plaintiff submitted a series of registered deed before the trial court which have not been exhibited in accordance with law and both the courts below failed to give emphasis on the issue of possession of the plaintiff as well as of the defendant in the suit land.

<u>17. It is true that in the schedule to the plaint the property has not been well defined. For such defect in the plaint the petitioner could not be deprived of getting relief. It appears that CS Plot No. 359 contains 111 sataks of land. The plaintiff in suit did not mention CS Plot No, 359 divided into how many RS plots but in the plaint .only given RS Plot No, 495 which .contains only 60 sataks of land. It is also true that the petitioner did not claim the entire property covered by RS plot No, 495. It is obvious that the plaintiff has claimed part .of the RS plot No. 495 and CS plot No, 359. The petitioner ought to have given definite and specific boundary in which portion of the plot he is in possession by giving a sketch map to the plain.</u>

<u>18. From perusal .of the judgment of both the courts below I find that in deciding the case of the plaintiff both the courts below differently found title of the plaintiff in the suit land which contradicts each other, The question of possession in the suit land has not at all discussed by the courts below on the basis of evidences on record; Mere mistake in the schedule to the plaint a party should not suffer and should not be deprived of getting relief as prayed for, From the facts and circumstances of the case, I find that the documents submitted by the plaintiff has' not been properly marked as exhibits and the evidences have not been properly appreciated in its true perspective.</u>

<u>19. This being the situation, I think that the plaintiff should be given. a chance for making proper prayers by way of amendment of the plaint and also adduce evidences in support of his claim and in that situation, the defendants also shall be at liberty to file additional written statement and necessary documents in support 'of their claim. Accordingly, I think that justice will be met if the case is sent back on remand to the trial court for fresh trial affording sufficient opportunities to the parties to place their respective cases and get the plaint amended if so advised.</u>

20. In the result, the rule is made absolute however there will be no order as to costs. The impugned judgments and decrees passed by both the courts below are hereby set aside. The case is sent back on remand to the trial court for fresh trial and disposal within a shortest possible time preferably within 6(six) months from the date of the judgment of this Court:

21. Communicate a copy of this judgment to the Court concerned.

Send down the lower court records at once.

End.

lawyer:
SR Karmaker, Advocate ----- For the Petitioner 
Md Shahidul Alam Chowdhury, Advocate ----- For the Opposite Parties.
parties:
Dayal Chandra Mondal and others ------ Petitioner
vs.
Assistant Custodian of Vested and Non-Resident Properties (L&B) and Additional Deputy Commissioner (Revenue), Dhaka and others ------ Opposite Party
full_judgment:
Gour Gopal Saha, J: This Rule is directed against the judgment and decree dated 26-11-86 (decree drawn on 2-12-86) passed by the learned Subordinate Judge, 4th Court Dhaka in Title Appeal No. 41 of 1985 affirming the judgment and decree dated 12-1-85 (decree drawn on 16-1-85) passed by the learned Munsif Savar in Title Suit No.153 of 1984 dismissing the suit.

2. Maran Mondal, predecessor-in-interest of the petitioners as plaintiff, instituted a suit in the 3rd Court of Munsif Dhaka being Title Suit No. 732 of 1981 subsequently re-numbered as Title Suit No. 153 of 1984 before Munsif. Savar for declaration of his title in the suit land measuring 0.82 acre of nal land as recorded in CS Plot No. 787 under CS Khatian No. 137/24 corresponding to SA Plot No. 198 under SA Khatian No. 198 and RS Plot Nos. 1194 and 1204 under RS Khatian No. 225 of Mouza Barakakar, PS Savar, District Dhaka. The plaintiffs case, in short, is that the suit land originally belonged to Lakshman Mondal, full brother of plaintiff Maran Mondal and the same was correctly recorded in the CS and SA Khatians in the name of Lakshman MondaI. Lakshman Mondal eventually died as a childless widower at his native village Kakabo PS Savar District Dhaka leaving the plaintiff as his only heir to succeed him and since then he has been owning and possessing the suit property peacefully on payment of rent to the Government Acquired Estate. The plaintiff’s further case is that while he has been in rightful possession of the suit property the same has been correctly recorded in his name in the finally published RS Khatian No. 225 following which he has been paying rent to the Government in his own name in respect of the suit property. It was in late 1975 that at the instance of some greedy and unscrupulous persons the defendants illegally tried to treat the suit property as a vested property and threatened to oust him from possession by sheer force and under threats of imminent forcible dispossession he was constrained to pray for yearly lease of the suit property under protest but at the same time he filed an application before the appropriate authority for releasing the suit property from the list of vested property. It has further been contended by the plaintiff that the SDO. Dhaka who is defendant No. 2 in the suit after proper enquiry clearly found in his order dated 5-10-76 Ext. 5 that the original tenant Laksham Mondal had died 15 years ago at his native village Kakabo, Savar leaving plaintiff Maran Mondal as his brother and only heir to succeed him. The learned SDO in his order dated 5-10-76 further found that there was no occasion to treat the suit property as vested property and recommended the release of the suit property from the list of the vested property. The learned ADC (Rev) Dhaka eventually rejected the said recommendation of the SDO Dhaka illegally and arbitrarily and this necessitated the filing of the suit for declaration that the suit property is not vested property and the plaintiff is the absolute owner of the same.

3. The Assistant Custodian Vested and Non-Resident Property (Land and Buildings) and ADC (Rev) Dhaka contested the suit by filing written statements denying the material allegations of the plaint and contended, inter alia, that the recorded tenant Lakshman Mondal left Bangladesh long ago and permanently settled in India as a result of which the suit property has become a vested property by operation of law. It was further contended that since the plaintiff himself took lease of the suit property from the vested property authority and unsuccessfully tried for release of the same from the authority concerned he is estopped from challenging the legality or propriety of the vested property proceedings and, as such, the suit is liable to be dismissed. At the trial the defendant did not appear and contest the suit either by cross-examining the plaintiffs witnesses or by adducing any witness in support of the defence case.

4. The learned Munsif by his impugned judgment dated 12-1-85 dismissed the suit without discussing any evidence oral or documentary. It is evident from the impugned judgment that the learned Munsif dismissed the suit in a most casual manner without discussing and considering any evidence adduced by the plaintiff and the legal incidence of the documents exhibited in the case in support of the plaintiff’s case. It also appears from Ext. 4 and 5 that these do not contain any khatian number but the learned Munsif appears to have discovered a khatian number in the said exhibits, the basis of which is not available on record arid discarded the plaintiff’s case with reference to the baseless khatian purported to have been mentioned therein.

5. Mr SR Karmaker the learned Advocate appearing for the plaintiff-petitioners submits that the learned Court of appeal below seriously erred in law in holding that the suit property is a vested property without any basis at all. The learned Advocate further submits that in the face of cleat assertions by the plaintiff and evidence led to substantiate the same to the effect that his brother Lakhman Mondal never left this country to settle in India and he died at his native village Kakabo leaving the plaintiff as his only heir and since then he has been owning and possessing the suit property and his name has duly been recorded in the finally published RS Khatian and he has been regularly paying rent to the Government Acquired Estate, there is absolutely no basis for treating the suit property as vested property on the basis of a VP Case started in late 1975. The learned Advocate further submits that in the face of the clear finding recorded by defendant No. 2 SDO Dhaka in Ext. 4 that the admitted tenant Lakshman Mondal had died in this country leaving the plaintiff to succeed him as his only heir and in the face of the unchallenged evidence of the plaintiff as PW 1 to the said effect the learned Court of appeal below evidently erred in law in arbitrarily ignoring the said evidence both oral and documentary by illegally shifting the onus of proof regarding the death of Lakshman Mondal and the same has resulted in error in the impugned decision occasioning failure of justice. Mr Karmaker further submits that from Exhibit 4 it is evident that the learned SDO Dhaka who is defendant No. 2 in the suit and himself conducted an enquiry in the VP Case himself found on local enquiry that Lakshman Mondal had died in this country as a citizen of the erstwhile East Pakistan and he never migrated to India and since Lakshman's death plaintiff Moran Mondal has been owing and possessing the suit property on payment of rent to the Government Acquired Estate and on such findings recommended the realse of the suit property from the list of the  vested property. the learned Court of appeal below evidently erred in law in completely ignoring these pieces of material evindence convincingly proving the plaintiffs case and the same has resulted in error in the impugned decision occasioning failure of justice.

6. Mr Karmaker has drawn my attention to Ext. 5 and the order dated 17-8-88 passed by the learned ADC (Rev) Dhaka wherein he called for opinion of the legal Adviser of Vested Properties in respect of release of the suit property from the list of vested properties. It also appears from Ext. 5 that before the opinion of the Legal Adviser of the Vested Property could be obtained as ordered by the learned ADC (Rev) the Superintendent of Vested Properties who is a much lessor officer and subordinate to the SDO could wishfully throwaway the definite recommendation of the SDO for release of the suit property by substituting the satisfaction of the SDO by his own satisfaction without any further material before him and the learned ADC (Rev). Dhaka simply acted mechanically at the bidding of the Superintendent of Vested Properties in rejecting SDO's definite recommendation and positive finding and completely ignoring the legal incidence of the finally published RS Khatian in the name of the plaintiff-Ext. 3 and the Government rent receipts Ext. 2 series in favour of the plaintiff.

7. The learned Advocate appearing for the opposite parties finds it difficult to support the impugned judgments and frankly concedes that in the facts and circumstances of the case and the evidence on record the impugned judgments do not appear to be proper and sustainable in law.

8. In support of his submissions Mr Karmaker has placed before me the case of Abul Khair vs. Bangladesh and others reported in 32 DLR (AD) 29 wherein their Lordships held that before a property could be treated as a vested property the authority concerned must prove that the original tenant migrated to India before the Enemy Property laws came into force in 1965. In the instant case there is absolutely no material on record to prove that Lakshman Mondal migrated to India at any point of time and settled there permanently but on the contrary there is convincing documentary and oral evidence to prove that the admitted tenant Lakshman Mondal had died in this country as its citizen leaving the plaintiff as his only heir to succeed him. The casual exercise made by the defendants in treating the suit property as a vested property without any legal basis whatsoever ostensibly at the instance of an irresponsible Tashilder who is accountable to none and an overzealous Superintendent lightly setting at nought the definite finding and recommendation of the SDO Dhaka must be held to be acts of malfeasance and witch-hunting at the cost of a citizen of the country whose name has duly been recorded in the finally published RS Khatian and from whom rent is being regularly accepted by the Government treating him as a tenant in respect of the suit property.

9. In the face of the SA Khatian standing in the name of Lakshman Mondal and the finally published RS Khatian standing in the name of plaintiff Maran Mondal and the Government regularly accepting rent from the plaintiff treating him as a tenant and there being no material basis and legal foundation for treating the suit property as an enemy property subsequently vested property on the basis of a case started in late 1975 the learned Courts below evidently erred in law in passing the impugned judgments on erroneous view of law.

10. In the present case the plaintiff never abandoned his rights in the suit property and the defendants were never misled by his prayer for taking yearly lease so as to change or alter their position to their detriment and the prayer for temporary lease being obviously under protest and without any prejudice to the rights of the parties the doctrine of estoppel or waiver has no manner of application in the present case. Now here in the whole spectrum of deliberations the learned Courts below appear to have addressed themselves to the vital question as to whether the mere unsubstantiated claim of the vested property authority at the instance of an ever-exuberant and irresponsible Tahsilder whose action is never authenticated by any responsible officer of the Government is sufficient to throw away the unchallenged legal evidence both oral and documentary convincingly proving that the recorded tenant Lakshman Mondal had died in his country as its citizen leaving the plaintiff to succeed him as his only heir and thereby clearly fell in error in deciding the moot question involved in the case by misplacing the onus of proof.

11. It is evident that the instant Vested Property case was started as late as in 1975 and before that time there was no occasion to treat the suit property as vested property. In the absence of any legal foundation whatsoever to treat the suit property as a vested property the whole exercise made in this direction appears to be a malafide and superficial one at the behest of some irresponsible officials unnecessarily landing a citizen of the country and the Government in costly vexacious and oppressive litigations for an unworthy cause. Exts. 4 and 5 from the VP Case in question were admitted into evidence without any objection and, as such, it was absolutely unnecessary for the plaintiff to call for the records of the said VP case for proving the genuineness of Exts 4 and 5. The objection of the learned Court of appeal below on Exts 4 and 5 is totally unwarranted in the facts and circumstances of the case. It is apparent that the learned Court of appeal below totally misconceived the law bearing on the subject and clearly erred in law in discarding the case of the plaintiff who successfully proved his title in the suit property and the baselessness of the Vested Property proceedings in question. On a complete misreading of Ext 3 and 4 the learned trial Court mis-directed itself to find that the land described in the schedule to the plaint is different from that mentioned in Ext. 3 and 4. Unfortunately, the learned Court of appeal below failed to scrutinize Exts 3 and 4 as they deserved and fell in error by committing the same mistake. The misreading and non-reading of the said material evidence has obviously resulted in error in the impugned decision occasioning failure of justice.

12. Mr Karmaker then refers to the case of Nitya Gopal Roy Barman VS. Pran Gopal Nandi and others respond in 32 DLR 11 wherein their Lordships held that a mere claim of the Assistant Custodian that the property of the deceased testator is an enemy property in respect of which an enemy property case was started in 1978 is not sufficient for coming to a conclusion that the property in question is an enemy property. In the instant case the Vested Property case was started as late as in 1975 and the same has been proved to be without any legal foundation and consequently the abortive attempt by the defendants to treat the suit property as a vested property must be held to be illegal and arbitrary.

13. Mr Karmaker also refers to the case of Arun Kumar Lal and others vs. Assistant Custodian of Enemy Property (Land & Buildings) and ADC (Rev) Dhaka reported in 1983 BCR 225 wherein his Lordship found that estoppel cannot operate against a statute. From the facts and circumstances of the case and the evidence on record it is evident that the plaintiff was threatened with dispossession in a summary way by the defendants and it was under the instant threats of forcible dispossession he had to pray for yearly lease of the suit property for saving his possession albeit under protest and lost no time in coming to the Court for vindication of his grievance. Under such circumstances the learned Courts below erred in law in holding that the plaintiffs claim in barred by estoppel.

<u>14. In this connection we may profitably refer to the principle which is incorporated in section 115 of the Evidence Act. The doctrine of estoppel in an equitable postulation which Jays down that if a person has acted to his detriment or altered his position on the basis of any declaration, act or omission of another that other person will not be allowed in any future suit or proceedings between himself and that other person or his representative to go back upon to the detriment of the opposite party. To establish a case of waiver or estoppel it is therefore, necessary to show that the party alleged to have waived his rights had acted in such a manner so as to lead the other side to believe that such rights will not be enforced in the future. Mere indulgence shown under exigency of circumstances in not enforcing one's legal rights or keeping the said rights suspended for the time being cannot constitute waiver or estoppel and give rise to the inference that the rights have been abandoned for all times. In the present case the plaintiff was always diligent in asserting his own title in the suit property and he never abandoned his claim of ownership over it nor the defendants were misled by his prayer for an annual lease so as to change or alter their position to their detriment and the prayer for temporary lease being obviously under protest and without any prejudice to the rights of the parties the doctrine of estoppel or waiver has no manner of application in the present case. The learned Court of appeal below acting on wrong premises evidently erred in law in holding that the suit is barred by estoppel and waiver.</u>

15. The learned Courts below left the field of fact and strayed to fiction by finding fault with the plaintiff for not producing the death certificate of Lakshman Mondal which is not a requirement of law for proving his death particularly when his death was well proved by other convincing and unchallenged evidence. The learned Courts below appear to have approached the case from a totally wrong angle of vision unsupported by the established principles of law and thus misdirected themselves to dismiss the suit on misreading and non-reading of the material evidence on record affecting the merit of the impugned decision.

16. Mr Karmaker then refers to the case of Laxmi Kanta Roy Vs. Upazila Nirbahi Officer and another reported in 46 DLR 136. In this case his Lordship found that since the law of enemy property itself died with the repeal of Ordinance 1 of 1969 on 23-3-1974 no further vested property case can be started thereafter on the basis of the law which is already dead. It is evident that the VP Case in question was started in late 1975 and before that time there was no occasion to treat the suit property as a vested property. In the absence of any legal basis whatsoever to treat the suit property as a vested property, the whole exercise made in this direction appears to be a mala fide and superficial one at the instance of utterly irresponsible officials unnecessarily landing a citizen and the Government in costly and vexatious litigations for an unworthy cause.

<u>17. Order VIII rule 5 of the Code of Civil Procedure provides that assertion of facts made in the plaint if not denied specifically or by necessary implication shall be deemed to be admitted. In our case under review the plaintiff clearly stated in the plaint that Lakshman Mondal had died in this country as a citizen of the erstwhile East Pakistan leaving the plaintiff as his only heir to succeed him and he led evidence to prove the said assertion by the unchallenged oral and documentary evidence and there being no contrary evidence on record the learned Courts below clearly erred in law in dismissing the suit ignoring the positive evidence on record by resorting to hypothetical assumptions and the same has resulted in error in the impugned decision occasioning failure of justice.</u>

<u>18. It may not be out of place to reiterate that laws relating to enemy properties now vested properties which are fairly well-settled by now by the consistent pronouncements by the highest Court of the country properties which assumed enemy character and became enemy properties by operation of law during the relevant time viz from 6-9-65 to 16-2-69 when emergency was formally lifted became vested properties and the Government may treat such properties as enemy or vested properties and take over possession thereof in accordance with law subject to the legitimate rights of co-owners co-sharers and the bonafide transferees in lawful possession therein. But before a property is treated as a vested property particularly on the basis of a VP Case started long after the lifting of emergency on 16th February, 1969 a heavy duty is cast upon the authority concerned to satisfy itself that the recorded tenant migrated to India before 1965 and settled there following which the property in question has really become vested property by conducting necessary enquiry into individual cases rather than relying on the stray noting of a petty Tahsilder who is accountable to none and whose report has never been verified by any responsible officer of the Government. There being as yet no authenticated and published enemy property list the scope for manipulations is wide open till now to unscrupulous officials to include any new property any time in the unending list of enemy property and play like toys with the rights of the citizens whose consequent engagements against the Government in protracted costly and oppressive litigations do not eventually serve any useful purpose either for the Government or for the members of the public the only beneficiaries being some capricious officials and the paraphernalia.</u>

<u>19. When challenged in a Court of law the onus is heavily on the Government to prove affirmatively that the property in question is in fact a vested property failing which some evidence to the contrary adduced by the successors-in-interest of the original tenant or the transferees showing that they are in rightful possession of the disputed properties is sufficient to take the same out of the ambit of enemy property laws. Mere claim by the Government or by the vested property authority that a certain property is a vested property without the necessary factual basis and legal foundation has no validity in the eye of law. The learned Courts below clearly erred in law in passing the impugned judgments ignoring the settled law on the subject.</u>

<u>20. There is yet another special feature of the case which has been overlooked by the learned Courts below. Admittedly the finally published RS Khatian stands in the name of the plaintiff and the Government is regularly accepting rent from him thereby recognising him as the tenant in respect of the suit land. A finally published record of rights revised under section 114A of the SAT Act has a presumption of correctness and that presumption continues till it is otherwise rebutted by reliable evidence. Nothing has been done by the contesting defendants to dispel the legal presumption that attaches to the finally published RS Khatian in the name of the plaintiff. Recognition of the plaintiff as a tenant in respect of the suit property by the Revenue Authority of the Government is binding upon the Vested Property Department and the latter cannot claim the suit land as a vested property summarily discarding the finally published RS Khatian in the name of the plaintiff. The action of the ADC (Revenue) Dhaka who is the de facto head of the Vested Property Department of the District indulging in oppressive litigations must be deprecated. The case of the Additional Deputy Commissioner (Rev) Narayanganj vs. AKM Latiful Karim and others reported in 17 BW (HCD) 249 lends instant support to this view. The impugned judgment cannot be sustainable on that ground as well.</u>

21. For the reasons stated above. I find substance in the submissions made by the learned Advocate for the petitioners and I hold that the impugned judgments suffer from serious legal infirmity and the same have occasioned failure of justice.

In the result, the Rule is made absolute. The impugned judgments are set aside and plaintiffs Title Suit No .153 of 1984 of the Court of Munsif, Savar in Dhaka is hereby decreed. There shall be no order as to costs.

Send down the lower Court records at once.

End.
