full_judgment:
Md Mozammel Hoque J: All the aforesaid seven writ petitions were heard together in view of the fact that identical question of facts as well as Jaws are involved in these cases and, as such, after hearing the same together the writ petitions are being disposed of by one judgment 

2. The Rule in Writ Petition No. 3025 of 1996 was issued calling upon the respondents to show cause as to way the proviso to sections 5 and 6 of Surplus Public Servant Ordinance No. (XXIV of 1985) should not be declared as ultra vires of Articles 27 and 29 of the Constitution and as to why the petitioner should not be absorbed in the BCS (Customs and Excise) Cadre with immediate effect and why the petitioner's seniority should not be counted from the date of his first joining the government service as per government's decision of seniority of surplus personnel as published in the office memorandum No. ED(R-11) S-59/77-25(500) dated 20-3-97 Annexure Z-6.

3. At the time of hearing of the Rule the learned Advocate for the petitioner prays that he does not press the prayer A in the writ petition. He   further submits that he is not also pressing the later portion of prayer 'B' of the writ petition. In all writ petitions he is now praying to the effect that as to why the petitioners should not be absorbed in BCS (Customs and Excise) Cadre with immediate effect.

4. It is stated in the application that by way of Notification under Memo dated 25th February, 1993 published in the official Gazette vide notification dated 16th February, 1993 by the Ministry of Establishment the petitioner along with others was recruited to the Bangladesh Civil Service Trade Cadre following his outstanding results in the 11 the BCS examination in which this petitioner came first in the order of merit. This notification dated 16th February, 1993 is Annexure-A (l). The petitioner joined his service on 1st April, 1994. After only 9 months of the period of the petitioner's service in the Ministry of Commerce as Assistant Director, Export and Import Control Section, the Government in its drive to reduce public expenditure, amalgamated the aforesaid Section of the Ministry with certain other section rendering it necessary for the petitioner and 8 other officers who were appointed under the said gazette notification to become Surplus Civil Servants. Respondent No.1, represented by the Establishment Division in an official Memo dated 27-5-93 inquired of the Ministry of Commerce, Respondent No.5, that in view of the recent recruitment in their cadre, whether they had any surplus officers and if so whether any assistance was needed for arranging for those officers to be absorbed in BCS (Tax) Cadre which Memo dated 27-5-93 has been annexed as Annexure-B to the writ petition. 

5. Respondent No. 5, Ministry of Commerce, wrote to respondent No.1 on 15-6-93 indicating that in case the recommendation of the Committee is implemented, then there is strong likelihood of the 9 appointees of the 11th recruitment becoming surplus as a result of the government's drive to reduce public expenditure. The Ministry of Commerce accordingly vide their above Memo recommended the absorptions of 9 officers including the petitioner to the BCS (Tax) Cadre and that letter dated 15-6-93 has been annexed as Annexure-C. On 14-6-93 respondent No. 2 Chairman, National Board of Revenue (NBR), wrote to the Ministry of Commerce informing that there are a number of posts vacant in the cadre of tax & customs and excise. Respondents No. 2 in the letter further invited respondent No.5, Ministry of Commerce, to forward the names of such surplus officers recruited on the basis of the results of the 11th BCS examination who could be absorbed in the cadre of BCS (Tax) or in the Cadre of BCS(Customs & Excise) and respondent No. 2 wanted such communication by 24th June, 1993: The said letter further clarified that the seniority of such absorbed officers would be based on the result of the original competition. A copy of the aforesaid letter dated 14-6-93 is annexed as Annexure-D. Respondent No. 5 Ministry of Commerce duly sent a reply to respondent No. 2's letter on 23-6-93 explaining the circumstances in which the 9 officers of 11th BCS examination recruitment in the trade cadre were about to become surplus. The letter of the Commerce Ministry also stated that in response to an earlier letter by the Establishment Division the said 9 officers' application for absorption into the Tax Cadre had already been sent. The Ministry of Commerce further sent the-list of the said 9 officers to respondent No.1 reiterating their earlier recommendation for taking necessary measure for the absorption of those officers in the Taxation as well as in the Customs & Excise Cadre and the letter dated 23-6-93 has been annexed as Annexure-E. 

6. Respondent No.6, Internal Resources Department of the Ministry of Finance, in a letter dated 22-9-93 informed respondent No.5 the Ministry of Commerce that it was decided in a meeting chaired by the Principal Secretary of the Hon'ble Prime Minister that if the 9 officers in the 'Trade Cadre were made surplus. then they could be absorbed 'in the Tax or Customs & Excise Cadres Therefore, the letter added that when the Ministry of Establishment announces the surplus status of the said 9 officers then the necessary steps could be taken for their absorption in the Tax or Customs & Excise Cadres. The copy of the aforesaid letter dated 22-9-93 has been annexed as Annexure-F. Respondent No.2 NBR further requested for transferring those officers including the petitioner to the National Board of Revenue on deputation pending the formalities to be observed for making them surplus and completion of the absorption procedure and this letter of respondent No.2 dated 16-1-94 has been annexed as Annexure-G to the Writ petition. The appointment, promotion and deputation section of the Establishment Division accordingly vide a notice dated 19-1-94 named the 8 of those 9 BCS Trade Cadre Officers, the petitioner being one of them, as being announced until further order, to be under Internal Resources Department in order to make arrangement for them to be appointed in the appropriate posts of the respondent No.2's organisation, namely, National Board of Revenue and the said notice dated 19~1-94 has been annexed as Annexure-H to the writ petition. The Internal Resources Division of the Ministry of Finance in a notice published in Bangladesh Gazette announced the names of7 BCS (Trade) Cadre Officers including the petitioner and they were thus appointed on deputation to the appropriate post in the National Board of Revenue and a copy of the said notice dated 1-2-94 has been annexed as Annexure-I Subsequently, on 3-3-94 the respondent No.2 NBR vide a notice duly published in the Bangladesh Gazette announced designations of the 7 officers including the petitioner. In the said notice it was stated that the petitioner had been appointed as Assistant Collector. Customs Excise and VAT Collectorate, Chittagong and the copy of the notice dated 3-3-94 has been annexed as Annexure-J. 

7. On 11-4-94 the Establishment Division being respondent No. 1 vide Memo dated 11-4-94 addressed to the Ministry of Commerce confirmed that the latter Ministry could take necessary step to announce the relevant officers surplus and make arrangement for them to be absorbed in other cadres and this Memo dated 11-4-94 has been annexed as  Annexure-K. Respondent No. 5 Ministry of Commerce in its reply dated 2-5-94 informed the respondent No.1 that in the relevant section of the Trade Cadre no post had yet been formally abolished and therefore asked whether in these circumstances it would. be appropriate to announce any officers surplus on the expectation that their post would be abolished in the foreseeable future and a copy of this letter dated 2-5-94 has been annexed as Annexure-L, Respondent No.1 in a Memo dated 2-4-95 informed the Ministry of Commerce (respondent No.5) that before declaring the 7 officers surplus it would be necessary to abolish their posts first, Further. it was suggested that steps could be taken for formally abolishing the 7 posts in question and the copy of the said Memo dated 2-4-95 has been annexed as annexure-M. Accordingly, the Ministry of Commerce in a letter to the Establishment Division respondent No.1 dated 3-5-95 formally requested them to abolish 23 trade Cadre posts including the post of the petitioner and 6 others who were already posted in the Customs & Excise Cadre as Assistant Commissioners. A copy of the letter dated 3-5-95 has been annexed as annexure-N to the writ petition. 
8. The Establishment Division, respondent No.1, duly wrote back to the Ministry of Commerce. respondent No.5, on 8-5-95 expressing their concurrence and agreement with the decision in compliance with relevant Rules in order to abolish 23 Trade Cadre posts which included the 16 posts which would become formally vacant when the   seven persons of 11th BCS Trade Cadre including the petitioner, would be announced surplus. In a similar letter dated 24-5-95 the Ministry of Finance, respondent No.6, also had not objected to the decision to abolish the 23 suggested posts. Copies of the letters dated 8-5-95 and 24-5-95 have been annexed as Annexure-O and 0(1). Accordingly, the Ministry of Commerce, respondent No.5, sent a' Memo on 29-5-95 to the Hon'ble Prime Minister recommending for abolition of the 23 posts while confirming that the legal requirement for abolition of these posts as laid down in BCS (Trade) Cadres Organogram and Cadre Regulation, 1980, have been adhered to, and in the circumstances such posts could be abolished. A copy of the said Memo dated 29-5-95 has been annexed as Annexure-P to the writ petition. On 13-6-95 respondent No 5 the Ministry of Commerce accordingly under a Memo No Bam/ Pro 4/BCS/ Trade 4-22/93/89 formally announced the abolition of the said 23 posts and confirmed that both this Ministry and Establishment Division agreed for abolition and the Ministry had duly granted the abolition of the said posts. On the same date the Ministry of Commerce issued another order, formally announcing the names of the 7 officers, declared as surplus public officers, after the earlier abolition of their respective posts. This list of names included the petitioner as one of the surplus officers of a post that had been abolished. 

9. Further, the said order issued under the same Memo with issue No. 96 stated that until the 7 officers were totally absorbed they would be entitled to draw their salaries/allowances from their working place under the National Revenue Board, respondent No.2. Copies of both the said Memos dated 13-6-95 have been annexed as Annexure Q and Q (1) to the writ petition. On 21-6-95 the Establishment Division in a letter addressed to the Internal Resources Division announced the selection of the 7 officers, including the petitioner, for absorption in the BCS (Customs and Excise) Cadre and made the necessary directions to the relevant Division for informing the Ministry of Establishment Division on completing the process of absorption and if there was any delay in this regard, to inform the Ministry the reasons for such delay. A copy of the said letter dated 21-6-95 has been annexed as Annexure-R to the writ petition. In the meanwhile the petitioner and six others have been working in their respective posts under the National Board of Revenue since February, 1994, its deputation in the National Board of Revenue having become operative months before the procedures for abolition of posts and declaration of surplus status were finalised. In the first month of his appointment the petitioner received intensive training on the system of imposing value added tax. This was followed by a month long field study regarding implementation and practice as to how to impose value added tax and the study and practical-know-how in the system itself. 

10. The petitioner's initial period of appointment with Customs, Excise and VAT Collectorate, Chittagong lasted until May, 1994 when he was transferred to Customs, Excise and V AT Collectorate (now Commissioner) Dhaka (North). The petitioner within a very short space of time became an outstanding officer in the field. In July 1994, he was instrumental in exposing a company, the name of Orian Laboratory Ltd who had illegally evaded Taka 40 lakh in value added tax. In the financial year 1994-95 whilst working under Tongi Division the petitioner earned for the country in revenue a sum of Taka 43,83 crore more compared to the previous year and the figure was Taka 23.10 crore more than the target for that year. As an acknowledgment of the petitioner's highly satisfactory performance on 2-1-95 the Collector of Customs, Excise and V AT Collectorate, Dhaka (North) sent him a message of congratulation. A copy of the congratulation letter date 2-1-95 has been annexed as Annexure-S to the writ petition. 

11. There was shortage of manpower to do the job in the department as the work is ever increasing with overflow of responsibilities. The petitioner therefore, since January, 1996, has been for all intents and purposes, holding charge of 3 posts simultaneously, namely, Assistant Collector (Establishment), Assistant Collector (Commodity and Services) and Assistant Collector (Bond). Due to superb performance and being surplus officer from another Ministry, the petitioner and the other 6 officers soon became a target of resentment by many of the officers of the respondent No.2. The interested group and vested lobby started a machination as to how this input of fresh blood could be excluded from Customs and Excise by denying them in the Customs, Excise and VAT Cadre. 


12. As part of this machination on 26-10-96 the respondent No, 2 in their weekly meeting made a decision regarding the 7 officers in the following terms, "That as a matter of principle the National Board of Revenue is not in favour of absorbing any officers from other Cadres except in the entry post. The Ministry of Establishment can be approached about the question whether the 7 officers are entitled to be absorbed in the BCS (Customs and Excise) Cadre and if so how should their seniority be determined. After receiving the reply from the Ministry of Establishment a final decision could be made about these officers on making proper evaluation about their performance whilst under deputation;" 

13. A copy of the minutes of the said meeting dated 26-10-95 has been annexed as Annexure- T to the writ petition. Accordingly, respondent No.3 in a letter dated 3-12-95 informed the respondent No.1 about their decision on absorption and asked for the opinion of the respondent No. 1 regarding the relationship between those 7 officers, petitioner being one of them, and the 13th BCS (Customs and Excise) Cadre vis-a-vis the question of seniority, this indicating that there is no principle so far laid down by the Government as contemplated under Section 6, A' copy of the letter of Respondent No.2 dated 3-12-95 has been annexed as Annexure-U to the writ petition. In reply vide a Memo dated 26-12-95 the respondent No. 1 wrote to both respondent Nos. 2 and 3 stating that in accordance with law these 7 officers had been declared surplus and they have been duly nominated by the Establishment Division for their posts and, as such, they are entitled to be absorbed into the respective nominated posts. The Establishment Division further stated that the question of seniority must be resolved by reference to the relevant rules and regulations in the subject and further referred to an earlier letter by the respondent No.2 addressed to the Ministry of Commerce (Annexure-D) stating that the absorbed officers' seniority would be based on the result of the original competition. A copy of the said reply dated 26-12-95 has been annexed as Annexure- V to the writ petition. 

 14. On 16-1-96 Customs and Excise Association dominated by the power lobby of a vested group interest held an emergency meeting of their Executive Committee. In that meeting the members expressed their concern about the respondent No. 2's failure to return the 7 officers to the Establishment Division in spite Of an earlier promise to do so. Further, in the meeting these 7 officers became the object of evident resentment of the officers who passed the relevant resolution as quoted in the application itself. A copy of the minutes of the meeting of the Association dated 16-1-96 has been annexed as Annexure-W to the writ petition. In order to  create illegal obstruction to the formal absorption of the petitioner along with other six officers the respondent No. 2 held an internal meeting on 5-2-96 and took decision to the effect that at one stage there was shortage of officers in the Customs and Excise Cadre and therefore the• 7 officers were brought on deputation. Then there are sufficient officers in that cadre and therefore the Establishment Division could be written for withdrawing those 7 officers. The Board was of the opinion that if those 7 officers were absorbed in the BCS (Customs and Excise) Cadre, then difficulties might arise about the question of seniority. This would have serious implication in the Administration. A copy of the minutes of the meeting dated 5-2-96 has been annexed as Annexure-X to the writ petition. 

15. It was further stated in the application that on the one hand respondent No. 2 who has been trying to get rid of these 7 officers on the plea of sufficiency of staff or on the question relating to seniority but on the other hand they are at the same time giving direction to the Internal Resources Division for making arrangement for filling up the vacant posts in the BCS (Customs and Excise) Cadre by recruiting officers through 17th BCS Examination. Clearly there is a sinister motive in this. The respondent No.2 is determined to fill up all possible vacant posts to create a further excuse for denying the petitioner and 6 officers' rights to be absorbed which should have taken place as soon as the Establishment Division recommended the same. A copy of the said Memo dated 5-10-94 has been annexed as Annexure- Y to the writ petition. Respondent No. 3 wrote to respondent No. 1 on 18-2-96 informing its decision made in the meeting dated 5-2-96 and asking them to take necessary measure for implementation. A copy of the said letter dated 18-2-96 has been annexed as Annexure-Z to the writ petition. On 13-5-96 respondent No. 1 wrote back to the respondent Nos. 2 and 3 that there was no scope for withdrawing the 7 officers, and therefore steps should be taken for absorption of those officers. A copy of the letter of respondent No. 1 dated 13-5-96 had been annexed as Annexure Z(I) to the petition. 

16. In the meantime the petitioner and other 6 officers found themselves in the most unenviable position. They entered the Bangladesh Civil Service with high hopes, expectations and dreams to playa part in their country's progress and development. However, as years went on, their dreams turned into nightmares as powerful lobby in collusion with the vested interests' worked to deny them of their legitimate rights and dues and had in effect caused serious uncertainty as to their future prospect in service by obstructing formalisation of absorption process and their seniority in the unbroken service record which is otherwise due as in the normal course under the law and equity. The petitioner and other 6 officers found that over more than 2 years they have been treated as' on deputation and not being absorbed though that was the main objective for being placed on deputation, the mere formality for completing the absorption process was thus about to be frustrated due to this unlawful and malafide intervention This has caused uncertainty about their future and those innocent 7 officers have been subjected to naked animosity displayed by the interested lobby because the petitioner and other 6 officers have been performing their duties in the National Board of Revenue with a high degree of efficiency and honesty. The honesty and efficiency thus have become the liability for their survival in the Cadre in which they are to be absorbed. One of the interested groups such as those recruited in the thirteenth batch and some of the senior officers and leaders of the Association informally held out a promise that the Association could withdraw its objection if those 7 officers including petitioner would concede their seniority to the 13th batch.

17. The petitioner on 2-12-95 wrote to the respondent No. 1 explaining about his high performance at work and seeking assistance in order to bring an end to the discrimination and unfairness of the uncertain position in which he has been kept for such a long time. A copy of the letter of the petitioner dated 2-12-95 has been annexed as Annexure-Z (2) to the petition. The petitioner being fully trained and effective in his post, having spent a long time in learning the expertise and having received in service training, etc. now if the illegal attempt to withdraw him from the National Board of Revenue succeeded then the country would be deprived of his expertise in the revenue matters and the training and experience that he had received, which would be totally wasted and as a result both the country and the petitioner himself as an individual would suffer. Bearing that fact clearly in mind and anxious to bring the uncertainty to an end, being fully aware that, most of the resentment and opposition to the petitioner and other six officers' absorption is due to the question of seniority, the petitioner and the other six officers were forced into a situation for making a grand sacrifice. The petitioner on 25-5-96 and other 6 officers separately on different dates wrote to the respondent No.2 stating that they would be prepared to forego their legal right of seniority and would accept seniority after the 13th BCS Batch. It is to be noted that this was a supreme sacrifice of legal rights made under duress with full awareness of the same by some highly intelligent and talented young officers being under extreme pressure, anxious just to retain the opportunity to simply serve their country in the capacity in which they have been trained, gained experience, proved, to be highly effective and beneficial to the country. A copy of the said letter dated 25-5-96 had been annexed as Annexure-Z (3) to the petition. After receiving that letter on 25-5-96 respondent No. 3 wrote to respondent No. i on 19-6-96 stating that the 7 officers have voluntarily accepted to be counted after the 13th BCS Cadre for the seniority purpose and if the matter is resolved in this manner then it is hoped that nobody would object to their absorption. Respondent No I replied on 8-7-96, reiterating that legally there was no scope for withdrawal of the 7 officers from' their present services. However, since it is stated that the officers had voluntarily foregone their seniority rights and that as a result there will not be any objection from anyone else then the matter can be resolved by wording the absorption order in the appropriate terms. A copy of the letter dated 8-6-96 has been annexed as Annexure-Z (5) to the petition. 

18. Thereafter on 31-7-96 respondent No.3 wrote to the respondent No. 1 stating that now the 15th BCS (Customs and Excise) Cadre objecting to the absorption of the 7 officers on the grounds of seniority vis-a-vis themselves, and that the National Board of Revenue is also in favour of withdrawing the said 7 officers. The letter further stated that the memorandum that the Board issued on 18-2-96 to the respondent No.3, Annexure-Z, requesting for making arrangement for withdrawal of the 7 officers and stating that, same had always been their stand. A copy of the letter dated 31-7-96 has been annexed as Annexure-Z (6) to the petition. It is submitted that the petitioner became a 'surplus public servant' after the abolition of his post by the Government for the purpose of administrative rearrangement to save public money, in accordance with section 2(e) of the Surplus Public Servants Absorption Ordinance, 1985. Thereafter, there is no dispute regarding the petitioner's status as surplus civil servant within the meaning of the law. It is further submitted that the petitioner once became a surplus public servant, he was duly nominated by the respondent No. 1 being the Establishment Division for the absorption in the post of Assistant Collector (presently Assistant Commissioner) in the BCS (Customs and Excise) Cadre in accordance with section 5 of the Surplus Public Servants Absorption Ordinance, 1985. There are no provisions at all for withdrawal of such nomination. Hence, the stand of respondent No.2 is malafide it being a malice in law as well as in fact to deny the equal opportunity to the petitioner in the service of the Republic. 

19. On behalf of the Government, respondent No.1, an affidavit-in-opposition has been filed. Another affidavit-in-opposition has been filed on behalf of respondent Nos. 2 to 4. In this case respondent Nos. 7 to 10 are the added-respondents who are already existing officers of the National Board of Revenue. Respondent Nos. 11 to 14 are also the added-respondents. These two groups of added respondents have filed their separate affidavits-in-opposition. On behalf of respondent Nos. 2 to 4 the affidavit-in-opposition has been filed, but no Advocate for respondent No.2, namely, National Board of Revenue has appeared in this case and advanced any argument. On behalf of other respondents their respective learned Advocate have appeared. In the affidavit-in-opposition the learned Advocates for the respondents had taken a common stand as regard maintainability of the writ application. In is their case that since the absorption in a Cadre is a service condition for enforcement of the same, the proper remedy of the petitioner is the Administrative Tribunal constituted under Article 117 of the Constitution and, as such, this writ petition is not maintainable. 

20. Mr Arnir-ul-Islam, the learned Advocate for the petitioners, submits that the present application is maintainable under Article 102 of the Constitution. His case is that in the instant case the petitioner being in the service of the Republic has not challenged any order passed by any Governmental authority to his detriment, and he is not aggrieved by any order of the Government as such. His case is that, the Government under law has issued a lawful order directing the respondent No.2 National Board of Revenue for absorption of the petitioner in BCS (Customs & Excise) Cadre being surplus in other service of the Republic, implementing and carrying out the lawful direction of the Government, namely, respondent No.1. He further submits that in the instant case he is praying for enforcement of Articles 27 and 29 of the Constitution in favour of the petitioner. Since he is praying for enforcement of fundamental right and since he is, in fact, praying for directing the respondent No. 2, National Board of Revenue, to obey and implement the lawful order of the Government, the application before the Administrative Tribunal is not maintainable. Rather the appropriate direction can be given by the High Court Division under Article 102 of the Constitution. It appears that the petitioner has not challenged any order of any Governmental authority by which he is aggrieved. No term and condition of his service is involved in the instant case. The petitioner was directed to be surplus and the Government, respondent No. 1 directed respondent No. 2, National Board of Revenue, to absorb him in the BCS (Customs & Excise) Cadre which the Government is empowered under section 5 of the Surplus Public Servants Absorption Ordinance, 1985. He further submits that as per law the present petitioner was nominated by the Government, respondent No. 1 and the Government repeatedly directed the respondent No.2, the National Board of Revenue, to absorb the petitioner following the procedure of law. Me Amir-ul-Islam further submits that the direction which this Court can give under Article 102 of the Constitution, cannot be given by the Administrative Tribunal. 

21. Since enforcement of fundamental right is involved and since the present petitioner is, in fact, praying for a direction to obey the lawful order of the Government by the National Board of Revenue in the instant case by absorbing the petitioner in BCS (Customs & Excise) Cadre, we are of the view that this application is maintainable under Article 102 of the Constitution inasmuch as the Administrative Tribunal is not competent to give a direction as the High Court Division is competent to give under Article 102 of the Constitution. Further, this relates to the policy of the Government which the Government is empowered to do under law. The terms and conditions of service, as such, are not involved. Rather the policy of the Government to absorb the surplus Government Servant in another Department is in question and for that the relevant law is also there. If one Branch of the Department of the Government is not following the lawful order of the hierarchy of the Governmental authority definitely the person who is aggrieved can come before this Court and pray for direction or declaration to implement, fulfill or obey the lawful order of the Government which the Administrative Tribunal is not competent to do. In this view of the matter we hold that the present writ petition is maintainable and the preliminary objection of the learned Advocate for the respondent is overruled. 	 

22. In this connection Mr Mahmudul Islam has referred to the case of Mujibur Rahamn vs. Government of Bangladesh, 44 DLR 111 and Civil Appeal Nos. 14-16 of 1995 in the case of Bangladesh vs. Saifuddin Ahmed [50 DLR (AD) 27 = 3 BLC (AD) 6J. We have gone through the judgment of the Appellate Division in both the cases. It appears that the facts and circumstances of this case are quite distinguishable from the facts and circumstances of the aforesaid two cases. Further, their Lordships of the Appellate Division held that for enforcement of fundamental right the High Court Division is competent to do under Article 102 of the Constitution which the Administrative Tribunal is incompetent to do. In this view of the matter we find that the objection of the learned Advocates for the respondents has no leg to stand on. 

23. Me Amir-ul-Islam has referred to sections 2(e), 4 and 5 of the Surplus Public Servants Absorption Ordinance, 1985. He submits that the petitioner in the instant case is a surplus public servant and he was on deputation under service of the National Board of Revenue, respondent No.2 Since there were vacancies and since the post of the petitioner was abolished and he was declared surplus, the respondent No.1directed the National Board of Revenue to absorb him according to Rules. But from the papers and documents which we have already referred earlier in this judgment and which have been annexed in the writ petition it appears that though the petitioner on deputation has been serving in the National Board of Revenue and though respondent No. 1 repeatedly directed respondent No.2 National Board of Revenue to absorb him, the National Board of Revenue on this plea or other is disobeying and/or showing disrespect to the lawful order of the Government, respondent No. I, who nominated the petitioner under sub-section (2) of section 5 of the aforesaid Ordinance. Mr Islam submits that section 5(2) of the aforesaid Ordinance provides that a surplus servant shall not be absorbed in any post unless he is nominated by the Ministry of Establishment. In the instant case, from the record, it appears that not only the Establishment Division, that is, respondent No. 1 had nominated the petitioner, but it repeatedly directed respondent No.2 National Board of Revenue, to absorb the petitioner after performing all the formalities. But the National Board of Revenue on this plea or that failed to obey and implement the order or the lawful authority. 

24. The learned Assistant Attorney General appearing for respondent No. 1 cannot dispute the submission of the learned Advocate for the petitioner. No one is appearing for respondent No. 2 the National Board of Revenue. But the learned Advocates for respondent Nos. 10 to 14 are disputing the absorption on the ground that they were already in the aforesaid Cadre and if the petitioner and 6 others are absorbed in their service and given seniority over them, then they will be highly prejudiced and their fundamental rights will be affected. In the facts and circumstances of the case it appears that the absorption is not the main question. The petitioner and six others have not yet been absorbed. If after absorption their seniority is fixed above added-respondents, then the question of being affected or aggrieved of these added-respondents will arise. But that stage has not yet arisen in the instant case. They are only apprehending that if they are absorbed and given seniority over them from date of their appointment, it will make these added-respondents junior to them. The added-respondents' grievance is that their fundamental right will be affected if the petitioner and six others are given seniority above them after absorption. 

25. In this connection we may refer to Paragraph 38 and Annexure-Z (3) of the writ petition. From the above it appears to us that the petitioner and six others have already written to the National Board of Revenue, respondent No.2 that if they are absorbed, they will not claim their seniority above the existing officers of the same cadre. Rather they will accept the seniority after the 13th BCS batch. Since the said averment has been made supported by this Annexure-Z(3), we are of the view that if the 7 officers including the present petitioner ar absorbed, the added-respondent Nos. 7 to 14 will have no objection as regards seniority and the application of the petitioner and others with regard to seniority filed before the National Board of Revenue may be accepted by the National Board of Revenue and in that case the added-respondents will have no grievance. 

26. Though as regards seniority the petitioner and six others have already expressed their mind to the National Board of Revenue, even then the respondent No. 2, National Board of Revenue, is not obeying the order of respondent No.1. This is very painful in view of the fact that if the petitioner and others are placed after the 13th BCS batch, then the existing officers who are already in the cadre will have no grievance. It is not disputed that the petitioner is on deputation in the National Board of Revenue with the consent of the National Board of Revenue. It is also not disputed that the posts of the petitioner and others were abolished in the BCS (Trade) Cadre and he was declared surplus along with others. It is also not disputed that there were vacancies in the BCS (Customs & Excise) Cadre and for that reason the National Board of Revenue had no objection to take them on deputation. After they were taken on deputation the post was abolished and they were declared surplus and thereafter with the concurrence of the Ministry of Finance and Ministry of Commerce, the Establishment Division had decided to absorb the petitioner and others in the BCS (Customs & Excise) Cadre in accordance with the provisions of the Surplus Public Servants Absorption Ordinance, 1985. So, the National Board of Revenue on the matter should have no objection to absorb them in accordance with law. 

27. Mr Mahmudul Islam, the learned Advocate appearing for respondent Nos. 7 to 10, has raised an objection as regards surplus Public Servant. He has referred to section 2(e) of the aforesaid Ordinance which provides the definition of surplus public servant. He submits that surplus public servant means the public servant whose post is abolished by the Government for the purpose of the administrative re-organisation. In the present case the administrative re-organisation has not yet been made. Since the administrative re-organisation has not yet been made, these alleged surplus employees cannot be absorbed in the BCS (Customs & Excise) Cadre under National Board of Revenue, respondent No.2. But Mr Islam has failed to notice that in the self-same section it is also provided that "or any other public servant the responsibility of whose absorption has been taken by the Government." In the instant case the Government had already treated the petitioner and six others as surplus public servant and Government directed the National Board of Revenue to absorb them. So, we do not find any violation of any law as submitted by Me Mahmudul Islam. It further appears that the abolition of the post in the BCS (Trade) Cadre were made and the petitioner and others were declared surplus with the concurrence of the Prima Minister. As soon as the Prime Minister, the head of the Government, has approved the proposal of the one Ministry the other Ministries or Department will be bound to obey it and in the instant case this respondent No.2 National Board of Revenue should have no lawful cause or reason to disobey or defy or dishonour the direction of respondent NO.1. In this view of the matter we find that this very action or attitude of respondent No.2, National Board of Revenue, is uncalled for and contrary to the direction of the Government, respondent No.1 as well as law. So, we are of the view that the National Board of Revenue, respondent No.2, is bound to obey and implement the lawful order of respondent No. 1 In the matter of absorption of the present petitioner and SIX others. 

28. This petitioner and six others are public servants and they were also appointed through competitive examination and they were appointed as public servants in the service of the Republic. Now this abolition of the post has rendered them, in a very precarious position. Before abolition they were taken on deputation in the National Board of Revenue. Now the post has been abolished and they are declared surplus. But they are still working under the National Board of Revenue with the same scale pay and allowances as they were getting before. They have been nominated, but they have not yet been absorbed. They are on deputation, but they are neither absorbed in the National Board of Revenue nor they were treated as Servants in the service of the Republic in a particular cadre. This has brought this petitioner and others, In a very uncertain position without any fault of their own. In this view of the matter the petitioner is really justified to file this writ application for justice inasmuch as though the Government directed to absorb them in the BCS (Customs & Excise) Cadre, they are not being absorbed by the National Board of Revenue, another Department of the Government. So, it appears to us that the present petitioner in fact has got a legal, lawful and genuine grievance for his survival. 

29. Since the case of the present petitioner and six other petitioners are on identical footing, since the facts and circumstance and the point of law as well as their grievance are same and similar and since all these seven petitioners are on deputation in the BCS (Customs & Excise) Cadre under National Board of Revenue and since their reliefs are same and similar, we are of the view that this judgment in Writ Petition No. 3025 of 1996 will cover the cases of other six writ petitioners and these other six petitioners will have the same and similar relief from this Court. 

30. Considering the facts and circumstances of the case and the documents and papers as annexed with the writ petition as well as affidavit- in-opposition we are of the view that this writ petition along with six others will succeed in the following manner. 

31. In the result, all the 7 Rule in write petitions are made absolute in the manner that  respondent Nos. 3 and 4 are here by directed to absorb all the seven writ petitioners in the BCS (Customs & Excise) Cadre according to the direction and nomination of respondent No. 1 in accordance with law, rules and regulations and they are also directed to issue necessary order and/or notification for absorption of the 7 petitioners in the aforesaid cadre service within thirty days from the date of receipt of the copy of this judgment. As regards the question of seniority for which respondent Nos. 7 to 14 are very, much concerned, we direct that the National Board of Revenue will be at liberty to consider the question of seniority of the petitioners and added-respondents according to the existing rules, regulations and also on consideration of the application of the petitioners   vide Annexure-Z (3) of the writ petition. Considering the facts and Circumstances of the  

 Case, we pass no order as to cost. 

End.

Mr. Jamiruddin Sircar, Advocate, Supreme Court, instructed by Mr. Md. Sajjadul Huq, Advocate-on-Record ----- For the Appellant. 
Mr. Abdul Hamid, Advocate, Supreme Court, instructed by Mr. M Nowab Ali, Advocate-on-Record -----For Respondent No. 1.

case_source: (From the judgment and order dated 6.8.85 passed by the High Court Division, Rangpur Bench, in Second Appeal No. 16 of 1974).
full_judgment:
MH Rahman J: This appeal at the instance of defendant No. 1 is directed against a judgment of reversal of the High Court Division, Rangpur Bench passed in Second Appeal No. 16 of 1974 setting aside the judgment and decree of the District Judge, Dinajpur, dated 28.7.1973 and restoring those of the Munsif, Dinajpur passed in OC Suit No. 162 of 1969 decreeing the plaintiffs suit.

2. Plaintiff-respondent No. 1 filed the suit for permanent injunction for restraining the defendants from entering into CS Plots Nos. 784 and 802 appertaining to CS Khatian No. 125 of Mouza Galtoir, PS Chirirbandar, District Dinajpur. His case is that the suit land originally belonged to Dinomoni Barmani who sold the land to her son-in-law, Janaki Nath Barman, by a kabala dated 18.1.1938. (Ext. 1 (a). The plaintiff purchased that land by a kabala dated 1.4.1957 (Ext.1) and got his name mutated and obtained rent receipts (Exts 2(a) to 2(h)). On 15.5.1969 the defendants in collusion with each other attempted to dispossess the plaintiff.

3. The defendant-appellant's case is that the suit land belonged to Dinomoni Barmani and Lalit Chandra Barman in equal shares and their names were correctly recorded in the CS Khatian No. 125 (Ext. B); that by an exchange Lalit Chandra Barman got Plot No. 801 of CS Khatian No. 133 of mouza Galtoir (Ext. B(1) from defendant No. 3 Buli Barmani and transferred to her the disputed Plot No. 784 and that the fact of exchange was noted in the CS Khatian. Defendant No. 3 sold Plot No. 784 by a kabala dated 2.12.1968 (Ext. A) to defendant No. 4 who was in possession of that land through his bargadar.

4. Defendants did not challenge the plaintiffs title and possession in Plot No. 802.

5. After finding that Dinomoni inherited the land of CS Khatian No. 125 from her husband, and that her son-in-law Janaki looked after her properties and that there was no basis for the noting of the alleged exchange in the CS Khatian the trial Court held that Janaki got his son Lalit's name included in the CS Khatian fraudulently; that Dinomoni had title to all the lands including plot No. 784 and that the presumption of correctness of the record of right was rebutted. The trial Court further found that in the kabala dated 18.1.1938 executed by Dinomoni in favour of Janaki, there was a reference to two other, plots besides the two suit plots; that Janaki asserted his title and possession in the suit lands and executed Ext. 1 the kabala dated 1.4.1957 in favour of the plaintiff who after purchase got his name mutated and got rent receipts. The trial Court also accepted the evidence of PW 2 and 3 in support of the plaintiffs case and rejected the evidence of the defendants' witnesses.

6. The appellate Court upheld the trial Court's decree with regard to Plot No. 802, but dismissed the plaintiffs prayer with regard to the other plot, namely, Plot No. 784, after finding that the plaintiff failed to prove his prima facie title and exclusive possession there.

7. In second Appeal tie High Court Division without considering the oral evidence of the witnesses of the parties set aside the judgment of the appellate Court. It laid much emphasis on mutation papers and the plaintiffs rent receipts which were not challenged by the defendants and held that the appellate Court ought to have presumed that the mutation, an official act, was duly done.

<u>8. In a simple suit for permanent injunction with regard to a disputed landed property the relief is available to a person who is in possession. The Court may enquire incidentally into the respective claims of the parties to the suit for determining whether the plaintiff has got a prima facie case i.e. whether he is in possession of the disputed property and entitled to the specific relief of permanent injunction. If the dispute involves complicated questions of title the plaintiff must establish his title by filing a regular suit for declaration of title. A simple suit for permanent injunction should not be allowed to be used as a testing device for ascertainment of title. In this case the plaintiff assails the presumption of the CS Khatian, a kind of exercise the Court in a simple suit for permanent injunction should ordinarily avoid.</u>

9. By mere assertion of the plaintiff that the disputed holding originally belonged to Dinomoni the subsequent fact of exchange between Dinomoni's daughter Buli Barmani and her grandson Lalit Chandra, reflected in the CS Khatian, cannot be rebutted in view of the clear statement of the plaintiffs own witness, PW 3, that Dinomoni, Lalit and Janaki got the record prepared. After considering the evidence of PW 3 and other wises of boththe parties, and the fact that the plaintiff did not pursue his case under section 144 of the Code of Criminal Procedure the appellate Court held that the plaintiff failed to prove his possession in plot No. 784. The High Court Division reversed this finding of fact of the last court of fact without considering the oral evidence in the case. It did not consider that there was nothing on record to show that notice with regard to the mutation proceeding was served on Lalit Chandra. The plaintiff got the rent receipts on the basis of that mutation. The High Court Division wrongly held that the appellate Court ought to have presumed that the mutation proceeding was duly done as an official act, without considering that the proceeding was initiated at the instance of a private party and if it was concluded without serving notice on necessary parties it would not have any legal effect.

In view of the above, the judgment and decree of the High Court Division are set aside and those of the Court of appeal below are restored. In the result, the appeal is allowed. No costs.

End.

case_source: (From the judgment and order dated the18th day of April, 2010 pass by the High Court Division, in civil Revision No. 3506 of 2007).
full_judgment:
Md Abdul Wahhab Miah J : This petition for leave to appeal is from the judgment and order dated 18-4-2010 and 19-4-2010 passed by a Single Bench of the High Court Division in Civil Revision No. 3506 of 2007 discharging the Rule.

2. Facts emerged from the judgment of the Appellate Court, the impugned judgment and order and the leave petition are that Halimon Bibi, predecessor-in-interest of the respondents as the plaintiff filed Partition Suit No.141 of 1962 in the Court of Sub or din ate Judge, Bogra (Now the Joint District Judge, First Court, Bogra) for partition of the suit land.

3. The suit was contested by defendant No.1, Ositullah @ Dasham Tullah Fakir, by filing a written statement.

4. At the trial, both parties adduced evidence. On conclusion of hearing of the suit, the trial Court by the judgment and decree dated 22-6-1964 decreed the suit in preliminary form on contest against defendant No.1 and ex-parte against the other defendants. Against the judgment and decree of the trial Court, defendant No.1, Ositullah Fakir, filed Partition Appeal No. 13 of 1964 in the Court of District Judge, Bogra. The predecessor of the petitioners also filed Partition Appeal No. 8 of 1964. During the pendency of the appeals, on 24-2-1969, the plaintiff-respondent filed an application in Partition Appeal No. 13 of 1964 for withdrawal of the suit with permission to sue afresh on the ground of formal defect. The learned District Judge, Bogra by the order dated 24-2-1969 allowed the application and thereby the suit stood withdrawn. Long after 33 years of the said order of withdrawal of the suit, the plaintiff-Halimon Bibi on 6-1-2002 filed an application in the trial Court for passing final decree pursuant to the preliminary decree dated 22-6-1964 and accordingly, a survey knowing Advocate was appointed as Commissioner who submitted his report, the report was accepted and the final decree was passed on 4-5-2002; the final decree was sealed and signed on 9-5-2004. Subsequently, the final decree was put into execution through Execution Case No. 1 of 2002.

5. The petitioners having known about the said final decree filed an application under section 151 of the Code of Civil Procedure (the Code) and section 44 of the Evidence Act for setting aside the final decree dated 4-5-2002 on the ground that the same was obtained fraudulently by suppressing the fact that the suit was withdrawn by the order of the learned District Judge dated 24-2- 1969 on the ground of formal defect and, in fact after withdrawal of the suit, there was no preliminary decree and also prayed for staying all further proceedings of the execution case till the hearing of the application. And all further proceedings of the execution case were stayed:

Eventually, the application was allowed by the order dated 14-10-2002 and the execution case was postponed. Being aggrieved by the said order, the plaintiff-Halimon Bibi filed Civil Revision No. 106 of 2003 before the High Court Division. A learned Judge of the Single Bench by the judgment and order dated 11-1-2004 made the Rule absolute, set aside order dated 14-10-2002 passed by the trial Court on the view that "since the suit has been finally disposed of-with the signing and sealing of the final decree, such decree can not be disturbed on an application under section 151 of the Code of Civil Procedure and thus the impugned order is not sustainable in law and liable to be set aside." The learned Judge further observed that "it appears that against the final decree there are specific provision for appeal the applicant if aggrieved have to avail such remedy by way of appeal against the final decree since the decree can be challenged in an appeal and the aggrieved party has other remedy available, the inherent power under section 151 of the Code of Civil Procedure cannot be invoked."

6. The defendants did not challenge the said judgment and order of the High Court Division before this Court and as per observations made therein filed Partition Appeal No. 15 of 2004 before the District Judge, Bogra against the final decree. The learned Additional District Judge, 1st Court, Bogra on hearing the appeal by the judgment and decree dated 25-6-2007 dismissed the appeal. Being aggrieved by the judgment and decree of the learned Additional District Judge, the petitioners filed Civil Revision No.2506 of 2007 before the High Court Division and obtained the Rule. The revision was heard by the same learned Judge who earlier disposed Civil Revision No.106 of 2003 and he, by the impugned judgment and order (dated 18-4-2010 and 19-4- 2010), discharged the Rule; hence this petition for leave to appeal.

7. Mr Abdul Quayum, learned Counsel for the petitioners, has submitted that after the withdrawal of the suit by the plaintiff in Partition Appeal No. 13 of 1964, there was no existence of the preliminary decree passed in the suit by the trial Court. Therefore, the final decree passed pursuant to the preliminary decree was without jurisdiction, but the learned Additional District Judge as well as the learned Judge of the High Court Division failed to consider that simple factual and legal aspect of the case and thus fell into an error in maintaining the final decree passed in the suit and, as such, the impugned judgment and order calls for interference by this Court by way of granting leave.

8. Mr Abdul Wadud Bhuiyan, learned Counsel entering caveat on behalf of respondent Nos. 1, 2, 4, 6, and 46, on the other hand, has supported the impugned judgment and order and has made submission to dismiss the leave petition.

9. Mr Abdul Quayum has placed the judgment and order passed in Civil Revision No. 106 of 2003, the judgment and decree of the Appellate Court in Title Appeal No. 15 of 2004, the orders passed by the learned District Judge in Partition Appeal Nos. 13 and 8 of 1964 and the impugned judgment and order.

<u>10. In the facts and circumstances of the case as stated hereinabove, two interesting questions are to be decided in this petition: (a) whether after withdrawal of the suit at the appellate stage, the preliminary decree passed in the withdrawn suit could be the basis for passing final decree and if any final decree passed any how in the context could be put into execution, (b) whether, in the instant appeal (Partition Appeal No. 15 of 2004) giving rise to the instant revision (Civil Revision No. 3506 of 2007), the Additional District Judge could sit over the order passed by the District Judge in the earlier appeal being Partition Appeal No. 13 of 1964 allowing the plaintiff-respondent to withdraw the suit with permission to sue afresh on the view that the order of withdrawal of the suit with permission to sue afresh passed in Partition Appeal No. 13 of 1964 was not legal and defective.</u>

11. To answer the questions, the most relevant materials to be considered are the two orders passed in Partition Appeal Nos. 13 of 1964 and 8 of 1964. With the additional paper book, the entire order sheets of the two partition appeals (Nos. 8 of 1964 and 13 of 1964) have been filed. From the order sheets of the two appeals, it appears that, in fact, the order of withdrawal of the suit with permission to sue afresh was passed in Partition Appeal No. 13 of 1964. The order of withdrawal of the suit was passed on 24-2-1969

The order reads as follows:

Respondent I entered appearance today. The appeal is taken up for hearing. Argument at length heard on both sides. Respondent at the close of the argument files application praying for withdrawal of the original Part. Suit with leave to sue afresh on grounds of formal defects. The suit, especially law to the amendment allowed at day end of the trial for formal defect since the prayer for withdrawal of the suit should be allowed. The court fees paid is sufficient. Hence it is

Order

That the plff respondent be permitted to withdraw the suit with liberty to bring a fresh suit if not otherwise barred. In view of the withdrawal of the suit there stand no decree and therefore there is no locus standi for the appeal which therefore is accordingly disposed of.”

12. From the order sheets of Partition Appeal No. 8 of 1964, it appears that the argument in the appeal was heard on 8-2-1969 and the judgment was reserved till hearing of Partition Appeal No. 13 of 1964 and on 24-2-1696 i.e. the date on which the order was passed in Partition Appeal No. 13 of 1964 allowing the plaintiff to withdraw the suit with permission to sue afresh the following order was passed in that appeal (8 of 1964)

"The original part, suit has been withdrawn by the plaintiff respondent in PA 13/64. The suit having been withdrawn there is no scope for this appeal which therefore be accordingly disposed of."

<u>13. From the two orders passed in the two appeals as quoted hereinbefore, it is clear that the plaintiffs suit for partition stood withdrawn on 24-2-1969 and with the withdrawal of the suit, the preliminary decree passed therein became non existent or non-est, even then in the order permitting the plaintiff to withdraw the suit with permission to suit afresh, it was specifically stated "I n view of the withdrawal of the suit there stand no decree. "And because of withdrawal of the suit, the appeals were not disposed of on merit. Against the order of withdrawal of the suit, the plaintiff did not take any step to set aside the order either on the ground of fraud or on any other illegality or irregularity, but after 33 years of the said order on 6-1-2002 filed on application in the suit to pass final decree pursuant to the preliminary decree though there was no existence of any preliminary decree on that date and the learned Joint District Judge, 1st Court, Bogra appointed an Advocate Commissioner to give saham to the plaintiff according to the preliminary decree, who submitted his report and on acceptance of the Commissioner's report submitted on 22-4-2002, passed the final decree 4-5-2002 and the final decree was sealed and signed on 9-5-2002 and then Execution Case No. 1 of 2002 was filed on 16-5-2002 for execution of the final decree.</u>

14. As quoted hereinbefore, the Rule in Civil Revision No. 106 of 2003 was made absolute on two grounds: (i) against the final decree, there was specific provision for appeal and if the defendants were, in fact, aggrieved, they had to avail such remedy by way of filing an appeal, (ii) since the final decree had been sealed and signed, the application under section 151 of the Code was not maintainable.

15. In the context, it needs to be mentioned that in Civil Revision No. 106 of 2003, the learned Judge of the Single Bench did not say anything about the propriety of the order passed in Partition Appeal No. 13 of 1964 permitting the plaintiff to withdraw the suit with permission of sue afresh. It is also an admitted fact that pursuant to the observations made by the learned Judge in the said civil revision (Civil Revision No. 106 of 2006), the defendants preferred Partition Appeal No. 15 of 2004 before the District Judge, Bogra. The appeal was heard by the learned Additional District Judge, 1st Court, Bogra and he dismissed the appeal on the findings, inter alia, that on examining the application filed for withdrawal of the suit, it appeared that there was no signature of Halimon Bibi and there was also no verification in the application; that the order dated 24-2-1969 allowing plaintiff-respondent No.1 to withdraw the suit with permission to sue afresh was passed through inadvertence and before passing the order no statement of the plaintiff-respondent to the effect that there was formal defect in the main suit was recorded which was logical and legal requirement, that the order permitting the plaintiff to withdraw the suit was not legal and was defective.

16. The learned Additional District Judge in his penultimate finding held that the order dated 24-2-1969 passed in Partition Appeal No. 13 of 1964 being a defective order from the legal point of view, there was no logic to maintain that order and therefore, it could not be said that there was no existence of the preliminary decree dated 22-6-1964. The learned Additional District Judge further held that since the preliminary decree was passed in the suit on detailed discussion and the lower Court did not give any finding that there was defect in the framing of the suit; there was no scope to withdraw the suit on the ground of formal defect, the final decree was rightly passed on 4-5-2002 on the basis of the application filed by the plaintiff pursuant to the preliminary decree.

17. The learned Additional District Judge observed that there was no straight order setting aside the preliminary decree in Partition Appeal Nos. 13 of 1964 and 8 of 1964 and in Civil Revision No. 106 of 2003, in fact, the preliminary decree and the final decree were confirmed. The learned Additional District Judge further observed that since defendant Nos. 9-11 and 15 did not contest the suit and the decree was passed against them ex-parte, they had no locus standi to file Partition Appeal No. 8 of 1964. The learned Additional District Judge further held that since defendant Nos. 9-11 and IS did not file any objection against the Advocate Commissioner's report the instant appeal (Appeal No. 15 of 2004) at their instance was not maintainable in law.

18. From the impugned judgment and order, it appears that the learned Judge of the Single Bench simply dittoed the view of the learned Additional District Judge, but in different language. However, the learned Judge added a new finding that the order of withdrawal of the suit with permission to sue afresh was obtained by practicing fraud upon the Court, and the reason in finding so were that in the application for withdrawal, there was neither any signature of the plaintiff nor there was any verification or affidavit as required under rule 19 of the Civil Rules and Orders and under Order VI, rule 15 of the Code of Civil Procedure, and that there was nothing on record to show that either summons of Partition Appeal No. 8 of 1964 was served upon the plaintiff-Halimon Bibi or she appeared in the said appeal. The learned Judge gave further finding that Title Appeal No.8 of 1964 was an independent appeal and though no application for withdrawal of the suit was filed by the plaintiff in that appeal, the order was passed withdrawing the suit.

19. In the above back drop, keeping in view the findings of the Court below and the learned Judge of the High Court Division, let us examine the two questions as formulated hereinbefore.

20. One thing is absolutely clear that the orders passed by the learned District Judge in Partition Appeal Nos.13 of 1964 and 8 of 1964 were very much in force with all their legal implication on the date of filing the application by the plaintiff on 6-1-2002 for passing the final decree pursuant to the preliminary decree and till date, those are in force with the same legal implication as stood on 6-1-2002. It is also a fact that the defendants in their application under section 151 of the Code along with section 44 of the Evidence Act categorically stated about the said fact of withdrawal of the suit by the plaintiff and the order passed by the Appellate Court. But the plaintiff as well as her heirs after her death did not take any step either to vacate or set aside the order. In the context, it is also necessary to state that the learned Additional District Judge gave finding that the order allowing the plaintiff to withdraw the suit with permission to sue afresh was defective from the legal point of view and there was no logic to maintain that order, but he failed to consider that the date on which the application for passing the final decree was filed, the date on which the Advocate Commissioner was appointed to give the saham, the date of submission of the report by the Advocate Commissioner arid the passing of the final decree, the order allowing the plaintiff to withdraw the suit with permission to sue afresh had all its legal implication and by no legal fiction, the trial Court could ignore that.

21. Be that as it may, the order allowing the plaintiff to withdraw the suit with permission to sue afresh having been passed in a completely separate appeal being Partition Appeal No. 13 of 1964, we failed to understand under what provision of law the learned Additional District Judge and the High Court Division sat over the order passed in that appeal. So long the order dated 24-2-1969 passed in Partition Appeal No. 13 of 1964 remained in force, neither the learned Additional District Judge nor the learned Judge of the High Court Division could by-pass or ignore the same as has been done by them.

<u>22. The learned Additional District Judge did not find any fraud in the order dated 24-2-1969 in Partition Appeal No. 13 of 1964 passed by the learned District Judge, what he found, was that the order was not legal and defective. But the learned Judge of the High Court Division found that the order withdrawing the suit was obtained fraudulently. Fraud is basically a question of fact and that has to be alleged by a party and, if alleged, the other side has to be given chance to controvert such facts, but in the instant case, no such allegation was made either by the plaintiff or by her heirs after her death. As stated earlier, neither the plaintiff nor her heirs ever made any application before the District Judge, Bogra to set aside the order dated 24-6-1969 alleging fraud in obtaining the order, because the order having been passed by the learned District Judge, only he could set aside or vacate the order if it could be established that the order was obtained by practising fraud upon him.</u>

23. From the judgment of the Appellate Court (Partition Appeal No. 15 of 2004), it further appears that the plaintiff-respondent claimed that she did not put her signature or left thumb impression in any application for withdrawal of the suit on the ground of formal defect or in the verification in support of the application, but she did not say that no application for withdrawal was filed by her learned Advocated and no allegation was also made that the application for withdrawal was filed by her learned Advocate in collusion with the learned Advocate of the other side or the appellants or that she never engaged any Advocate to appear on her behalf or that the learned Advocate who filed the application was not at all engaged by her or that she did not enter appearance in the appeal through the learned Advocate on 24-2-1969 who filed the application for withdrawal of the suit or that her learned Advocate did not participate in the hearing of the appeal (in the order dated 24-2-1969, it has been clearly stated that "Respondent No.1 entered appearance today. The appeal is taken up for hearing. Argument at length heard on both sides"). So, the question of obtaining the order dated 24-2-1969 by practising fraud as found by the learned Judge of the High Court Division does not arise at all.

24. From the above, it is clear that the plaintiff who was respondent No.1 appeared in Partition Appeal No. 13 of 1964 and because of the order permitting him to withdraw the suit with permission to sue afresh, the appeal was not disposed of on merit and for the same reason Partition Appeal No. 8 of 1964 was also not disposed of on merit. The application for making the preliminary decree final was filed long after 33 years, is it believable that when the plaintiff appeared in the appeal through her learned Advocate and the appeal was not disposed of on merit, she would not know about the disposal of the appeal, or keep any information about the appeal and so also the order of withdrawal of the suit, even if for argument's sake, it is accepted that in the application for withdrawal of the suit, she did not put any signature or left thumb impression and that the application was not verified by her and that before passing the order, her statement was not recorded.

<u>25. Similarly had the suit giving rise to the appeals not been withdrawn, defendant No.1 and the other defendants who filed the appeals would not sit idle. More so, had the suit not been withdrawn, the appeals would have been disposed of in some way, i.e. either on merit or by default, but nothing happened. Be that as it may, in no way, the learned Additional District Judge could sit suo moto over the order passed by the learned District Judge in Partition Appeal No. 13 of 1964 permitting the plaintiff to withdraw the suit with permission to sue afresh. The moment the suit stood withdrawn and the Appellate Court passed order to the effect "there stand no decree" by no legal fiction, the preliminary decree passed in the suit could be said or treated to be in existence and as such, no application could be filed to pass the final decree pursuant to the preliminary decree and for that matter to proceed under the provisions of Order XXVI, rules 13 and 14 of the Code. In other words, rightly or wrongly when the Appellate Court passed the order permitting the plaintiff to withdraw the suit with permission to sue afresh in the terms as quoted hereinbefore, there was no scope to say that the preliminary decree remained in existence after 24-2-1969, inasmuch as with the withdrawal of the suit whatever may be the preliminary decree passed therein became non existent and non-est. suit unfortunately, the learned Additional District Judge and the learned Judge of the High Court Division did not at all consider these factual and legal aspects of the case in maintaining the final decree passed on the non existent and non-est preliminary decree. Further, the lower Court's records were sent to the District Judge in connection with Partition Appeal Nos. 8 and 13 of 1964 as clearly noted in the orders dated 22-12-1964 and 27-3-1965 respectively passed in the appeals and after the disposal of the appeals, the records must have been sent to the lower Court and the result of the appeal must have also been communicated to the trial Court, but in acting on the application of the plaintiff to pass final decree pursuant to the non-est preliminary decree, the trial Court did not at all look at the order passed by the Appellate Court.</u>

26. Now, the finding or the High Court Division that "the suit or an appeal is independent and should be independently determined", but no application for withdrawal of the suit was filed by the plaintiff in Partition Appeal No. 8 of 1964 and that it did not find any service of notice of the appeal either upon the plaintiff or any other respondents. The finding of the High Court Division as to the non service of notice of appeal upon the plaintiff-respondent and' the other respondents is prima facie wrong, as order No. 3 of Title Appeal No. 8 of 1964 shows that notice of the appeal were served upon all the respondents. Order No. 3 reads as follows:

"Notices served upon all the respondents (respondents included principal and proforma-respondents) they do not appear. Court guardian of minor respondents 5 to 7 also does not apear. LCR not received. Issue this appeal." a reminder. To 22-12-1964 for LCR and order

The next order (Order No.4) dated 22-12- 1964 reads as follows:

"LCR received. To 26-3-1964 for settling the date of hearing."

27. Reading order Nos. 3 and 4 together, it is prima facie clear that notices of the appeal were duly served upon the respondents and after the receipt of the lower Court's records, the appeal was set for settling the date of hearing and it was heard on 8-6-1969. Thus it is clear that the appeal was not heard abruptly or without any notice upon the plaintiff who was allegedly made proforma defendant No.17 (as found by the High Court Division). Furthermore, the plaintiff never made any complaint either in the instant appeal (Partition Appeal No. 15 of 2004) or in Civil Revision No. 106 of 2003 that notice of Partition Appeal No. 8 of 1964 was not served upon her or she had no knowledge of the said appeal. In the context, it is very pertinent to state that after the service of notice of the appeal, option was with the plaintiff-respondent either to appear in the appeal or not. The High Court Division was also wrong in finding fault with the order of withdrawal or the suit on the ground that no application for withdrawal was filed in Partition Appeal No. 8 of 1964, because. both the appeals were filed against the judgment and decree passed in one suit being Partition Suit No.141 of 1962, so it was not necessary to file separate application in Partition Appeal No. 8 of 1964, when application was filed in Partition Appeal No. 13 of 1964. And, in fact, no 'order for withdrawal of the suit was passed in, this appeal. From the order dated 24-2-1969 (the order has been quoted earlier), it is also clear that this appeal (Partition Appeal No. 8 of 1964) was disposed with the observation that since the original partition suit had been withdrawn by the plaintiff-respondent in Partition Appeal No. 13 of 1964, there was no scope "for this appeal."

<u>28. The learned Additional District Judge and the High Court Division were also totally wrong in taking the view that since the appellants did not contest the partition suit by filing written statement, they could not file Title Appeal No. 8 of 1964, inasmuch as it is a well settled legal proposition that even if a 3rd party is affected by a decree, he can file an appeal against such decree and in the instant case, the appellants very much were parties to the suit. The only bar put by the legislature in a suit for partition as in section 97 of the Code is that where any party aggrieved by a preliminary decree does not appeal from such decree, he shall be precluded from disputing its correctness in any appeal which may be preferred from the final. decree. This bar was not applicable in, the instant case, as the defendants preferred Title Appeal No. 8 of 1964 before the District Judge against the preliminary decree and that appeal was not disposed of on merit on the ground that the suit out of which the appeal arose, had been withdrawn, so the instant appeal by the defendants against the final decree was quite competent and maintainable.</u>

29. The learned Additional District Judge and the High Court Division were also wrong in not entertaining the appeal on the ground that the defendants did not file any objection against the Advocate Commissioner's report inasmuch as there being no existence of the preliminary decree in the eye of law, the very appointment of the Advocate Commissioner to give saham to the plaintiff pursuant to the preliminary decree was without jurisdiction. Furthermore, in the application filed by the petitioners under section 151 of the Code before the trial Court to set aside the final decree, it was categorically stated that the plaintiff by suppressing the fact of withdrawal of the suit on 24-2-1969 filed the application for, making the preliminary decree final and by practising fraud upon the, Court and in a hurried manner made the non existent preliminary decree final on 4-5-2002 and the decree was sealed and signed on 9-5-2002, so there was no scope of filing the objection against the Commissioner's report.

<u>30. Now, the other 'legal questions which have to be addressed are whether the application for withdrawal of the suit was required to be signed by the plaintiff-respondent, whether the same also was required to be verified by her or supported by an affidavit and whether the statements of the plaintiff was needed to be recorded before passing the order allowing her to withdraw the suit with permission to sue afresh as held by the Appellate Court as well as by the High Court Division.</u>

<u>31. Rule 14 of Order VI of the Code has clearly provided that every pleading shall be signed by the party and his pleader (if any). The rule also provides that where a party pleading is, by reason of absence or for other good cause, unable to sign the pleading, it may be signed by any person duly authorized by him to sign the same or to sue or defend on his behalf. Rule 15(1) of Order VI has provided that save as otherwise provided by any law for the time being in force, every pleading shall be verified at the foot by the party or by one of the parties pleading or by some other person proved to the satisfaction of the Court to be acquainted with the facts of the case. (Sub-rules (2) and (3) of rule 15 are not relevant for the present purpose). And according to rule 1 of Order VI "pleading" shall mean plaint or written statement. So, by no stretch of imagination, the application for withdrawal of a suit can be treated or termed as pleading. Therefore, we do not see the requirement of verification in the application for withdrawal of a suit as found by the learned Additional District Judge and the learned Judge of the High Court Division. In this regard, it may be also stated that the applications/petitions which would require affidavit in support of the prayer made therein have been specifically mentioned in the Code such as, prayer for attachment before judgment under Order XXVIII, rule 5, prayer for temporary injunction under Order XXXIX, rule 1 of the Code. But nowhere in Order XXIII, sub-rules (1) and (2) of rule 1, which have dealt with withdrawal of suit or abandonment of part of claim the phraseology "affidavit" has been referred to or mentioned, when the Code is silent about the necessity or requirement of any verification or affidavit to make a prayer for withdrawal of a suit, the Court could not impose such a condition to file an application for withdrawal of a suit. So, the Appellate Court and the High Court Division were apparently wrong in finding that the application for withdrawal of the suit in Partition Appeal No. 13 of 1964 was defective as the same was not verified by the plaintiff or supported by any affidavit.</u>

<u>32. The learned Additional District Judge as well as the High Court Division found the order dated 24-2-1969 defective on the ground that the application for withdrawal of the suit was not signed by the plaintiff-respondent, Halimon Bibi. As already found hereinbefore, the application for withdrawal of a suit need not be verified by the plaintiff and that need not be signed by the plaintiff as well and it was enough if the same was filed by her learned Advocate. Admittedly, the application for withdrawal was filed by the learned Advocate for the plaintiff-respondent. An Advocate (in the Code still it is pleader) is the attorney of the plaintiff or the defendant as the case may be and he is legally quite competent to file any application in the suit including the application for withdrawal of a suit. In rule 1 of Order Ill of the Code, it has been clearly provided that any appearance, application or act in or to any Court required or authorized by law to be made or done by a party in such Court, may, except where otherwise expressly provided by any law for the time being in force; be made or done by the party in person, or by his recognized agent, or by a pleader appearing, applying or acting, as the case may be, on his behalf: provided that any such appearance shall, if the Court so directs, be made by the partly in person. In the context rule 4 of the order is very relevant and I consider it better to quote the rule in its entirety which is as under:</u>

<u>"4.(1) No pleader shall act for any person in any Court, unless he has been appointed for the purpose by such person by a document in writing signed by such person or by his recognized agent or by some other person duly authorized by or under a power-of- attorney to make such appointment.</u>

<u>(2) Every such appointment shall be filed in Court and shall be deemed to be in force until determined with the leave of the Court by a writing signed by the client or the pleader, as the case may be, and filed in Court, or until the client or the pleader dies, or until all proceedings in the suit are ended so far as regards the client.</u>

<u>(3) For the purposes of sub-rule (2) an application for review of judgment, an application under section 144 or section 152 of this Code, any appeal from any decree or order in the suit and any application or act for the purpose of obtaining copies of documents or return of documents produced or filed in the suit or of obtaining refund of monies paid into the Court in connection with the suit shall be deemed to be proceedings in the suit.</u>
