<u>(4) The High Court Division may, by general order, direct that, where the person by whom a pleader is appointed is unable to write his name, his mark upon the document appointing the pleader shall be attested by such person and in such manner as may' be specified by the order (5) No pleader who has been engaged for the purpose of pleading only shall plead on behalf of any party, unless he has filed in Court a memorandum of appearance signed by himself and stating-</u>

<u>(a) the names of the parties to the suit, (b) the name of the party for whom he appears, and</u>

<u>(c) the name of the person by whom he is authorized to appear.</u>

33. Provided that nothing in this sub-rule shall apply to any pleader engaged to plead on behalf of any party by any others pleader who has been duly appointed to act in Court on behalf of such party."

34. A reading of sub-rules (1) and (2) of rule 4 shows that in order to act by an Advocate on behalf of a person a vokalatnama duly signed by him has to be filed and in the instant case as stated earlier the plaintiff-respondent did not deny the fact that she made appearance in Partition Appeal No. 13 of 1964 through the learned Advocate who filed the application for withdrawal of the suit and in Order XXIII, sub-rules (1) and (2) of rule 1, it has not been stated that the application for withdrawal of a suit either simpliciter or with permission to sue afresh has to be filed by the plaintiff himself (s). So, the learned Advocate who filed the vokalatnama on behalf of the plaintiff-respondent 'was quite competent to file the application for withdrawal of the suit with permission to sue afresh and there was no necessity on the part of the plaintiff-respondent to sign the same and the learned District Judge rightly acted on it.

<u>35. Yet another legal point to be considered is whether, before passing the order allowing the application to withdraw the suit with permission to sue afresh, it was necessary to record the statement of the plaintiff-respondent that there was formal defect in the plaint for which she wanted to withdraw the suit. Rule 1 of Order XXIII of the Code reads as follows:</u>

<u>"1. (1) At any time after the institution of a suit the plaintiff may, as against all or any of the defendants, withdraw his suit or abandon</u>

<u>(2) Where the Court is satisfied-</u>

<u>(a) that a suit must fail by reason of some formal defect, or</u>

<u>(b) that there are other sufficient grounds for allowing the plaintiff to institute a fresh suit for the subject-matter of a suit or part of a claim, it may, on such terms as it thinks fit, grant the plaintiff permission to withdraw from such suit or abandon such part of a claim with liberty to institute a fresh suit in respect of the subject-matter of such suit or such part of a claim."</u>

36. In these two sub-rules, nothing has been said about the necessity of recording the statement of the plaintiff before according permission for withdrawing the suit either with permission to sue afresh or to withdraw a suit without permission to sue afresh. Only thing which has been provided in sub-rule (2) of rule 1 of Order XXIII is that in case of withdrawal of a suit with permission to sue afresh, the Court has to be satisfied that a suit must fail by reason of formal defect or that there are other sufficient grounds for allowing the plaintiff to institute a fresh suit for the subject matter of a suit or part of a claim. The satisfaction of the Court as spoken about in sub-rule (2) is relatable only to the question, there was some formal defect in farming of the suit for which the suit shall fail or that there are other sufficient grounds allowing the plaintiff to institute a fresh suit for the subject matter of a suit or part of claim, so the question of recording the statement of the plaintiff to the above effect as found by the learned District Judge and the High Court Division would not arise at all. It will not be out of context if we look at the provision of rule 3 of Order XXIII.

<u>37. This rule reads as follows:</u>

<u>"3. Where it is proved to the satisfaction of the Court that a suit has been adjusted wholly or in part by any law full agreement or compromise, or where the defendant satisfies the plaintiff in respect of the whole or any part of the subject-matter of the suit, the Court shall order such agreement, compromise or satisfaction to be recorded, and shall pass a decree to in accordance therewith so far as it relates to the suit."</u>

<u>38. A reading of this rule shows that before passing an order of agreement or recording a compromise, it has to be proved to the satisfaction of the Court that a suit has been adjusted wholly or in part by any lawful agreement or compromise. The phraseology used in this rule "Where it is proved to. the satisfaction of the Court" can very well be construed that to prove the satisfaction of the Court, as to the compromise of a suit, examination of the concerned party(s) is necessary, because the words "Where it is proved to the satisfaction of the Court" cannot be confined or related to the filing of an application for compromise and it would need something more, i.e. before allowing the prayer under the rule, it has to be proved by the party(s) concerned that they really compromised the matter and the terms of compromise are lawful, but in case of an application for withdrawal of a suit, the phraseology "Where it is proved to the satisfaction of the Court" has not been used. And it is being consistently followed by the Courts including the Apex Court (both the Divisions) that before recording compromise, the Court always examine the party(s) concerned to ascertain as to whether they really compromised the suit, as per terms of the solenama or the compromise petition, i.e. as per the language of the rule, whether a suit has been adjusted wholly or in part by any lawful agreement or compromise. But in sub-rules (1) and (2) of rule 1, the phraseology "Where it is proved to the satisfaction of the Court" being absent, it is only the satisfaction of the Court that a suit must fail by reason of some formal defect or that there are other sufficient grounds for allowing the plaintiff to institute a fresh suit for the subject matter of a suit or part of a claim. And the learned District Judge having allowed the plaintiff to withdraw the suit with permission to sue afresh, it has to be presumed that he was satisfied as to the formal defect of the suit and in any view of the matter, the learned Additional District Judge was not legally empowered to question the satisfaction of the learned District Judge as to the formal defect of the suit in the instant appeal as that was not the lis before him. Therefore, the view taken by the learned Additional District Judge as well as the High Court Division that the recording of the statement of the plaintiff-respondent to the effect that there was formal defect which was a requirement of law and logical, so the order allowing the plaintiff to withdraw the suit with permission to sue afresh was defective was absolutely erroneous.</u>

<u>39. For the discussions made hereinbefore, we are of the view that since there was no existence of any preliminary decree with the withdrawal of the suit, no final decree could be passed on a non-existent and non-est preliminary decree passed in the partition suit. Therefore, the impugned judgment and order calls for interference by this Court. And since both the parties have been well represented by their Senior Counsel, we consider it expedient to interfere with impugned judgment and order summarily without giving any leave, as if leave is granted, it would take long time to dispose of the matter and in the long run, it would endure to the sufferings of the parties. Since the cause of action for filing a suit for partition is recurring and the order of withdrawal of the suit with permission to sue afresh is still in force, the heirs of the deceased- plaintiff, Halimon Bibi, if so advised, can still file a suit for partition.</u>

Accordingly, the petition is disposed of in the following terms:

The impugned judgment and order affirming the judgment and decree of the learned Additional District Judge, 1st Court, Bogra in Partition Appeal No. 15 of 2004 and the final decree dated 4-5-2002 passed by the learned Joint District Judge, 1st Court, Bogra (the decree drawn and signed on 9-5-2002) in Partition Suit No. 141 of 1962, are set aside. The heirs of the deceased-plaintiff, Halimon Bibi, if so advised, may file fresh suit for partition.

End.

caseno: Appeal from Original Decree No. 43 of 1979.
lawyer:
SM Monir, Advocate ----- For the Appellants.
BK Das, Advocate ----- For Respondent No. 1
parties:
Shah Alam and others   ----- Appellants.
Vs.
Masuma Khatoon and others ----- Respondent.
full_judgment:
Kazi Ebadul Hoque, J.: This appeal at the instance of defendant Nos. 1 to 6 and 10 is directed against the judgment and decree dated 17.8.78 passed by the Subordinate Judge, 1st Court, Dhaka in Title Suit No. 27 of 1977 decreeing the plaintiffs suit for declaration of title in the 'A' schedule land and recovery of possession in. the 'B' schedule land of the plaint which is part of the 'A' schedule land.

2. Respondent Nos. 1 and 2 as plaintiffs filed Title Suit No. 27 of 1977 in the 1st Court of Subordinate Judge, Dhaka on the 26th, of January, 1977 against appellant Nos. 1-6 as principal defendant Nos. 1 to 6 impleading also appellant No. 7 and respondent Nos. 3-6 as proforma defendant Nos. 7 to 11 in the suit.

3. The case of the plaintiffs in short is that proforma defendant No. 7 Kadam Ali, father of proforma defendant No.8 Ahmmad Ali, proforma defendant No. 10 Alamat Ali and Julmat Ali husband of proforma defendant No.9 Mohammadi Begum, acquired right, title and interest in suit CS plot No. 313 of CS Khatian No. 362 Ext. 5(a) of Mouza Barabo along with other lands on the basis of a deed of heba-bil-ewaz dated the 17th December, 1935 Ext. 1 and A executed in his favour by Jamirjan Bibi and Annabi Bibi, widow and daughter respectively of late Alef and he was in peaceful possession of the said property. While in such title and possession defendant No. 7 transferred entire area of 2.51 acres of suit plot No. 313 to Mohammad Azizur Rahman by a registered deed of sale dated 16th April, 1957 Ext 2 and delivered possession of the said land to the said purchaser. While in such title and possession the said Azizur Rahman transferred eastern half of the suit CS plot No 313 to plaintiff No. 1 Mosammat Masuma Khatoon by a sale deed dated 7th July, 1958 Ext. 2(b) showing the purchased land as Block 'B' in the Map attached to the said sale deed and the western half of the said suit plot No. 313 to plaintiff No. 2 Mosammat Rezia Khatoon by sale deed dated 7th, July, 1958 Ext. 2(a) showing the said land as Block 'A' in the Map attached, to the said sale deed and made over khas possession of said land to the said purchaser plaintiffs. Thereafter the plaintiffs got their names mutated with the Government Tahsil office and have been paying rents since 1367 BS and onwards under separate rent receipts Ext. 4 sides. The said CS plot No. 313 has been recorded in the revisional survey operation in six separate plots. As there was wrong recording in respect of the area the plaintiffs fired an application on 25.3.74 Ext. 11 before the Revenue Officer, Dhaka for correction of the said mistake. Since the date of purchase the plaintiffs remained in exclusive khas possession of the suit plot No. 313 measuring an area of 2.51 acres by growing crops therein through their cultivators and bargadars openly, peaceably, and to the knowledge of all persons including the principal defendants and their predecessors-in-interest and of independent right, free from all encumbrances for more than 17 years and by adverse possession too.

4. Further case of the plaintiffs is that the principal defendants who are alleged to be purchasers from proforma defendant Nos. 8 to 10 illegally encroached upon the plaintiffs land and made a small thatched hut towards west of the suit plot No. 313 measuring 8X5 cubits and filled up earth in an area of 0.10 acre and dispossessed the plaintiffs therefrom on 9.2.76 for which plaintiffs lodged a GD Entry No. 491 dated 10.2.76 Ext. 6(a) with Mohammadpur PS. But in spite of repeated requests and demands the said defendants have not vacated the said shed as well as the dispossessed portion fully described in schedule 'B' of the plaint The plaintiffs have been in exclusive possession of the suit plot No. 313 and as such they acquired right, title and interest in the 'A' Schedule property by adverse possession too. The defendants and their predecessors-in-interest have no right, title and interest therein and the principal defendants are liable to be evicted from 'B' schedule of the suit property.

5. The suit was contested by principal defendant Nos. 1 to 6 by filing one joint written statement and by defendant Nos. 8 and 10 by filing another separate statement on identical grounds.

6. Their common case is that the suit is not maintainable in the present form and is bad for defect of party. They also denied the material allegations made in the plaint.

7. Their specific case, in short, is that one Alef was owner of 8.89 acres of land in raiyati jote right in mouza Barabo and the said Alef died leaving his widow Jamirjan Bibi and four daughters, namely, Aliman Bibi, Saliman Bibi, Kctabi Bibi and Annabi Bibi but during the CS operation the said land was recorded in CS Khatian No. 362 Ext. 5(a) wrongly in the name of Jamirjan Bibi alone. Jamirjan Bibi and Annabi Bibi created a Heba-bil-ewaz deed on 17.12.1935 Ext. 1 & A in respect of 3.43 acres of land of CS plot No. 313, 365 and 341 in favour of defendant No. 7 Kadam Ali son of Aliman Bibi. Saliman Bibi also created a Kabala dated 9.2.49 Ext B in respect of 2.60 acres of land of CS plot Nos. 313, 365 and 371 in favour of said Kadam AIi Sirajbi Bibi daughter of Ketabi Bibi sold .73 acre of land out of CS plot No. 313,365 and 371 to Ahmed Ali, Julmat Ali and Alamat Ali defendant Nos. 8 to 10 sons of Kadam Ali by sale deed dated 19.5.47 Ext. B(I) and delivered possession of the same then and there from CS plot No. 313 as per amicable arrangement Sirajbi Bibi by amicable arrangement with other co-sharers had been possessing 1.14 acres of land from the western side of CS plot No. 313 and defendant Nos. 8 to 10 were given possession out of Sirajbi Bibi's 1.14 acres of land from western side of that plot. Kadam Ali had been possessing 1.37 acres of CS plot No. 313 from the eastern side of that plot and he transferred some of his lands to Azizur Rahman who also transferred the same to the plaintiffs. The names of Jamirjan Bibi, Kadam Ali, Ahmed Ali, Julmat Ali, Almat Ali and the plaintiffs were recorded in SA Khatian No. 365 Ext. C(1). Julmat AIi died leaving defendant No.9 Mohammadi Begum and his father defendant No. 7 Kadam Ali as his heirs. Defendant Nos. 8 and 10 sold 0.30 acres of land from CS plot No. 313 to the defendant Nos. 1 to 4 by a registered kabala dated 27.7.76 Ext B(2) and delivered possession of the same then and there with their already constructed thatched hut. Defendant No.9 also sold .06 acres of land from said CS plot No. 313 to the defendant Nos. 5 and 6 by a sale deed dated 27.7.76 Ext. B(3) and delivered possession of the same to those purchasers then and there. Thus the defendant Nos. 1 to 6 are in possession of 0.36 acres of land and the defendant Nos. 8 to 10 are in possession of 0.37 acres and the plaintiffs are in possession of 1.37 acres and Sirajbi Bibi is in possession of 0.41 acres of CS plot No. 313 but the present RS record has not been properly prepared and the same is under dispute. The 'A' Schedule property of the plaint is ejmali property of the plaintiffs and the defendants as well as Sirajbi Bibi and as such plaintiffs' suit for declaration of title in the said land and recovery of khas possession from the 'B' schedule land which is part of the 'A' schedule land is not maintainable and is liable to be dismissed.

8. The learned Advocate for the appellants submitted that the land described in 'B' schedule of the plaint is vague and indefinite and on this ground alone plaintiffs' prayer for recovery of possession is liable to be dismissed. He further submitted that Sirajbi Bibi is an admitted co-sharer of the suit holding and on the basis of purchase from her in the year 1947 defendant Nos. 8 and 10 and their brother Julmat Ali became a co-sharer in the suit plot and by purchase from them the defendant Nos. 1 to 6 also became co-sharers in the suit plot with the plaintiffs. As such court below was not justified in declaring title of the suit 'A' schedule property in favour of the plaintiffs. The plaintiffs having failed to prove dispossession and the defendants being in possession on the basis of their purchase as well as entry in the SA Khatian they could not be evicted from the suit land.

9. In support of their case plaintiffs examined six (6) PWs including husband of plaintiff No. 2 as PW 1 and their borgader Tyeb Ali as PW 6 apart from documentary evidence Ext. Nos. 1 to l1 Contested defendants also in support of their case examined 4 witnesses including defendants 6 and 10 and also produced and proved documentary evidence Exts. A to E.

10. Is to the vagueness of suit property it is found from description of 'A' schedule to the plaint that the entire area of 2.51 acres of land of CS plot No. 313 of CS Khatian No. 362 of Mouza Barabo with boundaries has been mentioned. In the 'B' Schedule of the plaint the plaintiffs have described dispossessed 0.10 decimals of land to be lying to the west of CS plot No. 313 being the land filled up with earth having a thatched hut measuring 8x5 cubits buict thereon. The learned Advocate of the appellants contends that as there is no mention of boundary of the said decimals of land it is difficult to identify the same. The learned Advocate of the respondents in reply contends that 'though boundaries of the said 0.10 decimals of land have not been mentioned in the plaint no specific objection as to the identity of the said land was either taken in the, written statement or in the cross-examination of the PWs. On consideration of the written statement and the deposition of the witnesses we find that no such objection was taken as to the identity of the suit 'B' schedule land. Therefore we find no merit in the contention of the learned Advocate for the appellants in this respect.

11. It appears from the deed of Heba-bil-ewaz dated 17.12.35 Ext. 1 executed by Jamirjan Bibi widow of Md. Alef and Anna Bibi daughter of said Md. Alef that they transferred en tire 2.51 acres of land of suit SC plot No. 313 along with other lands to defendant No.7 Kadam Ali and delivered possession of the said land to him . It appears from Ext. 2. deed of sale dated 16.4.57 executed by Kadan Ali in favour of Md. Azizur Rahman that he transferred the entire 2.51 acres of land of suit plot No. 313 to the said purchaser for valuable consideration and delivered possession of the said land to him. It also appears from Ext. 2(a) sale deed dated 7.7.58 that the said Md. Azizur Rahman transferred western half of the said CS plot No. 313 to the plaintiff No. 2 Mosammat Rezia Khatoon and delivered possession to her in the block 'A' shown in the Map attached to the sale deed. Similarly from Ext. 2(6) it appears that the said Md. Azizur Rahman transferred eastern! half of suit CS plot No. 313 to plaintiff No. 1 Masuma Khatoon and delivered possession of the said land to her from Block 'B' of the map attached to the said deed defendant on the other hand claimed that Sirajbi Bibi was 10 possession of 1.14 acres of land from the western side of CS plot No. 313 and while in such possession by sale deed Ext B(1) dated 19.5.47 she transferred 0.73 acres of land out of CS plot Nos. 313, 365 and 371 to defendants 8, 10 and Julmat Ali husband of defendant No. 9 and delivered possession of the said land to the said purchasers from western side of CS plot No. 313 only. But neither in the recital nor in the schedule of the said kabala there is any mention that the said purchasers were given possession in the said 0.73 acres or from the western part of suit CS plot No. 313 alone. In view of the same the Claim of the said defendants 8 and 10 that they got possession in the said purchased land from the western side of suit CS Plot No. 313 is control to the recital of the said document and the oral evidence adduced by the defendants Contrary to the said recital cannot be relied on and rightly rejected by the trial Court. To reconcile the said defendants at the trial adduced evidence contrary to their claim as made out in paragraph No. 19(d) of the when statement that after purchase on the basis of the said deed dated 19.5.47 they got possession in their purchased land from the western side of suit CS plot No. 313 on the basis of amicable arrangement with their father Kadam Ali. This shows Kadam Ali had been in sole, possession of the suit plot No. 313. Moreover, Kadam Ali admitted in sale deed dated 16.4.57 Ext. 2 that he transferred the entire 2.51 acres of land of suit plot No.313 to Md. Azizur Rahman vendor of the plaintiffs and delivered possession to him who in his turn sold the same to the plaintiffs by sale deeds dated 7.7.58 Ext. 2(a) and 2(b) and delivered possession thereof to them. Thus oral evidence from the defendants side that Kadam Ali delivered possession of 0.73 acre of land to his sons defendants 8 and 10 and Julmat Ali by way of amicable partition after their purchase from Siraji Bibi is negatived by such admission of Kadam Ali in the said sale deed Ext. 2 There is no evidence that defendant No. 7 Kadam Ali has any strained relationship with his sons, and we find no explanation why he was not examined by the defendants in support of the contention that they got possession from him. This shows Kadam Ali was not willing to support the defendant. Rather documentary evidence discussed above clearly shows that Kadam Ali was in sole possession of entire land of suit plot No. 313 till his transfer to Azizur Rahman in 1957.

12. The appellant Nos. 1-6 have filed an application for amendment of paragraph No. 19(d) of the written statement filed by them as defendant Nos. 1-6 and also to add a new paragraph No. 19(i) in the said written statement the middle portion of the said paragraph No. 19(d) full stop after the words "as per amicable arrangement" is sought to be deleted and the words between Kadam Ali and his sons defendants 8,10 and Julmat Ali is sought to be added after the said full stop. It is also sought to be added in the new paragraph 19 if that Title Suit No. 501 of 1978 has been filed by Sirajbi Bibi in the First Court of Subordinate Judge, Dhaka for partition of the entire lands of CS Khatian No. 362 of mouza Barabo and subsequently renumbered as Title Suit No. 812 of 1985 of the Second Court of Subordinate Judge: Dhaka and the same is still pending. The learned Advocate for the respondents vehemently opposed this prayer for amendment on the ground that it is an afterthought to make their inadmissible evidence as admissible, We have already found earlier that the claim of the defendants that defendants 8, 10 and Julmat Ali got possession in their purchased land on the basis of amicable arrangement with their father Kadam Ali cannot be relied upon. Moreover, as pointed out by Mr. BK Das, the learned Advocate for the respondents that the said partition suit is no longer pending, rather it was decreed by the trial Court and on appeal by his clients the said decree was reversed by this court in First Appeal No. 843 of 1991. In view of the above, we find no merit in the said application for amendment of the written statement of defendant Nos. 1-6. Moreover, even if we allow this amendment the unamended written statement of defendant Nos.8 and 10 will remain intact in paragraph No. 19 (d) in the very same language as in paragraph No. 19 (d) of the written statement of defendant Nos. 1-6. They being mere subsequent purchasers from defendant Nos. 8 to 10 cannot make a contradictory claim with their vendors. Therefore, the application for amendment is rejected.

13. Now coming to the evidence of possession of the plaintiffs it is seen that PW 1 Syed Nuruddin Wahed Ali, husband of plaintiff No.2 has deposed in support of the plaintiffs' exclusive possession of the suit plot. He stated that the plaintiffs possessed the suit plot through their borgader Sultan Mia who at a subsequent stage executed a borga kabuliyat Ext. 3 in their favour and after him plaintiffs possessed through their borgader PW 6 Md. Tayeb Ali who executed borga Kabuliyat Exts. 3(a) to 3(c). He further stated that the plaintiffs paid rent from 1367 BS up to 1386 BS by mutating their names vide rent receipts Ext. 4 series. PW 1 is corroborated in respect of plaintiffs exclusive possession of the suit plot by a neighboring resident PW 2 Azharul Islam who is a retired Government servant. PW 6 Md. Tayeb Ali also corroborated the PW 1. PW 3 Mansur Ali who had a piece of land to the north of the suit plot and which he sold 8/9 years before and who is a resident of the locality stated that he saw Kadam Ali to possess the entire suit plot and defendant No. 1 had been possessing 10 or 11 decimals in the suit plot by sing a hut for the last 2 and 2½ years and prior to that PW 1 and his bhaira possessed the entire suit plot and the defendants did not possess any portion of the suit plot prior to 2 or 2½ years of course he stated in cross-examination that he saw sons of Kadam Ali to possess along with their father without stating the time. It must be before his sale of the land to Azizur Rahman. It is but natural for the sons to help their father in cultivatting the land. That does not mean their independent possession and the same is clear from his denial of defendants suggestion that the plaintiffs possessed 4½ pakhis in the east and the rest 1.14 acre in the west in the suit pot. PW 4, Kazi Fakhruddin Ahmed, a retired government servant and a surveyor measured the suit plot and prepared the map attached to plaintiffs' Kabalas Ext. 2(a) and 2(b) on the identification of husband of plaintiff No. 1. PW 5 Lal Mia who resides 500 feet away from the suit plot clearly stated in his deposition that he saw Kadam Ali to possess the entire suit plot. 'He further stated that while.in possession Kadam Ali sold it to one Azizur Rahman who sold to the plaintiffs who possessed through Sultan and at present Tyeb Ali has been possessing on plaintiffs behalf. But this witness also stated that 5/6 years after purchase by the plaintiffs sons of Kadam Ali possessed some portion in the western part of the plot. Relying upon this the learned Advocate for the appellants strenuously contended that the defendants Sifo and Julmat Ali possessed from western part of the suit plot as claimed by them on the basis of amicable arrangement with Kadam Ali From the cross-examination of DW 1 Almat Ali defendant No. 10) it is seen that the defendants 8 and 10 received compensation for 0.24 acres of land of plot No. 371 of their kabala land in LA case No. 41 of 1964-65 in which case plot Nos. 365 and 371 were acquired. This goes to show that PW 5 meant to say that sons of Kadam Ali were in possession in the land of plot No. 371 and not in the suit plot. This portion of the deposition of PW 5 inconsistent with his earlier statement in his deposition appears to us not to have been correctly recorded Almat Ali is defendant No. 10 and ow 3 Sirajul Huq son-in-law of Kadam Ali is defendant No.6. He also attested the sale deed executed' by Kadam Ali in favour of Azizur Rahman vendor' of the plaintiffs. They being interested in the result of the suit they cannot be relied upon without 'independent corroboration. DW 2 Haji Kala Chand Mia who claims to be a resident of Agargaon and an old man of 95 years is an over zealous witness. He stated that defendant No. 10 was 40 years-old at the time of Kabala Ext. B(1) whereas defendant No. 10 himself as OW 1 admitted that he was only 14/15 years old at 'that time. He also stated that defendant No. 1 is a Municipal Commissioner but denied the suggestion that he came to depose falsely to please him DW 4 Ali Mia who also claims to be a resident of Agargaon is another over zealous witness. He stated that Kadam Ali sold the eastern part and still owned western part of the suit plot though he stated on recall that he did not say that Kadam Ali possesses the western portion still now. How could sons of Kadam Ali possess their entire purchased 0.73 acres from plot No: 313 as deposed by DWs when as admitted by DW 1 that they received compensation for requisition and acquisition of plot No. 371? The statement of the Dws. that defendant Nos. 8,10 and Julmat Ali constructed the straw hut is belied by the recital in the kabalas Ext. B(2) and B(3) in favour of principal defendant Nos. 1-6 inasmuch as there is no mention of such straw hut in the said deeds. Therefore, it is difficult to rely upon the testimony of the said DWs contrary to recital in their sale deeds. In view of the above discussion of evidence record we are of the view that Kadam Ali had been in sole possession of the suit plot No. 313 till his sale in 1957 to Mohammad Azizur Rahman vendor of the plaintiffs and the plaintiffs got possession from him of the said land after their purchase in 1958 and the plaintiffs had been in exclusive possession of the entire suit plot till their dispossession of the 'B' schedule land measuring 0'10 acres on 9.2.76.

<u>14. The learned Advocate for the appellants relied on the decision in the case Abdul Jalil Sikder and others Vs. Khorshed Ali Dakua and others reported in 27 DLR (AD) 143 and in the case of Hazera Begum and others Vs. Rousan Ara Begum and others reported in 39 DLR (AD) 22 and contended that even if the plaintiffs are found to have been in sole possession of the suit plot No. 313 that will not amount to ouster of the co-sharer defendants however long their possession might be and title of the defendants, will not be extinguished in the suit plot by such possession of the plaintiffs and as such, court below was wholly wrong in declaring title of the plaintiffs in the entire land of suit plot No. 313. It is true that defendant No. 7 Kadam Ali being a descendant of the original owner and his sons also similarly being transferees from a descendant of the original owner sole possession of Kadam Ali could not have extinguished the title of his co-sharer sons. But the plaintiffs being strangers to the family and they having purchased from Azizur Rahman transferee of Kadam Ali and having got exclusive possession to the knowledge of the defendants and having mutated and recorded their name in assertion of their title denying title of sons of Kadam Ali and paid rents from the time of their purchase continuously in spite of objection by the sons of Kadam Ali their open possession is a notorious fact and nothing but ouster of the sons of Kadam Ali from the suit plot. Even if we accept defence case that sons of Kadam Ali also possessed the suit plot with their father as deposed by PW 3 fact remains that the plaintiffs had been in exclusive possession of the suit plot for 16 years as already found by us and this leads to the irresistible conclusion of their ouster from the suit plot. It may be noted that SA Khatian Ext. 5 prepared by merely revising the CS Khatian and recording names of sons of Kadam Alialong with the names of the plaintiffs even without omitting name of CS recorded tenant Jamirjan Bibi and the government acquired plots has no presumptive value and we find up merit in the contention of the appellants that they have interest in the suit property on the basis of the said SA Khatian. Moreover, it is pointed out by the learned Advocate for the respondents that in the judgment of FA No. 843 of 1991 between the same parties it has been found that corrected RS Khatian in respect of the suit plot was finally published in the name of the plaintiffs subsequent to the SA Khatian. Since the plaintiffs had been in exclusive possession of the entire land of CS plot No. 313 openly, notoriously and continuously for more than 16 years beyond the statutory period of limitation, right, title and interest if any of the sons of Kadam Ali in that plot had been extinguished by adverse possession before the alleged dispossession of the plaintiffs from the 'B' schedule land. Facts of the above decisions are distinguishable from the facts and circumstances of the present case and as such principle enunciated in those cases are of no help to the appellants.</u>

<u>15. When a co-sharer in sole possession transfers the land in his possession to a stranger to the family and such purchaser possesses the land in assertion of his title to the exclusion of other co-sharers of his vendor openly, notoriously and continuously denying title of such co-sharers by mutating and recording his name in the record of rights and paying rent separately the same will amount to ouster of such co-sharers and such possession for more than 12 years will extinguish title of such co-sharers by adverse possession.</u>

16. As to the grievance that actual dispossession of the plaintiffs from the 'B' schedule land has not been proved by evidence it is seen from Ext. 6(a) a copy of GD Entry No. 491 dated 10.2.76 that the plaintiffs complained against defendant No. 1 Shah Alam that he with the help of defendant Nos. 8-10 and 20/25 others forcibly trespassed and constructed a dochala thatched hut on 9.2.79 in the suit plot and attempting to cultivate the land. The said defendant No. 1 has not denied the said allegation. He appears to be owner of a Textile Mills. He being a rich man felt shy to depose falsely appearing before the court. DW 2 also indirectly supported the plaintiffs case of such dispossession by saying that about 2½ years ago defendant Nos. 8 and 10 repaired the straw hut. Kabala Ext. B(2) in favour of defendant Nos. 1-4 executed on 21.4.76 shows that defendant No. 1 purchased 0.11 acre of land and this also supports plaintiffs case. We therefore, find no merit in the contention that the plaintiffs failed to prove actual dispossession for the 'B' schedule property. We, therefore, find no merit in this appeal.

In the result, the appeal is dismissed with cost and the judgment and decree of the court below is affirmed.

End.

lawyer:
Mr. M. H. Khondker, Advocate with Mr. AJ Mohammad Ali, Advocate and Mr. Shareef Ahmed, Advocate -------- For the Petitioners. 
Mr. S. C. Das, Advocate ------ For the Respondent No.2 
Mr. Fakhrul Islam, AAG -------- For the Respondent No.1
parties:
Mustafa Kamal and others   -------- Petitioners [WP No. 207 of 1986)
Sebera Begum   -------- Petitioner [WP No. 208 of 1986)
Vs.
Director of Land Records and others  -------- .Respondents [In both the WPs]
full_judgment:
Qazi Shafiuddin, J.: This Rule Nisi issued in Writ Petition No. 207 of 1986 has been directed against the impugned order dated 31.3.1986 (Annexure E) passed by the Respondent No. 1 while the Rule in Writ Petition No. 208 of 1986 is directed against the impugned order dated 31.3.1986 (Annexure G to the petition) calling upon the respondents to show cause why the same should not be declared to have been made without lawful authority and of no legal effect.

2. Since identical question of facts as well as law having been involved in these two Rules the same are being heard and will now be disposed of by this judgment.

3. The petitioner's case in Writ Petition No. 207/86 is that they purchased the land in question from one Siddique Ahmed by a registered kabala dated 15.8.79. Originally the land was recorded in the name of its owner Abdur Rahman in RS khatian. Subsequently Fazar Rahman, the heir of Abdur Rahman, sold the same to one Nur Mohammad by registered deed of sale and Nur Mohammad sold the same in favour of one Siddique Ahmed by a registered kabala dated 3.12.69. The present petitioners purchased the suit land from the said Siddique Ahmed. The petitioners claim that the suit land be recorded in their names. That one Mohammad Harunur Rashid filed an objection under section 19(1) of the East Bengal State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, 1950 in objection Case No. 139 dated 15.10.1980 objecting the entry of the name of the respondent No.2 in the draft record of rights. The objection was not allowed.

4. Being aggrieved the petitioners and others filed an appeal case against his objection Case No. 139 dated 15.10.1980. The appeal case was numbered as Appeal case No. 25187/81. The appellate authority after complying with the due formalities and after obtaining the Survey Report and hearing the parties allowed the appeal and directed the inclusion of the names of the petitioners to the extent of 7 annas share in the draft record of rights. Thereafter a Review petition was filed by the respondent No. 2 against the order of the Appellate Authority dated 16.9.1984. The said petition was heard and disposed of by the appellate authority by rejecting the same and maintained the order passed by him in the appeal. The respondent No.2 finding no alternative filed a Second Review petition before the Director of Land Records against the order of the appellate authority dated 16.9.1984. The Director of Land Records by his order dated 31.3.1986 allowed the Second Review petition setting aside the order dated 16.9.1984 passed by the appellate authority and sent back the case to one Mr. Bazlur Rahman for hearing of the appeal afresh. Against this very order of the Director of Land Records dated 31.3.1986, the petitioners have filed this Writ Petition and obtained the present Rule.

5. The case of the respondent No.2, as it appears, is that respondent No.2 purchased 12 annas interest from Fazar Rahman the heirs of Hafizur Rahman by a registered Kabala dated 29.11.1976 and subsequently the respondent No.2 also purchased the share of Mofizur Rahman by a registered Kabala dated 2.6.80 and accordingly his name in the draft record of rights has been correctly recorded.

6. In Writ Petition No. 208 of 1986 the case of the petitioner Mosammat Sabera Begum is that one Bujarat was instituted by the respondent Nos. 2-3 impleading the petitioner as the second party before the Revenue Authority. The case was disposed of ex parte by order dated 23.6.77 wherein the name of the petitioner in the khatian was directed to be struck off and those of respondent Nos. 2-5 were to be recorded. Against the said order the petitioner filed objection case impleading the respondent Nos. 2-5 as opposite parties. The Revenue Officer considered the objection and disposed of the case by his order dated 31.5.79 maintaining the order recording the name of the respondents passed in the Biujarat dispute case. It is the case of the petitioner that the original owner of the case land was one Abdur Rahman and his name appeared in the RS khatian in Korfa right The said RS khatian was under khatian No. 25 of Jote No. 1 and the owner of the said jote No. 1 was one Abdul Aziz Sarang in raiyati right. The said Jotedar having defaulted in payment of revenue, the Jote was put to auction and ultimately the entire lands vested in the Government. One Abdus Salam prayed for re-settlement of the case land and his prayer was allowed and accordingly he became tenant directly under the Government Abdus Salam also defaulted in payment of rent and a Certificate case was started being Certificate Case No. 357 of 1945-46. The land in question was auction sold to one Ahmedur Rahman on 16.7.1946 and the sale was confirmed on 16.9.1946 and possession was delivered on 18.1.1948. The said Ahmedur Rahman got his name mutated in the RS khatian. The said auction purchaser while in possession sold the land to the petitioner by a registered kabala being kabala No. 4245 dated 21.6.1960 and since then she has been in possession of the case lands. The petitioner's name has been duly recorded in the SA khatian which has been finally published. The petitioner's name was also correctly recorded in the present khatian as per his title and possession. After the Field Survey the present respondent Nos. 5 filed a dispute case and managed to get their names recorded by suppressing notices.

7. The case of the respondent that the land originally belonged to one Abdur Rahman to the extent of 16 annas share and RS khatian No. 30/1 has been finally published in the name of the said Abdur Rahman. On his death, the respondent Nos. 2-5 were in possession of the case land as his heirs. That while in such possession they sold the land in favour of Jalalabad Housing Society and delivered possession to the said Society. As against the order the petitioner filed an appeal to the Revenue Authority and the case was registered as Appeal Case No. 23994/80. The Appellate Authority by its order dated 16.9.84 allowed the appeal and directed the recording of the name of the petitioner in the khatian by striking out the names of the respondents. Thereafter the respondent Nos. 2-5 filed a Review petition on 14.10.84 before the said appellate authority and the appellate authority heard the matter and considered the case rejecting the Review petition and maintained his earlier decision by order dated 16.9.84. That thereafter the respondent Nos. 2-5 filed a second appellation for review of the order dated 16.9.84 before the Director of Land Records. The Director of Land Records by the impugned order dated 31.3.86 allowed the second review petition of the respondents by setting aside the order dated 16.9.84 passed by the appellate authority.

8. Mr. MH Khondker, the learned Advocate appearing for the petitioner in both the Rules, has submitted that the order dated 16.9.84 in Appeal Case No. 25187/81 having already been reviewed by the learned Appellate officer by his judgment and order dated 27.3.1985, the entertainment of a review petition and of passing the order by the Director of Land Records in reviewing the earlier order of the appeal for the second time is absolutely without jurisdiction and is of no legal effect. Mr. Khandker argued that the Director of Land Records has not been vested with any statutory power to entertain and dispose of any review petition and as such his order is liable to be declared to have been passed without any lawful authority and the same is of no legal effect.

9. Mr. SC Das, the learned Advocate appearing for the respondents submitted that the Director of Land Records has been vested with full powers and authority to revise any order passed by any Revenue Officer under Rule 44 read with Rule 43 of the East Bengal Tenancy Rules, 1955 and as such committed no error of law.

10. We have heard the learned Advocates and perused the petition and affidavit filed by the respective parties. The only question that has cropped up in these two Rules is whether the Director of Land Records has been empowered under the statute to entertain and review any order passed by the appellate authority.

11. Under section 19 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, 1950 the Revenue Officer shall publish a draft of the record-of-rights so prepared or revised in the prescribed manner and shall receive and consider any objections relating to any entry therein during the period of such publication. By sub-section 2 of section 19 the forum for appeal is created and any aggrieved person by the order of the Revenue-Officer on any objection made under sub-section (1) of section 19 may appeal to the prescribed Revenue Authority not below the rank of an Assistant Settlement Officer in the manner and within such period as prescribed.

12. The petitioner in Writ Petition No. 207 of 1986 filed an appeal being Appeal case No. 25187/81 against the objection order passed in objection case No. 139 dated 15.10.80. The Appellate Authority by his order dated 16.9.84 allowed the appeal and directed the inclusion of the names of the petitioners to the extent of 7 annas share in the draft of record of rights.

13. It appears that the respondent No.2 filed a Review petition before the appellate authority who by his order dated 27.3.85 rejected the same and maintained the earlier order dated 16.9.84 passed in the appeal. Thereafter the respondent No. 2 moved the Director General of Land Records respondent No. 1 in a second Review. The Director General of Land Records by the impugned order dated 31.3.86 allowed the second review petition by setting aside the order dated 16.9.84 of the appellate authority directing fresh hearing by one Mr. Bazlur Rahman, an Appeal officer. The Director General appears to have exercised his powers under Rule 44 of the East Bengal Tenancy Rules 1955 and caused interference under Rule 42 of the said Rules by holding that he had powers to correct, modify or set aside any record of rights made or passed in any proceeding following Rule Nos. 28-32 of the said rules.

14. Let us have a look at Rule 44 of the East Bengal State Acquisition and Tenancy Rules, 1955 which reads as follows:

Powers vested in Director of Land Records and Surveys: "In respect of all operations under Chapter XVII of the Act Which have been placed under the administrative control of the Director of Land Records and Surveys. East Pakistan, he may discharge all the functions of a Revenue-Officer under the said Chapter and shall have all the powers of a Settlement Officer under rules 36, 38, 39, 40, 41,42, 42A and 42B,"

15. Chapter XVII of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, 1950 deals with maintenance of the Record-of-Rights. Section 143 of the said Act runs as follows:

"The Collector shall maintain up to date, in the prescribed manner, the Record-of-rights prepared or revised under Part IV, or under this Part by correcting clerical mistake and by incorporating therein the changes on account of:

(a) the mutation of names as a result of transfer or inheritance:

(b) the subdivision, amalgamation or consolidation of holdings.

(c) the new settlement of lands or of holdings purchased by the Government, and

(d) the abatement of rent on account of abandonment or diluvian or acquisition of land."

This matter has been placed under the Director of Land Records in his Administrative Control.

16. Rule 36 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Rules, 1951 speaks of Grant and Revision of certificate under section 20(4) which reads as follows:

"The authority for granting a certificate under sub-section (4) of section 20 shall be the Collector of the District, and a certificate so granted shall be subject to revision annually unless the Provincial Government by a special order otherwise directs in a particular case or class of cases."

Rule 38 speaks about Revision of record- of-rights under section 31 and Rule 39 deals with powers vested in Settlement and Assistant Settlement Officers and 40 deals with further power vested in Assistant Settlement Officer under Bengal Act V of 1875 and rule 41 empowers the Revenue Officer appointed with the additional designation of 'Settlement Officer' is also hereby vested with all the powers of superintendence of Survey under the Bengal Survey Act of 1875; Rule 42 of the Tenancy Rules reads as follows:

Special power of Revenue Officer appointed with the additional designation of Settlement Officer:

"A Revenue Officer appointed with the additional designation of 'Settlement Officer' may at any time before the publication of final record-of-rights, direct that any portion of the proceedings referred to in rules 28-32 in respect of any district, part of district or local area shall be cancelled and that the proceedings shall be taken up fresh from such stage as he may direct" From the aforesaid Rules it appears that the Director General of Land Records is vested with administrative control in respect of all operation under Chapter XVII of the Act and he may discharge all the functions of a Revenue Officer and shall have powers of a Settlement Officer under Rules 36, 38, 39, 42B as such the Director General of Land Records can be said to have at best co-equal powers with that of any Revenue Officer or Settlement Officer with regard to their powers whether they are designated as Additional Designation of Settlement Officer or not but this does not mean that the Director of Land Records has been vested with superior powers to sit over their orders or decisions and to annul the same. In a quasi judicial proceedings like the present one all that is competent to do is that he may exercise any of such powers as is vested in a Revenue or Settlement Officer under Rules 44 and 42 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Rules, 1955 in respect of a proceeding which has not attained finality, in either words, in a fresh proceeding the Director General is quite competent to assume his jurisdiction and dispose of the matter which is co-extensive with that of the Revenue or Settlement Officer. But in a matter which has already been disposed of by the Revenue Officer, namely Settlement Officer or Assistant Settlement Officer, in our view the Director of Land Records is incompetent and absolutely without power to lay his hands over such matters.

<u>17. In the present cases the Director General of Land Records has interfered with the decisions of the appellate Court which has been done under sub-section 2 of section 19. But in administrative matter under chapter 17 of the Act he has been placed in superior position in matters of control, management of Record of Rights as vested under Rule 44 of the State Acquisition & Tenancy Rules.</u>

<u>The Respondent No. 1 Director General of Land Records Bangladesh has exceeded his power in entertaining and disposing of the second review petitions reviewing the orders passed by the Settlement Officer in appellate jurisdiction and as such his actions cannot but be said to be without jurisdiction. The Rule 19(1) and 19(2) has vested a power to the Settlement Officer to entertain and hear an appeal arising out of any disputed proceeding and no further power has been provided by way of revision. Although the Code of Civil Procedure has allowed an appellate authority to review any decision but no second review is contemplated under the Rule ref. by any third party namely, the Director of Land Records. Sub-section 3 of section 19 has clearly stated that when all such objections and appeals have been considered and disposed of according to such Rules, the Revenue-Officer shall finally frame the record and shall cause record to be finally published in the prescribed manner and the publication shall be conclusive evidence that the record has been duly prepared or revised under this Chapter. So after the forum of appeal being exhausted, the only course left open to the Revenue Officer is to finally frame the record and such record be published in the prescribed manner. So this Rule also does not speak of any forum created for hearing a second review petition as the respondent No. 1 has entertained and disposed of. Since the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act of 1950 and the Rules made thereunder do not specifically confer on the Director of Land Records any power to revise the order passed in appeal, in our view, the impugned orders dated 31.3.86 Annexure E in Writ Petition No. 207 and 'G' in Writ Petition No. 208 of 1986 are illegal and void and as such are hereby declared to have been passed without lawful authority and the same are of no legal effect.</u>

In the result, both the Rules are made absolute without costs.

End.

lawyer:
AF Hasan Ariff with Faridul Alam Chowdhury -----For the Petitioner.
Shahabuddin Ahmad, Deputy Attorney-General -----For the Respondents.
parties:
Friends Corporation ------ Petitioner
vs
Commissioner of Customs and others ------ Respondents
full_judgment:
AM Mahmudur Rahman J: This Rule calls in question the levy of customs duty on the basis of tariff value instead of registration value pursuant to import particular registration scheme on the ground that imposition and levy of duty upon such basis without any lawful authority.

2. The petitioner, a firm, carries on business of import of Caustic Soda. It opened Letter of Credit on 21-1-1998 for importing 350 MT of Caustic Soda solid and 150 MT of Caustic Soda Flakes at the rate of US$ 250.00 per metric ton and 260.00 per metric ton respectively. On arrival of the consignment the petitioner through its clearing agent submitted bill of entry and certificate of registration for assessment of duties on the basis of invoice value. But respondent 2, appraiser, illegally and arbitrarily directed to assess the duties and charges on the basis of tariff value.

3. The petitioner contends that Kfixation of tariff value at US$ 375.00 per metric ton under HS Code No. 2815. 11.00 is arbitrary and baseless for the merchandise. The basis for determination of tariff value under delegated authority as provided in section 25(7) of the Customs Act, 1969 on the basis of Notification No. 38/97 Cus. dated 30-12-97 suffers from want of authority and, as such, the assessment of duty impugned is illegal. It is further contended that delegated power as conceived in section 25(7) of the Act has no relation with the normal market price and, as such, the basis for levy of duty in exercise of delegated power in the present case is without lawful authority. Farther, it was argued that sub-section (7) of section 25 is independent of other provisions of the section and there being no guideline for determination for fixing tariff value the impugned order is arbitrary and without lawful authority. It is further contended that as the petitioner being allured by the notification pursuant to import registration scheme dated 12-6- 97 opened letter of credit for import of the merchandise the customs authority imposed duty on tariff value against doctrine of promissory estoppel.

4. The learned Deputy Attorney-General, on the other hand, drawing our attention to the scheme itself argued that scheme provides that the exporter at least during 3 years is to export commodities to the tune of Taka 5 crore in order to obtain registration under the scheme. He drew our attention to the figure containing the export value for the year 1995-96 and 96-97 and submitted that it did not reach the target of Taka 5 crore. He also argued that mere registration is not enough to get the special benefit under the scheme. He contends that unless the price given by the exporter is approved by the registration authority, the customs authority has got sufficient power to determine the value of the merchandise on the basis of tariff value.

5. Before we enter into the contention we are inclined to examine the law itself. The Customs Act, 1969 has elaborately dealt with fixation of the price of imported goods, determination of tariff value, levy of customs duty. Section 25 is on value of the imported and exported goods. Sub-section (2) of this section provides for determination of normal price of any imported goods and for such determination certain conditions are to be followed section 30 is on the dated for determination of the value and rate of import duty. Section 30A which was inserted on July 1, 1995 is on value and effective rate of duty. According to sub-section (1) of section 25 normal value means price which the commodity would fetch on the date referred to in section 30 on a sale in open market between a buyer and seller independent of each other. The contention that as the petitioner on the basis of import registration scheme opened Letter of Credit and the invoice, supplied by the exporter mentioning price at a lower rate the duty assessed by the Customs authority on the basis of tariff value is without any sanction of law. This leads us to consider the provision of section 30A. Section 30A reads:

"30A Notwithstanding anything contained in any other law for the time being in force or any decision of any court for the purposes of section 30, the value and the rate of duty applicable to any goods shall respectively include the value as determined under section 25 and any amount of duty imposed under section 18, 18A or 18B and the amount of duties that may have become payable in consequence of the withdrawal of the whole or any part of the exemption or concession from duty whether before or after the conclusion of a contract or agreement for the sale 0 such goods or opening of a letter of credit in respect thereof".

<u>6. Section 30A sufficiently indicates that notwithstanding anything contained in the Customs Act the value and rate of duty applicable to any goods shall include the value as determined under section 25 of the Act whether or after opening the LC in respect of the goods. Although LC was opened pursuant to scheme which came into force on 12-6-97 but opening Letter of Credit is subject to section 30A for the expressions. "Whether or after" opening the Letter of Credit in respect thereof in section 30A of the Customs Act, 1969 which does not admit of any ambiguity. The expression "thereof’’ is of wide connotation and it includes any goods and the rate of duty is applicable to any goods. Therefore, cumulative effect of reading of sections 25(7), 30 and 30A together is that the levy of duty on the basis of tariff value giving go-by to the scheme and the rate as shown in the invoice by the exporter has been levied legally, properly and with lawful authority. Mr. Hasan Ariff contends also that other provision of law provides that if the ex-parte and importer give the higher value than the tariff value then higher value will be determined for assessing the duty and where the invoice value is less than the tariff value the determining factor for assessing customs duty is the invoice value. We cannot read such thing in section 25(7). We do not find any want of jurisdiction under section 25(7) on the part of the customs authority to assess the duty under challenge.</u>

7. A careful consideration of section 25A indicates that it contains provision for guideline to be made by notification in the form of SRO Therefore, in this case for the aforesaid provision of law vis-a-vis the Registration Import Particular Scheme we do not find any want of authority on the part of the respondent to assess the duty on the basis of tariff value. Secondly, we are called upon to decide whether the petitioner is entitled to the benefit under import Particular Registration Scheme dated 12-6-97. The Scheme says that any exporter is entitled to the benefit on fulfillment of the condition laid down therein. The petitioner filed an application for such relief under the Scheme. But the conditions could not be fulfilled. Therefore, the contention on the doctrine of promissory estoppel has got no role to play in the facts of this case. The principle laid down in Mannan's case, 42DLR 107 (AD), has no role to play in the present case inasmuch as section 30A was not on the statute when the Appellate Division decided the Mannan's case and that too was made on dissimilar-facts. By subsequent insertion of section 30A of the Customs Act, 1969 the mischief, want of authority, by the Parliament in subsection (7) of section 25 of the Act which was in existence has been removed, Thus, the contention that in the absence of any guideline no action can be taken as has been taken by the impugned order of assessment of levy of duty has no leg to stand. The observation made by the High Court Division in Nasiruddin case is merely an obiter and does not lay down any principle of law having any binding legal force. Moreover, in view of insertion of section 30A as has been held in the case of Collector of Customs vs Ahmed Hossain & others, 48 DLR 199 (AD), the contention seems to be bereft of any substance.

8. Mr. Deputy Attorney-General opposes this Rule on the ground of maintainability. He submits that as the petitioner himself stated that he having had taken appeal without exhausting that remedy this petition is not maintainable. We are also of the view that as the petitioner filed appeal against the order under challenge in this Rule without disposal of the appeal the Writ Petition is not maintainable and we should not exercise our jurisdiction as conferred under Article 102 of the Constitution in the instant case.

For the aforesaid reason, the Rule is liable to be discharged.

In the result, the Rule is discharged without any order as to costs.

End.

 Vs.

full_judgment:
Sharif Uddin Chaklader J: Having aggrieved by the judgment and decree dated 26-11-2000 passed by the learned Subordinate Judge, 2nd Court, Laxmipur in Title Appeal No. 21 of 1997 heard analogously with Title Appeal No. 50 of 1997 allowing the appeals thereby on reversing the judgment and decree dated 21-11-1996 passed by the learned Senior Assistant Judge, Additional Court, Laxmipur decreed Title Suit No. 56 of 1991.

2. Defendant Nos. 8 and 9 preferred these two Civil Revision No. 4016 of 2009 and Civil Revision No. 1148 of 2002 and both these revision having arisen from same suit and from same judgment and decree these two revisions are taken up together for disposal and this judgment would govern both these two rules.

3. Plaintiff-opposite party instituted the aforesaid suit praying for decree as:-

"অতএব বাদী প্রার্থনা করেন যে,

(ক) নিম্ন (ক) তপছিল ভূমিতে বাদীর রয়তি স্বত্ব ঘোষনার মর্মে ডিক্রি দেওয়ার মর্জি হয়।"

(খ) নিম্ন (খ) তপছিলে উল্লেখিত লক্ষ্মীপুর সহকারী কমিশনার ভূমি অফিসের ১৯৮৩/৮৪ ইং সনের ১ নং নামজারী ও  জমা খারিজ দরখাস্তে ২৭-৭-৮৩ ইং তারিখে ৪/৫ নং বিবাদীর নমে হোল্ডিং খতিয়ান খোলার আদেশ বেআইনী ও বাতিল ঘোষনার মর্মে ডিক্রি দানের মর্জি হয়। ১০(ম) (১) বাদী নালিশী রায়তিতে শেঃ ১০.৫ ডিং ভূমিতে মালিক ও দখলকার থাকায় উক্ত ভূমি বাবত বাবত বাদীকে পৃথক ছাহামের প্রদানে বন্টনের প্রাথমিক ডিক্রিদানের আজ্ঞা হয়। ১০(ম) (২) আদালতের নির্ধারিত সময়ের মধ্যে শরীফ বিবাদীগন আপোষে বাদীর অংশের ভূমি পৃথকভাবে বন্টন করিয়া না দিলে আদালত বাদী হইতে ক্ষয়াদি গ্রহণে জনৈক সিভিল কোর্ট কমিশনার নিযুক্ত ক্রমে চিটা নকশা ফিল্ড বুক ইত্যাদি প্রস্তুত ক্রমে বন্টনের ফাইনাল ডিক্রি দানের আজ্ঞা হয়।

(গ) সমস্ত আদালত ব্যায় বাদীর অনুকুলে বিবাদীর বিরুদ্ধে ডিক্রি দেওয়ার মর্জি হয়।

(ঘ) অথবা অবস্থা ও প্রমান দৃষ্টে বাদী অন্য যে ভাবে যে যে প্রতিকার পাইতে পারে তৎমর্মে ডিক্রি দেওয়ার মর্জি হয়।"

4. It is the case of plaintiff that suit land comprising 29 decimals of land of dag No. 3246 of District settlement khatian No. 458 and No. 63 Nancha Nagar Mouzajoma of dag No. 21 originally belonged to Amzad Khalasi. Amzad Khalasi sold 10.5 decimals of land out of 29 decimals of land to Abul Hasim. Joynal Abedin purchased 7.5 decimals, Sabina Khatoon also purchased 4 decimals and 7.5 decimals of land purchased by Bazaler Rahman from Amzad Khalasi. The suit land having been recorded in 63 No. Bancha Nagar Mouza in khatian No. 909 in the name of Abul Hasim 4 annas share in the name of Joynal Abedin 2 annas share, in the name of Sabina Khatoon 4 annas share, 4 ann as share in the name of Bazaler Rahman correctly. In getting settlement, in khatian No. 909, the name of Sabina Khatoon has been wrongly recorded. Sabina Khatoon out of her share, sold 4 decimals of land by saf kabala dated 27th Falgun, 1339 B.S. corresponding to 11-3-1933 to Arafatunnessa. Abul Hasim sold his 6 annas share comprising 10.5 decimals of land to Bazaler Rahman, Joynul Abedin in 4 annas share transferred 7.25 decimals of land to Bazaler Rahman. In this way, Bazaler Rahman with his 4 annas share, purchased 10 annas share, in total purchased 14 annas share of 25 decimals of land, died leaving 3 sons, defendant No. 1-3. Arafatunnessa having owner of 4 decimals of land died leaving 2 sons, Abdul Aziz Patwari and Abdul Hasim Patwari and daughter, Anwara Begum. Abdul Aziz Patwari purchased 6 decimals of land from Bazaler Rahman by kabala dated 17-4-1944. In this way Abdul Aziz Patwari having owner of 7.5 decimals of land by purchase and by inheritance, died, leaving son, Sherajul Islam, 3 daughters, Parul Begum, Minara Begum, Shamsur Nahar and wife, Fatema Bibi. Fatema Bibi, Sherajul Islam and Shamsur Nahar jointly by saf kabala deed No. 12950 dated 29-11-1990 transferred 3 and 5/8 decimals of land to plaintiff Sherajul Islam and Shamsun Nahar sold 3 and 5/8 decimals of land by registered deed No. 1295 dated 29-11-1990 to plaintiff. At the time of death of Hossain Ahmed, he was survived by son, Shahab Uddin and daughter, Sabina Khatoon. On the death of Anwara Khatoon, her two sons, Shah Alam and Bachu Mea became owner of her property. Shahab Uddin, Shah Alam and Bachu Mea sold 3 decimals of land by baina, which was converted to registered document dated 20-4-1991. In this way plaintiff become owner by purchase and by inheritance of the scheduled land. After purchase, plaintiff went to pay rent to the local Tahsil Office on 15-2-1991 and came to know that out of suit land, during MRR survey, 29 decimals of land recorded in the name of his predecessor of No. 63 Bancha Nagar Mouza, Khatian No. 767, dag No. 8351. For total land of 29 decimals, plaintiff came to know that for aforesaid land in Mutation Case No. 111983-84 of the court of Assistant Commissioner (Revenue) the name of Bazaler Rahman was replaced and was recorded in the name of defendant Nos. 4-5 in holding No. 2405, khatian No.2404 and holding No. 2395 and khatian No. 2396. It is further case of plaintiffs that for the aforesaid wrong recording either in the name of Bazaler Rahman or in the name of defendant Nos. 3-4 or defendant No. 1-5, title, interest and possession of plaintiff has not been effected as the plaintiff purchased the suit land finding title of his predecessor and plaintiff could not know of the aforesaid wrong recording. The aforesaid wrong recording a cloud has been cast upon title of plaintiff which required to be removed, as such, plaintiff instituted the suit. For the cause of action of suit plaintiff has stated as :-

"ঐ অবস্থায় বাদীর মালিকী দখলীয় নিম্ন তপছিল ভূমি ১-৩ নং বিবাদীর মৌরশ বজলের রহমনের নামে এম, আর, আর, জরিপে ভূল রেকর্ড হওয়ায় এবং উক্ত ভূমি বাবৎ ৪/৫ নং বিবাদিগন তাহাদের নামে ভিন্ন খতিয়ান খোলার ঘটনা করায়এবং তাহা এমন প্রকাশ পাওয়ায় নিম্ন তপছিল ভূমিতে বাদীর স্বত্ব দখলের উপর এক মেঘাবরন ঝুকিয়া পড়িয়াছে। উক্তকালিমা দুরীভূত হওয়া একান্ত আবশ্যক। তাই নিম্ন তপছিল ভূমিতে বাদীর রায়তি স্বত্ব ঘোষনার মর্মে অত্রাদালতে অত্র নালিশ দায়ের করিতে বাধ্য হইলেক।

তর্কিত ভ্রমাত্মক খতিয়ানের বিষয় বাদী যথা সময়ে কিছুমাত্র অবগত ছিল না চলিত ১৯৯১ ইং সনের ফ্রেব্রুয়ারী মাসের ১ম দিকে বাদী তহশিল অফিসের খাজনা দিতে গেলে উক্ত ভুল খতিয়ানের বিষয় অবগত হয়। এবং ভূয়া জমা খারিজ ও মানজারী মুলে ৪/৫ নং বিবাদীর নামে ভূয়া খতিয়ান খোলার বিষয়  অবগত হয়। "
