full_judgment:
This Rule was issued calling upon the opposite party to show cause as to why the judgment and decree dated 21.11.88 passed in SCC Suit No. 11 of 1985 of the court of Assistant Judge sitting as SCC Judge, Sadar Upazila, Comilla should not be set aside.

2. The opposite parties as plaintiffs instituted SCC Suit No. 11 of 1985 in the court of Assistant Judge-cum-SCC Judge, Sadar, Comilla for the eviction of the defendant-petitioner from the suit premises claiming that the defendant-petitioner is a monthly tenant under them and he is liable to be evicted on the ground of default for non payment of rent.

3. The case of the plaintiffs, in short, was that Rani Ragu Bangsha Dulari was the original owner of the suit premises and the defendant was a monthly tenant under her at a monthly rent of Tk. 37.00. While the tenant had been possessing the suit premises running a cloth business under the name and style "Bibekananda Store" Rani Ragu Bangsha Dulari executed a deed of power of attorney and exchanged the suit premises along with other properties with one Abdul Khaleque, a migrant from India. Before regularisation of exchange the suit premises was declared as enemy property and the defendant and other persons took lease of the same from the Assistant Custodian Enemy Property, Comilla. After the regularisation of the exchange of Abdul Khaleque the suit premises was released from the list of enemy property by the Assistant Custodian by a deed of transfer. Abdul Khaleque after becoming owner transferred the suit premises along with other properties to Shafiqur Rahman and others by registered sale deed dated 22.8.73 and Shafiqur Rahman and others in their turn transferred the same to the plaintiffs by a registered sale deed dated 8.7.75. The plaintiffs thus becoming the owner of the suit premises intimated the defendant about their purchase and claimed rent from him but the defendant did not pay any heed to it. Thereafter the plaintiffs sent a notice under section 106 of the TP Act to the defendant to quit the premises and thereby the tenancy was determined. Instead of vacating the suit premises the defendant sent a reply in which the title of the plaintiff was questioned.

4. The defendant-petitioner contested the suit by filing written statement contending, inter alia, that the plaintiff has no title and possession in the suit premises and the defendant petitioner is not a monthly tenant under him and no relationship of landlord and tenant does exist between the defendant and the plaintiff. It was stated by the defendant that under the Thakur Proshad Tewary Estate there were certain vacant land in Comilla town recorded in Khas khatian No. 1 in the name of the Estate owned and possessed by Rani Ragu Bangsha Dulari in Taluki right. Buildings were constructed and structures were raised by different persons on the said land with the permission of the landlord to carry on business as monthly tenants under the said Estate and the defendant-petitioner paid monthly rents in the Comilla Thakur Proshad Tewary Estate obtaining rent receipts. One Baikunta Chandra Paul, the predecessor-in-interest of the defendant-petitioner made constructions on the lands and started business therein under the name and style "Bibekananda Store" since 1332 BS. Baikunta Chandra Paul died in 1359 leaving Arjun Chandra Paul and Narendra Chandra Paul as his brother's son. Thereafter defendant-petitioner by way of inheritance from Arjun Chandra Paul and by way of purchase of the share of Narendra Chandra Paul has been carrying on business in the premises. It was also stated that the alleged power of attorney is forged and for that matter the subsequent transfers of the shops of the suit premises in the name of Shafiqur Rahman and thereafter in the name of the plaintiffs are all sham transactions. It was alleged that Abdus Sabur Khan, a Tahshildar of the enemy property office by exerting his influence created forged Power of Attorney in the name of Rani Ragu Bangsha Dulari in favour of Abdul Khaleque, a fictitious name, and created a sale deed in the name of his brother Shafiqur Rahman and other relations and then transferred the property to the plaintiffs and others. The Government having come to know about these underhand deals started criminal cases against Abdus Sabur Khan and Additional Deputy Commissioner (Revenue) and others and those cases are pending for disposal. The Government having acquired the estate of Rani Ragu Bangsha Dulari has virtually become the owner of the premises but has not been realising rent because of the said anti-corruption cases. The defendant instituted inter pleader suit No. 325 of 1986 for determination as to who is the real owner and the Government also contested the suit but the said was unfortunately dismissed on 15.11.88.

5. Four witnesses have been examined on behalf of the plaintiffs including the plaintiff No.1 as PW 1 while the defendant has examined himself as DW 1. The learned Trial Court after consideration of the evidence of the respective parties decreed the suit holding that the defendant is a habitual defaulter and as such liable to be-evicted. Being aggrieved by and dissatisfied with the judgment and decree of the SCC Judge, Sadar, Comilla passed in SCC Suit No. 11 of 1985, the defendant-petitioner filed an application under section 25 of the Small Causes Courts Act, 1887 and obtained the instant Rule.

6. From the case as given out in the plaint, written statement and the evidence of witnesses of the respective parties it appears that there is no dispute with regard to the case of the plaintiff that the suit premises originally belonged to Rani Ragu Bangsha Dulari and the defendant-petitioner's predecessors were monthly tenant under her on payment of rent. Admittedly the defendant did not pay rent of the suit premises since 1947. It is also not denied that the plaintiffs claimed the tenancy right in respect of the suit premises against the defendant by way of giving him the intimation of this acquisition of interest in the same and a notice under section 106 of the TP Act sent by the plaintiffs having been received, the defendant gave reply. In the reply the defendant denied the existence of relationship between him and the plaintiffs and also questioned the right, title and interest of the plaintiffs in the suit premises.

7. The learned SCC Judge framed the following issues for determination.

(1) Is the suit of the plaintiff maintainable in its present form and manner?

(2) Are the plaintiffs entitled to the reliefs claimed in the suit according to the prayer made in the plaint?

The plaintiff's case was that as the defendant was a tenant of the suit premises under Rani Ragu Bansha Dulari and the right, title and interest of the said owner having subsequently devolved on the plaintiff the relationship which the original owners had with the defendant also devolved upon the plaintiff on his acquisition of interest over the properties with all its rights and liabilities It was further stated that as the relationship of landlord and tenant subsists between the plaintiff and the defendant, the defendant is under obligation to pay rent to the plaintiff and, in default, he is liable to be evicted under due process of law from the suit premises. It was further stated that the defendant having only a tenancy right is estopped under section 116 of the Evidence Act from challenging the title of the plaintiff who is his landlord. From the defendant's side it was not denied that his predecessor-in-interest was tenant under the original owner Rani Ragu Bangsha Dulari. But the existence of relationship of landlord and tenant between the defendant and the plaintiff in respect of the suit premises were very much denied stating that neither the defendant nor his predecessor was inducted in the premises by the plaintiff or his predecessors, the alleged transferees from Rani Ragu Bangsha Dulari. The defendant also never admitted the plaintiff as his landlord by way of attornment or in any other manner. The defendant petitioner also challenged the very tide of the plaintiff stating that the SCC Court has no jurisdiction to entertain and decide the suit as complicated question of title is involved. Instead of returning the plaint on the ground of maintainability, the learned SCC Judge assumed jurisdiction to try the suit and thus found that the plaintiff has become owner of the suit premises as he derived his title through Abdul Khaleque who, in turn, became owner of the suit property by way of deed of exchange which was regularised by the Government through different process. The SCC Judge also found that the defendant having claimed only the tenancy right under the original owner and having not claimed title independently to that of the plaintiff, has no right to challenge the tittle of the plaintiff. It was further held that the defendant being a tenant in respect of the suit premises under the original owner has remained a tenant under the plaintiffs who have acquired right, title and interest in the suit premises and the defendant being a defaults has rendered himself liable to be evicted from the same.

<u>8. Mr. Abdul Quddus Mia, the learned Advocate appearing on behalf of the petitioner, submits that the learned SCC Judge has committed error of law: Firstly, for not returning the plaint under section 23 of the SCC Act on the ground that the suit is not maintainable as complicated question of title is involved in the suit. Secondly, for not framing an issue as to whether there exists any relationship of landlord and tenant between the contesting parties though the said question has seriously been agitated by the defendant in the written statement. The learned Advocate for the petitioner submits that without framing an issue and arriving at a finding as regards the relationship of the landlord and tenant the question of default in payment of rent to the plaintiffs could not arise. With regard to the point relating to maintainability let us have a look at the provision of section 23 of Small Causes Courts Act, 1887 which reads as follows:</u>

<u>"Notwithstanding anything in the foregoing portion of this act, when the right of a plaintiff and the relief claimed by him in a court of small causes depend upon the proof or disproof of a title to immoveable property or other title which such a court cannot finally determine the court may at any stage of the proceedings return the plaint to be presented to a court having jurisdiction to determine the title."</u>

<u>The section thus provides that if the reliefs claimed depend upon the proof or disproof of a title to the immoveable property or other title and the court is unable to determine such title finally it may return the plaint to be presented to the proper court having jurisdiction. So it is not incumbent on the court to return the plaint in all cases and whenever and in whatever manner the question of title is raised. The court may refuse to try the suit and return the plaint only when the relief claimed is dependent on the proof or disproof of complicated question of title. The provision of section 23 of the Act does not impose upon the court an absolute bar and if it is found that the points involved can be determined by way of dealing with it incidentally the court is left 'with the discretion to try the suit. In the present suit the plaintiffs has claimed ownership over the suit premises and the defendant has not claimed any right, title and interest over the same but only claimed the tenancy right. Thus the question of title is not in controversy by the claim and counter-claim of title of the parties so as to take the suit out of the jurisdiction of Small Causes Court. Only duty cast upon the SCC Judge was to determine whether the relationship of landlord and tenant created at the time of original owner continued and existed even at the time of filing this suit and for determination of such question the SCC Judge was quite competent to deal with and determine the question of title incidentally, if it was considered necessary. In support of his contention that the SCC Judge should have returned the plaint in a suit where question of title is involved Mr. Abdul Quddus Mia, the learned Advocate for the petitioner, referred to the case of Meraj Uddin Ahmed Vs. Anwarul Islam and another reported in 26 DLR 314 wherein it is held:</u>

<u>"Small Cause Court Judge, in case of question of title of property involved, may return the plaint, or it may not do so and try the case touching the question of title incidentally but not finally".</u>

<u>This principle is not applicable in all cases and, therefore, in the said case it has further been held: "The suit being one between alleged landlord and alleged tenant for an enforcement of certain rights of a landlord the simple question which is to be tried in such a suit is whether there is existence of any relationship of landlord and tenant. In such a case the question of title is not relevant at all".</u>

<u>In the case of Ahmed Shah Vs. A Bakar reported in 11 DLR 427 it is held :</u>

<u>"In a Small Causes Court suit between a landlord and a, tenant, the court has no power to go into the question of title except incidentally for the purpose of deciding the question raised in the suit which is absolutely necessary for decision of the case," and it is further held:</u>

<u>"A tenant inducted by the plaintiff landlord cannot deny the title of the landlord during the continuance of tenancy".</u>

<u>Thus from the reading of section 23 of the SCC Act and the principle laid down in a number of judicial pronouncements it becomes clear that the determination of the question of title is discretionary and the SCC Court has the power to decide the question of title incidentally in a suit, which is essentially of Small Cause nature and the court chooses not to return the plaint. Hence I am of the view that if the relationship of landlord and tenant is proved in favour of the landlord, the landlord's claim cannot be resisted whatever may be the state 01 things regarding the title of the property. On the other hand, if the landlord fails to establish the relationship as alleged by him he can not succeed in such a suit, even if he proves title to the property. The question of title is beyond the scope of such litigation.</u>

<u>9. Mr. Abdul Quddus Mia next submits that the determination of the question of relationship of the landlord and tenant between the plaintiff and the defendants was vital as it is asserted by the plaintiff but denied by the defendants and for that matter the SCC Court committed error of law in not framing a specific issue of the point for determination. As the derivative title of the plaintiff has been challenged the framing of such issue for determination of the above question was essential and, therefore, the learned Advocate submits that non framing of such a specific issue for the purpose of consideration and determination has caused prejudice to the petitioner. In support of his contention the learned Advocate referred to the case of Atauddin Mia and others Vs. Abdul Latif reported in 9 DLR 357 relevant page 361 wherein a Single Bench of this court held:</u>

<u>"There may well be cases in which some brief discussion or the reasons upon which a decision is based may be necessary. At any rate, when this court is called upon to determine as to whether that judgment is in accordance with law or not there must be something before this court from which is can satisfy itself that the Small Causes Court at least applied its mind to all the questions in controversy between the parties in the suit."</u>

<u>Mr. Md. A Karim, the learned Advocate appearing on behalf of the opposite party, by way of referring the Order 20 rule 4 of the Code of Civil Procedure, submits that the judgment need not contain more than the relevant points and decision thereon. He goes on to submit that non framing of issue under Order 41 rule 1 of the Code of Civil Procedure is merely an irregularity for which the judgment cannot be assailed. In the instant case evidence has been led into and the learned court has arrived at the conclusion on consideration of material points. In support of his contention the learned Advocate referred to the case or Amulla Kumar Ghosh Vs. Khama Prava Haldar reported in 34 DLR 267 wherein it is held :</u>

<u>"It is well settled that defective framing of issues or absence of issues being framed is merely an irregularity not affecting the merits of the case if evidence were led and the parties fought the case knowing the points to be answered causing no prejudice. Absence of proper issues could not affect the judgment and decree".</u>

<u>Mr. Karim has referred to the case of Nathosan Pilly Vs Berasraml Polly reported in AIR 1937 Mad. page 186 where it was held:</u>

<u>"Judgment is sufficient and a court can be said to conform with the Order 20 rule 4 if it states the main points for determination arid has made a statement sufficient to show that the judge has applied his mind to the main points and has recorded a decision on them".</u>

<u>Similar view was taken in the case of Bamunal and others Vs Newan Dual and others reported in AIR 1921 (Sind). 159 the Full Bench holding :</u>

<u>"Where the parties appear to have gone to trial knowing what the question between them was, any defect in the form of the issues is in no sense material",</u>

<u>In the case before us the learned SCC Judge though' has not framed any specific issue as to whether there exists; a relationship of landlord and tenant, the plaintiffs and defendant the said court has stated the main points for determination in his judgment and after consideration of those points arrived at his conclusion which does not show the absence of application of mind of the learned Judge. As the parties have adduced evidence and were fully aware about the question involved in the case no prejudice is seemed to have been caused to anyone of them, Moreover, the learned SCC Judge has given out the reasons for the decision though he was not bound to do so under the law. In the case of Saty adhyantirtha Swami Vs. Ragu Nath Daji Patil and others reported in AIR 1926 Bom 385 it is held:</u>

<u>"If there is no issue framed on a question but the parties have adduced evidence and discussed it before the court, and the court decides it as if there was an issue about it; the decree need not be set aside on the ground merely that no such issue was framed."</u>

<u>In the instant case though no issue was framed specifically from the judgment it becomes clear that the learned SCC Judge has taken for consideration the main points and has decided the same as if there was an issue on the points and hence the judgment can not be assailed only for not framing specific issue.</u>

10. Mr. Abdul Quddus Mia, then submits that though the defendant was a tenant under the original owner in respect of the premises the plaintiffs have not been accepted as landlord by any agreement or by way of payment of rent or by attainment, right of landlord has not accrued on the plaintiffs, though the plaintiffs have alleged that they have acquired derivative title over the suit premises by successive transfers and for that matter the law of estoppel under section 116 of the Evidence Act has no manner of application as no relationship of landlord and tenant between the plaintiffs and the defendant has been established either by way of attornment or otherwise. On the other hand, Mr. Karim argues that the tenancy of the defendant in respect of the suit premises existed with Rani Ragu Bangsha Dulari having not been determined by any act either from the side of the original owner or her successors or from the side of the tenant it will be deemed that the tenancy has been continuing and the plaintiffs have ownership over the suit premises with all its rights and liabilities by operation of law. The learned Advocate for the opposite party refers to the provision of section 116 of the Evidence Act which is as follows:

"No tenant of immovable property, or person claiming through such tenant shall , during the continuance of the tenancy, be permitted to deny that the landlord of such tenant had, at the beginning of the tenancy, a title to such immovable property, and no person who came upon any immovable property by the licence of the person in possession thereof shall be permitted to deny that such person had a title to such possession at the time where such licence was given".

In the case of Jogendra Lal Sarker Vs Mahesh Chandra Sadhu and others reported in AIR 1929 Cal 22 it is held :

"Estoppel would operate only as regards the denial insofar as it relates to the beginning of the tenancy and not to any other point of time. Though the tenancy may be continuing jt is quite open to the tenant to plead and show that his liability to pay the rent has wholly or partially or for a time ceased as such a plea does not amount to disputing the landlord's title but is really one of confession and avoidance, and is available to the tenant".

It was thus the duty of the defence to show that the tenancy which was in existence with the original owner Rani Ragu Bangsha Dulari was determinedly disclaimed but the defendant has not been able to prove the same therefore, it is held that the tenancy is continuing along with the suit premises and with the transfer of ownership of the suit premises the plaintiffs stepped into the shoes of the original landlord as they acquired the right over the same with all its appurtenances and privileges.

Mr. Abdul Quddus Mia, the learned Advocate for the petitioner, then submits that the defendant having not been inducted by the plaintiff in the suit premises and the defendant being in occupation of the said premises from before, having not attorned the plaintiff as his landlord, the relationship of landlord and tenant could not have been established entitling the plaintiff to claim rent and seek eviction of the defendant from the suit premises and therefore, the question of determination of tenancy of the defendant by serving notice under section 106, Transfer of Property Act does not arise. The learned Advocate for the petitioner referred to the case of Kumar Krishnan Prasadhal Singa Dev Vs. Baraball Coulo Concum Ltd. and others reported in AIR 1937 (PC) 251 where it is held:

"Section 116 of the Evidence Act does not deal with all kinds of estoppel or occasions of estoppel which may arise between the landlord and tenant".

It was further held:

"It provides that neither the tenant nor anyone claiming through tenant shall be heard to deny that particular landlord had at that date title to the property, what all such persons are precluded from denying is that the lessor had title at the date of lease, there is no exception to the case where the lease itself discloses the defect to title the principle does not apply to disentitle the tenant and deny the derivative title of the person who claims to have such because entitled to the reversion though in such cases there might be estoppel i.e. attornment and acceptance of rent, etc. In the same, the principle only applies to the title of the landlord who let the tenant in as distinct from any other person claiming to be reversioner. Nor does the principle apply to prevent a tenant from pleading that the title of the original lessor has since come to an end".

In reply to the above submission the learned Advocate for the opposite party has referred to the provision of section 109 of the Evidence Act which runs as follows :

Sestion 109: 	Rights of lessors transferee-If the lessors transfers the property leased or any part thereof; or any part of his interest therein, the transferee, in the absence of a contract to the contrary, shall possess all the rights, and if the lessee so elects, subject to all the liabilities of the lessor as to the property or part transferred so long he is the owner of it, but the lessor shall not, by reason of such transfer, use to be subject to any of the liabilities imposed upon him by the lease, unless the lessee selects to treat the transferee as person liable to him".

11. In support of his contention the learned Advocate has cited the case of Brij Behari Prasad Vs. Sm. Dewki Delli and others reported in AIR 1978 Pat, 117 wherein the following principle has been laid down :

"Whenever there is an assignment of the interest of a lessor or the interest of a lessee in a lease a new relationship comes into existence between the two sets of person one of whom was not party to the original agreement. In England at common law, an assignment was not complete without attainment by the lessee to the assignee of the original lessor, except when the assignment was by will. Later it was realised that this necessity of an attornment by the lessee was a restriction on the right of a lessor to transfer and assign his interest in a lease, and so this necessity of attornment was done away by legislative interference. This Law of Property Act, 1925, which replaced the earlier statute, has also made it clear that in such a situation, the attornment by the lessee was not necessary. In view of section 109 of the Act which says that if the lessor transfers the property leased, the- transferee in absence of a contract to contrary shall possess all the rights, and if the lessee so elects, be subject to all liabilities of the lessor as to the property so transferred, there is no requirement of attornment by the lessee. In view of this provision, the assignee of the lessor has against the lessee all the rights that he had and can enforee not only covenants but even conditions. The right to receive rent from the lessee in terms of the lease is one of such rights which passed to the assignee and a lessee cannot deny that he is not bound to pay the same as he used to pay merely because there is no privity of contract between him and the assignee who is not the landlord. The matter will be different if subsequent to the assignment, any fresh contract is entered into between the new assignees and the lesse to alter the terms of the lease, including the date of commencement of the monthly tenancy and rate of rent which will be payable".

12. Here in the present case there is no proof that the tenancy under the plaintiffs predecessor has come to an end, or that it has been determined by any act of the parties, or by lapse of time by operation of law and hence it cannot be said that on cessation of tenancy right the defendant-petitioner has become the absolute owner of the premises and therefore not answerable to the plaintiff or to anybody having better claim over the property so far it relates to the title in the same. The learned SCC Judge has in fact, dealt with the material questions in dispute and found to have decided the point after consideration of materials available on record. The learned SCC Judge discussed the question of title so far it was necessary for determining the points raised incidentally and not finally and therefore, no error is found to have been committed in this regard by the learned SCC Judge in his judgment. The point as to whether the relationship of landlord and tenant between the plaintiff and the defendant subsisted at the time of filing of the suit and whether the defendant paid rent to the landlord has also been decided by SCC Judge on consideration of the evidence and other materials on record. The evidence shows that the defendant was admittedly tenant under the previous landlord Rani Ragu Bangsha Dulari and there is nothing to show that the said tenancy came to an end by acts of the parties or by operation of law and that the defendant petitioner ever paid rents to the Government or to anybody claiming right, title and interest in the same.

13. For the reasons stated above, I find that the plaintiff has successfully proved his case and there is nothing which calls for interference with the judgment and decree of the learned SCC Judge which is hereby affirmed.

In the result, the Rule is discharged without any order as to costs.

End.

lawyer:

parties:
Farid Hossain Defendant ------ Petitioner
Vs.
Jahanara Begum and eight others ------ Plaintiffs-Opposite-Parties
full_judgment:
SM Mozibur Rahman J : This Rule was issued, at the instance of petitioner defendant No. 6 calling upon the opposite party plaintiffs Nos. 1-9 to show cause as to why the impugned Order dated 7-3-2013 passed by learned Joint District Judge and Arbitration Adalat, Dhaka in Title Suit No. 4890 of 2008 allowing the application dated 29-7-2012 in part filed by the plaintiff-opposite party Nos. 1-9 under section 151 of the Code of Civil Procedure for correction of deposition and cross examination of PW 1 and discharging the plaintiffs from submitting the Memorandum of Understanding should not be set-aside.

2. Short facts, necessary for disposal of the Rule, is that, the opposite parties No. 1-9 as plaintiffs filed Title Suit No, 4890 of 2008 before the learned District Judge, central filing section, Dhaka against the present petitioner and the opposite parties No. 10-14 impleading them as defendants Nos. 1-6 praying for recovery of khas possession after declaration of title in the suit land shown in the schedule of the plaint. Ultimately the suit was transferred to the Joint District Judge, 7th Court (Arbitration Adalat), Dhaka, for disposal.

3. The defendant Nos. 1-3, 4-5 and 4 and 6 contested the suit by filing three separate written statements and the defendant No. 6 stated in his written statement that the suit is not maintainable in its present form and manner and that the suit has no cause of action. The plaintiffs have not come to the court with clean hand; the plaintiffs filed the suit by suppression of facts; the suit is barred by law of limitation. The suit is bad for defect of parties, the suit is barred by section 42 of the Specific Relief Act; the suit is barred by estoppel, waiver, acquiescence and the plaintiffs have no right, title, interest, owner ship and possession in the suit land. The defendant No. 6 stated that he has been owning and possessing the suit land by way of purchase from its original owner since 1974 to the knowledge of the plaintiffs and other defendants. The defendant No. 6 also mutated the suit land in his name and has been paying the rent and taxes to the Government and City Corporation; that in the city survey the suit land was recorded in the name of the defendant No. 6 vide khatian No. 425, plot No. 3337; that in 1994 the Deputy Commissioner, Dhaka and others tried to evict the defendant No. 6 from the suit land claiming it as CS Plot No. 380; that challenging the said order of eviction the defendant No. 6 as plaintiff filed Title Suit No. 61 of 1994 before the Assistant Judge, 4th Court, Dhaka for declaration of title and permanent injunction against the Deputy Commissioner and others; that on 28-3-1995 the suit was decreed declaring that the suit land is situated at CS Plot No. 376 and that also a decree of permanent injunction was given in the said suit against the Deputy Commissioner and others restraining them from the suit land at CS Plot No. 376 in the name of CS Plot No. 380; that against the said decree for declaration of title and permanent injunction the Deputy Commissioner and others did not take any steps before the competent court.

4. In view of the above pleadings of the parties to the suit the learned Joint District Judge after framing issues as usual and observing all other legal formalities in this regard made the suit ready for trial. Accordingly, examination in chief of PW 1 was started on 24-7-2011 and taking long five days it was ended on 8-4-2012. Thereafter PW 1 was being cross-examined on and from 27-5-2012 and on 29-7-2012 he stated in cross that a Memorandum of Understanding was executed 15 days before the execution of power attorney Ext. 1 between the parties to the suit. On that date i.e. on 29-7-2012 petitioner filed a petition for a direction upon the plaintiff to submit the said Memorandum of Understanding. Learned Joint district Judge after giving both sides an opportunity of being heard allowed the petition directing the plaintiffs to submit the paper as the petitioner prayed for. On the other hand plaintiffs also filed a petition on 27-5-2012 long one year after the conclusion of examination in chief of PW 1 praying for correction of deposition made by PW 1 and this petition was heard and disposed of on 7-3-2013 allowing the petition for correction of deposition made by PW 1 one year ago. At the same time learned trial court exempted the plaintiffs from submitting the Memorandum of Understanding regarding which he passed earlier order to submit it on the basis of the petition of this petitioner defendant No. 6 exercising his inherent power envisaged in section 151 of the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908.

5. After hearing of both the parties, the Joint District Judge and Arbitration Adalat Dhaka, allowed the application of the plaintiffs in part by his impugned judgment and order dated 7-3-2013 correcting the deposition of PW 1 which he made one year ago as well as exempting the plaintiffs from submitting the Memorandum of Understanding in contrary to the order he passed earlier on 23-1-2013.

6. Being aggrieved by and dissatisfied with the impugned judgment and order dated 7-3-2013 passed by the learned Joint District Judge and Arbitration Adalat, Dhaka in Title Suit No. 4890 of 2008 petitioner moved the instant civil revisional application and obtained the Rule.

7. Mr Md Moin Uddin, the learned Advocate appearing on behalf of the defendant-petitioner, submits that that on 29-7-2012 at the time of cross examination PW 1 admitted that সমঝোতা চুক্তিপত্র সম্ভবত ১০-৩-২০০৮ ইং তারিখে স্বাক্ষরিত হয়, এটা রেজিষ্ট্রি হয় নাই। সমঝোতা চুক্তি সম্পর্কে আমি কোন ব্যাখ্যা দিব না। সমঝোতা চুক্তিপত্র দাখিল করিব প্রয়োজনে।As such, he submits that on the same date the petitioner filed an application for direction upon the plaintiffs to submit the said সমঝোতা চুক্তিপত্র for ends of justice. That on 23-1-2013 the Trial Court heard the both sides and allowed the application given by the petitioner for submitting Memorandum of Understanding. He further submits that the deposition of PW 1 was started on 24-7-2011 and ended on 8-4-2012 and cross examination was started on 27-5-2012 one year after the plaintiffs filed application for correction of the deposition of PW 1 and that PW 1 admitted in cross examination that he got Master Degree in Economics from Dhaka University; that subsequently on 7-3-2013 the Trial Court changed his mind and allowed the application of the plaintiffs given for correction of deposition of PW 1 and the learned Court below allowed the petition along with a separate order that plaintiffs are exempted from filing the Memorandum of Understanding in contradiction with his earlier order dated 23-1-2013 and as such the Trial Court committed error of law which is liable to be interfered with.

8. In support of his arguments, he cited the following decisions given in the case of Bangla-desh vs Luxmi Bibi reported in 2 BLT (AD) 1994 Page 183 = 46 DLR (AD) 158, the case of Harun-or-Rashid vs Quyum Khan reported in 7 BLT Page 34, the case of Abdul Noor vs Makhan Mia, reported in .60 DLR (AD) 39, the case of Harun-or-Rashid vs Gulaynoor Bibi reported in 19 BLC (AD) 123. Accordingly, he submits that in pursuance to the decisions given in the cases he referred the present Rule is liable to be made absolute for ends of justice.

9. Mr Md Mostafa, the learned Advocate appearing on behalf of the plaintiff opposite parties submits that the record of schedule land was prepared on the basis of settlement. But the plaintiff did not file any settlement case. The plaintiff has filed a photocopy of Khatian No. 14, plot No. 2479 of 2010 Joggasola Mouja. On the perusal of the photocopy of this record it appears that 5.00 acre land has been recorded in the name of plaintiff Nurul Islam. The plaintiff has filed some photocopy of rent receipt. The plaintiff did not file original copy of the rent receipt. These photocopies are not acceptable as a document. The plaintiff did not adduce any witnesses and produced any original document to prove the case. With regard to the impugned judgment and order he has clearly stated that the learned Court below did not commit any error of law.

10. In support of his arguments, he referred the case of Charandwip Bhumihin Krishi vs The Cox's Bazar reported in 1988 BLD (AD) page 63 = 40 DLR (AD) 213. Accordingly, he submits that the Rule issued earlier may be discharged for ends of justice.

11. In view of the above facts and circumstances of the case we have perused the Revisional application, impugned order dated 7-3-2013 and other documents/papers as available in record. It appears from the record that the Trial Court started recording examination in chief of PW 1 on 24-7-2011 and ended on 8-4-2012 cross examination of whom was commenced on 27-5-2012 when the plaintiff filed the petition for correction of deposition and cross examination of PW 1. After giving both sides an opportunity of being heard he allowed the petition on 7-3-2013 exercising his discretionary power conferred on him under section 151 of the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908.

12. Now pertinent question in the instant case before us is whether the Trial Court is correct in passing the impugned order dated 7-3-2013 allowing the plaintiffs petition for correction of deposition and cross examination of PW 1 as well as discharging the plaintiffs from submitting the Memorandum of Understanding respecting which he earlier allowed an application of the petitioner asking the plaintiffs to submit the said Memorandum of Understanding by his order dated 23-1-2013.

<u>13. We have carefully examined the impugned order dated 7-3-2013 passed by the learned Joint District Judge and found that in exercise of his power conferred on him under section 151 of the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908 he has arbitrarily allowed the plaintiff’s petition submitted for correction of one year old deposition of PW 1. Besides, he has exempted the plaintiffs from filing the memorandum of understanding reversing his own order dated 23-1-2013. It is long settled principle of law that where an alternative remedy exists a party cannot have recourse to the inherent jurisdiction of the court under section 151 of the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908. But in this case it is clearly seen that Trial Court passed the impugned judgment and order whimsically and arbitrarily without applying his judicial mind allowing the petition for correcting the deposition of the PW 1 as prayed for by the plaintiffs. Discretionary power of a court as has been inserted in section 151 of the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908 cannot be exercised where alternative remedies are available. After administering oath in the open court when the evidence of a witness is recorded by a trial court cannot be discarded or changed or corrected in the form of modification except recalling the witness following the prescribed provision of law enunciated in the Evidence Act, 1872.</u>

14. In the instant case we have observed that Trial Court did not follow the accurate provision of law in course of passing the impugned order dated 7-3-2013. He has manifestly acted at his own whim and caprice which is neither desirable nor acceptable in the eye of law.

15. On perusal of the impugned judgment and order it is further seen that Trial Court passed a suo-motu order exempting the plaintiffs from filing the Memorandum of Understanding in contravention of his earlier order dated 23-1-2013 in strength of which he directed the plaintiff to submit the Memorandum of Understanding on the basis of the application filed by the petitioner defendant. This portion of order passed by the Trial Court is also seen to be injudicious and not consistent with the existing provision of law provided to be applied in this regard as we have cited earlier.

16. We have gone through the cases referred by the learned Advocates for both sides as has been stated earlier and found that the facts and circumstances of the case cited by the learned Advocate of the opposite parties are not consistent with that of the instant case before us.

17. In view of the discussion made above we are of the view that the Trial Court committed an error of law in the impugned order resulting in an error in the decision occasioning failure of justice and as such the impugned order dated 7-3-2013 passed by the learned Joint District Judge and Arbitration Adalat, Dhaka in Title Suit No. 4890 of 2008 is set aside.

18. In the result, the Rule is made absolute without any order as to cost.

19. The order of stay granted earlier by this Court stands vacated.

Send copy of this judgment to the court below at once.

End.

parties:
Saifur Rahman ----- Petitioner
Vs.
Government of Bangladesh, represented by the Secretary, Ministry of Land Administration and Land Reforms, Dhaka and others ----- Respondents
full_judgment:
Naimuddin Ahmed J : In this Writ Petition arising out of an application under Article 102 of the Constitution an order passed by the Government, the respondent No. 1, under Memo No. 11-1/86/230 dated 5.6.86 (Annexure 'H') whereby the settlement of certain lands granted to the petitioner by the Deputy Commissioner, Bhola, some time in 1951, was cancelled and the Deputy Commissioner, Bhola, was directed to take steps for recognizing the respondent No. 4 and some others as co-tenants of those lands, and an order passed by the Government under Memo No. 11-1/86/438/1(3) dated 19.11.86 (Annexure 'J) whereby an application for review filed to the Government by the petitioner for reviewing the order contained in the memo first above mentioned was rejected, have been called in question.

2. The facts leading to this Writ Petition are somewhat lengthy.

3. It is alleged by, the petitioner that three plots of lands appertaining to RS Plot Nos. 557, 558 & 559 comprising a total area of 1261.95 acres corresponding to CS Plots Nos. 521 and 522 in the CS record of right were the lands of mauza Char Sitaram and were the khan lands of the Crown. These lands were lost by diluvian in the river, Tetulia, and during the RS operations conducted in the year, 1941, these lands were shown as river blocks outside the revenue survey. After remaining under the river, Tetulia, for over 20 years, these lands re-appeared in the year, 1951, and became vested in the Government. Thereafter, the Khasmahal Authorities of the then District of Bakerganj (now the District of Bhola) granted settlement of these lands with the petitioner and others in Miscellaneous Case No. 274 of 1947. The petitioner and other lessees, after due execution of their respective Kabuilyats, entered into possession therein. While the petitioner and his other co-tenants were in peaceful possession of these lands, one Rafiqul Huq Chowdhury made a claim over these lands as his own lands and tried to dispossess the petitioner. Having failed to enter into possession of these lands the said Rafiqul Huq Chowdhury filed an application before the then Sub-Divisional Magistrate, Bhola, with a prayer for drawing up a proceeding under section 145 of the Code of Criminal Procedure. The learned Sub-Divisional Magistrate drew up a proceeding and the present petitioner and others who were the opposite parties therein appeared and after hearing both the parties the Sub-Divisional Magistrate, by an order dated 3.1.57, found the petitioner and his co-tenants in possession of these lands and also found the said Rafiqul Huq Chowdhury out of possession, and, accordingly, declared the possession of the petitioner and his cotenants in the said lands. Against this judgment and order dated 3.1.57 a Criminal Motion being Criminal Motion No. 11(1) of 1957 was filed before the Sessions Judge, Bakerganj, by the respondent No. 4 of this writ petition. The said Criminal Motion was heard by the Additional Sessions Judge, 3rd Court, Bakerganj, and by his judgment and order dated 31.8.57 he dismissed the Criminal Motion. Against this decision of the Additional Sessions Judge, 3rd Court, Bakerganj, a revisional application being Criminal Revision No. 547 of 1957 was preferred before the High Court of East Pakistan, as it was then. The High Court also rejected the said revisional application upholding the order of the Additional Sessions Judge, 3rd Court, Bakerganj. The respondent No. 4 and his party-men then instituted a Title Suit being Title Suit No. 191 of 1959 in the Court of the Subordinate Judge, 2nd Court, Barisal, claiming only 75.00 acres of lands out of RS Plot Nos. 557, 558 and 559 with a prayer for establishment of title and khan possession. The present petitioner and the respondent No. 1, the Government of East Pakistan, as it was then, were made parties in the said suit. The respondent No. 1, the Government of East Pakistan, appeared and contested the suit disclaiming the alleged title of the respondent No. 4. The present petitioner also contested the suit by filing a separate written statement. A prayer was made in the said suit by the present petitioner and other defendants for temporary injunction for restraining the plaintiffs of that suit including the respondent No. 4 of this writ petition from entering into the disputed lands. The injunction matter was heard by the learned Subordinate Judge, 3rd Court, Barisal, and by his order dated 17.11.60 restrained the respondent No. 4 and other plaintiffs of that suit from entering into the disputed lands till the disposal of the suit. Thereafter, the Title Suit abated on 3rd April, 1973 under the provisions of President's Order Nos. 72, 135 and 137 of 1972 at the instance of the Government. As against the order of abatement a revisional application was filed before the High Court Division of the Supreme Court. This revisional application was allowed setting aside the abatement order and the suit was restored and remanded for trial to the Court of the Subordinate Judge, Bhola, and it was then re-numbered as Title Suit No. 10 of 1984. On 2.12.84 the respondent No. 4 preferred an application under Order 39 rules 1 and 2 of the Code of Civil Procedure read with section 151 of the Code praying for temporary injunction against the defendant No. 1 in the said suit (the Deputy Commissioner of Bhola), who is the respondent No. 3 in this Writ Petition, for restraining him from disturbing their alleged possession in the disputed lands and also for restraining him from obstructing them from harvesting the paddy standing thereon. The Defendant No. 1, the Deputy Commissioner of Bhola, contested the application for temporary injunction by filing a written objection wherein he denied title and possession of the plaintiffs in the disputed lands. By an order dated 11.12.84 the learned Subordinate Judge allowed the prayer for temporary injunction restraining the said defendant No. 1 from disturbing the alleged possession of the plaintiffs of that suit and from interfering with harvesting the paddy standing thereon by them. An appeal was preferred against the order of the learned Subordinate Judge, Bhola, before the District Judge, Bhola and this appeal was numbered as Misc. Appeal No. 71 of 1984. The learned District Judge heard the aforesaid appeal and by his judgment and order dated 31.1.85 affirmed the order dated 11.12.84 passed by the learned Subordinate Judge and dismissed the said appeal. Thereafter a revisional application was filed before the High Court Division, Barisal Bench, against the order of the learned District Judge on 31.1.85 in which Rule was issued and it was numbered as Civil Revision No. 25 of 1985. After hearing this revisional application the High Court Division, by an order dated 29.5.85, set aside the judgment and order passed by the District Judge on 31.1.85 and also the order passed by the Subordinate Judge on 11.12.84 and rejected the application for temporary injunction. As against this order of the High Court Division of the Supreme Court dated 29.5.85 an application for Special Leave to Appeal was preferred before the Appellate Division of the Supreme Court and this appeal was registered as Civil Petition for Special Leave to Appeal No. 149 of 1985. After hearing the parties the learned Appellate Division of the Supreme Court by its judgment and order dated 8.7.85, dismissed the petition upholding the judgment and order passed by the High Court Division of the Supreme Court after finding, it is alleged, that the Court did not find possession of the plaintiffs in the disputed lands.

4. Having thus failed to achieve their purpose the respondent No. 4 and his party-men filed an application before the respondent No. 3, the Deputy Commissioner, Bhola, and obtained an order in their favour passed by the Additional Deputy Commissioner (Rev.), Bhola, on 17.11.84 in Misc. Case No. 125 of 1984-85 and against this order the petitioner of this writ petition filed an application before the respondent No. 3, the Deputy Commissioner, Bhola, and on the basis of this application the respondent No. 3, the Deputy Commissioner, Bhola, by his order dated 28.11.84, directed the Magistrate-in-charge of the local police camp to ensure peaceful possession and harvesting of the paddy by the petitioner as a result of which the petitioner and others could peacefully harvest the crops grown by them in the disputed lands.

5. Thereafter, the respondent No. 4 filed an application, on 2.1.86 before the respondent No. 1, the Secretary of the Ministry of Land Administration and Land Reforms, Government of the People's Republic of Bangladesh, claiming title and possession in these lands. The respondent No: 1 asked the Deputy Lands Reforms Commissioner to hold an enquiry and submit a report. No notice of any such enquiry was served on the petitioner and others and it was reported that the Deputy Land Reforms Commissioner came to Bhola and visited the disputed lands on 19.2.86 accompanied by the Upazila Revenue Officer, Bhola, and held an enquiry from 18.2.86 to 20.2.86 and then submitted a biased report holding that these lands did not appertain to Char Sitaram and had been wrongly settled by the Khasmahal Authorities with the petitioner and others in the year, 1951. On the basis of this report the respondent No. 1 passed the impugned order under Memo No. 11-1/86/438/1(3) dated 19.11.86 cancelling the settlement granted to the petitioner by the Khasmahal Authorities in the year, 1951, and also directing to recognise the respondent No. 4 and others as tenants of the disputed lands. No notice was served on the petitioner and he was not heard by the respondent No. 1 before passing this order. On hearing about this order the petitioner filed an application before the respondent No. 1 for review of the order on various grounds and this application was also rejected by the Respondent No. 1 by his order dated 19.11.86 confirming the order dated 5.11.86. As against these orders passed by the Respondent No. 1 that the petitioner approached this Court and obtained the present Rule.

6. The Respondent No. 1, the Government of the People's Republic of Bangladesh, represented by the Secretary of the Ministry of Land Administration and Land Reforms, has filed an affidavit-in-opposition denying the allegations made by the petitioner. Briefly stated, the case of the respondent No. 1 is, that the three disputed plots, namely, plot Nos. 557, 558 and 559 never appertained to Char Sitaram. These three plots appertained to mouza Udaypur which belonged to the ex-rent-receivers namely, the Landlords of Ulania and the Bhuban Mohan Roy Chowdhury Estate, and as such, the settlement of these lands with the petitioner and his co-tenants by the Khas Mahal Authorities was illegal. It has also been stated in the affidavit-in-opposition that the petitioner has no title in these lands. An application was made by the Respondent No. 4 to the respondent No. 1 for holding an enquiry into the matter. An order was then passed directing enquiry by the Deputy Land Reforms Commissioner. The Deputy Land Reforms Commissioner held a detailed enquiry into the disputed lands and submitted a report opining that these three plots appertained to mouza Udaypur and not to mouza Char Sitaram. The Deputy Land Reforms Commissioner also opined that these lands belonged to two sets of ex-rent-receivers mentioned above. On the basis of this report and after hearing the parties the respondent No. 1 passed the impugned orders which were based on sound reasons.

7. The respondent No. 4 also entered appearance and contested the writ petition by filing an affidavit-in-opposition wherein, apart from general denial of the statements of the petitioner made in the writ petition, it has been contended that the three disputed RS plots were never part of mouza Char Sitaram. It has also been contended that these three disputed plots were part of mouza Udaypur belonging to the estates of the Landlords of Ulania and Bhuban Mohan Roy Chowdhury. After re-appearance of these lands from diluvian these ex-landlords entered into possession of these lands and granted settlement thereof with the respondent No. 4 and others. The respondent No. 4 also contends that since the settlement was made the respondent No. 4 and others have been possessing these lands peacefully. While admitting that one Rafiqul Huq Chowdhury filed a proceeding milder section 145 of the Code of Criminal Procedure against the petitioner he contends that he was not a party in the said proceeding and as such, he was not bound by any order passed therein. He also contends that while he along with his co-tenants was in possession in these plots, the Khasmahal Officer of Bhola tried to have these plots wrongly recorded within mouza Char Sitaram during the SA operations and as such, he instituted Title Suit No. 191 of 1959 in the 2nd Court of Subordinate Judge, Bakerganj, against the Government, the petitioner of this Writ Petition and others who were defendants Nos. 2-110. This suit is still pending after having been re-numbered as Title Suit No. 10 of 1984 in the Court of Subordinate Judge, Bhola. While the respondent No. 4 and others were in peaceful possession of these plots the petitioner and his party-men tried to disturb their possession and as such, the respondent No. 4 and other co-tenants filed an application before, the Additional Deputy Commissioner, (Revenue) Bhola and after hearing the parties the Additional Deputy Commissioner, (Revenue), Bhola passed an order on 17.11.84 in their favour. Thereafter, the present petitioner and other defendants of Title Suit No. 10 of 1984 filed Misc. Case No. 125 of 1984-85 before the Deputy Commissioner, Bhola and the Deputy Commissioner in collusion with the petitioner and his party-men passed an order on 28.11.84 directing a Magistrate, who was in charge in the police camp in the locality, to ensure possession of the disputed lands and harvesting of the paddy by the petitioner and his party-men who has taken settlement from the i3overnment and on the basis of this order, the petitioner and his party men forcibly harvested paddy from .50 acres of lands out of the three disputed 1Dlots. The respondent No. 4 then filed and (application before the Subordinate Judge, Bhola, in (title Suit No. 10 of 1984, praying for restraining the Deputy Commissioner of Bhola from deploying t any police force in the disputed lands and the prayer was allowed. There was an appeal against the order of the Subordinate Judge before the District Judge, 13hola, and the District Judge affirmed the order of the Subordinate Judge. The orders of the Subordinate nudge and the District Judge were set aside by the relight Court Division of the Supreme Court, Barisal Bench, in Civil Revision No. 25 of 1985. Azoetition for special leave to appeal against the order 2A. the High Court Division before the Appellate Division of the Supreme Court being Civil Petition for Special Leave to Appeal No. 149 of 1985 was also dismissed. The respondent No. 4 then filed an application on 2.1.86 before the respondent No. 1 and the respondent No. 1 directed the Deputy Lands Reforms Commissioner to hold an enquiry into the matter and submit a report. Accordingly, the Deputy Lands Reforms Commissioner visited the disputed land on 19.2.86 and submitted his report on 25.6.86 finding that the three disputed plots were parts of Char Sitarammouza, that granting settlement of these plots by the Khasmahal Authorities to the petitioner and others in the year, 1951, was done wrongly and illegally and that the respondent No. 4 and his party-men were the bonafide tenants in those plots. On the basis of this report and after considering the facts and circumstances of the case, the respondent No. 1 passed an order contained in Memo No. 11-1/86/438/1(3) dated 19.11.86 cancelling the settlement granted to the petitioner and his other co-tenants and directing the Deputy Commissioner, Bhola, to take steps for recognising the respondent No. 4 and others as bonafide tenants of these plots. It is also stated in the affidavit-in-opposition that the petitioner filed an application for review against the order under the aforesaid memo and this application for review was also rejected by the respondent No. 1 under Memo No. 11-1/86/438/1(3) dated 19.11.86. The aforesaid orders are absolutely lawful orders and, as such, cannot be interfered with.

8. Subsequently, the petitioner filed 2 affidavits-in-reply to the affidavits-in-opposition submitted by the respondent No. 1 and the affidavit-in-opposition submitted by the respondent No. 4 and in these affidavits-in-reply the facts narrated in the original petition have been re-iterated.

9. Mr. Shamsul Huq Chowdhury, the learned. Advocate appearing on behalf of the petitioner, first of all, attacked the impugned Memo No. 11-1/86/230 dated 5.6.86 on the ground that before passing this order whereby a right vested in the petitioner had been taken away, no notice was issued to him and he was not heard and as such, this order was in violation of the basic principles of natural justice.

10. The second ground taken by Mr. Chowdhury is that the respondent No. 1, or the Secretary, Ministry of Land Administration and Land Reforms or the Joint Secretary of the said Ministryis not empowered to pass the impugned order and in exercising the power with which they are not vested in law they acted arbitrarily and without jurisdiction.

11. The next ground of attack on the impugned orders by Mr. Chowdhury appears to be that when admittedly a litigation between the parties including the respondent No. 1 was pending in a court of competent jurisdiction to decide the issues in question it was not open to a party to the said litigation to take any step to the detriment of another party to the litigation. Mr. Syed JR Modassir Hossain, the Deputy Attorney-General, representing the respondent No. 1, argued, at first, that the respondent No. 1 was quite competent and empowered in view of section 146 of State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, 1951, to pass an order revising the order passed by a Revenue Authority and as such it cannot be said that the impugned orders were incompetent and without jurisdiction.

12. He has also argued that it was always open to the respondent No. 1, the Government of Bangladesh, to rectify and modify any order it deemed to have been wrongly passed by any officer subordinate to it.

13. He has also contended that the order of the respondent No. 1 being passed on an enquiry report submitted by a competent officer of the Government was passed on objective materials and, as such, was not arbitrary or biased.

14. Mr. Khandker Mahbubuddin Ahmed, the learned Advocate, representing the respondent No. 4, contended that the respondent No. 1 was vested under the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, 1950 with the power to pass such orders as the impugned orders.

15. He also contended that the pendency of the litigation between the parties in the Court of the Subordinate Judge, Bhola, could not be treated as a the against the right of the respondent No. 1 to rectify any error committed by any Officer appointed by the Respondent No. 1 and, as such, no exception can be taken to the impugned order on this ground.

16. Mr. Ahmed also contended that the order granting settlement to the petitioner and his co-tenants in 1951 by the Khasmahal Authorities being ability void the question of providing any opportunity to the petitioner to show cause against the impugned order cancelling the said settlement o, not arise as no question of natural justice was involved in such a case.

17. He, last of all, argued that in this writ petition vital disputed questions of facts are involved and as such this writ petition is not maintainable.

18. So far as the first ground taken by Mr. Chowdhury that before passing the impugned order under Memo No. 11-1/86/230 dated 5.6.86, which is virtually the impugned order, no notice was issued on him and he was not afforded any opportunity by the authorities of showing cause against the impugned order and of being heard by the respondent No. 1, is concerned, it is necessary to refer to the relevant portion of this order which is at Annexure 'H' and which runs as follows :

"There is no factual and documentary proof to treat these plots of Char Udaypurmouza as belonging to Char Sitaram which is under Lalmohan Upazila and disturb the petitioner tenants who had taken settlement from the ex-landlords of the Ulania-Joint Estate and Bhuban Mohan Roy Chowdhury Estate as far back as in 1950. That these plots belonged to Char Udaypurmouza and not Char Sitaram was a settled issue decided upon by the Assistant Settlement Officer and Objection Officer during last S.A. operation against which no appeal was preferred by the local administration.

2. The Government in the Ministry have, therefore, decided that :

(a) the disputed land in plots No. 557, 558 and 559 be treated as belonging to mouza Udaypur in lawful recognition of the existing records of rights, both RS and SA and admitted to be forming part of Touzi No. 2872 belonging to the Ulania Joint Estate and Bhuban Mohan Roy Chowdhury Estate before the State Acquisition.

(b) The Settlement of the Lands given by the Local Administration by treating the same as Government khas land and forming part of mauza Char Sitaram has been illegal and is, therefore, cancelled.

(c) The petitioner along with others claim to have taken settlement of these lands from the ex-proprietors. They were also in possession of 3 the lands until ousted therefrom by police force deputed by the District Administration.

The petitioners should, therefore, be recognised as tenants by the Local Revenue Authority after scrutiny and examination of their papers and also after withdrawal of the TS Case No. 10/84 pending in the Court of Sub-Judge, Bhola."

The aforesaid letter was addressed by the .respondent No. 1 to the Deputy Commissioner, 1Bhola. A perusal of the above letter shows that certain findings were recorded adversely affecting the linterests claimed by the petitioner in the disputed plots. It further appears that the settlement on the ,basis of which the plaintiff has been claiming title in these plots was cancelled by the respondent No. 1. It also appears that the respondent No. 1 directed some other persons including the respondent No. 4 to be recognised as lawful tenants in these plots under the Government. There is no doubt that these observations and the order of the respondent No. 1, adversely affected the interest claimed by the petitioner in the disputed plots since this order sought to take away some rights and title with which the petitioner claims to have been vested in the disputed plots on the basis of his alleged settlement from the Government. As such, the petitioner was certainly entitled to be heard before he order was passed, because, to take away one's right denying one the right to be heard is to deny one natural justice. It is not disputed that no opportunity if hearing was offered to the petitioner before passing the impugned order on 5.6.86. We are therefore, of the opinion that the principles of natural justice were not observed before the order Memo No. 11-1/86/230 dated 5.6.86 was passed by respondent No. 1. It is difficult at this stage to accept the contention of Mr. Ahmed that the settlement alleged to have been granted to the petitioner in the year, 1951, by the Khasmahal Authorities was void and as such, the petitioner was not entitled to be heard before cancelling a void order. It cannot be said that the alleged settlement vas ex facie void. The question of vires of the alleged settlement of the petitioner cannot be decided within the limited scope of writ jurisdiction as it would involve detailed investigation into various questions of fact which can only be decided by a Court of competent jurisdiction. So, we are unable to accept the proposition that no question of the principles of natural justice was involved when the respondent No. 1 dealt with the matter. In these views of the matter, we are of opinion that the impugned order under Memo No. 11-1/86/230 dated 5.6.86 (Annexure 'H') cannot be supported in law as it was passed in utter disregard of the principle, "Audi alteram partem."

19. Mr. Shamsul Huq Chowdhury then attacked the impugned order under Memo No. 11-1/86/230 dated 5.6.86 contending that the Government was not authorised under any provision of law and was, therefore, not competent to make the impugned order rescinding the order of the Revenue Officer granting settlement to the petitioner and his alleged co-tenants. In this connection, Mr. Chowdhury drew our attention to sections 147, 148, 149 and 150 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, 1950 which provide for appeal, revision and review of the orders passed by the Revenue Officers under the provisions of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, 1950. We carefully perused sections 147, 148, 149 and 150 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, 1950. Section 147 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, 1950, provides for preferring appeal against the orders of the Revenue Officers and this section shows that the Appellate Authority is the Collector, when the order is made by a Revenue Officer subordinate to the Collector, Commissioner of the division, when the order is made by the Collector of a district within the division and the Board of Land Administration, when the order is made by the Commissioner of a division. There is no other authority under section 147 to whom an appeal can be preferred. Section 148 provides for the period of limitation for an appeal under section 147. Section 149 provides for revision of an order passed by a Revenue Officer. Under this section, similar to an appeal, the Collector, the Commissioner and the Board of Land Administration have been vested with power of revision against the orders 0f the Revenue Officers. Section 149 does not empower the Government to revise, rescind or cancel any order passed by a Revenue Officer. Section 150 provides for review of an order by the Officer himself who passed the order.

<u>20. From the above, it appears that the Board of Land Administration is the final authority to entertain appeal and revision against any order passed under the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, 1950 by a Revenue Officer which includes an order granting settlement of land vested in the Government as in the case of settlement to the petitioner done by a regular proceeding under section 86 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, 1950.</u>

<u>21. Mr. Syed JR Modassir Hossain, the learned Deputy Attorney-General, tried to rely on sub-section (1) of section 146 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, 1950 and tried to argue that the general power of superintendence and control over the Revenue Officers empowers the Government to pass any order revising an order passed by a Revenue Officer. Sub-section (1) of section 146 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, 1950, as amended by Ordinance XXI of 1982 provides as follows :</u>

<u>"146(1) The general superintendence and control over all Revenue Officers shall be vested in and all such officers shall be subordinate to, the Board of Land Administration."</u>

<u>Section 146(1), therefore, shows that the general power of superintendence and control over all Revenue _Officers is vested in the Board of Land Administration and not in the Government. Moreover section 146(1) vests the Board of Land Administration with administrative control over the Revenue Officers and by no means empowers it to revise the orders passed by the Revenue Officers under the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, 1950. The powers of appeal, revision and review are in sections 147 to 151 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, 1950. The power in section 146 does not, therefore, include the power to revise the orders of a Revenue Officer and this aspect of the legal position was candidly accepted by Mr. Ahmed while arguing for the respondent No. 4. Nothing has been placed before us to show that the Government is empowered under any provision of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, 1950, to cancel or rescind any order passed by the Revenue Authorities. Consequently, there is no substance in the submission made by the learned Deputy Attorney-General.</u>

22. It, therefore, appears that the submissions made by Mr. Chowdhury that the Government was not empowered under any provision of law to pass the impugned order and revise the order passed by the Revenue Officer granting settlement to the petitioner and his co-tenants has substance. So the impugned order under Memo No. 11-1/86/230 dated 5.6.86 passed by the Respondent No. 1 being passed by authority not vested by law to make such order suit without lawful authority.

24. Lastly, Mr. Chowdhury submitted that by passing the impugned order under Memo No. 11-1/86/230 dated 5.6.86 the respondent No. 1 sought to settle a dispute pending before a Civil Court of competent jurisdiction. In Title Suit No. 10 of 1984 of the Court of Subordinate Judge, Bhola, precisely, the same question of law and fact are involved and in this suit the respondent No. 1 is also a party. As such Mr, Chowdhury wanted to say, the respondent No. 1 who is a party to the dispute which is sub judice before the Civil Court was not, in all fairness, entitled to take any action to the detriment of another party to the said litigation.

25. In relation to the last submission of Mr. Chowdhury it is necessary to refer to certain undisputed facts. One Rafiqul Huq Chowdhury, an alleged co-tenant of the respondent No. 4, filed a case under section 145 of the Code of Criminal Procedure claiming title and possession in the disputed plots on the same basis as the respondent No. 4. The copy of the order of the learned Magistrate in this proceeding is at Annexure 'A' to the Writ Petition. This order was passed as far back as on 3.1.57 and its concluding portion runs as follows : "From all these above facts and circumstances and from the evidence on record, I find that the disputed land appertains to Char Sitaram (Block 'B') and not Udaypur as alleged by the 1st party and I am satisfied that the 2nd party and 3rd party were in possession of the proceeding land at the date of the order u/s 145 CrPC and it is, hereby, declared by this that the 2nd party and the 3rd party are entitled to possession thereof until evicted therefrom in due course of law.

Any disturbance of such possession until such eviction is also forbidden by law."

26. The present petitioner was one of the third parties in the above proceeding. The respondent No. 4 was not, however, a party to the said proceeding and as such, the order in this proceeding did not bind him, but it is relevant at least as evidence of possession of the petitioner at the time when the order was passed. The order in this proceeding was unsuccessfully challenged in Criminal Motion No.111(1) of 1957 before the learned Sessions Judge, Bakerganj, and ultimately before the High Court in Criminal Revision No. 547 of 1957. Thereafter, the respondent No. 4 instituted Title Suit No. 191 of 1959 in the 2nd Court of Subordinate Judge, Barisal, against the petitioner and others for establishment of title and khas possession in the disputed lands and this suit is still pending as Title Suit No. 10 of 1984 in the Court of Subordinate Judge, Bhola. In this suit the petitioner and others filed an application for injunction for restraining the respondent No. 4 and the other plaintiffs of that suit from entering on the disputed lands and this application was allowed and the respondent No. 4 and the other plaintiffs were restrained from entering into the disputed lands by an order dated 17.11.60 as at Annexure 'C'. The respondent No. 4 then filed an application for temporary injunction against the respondent No. 3, the Deputy Commissioner of Bhola, who was the defendant No. 1 in that suit, for restraining him from disturbing the alleged possession of the respondent No. 4 and the prayer was allowed by the learned Subordinate Judge and the order of the Subordinate Judge was affirmed by the learned District Judge. The orders of the Subordinate Judge and the District Judge were reversed by the High Court Division of the Supreme Court in Civil Revision No. 25 of 1985 on 29.5.85 and the prayer of the respondent No. 4 was rejected finding that the respondent No. 4 and the other plaintiffs of the suit had no possession in the disputed lands till 1960. A petition for special leave to appeal being Civil Petition for Special Leave to Appeal No. 149 of 1985 was filed before the Appellate Division of the Supreme Court and was rejected by their Lordships of the Appellate Division. The order is at Annexure "E". His Lordship Shahabuddin Ahmed, J, as his Lordship was then, speaking for the Court observed "Mr. Khondker Mahbubuddin Ahmed, learned Advocate for the petitioner, has made strenuous efforts to convince us that the petitioners have been in possession all along on the basis of their settlement from the Ulania Joint Estate. But we find no evidence of any settlement from the ex-landlords. The suit land was recorded as Government khas land. Khondker Mahbubuddin Ahmed contends that this entry in the khatian is wrong in that the suit land was found by the Settlement Officer and the Pleader Commissioner to be included in "Udaypur Mouza." But whether the land falls within Udaypurmouza or Char Sitarammouza, there is no dispute about its identity and it is found to be the one and the same land, which is the bone of contention between the parties. In the absence of any prima facie prbof of the settlement from the ex-landlords, the petitioners are trying to make out a case that if the land appertains to Udaypurmouza it will necessarily follow that it was the former Zaminders to the petitioners (sic.) As to possession, in a previous proceeding under section 145 CrPC MR Case No. III of 1954 lessees of the Zaminders were not found in possession. Mr. Khondker Mahbubuddin Ahmed contends that in that proceeding the petitioners were not parties; but there is no dispute that the said proceeding was instituted in respect of this very land though it was filed by another set of claimants, and it is after the disposal of this proceeding that these petitioners filed the Title Suit claiming title and possession in respect of the same land. In these circumstances, the High Court Division prima facie found that the plaintiffs got no possession in the suit land and on that finding set aside the order of temporary injunction. We do not find any wrong in the finding of the High Court Division."

27. It is, therefore, clear that complicated and intricate question of title of the parties to the suit pending before the Civil Court is involved and this question of title can only be judicially resolved by a competent Court after due and proper consideration of the facts and law involved in the dispute. By the impugned order dated 5.6.86, the respondent No. 1 who is a party to the dispute pending in a competent Court virtually and substantially decided these disputed question of facts, law and title of the parties involved in the suit. The order of the respondent No. 1 also sought to frustrate the orders of the highest judicial forum in the country relating to the status quo of the parties in the disputed property during pendency of the suit in the Civil Court. Administrative interference by an incompetent authority in the matters pending for judicial determination, if encouraged, will augur the end of rule of law. Moreover, if a party to a litigation is allowed to take an action to the detriment of another party in respect of the subject-matter of the litigation it will be negation of the basic principles of administration of justice.

28. In the result, considering all the facts, circumstances and the submissions made by the learned Advocates we find that the impugned order under Memo No. 11-1/86/230 dated 5.6.86 is without lawful authority and of no legal effect. Consequently, the subsequent order under Memo No. 11-1/86/438/1(3) dated 19.11.86 which is virtually re-iteration of the former and direction to implement the former order is also without lawful authority.

29. Accordingly, the Rule is made absolute. 30. The impugned orders passed under Memo No. 11-1/86-230 dated 5.6.86 and Memo No. 11-1/86/438/1(3) dated 19.11.86 as at Annexure 'H' and 'J' are declared to be without lawful authority and are of no legal effect.

There is no order as to cost.

End.
