Vs.
Bholanath Guha & ors------Respondents
case_source: (From the Judgment and Order dated 7.7.82 Passed by the High Court Division in Civil Revision Case Nos. 951 to 955 of 1972).
full_judgment:
Chowdhury A.T.M Masud, J.- These five appeals arise out of five petitions for special leave to appeal preferred by the appellant against the judgment and order of the High Court Division passed in Civil Revision Case Nos. 951 to 955 of 1972. All the cases were disposed of by a single judgment. Common question of law being involved all the appeals are heard together and disposed of by this single judgment.

2. Respondent No. 1 filed Miscellaneous Case Nos. 1002 to 1005 of 1969, in the 2nd Court of Munsif, Tangail, for correction of rights under section 143A of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act. The case of respondent No. 1 was that the case land originally-belonged to Anath Bandhu Guna who died leaving four sons, namely, Akhil Sandhu Guha, Amar Bandhu Guha, Anil Bandhu Guha and Aghar Bandhu Guha as heirs and while the said heirs were owning and possessing the, land they, settled the same with respondent, No. 1 in 1353 B.S. by granting Pattannamas and realising rent by granting dakhilas. Further case of the plaintiff respondent was that the revisional record-of-right was wrongly prepared in the name of the said four sons of Anath Sandhu Guha overlooking the possession of the plaintiff on the basis of the settlement from the owners. The present appellant was made opposite, party No. 7 in the aforesaid Miscellaneous cases, and he contested the cases by filing written objection contending, inter alia, that the documents relied upon by the plaintiff were not genuine; that after the death, of Anath Bandhu Guha the land belonged to his four sons who left for India long before, and the case land vested ill the Custodian of Enemy Property. The learned Munsif allowed the Miscellaneous Cases and directed the correction of the Khatians, holding, inter alia, that the pattannamas Exts. 1 to 1 (b) and the Dakhilas Exts. 2 to 2(g) are genuine and that respondent had been in possession of the properties. On appeal by the present-appellant the learned Subordinate Judge, Tangail, set aside the judgment of the learned Munsif on the finding that the materials produced by the plaintiff were not sufficient for corning to the finding on the case land, He further held that complicated question of title was involved in the matter and that the question of possession was not a material issue in the present case.

3. The respondent then filed revisional applications before the High Court Division challenging the aforesaid judgment and order of the learned Subordinate Judge and obtained Rules. A Single Judge of the High Court Division by the impugned judgment and order reversed the decisions of the lower Appellate Court and restored those of the trial Court, holding, inter alia, that section 143A of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, is meant for, rectification of mistake in the entry of record-of-right and that the incidental reference to the plaintiff's title did not convert the proceeding into a title suit. The learned Judge further held that there was no, complicated question of title involved in the instant cases.

4. Leave was granted to consider as to whether the rectification of record-of-rights as contemplated under section 143A of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, 1950, would be allowed in a case, where the plaintiff's possession in the land in question is based Oil, unregistered Pattannamas and Dhakhilas claimed by the plaintiff to have been granted by owners thereof.

5. Mr. Moksudor Rahman, learned Deputy Attorney-General, appearing on behalf of the appellant argues that in view of the, clear finding of the Court of appeal below that a complicated question of title has arisen in the case, which cannot be decided in a summary proceeding as under section 143A of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, the learned Judge of the High Court Division on misinterpretation of the scope of section 143A reversed the decision of the lower appellate Court and allowed the Miscellaneous Cases.

6. Mr. B. N. Chowdhury, learned Counsel, appearing for the respondents, however, argues that lower appellate Court misconceived the scope of section 143A in holding that possession is not a material question in deciding an application under section 143A. He further contends that the lower appellate Court overlooked the reliefs sought for in the application which were not for declaration of title on the basis of Pattannamas and rent receipts but were applications for correction of the error in the records-of-rights due to the non-consideration of the fact of plaintiff's possession in the case land. The learned Counsel submits that the learned Munsif on consideration of evidence and report of the local investigation by Circle Officer (Dev) found plaintiff in possession and he also found prima facie title in favour of the plaintiff on the basis of Pattannamas and rent receipts and the High Court Division rightly restored the decision of the trial Court setting aside those of the lower Appellate Court.

7. Section 143A of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act since omitted by Ordinance LXIV of 1975 reads as follows:-

(1) Any person aggrieved by an entry or omission of entry in the record-of-rights prepared or revised and finally published under Chapter IV may, not-withstanding anything contained elsewhere in this Act, file an application along with necessary requisites, for the purpose of correcting mistakes in such record-of-rights in the civil court which would have jurisdiction to entertain a suit for possession of the land to which such entry relates or in respect of which such omission was made.

(2) An application filed under sub-section (1) shall be deemed to be a plaint 444 order passed thereon shall have the force of a decree under the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908.

(3) An application filed under sub-section (1) shall contain full particulars of persons likely to be affected by an order on such application and shall also contain the full particulars of the holding to which the entry relates or in respect of which the omission complained of was made.

(4) The Court shall, for the purpose of disposal of application filed under sub-section (I) follow the following procedure, namely.

Clause (b) of section (4) of the said section provides for a report of local inquiry by the Revenue Officer concerned on the subject matter of the application.

8. In the instant case the Circle Officer (Rev), submitted a report finding possession with the plaintiff. It is true that on an earlier occasion on 1969 the Circle Officer stated that possession was taken by the Government treating the Property as vested property. The learned trial Court however could not place any reliance on the earlier report on valid reason and relying on the later report along with the evidence, allowed the Miscellaneous Cases.

<u>9. For disposal of an application under section 143A, question of possession, the Pattannamas and rent-receipts, along with the report of the Revenue Officer were the relevant materials for consideration. The lower appellate Court did not consider the question of possession holding that it was not material for deciding a case under section 143A. The learned Judge of the High Court Division on consideration of the facts and circumstances of the case affirmed the finding of the trial Court holding that no complicated question of title appears in the case. He further heir that the lower appellate court was clearly in error in holding that the question of possession is not material issue and that the case involves a serious question of law which cannot be tried in a summary proceeding under section 143A.</u>

<u>10. An application under section 143A is not a suit for declaration of title but is a proceeding for rectification of mistakes in the records of right prepared on the basis of possession in the land in question. The scheme of the section show that possession is the material question. This was a special provision and this section was inserted after section 143 by E.P. Ordinance VIII of 1967. It was, however, omitted after a few years by Ordinance No. LXIV of 1975.</u>

<u>11. The lower appellate Court apparently misconceived the scope of an application under section 143A and the High Court Division rightly observed that with the scope of section 143A, there is hardly any ground for the appellant to challenge the title of the plaintiff. The learned Judge found that the appellant, Custodian of Enemy Property, had no document in his possession to claim the property as enemy property except the record of right containing the disputed entry. Before the High Court Division no one appeared on behalf of the present appellant. The learned Judge of the High Court Division having found the plaintiff's prima facie title and clear possession of the case land, rightly reversed the decision of the lower appellate Court and restored that of the trial Court No illegality could be pointed out calling for an interference\ with the impugned decision.</u>

<u>The appeals are dismissed without any order as to costs.</u>

End.

full_judgment:
This Rule is directed against the judgment and decree dated 22-1-2008 passed by the learned Special District Judge, Kushtia in Title Appeal No. 140 of 2005 affirming the judgment and decree dated 30-6-2005 passed by the learned Joint District Judge, First Court, Kushtia in Title Suit No. 92 of 1993 in decreeing the suit for specific performance of contract.

2. It may be noted that this revisional application was filed with a delay of 140 days and in that respect Civil Rule No. 583(Con) of 2008 was issued and subsequently the rule was made absolute by order of this court dated 17-2-2009.

3. The opposite-party Nos. 1-3 as plaintiffs instituted Title Suit No.92 of 1993 in the First Court of Joint District Judge, Kumarkhali, Kushtia impleading the present petitioner as defendant No.1 and others praying for a decree for specific performance of contract.

4. The plaintiff case, in short are that the suit land morefully described in the schedule of the plaint is under Mouza Damdama and Bagulat, Police Station-Kumarkhali, District Kushtia belongs to defendant No.1 Srimati Bhabani Bala. The defendant No.2 proposed to sell the land due to met funeral expenses and to pay the loan of her deceased husband. The defendant No.1 proposed to sell land and plaintiffs were agreed to purchase the same for a total consideration of Taka 1,65,000 and accordingly a bainanama was executed on receipt of Taka 1,25,000 on 27-1-1993. It was stipulated therein that on payment of balance consideration of Taka 40,000, the defendant will execute and register the sale deed. The plaintiffs requested to receive the rest of the money but in spite of repeated demand defendant did not execute and register the kabala and last demand was made on 1-8-1993 but she refused to register the suit land and hence the suit.

5. The defendant Nos.1 and 2 contested the said suit by filing a separate written statement denying the material allegations made in the plaint and contending, inter alia, that the suit is barred by limitation and also barred under the principles of waiver, estoppel. There is no cause of action of the suit and the plaintiff’s present suit is not maintainable under sections 39 and 42 of the Specific Relief Act. The positive case of defendant No.1 is that she sold some portion of land for repayment of loan of her deceased husband and also to met funeral expenses. At that time the plaintiffs purchased some non suited land on 3-3-1993 by two registered deed Nos. 272 and 1273 and also by another deed No.4370 dated 17-7-1993. The defendant No.1 had no such requirement to sell the aforesaid land there is no question to purchase the further land. At the time of execution and registration of the aforesaid deeds the plaintiffs took some signature of the defendant No. 1 in the some blank stamp papers and subsequently created those papers as the alleged binanama 27-1-1993. The defendant never sell the land in favour of the plaintiff and she never executed such bainanama in favour of the plaintiff after receipt of total consideration money Taka 1,65,000 and never delivered possession in favour of the plaintiff. It was further stated that the plaintiffs did not disclose about the said bainanama before filing of the suit. Even he did not serve any notice in accordance with the provision of law. The plaintiffs however instituted the present suit by converting the said blank papers into an alleged bainanama. With these averments, the defendant prayed for dismissal of the suit.

6. The defendant No. 3, Md Abul Hossain Mollah, subsequent purchaser from defendant No.1 contested the suit by filing separate written statement. The positive case of the defendant is that the area of land measuring '25 acres of SA Khatian No. 96 of Kalikatola Mouza belong's to defendant No. 1. Area of '26 acres under S.A. Khatian No. 14 of Bagulat Mouza, '21 acres of land from Plot No. 834, '09 acres of land from Plot No. 460, '25 acres of land from Plot No. 834 of Mouza Damdama Mouza, '25 acres of land from Plot No. 174 of Mouza Kalikatola in total 1.09 acres belongs to defendant No.1. She entered into an bainanama on 15-12-1992 for sale of the suit land for a total consideration of Taka 78,000 out of which the defendant No.3 paid Taka 50,000 as advance and delivered possession to defendant No. 3. Subsequently, defendant No.1 further received a sum of Taka 10,000 on 2-2-1993, Taka 8,000 on 3-3-1993, and Taka 7,000 on 4-4-1993 by putting her signature on the back side of the bainanama. Latter on he did not execute and register the Kabala after receiving the balance amount of Taka 3,000. The defendant No. 1 refused to register the kabala on 2-2-1994, then he filed a Title Suit No. 31 of 1994 in the Court of Assistant Judge, Kumarkhali impleading the defendant No.1 as defendant and got a decree on 22-8-1994 and after decree defendant No.1 withdraw Taka 3,000 deposited in the said suit. This defendant filed Title Execution case being No. 4 of 1994 and got a registered Kabala No.1032 dated 26-2-1995 through court and took possession on 3-12-1995. Subsequently, this defendant mutated the land through Mutation Case No. 532/9-2/94-95. The present plaintiff and one Abu Taleb Sk. filed Title Suit No. 56 of 1995 impleading present defendant as defendant No.1 and Bhabani Bala Chowdhury as defendant No.2 and prayed for a declaration that the Judgment and decree dated 22-8-1994 passed in Title Suit No. 31 of 1994 is illegal, collusive, inoperative, void and the deed is not binding upon the plaintiff. In that suit, the present defendant No.2, Bhabani Bala Chowdhury filed written statement and admits the bainanama dated 15-12-1992 and the Title Suit No. 31 of 1994 which is filed in respect of bainanama dated 15-12-1992. This defendant and Bhabani Bala Chowdhury contested in Title Suit No.56 of 1995 and the learned court was pleased to dismiss the suit on 24-6-1997. The plaintiffs have no right, title, interest in the suit land; that the land measuring 26 acres in schedule-1 and 0.58 acres of land described in scheduled-2 and the rest land have been in possession of the defendant No.1 for more than twelve years. The defendant No. 1 disclosed on 14th Magh, 1399 BS correspondence on 27-1-1993 that she did not execute any bainanama in favour of the plaintiff. That the plaintiff is aware about the bainanama executed between the defendant No. 3 and plaintiff. The plaintiff has filed this case just to harass the defendant. Hence, this defendant prays for dismissal of the suit.

7. In this suit plaintiff adduced four p.ws and defendant examined five P.ws to prove their respective case. The learned Joint District Judge, First Court, Kushtia after considering evidence and materials on record decreed the suit by judgment and decree dated 13-6-2005.

8. Against the aforesaid judgment of the learned Joint District Judge, First Court, Kushtia, the defendant No.1 preferred Title Appeal No. 140 of 2005 and defendant No.3 also preferred Title Appeal No.158 of 2005 before the learned District Judge, Kushtia. Eventually, on transfer both the appeals were heard analogously by the Special Judge, Kushtia, who by a single judgment dismissed both the appeal by judgment and decree dated 22-1-2008.

9. Being aggrieved by and dissatisfied with the judgment and decree dated 22-1-2008 passed by the learned Special Judge, Kushtia, the defendant No.1 moved this revisional application and obtained the present Rule.

10. Mr Shasti Sarker, the learned Advocate appearing on behalf of the defendant-petitioner submits that since the defendant denied the execution of the bainanama dated 27-1-1993 but the plaintiff by adducing any evidence failed to prove the bainanama, the appellate court has committed gross an error of law is not dismissing the suit. He further submits that both the courts below committed gross error of law in considering the report of the hand writing expert and that said report ought to have been cancelled because of the fact that the thumb impressions of bainanama are not the thumb impressions of defendant No. 1 He next submits that in a suit for specific performance of contract when the executant deny the execution of the bainapatra it is the duty of the plaintiff to prove the genuineness by comparing the signature with the admitted signature but in the present case same has not been done. He also submits that the scribe of the deed was not examined in the present case rather he was withdrawn as such the defendant will get advantage under section 114(g) of the Evidence Act. He further submits that the bainanama has been created by his obedient person who clearly appears that one thumb impressions over stamp papers on the right side and another one on the left side of the demi papers. He finally submits that the appellate court committed gross error of law in misreading, misconstruing, miss appreciating and non-consider the materials and evidence on record. In support of his submission, he cited certain decisions specially on the point of expert opinion reported in 50 DLR (AD) 88, 45 DLR 169, 1 BLC (AD) 85. It may be noted here that in support of his submission on the finger-print of the defendant No.1, he referred the Book "Disputed Documents Examination and Finger-prints Identification by HR Hardless", 5th Edition 1997, regarding the identity of the LTI in respect of 16 ridge characteristics. He also referred a decision reported in 17 BLD (AD) (1987) 156 in respect of onus on whom lies in a suit for specific performance of contract for sale of the property where the signatures in the documents recording the contract is admitted by the defendants pleading that the same was obtained by threat, intimidation and coercion.

11. On the other hand, Mr Md Nurul Amin, the learned Advocate appearing on behalf of the plaintiffs-opposite-parties by referring paragraph 8 of the written statement submits that since the defendant No.1 has made out an alternative case and denied the execution of the bainanama dated 27-1-1997 stating that: অন্য দলিল Execute করার সময় Black Stamp Paper's sign করে নেয়। In refuting the argument of the learned Advocate of the petitioner, he submits that whether the bainapatra is genuine one or not as the same is denied by the defendant No.1, it is solemn duty of the defendant to prove the said fact that at the time of bainanama some signatures /LTI were obtained by the plaintiff. In support of his submission Mr Md Nurul Amin relied upon the decisions reported in 42 DLR 344, 7 BLD (AD) (1997) 156 = 2 BLC (AD) 103 (which was also relied by the learned Advocate for the petitioner). He next submits that both the courts below concurrently found that the defendant failed to prove that no bainanama was executed in favour of the plaintiff on 27-1-1993 and both the courts below after considering the evidence of attesting witnesses PW 3 and PW 4 in respect of execution and payment of money proved the bainanama. On the contrary, the P.ws failed to prove the alternative story of obtaining LTI malafidely by the plaintiff on the so called bainanama. On this point the learned Advocate relied on the decisions reported in 64 DLR (AD) 133 and 17 BLD (AD) 199 = 2 BLC (AD) 134. He also submits that the defendant No.1 as d.w.1 failed to prove the alternative story stating in her pleadings but in the deposition he categorically stated that: বায়নার কথা জানি না DW 2 did not corroborate such fact.

12. Learned Advocate further submits that the decision which was referred by the learned Advocate for the petitioner reported in 2 BLC (AD) 285 has no manner of application in the present case because of the fact that the expert opinion must be considered with other materials on record and should not be considered expert opinion alone but in the preset case courts below considered expert opinion along with other evidence and materials on record. Mr Md Nurual Amin by referring the order sheet of the trial court specially order dated 13-10-2004 submits that the hand writing expert, court witness, SK Mostafizur Rahman submitted report dated 23.07.1998 but no objection was filed against the said report which will be clearly reveal from order No.51 dated 13-4-2004 but objection was raised when the suit was fixed for pronouncement of the judgment. So, the defendant being a indolent person, he should not get benefit for his own default/wrong, who slept over his own right. He finally submits that both the courts below after considering the evidence and materials on record clearly found that the bainaparta was genuine one. The PWs.1-4 specially PW 3, the attesting witness of the bainapatra clearly stated that: Baina পাঠ করে শোনানো হয় and PW 4 also corroborated by PW 2 and PW 3 in respect of execution and payment of consideration money. In this respect learned Advocate referred the case of Md Fazlul Haque vs BM Rahman @ Mahbubur Rahman reported in 1 MLR (AD) 418. In the said decision it has been held that whether the bainapatra upon which the plaintiff was relying was genuine or not was a question of fact and the learned Additional District Judge upon a proper consideration of the evidence on record including the bainapatra found the case of the plaintiff to be unacceptable. This being a finding of fact, the High Court Division rightly refused to interfere with the same in revision.

13. In the present suit the plaintiff was able to prove the bainanama dated 27-1-1993 executed by the defendant No.1 in favour of the present plaintiffs by his witness Emdad, Firoz and Johir Uddin. Since the LTI of the bainanama was challenged by the defendant and same was sent to the hand writing expert for examination and the hand written expert as court witness proved the report Exhibit-8 dated 7-8-1998 that LTI and bainanama with the admitted LTI of the defendant No.1 Bhabani Bala in sale deed No.1272 dated 3-3-1993 Exhibit-l (Ka) and sale deed No.4371 dated 17-7-1993 Exhibit-1(Kha) respectively. In this respect Mr Shasti Sharker tried to submit that since the bainanama was executed by Bhabani Bala being পর্দানশীল লেডী, the same was not proved in accordance with law. In support of this submission, he referred a decision reported in 50 DLR (AD) 80.

14. I have gone through the decision reported in 50 DLR (AD) 80 but the facts and circumstances of the cited case are totally different from the facts and circumstances of the present case. In the present case the plaintiff was able to prove the Bainanama dated 27-1-1993 (Exhibit-1) by oral and documentary evidence and specially by Exhibit-X, Exhibts-1(Ka)- 1(Kha) and l(Gha).

15. In this connection learned Advocate for the opposite-party by referring section 103 of the Evidence Act tried to submits that burden of prove as to the alternative story stated by the defendant No. 1 in the present case to the effect that at the time of execution of kabalas Exhibt-1(Ka)- 1(Gha), plaintiff obtained LTI from the defendant No. 1 in some blank stamp papers. Since the defendant has failed to prove the said particular fact in the present case of specific performance contract. In the present suit the court after obtaining some LTI of defendant No.1 and comparing that LTI with the LTI appearing the Exhibit-1(Ka)-1(Gha) and also the LTI of bainanama dated 27-1-1993 (Exhibit- 1) clearly found that the LTI appearing in the bainanama and other are admitted LTI of the defendant No.1 are same/similar. In this respect reliance may be placed in a case of Chand Mia (Md) vs Khodeza Bibi reported in 42 DLR 344 wherein it has been held: Burden of proof as to particular fact the defendant in a suit for specific performance contract admits her LTI in the agreement for sale and offers an alternative story as to how her LTI came to be put on the document. The onus lies on her to prove the alternative story.

16. In the present case plaintiff has produced the bainanama as Exhibit-1 from the rightful custody and the defendant No.1 has admitted her LTI therein. She has however given an alternative story as to how she came to put her LTI in alleged bainaparta. But the courts below clearly found that the defendant No.1 failed to prove her alternative story and primary onus has been satisfactorily discharged by the plaintiff as to the execution of the bainanama (Exhibit-1). In this regard, reference may be made to the case of Jahed Ali Mondal vs Jamini Kanta Dey reported in 7 BLD (1987) (AD) 156 it has been held: Onus-Onus on whom lies in a suit for specific performance of a contract for sale of property where the signatures in the documents recording the contract is admitted by the defendant pleading that the same were obtained from them by threat, intimidation and coersion-Law does not require that all facts alleged by the plaintiff shall be strictly proved, for burden of proof is often lightened by presumptions, admissions and estoppels-Primarily onus of course lies, in a civil proceedings, upon the plaintiff-In this case primary onus has been discharged satisfactorily by the plaintiff. Then onus has shifted upon the defendants to prove their particular fact that their signatures were extorted. This onus they failed to discharge. Consequently, the evidence adduced by the plaintiffs as to the execution of the documents stands.

17. In the present case primary onus has been discharged satisfactorily by the plaintiff. Then onus has shifted upon the defendant to prove the particular fact that her LTI/signature was extorted but the defendant failed to discharge her onus. Consequently, the evidence adduced by the plaintiffs as to the execution documents stands. Since both the courts below have concurrently found that the bainanama was executed by the defendant No.1 and such concurrent findings of fact are immune from the interference by this revisional court and the learned Advocate for the petitioner failed to pin point anything that the trial court, as well as of the appellate court misread or non-considered any material evidence on record. In this connection, I can place reliance on the case of Habibur Rahman Bhuiyan (Md) vs Galman Begum reported in 64 DLR (AD) 133 where in our apex court held under: "When a finding of fact is based on consideration of the materials on record, those findings are immune from interference by the revisional Court except there is non-consideration or misreading of the material evidence on record. The High Court Division has no jurisdiction to sit on appeal over a finding of fact."

18. In this respect we can also rely on the case of Amanatullah vs Ali Mohammad Bhuiyan reported in 17 BLD (AD) (1997) 199 = 2 BLC (AD) 134 in that decision it has been held: "A finding of fact whether concurrent or not arrived at by the lower appellate Court is binding upon the High Court Division in revision except in certain well-defined circumstances, such as non-consideration or misreading of the material evidence affecting the merit of the case."

19. I have gone through the decision of both the courts below although the learned Advocate was trying to submit that there was misreading and non-consideration of material evidence but he was miserably failed to point out any misreading and non-consideration of any materials evidence on record.

<u>20. Let us now consider the decision referred by the learned Advocate for the petitioner. The decision reported in 45 DLR 169 it was held that Examination of LTI—: It is true court itself can compare any signature or LTI of any concern person himself under section 73 of the Evidence Act, but it is better to have an expert's opinion also particularly in case of LTI. In the present case it appears that the expert opinion in respect of LTI of defendant No.1 in bainanama (Exhibit-1) and others admitted documents, Sale Deeds, Exhibits-I (Kha) - I (Gha) and Exhibit-X without given any objection from the defendant side. And it further appears that expert opinion (Exhibit-X) was submitted on 23-7-1998 and same was accepted. Against the said report of the hand writing expert no objection was raised by the defendant till 30-10-2004, when the suit was fixed for delivery of judgment. So, the decision of 45 DLR 169 will not any way help the learned Advocate for the petitioner. Learned Advocate for the petitioner also refers the case of 50 DLR (AD) 88 and 1 BLC (AD) 85 but citations as referred by the learned advocate for the petitioner has no manner of application in the facts and circumstances of the present case. Here in the instant case of the learned Advocate for the petitioner failed to point out that the impugned order has occasioned failure of justice to the present petitioner. The mere error of law without occasioning failure of justice cannot by itself be a ground for interference by this court under section 115(1) of the Code of Civil Procedure and in that view of the matter I find nothing to interfere with the same.</u>

21. Thus having regard to all aspects of the case and on careful and overall consideration of the entire evidence on record, provisions of law and the decisions cited above, I am of the opinion that the concurrent findings of the courts below should not be interfered with.

22. In the result, the Rule is discharged without any order as to costs.

Send down the lower court records expeditiously with a copy of judgment for information.

End.

full_judgment:
This Second Appeal at the instance of the contesting defendant No. 2, Province of East Pakistan, now Bangladesh is directed against the judgment and decree dated 14th February, 1968 passed by the learned Subordinate Judge, 1st Additional Court, Sylhet in Title Appeal No. 260 of 1967 reversing those dated 28.8.67 passed by the learned Munsif, Sunamgonj, Sylhet in Title Suit No. 43 of 1966.

2. The present respondent as plaintiff instituted the above suit for declaration of his title in the disputed land described in the second schedule of the plaint. Plaintiffs case is, interalia, that the lands of the 1st schedule were path. 25/26 years back and out of the said lands he took pattan of 11 kedars described in the second schedule of the plaint and started to reclaim the same; that one Narendra instituted a criminal case against him on false allegations of cutting away paddy but subsequently the complainant withdrew the same for non-availability of evidence; that there is a gopat to the west of the disputed lands and the said Narendra brought another criminal case against the plaintiff alleging that he (plaintiff) encroached upon the gopat and in that case a pleader Commissioner was appointed to ascertain whether there was any encroachment on the gopat; that the plaintiff admitted the gopat and remained in possession of the land lying to the west of the same; that thereafter he reclaimed the entire disputed land and possessed it from the time of reclamation and that subsequently the Court of Wards Estate realised rent from the plaintiff by a certificate proceeding, as the management of the estate of the ex-landlord, defendant No. 1 was given to the Court of Wards; that during the last settlement operation, Tahsildar of the Government acquired Estate demanded illegal gratification from the plaintiff but he failed to meet such demand, as a result the employees of the settlement department recorded the entire suit land except 24 decimals (25 cents) in favour of defendant No. 1 and then in the name of defendant No. 2; that the plaintiff was absolutely unaware of the record of right prepared in the name of the defendants and this wrong record clouded the plaintiff's title to the suit-lands and hence the present suit.

3. The defendant No. 2 the Province of East Pakistan now Bangladesh filed written statement to contest the suit denying the material allegations in the plaint and contending inter-alia that the suit-land was first recorded in the name of defendant No. 2 but subsequently on the objection filed by the plaintiff the land of plot no. 1788/1583 was recorded in his name; that the plaintiff had knowledge of the record of right from the beginning; that the suit-land was in khas possession of the ex-rent receiver defendant No. 1 and the same now vested in the Government i.e. the contesting defendant No. 2 under the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act as excess Khas land of the ex-rent receiver; that the suit-land was delivered on temporary borga settlement with one Abdul Karim and Yar Baksh who have been possessing the same since the date of their borga settlement and they have applied for permanent lease of the suit land in respect of which Misc. Case Nos. 181/64-65 and 222/64-65 are pending. It has been further alleged that the plaintiff has no title or possession in the suitlands and hence he is not entitled to any relief as prayed for. The suit is liable to be dismissed with cost.

4. The plaintiff examined including himself five PWs and filed some documents which were marked and numbered as Exts 1 to 6 and the contesting defendant No. 2 examined three DWs and filed some documents marked as Exts. A to G(2) in support of their respective cases. The learned Munsiff now Assistant Judge on consideration of the materials on record was pleased to dismiss the suit on contest with costs against the contesting defendant No. 2 and cxparte against the rest without costs by his judgment and decree dated 20.8.67.

Thereafter on appeal by the plaintiff, the learned Subordinate Judge, Sylhet reversed the judgment and decree of the trial Court and decreed the suit on contest with costs against the contesting defendant and ex parte against the rest and declared the jote right of the plaintiff in the suit-land under the Govt. by his judgment and decree dated 14.12.68.

5. Being aggrieved by the aforesaid judgment and decree of the lower Appellate Court, the contesting defendant No. 2 preferred the Second 1 Appeal in this Court.

6. Mr. Fazlul Huq, the learned Assistant Attorney-General appeared for the defendant appellant and Mr. SK Sinha, the learned Advocate appeared for the plaintiff respondent.

<u>7. At the hearing of this appeal I have been taken through the judgment of the courts below and also the evidence and other materials on record. The learned Assistant Attorney-General on behalf of the appellant firstly contended that the lower appellate Court committed error of law in not holding that the suit suffers from vagueness of the description of the suit-land about which the trial Court came to a finding to the effect that the suit was not identifiable and no effective decree could be passed in such a case. Mr. SK Sinha, the learned Advocate for the respondent on the other hand contends that the question of vagueness of the suit property was neither raised in the pleading i.e. written statement filed by the defendant No. 2 nor any issue was framed about the same by the trial Court. Hence this question should not have been discussed or decided by the trial Court. Besides its finding on the said question was bad and illegal and rightly reversed by the lower Appellate Court. In this connection he has referred to some decisions reported in 27 DLR 413 in the case of Md. Ibrahim Vs. Md. Alauddin and others and in the case of Abdul Hannon & ors Vs. Halima Khatun and others at page 465 of the said report and also another decision reported in AIR 1969, SC page 1291 in the case of Gappulal Vs. Thakurji Shriji Dawarkadheeshji and another relevant paragraphs 6 & 7. In the decision reported in 27 DLR at page 413 it has been observed as follows :</u>

<u>"In determination of questions of facts the parties should not be allowed to lead evidence without proper pleadings. It is no longer a mere technicality that material facts should be specifically pleaded and omission to do so:- would certainly deprive the other side of an-opportunity to meet the allegation. This salutary provision of law is designed as a safeguard so that one cannot be taken by surprise by the other side at the time of trial. In the decision reported in AIR 1969 SC page 1291, it has been observed in para 7 that" In the absence of any pleading and issue on this question the High Court was in error in recording the finding that the two shops were sub-let towards the end of 1947 after the Jaipur Rent Control 1947 came into force."</u>

8. Admittedly in the present case, the question of vagueness of the suit property was not taken or raised in the pleading and also no issue was framed by the trial Court on the same, but it appears that the trial Court on the basis of the submission of the learned Advocate of the contesting defendant came to a finding to the effect that "I agree with the learned Advocate for the defendant and opine that no effective decree can be passed when the subject-matter of the suit is unidentifiable." The lower Appellate Court of course framed a specific point for determination on this matter, namely the point No. 2 of his judgment which is as follows : "Whether the finding of the learned lower court as to non-maintainability of the suit over alleged vagueness of the disputed land is maintainable." and decided the same in favour of the plaintiff by reversing the finding of the trial Court and holding that "I can not see eye to eye with this contention of the learned lower Court as it is no body's case before him that the description of the disputed land was vague. The judgment shows that no such issue has been framed. Thus it. appears to me that the learned lower Court has found vagueness in the disputed land, although it was not contended by the contesting defendants. The DW 1 Md. Araf Miah is a Tahsildar attached to Painda Tahsil Office. In chief he deposed that the area of the disputed land is 4.63 acres. In the plaint the area shown in schedule 2 is 3.08 acres and it is to the western portion of schedule I land. So, I find that this land is to be taken out from the western side of the Schedule. I land. Hence it appears that there is no vagueness in the disputed land."

<u>9. Now, let me see whether there is any illegality in the aforesaid finding of the court of appeal below. It is true that matter which is not specifically raised in the pleading, the parties cannot be allowed to lead evidence on such matter. In the present case, the question of vagueness of the suit land has not been alleged by the contesting defendant and it appears from the plaint that in the schedules, the suit land has boon described by boundaries. It is also to be noticed that out of 4.63 acres in plot No. 1583 which was allegedly recorded in the name of defendant No. 1 and thereafter defendant No. 2, the plaintiff has claimed his title with respect to 3.08 acres of land (11 kodars) described in the second schedule of the suit land in plot No. 1583, but the trial Court without noticing the fact that the description of the suit lands has been given by the boundaries, came to an abrupt and arbitrary finding that the subject-matter of the suit was not identifiable whereas the lower appellate court has noticed the description of the suit-land given by boundaries and found that the same is quite identifiable and not vague, thus, it appears that the lower Appellate Court on proper scrutiny of the plaint schedules came to such finding and I think he has rightly reversed the finding of the trial Court on the said question. However, the facts of this case are quite distinguishable from the eases reported in 27 DLR and AIR 1969 SC. In the instant case no new fact required to be examined or proved by evidence to see whether the allegation of vagueness of the suit-land was correct or not. In this connection I may look to the provision of rule 3 of Order 7 of the Code of Civil Procedure which reads as follows :</u>

<u>"Where the subject-matter of the suit is immovable property, the plaint shall contain a description of the property sufficient to identify it, and, in case such property can be identified by boundaries or numbers in a record of settlement of survey, the plaint shall specify such boundaries". From the above it is clear that the description of the suit-land can also be given by boundaries for proper identification of the same and the Court may be satisfied with the same. In the instant case the trial Court possibly without noticing the above provision of law and the description of the suitland by boundaries wrongly held that the subject matter of the suit was not identifiable. The lower Appellate Court however took the correct view and rightly reversed the finding of the trial Court. Apart from that, the instant suit was a suit for declaration of title only and in fact for correction of the alleged wrong record of right in the Khatian and there was neither any prayer for confirmation of his possession nor recovery of possession of the suit and. From that point of view also it appears that the point of alleged vagueness was not so material for the adjudication of the present suit. So, I find no substance in the contention of the learned Advocate for the appellant in his first point. The next contention of the teamed Advocate for the appellant is that the impugned judgment is not a proper judgment of reversal as the lower Appellate Court has failed to advert to the reasoning of the trial Court in deciding the suit and also it has failed to take into consideration the material evidence particularly the documentary evidence of the contesting defendant, as a result there has been a serious miscarriage of justice. In support of his contention, the learned Advocate for the appellant has referred to a number of decisions reported in 35 DLR AD page 216 and 17 DLR pages 687, 547, 541 and 105. In elaborating his submission, the learned Advocate for the appellant has drawn my attention to the judgment of the trial Court as well as to that of the court of appeal below and also to the evidence on record. It has already been stated that both the sides adduced evidence, oral and documentary in support of their respective cases. From the side of the defendant appellant a number of documents were filed and they were marked as Ext. A to G(2); to these documents, the trial Court took into consideration, most of them along with the documents filed by the plaintiff and decided the question of title and possession of the parties over the suit lands, but it appears from the judgment of the lower Appellate Court that save and except document Ext. E of the contesting defendant, the learned Subordinate Judge has not taken into consideration any other documents of the defendant, but those documents appear to be quite material not only to support the defence case but also to test the genuineness of the plaintiffs document  of title particularly Ext. 1. Apart from that, it appears that the trial Court made some observation with regard to the question of adverse possession. But the lower Appellate Court is silent on the same. Besides, it is also the contention of the learned Advocate for the appellant that the lower appellate Court on a misreading and also upon material mistaken assumption of fact came to an illegal finding in respect of the right, title of the plaintiff. It appears from the judgment of the trial Court that it held while considering the question of possession as follows : "PW 4 Tozammul Ali has corroborated the evidence adduced by PWs 1, 2 and 3, I do not find any contradiction in their evidence. I therefore, accept their evidence and opine that the plaintiff has possession in the suit land. "But the lower appellate Court appears to have held apparently upon misreading and also mistaken assumption of fact that "PW 4 Tajammul Ali deposed in corroboration of the plaint case of settlement and possession of the disputed land by plaintiff". The lower Court found that there was no contradiction amongst the PWs in respect of plaintiff's case of settlement and possession. It is apparent that the trial Court in its observation did not refer to any settlement. In the observation of the lower appellate Court the word "settlement" was wrongly quoted. From the above, it appears that the lower appellate Court did not apply its judicial mind to the facts and circumstances of the case and the materials on record and arbitrarily found the mere submission of the learned Advocate for the plaintiff to be a view taken by the trial Court in respect of the alleged tenancy right of the plaintiff which is not correct. In the trial Court's judgment it has been observed by the learned Munsif as follows:— "The learned Advocate for the plaintiff has argued that he had called for all papers relating to the. suit land from the ex-landlord. The non-production of those documents by the defendant would lead us to presume that the plaintiff has tenancy right in the suit-land. The above fact by itself does not exonerate the plaintiff from proving ' his case. "The plaintiff in order to succeed must prove, beyond reasonable amount of doubt his title in the suit land."</u>

10. But with regard to this, the lower appellate Court observed as follows" "In this connection, it is to be noted that the plaintiff called for all necessary papers to prove his jote right from the ex-landlord. It was argued by the learned lawyer for the plaintiff that he called for all papers relating to disputed lands from the ex-landlord but none were produced and the non production of these documents by the defendants would lead us to presume that the plaintiffs had tenancy right in the suit land, observed by the learned lower Court." The learned Subordinate Judge without noticing the subsequent line of observation of the learned Munsif, it appears that he took the alleged presumption of the tenancy right of the plaintiff in the suit land as urged by the learned Advocate for the plaintiff to be an acceptance of the said right by the trial Court. Thus from an analysis of the facts and circumsatnces of the case and the materials on records I am of the opinion that the judgment of the Court of appeal below is not a proper judgment of reversal anal the same should be set aside. In view of the above, on setting aside the impugned judgment and decree, the appeal is generally sent back on remand to the Court of appeal below for rehearing and fresh decision in accordance with law, but as it is a very old suit of the year 1966 and when all materials are available on record, I feel that in the interest of justice this Court should exercise its jurisdiction under section 103 of the Code of Civil Procedure and decide the issues involved in the suit or the appeal on consideration of the materials on record. And this view of mine finds support from the decisions in the case of Khandakar Mohiuddin Vs. Syed Moin Ahmed reported in 28 DLR SC 85 and in the case Ajufannessa @ Aji Bibi and others Vs. Safar Miah and ors. reported in 30 DLR (SC) 41 and also in the case of Md. Altafur Rahman Vs. Tantijur Rahman reported in 30 DLR (SC) 236. In that view of the matter, I therefore want to decide the appeal afresh on consideration of the evidence on record and the facts and circumstances of the case.

11. Plaintiffs main case is that he took pattan (settlement) from the ex-landlord of the suit estate and on payment of rents he has been possessing the same after reclamation of the suit lands since 25/26 years back. To prove the case of his title, the plaintiff admittedly failed to produce any document save and except Ext. 1. He has stated that he has lost his dakhilas of payment of rents in respect of the suit-lands. He has submitted, of course one document namely Ext. 1 dated 5.7.53, a receipt of payment of rental of Rs. 11/4 annas to the Court of Wards which allegedly took over the administration of the same. According to the plaintiff, this is the only basic document to prove his title in the suit-lands. He has of course submitted some other documents namely Exts. 2 to 2(a). Exhibit 2 relates to an Advocate Commissioner's report in a proceeding in respect of Criminal Case No. 187 of 1943 of the Court of SDO Sunamganj between one Narendra Kumar Purakaysta as first party and Shamsher Ali and others as second party and Ext. 2(a) relates to a sketch map in respect of the same prepared by the said Advocate Commissioner, but there is nothing specific in these documents to show any connection with the suit-lands. Ext. 3 it appears to be a ceartified copy of an order dated 10.6.41 showing withdrawal of a case being-CR Case No. 575 of 1941 between one Naresh, Chandra Rai Vs. Shamsher under section 379 IPC and again this has-also no reference to the suit land. Ext. 4 another certified copy of judgment of another case being Cast No. 187 M/1943 between one Narendra Kumar Purakyastha Vs. Shamsher Ali and others under Section 147 CrPC dated 10.1.44. This appears to have also no reference to the suit-land but it has reference to a gopat. Ext. 5 is a certified copy of a plaint of Title Suit No. 19/65 between one Abdul Mannaf Vs. Shamser Ali and Ext. 6 appears to be a petition praying for an order of dismissal of the suit for non prosecution. This appears to have some reference with regard to possession over the suit-land but nothing about the title of the plaintiff over the same. All the above documents Exts. 2 to 6 have been filed by the plaintiff mainly in order to show his possession over the suit-lands. Exts. 3, 4 and 5 were admitted into evidence without objection but other documents namely Ext. 1, 2 to 2(i) and 6 were admitted into evidence after objection. The contesting defendant on the other hand filed Ext. A, a Fortified copy of the choice list and the list of excess khas land of the ex-landlord defendant No. 1 Dewan Obaidur Reza Chowdhury and Ext. B, is a certified copy of the khatian No. 49 not Paschim Haripur; Ext. C and C(1) are certified copies of Objection petition and the order sheet in Objection Case Nos. 18 of 1960 under section 19(1) of the EBS. A and Tenancy Act, filed by plaintiff Shamser Ali; Ext. D, D(1) are certified copies of the order sheet and the objection petition of plaintiff Sham= Ali under section 50 of East Bengal State Acquisition and Tenancy Act in Miscellaneous Case No. 37/64; Ext. E is a carbon copy of order regarding possession of certain property in Proposal case No. 215 of 1960 and Ext. F is a certified copy of settlement map and Ext. G to G(2) for petitions of submission of rayati settlement proposal of the suit-lands by one Karim, Yar-Baksh and Abdun Nur. Of these documents. Ext. B, and Exts. C-C(1), D,D(1) series have been admitted into evidence without objection. But Ext. AEF-G-G(g) series appeared to have been admitted into evidence after objection. The trial Court on consideration of the evidence on record found possession of the suit-lands with the plaintiff, but with regard to the alleged documentary evidence Ext. I he has observed that the same does not show that the payment of rent was made in respect of the suit-lands He has also observed that the plaintiff has failed to prove a single dakhila of rent either to the landlord or to the Government acquired Estate and also there is no reasonable and satisfactory explanation as to the non-production of the alleged dakhilas. Now, the lower appellate Court appears to have believed this document Ext. I and found that payment of rent by this document was made against claim in Certificate Case No. 359 of the year 1952-1953. Now, I have to see how far the finding of the lower appellate Court is correct and sustainable in respect of the alleged title of the plaintiff in the suit-lands. So far the question of possession over the suit-lands, both the Courts below on consideration of the evidence on record, oral and documentary came to a concurrent finding in favour of the plaintiff. In the Second Appeal, I have no authority to disturb this concurrent finding of fact on possession unless it is found to be perverse or contrary to the evidence on record. Furthermore, inspite of the finding on possession by the trial Court in favour of the plaintiff the contesting defendant did not prefer any cross objection against such finding. So, I, have nothing to interfere with the same.

12. Now, I have to see only which court is correct in deciding the question of title of the plaintiff over the suit-lands. It is contended by the learned Advocate for the plaintiff-respondent that the contesting defendant has failed to prove its plea that the suit-property vested in the Government and the Government got khas possession of the same from the ex-rent-receiver. It appears that in order to prove vesting of the suit property in the Government the defendant has produced Ext. A a certified copy of the order-sheet of the vesting case along with the list of excess lands of the ex-rent-receiver and examined a Tahsildar of the Tashil office as DW 1 and no other document has been filed in the Court in proof of vesting. Mr. SK Sinha, the learned Advocate submits that the defendant has failed to prove the vesting of the suit property, particularly when the Gazettee Notification in this connection has not been filed by the contesting defendant. The learned Advocate for the appellant on the other hand submits that by a Gazettee Notification, the wholesale acquisition of the interest of all the rent receivers was made and the rent-receivers were asked to submit their lists of choice lands, but so far this suit-property is concerned, the ex-landlord did not make any choice as a result the same vested in the Government as excess land by operation of law. As regards the non production of the Gazettce notification, he however could not give satisfactory explanation. Be that as it may, whatsoever weakness there might be in the defendant's case, the plaintiff must prove his own case satisfactorily to obtain a decree. In that view of the matter, let. me see how far the plaintiff has been able to prove his title in the suit lands. Admittedly, the plaintiff could not file any document of tide save and except Ext. I, of course he has led some oral evidence also, but those relate to his possession and not to his alleged claim of title in the suit-lands. As regards his other documents, it has been observed by the Court of Appeal below to the effect that "Besides these, certified copies of the order-sheet, judgment and plaint of other criminal cases and title suits are filed but they will not be of much help to the plaintiff." In finding title in favour of the plaintiff, a presumption has been tried to be drawn by the lower appellate Court in favour of the plaintiff's alleged tenancy right in the suitlands for alleged non-production of some documents by the defendants alleged to have been called for by the plaintiff from them.

13. The learned Advocate for the appellant however submits that nothing appears in the order-sheet of the trial Court that any such application was filed on behalf of the plaintiff calling for the alleged original documents from the defendants and that no officer of the Court of Wards Estate was cited as a witness to come to court with the original records of the said Estate. I have myself scrutinised the records and the order sheet of the suit but nothing is found in the order sheet. Only an application is found without any verification and without any date with a newly inserted page No. 22A citing the ex-rent receiver Abdur Reza Chowdhury and some other officers of the Court of Wards as witnesses. It is submitted by the learned Advocate for the appellant that it was a spurious act of the plaintiff and he somehow inserted this application in the record in collusion with the office staff subsequently and it was not at all placed before the Court and hence no order was made thereon. The said application appears to have been written by a Moharar but neither his signature nor the signature of the Advocate concerned can be identified. Apart from that the impressed seal also appears to be unrecognizable and nothing can be read on the said seal. Thus the submission of the learned Advocate for the appellant appears to be correct and no such application was actually presented before the Court in due course and hence no order was passed on the same. So, unless the ex-landlord or the staff or any officer of the Courts of Wards Estate as witness was summoned by the court asking him or them to produce the original documents a presumption of the tenancy-right in favour of the plaintiff in the suit-lands for non production of the same cannot bedrawn and this aspect of the matter has totally escaped the notice of both the courts below and as a result there has been a miscarriage of justice.

14. Now there is no denying of the fact that the plaintiff's success is dependant on the proof of genuineness of the document Ext I and its relation with the suit lands. On the face of it there is not specification or description of the land for which the alleged rent receipt was obtained. It appears that it was granted on behalf of the Court of Wards Estate by one Bhupesh Chandra Nag, but the plaintiff has neither examined that grantor Bhupesh Chandra nor he has given any explanation as to whether he was available in the country or not and why he has nt been produced in court as witness. Rather PW 2 says that the said Bhupesh is about 30/32 years who is alive. The document appears apparently to be related to the certificate case being No. 359/52-53, but the plaintiff has failed to bring any paper of such certificate case to show that the same related to the suit-lands. Besides from Ext I, it appears that the alleged payment of rent was made on behalf of Shamsher Ali by one Ainuddin of village Baishaber but that Ainuddin has not been produced. Similarly PW 3 says that one Janick Ali and Altafun assisted the plaintiff in reclaiming the suit land but they have also not been produced to support the plaintiffs case. Along with this, if we examine the document filed by the contesting defendant namely Exts C, C(1), D and D(1) which show that the plaintiff filed objection cases ups, 19(1) and 50 of the East Bengal State Acquisition and Tenancy Act before the Revenue Authorities against recording of the names of the ex-rent-receiver in the settlement khatians but the said petitions were disallowed. It appears that Exhibits C and D series relate to objection cases of the years 1960 and 1964 relating to plot No. 1583 but strange enough this document Ext I allegedly a document of title of the plaintiff which is dated 5.7.53, was not produced before the revenue authority for correction of the record and instead in Objection case No. 18 of 1960 a RR of Rs. 2/8/ dated 27.5.62 was produced before the revenue authority as revealed by Ext C(1). This smacks of the concoction of the document Ext 1. Had it been a genuine document in possession of the plaintiff, certainly it would have been placed before the revenue authorities in the objection cases to prove his title in the suit lands and to get the record of right corrected in his name. So, the trial Court very correctly disbelieved the claim of title of the plaintiff. But the lower appellate court wrongly relied on the said document Ext I and illegally found title in favour of the plaintiff. In this connection the oral evidence of the parties may also be taken into consideration. PW 1 is the plaintiff. He himself at the very inception of his deposition stated that the disputed land was formerly khas patit of the ex-landlord Dewan Obaidur Reza. Then he said that he had taken pattan of 11 kedars of land some 25/26 years ago. He stated that he lost his dakhilas but this statement was not made in the plaint. He admitted that he has no papers to prove taking of pattan of the suit land from the ex-landlord. The other PWs namely PW 2-4 deposed only about possession of the plaintiff over the suit land and not about his claim of title by way of pattan. So, there is no evidence to corroborate PW I in his claim of title over the suit lands. On the contrary DW 1 has come to say that the suit property belonged to ex-rent-receiver defendant No. 1 which subsequently vested in the Government defendant No. 2. As to possession of the plaintiff, of course both the Cburts below on consideration of the evidence on record came to concurrent finding in his favour. But it is not the case of the plaintiff that he acquired title by way of adverse possession. He tried to base his claim of title on his alleged pattan which he ultimately failed to establish. Besides, it has not been contended on behalf of the plaintiff that he has fulfilled the basic requirements of any claim of title by adverse possession over the suit lands. Thus having regard to all aspects of the case and on careful and overall consideration of the entire evidence on record and the facts and circumstances of the case, I am of the firm view that the plaintiff has totally failed to prove his right, title and interest in the suit land, though he has been found to be in possession of the same. For the reasons stated above, I therefore find that the impugned judgment and decree of the lower appellate Court can not be sustained in law and on facts and the same should be set aside.

In the result, the appeal is allowed. The impugned judgment and decree of the Court of appeal below are set aside and those of the trial Court are upheld. In the facts and circumstances of the case, there will be no order as to costs. Send down the lower courts' records immediately.

End.

case_source: (From the judgment and decree dated 6.12.1982 passed by 2. Defendants are the appellants Plaintiff the High Court Division, Rangpur Bench in respondent filed Title Suit No. 66 of 1966 in S.A. No. 1355 of 1968)
full_judgment:
Badrul Haidar Chowdhury, J.—This appeal by special leave is directed against the judgment and order passed by the High Court Division in Second Appeal No. 1355 of 1968.

2. Defendants are the appellants Plaintiff respondent filed Title Suit No. 66 of 1966 if the Court of Munsif, 2nd Court, Serajganj for declaration of title and recovery of possession. His case was that the suit land described in the schedule Ka and Kha of the plaint appertaining to Khatian Nos. 123 and 125 respectively of mouza Bhangari originally belonged to landlords Girija Sannyal and Aswini Kumar Sannayal. Basarat Akanda and Maidan Akanda used to cultivate the suit land in raiyati right as tenants paying half of the produce as rent. Maidan Akanda surrendered his land in favour of the landlords who in turn gave that land in borga to Bassarat Akand. Bassarat Akanda died leaving two sons namely Mofiz Akanda and Mahim Akanda who by inheritance got the land of Khatian No. 123 of Schedule 'Ka' as raiyati tenant at a rental of half of the produce and also possessed the land of Khatian No. 125 of Schedule Kha in borga like, their father. Having difficulties in paying rent in crop Mafiz and Mahim prayed to the landlords for conversion of Khatian No. 123 into money rent and further prayed for leasing out the land of Khatian 125 to them by fixing a jama. Narayan Chandra Roy, Manager of the Estate leased out 3.91 acres of land of Khatian Nos. 123 and 125 to the plaintiff Mofiz and Mohim at a rental of Rs. 15/8/- annas on 15th Chaitra, 1348 B.S. after receiving Nazarana and issued a Likhon in favour of Mahim and Mofiz who had been possessing the land as tenant on payment of rent to the Sanayal landlords. The present provisional rent Roll Khatian has been finally published in the name of Mahim and Mofiz who have sold two plots out of their jote to the plaintiffs by registered kabala dated 28.1.65. His further case was that the defendants cut and took away jute grown by the plaintiffs for which the criminal case was started but the case was dismissed and being encouraged by an order of acquittal the defendants dispossessed the plaintiffs from the suit land on 11.6.66.

3. The suit was resisted by the defendants who contended that Basarat Akanda and Maidan Akanda had no raiyati right in the suit land. Both of them were simple bargadars under the landlords namely Sannyals. Mohim and Mofiz never possessed the land in raiyati right. Therefore the plaintiff's purchase of the suit land from Mofiz and Whim did not confer any title on the plaintiff. Defendants, it was contended, were in possession and took pattan of the suit land by Amalnama. The trial Court on consideration of the evidence decreed the suit. Appellate Court, however, reversed the decision and allowed the appeal and found that the defendants are in possession by making an observation as under:

''The PRR in my opinion, has been correctly recorded in the names of Sannyals because they did not lease out to either party. It is their has land. Neither plaintiff's vendor nor defendants was able to record their names in the PRR and they could not do so as they actually bad no title and possession for the purpose of recording their names, defendants are found to be in possession, not known in what capacity".

In that view of the matter the appeal was allowed. In Second Appeal the High Court Division on analysis of the evidence found that the plaintiff had proved the tenancy right of Mofiz and Mohim and their settlement by Ext. 3. This Ext. was not considered by the Court of appeal below in correct perspective. Ext. 3 Likhon was issued in 134.8 B.S. for the lease of the land of both the Khatians. Appellate Court below considered that there was no corroborative evidence and accordingly disbelieved this Likhon. The High Court Division rightly pointed that there was positive evidence of P.W. 3 to substantiate the genuineness of the Ext. 3. It is found to be genuine as it has been found by the trial court, the High Court Division inferred that the suit was filed within 12 years from 1363 B.S. and the same was not barred by limitation. Next the kabala Ext. 1 of the plaintiff had been admitted by both P.Ws. Mofiz and Mohim. It is clear that the lower appellate court below wrongly set aside the judgment of the Munsif inasmuch as plaintiff's title has been amply proved by the oral evidence as well whereas the appellate Court below had found the possession in favour of the defendant by saying "not known, what capacity". When a dispute is brought before the Court for adjudication, it is necessary for the Court to come to conclusion this way or the other. The defendants have got no document of title. This was noticed by the appellate Court below as well. The defendants relied on an Amalnama Ext. C and C (I) and even the appellate Court below compared the signature of Aswin Sannayal on Ext. C series with dakhilas Ext. D series and found that Ext. C series were not genuine. Notwithstanding this finding that the defendant had got no document of title yet the judgment and decree of the trial court was set aside.

Mr. Pal appearing for the plaintiff respondents canvassed that the appellate Court below had reversed the decision of the trial court on misreading and dis-reading the positive evidence on record.

<u>4. Mr B.N. Chowdhury appearing for the defendant-appellant contended that the plaintiffs' vendors were mere borgadar and their tenancy could not be proved. The position of the defendants is worse. In the Khatian it is mentioned that the right of Sannyal was মধ্যস্বত্ব চিরস্থায়ী (illegible) and as such a lease holder under them would be tenant. But strangely enough in the Amalnama of the defendants Ext. C series, it shows that Korfa pattan. The trial Court concluded that the contention of the plaintiff that these were created after the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act when the Sannayal became raiyat by operation of law and on a mistaken notion thought that no lease could be granted to them and therefore korfa pattan was mentioned. This position shows that Ext. C series were created for the purpose of the suit the inference drawn from such document—is a question of law and there is no escape from the conclusion that the trial court was correct in drawing the conclusion as it did. Now the question of status of the plaintiff's vendor. In the case of Abu Nasser Sayedullah Vs. Abdul Malik alias Mala and another 12 D.L.R. 206 a single Bench considered section 3(17) proviso and held that a borgadar could become a tenant before the introduction of the provision to clause (17) of section 3 but cannot be so after its introduction unless the conditions in the exception are fulfilled. The decision was doubted in 14 DLR 801 in the case of Munir Mondal and others Vs. Paramatha Nath Chowdhury and others by a Division Bench and it was held that borgadar recorded in C.S. Khatian as tenant before introduction of the provision in 1928, can plead tenancy right after the introduction of the proviso. It was observed that the interpretation given in 12 DLR would create anomalous position namely once a tenant, he could not be considered as tenant for the subsequent period. Reliance was placed on high authority, A.I.R. 1940 P.C. 124 that such construction so unreasonable and imprecise ought not to have been preferred when another construction is open. Subsequently. In the case of Krishna Chandra Paul Vs. Khoyar Sardar, 20 DLR 745 another Single Bench took the view that a person who is holding land by giving a share of the crop must be doing so under the system know as Borga, Adhi or Bhag and, if the C.S. record show that before the amendment in 1928 the person was holding the land as a permanent raiyati and the rent was fixed at half the crop and that case is included in the rent which has been fixed, then it must be held that the person was not holding the land under the system of Borga, or adhi but he was a tenant with occupancy right and the rent was fixed by which the cess was also included.</u>

5. Proviso to section 3(17) may now be considered. It reads: "Provided that a person who, under the system generally known as "Adhi", Borga" or "Bhag" cultivates the land of another person on condition of delivering a share of the produce to that person, is not a tenant, unless—(i) such person has been expressly admitted to be a tenant by his landlord in any document executed by him or executed in his favour and accepted by him; or

(ii) He has been or is held by a Civil Court to be a tenant."

<u>6. Having considered these three decisions the opinion is that the 14 DLR 801 had correctly interpreted the law which was reiterated in 20 DLR. 746 and in that view of the matter there is no hesitation in saying that the plaintiffs' vendor was tenant of the landlords Sannyals and Ext. 3 is such document backed by Ext. 4 series and evidence of P.W. 3. The plaintiff has filed the dakhilas Ext. 4 series and P.W.3 Narayan Chandra Roy admitted that these dakhilas were written by Provash Chandra who was the Tahsildar of the Estate. The Appellate Court below had discarded these evidence without any reason. Next, on the possession, the appellate court below took the view that the defendant's possession had bee proved. Mr. Pal has placed the evidence P.W.5 on whom the appellate court relied for coming to its conclusion. On scrutiny, it is found teat the appellate Court had misread the evidence and no inference could be drawn as it did for finding possession of the defendant. Plaintiff purchased it by registered kabala from his vendors who were the tenants, therefore his title was rightly declared by the trial Court and the High Court Division took the correct view that the appellate Court below had drawn erroneous inference from the evidence and rightly set aside the judgment of the appellate Court below and restored the trial court's decision.</u>

<u>In the result therefore this appeal is dismissed with costs.</u>

End.

lawyer:
M. Quamrul Haque Siddique with AKM Alamgir Parvez, Advocates ----- For the Petitioner.
Rokanuddin Mahmud with Syed Mamun Mahbub, Advocates ----- For Respondent No. 1.
M. Khaled Ahmed with Md Ashiqur Rahman, Advocates -----For Respondent No.7.
parties:
Jamal Uddin (Md) ------ Petitioner
Vs.
Major General Abdus Salam (Retired) and others ------ Respondents
full_judgment:
Md Khurshid Alam Sarkar J: This Rule has been issued calling upon the respondents to show cause as to why the holding of the Office of the Member of Parliament (MP) from the constituency No. 154 Mymensingh-9 (Nandail) by respondent No. 1, as declared by the Election Commission, shall not be declared to have been held without lawful authority and of no legal effect and, further, to show cause as to why respondents No.2 and 4 shall not be directed to declare the seat of the Member of Parliament from the constituency No. 154 Mymensingh-9 (Nandail) held by respondent No. 1 vacant and thereby hold fresh election for the said seat with- in 90 days from the date of decision, and/or pass such other or further order or orders as to this Court may seem fit and proper.

2. Succinctly, the facts of the case, as stated in the writ petition and supplementary affidavit, are that the petitioner, by virtue of being an inhabitant of Village- Tashra, Upazilla-Nandail, District-Mymensingh, is a constituent of constituency No. 154, Mymensigh-9 (Nandail) wherefrom Major General (retired) Abdus Salam (hereinafter referred to as respondent No. 1) has been elected in the 9th parliamentary election and since then holding the post of Member of Parliament (MP). In the estimation and consideration of the petitioner, respondent No. 1 is a disqualified person to be elected and, thereby, to hold the public office of MP, as per provisions of our Constitution and Representation of the People's Order, 1972, and, as such, the petitioner has brought this application under Article 102(b)(ii).

3. It is stated that on 23-11-2008 respondent No.1 submitted his nomination paper as a candidate of 9th parliamentary election for the constituency No. 154, Mymensingh-9 (Nandail) and on 4-12-2008 the same was cancelled by the Returning Officer (hereinafter referred to as respondent No.9) on the ground of being a 'loan defaulter' and when an appeal was preferred by respondent No.1, the Election Commission (hereinafter referred to as respondent No.3) dismissed it on 10-12-2008.

4. Side by side, on 4-12-2008 respondent No. 1 filed the writ petition No. 9819 of 2008 (hereinafter referred to as 'other writ petition') challenging the legality and propriety of the action of Bangladesh Bank and others in inclusion of his name in the CIB report as a 'loan 'defaulter' and the same was though moved before this Court but was adjourned for 11-12-2008. Then, by filing a supplementary-affidavit as to the cancellation of his nomination paper, respondent No.1 prayed for giving a direction upon respondent No. 9 and respondent No.3 to accept his nomination paper and an interim order of direction was passed upon the said respondents to allow respondent No. 1 to contest in the aforesaid election albeit no Rule was issued on the orders cancelling the nomination of respondent No. 1 passed by the Election Commission and Returning Officer. Thereafter, when the 'other writ petition' was placed before a Division Bench of the High Court Division on 17-12-2008, the said interim order of direction dated 11-12-2008 was extended till disposal of the Rule. It is stated that respondent No.1, after obtaining the aforesaid favourable order from this Court, did never bother to take any step to get the 'other writ petition' heard. Having been won in the 9th parliamentary election, respondent No.1 took oath as a Member of Parliament and since then he has been holding the post of MP. It is stated that since respondent No. 1 did never challenge the legality of the orders of cancellation of his nomination paper either in this Court nor in Election Tribunal and, as such, orders passed by the Returning Officer on 4-12-2008 cancelling his nomination paper and the order passed by the Election Commission on 10-12-2008 affirming the Returning Officer's said order dated 4-12-2008 are still in operation and their findings of fact, on the CIB report published by the Bangladesh Bank that respondent No. 1 is a 'loan defaulter', do stand correct. It is stated that since the petitioner was a 'loan defaulter', he was not and, even, at present is not legally eligible and competent to be a Member of Parliament and to hold the said post. Therefore, having been aggrieved by the holding of the position of MP by respondent No.1, the petitioner seeks to challenge the authority of respondent No. 1 to the post of MP. Hence, this Rule.

5. While respondent No. 1 contested the case by filing affidavit-in-opposition, supplementary affidavit and placing relevant laws, references and arguments and respondent NO.7 (Janata Bank Ltd) opted to appear in the instant case by filing Vokalatnama only, the remaining respondents namely, Bangladesh Jatio Shangshad (hereinafter referred to as respondent No.2), Bangladesh Election Commission (hereinafter referred to as respondent No.3), Ministry of Law, Justice and Parliamentary Affairs (hereinafter referred to as respondent No.4), Credit Information Bureau of Bangladesh Bank (hereinafter referred to as respondent No.5), Dynamic Textile Industries Limited (hereinafter referred to as respondent No.8) and the Deputy Commissioner, and the Returning Officer, Mymensingh (hereinafter referred to as respondent No.9) did not avail of the opportunity of appearing before this Court.

6. Respondent No. 1 by filing affidavit-in- opposition contends, inter alia, that he participated in the 9th national parliamentary election as a valid candidate in pursuant to the order dated 11- 12-2008 passed by a vacation Bench of this Hon'ble Court in 'other writ petition' and was elected for the constituency No. 154, Mymensingh- 9 legally. It is stated that one Mr Advocate Abdul Hai was a nomination aspirant from Bangladesh Awami League and was willing to be a MP candidate from the same constituency but Awami League had nominated respondent No. 1 and having been unsuccessful in getting nomination from the party, he started to perturb respondent No.1, first time, by issuing a legal notice through his Advocate-on- Record on 14-12-2008 threatening that a Civil Miscellaneous Petition for Leave to Appeal is being awaited to be moved against the interim order dated 11-12-2008 passed by the vacation Bench of the High Court Division allowing respondent No. 1 to contest in the 9th parliamentary election and, now, it is the same person who, in disguise, have employed the present petitioner to file the instant writ petition after nearly 4 and half years.

7.
