case_source: (Form the Judgment and Decree dated 11 8.82 passed by the High Court Division in first Appeal No, 32 of 1978)
full_judgment:
Fazle Munim C. J.—This appeal arises from First Appeal No. 32 of 1974 passed by the High Court Division on 14 August 1982.

2. Appellants instituted Title Suit No. 36 of 1975 in the 4th Court of Subordinate Judge, Dhaka and was renumbered as Title Suit No. 1 of 1978 alter being transferred to 5th Court of the Subordinate Judge, Dhaka. Appellants prayed for declaration of their title and possession to the suit properties and also for declaration that the compromise decree obtained in Title Suit No. 107 of 1966 in the 4th court of Subordinate Judge, Dhaka on 20 August, 1966 was fraudulent, void and not binding upon them. Prayer for permanent injunction restraining the defendants from dispossessing the appellants from the suit premises was also made. Facts stated in the plaint are that the suit premises belonged to one Noor Mohammad Bepari who gave permission to the appellants to enter into end live in the suit premises. While in possession plaintiff-appellants entered into an agreement with the owner for selling the suit premises to them at a price of Tk. 20,000/-. On 20 September 1950 a bainapatra was executed and on the same day an amount of Tk. 18,000/-was paid to Noor Mohammad Bepari as earnest money. The owner was to execute the sale deed within 3 months from the date of agreement. Plaintiff appellants came to know that suit property was requisitioned by the Government of East. Pakistan as it then was but it could not take possession of the suit premises by evicting the plaintiff-appellants therefrom. Noor Mohammad Bepari did not, however, perform his part of the contract in spite of tender of the balance consideration money and requests of the plaintiff-appellants No suit for specific performance within time could therefore, be filed due to the dilatory tactless of  the owner to perform his part of the contract. Plaintiff appellants possession extended over a period of more than 12 years. In 1973 defendant No. 6, the Government of Bangladesh, issued a notice upon the plaintiff-appellants to vacate the premises who instituted Title Suit No. 47 of 1973 in the 1st court of Munsif, Dhaka for permanent injunction restraining the Government from interfering with the peaceful possession of the plaintiffs. On 27th February, 1975 they, however, withdrew the suit and filed the present suit.

3. Their further case was that defendant Nos. 1 and 2 filed Title Suit No.107 of 1966 in the 4th court of Subordinate Judge, Dhaka against one Syed Abdul Latif, defendant No.12 and another and obtained a compromise decree in collusion with each other on 22 August 1966. The predecessor of defendant Nos. 3-5 filed Title suit No.90 of 1967 in the same court for cancellation of the compromise decree but the plaint was rejected for non-payment of court-fee Defendant No.1 filed Title Suit No.56 of 1967 in the said court against the Government but withdrew the same. The predecessor of defendant Nos.3-5 also filed Title Suit No.105 of 1974 in the same court for cancellation of the compromise decree dated 23-8-66 but the same abated. The cause of action of the suit arose on 1st March, 1973 when the plaintiff-appellants received a notice of eviction from defendant No.6 and also on October 31, 1974 when defendant No.3 threatened them with dispossession. By filing three different written statements, three sets of defendants, namely, defendant No.1, defendants Nos. 3-5 and defendant No.6 contested the suit. The case of defendant No.1 was that Noor Mohammad Bepari settled the suit property to Syed Abdul Latif, defendant No. 12 who, in 1951, settled it with him and his sister defendant No.2 by executing an unregistered Amaluama on receiving a selami of Tk. 40,000/-. On the basis of compromise decree obtained by him in Title Suit No.107 of 1966 defendant No.1 got his name mutated in the S.A. record. The predecessor of defendant Nos.3-5 filed Title Suit No. 19 of 1967 for cancelling the compromise decree, but the suit was dismissed. Plaintiff No.2 and two others filed Title Suit No.82 of 1968 against defendant Nos.1 and 2 predecessor or defendant Nos.3-5 and defendant No.6 but the same was dismissed for default. The predecessor of defendant Nos.3-5 filed Title Suit No.307 of 1970 which was also dismissed for default. Plaintiffs filed Suit No.47 of 1973 in the 1st court of Munsif, Dhaka against the defendants but ultimately withdrew the same. The plaintiffs also filed Title Suit No.622 of 1973 against the same but this suit was also withdrawn. The predecessor of defendant Nos. 3-5 filed Title Suit No.104 of 1974 for cancellation of the compromise decree dated August 23, 1966 but it abated. Miscellaneous case filed for setting aside the order of abatement was also dismissed. The present suit has been filed by the plaintiff-appellants in collusion with defendant Nos. 3-5. The case of defendant Nos. 3-5 is that Noor Mohammad Bepari transferred the suit premises in favour of Nazrul Islam and Aminul Islam, defendant Nos.10 and 11, who transferred their interest in the suit property to them on 27 October 1974 by executing a kabala. Defendant No. 6, the Government of Bangladesh, contends that the suit premises was requisitioned on 23-7-47 by the then Government of Bengal and the same was allotted to Class IV employees of P.W.D. who were in possession. On receiving a notice of eviction plaintiff-appellants who were in unauthorised occupation of a portion of the house instituted Title Suit No. 47 of 1973 which they subsequently withdrew. The suit premises has been recorded in the name of defendant Nos.1 and 2 in the record of the Deputy Commissioner, Dhaka. Defendant Nos.10 and 11 challenged the compromise decree in Title Suit No.105 of 1974 but the same abated. Plaintiff-appellants were in unauahorised occupation of the suit premises and are, therefore, liable to be evicted under section 12A of the Emergency Requisition of Property Act. On March 14, 1978 the suit was dismissed by the learned Subordinate Judge, Dhaka. Plaintiff-appellants preferred First Appeal No.32 of 1978 before the High Court Division. Cross-objections were filed by defendant No.1 and defendant Nos.3-5. On 11 August 1982 the High Court Division dismissed the appeal and affirmed the judgment and decree of the trial court "with modification to the effect that the findings of the court below so far as the claim of the defendant No.1 and defendants Nos. 3-15 are concerned will be of no legal effect and are set aside".

4. Being aggrieved plaintiff-appellants moved this Court and obtained leave to consider whether the learned Judges of the High Court Division had incorrectly applied the law of part performance as contained it section 53A of the Transfer of Property Act.

5. Mr. M. H. Khondker, Counsel for the plaintiff-appellants, while challenging the correctness of the decision of the High Court Division and also that of the trial court concentrated his efforts mainly on two points, namely, (1) appellants being in possession of the suit premises in part performance of the contract is entitled to the decree; and (2) appellants possession being adverse has conferred upon him title to the suit premises.

6. In order to substantiate his contentions the learned Counsel tried his utmost to prove that the bainapatra, Ext.1, was a genuine document. This document has been considered by the learned Judges of the High Court Division and the trial court at some great length. In this connection the history of possession of the suit premises by the Government after it was requisitioned in 1947, the continued litigation by the appellants as well as the different sets of defendants since 1966, the oral and documentary evidence relating to the respective claim of each of these parties in those cases and the results thereof were fully considered by the Courts. Mr. Khondker referred to grounds Nos. 7 and 9 on the application of section 53A of the Transfer of Property Act to the facts and circumstances of the case. These grounds are as follows :

"VII. For that in view of the fact that no question of non-joinder of any party to the suit was raised by any of the contesting defendants and that Noor Mohammad Bepari had left no heir or that his only son died without leaving any heir behind him, the learned Judges of the High Court Division erred in making out a new and untenable case to hold that "it further appears that Noor Mohammad Bepari died in 1956 leaving some heirs. His heirs have not been impleaded in this suit, to claim hostile title against him or his heirs. In that view of the matter this claim of part performance on the part of Noor Mohammad Bepari cannot be sustained and that the finding is based on a misconception of the law of part performance as contained in section 53A of the Transfer of Property Act."

"IX. For that the suit as framed for declaration of title and not by way of defence for protection of possession under section 53A of the Transfer of Property Act and the First appeal being open on facts, the learned Judges of the High Court Division misdirected themselves in deciding the appeal on the wrong findings of the learned Subordinate Judge based on misconception of law, fact sand evidence on record assuming the suit as one for protection of possession under Section 53A of the T.P. Act."

7. Apart from invoking the doctrine of part performance as embodied in the aforesaid section, appellants' Counsel vehemently argued that the appellants' prayer for declaration of title in the suit on the basis of adverse possession should have been granted, He asserted that the appellants' possession over 12 years preceding the filing of the suit has been found by the Court.

8. Before dealing with the contentions raised by the learned Counsel it may be useful to refer to the findings arrived at by the trial court which have been upheld by the High Court Division. Ext. 1, the bainapatra, which was alleged to have been executed by Noor Mohammad Bepari, owner of the suit premises, on 20-9-50 for selling it for a consideration of Tk. 20,000/- has been found to be a spurious document. This document recites that on receiving Tk. 18,000/- as earnest money Noor Mohammad Bepari promised to execute and register the sale deed within 3 months after obtaining income tax clearance certificate In so far as no suit has ever been filed by the appellants for specific performance of contract and there has been no mention to the bainapatra in the several civil suits previously filed by the appellants in respect of the suit premises and unsatisfactory evidence regarding its execution by Noor Mohammad Bepari and interpolations as to the amount the trial court found that the bainapatra was "created for the purpose of this suit only to get the benefit of section 53A of the Transfer of Property Act". It was, therefore, found not to be a genuine document. These civil suits are: Title Suit No. 182 of 1968 filed by the plaintiff No.2 and others in the 1st court of Munsif, Dhaka for permanent injunction in respect of the suit premises. Plaintiff Nos. 1, 2, 3, 4 and 7-9 filed Title Suit No. 307 of 1979 in the 1st court of Munsif, Dhaka for permanent injunction. These two suits were dismissed for default. Plaintiff No.7 filed Title Suit No.622 of 1974 in the 1st court of Munsif, Dhaka. This suit was withdrawn with opportunity to use afresh.

9. As to the appellants' claim regarding the genuineness of the bainapatra, Mr. Khondker submitted that since there has been no challenge to the genuineness of the signature of Noor Mohammad Bepari on the document the finding arrived at by the Courts were wrong. Mr. Khondker has referred to a few cases in support of his contentions as to part performance of the contract. One who places reliance on the doctrine of part performance succeeds only where one has been able to prove a contract. This is clear from the provisions of the section itself which is as follows:

"53A. Where any person contracts to transfer for consideration any immovable property by writing signed by him or on his behalf from which the terms necessary to constitute the, transfer can be ascertained with reasonable certainty, and the transferee has, in part performance of the contract, taken possession of the property or any part thereof, or the transferee, being already in possession, continues in possession in part performance of the contract and has done some act in furtherance the contract, and the transferee had, performed or is willing to perform his part of the contract, then, notwithstanding that the contract, though required to be regretted, has not been registered, or, where there is an instrument of transfer, that the transfer has not been completed in the manner prescribed therefore by the law for the time being in force, the transferor or any person claiming under him shall be debarred from enforcing against the transferee and persons claiming under him any right in respect of the property of which the transferee has taken or continued in possession, other than a right expressly provided by the terms of the contract:

Provided that nothing in this section shall affect the rights of a transferee for consideration who has no notice of the contract or of the part performance thereof;

10. Mr. Khondker next contended that since the appellants have been in possession of the suit premises since 1950, asserting their independent title, the Courts should have found that they acquired title to the suit premises by adverse possession. In support, the learned Counsel referred to Ext.2, the identity card issued by the Camp-in-charge, Mohajereen Relief Camp, Dhaka in favour of Sk. Azhar Ali showing that he was living in the suit premises and that he arrived in East Pakistan on 18-3-50, Ext. 3 series which are electric bills paid by plaintiff No.2 during the period, 1974 to 1977, Ext.4 series, municipal tax receipts showing that plaintiff No.2 have been paying municipal rents for the suit premises through Marfatdars since 1975, Ext.5 series show that plaintiff No.4 paid water and sewerage charges for the suit premises in 1968. The learned Counsel also referred to a few other Exhibits to show that the appellants have been living in the suit premises. Of these Ext.6 series are of the year 1967 and 1968 Ext.7 is dated 10-9-75, Ext.10 is dated 15-11-63, Ext. 10(a) is dated 7-3-63. Besides, he referred also to the evidence of P.Ws. 3, 4, 5-7 and 9 in support of the appellants possession.

11. It, however appears that the suit premises was requisitioned by the Government on 23 July 1947 and was allotted to employees of Central P.W.D. for the purposes of residential accommodation. It also appears that Noor Mohammad Bepari, the owner of the premises, applied to the authority for enhancement of rent of the suit premises on 10-4-48. A formal agreement dated 23-2-51. Ext. 8, was made between him and the Estate Officer C & B Department, Dhaka. The employees to whom allotment was made occupied the suit premises on and from 1-9-47. The fact that some Government employees were in possession of a portion of the suit premises was admitted by Sk. Azhar Ali, plaintiff No.2, On considering these documentary evidence and the perfunctory manner in which the appellants have filed civil suits one after another and either allowed them to be dismissed for default or withdrew them, the trial court found that the appellants could not establish adverse possession of the suit premises by them. As to the motive for filing the civil suits the trial court observed as follows:

"It is evident from filing of as many as 4 title suits by the plaintiffs previous to this suit that whenever they apprehended their eviction by the Government agency they used to rush to the civil court with prayer for injunction. When their purpose was served they did not proceed with the suit. So taking recourse to litigation the plaintiffs appear to have been continuing in their unlawful possession in the suit premises. As such the plea of acquisition of title by adverse possession is of no avail. They have no right, title and interest in the suit property and they are merely trespasser therein".

12. Some cases on the doctrine of part performance may now be considered. In Pandit Ram Chander V. Pandit Maharaj Kunwar, AIR 1939 All. 611 facts were that the plaintiff was a lessee of certain properties under a deed of lease which was duly registered but was not signed by either the lessor or lessee in accordance with the provisions of S. 107. Nevertheless, plaintiff had obtained possession of the subjects leased. While the plaintiff was thus enjoying the possession, defendants demolished part of the property. Plaintiff brought a suit for injunction restraining the defendant from interfering with any of the rights of the plaintiff as lessee of those properties. It was contended by the plaintiff that as he had entered into possession of the properties in terms of the lease executed in his favour and was willing to perform his part of the contract of the lease though it was not entitled to eject him by process of law or otherwise. Upon a question whether plaintiff could rely upon the provisions of S. 53A, it was held that:

"It was defendants who were seeking to enforce their rights under the contract of lease. The plaintiff was only seeking to debar them from doing so and was thus merely protecting his rights. There was therefore no things the terms of Sec. 53-A which dis-entitled the plaintiff from maintaining the suit."

13. In the instant case before us facts are distinguishable inasmuch as the plaintiff-appellants here did not bring this suit to protect their possession as against Noor Mohammad who, according to them, entered into the agreement for sale on 20-9-50 but filed the suit for declaration that the compromise decree obtained by some of the defendants in Title Suit No. 107 of 1966 was fraudulently obtained and, therefore, void.

14. In Mrs. June Ferguson V. Ameenur Rasheed Chowdhury, (1973) 25 DLR 1, the learned Judges of the Dhaka High Court had to consider the scope of the provisions of section 53A of the Transfer of Property Act in a suit for possession of immovable property. Here, the question arose whether the plaintiff in defending his possession of the property can successfully invoke such provisions, the contention of the defendant being that the provisions of the aforesaid section in such a suit were available only to defendant and not to a plaintiff. It was held that such a suit could not be said to be not maintainable on the ground that the benefit of section 53A was not available to the plaintiff.

15. The principle laid down in this case is also not available to the plaintiff-appellants as the suit was not against the original owner of the suit premises. Moreover, as it appears from the facts of this case, the plaintiff-appellant did not succeed in proving the alleged agreement between him and the owner of the suit premises. In view of the finding by the High Court Division as well as the trial court that the agreement for sale, Ext.1, was not a genuine document the plaintiff-appellants' possession is not referable to it.

16. In another case cited by the learned Counsel for the appellants it was held that the registration of a contract to transfer immovable property is not required in law and is admissible in evidence to prove the contract to transfer or the terms thereof for the purposes of section 53A of the Transfer of Property Act. As the plaintiff-appellants' possession of the suit premises is not referable to the contract they were not entitled to the benefit of section 53A of the Transfer of Property Act, vide, Manjurul Hoque V. Newajan Bibi (1955-56) 60 CWN 714.

17. As regards the plaintiff-appellants' claim of title to the property on the basis of adverse possession for 12 years preceding the institution of the suit, the finding of the trial court as well as High Court Division is that they were aware that the suit premises was requisitioned by the Government for the accommodation of Government employees. They could not produce any papers whatsoever to show that the same had been derequisitioned and that they had been possessing the suit property since then claiming hostile title. Noor Mohammad Bepari who is alleged to have executed the bainapatra died some time in 1956 long before the institute of the present suit by the plaintiff-appellants. No claim of hostile title was ever made by them, nor in the various civil suits filed before the present one out of which this appeal has arisen any mention regarding the bainapatra was made. In such circumstances it cannot be said that the plaintiff-appellants have acquired title to the suit premises by adverse possession.

18. Yet their learned Counsel, Mr. Khondker, submitted that plaintiff-appellants have been able to prove their adverse possession for over 12 years prior to the filing of the present suit, though he failed to show against whom the assertion of hostile title was made and when, or whether such assertion was ever made. The only thing which appears from the conduct of the plaintiff-appellants is that whenever any notice was served by the Government upon them to vacate the suit premises they rushed to the Court and prayed for injunction but, as already observed, in none of case suits they ever claimed hostile title on the basis of their alleged adverse possession nor referred to the bainapatra. In addition, it appears from Ext. II that some of the plaintiff-appellants submitted a joint application for allotment of the suit premises.

19. From these facts and circumstances which have been fully discussed and considered by the trial court and the High Court Division, it appears that the plaintiff-appellants are not entitled to any declaration of their title by adverse possession for over 12 years. The principles defining the acquisition of title by adverse possession have been considered in numerous cases, but judging by the principles enunciated therein, the plaintiff-appellants case for adverse possession does not seem to have been made out.

<u>20. In Aditya Kumar Ray V. Dhirendra Nath Mondal, (1948-49) 53 CWN 879, principles regarding adverse possession have been referred to. The facts concerned show when the possession of the mortgagor's tenant became adverse to the mortgagee. It became adverse to the mortgagee when he was entitled to possession after purchasing the property in execution of the mortgage-decree; and the suit having been brought within 12 years, therefrom, was within time. Facts of this case are, therefore, distinguishable from those of the present case. However, in referring to the term "adverse possession" the court quoted with approval the following observations of Sanderson C.J. in another case, "the term 'adverse possession' implies that the person against whom adverse possession is exercised, is a person who is entitled to demand possession at the moment adverse possession begins".</u>

21. In Sadak Ali V. Suruj Ali, (1955) 7 DLR 94, a Single Bench of the Dhaka High Court in considering the provisions of Articles 28 and 142 of the Limitation Act, noted the differences between the two sections. It was observe that:

"Possession under a mistaken or invalid title is as effective as that of a trespasser and, if sufficient in length of time and continuity, gives the holder a title."

Further, it was observed:

"Under Article 142 of the Limitation Act lime begins to run against the rightful owner from the date of discontinuance of possession or dispossession, as. the case may be, and under section 28 of the Limitation Act the right is extinguished, if no wit for recovery is instituted by him within the statutory period.”

<u>22. In Ejaz Ali Qidwai V. Special Manager, Court of Wards, Balrampur Estate, AIR 1935 PC 53, the Judicial Committee of the Privy Council, while referring to the principle of law regarding adverse possession, observed that:</u>

<u>"a person, who bases his title on adverse possession, must show by clear and unequivocal evidence that his possession was hostile to the real owner and amounted to a denial of his title to the property claimed. This onus the appellants have failed to discharge."</u>

23. In Munnalal, minor V. Mst. Kashibai, (1916-17) 21 CWN 175, the Privy Council observe that:

"The general principle that the Court will always attribute possession to a lawful title applies where that is possible. Where the circumstances under which possession was assumed are known there is no room for drawing any presumption.

24. In another case, Hafiz Mohammed Fateh Nasib V. Sir Swarup Chand Hukum Chand, (1947) 52 CW19 382, the Judicial Committee of the Privy Council referred to principles regarding adverse possession:

"It is no doubt true that the claim of a mere trespasser to title by adverse possession will be confined strictly to property of which he has been in actual possession. But this principle has no application where the person is not a mere trespasser but was put into possession by an order of a Court, whether or not such order was rightly made"

Further, it was observed:

"The correct test to be applied in a case of this nature is, whether the claimant exercised such dominion over the property as to justify the inference that he was in possession of the whole. It is not necessary for him to prove that he was in physical possession of every square inch."

2S, In the present case there is no evidence to show that the plaintiff-appellants ever claimed any title to the suit property on adverse possession, nor when their possession became hostile to Noor Mohammad Bepari, the owner of the suit property. Also, they never asserted hostile title against him. On the contrary, it is admitted by the appellants that they entered the suit premises with the permission of the owner who, however, allowed it to be. requisitioned by the government for the accommodation of government employees. From the government papers produced by the learned Additional Attorney-General, it is to seen that the suit premises are still under requisition. Moreover, the present suit is not for declaration of plaintiffs' title on adverse possession, but for the declaration that the compromise decree obtained by some of the respondents in Title Suit No.107 of 1966 in the 4th Court of Subordinate Judge, Dhaka is fraudulent, void and not binding upon them. In this suit, therefore, plaintiff-appellants are not entitled to any relief's whatsoever.

26. None of the three sets of defendants namely, defendant Nos. l and 2, defendant Nos. 3- 5 and defendant No. 6 is entitled to any relief.

The appeal is dismissed. There will be no order as to costs.

End.

full_judgment:
This Rule under section 115 (1) of the Civil Procedure Code is directed against the judgment and decree of the learned Sub-ordinate Judge, 3rd Court, Chittagong, passed in Title Appeal No. 166 of 1979 reversing those of the learned Munsif, North Rauzan, Chittagong passed in other Suit No. 250 of 1914.

2. The petitioners as plaintiffs filed the suit against the defendants opposite-parties praying for the following reliefs:— Civil Revision No. 194 of 1983.

(ক) নিম্ন তপসীলের পুকুরের ৮৭৪৬ দাগের RS খতিয়ানের মন্তব্য ঘরের লিখিত ৭/৯ অংশ সংক্রান্ত ১,০৮,৮/১ শতক জমিতে মুল বিবাদীর পূর্ববর্তী ক্রমে কোন স্বত্ব স্বামিত্ব না থাকায় উচ্চারনের ডিক্রি প্রচারিত হয়।

(খ) উক্ত ১/২নং তপসীলের সম্পূর্ণ পুকুরে বাদী ও মোঃ বিবাদী এজমালে দখল থাকার প্রতিকুলে মুল বিবাদী কোন বিঘ্ন না জমাইবার স্বত্ববান নহেন উচ্চারিত হয়।

(গ) বাদী ও মোকাবিলা বিবাদীর স্বত্ব দখলীয় উক্ত পুকুরে মুল বিবাদী অনাধিকার প্রবেশ না করিবার জন্য এবং তৎপ্রতি হস্তক্ষেপ না করার জন্য তদুপরি negative specific relief of permanent injunction জারী হয়।

(ঘ) মোকদ্দমা দায়ের অবস্থায় (গ) প্রার্থনা মতে বাদী ও মোঃ বিবাদীর ১/২ নং তপসীলের পনীর উক্ত জমিতে প্রবেশ না করার ও তাহার প্রতি হস্তক্ষেপ না করার জন্য অস্থায়ী নিষেধাজ্ঞা জারী হয়।

(ঙ) বাদী ও মোঃ বিবাদী অশুদ্ধ RS ৩২৭৪ নং ৩২৮৭ নং খতিয়ান এবং অশুদ্ধ RS খতিয়ান দ্বারা বাধ্য না হওয়া উচ্চারিত হয়।

(চ) মোকদ্দমার খরচ আপত্তিকারী বিবাদীর বিরুদ্ধে ডিক্রি হয়।

3. The plaintiff's case in short is that the disputed tank belonged to Bakar Ali, Gul Banu and Bhagyabati Gul Banu and Bhagyabati had no heir except Bakar Ali. Bakar Ali was great grandfather of plaintiff No. 1. Maghi survey was made in the names of Bakar Ali, Gul Banu and Bhagyabati. CS Khatian stands recorded in the name of Uzir Ali who was son of Baker Ali. MS plot No. 6998 corresponding to CS plot No. 7190 was in possession of Md Waresh Ali who was in Chasha (cultivator) under plaintiffs predecessors. RS Khatian was wrongly prepared in respect of the disputed tank and it was recorded as RS plot 8746. Recording of 7/9th share in the names of defendants predecessors was wrong. Uzir Ali died leaving sons Asmat Ali, Ismat Ali and Hamdu Meah. The plaintiff No. 2 and proforma defendant 43 are the heirs of Hamdu Meah. lsmat Ali died leaving sons, plaintiff No. 1 and proforma defendant No. 42. The plaintiffs are possessing the disputed tank for generations. PS and BS khatian also are wrongly recorded. The plaintiffs transferred 2 gondas of land to Gura Meah and 2 gondas of land to Yakub Ali. The defendants have no share in the disputed tank.

4. The defendants 2 and 8 contested the suit by filing joint written statement contending, inter-alia, that the suit is not maintainable and it barred by limitation. The defendants are the heirs of Gut Banu and Bhagyabati. Gul Banu and Bhagyabati were not related to Baker Ali Md Zaman was the husband of Gul Banu and Hari Chand was the husband of Bhagyabati. Gul Banu died leaving son Abdul. Abdul died leaving two sons namely, Mohsen Ali and Malekazzaman. Mohsen Ali died leaving two sons namely, Torab Ali and Amjad Ali. Torab Ali died leaving three sons namely, Chunnu Meah, Sultan Ahmed and Lal Meah. Sultan Ahmed died leaving widow Abeda Khatun and daughter defendant No. 1 Gul Safa Khatun. Lal Mueah died leaving widow Sanwara Begum and brother Chunnu Meah. Chunnu Meah transferred his share to defendant No. 2 Lal Meah Amjad Ali died leaving three namely, Chunnu Meah Yakub Ali and Akmal Ali. The defendants Nos. 6 to 11 are the heirs of Yakub Ali, Abdul Sobhan purchased the share of Malekazzaman for his heirs. Bhagyabati died leaving Md. Waresh Md. Waresh died leaving Mubarak Ali Mubarak Ali died leaving daughter Amirun Nessa who sold her share to Abdul Malek. CS. Khatian was recorded in the names of predecessors of the plaintiffs, and the defendants. RS. Khatian was recorded correctly. PS. Khatian and BS Khatian are prepared in the names of defendants. The principal defendants (1-10) are in possession of 7/9the share of the disputed tank. The principal defendants have graveyard on the eastern and western banks of the disputed tank. The principal defendants have cowshed and haystack on the western bank of the disputed tank. They have 4 outer houses on the western bank of the disputed tank. The Plaintiffs and proforma defendants (41-56) got 2/9th share of the disputed tank.

5. The learned Munsif found that the plaintiffs having paid the advalorem court fees as per Courts Direction in the plaintiff’s prayer "for declaration that the recording of 7/9th share in the disputed tank in RS. Plot No. 8746 is wrong and also for declaration that in spite of that wrong recording the plaintiff's right and interest has not been affected" the suit for declaration of title and confirmation of possession and, as such, the suit as framed was maintainable. The learned Munsif further found that Maghi Chitta is a document of title, that Gul Banu and Bhagyabati were the predecessors of the plaintiffs 41-56, that the defendants suggestion that Md. Waresh Ali, the predecessor of defendants 23-29, 33-35 and 37-40, was the son of Bhagyabati was disproved by CS Khatian Exhibit 1(f) and a and that the descendants of Chasa Md. Waresh Ali got their names recorded with their masters' descendants. He also found that the recording of the 7/9th share in the names of the defendants' predecessors during the RS. Operation was wrong and the plaintiffs are entitled to get a declaration to that effect and that the suit having been filed within 6 years from 15-5-74 on which date defendants threatened the plaintiffs with dispossession on the basis of wrong entry in the RS Khatian, the suit was not barred by limitation or adverse possession. Accordingly the learned Munsif decreed the suit in part declaring that the recording of RS Khatian, Exhibit A (1) and A (2) to the extent of 7/9th share in the names of the defendants' predecessors was wrong and that the right of the plaintiffs and proforma defendants Nos. 41 to 56 to the extent of 16 annas share in the disputed tank has not been affected by RS. Khatians in dispute and further declaring that the plaintiffs and the proforma defendants joint possession with defendants who had purchased 4 gandas of land out of the disputed tank appertaining to RS Plot No. 8746 from the plaintiff No 1 be confirmed. Against the judgment and decree of the learned Munsif the contesting defendants 2 and 8 prepared the appeal and the plaintiffs-respondents in the appeal filed cross-objection for cost of suit. On consideration of the facts and circumstances of the case and evidence on record, the learned Sub-ordinate Judge found that in the plaint there is no clear mention of declaration of title in the disputed property, that two negative prayers in prayer (kha) make it affirmative i.e. it tantamount to the position that the principal defendants have got right to disturb in the possession of the entire disputed tank of schedules 1-2 of the plaint, that from the prayer portion of the plaint it appears that schedule 1 property is disputed i.e. 7/9 th share and schedule 2 i.e. 2/9th share is not disputed and thus it creates contradiction in the prayer (kha) and that the negative specific relief of permanent injunction in prayer (ga) is a vague term. The learned Sub-ordinate Judge further found that the recording of RS Khatian in the names of principal defendants is correct, that the principal defendants have possession in the disputed tank, that the Maghi Chitta cannot alone create title in favour or the plaintiffs for the disputed tank and that the plaintiffs side having not rectified the recording of the RS Khatian by filing any suit/case the question of limitation for challenging the RS Khatian also arises, that the plaintiffs and the proforma defendants have joint possession in the disputed tank along with the principal defendants, that the RS Khatian cannot be rectified as the plaintiffs did not take to correct it within the period of limitation, that in the absence of direct evidence the presumption of RS Khatian cannot be rebutted that there is no clear claim by the plaintiff's side that they have title in the entire disputed tank, that the suit is not maintainable and it is barred by limitation. Accordingly he allowed the appeal and rejected the cross-objection and dismissed the suit in reversal of the judgment and decree of the learned Munsif. Against the judgment and decree of the learned Sub-ordinate Judge the plaintiffs have obtained the present Rule.

6. Mr AKM Shafiqur Rahman, the learned Advocate appearing for the plaintiffs-petitioners, has contended that the trial Court having directed the plaintiffs to pay advalorem Court fee and the plaintiffs having done so, the suit as framed is maintainable and the finding of the trial Court as to the maintainability of the suit having not been adverted to or reversed by the learned Subordinate Judge the decision of the learned Sub-ordinate Judge that the suit is not maintainable is not sustainable in law. In sup-port of his contention he has relied upon the case of Pakistan vs Muhammad Abdul Kuddus, Income Tax Officer, (1968) 20 DLR 332 and the case of Mst. Rabeya Khatun vs Md. Elias Molla and others, (1976) 28 DLR (HC) 181. In the case reported in 20 DLR 332 the plaintiff prayed for declaration that the order posting his as Income Tax officer be declared illegal and inoperative and it was held in that case that the plaintiff was entitled to a declaration that his appointment as Income Tax Officer. Class 11, Grade 111 was illegal, void and inoperative although the declaration sought for was couched in a negative form, namely that order posting him as Income Tax Officer be declared illegal and inoperative. In the present case as correctly noted by the learned Sub-ordinate judge the plaintiffs did not pray for declaration of title and confirmation of possession and made two negative and contradictory prayers in prayer (kha)of the plaint and a prayer for a negative specific relief of permanent injunction in a vague term in prayer (ga) of the plaint. Thus the facts of the case reported in 20 DLR 332 are distinguishable from those of the present case and, as such, the proposition of law enunciated in 20 DLR 332 is not applicable in the present case. In the case reported in 28 DLR 181 upon the facts that the plaintiff prayed for a decree that a sale deed executed by the defendants 1-2 in favour of defendant No. 3 relating to self-same property was void, illegal, inoperative, collusive and the defendants 1-2 acquired no interest in the said property and hence not binding on the plaintiff, it was held: "the prayer in the plaint, though not drafted happily, leaves no doubt that what the plaintiff was essentially seeking in the suit was a declaration that their right, title and interest have not been affected by transaction of sale in favour of the defendants Nos. 1 and 2 or in favour of defendants No. 3. We cannot therefore, say that the suit as framed does not fall within the purview of section 42 of the Specific Relief act and that should be thrown out as not maintainable." In the case of Mst Rabeya Khatun vs Md. Eleas Molla and others 28 DLR 181 the prayer in the plaint left no doubt that what the plaintiff was essentially seeking in the suit was for declaration that their right, title and interest were not affected by the transaction of sale but in the present case the plaintiffs have not at all prayed for declaration of title and confirmation of possession and have made negative contradictory and vague prayers. Thus the facts of 28 DLR 181 are different from the facts of the present case and, as such, the principal laid down in the case reported in 28 DLR 181 has no application in the present case.

7. Mr. SC Das, the learned Advocate appearing for the OPs 1 and 2, has contended that the learned Munsif has erred in proceeding to dispose of the case from a wrong premise namely, that the suit is one for declaration of title and confirmation of possession though from the pleadings and the reliefs prayed for it is nowhere found that it is a suit for declaration of title and confirmation of possession as the plaintiffs have not prayed for declaration of title and confirmation of possession.

8. It is found that the learned Sub-ordinate Judge has reversed the finding of learned Munsif that the suit was one for declaration of title and confirmation of possession inasmuch as, the plaintiffs in their pleading relief prayed for did not pray for declaration of title and confirmation of possession and has found that the suit is not maintainable. It cannot be said that merely because the plaintiffs paid the advalorem court fees as per direction of the Court, the suit in effect became a suit for declaration of title and confirmation of possession and, as such, maintainable in the absence of prayer for declaration of title and confirmation of possession in the pleading or in the reliefs prayed for. The finding of the learned Sub-ordinate Judge that the suit is not maintainable in due to the negative, contradictory and vague prayers of the plaintiffs in the reliefs prayed for in the plaint. For the above reasons, I am of the opinion that the learned Sub-ordinate Judge has correctly found that the suit as framed is not maintainable in as, much as, no relief can be given to the plaintiffs as per their negative, contradictory and vague prayer in the plaint.

9. On the point of limitation the learned advocate for the petitioner has contended that the suit having been instituted within 6 years from the date of threatened dispossession on 15-5-74, the suit is in time. In support of his contention he has relied upon the case of Rai Kiran Chandra Ray Bahadur vs Tarak Nath Gongopadhy, 40 CWN 566 which were relied upon by the learned Munsif. In the case reported in 40 CWN 566 it was held: If there is an entry adverse to the plaintiff he is not bound to institute suit for declaration that the entry is wrong. He can wait and when an invasion on his right is made on the basis of the entry, he can come and sue for a declaration of his title on the ground that the record is wrong. Such a suit will be in time if brought within 6 years of the threatened invasion.

10. Mr SC Das, the learned Advocate for the opposite-parties 1 and 2 has further contended that the RS record showing that the predecessors of principal defendants and proforma defendants have been in possession of 7/9th share of the suit tank and the suit having not been instituted within 12 years it is barred by limitation and in the absence prayer for consequential relief by way of recovery of possession the suit is not maintainable. The learned Sub-ordinate Judge having found that the plaintiffs and proforma defendants are in joint possession of the disputed tank, along with the principal defendants and thus the principal defendants having become co-sharers of the plaintiffs and proforma defendants, I think the question of adverse possession and the prayer for consequential relief by way of possession does not arise in the present case and plaintiffs having instituted that suit within six years from the date of threatened dispossession on 15-5-74 as per finding of the learned Munsif which is neither adverted to nor reversed by the learned Sub-ordinate Judge I opine in the light of the case reported in 40 C W N 566 that the suit is within time under Article 120 of the Limitation Act.

<u>11. In support of the finding of the Sub-ordinate Judge that the Maghi chitta does not create title, Mr. SC Das, the learned Advocate for the opposite-parties 1-2 refers the case of Fazlur Rahim vs Nabendra Krishna Roy and others 17 CWN 151 and the case of Prodyot Kumar Sen Gupta vs Nagendra Kumar Chowdhury, 52 CWN 72. In 17 CWN 151 it was held that a chitta prepared by the Government when interested as a proprietor of the estate concerned could not be said to be a public document and that no special presumption attached to these chittas. In 52 CWN 72 it was held:-It is not necessary for us to hold that Maghi Chitta is wrong. Each record must be presumed to be correct at its date, and since the position indicated by the entries in the chittas could, during the interval, well change into the position indicated by the cadastral and revisional survey records, the latter position is not shown to be impossible or invalid in law, as the learned Sub-ordinate Judge erroneously supposed." In the light of the above cases reported in 17 CWN 151 and 52 CWN 72 it can safely be held that Maghi chitta did not create title in favour of the plaintiff in the disputed tank as has been correctly found by the learned Sub-ordinate Judge and the latter position indicated by the RS record is valid in law. As to the presumption of RS khatian and its rebuttal the learned Advocate for the opposite-parties 1-2, has referred to the case of Akrab Ali vs Zahiruddin Kari, 30 DLR (AD) 81 and the case of Meherjan Bibi vs Naimuddin Dhali being dead Raisuddin and others 33 DLR 127 in the case reported in 30 DLR (AD) 81 it is held that according to section 103B(5) of the Bengal Tenancy Act every entry in a record of right finally published shall be evidence of the matter referred to in such entry and shall be presumed to be correct until it is proved to be incorrect. In 33 DLR 126 it is held that the presumption of correction as available on the strength of section 103 B (5) of the Bengal Tenancy Act, has got to be rebutted by the person who alleges it. In the light of the proposition of law enunciated in the Appellate Division case reported in 30 DLR (AD) 81 the RS Khatian in the present case raises a presumption of its correctness until proved to be incorrect and in view of the decisions in 33 DLR 126 the onus is on the plaintiffs to rebut the presumption of the correctness of the RS khatian in the present case in as, much as, the plaintiffs have alleged that the entry of the RS khatian is wrong. The learned Sub-ordinate Judge has correctly found that there is no direct evidence in the case to rebut presumption of the RS khatian. As such the correctness of the entry of the RS Khatian is not rebutted in the present case.</u>

For the reasons stated above, I am of the opinion that the learned Sub-ordinate Judge has correctly held that the suit is not maintainable, that the Maghi chitta created no title in favour of plaintiffs and the RS recording is correct but he is not correct in holding that the suit is barred by limitation.

In the result, the Rule is discharged without any order as to costs. The connected Civil Rule No. 39 (R) of 1984 is discharged.

End.

caseno: Appeal from Original Decree No.8 of 1979.
lawyer:
MihirKanti Majumder with Hemayet Hossain, Jatirmoya Deb for Jitendra Narayan Deb, Advocates ----- For the Appellants,
BK Das, Advocate ----- For the Respondents.
parties:
Madaris Ali and others ----- Appellants
Vs
Biswamber Das Being dead his heirs ----- Respondents
full_judgment:
Kazi Ebadul Hoque, J.: This appeal at the instance of the principal defendant defendant Nos. 1 to 13 is directed against the judgment and decree dated 30th November, 1977 passed by the Subordinate Judge, First Additional Court, Sylhet, in Title Suit No. 43 of 1977 decreeing plaintiffs suit for declaration of title in the suit land.

2. Case of the plaintiff-respondent Nos. 1 to 36, in short, is as follows:

The suit land masuring 26.22 acres originally belonged to Syedunnessa Chowdurani and Khan Bahadur Gousuddin Ahmed Chowdhury and their co-sharers, predecessors of the proforma defendant Nos. 14 to 21. The said land was lying vacant and is situated far away from the houses of the landlords. The plaintiffs took settlement of the suit land from the landlords 49 years ago at an annual rental at the rate of half a maund of paddy per kedar. The plaintiffs, thereafter, reclaimed the suit land and grew paddy and they paid rent to the Zamindars through the Morals and some of the landlords received sale proceeds after selling paddy rent collected by the Morals, Share of the plaintiffs in the suit land is equal and subsequently for convenience of possession they got the same partitioned by 'Ails' but continued to pay paddy rent together.

3. Further case of the plaintiffs is that they being illiterate simple village folk they entrusted Morals and employees of the Zamindars with recording of their names during the settlement operation and they believed that their names were correctly recorded in the settlement papers. Principal defendants disclosed on 1st/2nd Chaitra, 1381 BS that they purchased the suit land from the proforma defendants and asked the plaintiffs to make over possession of the same to them. Plaintiffs doubted their claim and enquired into the Tahsil Office and came to learn that the employees of the landlords in collusion with the settlement staff got the suit land recorded as Khas Dakhuli land of the landlords. Proforma defendants never claimed the suit land on the basis of the wrong records nor did the same affect their title. Principal defendants obtained void, fraudulent, collusive sale deed from some of the greedy proforma defendants after coming to learn about the recording of the suit land in their names and thus clouded the title of the plaintiffs in the suit land. The plaintiffs on the basis of their settlement and adverse possession beyond the statutory period of limitation to the knowledge of all acquired title in the suit land and, as such, they are entitled to get their title declared.

4. Defendant Nos. 1 to 8, 10 and 13 contested the suit by filing a joint written statement. Proforma defendant Nos. 14 to 19 also filed a joint written statement but they ultimately did not contest the suit.

5. Contesting defendant Nos. 1 to 8, 10 and 13 denied the material allegations made in the plaint. They further averred that the plaintiffs suit is not maintainable and barred under section 42 of the Specific Relief Act. Their specific case is that Syedunnessa Chowdhurani, Khan Bahadur Gousuddin Ahmed Chowdhury and others did never settle the suit land 40 years ago or at any time with the plaintiffs at an annual rental of half a maund of paddy per kedar or any rent nor they realised any rent from them. Suit land was Khas dakhali land of the said landlords and the same was fallow land even during the land settlement operation and recorded as such in the name of the proforma defendants in the khatians. In 1380 BS principal defendants entered into an agreement with the proforma defendants to purchase the suit land at the rate of Tk. 1250.00 per acre and with the permission of the said owners principal defendant Nos. 14 to 19 sold 24 acre of the suit land in their 14 annas 12 gondas 35 tils share at a consideration of Tk. 30,000 to the principal defendants by a registered sale deed dated 22nd Falgoon, 1381 BS (27.3.75) and the said sellers relinquished all their right, title and interest in the said land in favour of defendants 1 to 13 and the principal defendants have been possessing the same along with 1 anna 7 gondas 3 koras 5 tils shares of proforma defendants 20 and 21 who could not execute and register the sale deed for some difficulties but made over possession of the same to the defendants 1 to 13. Plaintiffs failed to purchase the suit land as the principal defendants offered more money than they had offered and they filed the suit on false allegation of settlement. They had never any title and possession in the suit land.

6. Plaintiffs examined 6 witnesses including plaintiff No. 3 Mobarak Ali as PW 1 and also produced and proved some Toka Farags Exts. 1 to 1 (r) in support of their case. Contesting defendants examined 5 witnesses including defendant No. 7 Rowab Ali as DW 1 and also produced and proved some documents such as finally published Khatians Ext. A (2), the government rent receipts Ext. B to B(2) and certified copy of their kabala Ext. C.

7. Oil consideration of the said evidence court below decreed the suit after arriving at the following conclusion:

"In spite of all the defects in" the Toka farags it has now become clear that the plaintiffs have their legs on the suit land and whatever defects crept in the Toka farags have since been perfected by the long user of the suit land by the plaintiffs beyond the statutory period of limitation to the knowledge of the original owners. Khatian Ext A is found to be erroneous and kabala Ext. C is found to have no legal effect. As the plaintiffs have clear title and possession in the suit land the suit is found to be maintainable in the present form."

8. Mr. Mihir Kanti Majumder along with Mr. Hemayet Hossain and Mr. Jotirmoya Deb. learned Advocates, appearing on behalf of Mr. Jitendra Narayan Deb for the appellants, placed before us plaint, written statement, deposition of the witnesses, impugned judgment and other materials on record. The learned Advocate submitted that the plaintiffs failed to establish their alleged claim of settlement of the suit land on the basis of Toka farags Ext. 1 series which are neither in the name of any of the plaintiffs nor any particulars of the suit land mentioned therein. He further submitted that the plaintiffs also failed to establish their alleged adverse possession beyond the statutory period of limitation. He further submitted that the suit land was recorded in the name of predecessor-in-interest of the proforma defendants in finally published Khatians after factual field survey in the locality and the suit land has been recorded as fallow land (layek-patiti/ Layek ura).

9. Mr. BK Das, learned Advocate appearing for the respondents, on the other hand, strenuously argued that the plaintiffs are in possession of the suit land for the last 40 years beyond the statutory period of limitation and thereby acquired title in the suit land by adverse possession, even if they failed to establish their settlement of the same from the landlords. He further submitted that the kabala Ext. C of the principal defendants shows that the suit land is cultivable land and not fallow land at the time of their purchase and defendants' story that the suit land was fallow Khas land of the landlords is belied by such recital in their sale deed.

10. In this case admittedly the suit land belonged to the predecessors-in-interest of the proforma defendants and it was their vacant Khas land and finally published khatians Ext. A series recorded the same in the name of the said landlords as their Khas land. The question in whether the said landlords settled the same with the plaintiffs and or the plaintiffs acquired title therein by adverse possession.

11. PW 1 in his deposition stated that the suit land was lying fallow, situated far away from the house of the landlords and near their house and they took settlement of the same about 40 year before and they reclaimed the same and made it fit for seedling bed. No other witness supported the PW 1 in this respect. There is no particular as regards date, time, place and persons from whom and in whose presence plaintiffs took settlement of the suit land. There is also no document in support of such settlement of the suit land in favour of the plaintiffs. Of course, the plaintiffs have produced some Toka farags or receipts Ext.1 series but none of those Toka farags are in the name of any of the plaintiffs nor there is any particular of the land in respect of which rent was realized by the said Toka farags PW 6 Dinash Chandra Chakrabarty who claimed to have served in the Sheristha of the said landlords from 1329 BS to 1349/1350 BS formally proved Toka farags dated 21.2.55 BS Ext. 1(L), 4.9.59 BS Ext. 1(10), 12.8.59 BS Ext. 1(q) and 2.3.59 BS Ext 1(r) to be in the handwriting of Abdus Shahid, another employee of the Zamindars. He also proved Toka farag dated 7.3.62 BS Ext. 1(n) to be in the handwriting of Naresh another employee of the said Zamindars and also Toka farag dated 7.5.61. BS Ext. 1(k) to be in the handwriting of Surendra, another employee of the said Zamindars. He did not say that the said Toka farags were granted in his presence. He admitted in cross-examination that the landlords had a big sheristha and had printed farags and dakhilas and other registers. As we have already noticed that the said Toka farags are neither in the name of any of the plaintiffs nor in respect of the suit land. Merely because the said Zamindars are not coming to dispute the claim of the plaintiff it could not be said that the plaintiffs got settlement of the suit land on the basis of the said Toka farags. We, therefore, hold that the plaintiffs failed to prove that they took settlement of the suit land from the then landlords predecessors-in-interest of the proforma defendant Nos. 14 to 21 about 40 years ago or at any time.

12. Plaintiffs claimed title in the suit land on the basis of their settlement as well as adverse possession. As the plaintiffs failed to prove their settlement of the suit lands now let us see whether they have been able to prove their possession beyond the statutory period of limitation adversely to the true owners.

13. There is no case of the plaintiffs that they entered into the suit lands forcibly at any point of time to the knowledge of the said landlords, who admittedly reside far away and who has no tahsil office in the locality, denying title of the said landlords. Admittedly suit land was recorded in the name of the landlords Sayedunnessa Chowdhurani and Khan Bahadur Gousuddin Ahmed Chowdhury and others in Khatian Nos. 16 and 112 of mouza Purnakhola and Khatian No. 581 of Mouza Chaluia Exts. A-(2) and the said land has been recorded as fallow land in khas possessions of the said persons. It is admitted by the learned Advocates of both the parties that at the time of acquisition of rent receiving interest under the SAT Act field survey operation for preparation of record of rights under the provisions of Sylhet Tenancy Act 1936 in the suit locality was going on and ultimately the record of rights were prepared and finally published under the provisions of State Acquisition and Tenancy Act as there was no previous settlement operation in the District of Sylhet. Relying on the evidence of PW 1 the learned Advocate for the respondents contended that the said Khatians were wrongly prepared in the name of the landlords. PW 1 in his deposition stated that during last settlement operation they entrusted Morals and Karmacharies of landlords to record the suit land in their name. But in cross-examination he admitted that he has other lands besides the suit land and those were correctly recorded in his name. We have already seen that there was no tahsil office of the Zamindars in the locality and as such entrusting Karmacharies of the Zamindars cannot be relied on. None has corroborated the PW 1 in this respect and he also failed to name the Moral or Karmachari whom the plaintiffs had entrusted for the purpose. Moreover, the plaintiffs never took care to enquire about the Khatians within the period of 12 years from the date of final publication of the Khatians in 1963 and they only enquired about the Khatians in 1975 when they came to know from the principal defendants about the sale of the suit land by the proforma defendants to the principal defendants. The plaintiffs neither claimed to have paid any rent to the Government from 1363 BS till the time of filing the suit in 1382 BS nor produced and proved any rent receipts. In view of the above it is difficult to hold that the said Khatians were not correctly prepared in the name of said Zamindars. Such finally published SA Khatians prepared after field survey operation stand on much better footing and more reliable than the SA Khatians made by merely revising the CS Khatians.

14. Now coming to the evidence of possession it is seen that PW 1 simply said that they reclaimed the suit land and made it fit for seedling bed, whereas the plaint case is that they grew paddy in the suit land after reclaiming the same. He even failed to give number and area of the suit land and area under possession of other plaintiffs or quantity of paddy delivered as rent. Though he said that Majid Moral now deceased realized paddy but admitted that he did not grant receipt of paddy. PW 2 simply said that the plaintiffs have been possessing the suit land for about 40 years. PW 3 stated that he has been seeing the plaintiffs' possession in the suit land since dawn of his knowledge. PW 5 stated that the plaintiffs have been possessing the suit land. But none of those witnesses stated that the plaintiffs have been possessing the suit land by growing paddy or as seedling bed. Only PW 4 who is a relation of plaintiff No. 11 Asmat Ali stated that the suit land Laye kpatit formerly and yield boro paddy and the plaintiffs have been possessing the same. PW 2 claimed himself to be 80 years old but in cross-examination he said that he had been seeing possession of the plaintiffs in the suit land since his boyhood which is contrary to the plaint case. He is resident of a different village Daudpur and his homestead is half a mile away from the suit land. He has no land near the suit land. PW 3 is an old man of 65 years. In cross-examination he has stated that knowledge dawned in him at the age of 7/8 years. He is also a resident of a different village Daudpur half a mile away from the suit land. He has also no land near the suit land. It is clear that according to him plaintiffs has been possessing the suit land for 57 years which is contrary to the plaint case. Thus, PWs 2 and 3 are nothing but over zealous witnesses. It is difficult to rely upon the evidence of PWs. 2 and 3 regarding plaintiffs claim and possessions of the suit land. We have already noticed that PW 4 is a relation of plaintiff No. 11 and PW 5 is a man from a different village 3 miles off from the suit land and from his cross-examination it is clear that he is quite ignorant about the possession of PW Mobarak Ali or other plaintiffs. Court below, therefore, did not rightly rely upon the evidence of PWs 4 and 5. Except PW1 none of the other PWs. said anything about reclamation of the suit land by the plaintiffs. In the absence of any evidence to corroborate the PW 1 as to reclamation of the suit land by the plaintiffs statement of the PW 1 who is interested in the result of the suit in this respect cannot be relied upon. There is no averment or evidence on the side of the plaintiffs when they denied the title of the said landlords in the suit land and began to possess the same adversely to them.

<u>15. From the above discussion, it is clear that the plaintiffs' failed to prove their possession in the suit land Plaintiffs claim that they made the suit land fit for cultivation 40 years ago after taking settlement and grew paddy therein is also belied by the entry in the khatians Ext. A series classifying the suit lands as Layak patit layck/ura i.e. follow land in Khas possession of the predecessor of the proforma defendants. It is well settled that possession follows title. Even occasional surreptitious acts of possession on the part of the plaintiffs behind the back of such recorded owners who were admittedly residents of a distant place in the absence of any evidence of forcible entry in the land in denial of title of such owners cannot amount to adverse possession of the plaintiffs in the suit land.</u>

16. Court below did not assign any reason for finding the khatians Ext. A series to be erroneous and kabala Ext. C to have no legal effect, admittedly Syedunnessa Chowdhurani and others were the owners of the suit land and proforma defendants 14 to 21 as their heirs inherited the same. As the plaintiffs failed to establish their settlement of the same from the said landlords we find no reason how the court below could hold the said khatians in the names of the said landlords to be erroneous and the kabala in favour of the principal defendants to have no legal effect. Had the plaintiffs acquired any title in the suit land they would have paid rent for the same to the Government from 1363 BS after the acquisition of rent receiving interest. They utterly failed to make out any such case of payment of rent to the Government. How could the plaintiffs enjoy the suit land from 1363 BS till the time of filing the suit as claimed by them without paying rent to the Government? Any lay cultivator is quite conscious that he cannot enjoy the land without paying rent to the Government. Had the plaintiffs acquired any interest or title in the suit land they would have endeavored to pay rent to the Government and would have taken steps at the earliest opportunity to get the Khatians corrected in their names. But they have been sitting idle and now have arisen from their deep slumber after lapse of such a long time when the principal defendants purchased the suit land from the proforma defendants. On the other hand, we find from Ext. B series that the contesting defendants paid rents for the years 1379-82 BS vide Ext. B series. These go to show that all previous rents were paid by the recorded owners of the said land as stated by the DW 1 in cross-examination.

<u>17. It is true that in the kabala Ext. C the suit land has been described as Halichara i.e. seedling bed. As the plaintiffs failed to prove their possession in the suit land merely because the suit land has been described in defendants kabala as Halichara land will not lead to the necessary inference, that the plaintiffs had been or are in possession of the said land. Moreover it is not the case of the plaintiffs that the suit land is Halichara rather their case is that the suit land is paddy land which they failed to prove.</u>

18. In view of the above, we are of the opinion that the plaintiffs failed to prove their case of settlement of the suit land in their favour 40 years before the filing of the suit or that they acquired title in suit land on the basis of adverse possession beyond the statutory period of limitation. As the plaintiffs failed to prove their possession in the suit land their simple suit for declaration of title is barred under the proviso to section 42 of the Specific Relief Act for want of prayer for further relief. The suit as framed is not also maintainable.

In the result, the appeal is allowed and the judgment and decree appealed from is set aside and the plaintiffs suit is dismissed. In the facts and circumstances of the case parties shall bear their respective cost all through.

End.
