case_source: From the judgment and order dated 25-3-82 passed by the High Court Division in Civil Revision Case No. 358 of 1980.

lawyer:
S.K. Sinha for B.N. Chowdhury ------ For the petitioner in all the three Rules. 
M. Shehabulla with Syed Mahmud Hossain  ------ For Opp. Party No. 1 in all the three Rules.
parties:
Haladhar Dutta ------Petitioner
Vs.
Abdul Rob Choudhury and ors ------Opposite party
case_source: (In the meter of an application under section 115 (2) of the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908 for setting aside the order date 27.12.1980 passed by Sub-Judge, Noakhali in Misc. Appeal No 122, 121, 123 of 1978 affirming those of Munsif, 2nd Court, Feni in Misc. Case Nos. 129, 128 and 139 of 1972 passed on 30.6.78 )
full_judgment:
These three Rules have been obtained by the pre-emptor-petitioner calling in question the judgment and order dated 27.12.80 by the learned Subordinate Judge, Noakhali in Miscellaneous Appeals No. 121, 122 and 125 of 1978 affirming the judgment and order dated 30.6.78 passed by the learned Munsif, 2nd Court, Feni in Miscellaneous Cases No. 128, 129 and 139 of 1972 rejecting the prayer for pre-emption, made under section 96 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, Since all the Rules have arisen out of the same judgment, the same have been heard analogously and this judgment shall govern all the cases.

2. The common case of the petitioner in all the three miscellaneous cases is that he is the co-sharer by inheritance in C.S. Khatian No. 803 of mouza Chandpur and lands recorded therein originally belonged to Shafi Kumar, Kali Kumar, Krishna Chandra, RajKumar, Nakshatra and Sharoda and that he is the son of Krishna Chandra and that opposite party No. 2 is also a co-sharer by inheritance in the aforesaid C.S. Khatian No. 803, that the opposite party No. 2 by three different kabalas sold some portion of the disputed plot to the opposite party No. 1 in the year 1972 and .did not serve any notice of such transfer to him and that the opposite party No. 1 is a stranger-purchaser, that he is in possession of some portion of the disputed plot in his maliki right. Thus he is entitled to pre-empt the disputed lands.

3.  The pre-emptee opposite party No. 1 contested the cases by filling written objection and alleging, inter alia, that the petitioner was not a co-sharer in respect of the disputed property with regard to which two khatians under S.A. operation, namely Khatian Nos. 844 and 845 have been prepared and the disputed land has been recorded in new Khatian No. 845 and that the land recorded in Khatian No. 844 belonged to the petitioner. Thus after splitting up of the original khatian i.e. C.S. Khatian No. 803 the petitioner is not entitled to claim himself as a co-sharer. tenant in the disputed khatian No. 845. The further cases of the opposite party No. 1 is that the land in dispute is a debuttor property and as such the petitioner is not entitled to claim any pre-emption under section 96 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act.

4. The learned Munsif dismissed the pre-emption petitions upon holding that the vendors of opposite party No. 1, namely Phani and Khogendra, are the tenants in the separately recorded M.R.O.R. Khatian No. 845 at jama of Tk. 7/14 annas and the M.R.O.R. Khatian No. 844 stands recorded in the name of the petitioner along with his other co-sharers. Thus the interest of the vendors of the opposite party No. 1 in their parent C.S. Khatiaa No. 803 was no longer in existence while the impugned transfer took place. The learned Munsif also declined to consider whether the parent Khatian No. 803 was legally spitted up into two khatians, namely, M.R.O.R. Khatian Nos. 844 and 845. Thus the learned Munsif  held that the petitioner has no locus standi to claim pre-emption in respect of the disputed land.

5. Against the judgment and order of the trial Court the petitioner preferred the above mentioned miscellaneous appeals and the lower appellate Court by the impugned judgment and order dismissed the appeals and affirmed the judgment of the trial Court upon taking the same view that the parent khatian i.e C.S. Khatian No. 805 having been separated into two khatians and the disputed land having been recorded in the new khatian No. 845, the petitioner is not a co-sharer in respect of the disputed land.

6. Mr. S.K. Sinha, the learned Advocate appearing for the petitioners has raised two points for all the three Rules. Firstly, that the opening of two separate jamas under the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act by way of sub-division of the original jama i.e. C.S. Khatian No. 801 having not been done in accordance with law, the Courts below committed an error of law in holding that on the basis of two separate khatians the pre-emptor, although is admittedly a son of the original owner, lost his right of claim to be a co-sharer in respect of the disputed property. Secondly, that the petitioner also claimed that he is the contiguous owner of the disputed land but the Courts below failed to consider his case as to whether he could prove his claim as the contiguous owner of the disputed land.

7. Mr.M. Shehabullah, the learned Advocate appearing for the opposite party No. 1 contends that the parent jama was separated at the instance of the pre-emptor as well as his other co-sharers and on the basis of separate khatians, namely, Khatian Nos. 844 and 845 they have been paying rents in respect of the disputed land. Thus the Courts below legally held that the pre-emptor lost his right of claiming pre-emption as a co-sharer. The learned Advocate further submits that the pre-emptor in his petition for pre-emption did not specifically plead that he is also a contiguous owner of the disputed land and nothing also transpires from the judgments of the Courts below that the pre-emptor also pressed his claim that he is entitled to pre-empt the land as contiguous owner. The learned Advocate in his affidavit-in-opposition has annexed true copy of the petition of miscellaneous case No. 128 of 1972 and in paragraph 8 of the said-affidavit it is stated that the petitioner did not claim his right of pre-emption as a contiguous owner too.

8. At the time of issuance of the Rules records were not called for. But on being asked the learned Advocate for the petitioner produced the certified copy of the depositions of the witnesses. Since nothing has been mentioned in the judgments of the Courts below regarding the oral evidence of the parties, for my personal satisfaction have perused the evidence of the witnesses of both The sides from the certified copies of the depositions. It is evident from the Annexure-1 of the affidavit-in-opposition that the petitioner has stated that he along with the vendor of the opposite party No. 1 is co-sharer by inheritance in C.S. Khatian No. 803 and that he is in possession in some portion of the disputed plot in his maliki right. In the Schedule be has mentioned the original Khatian No. 803 as well as the present Khatian No. 845. The disputed plots are Plots No. 846 and 850 measuring the total area of 1.84 and, 69 decimals respectively.

<u>9. Admittedly, two separate khatians under the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act have been prepared in respect of the land of the original jama i.e. C.S. Khatian No. 803. The Courts below have observed that these two khatians are the modified record-of-right Nothing transpires either from the evidence 91 the parties or from the judgments of the Courts below that those khatians have been-finally published and accepted under the provisions of State Acquisition and Tenancy Act as final. There are two provisions under the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act regarding preparation of the record-of-rights. Under section 19 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act in view of the notification of the Government under section 17 of the Act a draft record-of-right was prepared for the purpose of acquisition of the rent-receiving interest or under the same provisions the record of right that was prepared under Chapter X of the Bengal Tenancy Act would have been revised in respect of any district, part of a district or of any local area as the Government would deem fit and necessary; The particulars which are required to be incorporated under those draft record-of-rights have been mentioned in the rules framed for the purpose. A judicial notice can be taken that the draft or the revised khatians that were directed to be prepared under section 19 of the Act was not finally published since before coming into force of Part V or the Act, which came into operation in the Noakhali district on 1.8.63. After coming into force of whole of the Part V a radical change in the scheme of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act was brought in, whereby in view of sub-section (8) of section 82 the words 'raiyati' or 'tenant' as well as 'rent' were to be deemed to have been substituted by the words 'milk' an 'land revenue'. Chapter V of the Act also brought in the incident of tenancy including the right of occupancy as well as devolution of interest by way of inheritance. In view of sections . 83 and 84 of the Act. Thus question of status of the malik as well as the co-sharer malik, as are to be read in section 96(1) of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act in view of the, provisions of section- 82 (8) of the Act, gave a new dimension in the rights and liabilities including the right to pre-empt by a co-sharer malik in respect of the transfer of any holding or portion thereof by a ma to any stranger. Section 96 has also brought a new right of pre-emption for the owners of the contiguous lands. Under section 19 provisions have been made only to prepare a draft record-of-right or to revise the re-cord-of-right prepared and finally published under Chapter X of the Bengal Tenancy Act. After coming into force of Part-V and giving the raiyats of different natures to a single status of malik, the right to hold or occupy such land for agricultural or horticultural purposes on payment of revenue direct to the Government. The word 'tenant' as has been defined under section 2(27) of the Act lost is connotation as was initially defined. It is evident that in Part—V provision has been made under section 117 of the Act for amalgamation, consolidation or subdivision of holdings. In .case of amalgamation or consolidation of holdings under section 117 (1) (a), (b) the revenue officer either of his own motion or upon any application made to him in that behalf is entitled to amalgamate or consolidate the holdings. But so far the sub-division of holdings is concerned under section 117(1) (c) of the Act it has been made imperative that the sub-division of joint tenancy for distribution of rent thereof can be made by the revenue officer only upon an application made to him by one or more co-sharer tenants and no order for such sub-division shall be passed unless reasonable notice is given to the parties concerned to appear and to be heard by him in the matter. It has further been provided under sub-section (3) of section 117 that that when an order under sub section (1) has been passed sub-dividing a joint holding, such sub-division may be demarcated on the ground and shown on the cadastral survey map. Thus the scheme of sub-division is very much clear for the purpose of adjudication that has been provided under Chapter XII of Part-V of the Act.</u>

<u>10. The modified record-of-right, as in evident from the provision of sec. 46 of the Act, was required to be prepared and considered for the purpose of final publication of the compensation assessment roll regarding acquisition of all kind of rent receiving interest under the Act. The record of right derives its presumptive value of correctness both under section 19 of the Act as well as section 144 of the Act. In the absence of any final publication of the record of right which have been prepared under the Act either under section 19 or under section 144, there cannot be any presumptive value of its correctness which is required to be rebutted. It does not a from the judgments of the Courts below that they considered as to whether this sub-division of the original jama was done upon the application of the pre-emptor or with notice to him as provided under section 117 (1) (c) of the Act. Preparation of the record-of-right under Chapter IV was for the purpose of acquisition of rent receiving interest whereas the purpose of preparation of the record-of right under Part-V, Chapter-XIV is for maintaining the proper and up-to-date settlement rent roll. It should be significantly noted that whenever the raiyat or under raiyat or any other raiyat as they had been under the Bengal Tenancy Act, alter coming into force of Part-V of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, 1950 have been merged into a single status of malik having their equal rights and liabilities including the right to pre-empt any land under section 96 of the Act. Thus in the absence of any material or evidence on record that such separation of original jama was done in accordance with section 117(1) (c) of is not at all safe to oust a co-sharer malik from exercising his vested right only on the basis of two M.R.O R. Khatians which were prepared initially for the purpose of realisation of rent pending final publication of record-of-right as has been contemplated under the scheme of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act.</u>

<u>11. It has been submitted by the learned Advocate for the opposite party that on the basis of two new khatians the vendors of the opposite party as well as the pre-emptor have been paying rent separately but it does not appear from the judgments of the Courts below that they had the opportunity of considering any materials regarding such payment of rent which would give some light as to the point of time since when they started paying rent. The Courts below have proceeded on the footing that so far the exercising of the right of pre-emption is concerned under section 96 of the Act on the basis of the claim of co-shareship in the holding, mere showing the payment of land revenue under two different numbers in the tenants ledger is sufficient to give a complete negation to any vested right of pre-emption. There cannot be doubt, of course, whenever all the co-sharers of the original C.S. Khatian amicably, split up the jama for the purpose of facilitating payment of land revenue that can be construed as very much identical to the amicable partition amongst such co-sharers. In such a case by their conduct amongst them-selves the co-sharers would dis-entitle them-selves from claiming any benefit of a joint tenancy in view of the doctrine of estoppel, as has been provided under section 115 of the Evidence Act. "</u>

<u>12. Thus in resolving the dispute in the instant case, in my opinion, it is necessary to look into the legality of the sub-division of the original holding in the light of the provisions of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act. since in a application for pre-emption the Court of law is under the legal obligation to decide-certain basic rights of the parties.</u>

<u>Moreover, the pre-emptor in the application for pre-emption has asserted that he is in possession in a portion of the disputed plots in his maliki right and two of his witnesses, namely, P.Ws. 2 and 3 have deposed that the pre-emptor has the land contiguous to the disputed plots. Thus it was also the duty of the Court below to consider as to whether the pre-emptor is a contiguous owner of the disputed plots, since it is not the case of either of the party that such sub-division was finally effected under section 117(3) of the Act. I do not find any light from the judgments of the Courts below as to whether the land of the plots under pre-emption has also been recorded in the other M.R.O.R. Khatian No. 844. In support of the contention, Mr. M. Shebabullah. the learned Advocate has referred to a decision reported in 29 DLR. 153 in which the original C.S. Khatian was split up into four different khatians and in respect of such split up khatians pre-emption was sought for by the owner of the other khatians, where it has been decided that since those khatians were amicably allowed to be prepared out of the parent khatian, the pre-emptor and his other co. sharers virtually waived their right to claim co-sharership into the disputed khatians. Since I do not find any material that in the instant case the two khatians were allowed to be prepared amicably by the co-sharers, in my opinion, the decision reported in 29 D.L R. is distinguishable on facts. Mr. S.K. Sinha, learned Advocate in support of his contention has also cited a decision reported in 33 D.L.R. (A. D.) 323 in the case of Md. A. Rouf and others vs. Mahmuda Khatun and others. He has also referred to another case reported in the same volume of 33 D.L.R. (A.D.) 309. from the decision reported in 3 D.L.R (A. D.) it is clear, so far as the sub-division of the original holding is concerned under section I l7(1)-c) of the Act, that it is mandatory to notify all other co-sharers before passing order for such subdivision. In the instant case since no material is available from the judgments of the Courts below that such sub-division of holding was done either amicably or by an application under section 117(1)(c) of the Act, I am afraid to come to any definite conclusion that the pre-emptor has either lost his right of pre-emption as a co-sharer or his interest in the original jamal still exists. In such view of the matter I am of the opinion that for the interest of justice the applications for pre-emption should be heard by the trial court afresh.</u>

13. For the reasons as started above, I find substance in these Rules and, accordingly, I make these Rules absolute and set aside the judgments and orders of the Courts below and send back the miscellaneous cases to the trial court on remand for rehearing on the basis of materials on record and allow the parties of opportunity to adduce further evidence for the purpose of the Court to adjudicate upon the dispute effectively and completely between the parties.

In the facts and circumstances of the case there will be no order as to costs.

End.

full_judgment:
Fazle Munim C.J.-I have gone through the judgments of Ruhul Islam and Shahabuddin Ahmed JJ and I concur with the decision of Ruhul Islam J.

Ruhul Islam J.- This appeal by special leave which arises out of a pre-emption proceeding under section 24 of the Non-Agricultural Tenancy Act, 1949. The respondents filed application under section 24 of the Non-Agricultural Tenancy Act, 1949 for pre-emption of the auction sale on 24-10-1973 in Certificate Case No 408 of 1967-1968 held by the Certificate Officer, Chittagong, for arrear rent dues from H E Percival, the recorded tenant, transferring land of P.S. Plot No. 108 of P.S. Khatian No. 14. The respondents claimed to be co-sharers of the Certificate Debtor by purchase of 1 kani 10 gondas of land of plot Nos. 107 and 87 appertaining to said Khatian No. 14, from H.E. Percival by registered kabala dated 29-12-1965 and their names were duly mutated in Khatian No. 14, which has been described in Schedule No. 2, which is part of Schedule 1 containing P.S. Khatians Nos. 14, 18, 20 and 24 owned by H.E. Percival in Mouza Kashim Bazar, P.S. Kotwali Chittagong, Their further case is that in the Oerti6cate Sale it was wrongly shown that P.S. Plot No. 108 appertained to P.S. Khatian No. 18 created after amalgamation and consolidation of the holdings held by H.E. Percival, because, such ambulation was done without giving any notice to the co-sharers. The pre-emption case was contested by the pre-emptee contending inter alia that the pre-emptors though were co sharers of the P.S. Khatian No. 14, but they ceased to be co-sharers after the lands in different plots in Kbatian Nos. 14, 18, 20 and 24 in Mouza Kashim Bazar still owned and possessed by H.E. Percival were amalgamated and consolidated in one Khatian, namely Khatian No. 18 and the auction sale was held on the basis of the new Khatian No. 18, wherein they were not co-sharers of the Certificate Debtor.

2. The pre-emption case was dismissed by the learned Subordinate Judge and on appeal the learned District Judge. Chittagong allowed the pre-emption case in part and remanded the case to the trial Court for assessment of the cost of improvement in the case land. The appellant unsuccessfully moved the High Court Division in revision and thereafter obtained leave from this Court. Leave was granted to examine the question whether after creation of a new tenancy by amalgamation and consolidation of holdings the respondent pre-emptors could rightly claim to be co-sharers of the recorded tenant H.E. Percival. Leave was also granted to consider the question whether a person claiming to be co-sharer in the holding, and not in the land transferred, could validly, maintain an application for pre- emption under section 24 of the Non-Agricultural Tenancy Act, 1949.

3. The appellant purchased the entire holding on 24-12-73 belonging to H. B. Percival recorded in P.S. Khatian No. 18 consisting of P S. Plot No. 108, 116, 117, 119 and 121 when the said holding was sold for arrears of rent under the Public Demands Recovery Act. Possession was delivered to the appellant on 11-2-74 and since then he was exercising various acts of possession. In the pre-emption proceeding the pre-emptors challenged validity of the amalgamation of different plots of different holdings in one holding, namely, Kbatian No. 18 in Miscellaneous Case No. 89 of 1972-73. Main ground of attack being that the amalgamation and consolidation was illegal, because, this was done without serving any notice upon the co-sharers in the holding, namely the pre-emptors, On consideration of the materials on record the learned Subordinate Judge came to the finding that notices of the Miscellaneous Case No. 89 of 1972-73, were duly served upon the co-sharer/joint tenants in those holdings and as such the order allowing amalgamation and creation of a new khatian in the name of H.E. Percival alone was validly made, and the pre-emptors ceased to be co-sharer of H.E. Percival. The learned District Judge however took the view that amalgamation and separation of land was made without giving notice to the co-sharers, and as such the purported amalgamation was null and void and such order need not be avoided by a separate proceeding, as in the eye of law it was no order. He also took the view that since the petitioner had been paying rent at old rate; and it was accepted by the Tahsil office, it may be said that the separation and amalgamation was not acted upon also. The learned Single Judge of the High Court Division agreeing with the above views affirmed the decision of the District Judge.

4. Mr. Hamidul Huq Chowdbury, the learned Counsel appearing for the appellant submitted that amalgamation and consolidation of holdings having been made by the Revenue Officer in due course of his official duties, it should be presumed that it was validly done and in accordance with law, besides it is not correct to say that a new tenancy in P.S Khatian No. 18 in the name of H.E. Percival as the sole owner was made in the absence of any written application by the recorded tenant H.E. Percival in this regard; and the order was made without giving any notice to the co-sharers of H.E, Percival. With reference to different documents on record the learned Counsel submitted that the record would show that the amalgamation proceeding was initiated at the instance of H. E. Percival. When Certificate Case No. 408/67-68 and six other Certificate Cases were started against H.E. Percival by the Certificate Officer Chittagong for realization or arrear rents, on 12-3-69, the certificate debtor filed an application under section 9 of the Public Demands Recovery Act. in the aforesaid 7 Certificate Cases denying his liability for the huge arrear revenue dues on the grounds, inter alia that the lands of some of the khatians had been acquired by the Government and some of the lands bad been transferred by him to different persons; and praying for permission to pay the proportionate amount of the rent dues for him existing land in different khatians. On this application an order was passed by the Certificate Officer on 21-6-1973 directing the Tahsilder concerned for filing revised certificate on fresh assessment of correct rental dues, after amalgamation and consolidation of the lands in deferent khatians still in the possessions of H.E. Percival. The learned Counsel submitted that a regular case under Chapter XV of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act was started by the Revenue Officer concerned and as a result new khatian No. 18 solely in the name of H.E. Percival was created, and on the basis of this khatian revised certificate was filed. The learned Counsel further submitted that auction was held on the basis of this amalgamated newly created khatian No. 18 wherein the respondents not being co- sharer are not entitled to pre-empt the certificate sale

5. On perusal of the material on record it appears that admittedly the land of khatian No. 18 was sold in auction for arrears of rent and the pre-emptors were not co- sharers in the said khatian. H.E. Percival was a recorded tenant in respect of khatian Nos. 14, 18, 20 and 24, and for recovery of a huge arrear of rent in respect of those khatians Certificate Case Nos. 408, 109, 411, 412, 413 and 414 of 1967-68 were started. H.E. Percival filed an application under section 9 of Public Demands Recovery Act, 1913 on 12-3-69 stating inter alia that he was not liable for the entire arrear rent dues, because some of the lands had been acquired by the Government and some of the lands had been transferred by him to different persons. He stated therein that he was prepared to pay the proportionate rent for the lands still in his possession. This application was duly signed by H.E. Percival. On this application, it appears from the order sheet that the relevant Revenue authority took certain actions on the direction of the Circle Officer (Revenue) and a proposal for consolidation and amalgamation of several holdings of H.E. Percival was submitted, and on the basis of this recommendation for amalgamation and consolidation the relevant Revenue Officer passed the order. From the Circular of the Board of Revenue dated 26-6-69 it appears that the district authorities were instructed to the effect that the work of amalgamation of holdings should be started in all the circles in the month of July and complete by the end of October, 1969. Mr. Hamidul Huq Chowdhury, rightly pointed out with reference to the Circular that the amalgamation of the lands belonging to H E. Percival was not a solitary case, because, the process of amalgamation and consolidation had already been started in the district There is no doubt the action was taken at the instance of H.E. Percival, and it was taken up in this background Chapter XV of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act provides for amalgamation, sub-division and consolidation of holdings. Section 116 provides that where various parcels of land are held by One tenant within one village, and such parcels of land or some of them are the subject of separate tenancies, such parcels of land shall under the orders of the Revenue- officer, be amalgamated into one tenancy. Section 117 provides the at notwithstanding anything contained elsewhere in this part, the Revenue-officer may.-

"(a) for the purpose of amalgamation of tenancies under section 116, either on his own motion or on an application made to him by one or more co-sharer tenants, in that behalf, or

(b) for the purpose of consolidation of holdings of a Malik, under section 119, either on his own motion or on an application made to him, in that behalf, or

(c)for the purpose of sub-division of a joint tenancy for distribution of rent thereof, on an application made to him by one or more co- sharer tenants..................’'

Chapter XVII of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act provides for maintenance and revision of the record- of fights. Section 143 of the Act provides that the Collector shall maintain up-to-date, in the prescribed manner, the record-of rights prepared or revised under Part IV or under this Chapter by correcting clerical mistakes and by incorporating therein the changes on account of-

(a) the mutation of names as a result of transfer or inheritance;

(b) the sub-division, amalgamation or consolidation of holdings;

(c) the new settlement of lands or of holdings purchased by the Government; and

(d) the abatement of rent on account of abandonment or dilution or acquisition of land.

6. With reference to section 117 of the Act Khondkarm Mahbubuddin Ahmed submitted that the entire proceedings and the purported amalgamation and consolidation of holdings as claimed by the appellant being not in accordance with Jaw, was illegal, and as such the new khatian 18 having no legal basis, it should be presumed that the khatians 14, 18, 20 and 24 continued to be the existing khatians and khatian 14 to which Plot No. 108 appertained, the respondents continued to be co-sharers of H.E. Percival in the said, holding, and it is not correct to say that H.E. Percival was the sole owner of Plot No. 108 without any co-sharer, He also argued that the purported amalgamation and consolidation of holdings under section 116 of the Act was done without giving any notice to the co-sharers. In the absence of any notice upon the co-sharers the alleged amalgamation and consolidation of holding is not tenable in law. Mr. Hamidul Huq Chowdhury, however submitted by pointing out from the record that the noting in the order sheet of Miscellaneous Case No. 89 of 1972-73 (under Chapter XV of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act) sufficiently showed that amalgamation and consolidation of holdings of HE. Percival was made after the service of notice on all the parties concerned as per provisions of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act.

7. At the healing of the appeal we had the advantage of going through the entire original record called for by the Court. Thepapers in the record substantially support the contention of Mr. Hamidul Huq Chowdhury that the lower Appellate Court as well as the learned Judge, of the High Court Division did not accept the case of the pre-emptee as a result of faulty reading of the relevant papers in the record of Miscellaneous Case No. 89 of 1977-73. The learned District Judge on perusal of record made the following observation:

"The total papers according to Firisti appear to be in tact with the record.It is not that any piece of paper was missing from the record. So mere noting in the record that notices were duly served is not sufficient to show that notices were duly served and it is not known at whose instance or under what circumstances it was noted in short, it may be said that such noting of due service of notices was made without any basis. When it is patent on the face of the record and it is admitted that petitioner Mr. Percival himself died before the order of separation and amalgamation passed and. no notice was actually served upon the petitioner appellants co-sharers, the order of separation and amalgamation was null and void and such order need not be avoided by separate proceeding, as in the eye of the Jaw it was no order."

The learned Judge of the High Court Division as it appears from the judgment, proceeded on the assumption that the Miscellaneous Case No 89 of 1972-73 was started suo motu without having any application filed by H.E. Percival, and the record of Miscellaneous Case shows that it commenced with a typed copy of the application under section 9 of the Public Demands Recovery Act, filed by H.E. Percival for disposal of the certificate cases. The learned District Judge as well as the learned Judge of the High Court Division while perusing the record missed to notice that initial order for starting a proceeding for amalgamation and consolidation of holdings was made on the original application under section 9 of the Public Demands Recovery Act filed by H.E. Percival. This application dated 12-3-69 under section 9 of the Public Demands Recovery Act was duly stamped and signed by H.E. Percival. The original application bears the following noting;

"This is in connection with amalgamation of land owned by H.E. Percival. Copy of the petition may be sent to Tahsildar Sadar for necessary action, Submitted.

Sd/- Illegible.

17-3-73

As proposed. 	Sd/-Illegible

C.O.

17/3

The record of the Miscellaneous Case No. 89 of 1972-73 shows that on the same day i.e. 17-3-73 the Revenue Officer started a Miscellaneous case with the following order:

"17-3-73. This case is started on the basis of the prayer of the petitioner H.E. Percival for the separation and amalgamation of his landed property on which he has possession. It is stated by him that major portion of his property has been acquired by the Government.

Ask Tabsilder Sadar to submit report in prescribed form for taking necessary action, To 2-4-73."

"2-4-73. Seen the report of Tahsildar in the prescribed form hence issue notice upon all concerned fixing 24.4.73." "24-4-73. Notice duly served, no objection filed. Seen the papers produced in support of the claim of the petitioner. He is a recorded tenant in the proposed khatians hence on the basis of his petition separation and amalgamation of

jama is therefore allowed as proposed by Tahsildar in respect of property as shown at mouza Kashim Bazar.

18 				119 	.3706

20 				116. 	.1790

7A. The order-sheet of Certificate Case No. 468 of 1967-68 shows that on consideration of the grounds raised by the Certificate Debtor H. E. Percival in his petition under section 9 of the Act denying his liability for the dues shown in the notice under section 7. the Certificate Officer, who is also the Revenue Officer, passed an order on 21-6-73, wherein after nothing the lands still in possession of the Certificate Debtor gave direction upon the Tahsildar concerned to file fresh certificate after amalgamating P.S. Plot Nos. 117, 116 and 108 and 121 under Khatian Nos. 20, 24 and 14 along with Khatian No.18 of this case and assess correct rental demand for realization of Government rental dues immediately. After an the lands still owned and possessed by H.E. Percival appertaining to khatian Nos. 20.24.14 and 18 were amalgamated and consolidated into one khatian, namely, khatian No.18 fresh assessment of correct rent dues against H.E. Percival was made and fresh notice under section 7 of the Public Demands Recovery Act was prepared. Since in the meantime it was reported that the Certificate Debtor had died, notice under section 43 upon the legal heirs of the Certificate Debtor were issued. Auction sale was l1eld for realization of the rent dues as assessed on the basis of the amalgamated khatian that is khatian No. 18.

<u>8. In view of the circumstances as noted above, it would not be correct to say that the proceeding for amalgamation and consolidation of holdings under sections 116 and 117 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act was initiated suo motu without having any basis. In the auction sale P.S. Plot No. 108 as appearing appertained to new P.S. Khatian No. 18 was sold. It is admitted that plot No. 108 previously appertained to khatian No. 14, and in its 16 annas belonged to H.E. Percival. So separation of plot No.108 from khatian No. 14 and its amalgamation in khatian No. 18, could not prejudice the pre-emptors who claimed to be a co- sharer in khatian No. 14 on the basis of their purchase from H.E. Percival. Apart from that there is a presumption under the law that all official acts are presumed to have been rightly and regularly done.</u>

9. Chapter XV of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act deals with "Amalgamation Sub-division and Consolidation of holdings." Section 116 provides for amalgamation of holding of a tenant in the same village. This section requires that where various parcels of land are held by one tenant within one village and such parcels of land or some of them are the subject of separate tenancies such parcels of land shall under the orders of the Revenue-officer, be amalgamated into one tenancy. This section however provides that if the tenant concerned has any objection thereto which appears to such officer to be reasonable and sufficient no such amalgamation shall be ordered by the Revenue-officer. Section 116 read with section 117(1) (a) provides that amalgamation and consolidation can be taken by the Revenue-officer, either on his own motion or on an application made to him, in that behalf Section 17(1)(c) contains the provision for sub-division of a joint tenancy for distribution of rent thereof subject to the conditions indicated therein. On examining sections 116 and 117 Hind that the learned Judge of the High Court Division is completely in error in taking the view that it is a case of sub-division of a joint tenancy as provided under section 117(1)(c) for which an application was required to be filed; and in the absence of an application by the parties the Revenue officer had no authority of his own motion to sub-divide a joint tenancy. He was however conscious that "Amalgamation and consolidation as have been referred in the section may begin for the purpose of collection of revenue and for that purpose the Revenue-officer may on his own motion exercise jurisdiction." The relevant finding of the learned' Judge is quoted below:

"So I am of the view that for the purpose of sub-division of a joint tenancy an application must be filed by the tenant concerned. In the instant case the typed copy of the application dated 12.3.69 in the certificate case before the Certificate Officer at Chittagong under section 9 of the P.D.R. Act for dismissing the certificate cases could not be suo motu brought in the Miscellaneous case No. 89/72-73 by the Revenue Officer"

<u>10. Khondkar	Mahbubuddin	Ahmed only faintly argued that as a matter of fact this was a case of sub-division of a joint tenancy. He however failed to give sufficient reasons in support of this view. Prior to amalgamation Khatian No. 14 contained plot Nos. 108, 107, 87 and 124; Khatian No. 20 contained Plot No. 116; and Kbatian No. 24 contained plots 117 and 121. By the process of amalgamation and consolidation Plot 108 of Khatian 14, plot 119 of khatian 18, plot 16 of khatian 20 and plots 117 and 121 of khatian 24 were amalgamated and consolidated into one khatian, that is khatian 18. This sufficiently shows that it was a case of amalgamation and consolidation as contemplated under section 116 read with section 117(1)(a) and not a case of sub-division of a tenancy recorded in kbatian 14, as provided in section 1l7(1)(c). The order of the Certificate officer who was also the Revenue Officer, shows that the action for amalgamation and consolidation was taken at the instance of the tenant when it was considered necessary for the purpose of collection of revenue. Plot 108 solely owned and possessed by H. E. Percival was amalgamated with Plot No. 119 of khatian 18 plot No. 116 of Khatian No. 20 and plot Nos. 117 and 121 of khatian 24 and thereby new khatian 18 was brought into being and a new jama was fixed for the amalgamated and consolidated khatian. Endorsement on khatian 14 filed by the respondents itself shows that separation of plot No. 108 from that khatian and its amalgamation to khatian 18 was noted on it. Payment of rent at the old rate even after the amalgamation and consolidation as claimed by the respondents cannot set at naught the process and the order of amalgamation and consolidation which was duly made and acted upon. The learned Subordinate Judge took the correct view on this question saying:-</u>

<u>“As there was no short payment it was accepted when the petitioners paid rent at the old rate. This payment of rent at the previous rate itself does not show that the amalgamation and separation of tenancy was not given effect to."</u>

<u>11. There is another point to be discussed which is that the learned District Judge as wen as the learned Judge of the High Court Division took the view that the so called amalgamation and consolidation of holdings suo motu and that too after death of H.E. Percival cannot be said to have any legal sanction and must be treated as a void one and need not be avoided. Mr. Hamidul Huq Chowdhury In support of his submissions that the order of amalgamation and consolidation was made in accordance with law, further submitted that when such an order has been passed by the competent authority and in accordance with law, its validity cannot be challenged in the pre-emption proceeding. In support of this proposition he relied upon a decision of this Court in the case of Md. Jabed Ali Vs. Pakhal Chandra Mondal, 33 DLR (AD) 309. This is a case of separation of jam a under section 117(1) (c) of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act and not a case of amalgamation and consolidation, but the principle laid down therein provides the necessary guidance. In that case it has been held as follows:-</u>

<u>"When such a valid order under section 117 is on record and the order has been given effect the Civil Court is not competent to ignore the order on the ground of finding some irregularity in the same as a Court of appeal while dealing with the application under section 96 of the Act for pre-emption."</u>

<u>12. The principle of law laid down in the above noted case may be fully reiterated in the facts of the present case. The learned Judge also made a mistake in not taking into consideration that the noting on the petition itself and the order-sheets of Certificate Case No. 408 of 1967-68 and Miscellaneous Case No. 89/72-73 show that the case was started on 17-3-73 before it was reported on 5-7-73 that H.E. Percival bad died. Besides the Miscellaneous case being one for amalgamation and consolidation of holdings and not a case of sub-division as provided in section 117(1)(c), the Revenue-officer was competent to take action suo motu. Amalgamation of tenanciesmade in Miscellaneous Case No. 89/72-73 under sections 116 and 117(1)(a) was given effect by amending khatia. No. 14 after excluding plot No. 108 therefrom and revenue was collected on the basis of the new khatian No. 18 Prima facie the order was a valid one, its validity could not be challenged for a collateral purpose that is in a proceeding of pre-emption. The Civil Court while dealing with altogether a different matter cannot ignore the order passed by a competent Revenue-officer under section 117 of the Act,</u>

13. So far as the second point is concerned Mr. Hamidul Huq Chowdhury did not think it necessary to address the Court on this ground. So the second point is left undisguised. For the reasons stated above the judgment of the learned District Judge and that of the learned Judge of the High Court Division cannot be sustained, and the order of the learned Subordinate Judge must be restored. Therefore the appeal is allowed and the judgment of the learned District Judge and that of the learned Single Judge of the High Court Division are set aside and the Judgement of the trial Court restored, I make no order as to costs.

Badrul Haider Chowdhury J.- I have ad- vantage of going through the judgments written by my learned brothers Ruhul Islam and Shahabuddin Ahmed JJ.and I concur with the judgment of Ruhul Islam J.

Shahabuddin Ahmed J.- I have gone through the judgment proposed to be delivered by my learned brother Ruhul Islam J. As I find difficulty to agree with him I am giving views of my own as follows.

14. The land under pre-emption is plot No. 108 of Khatian No. 14 which belonged to one Percival. Khatian No. 14 consisted of three plots, Nos. 87, 107 and 108 and this Khatian, it is needless to say, constituted a non-agricultural holding under Percival. Respondent, pre-emptor purchased Plots Nos. 87 and 107 by a registered kabala dated 29 December 1965 and thereby became a co-sharer in the holding and in due course his name was mutated as Percival's co-sharer under a joint Jarna of Rs.4 and annas 7. Percival also held many other parcels of land such as in Khatians Nos. 18, 20 and 24, but the Respondent is not interested in those lands as he is not a co-sharer there. A Certificate Case being C.C. No. 408 of 1967-68 along with other such cases was filed against Percival for recovery of money due asarrear of rent under the Public Demands Recovery Act, 1913 and this case was pending when he die in August, 1971. Two years five months after his death that is, on 24 December 1973, the appellant-pre-emptee, a stranger, auction purchased Plot No 108 along with other lands of Percival in connection with that Certificate Case. Respondent filed the pre-emption case on 15 April 1976, under section 24 of the Non-Agricultural Tenancy Act alleging that he had come to know of the sale for the first time on 3 January 1976. He further alleged in his application that by an inquiry be had ascertained that, for the purpose of avoiding pre-emption, the pre-emptee had, by collusion with the Revenue Officer, got a Mutation case, being Miscellaneous Case No. 89 of 1972-73, started and thereby made a show of separation of Plot No. 108 from the joint tenancy under Khatian No. 14 and amalgamation of the separted hare with the other lands of late Percival, which were shown constipated as a new tenancy under Khatian N.18. Separation of this plot from the original holding having been made in total disregard of mandatory provisions of section 117(c) of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, the pre-emptor alleged, the separation is void and not binding upon him and that he continued to be a co-sharer of the holding in Khatian No. 14.

15. The application for pre-emption was resisted on grounds of limitation and maintainability, particularly the latter. It was contended that "the separation and amalgamation" was effected by the Revenue Officer in accordance with law and that the Revenue Officer's order could not be challenged in a collateral proceeding like the pre-emption case. The trial Court accepted both the grounds and refused pre-emption holding the pre-emptor ceased to be a co. sharer in the holding since 24 April 1973 when plot No. 108 of Percival was validly separated from the original holding. But on appeal the learned District Judge reversed the findings on both the points and allowed the pre-eruption subject to payment of compensation for improvement of the land the amount of which was to be determined on remand after arriving at the findings that the Revenue Officer's order for separation of Percival's share was void in that the said order was passed by the Revenue Officer "on his own motion's and not upon any application from a co-sharer and that no notice of the 'Separation' was served upon the other co-sharer and further that the order was also acted upon as rent of the joint tenancy continued to be paid at the old rate. A learned Single Judge of the High Court Division did not find anything to interfere with the District Judge's order in revision.

<u>16. Leave was granted on both the grounds, limitation and maintainability, but the ground as to the limitation was not pressed. Mr. Hamidul Huq Chowdhury, learned Counsel for the appellants directed his arguments on the question of maintainability of the application for pre-emption contending that the respondent ceased to be a co-sharer in the holding since the separation of Percival's share and creation of a new tenancy comprising the separated portion and other lands of Percival. Mr. Chowdhury next contends that when the Record of the Revenue Officer prima facie shows the separation and amalgamation according to law, his order cannot be challenged in a collateral proceeding like the instant one. Yes, if the original holding under Khatian No.14 were subdivided and plot No. 108 were separated therefrom according to law, then the pre-emptor got no case, as on sub-division of an original holding the former co-sharers cease to remain co-sharers with right to pre-emption. This is a settled law; reference. if at all necessary, may be made to the decision of the Supreme Court of Pakistan in the case of Begum Asia Rahman, 26 D.L.R, (S.C ) 58, and the decision of this Court in the case of Mofizuddin Patwary; 33 D.L.R. (AD) 305. But the question is whether the alleged separation of Plot No. 108 from Khatian No. 14 was made in conformity with law and to determine this question to what extent a civil court can go into the matter in a collateral proceeding such as the one at hand.</u>

<u>17. It appears that some confusion has crept in during the bearing of this appeal because of using, in a loose sense, the terms "separation" and "amalgamation" of holdings. These are quite distinct things each having specific meaning and implication; and as such, these terms should be understood in their proper perspective. For this purpose section 116 and 117(a), 117(c) of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, which are relevant in this case, are quoted below:</u>

<u>"116. Where various parcels of land are held by one tenant within one village, and such parcels of land or some of them are the subjects to separate tenancies such parcels of land shall under the orders of the Revenue Officer, be amalgamated into one tenancy."</u>

<u>"117.Notwithstanding anything contained elsewhere 10 this part, the Revenue Officer may,-</u>

<u>(a) for the purpose of amalgation of tenancies under section 116, either on his own motion or on an application made to him by one or more co-sharer tenants, in that behalf, or</u>

<u>(c) for the purpose of subdivision of a joint tenancy for distribution of rent thereof, on an application made to him by one or more co-sharer tenants, direct, by order in writing, such subdivision of a joint tenancy amongst the co-sharer tenants and distribution of rent thereof, including arrears of rent, if any as he may consider fair and equitable:</u>

<u>Provided that no such order shall be passed unless reasonable notice is given to the parties concerned to appear and be heard in the matter."</u>

<u>18. It appears clearly that 'amalgamation' means joining of various parcels of lands held by only one tenant so as to constitute one tenancy; and as such it is that tenant's problem alone. No other person, such as his co-sharer, is interested in it and that is why it may be ordered by the Revenue Officer either on his own motion or on an application made to him by the tenant; no notice of the amalgamation is required to be served upon anybody. Sub-division on the other hand, means physical division of a joint-tenancy as well as distribution of the rent thereof among the co-sharer tenants. Sub-division can be made by the Revenue Officer only on an "application made to him by one or" more co-sharer tenants". It shall not be ordered by the Revenue Officer "on his own motion". Secondly, notice of the sub-division shall be served upon all other co-sharers. Non-fulfillment either of these two requirements shall render the order of sub-division void. The term 'separation' is not a legal term like "amalgamation" or "sub-division"; it is not used in section 116 or 117, but nevertheless it denotes in general sense, separation of a share from a joint tenancy and as such 'separation' necessarily means subdivision of a joint tenancy and falls under, and is governed by clause (c) of section 117 Effect of separation of a share from the joint holding falls upon all co-sharers who, after separation, cease to be co-sharers of the original holding. A co-sharer after getting his share separated may get his portion constituted into a new tenancy or he may tag this share with his other land, if any, and if he does so, his case may be referred to as a case of 'separation and ‘amalgamation' for the sake of convenience though the two terms are quite different. His former co-sharers are not interested in such amalgamation. But whether amalgamation or not, for separation of a share from a joint tenancy the two mandatory provisions of clause (c) of section 117 must be first complied with. These provisions cannot be avoided or bypassed by saying that it is not a case of subdivision but it is 'separation and amalgamation'. An undivided share in a joint tenancy cannot be amalgamated with other independent holdings of a co-sharer without first getting his undivided share separated from the joint tenancy. This procedure shall apply even if he has applied for both in the same application. 'Amalgamation' cannot precede 'separation' as cart cannot be put before horse. It is the very case of the appellant that the respondent ceased to be a co-sharer in Khatian 14 from 24 April 1973 when plot 108 was" taken out and constituted into a new tenancy along with his other lands. If the original tenancy was not subdivided how the respondent ceased to be a co-sharer as the appellant claims? Revenue Officer's order shows that the original jama was also divided, out of Tk. 4.45 respondents jama was re-fixed at Tk. 2 55 and that of Percival at Tk. 1.90, which thereafter was added to the jama of the other holdings making his total jam a at Tk. 18.60 for the newly created separate tenancy under Khatian No. 18. This is subdivision pure and simple of the original holding under Khatian No.14. Again, whether a case attracts clause (c) depends upon its nature and implication and not upon how it has been described or designated by the Revenue Officer, The Revenue Officer took this case as 'separation and amalgamation'; but separation as shown above resulted necessarily in subdivision of the old tenancy. 'Separation' is synonymous with 'subdivision' under clause (c) of section 117 The argument that the original holding was not subdivided but was separated and amalgamated is self-defeating and self-contradictory.</u>

19. Khandker Mabbubuddin Ahmed, the learned Counsel for the respondent contends that for separation of Plot No. 108 Percival filed no application whatever to the Revenue Officer or any notice about separation was served upon the co-sharer, respondent, and as such the order for separation is void ab initio. He next contends that the order for separation was also not acted upon in that the rent was being paid for the joint holding at the old rate. Record of the Miscellaneous Case No. 89 of 1973 started by the Revenue Officer has been relied upon by the learned Counsel in support of his contentions. This record shows that Percival did not address any application to the Revenue Officer praying for separation of his share from Khatian No. 14 but it shows that a Certificate Case was filed against him to the Certificate Officer in 1967 (C.C. No. 8 of 1967-68) under the Public Demands Recovery Act. Percival in that case filed an Objection Petition on t 9-3-69 denying his liability under section 9 of the said Act alleging that most of the land for which rent was claimed had been alienated. He however stated that he was ready to pay up the dues for the lands in his possession'. Thereafter he died in August 1971. A carbon copy of that objection petition somehow found its way to the Office of the Circle Officer (Revenue) on 1st March 1973. On the left hand margin of that copy which was not signed by anybody, the Dealing Assistant Doted: "This is in connection with amalgamation of land acquired by Percival. This may be sent to Tahshilder for necessary action". The Circle Officer (Revenue) on the same day passed the following order:

"Seen the above note of Dealing Assistant Ask the Tahshilder to submit necessary proposal in the prescribed form for amalgamation at an early date"

<u>20. 00 24 April 1973 the Circle Officer (Revenue) passed the final order on receipt of the Tahshilder's report allowing 'separation and amalgamation on the basis of his (Percival's' petition' The trial Court treated the carbon copy of the Certificate Debtor's objection petition as an application for separation of his share in the joint tenancy; but the lower Appellate Court and the High Court Division held that the unsigned carbon copy of an objection petition denying liability in a certificate proceeding under the Public Demands Recovery Act can, under no circumstances. be treated as an application for subdivision or separation of a joint tenancy under the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act. In that objection petition, the Certificate debtor did not pray for 'separation or amalgamation' but expressed his readiness to pay the proportionate rent; the objection was filed in 1969 by Percival but he died in August 1971. This objection petition could not have been treated as an application for separation of his share in the joint holding two years after his death. Even if it is taken that Percival while filing the objection petition also intended the petition to be an application for separation of his share in his joint tenancies it abated on his death in 1971 whereupon his legal, representatives were not substituted. In the Certificate proceedings however his legal representatives were brought on record. From the proposal submitted by the Dealing Assistant and the order of the Revenue Officer starting the proceeding for separation and amalgamation, it is crystal clear that the Revenue Officer, whatever might have prompted him, had initiated the matter on his own motion. Had it been the case of mere amalgamation under clause (a) it would have been perfectly lawful. But this being a case of separation first, it comes well within the mischief of clause (c), and the 'separation' not having been made on an application it is void.</u>

21. As to the contention about non service of notice-another mandatory provision for separation of the share-it is only the order-sheet of the Mutation case, which shows "notice duly served" Khandker Mahbubuddio Ahmed con- tends that the Record does not contain the. Service Return nor the name and address of Percival's co-sharer were stated in the carbon copy petition nor in any other document or paper of the Record and the Firisti of documents forming the record does not show any paper missing either. In these circumstances, the learned Counsel contends that prima facie this mandatory provision was not complied with by serving notice upon the respondent, The learned Counsel has in this connection relied upon a decision of this Court in the case Abdur Rouf Vs. Amuda Khatun, 33 D.L. R. (A D) 323, wherein if was held that the splitting,up of a joint tenancy effected behind the bat of a co-sharer was void. Mr. Harnidul Huq Chowdhury however, contends that the entry in the order-sheet of the Mutation Case made in usual course of official business is sufficient proof of prima facie service of notice and that in the proceeding for pre-emption the Court is not competent to go further into the matter to ascertain whether the notice the actually served in support of this contention the learned Counsel has referred to another decision of this Court in the case of Md. Jabed Ali Vs. Rakhal Chandra Mondal 33 D.L.R. (A.D.) 309. The purport of that decision is that when an order is passed by a competent Revenue Officer under section 117 of the Act and the order is inconformity with the statutory requirements and the order has been given effect to by the co-sharer tenants of the holding the holding stands separated under law and.................the civil court is not competent to ignore the order on the ground of finding some irregularity in the same as a court of appeal while dealing with the application under section 96 of the Act for pre-emption", I do not find any conflict between these two decisions. The questions raised there related to prima facie compliance of mandatory provisions as to splitting up of a joint tenancy by a competent Revenue Officer and the scope of enquiry in a collateral proceeding. In one case the order for splitting up was found prima facie valid and in the other the order was not so found. These cases were decided on their respective facts and circumstances. In the instant case apart from the question of compliance with the two statutory requirements, there is the question of giving effect to the order for splitting up of joint jam a of Khatian No.14. Though Plot No. 108 was separated and constituted into a new tenancy with effect from 24 April 1973 as alleged by the appellant, the record or right was not amended accordingly until two years after the filing of this pre-emption case. Mr. Hamidul Huq Chowdbury relies upon Ext. R which is purportedly the amended Khatian No. 14 showing the splitting up of the joint tenancy between Percival and the respondent by an order of the Revenue Officer dated "28-1-67". But it also shows that this splitting up of the original jama was made on the basis of the Mutation Case. No. 89 of 1972-73. How the amendment was made six years before the filing of the Mutation Case its basis? Obviously, Ext. R bas been created for the purpose of this instant case and as such is not reliable. As to its rent it continued to be paid at the old rate of Tk. 4.45 till 1978. Tile trial Court is of course right in its observation that mere non-payment of rent at the new rate will not affect the splitting up; but this omission is a factor which must be considered when the question is whether the splitting up order was given effect to as against the consistent claim of the respondent that everything was done behind his knowledge in the Dame of a dead co-sharer. Facts of this case attract Abdur Rouf Vs. Amuda Khatunand not "Jabed Ali Vs. Rakhal Chandra Mondal:" The order of Revenue Officer splitting up a joint-tenancy whichever way it may be designated if it serves the old relationship of its co-sharers and thereby destroys a co-sharer's statutory right of pre-emption, must be examined by the Court in a pre- emption proceeding in order to be satisfied that prima facie the order was passed in accordance with law, that is to say the mandatory provisions of section 117(c) were complied with on the face of the record. The scope of this examination cannot be so limited as to ask the Court to keep its eyes closed and to accept without hesitation whatever order is placed before it simply because the order was passed by a competent Revenue Officer. Khandker Mahbubuddin Ahmed has submitted that the scope of enquiry in a case for pre-emption is wide enough to include the question of benami transaction in certain cases placing his reliance upon the case of Balai Chandra Mondal Vs. Nibaran Chandra Das 51 C.W.N. 644. In that case two long lines of cases, one line reo presenting the view that question of benami was outside the scope of s. 26F of the Bengal Tenancy Act and the other line representing the contrary view were elaborately discussed and considered and it was held that the question of benami transaction fell within the scope of s. 26F only in two classes of cases. In one class, the transfer is made to a co-sharer tenant in the benami of a stranger, and in the other class no transfer at all takes place but a show of transfer is made as in the case of plaintiff Nibaran. The suit was decreed and the order of pre-emption was declared void.

<u>22. In the instant case it has been argued, the aggrieved co-sharer got proper remedy against the Revenue Officer's order by appeal. But his case is that the whole matter was manipulated after Percival's death and behind his knowledge and as such he got no opportunity to seek remedy by appeal. Be that as it may, on perusal of the records of the Miscellaneous case I find no difficulty to bold that the proceeding for separation of Plot No. 108 from Kbatian No. 14 was void ab initio as it was taken suo motu by the Revenue Officer and behind the co-sharer's knowledge and consequently the joint tenancy was Dot divided but it still continues and this being the position the pre-emption is a co-sharer in the holding having right to pre-emption. I find nothing to interfere with the order of the High Court Division which rightly confirmed that of the lower appellate Court. I would therefore dismiss the appeal' with costs.</u>

Chowdhury A.T.M. Masud J.-I have had the privilege of going through the judgments delivered by my learned brothers, Ruhul Islam and Shahabuddin Ahmed JJ. I concur with the judgment of Rubul Islam J.

Order of the Court

By the majority decision the appeal is allowed. The judgment of the learned District Judge and that of the High Court Division are set aside and the judgment of the trial Court restored. There will be no order as to costs.

End.

full_judgment:
Md Khurshid Alam Sarkar J: This Rule was issued calling upon the respondents to show cause as to why the impugned decision taken by respondent Nos. 1 and 4 upon showing the petitioner's financial proposal to be non-responsive in relation to the tender under reference No. 2781- BPDB (Sets)/Dev-205/2011 for engineering, design, manufacturing, inspection, supply, installation, erection, testing & commissioning of Chapai Nawabganj 100 MW ± 10% Power Plant (HFO fired Engine Generating Sets.) Project on turnkey basis in Amnura, Chapainawabganj, Bangladesh, shall not be declared to have been taken without lawful authority and of no legal effect and, further, to show. cause as to why respondent Nos. 1 and 4 shall not be directed to declare that the petitioner's financial proposal is responsive as well as the lowest and thereby to award the tender under reference No. 2781/2011 BPDB (Shct.)/Dev-205/2011 in favour of the petitioner as the same is technically responsive and financially the lowest and/or pass such other or further order or orders as to this Court may seem fit and proper.

2. The facts of the case, as stated in the writ petition, are that the petitioner being incorporated as a company in the year 1982 engaged itself in carrying out engineering, construction and various large scale development programs in Highway, Bridge, and Building including the land mark construction and maintenance of Dhaka- Chittagong Highway, Dhaka-Sylhet Highway, Highways of Dinajpur, Rangpur, Rajshahi and Khulna, 300fts wide Purbachal link road and, eventually, the petitioner diversified its business from infrastructure to Power Generation from 2007 and pursued several powers projects. When respondent No. 1 invited tender on 9-10-2011 for engineering design, manufacturing, inspection, supply, installation, erection, testing & commissioning of Chapai Nawabganj 100 MW ±10% Power Plant (HFO fired Engine Generating Sets.) project on turnkey basis at Amnura, Chapai-nawabganj, Bangladesh, the petitioner participated in the said tender by submitting the 'Technical Proposal' to which the commitment letter from the financier was appended and the 'Financial Proposal' as per the procedure prescribed in the tender document. On 25-6-2012 the respondents opened the Technical Proposals and found 5 bidders, including the petitioner company, to be technically responsive and, then, respondent No. 2 vide letter dated 14-10-2012 notified the petitioner that their 'Financial Proposal' would be opened on 2I -10-2012 at 11 am local time in respondent No. 1,s Board room. After opening up the 'Financial Proposal' of the technically responsive 5 bidders, there were communications from Hardy Capital Corporation, which is the financier of the petitioner company. On 3-12-2012 to respondent No.1 in order to provide a reassurance of funding the project and vide letter dated 17-12- 2012 the said financier company provided certain clarifications to respondent No. 1 in relation to the anomalies as to the letterhead and logo of their company. It is stated that though the bidders were notified that the 'Financial Offer' would be opened on 21-10-2012 but nothing was notified to any of the bidders as to their financial offers. It is alleged that the respondents failed to show any transparency in dealing with the said tender and making the bidders financially responsive or non- responsive given that from the date of finding the petitioner to be technically responsive, there was no communication between the petitioner and the respondents. When on 25.02.2013 'The Daily Star', a leading daily newspaper of the land, published news under the title "Harbin Deal Gets Government Nod Again", only then the petitioner had the opportunity to know that the Purchase Committee approved the aforementioned project in favour of the China Company Hubei Electric Power Survey and Design i.e. respondent No.5 for a price of Taka 948 crores. The petitioner then managed to obtain a copy of the summary of the purchase proposal, which was prepared on the basis of the evaluation report of the Tender Evaluation Committee (hereinafter referred to TEC), wherein the TEC considered the financial proposal of all the 5 technical responsive bidders and found the petitioner's financial proposal to be non-responsive.

3. It is alleged that the petitioner offered Taka 200 crores less than that of respondent No.5 who was recommended the award but on the ground of lacking some frivolous and petty requirements the petitioner was made financially non-responsive just to favour respondent No. 5 purposefully and the action of respondent Nos. 1 & 2 in offering the tender to respondent No. 5 demonstrates mala fides as the petitioner has been deprived of getting the award for the personal gain of the respondents and against the financial interest of the State at the cost of huge loss of Bangladesh. The petitioner on 27-12-2012 notified respondent Nos. 1 &2 about the action of respondent No. 4 when the latter explained its position to the former stating that the petitioner's financial proposal was not found responsive for the reasons stated in the minutes of the meeting of TEC on 8-1-2013. It is stated that since the petitioner was not supplied with any decision, she was not in a position to prefer an appeal to the appellate authority and under the circumstances the petitioner was compelled to approach this Court for vindication of her legal rights. By filing a supplementary affidavit on 06-10-2013, the petitioner stated that though this Hon'ble Court issued Rule on 10-3-2003 with a verbal direction upon the respondents to maintain statusquo, respondent Nos. 1-3 issued Notice of Award in favour of respondent No.5 on 14-3-2013 and the same was accepted by the latter on 18-3-2013 and, thereafter, on 31-3-2013 they sealed the agreement. The petitioner terms the aforesaid actions of the respondents to have been taken in sheer disregard of this Court's honour and practice.

4. Bangladesh Power Development Board (BPDB) is respondent No. 1, the Secretary of Bangladesh Power Development Board is respondent No.2, the Tender Evaluation Committee (TEC) of Bangladesh Power Development Board is respondent No.3, the Government of the People's Republic of Bangladesh represented by the Ministry of Power, Energy and Mineral Recourses Division is respondent No. 4 and HUBEI Electric Power Survey and Design Institute of China is respondent No.5 in this writ petition. Respondent Nos. 1-3 have entered their appearances and contested the case by a filing an affidavit-in-opposition followed by supplementary thereto and respondent No.4, though did not file any separate affidavit-in-opposition, adopted the statements and submissions of respondent Nos. 1-3. Respondent No.5 contested the Rule by filing a separate set of affidavit-in-opposition with a supplementary thereto.

5. In the affidavit-in-opposition filed by respondent Nos. 1-3, it is stated that BPDB invited Tender under 'Single-Stage Two-envelop Tendering Method' for engineering, design, manufacturing, inspection, supply, installation, erection, testing & commissioning of Chapai Nawabganj 100 MW ±10% Power plant (HFO fired Engine Generating sets project on turnkey basis including 2 years warranty period along with LTSA for next 4 (four) years under the heading of "Construction of Chapai Nawabganj 100 MW. ± 1 0% Power plant (HFO fired Engine Generating sets) project "on 9-10-2011 vide Tender Ref. No. 2781-BPDB (Sect)/Dev-2051 2011 dated 9-10-2011. The said Tender Notice was published in several daily newspapers on 10- 10-2011, 13-10-2011 and 15-10-2011.

6. As per the Tender Notice and subsequent addenda, the Technical and Financial proposals, separated in two sealed envelopes, were to be submitted to BPDB by 10-00 hrs. BST on 25-6-2012. The Tender opening committee headed by the Secretary of BPDB was to open the Technical proposal at the same date and read out the names of the Tenders. The following 5(five) tenderers namely, 1.M/s.CCC:ETERN-FUJIAN JV (CFFJV), China, 2. M/s. HUBAI Electric Power Survey and Design Institute, China, 3. M/s. Energypac Power Generation Ltd. Bangladesh, 4. M/s. Concord Pragatee Construction Ltd, Bangladesh and 5.M/s.Dong Fang Electric International Corporation, China were received. All the Tenderers' representatives were present. As per clause 25 of the Tender documents, the Technical proposals submitted by the bidders were to be evaluated first and then the "Financial Proposals" of the Tenderers whose "Technical Proposals" found to be responsive would be opened and to be evaluated only. The technical proposals were evaluated by the TEC which was formed by the Power Division, Ministry of Power Energy and Mineral Resources and the said Committee recommended all the said tenderers as technically responsive after receiving requisite clarifications from them and, accordingly, further recommended to open their Financial Proposals which were finally approved by the BPDB and the concerned Ministry (MEMR).

7. Then the Financial Proposals of all the technically responsive tenderers were opened on 21-10-2012 and the evaluation of the financial proposals was done as per the instructions set forth in the tender document and subsequent addenda. As per the assessment of the TEC, only 2 (two) tenderers' financial proposals were found to be responsive namely: (1) M/s. CCC:ETERN- FUJIAN JV(CFFJV), China and (2) M/s. HUBEI Electric Power Survey and Design Institute, China and the following tenderers' Financial proposals were found to be non-responsive- (1) M/s. Energy Pac Power Generation Ltd. Bangladesh, (2) M/s. Concord Pragatee Construction Ltd, Bangladesh and (3) M/s. Dong Fang Electric International Corporation, China. The Financial proposal of M/s. Concord Pragatee Consortium Ltd. Bangladesh (the petitioner) was found non- responsive since her offer was confusing and conditional which falls under material deviation and the said decision was communicated to the petitioner vide memo No. 27/BPDB(Secy.) /Dev- 205/2011 and dated 3-1-2013. As the financial proposals of the petitioner and two other tenderers were found non-responsive, the same were not considered for further evaluation. The specific reasons for non-considering the writ petitioner's financial offer is given in the minutes of the meeting of TEC held on January 2013 (annexure-I to the writ petition).

8. The financial proposals of 2 responsive tenderers were evaluated by the TEC and after threadbare discussions and considering the facts and factors the said Committee recommended to accept the financial offer (EPC cost) of technically and financially responsive 1st Lowest Bid of M/s. HUBEI Electric Power Survey and Design Institute, China, (respondent No.5) which was subsequently recommended by BPDB and then was approved by the Purchase Committee and, finally, was received nod from the Hon'ble Prime Minister of the Government of People's Republic of Bangladesh. Thereafter, on 14-3-3013 the Notification of Award was issued in favour of respondent No.5 who accepted the same on 18-3- 2013 and submitted performance Guarantee (PG) on 28-3-2013 and thereafter a contract was signed between the BPDB and respondent No.5 on 31-3- 2013.

9. Out of 3 financially non-responsive tenderers, one M/s. Dong Fang Electric International Corporation went to the Review Panel invoking the provisions under sections 29 and 30 of the Public Procurement Act-2006 (PPA, 2006) and Public Procurement Rules-2008 (PPR, 2008) to seek redress for their grievance and after hearing both the sides the Review Panel rejected the said appeal on 10-2-2013. However, the writ petitioner, without exhausting the said provisions of law for settlement of her grievance, filed the instant writ petition and obtained the present Rule. It is started that as per clause 2. of the Tender Documents, Specimen Form of the Proposal (Form of Tender) 'without price' needed for technical proposal and Specimen Form of Tender 'with price' needed for financial proposal are furnished in Appendix-2 of the Tender Documents. As such, it cannot be said that the financial credit proposal of the writ petitioner has been evaluated with her technical proposal. It is further stated that when the writ petitioner's financial offer was found non-responsive she filed an application to respondent No.2 on 27-12-2012 and respondent No.2 after examining the matter rejected the said application of the writ petitioner on 3-1-2013 and, hence, it cannot be said that the writ petitioner was not informed about her financial offer as non- responsive.

10. In the affidavit-in-opposition filed by respondent No.5, it is contended that the claim of the petitioner as to making the lowest offer by a margin of Taka 200 crores appears to be based on the 'read-out' price as stipulated in the financial proposal of the submitted tender documents. It was mentioned by respondent No.5 that the readout price is not the final price to be accepted for determining the successful bidder. The 'present tender in question involves such method Of, procurement where the bidder will arrange finance for the tendered project and, therefore, in 'addition to read-out price, rate of interest, repayment period, arrangement' fees and other bank charge set should be taken into consideration for final evaluation of the financial proposal. Read- out price is actually the cost of Engineering, Procurement and, Construction Cost (EPC) and does' not include rate of interest, repayment period; arrangement fees and other charges and expenses as may be incurred. The petitioner, in his financial offer, has Claimed 5% as 'Lender Fee" culminating 4.25 million in Euro which is not included in the read-out price. 20. Mr Razik Al Jalil, the learned advocate appearing for respondent Nos. 1-3, and Dr. Shahdeen Malik, the learned advocate appearing for respondent No.5, both of them opted to adopt the submissions advanced by Mr. Murad Reza. However, Dr. Malik, added a further submission that respondent Nos. 1-4 are government functionaries and in course of carrying out their routine tasks they have made a decision in favour of respondent No.5 in accordance with law and it is the settled principle of law that presumption on the decision made by a government functionary should be that the same has been taken bonafide unless any aggrieved person makes out a clear case of malafide by categorically stating the motive or dishonesty of the concerned government functionary. He submits that there is no specific allegation against the respondents in leveling blame against them that they have been influenced by extraneous consideration. By referring to the case of Farzana Haque vs University of Dhaka 42 DLR 262, he submits that malafide must be pleaded in clearer terms in a writ petition and requires to be proved by material evidence and, thus, malafide must not be readily inferred.
