65. From a concurrent reading of Rules 119- 121 of the PPR, it is our understanding that the TEC is required to prepare a score sheet containing the scores of each of the bidders which they were awarded on their technical proposals. The minimum score set for passing through the technical stage is to be obtained by a bidder in order to qualify for its financial offer to be opened up and, thereafter, the TEC shall show the bidders the cumulative score they have obtained but nothing was produced before this Court by the respondents to corroborate their claim that respondent No, 5 got the highest score in the technical offer as well as in the financial offer and it was awarded contract as the highest scorer in the combined score sheet.

66. In addition to the violation of the provisions of the PPA, 2006 and PPR, 2008 heavy emphasis were given by the petitioner on the non- compliance of the Clauses 17 & 25 of the Instructions of Tender Document in making the petitioner financially non-responsive.

67.	Let us look at the aforesaid Clauses. Clause No. 17: Source of finance will be from Tenderer's Financing. For Tenderer's financing, firm commitment letter from the financial unit/lender about Tenderer's credit financing shall be submitted with 'Technical proposal' at the time of bid. submission, otherwise the Tender shall be considered technically non-responsive. The credit amount shall cover 100% of the turnkey price (both foreign and local currency portion of the offered price). The Tenderer shall enclose a complete and firm financing proposal. The Credit Proposal shall mainly include the followings:

a)	Offered credit

b)	Rate of interest

c)	Repayment period

d)	Grace period etc.

The Financial proposal should also include 3 (three) amortization schedules considering above mentioned features of credit,

1 (one) for CIF value of Schedule-l in foreign currency, 01 (one) for remaining portion of foreign currency (except DIF value, 1 (one) for local currency. BPDB will provide Corporate Guarantees against the credit financing.

Claus No. 25: The Technical proposals submitted by the bidders shall be opened first in presence of the Bidders. At the same time the envelope marked "Financial Proposal" submitted by the respective Bidders will be noted for record and kept unopened in proper custody of the Secretary, BPDB until the Technical Proposals are completely evaluated. Considering all the aspects (in connection with specified work) offered by each Bidder as well as the date and information submitted and on proper judgment of the capability of individual Bidders, technically qualified proposals shall be selected amongst them and listed. The technical qualifications and overall capability of the Bidder for carrying out the work as specified as well as the specifications of the equipment/materials offered and fulfillment of the key dates shall be the essence for selection of technically qualified Bidders. 	.

The technical qualifications and overall capability of the Tenderer for carrying out the Words as specified as well as the Specifications of the equipment/materials offered and fulfillment of key dates shall be the essence for selection of qualified tenderers.

In the process of evaluation, tender may be considered as responsive only if it is submitted in compliance with the mandatory requirement set out in the tender document, without material deviation or reservation.

A material deviation or reservation is one:

a)	Which affects in any substantial way the scope, quality or performance of the works,

b)	Which limits in any substantial way, inconsistent with the tender document, the procuring entity's rights or the tenderer's obligations under the contract

c)	Whose rectification would affect unfairly the competitive position of other tenderers presenting responsive tenders.

68. From a bare reading of Clause 17 it appears that 'Firm Commitment letter" is a component or part of the 'Technical Proposal' which the petitioner had submitted with 'Technical Proposal' vide annexure-C dated 5-6-2012 which assures that credit amount shall cover 100% of the price which is completely ready for immediate use. The respondents having been satisfied with the same declared the petitioner to be a technically responsive bidder. However, since the respondents are empowered under Rules 120 & 121 to take into consideration the combined score, the Review Panel is to consider as to whether the petitioner's offer with 5% lending fees or commitment fees of $ 1,00,000 cumulatively stand as a poor offer (albeit with a margin of 200 crores Taka) than that of respondent No.5.

69. And from the perusal of Clause 25 it appears that a tenderer shall be qualified for being responsive only when her proposals will be found in compliance with the 'mandatory requirement' set out in the Tender Document without being in 'material deviation'. The Review Panel is to assess as to whether the grounds taken by the TEC in rejecting the petitioner's financial proposal comes within the mischief of (a), (b) or (c) of the definition of 'material deviation' under Clause 25 of the instructions of 'Tender Document'

70. If the petitioner approaches the Review Panel following the disposal of this case, the Review Penal may take the anomalies indicated hereinbefore into its consideration upon condoning the delay in preferring an appeal before it under section 30(2) of the PPA, 2006 as an exceptional case in view of the statements made by the petitioner in this Court that she had never received the annexure-7 (decision of the respondents on the petitioner's representation). The Review Panel may also ask the respondents to produce the score sheets of all the bidders who were declared technically responsive and the combined score sheets of the financially responsive bidders to examine the allegations of the petitioner in details and, thereby, make its observation as to whether the provisions of Section 59 of the PPA, 2006, Rules 199-121 and the instructions contained in the Tender Documents, particularly the instructions laid down in Clause Nos. 17 and 25 thereof, have been followed. In the event that the Review Panel finds the decision of the TEC to have been taken in violation of any provisions of the PPA, 2006 and. PPR, 2008, it shall pronounce its decision under the provisions of Rule 60 of the PPR, 2008 with necessary ancillary relief/s to the parties of this case whatever may deem fit and appropriate to the adjudicators. The fact that the respondents have already awarded contract in favour of respondent No. 5 and, now, the works for construction and installation of the project is going on in full speed, which ought not to have been done by the respondents during pendency of the Rule, may be mitigated by compensating either respondent No. 5 for the works already she has carried out if the Review Panel decides for cancellation of the contract executed between respondent No.5 and the respondents. Or, in the alternative, allowing respondent No. 5 to continue with the construction and installation of the project works at the rate quoted by the petitioner to protect the financial interest of the state and, in that event, the petitioner should be entitled to be compensated sufficiently by the government authorities and respondent NO.5. Here it is pertinent to refer to the facts and dictum of the case of RAJUK vs Abdur Raul Chowdhury 61 DLR (AD) 28 where the writ petitioner Mr. Abdur Rouf Chowdhury constructed a 22 storied building near the Tejgaon Airport and RAJUK alleged that the same has been done without obtaining any planning per- mission from them and, eventually, it threatened to dismantle the building when the High Court Division though made the Rule absolute but on an appeal the Apex Court ordered for demolishing the building. The purpose of referring this case here is that the Court can pass an order to demolish a project if it is required for protection of the national interest. However, in this case there should not be any order to demolish the project for the protection of financial interest of the state. In the cited case, the order of demolition was passed in order to protect the interest of the state i.e. to protect the Tejgaon Airport and, here the national interest is installation of the project with the minimum cost and maxim quality. Thus, if it is required in this case any appropriate order may be passed by the Review Panel without hampering the ongoing construction and installation work of the project upon unhesitatingly detecting the illegality and lack of transparency, if there is any, towards adjudication of this sensitive public procurement related complaint.

71. Though this Court declined to exercise its power of judicial review for now, however, this judgment shall not operate as a bar (res judicata) to seek the 'certification' (certiorari) from this Court on the Review Panel's decision, if the petitioner wishes to revert back to this Court following the Review Panel's verdict in favour of the respondent and the petitioner finds herself dissatisfied and aggrieved with the same. In that event this Division shall be fully competent and will be in a better and convenient position to exercise its power of judicial review on the said decision of the Review Panel.

72. In our jurisdiction the power of judicial review of this Court flows from the mandate of Article 102 of our Constitution unlike the UK where inspite of not having any written legal man- date, their judiciary exercises this power. However, the British judiciary since long has formulated some rules, principles/guidelines as to where the judicial power should be exercised. Among them, one rule is constantly being followed by them that if there is any forum created by any law, the UK judiciary does not entertain the judicial review application.

73. In our jurisdiction as well, our Apex Court has repeatedly reminded the High Court Division to be skeptical in entertaining writ petition where there is an alternative forum. In a series of decisions our Apex Court disapproved invocation of writ jurisdiction by circumventing the alternative forum. In a recent case, ACC vs Enayetur Rahman, 64 DLR (AD) 14, when the ACC filed charge-sheet against the petitioner he invoked the writ jurisdiction for quashing the criminal proceedings and the High Court Division quashed the proceeding but the Appellate Division set-aside the verdict on the ground that the High Court Division should not have entertained the writ petition when there is an alternative forum.

74. In another recent case, Government of Bangladesh vs M Anwar Hossain 32 BLD (AD) 36 =16 BLC (AD) 155, when High Court Division entertained the writ petition on the grievance of the petitioner that his mutation case is being kept pending without disposing of the same for malafide purpose, it was held that-

What's more, the writ petitioners have also alternative remedy against the inaction of the Assistant Commissioner (Land), if there be any, for mutating their names. Where an alternative remedy is available, the remedy under Article 102(2) being discretionary High Court Division should refuse to grant relief to the aggrieved person. Where the alternative remedy could not be equally efficacious the exercise of discretionary power by the High Court Division is called for. The writ petitioners failed to make out any case that the alternative remedy available to them is not efficacious.

<u>75. Since, this Court has held that the Review Panel is equally efficacious forum for adjudication of the grievance of the petitioner, the present Rule is liable to be discharged only on the ground of maintainability without embarking upon other issues under the law of contract for examination as has been advanced by the learned Additional Attorney-General.</u>

<u>Accordingly, the Rule is discharged without any order as to costs.</u>

End.

lawyer:
M Golam Rabbani with AKM Asaduzzaman, Advocates ----- For the Appellants.  
AY Salehuzzaman, DAG  ----- For the Respondents.
parties:
Noor Mohammad Khan & ors ----- Appellants  
Vs. 
Government of the People's Republic of Bangladesh & ors ----- Respondents
full_judgment:
Kazi Ebadul Haque J: This appeal is at the instance of the plaintiff against the judgment dated 28th August, 1982 passed by the learned Subordinate Judge, Second Court, Dhaka in Title Suit No. 401 of 1979.

2. The case of the plaintiffs, inter alia, was that the suit plot No. 5 measuring an area of 45.93 acres of land belonged to Dhaka Nowab Court of Wards Estate as the recorded owner in the CS Khatian No. 1 of mouza Chowbaria under Police Station Savar, District Dhaka and the said Court of Wards Estate settled the said land in rayoti right to the plaintiff No. 1 on 20.6.1353 BS by granting Amalnama and rent receipt in his favour on receiving salami; that the plaintiff No. 1 settled part of the suit land to some tenants and he remained in possession of 28.79 acres of land after such settlement; that the plaintiff No. 1 subsequently gifted another portion of the suit land to his children, plaintiff Nos. 2-5 and thus all the plaintiffs remained in possession of the suit land; that at the initial stage of the SA settlement operation the suit land was recorded in the name of the plaintiff No. 1 but the defendant No. 2 most illegally and behind the back of the plaintiff No. 1 got the suit property recorded in SA khatian in the name of the defendant No. 2; that subsequently in RS khatian the same mistake was committed by recording the land in the name of the defendant No. 2; that the plaintiff No. 1 who was away from the country could not know about the wrong recording of the name of defendant No. 2 in the SA as well as RS Khatian; that the wrong recording of the suit land in the RS Khatian cast cloud over the title of the plaintiffs in the suit land giving rise to the cause of action of the suit.

3. Defendant Government of Bangladesh contested the suit by filing a written statement denying material allegations and stating, inter alia, that the suit is barred under section 42 of the Specific Relief Act and is not maintainable; that the defendant government further denied that the Dhaka Court of Wards Estate settled the suit plot to the plaintiff No. by granting amalnama or rent receipt on receipt of salami or that the plaintiff No. 1 leased out some portions of the suit plot to some tenants and the suit land remained in his possession or that the plaintiff No. 1 gifted some portion of the suit property to plaintiff Nos. 2-5 or that the plaintiffs have been owning and possessing the same peacefully. The further case of the defendant Government is that the suit plot was declared as reserved forest under Gazette Notification No. 3125 dated 13.4.55 published in the Dhaka Gazette on 5th May, 1965 and subsequently the Nowab Estate was acquired by the Government under the provision of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act. Since the aforesaid Gazette Notification suit plot is in peaceful possession of the Forest Department. The Exlandlord of Dhaka Nawab Estate entered into an agreement with the Collector of Mymensingh and Dhaka on 26.1.1923 for the management of the forest and as such ex-landlord had no right to settle the suit plot to the plaintiff No. 1. The suit plot having been correctly recorded in the name of the Forest Department in the SA and RS Khatian, the suit is barred under section 144B of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act. The plaintiffs in order to grab the forest land of the Government have filed the suit on the basis of forged, fabricated, ante-dated and fraudulent papers. The plaintiffs did not acquire any right, title, interest or possession in the suit land on the basis of the alleged amalnama and rent receipt.

4. In the trial Court plaintiffs examined 5 witnesses including plaintiff No. 1 and also adduced some documentary evidence which have been marked as Exhibits. Though the defendant Government cross-examined plaintiffs' witnesses but it did not adduce any witness nor produced any document except producing the relevant Gazette Notification.

5. After trial the learned Subordinate Judge by judgment dated 28th August, 1982 dismissed the suit.

6. The learned Advocate for the appellants have taken us through the plaint, written statement, deposition of the PWs and the judgment of the court below.

7. Mr. M Golam Rabbani, the learned Advocate appearing for the plaintiff appellants, submitted that the court below was wholly wrong to hold that the basic documents of the plaintiff could not be satisfactorily proved and that plaintiffs also failed to prove their physical possession in the suit land inasmuch as the plaintiff No. 1 as PW 1 proved the document marked Ext. 1, receipt showing payment of salami, Ext. 2, the Amalnama and Ext. 3 series, rent receipts granted to him by the Dhaka Nowab Court of Wards Estate for the years 1353, 1354 and 1358 B.S. He further submitted that the court below was wholly wrong to find that PW 5 utterly failed to prove the documents as he does not know how to read and write when PW 5 simply corroborated the statement of PW 1 as regards settlement of the suit land to the plaintiff No. 1. He further submitted that the plaintiffs did not attempt to prove the document through PW 5. He further submitted referring to section 47 of the Evidence Act that documents could be proved by a witness who knows the hand-writing of the person writing the document and signature of the person who signed the same. He also referred to a decision reported in the case of Ram Chandra and another Vs. Jaithmal and others reported in AIR 1934 All at page 990 wherein it was held that a person who cannot read and write certain characters may prove the hand-writing of another in those characters. The learned Advocate next submitted that the plaintiffs having discharged the onus lying on them by proving the documents in support of their title in the suit land onus shifted on the defendants to rebut the same by producing the counter-foils of rent receipts lying in their custody and the defendants though challenged the genuineness of plaintiffs documents failed to produce any oral as well as documentary evidence to disprove the same. The learned Advocate also referred to Order 18 rule 2 of the Code of Civil Procedure in support of his contention. The learned Advocate next submitted that the court below was wholly wrong in holding that the plaintiffs failed to prove possession in the suit land inasmuch as the plaintiffs must be presumed to be in possession as they proved their title thereof specially when defendants failed to prove their possession by adducing any evidence inasmuch as the plaintiffs adduced some evidence in support of their possession in the suit land. The learned Advocate for the appellant further submitted that the notification under section 4 of the Forest Act could not vest the suit property with the Government or the Forest Department.

8. Mr. AY Salehuzzaman, the learned Deputy Attorney-General appearing for the defendant Government, submitted that in paragraph Nos. 5-7 of the plaint the plaintiff asserted that SA Khatian as well as RS Khatian in respect of the suit land was wrongly recorded in the name of the defendant Government. Under section 144A of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, there is presumption of correctness of the entry made in the RS Khatian and as such presumption of possession of the suit land is in favour of the defendant Government and the plaintiffs having failed to satisfactorily prove their possession in the suit land, the suit for mere declaration of title without prayer for consequential relief by way of either confirmation or recovery of possession of the suit land is barred under the provision of section 42 of the Specific Relief Act. The learned Deputy Attorney-General further submitted that the plaintiffs asserted in the plaint that at the initial stage of preparation of record of rights the name of plaintiff No. 1 was re-corded in the S.A. khatian and subsequently the same was wrongly recorded in the name of the defendant No. 2 and R.S. khatian is simply a copy of the S.A. khatian and that part of the suit plot was leased out by the plaintiff No.1 to some of the tenants and the same were recorded in their names but the plaintiffs failed to produce any khatian to show that part of the suit plot was recorded in the name of the alleged tenants of plaintiff No. 1 or compensation assessment roll for payment of compensation to the plaintiff No. 1 for the said tenanted land was prepared in the name of the plaintiff No. 1. Moreover, the plaintiffs could not produce any rent receipt granted either to them or to their tenants after the acquisition of Dhaka Court of Wards Estate by the Government. He further submitted that as the plaintiffs failed to prove their case there was no question of discharging onus by the defendant Government by adducing oral evidence or by producing counter-foils of rent receipts genuineness of which was challenged by the defendant Government.

<u>9. Before considering the respective contentions of the learned Advocates we find from the plaint that the suit is in respect of 28.79 acres out of 45.93 acres of suit plot No. 5. In the schedule of the plaint the plaintiffs have not given any boundary or other specification of the suit land to identify the same and thus the suit land is vague and unspecified portion of the suit plot. Under the provision of Order 7 rule 3 of the Code of Civil Procedure the plaintiffs shall give clear description of the suit land in the plaint sufficient to identify the same. We are of the view that the plaintiffs having failed to comply with the mandatory requirement of law in giving clear description or boundary sufficient to identify the suit land the plaintiffs are not entitled to any decree for such defect in the plaint even if they can succeed in proving their title to the suit land as no court can pass decree for unspecified land.</u>

<u>10. We are to consider here whether the plaintiffs have been able to prove their title to the suit land. Ext. 1 is the receipt for payment of salami to the Dhaka Nowab Court of Wards Estate. Ext. 2 is the alleged Amalnama granted by the said Estate settling the suit land to the plaintiff No. 1 and Ext 3 series are the rent receipts granted for the years 1353, 1354 and 1358 B.S. by the said Estate. The appellants have not included the said documents in the Paper Book though the Rules provide that part II of the Paper Book shall consist of exhibits and no finding or conclusion in the decision appealed from will be permitted to be challenged at the hearing of the appeal unless the materials on which such challenge is based is included in the Paper Book. As such we are not bound to consider the said documents. However, we have perused the said documents in the lower court records. The contents of Exts. 1 and 3 series were written with pencil and Ext. 2 with ink as pointed out by the learned Deputy Attorney-General. He also pointed out that the receipts were rubbed to make the same appear old and the same were written with pencil instead of ink so as to avoid the same from being checked. We have noticed from Ext. 1 that the amount of salami was received subject to the approval of the Chief Manager and from the remarks in the bottom of the said Ext No. 1 it appears that salami and rents received without approval of the Chief Manager will not have the effect of settling the land of the Estate to the person paying the same. We find from Ext. 2 that it is a form of proposal for settlement of the land of the said Estate and there was no approval of the Chief Manager. We have also noticed from Ext. 3 series, rent receipts that unless settlement is approved by the authorised officer of the Estate claim or settlement of land cannot be made on the basis of payment of rent. In Ext. 2 it has also been clearly written that the proposal for settlement of land will not be effective unless the tenant executes kabuliyat in favour of the landlord. The plaintiff No. 1 as PW 1 stated that the receipt for payment of salami was signed by Gobinda Chandra Roy, Cashier of Dhaka Nowab Estate in his presence and the said receipt was marked Ext. 1. The said witness further stated in his deposition that the suit land was leased out to him by the document of lease executed by the officers of Nowab Estate including Assistant Manager, Dhaka Nowab Estate by signing before him and the document was marked Ext. 2. He further stated that these are the signatures of the Head Assistant and Assistant Manager in the said document marked Exts. 2(i) and 2(ii). He further stated that he paid rent to the Nowab Estate afterwards and rent receipts were granted by the Dhaka Nowab Estate and the same were marked Ext. 3 series. From the cross-examination of this witness we find that he was a school student at the relevant time of taking lease and that he did not pay any rent from 1359 BS upto date. PW 5, who claimed himself to be an ex-employee of Dhaka Nowab Court of Wards Estate as orderly of the then Assistant Manager, stated in his deposition that the Assistant Manager Abul Kashem executed Ext. 2 in his presence and proved his signature marked Ext. 2(ii). He further stated that receipt of salami Ext.1 and rent receipts were granted by Dhaka Nowab Estate. From his cross-examination, we find that he is an illiterate person and he could not satisfy the court that he ever worked as orderly of the said Estate. We are unable to place any reliance on the testimony of PW 5. He appears to be a procured witness who does not know how to sign his name and put his thumb impression in the deposition sheet. PW1 being the plaintiff and a school student at the relevant time on his own admission cannot also be relied on as he is interested in the result of the suit. The contents of the said documents were not even attempted to be proved by the PW1. Considering the evidence of the said witnesses we arc of the view that the said documents were not legally proved as writing of the said documents could not be proved by examining any witness. We are unable to appreciate the argument of the learned Advocate of the appellants that the said documents were legally proved. The decision referred to by the learned Advocate has no manner of application in the facts and circumstances of the instant case. From the very look the said documents appear to be spurious and manufactured for the purpose of the suit in collusion with the interested persons. Even if these documents are accepted as genuine the same could not create title in favour of the plaintiffs in the absence of the approval by the Chief Manager and execution of kabuliyat in compliance thereof. It appears that the alleged settlement by the said document were not acted upon as the plaintiffs failed to produce any rent receipts granted by the Government after the acquisition of rent receiving interest nor they could produce any khatian alleged to be prepared in the name of their alleged tenants in respect of part of the suit plot or any compensation assessment roll in the name of the plaintiffs or in respect of the said tenanted land or any khatian alleged to have been prepared in the name of the plaintiff No. 1 at the initial stage. Moreover, the PW 1 himself admitted that he did not pay rent from 1359 BS upto date.</u>

<u>11. Thus the plaintiffs having failed to prove their case there is no question of failure of the defendant Government to discharge any onus as the defendant Government did not admit plaintiffs' case of settlement of the suit land to the plaintiffs by setting up any counter case. In the trial Court the plaintiffs rightly began their case first and examined their witnesses in support of their case. In this case, we find that the defendant Govt. did not adduce any evidence except cross-examining the PWs. Order 18, rule 2 of the Code of Civil Procedure deals with order of production of evidence by the parties and not with onus which depends on the pleading of the parties. Plaintiffs' case having been totally denied by the defendant Government in the written statement, the onus to prove the case was entirely on the plaintiffs and the plaintiffs having failed to prove their case there was no onus on the defendant Government to discharge by producing either oral or documentary evidence. As the plaintiffs neither adduced any evidence to show that counterfoils of the rent receipts produced by them were in the custody of the defendant Govt. nor they called for any such counterfoils from the defendant Government, so we find no reason to form an adverse presumption against the defendant Government for non-production of any such documents existence of which were denied by the Government.</u>

<u>12. The plaintiff No. 1 as PW 1 simply stated in his deposition that he is in possession of the suit land without giving any details how he possessed the same but PW 2, who is aged about 30 years and claimed to be a servant of the plaintiff, stated that he had been looking after the properties for last 8 years and before him Ali Ahmed used to manage the affairs of the plaintiffs for 15 years. But in cross-examination he stated that he cannot tell total area of the suit plot. PW 3 who is a resident of a distant village Banpura under PS Banani stated that the plaintiffs are in possession of the suit land. In cross-examination he admitted that formerly he was a Mohrar and he has case in court. PW 4 who also hails from Chand Road, PS Banani far away from the suit land stated that the plaintiffs are in possession of the suit land through their own man, In cross-examination he stated that Rahman Shaheb (possibly he meant Rahmutullah PW 2) holes after the suit land for the last 20/2 years. Both the PWs 2-3 stated that the plaintiffs have residential and other houses in the land and chowkidari tax for the same are paid. PW 4 also stated that plaintiffs have residential and other houses in the suit land. Plaintiffs in support of their possession could not produce any rent receipts or chowkidari tax receipts. PW 2 being servant of the plaintiff and PWs 3 and 4 being men of different locality and all of them being more zealous than the plaintiff PW 1 to state what the PW 1 did not state in his deposition cannot be relied upon and as such we are of the view that the plaintiffs failed to prove their possession in the suit land. Therefore, simple suit for declaration of title by the plaintiffs in the absence of prayer for recovery of possession in the suit land is also barred under the proviso to section 42 of the Specific Relief Act and as such the present suit is also not maintainable.</u>

<u>13. Though the Government did not examine any witness they produced copy of Dhaka Gazette dated May 5, 1955 publishing Notification No. 3125-For-13th April, 1955 under section 4 of the Forest Act, 1927 in respect of the suit plot No. 5 of Mouza Chowbaria. This Notification is a preliminary of vesting of the land contained in the said notification. The Government did not take any step to produce the Notification under section 20 of the Forest Act which is a natural culmination of a preliminary Notification under section 4 of the Forest Act. As we have already found that the plaintiffs failed to prove their title or possession in the suit land there is no necessity of deciding whether the suit land vested in the Government as reserved forest land. Admittedly SA khatian and subsequently prepared and published RS khatian are in the name of the defendant No. 2 Forest Department. RS khatian prepared under the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act has presumption of correctness under section 144A of the said Act. The plaintiffs having failed to displace the said presumption by proving their title and possession in the suit land the plaintiffs are not entitled to any decree and the learned Subordinate Judge rightly dismissed the suit.</u>

In the result, the appeal is dismissed without any order as to costs and the judgment and decree of the learned Subordinate Judge are hereby affirmed.

End.

caseno: Appeal from Appellate Decree No. 770 of 1959.
lawyer:
Shehabullah  with Moqbul Ahmed ----- For the appellants.
A.K.M. Shafiqur Rahman with Faruque Ahmed ----- For the respondents.
parties:
Abdul Hamid & ors ----- Appellants
Vs.
Abul Hossain Mir being dead, his heirs: Abdus Sobhan Mir & ors ----- Respondent
case_source: Appeal against the Decree of G. Mowla, Additional District Judge of Zilla Tippera (now Comilla) dated 10th day of December. 1958 passed in Title Appeal No. 29 of 1957 affirming the decree of Mr. M.H. Chowdhury, Subordinate Judge, 1st Court, Comilla dated 18th day of December, 1956- in Partition Suit No. 127 of 1956/108 of 1954.
full_judgment:
This appeal by the defendants is directed against the Judgment and decree passed by the learned Additional District Judge, Comilla (Tripura) affirming those of the learned Sub-ordinate Judge, Comilla in a suit for partition.

2. Plaintiffs have alleged that the suit properties belonged to Arman Mir and Jamiruddin Mir and that the two brothers who were in ejamali possession of the properties had 8 annas share each therein. On the basis of geneology through Jamiruddin Mir the plaintiff have jointly claimed 4 annas 2 gondas 1 kara 5 krantis share in the properties. The plaintiffs have further alleged that C S. dag Nos. 100 and 10l have been wrongly recorded in the suit khatian No. 146 and that these two plots have been acquired by the sons of Jamiruddia from one Barkat by a kabala dated 24th Ashar 1306 B.S, and these plots have been wrongly recorded in the khatianas properties owned by the co-sharers on the basis of inheritance from Arman Mir and Jamiruddin Mir.

3. The defendant Nos. 2, 19, 35 and 45 by two separate written statements contested the suit They have alleged that Arman Mir and Jamiruddin Mir were not full brothers but they were step brothers: they lived in a different village; Arman Mir first came over to this village and settled down and acquired the properties thereafter Jamiruddin Mir came to reside with his step brother Arman Mir and that both of them acquired sepal rate independent properties. Subsequently there had been a partition between the superior landlords under the Estate Partition Act in which the personal properties acquired by Arman Mir were recorded in the Batwara Khatin No. 38 and the other properties belonging to Jamiruddin Mir and Arman Mir in equal shares were recorded in the Batwara Khatian No. 39 it has been contended that during the last C S. operation, the properties of Batwara Khatian Nos. 38 and 39 were fraudulently recorded in the suit khatian. i.e. C.S. Khatian No. 146; properties recorded in Batwara khatian No 38 have been wrongly included in the suit kharian No. 146 of Dhaneswar Mouja; and these are not liable to be partitioned in this suit.

In the trial the principal point for determination was whether the lands in Batwara Khatian No. 38 were self-acquired properties of Arman Mir or joint properties of the two brothers and which khatian would prevail over the other.

4. The trial court on consideration of evidence found that suit properties were Joint properties of the two brothers Arman Mir and Jamiruddin Mir and that Arman Mir and Jamiruddin Mil were not step- brothers but they were full brothers. The trial court also found that there is no evidence that Arman Mir and Jamiruddin Mir came to the suit village from a southern country. The learned Subordinate Judge on consideration of all these evidences oral and documentary as found that the suit properties originally belonged to Jamiruddin Mir and Arman Mir in equal shares. On appeal the learned Additional District Judge affirmed the decision of the trial court and dismissed the appeal.

5. Mr. Shehabullah with Mr. Moqbul Ahmed the learned Advocate appearing on behalf of the defendant-appellants has submitted that the court of appeal below committed an error of law in affirming the decree of the trial solely on the basis of entries in the C.S. Khatian inasmuch as that when the court has embarked upon an investigation of the title of the respective parties to the suit properties the entry in the khatian lost its weight and more so when the plaintiffs have failed to prove the basis of the eatries in the khatian. He has submitted that the plaintiffs having failed to produce any evidence as regards the basis of the entries in the khatian both the courts below committed an error of law in decreeing the suit on the basis of the entries in C.S. Khatian alone. In support of his contentions he has referred to the decisions reported in 17 DLR (SC)-398, 14 DLR 725 and 27 DLR 589. He has also submitted that the courts below ought to have accepted the entries in the batwara khatians and the rent receipts in support of the contentions of the defendant that the properties in batwara khatian No. 38 were the self-acquired properties of Arman Mir.

6. Mr. A.K.M. Sha6qur Rahman, the Jearned Advocate appearing on behalf of the respondents has submitted that presumption of khtians loses its weight with the passage of time and that the entries in the subsequent khatian would be more acceptable to a court than the entree in the earlier khatian. According to him the latter Khatian should relatively have more weight than the previous one. He has further submitted that the presumption of the C.S. Khatian which is subsequent in point of time was rightly accepted by the courts below than those in the batwara khatian; according to him the C.S. khatian having been prepared subsequently in 1915-18 should prevail over the batwara khatian prepared in 1908 inasmuch that the earlier Batwara khatian must be deemed to have been considered and rejected. He has also submitted that the court of appeal below accepting the evidence of the witnesses of the P.Ws. has found that the plaintiffs’ predecessor Jamiruddin Mir possessed the suit land i.e. the lands of batwara khatain No. 38.

7. As regards the presumption of the C. S. Khatian upon which the courts below have held that the suit properties originally belonged to Arman Mir and Jamiruddin Mir, it appears that apart from the presumption of the C.S. Khatians, the trial court has elaborately considered the oral evidence of the witnesses of the plaintiff. Court of appeal below has considered the evidence of P.W. Wasuddin aged about 90 years. This witness has denied that Amiruddin Mir and Jamiruddin Mir came to this place from a southern country. He has deposed that Arman Mir and Jamiruddin Mir are the sons of Dhanai Mir. Other witnesses of the plaintiff have deposed that the suit lands were possessed by the heirs of Arman Mir and Jamiruddin Mir. The trial court has also considered the oral evidence of the witnesses for the defendants

8. Defendants have alleged that properties described in batwara khatian No. 38 appertaining to jote No. II were the self-acquired properties of Arman Mir and that the properties in Batwara khatain No. 39 were the joint properties of Arman Mir and Jamiruddin Mir. The defendants have alleged that properties in batwara khatian No. 39 also belonged to Arman Mir but since these comprise of homestead and sat lands Arman Mir allowed Jamiruddin Mir to stay there and ultimately gave the said land to the latter and as such the names of two brothers Arman and Jamiruddin Mir have been recorded in the Batwara Khatian No. 39. In support of the tenancy of Arman Mir in respect of khatian No. 39 the defendants have produced some rent receipts B series, to prove original tenancy of Arman Mir with respect to the lands of Batwara No. 38. Court of Appeal below in this connection observed that by the dakhilas ext. B series showing payment of rents with respect to the entire lands of the khatians, the interest of the co-sharers remain unaffected. It is also seen from the dakhilas that all the heirs of Arman Mir have not paid rents by these dakhilas. Be that as it may the payment of rent by itself does not prove that heirs of Arman Mir only were the tenants of the land of C.S. Khatian No. 146.

9. The batwara khatian has been prepared in 1908 whereas the C.S Khatian has been prepared in 1915-18. The C.S. Khatian having been prepared subsequently in point of time is more acceptable than the earlier khatian. In a decision reported in 38 C.W.N. 268 it has been held that in case of assessment of relative value of two khatians, the latest khatian should prevail over the earlier khatian. On this question their lordships in that decision has held as follows:-

"The subsequent record of right which is in favour of the appellants has not been considered at all. Even when the competition is between an earlier record-of rights and a subsequent record-of- rights, it has been held that the earlier record-of- rights cannot ipso-facto disprove the latter; indeed, it is the subsequent record of rights which ought to prevail inasmuch as the earlier record must be deemed to have been considered and rejected."

10. In my view the presumption that was attached to the batwara khatian lost its relative weight after C S. Khatian came into being in 1915-18. In the absence of any other evidence the latter khatian was rightly accepted by the courts below in proof of the state of affairs existed at the time when the records were prepared and that the presumption of the C.S, Khatian in my view could not be rebutted by the defendants by any cogent evidences and the courts below correctly accepted the entries in the C.S. records. I am further of the opinion that the presumption of the C.S. Khatian did not lose its weight because of absence of evidence as to its basis (14 D.L.R. 725). It further appears that the trial court has also noticed the evidence of D.Ws. 7 and 8 who are heirs of Arman Mir. They have claimed their saham on the basis that the properties belonged to Arman Mir and Jamiruddin Mir. If they have supported the case of the defendants they could claim a double share than what they have claimed by an application for saham.

In this view the contentions of the learned Advocate for the appellants appear to be without any substance. I do not find any error of law or of procedure in the judgment.

This appeal is accordingly dismissed without any order as to cost.

End.

caseno: Appeal from original Decree No. 165 of 1965
lawyer:
Anil Chandra Sarker -----For Appellant in F. A. No. 1 69 of 1965 and for respondent in F. A. No. 165. 
Nizamuddin Haider with A.B.M Abbasuddin -----For Respondent in F. A. No. 169 of 1965 and for Appellant in F.A. No. 165 of 1965.
parties:
Imanuddin Rarhi ----- Appellant in F A No 169 and Respondent in F.A. No. 165/65.
Vs.
Lilabati Das ----- Respondent in F.A. 169 and Appellant in F.A. No. 165/65.
case_source: Appeal against the judgment, order and Decree dated 23rd January 1965 passed by Mr. R. K. Biswas, Subordinate Judge of the First Court at Barisal, in Bakerganj in Title Suit No. 376 of 1963 of the said court declaring the decree in T. S. No. 449/69.
full_judgment:
Abdul Wadud Chowdhury J: These two appeals are directed against the judgment and decree passed by the learned Sub-ordinate Judge, Barisal dated 23-1-1965 in Title Suit No. 367 of 1963 and arises out of a suit for declaration of the plaintiff's raiyat right in Kha schedule land as also for a further declaration that the ex-parte decree that was passed in Title Suit No. 449 of 1961 of the Court of Sub-ordinate Judge. Barisal, detailed in schedule 'Ka' of the plaint is void, inoperative and not binding upon the plaintiff.
2. The Plaintiff's case to the effect that the suit properties described in 'Kha' schedule of the plaint was acquired by the plaintiff in the benami of Sudhendu Roy Chowdhury and Serala Sundari Basu by virtue of two pattas and Kabalas of different dates. The Plaintiff, however, took settlement of the suit land from Sudhendu Nath Roy Chowdhury by a patta dated 22nd Jaistha, 1348 BS corresponding to 5-9-35 AD in the name of Serala Sundari Basu. She paid selami of Rs. 475 for the patta. The plaintiff again took settlement of land from Sarala Sundari Basu in the benami of Sudhendu Nath Roy Chowdhury by a patta dated 19th Kartick, 1360 BS (5-11-53) and she paid the selami for the same. Both the pattas were in the custody of the plaintiff. After the said pattas Sarala Sundari sold her superior right to" the Plaintiff by a kabala dated 21st Kartick, 1360 BS (7-11-53) and the said kabala was taken in the benami of Sudhendu Nath Roy. Consideration money was paid by the Plaintiff. As such three documents were executed in the benami of Sudhendu Nath and Sarala Sundari with the money and in the interest of the Plaintiff and Sudhendu Nath Roy and Sarala Sundari were mere name lenders of the Plaintiff being near relations of her. The Plaintiff thus acquired the suit property in the benami of Sudhendu Nath Roy and Sarala Sundari Basu. During the RS operation the suit properties were recorded in the name of the said two benamders at her instance. Subsequently since Sudhendu Nath Roy and Sarala Sundari did not execute any Nadabi Patia, she brought Title Suit No. 267 of 1960 before the Court of the Sub-ordinate Judge, Barisal for declaration of her title with respect to the disputed properties and obtained an ex-parte decree on 2-9-60. Thereafter, the Plaintiff got her name mutated in place of those persons before the acquired Estate and the name of the benamders were struck off from the settlement record. The Plaintiff later on came to know from her husband that the defendant obtained a decree in respect of 'Kha' schedule land in Title Suit No. 449 of 1961 of the Court of Sub-ordinate Judge, Barisal on 9-3-65 although the defendant No. 1 had no right, title or possession in the suit property. No summons of the said suit was served either on Sudhendu Nath Roy or Sarala Sundari Basu as those two persons were Indian citizens. As such, the alleged ex-parte decree is fraudulent and not binding on the plaintiff. The defendant No. 1 got the summons of the said suit served on one Mafizuddin alleging him to be Karmachari of Sudhendu Nath Roy and Sarala Sundari Basu though he was not so. The defendant has no title or possession in the suit properties and the story of settlement from Sudhendu Nath Roy and Sarala Sundari is false. There was no settlement of the suit properties by Sudhendu Nath and Sarala Sundari in favour of defendant No. 1 and no possession was delivered to the defendant No. by them. As such the defendants did not acquire any title to the suit property by virtue of the said decree which is fraudulent. The plaintiff acquired right, title and interest in the suit property by virtue of her pattas and kabala and subsequently by virtue of her ex-parte decree obtained against Sudhendu Nath Roy and Sarala Sundari. In that view of the matter, the plaintiff has filed the present suit for declaration as above as a cloud has been cast upon the title of the plaintiff.
3. The defendant No. 1 contested the suit contending, inter alia, that the suit is not maintainable in its present form the plaintiff's story of acquiring of title on the basis, of said pattas and the Kabalas are denied by the defendant No. 1. He further contended that the said three documents were not benami transactions and neither Sudhendu Nath Roy nor Sarala Sundari was the benamider of the plaintiff. No consideration did pass at the instance of the plaintiff herself with regard to the said three documents. It was further contended by the Defendant that the plaintiff was never in possession of the suit properties and she acquired no title in the same as benamder of Sudhendu Nath Roy and Sarala Sundari. The defendant further contended that Sudhendu Nath and Sarala Sundari acquired the suit properties in their own names with their own modify and the RS records were correctly prepared in their names. While thus in possession on the owners i.e. Sudhendu Nath and Sarala Sundari settled the suit property with the defendants on 28th Chaitra 1360 BS at a jama of Rs. 15 and delivered possession to him. The defendant No. 1 is in possession of the suit land since the settlement in his favour. As SA Khatian did not record the name of the defendant in spite of his settlement he brought Title Suit No. 449 of 1961 before the court of Sub-ordinate Judge, Barisal against Sudhendu Nath and Sarala Sundari and obtained a decree after due service of summons upon the said two persons. The said decree was bonafide and could not be called into question by the plaintiff. As Sudhendu Nath Roy and Sarala Sundari leased out the suit property to the defendant No. 1, the husband of the plaintiff subsequently obtained the original pattas and kabala clandestinely and brought Title Suit No; 267 of 1960 and obtained a fraudulent decree against Sudhendu Nath and Sarala Sundari in respect of the suit property. Neither the plaintiff nor her husband ever posseted the suit property or realised any rent from tenants. The defendant further contended that the decree obtained by the defendant against Sudhendu Nath and Sarala Sundari was bonafide and valid decree after due service of summons upon them at their Barisal residence. The husband of the plaintiff is the proprietor of the Sonali Cinema Hall. His business is to acquire properties of thereon resident Hindus and to prepare false and forged documents in his name from the aforesaid non-resident Hindus. It was further staged that the suit of the Plaintiff is hit by Ordinances I and VI of 1964 and the Plaintiff has no locus standi or any legal character to file the present suit.
4. The learned Sub-ordinate Judge dismissed the suit of the Plaintiff holding that the plaintiff could not prove her title by benami purchase in the name of Sudhendu Nath Roy and Sarala Sundari. He found that the ingredients of benami have not been proved. He also found that the plaintiff's ex-parte decree in Title Suit No. 267 of 1960, the sheet anchor of the plaintiff's title, was tinged with fraud in view of the fact that though the defendants of that suit i.e. Sudhendu Nath and Sarala Sundari were not in the then Pakistan and were Indian citizen yet notices were served upon them at Barisal through one Daruba Nath PW 3. Though Daruba Nath has admitted that he had no interest in the suit proper-ties yet he was made a defendant in the said suit. In that view of the matter, he found that the plaintiff did not acquire the suit properties in the benami of Sudhendu Nath and Sarala Sundari. He also found that the decree obtained by the plaintiff in the Title Suit No 267 of 1960 against Sudhendu Nath and Sarala Sundari. In respect of the suit properties is nothing but fraudulent and, as such, the plaintiff has got no title in the 'Kha' schedule properties and the case of benami has not been proved. He has, however, found that the plaintiff has proved his present possession from the time of the ex-parte decree obtained by him. The learned Sub-ordinate Judge after deciding that the plaintiff has no title or interest in the suit land and that the ex-parte decree obtained by him against Sudhendu Nath and Sarala were fraudulent, also considered the decrees obtained by the defendant No. 1 was also fraudulent and collusive as such he dismissed the suit of the plaintiff with the finding that the ex-parte decree passed in Title Suit Nos. 449 of 1961 and 267 of 1960 of that court was also declared to be null and void. As against the said judgment and decree passed by the learned Sub-ordinate Judge, both the plaintiff and the defendant No. 1 preferred two appeals. The plaintiff's appeal is FA No. 169 of 1965 and the defendant's appeal is FA No. 165 of 1965. The Plaintiff's appeal was against the dismissal of his case as also against the declaration that his ex-parte decree in Title Suit No. 267 of 1960 was fraudulent and null and void. The delft's appeal was against the findings of the learned Sub-ordinate Judge that the Title Suit No. 449 of 1061 obtained by him against Sudhendu Nath and Sarala Sundari was fraudulent and, as such, null and void. As these two appeals arise out of the same judgment and decree and is with regard to the same suit land we dispose of both these appeals by this judgment.
5. Mr Anil Chandra Sarkar appeared on behalf of the plaintiff appellant in FA No. 169 of 1965 and Mr. Nizamuddin Haider with Mr. ABM Abbasuddin appeared on behalf of the defendant No. 1 appellant in FA No. 165 of 1965. Mr Anil Chandra Sarker learned Advocate appearing on behalf of the Plaintiff appellant in FA No. 169 of 1965, submits that the learned Sub-ordinate Judge erred in law and against the weight of evidence on record in holding that the plaintiff has not been able to-prove her title by benami purchase. He then submits that the trial court should not have decided the propriety or otherwise of the ex-parte decree passed in favour of the plaintiff in Title, Suit No. 267 of 1960 in view of the fact that no specific issue has been raised as regard the said decree and no particulars of fraud have been alleged in the written statement and no evidence of fraud have been given by the defendant. He further submits that the said ex parte decree ought to have been accepted by the court below as valid. He also submits that the benami character of the suit land cannot be set-aside without setting aside the ex-parte decree and the ex-parte decree cannot be act aside at the instance of the defendant No. 1 who could not challenge it because he was not a party to the said suit Mr Sarkar learned Advocate further urged that in view of the finding of possession arrived at by the trial court he is entitled to a declaration to the effect that the defendant's decree was fraudulent and void. Mr Nizamuddin Haider the learned Advocate, on the other hand, submits that the trial court's findings so far as the question of benami and declaration to the effect that the plaintiffs ex parte decree was fraudulent are based on sound principle of law and should be maintained but so far as the decree declaring the defendant's decree in Title Suit No. 449 of 1961, to be fraudulent and null and void is not maintainable in view of the fact that the plaintiff is to succeed on his own case and she having failed to prove her title in the suit property. She has no legal character and as such she is not entitled to any such declaration that the decree obtained by the defendant was forged, null and void. As regards the first point urged by Mr Sarker that he has been able to prove benami character of the said documents. We find from the judgment of the court below that he has considered about the benami character of those documents. He has found out that the plaintiff had no relationship with Sudhendu Nath & Sarala Sundari. He also found that there is no evidence of payment by the plaintiff of the consideration money. As regards the custody of the document the learned Sub-ordinate Judge has found that those documents came into possession of the plaintiff in connection with the purchase of land from a co-sharers of Sudhendu Nath i.e. Defendant No. 2, Jatindra Nath Roy the brother of Sudhendu Nath Roy. He also found that that the Plaintiff could not prove any motive for the said alleged benami transactions. We have considered the evidence on record; we do not find that the learned Sub-ordinate Judge has committed any error in coming to such finding. We also, on consideration of evidence on record, find that the plaintiff has not been able to prove the ingredients of benami. In that view of the matter the learned sub-ordinate Judge was correct in holding that the plaintiff had no right, title and interest in the suit land. In the light of the said finding it was necessary for the court to come into the question as to how the ex-parte decree was obtained by the plaintiff in Title Suit No. 267 of 1960. The plaintiff claimed title, by virtue of benami purchase and the ex-parte decree. The ex-parte decree was obtained on the basis of the benami. So when it has been found that the plaintiff could not prove benami character of the transacting it could not be said that the ex-parte decree has any leg to stand upon. In order to find out whether the plaintiff had any right, title and interest in the suit land, the consideration as to whether the said-decree was validly obtained or not was necessary. It cannot be said that since the decree has been passed in Title Suit No. 267 of 1960 the court cannot go into the question of the validity of the decree. In order to arrive at a finding as to whether the Plaintiff had any right, title or interest in the kha schedule property the court has of necessity to go into the question of the question of the genuineness of the ex-parte decree and to Come to a finding whether the same was a valid decree or not. In that view of the matter the objection taken by the learned Advocate for the appellant that since no issue has been raised on the quest ion of validity of the said ex-parte decree the same could not be considered by the trial count and the decree cannot be set aside. We are unable or accept the said contention of the learned Advocate for the appellant. The court was within his province in sifting the evidence or record as to whether the ex-parte decree was genuine or tinged with fraud. It is of no consequence whether the defendant raised any objection with regard to the said ex-parte decree. The Plaintiff was to prove her case and in proving heir case she has to adduce evidence as to whether the said decree which was the sheet-anchor of her title was valid or not. When the court on consideration of the facts, circumstances and evidence led in the case came to the conclusion that the transfers were genuine and not benami and the plaintiff did not acquire the property in the benami of Sudhendra Nath and Sarala Sundari, obviously it has to see whether the ex-parte decree obtained on the basis of the said allegation of benami has legs to stand upon. So we do not find any illegality in the findings of the learned Sub-ordinate Judge in considering the genuineness of the ex-parte decree. In that view of the matter we do not find any sub-stance in the argument advanced by the learned Advocate for the appellant that the decree could not be assailed or set-aside by the learned Sub-ordinate Judge in the present suit. Moreover, the evidence on record discussed by the learned Sub-ordinate Judge as discussed in the judgment tends to show that the decree obtained in Title Suit No. 267 of 1960 was fraudulently obtained because of the fact that though there is evidence on record to the effect that Sudhendu Nath and Sarala Sundari were Indian citizens and were not living in the then East Pakistan for a long time, curiously enough the summons were served on them at Barisal through PW 3 Daruba Nath. This Dhruba Nath was made party in that suit though he admitted in his deposition here that he had no interest whatsoever in the suit land and Dhruba Nath PW 3 was an employee of the husband of the plaintiff. This alone is enough to come to a finding that the decree was fraudulent. It has been argued by Mr Sarkar, the learned Advocate that since no fraud has been alleged by the defendant the court suo motu could not go into that question and set-aside the decree. But as we have stated earlier, the genuineness or otherwise of the said decree was very much in issue in deciding the title of the plaintiff as it was found that the plaintiff could not prove benami character-of the documents. In that view the nature and character of the ex-parte decree required scrutiny and the court on scrutinising the same has found that the said decree was obtained fraudulently. We do not find any illegality in the treatment of the case by the learned Sub-ordinate Judge on this account.
6. Mr Sarker, the learned Advocate for the appellant has further submitted that in view of the fact that the court has found possession of the suit land with the plaintiff he had a legal character and he was entitled to a declaration that the defendant's decree was fraudulent and null and void. Let us now examine section 42 of the Specific Relief Act. Section 42 of the Specific Relief Act is as follows:—
"Any person entitled to any legal character, or to any right as to any property, may institute a suit against any person denying or interested to deny, his title to such character or right, and the court may in its discretion make therein a declaration that he is so entitled and the plaintiff need not in such suit ask for any further relief; Provided that no court shall make any such declaration where the plaintiff being able to seek further relief than a mere declaration of title, omits to do so"
<u><u>7. The Plaintiff may ask for relief under that section provided that the plaintiff must at the time of the suit be entitled to any legal character or to any right to any property. Section 42 must be construed strictly. The courts are only to grant such declaration which came within the terms of that section where the plaintiff has asked for a declaratory decree, namely a declaration that the decree obtained was fraudulent and void. Such a simple declaration could not be given within the provisions; of section 42 as such the suit on the face of that section has to be dismissed. In the present case we find that the plaintiff could not prove her title to the suit land although the learned Sub-ordinate Judge has found that he was in possession of the same since the passing of the ex-parte decree in his favour. Mr Sarker, the Learned Advocate has referred to a decision of this court in the case of Aminul Islam vs M/s Kilburn & Co. reported in 18 DLR 691 where it has been held that if a possessor owner is wrongfully deprived of the thing by person other than the true owner he can recover khas possession of it, after evicting the defendant from the land on the basis of possessory title even if he has not acquired any valid title. The facts of that case are completely different from the present case. In the reported case the suit was filed under section 9 of the Specific Relief Act on the averment that the plaintiff was in possession and he has been subsequently dispossessed from the suit land on encroachment by the defendant. There it was held that thought the plaintiff did not acquire any valid title, he was entitled to recover khas possession. Of course, in that case the plaintiff acquired goodwill and all interest of the original owner by virtue of an agreement. In the agreement it was stated that consideration of the goodwill and the assets of the original owner passed to the plaintiff and he would be paid by allotment of shares. In consequence of that transaction they were in possession of the suit land. It was found that the original Company validly transferred the disputed land to the plaintiff till they were dispossessed by the defendant. It was found there that the plaintiff did not acquire valid title to the suit land as no instrument of transfer was effected between the plaintiff and the original owner. But in the context it was held that plaintiff was entitled to a decree for khas possession. But in the present case the plaintiff did not file any suit for khas possession or anything of that sort and there is also nothing to show that the owners of the land transferred the suit land in favour of the plaintiff. But on the other hand, it has been found by the court below as also by us that the plaintiff could riot prove the benami nature of the document. Rather the findings of the court below are to the effect that the plaintiff went into possession of the suit land after the passing of the ex-parte decree. In that view of the matter, the decision cited by Mr Sarker is of assistance to this case. The Plaintiff has prayed for a declaration to the effect that the decree obtained by the defendant was fraudulent and collusive and not binding against the plaintiff. The plaintiff having failed to prove her title and having no legal character in the subject matter of the suit land, was not entitled to any declaration with regard to the defendant's decree to which she had no connection. If however, it transpires from the evidence on record that the decree obtained by the defendant was also tainted with the same defect as that of the plaintiff though in the present suit. We do not hold that the plaintiff was entitled of any such declaration with regard to the defendant's decree since the matter is not before us. In the interest of justice we notice that the defendant No. 1's decree was also not in accordance with law, Summons of the suit was served on a person who had no interest in the suit and admittedly the defendants of that suit were Indian citizens, but their addresses in the suit were given to be in East Pakistan. From all these the learned Sub-ordinate Judge was correct in holding that the defendant's decree also suffers from the same defect as that of the Plaintiff. However, since the plaintiff has no locus standi to challenge the same and Sudhendu Nath and Sarala Sundari were not parties in the present suit we do not declare in the present suit the defendant's decree to be a nullify. Another factor to be noticed in the present case was that Sudhendu Nath and Sarala Sundari were impleaded as deft. Nos. 2 and 3 in the present suit but ultimately their names were struck off. The title to the suit land remained with Sudhendu Nath and Sarala Sundari, as such, they having not been implicated, their names having been struck off; the learned Sub-ordinate Judge has correctly dismissed the suit holding that the present suit was not maintainable in the absence of the real owners.</u></u>
8. The result, therefore, is that the judgment and decree passed by the learned Sub-ordinate Judge dismissing the suit of the plaintiff are hereby affirmed the appeal No FA 169 of 1965 is hereby dismissed and the judgment and decree passed by the learned sub-ordinate Judge are affirmed. The appeal No FA 165 of 1965 is allowed with the observations made in the body of the judgments the parties will bear their respective costs.
End.

caseno: Appeal from Appellate Decree No. 595 of 1963
lawyer:
Shahabuddin Ahmed with A. Halim—For the appellant.
B. N. Chowdhury—For the respondent.
parties:
Meherjan Bibi ------- Appellant
Vs.
Naimuddin Dhali being dead, one of his heirs: Raisuddin Dhali and others ------- Respondents
case_source: Appeal against the decree of Mr. Anisuddin Ahmed, Additional District Judge 3rd Court of Zilla Mymensingh.
full_judgment:
The plaintiff obtained a preliminary decree in the trial Court for petition of the mil land against the defendant No. 32 on content with costs and expert against the rest. On appeal by the defendant No. 32 the appeal was allowed and the decree of the trial Court was modified. The plaintiff the appellant in this Second Appeal.

2. The plaintiff's case shortly is that the suit lands originally belonged to Adam Munshi, Adam Munshi died leaving a son Ismail and three daughters; Bajiterma, Hakimerma, and Kaluarma as his heirs, Ismail left two sons Bulurbap and Asmat, a daughter Meherjan Bibi (plaintiff) and a widow Pirjan as his heirs. Next to die wee Bulurbap who left as a widow Tearma mother Pirjan brother Asmat and sister plaintiff. Pirjan died next leaving a son Asmat and daughter plaintiff Asmat also died leaving defendant. 4 as Tearma died leaving defendants 6-9 an heirs Defendants 10 and 11 are the heirs of Bajiterma, Defendants 12-16 are heirs of Hakimerma who is also dead. Kaluarma died leaving defendants 17-23 as heirs. Defendants 24-29 are heirs of Kaliarma, who is one of the daughters of Kaliarma. Other defendants including the contesting defendant No. 32 are purchasers from the original owners. Defendant No. 32 agreeing with the gemology only asserts that the original owner of the suit land was Sada Dhali who died leaving a son Adam Munshi, and 2 daughters Elemjan and Afarjan Into consideration the plaintiff's share in the suit land stands reduced, according to the defendant No. 32.

3. The undisputed position in the case is that if Adam Munshi Is found to be the original owner the plaintiff's claim to the suit land becomes to 2.11.3-1.4/5th kranti as decreed by the trial Court but if Sada Dali is found to be the original owner the plaintiff's share comes to 1.8 3-1/2 kranti as decreed by the appellate Court below.

4. At the trial of the suit the plaintiff produced C S. Khatian Est. 1 showing that the suit land wan recorded in the name of Adam Munshi alone. It also shows that one Jogesh Chandra Chakraborty was the superior landlord of the suit land. The concealing defendant No. 32 produced two Chittas Exts. B and B(I) prepared in 1883 in a case between one Uma Sundar Debya and one Amal Prasanna Bal and other by an Amin of the Collectorate in connection with partition of Touzi No 115 under the Estate Partition Act. The trial Court held that only parts of the suit land are covered by Chitta Dags in some of which Sada Dhali were found to be in possession with Abbas Dhali and in some with others. Only in some of the Chitta Dags, Sada Dhali was found to be in exclusive possession. The Trial Court held that under no circumstance could it be said that the suit land in their entirely belonged to Sada Dhali at any time; There were other interested persons also. Apparently, the trial Court held, three were great changes in possession.

4A. The appellate Court Into observed that the plaintiff has not stated how Adam Munshi acquired the suit land. It analysed the evidence of the Pleader Commissioner who was appointed to relay the Chitta Dags with C. S. P plots in suit. Suit land contained 12 C S plot. Out of 12 plots the defendant has not furnished Chitta papers of 2 plots for repayment 2 C. S. plots are fully attracted by the Chitta Dags, The remaining 8 C. S. plots are pertly attracted by the Chitta Dags. The appellate Court below finds that 10 suit plot are 'substantially' attracted by Chitta Dags. As the plaintiff flied no basic document to show that the remaining 2 C S. plots were self-acquired properties of Adam Munshi, it held that these plots also were in possession of Sada Dhali. It came to the conclusion that Sada Dhali was the owner of the entire suit land.

5. Mr. Shahabuddin Ahmed, the learned Advocate for the appellant, contended that the appellate Court below erred in coming to finding that Sada Dhali was the owner at the time of  reparation of CS record without there being any evidence on record to that effect. It erred in law in relying upon the Ext. B and B(I) which have got no relevance at all to the facts and circumstances of the case. Ext. 1 the CS khatian which was prepared some time in 1910 or 1911 shows that Jogesh Chandra Chakraborty was the superior landlord and Adam Munshi alone was in possession of the suit land. Exts. B and B(I) were prepared in 1883 ie. about 30 years before the C. S. operation. In a case between one Uma Sundar Debya and Kamal Prosonna Bal and others. The defendant adduced no evidence to show that Jogesh Chakraborty was in any way connected with either Uma Sundar Debya or Kamal Prosonna Bal, Sada Dhali might have been in possession of some suit plots in 1893 under a different landlord but in the meanwhile with in the course of 30 years the superior landlord of the suit land changed and with the change of the landlord tenants also changed. There is no evidence at all that Sada Dhali continued to be in possession of the entire suit land for the next 30 years. Mr Shahabuddin Ahmed submits that no evidence having been adduced by the defendant as to what happened in the meanwhile the presumption of correctness of entry in the record of rights stand unrebutted.

6.. Mr. B. N. Choudhury, the learned advocate for the respondent, has contended that the question whether the presumption as to correctness of entry in the record of rights has been rebutted or not is a question of fact and however erroneously the appellate Court below might have come to that finding of fact, it cannot be interfered with In a second appeal. He had cited several decisions to that effect.

7. In a case where the plaintiff relies upon the entry in the record of rights for the basis of his title it is not necessary for him to show the basis of his title of the entry in the record or right. As was held in the case of Alamuddin Munshi and others vs. Mainuddin Talukder and others reported in 14 D.L.R. 725.

"Merely because there Is no evidence to show the basis of the entries in the record of rights, the presumption is not rebutted to view of the provision of section 103(B) of the Bengal Tenancy Act, and also the procedure as laid down in the several sections of the Bengal Tenancy Act followed by the other concerned while preparing the final records of rights. There must be further evidence to show that the entries are incorrect. The absence of evidence for the basis of the entries may be a circumstance which along with other evidence may go to show that the presumption has been rebutted”.

<u>8. Yet, the appellate Court below merely because the plaintiff failed to produce any basis of the C.S Khatian held that Sada Dhali was in possession of at least 2 C.S. plots in respect of which the defendant did not file any Chitta papers. This finding cannot be sustained. For it is well settled, as has been held in the case of Aminuddin Biswas Vs, Miajan Biswas, reported in 12 D L R. 103. 'The presumption of correctness, as available on the strength of section 103 B (5) of the Bengal Tenancy Act has got to be rebutted by the person who alleges it.". There was no evidence at all in respect of the said 2 plots that Sada Dhali was in possession even in 1883. In respect of the 10 remaining suit plots the appellate Court below in common with the trial Court held that in some plots Sada Dhali is found to be in exclusive possession and in some other plots he is found to be in Joint possession with Abbas Dhali and others. While the trial Court held that apparently there were great change in possession after the Chitta Dags were prepared, the appellate Court below without any further evidence on record came to hold that Sada Dhali was the owner of the entire suit land. It is no doubt well settled, contended by Mr B.N. Chowdhury that where evidence was led in rebuttal of the presumption of correctness of entry in the record of rights and the appellate Court below comes to a finding that the preemption stands rebutted, that finding is final and cannot be interfered with in the second appellate jurisdiction. In all the decisions cited before me, namely, the case of Wali Mohammad and others Vs. Mohammad Bakhsh, reported in 51 C.L J. 518 Ghulam Mohammad Vs. Secretary of State reported in A.I.R 1938 (L) 445-and Charu Bala Rudra Vs. Narayan Prasad Sen reported in 14 DLR 159 the presumption was rebutted on the basis of relevant evidence on record. In the present case, however, the defendant had not adduced any evidence at all as to what was the state of possession of the suit land at the time of C S. records or approximately earlier to that Mr. B N. Chowdhury submits that by producing Exts. B and B (I) the defendant has discharged the onus of proving that CS khatian has no basis. Thereafter, he argue, it is for the plaintiff to show that her predecessor in interest was in possession of the suit land at the relevant lime. It is difficult to agree with Mr. B.N Chowdhury. By adducing evidence of certain state of affairs 30 years back, how can it be said that the basis of C.S. khatian has been shaken? All that the attendant has produced in this case in the state of affairs relating to 10 out of 82 suit plots as far back as in 1883 which shows superior ownership and possession in the names of a different set of persons. How that evidence is evidence at all in rebuttal of the presumption of correctness of entry in the record of rights is difficult to appreciate. Mr. B.N. Chowdhury has failed to cite a tingle decision to show that evidence of such remote chamber has any bearing upon the presumption of correctness of entry in the record of rights. Mr. Shahabuddin Ahmed has cited the case of Maurabgi Tewari Vs. Kanhaiya Tewari reported In 123 IC 390 in support of his contention that when Chitta Dags and C.S. record show plan of two different persons it must be presumption that at some time between the two periods the person recorded In in the Chitta Dags lost their possession and that the person whose name appears in the C.S. khatian obtained possession, although there Is no presumption regarding the exact time at which the change of affairs took place. I entirely agree with the ratio decidendi of that decision.</u>

<u>While the trial Court rightly held that apparently were great changes in possession. In the meanwhile, the mining link in between the slate of affairs in 1883 and the C.S operation In 1910 or 1911 has been filled up by the appellate Court below by conjectures and surmises. It surmised that there was a division or partition for convenience of pollution between Sada Dhali and Abbas Dhali. It conjectured that an excess area of .04 acre in C.S. plot Nos 1088 might have accrued due to encroachment on adjoining laud and it also surmised as to how the suit property devolved relying upon a stray observation of P W. 4.</u>

<u>In such circumstances the finding of the appellate Court below that Sada Dhali was the owner of the suit land cannot be sustained.</u>

<u>In the result, the appeal is the judgment and decree of the Court below are set aside and those of the trial are restored.</u>

<u>There will be no order as to costs.</u>

End.
