35. With regard to his statement made in the written statement the plaintiff admitted that he filed a written statement but when a certified copy of it was shown to him he could not say if it was this, he, however, stated that in that suit a solenama was filed and without reading the solenama he signed the statements made by the plaintiff in the above mentioned title suits.

36.The statements made in the said suits are relevant for adjudication of the issue- "Is the suit barred by principle of estoppel, waiver, acquiescence and conduct ?" Certified copies of the preliminary decree and final decree made in the said suits are admissible in evidence for determining the ownership of the suit properties. From the judgments of the trial Court and that of the High Court Division it does not appear that any serious consideration was given to this aspect of the case. The suits being partition suits wherein the present plaintiff and defendant were impleaded as parties, the decrees having been passed therein in their presence, they are bound by the same. The statements made in the solenama, upon which the suits were disposed of carry a legal presumption that the statements were consciously made. However, the presumption is rebuttable but the plaintiff did not offer any explanation by way of rebuttal. The learned Counsel has correctly submitted that in absence of any evidence rebutting the presumption, the admissions are binding upon the plaintiff. With regard to subsequent conduct of the parties it has been found that it was the defendant who was although exercising her right as the owner in possession and the plaintiff could not produce any evidence to support his case of exercising his right to possession in the suit properties. In my opinion the plaintiff is estopped from challenging the title of the defendant in the suit properties calling her as his benamdar,

<u>37. Before concluding I like to observe that in the case of benami transactions, although the source of purchase money is an important criteria but it is not conclusive where there are other circumstances showing that the purchaser intended the property to belong to the person in whose favour the sale deed is executed. So it is the intention of the parties which practically determines the question as to who is the owner of the property. It has been already noticed that the defendant succeeded in showing that she had the capacity to pay the consideration for the properties acquired by her and the sale deeds were executed in her favour. In this context reference may be made to the decision of the Supreme Court of India in the case of Kanakarathanammal v V.S. Loganatha Mudaliar, AIR 1965 S.C. 271, In this case the question for consideration was whether in transaction where purchase was made by the wife and consideration money was paid by the husband, wife shall be treated as the benamdar of her husband in respect of the property purchased by her. In determining this question subsequent conduct of the parties was taken into consideration; and mainly on consideration of the conduct of the parties regarding possession of the property, the statements made by the husband on different occasions in respect of the properties in suit it has been held that the property had been purchased by the wife in her own name though the consideration which was paid by her had been received by her from her husband. From the reported case it appears that the learned Judges while examining the question of benami remarked that the High Court did not correctly appreciate the effect of the admissions made by the husband. The finding of the trial Court, approved by the High Court was reversed. In the instant case position is more or less the same. What is the effect of the admission made by the plaintiff in Title Suit Nos. 163 and 183 of 1949 has not been properly appreciated. Admissibility of the written statement filed by the plaintiff in. the above mentioned title suits and his statement in the petition of objection filed by him to oppose the petition for appointment of Receiver and the statement made in the solenama to which he was a party, has not been disputed. In the absence of rebuttal of the presumption that the admissions were consciously made by the plaintiff, in law his admission operates against him in his claim against his wife over the suit property which were acquired by exchange of the Park Street and Dum Dum Road properties. In short, the plaintiff is estopped from putting up the claim that the properties were acquired by hem for himself and that the defendant was his benamdar.</u>

38. The law of benami has not been properly applied to the facts of this case by either the learned Subordinate Judge or the learned Judges of the High Court Division. In the absence of proper application of the law of benami the course of justice has been misdirected, and because of this, notwithstanding the concurrent finding of facts it called for examination of the evidence. It has been already mentioned above that the trial Court accepting the plaintiff's case that the suit properties were acquired in the benami of the defendant and the judgment of the High Court Division affirming the same are mainly based on the conclusion deduced from the source of the consideration money but the materials on record do not warrant the findings. The question of benami, in the facts and circumstances of this case, has not been correctly decided on proper application of the law of benami. So, the judgments in favour of the plaintiff cannot be sustained. In the result the appeal is allowed Judgment and decree of the trial Court and those of the High Court Division are set aside and the suit is dismissed with costs.

End.

lawyer:
Shah Mohammad Munir Sharif with AKM Nurul Alam-----for the petitioner: 
Dr Naim Ahmed ----- For the Opposite Party No.1.
parties:
Khulna Zilla Parishad ------ Plaintiff-Petitioner 
Vs.
Kamol Kumar Chakrabarti and another ------ Defendant-Opposite-Parties
full_judgment:
This Rule, on an application under section 115(4) of the Code of Civil procedure (in short, the CPC) at the instance of the plaintiff-petitioner was issued calling upon the opposite parties to show cause as to why the impugned judgment and order dated 24-8-2010 passed by the learned Additional District Judge, 2nd Court, Khulna in Civil Revision No.9 of 2010 affirming the order dated 18-11-2009 passed by the learned Assistant Judge, 8th Court, Khulna in Title Suit No. 1321 of 2008 shall not be set-aside and/or pass such other or further order or orders as to this Court may seem fit and proper.

2. The facts leading to the issuance of the Rule, in short, is that the present petitioner as plaintiff filed the above numbered suit against the defendant-opposite parties being No. 1321 of 2008 before the learned District Judge, Khulna as part of the central filing system, prevailing at the relevant time though the suit was triable by the Assistant Judge, for declaration that the judgment dated 30-9-1958 and the decree dated 6·11·1958 in Title Suit No. 160 of 1957 passed by the then Subordinate Judge, Khulna is void, illegal and not binding upon the plaintiff.

3. It was averred that the suit land was an acquired property of the plaintiff, the same was correctly recorded in his name who has been possessing the same for the last 80 years by establishing technical school and residence of the Superintend thereof, But Indra Sekhar Chakrabarti, the predecessor of the opposite party No. 1 preferred Title suit No. 160 of 1957 in the Court of Subordinate Judge, Khulna against the plaintiff-petitioner and opposite party No.2 and obtained a fraudulent and collusive decree against them.

4. The said suit was contested by the then Province of East Pakistan who filed a Civil Appeal being No. 57 of 1959 in the High Court of East Pakistan and in the appeal the judgment and decree of Title Suit No. 160 of 1957 was affirmed.

5. The petitioner had no knowledge of the said suit. All on a sudden on 13-6-2007 the process of Title Execution Case No 5 of 2007 was served upon the plaintiff petitioner and only then the petitioner for the first time came to know about the suit. Thereafter the petitioner collecting papers on 13-7-2008 became sure of the said suit, hence the present suit.

6. After filing of the suit the petitioner filed an application In the trial Court on 27·1·2009 under section 151 of the Code of Civil Procedure for staying the operation of the Judgment and decree dated 30-9-1958 and 6-11-1958 of the Title suit No. 160 of 1957. But the trial Court was pleased to reject the said application by his order dated 18-11-2009.

7. The petitioner against the said order dated 18-11-2009 preferred Civil Revision No.9 of 2010 before the learned District Judge, Khulna which has been ultimately heard by the Additional District Judge, 2nd Court, Khulna who by his impugned judgment and order dated 24-8-2010 dismissed the revision affirming that of the order of the trail Court dated 18·11-2009. The petitioner being aggrieved by and dissatisfied with the impugned judgment and order dated 24-8-2010 passed by the learned Additional District Judge, 2nd Court, Khulna moved this Court and obtained the present Rule. The Rule is resisted by the opposite party No.1.

8. Mr Shah Mohammad Munir Sharif with Mr AKM Nurul Alam, the learned Advocate appearing on behalf of the plaintiff-petitioner supports the Rule. He submits that both the trial Court and the appellate Court below being misconceived of the fact and also on the misconception of law came to a wrong findings and conclusion that the plaintiff-petitioner is to prove that the summons and process of the former suit were served upon him. He also submits that whenever the present plaintiff-petitioner filed the present suit claiming that the summons and process of the former suit have not been served upon him, the onus heavily lies upon the plaintiff of the former suit to prove that the summons and process were duly served upon the defendant (the present petitioner) of that suit. He also submits that a negative fact and matter cannot be proved because the same bears no existence. But who claims some- thing positive on that fact he is to prove the existence of that particular fact and in that view of the matter the plaintiff of the former suit was under duty bound to prove that the summons was served upon the defendant of that suit.

9. He also submits that in fact immediately after filing of a suit it was neither practicable nor, desirable for any party of the suit to prove the same fact and the same fact cannot be proved without trial but during the trail, the operation of the judgment of the former suit requires to be stayed. He adds that after almost 19/20 years of the judgment of the impugned suit, the execution case was filed but in view of Article 182 of the Limitation Act read with section 48 of the Code of Civil Procedure, the execution case was not maintainable and the filing of the execution case after such a long gap signifies and indicates about the collusiveness of the decree. So, the Courts below should have stayed the operation of the judgment and decree of the disputed suit till disposal of the present suit and if the operation of the judgment and decree of the disputed suit is not stayed the purpose of filing of the present suit may be frustrated. So, the impugned judgment and order, complained of, in this revisional application may kindly be set-aside staying the operation of the judgment and decree of the former suit being Title Suit No. 160 of 1957.

10. 'On the other hand, Dr. Naim Ahmed, the learned Advocate appearing on behalf of the opposite party No.1 opposes the Rule. He submits that Indra Sekhar Chakraborti, the predecessor of the opposite party No. 1 as plaintiff filed the impugned title Suit being No. 160 of 1957 for declaration of title and permanent injunction into 4 bighas of land fully described in the schedule of that suit and in the said suit the then Province of East Pakistan was the defendant No. 1 and District Board, Khulna was defendant No.2 and the suit was decreed on contest by a judgment dated 30-9- 1958. Against the said judgment, the Government of the then East Pakistan preferred an Appeal being Title Appeal No. 57 of 1959 before the High Court and the High Court ultimately by its judgment dated 12-12-1978 affirmed the judgment of the trial Court. The opposite party No. 1 being the legal heirs of the said Indra Sekhar Chakrabarti while was in possession of the suit land all on a sudden on 2-8-2005 the present petitioner, that is the Khulna Zilla Parishad had entered into the suit land forcibly and started making semi pucca construction and under the said compelling circumstances the opposite party No. 1 filed Execution Proceeding No.5 of 2007 before the Joint district Judge, 1st Court, Khulna under Order XXI Rule 32 and section 151 of the CPC. He submits that though the District Board, Khulna, that is, the defendant No.2 of that suit did not contes.t in the suit but the Government of the then East Pakistan contested the suit. So, the interest of the defendant No.2 has been rightly protected by the defendant No.1. So, the defendant No.2 at this stage cannot file a suit taking the ground of fraud, collusiveness or any other grounds and the suit was filed after almost 50 years of the decree with a malafide intention to cause harm to the opposite party No .I and both the Courts below being convinced of the said fact did not stay the operation of the judgment and decree of the former suit dated 30-9-1958 which was affirmed by the High Court even. So, the Courts below particularly the learned Additional District Judge, 2nd Court, Khulna on due consideration of the facts and circumstances of the case did not commit any error of law by his impugned order occasioning failure of justice to the petitioner. So, the Rule is liable to be discharged with costs,

11. I have considered the above submission of the learned Advocates of both the parties with profound attention and have gone through the materials on record.

12. Ongoing to the materials on record and also on going to the judgment of the former suit being Title Suit No. 160 of 1957 it appears that the present petitioner Khulna Zilla Parishad was the defendant No.2 in the form as District Board, Khulna. There appears a common narration in the judgment of Title Suit No. 160 of 1957 that the suit was decreed on contest. The language of the Court denotes as the suit was contested by all the defendants of that suit. But on meticulous perusal of the judgment of Title Suit No. 160 of 1957 it appears that the suit was contested by the defendant No.1 of that suit. But that was not correctly articulated in the ordering portion of the judgment of that suit. However, be that as it may, it is fact that the suit was not contested by the defendant No.2 of that suit.

13. The former suit was in fact decreed on contest against the defendant No.1 and ex-parte against the defendant No.2 who is the present petitioner in this Rule. The petitioner filed the Title Suit No. 1321 of 2008 on two counts. The first count is that the summon of that suit was suppressed upon him and the second count is that the ex-parte decree was obtained collusively and fraudulently against him by the plaintiff of that suit.

14. In the case of 10 MLR (AD) 167 it was held by our Apex Court that a defendant may file an independent suit for setting-aside the ex-parte decree when he alleges that the decree was obtained by practicing fraud, but when he alleges that there was no service of summon upon him, remedy lies in filing a proceeding under order IX of Rule 13 of the CPC on the ground of non-service of summons and in that case no independent suit will lie.

15. In the fact of the present case I find both the grounds are in the luggage of the plaintiff-petitioner as such there appears no prima facie bar in filing a regular suit challenging the decree of the former suit. Both the trial Court and the revisional Court below held that onus lies upon the plaintiff-petitioner to prove that no summons and process of the original suit was served upon him. In fact, this sort of findings and decisions of the Courts below is against the spirit of the set principle of law.

16. In the case of 40 DLR (AD) 193 it was held that if the defendant alleges that the summons was not duly served upon him in that case the plaintiff of the original suit will be required to prove that summons was duly served upon the defendant of the original suit. And the same views have been endorsed by the apex Court in numerous cases including in the case of 1 BLC (AD) 179, 1 MLR (AD) 137=48 DLR (AD) 159 and 9 MLR (AD) 158. But it is very unfortunate that both the Courts below came to a wrong conclusion that the plaintiff-petitioner could not prove that the summons of the original suit was not served upon him.

17. In the facts and circumstance of the case it is also pertinent to point out that immediate after filing of a suit it is neither practicable nor desirable for any particular party to prove the said fact. It is a fact which can only be addressed at the trial of the said. However, in my consideration the Courts below were net justified in coming to a conclusion at the prematured stage of the suit that the plaintiff-petitioner (defendant of the former suit) could not prove the service of summons upon him although the same was the matter of trial.

18. Since the present plaintiff-petitioner occupies the right to file a suit challenging the decree of the former suit and, as such, if the operation of the decree of the former suit is not stayed the purpose of filing of the present suit may be frustrated and in such a case the purpose of the ends of justice would be best served if the operation of the decree is stayed for a limited period enabling the trial Court to dispose of the present suit within the said period. If the operation of the judgment and decree of the former suit are allowed to continue and run during the pendency of the present suit parallelly that may create a clash a chaotic situation between the parties.

19. At the time of hearing of this Rule, the learned Advocate for the petitioner seriously raised question as to the maintainability of the execution proceeding being No. 5 of 2007. He referring the provision of Article 182 of the limitation Act as well as section 48 of the CPC submits that almost after 20 years of the original suit, the .plaintiff preferred the execution case which ought to have been filed within 3 years and after filing of the execution case though original plaintiff was entitled to maintain his execution case up to 12 years but he did not even come within 12 years. So; the execution case was not at all maintainable.

20. In my consideration whether the execution proceeding is maintainable or not is not the subject matter of the present Rule. But the learned Advocate appearing for the opposite party No.1 made his submission that the execution case was not filed under Article 182 of the Limitation Act nor under section 48 of the CPC rather since the original suit was decreed for permanent injunction and since after a long gap the defendant made invasion in the decreetal land of the plaintiff, they had come to the Court seeking relief under Order XXI of Rule 32 of the CPC. As I have already noted it earlier that the maintainability of the execution proceeding is not the subject matter of the present Rule.

<u>21. Since a title suit has been filed by the present plaintiff-petitioner challenging the decree of the former suit being No. 160 of 1957 and since apparently there appears no legal bar in filing of such a suit, so, the present suit and the operation of the decree of former suit cannot run simultaneously and if it is allowed to continue that will create judicial anarchy. So, the ends of justice would be best served if the operation of the judgment and decree of the former suit be stayed for a specific period directing the trial Court below to dispose of the suit within such period and that will be the best option for both the parties.</u>

22. In the result, the Rule is made absolute. The impugned judgment and order dated 24-8- 20 10 passed by the learned Additional District Judge, 2nd Court, Khulna in Civil Revision No.9 of 20 10 is set-aside and the operation of the judgment and decree of the former Title Suit being No. 160 of 1957 is stayed for I(one) calendar year from the date of receipt of the copy of the judgment and the trial Court below is directed to dispose of the present suit being No. 1321 of 2008 within 1(one) year with a further direction that the present plaintiff-petitioner will not get any adjournment in the suit.

Let a copy of this judgment and order be sent to the Court concerned for information and necessary action.

End.

caseno: Writ petition Nos. 425 of 1985 and 1634 of 1988 with contempt petition No. 3 of 1987
lawyer:
Md. Hannan with M. Khaled Ahmed. Advocates ------ For the Petitioners in W.P. No. 425/85 and Contempt Petition No.3/87 and for the Respondents in W.P. No. 1634/88 

Khondaker Mahbubuddin Ahmed with Mirza Hossain Haider and S.M. Moonir, Advocates ------ For the Petitioners in W.P. No. 1634/88 for the Respondents in W.P. No. 425/85 and for the respondent in Contempt Petition No. 3/87. 

Fakhrul Islam, A.A.G. with Md. Delwar Hossain. A.A.G ------ For the Respondent No. 3 in W.P. No. 425/85 and Contempt Petition No. 3/87
parties:
Syed Ashfaque Hossain & others  ------ Petitioners in W.P. No. 425 of 1985
Syed Mohsen Ali &others ------ Petitioners in W.P. No. 1634 of 1988
Vs. 
Bangladesh, represented by Secretary, Ministry of Land Administration and Land Reforms and others ------ Respondents in W.P. No. 425 of 1985
Board of Land Administration and others ------ Respondents in W.P. No. 1634 of 1988
Syed Ashfaque Hossain and others ------ Petitioners in Contempt Petition No.3 of 1987
Deputy Commissioner, Moulvibazar and another ------ Contemned in Contempt Petition No. 3 of 1987
full_judgment:
Mustafa Kamal, J: These two Rules Nisi and the contempt petition have been heard together and will be disposed of by this common judgment as they arise out of the same transaction and involve common questions of fact and law. 

2. In Writ Petition No. 425 of 1985 the petitioner obtained the Rule Nisi challenging two Memos, namely, a Memo dated 24.4.85 (Annexure M) and a Memo dated 26.10.85 (Annexure N 1) both is- sued by the respondent No.2, Deputy Secretary, Ministry of Land Administration and Land Reforms. 

3. The petitioners' case is that they had their ancestral home on 2.65 acres out of a total of 5.80 acres of Khatian No. 1358 of mouzaMoulvi Bazar Town which comprises several houses, tank, graveyard, gardens etc. wherein the petitioners have been living for generations now. The respondent No.4 Syed Mohsin Ali, his six brothers, two sisters and mother mutated their names in respect of the entire land of 5.80 acres of the above khatian No. 1358 on the basis of a registered Kabala No. 5879 executed and registered on 31.10.55 by one Keramat Ali in favour of Syed Ashraf Ali, deceased father of the said respondent No.4. The said Keramat Ali auction purchased the entire land of 5.80 acres of the said khatian No. 1358 on 25.9.54 for arrears of rent. The auction purchaser Keramat Ali however sold only 3.15 acres of the khatian land out of 5.80 acres to late Syed Ashraf Ali, father of the respondent No.4. The balance 2.65 acres of ancestral homestead continued to remain in the possession of the petitioners and their predecessors. The predecessors of the petitioners obtained a registered Muktipatra dated 8.5.79 from one of the sons of auction purchaser Keramat Ali, namely HabiburRahman. Thereafter the predecessors of the petitioners by executing and registering three separate deeds of gift, all dated 5.11.78, transferred their right, title and interest in the case land to the petitioners and delivered physical possession thereof to them. The petitioners thereafter instituted Mutation Case Nos. 91, 92 and 93 of 1979 be- fore the Circle Officer (Revenue), Moulvibazar. After compliance of necessary formalities all the three mutation cases were allowed vide order dated 13.11.79. The respondent No.4 Syed Mohsin Ali and his 5 brothers filed an objection petition before the Circle Officer (Revenue), Moulvi Bazar whereupon Miscellaneous Case No. 38 of 1979 was started. The par- ties were notified. After hearing the parties the Circle Officer forwarded the case record to the Additional Deputy Commissioner (Revenue), Sylhet for necessary action with a detailed report as he found the case to be complicated. Then the respondent No.4 preferred an appeal before the Additional Deputy Com- missioner (Revenue), Sylhet under section 147 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, 1950, shortly the Act, against the Order dated 13.11.79 passed by the Circle Officer (Revenue), Moulvi Bazar whereupon Mutation Appeal Case No. 24 of 1979- 80 was started and the petitioners were notified. By his order dated 10.9.80 the Additional Deputy Com- missioner, Sylhet after hearing the parties rejected the appeal of the respondent No.4 and upheld the or- der dated 13.1l.79 passed by the Circle Officer (Revenue), Moulvibazar in Mutation Case Nos. 91, 92 and 93 of 1979. Against the aforesaid order of the Deputy Commissioner (Revenue), Sylhet the respondent No.4 preferred an appeal before the Com- missioner, Chittagong Division being Miscellaneous Appeal No. 223 of 1980 under section 147 of the Act which was heard and disposed of by the Additional Commissioner, Chittagong Division by his order dated 15.12.82 dismissing the same and con-firming the order dated 10.9.80 passed by the Additional Deputy Commissioner (Revenue), Sylhet. 

4. In the meanwhile the Board of Land Administration Act, 1980 (Act No. XIII of 1981), shortly the Board Act, came into force on 30th June, 1981 whereby a Board of Land Administration was constituted with the authority to dispose of all statutory appeals vide memo No. lOM-13/82/1224-Estt. dated 3.9.82 (Annexure I). The respondent No.4 being aggrieved by the order dated 15.12.82 passed by the Additional Commissioner Chittagong Division preferred an appeal before the Board of Land Administration. The appeal was admitted, reports were called for from the Additional Commissioner, Chittagong Division and the Additional Deputy Commissioner (Revenue), Sylhet. Upon perusal of the reports and hearing the parties the Board of Land Administration in Appeal Case No. 43 of 1983 by order dated 1l.l.84 contained in memo No. VI-43/ 83/92-Appeal dated 24.l.84 (Annexure K) rejected the appeal. Under section 4 of the Board Act a right of review within 60 days of the order has been provided for but the respondent No. 4 did not prefer any application for review. Instead, he preferred an incompetent appeal before the Ministry of Land Ad- ministration and Land Reforms which was admitted by the Secretary, Ministry of Land Administration and Land Reforms, respondent No.1, on 13.1l.84 and records were called for. No notice however was served on the petitioners. In the light of orders of the Board of Land Administration (Annexure K) the petitioners went to Tahsil Office, Moulvi Bazar for payment of rent for 1392 B.S. in the last week of May, 1985 when to their surprise they came to know that the Ministry of Land Administration and Land Reforms has since reversed the order of the Board of Land Administration exercising appellate powers under section 147 of the Act in a mutation proceeding under section 143 of the Act, allowing the objection of the respondent No.4. The petitioner No.1 came to know definitely about the aforesaid order on 2.6.85 when he came to Dhaka. A true copy of the said order was annexed as Annexure M which is the first impugned order. 

5. On 6.6.85 the petitioners filed an application before the respondent No. 1 for setting aside the ex parte impugned order Annexure M on review on grounds, inter alia, of want of jurisdiction and palpable illegality. But by memo No. VUI-604/85/1054/ 1(2) dated 26.10.85 the respondent No.1 rejected the review application, which is Annexure N1, the second impugned order. 

6. In this Writ Petition the only ground urged upon by Mr. Md. Hannan, learned Advocate for the petitioners, is that the Government had no power and jurisdiction of entertaining either any appeal or revision from the final order of the Board of Land Ad- ministration and therefore both the impugned orders Annexures M and Nl are without jurisdiction. We shall revert to the submission later on. 

7. An affidavit-in-opposition has been filed on behalf of the respondent No.4. 

8. It is stated therein that the aforesaid 5.80 acres of land of the aforesaid khatian originally be-longed to Syed Ashraf Ali, the father of respondent No.4, and Syed Ashraf Ali gifted the same to his wife SyedaAktarunnessaKhanam in lieu of her dower. The said property was sold in auction for arrears of rent and was purchased by Keramat Ali when Syed Ashraf Ali and his wife were living in Calcutta. Coming to know of the auction sale Syed Ashraf Ali obtained a kabala in his own name for valuable consideration from the said auction purchaser Keramat Ali in respect of the whole of the auction sold property, namely 5.80 acres, by kabala No. 5879 dated 31.10.55. But unfortunately the deed writer through bonafide mistake wrote 3.15 acres in place of the whole of the auction sold property, namely 5.80 acres. The recipient of the said kabala, Syed Ashraf Ali, was not aware of the said mistake in the deed as he remained in possession of the whole of 5.80 acres all along, including the period from the date of auction upto the date of the aforesaid kabala. 

9. During the rent roll operations in 1958 the entire 5.80 acres of land was wrongly recorded in the names of Syed Ashraf Ali and his brother Syed Ankar Ali, the latter having no title to or interest in the aforesaid property. In 1964 Syed Ashraf Ali allowed his nephews, namely, Syed Abdul Mannan, Syed Mozammel Ali and Syed SalehMasud to live in a portion of the aforesaid property having structures thereon, as his licencees. In 1965 Syed Ashraf Ali corrected the khatian by filing Case No. 331 of 1965 before the Circle Officer (Revenue), Moulvi Bazar by striking out of the name of his brother Syed Ankar Ali from the khatian. It is therefore absolutely incorrect that the balance 2.65 acres of ancestral home- stead continued to remain in possessive of the petitioners and their predecessors. Three nephews of Syed Ashraf Ali were only in possession of a part of the property in question. Syed Ashraf Ali died in 1970. Thereafter the heirs of Syed Ashraf Ali, namely, the respondent No.4 and his brothers and sisters requested the said licencees to surrender possession of the structures to them. At this stage they became hostile and instead of complying with the request they approached one of the sons of auction purchaser Keramat Ali, namely HabiburRahman, and obtained a so-called Muktipatrafrom him in respect of 2.65 acres out of the khatian taking advantage of mistake in respect of area in Syed Ashraf Ali's kahala dated 31.10.55 The said Muktipatra dated 8.5.79 was obtained in the names of the three licencees of Syed Ashraf Ali and another, namely Syed Abdun Noor. The Muktipatra is collusive and fraudulent. Later, Syed Abdun Noor purported to gift .64 acres of land in favour of his brother's son, namely petitioner No. 1, on 26.10.79. Syed Abdul Mannan purported to gift .65 acre on the same day to his wife who is the petitioner No. 2. Syed SalehMasud purported to gift .65 acres of land on the same day to his wife, petitioner No.3. The said donors being mere licencees and having no title to the land in question, the petitioners got no title to or interest in the lands purported to have been gifted to them. It has also been stated that after completing the aforesaid collusive and fraudulent transactions the petitioners applied to the Circle Officer (Revenue), Moulvi Bazar for mutation of their names whereupon their names were mutated in respect of 1.95 acres by an ex parte order dated 13.11.79. No notice of the aforesaid mutation ease was either issued or served upon the respondent No.4 and the order of mutation was passed in spite of objection raised by the Tahsildar which will appear from the records of the Mutation Case Nos. 91, 92 and 93 of 1979. Thereafter the respondent No.4 has more or less accepted the petitioners' description of the progress of the case from the stage of the Circle Officer (Revenue), Moulvi Bazar upto the Board of Land Administration. The said respondent however justifies his appeal before the Ministry of Land Administration on the ground that the law does not oust the Government's authority to decide a matter in respect of which the Board of Land Administration exercises appellate power.

10. However to protect his interest in the matter the respondent No.4 along with his other brothers instituted Writ Petition No. 1634 of 1988 against the petitioners as respondents and against the Government and its functionaries and obtained a Rule Nisi on 13.11.88 calling into question the or- der of the Chairman of the Board of Land Administration dated 11.1.84 passed in Appeal Case No. 43 of 1983 and which is Annexure D(2), i.e. the impugned order, in Writ Petition No. 1634 of 1988. The respondent No.4 claims that if the Rule is made absolute in Writ Petition No. 425 of 1985, then his case against the final order of the Board of Land Ad- ministration should be considered in Writ Petition No. 1634 of 1988. 

11. The averments made by the petitioners in Writ Petition No. 1634 of 1988 are the same as the averments of respondent No.4 in the affidavit-in- opposition filed in Writ Petition No. 425 of 1985. The petitioners of Writ Petition No. 425 of 1985 are respondent Nos. 4-6 in Writ Petition No. 1634 of 1988. Only respondent No.5 has filed an affidavit- in-opposition therein. The averments contained therein are almost the same as the averments contained in Writ Petition No. 425 of 1985. 

12. We shall now dispose of the petitioners' only contention in Writ Petition No. 425 of 1985, namely, that after Board of Land Administration dis- poses of an appeal under section 147 of the Act no other appeal or revision lies before the Government and therefore both the impugned orders Annexure M and N1 have been passed without jurisdiction. 

13. Section 147 of the Act, as amended up-to- date, is as follows :-"147, Appeals. Subject to any special pro- visions for appeal made in this Part or in any rules made under this Act, an appeal shall lie from every original or appellate order made un- der any of the provisions of this Part by a Revenue-officer as follows, namely :- (a) to the Collector, when the order is made by a Revenue-officer subordinate to the Collector; (b) to the Commissioner of the division, when the order is made by the Collector of a district within the division; and (c) to the Board of Land Administration, when the order is made by the Commissioner of a division". 

It may be stated that formerly appeal lay to the Government against an order made by the Commissioner of a Division but by the Laws (Amendment) Ordinance, 1982 (Ordinance No. XLI of 1982) in place of the word 'Government' the words 'Board of Land Administration' were substituted. 

14. In this connection the provisions of the Board Act may be considered. Section 3 provides that as soon may be after the commencement of this Act, the Government shall constitute a Board to be called the Board of Land Administration. It shall consist of a Chairman and not more than two other members to be appointed by the Government. The Board shall 'exercise such powers and perform such functions as may be entrusted to it by the Government or under any law. The petitioners in Writ Petition No, 4 1985 have annexed Annexure I, namely an order of the Ministry of Land Administration and Land Re- forms No. 1O-13/82/1224-Estt. dated 3.9.82 in which it has been provided under the provisions of sub-section (3) of Section 3 of the Board Act that the Board will decide all statutory appeals and revisions and perform other functions as may be provided by law. Section 4 of the Board Act however provides that within 60 days from the date of any order of the Board, an aggrieved person may apply to the Board for a review of the same. 

15." Mr. Md. Hannan submits that the respondent No.4 could have applied to the Board for a re- view of the Board's order (Annexure K) within 60 days of the same but he did not do it. He filed an appeal to the Ministry of Land Administration and Land Reforms. There is no provision for such appeal. The Ministry was coram non juice in the matter. 

16. In this connection it may be mentioned that section 149 of the Act deals with revisions. Sub-section (3) of section 149 originally provided that the Government may, of its own motion, within six months of the date of any order passed under this Part by the Commissioner of a division or on an application made in that behalf within six months of the date of such order, revise such order. But by the Laws (Amendment) Ordinance, 1982 (Ordinance No. XLI of 1982), for the word "Government", the words "Board of Land Administration" were substituted. As such even the power of revision was parted with by the Government and the provisional power was entrusted to the Board not by any executive order but by a statutory amendment. 

17. Similarly under sub-section (4) of section 149 of the Act the Government had the power to or- der at any time the correction of any entry in a record-of-rights provided that no appeal under this section had been preferred against such order. By the said Ordinance No. XLI of 1982 in place of the word "Government", the words "Board of Land Administration" have been substituted in sub-section (4) as well. 

18. Me. Khondaker Mahbubuddin Ahmed, learned Advocate for the respondent No.4 in WritPetition No. 425 of 1985, faced with this difficulty, feebly argued that in spite of the statutory amendment relegating to the Board of Land Administrationthe powers of hearing and disposal of appeals and revisions, the Government, as the overall supervisory authority of all revenue officers and revenue administration, possesses the inherent jurisdiction to revise and modify any order passed by the Board of LandAdministration. Therefore, even if the appeal of the respondent NO.4 to the Ministry of Land Administration and Land Reforms was incompetent, it can be treated as a provisional application and the Government should be deemed to have exercised its inherent provisional power in disposing of the same. 

19. Apart from the fact that we do not find any final provisional power within the four comers of the Act itself, we consider it to be a hazardous leap into the dark to invest the Government with an imaginary power by way of a bonus. The Government itself possessed the full powers of an appellate and provisional body. It handed over those powers to the Board by a statutory amendment, without reserving any residuary power to itself to act as an authority of last resort. In the absence of any legislative intention investing the Government with the authority of a residuary power we arc frankly unable to see how the Government could have exercised the appellate or re- visional power in respect of the application of the respondent No.4. The order of the Board of Land Administration, Annexure K in Writ Petition No. 425 of 1985, appears to have drawn the certain of finality in the proceedings and the matter, it appears, cannot be dragged any further, except by way of a challenge under Article 102 of the Constitution. 

20. In that view of the matter we are of the opinion that the Rule Nisi in Writ Petition No. 425 of 1985 ought to be made absolute. 

21. With regard to Writ Petition No. 1634 of 1988 it is the contention of Mr. Khondaker Mahbubuddin Ahmed, learned Advocate for the petitioners, that the Board of Land Administration by the impugned order; Annexure D(2), has addressed itself to   a wrong question which has gone into the root of its jurisdiction. He submits that Mutation Case Nos. 91,92 and 93 of 1979 are themselves without jurisdiction, not maintainable under section 143 of the Act and the Board has failed to address itself on this question. He has cited no decision in support of his argument. Section 143 of the Act, as amended up-to-date, is as follows:-	

143. Maintenance of the Record-of-rights. The Collector shall maintain up-to-date, in the prescribed manner, the record-of-rights prepared or revised under Part IV of under this Part by correcting clerical mistakes and by incorporating therein the changes on account of - 
(a) the mutation of names as a result of transfer or inheritance.
(b) the subdivision, amalgamation or consolidation of holdings; 
(c) the new settlement of'lands or of holdings purchased by the Government ; and 
(d) the abatement of rent on account of abandonment or diluvia or acquisition of land." 

22. Indeed we find that the petitioners have all throughout agitated that the alleged transfer by the predecessors of respondent Nos. 4-6 having not been effected by a recorded tenant, proceedings under section 143 are entirely misconceived. 111is is what the petitioners specifically argued before the Circle Officer (Revenue), Moulvi Bazar (vide Order dated 28.11.79 in Miscellaneous Case No. 38 of 1979 Annexure F of Writ Petition No. 425 of 1985), in their Memo of Appeal before the Commissioner, Chittagong Division (ground Nos. 2 and 3 of Annexure H in Writ Petition No. 425 of 1985) and also before the Board of Land Administration (ground No. IV of the appeal petition Annexure J in Writ Petition No. 425 of 1985) 

23. The Additional Deputy Commissioner (Revenue), Sylhet, the Additional Commissioner, Chittagong and the Board of Land Administration in their respective orders came to a finding that Keramat Ali auction purchased the entire 5.80 acres of case khatian. Syed Ashraf Ali purchased only 3.15 acres from him. After Syed Ashraf Ali's death, names of his heirs were mutated, but they are entitled to have their land mutated to the extent of purchase by their predecessor-in-interest. It is for them to establish in a Court of law that Syed Ashraf Ali actually purchased 5.80 acres. The respondent Nos. 4-6 and their predecessors were and are in possession of the remaining portion. So they are entitled to mutate their names. 

24. The question is, is such mutation permit- ted under section 143 of the Act? Chapter IV of the Act contains an elaborate procedure for preparing the record-of-rights and also for hearing objections from parties concerned. S.A. khatian No. 1358 was pre- pared in the joint names of Syed Ashraf Ali and his brother Syed Ankar Ali during the rent roll operations in 1958. No objections were filed by the predecessors of the respondent Nos. 4-6. Thekhatian was corrected in 1965 by Syed Ashraf Ali and thereafter it stood in his sole name. After his death in 1970, his heirs and successors mutated their names in Mutation Case No. 75 of 1973-74. No objections were filed at that time. 

25. Section 143 of the Act is attracted only when a clerical mistake is to be corrected or, inter alia, the mutation of names as a result of transfer or inheritance is necessary. It is not attracted when the record-of-rights is to be corrected after a finding to be given as to the title of the holders or the challengers. The examination of title deeds for purposes of determination title or the holder of record of rights is not permitted under section 143. The word "transfer" referred to in clause (a) of section 143 is limited to transfer by the recorded tenant, not by other persons. The respondent Nos. 4-6 applied for mutation not because the recorded tenant transferred the lands to them, but because some persons, unconnected with record of rights, transferred the lands. Clause (a) of Section 143 is not attracted under these circumstances. 
26. By E.P. Ordinance No. VIII of 1965 section 143A was inserted into the Act which reads as follows:- "(1) Any person aggrieved by an entry or omission of entry in the record-or-rights pre- pared or revised and finally published under Chapter IV may, notwithstanding anything contained elsewhere in this Act, file an application along with necessary requisites for the purpose of correcting mistakes in such record-of-rights in the Civil Court which could have jurisdiction to entertain a suit for possession of the land to which such entry relates or in respect of which such omission was made." 

27. It is not- necessary to quote the other pro- visions of section 143A. 

28. Section 143A was omitted by Ordinance No. LXIV of 1975 

29. The respondent Nos. 4-6 and their predecessors, claiming as they do the disputed property as their ancestral property from time immemorial, had a remedy from 1965-1975 to file an application in the Civil Court for the purpose of correcting mistakes in the record-of-rights. The question could have been decided on the basis of possession only. This they failed to do. Now that Syed Ashraf Ali is the recorded tenant and his heirs and successors have also been substituted after his death, transferees of persons unconnected with the record of rights do not have any locus standi under section 143 of the Act to maintain an application for mutation. Such transferees have now to take recourse to Civil Court for establishment of their predecessors' right, title, interest and possession and it is only when they do so establish that the question of mutation will arise. 

30. It is well-established that a determination that is erroneous in law can be set aside if the error goes to jurisdiction or if the error is apparent on the face of the record. We find that the Board of Land Ad- ministration has misdirected itself as to the question of law involved in this case and has decided matters which are not within its jurisdiction to decide under scction143. We arc of the opinion that under such circumstances the decision of the Board of Land Administration is liable to interference by this Court. 

31. At one time section 143 of the Act stood as follows:- "143. The Collector shall maintain up-to-date, in prescribed manner, the record-of-rights prepared or revised under Part IV under this Part by correcting bonafide mistakes and by incorporating therein the changes on account of- 
(a) the mutation of names as a result of transfer or inheritance; 
(b) the subdivision, amalgamation or consolidation of holdings; 
(c) the new settlement of land or holdings purchased by the Government; and 
(d) the abatement of rent on account of abandonment or diluvium or acquisition ofland." 

32. In the unreported decision of the Appellate Division in the case of Bangladesh and others-Vs- MariumKhatun and others (Civil Appeal No.8 of 1972) the facts are that the respondent who, along with others took settlement of land from Zaminders and were in in possession thereof, challenged the or- der of the Additional Deputy Commissioner (Revenue), Faridpur cancelling the names of the respondent and his co-sharers from the record of rights which were recorded in the name of the then Province of East Pakistan. By four different orders from 1960 to 1963 the Revenue Settlement Officer corrected the record of rights and inserted the names of the respondent and his co-sharers in the disputed khatian. The Deputy Commissioner of Faridpur purchased some of the land in dispute from the respondent in 1964, but on 17.10.66 the respondent and his co-sharers were served with notice to show cause why the record of rights shall not be changed in favour of the Province of East Pakistan. The respondent showed cause but the Additional Deputy Com- missioner (Revenue), Faridpur cancelled the names of the respondent and his co-sharers by order dated 13.7.67 and inserted the name of the Province of East Pakistan in respect of the disputed Khatian. The case of the Province of East Pakistan was that the names of the respondent and his co-sharers were re- corded as a result of fraudulent transaction between the respondent and his co-sharers on the one hand and some of the revenue authorities on the other. 

33. The Appellate Division quoted with approval the judgment of the then Dhaka High Court in Writ Petition No. 386 of 1967 arising out of the above proceeding as follows :- 

"The scope of section 143 of the Act is, in our opinion, of a very limited nature. It authorizes the Collector to maintain up to date record of rights and to make such correction as occurred as a result of bonafide mistake committed in preparing the record of rights. It does not, in our opinion, authorise the Collector to correct the record-of-rights which affects the question of title or possession relating to disputed question of fact. Bonafide mistake, as contemplated under section 143 of the Act, in our opinion, relates to the mistake of the nature where a mistake has crept in which is not supported by the records or where there has been a mistake in recording quantum of the land which again is not supported by facts but where name of a person stands recorded and another person challenges that such entry cannot be said to have been made as a result of bonafide mistake, and that cannot be corrected by the Collector under section 143 of the Act." 

34. The Appellate Divisionwas unable to find fault with or take exception to the views so expressed. The Appellate Division held that the facts which were required to be determined prior to correcting the record-of-rights by a proceeding under Section 143 of the Act involved the examination of documents of title relating to the lands in dispute, commission of fraud, if any, and the interpretation of various sections of the Act. The summary method under section 143 cannot be strained to consider question relating to such facts. 

35. In the present case also the questions, for example, whether Syed Ashraf All purchased 5.80 acres or only 3.15 acres, whether the predecessors of respondent Nos. 4-6 were possessing the remaining 2.65 acres as ancestral land and if so under what title, whether the Muktiptara dated 8.5.79 created any title in favour of the predecessors of respondent Nos. 4-6 and other questions can be determined only after examining witnesses and documents in a full-scale title suit. None of these things can conveniently or even suitably be done by the Collector 'under the terms and provisions of aforesaid section 143, as it now stands. If "bonafide mistake" was not covered by the facts disclosed in the aforesaid Civil Appeal No. 8 of 1972, we fail to see how "clerical mistake" can be found in the present case. 36. In the Rule Nisi obtained in Writ Petition No. 1634 of 1988 the respondents have also been asked to show cause why direction should not be issued for cancellation of the Board's order and restoration of the record in the names of the petitioners to the extent of 5.80 acres. 
37. From the above we are of the opinion that the petitioners arc also entitled to get the said direction in full. 

38. In Contempt Petition No. 3 of 1987 the petitioners of Writ Petition No. 425 of 1985 have alleged that while obtaining a Rule Nisi on 13.11.85 in Writ Petition No. 425 of 1985, the petitioners obtained a stay of operation of the impugned orders Annexure M and Ni. But violating the order of stay the Deputy Commissioner of Moulvi Bazar and the respondent No. 4 mutally and in collusion with each other caused an amendment in the record-of-rights showing the respondent No. 4 as the recorded tenant. As a proof thereof the petitioners have annexed in their supplementary affidavit Annexure 6 showing that on 19.2.87, i.e., about 2 years after issuance on the Rule Nisi and stay order, the record-of-rights was corrected in favour of the respondent No. 4 in pursuance of the impugned order Annexure M passed by the Ministry of Land Administration and Land Re-forms.

 39. In a counter-affidavit the respondent No. 3, the Deputy Commissioner, Moulvi Bazar has denied the allegations and has stated that he did not pass any order for the alleged correction of records. 

40. We find that the Contempt Rule was is-sued not by name upon any particular officer but by designation upon the Deputy Commissioner, Moulvi Bazar. The law of Contempt acts in persona and therefore the issuance of the Rule upon an office is of no consequence. That leaves us with the question as to whether the respondent No. 4 himself has taken any part in the correction of records after the High Court Division passed an order of stay on 13.11.85. We do not find any material in support of the allegation that the respondent No. 4 himself was responsible or was instrumental in effecting any correction.

 41. In that view of the matter we do not find any substance in this Rule.

 42. In the result the Rule Nisi in Writ Petition No. 425 of 1985 is made absolute without any order as to costs. Annexures M and Ni thereof are declared to have been passed without lawful authority and to be of no legal effect. The respondent No. 1 is directed to cancel/rescind and/ or withdraw the impugned orders. 
	
43. The Rule Nisi in Writ Petition No. 1634 of 1988 is also made absolute without any order as to costs. It is declared that the, impugned order Annexure D(2) has been passed without any lawful authority and is of no legal effect and the respondent No. 1 is directed to cancel the same and the respondent No. 3 is directed to restore the records in the names of the petitioners to the extent of 5.80 acres as it originally stood. 

44. The Rule in Contempt Petition No. 3 of 1987 is discharged. 

End.

full_judgment:
This Rule is directed against the appellate decree in a suit for declaration of the plaintiff's title to 2.39 acres of land representing 8 annas share in the holding recorded in C. S. Khatian No. 27 corresponding to R. S. Khatian No. 65 and S. A. Khatian No. 178 of Mouza Uttar Shubidkhali, under P.S Mrijagonj. The learned Munsif, 3rd Court, Patuakhali decreed the suit. On appeal the learned District Judge, Patuakhali reversed the judgment and decree of the learned Munsif and dismissed the suit.

2. It is undisputed that 4.94 acres of land in 18 different plots recorded in C.S. Khatian No. 27 belonged to Dhalai and Arabdi in equal shares. The plaintiffs are the successive heirs of Arabdi. Defendant Nos. 1.6 are the successive heirs of Dhalai and defendant No. 7 is the heirs of one Mokim Mridha. The lands of the disputed holding with a diminished area of 4.78 acres have been recorded in both the R S. and S.A. Khatians in the names of defendants 1-6 who are heirs and successors of Montazuddin, son of Dhalai, as well as in the name of Mokim Mridha, predecessor-in-interest of defendant No. 7. The plaintiffs were unaware of the wrong recording until 1.12.76 when the defendants denied their interest on the basis of the wrong record. The plaintiffs claimed that they were in continuous possession of their 8 annas share in the suit properties by cultivating paddy and living on the homestead plot.

Only the defendant No. 2 contested the suit by filing a written statement and denying the plaintiffs title and possession in the suit lands; He contends that Arabdi's son and only ultimate heir Tomiruddin mortgaged his 8 annas interest in the lands of the disputed khatian to one Nimchand Roy who in Mortgage Execution Case No. 117/18 auction purchased Tomiruddin's interest on 6.9 18 and took khas possession thereof on 13.4.1919. Thereafter he sold the interest under a registered kabala dated 19.5.1919 in favour of Dhalai who possessed the same. After the death of Dhalai his heirs and successive heirs including the defendants possessed the same. Ainuddin, a deceased grandson of Arabdi took settlement of .42 acres of land of the disputed holding for 12 years on payment of Tk. 50 as salami and at an annual rental of 9/- executing a registered kol karsha kabuliyat on 18.9.29 in favour of Montaruddin, son of Dhalai. The Kabuliyat was executed by Ainuddin on his own behalf and on behalf of plaintiff Nos. 1 & 2, then minors. This under-tenancy fell into arrears of rent and in Rent Execution Case No. 273/44 Montazuddin auction purchased the land and took delivery of possession thereof on 19.6.44 by evicting the plaintiffs and since then the defendants are in possession of the lands of the entire holding.

3. The plaintiffs examined 4 P.Ws. and the contesting defendant examined 3 D.Ws and exhibited several documents in support of their respective cases. The learned Munsif on consideration of the oral evidence on record found that the plaintiffs were in possession of suit land. The learned District Judge, on the other hand, considered the exhibits filed by the contesting defendant showing that Nimchand Roy, the decree-holder auction purchased the 8 annas share of Tomiruddin, heir of Arabdi and also showing that he took delivery of possession through Court on 13.4.1919. He noticed the certified copy of the sale certificate. He also noticed the registered kabala dated 19.5.1919 executed by Nimchand Roy in favour of Dhalai in respect of his auction purchased 8 annas share. The karsha kabuliyat executed by Ainuddin was also noticed by the learned District Judge. He also noticed the certified copy of the writ of delivery of possession of .42 acres of land on 19.6.44 by evicting the plaintiff Nos. 1 & 2 and Ainuddin. The learned District Judge found that the registered kabala dated 19.5.1919 and the registered kol karsha kabuliyat came from proper custody and the other documents were certified copies of Court documents. He then discussed the evidence of P.Ws. and found that they were not competent to say anything about the transactions of mortgage and auction sale taking place as far back as in 1918 and 1919. The learned District Judge also found that except for homestead plot No. 1388 the plaintiff's evidence on possession was not convincing On the other hand, the contesting defendant's evidence on possession was satisfactorily proved by the D.Ws., except with regard to homestead plot No. 1388 which, even according to D.W. 2, was in possession of the plaintiffs. The learned District Judge held that since the defendants' possession in at least 8 annas share of the disputed khatian is undisputed, the plaintiffs have the burden to prove that they possess the remaining 8 annas share in suit They have failed to prove the same, except that they are in possession of homestead plot No. 1388. The learned District Judge was also of the view that the plaintiffs have failed to rebut the presumption that the R.S. and S.A. records were correct. He, however, held that the suit was not barred by limitation. The learned District Justice set aside lodgment and decree of the learned munsif with the modification that the plaintiffs right, title and interest in plot no. 1388 in suit was declared and the suit was decreed to that extent only. Thereafter the plaintiffs obtained the present Rule.

4. Mr. Khondkar Mahbubuddin Ahmed, learned Advocate for the petitioners submits that the court of appeal below committed an error of law apparent on the face of the record by approaching the suit from a wrong view of onus which has completely vitiated his findings. Mr. Ahmed submits that admittedly the C.S. Khatian record Arabdi, the predecessor-in-interest of the plaintiffs as 8 annas co-sharer of the disputed khatian. If it is the case of the defendants that a mortgage, a mortgage execution case, an auction sale, a sale of the auction purchased land, a kol karsha kabuliyat of a part of the purchased land and finally a rent execution case in respect of the kabuliyat lands took place subsequent to the C.S. operation, the onus was on the contesting defendant not only to prove these subsequent developments but also conclusively to prove that after each alleged event the defendants predecessor had obtained actual physical possession of the 8 annas share of Arabdi. Instead, the learned District Judge has proceeded from the wrong standpoint that since till defendants are in possession of their 8 annas share, which is undisputed, it is for the plaintiffs to prove that they possessed the remaining 8 annas share in suit. It is this wrong view of onus which has prompted the court of appeal below to merely weigh on balance the evidence of P.Ws. and D.Ws. on possession of the suit land except the homestead plot No. 1388. Had the learned District Judge approached the question from the right standpoint, namely, that it is for the contesting defendant to prove the transactions subsequent to C.S. operation as well as possession be would have looked into the evidence of actual physical possession of the predecessors of the defendants after each alleged event. He having not done so, Mr. Ahmed submits, the appeal should be re-heard by the appellate Court below keeping the question of onus uppermost in view.

5. It is true that the plaintiffs have based their claim on the simple proposition that they are the heirs and successors of the 8 annas recorded tenant in the C.S khatian The C.S. khatian supports their case. It is however the contesting defendant's case that several developments have taken place after the C.S. operation resulting in the transfer of ownership and possession of the 8 annas share of Arabdi in the hands of the defendants predecessor. To prove that point, the defendants have filed a number of documents, as already stated, which have been believed by the Court of appeal below. The presumption of correctness of entry in the C.S. Khatian was never in doubt. The defendants also admit the correctness of the entry in the C.S. Khatian. The defendant’s documents have convinced the Court of appeal below that subsequent to the C.S. operation the defendants' predecessor acquired ownership and possession of the 8 annas share of Arabdi. What the Court of appeal below held in substance is that the latter developments after the C.S. operation have been proved by the contesting defendant. Under the circumstances, it is difficult to hold that the defendant has not discharged his onus to prove the subsequent developments.

<u>6. As far as possession is concerned both sides have adduced evidence. When both sides adduce evidence the question of onus loses it importance and the court has to weigh the evidence on record and come to a decision on the basis of preponderance of evidence. Obviously the Court of appeal below was not impressed with the evidence of P.Ws. on the subject. His council that the plaintiffs were not in possession of the suit land except the homestead plot No 1388 is therefore based on an appreciation of evidence over which this Court sitting in the revisional jurisdiction will not interfere.</u>

7. Mr. Ahmed's next submission is that the Court of appeal below committed an error of law apparent on the face of the record by dismissing the plaintiffs suit against the defendant Nos. 1 and 3-7 who did not contest the suit. It is only the defendant No. 2 who contested the suit by filing a written statement. The defendant No. 2 did not contest the suit on behalf of the other defendants. He filed power only on his own behalf and the written statement was also signed only by him. The other defendants were, therefore, non-contesting defendants and since they did not contest the suit at all, the learned District Judge should have decreed the suit against them. Mr. Ahmed refers to Order 1, rule 12 of the Code of Civil Procedure which provides that where there are more defendants than one, any one or more of them may he authorised by any other of them to appear, plead or act for such other in any proceeding. If the defendant No. 2 was so authorised by the other defendant then his defence would have been the defence of the other defendants, and the other defendants would have stood or fallen along with the defendant No. 2 But in the present case. Mr. Ahmed submits the defendant No. 2 was not authorised in terms of Order 1, rule 12 of the Code of Civil Procedure. Mr. Ahmed next draws my attention to Order 15. rule 2 of the Code of Civil Procedure which provides that where there are more defendants than one, and any one of the defendants is not at issue with the plaintiff on any question of law or of fact, the Court may at once pronounce judgment for or against such defendant and the suit shall Proceed only against the other defendants. Mr. Ahmed argues that the expression "any one of the defendants" not at issue with the plaintiff" refers to the non-contesting defendants as well, because they are not at issue with plaintiff.

<u>8. The argument is attractive, but hardly commends to me In my view a defendant is "not at issue with the plaintiff" only if before or during framing of issues he comes and tells the Court either by filing a written statement or orally that he does not pick up any issue with the plaintiff Thus, in a money suit the defendant may come and tell the Court that he admits the claim of the plaintiff but only asks for installments. To make a defendant one who is ''not at issue with the plaintiff" he must appear and say so. A non-correcting defendant has several options up his sleeves. He can come up any moment to say that he did not receive the summons of the suit. He can come at the close of the trial to say that he received information about the suit only recently and he wants to contest the suit. At the first hearing of the suit which is the subject matter of Order 15, rule 2 of the Code of Civil Procedure it cannot be presumed against the non-contesting defendant that he was not at issue with the plaintiff.</u>

<u>9. Moreover, the plaintiff may file a suit against several defendants and none of them may appear. The plaintiff has still the burden to prove his own case in an ex parte proceeding. If he cannot prove his own case even in an ex parte proceeding the suit cannot be decreed against the non-contesting defendants.</u>

10. In the present case the plaintiffs have not been able to prove their case of tide and possession not only in so far as the contesting defendant No. 2 is concerned, but also in so far as the other non-contesting defendants are concerned. Can it be said then that the suit should be decreed against the non-contesting defendants, simply because they did not contest the suit? I am clearly of the opinion that the suit cannot be so decreed.

For all the above reasons I do not find any ground for interference in the Rule.

In the result the Rule is discharged without any order as to costs. The judgment and decree of the learned district Judge are affirmed.

Let the records be sent down immediately.

End.
