case_source: From the judgment and order dated 14.2.1977 passed by the High Court in Civil Revision Case No. 1696 of 1968.
full_judgment:
Ruhul Islam, J.—This appeal by special Ism arises from the judgment dated February 14 1977 of the High Court of Bangladesh in Civil Revision Case No. 1696 of 1968 in connection with the pre-emption case under section 96 of the East Bengal State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, 1950.

2. The short question for consideration In this appeal it whether the learned Single Judge of the High Court correctly appreciated the ratio decidendt of the decision of this Court in Motilal Sikder vs. Benodini Dasi, 28 DLR (AD) 5, and whether the same has been correctly applied to the facts and circumstances of this case.

3. Facts relevant for disposal of the appeal are that the pre-emptor respondent No. 1 filed an application claiming to be a co-sharer in the holding and prayed for pre-emption of the transfer of .45 acres of land dated October 25, 1965 made by respondent No. 3 Abdul Huq Sarker in favour of the appellants who are strangers to the holding, at Taka 1000/- without serving notice of the sale. The pre-emptor respondent claimed that he came to know about the sale on October 30, 1965 and filed the pre-emption case on February 23, 1966. The appellants contested the case by filing two sets of written objection contending, inter alia, that the case Is not maintainable on account of defect of parties, as many of the co-sharers by inheritance in the case holding have not been impleaded. They further contended that they are not the actual purchasers but they are the benamdars of their mother Afronnessa who being a co-sharer by inheritance in the holding made the purchase in the benami of her minor sons, and, as such, the sale cannot be made subject-matter of pre-emption. Their further case is that the original holding was never auction-sold nor any fresh settlement was taken by the original tenants and no fresh or separate holding was created in respect of the case land.

4. The pre-emption case was allowed by the Munsif, Jamalpur, and on appeal by the appellants, the judgment was reversed by the Subordinate Judge, Second Court, Mymensingh. The learned Subordinate Judge held that the pre-emption case was not maintainable in the absence of some of the co-sharers by Inheritance. On a revisional application filed by the pre-emptor-respondent under section 113 of the Code of Civil Procedure the learned Single Judge of the High Court of Bangladesh set aside the judgment of the lower Appellate Court holding that the pre-emption case should not be dismissed on the ground of non-joinder of necessary parties. It is not necessary that all the co-sharers of the holding should be impleaded in the pre-emption proceeding. In taking this view the learned Judge referred to the decision In Motilal Sikder vs. Benodini Dasi. The learned Judge held that the provision of sub-section (2) of section 96 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, 1950 regarding parties to the proceeding is directory, and not mandatory; and, as such, the pre-emption application was not bad for defect of parties. On this view the judgment of lower Appellate Court was set aside.

5. From the judgment of the learned Single Judge it appears that he agreed with the finding of the lower Appellate Court that some co-sharers by inheritance in the holding were omitted from the proceeding, but he condoned this defect on the ground that the requirement with regard to the making of parties in a pre-emption proceeding as provided in sub-section (2) of section 96 of the Act is directory and omission of some of the co-sharers from the proceeding cannot be fatal to the same. The learned Judge quoted certain passage from the decision in Motilal Sikder vs. Benodini Dasi which runs as under:

"It does not appear from a perusal of the provisions of section 96 that it was the intent of the legislature that the penalty for non-impleading a person as contemplated in sub-section (2) Is the invalidity of the order which may ultimately be made in the said proceeding. The question whether a person re a necessary party under sub-section (2) is a question of fact and the object of this provision seems to provide the co-sharer tenants and the holders to the contiguous lands with the opportunity of availing of the provision of the said sub-section. Since the benefit conferred under the said provision is meant for certain individuals, they can very well of waived. In that view of the matter the positive injunction contained in the said sub section as to the making of parties in spite of its being couched in mandatory language, should be read as directory".

6. Mr. Akram Hossein Amin, the learned Advocate on Record appearing for the appellants submitted that the learned Single Judge of the High Court failed to make proper appreciation of the ratio decidendt of the judgment in Motilal Sikder Vs. Benodini Dasi. He elaborated his submission stating that the observations made in the decision or Motilal Sikder Vs. Benodini Dasi do not give the indication that their Lordships were taking the view that the provision as contained in sub-section (2) of section 96 regarding making parties In a pre-emption case is directory and not mandatory.

7. On perusal of the judgment in Motilal Sikder Vs. Benodini Dasi it appears that in the context of the facts and circumstances of that case the following observation has been made:

"Since the benefit conferred under the said provision is meant for certain Individual, they can very well be waived. In that view of the matter the positive injunction contained in the said sub-section as to the making of parties In spite of its being couched in mandatory language, should be read as directory."

8. For proper appreciation of the ratio decidendi of the said decision in Motilal Sikder Vs. benodini Dasi some facts of the case are necessary to be stated. An application for pre-emption under section 96 of the East Bengal State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, 1950 was filed by the appellants claiming to be owners of the lands contiguous to the land sold by a registered kabala for consideration. The application was contested by the transferee contending, inter alia, that the applicants were not owners of contiguous lands; and that the application was not maintainable in the absence of contiguous land owners as named in the written objection. To meet this objection the appellants impleaded the persons whose names were supplied by the pre-emptee. At that trial only two points were pressed, namely whether the petitioners were the owners of the contiguous lands and whether the application was barred by limitation. On both the points the learned Munsif found, on consideration of the evidence, in favour of the pre-emptors. On the question of defect of partied the learned Munsif observed:

"An objection as to the defect of parties was stated in the written objection but the same was not pressed".

9. On appeal the decision was affirmed by the Subordinate Judge. No objection as to the defect of parties was canvassed before the said Court at the hearing of the rule issued on a revisional application filed by the pre-emptee. An application was filed on behalf of the pre-emptee praying for consideration of an additional ground which was as under: For that the Courts below acted without jurisdiction in allowing pre-emption that the preemption case is not duty constituted due to want of impleading of necessary parties as on showing all the pre-emptors by Exhibit 1 (e)."

10. The learned Single Judge allowed the petitioners to urge the additional round. II was contended that one Mozaffar Ali Khan who happened to be the co-purchaser with one Ledu Khan in the kabala Exhibit 1(b) by which the said Ledu Khan claimed to have acquired interest in the land contiguous to the land under pre-emption, and as such the said Mozaffar Ali Khan was a necessary party, in whose absence the application for pre-emption was not maintainable. The learned Single Judge relying upon the decision of a Division Reach of the Dacca High Court in Syed Abdul Karim vs. Harendra Chanara Dhupi. 14 D L.R 847, accepted the contention and dismissed the application for per emption. Special leave to appeal was granted to the appellants to consider whether cue objection chat Mozzaffar Ali Khan was a necessary party which was taken for the first time in the High Court should have been entertained and whether in any view of the matter the case should have been remanded for Investigation whether he was a necessary party.

11. While considering the ground upon which the leave was granted his Lordship observed that the question of joinder of partner is essentially a matter of procedure and some detailed rules have been provided in the Code of Civil Procedure. On the question of joinder of parties, in the course of discussion of this question, his Lordship observed that Order I of the Code of Civil Procedure deals with the question of the parties to a suit and by virtue of section 141 of the Code, the said provisions are applicable to a proceeding of original nature like the one under section 96 of the East Bengal State Acquisition and Tenancy Act. The discussion, however, mainly centred on the rules of pleading which provide that any objection as to the maintainability of a suit which requires investigation of acts must be taken in the pleading before the framing of the issues. So that the other party may not be taken by surprise and is prejudiced in the matter of taking steps to meet the objection. According to his Lordship the principle relating to a partition suit has got no application to a proceeding for pre-emption His Lords ship referred to a decision of a Single Judge of the High Court in the care of Syed Abdul Karim vs. Harendre Cnandra Dhupi, 14 DLR 847 which contains the following observation:

"In the case of pre-emption because of the special provision of the Act, rights of the parties cannot be deter-mined without considering the right of others. The principle of Order 1, rule 9 of the Code cannot be made applicable. In the circumstances, it cannot be said that the tenants holding lands contiguous to lands transferred are not necessary parties as they are persons whose presence is necessary for the proper constitution of the pre-emption application, Their presence is not only a matter of convenience but of absolute necessity to enable the Court to adjudicate more effectively and completely. Order 1, rule 9 of the Code does not apply when a cause of action arises against a number of persons jointly because when one of such persons is eliminated no cause of action subsists against other as in the suit for partition. In the case of preemption under section 96 of the Act, the cause of action arises not only against the transferee but also against the co-sharer and other holders of contiguous lands".

12. According to his Lordship the analogy drawn in the above noted decision between a suit for partition and the proceeding for pre-emption does not appear to be based on sound reasoning. His Lordship however approved another principle laid down in the said decision with the following observation:

"It should, however, be noticed that in the said case reported in 14 DLR 847 the Dacca High Court laid down another principle which appears to be substantially correct. Reading sub-sections (2) and (4) of section 96 together, the said Court took the view that only those of the co-sharer tenants and the holders of contiguous lands, whose right of pre-emption had not been barred under subs section (1) of section 96 were necessary parties within the meaning of sub-section (2) of the said section. Although we have been unable to concur in the other view expressed in the said case as to the analogy between a suit for partition and the proceeding for pre-emption, but the aforesaid principle as to a necessary party in a proceeding for pre-emption has been, in our opinion, correctly pronounced. From sub-section (4) of section 96 it Is clear that the said provision was obviously made for the purpose of providing the facility of pre-emption to the persons interested, who have not lost their right of pre-emption under sub-section (1) of the said section"

13. The above quotations provide sufficient indication as to the manner how the appeal under consideration was disposed of. The petitioners were allowed to take an additional ground showing defect of party at the hearing of the rule which was not taken at the trial of the pre-emption case and objection on the ground of non-joinder of necessary parties was not pressed at the trial. The pre-emption application was dismissed only on accepting the objection which was taken for the first time in revision and without sending the case back to the trial Court to find out as to whether the said persons omitted from the proceeding had any subsisting interest in the land as shown by the pre-emptee. The uncontroverted statement of the appellants made in respect of the subsisting interest of Mozaffar Ali Khan was accepted. It was stated that there was a subsequent partition of the lands purchased by Exhibit 1 (b) between the two brothers and the portion which fell in the share of Ledu Khan was contiguous to the land under pre-emption and the portion which was allotted to Mozaffar Ali Khan was not contiguous to the said lands. In this background the appeal was allowed and judgment of the High Court was set aside and the judgment of the Courts below were restored.

14. With one respect I must say that the above noted opinion that the positive injunction contained in sub-section (2) of section 96 as to making parties is to be read as directory and not mandatory as its language indicates, is limited to the particular facts of the case.

Sub-section (2) of section 96 reads as under:

“In an application made under subs section (1) by a co-sharer tenant or co-sharer tenants, all other co-sharer tenants of the holding and the transferee shell be made parties and in such an application made by a tenant holding land contiguous to the land transferred, all the co-sharer tenants of the holding and all the tenants holding lauds contiguous to the land transferred and the transferee shall be made parties"

<u>15. The right of pre-emption as provided under sub-section (1) of section 96 is a statutory right. The cause of action for pre-emption of any transfer accrues to the co-sharer tenants and contiguous land owners This right of the applicant or applicant claiming to be cc-sharer tenants or owner of contiguous land, is not absolute but subject to the right of other co sharers and other holders of land contiguous to the land transferred, as the case may be, for proper adjudication. To give fall effect to the statutory provision, all the necessary parties must be impleaded, because relief cannot be given in the absence of such party.</u>

<u>16. The right to purchase the land transferred as contemplated under section 96 is a statutory right and it is to be exercised within 4 months of the service of notice under section 89, or if no notice has been served under section 89, within four months of the date of knowledge of the transfer. The right to purchase the land has been very clearly and unambiguously spelt out by the legislature in the section. The language of the provisions in different parts of the section shows that the right to purchase conferred upon the co-sharer tenants or the contiguous land owners is not by any means dependent upon initiation of the pre-emption proceeding either by a co-sharer tenant or owner of the land contiguous to the land of transfer. However, the section does not cast any duty upon the Court to find out through process of enquiry all the non-notified co-sharers if any or all the non-impleaded contiguous land owners, and for complete adjudication implead them In the proceedings, Sub-section (2) requires that all the co-sharer tenants of the holding are to be impleaded in the application failing under the first part of sub-section (1). Similarly, all the contiguous land owners are to be made parties in the application failing under the second part of sub-section (1), Sab-section (4) provides the period of limitation for the remaining co-sharer tenant or the tenants holding land contiguous to the land transferred, to join in the pre-emption proceedings. This period of two months begins to run from the service of notice of the application for pre-emption. The different provisions of section 96 clearly point out that a duty has been cast upon the pre-emptor, if he is a co-sharer tenant, to make all the remaining co-sharer tenants, and if he is a tenant holding land contiguous to the land transferred, all the remaining tenants boiling lands contiguous to the land transferred and the transferee, parties to the application. Object of sub-section (2) is to have all the co-sharer tenants or all the tenants holding lands contiguous to the land transferred, before the Court for proper and complete adjudication in accordance with law. A co-sharer tenant or tenants holding land contiguous to the land transferred may waive his right to purchase the land, but on this consideration there is hardly any scope for taking the view that the requirement of sub-section (2) is not mandatory but is me rely directory. Second Part of sub-section (4) clearly indicates that a co-sharer tenant or a tenant having land contiguous to the land transferred failing to join in the pre-emption proceeding within the given time, shall not have any further right to purchase under this section. Waive of the right is one thing, but defeating the right by deliberate omission in the pre-emption application is a different thing. There is hardly any scope to doubt that the clear object, of legislation is that all the parties having right of pre-emption should be before the Court for adjudication of the right or rights of pre-emption in accordance with law.</u>

17. Now the question is whether the omission of any necessary party in the pre-emption proceeding entails automatic failure of the proceeding. In Motilal Sikder Vs. Benodini Dasi an attempt has been made to lay down the principal that the provision as contained in sub-section (2) of section 96 is not mandatory but merely directory, in other words, no duty cast upon the pre-emptor to implead all the parties who are, as contemplated under section 96, necessary parties. This view is mere founded on the provision of procedure as provided under Order 1, rule 9 of the Code of Civil Procedure than strict interpretation of the language of the section.

18. The procedure with regard to misjoinder and non-joinder of parties in a suit or a proceeding in any Court of civil jurisdiction, in view of section 141 of the Code of Civil Procedure, Order 1. rule 9 is applicable. Order 1, rule 9 reads as under:—

"No suit shall be defeated by reason of the misjoinder or non-joinder of parties, and the Court may in every suit deal with the matter in controversy so far as regards the rights and interest of the parties actually before it."

<u>19. The question of non-joinder of necessary party affecting framing of a pre-emption application is to be decided keeping in view the requirement of the different sub-sections of section 96 along with the provisions as contained in Order 1, rules 9 and 10 of the Code of Civil Procedure, because, Pre-emption proceedings being one of the proceedings as contemplated under section 141 of the Code of Civil Procedure the procedure of law in Order I, rule 9 is applicable. On account of omission of necessary party a preemption case shall not be dismissed outright keeping In view the provision of Order 1, role 9, inasmuch as non-joinder of necessary party will not by itself defeat a suit proceeding However, the special statutory provision in sub-section (2) as to the necessary parties to be impleaded is mandatory. In clear language it mentions the persons to be impleaded in an application made under sub-section (1) by a co-sharer tenant: and in an application made by a tenant holding land contiguous to the land transferred. Requirement of the statutory provision cannot be minimised by the procedural law as contained in Order 1, rule 9. The special provision in sub section (2) is not controlled by Order 1, rule 9, which merely provides that a suit shall not be dismissed by reason of mere non-joinder of necessary parties. Order 1, rule 10 provides for addition of party at any stage of the proceedings, either upon or without the application of either party. Where there is non-joinder of a necessary party the Court is ems powered to add the necessary party under rule 10 at any stage of the proceeding, either upon or without the application of either party. The objection as to non-joinder of necessary parties must be taken at the earliest opportunity by the defendant. Such objection provides an opportunity to the plains tiff to remove the defect by adding parties who were omitted. In taking objection on the ground of non-joinder of necessary parties the defendant is required to furnish the names and particulars of the parties who were omitted from the suit. On the refusal of the plaintiff to implead the parties mentioned in the written statement, the question becomes an issue for adjudication by the Court and on adjudication the question becomes decided. In such an event the consequences must follow, that is, the suit becomes liable to be dismissed on the ground of non-joinder of necessary party. In the case of a pre-emption preceding the law regarding procedure cannot be treated as different. If the pre-emptee or for that matter any of the parties disclose existence of a necessary party and furnishes the necessary particulars, but the pre-emptor still insists not to implead him as a party, consequence on adjudication is the same. It has already been mentioned that such objection regarding non-joinder of necessary parties should be taken at the earlier opportunity, before the trial, because an enquiry on this question may be necessary. Of course, in an appropriate case such objection may be allowed to be raised in the appeal. This may be done on the ground that the appeal is continuation of the suit or proceeding. But there is no scope for raising the question of defect of party on account of non-joinder of necessary parties, for the first time in revision.</u>

20. In the instant case written objection was filed by the appellants contending; inter alia, that the case was not maintainable due to defect of parties, as many of the co-sharers by inheritance in the holding were omitted. It was, inter-alia, stated that their mother Afronnessa who being herself one of such co-sharers by Inheritance In the holding was a necessary party, and In her absence the pre-emption case was liable to be dismissed. The learned Munsif overruling the objection allowed the pre-emption case with the following observation:

"In view of my finding in the foregoing pares I do not find any prima facie evidence to the effect that the said Afronnesse is a co-sharer of the holding. And these are serious , questions of title involved in this case in the way of determination of Afronnessa or anybody else named in w/s has any share in the case holding or not. And these questions cannot be decided in this Miscellaneous Case without properly being framed in title suit".

21. On appeal the main question for consideration was whether the application for pre-emption was maintainable or whether it was bad for defect of parties. The learned Subordinate Judge on consideration of the materials on record found that the question was not properly adjudicated by the learned Munsif inasmuch as he based his decision upon a wrong assumption that the S.A. Record should be presumed to be correct and that there is no need of scrutiny as to its correctness. The learned Subordinate Judge found that some of the co-sharers by inheritance in the holding including the appellant's mother Afronnessa were not impleaded in the preemption case, although this objection was taken by she pre-emptees at the earliest opportunity. The learned Subordinate Judge after consideration of the evidence arrived at the following finding:

“Thus, upon the evidence on record I find that the case is legally not maintainable due to defect of parties as several co-sharers by inheritance have not been brought on record".

22. On the basis of the finding that several co-sharers in the holding were omitted in the pre-emption case and they were not brought on record in spite of objection taken by the pre-emptees in this respect, set aside the order of the Munsif and dismissed the pre-emption case.

23. The learned Single Judge of the High Court Division however set aside the judgment of the lower Appellate. Court on taking the view that on account of defect of parties the case should not have been dismissed. He practically acted on the authority of the decision in Motilal Sikder vs. Benodini Dasi, wherein the following observation occurs:

"The expression a positive injunction contained in the said sub-section as to the making of parties in spite of its being couched in mandatory language should be read as directory".

24. The provision of law as contained to sub-section (2) should be followed without minimising its requirement. The requirement as to making of parties is undoubtedly positive. It is the duty of the pre-emptor to implead the necessary parties as I have already observed above that this requirement of law should be enforced keeping in view the provisions of Order 1, rules 9 and 10 if the prey emptor, after getting an opportunity, fails to amend his application by impleading the necessary parties as pointed out by the pre-emptee, and on evidence if it is found that the application suffers from defect of parties, in that event the application cannot succeed and must be dismissed. I fully agree with the view expressed in the case reported in 14 DLR 847 that presence of the persons mentioned in sub-section (2) of section 96 " is not only a matter of convenience but of absolute necessity to enable the Court to adjudicate more effectively and completely". Otherwise, a non-notified co-sharer or a contiguous land owner may have an occasion to challenge the decision and to try to re-open the matter. The decision in Motilal Sikder vs. Benodini Dasi, should be read in the light of the observations made above.

<u>25. The learned Single Judge while upsetting the decision of the lower Appellate Court omitted to notice that the pre-emption case was dismissed mainly on the ground that the pre-emptors failed to implead the necessary parties in spite of opportunity given to them by supplying the names in the written objection; and that on evidence it was found by the lower Appellate Court that the persons named in the written objection were co-sharers by inheritance having subsisting Interest in the holding, and In their absence the pre-emption case was not maintainable. The learned Judge in considering the question whether the sub-section (2) is directory or mandatory observed that non-inclusion of the persons named by the pre-emptees does not affect the application for pre-emption. "since the benefit of pre-emption is an individual opportunity and, as such, may be waived". Right to purchase a land may be waived, but that cannot be made a ground to relax the mandate of the statute to implead the necessary parties in the proceeding. A co-sharer in the holding cannot be allowed to purchase the entire land without impleading the other co-sharers and thereby depriving them from getting their share Similarly, a tenant owning land contiguous to the land transferred cannot be allowed to purchase the entire land transferred without impleading the other tenants holding lands contiguous to the land transferred, and thereby depriving them from exercising their right in the case of second category of pre-emptors presence of other tenants or tenants holding land contiguous to the land transferred is necessary for the purpose of determination of the order of priority as among the tenants in the manner as indicated in clause (b) of sub-section (5). So, presence of all the persons mentioned in sub-section (2), as the case may be, is more a matter of absolute necessity than of mere convenience. Their presence is necessary, so that the Court can adjudicate the claim of pre-emption more effectively and completely.</u>

26. In the instant case as I have already indicated above the pre-emptors got sufficient opportunity to remove the defect by impleading the persons named in the written objection but they failed to remove the defect, and, consequently, the application must be treated as not properly constituted. The pre-emptors cannot succeed on such an application. In that view of the matter the judgment of the learned Single Judge cannot be sustained, therefore, the appeal is allowed with costs and the judgment of the High Court set aside. Judgment and order of the lower Appellate Court are restored.

End.

case_source: Appeal against the order of Mr. D.N. Chowdhury, Subordinate Judge of Zilla Noakhali, dated the 23rd of April, 1969 in Title Suit No. 150 of 1967.
full_judgment:
Sultan Hossain Khan, J. - This appeal arises out of an order passed by the learned Subordinate Judge, Noakhali rejecting an application for temporary injunction in a suit for declaration that auction sale of certain bazar was premature illegal and without jurisdiction and that certain tanks are retainable as khas under the provisions of section 20(2a) of the East Bengal State Acquisition and Tenancy Act.

2. Facts of the case, in short, are that the plaintiffs, who are the deities installed by the fore-fathers of the sebaites, instituted the suit against the Government and others for a declaration as follows:

(a) declaring that the auction sale of the Battapars Chowdhury Bazar in lzara lease for the remaining period of 1374 B.S. held on 4.10.67 A.D. in sairat case No. 12/1967-68 was premature, illegal, without jurisdiction and null and void.

(b) declaring that the two tanks covered by C.S. Plot 1628 of village Dattapara and C.S. Plot 13 of Village Darjipara, P.S. Lakshimpur are retainable khas land of the plaintiffs.

3. The plaintiffs have alleged that the land constituting the bazar known as Dattapara Chowdhury Bazar was owned by to debattars created by the predecessor of the Soebaites in favour of the deites long before. This bazar it has been alleged comprises a part of the suit lands. Plaintiffs have alleged that they had been in possession of the bazar but the Government without any possession had put the bazar to izara sale, and that the auction sale of the bazar was illegal and without jurisdiction. The plaintiffs have also prayed for an order of temporary injunction restraining the defendants from giving effect to the lease of the bazar for the remaining period of 1274 B.S.

4. The plaintiffs have further alleged that the two tanks as recorded in C.S. dag No. 1628 of Mouza Dattapara and dag No. 13 of Darjipara are retain able khas of the plaintiffs and that it should be so declared. The plaintiffs also prayed for an order of temporary injunction restraining the Government from leasing out the two tanks till the disposal of the suit.

5. Defendant No. 1 has opposed the application. They have alleged that the bazar in question has vested in Government under law and that the defendant are realising tolls from the bzar and that the bazar has been put to auction and that the izara had been taken by defendant No.6. With regard to the tanks the defendant has alleged that those have been used as a part of the bazar and as such these tanks have vested in the Government.

6. As regards the bazar it appears to us that neither of the parties could place anything before us as to the extent of the bazar as contemplated in section 20 (2a) of E.B.S.A.T. Act. For the purpose of the appeal we would say that any bazar which includes any land, building or hut therein cannot be retained by any rent-receiver or raiyat or tenant and as such the plaintiffs are not entitled to any injunction with respect to the bazar. With regard to the area or extent of the bazar as said earlier it should be left open to be determined in the trial. As regards the two tanks the plaintiffs have claimed them on the ground that these tanks are their khas land and as such they are entitled to retain them under section 20(2)(b). Defendants have alleged that those two tanks are part of the bazar and as such those could not be retained by the plaintiffs. Plaintiffs have alleged that these tanks are pot part of the bazar for they have been excavated long before the creation of the bazar in 1934. Undoubtedly these tanks are not natural formation and these have been excavated and the owners had been using the tanks for rearing and catching fish.

7. In our opinion tanks in which fish is reared are retainable in view of the provision of section 20(2a) of the Act. Although the plaintiffs have averred that people of the bazar and villagers use the water of the tanks, yet in our opinion it does not make the tanks part of the bazar. By use of water of the tanks no right whatsoever has been created in favour of the users.

In our view plaintiffs have succeeded in establishing a prima facie case that the tanks are retainable khas tanks of the plaintiffs.

Mr. J.R. Mudasir Hossain has submitted that compensation with respect to the lands of khatian No. 349 have been prepared and finally published and that compensation for acquisition of the suit lands have been received by the landlords.

8. We have perused the certified copy of the khatian placed before us. In this khatian we find that there are tanks and khas lands owned by the shebait on behalf of the deities. In the khatian there are tenanted lands as well. In our view compensation assessment roll must have been prepared with respect to re It receiving interests in the khatian. Nothing could be shown that the compensation assessment roll have been prepared and compensation has been received by the landlords with respect to the khas lands of the khatian.

9. In these views of the matter the order of the learned Subordinate Judge so far as it relates to the granting of temporary injunctions with respect to the bazar is affirmed and with respect to the two tanks are set aside. The defendants are restrained by way of an injunction from leasing out the suit tanks to anybody till the disposal of the suit.

10. In the result this appeal, is allowed in part. The judgment and order passed by the learned Subordinate Judge rejecting the application for injunction with regard to the bazar are affirmed and that relating to the suit tanks are set aside and the injunction prayed for with regard to the tanks is granted.

11. In the facts and circumstances of the case the parties are directed to maintain statuesque with regard to plot Nos. 6, 7 and 8 of Mouza Darjipara on which temple, Asram and the pathway are situated. In the facts of the case there will be no order as to cost in this appeal.

The learned Subordinate Judge is directed to dispose of the suit within six months from the date of the receipt of the records.

Mohammad Abdur Rouf J.-I agree.

End.

case_source: (From the judgment and Order of the High Court Division dated 4.10.72 passed in Criminal Appeal No. 472 of 1969).
full_judgment:
Ahsanuddin Choudhury, J.-These two appeals by special leave are against a judgment of a learned Single Judge of the erstwhile High Court of East Pakistan passed in Civil Revision Case Nos. 181 and 182 of 1964. They arise in the following circumstances.

2. One Fariduddin Ahmed, predecessor of respondents 1(a) to 1(f), and respoadent No.2 Ashrafuddin Ahmed filed in the Court of the Munsif at North Raozan, Chittagong two cases, being No. 134 and 135 of 1962, under section 26F of the Bengal Tenancy Act (hereinafter referred to as the (B. T. Act) for pre-emption of certain land purchased by appellants Anwara Begum Chowdhurani and her husband Shamsul Huda Chowdhury. Their case was that they were co-sharers in the occupancy raiyati holding to which the said land appertained. The appellants contested those two cases on the ground that the land which the respondents sought to pre-empt appertained to a Korfa (under-raiyati) holding and, as such, pre-emption under section 26F of the B. T. Act was not available .

3. The learned Munsif, on evidence adduced before him, found that the holding was an occupancy raiyati holding and accordingly he allowed both the cases for pre-emption. The learned District Judge, on appeal, set aside the judgment and order of the learned Munsifand dismissed those cases and disallowed pre-emption on a finding that the holding was a Korfa (under-raiyati) holding with occupancy right and that pre-emption under section 26F of the B. T. Act was not available. Thereafter the respondents, i.e., the pre-emptors, obtained two Rules. A learned Single Judge of the Dacca High Court made the Rules absolute on a finding that the Korfa (under-raiyati tenancy) under pre-emption was "upgraded to a raiyati tenancy since 14.4.56 as the rent-receiving interests of  the immediate landlord, who was a raiyat, stood acquired with effect from 14.4.56 under general Notification under section 3 of the East Bengal State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, 1950. He further found that section 26F of the B. T. Act was fully applicable to these cases as the sale took place on 4.12.1959 and, 5.12.1959 and the applications for pre-emption were filed on 3.12.1962 when B. T. Act was in force and was still governing the field.

4. Leave was granted to consider (1) whether prior to coming into operation of Part V of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act (hereinafter referred to as the Act), the Korfa (under-raiyati) tenancy became upgraded to a raiyati tenancy on and from 14.4.56 simply because by the general Notification under section 3 of the Act the rent-receiving interests stood acquired with effect from 14.4.56 and (ii) whether, in case of upgrading of under-raiyati to a raiyati in the above circumstance, pre-emption under section 26F of the B. T. Act was available in the instant case.

5. Mr. Siddique Ahmed Chowdhury, learned Counsel for the appellants firstly contended that it was wrong to hold that the Korfa (under raiyati) tenancy was upgraded to a raiyati tenancy since 14. 4. 56 when by a general Notification under section 3 of the Act all rent-receiving interests were acquired by the Government. He urgued that even after acquisition of the rent-receiving interests of the raiyat under section 3 of the Act, the Korfa tenant, that is the under-raiyat who was a. tenant under the raiyat, continued to be so under the B. T. Act till Part V of the Act came into operation. The learned Counsel pointed out that in the District of Chittagong wherein lies the land in question, Part V of the Act came into operation on 1.8.63 and since that date B. T. Act stood repealed as provided in section 80 of the Act. So, it was contended that prior to 1.8.63, B. T. Act was in force in that area with all incidents of tenancies thereunder and that the under-raiyat retained the status of an under-raiyat within the meaning of section 4 of the B. T. Act till 1.8.63. The learned Counsel thereby tried to impress upon us that it is not correct to say that the rent-receiving interest of the raiyat having been acquired, the raiyat disappeared from the field and that the under-raiyat was upgraded to the status of a raiyat. In support of his contention reference was made to some provisions of the Act as well as to some Rules with particular reference to sub-section (J) of section 24 of the Act and rules 18 and 61 of the State Acquisition Rules, 1951 (herein-after called the Rules) to show that the original status of the different kinds of tenants remained unchanged till Part V of the Act came into operation. In order to appreciate the contention of the learned Counsel, sub-section (1) of section 24 of the Act. and rules 18 and 61 of the Rules are quoted below :-

Sub-section (I) of section 24 :-.

"In preparing or revising a record-of-rights under this Chapter, the Revenue-officer shall, subject to the provisions of sub-sections (2), (3) and (4), presume the rent, payable in respect of any land held by a raiyat or an under-raiyat in the area to which such record relates at the time of preparation or revision of such record, to be fair and equitable."

Rule 18 :-

"Where an order is made under section 17 for the preparation or revision of a record-of-rights, the particulars, to  be recorded shall include, either without or in addition to other particulars, some or all of the following, namely :- .

(a) the name, father's name and address of each tenant or occupant;

(b) the classes to which each such tenant or occupant belongs that is to say, whether he i.s a proprietor, tenure-holder raiyat holding at fixed rates, settled raiyat, occupancy raiyat, non-occupancy raiyat, under-raiyat with or without a right of occupancy, or a non-agricultural tenant, and if he is a tenure holder, whether he is a permanent tenure-holder or not, and whether his rent is liable to enhancement during the continuance of his tenure .... .,

Rule 61 :-

"After the final publication of the compensation-assessment-roll, the Collector shall assign a touzi number to all the lands under one Tahsil and inform the Revenue Officer accordingly. The Revenue Officer shall, thereafter, re-arrange the khatians under that touzi number by eliminating therefrom the entire chain of interests of rent-receivers and showing therein only the tenants who will come directly under the provincial Government."

6. It appears that mention of the different classes of tenants or occupants has been made in the above quoted provisions of law. It was argued that sub-section (1) of section 24 of the Act clearly indicates that on under-raiyati holding would remain in existence at the time of the preparation of the record-of-rights which would be subsequent to the Notification under section 3 of the Act. Rule 18 provides for the preparation or revision of the record-of-rights on the basis of which the compensation Assessment-roll would be prepared and published and rule 61 says that the different classes of tenancies would not cease to exist with publication of the Notification under section 3 of the Act and that entire chain of interests of rent-receivers would be eliminated only after the publication of the Compensation Assessment-roll. Thereafter a Notification would be published under sub-section (2) of section 43 declaring that the compensation assessment-roll in respect of that area had been finally published and after this publication of Notification, the whole of Part V of the Act would come into operation. The sum and substance of the contention of the learned Counsel is that raiyaji interest did not cease to exist and that under-raiyat was not upgraded before Part V came into operation. With a view to strengthen his argument the learned Counsel relied on a decision in Afran Ali Sheikh's case reported in 14 D.L.R. (Dacca)791. It is a Single Bench decision by Idris, J. of the Dacca High Court. The said case was under section 26P of the B. T. Act. In that case the question arose as to whether there was an automatic elevation of under-raiyats to the status of raiyats with effect from 14.4.56 when all rent-receiving interests vested in the Government. The learned Judge held that publication of Notification under section 3 of the Act did not eliminate the different classes of tenancies till publication of the compensation assessment-roll, i.e., till Part V of the Act came into operation. In coming to that decision Idris, J. it appears, relied on an unreported decision by Asir, J., in Civil Revision Case Nos.1129 and 1130 of 1960 of the Dacca High Court. On the authority of the decision of Idris, J. and the provisions of law referred to above, the learned Counsel submitted that pre-emption was not available in the present case to an under-raiyati even if he had occupancy right.

<u>7. On the other hand, Mr. M. A. Rouf, appearing for the respondents argued that in deciding this point, the general scheme of the Act is to be taken into consideration. The general scheme of the Act is that for the purpose of taking over all interests that are liable to be acquired under the Act, preparation of record-of-rights is to be made and after final publication of the record-of-rights, assessment of compensation of the acquirable interests is to be made and finally published. It, however, seems that an exception has been made with regard to rent-receiving interests and special provisions for acquisition of the interests of certain rent-receivers have been made in Chapter II of Part II of the Act. According to the provisions of this Chapter, rent-receiving interests can be acquired by publication of Notification under section 3 of the Act even before the general provisions of the Act are given effect to, that is, before preparation of the record-of-rights and preparation and publication of the Compensation Assessment-roll. It may also be pointed out that according to the provisions of section 3 of the Act, before introduction of the sub-section (2a) in section 3 by way of amendment, Notification under section 3 was to be published with reference to particular estates, taluks, tenures, holdings and tenancies and in respect of all rent-receivers whose properties were under the management of Court of Wards Act, 1879. Sub-section (2a) was enacted and introduced in section 3 of the Act by Ordinance No. III of 1956. This provision, namely, sub-section (2a) empowers the Government to publish Notification under section 3 in respect of rent-receivers by name or by reference to areas wherein they have interests or in such other manner as the Government might determine. It is after this amendment that general Notification dated 2nd April, 1956 were issued District-wise in regard to all rent-receiving interests which thereafter vested in the Government with effect from 14.4.56 in terms of those Notifications. So, Mr. Rouf submitted that it was futile to argue that these interests, which were the subject-matter of the general Notifications, contained even after 14th April, 1956 and that they did not vest in the Government. His contention was that in the instant case the rent-receiving interests of the raiyat legally vested in the Government which became the proprietor by virtue of acquisition of the said interests. Accordingly, from 14. 4. 56 the Government alone became entitled, under the law, to receive the rent. The previous rent-receivers became divested of the right to receive rent and consequently they disappeared from the scene. On this point reference was made to sub-section (4)(e) of section 3 which runs thus :—</u>

<u>"all tenants holding lands in such estates, taluks, tenures, holdings or tenancies directly under the rent-receiver specified in the notification under sub-section (1), shall become tenants directly under the Provincial Government and shall pay rent at the existing rate, in respect of the rent-paying lands so held by them to the Provincial Government and not to any body else."</u>

8. In support of the argument advanced by Mr. Rouf reliance was placed on a decision of a Division Bench of the Dacca High Court in the case of Mubashor Ali in 19 D.L.R. (Dacca) 271 in which it was held that after the general Notification under section 3 of the Act which came into operation on 14. 4. 56 all rent-receiving interests stood acquired by the Government and that there was automatic elevation of under-raiyats to the status of raiyats. It was pointed out by Mr. Rouf that the decision of Idris, J., and that by Asir, J., were noticed by the Division Bench in Mubasher Ali's case. It is to be noted that similar contentions, as have been pressed in the instant case by the learned Counsel for the appellants, were urged in Mubasher Ali's case too. The Division Bench, it appears, considered the provisions of the Act which were considered by Idris, J. The said Bench also considered the provisions of sub-section(2) of Section 43 and those of sections 79 and 80 of the Act and observed as follows :—

"We fail to see why the upgrading in status as urged on behalf of the petitioner cannot take place simply because Part V of the Act did not come into force at the relevant time and why the Bengal Tenancy Act can-not govern the relationship of the upgraded tenant and the Provincial Government till then."

9. The learned Judges relied, among other rases, on the case of Ramehandra Sutradhar A.I.R. 1934 Calcutta 852. In that case there were under-raiyats under the raiyats. The immediate landlord of the raiyats auction purchased the raiyati interest. It was held that after the auction-purchase of the raiyati interest by the immediate landlord the under-raiyats ceased to be under-raiyats and were automatically raised to the status of raiyats.

10. Mr. Rouf submitted that from the decision made in Mubasher Alis case it is clear that the Division Bench did not agree with the view expressed by Idris, J. in Arfan Ali Sheikh's case. In view of the said decision, Mr. Rouf tried to impress upon us that the effect of acquisition of rent-receiving interests under section 3 of the Act was the total elimination of all rent-receivers and that those who had no rent-receiving interests, remained on the land as tenants under the Government. In the instant case the immediate rent-receiver was the raiyat who, on account of acquisition of his rent-receiving interests, disappeared from the class of tenants and the under-raiyat under him became the raiyat under the Government and became legally entitled to claim pre-emption, if not otherwise barred.

11. Learned Counsel for the appellants, however, contended that there being conflicting decisions of the High Court on the above question, it is desirable that this Court should finally settle the conflict. According to him, till Part V of the Act comes into operation, the different classes of tenants under section 4 of the B. T. Act would continue in spite of acquisition of the rent-receiving interests by Notification under section 3 of the Act. In support of his contention, reference was made to sub-section(1) of section 81 of the Act. Sub-section (1) of section 81 of the Act occurs in Part V thereof and reads as follows :—

"On and from the date of coming into force of the whole of this Part in any area, there shall, within that area, be only one class of holders of agricultural land, namely, maliks, and the rights and liabilities of every such land-holder shall be regulated by the provisions of this Part."

This Sub-section (1) was substituted for the original sub-section (1) of section 81 by East Bengal Act No. VI of 1952. The original sub-section (1) read as follows :—

"(1) On and from the first day of the agricultural year immediately following the publication of a notification in the official Gazette under sub-section (2) of section 43 declaring that a Compensation Assessment-roll has been finally published, there shall, within the area to which such roll relates, be only one class of tenants of agricultural land, namely, raiyats, and the rights and liabilities of every such raiyat shall be regulated by the provisions of this Part."

12. It is evident that the word "raiyats" in the original sub-section (1) was later substituted by the word "maliks". Whatever may be nomenclature of the holder of the land under the Government, there is no dispute that the only authority which is entitled to get rent is the Government. Virtually the holder of the land paying rent to the Government is a tenant according to the definition under section 2(27) of the Act. The provision of the present sub-section (1) of section 81 merely indicates that after acquisition of rent-receiving interests those who would remain on the land would pay rent for the land to the Government and would hold the land under the Government as maliks and the different classes of tenants under section 4 of the B. T. Act would go and the B. T. Act would be repealed as a whole. Accordingly, the raiyati interest which was a rent-receiving interest in the instant case, vested in the Government by virtue of the acquisition of the said interest and the under-raiyat, in view of the sub-section (4)(e) of section 3 of the Act, became a tenant directly under the Government. This tenant under the original sub-section (1) of section 81 was designated as raiyat and under the present sub-section (1) of section 81 as "malik."

<u>13. The next contention urged by the learned Counsel for the appellants was that in the absence of any specific provision in the Act conferring the right of pre-emption to an upgraded under-raiyat as a raiyat, no right of preemption under section 26F of the B.T. Act can be available to such a raiyat under the said Act and that in claiming pre-emption in the instant case the respondents sought to take advantage of two laws, i.e., section 96 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act and section 26F of the B. T. Act. It was pointed out that the respondents firstly claimed that under the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act the status of the under-raiyat was raised to that of a raiyat after acquisition of the rent-receiving interests of the latter and accordingly secondly, they sought to obtain pre-emption of the raiyati interest under section 26F of the B. T. Act. It was, therefore, submitted that the respondents should not be allowed to take advantage of both the laws according to convenience only to suit their purpose, r.e., the upgrading of the under-raiyat to the status of a raiyat under the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act and the relief by way of pre-emption under the B. T. Act. lie accordingly urged for dismissal of the applications for pre-emption of the disputed land. This contention of the learned Counsel does not appear to be tenable inasmuch as the right which  became available to the respondents was not their own creation. The said right was created by a statute. It is all undenying fact that the raiyati interests in the present case in view of the under raiyat there under was a rent-receiving interest within the meaning of the Act. The rent-receiving interests of the raiyat, as already stated; vested in the Government. The Government became the proprietor by virtue of acquisition of the said interests. Thereafter the rent-receiving raiyat was divested of his right and consequently disappeared from the field. Naturally the under-raiyat was automatically upgraded as a raiyat under the Government, there being no intermediate interest in between. Part V of the Act not having come into operation at the time the transfers in the instant case were made and the applications for pre-emption having been filed when the B.T. Act was in force, the right to claim pre-emption could be exercised under the law in force.</u>

<u>14. Having considered the contentions of the learned Counsel with reference to the provisions of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act as well as the relevant provisions of the B, T. Act, we are inclined to hold that the view expressed in the case of Mubasher Ali that after the Notification issued under section 3 of the Act, the status of the under-raiyat became upgraded to that of raiyat, was correct and the impugned judgment of the learned Single Judge of the High Court, being based upon that view, calls for no interference.</u>

In the result, the appeals are dismissed but without any  order as to costs.

End.

M. Fazlul Karim With Nurul Islam Chowdhury ----- For the Appellant. 
Sharifuddin Chaklader ----- For the Respondent
parties:
Abdur Razzak ----- Appellant
Vs.
Rabeya Khatun ----- Respondent
full_judgment:
This appeal at the instance of the plaintiff is against the decision of the learned Subordinate Judge, reversing those passed by the learned Munsif, Second Court, Chittagong, in a suit for partition.

2. The plaintiffs case in short is that the land in suit previously belonged to one Wahed Ali who executed a deed of gift in the year 1925 A.D. in favour of his sisters sons Thanda Mia and Omra Mia defendant Nos. 2 and 5 respectively and delivery of possession of the same to them. The defendants Nos. 1 and 5 since the gift continued to remain in possession of the suit land and the said property was recorded in C.S. record of right in the name of both the defendants in 4 annas share each of the entire land being the gifted property. The remaining 8 annas share of the property was recorded in the names of his 2 daughters namely Ambia defendant No. 3), Rabya Khatun (defendant No. 1) and his wife. When defendant Nos. 1 and 5 had been in possession of the gifted property the plaintiff purchased the 4 annas of defendant No. 5, Orma Mia by a registered sale deed in the year 959 A.D. vide Ext. 1 and his name had been recorded in the S.A. khatian to the extent of his purchase. But as there was difficulty in possessing ejmali he demanded partition, but being refused he brought the suit for partition and for separate saham of his purchased share.

3. Rabya Khatun, the daughter of Wahed Ali, being defendant No. 1 contested the suit by filing a written statement, denying all the material allegations made in the plaint, contending, inter al in that the deed of gift executed in 1925 A.D. by her father in favour of the defendant No. 2 and 5 was not a gift but a will which was subsequently cancelled by her father by another deed of cancellation in the year 1930 A.D. and therefore she along with her other sister Ambia Khatun and her mother became the sole heirs of Wahed Ali after his death and the defendants 1 and 5 having lost all interest in any portion of the suit land the plaintiff acquired no interest by his purchase from Omra Mia in 1959 A.D. vide Ext. 1 and he being not a co-sharer no question of partition could arise.

4. On these pleadings the parties fought out the suit. The court of first instance on a consideration of the pleading of the parties and the evidence on record came to the view that the disputed document namely, Ext. A (1) was not a Will but a Gift which could not be cancelled subsequently after the gift took its effect and the said deed of gift having all legal force the plaintiff was entitled on purchase from Omra Mia, 4 annas share and on a further finding that the gift in the favour of defendant Nos. 1 and 5 having been followed by delivery of possession, the condition attached to the deed of gift as to the provisions of reserving life usufruct of the said property with the donor would be void and in that view of the matter the suit was decreed directing separate saham of the plaintiff on partition. On appeal the said was revered by the Subordinate Judge, on a finding that the said gift having reserved the usufruct and control of the said property with the donor it was a gift to take effect. In future and as it was not accompanied by delivery of possession the said would not operate until the death of Wahed Ali. In that view of the matter the court of appeal below came to a finding that the gift was absolutely void. The court on further finding that the plaintiff's possession, if any, was not on the strength of the gift allowed the appeal with cost. The judgment and decree of the court of first instance were set aside and plaintiff's suit was dismissed with costs. As against that the plaintiffs have preferred this appeal to this court.

5. Mr. Nurul Islam Chowdhury, the learned Advocate appearing in support of the appeal having taken me through the judgments of both the courts below and evidence on record, has urged that the court of appeal below erred in law in holding that the condition as mentioned in the deed of gift reserving usufruct to the donor of life would invalidate the gift. He has further urged that the court of appeal below on a misconstruction and misreading of the deed of gift came to an erroneous finding that it provided no scope for any possession for the plaintiff and upon a non-consideration of such evidence on record as to plaintiff's possession came to an erroneous finding that the plaintiff was not in possession on the strength of the deed of gift. The said finding having been arrived at upon a misconstruction of the title deed of the plaintiff and upon non-consideration of the material evidence on record, needs to be set aside.

6. Mr. Sharifuddin Chaklader, the learned Advocate for the respondent No. 1, has, on the other hand, urged that a gift by a Muslim is never valid if not accompanied by delivery of possession and, in support of this contention he has referred to the decision reported in 98 I.C. at page 285, A.I.R. 1926 Born at page 559 and I.L.R. Cal. at page 138.

7. In this appeal the point of law that arises from determination is simple. This is whether a gift reserving usufruct in favour of the donor for life would be a void. There is no dispute to the proposition of law that a gift by a Mohammaden, whether registered or unregistered, would not take affect as a valid gift unless accompanied by delivery of possession and that a gift which purports to postpone possession to a future date would be void. The decisions relied upon by Mr. Sharifuddin Chaklader, reiterated, that principle of law with which I am in respectful agreement.

<u>8. In the case of a transfer by way of gift it is the duty of a court to look into the deed itself in order to find out the scope of the same and the intention of the donor as spelt out in the deed itself because the essential conditions of a valid gift are that the donor must have intended a gift and an immediate gift intending to transfer the ownership of the property without consideration voluntarily and accepted by the donee being accompanied by delivery of possession of the corpus. For that purpose one has to look at the instrument creating the gift and construe the same as one finds it without changing or altering the terms of the deed by outside evidence. On a reference to the deed or gift as evidence by Ext. A (1) it is seen that the recital of the said deed in the relevant portion runs thus:"</u>

<u>"You being my daughters sons I have a great love for both of you and having satisfied with the care you have taken of me during my illness I hereby make this gift to you of the property in schedule but the said property would be kept for my maintenance till my death and after my death you will have all the right in the land gifted to you."</u>

<u>From a clear reading of the said it would be evident that by the said recital in the deed the donor only reserved a life interest as to the usufruct. The said reservation of the usufruct is not prohibited under the principle of Mohammadan law as under the Mohammadan law the corpus may be vested in one person and the usufruct vested on another person. Under the principle of Mohammadan law: When a gift is made with a condition which derogates from the completeness of the grant the condition would be void and the gift will take effect as if no conditions were attached with. Thus, a gift restraining delivery of immediate possession of the corpus would be derogatory to the completeness of the grant and the said condition would be void but reserving usufruct for the life with the donor would not be a condition derogatory to the completeness of the grant, as under the Mohammadan law as stated herein before, the corpus may rest in one person and the usufruct on another person. Under the Mohammadan law a life interest thus, can be created by means of a gift in favour of the donee in the gifted property and in same way the usufruct of the gifted property could also be kept with the donor for life and in the latter the gift will take effect subject to the condition of reserving the usufruct with the donee for life as in that case the usufruct will vest in one person and the corpus in another person. If the donor transfers a property to the donee by a deed of gift without reserving any domination over the corpus, merely the existence of a condition that the whole or a part of the usufruct would be paid to the donor or would be kept for his use during his life the said would not invalidate the transfer by gift. Similarly, if a Muslim makes a gift to one person of certain property on condition that the income of the property or a part of the income of the property gifted shall not belong to the donee but shall he used for the benefit of another person during his life time, the said gift shall also be valid.</u>

9. In the view I have taken herein before I am supported by a number of decisions and of good authorities. Sir John Wedge in delivering the judgment of the Judicial Committee of the Privy Council in the case of Mohammad Abdul Ghani Vs. Fakher Jahan Begum and others, reported in 49. Indian Appeals, at page 195 in the relevant portion of the judgment observed thus:

"The reserving of the usufruct did not by itself make the gift of the property now in question void under Muslim law .....For a valid gift under Mohammadan law three conditions are necessary, which their Lordships consider have been correctly stated thus;- (a) manifestation of the wish to give on the part of the donor; (b) the acceptance of the donee, either impliedly or expressly; and (c) the taking of possession of the subject matter Of the gift by the donee, either actually or constructively. The question is did Lutf Ullah Khan actually or constructively take possession of the property in question in this suit. That he did not, until Munni Bibi's death in 1906, take physical possession of Mouza Mundia Misir, the 4 annas 5 pies share in Gundia or the two groves, house and sir land in Jalalpur, or apply for mutation of names in his favour in respect of these particular properties, is admitted. On the execution of the deed of gift in 1884, Lutfullah Khan did obtain mutation of names in his favour of all the other Zamindari property, and from March, 7, 1884 until Munni Bibi died in 1906 he paid the Government revenue which became due in respect of the talukdari part of the property now in question. If Lutfullah Khan had received after March 7, 1884, and before Munni Bibi died in 1906, any of the rents or profits of the property now in question he would be held to have received them as a trustee for Munni although the title to the corpus of the property was in him. In their Lordships opinion Lutfullah Khan must be regarded as having been constructively in possession although not in physical possession of the corpus of the property now in question from 1884 until 1906, and the gift was valid gift".

<u>10. I am in respectful agreement with the observations as above to the effect that reservation of usufruct by the deed itself would not invalidate a gift made by a Mohammadan under the Mohammadan law and that the possession of a donee could be affected either by actual possession or by constructive possession which constructive possession could be evidenced by the mutation of the records of right in the name of the donee are in complete accord with the view I have taken herein before.</u>

11. In support of this principle reference may also be made to the decision of the Privy Council in the case of Newarish Ali Khan Vs. Ali Reza khan. In that case a similar point was involved and their Lordships of the Judicial Committee of the Privy Council held in the relevant portion of the judgment as under:- "What Muslim law does recognise and insist upon is. the distinction between the corpus of the property itself and the usufruct in the property. Over the corpus of the property the law recognises only absolute dominion heritable, and unrestricted in point of time and where a gift of the corpus seeks to impose condition inconsistent with such absolute dominion, the condition is rejected as repugnant but interest limited in point of time can be created in usufruct of the property and the dominion over the corpus takes effect subject to any such limited interest."

12. The principle thus enunciated was followed in the case of Mst. Khan Bibi Vs. Mst. Sufia Begum, reported in P.L.D. 1969 Lah. at page 388, Lad Jan Vs. Mohammad Shaft Allan, reported in I.L.R. 34 All at page 478. Following those authorities as quoted above I find that the finding of the court of appeal below to the effect that the said condition reserving the usufruct for the life time of the donee and control over said usufruct would make the gift a contingent gift purported to take effect in future and thus a void gift is wholly erroneous as in the said document (Ext. A (1) there is nothing to how that the possession or dominion over the corpus of the said property was also reserved or postponed to a future date. That the said was not the intention would be evident by the entry in the records of right of the entire gifted property of the donor in the name of the donee namely, Thanda Mia and Omra Mia in the R.S. Records. The said R.S. khatian was prepared in the year 1929 and completed in 1930 immediately after the deed of gift was executed and registered in 1925 without any objection from the donor. An entry in the khatian is not an evidence of title by itself but it is an evidence of possession and a strong presumptive evidence of title also (Ref: 30 D.L.R. (S.C.) 81 and following the principle as enunciated by the Privy Council in the case referred to earlier the donee would be considered to be in constructive possession of the said gifted property and would be construed that the said gift was in fact followed by possession as evidenced by the entry in the C.S. khatian in the names of the donee. There is evidence on record that the donor died long before and the defendants donee had been in possession of the suit land since after the death of Wahed Ali.

The court of appeal below had not considered this legal aspect of this matter.

13. The court of appeal below however took notice of the fact that the name of the plaintiffs vendor was recorded in the R.S. khatian and having taking notice of the said the learned court took the view that through the said was recorded as such the said entry was absolutely void and without basis as the gift itself was void ab initio. If the deed of gift was a valid one, the said entry perhaps could have been taken into consideration by the court of appeal below, in proving prima facie the plaintiffs vendors possession of the gifted suit land, to the extent of his 4 annas share.

<u>14. The construction of a title document is a question of law. Findings of fact arrived at by misconstruction of a document are liable to be set aside in second appeal but only when the said document was a document of title and was the foundation of a suit, being in the nature of a contract or a document of title and hence the construction of a kabuliyat or the construction of an entry in a khatian used as a document of title or the construction of a deed, purporting to be a deed of gift would amount to a question of law (Refer 120 I.C. at page 557). In the instant case the court of appeal below arrived at the finding of fact to the effect that the gift was not a void gift as it purported to take effect in future by reserving the usufruct was arrived at on a misreading and misconstruction of the document of gift and upon a wrong view of the law, causing an error of law affecting the merits of the case and thus it needs to be set aside. The finding of the court of appeal below as to possession was also arrived at only on a consideration of the fact that as the gift was void there could not be any question of possession on the strength of the gift which was again erroneous as it was arrived at without taking into consideration the presumption of correctness attached to an entry in the R.S. khatian and without taking into consideration the evidence as to the possession of the plaintiff evidenced by the entry in the R.S. khatian and the evidence on record and without taking into consideration the legal position that even a possession under a document of title which subsequently proved to be a void document, would create a title in favour of the possessor if possessed for a period of more than 12 years, by adverse possession. On the premises above I find enough substance in this appeal and the said need to be allowed.</u>

In the result, this appeal is allowed. The judgment and decree of the court of appeal below are set aside and those of the trial court is restored. But in the facts and circumstances of the case there will be no order as to costs before this court.

End.
