full_judgment:
The plaintiff appellant instituted a suit for redemption of the suit property mortgaged on 22-4-1924 during his minority by his sister's husband Prankrishna, as his guardian, to Abdur Rashid the predecessor of defendants 1 to 8. As the loan together with interest was satisfied out of the usufruct of the land enjoyed by defendants Nos. 1 to 8 the plaintiff demanded back the land, but was refused.

2. Defendants asserted that the lands were acute n purchased by defendant No. 9 in a rent suit with his money and for his own benefit and, while he was in possession defendant No. 8 purchased the same from him.

3. The trial court dismissed the suit and held that the plaintiff knew about the rent sale for a long time and he was estoppel by his own conduct from claiming redemption of the suit property. It was considered that as the rent suit related to arrear rent of a period prior to the mortgage the mortgagee was not responsible for the payment of that arrear rent, and the subsequent acquisition of the property by the heirs of mortgagee could not be held to be for the benefit of the mortgagor.

4. The lower appellate court affirmed the decree of the trial court. It considered that the sale certificate dated 15-12-25, Ext. B, showed that the balding relating to the Suit land was in arrear for rent for which the landlord brought Rent Suit No. 513 of 1924; that the rent suit must have been for arrear of rent due prior to April; 1924 that in the deed of the mortgage mortgagee did not undertake any obligation to pay arrear rents ; that there was no evince that defendant No. 9 was a benamdars of defendants 1 to 8; shat the name of the suction purchaser Hamid Ali Defendant No. 9, was recorded in the R.S. Khatian which prima facie proved his possession in the Suit land; that the R. S. Khatian, Ext. D and D(1) were prepared and finally published to the knowledge of the plaintiff or his guardian; that the plaintiff stated in the plaint that he was demanding the Suit land for the last 35 years, but in the court he reduced the period from 35 years to 16/17 years; that the defendants were claiming to be in possession in a different right other than one under the mortgage at least for 16/17 years; that they acquired an Indefeasible right against the plaintiff and the plaintiff's suit was time barred.

5. Mr. M.A. Muttalib, the learned Advocate for the appellant, has submitted that the mortgagee Abdur Rashid, in the absence of any contract to the contrary, having defaulted to pay the arrear rent accruing due in respect of the suit land during his possession and in default of such payment of arrear rent the suit land having been sold and the same having been purchased by his cousin defendant No. 9, and subsequently by his wife, defendant No. 8, the benefit accrued thereby will ensure to the mortgagor; that the admitted fact being that the relationship between the plaintiff and Abdur Rashid being that of mortgagor and mortgagee and the suit being governed by Article 148 of the Limitation Act, the mortgage and subsequent transfer having taken place within 60 years from the date of the mortgage the equity of redemption is available to the plaintiff-appellant; and that in view of the evidence and circumstances the mortgagee Abdur Rashid taking advantage of his fiduciary position all, wed the suit land to be sold for arrears of rent and same having been purchased in the names of his cousin and wife subsequently, the subsequent transferees are constructive trustee of the mortgagor and the plaintiff appellant is entitled to redeem the suit land.

6. Mr. Kazi Ebadul Huq, the learned Advocate for the respondent, has submitted that the lower appellate court found no evidence that defendant No. 9 was the benamdar of defendants 1 to 8 and that as the property, purchased by defendant No. 9 was recorded in his own name in R.S. khatian and it was long after transferred to defendant No. 8 that transfer did not or could not revive the plaintiff's right of redemption which had totally been extinguished by the rent sale. He has further contended that the mortgagee was not under any obligation to pay arrear rent for which the land could be sold in rent sale.

7. The deed of mortgage was executed on 29-4-24. Rent suit No. 513 of 1924 was disposed of on 22-12-24. The lower appellate court rightly held that the rent suit must have been for arrear of rent due prior to April, 1924. The deed of mortgage does not show that the mortgagee undertook the obligation to pay arrear rent.

8. Clause (c) of section 76 of the Transfer of Property Act, 1882, provides that a mortgagee will be under obligation in the absence of a contract to the contrary, to pay the Government revenue, all other charges of a public nature and all rent accruing due in respect of the mortgaged property during such possession and any arrear of rent in default of payment of which the property may be summarily sold.

9. In the present case the property was not summarily sold and as the rent was for a period prior to the mortgagee entered into the possession of the mortgaged property he was not under any obligation to pay arrear rent for which the land was not summarily sold, but sold in execution of a rent suit. In Jagat Mohan Nath Sahi Deo Vs. Sheonarsin Marwari and others, AIR 1938 Patna 197. It was held that the word 'summarily' occurring in the latter portion of section 76(c) of the Transfer of Property Act implied that the proceedings for realisation of rent by sale of the property were of a summary nature, for instance, as in the case of a certificate proceeding under the Public Demand Recovery Act. This view was later followed in Jay Prasad Choubey Vs. Mt. Jasoda and others, AIR 1958 Patna 649.

<u>10. In this case the mortgagor defaulted to pay the arrear rent and the mortgagee was not under any obligation either in law or in contract to pay the arrear rent for which the land was sold out in the execution of a rent decree and the right of redemption of the mortgagor was extinguished. In Gauri Shankar Sahu Vs. Sheotshal, AIR 1936 Patna 434, it was held that the rent sale extinguished the mortgagor's equity of redemption when it was not proved to be fraudulent. The same view was followed in Fekua Mahto Vs. Babu Lal Sahu, AIR Patna 382. In the present case the plaintiff's equity of redemption was extinguished for his own default to pay arrear rent and there is no evidence to show that the mortgaged property was collusively or fraudulently sold out for any default of the mortgagee.</u>

11. The next question that calls for determination in this case is whether defendants No. 1 to 8 can be held as constructive trustees under section 90 of the Trusts Act, 1882. Mr. Muttaleb has referred to the case of Jamila Khatun Choudhury Vs. Mahmud Khatun Choudhury, AIR 1918 Cal. 192. In that case the defendant, a mortgagee in possession of a share in a taluk, had undertaken to pay the Government revenue, but

made default in payment of the revenue, and the taluk was sold for arrears of revenues and was purchased by one Abdul Bari, who shortly afterwards sold it to the defendant, and the plaintiff, a purchaser from the mortgagor, sued to recover possession of the taluk from the defendant on Redemption, it was held that the sale for arrears of revenues and the subsequent sales to the defendant were collusive transactions engineered by the defendant for the purpose of obtaining possession of the taluk as owner this case has got no relevance in the case before me.

<u>12. In the present case the mortgagee or his heirs had not undertaken any obligation to pay arrear rent for which the land was sold in a rent sale and there was no evidence to show that the suit property was sold in the execution of a rent decree because of any default or any collusion of the mortgagee or their heirs Defendant No. 9 auction purchased the suit land on 15-12-25. His name was recorded in R.S. Khatian and, much later, on 14th Chaitra, 1290 M.E. corresponding to 2-4-1929 AD defendant No. 8 purchased the suit land from defendant No. 9. Mr. Ebadul Huq has referred to the case of Isar Nonia Vs. Karinam Panday, AIR 1958 Patna 353 and that of Jay Prosad Choubay vs. Mt Jasoda reported in the same, volume of the report at page 649 in support of his contention that section 90 of Trusts Act could only apply where the mortgagee in possession gained some advantage by availing himself of his position. Defendant No. 8 purchased the suit property from defendant No. 9 long after the equity of redemption in the mortgaged property was extinguished and hence, she or other heirs of Abdur Rashid could not be liable to hold the property for the benefit of mortgagor just because the subsequent transfer took place within the time prescribed for a suit of redemption of a mortgage. Had the mortgaged property been purchased by defendant No. 8 or had defendant No. 9 purchased the property in the benami of the heirs of Abdur Rashid or in collusion with them, then by operation of section 90 of the Trusts Act defendant Nos. 1 to 8 could be held responsible for holding the property for the benefit of the mortgagor and a fiduciary relationship between the mortgagor and mortgagee would have subsisted and the suit would have been within time under Article 148 of the Limitation Act. But as the facts are otherwise I must hold that the plaintiff's right of redemption was extinguished long ago when the mortgaged property was sold in execution of a rent decree.</u>

In view of the above, the appeal is dismissed with costs. Leave prayed for under clause 15 of the Letters Patent is refused.

End.

case_source: in the matter of an application under Section 115 of the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908  for setting aside the order dt. 6-1-75 and 15.1.75 of the Munsif, 2nd Court Satkhira, Khulna passed in Misc. case No. 235/73, 244/73.
full_judgment:
These two Rules are directed against two orders of the learned Munsif in two different proceeding under section 143A of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act. The learned Munsif rejected the application for addition of parties in each of the proceedings.

2. One Ruhul Amin Sardar filed an application under section 143 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act for correction of record of right in respect of the properties mentioned in the schedule to the application. It is Khatian No. 2184 Plot No. 2594 measuring 11.97 acres. This land has been recorded in S.A. Khatian No. 1 in the name of the Deputy Commissioner. In this application Bangladesh has been impleaded as opposite party No. 1 and Sailuddin Sardar, Golam Rabbani and Ramjan Ali, the three brothers of Ruhul Amin have been impleaded as opposite parties 2 to 4 (preform) The allegations made in the petition are that the land in question originally belonged to Roy Harendra Nath and others in khas under the anent-merit and the petitioner Ruhul Amin and his three other brothers took settlement of Plot No. 2594 at a rental of Rs 90-8 annas in 1332 B S. and continued to possess the same along with other lands. The said lands have been wrongly recorded in the impugned current khatian.

Prayers have been made in the following terms:

(ক) ছায়েলের আরজির বর্ণনামতে তফসিল বর্ণিত ১১০৯৭ শতাংশ জমিতে ছায়েলের আরজির বর্ণিত রায়তি জমার স্বত্য প্রকাশ হয়।

(খ) দাবীকৃত জমি সম্পর্কে Record ছায়েলের বিরুদ্ধে বাধ্যকর না থাকা প্রকাশ হয়।

(গ) দাবীকৃত জমি সম্পর্কে Co (Rev.) সাহেবের Report দৃষ্টে ছায়েলেরকে ডিগ্রি দিতে মর্জি হয়।

(ঘ) বর্তমান মকদ্দমার যাবতীয় খরচ ছায়েলখান।

(ঙ) যুক্তি মতে ছায়েল আর যে কোন প্রতিকার চান তাহাও পান।

On this application Miscellaneous case No 235 of 1973 (143A) was started.

3. Sailuddin Sardar Golam Rabbani and Ramjan Ali as petitioners filed a similar petition under section 143A of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act on the allegations inter alia that they have tenancy in respect of 12.71 acres of land which has been recorded in S.A. Khatian No. 1 in the name of Deputy Commissioner. Reliefs have been prayed in the same terms as in the case of Ruhul Amin Sardar. In this case Bangladesh has been impeladed as opposite party No. 1 and Ruhul Amin has been impleaded as opposite party No. 2 (proforma) and on this application Miscellaneous case No. 244 of 1973 (143) was started.

4. The Bangladesh appeared in both the cases and filed written objection. Thereafter the order sheets indicates various other developments of the proceedings. Upon application of the instant petitioners for addition of parties under Order 1 rule 10 of the Code of Civil Procedure, the learned Munsif heard the parties and rejected the application in both the cases. According to the learned Munsif, the application was not maintainable and Tenancy Act does not provide for addition of opposite parties. Against the aforesaid order of the learned Munsif the instant Rules were obtained. It appears that an order has been recorded for analogous bearing of, the two Rules. Accordingly, both the Rules are taken up together for bearing.

5. Mr. A.F.M. Shahid, the learned Advocate appearing in support of the Rules has contended that the learned Munsif acted illegally and with material irregularity in the exercise of jurisdiction in rejecting the prayer for addition of parties. According to the learned Advocate, Order 1 rule 10 of the Code of Civil Procedure was applicable and the learned Munsif acted illegally in the exercise of jurisdiction in holding that the petition was not maintainable. Mr. Shahid submits that section 143A contemplated a civil proceeding and as such section 141 of the Code of Civil Procedure applies. Since no provision has been specifically made in section 143A for addition of opposite parties, according to Mr. Shahid, Order 1 rule 10 of the Code of Civil Procedure is the appropriate provision enabling the applicants to seek the remedy prayed for.

6. Mr. M.B. Rahman, the learned Advocate appearing for the opposite parties in both the Rules, contends that section 141 of the Code of Civil Procedure and Order I rule 10 have no application in the special provisions for correction of record of right under section 143A of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act. According to Mr. Rahman the applications for addition of parties are misconceived and not maintainable. It is, therefore, necessary to consider what section 143A stands for. It runs as follows:

"(1) Any person aggrieved by an entry or omission of entry in the record-of-rights prepared or revised and finally published under Chapter IV may, notwithstanding anything contained elsewhere in this Act, file an application along with necessary requisites, for the purpose of correcting mistakes in such record of rights in the Civil Court which would have jurisdiction to entertain a suit for possession of the land to which such entry relates or in respect of which such omission was made.

(2) An application filed under sub-section (1) shall be deemed to be a plaint and order passed thereon shall have the force of a decree under the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908.

(3) An application filed under sub-section (1) shall contain full particulars of persons likely to be affected by an order on such application and shall also contain the full particulars of the holding to which the entry relates or in respect of which the omission complained of was made.

(4) The Court shall, for the purpose of disposal of application filed under sub-section (1), follow the following procedure, namely :

(a) the Court shall reuse notice to be served on the persons named in the application in the manner as provided in the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908.

(b) the Court shall, within seven days of the filing of an application under sub-section (I), send a copy thereof by registered post at the applicant's cost to the Revenue Officer concerned for holding a local inquiry, in presence of the parties concerned, on the subject-matter of the application and the Revenue Officer shall within fifteen days of the receipt of the copy, hold inquiry and submit the report to the Court.

(c) the Court may allow such reasonable time as it may think fit to file objection to the inquiry report referred to in clause

(b) and, if no appearance is made by the opposite party within the time mentioned in notice, and, if no objection is filed to the inquiry report within the time so allowed, the court may proceed ex-parte with disposal of the application after taking into consideration the said report and other material evidence on record, and

(d) where the report referred to in clause (b) is not submitted, or where objection referred to in clause (c) is filed, the Court shall fix a date for hearing and on that date after hearing the parties and taking into consideration the report, if any, and other evidence which may be adduced by the parties in this behalf, shall pass such order as it may think just and proper.

(5) Any person whose interest has been affected by reason of an entry or omission in the record-of-rights, referred to in sub-section (1), may within fourteen days of the filing of an application under sub-section (1), appear to be added as co-applicant.

(6) The Revenue Officer shall, for the purpose of an inquiry under sub-section (4), have the same power as vested in a civil court under the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, including the power of:-

(a) enforcing attendance of any person, and examining him on oath, and

(b) compelling the production of any document.

(7) Within thirty days from the date of an order under sub-section (4), an appeal from that order shall lie to the District Judge who may, either himself bear the appeal or transfer it to any other court subordinate to him but not below the rank of a Subordinate Judge for hearing.

(8) Decision under sub-section (4), if no appeal is preferred from it, or under sub-section (7), shall be final and conclusive.

(9) Where the Court passes an order under sub-section (4) or sub section (7) revising the 	entries or rectifying the omission complained of under sub-section (1), it shall notify the same to the Collector and the Collector shall correct the record of rights accordingly.

(10) Any person interested may produce a certified copy of the orders referred to in sub-section (4) or sub-section (7) to the Revenue Officer and the Revenue Officer shall make such alterations in the record of rights as may be necessary to give effect to such orders.

(11) The record of rights corrected under sub-section (9) or subsection (10) shall be deemed to have been prepared and finally published under chapter IV of this Act.

(12) An application under subsection (1) or memorandum of an appeal under sub-section 	(7) shall, notwithstanding anything contained in the Court Fees Act, 1870, bear a fixed court fee of rupee one.

(13) For the purpose of an application, appeal, review, revision and consequence of 	nonappearance, relevant provisions of the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, shall mutatis mutandis apply".

7. Mr. Shahid has referred to sub-section (21 which according to him makes the proceeding a suit since the application is to "be deemed to be a plaint and the order passed thereon shall have the force of a decree under the Code of Civil Procedure". Accordingly, he contends that section 143A contemplates a decree and the proceeding is to be deemed to be a suit. That being so, his further contention is that section 141 and Order / rule 10 of the Code of Civil Procedure have application in proceeding under section 143A, Section 141 of the Code of Civil Procedure runs as follows :

"The procedure provided in this Code in regard to suits shall be followed, as far as it can be made applicable, in all proceedings in any court of civil jurisdiction".

Rule, 10, Order I reads as follows:-

"Where a suit has been instituted in the name of the wrong person as plaintiff or where it is doubtful whether it has been instituted in the name of the right plaintiff, the Court may at any stage of the suit, if satisfied that the suit has been instituted through a bonafide mistake, and that it is necessary for the determination of the real matter in dispute so to do, order any other person to be substituted or added as plaintiff upon such terms as the court thinks just.

(2) The Court may at any stage of the proceedings, either upon or without the application of either party, and on such terms as may appear to the Court to be just, order that the name of any party improperly joined, whether as plaintiff or defendant, be struck out and that the name of any person who ought to have been joined, whether as plaintiff or defendant or whose presence before the Court may be necessary in order to enable the Court effectually and completely to ad-judicator upon and settle all the questions involved in the suit be added.

(3) No person shall be added as a plaintiff suing without a next friend or as the next friend of a plaintiff under any disability without his consent.

(4) Where a defendant is added, the plaint shall unless the court otherwise directs, be amended in such manner as may be, necessary, and amended copies of the summons and of the plaint shall be served on the new defendant and, if the court thinks fit, on the original defendant.

(5) Subject to the provisions of the Indian Limitation Act, 1877, section 22, the proceedings as against any person added as defendant shall be deemed to have been only on the service of the summons".

<u>8. Assuming, as Mr. Shahid contends, that in the instant proceeding Order 1 rule 10 shall apply, evidently, sub-rule (1) has no manner of application. In terms of sub-rule (2) the court jurisdiction to add a party whose presence before the Court may be necessary in order to enable the Court effectually and completely to adjudicate upon and settle all questions involved in the suit. In the background of the above provision, can it be said that section 143A contemplates a proceeding of such nature or is a proceeding which is deemed to be a suit where all questions involved in the suit or proceeding may be effectually and completely adjudicated upon ? Obviously section 143A contemplates a summary power to be exercised by the Civil Court within the prescribed limits. The purpose of introducing this special provision is "correcting mistakes". The special provisions made in section 143A are intended for a definite and limited purpose. The legislative intent is clearly available from the language used in sub-section (I) of section 143A. Sub-section (2) contains the statutory fiction for extending the meaning of the terms "application" and "order" which they do not in reality imply but the statute requires them to be as such. Sub-section (2) does not enlarge the scope, object and purpose of sub-section (1). The procedure prescribed in the subsequent sub-sections is intended for the purpose of carrying out the purpose and object of "correcting mistakes". Sub-section (13) indicates that relevant provisions of the Code of Civil Procedure shall mutatis mutandis apply for the purpose of an application, appeal, review, revision and consequence of non-appearance. It is difficult to conceive that the Code of Civil Procedure has been made applicable in its terms and as a whole. Therefore, the contention of Mr. Shahid that section 143A. not bring exhaustive and in the absence of provision for addition of opposite parties there in, the provisions of Order 1 rule 10 of the Code of Civil Procedure shall apply on the strength of section 141 of the Code does not appear to stand on a sound footing within the meaning and scope of, section 143A of the State Acquit sit ion and Tenancy Act. Thus, the application under Order 1, rule 10 C.P.C. does not appeal to be maintainable. The learned Munsif in this behalf appears to have rightly rejected the petition for addition of parties.</u>

<u>9. Mr. Shahid has next contended that the applicants are some of the members of the public and they came to protect a public right in the nature of easement in respect of the suit land. The scope of enquiry under section 143A of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act relates to correcting mistakes in respect of an entry or omission of entry in the record-of-rights prepared or revised and finally published under Chapter IV of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act. Therefore, the right of the applicants, if any, cannot be adjudicated in the instant proceeding. The applicants not being parties can never be affected by an order passed in the proceeding. According to Mr. Shahid the members of the public have been enjoying a right recognised by the Government. It does not appear that the Government has denied the right of the public The alleged right of easement is sought to be confirmed by the applicants In the instant proceeding but this question is absolutely beyond the scope of investigation under section 143A.</u>

10. Mr. Shahid has finally contended that the addition of parties is necessary for avoiding multiplicity of proceedings. This is being the question. Since section 143A does not permit adjudication of the alleged right of easement, there is no question of avoiding multiplicity of proceedings.

<u>11. It must, however, be pointed out that section 143A is not intended to be misused in the way it has been sought to be done in the instant applications. In paragraph 5 of the respective petition, certain prayers have been made in declaratory form with regard to title of the petitioner or petitioners. It does not appear that section 143A contemplates such a relief as prayed for in the two cases. It further appears that the trial court proceeded to deal with the two cases as if these are suits for title. It appears that an Advocate Commissioner was appointed and he submitted certain report. Could the question, be decided within the scope of section 143A. The reply evidently is in the negative. Caution should be taken by the Court below not to encourage adjudication of disputed title and possession under the garb of a proceeding under section 143A. A complete end effectual adjudication with regard to title and possession must be left open for properly constituted suit. A proceeding under section 143A of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act should not be allowed to transcend its limited scope expressly provided by statute itself. The legislative intent and purpose should not be overlooked. It is not necessary for me to express my views on the applications under section 143A, since they have to be disposed of by the trial court according to law. The observation made by me are meant for guidance of the learned Muncie who is however free to dispose of the matters on consideration of necessary questions and according to law.</u>

<u>For the reasons stated above there is no ground for interference under section 115 of the Code of Civil Procedure.</u>

The result, therefore, is that the Rules are discharged without any order as to costs.

End.

caseno: Appeal from Appellate Decree No. 380 of 1965.
lawyer:
A.T. M. Kamrul Islam ------- For Appellant.
B.N. Chowdhury ------- For Respondent.
parties:
Osman Ali Talukder ------- Appellant.
Vs.
Sukumar Majumder  ------- Respondent.
full_judgment:
This appeal, by defendant No.1; is directed against the decision of the Subordinate Judge, Bogra, in Title Appeal No. 36 of 1963 reversing that of the Munsif, 3rd Court, Bogra in Title Suit No. 183 of 1961.

2. The plaintiff respondents filed a suit for declaration of title and recovery of khas possession in the suit land by evicting the defendants. The plaintiffs' case, in short is that the suit land was recorded in C.S. Khatian No. 160 of mouza Borai and the plaintiffs, by an amicable partition amongst themselves and pro-defendants, were possessing the same; that during the last c.s. operation Jasmat Sardar  was possessing the suit land as a barga darunder Girish Chandra and others, the plaintiffs predecessors, on delivering half of the produce of the land from year to year; and that during Jasmat Sardar's life time the land was taken and given borga bandabosta to others. As Jasmat was possessing the land as borgadar his name was wrongly recorded in the C.S. record as tenant paying borga rent though he was never recognized as a tenant by the plaintiffs' predecessors. Acting on rumors, that lands recorded in the names of bargadars paying half the produce as rent, had vested in the bargadar's ; defendants, 1, 2, and 3, got fraudulent kabala from Jasmat's daughters, defendants 4 and 5 and forcibly dispossessed the plaintiff's from the suit land in Baishak, 1364 B.S. and hence the suit.

3. Defendant 1 contested the suit by filing a written statement where he stated, inter alia, that Jasmat Sardar was a recorded occupancy raiyat and defendants 3, 4 and 5 were the heirs of Jasmat Sardar  and he derived good title by purchase from them. His further case is that the landlords were present at the time of the preparation of the settlement records, that neither Jasmat nor his heirs over gave up possession of the land and the plaintiff never possessed the land by their borgadars, that during the revisional settlement operation the suit land had been recorded in the names of defendants 3,4 and 5 and they possessed the same on payment of money rent and that the suit was barred by limitation.

4. The learned Munsif dismissed the suit after finding that the C.S. record (Ext. 2) indicated that Jasmat Sardar has acquired a tenancy right in the suit land and that there was no evidence that during his life the land was taken back from him and given to some other persons as borga by the plaintiffs predecessors, that the plaintiffs had no possession within 12 years before the date of the institution of the suit.

5. The learned Subordinate Judge reversed the decision of the trial Court after finding that the C.S. recorded was not correctly recorded, and Jasmat was a borgadar and he was in possession till his death, 6/7 years back, and hence the suit was within 12 years of possession of the last recorded borgadar, and the transferee-defendants had no saleable interest in the suit land and as such the defendants were liable to be evicted.

6. Mr. A.T.M. Kamrul Islam, the learned Advocate appearing for the appellant, has submitted that the learned Subordinate Judge misinterpreted the decision in the case of Kumir Mondal Vs. Pramatha Nath Chowdhury (1962) in 14 DL:R 801 in as much as the principle laid down in the said case is that a borgadar recorded in the C.S. Khatian as tenant before the introduction of the proviso to clause (17) of section 3 of the Bengal Tenancy Act, 1885 by the amending Act of 1928 can plead tenancy right even after the introduction of the proviso. He has further submitted that the presumption of correctness of the entry in the C.S. Khatian cannot be held to have been rebutted merely because there is no evidence to show the basis of the entry. Mr. Islam, in support of his contention, has relied on Alimuddin Munshi Vs. Mainuddin Talukdar (1962) 14 DLR 725.

7. Mr. B.N. Chowdhury, the learned Advocate for the respondent has submitted that the presumption of the correctness of the record of right has been lost by passage of time, and that where it is on record that Jasmat Sardar  gave kabuliyat to the landlords as a borgadar before the preparation of the C.S. record and there is no other evidence that there had been any other agreement creating a tenancy in favor of Jasmat Sardar  the C.S. record must be held to have been wrongly prepared.

8. The case of Kumir Mondal and ors Vs. Pramatha Nath Chowdhury and ors (1962) 14 DLR 801 went up to the Pakistan Supreme Court and the decisionis reported in 17 DLR (SC) at 392. After referring to the history of the legislation of the Bengal Tenancy(Amendment) Act, 1928 and a number of decisions of the Calcutta High Court as well as of the Dacca High Court the Pakistan Supreme Court held:

"that this proviso does not debar a person against whom a suit is now filed for recovery of a share of the crop as a bargadar, to set up the defense that he is not a bargadar but a tenant. In such a suit the presumption of correctness of the record of rights may also be invoked in aid as a circumstances supporting the defense but this will certainly not be a conclusive presumption. The presumption that attaches to a record of right under section 103 -B of the Bengal Tenancy Act is only this that the entry in the record of right represents the correct stale of affairs on the elate that it was prepared. Whether that state of affairs is continued even afterwards is not a presumption which arises under this section; but under section 114 of the Evidence Act, and its probative value diminishes progressively with the lapse of time. The older the record the less is its presumptive value. This is a matter therefore, of proof and it merely has the effect of shifting the onus upon the other side. It is certainly not a conclusive proof".

9. The C.S. Khatian recorded Jasmat Sardar  as a borgadar as well as a rayotisthitiban under Girish Chandra Majumdar and others at a rental of half of the produces inclusive of cess. The learned Subordinate Judge has found that Jasmat took borga settlement by a kabuliyat (Ext. 1) for a term of 7 years from 1321 B.S. and the preparatory works of C.S. operation started in the locality after 1327 B.S. and the record of rights was finally published in 1925 corresponding to 1332 B.S. He has observed that "it is quite likely that the settlement operation actually began at a stage when the term of the barga lease did not expire. It is, therefore, clear borga has been mentioned in the khatian. In the absence of any other stipulation between the parties Jasmat would be deemed to have continued in possession as a borgadar on the principle of holding over as enunciated in section 116 of the T.P. Act and as enunciated in principle in section 51 B.T. Act".

10. Mr. B.N. Chowdhury has empathetically urged that a finding as to the rebuttal of a statutory presumption is a finding of a fact and cannot be challenged in second appeal. In support of his contention he has referred 10 Aminuddin Biswas Vs. Miajan Biswas, (1960) 12 DLR 103, CharuBalaRudra Vs. Narayan Prosad Sen(1962) 14 DLR 159 and Dabiruddin Molla Vs. Prem Dasi(1967) 19 DLR 371.

<u>11. A finding as to a rebuttal of a statutory presumption is no doubt a finding of fact and it should not ordinarily be disturbed in second appeal. In the present case, however, the finding as to the rebuttal of the presumption of the C,S. record is based on a material mistaken assumption that Jasrnat Sardar would be deemed to have continued in possession as a bargadar on the principle of holding over as enunciated in Section 116 of the Transfer of Property Act and as enunciated in principle under section 51 of the Bengal Tenancy Act. Mr. B.N. Chowdhury has conceded that neither section 166 of the Transfer of Property Act nor section 51 of the Bengal Tenancy Act is applicable to a bargadar. He has, however, contended that the principle of holding over has been applied by way of analogy. The right of holding over, unless conferred by a statute, cannot be implied or inferred by analogy. Long five years after the terms of the borga kabuliyat expired, the C.S. Khatian was published on 6-9-25. The assumption of the Court of appeal below that the settlement operation actually began at the stage when the terms of the borga lease did not expire is based on no evidence.</u>

12. Again the learned Subordinate Judge seems to have proceeded on the view that the term 'borgadar' itself is a negation of the right of tenancy. I may refer to the following observation made by D.C. Bhattacharya, J. In Soda Mia Vs. MomrajBhuiya(1974) 26 DLR 245.

"It has not been defined anywhere what a 'bargadar is? We find in Wilson's Glossaries, that the term 'barga' has been defined as an agreement by which the cultivator engages to pay the landlord half of the produce, the latter providing half of the seed and paying the whole of the rent, from the definition of 'tenant' as given in section 3, . clause (17) of the Bengal Tenancy Act, as it stood before the amendment of 1929, we find that a tenant means a person who holds land under another person, and is, or but for a special contract would be liable to pay rent for that land to that person, and in clause (13) of the same section 'rent' has been defined as whatever is lawfully payable or deliverable in money or kind by a tenant to his landlord on account of the use or occupation of the land held by the tenant, So we find that there is nothing in clause (13), or clause (17) of section 3 which militates against a bargadar being a tenant, Rent, according to clause (13) of section 3 as we have seen may be in money or in kind and it need not be a fixed amount, there is nothing in law to prevent a landlord from accepting a variable or fluctuating quantity of the produce of land as rent, Therefore, according to the provisions of law, as were in force before 1929, there was nothing inherently inconsistent between the characters of a bargadarand a tenant, "

13, In 1929 by an amendment of the Bengal Tenancy Act, the Legislature sought to bring about a certain change with regard to presumption about the status of a person who used to cultivate lands under barga system, by adding the following provision to the definition of 'tenant' to section 3(17) of B,T. Act.

"Provided that a person who, under the system generally known as adhi, bargaor bhag cultivates the land of the produce to that person, is not a tenant, unless

(i) Such person has been expressly admitted to be a tenant by his landlord in any documents executed by him or executed in his favor and accepted by him, or

(ii) he has been or is held by a Civil Court to be a tenant."

14. Hamoodur Rahman, J. as he was then, delivering the judgment in the case of Promotha Nath Chowdhury and others Vs, Kumir Mondal and others observed as follows:

"It seems to us that the only change that the Legislature has labored to bring about is 10 lay down that; only in the first instance there will be a presumption 'that" a person holding under a system of adhi, barga or bhogis not a tenant, but this presumption will be rebutted only if it is established that he has been admitted by the landlord to be a tenant or is declared in a previous suit to be a tenant or if he can in a suit where this question is put in issue establish status as such tenant, In effect it seems that the Legislature has labored in in vain or worse avoided its responsibility and really thrown the burden upon the Court to resolve this question, for the net result appears, in substance, to leave the question where it was, apart from shifting the burden of proof on the tenant. To this extent possibly there has been a departure from the old principle."

Thus even after the amendment a bargadar can raise a contention in any suit that he is a tenant.

15. In Alimuddin Munshi Vs. Mainuddin Talukdar (1962) 14 DLR 725 it has been held:

“Merely because there is no evidence to show the basis of the entries in the 'record-or-rights, the presumption is not rebutted in view of the provision of section l03(B) of the Bengal Tenancy Act, and also the procedure as laid down in the several sections of the Bengal Tenancy Act followed by the officer concerned while preparing the final records-of-rights. There mutbe further evidence to show that the entries are incorrect. The absence of evidence for the basis of the entries may be a circumstance which along with other evidence may be to show that the presumption has been rebutted. "

The learned Subordinate Judge has not adverted to this case, though relied on by the learned Munsif. For want of proper approach to the material question in the matter and non-appreciation of the evidence on the records particularly the evidence of the D.Ws. he has arrived at an erroneous decision. In the present case, apart from merely asserting that the C.S. Khatian was 'Wrongly recorded, the plaintiff did not adduce any other evidence in support of his contention. There was no averment that Jasmat continued to possess the land on the expiry of the terms of the kabuliyat on the same terms and conditions. In fact there is no mention of a borga kabuliyat in the plaint. On the other hand, defendant No.1, apart from relying on the C.S. record, produced Defendant 2, the Tahsildar of the landlords, who stated that at the time of C.S. operation he himself and another amin looked after the preparation of the C.S. record and the suit land belonged to Jasmat on payment of paddy lent to the landlords. This witness admitted the kabuliyat to be written in his hand. He further stated in cross-examination that he held some lands of the landlords as bargadar but his name was recorded as mere borgadar possessor with an entry in the rent column.

16. I, therefore, hold that the presumption of correctness of the C.S. record has not been rebutted in this case. The next question is whether the presumptive value of the C.S. record, under section 114 of the Evidence Act, has been destroyed in this case or whether its presumptive value is still available to defendant 1.

The suit is of 1961. Instead of remanding the case I think I should dispose of this appeal under section 103 of the Code of Civil Procedure.

17. D.W. 1 Osman Ali, stated that Jasmat possessed the land as tenant and after his death his heirs defendants 3,4 and 5 got the suit land ; that he purchased the interest of defendants 3, 4 and 5 by registered kabalas Ext. 1 and l(a); that the suit land was at first recorded in the names of defendants 3, 4 and 5 and the Majumdar landlords filed an objection, under section 19(1) of East Bengal State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, and got their names recorded but the defendants, 3, 4 and 5 preferred an appeal, under section 19(2) of the said Act, and the land was again in their names. Ext. C is the certified copy of that judgment of the appellate officer. The Government also collected rent from the defendant No. 4 vide Ext. B Defendant's categorical statement that Jasmat got tenancy right in the suit land and after his death his heirs were possessing the same before his purchase are corroborated by D.W. 2 Haji Monsurulla, the tahsildar and D.W. 2 Majan Shah who held land contiguous to the suit land.

18. P.W. 1 is the only witness on behalf of the plaintiffs. He stated that the suit land was taken from Jasmat and was given borgabandabast to others. He did not state who used to cultivate the land after Jasmat but merely stated that when the defendant disposed the plaintiff Morlan Shah was the bargadar. Madan Shah according to D.Ws. 1 and 3 left for India long ago. Though P.W. 1 stated he had an account book for borga receipts he neither produced the account book nor any borga receipt. In the present case the presumptive value of the C.S. record under section 114 of the Evidence Act must be held to be still available to contesting defendant.

19. From the evidence on record it is clear that the predecessors of Defendant 1 never possessed the land as a bargadar of the plaintiffs and the defendant’s assertion that Jasmat and his heirs possessed the land in their own rights has been amply substantiated by the evidence on record. From Ext. 1it cannot be said, though contended by Mr. B.N. Chowdhury, that the subsequent possession of Jasmat was one of a bargadar . I do not find any mention of the kabuliyat in the C.S. Khatian. The learned Subordinate Judge has assumed, on a total misrepresentation of evidence on the record, that since Jasmat died 6/7 years back the sui t is within twelve years of possession through a recorded bargadar. From the evidence on record it is clear that the plaintiffs had no possession within 12 years before the institution of suit. The learned Munsif rightly dismissed the suit.

20. In the result, the appeal succeeds and is hereby allowed. The decision of the learned Subordinate Judge is set aside and that of learned Munsif is restored. There will, however, be no order as to costs.

End.
