full_judgment:
This Rule was issued calling upon the opposite parties to show cause as to why the judgment and decree dated 30-5-1993 and 8-6-1993 respectively passed by the District Judge, Gazipur in Title Appeal No. 92 of 1989 setting aside and reversing the judgment and decree dated 23-2-1989 and 28-2-1989 respectively passed by the Additional Assistant Judge, Gazipur in Title Suit No. 22 of 1987 should not be set aside.

2. The fact for the disposal of the Rule is as follows:

The plaintiff-opposite party i.e. Government of Bangladesh and the District Forest Officer, Dhaka Division, filed Title Suit No. 22 of 1987 in the Court of Munsif, Gazipur for decree declaring the plaintiffs full right, title and interest in the suit land measuring 19.29 acres of CS Plot Nos. 440, 465, 475, 215, 208 of mouja Sarabo Police Station Joydevpur, District Gazipur (formerly in the District of Dhaka) and holding that the ex parte decree dated 28-12-1981 passed in Title Suit No. 860 of 1981 of the Assistant Judge Court, Gazipur was fraudulent, void, collusive and without any legal effect.

3. The case of the plaintiff-opposite party was as follows:

The landed properties described in the schedule, here-in-after referred to as the suit land, originally belonged to Zaminder Rai Bahadur Arun Goure Prashad Roy Chowdhury and the Government had taken over the suit land under notification Nos. 2846 of 25-3-1953 and 16188 dated 15-12-1953 and subsequently proposed for its reservation as forest under Forest Act of 1927 by notification No. 3735(2)18-12-dated 15-9-1967. The Government had been and was still in possession of the suit land through the Forest Department of the Government. The defendant-petitioner had filed suit being Title Suit No. 860 of 1981 for declaration of his title in the suit land and it was alleged that by suppressing service of summons in collusion with the process server and other employees of the court fraudulently obtained an ex parte decree on 28-12-1981. The plaintiff-opposite parties stated that they came to know about the same in 1983. Thereupon they filed Misc. Case No. 26 of 1983 for setting aside the ex parte decree. The Misc. case was filed on 27-2-1983, which was dismissed on 16-5-1984, and because the defendant-petitioner thereafter gave an undertaking to the plaintiff that he would not come to the suit property in future no appeal was preferred against the order of dismissal of Misc. Case No. 26 of 1993. However, it was alleged that the defendant again claimed the suit land without any legal basis and only on the basis of the said ex parte decree which was alleged to have been collusively obtained by exercising fraud upon the court without the knowledge of the plaintiffs. It was further alleged that the defendant-petitioner had no right, title, interest in the suit land and he never got possession, but since the defendant started putting up claim again in March 1986, the plaintiff was constrained to file the present suit to remove the cloud on the title of the plaintiff in the suit land and prayed for a decree as stated above.

4. The defendant-petitioner contested the suit by filing written statement stating, inter alia, that the defendant petitioner filed Title Suit No. 860 of 1981 in the Court of Assistant Judge, Gazipur stating that the suit property originally belonged to Zaminder Prashad Roy Chowdhury and Gouri Prashad Roy Chowdhury of Kashimpur Estate, PS Savar, District Dhaka belonging to Touzi No. 27. The CS record of rights was prepared in the name of Saroda Prashad Roy Chowdhury and others, the heirs of the said Gouri Prashad Roy Chowdhury, as owners in possession of land measuring 19.29 decimals of land of CS plot Nos. 440, 465, 575, 215 and 208 of CS Khatian No. 6 of the Mouja Sarabo. The Zamindary Estate of Kashimpur was divided into two Hissa i.e. 8 Annas 17 Gandas, 3 Karas, 1 Kraniti share and 7 Annas 2 Gondas 2 Kranti 2 Danti share, popularly known as 9 Annas and 7 Annas shareholders and they possessed the suit land. On the 12th Poush 1338 BS the defendant took settlement of the suit land from 9 Annas hissa and on the 7th day of Magh 1338 BS the defendant took settlement of the suit land also from the owners of 7 Annas hissa on payment of proper salami of Rs. 291.00 only and took delivery of physical possession of the suit land and is enjoying the same upon payment of rent. It is stated that the defendant being an illiterate cultivator could not get his name recorded during the SA khatian to the negligence of Jinnat Ali Moulavi of Saradaganj on whom the defendant trusted for the purpose. During the RS operation the defendant appeared before the officer who went to the locality for the purpose and after examining the defendant's papers of title, assured that the defendant's name would be duly recorded in the RS Khatian and subsequently gave an attested copy of the DP khatain No. 19 prepared in the name of the defendant but subsequently it transpired that the RS record had been prepared in the name of the plaintiff and the defendant's name was not entered therein. Hence the defendant filed the said Title Suit No. 860 of 1981 in the Court of Munsif, Gazipur for a declaration of the defendant's-/16/-Annas right, title and interest in the suit land. Title Suit No. 860 of 1981 was decreed ex parte on 28-12-1981 not by suppression of summons which was duly served on 27-6-1981 and 29-6-1981 but in the presence of the Government Advocate Gazipur. The Misc. case No. 26 of 1983 for setting aside the said decree was filed on 27-3-1983 i.e. fourteen months thereafter with no.explanation or prayer for condonation of delay, therefore the Assistant Judge, Gazipur rejected the said Misc. case on contest on 28-3-1984 and the plaintiffs did not prefer any appeal therefrom. The defendant denied that he gave any undertaking that he would not possess the suit land after the dismissal of the Misc. case No. 26 of 1983 that is after the plaintiffs finally lost the case. The defendant after obtaining decree in the Court of Munsif, Gazipur started the Misc. case No. 124 of 1982 before the ADC (Rev), Dhaka which case was transferred from Dhaka to Gazipur and renumbered as Misc. case No. 46 of 1984 for correction of records in the name of the defendant. In the said Misc. case No. 46 of 1984 the learned CO Revenue, Gazipur twice conducted on the spot enquiry in the case land on visiting the suit land. The CO Revenue, Gazipur and after him the ADC (Rev), Gazipur also visited the suit land and made an on the spot enquiry and all the officers found the plaintiff to be in possession of the suit land. Thus found that this defendant was in possession of the suit land by construction of homestead, digging pond and that there was no Gazari tree or forest anywhere in the suit land. The local GP also gave his opinion that the suit land belonged to the defendant and not the plaintiff legally. Upon hearing this defendant and also because the plaintiff had no objection in the record being corrected in his name and as this defendant was in possession of the case land the ADC (Rev). Gazipur by his order dated 12-3-86 passed in Misc. case No. 46 of 1984 allowed correction of record in favour of this defendant. Thereafter there was again an on the spot survey and demarcation of the suit land by Government surveyor Mofizuddin, Revenue Department, Gazipur on 26-8-86 where the officers of the plaintiff and local Chairman were present, and the plaintiff's representative consented to the demarcation as per possession of this defendant. It was therefore submitted that the plaintiff had no right, title, and interest in the suit land and some other interested persons with ill motive started this false and frivolous suit although there was no Gazari tree anywhere in the suit land as falsely claimed in para 5 of the plaint as it appeared from the plaint. Further, none of the plaintiffs signed the plaint of the present suit.

5. The learned Additional Assistant Judge, Gazipur upon hearing the parties and perusing the document dismissed the suit of the opposite parties with the finding that it is not a fact that the summons were suppressed in Title Suit No. 860 of 1981, rather the suit was decreed in presence of the opposite parties on 28-12-1981 as it appeared from the Ext. "cha" the order sheet, and also that the plaintiff opposite parties filed the Misc. case No. 26 of 1983 which was dismissed on contest on 28-3-1984 and that as the plaintiff opposite parties did not file any appeal against the dismissal of the Misc. case No. 26 of 1983 on contest against the plaintiff opposite parties, the plaintiff opposite parties were debarred from instituting a fresh suit in respect of the same matter which was res judicata. With the said findings the learned Additional Assistant Judge, Gazipur dismissed the Title Suit No. 22 of 1987 on 23-2-1989.

6. Being aggrieved and dissatisfied with the said judgment and decree dated 23-2-1989 passed by the Additional Assistant Judge, Gazipur in Title Suit No. 23 of 1987 the plaintiff opposite parties filed Title Appeal No. 92 of 1989 in the Court of District Judge, Gazipur. The learned District Judge reversed the judgment and decree passed by the Additional Assistant Judge, Gazipur by the impugned judgment and decree dated 30-5-1993 and 8-6-1993 respectively against which the defendant petitioner has obtained the present Rule.

7. Mr. Alimuzzaman Chowdhury, the learned Counsel appearing for the defendant-petitioner, has submitted a number of grounds whereby the appellate Court committed error of law on the face of the record leading to wrong decision and injustice on the defendant-petitioner. It is submitted that the suit land is not Gazari land and the same cannot be treated as Forest Land as had been recorded in CS Khatian No. 6 Ext. Gha in which the suit land has been described as Chala and Teek land and the schedule also supported the same. The land mentioned in the schedule of the plaint was never published in the Gazette by the Government as forest land under any provision of the Forest Act, 1927 and the learned District Judge's finding that it was forest land published in the Gazette under the provision of Forest Act, 1927 was baseless, misconceived and wrong. The only paper Ext. 1 produced by the PW 1 as notification containing some other plots than the suit plot, mere departmental notification under the provision of East Bengal Private Forest Act, 1949 and not under the provisions of Forest Act, 1927 as has been wrongly stated and observed by the learned District Judge, Gazipur. The appellate Court below committed serious error of law while reversing the finding of the trial Court that the ex parte decree having been passed upon service of summons on 28-12-1981 in Title Suit No. 860 of 1981 in the Court of Assistant Judge, Gazipur, the plaintiff opposite party preferred a Misc. case for setting aside the said ex parte decree under Order 9 rule 13 of the Civil Procedure Code being Misc. case No. 26 of 1983, the restoration of the suit to its original file and number and having lost the Misc. case no. 26 of 1983 on contest on 28-3-1984 and the plaintiff-opposite party having not preferred any appeal against the said order passed in the Misc. case was debarred from filing a fresh suit between the same parties and in respect of the same property in 1987, and in not finding that the ex parte decree unless set aside also operated as res judicata in the matter. It is further submitted that a Gazette notification published on 11-7-85 and a photo copy of the same showed that the suit land was not included as forest land. A photocopy of the departmental notification dated 15-12-1953 Ext. 1 which was relied upon by the plaintiff-opposite parties was only a departmental circular and not a notification as required under section 4 of the Forest Act, 1927. It is also submitted by the learned Counsel appearing for the defendant-petitioner that the learned District Judge without considering the above facts found that the GP and the Assistant Judge had favoured the defendant petitioner who were illegally influenced by bribe and share of land. The judgment, it is submitted, is vitiated by irrelevant observation in the name of judicial notice and baseless as portion of all the concerned Government officials and the subordinate judiciary.

8. We will now consider the points raised by the learned Counsel for the defendant-petitioner. It appears from Ext. 'Gha' which is CS Khatian No. 6 that the suit land comprising of Plot No. 208, 215, 440 and 475 are described as Chala and Teek land. There is no mention that any of the lands was Gazari land. This has not been disputed by the plaintiffs. If these lands, were not forest land then they could not have been declared as land for reserve forest. It is the plaintiffs case that the suit land was taken over by the Government under State Acquisition and Tenancy Act by Notification No. 2846 of 25-3-1953 and Notification No. 16188 of 15-12-53 and subsequently for reservation as forest under Forest Act, 1927. If it was forest land then section 20 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act would not apply, as forest land vested in the Government without any notification of all CS recorded forest land vested in the Government as per proviso to section 20 of the Forest Act, 1927. If on the other hand the plaintiffs claim that the suit land was Gazari land is accepted, then giving notice under section 4 of Forest Act 1927 and the procedure laid down from section 4 to section 20 of the said Act has to be complied with. In the instant case although the appellate Court has referred to Gazette notification there is nothing on record to show that there was any Gazette notification under section 4 which requires there has to be a notification in the official Gazette. Ext. 1 upon which the plaintiffs have relied is a departmental notice which cannot be said to be an official notification as envisaged in section 4 of the Forest Act, 1927. In the case of Hazi Nurul Islam vs. Serajul Islam and ors. reported in 1984 BLD (AD) 36 the Appellate Division while considering the fact of Government circular in respect of principles of lease of Government fisheries held that the Matter did not have any statutory force nor were they published in the official Gazette for general information to the members of the public, so as to saddle them with the knowledge of the principles regulating the leasing out of fisheries. At best, this offered a guideline for the use of the officers of the department without prescribing any sanction against the violation of the principles contained therein as far as the members of the public are concerned.

<u>9. In the present case Ext. 1 appears to be nothing but a departmental notification which could not affect the right of the public. Further the notification was not published in the official Gazette as specifically required under section 4 and section 6 of the Forest Act, 1927. The appellate Court obviously came to an error in holding that a Gazette notification was published in respect of the suit land although no such Gazette notification appears in the record filed by the plaintiff. A photocopy Gazette notification was filed by the defendant which was published in 1985 and the suit land does not appear to be included in the said notification under section 6 of the Forest Act, 1927.</u>

<u>10. It appears from the record that the defendant filed suit being Title Suit No. 860 of 1981 for declaration of his title in the suit property. In the said suit the plaintiff opposite parties as defendant filed a petition praying for time to file written statement on the ground stated therein. The learned Asstt Judge, Gazipur rejected the petition on the ground that it could not be considered at that stage. The suit was therefore decreed ex parte in favour of the defendant-petitioner on 23-1-1982. Thereafter the plaintiff opposite party filed a petition under Order 9 rule 13 of the Civil Procedure Code being Misc. case No. 26 of 1983. The said Misc. case was dismissed on contest on 28-3-1984. It would thus appear that the plaintiff-opposite party's lawyer being present and having filed a petition for time had full knowledge of the ex parte decree when it was passed on 23-1-82. The Asstt. Judge took this into consideration while dismissing the Misc. case No. 26 of 1983 on the ground that it had been filed 14 months after the ex parte decree which was beyond the limitation period prescribed by law. It thus appears clear that it was found on contest that there had been no suppression of notice on the plaintiff-opposite party nor any fraud committed in the proceedings of the court. It also appears that no revision/appeal was filed by the plaintiff opposite party against the dismissal of Misc. case No. 26 of 1983. After a long lapse of 4 years the plaintiff-filed the present suit being Title Suit No. 22 of 1987 for setting aside the ex parte decree in Title Suit No. 860 of 1981. It was alleged by the plaintiff that the ex parte decree was obtained collusively. The learned Asstt. Judge dismissed the suit, inter alia, holding that the ex parte decree had been passed with the knowledge of the present plaintiff and the Misc. case filed by the plaintiff having been dismissed on contest and there being no appeal or revision filed against that judgment and order of dismissal under Order 9 rule 13 of the Civil Procedure Code that the ex parte decree in Title Suit No. 860 of 1981 was res judicata under section 11 of the CPC as subject matter of the present suit was the sane and between the same parties. The appellate Court has alleged bribery and collusion between the defendant petitioner, the GP and the trial Court, but without any evidence in support thereof. He has presumed that the ex parte decree was obtained by fraud by bribing officers in the department of Forest, the GP and also the Court. He has also presumed that the delay in filing Misc. case under Order 9 rule 13 and then not filing any revision or appeal against the order of dismissal of the Misc. case was also obtained by bribery and collusion to have a share on the suit land. These observations appear to be the feelings of the appellate Court without any legal basis or evidence. They are presumptive. The authorities concerned the GP and the Assistant Judge were not parties in the suit and, as such, the observation of bribery and collusion against them is uncalled for. In the case of Mrida Begum and others vs. Moulavi Md. Hasan and others reported in 10 BLD 1990 page 334 it was held that fraud cannot be imputed against authorities exercising judicial function either as Court or Tribunal. We have noted that there was nothing to show that the plaintiffs in the suit were prevented from appearing in Title Suit No. 860 of 81 which was decreed ex parte with full knowledge of the plaintiffs’ lawyer who had applied for time for filing written statement, but was rejected. In the absence of any fraud committed in the proceeding before the trial Court the ex parte decree unless reversed is res judicata to subsequent suit filed on the same subject and between same parties.</u>

11. We may discuss some cases on the subject. In the case of Rangalal Sutradhar vs. Satish Chandra reported in 11 DLR (1959) 376; it was held that as ex parte decree cannot be re-opened in a later action brought to set aside on the ground of fraud simply because the claim decreed ex parte was false. The only ground on which a decree in a previous suit can be successfully challenged in a suit for setting aside the decree is that the plaintiff was prevented by the fraud of the decree holder in the previous suit before the court. In the instant case that does not appear to be the position.

12. In the case of Kumar Begum Roy vs. Panna Debi and others reported in 1982 BLD (AD) 54 the Appellate Division held that fresh suit for achieving the same result by adopting indirect method is not permissible order of dismissal for default passed by the Calcutta High Court on September 1, 1949 in a suit filed by the plaintiff in 1944. The Appellate Division held as follows:

"By filing the present suit the appellant has merely adopted an indirect method to achieve in her suit filed in the Calcutta High Court. What she failed to achieve directly, she now wants to achieve indirectly. Law does not allow it to be done. It also appears that in the Calcutta High Court she did not proceed with the suit which was allowed to be dismissed for default on account of her non-appearance. She did not take any further step to have the orders of dismissal for default set aside. Under the provisions of Order 9, rule 9 CPC the present suit is barred."

In the instant case there was ex parte decree against which the plaintiff filed a Misc. case which was dismissed on contest. The plaintiff did not take any step by way of revision/appeal against the said dismissal order and instead has filed the present suit alleging collusion. This is a similar case when the plaintiff having failed to achieve directly by filing the Misc. case under Order 9 rule 9 is trying by filing the present suit for setting aside the ex parte decree on the ground of collusion.

13. In the case of Khan Sahed vs. Abdul Khaleque Sowdagar, Proprietor, Chittagong Rice Mills & Co. vs. Majutar Rahman Khan, reported in 12 PLR 421, it was held by Division Bench of the High Court as follows :

"(1) An ex parte decree can be set aside by new action, when the Court passing it had been misled by fraud. It must be actual and positive fraud relating to the proceeding of the court, a premeditated and intentional contrivance to keep the parties and the court in ignorance of the real and material facts of the case in order to obtain decree by that contrivance.

(2) Falsity of claim by itself is no ground for setting aside decrees on the ground of fraud nor perjured evidence, by which the decree might have been procured, can be ground for setting aside the ex parte decree in a new action.

(3) A decree obtained through suppression of material facts or on perjured evidence cannot be a ground for maintainability of a separate suit setting aside the decree as these omissions do not prevent the relevant party from appearing and placing his case before the Court."

In the case before us there is nothing to show that trial Court had been misled by fraud or that there has been actual and positive fraud relating to the proceeding of the Court or a premeditated or intentional contrivance to keep the parties and the court in ignorance of the real and material facts in order to obtain decree by that contrivance. Nothing of the kind appears to have been found by the appellate Court. There is simply finding on presumption that the decree was obtained by bribery and corruption without evidence.

14. In the case of Bangladesh vs. Rahimuddin reported in 1987 BLD 307 the question was whether ex parte decision in a former suit between the parties over the same matter will operate as res jusdicata. In the former suit the issue regarding acquisition of customary right of pasturage over the suit land by the plaintiffs was raised and finally decided though the suit was decreed ex parte. It was held that the decision of the former suit will operate as res judicata. The decree even if ex parte will operate as res judicata. A Single Bench of the High Court Division in the case observed:

"Now the question that arises for consideration is whether ex parte decree passed in OC Suit No. 55 of 1949 can operate as res judicata and the defendants are estopped from raising the same question that is, whether plaintiffs acquired customary right of pasturage in the suit land. In the former suit this issue was raised and finally decided though the suit was decreed ex parte. Therefore, decision of the former suit will operate as res judicata inasmuch as the pleadings and the prayer made in the former suit gave express notice to the defendant appellant Government that the question would or might be decided. A decree even if ex parte will operate as res judicata in respect of all grounds on defendants against actual claim in the suit as also matter insistent in the suit that claim which might or ought to have been raised. In the absence of fraud or irregularity a decree obtained ex parte is binding for all purposes as contested decree."

<u>15. In the instant case as pointed out, the ex parte decree was not obtained by fraud and the Misc. case under Order 9 rule 13 filed by the plaintiff was also dismissed on contest. Therefore the ex parte decree in the instant case would operate as res judicata on the present suit.</u>

16. The learned Advocate appearing for the petitioner pointed out that it appears from the record that the defendant-petitioner had paid rent and has referred to Exhibits on record. He has argued that once the Government accepts the rent it is estopped to challenge the title in support. In support of his contention he has referred to the case of Bangladesh vs. Askar Ali reported in BCR 1988 (HCD) 179. In the said case land was recorded in the name of the plaintiffs as tenants under the order of SDO. The Tahsilder accepted rent of the suit land from the plaintiffs and granted rent receipts since the plaintiffs were in possession of 9 bighas of the suit land. So it was held that obviously the claims of the plaintiffs were partially admitted by the defendants. Once the record of right was corrected and Government accepted rent from the plaintiff for the entire suit property, the Government is estopped to challenge the title of the plaintiff and the plaintiff had good title in the suit land.

<u>17. In the instant case the Government having accepted the rent from the defendant petitioner it was estopped from challenging the title of the defendant petitioner. The appellate Court without any basis held that the officer concerned was corrupt and therefore did not consider the facts disclosed in exhibit "ঝ" The said exhibit showed that the Revenue Officer, Gazipur had visited the suit land and found the defendant-petitioner to be in possession of the suit land and had constructed houses thereon. On enquiry it was found that the suit land was in possession of the defendant with a house and that there was no Gazari land. The Department of Forest was not present in spite of several notices to them. The ADC (Rev.) thereafter directed payment of rent of the suit land by the defendant petitioner. In doing so it accepted the title and interest of the defendant petitioner.</u>

18. In the light of my above observation I must hold that the appellate Court committed error in law leading to wrong decision and causing injustice to the defendant petitioner.

19. In the result the Rule is made absolute. The judgment and decree dated 30-5-1993 and 8-6-1993 passed by the District Judge, Gazipur in Title Appeal No. 92 of 1989 setting aside and reversing the judgment and decree dated 23-2-1989 and 28-2-1989 respectively passed by the Assistant Judge, Gazipur in Title Suit No. 22 of 1987 is set aside. The judgment and decree dated 23-2-89 and 28-2-89 passed by the Assistant Judge, Gazipur in Title Suit No. 22 of 1987 is hereby restored.

End.

Mahfuza Begum Assistant Attorney-General instructed by B Hossain, Advocate-on-Record ----- For the Respondent.

case_source: (From the judgment and Border dated 25th of March, 2001 passed by the High Court Division in Reference Application No. 43 of 1997)
full_judgment:
Md Imman Ali J: The Civil Appeal, by leave, is directed against the judgment and order dated 25-3-2001 passed by a Division Bench of the High Court Division in Reference Application No. 43 of 1997 rejecting the reference.

2. The facts of the case, in brief, are that the appellant filed return for the assessment year 1991-92 showing gross profit at the rate of 11.77%. Notice was served upon him fixing date of hearing but he did not appear at the time of hearing and the Deputy Commissioner of Taxes took the matter for ex-parte hearing and held that the assessee intentionally avoided attending the case and made assessment under section 84 of the Income Tax Ordinance, 1984. The Deputy Commissioner of Taxes considered the audit report submitted by the company but found that supporting papers including vouchers have not been filed and made the assessment fixing 64.70% as the rate of gross profit.

3. Against the said order the appellant filed an appeal being IT Appeal No. 56/coy-2/94-95 and the same was heard by the Commissioner of Taxes (Appeal) who by, his order dated 30-10-1995 reduced the gross profit to 25% and also allowed deduction of Taka 17,50,000 but rejected the claim for rebate of 60% as a garments manufacturer and exporter.

4. Against the said order the assessee appellant filed ITA No. 1831 of 1995-96 before the Taxes Appellate Tribunal. The Tribunal directed the revenue authority to accept the sale as disclosed by them and also, reduced the rate of gross profit to 20% from 25% holding that the decision was taken by the appellate authority on com parson of records with parallel cases.

5. Against the said order the appellant filed an application under section 160 of the Income Tax Ordinance before the High Court Division stating that the Taxes Appellate Tribunal has illegally fixed gross profit at the rate of 20% instead of 11.77% the question of law under reference was couched in the following terms:

"Whether in the facts and circumstances of the case the Taxes Appellate Tribunal was justified in directing adoption of gross profit at 20% in view of the fact that the petitioner's accounts are audited and verifiable, contrary to Income Tax Law and Procedure."

6. By the impugned judgment and order, the High Court Division rejected the reference application.

7. Against the said judgment and order dated 25-3-2001 the appellant filed a civil petition for leave to appeal.

8. Leave was granted to consider the following grounds:

I. Whether the High Court Division acted illegally in holding that no question of law arose for their decision in considering the reference formulated and placed before them;

II. Whether the respondent having not filed any affidavit-in-opposition in the reference application disputing the question of law as formulated nor suggesting any new question of law, the High Court Division acted illegally in holding that no question of law arose out of the order of the Tribunal; as such the reference application was not maintainable; and

III. Whether the High Court Division could itself have formulated the question referred by way of reference.

9. Mr Rafiq-ul-Huq, learned Senior Advocate appearing on behalf of the appellants made submissions in line with the grounds upon which leave was granted. He submitted that the High Court Division acted illegally in not considering that the Tribunal applied GP at the rate of 20% without taking into consideration the evidence on record when the misreading and non-consideration of evidence are questions of law and, as such, the appeal is liable to be allowed. The learned Advocate further submitted that the audit report was supplied containing a certificate from a Chartered Accountant certifying the correctness of the true income of the assessee, and, as such, the Tribunal was bound by the evidence given by the Appellant under section 82 of the Income Tax Ordinance and, as such, the High Court Division acted illegally in holding that no question of law had arisen in the reference application for their decision. He also submitted that the High Court Division acted illegally in not formulating any question of law as prayed for by the appellant. The learned Advocate lastly submitted that the question of law as formulated in the Reference Application does arise from the order of the Tribunal and, as such, the High Court Division acted illegally in holding that question of law does not arise for their decision in the instant Reference Application and the impugned judgment is liable to be set-aside and the appeal may be allowed.

10. Mrs. Mahfuza Begum, learned Assistant Attorney-General appearing on behalf of the respondent submitted that the High Court Division on perusal of the materials on record has rightly held that no question of law has been raised before it because the determination of the rate of gross profit is not a question of law. In support of her contention she referred to the decision in the Case of Commissioner of Income Tax A-Range, Chittagong vs Harendra Kumar Shil reported in 34 DLR (AD) 298, where it was held that:

"Determination of rate of gross profit for the particular year in respect of the particular business or trade, is purely a question of fact, and that being so it could not be made a ground for making reference under section 66(1) of the Income-tax Act."

11. She further submitted that the question of fact does not require to be controverted by filing an affidavit-in-opposition. As there was no requirement to controvert the question of fact raised before the High Court Division, the Revenue Department did not file any affidavit-in- opposition and for non-filing of affidavit-in-opposition by the respondent, the appellant cannot be benefited in any manner. The learned AAG lastly submitted that the audit report was not accepted by the Deputy Commissioner of Taxes for want of supporting papers and the appellant having not furnished any supporting papers either before the Commissioner (Appeal) or the Tribunal, their claim for being assessed at the rate of 11.77% in respect of gross profit is not tenable and thus suggestion for reformulating the alleged question of law as claimed by the appellant does not arise.

12. During the course of hearing Mr. Rafique-ul-Huq, learned Senior Counsel submitted that the appellant supplied accounts certified by Chartered Accountants which under section 82 of the Income Tax Ordinance, 1984 is sufficient to deem the return as correct.

13. On the other hand, Mrs Mahfuza Begum, learned AA G submitted that the provisions of section 82 is only applicable if the certificate of the Chartered Accountants is furnished on the prescribed form under Rule 64A of the Income Tax Ordinance Rules, 1984.

14. We have considered the submissions of the learned advocates appearing for the parties concerned and perused the impugned judgment as well as other evidence and materials on record.

15. The relevant portions of section 160 of the Income Tax Ordinance provides as follows:

160 Reference to the High Court Division ( 1) The assessee or the Commissioner may, within 60(sixty) days from the date of receipt of the order of the Appellate Tribunal communicated to him under section 159, by application in the prescribed form, accompanied, in the case of an application by the assessee, by a fee of 100 (one hundred taka), refer to the High Court Division any question of law arising out of such order:

Provided further that the Board may, on an application made in this behalf modify or waive, in any case, the requirement of such payment.

(4) on receipt of the notice on the date of hearing of the application, the respondent shall, at least seven days before the date of hearing submit in writing a reply to the application; and he shall therein specifically admit or deny whether the question of law formulated by the applicant arises out of the order of the Appellate Tribunal:

(5) If the question formulated by the applicant is, in the opinion of the respondent, defective, the reply shall state in what particular the question is defective and what is the exact question of law, if any, which arises out of the said order; and the reply shall be in triplicate and be accompanied by any documents which are relevant to the question of law formulated in the application and which were produced before the Deputy Commissioner of Taxes, the Inspecting Joint Commissioner, the Appellate Joint Commissioner, the Commissioner (Appeals) or the Appellate Tribunal, as the case may be, in the course of any proceedings relating to any order referred to in sub-section (2) (a) or (b).

16. The High Court Division observed that no audited accounts and papers relating to the applicant's accounts were either before the Commissioner of Taxes (Appeal) or before the Taxes Appellate Tribunal.

17. Having examined the reference application as well as the order of the Taxes Appellate Tribunal the High Court Division held that no question of law had arisen from the said order and the assessee-applicant had not been able to formulate any point of law. In this regard the learned AAG has referred to the decision in the case of Commissioner of Income Tax A-Range, Chittagong vs Harendra Kumar Sil reported in 34 DLP (AD) 298, where it was specifically held that the determination of rate of gross profit is purely a question of fact and could not be made a ground for making reference. Since that was the only point of reference made by the appellant before the High Court Division, we are constrained to agree with the submissions of the learned AAG that the respondents were not required to controvert the same by filing an affidavit-in-opposition. We also note that under sub-section (4) the respondents are required to specifically admit or deny whether the question of law formulated by the appellant arises out of the order of the Appellate Tribunal. 'Since in view' of the above mentioned decision of this Division, no question of law arose in the reference the respondents were not required to admit or deny the reference. Similarly the question of reformulating the question referred by the applicant would only arise if the reference was indeed on a question of law.

18. We are of the view that the High Court Division correctly found that no question of law had arisen.

<u>19. With regard to the submission of learned Counsel for the appellant that the High Court Division itself could have formulated a point of law in the manner, suggested, we are of the view that section 160 of the Ordinance does not provide for any such action. Clearly it is for the assessee to formulate any point of law and make the reference to the High-Court Division in the prescribed form. Under section 161 (2) the High Court Division is required only to hear and decide the question of law raised and, thereafter, deliver its judgment stating the grounds on which the decision is founded.</u>

20. In the instant case the High Court Division found that no question of law had arisen, which is fully in accordance with the decision reported in 34 DLR (AD) 298, mentioned above.

We do not find any illegality or infirmity in the .impugned judgment and order of the, High Court Division, accordingly, the appeal is dismissed without however any order as to costs.

End.

full_judgment:
This Rule issued in an application under section 115 of the Code of Civil Procedure calls in question a judgment and decree dated 26 September, 1990 passed by learned Additional District Judge, Cox's Bazar in Other Appeal No.94 of 1986 reversing those dated 17 May, 1986 passed by learned Upazila Munsif, Ukhiya, Cox's Bazar, in Other Suit No.26 of 1984 awarding decree in favour of the plaintiff side.

2. The Rule has been obtained by the petitioners raising the question as to whether the judgment of the lower appellate Court reversing the judgment of the trial Court was well founded on law.

3. For the purpose of answering to the said question posed, the relevant facts are stated briefly, which are as follows:

The predecessor of the opposite party Nos. 1-11 Eshaque Ahmed Sikder as sole plaintiff on 30-9-1980, instituted a suit being Other Suit No.471 of 1980 in the Court of Munsif, Cox's Bazar for declaration of title and confirmation of possession over 0.29 acre of land described in the schedule to the plaint. The schedule land is hereinafter referred to as the suit land. The suit was, thereafter, transferred to the Court of Upazila Munsif, Ukhiya and re-numbered there as Other Suit No.26 of 1984.

4. Sur Ali, Muklesh, Musa Ali and their mother, Ali Bibi were the owners of the suit land and the record of right was prepared in their names. The plaintiff purchased the said land by way of two sale deeds dated 31-1-1946 and 18-5-1952 from the heirs of the said recorded owners. RS record was prepared in the name of Sur Ali and other owners. The plaintiff had no knowledge of the wrong record in the name of Sur Ali and others, The MRR Khatian had been also prepared in the name of Sur Ali and others and the said record is absolutely wrong. The suit land was sold in auction for arrears of rent due to the Government in a certificate case of the year 1960 and was purchased by the defendants. The certificate case was stated making the recorded owners Sur Ali and others as certificate debtors. The certificate proceeding is collusive, illegal, void and without jurisdiction. The certificate sale was not acted upon and the auction purchaser did not acquire any right, title and possession on the suit land and the right, title and interest of the plaintiff has not been affected by the auctions sale. The defendants, though purchased the suit land from the auction purchaser, got no title and possession there and the suit land is possessed by the plaintiff. The cause of the suit arose on 8th Aswin, 1387 BS when the defendants, in the event of plaintiff''s dispossession over the suit or a portion of the suit land by the defendants.

6. The sole plaintiff having been dead, his heirs were substituted in his place as plaintiffs in the suit who are opposite party Nos. 1-11 in the Rule.

7. The defendant Nos. 5-7 entered appearance in the suit and contested the same by filing written statement traversing all the material allegations made in the plaint. It is the case of the defendant that the suit land originally belonged to Sur Ali and others and RS Khatian was prepared in their names. On the acquisition of rent receiving interest by the Government, they became tenants under the Government and MRR Khatian was correctly prepared in their names. For arrear of rents due to the Government with respect to the suit land, Certificate Case No.7402 of 1959-60 was started against the recorded owners of MRR Khatian and the land was put to auction and one Mir Ahmed auction purchased the suit land and got actual physical possession on 7-11-1962 through a Miscellaneous Case No. 53 of 1962-63 and possessed the land on payment of rents to the Government. The auction purchase Mir Ahmed transferred the auction purchased land to one Khatun and the said Khatun also exercised acts of possession over the suit land and on her death, the same was inherited by the defendant Nos. 1-4 and Mohammad Hussain, Shafiqur Rahman and Azizur Rahman. Mohammad Hussain, Shafiqur Rahman and Azizur Rahman transferred land of their share in favour of defendant Nos. 5-7 by four registered sale deeds on different dates the defendants encircled their purchased land with boundaries made a Kuria on some portion of the land and exercised acts of possession over the rest land. The defendant Nos. 1-4 sold land of their share to one Noorjahan.

8. Further case of the defendants is that, the alleged kabala deeds of the plaintiffs got no legal existence and those are forged, created and collusive deeds. The plaintiff, on the basis of those forged kabala deeds, did never exercise any act of possession on the suit land. MRR Khatian had been prepared 22 years back but the plaintiff did never make any attempt to have the MRR Khatian corrected. The plaintiff did not put forward any claim within twelve (12) years of the date of auction purchase and also of taking of the delivery of possession on the auction purchased land by the auction purchaser and the plaintiff claim and the suit stood barred by limitation. The plaintiff got no cause of action to file the suit against the defendants. The suit as framed is also not maintainable.

9. On these pleadings, the parties fought out the suit.

10. The learned trial Judge held that it had been proved that Mir Ahmed purchased the land in auction and went into possession by filing Miscellaneous Case No. 53 of 1962-63 and after that the defendants acquired title and possession over the suit land by virtue of sale deeds. The trial Judge further held that it had been proved that by the sale deeds, Exhibit-3 and 4, the plaintiffs did not get into possession over the suit land and the suit land by and the said deeds were not acted upon and by the auction sale, the title of the plaintiffs, if any, had been extinguished. The trial Judge held, further, that all the PWs admitted that the defendants possessed some portion of the suit land by encircling the same with fencing and that had been also proved by Exhibit-5, the Report of the Advocate Commissioner and some PWs admitted that the defendants were in possession over the entire suit land and the defendants grew ''pelong dal'' there. The trial judge came to the finding that MRR Khatian had been prepared long after the plaintiff obtained sale deeds but no attempt had been made by him to have the MRR Khatian, corrected. The trial judge found, further, that it was natural that the recorded owners of the suit land would be the certificate debtors. The trial judge found that the plaintiffs though were required to file suit for setting the sale did not do that. The trial judge, ultimately, expressed the view that the suit as framed was not maintainable and the same was barred by limitation. With the above findings, the trial judge negative the claim of the plaintiffs and dismissed the suit.

11. The plaintiffs, being aggrieved by the decision of the trial judge, carried an appeal to the Court of learned District Judge, Cox''s Bazar. The learned Additional District Judge heard the appeal set aside the judgment and decree passed by the trial Court and decreed the suit in favour of the plaintiffs.

12. The appellate Court in reversing the decision of the trial Court held that trial Court unnecessarily emphasized the question of possession of the suit land and the question of possession was not the subject matter of the suit but at the same time held that since the suit was for recovery of khas possession, the question of dispossession is significant. The appellate Court further held that the exhibits-3 and 4, the sale deeds of the year 1946 and 1952, were self-exhibited documents and those documents strengthen the claim of the plaintiffs. The appellate Court next found that the sale deeds in favour of Fatema Khatun had not been produced in the Court and thus the acquisition of title over the suit land by Fatema Khatun had not been proved. The appellate Court again found that the plaintiffs went into possession after purchase and since the plaintiffs were in possession, there was no question on the part of Mir Ahmed to go into possession over the suit land in the year 1962. The appellate Court further held that the certificate case was required to be filed against the persons who were in possession of the land and not those whose name had been recorded in the record of right and by the auction purchase no right accrued to the auction purchaser, Mir Ahmed. The appellate Court further held that the defendants, after creating some deeds, dispossessed the plaintiffs from the suit land and the suit had been filed within the period of dispossession.

13. The defendants being aggrieved by the aforesaid decision of learned Additional District Judge moved this Court in an application under section 115 of the Code of Civil Procedure and obtained the present Rule.

14. Ms Naima Haider, learned Advocate appearing in support of the Rule, directed her arguments in assailing the impugned judgment of the lower appellate Court and contended that the lower appellate Court having not at all adverted to the reasoned decision on which the trial Court''s judgment rested and the impugned judgment having not been a proper judgment of reversal, the same cannot be sustained in law.

15. Ms Naima Haider contended, first, the plaintiff-opposite-parties did not seek any relief with respect to the auction sale held in the certificate proceeding and in the event of subsistency of the auction sale, plaintiff-petitioners were not at all entitled to have any declaration of title and confirmation of possession or in the alternative of recovery of khas possession over the suit land and the suit, thus, was at all maintainable.

16. The next contention advanced on behalf of the defendant-petitioners is that, the lower appellate Court did not find at what point of time the alleged dispossession of the plaintiffs occurred and whether the plaintiff's suit was instituted within 12 years of the date of dispossession as alleged by the plaintiffs.

17. The next argument addressed from the side of the petitioners is that the lower appellate Court committed a substantial error of law in finding that the question of possession was not material in the suit and that the learned trial Court was wrong in over emphasizing the question of possession in as much as the suit having been for declaration of title with confirmation of possession or recovery of khas possession, the question of possession was very much material specially when the trial Court categorically held that the kabalas in favour of the plaintiffs were never acted upon and the findings and reasons of the trial Court were neither adverted to nor reversed by the lower appellate Court.

18. Mr Abdul Kalam Azad, learned Advocate representing the plaintiff-opposite parties, on the other hand, submitted that the findings of the trial Court were not based on evidence and materials on record but the findings of the lower appellate Court were based on proper assessment and consideration of the evidences and other materials on record and, as such, the impugned judgment cannot be said as not being, a proper judgment of reversal. It is the further contention of the learned Advocate that the plaintiffs were required to be made parties in the certificate case as certificate debtors and in the absence of the plaintiffs as certificate debtors in the certificate case, the same could not be binding upon them.

19. It is further canvassed on behalf of the plaintiff-opposite parties that the sale deed of Fatema Khatun from the auction purchaser Mir Ahmed has not been filed in the Court by the defendants and the title deeds of the defendants cannot be considered unless the title deed of their vendor, Fatema Khatun is produced before the Court.

20. In the wake of rival contentions raised from both the sides, let me now consider the soundness of the contentions raised.

21. The mandate of law is that the lower appellate Court being the last and final Court of fact, is required to discuss and consider the evidences of the parties and other materials on record and in reversing any judgment of the trial Court, it is required to advert to the findings and decisions on which the trial Court''s judgment rested. Keeping in view of this mandate of law, let me see whether the judgment of the lower appellate Court reversing the decision of the trial Court can be sustained in law or not.

<u>22. Plaintiff in paragraph No. 4 and 5 of the plaint pleaded that the defendants expressed that the suit land i.e., the land of RS Khatian, for arrears of rents, was sold in auction in 1960 and they purchased the land from the auction purchaser and in the event of disclosure of any Bainama (sale certificate) and Dakhalnama (Writ of delivery of possession), those will be regarded as illegal, ineffective and baseless and the said auction sale was not acted upon and the auction purchaser and his successors did not acquire any title. PW 1 in his evidence stated that the whole auction matter is absolutely false and the auction sale was not acted upon and the auction purchaser did not exercise any acts of possession over the auction purchased land. The defendant-petitioners in the written statement clearly stated that the suit land, for arrears of rents was put to auction in a Certificate Case No. 7402 of 1959-60 and one Mr Ahmed auction purchased the land and got actual physical possession on 7-11-1962 through Miscellaneous Case No. 53 of 1962-63 and possessed the land on payment of rents to the Government. It was further pleaded that the auction purchaser Mir Ahmed transferred auction purchased land to one Fatema Khatun and on the death of Fatema Khatun, her heirs being the owners of the land, transferred their share to the defendant Nos.5-7 and Noorjahan Evidence had been also led in support of the auction sale and possession of the defendants following auction purchase. Exhibit-Ka is the writ of delivery of possession in favour of the auction purchaser Mr Ahmed on 7-11-1972 in Miscellaneous Case No. 53 of 1962-63. The trial Court on consideration of the evidences and materials on record came to the finding that it has been proved that suit land was auction sold for arrear of rent due to the Government and it was the responsibility of the plaintiffs to file suit seeking relief against the auction sale which the plaintiffs did not do so. On perusal of the impugned judgment, it does not appear that the appellate Court below has adverted to this most important aspect of the case. It appears that the lower appellate Court has not addressed itself to the clear finding arrived at by the trial Court that it was the responsibility of the plaintiffs to seek relief against the auction sale. The appellate Court did not come to any positive finding whether the plaintiffs were required to seek relief against the auction sale. The Power appellate Court simply found that the decisions arrived at by the trial Court to the effect that the claim of the plaintiffs could not be eatertainable as because plaintiffs, on getting knowledge of the auction purchase, did not file any suit against the auction purchase, were not proper but it did not meet the positive finding arrived at by the trial Court that it was the responsibility of the plaintiffs to file suit against the auction sale.</u>

<u>23. It had earlier been pointed out that plaintiffs did not seek any relief against the auction sale. The plaintiff also did not seek any relief with respect to the kabala deeds of the defendants dated 124-1977, 21-6-1997, 28-9-1978 and 22-12-1981. No issues were framed on auction sale and the sale deeds of the defendants.</u>

Issues framed in the suit were as follows:

১। অত্র মোকাদ্দমা বর্তমান আকারে সচল কি না?

২। অত্র মোকদ্দমা তামাদিতে বারিত কি না?

৩। অত্র মোকদ্দমা পক্ষ দোষে দুষ্ট কি না?

৪। মামলাটির উচিৎ মূল্যায়নে যথার্থ কোর্ট ফি আদায় করা হইয়াছে কি না?

৫। নালিশী জমিতে বাদীদের কথিত মতে স্বত্ব দখল আছে কি না?

৬। বাদীগণ তাহাদের প্রার্থীত মতে অত্র মামলায় ডিক্রি পাইতে পারে কি না?

The PW 1 who gave evidence for himself and also on behalf of other plaintiffs, in evidence sought decree of declaration of Rayati right and confirmation of possession over the suit land.

Relief sought for is extracted below:

প্রার্থনা নালিশী তফছিলের জমিতে বাদীদের খরিদা রায়তী স্বত্ব সাব্যস্তে দখল স্থিরতরের ডিক্রি চাই।

So, it is manifestly clear that plaintiff side, neither in the plaint nor in the evidence sought the relief against the auction sale and the sale deeds of the defendants with respect to the suit land but the lower appellate Court in the impugned judgment granted decree declaring the auction purchase in the name of Mir Ahmed and the sale deeds in the names of the defendants with respect to the suit land illegal. The lower appellate Court, thus, appeared to have traveled beyond the pleadings and evidences of the parties and, thus, committed substantial error of law resulting in an error in the decision occasioning a failure of justice.

24. Admittedly, Revisional Settlement (RS) Khatian had been prepared in the name of Sur Ali and others. The original plaintiff Eshaque Ahmed Sikder claimed to have purchased the suit land by way of two sale deeds registered on 5-2-1946 and 21-8-1952. Exhibits 3 and 4. MRR Khatian had been prepared long after the date of registration of the sale deeds of the plaintiffs. In the MRR Khatian, the name of the original plaintiff Eshaque Ahmed Sikder had not been recorded, rather the names of the RS recorded owners Sur Ali and others had been recorded in the Said MRR Khatian. The original plaintiff Eshaque Ahmed Sikder did not take any step to have the MRR Khatian corrected in his name. The trial Court found that the plaintiff did not make any attempt to have the record of right corrected in his name. The lower appellate Court also found that immediately after purchase, the plaintiff was required to get his name mutated in the connected record of right and due to non-recording of his name in the record of right, the certificate proceeding had been started. The certificate case had been started showing the recorded owners of the MRR Khatian as certificate debtors. The certificate officer was not supposed to know whether there had been any subsequent transfer from the recorded owners and whether the transferee was in possession on the suit land. So, it is natural that only those persons whose name had been recorded in the Khatian would be made parties i.e., certificate debtors in the certificate proceeding. The trial Court appears to have duly considered this aspect of the matter but the lower appellate Court misdirected itself in its approach on this aspect of the matter and the observation made by the lower appellate Court does not appear to be a proper and sound observation.

25. It is worth noting here that the plaintiff side, though, appears to have claimed title over the suit land since purchase in the year 1946 and 1952, did not file any rent receipt showing payment of rent either to the Superior Landlords or to the Government Acquired Estate. The plaintiff produced seven (7) rent receipts showing payment of rents to the Government for the suit land, Exhibit-series. Exhibit 2(Chha) is a rent receipt dated 25-8-1977 which is prior to the institution of the suit but all other rent receipts are of the year 1980, 1981, 1982, 1983, 1984 and 1985, after the institution of the suit. The suit is filed on 30-9-1980. The trial Court held that the plaintiff, even if, acquired title over the suit land on the basis of sale deeds Exhibits-3 and 4, but, he having defaulted in payment of rent, the suit land was put to auction and Mir Ahmed auction purchased the land and got possession thereon. This finding arrived at by the trial Court was not met by the lower appellate Court.

26. Let me now turn back to the vital question, which is, whether the plaintiff side was entitled to get a decree of recovery of khas possession and also, whether the suit was barred by limitation.

27. The trial Court found that plaintiff side got no right, title and possession over the suit land and the auction purchaser, Mir Ahmed after getting actual physical possession over the land, got into possession and from him, the subsequent transferees including the defendants exercised acts of possession over the suit land. The trial Court, also, found that plaintiffs were in clear knowledge of the auction sale since the year 1962 and the suit was barred by limitation. The lower appellate Court found that the defendants after creating some deeds with respect to the suit land dispossessed the plaintiff from the said land and established their possession. The lower appellate Court, also, found that the suit had been filed within the prescribed period of dispossession and also within the stipulated period of the knowledge of the auction sale.

28. In the plaint the plaintiff, asserting possession on the suit land, prayed for declaration of title and confirmation of possession thereon. Relief ''Ka'' (T) is as follows:

(ক) নিম্ন তফছিলের জমিতে বাদীর খরিদ, কোর্কা, হাল রায়তী স্বত্ব সাব্যস্তে দখল স্থিরতরের ডিক্রি দেওয়ার।

The alternative relief of recovery of khas possession over the land from which the plaintiff would be dispossessed was sought, subsequently, by way of amendment, as pointed out earlier. Amended portion is extracted below:

বিকল্পে ইতি মধ্যে বিবাদীগণ বাদীকে নালিশী জমি কিংবা নালিশী জমিতে বাদীর রায়তী স্বত্ব সাব্যস্তে বিবাদীর অন্যায় যবর দখল উচ্ছেদে বাদীর বাস দখল দেওয়ার ডিক্রি হয়।

<u>29. From the above, it appears that plaintiff''s suit was for possession and subsequent dispossession and the case was squarely covered by Article 142 of the First Schedule to the Limitation Act. Now I am to refer to the relevant oral evidences on record to decide the factum of possession of the plaintiff and the defendants over the suit land. Plaintiff 1(ka) as PW 1 gave evidence for himself and for all the plaintiffs. He was aged about 30 years on 5-3-1986 when the evidence was recorded. This PW 1 stated that he did not file any case for setting aside the auction sale. He further stated that the rent receipts filed in the Court were subsequent to the filing of the suit. PW1 further gave evidence that defendant Nos. 5-7 forcible entered into the suit land and were in possession over some portion of the suit land. Again, he stated that on his prayer dated 6-5-1981, Advocate Commissioner was appointed and Advocate Commissioner reported that defendants were in possession over some portion of the land. PW1 did not state the date of dispossession from the suit land. PW 2 was aged about 35 years. In his evidence he stated that the defendants forcibly took over possession over 6/7 karas of land 4/5 years back. He could not say the Khatian and plot number of the suit land. This witness, further, stated that the defendants possessed land by erecting fencing. This witness further stated that he could not say on which date the defendants dispossessed the plaintiff. PW 3 gave evidence that the defendants, 4/5 years back, forcibly possessed about 8 karas of land. This witness again stated that the defendants erected house over the suit land 8/10 years back. PW 4 testified that 2-4 years back, the defendants forcibly possessed the entire suit land. PW 5 testified that the defendants, 3-4 years back, forcibly possessed some land. PW 6 testified that the defendants forcibly possessed 7/8 karas of land out of the suit land. PW 7, the learned Advocate Commissioner, gave evidence that he found a 'Kuria' over the suit land.</u>

<u>30. On the other hand, defendant No. 5 as DW 1, gave testimony that the auction purchaser, Mir Ahmed got into possession over the auction purchased land through the process of law in Miscellaneous Case No. 53 of 1962 and he exercised acts of possession over the suit land. He gave further testimony that auction purchaser, Mir Ahmed sold the suit land to one Fatema Khatun and on the death of Fatema Khatun her heirs transferred the suit land to the defendant Nos. 5-7 and to other persons. He stated that the suit land is under their possession and the suit land is surrounded by fencing. He further stated that plaintiff side got no title and possession over any portion of the suit land. The evidence of DW 1 was corroborated by other DWs DW 4 Ahmed, the auction purchaser, gave evidence that on the basis of auction sale, he possessed the suit land and after him, Fatema Khatun, on the basis of a sale deed from him, possessed the land and on the death of Fatema Khatun, the defendant No. 5 possessed the suit land on the basis of sale deeds from the heirs of Fatema Khatun. DW 4 further testified that the process server by beating of drum inducted him in physical possession on the auction purchased land. This witness further stated that he transferred the auction purchased land to Fatema Khatun by way of a sale deed.</u>

<u>31. On an analysis of the evidence of the PWs it become evidently clear that, though, the plaintiffs pleaded possession over the suit land on the date of the institution of the suit, they were out of possession on the suit land, at least, with respect to some portion of the land, PW 4 admitted the possession of the defendants over the entire suit land. The evidences of other PWs on the question of dispossession from the suit land by the defendant suffer from contradictions and inconsistencies. Some PWs gave evidence that dispossession took place 2-4 years back whereas some PWs testified that dispossession took place 7-8 years back i.e., prior to the institution of the suit. It is significant to note here that plaintiff''s exclusive possession over the suit land since the year 1946 i.e. since the execution and registration of the first sale deed till the institution of the suit could not also be proved by any aged reliable witness. On the other hand, the possession of the auction purchaser and after him, the possession of Fatema Khatun and thereafter of the defendants over the suit land since the taking of the actual delivery of possession 7-11-1962, has been substantiated by legal evidences, Exhibit-'Kha' is the right of delivery of possession evidence in handing over of the possession of the suit land by the Process Server to the auction purchaser, Mir Ahmed and the legal effect of this Exhibit-Kha cannot be overlooked. It had been earlier pointed out that except one rent receipt, Exhibit 2(Chha), all other rent receipts were subsequent to the date of the institution of the suit. The defendant also filed a rent receipt dated 19-3-1980 showing payment of rent for the year 1385-1386 BS and this rent receipt is prior to the institution of the suit.</u>

<u>32. In RS Khatian No. 967 corresponding to MRR Khatian No. 9029, the plot No. being 4021, total land is 0.29 acres. Exhibit 3 is a Kabala deed dated 5-2-1946 executed by Musa Ali, Moklesur Rahman sons of Waziuddin, Mokbul Ali and Alimuddin sons of Sur Ali in favour of plaintiff Eshaque Ahmed transferring total 0.29 acre of land from the said plot and Khatian. Exhibit-4 is the Kabala deed dated 21-8-1952 registered by Suya Bibi and Anabibi other owners of the land, in favour of the said Eshaque Ahmed transferring 0.08 acre of land from the said plot Khatian No. Thus, the total land transferred came to 0.37 acres of land but there were only 0.29 acres of land in the said plot and Khatian. On scrutiny of the two Kabala deeds, Exhibit 3 and 4 it transpires that Exhibit-3 is only one page Kabala deed and Exhibit-4 is only one and a half page Kabala deed. MRR Khatian has been prepared long after the sale deeds of the plaintiffs and admittedly, the plaintiff did not make any step to have the MRR Khatian corrected. The trial Court, on a consideration of the two ''deeds Exhibits-3 and 4, the MRR Khatian, legal evidences and other materials on record came to the decision that the plaintiff, as a matter of fact, did not get into possession over the suit land and the said two sale deeds were not acted upon and the suit, having not been filed within the period of limitation prescribed by law, the same stood barred by limitation. The lower appellate Court does not appear to have reversed the said findings of the trial Court property. The appellate Court in a sweeping way without considering the legal evidences and other materials on record found that the cause of action had been proved and the suit had been filed within the period of dispossession. It needs be mentioned here that the trial Court on a proper discussion of the oral evidences of both the PWs and DWs came to a decision and dismissed the suit. It is surprising that the lower appellate Court in reversing the decision of the trial Court did not discuss the oral evidences of PWs and DWs which it was required to do being the last and final Court of fact. The appellate Court simply stated that the PW 1 admitted that the defendants prior to the institution of the suit forcibly possessed some portion of the suit land. The lower appellate Court was required to find on which date the plaintiff was dispossessed from the suit land and whether the suit was filed within 12 years from the date of dispossession to get a decree for recovery of Khas possession. My considered view is this that the question of limitation had not been properly treated by the lower appellate Court.</u>

<u>33. The lower appellate Court granted the relief of recovery of Khas possession over the entire suit land, although, the plaintiff did not seek the relief of recovery of Khas possession over the entire suit land. Rather, from the amendment, it transpires that recovery of khas possession was sought in a portion from where the act of dispossession would occur but curiously, it is pointed out that the area of the specific portion from where the alleged dispossession occurred, had not been stated in the amendment. So, awarding a decree of recovery of Khas possession with respect to the entire suit land, not sought for by the plaintiff, suffers from a gross illegality and also legal infirmity.</u>

34. The lower appellate Court found that the sale deed executed and registered by auction purchaser Mir Ahmed in favour of Fatema Khatun had not been submitted in the Court and the acquisition of title and possession over the suit land by Fatema Khatun as stated by the defendant, had not been proved. This finding of the lower appellate Court got no basis and the same, also, suffers from a gross error. On perusal of the record, it is found that the kabala deed executed registered on 5-1-1965 by the auction purchaser Mir Ahmed in favour of Fatema Khatun had been filed in the Court under regular Firisti on 21-4-1986 and the original Kabala deed is in the record. The finding arrived at by the lower appellate Court as to the non-production of the kabala deed of Fatema Khatun in the Court is the result of non-application of mind of the said Court. In this context, it is mentioned here that Mir Ahmed, the auction purchaser as DW 4 gave evidence that he transferred the land in favour of Fatema Khatun and on her death, her heirs transferred the suit land in favour of the defendant Nos. 5-7 and other persons.

35. The lower appellate Court at one time came to the finding that it was not the principal subject matter who possessed the suit land presently and at the same time found that since the suit was for decree of Khas possession, the act of dispossession was a matter of vital importance. The lower appellate Court found that it was to be decided on whom lawful title vested but found fault with the trial Court in making remarks that the lower Court unnecessarily gave importance on the factum of possession over the suit land and at the same time found that it could not be denied that the question of possession would be the decisive factor in determining the title. The findings of the lower appellate Court suffer from patent inconsistencies.

<u>36. Admittedly, MRR Khatian had been prepared long after the alleged kabala deeds of the plaintiffs and MRR Khatian stands in the name of the original owners Sur Ali and others. The MRR Khatian got a presumption of possession, at least, at the time when the same had been prepared and the correctness of the presumption of possession did not appear to have been rebutted by the plaintiff's side.</u>

37. It may be profitably pointed that the finding arrived at by the lower appellate Court that at the time of purchase of the suit land by the plaintiff, there had been no other claimant for the suit land and, as such, there could not be and believable ground for not going into possession over the suit land by the plaintiff any it had been proved that the title and possession of the suit land vested with the plaintiff since their purchase and the defendants created some deeds with respect to the suit land and by that it had been proved that at the relevant time after creating the said deeds, the defendant dispossessed the plaintiff from the suit land and established their possession there are not borne out from the evidences and materials on record. The appellate Court did not give any reasons in coming to those findings and the findings are vitiated by error of law.

38. It is well known that the finding of fact arrived at by the appellate Court, being the last and final Court of fact, shall not be disturbed by the High Court but it is equally, also, well known that the finding of fact, to attain immunity from attack must be based on evidences and materials on record. If a finding is not based on evidence or if it is based on inadequacy of evidence, then interference is justified. The finding of fact not supported by any cogent reason is not finding in the eye of law. It has already been pointed out that the lower appellate Court as the last and final Court of fact, though required to discuss the evidences of the witnesses of both the parties, did not discuss the evidences of the witnesses of both the parties and, thus, committed an error. It has also been noticed that the findings of the lower appellate Court suffered from patent inconsistencies and those were vitiated by grave error of law. It has, also, been noted that the findings were not justified from the evidences and materials on record and the impugned judgment suffered from gross illegality and legal infirmity and the same could not be said to be a proper judgment of reversal. And by all these errors and illegalities, the ultimate decision in the appeal has been seriously affected. My considered view is that since the decisions arrived at by the lower appellate Court had been vitiated by error of law, those cannot claim immunity from being attacked in the exercise of jurisdiction under section 115 of the Code of Civil Procedure. Interference is, therefore, called for.

39. In view of the discussions made herein above, I find that the Rule got substance and the same, thus, succeeds.

40. In the result, the Rule is made absolute. The impugned judgment and decree dated 26-9-1990 passed in other Appeal No.94 of 1986 of the Court of Additional District Judge, Cox's Bazar is set aside and the judgment and decree passed in other Suit No. 26 of 1984 passed by Upazila Munsif, Ukhiya, Cox's Bazar is restored.

41. Having regard to the facts and circumstances of the case, I direct the parties to bear their respective costs.

LCR be sent down immediately.

End.
