with
(From the judgment and order dated 18 March 2000 passed by the High Court Division in Writ Petition Nos. 3085, 3086, 3427, 3428, 3429, 3430, 3431, 3432, 3433, 3434, 3435, 3436, 3606, 4756 and 3283 of 1997)
full_judgment:
Mainur Reza Chowdhury, CJ: These civil appeals by the Commissioner of Customs, Customs House Chittagong and others are against the Single judgment and order passed by a Division Bench of the High Court Division in Writ Petition Nos. 3252, 3077, 3099, 4148, 3226, 3230, 3228, 3050, 3051, 3108, 3683 and 3676 of 1997 and passed by another Division Bench of the High Court Division in Writ Petition Nos. 3085, 3086, 3427, 3428, 3429, 3430, 3431, 3432, 3433, 3434, 3435, 3436, 3606, 4756 and 3283 of 1997. Both the Benches made the Rules absolute.

2. The High Court Division while issuing the Rule called upon the present petitioners to show cause as to why the orders passed by them on different dates directing for assessment of duties and taxes on the imported goods after fixing tariff value thereon by notification No. SRO No. 113 AIN/ 97/ 1705/Shulka dated 11-5-1997 withdrawing the scheme of CRF from the imported goods. At the time of issuing the Rules, the respondents were allowed to release their respective consignments by paying customs duties and other taxes on the basis of CRF and furnishing bank guarantee for the difference of the customs duty and other taxes on the basis of tariff value as per the impugned orders. The case of the respondents as writ petitioners was that they opened letters of credit when schedule 1 of the Pre-shipment Inspection of Goods Rules 1996 as notified by SRO No. 244 dated 31-12-1996 contained only 12 items to which CRF Certificates issued by pre-shipment inspection agencies were not to be applicable and the said 12 items did not include consignment of the respondents. Relying on the situation and facilities then prevailing the respondents opened letters of credit for import of various items not included in the aforementioned SRO No. 244 dated 31-12-1996. After inspection CRF Certificates were duly issued in terms of the provisions of section 25A of the Customs Act 1969 and the relevant Rules of 1996. Long after the letters of credit were opened relying on SRO No. 244 dated 31-12-1996, the aforesaid SRO No. 113 dated 11-5-1997 was issued which among other items included the items imported by respondents in schedule 1 of the said 1996 Rules. Since the respondents opened the letters of credit long before SRO No. 113 dated 11-5-1997 which came into effect from that date i.e. 11-5-1997 the respondents had acquired vested right to be assessed on the basis of the rules which existed when the letters of credit were opened by them and the present petitioners by issuing SRO No. 113 dated 11-5-1997 could not take away the said vested right of the respondents in view of the principles as laid down in the decisions reported in 42 DLR (AD) 167, 48 DLR (AD) 199 and also the judgment dated 11-5-1998 passed by this Division in Civil Appeal Nos. 6, 7, 8, 9, 10, 11 and 12 of 1995.

3. The learned Deputy Attorney-General appearing on behalf of the present petitioners submitted that in terms of the provisions of section 30 and 30A read with section 35(7) of the Customs Act 1969 the customs authority had power to fix the tariff value of the imported goods at the rate prevailing at the time of presentation of the Bill of Entry which in all the Rules were filed after 11-5-1997 and in any view of the matter the bar provided in section 30A of the Customs Act 1969, the order for fixation of the value of the consignment on the basis of tariff value fixed under section 16(7) of the Customs Act, calls for no interference. The High Court Division after considering the provisions of section 25A of the Customs Act 1969 and the fact that the respondents before us opened the letter of credit in terms of SRO No. 316 dated 3-11-1994 provided for the release of the goods on the basis of CRF Certificate was in operation and respondents got their goods inspected by the approved Pre-shipment Agency who after inspecting the goods issued CRF certificate in their favour as per provision of said SRO No. 316 dated 3-11-1994 and whereas SRO No. 113 dated 11-5-1997 came into operation long after letters of credit were opened by the respondents it was of the view that the respondents before us had acquired vested right to have the customs duty assessed on their imported goods on the basis of CRF Certificates issued by PSI Agency and letter of credit opened in terms of SRO No. 316 Ain/94 /1568 /Shulka dated 31-12-1994. The SRO No. 113 dated 11-5-1997 having been issued subsequent to the opening of the letters of credit the respondents vested right of assessment of customs duty of their imported goods as per SRO No. 316 dated 3-11-1994 and SRO No. 244 dated 31-12-1996 could not be taken away. The High Court Division found that their view was supported by the decisions given by this Division in the case of Collector of Customs vs A Hannan reported in 42 DLR (AD) 167 and also in the case of Collector of Customs vs Ahmed Hossain reported in 48 DLR (AD) 199 and Mostafizur Rahman vs Government of Bangladesh case reported in 51 DLR (AD) 40. The High Court Division therefore held that the present petitioner acted illegally, arbitrarily and without lawful authority in refusing to release the imported goods on the basis of CRF Certificate issued by the pre-shipment inspection agency and that the SRO No. 113 dated 11-5-1997 could not affect the vested right which accrued to the respondents pursuant to SRO No. 316 dated 3-11-1994 and SRO No. 244 dated 31-12-1996. Accordingly, the impugned orders refusing to accept CRF certificate and directing to fix the customs duties and other taxes on the imported goods on the basis of tariff value were declared to have been passed without any legal basis and of no legal effect. The consignments imported by the respondents were liable to be assessed on the basis of CRF certificate. The petitioners were directed to release the goods against bank guarantees to be furnished by the respondents.

4. This Division granted leave to appeal to consider the submission made by the appellants that the present cases being cases in which the imported goods have been excluded from purview of section 25A of the Customs Act and not being a case of withdrawal, reduction or exemption of duty under section 19 of the Customs Act the decisions reported in 42 DLR (AD) 167 and 48 DLR (AD) 199 have no application in the present cases and the High Court Division committed error of law in making the Rules absolute relying on the aforesaid decisions. Leave was also given on the submission that the imported goods having been excluded from the purview of section 25A of the Customs Act, the value of imported goods is to be assessed in terms of section 25 in view of the provisions of section 30 of the Customs Act and, as such, the High Court Division was wrong in holding that duty has to be paid on CRF value of the goods and that the cases were fully covered by the decision reported in 52 DLR (AD) 149.

<u>5. Since in all these civil appeals common question of law and similar fact are involved the appeals were taken up together for hearing and are being disposed of by this single judgment. Admittedly, the respondents opened letters of credit prior to SRO No. 113 dated 11-5-1997 and arranged for pre-shipment inspection of the imported goods by the approved pre-shipment agencies who after inspecting the imported goods issued clean report of finding (CRF) for the imported goods for the purpose of assessment of customs duties and other taxes in terms of section 25A of the Customs Act 1969 and the relevant Rules 1996 referred earlier. It also appears that the Customs Authority acknowledged the receipt of CRF Certificates but took the view that by SRO No. 113 dated 11-5-1997 the CRF scheme was withdrawn in respect of the imported goods and accordingly, the provisions of CRF under section 25A of the Customs Act 1969 was not applicable to the goods imported by the respondents.</u>

6. It appears that in terms of section 25A read with section 219(1) of the aforesaid Customs Act, the Government issued SRO No. 244 dated 31-12-1996 framing the Pre-shipment Inspection of Goods Rules 1996 making provision for issuance of clean report of finding certificate (CRF) by approved pre-shipment inspection agencies and schedule 1 of the said Rules initially containing descriptions of only 12 items to which the CRF was not applicable. Subsequently, other items were included in the said list as it appears by SRO No. 113 dated 11-5-1997. The imported goods of the respondents were also included in schedule 1 and thereby imported consignments were excluded from the purview of the CRF scheme and relying on this SRO No. 113 dated 11-5-1997 the petitioners by the impugned orders, refused to accept the CRF in respect of the imported goods of the respondents. We are now to examine whether by obtaining CRF certificate under provisions of section 25A of the Customs Act the respondent importers acquired vested right to be assessed at the rate of duty prevailing on the date of opening of the letters of credit similar to the right acquired under section 19 of the Customs Act as found by this Division in 42 DLR (AD) 167 and in 48 DLR (AD) 199 which could not be taken away by issuing another SRO subsequent to the date of opening of the letters of credit canceling or reducing the exemption as provided earlier. This Division in its judgment dated 10th May 1995 passed in Civil Appeal Nos. 6, 7, 8, 9, 10, 11 and 12 of 1995 also applied the above principles as laid down in the above two cases of fixing or re-fixing of tariff value of the goods holding that the mode of valuation and or the rate of value as prevailing on the date of opening of the letter of credit, have to be taken into consideration while assessing customs duties and other taxes and the subsequent notification enhancing or fixing of tariff value cannot affect the vested right of the importer regarding fixation of the valuation of goods as per any notification or any matter prevailing at the time of opening of the letter of credit. Relying on the principles as laid down by this Division in the above cases the High Court Division was of the view that since in the present cases the respondents opened letters of credit in February/March 1997, the sub-sequent notification No. 113 dated 11-5-1997 could not affect the vested right of the respondents and the customs authority was under obligation to accept the CRF certificates. It noted that section 30A of the Customs Act 1969 came into effect from 1-7-1995 and present goods were imported subsequent to that date and that the sections 30A and 25A came into operation on the same date i.e. on 1-7-1995. But in section 30A there is no clause excluding the operation of section 25A and therefore, was of the view that the provisions of section 30A of the Customs Act was not applicable to the provisions of section 25A of the Customs Act relating to the CRF and the Rules framed and notifications issued thereunder.

7. This Division in the case Bangladesh vs Mizanur Rahman reported in 52 DLR (AD) 149 took a different view on the question of acquiring vested right under notification of tariff prior to the opening of the letter of credit. It was, inter alia, held:

"That section 25(1) of the Act provides for determination of value of imported goods on the basis of normal price and sub-section (7) provides for fixing of tariff value by the Government by notification published in the official gazette for the purpose of levying of customs duty and as section 25(7) was not interpreted in 48 DLR (AD) 199 it is difficult to hold in the fact of sections 25(7) and 30 that earlier SRO will prevail when the letter of credit was opened and not the subsequent SRO when new tariff value was declared for levying customs duty. The argument of acquiring vested right may be tenable in case of exemption granted in a special circumstances as in Hannan's case but it is difficult to understand that normal importer would acquire vested right in the invoice value or the tariff value prevailing at the time of opening of letter of credit. The Government has the power to fix tariff value by publishing notification in the official gazette and this power has been vested in the Government under sub-section (7) of section 25 of the Act to fix tariff value of imported or exported goods by notification. As a matter of fact the then Attorney-General could not bring to our notice the distinguishing feature between Hannan's case and the case of Mustafizur Rahman, 51 DLR (AD) 40 which was a case under section 25(7) of the Act. As the present case is under section 25(7) of the Customs Act we are of the view that customs duty is payable by the importer-respondent on the basis of tariff value in force on the date of presentation of the bill of entry and not on the basis of invoice or tariff value in force at the time of opening of letter of credit. So the decision in 51 DLR (AD) 40 appears to us to be not correctly decided due to the failure of the then Attorney-General to point out the distinction between 42 DLR (AD) 167 and 48 DLR (AD) 199 on the one hand and the case of Mustafizur Rahman on the other. Even he failed to bring to our notice the case of Khairul Bashar vs Collector of Customs, 50 DLR 225 in which the High Court Division correctly noticed the distinction between exemption under section 19 of the Act and declaration of tariff value under section 25(7) of the Act and did not follow the ratio decidendi of 42 DLR (AD) 167 and 48 DLR (AD) 199 and held that importer acquires no vested right in the invoice value or the tariff value existing at the time of opening of letter of credit. We therefore, review our opinion expressed in that decision in 51 DLR (AD) 40 and hold that no vested right is acquired by the importer to pay sales tax and customs duty on the basis of tariff value declared by notification in force on the date of opening the letter of credit. The importer has to pay tax and duty on the basis of tariff value in force on the date on presentation of bill of entry."

8. We notice from the above judgment that this Division while making a distinction between Hannan's case (42 DLR) and Mustafizur Rahman Case (52 DLR) has observed that argument of acquiring vested right may be tenable in case of exemption granted in special circumstances as in Hannan's case. In that case this Division considered the contention of the appellants Collector of Customs that the notification under section 19 of the Customs Act is always subject to the provision of section 30 which would prevail over the notification issued under section 19 of the Customs Act. The facts in that case were that by a notification issued under SRO it was notified that in exercise of the powers conferred by section 19 of the Customs Act 1969 (IV of 1969) and section 4(1) of the Sales Tax Ordinance, 1982 (XVIII of 1982), the Government was pleased to exempt sugar from so much of customs duty and sales tax liable thereon as is in excess of 50% and 10% respectively, subject to the fulfillment of the terms and conditions specified in the Public Notice No. 28 (84-85) Import dated 3-10-1984, issued by the Chief Controller of Imports and Exports, Dhaka. The importer opened his letter of credit relying on the exemption which was withdrawn prior to the presentation of the bill of entry. The importer had relied upon vested right on credit under section 19 of the Customs Act. It was held by this Division in that case that the notification under section 19 was issued without any condition, limitation or restrictions excepting those which have been mentioned as "terms and conditions" therein. Several cases were discussed one being the case on Union of India vs Anglo Afghan Agencies AIR 1968 (SC) 718 in which it was inter alia, observed that even assuming that the provisions relating to the issue of Trade Notices offering inducement to the prospective exporters were in character executive, the Union Government and its officers were not entitled at their mere whim to ignore the promises made by the Government. It could not be said that the Textile Commissioner was the sole judge of the quantum of import licence to be granted to an exporter, and that the Courts were powerless to grant relief, if the promised import licence was not given to an exporter who had acted to his prejudice relying upon the representation. Hence, the persons aggrieved because of the failure to carry out the terms of the Scheme were entitled to seek resort to the Court and claim that the obligation imposed upon the Textile Commissioner by the Scheme be ordered to be carried out. After reviewing certain English cases the Supreme Court of India observed:

"That even though the case did not fall within the terms of section 115 of the Evidence Act, it was still open to a party who had acted on a representation made by the Government to claim that the Government shall be bound to carry out the promise made by it, even though the promise was not recorded in the form of a formal contract as required by Article 299 of the Constitution."

9. This Division therefore held that this case completely demolished the argument of the learned Additional Attorney-General that no formal contract was executed between the parties. It was taken into account that the respondent in Hannan's case had clearly acted upon the Government's assurance, and imported sugar, and because of such assurance the Government was estopped from denying such position. The respondent acting upon the solemn promise made by the appellant incurred huge expenditure and if the appellant was not held to its promise, the respondent would be put in a disadvantageous position and, therefore, the principle of promissory estoppel could be invoked in the case. Hannan's case was distinguished from Mizanur Rahman's case where this Division held that no such vested right acquired nor a promise could be implied to determine the normal value on the basis of the invoice of tariff value in force at the time of the letter of credit and therefore, customs duty was payable by the importer on the basis of tariff value in force on the date of presentation of the bill of entry.

10. The present case before us is on the question whether any vested right was created when the letters of credit were opened on the basis of CRF under section 25A of the Customs Act. Section 25A provides for pre-shipment inspection agencies and assessment on the basis of their certificates. Section 25A of the Customs Act 1969 as amended till 1-7-1995 which applies to the present case reads as follows:

"Notwithstanding anything contained in any other section of this Act, the Government may, by notification in the official gazette, declare that the quality, quantity, price and customs classification of goods verified and certified in the prescribed manner by an approved pre-shipment inspection agency will be accepted as the basis for assessment.

Explanation—For the purpose of this section, 'price' shall mean the normal price determined in accordance with sub-sections (1) and (2) of section 25."

After amendment in 1999 section 25A reads as follows:

(1)	For the purposes of this Act, the Government may, in the prescribed manner, appoint pre-shipment inspection agencies and determine the scope and manner of their certification and related matters.

(2)	The Government may, by notification in the official gazette, declare that the quality, quantity, price, description and customs classification of any goods verified and certified in the prescribed manner by a pre-shipment inspection agency shall be accepted as the basis for assessment.

(3)	For the purpose of this section, 'price' means value of the goods determined in accordance with sub-sections (1) and (2) of section 25.

11. We have seen that this Division in Mizanur Rahman's case has accepted that the argument of vested right may be tenable in specific circumstances as reduction or exemption of customs duty under section 19 of the Customs Act. It has been recognised by superior Courts of the sub-continent that specific assurance made by the Government may give rise to equitable protection under promissory estoppel. The question is whether a notification under section 25A of the Customs Act gives rise to a vested right and protection under promissory estoppel. Section 25A as amended till 1995 provides that the price verified and certified in the prescribed manner by an approved pre-shipment inspection agency will be accepted as the basis for assessment and the price verified and certified in the prescribed manner by an approved pre-shipment inspection agency will be accepted as the basis for assessment and the price under this section means the value of the goods determined in accordance with sub-sections (1) and (2) of section 25. The respondents relying on the notification under this section acted to their detriment by having their goods inspected by inspectors appointed by the Government and by incurring expenses for such inspection. Would in such special circumstance of Government's assurance that the price so determined by the inspection would be accepted by them as the basis for assessment create a vested right? Would it be inequitable and unjust to allow the government to treat such inspection certificate as an idle exercise and a scrap of paper having no value at all? The promise of accepting the price having been made by the appellant under a law, should the Government be bound by such a promise when the other side has acted bonafide and to his detriment relying on that promise?

12. In the case of MP Sugar Mills vs State of UP reported in AIR 1979 SC 621 Justice Bhagwati has elaborately, inter alia, discussed the meaning of promissory estoppel and to what extent the parties including the State are bound by the principle of promissory estoppel. He has referred to and discussed several decisions of the English Courts on the subject. He has referred to Mr. Justice Denning as he then was, in High Trees case who observed: "that a promise intended to be binding, intended to be acted on and, in fact, acted on, is binding so far as its terms properly apply." Lord Denning added a qualification that though in the circumstances set out, the promise would undoubtedly be held by the courts to be binding on the party making it, not understanding that under the old common law it might be difficult to find any consideration for it, "the courts have not gone so far as to give a cause of action in damages for the breach of such a promise, but they have refused to allow the party making it to act inconsistently with it." Lord Denning also pointed out in Combe vs Combe, (1951) 2 KB 215 "Much as I am inclined to favour the principle stated in the High Trees' case, it is important that it should not be stretched too far, lest it should be endangered. That principle does not create new causes of action where none existed before. It only prevents a party from insisting upon his strict legal rights, when it would be unjust to allow him to enforce them, having regard to the dealings which have taken place between the parties..... ". He also referred to what Buckley, J said in the case of Beesly vs Hallwood Estates Ltd (1960) 2 All ER 314. "The doctrine may afford a defence against the enforcement or otherwise of enforceable rights: it cannot create a cause of action." Commenting on this observations Justice Bhagwati said:

"It is however, necessary to make it clear that though this doctrine has been called in various judgments and text books as promissory estoppel and it has been variously described as 'equitable estoppel', quasi estoppel and 'new estoppel, it is not really based on the principle of estoppel, but it is a doctrine evolved by equity in order to prevent injustice where a promise is made by a person knowing that it would be acted on by the person to whom it is made and in fact, it is so acted on and it is inequitable to allow the party making the promise to go back upon it. They are really promises, promises intended to be binding intended to be acted upon and in fact acted upon. It is an equitable principle evolved by the courts for doing justice and there is no reason why it should be given only a limited application by way of defence."

13. Justice Bhagwati also discussed various cases against the Crown. He found that the doctrine of executive necessity propounded by Rowlatt, J., was, in fact, disapproved by Denning, J., as he then was, in Robertson vs Minister of Pensions (1949-1 KB 227) where the learned Judge said:

"The Crown cannot escape by saying that estoppels do not bind the Crown for that doctrine has long been exploded. Nor can the Crown escape by praying in aid the doctrine of executive necessity, that is, the doctrine that the Crown cannot bind itself so as to fetter its future executive action. " It is true that the decision of Denning, J., in this case was overruled by the House of Lords in Howell vs Falmouth Boat Construction Co Ltd 1951 (SC) 837 but that was on the ground that the doctrine of promissory estoppel cannot be invoked to "bar the Crown from enforcing a statutory prohibition or entitle the subject to maintain that there has been no breach of it." The decision of the House of Lords did not express any disapproval of the applicability of the doctrine of promissory estoppel against the Crown nor did it overrule the view taken by Denning, J., that the Crown cannot escape its obligation under the doctrine of promissory estoppel by 'praying in aid the doctrine of executive necessity'. The statement of the law by Denning, J., may, therefore, still be regarded as holding the field and it may be taken to be a judicially favoured view that the Crown is not immune from liability under the doctrine of promissory estoppel."

<u>14. Among the conclusions drawn by the Supreme Court of India in MP Sugar Mills vs State of UP are</u>

<u>"Doctrine of promissory estoppel has been variously called 'promissory estoppel', 'requisite estoppel', 'quasi estoppel' and 'new estoppel'. It is a principle evolved by equity to avoid injustice and though commonly named 'promissory estoppel', it is neither in the realm of contract nor in the realm of estoppel. The true principle of promissory estoppel seems to be that where one party has by his words or conduct made to the other a clear and unequivocal promise which is intended to create legal relations or effect a legal relationship to arise in the future, knowing or intending that it would be acted upon by the other party to whom the promise is made and it is in fact so acted upon by the other party, the promise would be binding on the party making it and he would not be entitled to go back upon it, if it would be inequitable to allow him to do so having regard to the dealings which have taken place between the parties, and this would be so irrespective of whether there is any preexisting relationship between the parties or not. The doctrine of promissory estoppel need not be inhibited by the same limitation as estoppel in the strict sense of the term. It is an equitable principle evolved by the courts for doing justice and there is no reason why it should be given only a limited application by way of defence. There is no reason, logic or principle why promissory estoppel should also not be available as a cause of action, if necessary, to satisfy the equity."</u>

<u>15. Having discussed the relevant law and decisions with regard to vested right and promissory estoppel we are of the view that the position of the parties in the present case is like those arising out of promise made under section 19 of the Customs Act to exempt the import taxes and duties under special circumstances. The importers having acted on the promise made by the appellant under section 25A of the Act to accept the price determined by the government appointed inspectors and the appellants cannot go back on that promise as it was meant to be binding on them.</u>

<u>16. We may note here that section 30A of the Customs Act 1969 came into effect from 1-7-1995 and the present consignment were imported subsequent to that date. However it also appears that both section 30A and section 25A, came into operation on the same date i.e. on 1-7-1995 but in section 30A there is nothing to suggest that it excluded the operation of section 25A of the Customs Act. It is further noticed that section 25A (subsequently amended by F 16 of 1999 with effect from 1st July 1999) that at the relevant time the section contained non-obstantive clause like "Notwithstanding anything contained in any other section of this Act which means that it included section 30A of the Customs Act. Therefore, section 25A would prevail over all other sections including sections 25(7) and section 30A of the Customs Act. The High Court Division observed that section 30A of the Customs Act is a fiscal law putting restrictions; it is liable to be interpreted restrictively. In view of the matter they were of the view that provision of section 30A of the Customs Act will not be applicable to the provisions of section 25A of the Customs Act and also to the Rule framed and notifications issued thereunder.</u>

<u>17. In the light of our discussion and observation of our discussion we are in agreement with the decision of the High Court Division that Notification No. 113 dated 11-5-1997 cannot affect vested rights of the respondents to be assessed on the basis of CRF price and the impugned orders passed in Writ Petition Nos. 3052, 3077, 3099, 4148, 3226, 3230, 3228, 3050, 3051, 3108, 3683 and 3676, of 1997 respectively on 27-5-1997, 25-5-1997 and 25-5-1997, 28-5-1997, 24-6-1997, 29-5-1997, 1-6-1997 and 25-5-1997, 28-5-1997, 27-5-1997, 26-5-1997, 24-5-1997, 16-6-1997 and 17-6-1997 refusing to accept CRF certificate and directing for fixing customs duty and other taxes on the imported goods on the basis of the tariff value, are declared to have been passed without any legal basis and are of no legal effect.</u>

All the appeals are dismissed without any order as to costs.

End.

case_source: (From the judgment and Decree date 24-2-1966 passed by the Dacca High Court in S. A. No. 1917 of 1961).
full_judgment:
Kemaluddin Hossain, J. This is a Defendant's appeal by special leave arising out of a suit for recovery of possession of the suit land upon declaration of the plaintiffs title therein. The suit land is R.S. Plot No. 158 of mouza Madar Bari, Chittagong recorded in Khatian No. 234. Plaintiff says that the suit plot was recorded in raiyati right of Abdus Subhan. Plaintiff took, long lease of the land from the heirs of Subhan. This land is to the contiguous east of other lands of the plaintiff. They were wrongfully taken possession of by the defendants but the plaintiff succeeded in obtaining a decree for their eviction in Title Suit No. 5 of 1947. Out of spite for eviction, the defendants dispossessed the plaintiff by dismantling collie huts on the disputed lands 10 May, 1955. Hence the suit.

2. The appellant who is defendant No. 1 alone contested the suit. He denies plaintiff's title and the case of possession and dispossession. He challenges the correctness of the entry in the record of rights in the mine of Subhan He sets up his inherited tenancy right from his grandfather Ramzan Alternative he asserts that the suit is barred by adverse possession.

3. The learned Subordinate, Judge who tried the suit dismissed it, holding that the plaintiff failed to make out his title, and that the suit was barred by limitation, as the defendants were in adverse possession of the suit land for over 12 years.

4. On appeal by the plaintiff the first appellate Court found that the defendant's claim of title on the basis of Ext. B, Kabuliyat standing in the name of Ramzan did not subsist. He referred to two judgments, one in Title Suit No. 5 of 1941, and the other S.C.C. Suit No. 290 of 1941, Ext. 7(a) and 11. He also referred to Ext. F, written statement of Abdul Majid, father of defendant No. 1. Along with them, he considered Ext. 10, Khatian No. 234, relating to the suit land, and came to the conclusion that from these papers it was established that Ramzan's 5 years tenancy on the basis of Ext. was terminated by his superior landlord, Moifula Khatun, who in her turn settled the land with other tenants. The decisions of the aforesaid suits were binding on defendant No. 1 regarding this claim of title, As. regards plaintiff's title he differed with the, trial Court on the presumptive value of Khatian and treated it is evidence of title as well. He thereafter considered the oral and documentary evidence of both the plaintiff and defence on possession. He considered Ext. A to A4 Municipal demand register, Ext. C to C-7 the Municipal Tax receipts, Ext. G and G-l sale deeds, Ext. D and Ext. E filed by Defendant No. 1 and hold that they did not establish adverse possession of the defence on the suit land. He held so, after rejecting the second pleader commissioner's report. Earlier, a pleader commissioner's report had been rejected. The reason for rejecting the second report was that it was not prepared by surveying the land or with reference to the Municipal map. He disbelieved the defence witnesses but believed the plaintiff's witnesses, and found that the plaintiff succeeded in proving his dispossession in 1955 He hold that defendant No. 1 erected pucca and katcha structures on the land after dispossession of plaintiff. He also held that the plaintiff's suit was not barred by limitation. He reversed the decision of the Trial Court and decreed the suit.

5. The defendant No. 1 preferred a second appeal to the East Pakistan High Court and it was heard by a Division Bench. The High Court concurred with the First Appellate Court both as regards title and possession In favour of plaintiff and dismissed the appeal. The defendant No.1 appeal obtained leave from the Supreme Court of Pakistan to consider the following points.

i)Whether the plaintiff has failed to prove his title to the suit land and

ii)Whether oral and documentary evidence adduced by the defendant to prove his possession of the suit land for the statutory period, and which was accepted by the Subordinate Judge, did not receive due and full consideration in the appellate Courts.

6. Mr. B.N. Chowdhury has appeared on behalf of defendant No. 1 appellant and Mr. M.H. Khandker for the plaintiff-Respondent. Learned Counsels of both sides have advanced lengthy, and learned arguments. We however, do not feel the necessity of adverting at length to them as we find that the question involved in this appeal should be disposed of with reference to points raised in the leave order.

<u>7.The points referred to in the leave order, though mentions question of title, and possession separately, yet in facts of the present case, the two questions are interdependent arid should be treated as such. It is to be remembered that the suit plot viz., R.S. 158 of Khatian No. 234 is part of the Kabuliyat land of Ramzan, grandfather of the appellant. We are to proceed with the questions of title and possession, keeping this basic fact in view. Both the plaintiff and defendant No. 1 claim tenancy right in the land. They also claim possessory right over the land, defendant No. 1 claims expressly adverse possession, and plaintiff by implication, in tracing his title from Subhan. Plaintiff, however, came with the. story of possession followed by dispossession and is seeking eviction of defendants from the suit land. It is well settled that when a defendant is in possession, he could be evicted only by person having a better title than he. In such suit, plaintiff can only succeed by proving his better title over suit land. Has the plaintiff succeeded in doing so in the present case ?</u>

8. This question requires investigation and before we undertake it, it may be observed, that the concurrent findings of courts below cannot now be disturbed, regarding defendant No. 1's claim of tenancy right that it has failed. Evidence, documentary and oral, is ample to show that the Kabuliyat Ext. B of 1915 in favour of Ramzan, grandfather of Defendant No. 1 was terminated by the superior landlord, Moifula Khatun, who settled the land thereafter, with other tenants. In this view, a detailed discussion on defendant's title is not called for. But that does not automatically create title in favour of the plaintiff.

9. Plaintiff claims a derivative title from Subhan. According to him Subhan held the suit land in rayati right which was inherited by his heirs, two sons and wife, and they, by a patta, Ext. 4 dated 28-7-54, settled the land with him. Plaintiff in 1955 purchased the superior rayati right of his lessors, and thereby succeeded to the sixteen annas title of Subhan in the suit land. No doubt plaintiff.has produced the Patta Ext. 4, and the Kabla received from the heirs of Subhan one in 1954, and the other in 1955. The question is not the validity of the patta, but whether the lessors of the plaintiff had any transferable right. That again depends upon the fact whether they inherited any such transferable right from their predecessor, Subhan. Is there any evidence to show that Subhan held any tenancy right as claimed by the plaintiff ? The plaintiff except making his own bare assertion, and reliance on R.S. Khatian, Ext. 10, has adduced no evidence, oral or documentary. Plaintiff being a transferee from the heirs of Subhan, has not and cannot claim direct knowledge of the creation of tenancy in favour of Subhan. He could, however, lead evidence to prove the creation of tenancy. That he has not done. His case of title rests on the alleged presumption of correctness of settlement records.

10. The High Court has taken a view that although, an entry in the record of right would indicate the possessory right of the person whose name appears therein, but this also lends support to the claim of title made by the plaintiff. It seems to us, that this view of the High Court does not state the correct view of law on the presumption arising from the record of right. Both the learned counsel have on this point, cited a number of decisions. Apart from the cited decisions, there are a large number of authorities on this point, Some of them may be mentioned. Rani Harshamukhi Vs. Kshitindra, 47 C.W.N. 662, Anup Mahto Vs. Mita Dusadh 38 C.W.N. 365 (P.C.), Sri Nath Rai Vs. Pratap Udai Nath Sahi Deo, 28 C.W.N. 145 (P.C.), Pankajini Debi Vs. Suair Dutta 60 C.W.N. 793, Munnalal Vs. Mst. Kashibai 51 C.W.N. 175, Narendra Vs ( Rajendra 45 C.W.N. 654 ; Rai Kiran Chandra Roy Bahadur Vs. Srinath Chakrabarti 31 C.W.N. 135, Kumar Rai Vs. Baraboni Coal A.I.R. 1935 Calcutta 368, Jemarat Ali Vs. Rahman Sardar 17 D.L.R. Dacca 589, Pramatha Nath Vs. Kamir Mondal 17 D.L.R. (S.C.) 392.

11. Not all the cited authorities are. directly on the question before us, nor do we feel the necessity of referring to all of them in detail. From the cited decisions, we find that the preponderance of the judicial opinion is that the presumption of correctness arsing from the record of right under s. 103B of the Bengal Tenancy Act raises a presumption of possession in favour of person whose name is recorded therein at the time of its final publication. No forward or backward presumption arises from correctness of record of right. For drawing backward presumption there must be some evidence. Forward presumption however is not available from the s. 103B of Bengal Tenancy Act, but a presumption of continuity may be drawn under s. 114 (d) of the Evidence Act. This forward presumption becomes weaker with the passage of time, and its probative value diminishes progressively with the lapse of time.

<u>12. Record of right is not a document of title. It does not create or extinguish title to land. At best, along with other evidence, it may support an evidence of title. By itself, it is not an evidence of title. The view of the High Court seems to have been overstated.</u>

13. We may now turn to the facts of the case. R.S. Khatian of the plot, Ext. 10, shows a tenancy was recorded in the name of Subhan under, Moifula Khatun. The record of right was published some time in 1927. Initial presumption of correctness of recording of possession of 1927 in favour of Subhan is there. Barring Khatian, the plaintiff has led no evidence on the creation of tide of Subhan. Plaintiff leading no evidence, either oral or documentary, cannot use the Khatian as evidence of title in favour of Subhan. The High Court was wrong in presuming title in favour of Subhan barely relying on Khatian. Bereft of this Khatian, there is no evidence of creation tenancy in favour of Subhan. The plaintiff has failed to prove that the heirs of Subhan acquired any transferable right to confer upon plaintiff by patta Ext. 4 Plaintiff has therefore valid to make out a valid title in his favour on the basis of Patta,

14. We have observed earlier that the questions of possession and title are interlinked in this case, and therefore the second question raised in the leave order is to be discussed along with the first question.

<u>15. With regard to possessory title, we find defendant No. 1 has expressly and the plaintiff impliedly claimed so. The First Appellate Court and the High Court no doubt have discussed the question of adverse possession of the defendant. They have also made a thorough discussion of the evidence as to dispossession of the plaintiff, and these findings cannot be assailed now. But then, unless the plaintiff can make out his title, he cannot recover possession, now that the Defendant-appellant is on the land. Mr. B.N. Chowdhury has made strenuous effort in challenging the findings of the appellate Courts below, but a reference to the records reveals, that all relevant papers and oral evidence called by the appellant, have been thoroughly discussed the grievance of Mr. Chowdhury amounts to reconsideration of evidence afresh, a submission which is difficult to sustain.</u>

<u>16. Defendant No. 1’s claim both as regards title and adverse possession has failed; still then for the plaintiff to succeed, he has to make out a title in his favour. Though the plaintiff has failed on the acquisition of his title from Subhan's heir on the basis of Patta Ext. 4 yet prescriptive title of his predecessors may nonetheless subsist by continuous possession of Subhan and his heirs Plaintiff's registered patta Ext. 4 as a genuine document remains unchallenged, and so, if, he can show possessory title of his predecessors for the prescriptive period, he can still succeed in showing the acquisition of title in his favour. It appears, that this question bas not drawn the attention of either the First. Appellate Court or the High Court since they found title for plaintiff on the basis of patta But that finding having failed, this question assumes importance, and has now become decisive. It will be open to plaintiff to show the continuous possession of Subhan and his heirs, either direct or constructive on the Suit land for the prescriptive period before the grant of Patta in his favour. We feel that a determination of this question is necessary for complete adjudication of dispute between the parties. It is a mixed question of law and fact. We think therefore, the case should be remitted to the First appellate Court for decision of this narrow question; whether Subhan and his heirs were in possession direct or constructive at least from 1927, the year of publication of the Khatian till the Patta in 1954 was granted in favour of the plaintiff. Alternatively the plaintiff can show Subhan and/or his heirs were in possession for over the prescriptive period of 12 years prior to the grant of Patta on 28-7-54. Plaintiff, succeeding in establishing any of the alternatives, will be entitled to a decree for eviction on declaration of his title, as all other relevant questions have concurrently been held by the appellate Courts below in his favour. In this view of the matter, we refrain from making any observation on this question. The Court shall proceed to decide on the evidence already on record.</u>

17. In the result we allow the appeal in part. The decisions of the first appellate Court and the High Court regarding (a) the defence case of title and adverse possession have failed, and (b) the plaintiff has proved dispossession in May, 1955 are affirmed. The decisions of the said Courts below regarding the title of plaintiff are set aside and the appeal remitted back to the First Appellate Court to dispose of the question in the manner indicated above and in accordance with law. The First Appellate Court shall be at liberty to allow the parties to call such additional evidence on the question as it may deem fit.

In the circumstances of the case we make no order as to costs.

End.

full_judgment:
Gour Gopal Saha J: This appeal is directed against the judgment and decree passed by the 2nd Court of Sub-Judge, Chittagong in partition suit No. 3 of 1969 decreeing the suit. By this impugned judgment the learned Subordinate Judge, allotted a saham for 37.06 acres of land to the plaintiffs and a separate saham to defendant Nos. 1-18, 20-30 and 31 for 39.70 acres of land.

2. The case of the plaintiffs, in short, is that the suit land measuring 17 drones 5 kanis 1 gonda and 1 kara as described in schedules to the plaintiff originally belonged to Fazal Karim Khan, who possessed the same in khas. While being the rightful owner-in-possession Fazal Kabir settled 14 drones of the land with Md Putan by a registered patta dated 2nd Falgoon, 1308 BS and since than he owned and possessed the same. The said suit land was, of course, acquired by Putan in the benami of his son Ali Hossain on 1-2-1901 but he was the real ostensible owner of the land as it was acquired with his own money and for his own benefit. After taking settlement Md Putan possessed the suit land in khas on payment of rent to the landlords. After some time landlord Fazal . Khan forcibly dispossessed Mr Putan from the said land whereupon Md Putan filed. TS No. 111 of 1906 against the said Fazal Kabir Khan for recovery of khas possession in the said 14 drones of lands out of the suit land on declaration of his title thereto and the said suit was eventually decreed on contest on 18-3-1907. Against the aforesaid Judgment and decree Fazal Kabir Khan filed Title Appeal No. 161 of 1911 but the said appeal was allowed due to formal defects in the plaint. Ali Hossain, a son and benamder of Md Putan for the aforesaid 14 droned of lands out of the suit land was added as a pro-forma defendant in the aforesaid Title Suit No. 89 of 1909. During the pendency of the aforesaid Title Appeal No. 161 of 1911 Fazal Kabir Khan transferred his superior interest in the aforesaid 14 drones of lands and khas interest in 3 drones 5 kanis 1 gonda and 1 kara of lands out of the suit land to his wife Ruh Afza alias Alimannessa by a registered deed of gift acted 18th Magh, 1316. BS. In this way the right, title, interest and possession of Md Putan in the 14 drones of lands were clearly established. Subsequently, the aforesaid Ruh Afza alias Alimannessa transferred her superior interest in the 14 drones of lands and khas interest in 3 drones 5 kanis 1 gonda and 1 kara of land out of the suit land to Md Putan by a registered kabala dated 10-6-1912, corresponding to 26th Baishak 1319 BS on receipt of proper consideration and he duly delivered possession thereof to Md Putan. In this way Md Putan owned and passed the entire suit land by way of settlement from Fazal Kabir Khan and by way of purchase by registered kabala from his wife Ruh Afza alias Alimannessa. In course of time, Md Putan executed a power of attorney in favour of his eldest son Ali Hossain for management of the suit property for its proper management and administration as he was unable to look after it properly due to his old age. Thereafter Ali Hossain kot mortgaged the suit property with one Sultan Ahmed Bahaddar on behalf of his father Mr Putan, on the strength of the said power of attorney, in order to save the suit property from auction sale for arrears of land revenue. Subsequently, Md Putan died in 1919 leaving Ali Hossain, Omar Ali, Ali Akbar, the predecessor of plaintiffs, Nos. 1-3 and defendant Nos. 1-6, 8-10 and 12-19, 20 and 30 as 3 sons and Khatijan, Johra and Fatema, the predecessor of plaintiff Nos. 4-15 and defendant No. 7 and 1 as 3 daughters as. his heirs and heiresses. In this way, each son of Md Putan acquired 2/9 share and each daughter of Md Putan acquired 1/9 share in the suit property. Then Khadeja died leaving Ejahar Meah and the predecessor of plaintiff Nos. 11-15, as two sons to succeed her. Thereafter Johara died leaving plaintiff Nos. 6-10 and defendant No. 7 as her heirs. Then Fatema died leaving plaintiffs Nos. 4-5 as her heirs. Thus the plaintiffs have calmed right, title and interest in 6 drones 6 kanis and 19 gondas of land out of the suit land by inheritance from Ali Akbar, son of Md Putan and Khadeja, Johara and Fatema, the 3 daughters of Md Putan, Omar Ali, son of Md Putan died leaving defendant No. 8 as son and defendant Nos. 9-10 and 12 and one Mahmuda Khatun as 4 daughters to succeed him. Thereafter, Mahmuda Khatun died leaving defendant Nos. 13-14 as heirs. Ali Hossain died leaving defendant Nos. 15-17 as 3 sons and defendant Nos. 18, 20, and 30 as 3 daughters and Pear Jan as wife. Defendant No. 31 has acquired the share of Pear Jan in the suit land by purchase by a registered kabala. Defendant No. 32 acquired the share of defendant No. 20 in the suit land by, purchase. Ali Akbar died leaving plaintiff Nos. 1-3 and defendant Nos. 1-6 to succeed him. After the death of Md Putan one Makbul Ali created a fraudulent and collusive kabala in respect of the suit land from Fazal Kabir Khan. Thereafter one Elahadad Chowdhury, father of defendant No. 27 and the brother''s son of said Makbul Ali acquired the kot mortgage interest in the suit land from Sultan Ahmed Bahaddar by a registered kabala dated 11-9-1924 corresponding to 26th Jaistha 1286. BS on payment of proper consideration and he possessed the suit land in khas as the mortgagee under the heirs and heiresses.of Md Putan through Sultan Ahmed Bahaddar. Makbul Ali acquired no right, title and interest in his suit land by his alleged kabala from Fazal Kabir Khan, who had already transferred his right, title and interest in the suit land to his wife Ruh Afza by a registered deed of gift and the said Ruh Afza in her turn, transferred her right, title and interest in the suit land to Md Putan. Ali though Md Putan became the absolute owner of 14 drones of land, the names of his heirs and heiresses were not recorded in the RS Khatian due to sheer inadvertent mistake. The RS record was prepared in the names of Ali Hossain and Elahadad Chowdhury as the mortgagees. The RS Record is evidently wrong and it is not binding upon the plaintiffs. As the aforesaid Elahadad Chowdhury being in possession of the suit property on the basis of purchase of the kot mortgage interest of Sultan Ahmed Bahaddar by registered kabalas, failed to pay rent for the suit land to the landlords the suit property was put to auction sale for arrears of rent and the said Elahadad Chowdhury fraudulently auction purchased the suit property in the benami of his uncle Jinnat Ali on 20-5-1931. Thereafter the said Elahadad Chowdhury created a collusive deed of relinquishment in his favour for the suit land in collusion with his uncle Makbul Ali and Jinnat Ali and, as such, Elahadad Chowdhury acquired no right, title and interest in the suit property. Elahabad Chowdhury then created a fraudulent, collusive and void deed of partition in respect of the suit property with some heirs of Ali Hossain on 25-2-1940 following which one of the heirs of Ali Hossain filed CS No. 13 of 1951 against the heirs of Ali Hossain and Elahadad Chowdhury for redemption of mortgage of the suit property and the said suit was eventually decreed on compromise in terms of a solenama filed by the heirs of late Elahadad Chowdhury and defendant Nos. 15-18 in the suit but the plaintiffs were not made parties in the aforesaid suit. Now coming to the documentary evidence adduced by the contending parties in support of their respective claims of title and possession we are to consider how far the contending parties have been able to substantiate their claims with reference to the exhibited documents. The case of the plaintiffs is that the suit land comprising 17 drones 5 kanis 1 gonda and 1 kara as fully described in schedule Ka'' to the plaint formerly belonged to Fazal Kabir Khan who possessed the same in khas. In course of time, the said Fazal Kabir Khan settled 14 drones of land with Md Putan, the predecessor-in-interest of the plaintiffs and some of the defendants, by a registered patta dated 1-2-1919 in the benami of his son Ali Hossain, who owned and possessed the same. Thereafter, Fazal Kabir Khan transferred the said 14 drones of land along with other 3 drones 5 kanis 1 gonda 1 kara of land to his wife Ruh Afza by a registered deed of gift whereby he transferred the rent receiving interest to his wife in the 14 drones of land and the jote right in 3 drones 5 kanis and 1 kara of land. The said Ruh Afza thereafter sold her entire interests of the suit property to Md Putan by registered kabalas. Although this land was acquired by registered kabala by Md Putan in the benami of his son Ali Hossain, the latter was simply a name lender and Md Putan owned and possesAd the disputed land in his own right and for his own benefit. The contention of defendant No. 21, on the other hand, is that Md Putan and Ali Hossain jointly acquired 14 drones of the land out of the suit land from Fazal Kabir Khan by way of settlement by a registered patta dated 1-2-1901 by which they acquired the rent receiving interest in the said land and khash interest in 3 drones 5 kanis, 1 kara and 1 gonda of land by purchase from Ruh Afza, wife of Fazal Kabir Khan. The plaintiffs and defendant Nos. 1-18, 20 and 30 are the heirs and sons and daughters of Md Putan. The contending defendant No. 21 admitted that Md Putan acquired 14 drones of land in the suit land by way of settlement from Fazal Kabir Khan in Dar Jote right by a registered patta. Md Putan also acquired the rent receiving interest in the said 14 drones of land and jote interest in only 3 drones 5 kanis 1 gonda and 1 kara by way of purchase by a registered kabala from Ruh Afza in the benami of his son Ali Hossain. The plaintiff''s, witnesses uniformly stated that Ali Hossain was simply a benamder in respect of the suit land covered by registered patta dated 1-10-1921 and by registered sale deed from Ruh Afza, wife of Fazal Kabir Khan. On detailed consideration of the evidence on record, both oral and documentary, the learned Subordinate Judge found that except the solitary and uncorroborated statements of DW 1 there is no other evidence on record to prove that Ali Hossain and Ali Akbar acquired the Dar Jote right in the suit land along with their father Md Putan by settlement from Fazal Kabir Khan on the basis of registered patta dated 1-2-1901. The contesting defendant also failed to prove that Ali Akbar, Ali Hossain and Omar Ali acquired the jote right in the suit land by purchase from Ruh Afza, wife of Fazal Kabir Khan with their own money and for their own benefit and that with the income of the said property. On proper appreciation of the evidence on record the learned Subordinate Judge came to the firm finding that Md Putan acquired the jote right in the suit land by way of settlement from Fazal Kabir Khan by registered patta dated 1-2-1921 as well as by way of registered kabalas from Ruh Afza, who had earlier acquired the said land by way of gift from her husband Fazal Kabir Khan by a registered instrument. The learned Subordinate Judge also found that Md Putan acquired 16 annas interest in the suit land in Dar Jote right as well as in jote right.

27. The main contention between the contending parties appears to be entering around the question as to whether Md Putan acquired the suit property in 14 drones with his own money and for his own benefit and Ali Hossain was simply his benamder and a constituted attorney or the said property was actually acquired by Ali Hossain with his own money and for his own benefit. Ali Hossain, of course kot mortgaged the said land with Sultan Ahmed Bahaddar for payment of rent of the suit land to the landlords. Subsequently, the said Sultan Ahmed sold his mortgage right in the suit land to Elahadad Chowdhury but thereafter the said mortgage was redeemed amicably. This has been contended by the contesting defendant that Md Putan and Ali Hossain transferred 9 drone 4 kani of land from the suit property to Tripura and Prosanna by kot mortgage, who subsequently filed Mortgage Suit No. 25 of 1921 for realisation mortgage money and got a preliminary decree therein and in execution of the mortgage decree their mortgage interest was sold to Jinnat Ali. In this way Jinnat Ali purchased the decree of the mortgage suit, being Mortgage suit No. 61 of 1921, from Tripura and Prassana. The sale certificate has been marked as Exhibit C(1) and the corresponding writ of delivery of possession has been marked as Exhibit D(1), but which Jinnat Ali is alleged to have purchased the suit land in auction on 12-5-1925 in Mortgage Execution case No. 14 of 1925 filed by Tripura and by Tripura and Prassana against the heirs of Ali Hussain and some of the heirs of Md Putan. The certificate case No. 214 of 1930-31 was instituted by the Khas Mahal Estate for arrears of land revenue against the heirs of Ali Hossain and Elahadad Chowdhury, following which Jinnat Ali purchased the suit property in the aforesaid certificate case. Defendant No. 21 contends that his father Elahadad Chowdhury acquired the suit land on partition by a registered deed of partition dated 27-9-1933 Exhibit E concluded between Elahadad Chowdhury, Jinnat Ali and others. There is nothing on record to show that Elahadad acquired any interest in the suit land before 27-9-1933 and as such Exhibit E is merely a paper transaction. The name of the Elahadad Chowdhury was recorded in the RS Khatian as a mortgage. The RS Khatian has been marked Exhibit 2 and Elahadad Chowdhury is the certificate debtor in certificate case No. 214 of 1930-31, but Tripura, Prassana and Jinnat Ali were not the certificate debtors in the certificate case. From all these the learned Subordinate Judge concluded that Elahadad Chowdhury acquired only kot mortgage right in the suit jote from Sultan Ahmed Bahaddar, who had acquired the same from Ali Hossain and Putan in only kot mortgage right and consequently the sale certificate Exhibit C the RS Khatian Exhibit 2, Kabala Exhibit 6 clearly falsify the case of defendant No. 21 that Ali Hossain and Md Putan transferred the suit land to Prassana and Tripura. Moreover, it appears from the record that Md Putan and his heirs and heiresses were not certificate debtors in certificate case No. 214 of 1930-31, although defendant No. 21 admitted that Md Putan had one third share in the disputed jote. It is also found that only the heirs of Ali Hossain and Elahadad Chowdhury were made parties in Certificate case No. 214 of 1930-31. On consideration of all these documents the alleged sale of the suit land to Jinnat Ali in Certificate case No. 214 of 1930-31 vide Exhibit C has been found by the learned Subordinate Judge as fraudulent, oollusive and void as a result of which Jinnat Ali acquired no interest in the suit land against Ali Hossain and Elahadad Chowdhury. The contention of the plaintiffs that Md Putan transferred the suit land to one Sultan Ahmed Bahaddar by a registered kot mortgage deed in mortgage right, who subsequently sold the said mortgage right to Elahadad Chowdhury, father of the appellant, acquired only the kot mortgage interest of Md Putan in the suit land by registered kabala dated 9-7-1926 (Exhibit 6 this kabala Exhibit 6) and the RS Khatian Exhibit 3 clearly prove that Md Putan transferred the suit land to Sultan Ahmed Bahaddar in kot mortgage right and Elahadad Chowdhury, purchased the said right of Sultan Ahmed by registered kabala Exhibit 6 and as such his mane was recorded in the RS Khatian as a mortgagee. It is also found from the record that the Khas Mohal Estate filed certified case No. 214 of 1930-31 against Elahadad Chowdhury for realisation of arrear of rent in respect of the suit land Exhibit C but the names of Tripura, Prassana and Surrendra and Jinnat Ali, Abdur Rashid do not appear in the RS Khatian as mortgagee and they were not parties in certificate case No. 214 of 1930-31, while Elahadad Chowdhury alone was a party in the suit certificate case. The basis of the claim of the appellant is that Elahadad Chowdhury acquired right, title, interest and possession in the suit land by deed of partition dated 27-9-1933 with Jinnat Ali and others, in which Elahadad Chowdhury had no title whatsoever, this deed of partition Exhibit E has rightly been found to be a fraudulent and collusive one, created for the purpose of the suit.

28. The learned trial Court on consideration of the evidence on record found that there is nothing on record to prove that Elahadad acquired kot mortgage right in 4 drones 12 kanis of lands out of the suit land by way of purchase from Surrendra in the benami of Abdur Rashid and possessed the same as a mortgagee. From all these the learned Subordinate Judge found that kabala Exhibit 6, RS Khatian Exhibit 2 and the sale certificate Exhibit C do not support the claim of the contesting defendant that Md Putan sold 9 drones 4 kanis of the suit land to Tripura and Prassanna by a kot mortgage deed and they possessed the same as mortgage of land and thereafter Jinnat Ali purchased the same in Mortgage suit No. 14 of 1926. We find no cogent reasons to take a different view in the matter as this finding is well supported by convincing documentary and oral evidence.

<u>29. The learned Subordinate Judge also found that Surrendra, Prassanna and Tripura never possessed the suit property as mortgagees and the alleged mortgage decree in Mortgage suit No. 65 of 1921 is collusive and fraudulent. The learned trial Court further found that the kot mortgage deed Exhibit A -and A(1), kabala Exhibit B and the sale certificate Exhibit C(1) and the writ of delivery of possession Exhibit D(1) are all collusive and fraudulent paper transactions and these were never acted upon. This findings are based on evidence on record and are well reasoned. From those the learned trial Court found that the purchase of the suit land in auction by Jinnat Ali in Certificate case No. 214 of 1930-31 vide Exhibit C is out and out a fraudulent exercise and he never possessed the suit land. The learned trial Court also found that kabala Exhibit 6 the RS Khatian Exhibit 2 made it manifestly clear that Elahadad Chowdhury acquired only the mortgage right in the suit land from Sultan Ahmed Bahaddar, who had acquired the same from Md Putan through his Attorney Ali Hossain. The plaintiff and defendant Nos. 1-18, 20-30 contended that Elahadad Chowdhury acquired the suit land in kot mortgage right by way of purchase from Sultan Ahmed Bahaddar by kabala Exhibit 6 but subsequently he fraudulently purchased the suit land in auction in certificate case No. 214 of 1930-31 in the benami of his uncle Jinnat Ali and thereafter collusively created deed of partition Exhibit E with Jinnat Ali which is out and out a fraudulent transaction. This finding of the trial Court is also well supported by the evidence on record, both oral and documentary. The learned Subordinate Judge further found that the certificate sale of the suit land in certificate case No. 214 of 1930-31 was collusive, fraudulent and void sale which did not in any way affect the right, further interest and possession of the heirs of Md Putan, particularly his 3 daughters namely Khodeja, Fatema and Jahura, and consequently Jinnat Ali acquired no-interest in the suit property by the aforesaid sale. The contesting defendant filed the certified copy of an Ewaznama dated 26-12-1940. Exhibit F, which purports to show that Ali Akbar, Omar Ali and Ali Hossain acquired 3 drones 1 kanis 11 gondas out of the suit land from Elahadad by this deed of Ewaznaina. It has been stated in paragraph 19 of the written statement by defendant No. 21 that Jinnat Ali filed other suit No. 20 of 1929 in the court of Munsif at Cox''s Bazar for.recovery of the khas possession in the suit land on the strength of the alleged purchase in Mortgage suit.No. 14 of 1925 against Ali Akbar, Omar Ali and heirs of Ali Hossain and the said suit was decreed. It was further stated that Ali Akbar and the heirs of Ali Hossain amicably redeemed the mortgage of the suit land from Elahadad Chowdhury executing an Ewaznama Exhibit F by which Ali Akbar, Omar Ali and some other heirs of Md Putan got 3 drones 11 kanis and 11 gondas of land while Elahadad Chowdhury got the remaining portion of the suit property. But in this Ewaznama Exhibit F the three daughters of Md Putan named Khodeja, Fatema and Johura were not parties and as such the same is never binding upon them although the same is binding upon the parties thereto. It is thus evident that the right, title, interest and possession of plaintiffs Nos. 4-15 and defendant No. 7 and 11, the heirs and heiresses of Khatija. Fatema and Johura. The three daughters of Md Putan, remained totally unaffected by the alleged purchase of the suit land by Jinnat Ali, uncle of Elahadad Chowdhury, in mortgage Execution case No. 14 of 1925, by the alleged certificate purchase of Jinnat Ali in certificate case No. 214 of 1930-31, by the alleged partition deed Exhibit F between Jinnat Ali and Elahadad Chowdhury and by the so called Ewaznama deed Exhibit F. It is also found that the compromise decree dated 26-11-52 Exhibit H obtained in 0 S No. 13 of 1951 filed by Moherunnessa daughter of Ali Akbar, against defendant No. 21 and others for redemption of the kot mortgage right in the suit land did not at all affect the interest of the heirs and heiresses of Khodeja, Fatema and Johura, 3 daughters of Md Putan as they were not made parties to the said suit but the said compromise decree dated 16-9-42 in OS No. 13 of 1951 is binding upon the heirs of Ali Hossain, Ali Akbar and Omar Ali. Thus the interest of plaintiffs Nos. 4-15 and defendants 7 and 11 remained totally intact to the extent of 3rd share in the suit property. It is also found that by the compromise decree Exhibit H defendant No. 21 and other heirs of Elahadad Chowdhury became co-sharers in the suit land.</u>

30. The definite case of the plaintiffs is that the heirs of Elahadad Chowdhury delivered possession in the 5 drones of the suit land as described in schedule Ka to the plaint to plaintiff Nos. 4-15 in the middle of Baishak, 1355 BS on their demand and the deed of mortgage was accordingly redeemed amicably and since then they have been owning and possession of the suit land in their own right. The possession of the plaintiffs in the suit land has been proved by consistent and corroborative evidence of PWs 1-5 and the finding of the learned trial Court on the question of possession is based on proper appreciation of the evidence on record. It appears that by the compromise decree in OS No. 13 of 1951, Exhibit H Elahadad Chowdhury became a co-sharer to the suit jote with the plaintiffs and defendant Nos. 1-18, 20-30 and as such he is entitled to the said land.

31. Mr Fazlul Karim, the learned Advocate appearing for the appellant submits that since defendant No. 21 is a stranger to the suit land and his possession therein has been admitted by the plaintiffs themselves, a simple suit for partition without a prayer for declaration of title and confirmation of possession and for recovery of khas possession is not maintainable in law. In support of his contention, Mr Karim has referred to the case of Gagan Chandra Hazra and another vs Surendra Nath Khamral and others reported in AIR 1951 Calcutta 410. The cited decision is obviously of no assistance to the appellant as we have already found that Elahadad Chowdhury is not a stranger to the suit jote but a co-sharer thereto on the basis of the decree obtained in 0 S No. 13 of 1951. Exhibit H. This case has a chequered career starting from 1910 when Fazal Karim Khan settled the suit land with Mr Putan by registered patta dated 2nd Falgoon. 1308 BS. Soon thereafter the said landlords dispossessed Md Putan form the suit land which necessitated the filing of Title Suit No. 142 of 1906 by Putan against Fazal Karim Khan for declaration of title and recovery of khas possession. The said suit was eventually decreed on contest on 18-3-1907. The appeal by Fazal Karim Khan against the aforesaid judgment and decree in favour of Md Putan was allowed due to some formal defects in the plaint. Thereafter Md Putan filed title suit No. 89 of 1908 against Fazal Karim Khan as a principal defendant and Ali Hossain, his son, as a pro-forma defendant, for declaration of title and recovery of khas possession in the suit land and the said suit was decreed on 23-1-1911. Title appeal No. 101 of 1911 filed by Fazal Karim Khan against the aforesaid decree was dismissed on contest and right, title and interest of Md Putan was confirmed. In the mean time Fazal Karim Khan transferred his superior interest in 14 drones of the suit land and khas interest in 3 drones 5 kanis 1 gonda and 1 kara of land, out of the suit land, to his wife Ruh Afza alias Alimannessa by a registered deed of gift dated 18th Magh, 1316 BS. Thereafter Ruh Afza transferred her superior interest in 14 drones of the suit land and khas interest in 3 drones 5 kanis 1 gonda and 1 kara of land to Md Putan by registered kabala dated 10-6-1912 Mr Putan acquired the suit property in the benami of his son Ali Hossain but it was acquired with his own money and for his own benefit and Ali Hossain as simply a namlender, have no interest of his own therein. Due to his old age Md Putan appointed his son Ali Hossain as his constituted attorney for the management of the suit property as he himself could not look after the same due to physical infirmity. In course of time, Ali Hossain kot mortgaged the suit property with one Sultan Ahmed Bahaddar on behalf of his father Md Putan for saving the suit property from auction sale initiated for arrears of land revenue. Md Putan died in 1919 leaving his son Ali Hossain, Omar Ali, and Ali Akbar as his 3 sons and Khodeja, Johura and Fatema as his three daughters to succeed him. Defendant Nos. 1-6, 8-10, 12-19 and 20, 30 are the heirs and heiresses of the aforesaid 3 sons of Md Putan while plaintiff Nos. 4-15 and defendants 7 and 11 are the heirs and heiresses of Khodeja, Johura and Fatema, 3 daughters of Md Putan and they own and posses the suit property in ejmali. Md Fazal Kabir Khan and his heirs having greedy eyes over the suit property nevertheless undertook numerous abortive attempts and made unrelenting efforts and resorted to various exercises for laying claim upon the suit property by setting up their relation. Jinnat Ali and others. Fazal Karim Khan purchased the kot mortgage right in the suit property in Mortgage suit No. 25 of 1921 in the benami of Jinnat Ali in Mortgage Execution case No. 14 of 1925, certificate case No. 214 of 1930-31 was instituted by the Khas Mahal Estate for arrears of land revenue against Ali Hossain and the suit property was purchased by Jinnat Ali. Thereafter Elahadad Chowdhury created partition deed dated 27-9-1933 Exhibit E'' in collusion with uncle Jinnat Ali and others, although he had no interest in the suit land. This Exhibit E'' is evidently a paper transaction designed to create false show of interest in the suit property in favour of Fazal Kabir Khan. The learned trial Court rightly found that Elahadad Chowdhury acquired only kot mortgage right in the suit jote from Sultan Ahmed Bahaddar and nothing more than that. This auction sale in question has clearly been found to be fraudulent and collusive as the heirs and heiresses of Md Putan were not made parties as certificate debtors in certificate case No. 214 of 1931, although admittedly Md Putan had one third share in the suit Jote. Inspite of all these exercises by Fazal Kabir Khan, and Elahadad Chowdhury, the heirs and heiresses of Md Putan have been able to successfully withstand their onslaughts and managed to hold on to the suit land in assertion of their own title and interest. Fazal Kabir Khan and his successor want to the extent of entering into special deals with some of the heirs and heiresses of Ali Hossain and his heirs in their bid to dislodge the plaintiff from their unassailable position. In the facts and circumstances in the case and the evidence on record, we are satisfied that the plaintiffs have been able to prove their case by cogent and reliable evidence and the learned Subordinate Judge rightly decreed the suit on proper appreciation of the evidence on record. We do not find any justifiable ground to interfere with the impugned judgment and decree which are well reasoned and well supported by the evidence, we do not thereafter find any substance in the appeal. The impugned judgment is found to be based on proper appreciation of the evidence on record and correct principle of law. The submission made by the learned Advocate for the appellants are consequently found to be of substance and the same are accordingly repelled.

In the result, the appeal is dismissed with costs and the judgment and decree passed by the learned Subordinate Judge, 2nd Court, Chittagong in Partition Suit No. 3 of 1969 in preliminary form are affirmed.

Send down the lower court records at once.

End.
