full_judgment:
Sheikh Hassan Arif J: Since the questions of law and facts involved in the aforesaid three writ petitions are almost same; they have been taken up together for hearing, and are now being disposed of by this single judgment.

2. Rules in the aforesaid Writ Petitions were issued in similar terms, namely calling upon the respondent-lender banks and Bangladesh Bank to show cause as to why-inclusion and/or circulation of petitioners' names in the report of Credit Information Bureau (CIB) of Bangladesh Bank as 'defaulter-borrower' should not be declared to be without lawful authority and of no legal effect and. as to why the respondents should not be directed to delete the names of the petitioners from the said report of CIB.

3. Short facts, relevant for the disposal of the aforesaid Rules, are narrated below:

In Writ Petition No. 9158 of 2012, the petitioner was the Managing Director of two limited companies, namely Mystic Pharmaceuticals Limited and Russel Lodge Holding Limited (hereinafter called "Mystic" and "Russel Lodge"). In Mystic the petitioner was the holder of 3,000 (three thousands) shares out of total 9,000 (nine thousands) shares and in Russel Lodge he held 500 (five hundred) shares out of total 3,000 (three thousands) shares, Mystic obtained credit facilities from Sonali Bank (respondent No.4) vide sanction letter dated 25-9-2004, and in obtaining such credit facilities, the petitioner executed personal guarantee. On the other hand, Russel Lodge obtained credit facilities from Mercantile Bank Limited (respondent No.5) vide sanction letter dated 6-5-2007. In this transaction as well, the petitioner stood guarantee for the said loan by executing personal guarantee. Russel Lodge obtained further credit facilities from Prime Finance and Investment Limited (respondent No.6), and here as well, the petitioner stood guarantee for the said loan by executing personal guarantee. As against the above transactions, both the Mystic and Russel Lodge failed to repay the said loan and, accordingly, the names of those companies were sent to the Bangladesh Bank along with the name of the petitioner for publication of the same in the report of the Credit Information Bureau (CIB) of the Bangladesh Bank. Thus, the name of the petitioner appeared in the said report as 'defaulter-borrower' under Borrower Code Nos. 62653, 146221 and 802473 showing the said credit facilities as 'bad loans'.

4. In Writ Petition No. 10472 of 2012, the petitioner was the Managing Director of Anowara Jute Mills Limited. In the said company, the petitioner was the owner of 10% shares. After liberation of Bangladesh, the said company was nationalized followed by subsequent denationalization through an agreement between the government and the said company. According to the said denationalization agreement, all the liabilities of the said company were taken over by the said denationalized company. The said company obtained further credit facilities from respondent No.4 to 6, namely Uttara Bank Limited, Bangladesh Shilpa Rin Sangstha and Agrani Bank. In obtaining those credit facilities, the petitioner mortgaged his properties and stood guarantee by executing personal guarantee for securing the said liabilities. The company, subsequently, having failed to repay the said liabilities, it took initiative for winding up and, accordingly, filed Company Matter No. 60 of 1999 before the Company Bench of the High Court Division. Thereafter, one of the lenders, namely Uttara Bank (respondent No.4) filed Mortgage Suit No. 25 of 2000 (renumbered as Artha Rin Suit No. 268 of 2003) against the company and others including the petitioner before the concerned Artha Rin Adalat for realization of loan granted by it. However, at the instance of the company, the Company Bench of the High Court Division, vide order dated 2-6-2009 passed in the said Company Matter No. 60 of 1999, stayed further proceedings of the said Artha Rin Suit till disposal of the said winding up proceedings.

5. In Writ Petition No. 10093 of 2013, the petitioner was the Managing Director of Hoque Food Limited and proprietor of Hoque Food Agency, the former being a limited company and the later being a proprietorship firm. In the Hoque Food Limited, the petitioner held 200 shares out of total 1,000 shares. Both Houqe Food Limited and Houqe Food Agency obtained credit facilities from the Export Import Bank of Bangladesh Limited (EXIM Bank) (respondent No.5) and the petitioner stood guarantee for the said loan by executing personal guarantee in favour of the said bank. Since both the Houqe Food Limited and Houqe Food Agency failed to repay the said loans, the Exim Bank filed Artha Rin Suit No.410 of 2004 before the concerned Artha Rin Adalat impleading the petitioner as defendant No.3. Accordingly, the said suit was decreed in favour of the bank and the bank filed Artha Execution Case No.239 of 2005 for execution of the said decree. At one stage of the execution process, the judgment-debtors including the petitioner filed application before the concerned Adalat for allowing them to repay the ,entire decreetal amount without interests by installments in view of the provisions under section 49(1) of the Artha Rin Adalat Ain, 2003. Thereupon, the Adalat allowed the same and, accordingly, the debtors started repayment of installments as allowed by the Adalat. Being aggrieved by the said order of the Adalat allowing such installments without interests, the Exim Bank filed Writ Petition No. 9249 of 2010, whereupon the High Court Division issued Rule and stayed further proceedings of the said execution case. According to the petitioner, the said judgment-debtors have in the meantime paid the entire decreetal money, however, without interests.

6. As against the aforesaid circumstances and backgrounds, since the petitioners' names were published as defaulter-borrower in the CIB report of the Bangladesh Bank, they moved this Court and obtained, the aforesaid Rules. At the time of issuance of the Rules, this Court, by different orders, stayed operation of the said CIB report in so far as the same was concerned with the publication of the names of the petitioners as defaulter-borrower,

7. The Rules are contested by the respective lender banks and financial institutions as well as the Bangladesh Bank by filing separate affidavits-in-opposition through learned Advocates.

8. Mr Munir Sharif, learned advocate appearing for all the petitioners, mainly submits that since the letters of guarantee concerned were executed by the petitioners before the amendment of 2013 to the definition of the term "defaulter-borrower" as provided under section 5 Ga Ga of the Bank Companies Act, 1991 ("the said Act") and the respective companies or establishments of the petitioners had become defaulters before such amendment came into force, the rights of the petitioners not to be included in the definition of 'defaulter borrower' as prevailing at the relevant time had already accrued in their favour, and, as such, in view of the provisions under section 6 of the General Clauses Act, 1897, the amendment to the said section 5 Ga Ga inserting two more categories therein, namely 'guarantor' and 'director', will not be applicable retrospectively in respect of the petitioners. According to him, since the petitioners were not liable to be included in the definition of the 'defaulter-borrower' at the relevant time, so long as the said personal guarantees continue, no amendment inserting those categories in the said definition can take retrospective effect. In support of his submissions. Mr Sharif refers to various decisions of this Court as well as the Superior Courts of this sub-continent, namely Nazimuddin vs State, 30 DLR 49, State of Punjab vs Mohar Sings, 1955 AIR (SC) 84, Sangam Spinners vs Regional Provident Fund Commissioner-I (2008) 1 SCC 291. In respect of the petitioner in Writ Petition No. 10093 of 2013, Mr Sharif submits that since pursuant to the order given by the Artha Execution Adalat, the judgment-debtors have already paid the entire decreetal money except the interests, the matter should have been resolved long ago, but through the said writ petition filed by the lender-bank the matter is still pending. Thus, he submits, the name of the petitioner should not be published in the CIB report anymore. However, in respect of Writ Petition No. 9158 of 2012 and Writ Petition No. 10093 of 2013, Mr Sharif frankly concedes that the arguments as to the retrospective effect of the amendment to section 5 GaGa of the said Act is not applicable in respect of the petitioners in those writ petitions as admittedly the petitioner in Writ Petition No. 9158 of 2012 held more then 20% shares in Mystic bringing him even under the un- amended definition of the 'defaulter-borrower' and the petitioner in Writ Petition No. 10093 of 20iJ, being proprietor of Hoque Food Agency, was also liable to be included in the said un- amended definition of 'defaulter-borrower' even before the said amendment. Further, referring to the larger Bench decision of this Court in Quazi Nasibul Hassan vs Bangladesh Bank, 61 DLR 96, Mr Sharif argues that the issue whether the guarantor would be included in the definition of 'defaulter-borrower' having already been settled by a decision of a larger Bench of this Court holding that the guarantors would not be included in the said un-amended definition of 'defaulter-borrower', they were not liable to be referred to the Bangladesh Bank under section 27 KaKa of the said Act for publication of their names in the CIB. This being so, he continues, unless the amendment to section 5 GaGa of the said Act is applied retrospectively to the petitioner in Writ Petition No. 10472 of 2012, the petitioner's name cannot be published in the CIB report of Bangladesh Bank as, though he was a Director, he was holding only 10% shares in the borrower company and executed personal guarantee. But, he submits, by inclusion of the word 'director' in the definition of defaulter-borrower' by the said amendment, he is now affected on both counts, namely as 'director' and as 'guarantor'.

9. In writ petitioner No. 10472 of2012, Mr Hironmoy Halder, learned Advocate appearing for respondent No. 6 Bank, submits that since the petitioner was the Managing Director of the borrower company and executed personal guarantee, in view of the amended definition of  'defaulter-borrower' his name should be published in the CIB as defaulter-borrower. Ms Hosneara Begum, learned advocate appearing for Sonali Bank in Writ Petition No. 9158 of2012, submits that since the petitioner admittedly held more than 20% shares in one of the borrower companies, he was liable to be included in the definition of defaulter- borrower even before amendment and, as such, the submissions as to the retrospectively of the amended definition of 'borrower-defaulter' has no manner of application in her case. In Writ Petition 10093 of 2013,Mr Kowser Ali, learned Advocate appearing for Exim Bank, submits that since the petitioner was admittedly the proprietor of one of the borrowers, namely Hoque Food Agency, even under the un-amended definition of defaulter- borrower', he was liable to be included in the said definition and, as such, publication of petitioner's name in the CIB was not without lawful authority. Mr Kawsar further submits that the submission as to the retrospective effect of the amended definition of 5 GaGa does also not have any manner of application in respect of the petitioner in the said writ petition, Referring to a decision of our Appellate Division in Abul Kashem. Vs Mahmudul Hasan, 64 DLR (AD) 65, Mr Kowser submits that the Appellate Division under paragraph 26 of the said reported case, while interpreting the term defaulter-borrower as provided by section 5 GaGa of the Bank Companies Act, 1991, even held that the guarantors would also be included in the definition of the same.

10. Mr Zubair Ahmed, learned Advocate appearing for the Bangladesh Bank in all the writ petitions, submits that the comparison between the un-amended and the amended definition of the term 'defaulter-borrower' reveals that the said amendment of 2013 is a clarificatory and declaratory amendment to avoid confusions prevailing among, general public, and, as such, according to the long standing rule of interpretation as confirmed by the Superior Courts of the subcontinent, the same should be made applicable retrospectively. Mr Zubair further argues that since different Benches of the High-Court Division gave conflicting opinions on the definition of the term 'defaulter-borrower' as provided by the un-amended provision of section 5 GaGa and a larger Bench of this Court held that the 'guarantor' would not be included in the said definition, the Legislature was fully competent to legislate in clarificatory and declaratory form to confirm it's original intention by amending section 5 GaGa and thereby inserting the 'directors' and 'guarantors' within the scope of the said definition. According to him, since the said amendment in 2013 has only clarified the earlier definition of the term 'defaulter-borrower' in order to remove the confusion created because of the conflicting decisions of different benches of this Court, the same should be regarded as clarificatory and declaratory amendment and, as such, the same should be made effective retrospectively. This being so, he submits, the name of the petitioner in Writ Petition No.10472 of2012 is now liable to be published in the CIB as defaulter-borrower by retrospective effect of the said declaratory amendment to section 5 GaGa and, as such, after the said amendment, the petitioner has got no case to argue before this Court. In support of his submissions, Mr Zubair refers to three decisions of Indian jurisdiction, namely Pannirselvam vs Veeriah Vandayar AIR (1931) Mad-83, Balmakund vs Pirthiraj Ganesh Das AIR (1951) Patna- 333 and Jethanand vs State of Delhi AIR 1960 (SC) 59.

11. Considered the submissions of the learned Advocates and perused the materials on record including the relevant provisions of law. Since, admittedly, the amendment to section 5 GaGa does not in any way affect the petitioners in Writ Petition No. 9158 of2012 and Writ Petition 10093 of 2013, as the petitioners in those writ petitions were liable to be included in the definition of 'defaulter-borrower' by their respective position in the borrower company or proprietorship firm, we do to need to discuss their case in great detail except that even under the un-amended provisions of section 5 GaGa they do not have any case before this Court. The petitioner in Writ Petition No. 9158 of 2012 was admittedly the owner of more than 20% shares in Mystic and he executed personal guarantee to secure loan. Thus, even if he was not attracted within the definition of defaulter-borrower for execution of personal guarantee, he was still liable to be included in the said definition because of such admitted position that he was the owner of more than 20% share in the Mystic Pharmaceuticals Limited, one of the borrowers. Again in Writ Petition No. 10093 of 2013, the petitioner was, admittedly, the proprietor of Hoque Food Agency, a proprietorship firm, and it is also admitted that the said Hoque Food Agency was one of the borrowers of the EXIM Bank (respondent No.5) and defaulted in re-payment. This being so, the petitioner himself was the defaulter-borrower. Accordingly, we do not find any merit in the Rules issued in the said two Writ Petitions, namely Writ Petition No.9158 of 2012 and Writ Petition No.10093 of 2013, and, as such, the same should be discharged.

12. Since Mr Sharif has raised an important legal issue through his arguments in Writ Petition No. 10472 of2012, we should discuss the same in detail for reaching a proper decision.

13. As stated earlier, the petitioner in Writ Petition No. 10472 of 2012 was the Managing Director holding less than 10% shares in the company and executed personal guarantee to secure the credit facilities obtained by the company. Thus, the question as put-forward by Mr Sharif before this Court is whether the amended definition of section of 5 GaGa inserting therein two new categories of persons in the definition of the term 'defaulter-borrower' would be applicable in respect of the petitioner retrospectively as the execution of his personal guarantee and his holding of the position as the Managing Director were events which occurred before the said amendment and the defaults of the said borrower company in repayment also occurred before such amendment. To examine this issue, we should first see what changes have been made by the said amendment, namely the Act No. 27 of 2013 as published in Gazette dated 22-7-2013, to the said definition of 'defaulter-borrower'. For the convenience of our references, both the provisions under section 5 GaGa of the Companies Act, 1991, before and after amendment, are quoted below;

Before amendment:

৫(গগ) "খালাপী ঋণ গ্রহিতা" অর্থ কোন ব্যক্তি বা প্রতিষ্ঠান যাহার নিজের বা স্বার্থ সংশ্লিষ্ট প্রতিষ্ঠানের অনুকুলে প্রদত্ত অগ্রিম, ঋণ বা উহার অংশ বা উহার উপর অর্জিত সুদ বাংলাদেশ ব্যাংক কর্তৃক জারিককৃত সংজ্ঞা অনুযায়ী মেয়াদোত্তীর্ণ হওয়ার ৬ (মাস) অতিবাহিত হইয়াছে।

তবে শর্ত থাকে যে, খেলাপী ঋণগ্রহিতা কোন পাবলিক লিমিটেড কোম্পানীর পরিচালক না হইলে অথবা উক্ত কোম্পানীর তাহার বা উহার শেয়ারের অংশ ২৫% এর অধিক না হইলে, উক্ত পাবলিক লিমিটেড কোম্পানী স্বার্থ সংশ্লিষ্ট প্রতিষ্ঠান বলিয়া গণ্য হইবে।

আরো শর্ত থাকে যে, পাবলিক লিমিটেড কোম্পানী ব্যতীত অন্য কোন প্রতিষ্ঠানে এই দফার অধীন স্বার্থ সংশ্লিষ্ট প্রতিষ্ঠান বলিয়া গণ্য হইবে না।

After amendment:

৫(গগ) "খালাপী ঋণ গ্রহিতা" অর্থ কোন দেনাদার ব্যক্তি বা প্রতিষ্ঠান বা কোম্পানী যাহার নিজের বা স্বার্থ সংশ্লিষ্ট প্রতিষ্ঠানের অনুকূলে প্রদত্ত অগ্রীম, ঋণ না অন্য কোন আর্থিক সুবিধা বা উহার অংশ বা উহার উপর অর্জিত সুদ বা উহার মুনাফা বাংলাদেশ ব্যাংক কর্তৃক জারীকৃত সংজ্ঞা অনুযায়ী মেয়াদোত্তীর্ণ হওয়ার ৬(মাস) অতিবাহিত হইয়াছে।

ব্যাখ্যা- এই দফার উদ্দেশ্যে পূরণকল্পে কোন ব্যক্তি বা, ক্ষেত্র মত, প্রতিষ্ঠান বা কোম্পানী অন্যকোন প্রতিষ্ঠানের

পরিচালক না হইলে অথবা উক্ত প্রতিষ্ঠানে তাহার বা উহার শেয়ারের অংশ ২০% এর অধিক না হইলে অথবা উক্ত প্রতিষ্ঠানের ঋণের জামিনদাতা না হইলে, উক্ত প্রতিষ্ঠান তাহার বা উহার স্বার্থ সংশ্লিষ্ট প্রতিষ্ঠান বলিয়া গণ্য হইবে না;"

14. For comparison of these two defamations, before and after amendment, of the same term 'default-borrower(খেলাপী ঋণ গ্রহীতা)  we should mention here that unless some one comes under the definition of the said term defaulter-borrower, his or its name is not liable to be sent by any bank or financial institution to the Bangladesh Bank for publication of the same in the CIB report in view of sub-section (1) of section 27 KaKa of the said Act, and unless such publication of the name of any individual or establishment is done by the CIB report, that individual or establishment will not be deprived of getting any credit facilities from other banks or financial institutions in view of the provisions under sub-section (3) of section 27 KaKa. The grievances of the petitioners in the aforesaid writ petitions lie here as the publication of their names in the CIB report have already deprived them of getting any credit facilities from any other banks or financial institutions in view of sub-section (3) of section 27 KaKa of the said Act.

15. From the above quoted definitions of the term “খেলাপী ঋণ গ্রহীতা”,before and after amendment, it appears that though the term 'guarantor' was not specifically mentioned in the said definition before amendment, owners of 20% shares in an establishment were always included in the said definition and, as such, their names were liable to be published in the CIB for the default of their interested establishment (স্বার্থ সংশ্লিষ্ট প্রতিষ্ঠান) in repayment as per the definition of Bangladesh Bank. However, by the amended definition of the term “খেলাপী ঋণ গ্রহীতা”, the Legislature made the definition shorter and simpler in that by providing a simple explanation to the main definition of “খেলাপী ঋণ গ্রহীতা”, the Legislature included two categories of individuals in clear terms, namely 'director' and 'guarantor', in the said definition. Therefore, if this amendment is applied prospectively, according to the submissions made by Mr Sharif, the petitioner in Writ Petition No.10472 of 2012 would not be attracted by it and, as such, he would not be liable to be referred to the Bangladesh Bank for publication of his name as 'defaulter-borrower' in the CIB. Thus, according to him, the petitioner is directly affected by this amended definition as the petitioner was the Managing Director as well as the 'guarantor' of the said borrower company since long before amendment in 2013, in particular at the time when the said company defaulted in repayment.

16. The question of retrospectively of a particular amendment or enactment depends on the nature of the said amendment and/or enactment. Sometimes Legislature enacts a law by substituting the entire existing Act. In other cases, the Legislature, through amending Act, amends some provisions of the existing Act by adding or removing something from the said provisions. The amendment in question vide Act No. 27 of 2013 falls under the later type of enactment, as by this amending Act the Legislature has made various amendments to several existing provisions of the Bank Companies Act, 1991. One of such amendments is the amendment to the definition of “খেলাপীঋণগ্রহীতা”,(defaulter-borrower) as provided by section 5 GaGa of the said Act. Since we are only concerned with the definition of খেলাপীঋণগ্রহীতাas amended by section 4 of the said amending Act, we should refrain from discussing the effects and impacts of other amendments made by the said amending Act to the Bank Companies Act, 1991.

17. The issue of retrospectively of an amendment or enactment has been taken care of by section 6 of the General Clauses Act, 1897 to some extent. It is provided by section 6 of the General Clauses Act that such amendment or enactment cannot take away the rights already accrued or liabilities incurred under the un-amended provisions of law, and in that case the amended provision will not apply to such rights and liabilities. However, different aspect of retrospective applications of amended provisions have been interpreted by the Superior Courts in various directions depending on the nature of such amendments. The general pre-pendency of such interpretation is that once any substantive right is accrued in favour of a particular individual or person under exiting law, that accrued right cannot be taken away by subsequent amendment. As for example, a person cannot be punished under a new offence when the said offence did not exist at the time of commission of the said offence. However, according to the learned author, Advocate Mahmudul Islam, section 6 of the General Clauses Act does not apply to inchoate acts done under an Act before it ripens into accrued rights or incurred liabilities and such rights or liabilities cannot survive the repeal of the Act or amendment [see Mahmudul Islam, Interpretation of Statutes and Documents, Mullick Brothers (2009), page. 288-289]. In our jurisdiction, namely in MA Ghani vs Nasir Ahmed, 21 DLR 451, the then East Pakistan High Court, relying on a Pakistan Supreme Court's decision reported in 16 DLR (SC) 380, held that granting of exemption under the provisions of a statute lapses with the repeal of the said statute unless it is saved by the repealing statute. In the said referred case of 16 DLR, as decided by the Supreme Court of Pakistan, even a property which was not liable to be requisitioned under the un-amended provision and on the basis of such exemption an individual constructed a wall and structure on the land, the said property was subsequently requisitioned by the government after withdrawal of such exemption by amendment and such requisition was held to be valid requisition.

18. In some cases, the English Courts even held that if the object of the amending statute is not to inflict punishment but to protect the public from the activities of undesirable persons who bear the stigma of a conviction or misconduct on their character, the conviction or misconduct of such person before the operation of the statute may be relied upon. As for example, in Queen vs Vine (1875) 10 QB-195, the question was related to the construction of section 14 of33 & 34 Vict.c. 29, which enacted that every 'person convicted of felony shall be for ever disqualified from selling spirit by retail'. It was held that the disqualification applied to every convicted felon irrespective of whether he was so convicted prior to or after the Act came into operation. In the course of his judgment, Cockburm, CJ, observed:

"Here the object of the enactment is not to punish offenders, but to protect the public against public houses in which spirits are retailed being kept by persons of doubtful characters-, On looking at the Act, the words used seem to import the intention to protect the public against persons convicted in the past as well as in future: the words are in effect equivalent to 'every convicted felon'."

19. Again, in Re, A Solicitor s Clerk (1957) 3 All ER 617, the question was related to disqualification regarding employment as a solicitor's clerk. By section 16(1) of the Solicitors Act, 1941, it was provided that where a Solicitor's Clerk has been convicted of certain offences including larceny in respect of any money or property which belong to his employer or to a client of his, an application may be made on behalf of Law Society to the disciplinary committee for an order that no solicitor shall employ the said person without the written permission of the Law Society. This provision was amended by the amending Act of 1956, which allowed the Society to apply for an order where a clerk 'has been convicted' of larceny irrespective of whether the money or property belong to his employer or one of his clients or to someone else. A clerk, who was convicted of larceny in 1953 of property which belonged neither to his employer nor to his client, was proceeded against under the amended section, and it was contended by him that the amending Act of 1965 was not retrospective so as to apply to convictions before its operation. In rejecting the contention, Lord Goddard, CJ observed:

"In my opinion, this Act is not in truth retrospective. It enables an order to be made disqualifying a person from acting as a solicitor's clerk in the future and what happened in the past is the cause or reason for the making of the order; but the order has no retrospective effect. It would be retrospective if the Act provided that anything done before the Act came into force or before the order was made should be void or voidable, or if a penalty were inflicted for having acted in this or any other capacity before the Act came into force or before the order was made. This Act simply enables a disqualification to be imposed for the future which in no way affects anything done by the appellant in the past. Accordingly, in our opinion, the disciplinary committee had jurisdiction to make the order complained of."

20. In Indian jurisdiction, in State of Bombay vs Vishnu Ramchandra, AIR 1961 (SC) 307, the question was whether a person convicted in 1949 of theft could be directed to remove himself outside specific area under section 57 of the Mumbai Police Act, 1951, which authorized removal of a person who has been convicted of certain offences including theft. The contention raised was that the conviction being prior to the Act, no removal could be founded on such a conviction. In overruling the High Court, where the above contention had found favour, Hidayatullah, J, for the Supreme Court, stated:

"Section 57 of the Bombay Police Act, 1951, does not create a new offence nor makes punishable that which was not an offence. It is designed to protect the public from the activities of undesirable persons who have been convicted of offences of a particular kind. The section only enables the authorities to take note of their convictions and to put them outside the area of their activities, so that the public may be protected against a repetition of such activities. An offender who has been punished may be restrained in his acts and conduct by some legislation, which takes note of his antecedents; but so long as the action taken against him is after the Act comes into force, the statute cannot be said to be applied retrospectively. "

21. Stepping further ahead is the case of declaratory statutes or amendments, which are far more inclined in favour of applicability of the same with retrospective effect. According to the author, Justice GP Singh, the usual reason for passing a declaratory Act is to set-aside what Parliament deems to have been a judicial error whether in the statement of the common law (Judge made law) or in the interpretation of statutes [see Justice GP Singh, Principals of Statutory Interpretation, 11th edition, 2008 Wadhwa & Nagpur]. It was held by the Indian Supreme Court in Channan Singh vs Jai Kuar (Smt.) AIR 1970 SC 349, page-35] that it is well settled that if a statute is curative or merely declaratory of the previous law, retrospective operation is generally intended. In another case, namely Punjab Traders vs State of Punjab, AIR 1990 SC 2300, page 2304, the Supreme Court observed an amending act may be purely clarificatory to clear a meaning of a provision of the principal Act which was already implicit. A clarificatory amendment of its nature will have retrospective effect and, therefore, if the principal Act was existing law when the constitution came into force, the amending Act also will be part of the existing law.

22. Almost similar to our case in hand, the term "owner of house property" was taken up for interpretation by the Indian Supreme Court in Commissioner of Income-tax, Bombay vs Podar Cement Pvt. Ltd., AIR 1997 SC 2523, wherein the Indian Supreme Court held that amendments introduced by the Finance Act, 1987 in so far they related to section 27 (iii), (iiia) and (iiib) which defined the expression "owner of house property", in respect of which there was a sharp divergence of opinion amongst the High Courts, was c1arificatory and declaratory in nature and consequently retrospective. Again, in Brij Mohon Das Laxman Das vs Commissioner of Income Tax, AIR 1997 SC 1651, relevant page-165. Explanation 2 added to section 40 of the Income Tax Act, 1961 from 1-4-1985 on a question on which their was a divergence of opinion was held to be declaratory in nature and, therefore, retrospective. Maxwell has given much more better examples of such declaratory or clarificatory provisions which take effect retrospectively [see Maxwell on The Interpretation of Statutes, 12th edition, P. SU. Langan, Lexis Nexis, Butterworth (2007)], wherein an example was given referring to the case Re Lovell and Collard's Contract (1907) 1 CH 249. In that case section 6 of the Finance Act, 1898 provided for the removal of doubt that the definition of "conveyance on sale" in the Stamp Act, 1981 included an order for foreclosure. It was held that section 6 was declaratory and therefore retrospective so that an order of 1896 foreclosing a legal mortgage required stamping as a 'conveyance on sale'.

23. From the above short discussions of relevant rules of interpretation, it appears that though the substantive rights accrued or liabilities incurred already before the amendment is not allowed to be taken away by the amendment through its retrospective effect, the Superior Courts preponderantly held that this rule of retrospectively would not apply in some cases including the cases of declaratory or clarificatory amendments or statutes.

24. In our country, the history of interpretation of the un-amended provision of section 5 GaGa of the Bank Companies Act, 1991 reveals that different Benches of the High Court Division initially gave conflicting decisions as to whether the guarantors would be included in the term 'defaulter-borrower' and, accordingly, whether they would be referred to the Bangladesh Bank in view of the provisions under section 27 KaKa of the said Act for publication of their names in the CIB report. A division bench presided over by his Lordship Mr Justice Md Abdur Rashid in IFIC Bank Limited vs Beximco Holdings Ltd., 57 DLR (2005) 154 held that the- guarantor would also be included in the definition of 'defaulter-borrower' as provided by the un-amended provisions of section 5 Ga Ga. However, another division bench presided over by his Lordship Mr Justice Tariq-ul-Hakim held the contrary view, namely that since the word 'guarantor' was not specifically mentioned in the definition of 'defaulter-borrower' as provided by the said un-amended provisions of section 5 GaGa, the name of guarantor was not liable to be published in the CIB as 'defaulter-borrower'. As against this back ground, a larger bench was constituted comprising of three Hon'ble Judges of this Court and the said bench took up the issue in Quazi Nasibul Hassan vs Bangladesh Bank, 61 DLR 96 and agreed with the conclusion reached by the division bench presided over by his Lordship Mr Justice Tariq-ul-Hakim. However, it is interesting to note that, the larger bench was itself constituted comprising of the three Hon'ble Judges including his Lordship Mr Justice Tariq-ul-Hakim. Since the larger bench decision is the final unless and until it is interfered with by the Appellate Davison, we are also bound by that decision. However, the case before the larger bench was heard and decided long before the amendment in question of 2013 to the said section 5 Ga Ga.

<u>25. As stated earlier, by this amendment the Legislature, by adding an explanation to the definition, has provided that the 'guarantor' and 'director' of a company, irrespective of public or private, would be regarded as 'defaulter-borrower' for the default of the borrower-establishment or individual in repayment of liabilities, and in that case the borrower-establishment would be regarded as an interested-establishment (স্বার্থ সংশ্লিষ্ট প্রতিষ্ঠান) of the said guarantor or director. Upon comparison of the definitions of the 'defaulter-borrower' before and after amendment, it appears that the Legislature has in fact expressed its original intent by amending this section 5 GaGa as, in the meantime, the litigants as well as the people at general were suffering from confusion because of the divergent opinion of different benches of this Court followed by the said larger Bench decision. If we compare the decision of the aforesaid larger bench with the definition given in the amended provision of section 5 GaGa, the said intention of the Legislature would be evident in that the Legislature deliberately included two new categories, namely 'directors' and 'guarantors', in the definition of the term 'defaulter-borrower' to remove those confusions. This being so, we have no option but to hold that this amended definition of "defaulter-borrower" under section 5 GaGa is a declaratory and clarificatory amendment and, as such, it should be regarded to be already in place in the Bank Companies Act, 1991. Thus, in view of the decisions of the superior Courts applying declaratory and clarificatory amendments retrospectively, in particular relying on the last two examples of such application of declaratory amendments, we are of the view that this amended provision under section 5 GaGa should have retrospective effect and, as such, should apply to the petitioner in Writ Petition No. 10472 of 2012 retrospectively. This retrospective application of the amended definition of "defaulter-borrower" may also be viewed as subsequent withdrawal of exemptions by the Legislature as has been viewed by the Pakistan Supreme Court in the above cited case reported in J 6 DLR (SC) 380 and as was relied upon by the High Court in the case of MA Ghani as reported in 21 DLR 451.</u>

26. It may be mentioned that we have also considered and examined the decisions as referred to by Mr Sharif. It appears that in Nazimuddin's case, the question of applicability of amendment to substantive right of appeal was involved. Since we have already mentioned that substantive fight of appeal accrued in favour of an individual cannot be taken away by amendment in view of sec- tion 6 of the General Clauses Act and further held that the amended section 5 GaGa is a declaratory and c1arificatory amendment, the said case has no manner of application in the facts and circumstances of the instant case. Again, in State of Punjab vs Mohar Sings case, as referred to by Mr Sharif, the offence of giving false statement by a refugee under the Ordinance and punishment given by Magistrate under the amending Act replacing the said Ordinance was involved. In that case, applying section 4 of the Act it was held that the punishment was valid mainly on the ground that the provisions under the Ordinance and the Act were same. This being so, we do not see any reason as to how this decision should be applicable in the case before us. In the third case, namely Sangam Spinners case, as referred to by Mr Sharif, the infancy period providing some benefits to the newly established factories were omitted by subsequent amendment and it was held that the existing benefits already accrued to the newly established factories could not be taken away by retrospective effect of the amendment. We are not inclined to apply this case in the facts and circumstance of the present case as we have already held that the amended provision of section GaGa is a declaratory and c1arificatory provision and it will always have retrospective effect. Further, though Mr Zubair has also relied on one decision of our Appellate Division arising out of a case decided by the International Crimes Tribunal, widely known as Kader Molla's case, wherein the Appellate Division allowed the prosecution to prefer appeal before the Appellate Division against the judgment of the Tribunal through amendment subsequent to the conviction to the ICT Act incorporating provision for such appeal, this case should not be made applicable in the present case as the same was basically decided relying on the protection given to such amendments by Article 47 of the Constitution. Again, though Mr Kawser, learned Advocate, referred to Abul Kashem's case wherein our Appellate Division, in paragraph-26 of the reported case, while clarifying the definition of 'defaulter-borrower' included the term 'guarantor' therein, after reading paragraphs 26 and 27 and the entire decision of the Appellate Division it is evident that the said word 'guarantor' was in fact accidentally included therein and, as such, we are also not inclined to rely on that decision.

<u>27. As stated above, the preponderant view of the superior Courts being in favour of giving retrospective effect to the declaratory and clarificatory amendments, we have no option but to hold that this amended definition of 'defaulter-borrower' as provided by section 5 GaGa of the said Act will also be applicable to the petitioner in Writ Petition No. 10472 of 2012 as the same is a declaratory and clarificatory amendment of the term 'defaulter-borrower'.</u>

28. Regard being had to the above discussions of law and facts, we find no merit in the aforesaid Rules and, as such, the same should be discharged.

In the result, all the Rules are discharged. The orders of stay granted earlier by this Court at the time of issuance of the said rules, thus, stand recalled and vacated

Communicate this.

End.

Syed Mokaddas Ali with Rowshan Ara Begum, Advocates — For the Opposite Parties.

full_judgment:
This Rule at the instance of the defendant Nos. 9 and 15 arising out of an application under section 115 of the Code of Civil Procedure calls in question the judgment and decree dated 20-1-1993 passed by the Sub-ordinate Judge, Patuakhali in Title Appeal No. 83 of 1989 reversing the judgment and decree dated 26-7-1989 passed by the Assistant Judge, Bauphal Upazila in Title Suit No. 7 of 1987 dismissing the suit.

2. Fact relevant for the disposal of the present Rule is that, the plaintiff-opposite parties filed the aforesaid title suit for a declaration that the order of mutation passed in Mutation Case No. 193(11) Bau-68-69 and order dated 18-11-86 passed in Miscellaneous Case No.32 BPL/83-84 are illegal and not binding on them alleging, inter alia, that they are the heirs of the SA recorded tenants and are all along in possession of the suit land. The plaintiff opposite parties for the first time came to learn in 1984 from the local Tahsildar that the suit lands were mutated in the names of the defendant-petitioners. Accordingly, plaintiff-opposite parties made an enquiry into the matter and came to know that the defendant-petitioners managed to mutate their names in respect of the suit land in the aforesaid Mutation Case No. 193(11) Bau-68-69 on the basis of some false and manufactured documents showing that the defendant-petitioners auction-purchased the suit land pursuant to Mortgage Execution Case No. 32 of 1951 on the basis of a mortgage decree in Title Suit No. 102 of 1949 and that the mutation was done without serving any notice on them. Accordingly, the plaintiff-opposite parties filed Miscellaneous Case No. 32 BPL/83-84 before the Revenue Authority concerned for reconsideration of the aforesaid mutation order. But the Revenue Authority refused to reconsider its earlier order passed in favour of the defendant-petitioners in 1969. The plaintiff-opposite parties asserted that the aforesaid mortgage suit, mortgage decree and auction-purchase of the suit land and delivery of possession thereof in favour of the defendant-petitioners were all false and manufactured and the defendant-petitioners did not have any possession of the suit land at any time.

3. The petitioners as defendant Nos. 9 and 15 only contested the suit by filing written statement, contending, inter alia, that they auction purchased the suit land in auction in Mortgage Execution Case No. 32 of 1951 arising out of a mortgage decree passed in Title Suit No. 102 of 1949 and accordingly, they obtained mutation order in their names as far back as in 1969 under section 143 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act by the relevant revenue authority and as such the suit was liable to be dismissed.

4. The plaintiff-opposite parties examined 4 PWs and the defendant-petitioners, on the other hand, examined 2 DWs in support of their respective case. During the trial the plaintiff-opposite parties proved and exhibited SA and RS Khatians and the defendant-petitioner filed and proved relevant documents showing that there was a mortgage suit and the suit land was subsequently purchased in auction-sale by them in execution of a mortgage decree by filing an execution case and got possession thereof.

5. The trial Court, however, dismissed the suit on the finding that the plaintiff-opposite parties ought to have challenged the auction-purchase by the defendant-petitioners pursuant to the mortgage decree and not the order of mutation made in the year 1969 and that the plaintiff-opposite parties had no possession of the suit land.

6. On an appeal by the plaintiff-opposite parties the appellate Court below decreed the suit by reversing the judgment and decree of the trial Court only on point of law namely, that the order of mutation passed by the revenue authority in 1969 under section 143 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act in favour of the defendant-petitioners setting aside the entries in the SA Khatian was without jurisdiction and was thus liable to be set aside.

7. Mr Abdul Quayum, learned Advocate for the defendant-petitioners, submits that since the instant suit is not maintainable being hit by section 42 of the Specific Relief Act, the trial Court rightly dismissed the same and the appellate Court below committed an error of law by decreeing the same when it was liable to be dismissed in limini. The learned Advocate elaborating his augment submits that the plaintiff-opposite parties had no locus standi to file the present suit inasmuch as they could not be said to have any legal character or right to property in respect of the suit land inasmuch as SA Khatian standing in their names had no presumptive value as regards proprietary right to the suit land. It is also contended by the learned Advocate that the suit is not maintainable under section 42 of the Specific Relief Act as the plaintiff-opposite parties failed to seek any declaration as to their own status and also failed to pray for a further or consequential relief by way of possession. In support of his aforesaid submissions the learned Advocate referred to and relied on the cases reported in 18 DLR 706, to show that the plaintiff must have legal character or right to property, 6 BCR (AD) 57 showing that mere declaration in the absence of consequential relief is fatal, 42 DLR 24 and 13 DLR 676 showing that symbolical possession by defendant requires plaintiff to seek relief for recovery of possession. The learned Advocate also relied on the case reported in 19 DLR 9 in support of his contention that the SA Khatian does not give rise to any presumption of title to the suit land.

8. Mr Syed Mokaddas Ali, the learned Advocate for the plaintiff-opposite parties, submits opposing the Rule that since the impugned order of mutation passed by the revenue authority in 1969 purportedly under section 143 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act was without jurisdiction the appellate court below rightly decreed the suit by reversing the judgment and decree passed by the trial Court. The learned Advocate also submits that the plaintiff-opposite parties being the heirs of SA recorded tenants in respect of the suit land had locus standi to file the suit for declaration to the above effect and in view of the nature of declaration sought for there was no necessity to pay for any further or consequential relief.

<u>9. Admittedly, both the SA Khatians as well as RS Khatians in respect of the suit land stand in the names of the predecessors-in-interest of the plaintiff-opposite parties and also in some of their names. It is true that the SA records, in view of section 19(3) of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, do not provide conclusive evidence as regards title but it provides conclusive evidence as regards their preparation and revision. But entries in the SA records; in my opinion, provide a prima facie evidence as regards title. In order to maintain a suit for declaration under section 42 of the Specific Relief Act, the plaintiff is required to have prima facie evidence showing that he has a legal character or right to a property in respect of the subject matter of the suit and granting or refusal to grant a decree in such suit shall always depend on final adjudication thereof on evidence. Since the SA records vide Exts 3 and 3(Ka) stand in the names of the predecessor-in-interest of the plaintiff-opposite parties and also in some of their names it should be taken to be a prima facie evidence of title of the plaintiff-opposite parties in respect of the suit land and, as such, the plaintiff-opposite parties were competent to file the present suit. I do not dispute the legal principles deduced in the aforesaid cases cited by the learned Advocate for the defendant-petitioners. Since the present suit was not for a declaration of title but for a declaration of the act of the revenue authority namely, the order of mutation outside the purview of law as illegal the same is certainly maintainable. Reference may be made in this connection to the case reported in 16 DLR 298.</u>

10. Section 42 of the Specific Relief Act is not exhaustive but it does not sanction every form of declaration but only a declaration that the plaintiff is entitled to a specific legal character or right as to the property. In other words, a suit under this section cannot be maintained unless the plaintiff is a person entitled to some legal character or to such right as to property.

<u>11. In terms of the proviso to section 42 of the Specific Relief Act the court shall in exercise of its discretion refuse to grant any declaration if the plaintiff being in a position to seek further relief than a mere declaration of title fails to do so. Because the object of the proviso is to avoid multiplicity of suits and to prevent a person from getting a mere declaration of his rights in one suit and to resort to any remedy which was already available to him. A consequential relief is one which directly flows from the decree passed. A consequential relief within the meaning of section 42 of the Specific Relief Act, however, must fulfil another condition namely, the relief must be asked for as an incidental to the declaratory decree. In the present case the plaintiff-opposite parties being SA recorded tenant merely sought for a declaration that the mutation order which was passed in 1969 affecting their proprietary right in respect of the suit lands was bad in law. If a decree is passed to the above effect the purpose of the plaintiff-opposite parties would be served and they are not required, in my view, to ask for any consequential or further relief by way of recovery of possession. Because such further relief is not at all necessary in view of the declaratory relief granted in this case.</u>

<u>12. A suit for declaration simpliciter in a case, such as the present one, is maintainable without any further or consequential relief by way of recovery of khas possession, since the mutation order was challenged as made in excess of jurisdiction in the interest of maintenance or preservation of legal and proper act namely, the preparation of SA record.</u>

13. The Revenue Authority in this case is palpably without jurisdiction in disturbing the entries in the SA record in the name of mutation at the instance of the defendant-petitioners in purported exercise of powers under section 143 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act.

<u>14. Section 143 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act is attracted only when clerical mistake is required to be corrected or a mutation of names is to be made as a result of transfer or inheritance. It is not attracted when the record of right is to be corrected after a finding to be given as to the title of holders or challengers. The examination of title deeds for the purpose of determining title to the holder of record of rights is not permissible under section 143 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act. The word ''transfer'' in Clause (a) of section 143 of the said Act is limited to transfer by the recorded tenants and not by other persons. In the present case the mutation was sought for by the defendant-petitioners not because of the transfer by the plaintiff-opposite parties, but on account of auction sale at the instance of the court due to a mortgage decree. In that view of the matter, the impugned mutation order in favour of the defendant-petitioners by the revenue authority was without jurisdiction. Moreover, all the four PWs as well as DWs 1 and 2 have stated in their evidence that the plaintiff-opposite parties are in possession of the suit land. The appellate Court below has, therefore, rightly decreed that suit in favour of the plaintiff-opposite parties.</u>

In the result, the Rule is discharged and the judgment and decree passed by the appellate Court below decreeing the suit is hereby confirmed without any order as to costs.

End.

full_judgment:
The Rule issued calling upon the opposite party Nos.1 and 2 to show cause as to why the impugned judgment and decree dated 11-6-2012 and 21-6-2012 respectively passed by the learned District Judge, Noakhali in Title Appeal No. 114 of 2011 disallowing the appeal by upholding the judgment and decree dated 31-10-2011 and 3-11-2011 passed by the learned Assistant Judge, Chatkhil in Title Suit No.124 of 2006 should not be set-aside and/or pass such other or further order or orders as to this Court may seem fit and proper.

2. The facts leading to the issuance of the Rule in a nutshell can be; stated thus, the present opposite party No.1 and 2 as plaintiffs instituted the Title Suit No.124 of 2006 in the Court of learned Assistant Judge, Chatkhil, Noakhali against the present petitioners and opposite parties No.3-40 impleading them as defendants praying for declaration of title and further declaration that the deed of exchange Nos. 22 and 23 dated 2-1-1971 are forged, fraudulent, collusive and not acted upon contending infer alia, that the suit land appertaining to CS khatian No.359 corresponding to SA khatian No.372 measuring an area of 77 decimals of land in plot No.1735 under Mouza Topga originally belonged to one Yousuf Mollah who died leaving behind three daughters namely Syedunnessa, Rubitunnessa and Faridunnessa. Yousuf Mollah had another daughter namely Khairunnessa who died before him. The SA khatian was prepared in the name of Yousuf Mollah. He executed a waqf deed being No.782 dated 4-3-1916 in the name of his aforesaid three daughters and one grandson namely Ahmed Ullah. Saydunncssa died leaving behind three sons Waziullah, Aman Ullah, Fazley Rahman and one daughter Fatema Begum. By amicable settlement, Syedunnessa got 77 decimals of land of suit plot No.1735 and at the demise of Syedunnessa her property was amicably settled among her heirs and the suit plot No.1735 fallen into the saham of Waziulla, who died leaving behind two sons namely Mustafizur Rahman and Enaytur Rahman and they were owning and possessing the same. The son of Syedunnessa namely Fazlur Rahman died leaving, three sons namely Abdul Momen, Abdul Matin and Harunur Rashid. Abdul Matin died leaving behind two sons Mizanur Rahman and Muksudur Rahrrlan and two daughters namely Noorjahan Begum and Shahinur Begum. The son of Syedunnessa namely Amanullah died leaving behind three sons namely Mostafa, Helal Uddin, Zahiruddin and two daughters Shefali Begum and Shetera Begum. Rabitunnessa died leaving one son Aman Ullah and one daughter Halima Begum. That the son Faridunnessa Abdul Fattah died leaving behind one son Tariqul Islam and two daughters Kamrun Nahar, Ohidun Nahar. The son of Faridunnessa namely Abdur Rahim died leaving one son Abul Khair and one daughter Ajkarnessa and in this way the plaintiffs are the heirs of Waziullah, the son of Syedunnessa. The other heirs of Syedunnessa i.e, the defendant's No. 34-51 and Waziullah got 77 decimals of land in suit plot No.1735. In the suit land the defendants had no right, title and possession but they are claiming the suit land by way of collusive exchange deeds. Further case of the plaintiffs is such that after getting the certified copy of the deeds, they came to know that one Mobarakullah and Nurul Amin being the1st party exchanged the suit land with one ABM Takdir Hossain Bhuiyan showing him, in party but in fact the 1st party had no right, title and possession in the land of exchange it appears from the certified copy of the deed that Takdir Hossain Chowdhury, son of Alhaj Ramjan Ali Miazi is the recipient of the said deed and not Takdir Hossain Bhuiyan, son of Ator Ali. On the basis of the aforesaid collusive deed of exchange the defendants denied the title of the plaintiffs which constrained the plaintiffs to institute the original suit.

3. The contrary case of the defendants No.2, 4, 6, 18-21, 25, 26, 28 and 32 in short is thus, that the suit land is situated at Mouza-Topga under Police Station-Ramganj of District Noakhali which is recorded in CS khatian No.359, MRR No.372,plot No.1735 and total area 77 decimals out of38.50 acres of land. Further case of the contesting defendants is such that 1 anna, 6 gandas, 2 koras, 2 krantis were recorded in the name of Abdur Rashid and 2 annas, 13 gandas, 1kara, 1 kranti was recorded in the name of Abdul Latif and the rest 12 annas was recorded in the name of Yusuf Mollah. That non suited land of the said khatian of plot No.1179 measuring an area of 26 decimals was recorded in the name of Abdur Rashid and plot No.1180 comprising an area of 24 decimals was recorded in. the name of Yusuf Mollah and in plot No.1201 comprising an area of 76 decimals, In plot No.1306 an area of 19 decimals, in plot No.1316 an area of 42 decimals arid in plot No.1318 an area of 62 decimals was recorded in the name of Yusuf Mollah and the suit plot No.1735 comprising an area of 76 decimals of land was recorded in the name of Yusuf Mollah and thus Yusuf Mollah become the owner of 2.38 acres of land in all. Subsequently, Yusuf Mollah died leaving behind four daughters namely Jamila Khatun @ Khairunnessa, Syedunnessa, Rahimunnessa and Faridunnessa. Jamila Khatun @ Khairunnessa was married with one Raja Mia and she was living with her husband. Those other three daughters of Yusuf Mollah got married but they use to live in their father's residence. At the time of preparation of MR Rkhatian No.372 the suit land was wrongly recorded in the name of two daughters and legal heirs of one daughter omitting the name of Jamila @ Khairunnessa. By amicable settlement Jamila Khatun @ Khairunnessa got 38.50 acres of the suit land and for such wrong record, the right of Jamila Khatun @ Khairunnessa was extinguished. Jamila Khatun died leaving behind two sons Mobarakullah and Siddiqullah. Siddiqullah died leaving behind one son Nurul Amin. Mobarakullah and Nurul Amin have been owning and possessing 38.50 acres of land of suit plot No.1735 for about 40 years. Thereafter, on 2-1-1971 they made two exchange deeds being No. 22 and 23 with one ABM Takdir Hossain Bhuiyan and they made over possession of the suit land to Takdir Hossain. Thereafter Takdir Hossain died leaving behind the defendants No. 25-12 who had been owning and possessing the suit land for about 32 years. The plaintiffs had no right, title, possession in the suit land in any manner. Besides this, there exist a road to the eastern side of the suit plot which include 41/2decimals of land and 34 decimals was owned and possessed by defendants No.25-32 and in the recent survey khatian No.747, Plot No. 6033 was recorded in the names of defendants No.25-32. The plaintiffs did not file any objection under sections 30/31 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, 1955. The plaintiffs had no right, title and possession in the suit land. The plaintiffs have no locus standi to file the suit.

4. The learned trial court i.e. the Assistant Judge, Chatkhil during trial of the original suit after examining witnesses from the sides of the respective parties decreed the suit on contest by his judgment and decree dated 31-10-2011. Being aggrieved, the defendants preferred an appeal being Title Appeal No. 114 of 2011 in the court of earned District Judge, Noakhali and the learned District Judge, by the impugned judgment and decree dated 11-6-2012 disallowed the appeal' affirming the judgment and decree passed by the trial court.

5. Being aggrieved by and dissatisfied with 	the impugned judgment and decree this revisional application is preferred from the side of the defendant-appellant-petitioners under section 115(1) of the Code of Civil Procedure and obtained the Rule with an interim order of stay.

6. Mr Moin Uddin, the learned Advocate appeared on behalf of the petitioners while Mr Md Abdul Halim Mondal, the learned Advocate appeared on behalf of the opposite parties.

7. The learned Advocate appearing on behalf of the petitioners submits that both the courts below during disposal of the original suit and its subsequent appeal committed gross illegality and irregularity. The learned Advocate further submits that the appellate court below during passing the impugned judgment and decree violated the provisions laid down in Order XLI, rule 31 of the Code of Civil Procedure. There is no assessment of evidence and appreciation of law in its true perspective. The learned Advocate submits that the trial court as well as the appellate court during deciding the fate of the suit and its subsequent appeal misconstrued the actual position of law and without proper sifting of evidence arrived at an erroneous finding resulting in an error in the decision occasioning failure of justice. During trial of the original suit the plaintiff-opposite parties have utterly failed to discharge their onus in proving their case by any dependable evidence and the evidence adduced from the side of the plaintiffs are not trustworthy, rather they have falsified the case of the plaintiffs on title and possession. The learned Advocate submits that the title documents of the defendants i.e. the deeds of exchange are more than 30 years old and its proper custody inasmuch as was proved, under section 90 of the Evidence Act it is presumed to, be correct. In this context; the learned Advocate cited several decisions of our Apex Court.

8. The learned counsel on behalf of the petitioners during his argument submits that the plaintiffs in their testimony admits that the record of right stands recorded in the name of the defendants. The so called possession witnesses of the plaintiffs are not competent, credible, disinterested and trustworthy. The witness No.1 is the plaintiffs No.1 himself and the witnesses No.2-4 are the possession Witnesses of the plaintiffs who has totally failed to establish the plaintiff's possession, right and title over the suit land. On the contrary the defendants in support of their case have adduced 5(five) witnesses who have successfully proved the case of the defendants as stated within the contents of their pleadings. All the title documents of the defendants have been marked as Exhibits after proof without objection and there are no discussions and findings of the courts below on the said documents which has been proved and marked as Exhibits without objection. The learned Advocate lastly submits that the defendants in respect of the suit land mutated their names and have been paying rents regularly to the government. In respect of 'Ga' schedule land of the plaint the plaintiffs are claiming title but the land as described in that schedule is without specification and, as such, under section 42 of the Specific Relief Act the plaintiff's suit is barred. The deeds of exchange which has been challenged from the side of the plaintiffs in the suit were not challenged earlier and as a result of that under Article 91 of the Limitation Act as within three years from the date of the documents those were not challenged, the plaintiff's claim is barred by limitation.

9. As against the aforesaid submissions of the learned Advocate for the petitioners the learned Advocate appearing on behalf of the opposite parties opposing the Rule controverted the argument  advanced from the side of the learned Advocate for the petitioners and submits that both the courts below during disposal of the original suit and Its subsequent appeal after proper assessment of evidence and appreciation of law decided all the matters-in-issue concurrently in favour of the plaintiffs and against the defendants. The learned Advocate further submits that there is no illegality or irregularity and no misreading or non-reading of evidence and non-consideration of material facts resulting in an error in the decision occasioning failure of justice by which the impugned judgment and decree can be interfered with. The learned Advocate also submits that the deeds of exchange which are the basic documents of the defendants are forged, created and not acted upon which would be apparent from the name of the executant of the deed and from the deposition of the witness No. 1 of the defendants and thus it is clear that the executant is a fictitious person. The certified copy of the deed being No. 3039 has been falsified from the defendant Md Zahangir Hossain who has stated that Yousuf Mollah left behind four daughters namely Khairunnessa @ Jamila, Syedunnessa, Rabidunnessa and Farid-un-nessa. He further states that Khairunnessa @ Jamila lived with her husband Raja Miah separately and the MRR Khatian was prepared omitting her name but the recent khatian has been prepared in the name of his brother Takdir Hossain Bhuiyan. From the face of the documents it appears that not Takdir Hossain Bhuiyan but one Takdir Hossain Chowdhury, son of Alhaj Ramjan Ali Miazi is the recipient of the deed No.3039 which has been marked as Exhibit-4 and the matter has been properly addressed by the learned lower appellate court during disposal of the appeal. The learned Advocate lastly submits that the courts below in their observation and findings concurrently decided that the deeds of exchange are forged, collusive and manipulated. The learned Court have cited some reasons within the findings which are consistent with the evidence on records and, as such, there is nothing to interfere with the impugned judgment and decree.

10. Heard the learned Advocates of both the sides, perused the case records, exhibited documents, deposition of the witnesses and all other connected papers.

11. On perusal of the case records it transpires that admittedly the suit land originally belonged to one Yousuf Mollah and it is the case of the plaintiffs that Yousuf Mollah died leaving behind his three daughters. His another daughter died during his life time leaving one son Ahmed Ullah and Vis-a-vis it was contended from the side of the defendants that at the demise of Yousuf Mollah his four daughters namely Khairunnessa @ Jamila, Syedunnessa, Rabidunnessa and Faridunnessa inherited the property left, behind by Yousuf Mollah. Khairunnessa married with one Raja Miah and by way of amicable settlement among the heirs in all 38 and 1/2 decimals of land in plot No.1735 lies in the saham of Khairunnessa @ Jamila who died leaving two sons Siddiqullah and Mobarakullah.

12. Having gone through the papers on records it transpires that the courts below in their observation and findings decided that the deed of exchange Nos.22 and 23 dated 2-1-1971 which stands registered in favour of the defendants are forged, collusive and anti-dated. Vis-a-vis, it was contended from the side of the defendants that the plaintiffs are stopped from challenging these documents as their claim is barred under Article 91 of the Limitation Act since within three years from the year of documents those were not objected and long after 40 years the plaintiffs are challenging the same. It is a fact that the deeds has been marked as Exhibit-kha and kba(1) which appears to be more than 30 years old documents.

13. I have come across the evidence adduced from the sides of the respective parties that to substantiate the plaintiff's case they have adduced four witnesses. The witness No. 1 is the plaintiff No.1 himself Md Mostafizur Rahman. The plaintiff No. 1 in his testimony admits at a stage that the deeds of exchange are of more than 38/39 years and the recent survey was completed in their area in the year 1990-91 and the suit land of SA plot No.1735 has been recorded in recent survey as plot No.6033 and in 41/2 decimals of land of the suit plot there is a road by which the villagers move. He also admits that in the recent settlement plot No.6033, 34 decimals, of land have been included in field survey khatian No.2019 and in DP khatian No.787 which has been prepared in the name of the defendant's father and against that they did not file any case under sections 30/31 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act. In respect of the disputed exchange deeds the plaintiff No.1 states that his father died in the year 1993 and the deeds were executed and registered in the year 1971. During the life time of his father he did not file any case and after 40 years of the deeds they have 'instituted the original suit. Admittedly, the plaintiffs have failed to produce any Rent Receipt showing payment of rent in respect of the suit land and as regard their possession the witnesses who deposed as witness Nos. 2,3,4 and 5 tried to establish the case of the plaintiffs but from the examination-in-chief of these witnesses it is apparent from the face of the papers that the witnesses have failed to describe the actual identity of the suit land including its specification and as regard boundary they have totally failed to state anything. On the other hand, the defendants in support of their case have adduced five witnesses and among them DW1 is the defendant No.26 who tried to corroborate their pleading in his testimony. It is to be noticed that the established principle of civil law is such that it is the plaintiffs who in order to obtain a decree in their favour shall have to discharge their onus in proving their case, but on critical analysis of evidence I find that in respect of title and possession of the plaintiffs they have totally failed to prove their case by any tangible evidence and the evidence led from their side is not at all trustworthy, credible and competent.

14. Besides this, the proposition of law is such that under section 90 of the Evidence Act if a document is 30 years old or more than that, be produced from. a proper custody is presumed to have been signed and written by the person whose signature and writings are found and to have been executed and attested duly. No proof of any of these facts is required and the document, if it is thirty years old or more will prove itself provided it is produced from proper custody. In this context, the learned Advocate of the petitioners cited two decisions of our Apex Court passed in the case of Syed Abdul Haque vs Surendra Nath Majumder reported in 59 DLR (AD) 111 and the decision given in the case of Additional Deputy Commissioner (Revenue), Pabnavs Md Reazuddin Pk. reported in 8 BLT (AD) 185 = 5 BLC (AD) 76 law enjoins that without establishing the plaintiff's own title and possession they are not entitled to challenge any other deeds by way of simple declaration within the ambit of section 42 of the Specific Relief Act and in this context a decision is referred from the petitioner's side of our Appellate Division in the case of Ratan Chandra Dey vs Jinnator Nahar reported in 2XP (AD) 313. Apart from this, under the purview of section 42 of the Specific Relief Act with regard to a suit for declaration of title to an unspecified portion of land a decision is referred from the side of the petitioners of our Apex Court reported in 2XP (AD) 68 and the decision given by this Court in the case of Bashiur Rahman Biswas vs Md Hanif Ali Biswas reported in 21 BLD 89 = 7 BLC186.

<u>15. Having regard to the decisions referred to above I may not be out of place to advert the provisions laid down in Order VII, rule 3 of the Code of Civil Procedure regarding the specification and identification of the suit land which is badly required for having a declaration of title. The description of the land must be specific with its boundary and if it is found that the land described in the schedule of the plaint suffers from any vagueness or un-specification the plaintiff must suffer. Furthermore, the plaintiffs in order to succeed must establish their own case by credible evidence and weakness of the defendants is no ground for awarding a decree in favour of the plaintiffs.</u>

16. In the instant case; as I have already referred to above, that in respect of a particular portion or land described in schedule 'ga' of the plaint the plaintiffs have sought for a declaration of title and the witnesses have totally failed to discharge their onus in proving the respective case of the plaintiffs as to their alleged possession and identification of the land. Besides this, having gone through the impugned judgment and decree it is evident to note that the lower appellate court i.e. the learned District Judge, Noakhali at the time of disposal of the appeal on merit have utterly failed to assess the evidence on records and there is no discussion of evidence and no sifting of the same in its true perspective. Under the ambit of Order XLI, rule 31 of the Code of Civil Procedure it is the incumbent duty upon the appellate court below while affirming or reversing the judgment of the trial court that, the appellate court shall state the reasons for the decision after proper evaluation and assessment of evidence on records. Our Apex Court in the case of Hajarilal Mondal vs Md Mozaffor Bepari reported in 8 BLC (AD) 77 held that it is the principle of law that the lower appellate court being the final court of fact will have to discuss and re-assess the evidence on records independently while either reversing or affirming the findings of the trial court. But in the instant case as I have cited above that the learned District Judge have totally failed to scan the evidence on records by his discussion and evaluation of both oral and documentary evidence.

17. Before parting, however, I like to advert that with regard to the name of 'Takdir Hossain Bhuiyan' and 'Takdir Hossain Chowdhury' as it appears meanwhile that the proposition of law made herein above has imposed legal embargo upon the plaintiffs in getting the relief as prayed for it is needless to discuss more inasmuch as it is immaterial at this stage. Be that as it may, I find that the plaintiffs to the suit in order to succeed must have to establish their case and to stand on their own legs. But analyzing the evidence led from their side it is crystal clear that the plaintiffs have totally failed to discharge their onus in proving their right, title, interest and possession over the suit land by adducing credible, cogent, tangible evidence which can be treated trustworthy.

18. Having regard to the facts, circumstance and discussions referred to above I am constrained to hold such a view that the submission advanced from the side of the learned counsel for the petitioners accompanied by series of decisions of this Court and our Apex Court have got every nexus in the instant case.

19. In the result, the Rule having much merit is made absolute without any order as to costs. The impugned judgment and decree dated 11-6-2012 and 21-6-2012 respectively passed by the learned District Judge, Noakhali in Title Appeal No. 114 of 2011 disallowing the appeal by upholding the judgment and decree dated 31-10-2011 and.3-11-2011 passed by the learned Assistant Judge, Chatkhil in Title Suit No. 124 of 2006 is hereby set-aside. The original suit be dismissed on contest without cost.

20. The order of stay granted earlier by this court at the time of issuance of the Rule stands vacated.

Communicate the judgment and order immediately and send back the lower Court's record at once.

End.
