case_source: (From the Judgment and Order dated August 24,1999 passed by the High Court Division in Civil Revision No. 1358 of 1995)
full_judgment:
Md. Ruhul Amin, J: This is plaintiff's appeal, by leave, against the judgment and order dated August 24, 1999 of a Single Bench of the High Court Division in Civil Revision No. 1358 of 1995 making the Rule absolute upon setting aside the judgment and decree dated February 26, 1995 of the 2nd Court of Additional District Judge, Chuadanga, in Title Appeal No. 22 of 1994 affirming those of dated February 24, 1994 of the Court of Senior Assistant Judge, Damurhuda, Chuadanga, in Title Suit No. 30 of 1985 decreeing the suit which was filed seeking declaration of title, confirmation of possession, recovery of khas possession of some portion of land in suit and for a further declaration that the kabala in the name of defendant No. 8 is void and not binding upon the plaintiff and that the SA record in the name of defendant No. 9 and RS record in the name of defendant No. 8 are incorrect.

2. Plaintiff averred that land in suit belonged to CS recorded tenant Monohar Ghosh and on the death of Monohar Ghosh his interest devolved upon his daughter Charubala who settled 41 decimals of land (including the land in suit) to one Taiyab Ali on 10th Baisakh, 1357 BS and in his name SA record was prepared and he possessed the land on payment of rent to the Government. Plaintiff by the kabala dated August 6, 1963 purchased from Taiyab Ali 41 decimals of land and out of that 14 decimals were acquired by C&B Department and thereupon he remained owner and possessor of 27 decimals of land. It was further averred that during the War of Liberation he left Bangladesh and in his absence structures including dwelling house in the land in suit were destroyed and after emergence of Bangladesh he returned and he started to possess the land and while he was so possessing the defendant No. 1 threatened him to dispossess and thereupon he filed Criminal Miscellaneous Case No. 89 of 1975 under section 144 of the Code of Criminal Procedure on June 11, 1975 and the said proceeding was made absolute. Thereupon, the defendant No. 1 filed Title Suit No. 626 of 1975 in the Court of Munsif, Chuadanga, seeking declaration of title and for a further declaration that the SA khatian as regard the land of the said suit (which is the subject matter of the Title Suit No. 30 of 1985) is erroneous. The said suit having been dismissed on June 30, 1979, the defendant No. 1 filed appeal No. 92 of 1979 and the same was dismissed on April 7, 1981. It was also averred that during the pendency of the Title Suit No. 626 of 1975 the defendant No. 1 on May 1, 1979 dispossessed the plaintiff from the part of the land of the instant suit and erected one but and that during the pendency of the Appeal No. 92 of 1979 the defendant No. 1 converted the hut erected earlier into a 'chouchala' hut and also erected some other huts. It is the case of the plaintiff since he has been dispossessed from the portion of the land in suit on May 1, 1979, same has necessitated him to file the suit.

3. The suit was contested by the defendant Nos. 1-6 and 8 by filing separate set of written statements.

4. It was the case of the defendant Nos. 1- 6 that defendant No. 9 (Nurul Islam) took settlement of 21 decimals of land of plot No. 1049 from Charubala on 15th Chaitra, 1359 BS and therefrom 12 decimals of land was acquired by C & B Department and thereupon SA record in respect of 9 decimals of land was prepared in his name. Defendant No. 9 sold said land on October 20, 1979 to Chahiruddin (defendant No. 8) and in his RS record has been prepared and he allowed the defendant No. 1 to stay therein as licensee. It was also the case of the defendant No. 1 that C & B Department acquired 16 decimals of land out of 41 decimals of land of plot No. 1050 and the remaining 25 decimals of land was acquired by Bahar Ali upon obtaining settlement in Ashwin, 1360 BS from Charubala and Bahar Ali died leaving 3 sons - Rahim Ali, Taiyab Ali and Ayub Ali and the defendant No. 1 purchased 27½ decimals of land from Ayub Ali and Rahim Ali, sons of Bahar Ali by the kabala dated January 22, 1975 and since purchase he is possessing the land by constructing huts and is living therein with the members of the family. It was further contended by the defendant Nos. 1-6 that plaintiff has got no right, title and interest in the land in suit and he is not in possession of the land of suit plots, and they have not constructed any but in the land of the plaintiff. It was also the case of the defendant Nos. 1-6 that they are exercising act of possession in 16 decimals of land of SA plot No. 1142 which later on recorded in RS plot Nos. 2323 and 2324 and the plaintiff on the basis of his purchase from Taiyab Ali is possessing 9 decimals and the defendants have got their names mutated and upon obtaining receipt paying rent to the Government.

5. The case of the defendant No. 8 was almost similar to the case of defendant Nos. 1- 6.

6. The trial Court decreed the suit on the finding that the suit of the plaintiff as framed is maintainable and not bad for defect of parties and also not barred by limitation and that plaintiff has right, title and interest in the land in suit and defendant Nos. 1-6 in 1979 dispossessed the plaintiff from part of the land in suit and the SA record in the name of defendant No. 9 is erroneous and the purchase by the defendant No. 9 from defendant No. 8 is not binding upon the plaintiff and the RS record in the defendant No. 8 is incorrect.

7. Defendant Nos. 1-6 filed appeal. The appellate Court affirmed the judgment and decree of the trial Court on the findings that the defendants' contention relating to quantity of land of plot No. 1050 measuring 41 decimals of land is not correct, rather the defendants have introduced the said case to mislead the Court. The appellate Court disbelieved the defendants' contention of taking settlement from Charubala by Nurul Islam being fictitious since period in which Nurul Islam is said to have taken settlement he was a mere child and he had no source of income and moreover, the fact of taking settlement was not proved by calling competent witness. The appellate Court also concurred with the finding of the trial Court that transfer by Nurul Islam to Chahiruddin was a mere paper transaction and that plaintiff was dispossessed by the defendant Nos. 1-6 in the year, 1979 and as plaintiff has right, title and interest in the land in suit he is entitled to have a decree for recovery of khas possession upon evicting the defendant Nos. 1-6.

8. The defendant Nos. 1-6 moved the High Court Division in revisional jurisdiction against the judgment and decree of the appellate Court. The High Court Division made the Rule absolute on the finding that the appellate Court as well as trial Court were in error in decreeing the suit on the basis of Exhibits 4 and 6 (judgment and decree in Title Suit No. 626 of 1975 and in Title Appeal No. 92 of 1979 respectively) considering them as the good piece of evidence in support of the claim of title of the plaintiff and that appellate Court having had expressed view doubting genuineness of the documents on the basis of which plaintiff claiming title was in error in decreeing the suit basing its judgment thereon. The High Court Division was also of the view that the judgment in the Title Suit No. 626 of 1975 and in the Title Appeal No. 92 of 1979 were not being the judgment of the kind as contemplated by the provision of section 41 of the Evidence Act and that also not being the judgment as regards the matter as contemplated by the provision of section 42 of the Evidence Act and consequently, as the judgments of the aforementioned suit and the appeal cannot "be considered as a conclusive proof of the fact they stated and, as such, they were also not acceptable as relevant evidence under section 42 of the Evidence Act" and consequently, findings and decisions made by the trial Court as well as by the appellate Court placing reliance of the said judgments as regard the title and possession of the plaintiff in the land in suit are not sustainable in law. The High Court Division also held that the finding made by the trial Court as well as by the appellate Court in respect of the deed of defendant No. 8 placing reliance on the judgment of the Title Suit No. 626 of 1975 and Appeal No. 92 of 1979 was bad in law. The High Court Division further was of the view that the land as to which decree for khas possession sought for is unspecified and indefinite.

9. Leave was granted to consider the contentions that the High Court Division was in error in holding that the judgment on the basis of Exhibits 4 and 6 is incorrect in that decision as regard the case of the respective parties in the suit was made by the trial Court as well as by the appellate Court upon discussions of the evidence, both oral and documentary, brought on record and that not solely on the basis of Exts. 4 and 6, that in spite of remark made by the appellate Court, the said Court considered the evidence, both oral and documentary, and on the basis of the evidence so discussed arrived at the finding as regard the title and possession of the plaintiff, but the High Court Division did not consider the materials that weighed with the appellate Court and that the High Court Division was in error about the admissibility of Exhibits 4 and 6, the previous judgments relating to the land in suit and misconstrued the provision of section 41 of the Evidence Act and wrongly placed reliance in the decision reported in 41 DLR (AD) 97 though the said decision relates to admissibility of the previous judgment.

10. The learned Counsel for the appellant submitted that the High Court Division was in error in reversing the judgments of the courts below upon taking the view that plaintiff's case was disposed of on the basis of the judgments in the previous suit and the appeal therefrom although both the courts below on consideration of the evidence brought on record by the plaintiff, both oral and documentary, other than the judgments of the previous suit, is Title Suit No. 626 of 1975 and the appeal therefrom, arrived at the finding that alleged settlement of defendant No. 9, Nurul Islam from Charubala was fictitious one and that purchase from defendant No. 9 by defendant No. 8 was a mere paper transaction and that purchase by the defendant No. 1 from the heirs of Bahar Ali who is said to have taken settlement in 1360 BS from Charubala was also found fictitious and that plaintiff's purchase being of the year, 1963 the defendant No. 1 by purchase in 1975 from Bahar Ali's heirs did not acquire any interest in the land in suit. The learned Counsel further submitted that judgment of the previous suit i.e. 626 of 1975 and the judgment in the appeal therefrom were considered as the fact relevant being the judgment inter parties is plaintiff and the defendant No. 1, and also in connection with consideration of the question of possession of the plaintiff and the defendant No. 1 in the land in suit. The learned Counsel also submitted that the judgment in the previous Title Suit No. 626 of 1975 and the judgment in the appeal therefrom (Exhibits 4 and 6) were referred to by the trial Court as well as the appellate Court in the context of the claim of the parties in the suit i.e. plaintiff and the defendant No. 1, to the land in suit relating to title and possession. The learned Counsel continued that the High Court Division was in error in holding that the land as regards which recovery of possession was sought for unspecified and indefinite in that in the schedule to the plaint the land as regard to which recovery of possession has been prayed for specifically described.

11. The learned Counsel submitted that High Court Division was in error in observing that the judgments in the earlier suit i.e. in Title Suit No. 626 of 1975 and the appeal therefrom "were not relevant" in the instant suit, nor the same could be considered as "the conclusive proof of fact stated therein" upon placing reliance on the provision of sections 41 and 42 of Evidence Act as under section 43 of the Evidence Act in the background of the contentions of the parties in the instant suit the judgment of the earlier suit was a fact in issue as well as was a relevant fact. The learned Counsel lastly, submitted that the High Court Division was in error in holding that though the appellate Court entertained doubt as to the genuineness of the papers on the basis whereof plaintiff claiming the right, title and interest and the suit but still then affirmed the decree of the trial Court upon overlooking the material part of the judgment of the appellate Court wherein the said Court discussed the case of the parties in the background of the materials placed on record and arrived at the finding that the claim of the plaintiff in the land in suit is acceptable in the absence of any claim from the Government in the land in suit, than that of the defendant. The finding so arrived at is based on evidence both oral and documentary and the High Court Division totally ignored the evidence on which the appellate Court based its judgment while making observation that appellate Court in spite of entertaining doubt as to papers of the plaintiff affirmed the judgment of the trial Court.

12. The learned Advocate-on-record appearing for the respondent Nos. 1-6 submitted that since settlement claimed by Taiyab Ali was not proved and thus plaintiff by purchase from Taiyab Ali as did not acquire any right, title and interest in the land in suit the decree passed by the trial Court and affirmed by the appellate Court was rightly set aside by the High Court Division. He also submitted that land as regards which recovery of possession has been sought for as not specific the decree passed in the suit was not sustainable in law. He lastly, submitted that the judgment in the previous suit relied upon by the trial Court as well as by the appellate Court in decreeing the suit being not relevant, the High Court Division was quite right in setting aside the decree passed in favour of the plaintiff.

13. The contention of the contesting respondents that the land as to which recovery of possession has been sought for is unspecified and the finding of the High Court Division in that regard appears to be upon perusal of the schedule to the plaint and the description of the land, recovery whereof has been prayed for, given therein is not correct. On perusal of the schedule we are of the view the land as regards which decree for recovery of possession has been passed is identifiable and specifiable. The other contention of the respondent that settlement taken by Taiyab Ali from Charubala as was not established, the plaintiff by purchase from Taiyab Ali in the year 1963 did not acquire any right, title and interest in the land in suit and consequently as the courts below were in error in decreeing the suit the High Court Division committed no error in setting aside the said decree is also of no merit as the trial Court as well as the appellate Court on consideration of the evidence, both oral and documentary, have arrived at the concurrent finding that Taiyab Ali, vendor of the plaintiff, took settlement of the land in suit from the admitted owner. It may be mentioned High Court Division while setting aside the decree in the suit failed to advert itself to the materials upon placing reliance whereon the Court of first instance and the appellate Court arrived at the finding that Taiyab Ali, vendor of the plaintiff, took settlement in 1357 BS of the land in suit and in his name SA record was prepared and the plaintiff purchased the land in the year 1963. The High Court Division also failed to notice the fact that while settlement to Nurul Islam by Charubala in the year 1359 BS was not established as genuine then the claim of the defendant No. 1 in respect of the land in suit by purchase from the person who said to have taken settlement in 1359 BS did not vest any title in him. The fact of dispossession of the plaintiff from the land in suit has been noted in the RS khatian prepared in the name of the plaintiff in respect of the land in suit and that has also been established by oral evidence and while in the instant suit the question of dispossession of the plaintiff by the defendant No. 1 came up for consideration the trial Court as well as the appellate Court in disposing of the issue of dispossession referred to the judgments, Exhibits 4 and 6, wherein it was held that defendant No. 1 dispossessed the plaintiff in 1979.

<u>14. There remains the question of taking into consideration judgment in the previous suit ie judgment in Title Suit No. 626 of 1975, and the appeal therefrom (Exhibits 4 and 6). In the light of the provision of sections 43 and 13 of the Evidence Act, Exhibits 4 and 6 are relevant in the instant suit since the question of dispossession is a material question for consideration for maintainability of the suit or, in other words, as regards presence of cause of action and also in the context of noting in the RS record to the effect that the defendant No. 1 is in forceful possession of portion of the land in suit as well as finding in the previous suit that defendant No. 1 dispossessed the plaintiff from the land in suit in 1979 during the pendency of Title Suit No. 626 of 1975. The law is now settled that a judgment whether inter parties or not may be conclusive evidence against all persons of its existence, date and legal effect, as distinguished from the accuracy of the decision rendered. The former judgments and decrees were not themselves a transaction or an instance within the meaning of section 13 of the Evidence Act, but the suit in which they were made was a transaction or an instance in which the defendant's right of possession was claimed and recognised and that to establish that such transaction or instance took place the previous judgment (s) was the best evidence 41 DLR (AD) 97. The question as to admissibility and relevancy of the previous judgment in a subsequent suit in the changed position of the parties as regards the matter, which is common in the previous suit as well as in the latter suit, came up for consideration in the case of Malik Din and another vs Mohammad Aslant reported in 21 DLR 95 and therein it has been observed "Judgments, whether inter parties or not, are conclusive evidence for and against all persons whether parties, privies, or strangers of its own existence, date and legal effect, as distinguished from the accuracy of the decision rendered. In other words, the law attributes unerring verity to the sustentative as opposed to the judicial portions of the record. But where the judgment is inter parties, even recitals in such a judgment are admissible. A previous judgment is admissible also to prove statement or admission or an acknowledgement made by a party or the predecessor in interest of a party, in his pleadings in a previous litigation. Similarly, a judgment narrating the substance of the pleadings of the parties to a litigation is admissible to establish the allegations made by them on that occasion". As to admissibility of the previous judgment under section 43 of the Evidence Act it has been observed in the case of Alauddin Mia and another vs Abdul Latif and others reported in 9 DLR 357 as follows: "Under this section, judgments are admissible in evidence only if the existence of such judgment is a fact in issue or if it is relevant under some other provision of the Evidence Act ....  that judgments, not inter parties, were admissible in evidence for and against everyone under section 13 of the Evidence Act. They are thus admissible either as evidencing 'transaction' by which a right or a custom in question is created, claimed or modified, recognised, asserted or denied or as 'particular instances' in which the right or custom in question was claimed or modified, recognised, asserted or denied .....  judgments, not inter parties, are admissible in evidence under section 13 of the Evidence Act".</u>

<u>15. It may be mentioned in the previous suit is Title Suit No. 326 of 1975, defendant No. 1 was the plaintiff and the plaintiff of the instant suit was defendant No. 6 and the vendor of the plaintiff was defendant No. 1 and in that situation the judgment in the previous suit even if may not strictly be considered as the judgment inter parties but the same has been certainly admissible in evidence to show that there was a litigation between the plaintiff and the defendant No. 1 who were parties in the previous suit and in that suit the specific contention of the parties as to whether plaintiff of that previous suit (defendant No. 1 herein) has right, title and interest in the land in suit and the Court had found in that suit that said plaintiff had no right, title and interest in the land in suit which is the subject matter of the instant suit. In the background of the facts of the instant case the trial Court as well as the appellate Court while considering the question of right, title and interest and claim of possession of the plaintiff, which was denied by the defendant Nos. 1-6, the said Courts in deciding the question of right, title, interest and possession of the plaintiff were not in error in considering the judgment in the previous suit along with the other evidence, both oral and documentary, and decreeing the suit and that being the position the High Court Division without considering the evidence other than Exhibits 4 and 6 (previous judgment) placing reliance whereupon judgment by the trial Court was made and the appellate Court affirmed was in error in reversing the judgment of the appellate Court affirming the judgment and decree of the trial Court on the view that the said Courts decreed the suit solely on the basis of previous judgments which, according to the High Court Division, was not relevant.</u>

<u>In view of the discussions made hereinabove the appeal is allowed. The judgment and order of the High Court Division is set aside and the judgment and decree of the appellate Court affirming the judgment and decree of the trial Court is restored.</u>

There is no order as to costs.

End.

full_judgment:
These Rules obtained on an application under section 115 of the Code of Civil Procedure is directed against the judgment and decree dated 30-8-92 passed by the learned Additional District Judge-in-charge, First Court, Sylhet, in Title Appeal No. 39 of 1987 which was analogously heard with Title Appeal No. 40 of 1987 dismissing both the appeals on affirming judgment and decree dated 17-11-86 passed by the learned Subordinate Judge, Second Court, Sylhet, in Title Suit No. 308 of 1984 decreeing the suit.

2. The plaintiff opposite party No. 1 filed Title Suit No. 382 of 1967 in the Second Court of Subordinate Judge, Sylhet, against the petitioner and others praying for principal relief of simple declaration of title of the plaintiff Deity to the properties described in the schedules 1 and 2 including the properties of schedule 3 which is within schedule 1(one). In the said suit the present petitioner, late Durga Namasudarani and late Sekandar Ali who is the predecessor-in-interest of the opposite party Nos. 2-10 were impleaded as principal defendant Nos. 1, 2 and 3 respectively and the number of the defendants in the said suit were 12 in all. The said suit was subsequently transferred to the 2nd Additional Court of Subordinate Judge, Sylhet and on 10-2-69 re-numbered therein as Title Suit No. 5 of 1969. On 15-3-69 the learned Subordinate Judge heard the application of the defendant Nos. 1-3 filed in the suit about its maintainability and on consideration of the evidence, both oral and documentary, he found the plaintiff-opposite party out of possession of the entire suit land from before the institution of the suit and also found that the suit was grossly under valued. Consequent upon the aforesaid judgment and order dated 15-3-69 passed in Title Suit No. 5 of 1969 in respect of its maintainability and valuation, the plaintiff opposite party No. 1 by an application dated 26-3-69 amended the plaint and after such amendment the principal relief in Paragraph No. Ka(1) and Ka(2) of Paragraph No. 11 of the plaintiff stood as follows :

১১। (ক)(১) তপশীল বর্ণিত ভুমি সহ নিম্ন ১ম ও ২য় তপশীল ভূর্মাদিত বাদী দেবতার স্বত্ব সাব্যস্ত হইয়া সদর মুরসেফী ২য় আদালতের ১৯৬৬ ইং ৩১১ নং স্বত্ত্বের মোকদ্দমার বাদীর সেবাইত বলিয়া প্রচারিত সুলেনামাপন্ড আর্কষন প্রাবনিষ্ঞক অবৈধ প্রতিপত্তি মূলে প্রভাবান্বিত ঘোষনার বহিত হইয়া বিরোধীর ভূর্ম্যাদিত বাদী দখল স্থিরতর থাকার এবং বেদখলার অংশ হইতে গ্রহাদি বাধা বিঘ্ন অপসারনের মূল বিবাদীগনকে অনধিকারী গনে তকাইয়া দিয়া বাদী তাহাতে খাস দখল পাওয়ার।

১১। ক(২) বাদী বিগ্রহের তৎকালীন সেবাইত মন মহন দাস বিরুদ্ধে ১/২ নং বিবাদী গনের দায়ের সদর মুনসফী ২য় আদালতের ১৯৬৬ ইং ৩৩১ নং স্বত্ন (নিষধাজ্ঞার) মোকদ্দমার মন মোহন দাস সম্পাদিত প্রচারিত সুলেনামা ভিত্তিক এই মোকদ্দমার ২৪-৫-৬৭ইং ও ৩০-৫-৬৭ ইং ও ৩-৮-৬৭ ইং তারিখে দাখেলী সুলেনামা ভিত্তিক বিগত ৩-৬-৬৭ ইং তারিখের আদালত প্রদ্ত্ত ডিক্রীপন্ড অর্কধন্য প্রাবন্ধিক ও অবৈধ ঘোষনায় রহিত হওয়ার।”

3. The plaintiff's substantive case is that, the suit land belonged to Radha Krishna Deity which has been in existence over the land of schedule 1 (one) for over 100 years. The local members of the Namasudra community installed the plaintiffs Deity in an akhra within the land of schedule 1(one) of the plaint, one Joyram Baishnab was the 1st Shebayet of the plaintiff Deity. Thereafter, his disciple Saran Das Baishnab became the Shebayet who acquired some lands with the income of the plaintiff Deity. Saran Das died leaving behind his disciple Kaluk Das Baishnab who became the next Shebayet of the plaintiff Deity. Kaluk Das Baishnab also acquired some lands mentioned in schedule 2 (two) of the plaint with the income of the properties belonging to the plaintiff Deity. After the death of his father the defendant No. 1 petitioner was brought to the Akhrabari by Muluk Das Baishnab and the latter permitted him to stay in a place near the Akhra and since then he had been living therewith the permission of Kuluk Das Baishnab. The original defendant No. 2 late Durga Namasudrani, wife of Domai Namasudra (real name being fugal Namasudrani wife of Kuluk Das) used to reside as a widow at the Akhra of the plaintiff Deity and performed the duties of a maid servant. Kuluk Das Baishnab died in Chaitra, 1371, BS without leaving behind any disciple. In the circumstances the members of the Namasudra Community as well as the defendant No. 1 petitioner Jogendra Ram Namasudra brought Shebayet Mon Mohan Das Baishnab in the Akhra of the plaintiff Deity for performing the duties of a Shebayet of the plaintiff Deity inasmuch as he was a Baishnab from before. In Chaitra, 1372, BS Mon Mohan Das Bishnab took charge of the plaintiff Deity and its properties. At the instance of Mon Mohan Das Baishnab the name of the Shebayet was mutated in Government papers. Thereafter, trouble arose with the defendants and at the instance of the defendants Mon Mohan Das Baishnab was in Hajat for several days on the allegation of the defendant No. 1 petitioner to the effect that Mon Mohan Das Baishnab was an Indian national. Defendant No. 1 petitioner Jogendra Ram Namasudra filed a false arson case against Mon Mohan Das Baishnab which was ultimately dismissed. Thereafter, the defendant No. 1, petitioner filed one case bearing. No. 448 or 1966 against Mon Mohan Das Baishnab under section 145 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, defendant Nos. 1 and 2 also filed Title Suit No. 331 of 1966 in the Second Court of Munsif, Sylhet, against Mon Mohan Das Baishnab who filed written objection. Defendant No. 1 petitioner Jogendra Ram Namasudra with others obtained the signature of Mon Mohan Das Baishnab by criminal intimidation and then prepared a Solenama and filed the same in Title Suit No. 331 of 1966 and in the said criminal case under section 145 or the Code of Criminal Procedure. The plaintiff Deity was not a party either to the aforesaid Title Suit No. 331 of 1966 or to the aforesaid proceeding under section 145 of the Code of Criminal Procedure. The alleged sole decree in title suit No. 331 of 1966 was fraudulent. The defendant No. 3 (late Sikandar Ali) made fraudulent auction purchase of some properties of schedule 1(one) of the plaint which has been described in schedule 3 of the plaint. With these allegations the plaintiff Deity party prayed for declaration of the title to the disputed land as well as for confirmation of possession therein and in the alternative prayed for recovery of possession from any portion of the suit land by removing all constructions there from. The plaintiffs Deity also prayed for a declaration that the 2(two) Solenamas filed in Title Suit No. 331 of 1966 as well as in the aforesaid criminal case are fraudulent, void and are of no legal effect.

4. The present petitioner Jogendra Nath Namasudra as defendant No. 1 together with the original defendant No. 2 and defendant No. 3 filed a written statement denying all material allegations made in the plaint. Their case is that Kuluk Das adopted the defendant No.1 petitioner as his son about 27/28 years ago and since that time he has been living in his house as his adopted son. There is no Deity of the name of Radha Krishna in his house and there is also no existence of any Akhra in the house of Mulak Das Baishnab over the land of schedule 1 (one). Kulak Das inherited his house with some properties in suit from his maternal uncle Saran Das Baishnab. Kulak Das acquired the remaining suit land by purchase with his own money and means. Both Saran Das and Kuluk Das did not renounce worldly affairs and relinquish properties. Both of them were married. Kuluk Das married the defendant No. 2 Jugal Namasudarani after the death of his first wife. The name of the defendant No. 2 is not Durga Namasudarani as is falsely shown in the plaint. Her actual name is Jugal Namasudarani. The defendant No. 3 namely, late Sikander Ali, auction purchased some lands of Kulak in a court sale mentioned in schedule 3 of the plaint and has been possessing the same. The defendant No. 1 petitioner has been living in the house of Kulak with his wife and 4(four) children and his mother defendant No.2. The so-called Shebayet Mon Mohan Das was not in possession of any inch of the suit land. The defendant No. 1 petitioner has been in possession of all the suit land excepting the lands of schedule No. 3. Hakshmi Narayan Deity was the private Deity of Kulak Das. Mon Mohan Das was never installed as a Shebayet and he filed bonafide the Solenama in Title Suit No. 331 of 1966 as well as under the said section 145 of the Code of Criminal Procedure proceeding disclaiming any interest of the so-called plaintiff Deity. The suit is not maintainable in its present form and manner as well as for want of cause of action and the plaintiff has no possession whatsoever in the suit land. Mon Mohan Das being a Sudra is not entitled to become a Baishnab and he being an Indian citizen cannot get any relief in this suit, he has also not been appointed as a Shebayet maintaining due procedure and, as such, cannot conduct the suit on behalf of the Deity Rada Krishna Bigraha and as such the suit is liable to be dismissed with costs to the answering defendants.

5.. During the trial both the parties adduced both oral and documentary evidence. From the side of the plaintiff many persons were initially examined as PWs and from the side of the defendants 7 persons were examined as DWs. The plaintiff Deity was represented by its Shebayet Mon Mohan Das, Baisbab and he examined himself as PW 1. The learned Subordinate Judge on consideration of the evidence and materials on record dismissed the suit by a judgment and order dated 31-12-69, holding, inter alia, that the plaintiff opposite party had not succeeded in proving his alleged title to the suit land. Against the aforesaid judgment and order dated 31-12-69 the plaintiff opposite party No. 1 preferred First Appeal No.199 of 1970 on 23-4-70 in the High Court Division of the Supreme Court of Bangladesh and in the Memorandum of Appeal the plaintiff Deity was represented by Mon Mohan Das Baishnab upon whose death the plaintiff Deity was represented by Gopal Das Baishnab alias Kamal Das Baishnb. That first Appeal was heard by a Division Bench of the High Court Division and the same was allowed by the judgment and order dated 9-7-80 holding that without declaration that the sole decree obtained in Title Suit No. 331 was obtained by intimidation and undue influence therefore no relief could be given to the plaintiff opposite party and remanded the case back to the trial Court for giving opportunity to the parties to amend the plaint suitably and to bring on record the necessary elements to show that the sole decree obtained in Title Suit No. 331 of 1966 was obtained by intimidation, undue influence and coercion and it was further observed that there was insufficient evidence as regards nomination of a person to hold the post of Shebayet in case a Shebayet died without a disciple as alleged in the plaint and kept the entire matter open for the trial Court to arrive at a decision in accordance with law. Against that judgment of the High Court Division a Civil Petition for leave to appeal No. 17 of 1981 was preferred by the defendant No. 1 alone and that application was summarily rejected by the Appellate Division by its order dated 23-1-81 and upheld the judgment and order passed by the High Court Division. Ultimately, the record of the suit was sent back to the trial Court and the plaint was amended and additional written statement was filed by defendant No.1 and the opposite party No. 12, that is, defendant No.5(ka) who is son of late Sekandar Ali denying all material allegations made in the amendment petition. The opposite party Nos. 26-27 namely, Mahmud Ali and the Government of Bangladesh respectively who were added as defendant Nos.13 and 15 respectively also filed separate written statement denying all material allegations in the plaint.

6. The substantive case of the Opposite Party No. 26 that is, the defendant No. 13, is that there is no cause of action for the suit which was barred by limitation as well as for defect of parties and also barred by estoppel, waiver and acquiescence. There was no proper representation of the so-called Deity and Gopal Das Baishnab had no right to represent the Deity. Plot No. 459 really corresponds to item No. 11 of schedule 1(one) of the plaint. The 1st and 2nd schedule land never belonged to the plaintiff Deity which were the personal self acquired property of Kulak Das Namasudra and late Sikandar Ali during the life time of Kulak Das Namasudra purchased the property mentioned in schedule 3(three) of the plaint in money execution case No. 12 of 1950 of the Second Court of Sadar Munsif, Sylhet and on 10-1-51 he obtained a sale certificate in respect or his purchase through court and on 29-2-51 delivery of possession through court was made to him and he having remained in possession peaceably and adversely for well over 12 years sold an area of 10.5 and odd bighas of land by a registered deed dated 3-4-67 out of schedule 3(three) to the defendant Nos. 13 and 14 and defendant No.14 on 31-3-80 sold his share to the defendant No.13 and, as such, the suit can not be maintained.

7. In view of the pleadings of the parties the issues were recast and additional evidence from the side of the plaintiff opposite party No.1 as well as from the side of the opposite party No.26, that is, the defendant No.13 were also taken by the trial Court and on a review of the evidence and materials on record the trial Court decreed the suit vide its judgment and decree dated 17-11-86. Being aggrieved by the aforesaid judgment and decree of the trial Court the defendant No. 1 that is, the present petitioner as appellant preferred Title Appeal No.29 of 1987 while the opposite party No. 26, that is, the defendant No. 13 preferred Title Appeal No. 40 of 1987 in the court of the learned District Judge, Sylhet and both the appeals upon transfer were heard analogously by the learned Assistant District Judge, First Court, Sylhet who disallowed both the aforesaid appeals by one and the same judgment and decree dated 30-8-92. The present petitioner that is, defendant No. 1, being aggrieved by the aforesaid judgment and decree passed by the appellate Court below preferred the instant revisional application and the present opposite party No. 26, that is, defendant No. 13, preferred another revisional application which is numbered as Civil Revision No. 3229 of 1992 and both the revisional applications relate to the aforesaid judgment and decree dated 30-8-92 and, as such, both the Rules were heard together and are being disposed of by this judgment.

8. Dr Rafiqur Rahman, the learned Advocate appearing for the petitioner in both the Rules, submits that the trial Court decided the issues in question without proper assessment of evidence on record. The learned Advocate further submits that the prayer is vague and unspecific and, as such, it is incapable of execution but the courts below overlooked that aspect of the case and erroneously decreed the suit finding title of the Deity in the suit land and for confirmation of possession also for recovery of possession from the portion of the suit land which is found to be in possession of the defendant No. 1 Jogendra. The third plank of attack made by Dr Rafiqur Rahman is that the trial Court in decreeing the suit did not consider the documentary evidence filed by the defendant petitioner except Ext. M and M(1) and that has caused miscarriage of justice. The learned Advocate further submits that there is no specific averment either in the plaint or in their evidence as to when the plaintiff Deity was dispossessed from the suit land and there is also no averment that the plaintiff Deity was in possession of the suit land within twelve years from the date of dispossession and, as such, the instant suit is hit by both articles 142 and 144 of the Limitation Act but both the courts below misconceived the scope of the suit for possession and, as such, the impugned judgment and decree is liable to be set aside. The further submission of Dr Rafiqur Rahman is that neither of the courts below have considered Ext. O, a report of local investigation filed by the Advocate Commissioner in an earlier suit filed by the defendant No. 1 and the impugned judgment suffers from illegality on that score as well. The learned Advocate further submits that the judgment suffers from non-consideration of auction purchase particularly the date of delivery of possession. The learned Advocate emphatically submits that without framing any issue on the auction sale of the suit property the courts below committed an illegality in adverting to that aspect and decreeing the suit particularly in view of the fact that the defendant No. 3 took possession of the purchased land through court through execution case. The learned Advocate next submits that the impugned judgment is not tenable in law in view of the fact that it is asserted by the plaintiff Deity that the second schedule property was purchased out of the income of the Deity's property but there is no document of any kind to show that the second schedule property was purchased with the income of the Deity''s property and non-consideration of this aspect of the case also calls for interference with the impugned judgment. The learned Advocate further submits that the impugned judgment cannot be upheld in view of the fact that there is no finding by the courts below as to the existence of Deity and, as such, finding of the courts below that the suit property belongs to the Deity is absolutely erroneous and misconceived. The learned Advocate further submits that the suit as framed is not maintainable without a prayer for declaration that the auction purchase made by defendant No. 3 is null and void but a paper transaction and not binding upon the plaintiff. The final submission of Dr Rahman is that it appears from the record that the present Shebayet in fact is not contesting in this revisional application and one Abdul Ahad who is allegedly a constituted attorney of the Deity is taking all steps in the courts and swearing the necessary affidavits as and when necessary and in fact it is this Abdul Ahad who is pursuing this litigation in the name of the Deity and it is also significant to note that none is coming from the Namasudra Community to make tadbir in this case on behalf of the Deity other than a Muslim and in this case a serious doubt arises on the whole case of the plaintiff opposite party No. 1.

9. Mr Azizur Rahman Chowdhury, the learned Advocate appearing for the plaintiff opposite party No. 1 in both the Rules, submits that the plaintiff Deity has been successful in proving her case, title and possession in respect of the suit land and the alleged sole decree obtained by the defendant in their earlier title Suit No. 331 of 1966 along with the order in Miscellaneous Case No. 448 of 1966 under section 145 of the Code of Criminal Procedure was collusive, fraudulent and not binding upon the plaintiff opposite party No. 1 inasmuch as the plaintiff Deity opposite party No. 1 was not a party in those proceedings. The learned Advocate further submits that the alleged auction sale in favour of defendant No. 3 Sikandar Ali was also collusive and fraudulent and without covering any actual possession or title to him and the alleged sale is nothing but a mere paper transaction as per own admission of the alleged auction purchaser defendant No. 3 and his alleged subsequent transferee, the defendant No. 13 Mohammad Ali, whose deposition, on the other hand, will speak for itself to show that the story of auction purchase is nothing but a paper transaction. The learned Advocate further submits that it is claimed by the defendant No. 1 that he is the adopted son of Kulok but there is no evidence on record in respect of ceremony of giving and taking him as adopted son and the defendant-petitioner has miserably failed to prove his adoption. The learned Advocate further submits that it is true that there is no document to show that the suit property is a Dabottar property but Ext. 2 series, the CS records and Ext. 1 series, the name BAND. go to show that the suit property was recorded successively in the names of Baishnabs as disciple of Guru and there is no description of the father's name of the Baishnabs which consequently prove that the suit property belonged to the Deity for more than 100 years and these documents, that is, the CS Khatian and the Jama Bandi are the admitted documents and their genuineness arc not disputed by the defendant-petitioner. From Ext. 1 CS Khatian No. 251 it is found that Kulak Das Boishnab has been described as disciple of Joyram Boishnab and there is a homestead and from the materials coupled with the oral testimony of PWs conclusively established that the suit properties are not secular or personal properties of Kulak Das or of the defendant No. 1 but are dedicated properties and owned by the plaintiff Deity opposite party No. 1. The learned Advocate further submits that besides Exts. 1 and 2 Ties there are sufficient oral evidence on record to show that the suit property is debottor property inasmuch as PWs 4, 5 and 11 have categorically stated that from time immemorial the property is being used for the Sheba Puja of the Deity and the Puja offered by the Shebayets, as such, the plaintiff opposite party No. 1 has been able to prove by sufficient oral evidence that the suit property is being used for the Deity for a long period of over 100 years and the legal position is that if the property is used for a period of 50 years or more for performing Sheba Puja to a Deity that becomes Debottar property and in the instant case the oral evidence of the PWs coupled with the Ext. 1 and 2 series established it beyond any doubt that by long user for over long 50 years the suit property has become Debottor property and in that view of the matter, the trial Court rightly relied on the decision reported in 11 DLR 372,16 DLR (SC) 457; 24 DLR (SC) 36 and in addition to that the learned Advocate also refers to and relies on the decision reported in 36 DLR 47 and the case reported in AIR 1957 (SC) 797. The learned Advocate then submits that it is true that the defendant No. 1 petitioner has been residing in portion of the outer house to the south of the Deity house as servant of the Shebayet and Mon Mohan Das was installed as Sebayet of the Deity and has been in possession of the entire suit land on behalf of the Deity and, as such, the defendant No. 1 has been in possession of a part of the ditch land, that is, the portion of the house he has been living in just as a servant and he had every right over the same. The learned Advocate next submits that there are overwhelming evidence on record to show that the alleged Solenama obtained in Title Suit No. 331 of 1966 and the Solenama executed in Miscellaneous Case No. 448 of 1966 under section 145 of the Code of Criminal Procedure were obtained by the defendant petitioner through coercion, threat, intimidation by filing series of cases against Mon Mohan Das one after another both Civil and Criminal. The learned Advocate further submits that the Solenamas were obtained by coercion, threat, intimidation and undue influence is clear from the fact that immediately thereafter the then Shebayet Mon Mohan Das instituted the instant suit for declaration of title of the Deity to the suit property and for further declaration that the Solenamas were obtained by coercion, threat, intimidation, undue influence and not binding upon the plaintiff. The learned Advocate further submits that in the instant suit both the courts concurrently found that the suit is not hit by article 142 or 144 and the plaintiff opposite party No. 1 has instituted the same well within the period of limitation and both the courts below on proper appreciation of materials on record arrived at a finding to that effect and question of limitation is a question of fact and since the concurrent finding of both the courts below is based on materials and evidence on record there is no scope for this court to interfere with that finding of fact which by no stretch of imagination is perverse. The learned Advocate repels the submission of Dr Rafiqur Rahman that there is no evidence on record to show that the second schedule property was purchased by Kulak Das with the income of the Deity's property inasmuch as the defendant No. 1 himself as PW 1 categorically admitted in his cross-examination that Kulak purchased the second schedule property from the income of the property which he got from Saran Das Boishnab his Guru, and the name of this Saran Das Boishnab also appears in the record of right as Boishnab as disciple of his Guru. The learned Advocate further submits that in view of the admission of DW 1 himself that the second schedule property was purchased with the income of the property of Saran Das and the absence of any documentary evidence from the side of the plaintiff Deity that the second scheduled property was purchased by Mulak Das as Shebayet of the Deity is not fatal and this will have no material bearing on the title of the Deity in respect of the second schedule property as the defendant No. 1 has admitted that the property was purchased with the income of the first schedule property. The learned Advocate then submits that it is true that no issue has been framed on the alleged auction purchase of the third schedule land but this story of auction purchase of the third schedule land was not in the original written statement which had earlier been filed by the defendant Nos. 1-3 jointly and it is only when the suit came back to the trial Court on remand the defendant No. 3 for the first time introduced the story of auction purchase and sale to defendant No. 13 who is opposite party No. 26 in Civil Revision No. 3228 of 1992 and petitioner in the next revision, namely, Civil Revision No. 3229 of 1992. The parties led evidence on the point and the courts below taking into consideration the evidence on record, both oral and documentary, have concurrently found that the auction sale is nothing but a sham transaction and the original defendant No. 3 did never get possession of third schedule land through court in execution proceeding arising out of the money suit and the appellate Court below taking into consideration the evidence of defendant No. 3 himself arrived at a positive finding that the alleged auction sale is nothing but a paper transaction and the defendant No. 2 did not acquire any right, title and interest in respect of the third schedule land and the alleged sale made by him to defendant Nos. 13 and 14 on 3-4-67 did not create any right, title and interest in their favour. The learned Advocate next submits that both the courts below rightly found that the suit is not barred by limitation inasmuch as mainly it is a suit for declaration of title and recovery of possession and admittedly Kulak died on 25-12-1372. BS that is, some time in early part of 1965 and thereafter, the defendant No. 1 claiming himself as adopted son of Kulak filed a suit for permanent injunction, that is Title Suit No. 331 of 1966, and that suit was filed on 7-9-66 and it is alleged by the plaintiff Deity that the sole decree in suit No. 331 of 1966 has been obtained by threat, coercion, intimidation and undue influence and, as such, the Deity filed the present suit on 4-12-67 for declaration of its title and recovery of possession as well as for declaration that the sole decrees are null and void and obtained by threat, coercion, intimidation, and not binding upon the Deity and, as such, the suit was filed within two years from the date of death of Kulak. The learned Advocate further submits that the defendant No.13 purchased the suit land on 3-4-67 and the defendant No. 13 also purchased some portion of the suit land from third schedule land from Sikandar on 3-4-67 and some other portions of the third schedule land from defendant No. 14 on 31-3-80 and the suit was filed well within 12 years from the date of this transaction and, in that view of the matter, the courts below did not commit any illegality and concurrently found that the suit is not barred by limitation under article 142 or 144 of the Limitation Act. The learned Advocate further submits that it is true that none of the courts below considered Exhibit 0 but on a perusal of Ext. ''O'' it appears that this document, in fact, supports the case of the plaintiff Deity. In Ext. ''O'' it is stated that the defendant No.1 resides in the outer house which is situated within the suit land and it is also seen from Ext. ''O'' that there is a temple there though it has not been specifically mentioned that there is a Deity in the temple, but fact remains that a temple cannot be without any Deity and this shows that there was a Deity in the temple and on top of that there are oral evidences of the PWs to show that there is a Deity in the temple and Seba Puja is performed during Rath Jatra. Rash Jatra and Jhulan Jatra by the devotees and Shebayets of the Deity. The learned Advocate emphatically submits that the plaintiff opposite party No. 1 in the instant suit has paid ad-valorem court fees and prays for recovery of possession of the entire suit land and it is only after review of the evidence by the courts below they have found that the plaintiff Deity is not ousted from the entire suit land and is still in possession of the major portion of the suit land and, as such, decreed the suit declaring title of the Deity to the suit land, followed by confirmation of possession in respect of the land which are in possession of the Deity and decree for delivery of khas possession for that portion of the suit land where the defendant No. 1 is found to be in possession. Since the plaintiff has paid ad-valorem court fees on the entire suit land and since the plaintiff Deity has been successful in establishing her title to the suit land, it is immaterial in which portion or to what extent, the defendant petitioner is in possession of the suit land and since the plaintiff opposite party No. 1 is entitled to get recovery of possession of the entire suit land, it is immaterial to what extent, the defendant petitioner is in possession of the suit land and the suit cannot be dismissed for not specifying the exact areas which is in possession of the defendant petitioner. The learned Advocate further submits that the omission to specify the exact area which is in occupation of the defendant petitioner is not fatal in the instant case, inasmuch as title of the plaintiff opposite party No. 1 has been found in favour of the Deity and the suit is filed within the period of limitation. The learned Advocate next submits that the courts below did not commit any illegality in passing a decree for khas possession after evicting the defendant petitioner from the portion of the suit land which is found in his possession because under Order 7 rule 7 of the Code of Civil Procedure a court is empowered to grant any relief to a party if it is found on consideration of the materials and evidence on record that the plaintiff has been able to establish his case to that effect and in support of his submission he relies on the decision reported in AIR 1963 (Punjab) 538, AIR 1942 (Pat) 247; AIR 1952 (SC) 47; 16 DLR 510; 14 DLR 307; AIR 1970(M) 40; AIR 1957 (All) 784. The learned Advocate finally submits that even if there be some lacuna in the impugned judgment this court sitting under section 115 of the Code of Civil Procedure is competent to go through the records and the evidence adduced by the parties and on appraisal of the same if the court is of opinion that there are sufficient materials and evidence on record to ultimately sustain the impugned judgment, this court will not interfere with the same. The learned Advocate further submits that in an appropriate case, this court is entitled to enter into the merits of the case and decide the same finally, when the entire records are before it and this is the consistent view of our Appellate Division as has been taken in decisions, reported in 16 BLD (AD) 31; 43 DLR (AD) 78, 82, 125, and 44 DLR (AD) 98. The learned Advocate finally submits that on a perusal of the evidence and material on record, it is crystal clear that there are sufficient evidence and materials on record to show that the suit property actually belonged to the Deity opposite party No. 1 and the successive Boishnabs were managing the property as Shebayet of the Deity and applied the income of the suit property in performing Seba Puja of the Deity and therefore, the courts below did not commit any illegality in finding title of the Deity to the suit property and also in finding that the auction purchase is nothing but a paper transaction and that the suit is filed within time and the materials and evidence on record clearly supports the case of the plaintiff Deity. As such, there has been no error of law resulting in an error in the decision occasioning failure of justice calling for any interference by this court.

10. In course of reply Dr Rahman refers to exhibit H, and K and F-2, and submits that if the period of limitation is reckoned from these documents then it is crystal clear that the instant suit is hopelessly barred by limitation and the plaintiff cannot succeed in the instant suit without setting side the auction sale.

<u>11. Although in the normal course I should advert to the impugned judgment but in the instant case I would like to address myself about the judgment of the trial Court first because most of grievance agitated by Dr Rahman are in respect of the trial Court judgment. On a perusal of the trial Court judgment, it appears that the trial Court framed as many as 8 issues and there is no issue on the point of auction sale and this fact of auction sale was introduced by the original defendant No. 3 in the additional written statement, after remand of the suit to the trial Court. It further appears that no such issue was ever suggested by the defendant petitioners before the Court. Be that as it may, it would have been proper for the trial Court to frame an issue on that point but fact remaining that although no issue was framed on that point yet both the parties in the suit led evidence on that point and unfortunately, the trial Court did not advert to that aspect of the case and refrained from giving any finding on that point but that defect of the trial Court judgment has been cured by the impugned judgment inasmuch as the appellate Court below taking into consideration the evidence of defendant No. 3 arrived at a definite finding that the auction purchase is nothing but a paper transaction. In this connection it may be stated that no doubt exhibit H the sale certificate dated 10-1-51 Ext, ''Ka'' Writ of delivery of possession dated 29-3-91 and exhibit. F-2 order confirming the delivery of possession show that after auction sale the delivery of possession of the property was duly handed over to the defendant No. 3 by the court in pursuance of the money execution case but the appellate Court below on consideration of the materials and evidence on record, particularly the evidence of the defendant No. 3, auction purchaser himself, came to a definite finding that the alleged auction sale and subsequent delivery of possession to the auction purchaser was collusively obtained beyond the knowledge of the plaintiff Deity and the Baishnabs and it is nothing but a paper transaction. In this connection, it may also be stated that the evidence of defendant No. 3 coupled with the evidence of defendant No. 1 also show that the story of auction purchase is nothing but a sham transaction. On top of that, it is alleged by the defendant No. 3 that he purchased the land in 1951 but it is admitted by him that he made no mutation after alleged purchase in 1951 and did not pay any rent in respect of this land since 1951 until 1967 when he transferred major portion of the auction purchased land to defendant Nos. 13 and 14. There is another aspect in this case that this defendant No. 3 did not however contest the case at the High Court before remand and it appears that in 1967 he sold 10½ bighas of land to the defendant Nos. 13 and 14. Thereafter 4½ bighas of land is still retained by him but in the instant suit after his death his heirs are not contesting the same even though they are brought on record. Thus it has been rightly found by the appellate Court below that the story of auction purchase is nothing but a paper transaction and that the same is collusive and obtained beyond the knowledge of the Baishnabs and the Deity and it is immaterial whether there is any prayer made by the plaintiff for setting aside the auction sale or not, because the auction sale is nothing but a sham transaction and has no existence in the eye of law. On top of that, it should be remembered that in the money suit or in the execution case, the Deity, that is, the plaintiff opposite party No. 1, was not a party and, as such, that auction purchase is also not binding upon the Deity itself and here it may further be mentioned that the decree obtained in the money suit was an ex parte decree and the defendant No. 3 himself admitted in his evidence before the trial Court that he could not say how the summons of the suit was served on Kulak and what amount Kulak took as loan from him and these facts stare in the face of the defendant No. 3 and lend support to the finding of the appellate Court below that the auction purchase is, in fact, nothing but a paper transaction, collusively obtained by the defendant No. 3.</u>

<u>12. One of the grievances of Dr Rafiqur Rahman is that the trial Court without proper discussion of evidence decreed the suit. I had gone through the judgments of both the the courts. It is true that the trial Court in decreeing the suit did not refer to the evidence of all the PWs in detail but, nevertheless, on discussion of the relevant documents and materials and oral evidence and after proper consideration of the same arrived at a positive finding that the suit property is Debottor property and the suit land belongs to the Deity. On a perusal of the impugned judgment as well it appears that the appellate Court below discussed about the evidence adduced by all the PWs and discussed about some of the documents and although did not discuss about the evidence of all the DWs, but on a perusal of the evidence adduced by the DWs vis-a-vis the evidence of the PWs and materials on record, concurred with the findings of the trial Court and on a perusal of the records I am of the opinion that there are sufficient evidence on record for both the courts below to arrive at a finding at which they have so arrived. Thus it cannot be said that the decision given by the courts below are not based on proper discussion of evidence on record.</u>

<u>13. The second plank of attack made by Dr Rahman is that the prayer is vague and unspecific. The plaintiff Deity did not specifically state in her plaint as to when and from what portion of the suit land she was dispossessed by the defendant No. 1 and, as such, the decree passed by the courts below is not sustainable in law. It appears that the instant suit is a suit for declaration of title and recovery of khas possession and the plaintiff has paid ad valorem court-fees on the entire suit land, and initially prayed for recovery of possession of the entire suit land after evicting the defendant No. 1 from the suit land. Both the courts below concurrently found that the plaintiff is in possession of the suit land except certain portion where the defendant No. 1 lives in the homestead plot and, as such, decreed the suit is favour of the plaintiff and passed a decree for recovery of khas possession after evicting the defendant No. 1 from that portion of the suit land where he is found in possession. The case of the defendant No.1 is that he is in possession of the entire suit land, where as the case of the plaintiff opposite party No. 1 is that he is in permissive occupation of the suit land and he has no right, title and interest in the suit land and the defendant No.1 admittedly was brought to the suit land by Kulak. The further case of the plaintiff is that he was brought to the suit land by Kulak, the then Shebayet of the Deity and he used to perform the domestic work. The dispute arose between the parties only after the death of Kulak, when the defendant No. 1 claimed himself as the adopted son of Kulak and claimed the suit property as personal property of Kulak and he filed Title Suit No. 331 of 1966 and thereafter, the then Shebayet Mon Mohan Boishnab filed the instant suit in 1967. It is also admitted fact that Kulak Das died on 25th Chaitra, 1372, BS. It thus appears that the plaintiffs brought suit within 2 years from the date of death of Kulak and when the plaintiff No. 1 raised his claim to the suit property as his own property as heir of Kulak. It has already been noted that the appellate Court below on due consideration of the material and evidence on record found that the auction purchase is a sham transaction and that did not create any right, title and interest in favour of the defendant No. 3 in respect of land of schedule 3. Besides defendant No. 3 sold the suit land in 1967 to defendant Nos. 13 and 14 and defendant No. 13 purchased some portion of the third schedule land from defendant No.14 in 1980. It is, thus crystal clear that the finding of the appellate Court below that the suit is not barred by limitation is borne out by sufficient materials and evidence on record. Since the suit is a suit for declaration of title followed by recovery of possession both the courts below, in my opinion, did not commit any illegality by passing a decree declaring title of the Deity to the suit land followed by claim of possession in the suit land and also by passing a decree for khas possession of that portion of land which is found to be in occupation of the defendant No. 1. Since the plaintiff Deity has paid ad-valorem court fees for the entire suit land, if her title is established in the suit land she is entitled to get recovery of possession of the entire suit land and since she is already in possession of major portion of the suit land, she is entitled to get recovery of possession of that portion of land which is in possession of defendant. In that view of the matter I do not find any substance in this submission of Dr Rahman.</u>

14. Another plank of attack made by Dr Rahman is that in decreeing the suit the trial Court did not discuss the documentary evidence of the defendants except Ext. M and M-1. But during the course of argument he failed to point out what are the other documentary evidence, non-consideration of which vitiated the judgment. It appears from perusal of the trial Court judgment that besides Ext. M and M-1 he has also considered Ext. C series and B series along with Ext. 1 series and 2 series and the oral evidence of PW 1 and PW 4, and on perusal of the appellate Court judgment it appears that although he has not referred to all the documentary evidence in detail but it appears that he has considered the oral and documentary evidence adduced by both the parties and after considering the entire evidence adduced by both the parties the appellate Court below arrived at a positive finding that it is true that there is no documentary evidence to show that the suit land belongs to Deity plaintiffs or that the suit lands were recorded in the record of rights in the names of the Baishnabs as Shebayets of the Deity, but taking into consideration the evidence and circumstances of the case, the appellate Court below came to a finding that for three generations the suit lands were recorded in the record of rights in the names of Baishnabs, as disciples of other Boishnabs, which points out that the suit land is nothing but a dedicated property and the Baishnabs were holding that property as Shebayets of the Deity. Besides, Ext. B dated 24-11-1908 and Ext. 5, a registered deed of lease dated 17-6-1935 also show that both Saran Das and Kulak Das were described as Shebayets of the Deity and their occupation was shown as servant of the Deity. In that view of the matter the concurrent finding of both the courts below that the suit land belonged to the Deity plaintiffs opposite party No. 1 is also backed by sufficient materials and evidence on record; I have already pointed out that the instant suit was filed within 2 years from the date of death of Kulak. As such the omission of the plaintiff Deity to mention as to the date of possession and dispossession in respect of the suit land is immaterial and does not have any bearing on this suit because admittedly the defendant No. 1 was brought to the suit land by Kulak and during his lifetime he used to live with Kulak. It is only after the death of Kulak the defendant No.1 claimed himself to be the adopted son of Kulak and also claimed the property as personal property of Kulak but facts remain that the defendant petitioner No. 1 has miserably failed to show that he was the adopted son of Kulak Das Baishnab. It is clear from Ext. 4(Ka) dated 10-6-61 and ext. 8 dated 18-11-66 that defendant No. 1 has been described in these documents as son of one Kanak, his natural father and not of Kulak, the alleged adopted father. Besides, from the Solenama Ext. "E" which relates to Title Suit No. 331 of 1966, it appears that there is mention of Akhrabari and the Deity Radha Krishna and that they are the Boishnabs but it is stated that the property is not being claimed as the property of Deity. It thus appears that both the courts below rightly arrived at a finding as to the title of the Deity to the suit land.

15. One of the main grievance of Dr Rahman is that there is total non-consideration of the fact that delivery of possession of the third schedule land was given to defendant No.3 through court in pursuance of auction sale. It is true the trial Court did not advert to that ex parte auction sale but nevertheless the appellate Court below after taking into consideration the relevant averments made by the parties in their pleadings vis-a-vis the evidence adduced by the parties on that point arrived at a definite finding that no actual delivery of possession was ever given to the defendant No. 3 in pursuance of the ex parte auction sale and that was a sham transaction. I am of the view that the suit would not fail in the absence of any prayer for declaration that the auction purchase is null and void, collusive, inoperative, a mere paper transaction and not binding upon the plaintiff because it has been found by the appellate Court on proper scrutiny of the materials and evidence on record that the auction purchase is nothing but a paper transaction and the same was collusively obtained by defendant No. 3. It has already been noted that although no issue on auction purchase was framed by the trial Court but the parties were conscious about the plea of alleged auction sale and both the parties adduced their evidence on the point and the appellate Court below after taking into consideration the evidence adduced by both the parties arrived at a finding that the alleged auction sale is a sham transaction and in that view of the matter I am of the opinion that since the title of the plaintiff Deity has been found in favour of the plaintiff opposite party No. 1, omission on the part of the plaintiff to pray for declaration that the alleged auction purchase is null and void can not have any bearing on the merits of the suit.

16. Another major point of argument of Dr Rahman is that although it is claimed by the plaintiff Deity that second schedule land has been purchased with the income of the dedicated property but there is no documentary evidence to show that the schedule property was purchased with the income of the Deity's property. It is true that documentary evidence is wanting in this case on that point but there are oral evidence to show that the second schedule property was purchased by Saran and Kulak during their time as Shebayets with the income of the Deity''s property and nobody other than DW 1 himself also admitted in his cross examination Kulak Das purchased second schedule land with the income of property of Saran Das Boishnab. Thus, it appears to me that the absence of any documentary evidence to show that the second schedule property was acquired with the income of the Deity's property is not fatal in the instant case inasmuch as there is unimpeachable oral evidence to show that the second schedule land was acquired with the income of the Deity's property and it further appears from Ext. 1 (B) that the second schedule land is also recorded in the name of Kulak as disciple of Saran Das Boishnab which indicates the property as a dedicated one and not as secular or personal property because if it had been his personal property then his name would have been recorded as Kulak Das with his father's name.

17. Now I come to the point that, there is no finding as to the existence of the Deity. On a perusal of both the judgments of courts below it appears that in so many clear words the courts below did not observe that there was Deity named Radha Krishna Bigraha.

18. From a close scrutiny of both the judgments it appears that on consideration of oral evidence coupled with the documentary evidence they have arrived at a concurrent finding that the suit property belongs to the Deity plaintiff opposite party No. 1 and 3 successive Baishnabs were, in fact, Shebayets of the Deity and this observation leads to the irresistible conclusion that there was a Deity in existence otherwise how the property could belong to Deity. Besides there are evidence adduced by the PWs namely, PWs 1, 3, 4 and 11 who in a voice stated that there is a Deity installed in the Akhrabari in the suit land and the Shebayets used to perform Seba Puja, namely, Rath Jatra, Rash Jatra and Jhulan Jatra and other Sectional Festivals and it is further noted by the learned appellate Court below that the oral evidence on this point is unshakable and the evidence adduced by the PWs cannot be brushed aside on any grounds and the trial Court, as well, categorically observed that he did not find any reasons to disbelieve the testimony of PW 1, one of the Shebayets, and PW 4, so there are sufficient evidence on record to show that there is a Deity in the Akhrabari within the suit land. In this connection we may also refer to Ext ''O'' a report of Advocate Commissioner filed in connection with earlier suit in respect of the self same property filed by defendant No. 1 himself and Ext ''O'' shows that there is a temple in the suit land. On top of that even the alleged Solenama of Title Suit No. 331 of 1966 Ext ''E'' also shows that there is a Akhrabari and Deity Rada krishna, so, in my opinion, there are overwhelming evidence on record to show that there is a Deity in the suit land in the Akhrabari namely, Radha Krishna Bigraha installed by the Baishnavs of the locality long long ago.

19. In view of my aforesaid discussions, I do not find any substance in these two revisional applications and I find substance in the submission made by Mr Azizur Rahman Chowdhury.

20. In the result, both the Rules are discharged with no order as to costs.

The order of stay of operation of the judgment of the appellate Court below granted by this Court earlier is vacated.

End.
