full_judgment:
ABM Altaf Hossain J: The Rule under Adjudication, issued on 22-1-2012 was in following term:-

"Let a Rule Nisi be issued calling upon the respondents to show cause as to why the eligibility criteria for promotion against the posts of sub-Registrar from/amongst the posts of Head Assistant and Upper Division Assistants of-Registration-Directorate and Head Clerks/Head Assistant of District Registration Office as contained in as contained in the schedule-I, (SL No.6 Column- 5) of the Gazetted Officers (Registration Department) Recruitment Rules, 1979 (the Rules 1979) as contained in SRO No. 156- Ain/96 dated 27-8-1996 (Annexure-A) requiring the petitioners to have a Bachelor's Degree from a recognized University with at least 10 (ten) years service in the feeder posts or the aforesaid posts shall not be declared to be ultravires of the Constitution of the People's Republic of Bangladesh so far as it relates to the petitioners and as to why the respondents shall not be directed to apply the unamended/original Rules 1979 (Annexure A-1) for promotion of the petition of the petitioners against the posts of sub-Registrar and/ or pass such order of further order or orders as to this court may seem fit and proper".

2. Averments figured in the Rules generating instruments are narrated below in conspectus.

3. The petitioners are all qualified persons having discharged their duties diligently with unblemished records and joined the Registration Directorate with the different ranks on various dates. The petitioners were appointed in accordance with Gazetted Officers (Registration Department) recruitment Rules 1979 (briefly Rules 1979"). The schedule-I, (SL No.6, Column -5) of the Gazetted Officer (registration Department) Recruitment Rules, 1979 provides that the eligibility criteria for the posts of Sub-Registrar was to be filled up by way of promotion from/ amongst the Head Assistants and Upper Division Assistants of the Registration Directorate and Head Clerks/Head Assistants of the District Registration Officers having five 'years' experience in the feeder posts and/or the said post. Five years experience was required to consider the case of the promotion of the petitioners. The petitioners have been performing their duties with the hope to get promotion as Sub-Registrar, which is a class-1 post.

4. In the meanwhile, the Rules 1979, has been amended Vide SRO No. 156-Law/96, dated 31-8-1996 (briefly "Amended Rules 1979"). In the said amendment Rules 1979, the, eligibility criteria for promotion against the posts of Sub- Registrar is now Batchelor's Degree from a recognized University with at least 10(ten) years' Service in a feeder post or the aforesaid posts specified in Column-4 and, thus, the petitioners who were previously eligible for promotion under the unamended Rules 1979 have become ineligible  and debarred for promotion. Thus being aggrieved by and dissatisfied with the eligibility criteria of amended Rules 1979, petitioners filed this writ petition and obtained the present Rule.

5. The name of the petitioner No. 21 is already deleted from the instant writ petition, so we will not consider his interest accordingly.

6. Mr Md Mutahar Hossain, with Mr Ali Asif Khan with Mr Md Muddasir Hossain, the learned Advocates appearing on behalf of the petitioners. Mr Mutahar Hossain submits that the petitioners having rendered their services for the Registration Directorate since long and unamended Rules 1979 having originally provided that the existing personnel would be able to get promotion for the post of Sub-Registrar from/amongst the post of Head Assistants/Upper Division Assistant upon completing five years' experience in the said posts which has been created legitimate expectation of the petitioners. Mr Hossain also submits that on act and/or Rule cannot be given any retro respective effect so as to take away and/or cancel and substantial vested right of any individual and, hence, the Amended Rules 1979 is ultra vires the Constitution since if effectively creates an embargo who were appointed prior to the amended date 31-8-1996. Further to that Mr Hossain submits that by amending Rules 1979 some body shall get benefits which against the principle of unjust enrichment. Mr Hossain further submits that if the amended Rules 1979 is condemned as ultravires, then that will invariably lead to' setting-aside of the impugned Gazette, because it is indeed the amended Rules admittedly ignited the promotion of the petitioners. So, if the Amended Rules falls through, the impugned Gazette has no leg to stand it.

7. Mr Hossain-relied upon the citation of Motiur Rahman Chairman, BADC vs Chowdhury Md Mahfuzul Islam reported in 8 MLR (1D) 217 = 55 DLR (AD) 104 and an unreported Judgment in Writ Petition No. 1164 of 2011.

8. Mr Biswajit Roy, the learned Deputy Attorney General (briefly "DAG") with Mr Amatul Karim, learned Assistant Attorney- General appeared on behalf of the respondents, however without any affidavit-in-opposition. Mr Roy, the learned, DAG submits that the Rules 1979 gives the respondents fights to modify, cancel or amend the provision of the same with the approval of the Government. Again, he submits that the respondents have been changed the terms and condition of the petitioners rightly.

9. At the time of hearing we have considered the submissions of learned Advocate for the petitioners and the learned DAG and also perused the Writ Petition along with others material on records.

10. In order to attain a proper adjudication, we would first consider the issue of legitimate expectation.

11. The doctrine of legitimate expectation imposes in spirit aduty on public authority to act fairly by taking into consideration all relevant factors relating to, such legitimate expectation. The doctrine is still at a stage of evolution but it has generated a significant body of case law.

12. The doctrine of legitimate expectation has been judicially recognized by the apex Court of the different jurisdictions in Commonwealth Countries and this recognition has paved the way for the development of a broader and more flexible doctrine of fairness.

13. In the Common law jurisdiction the doctrine had been traced to an obiter dictum of Lord Denning MR in Sehmidt vs Secretary of Home Affairs reported in (1969) 1 All ER 904. Lord Denning observed in Sehmidti :-

"The speeches in Ridge vs Baldwin show that an administrative body may, in a proper case, be bound to give a person who is affected by their decision an opportunity of making representations. If all depends on whether he has some right or interest or would add, some legitimate expectation, of which it would not be fair to deprive him without hearing what he has to say "

14. The legitimate expectation referred to in, Sehmidt did not give the foreign students an enforceable right to stay for the time originally permitted but an enforceable right to be heard before the decision to revokes his permit was taken: a procedural protection only.

15. In this case, the Plaintiffs, on behalf of themselves and 50 other alie students of the college, claimed declarations against the defendant that his decision' not to consider further similar applications for extension of stay was unlawful, void, and of no effect and the defendant was bound to consider such applications on their merit and in accordance with the principles of natural justice.

16. The Court of appeal held that they had no legitimate expectation of extension and therefore no right to hearing, though revocation of their permits within the earlier granted period of permit would have been contrary to legitimate expectation.

17. It is significant to note that in his judgment in Schmidt vs Secretary of Home Affairs, Lord Denning makes no cite of any authority, judicial or otherwise, upon which the concept of legitimate expectation could be founded.

18. In a letter to Prof. CF Forsyth, quoted in Cambridge Law Journal, 47(2), July 1988, at 241 that he feels "sure it came out of my own head and not from any continental or other source." The later cases do not suggest any other origin. Presumably, therefore, the origin of the concept lies within Lord Denning's justly legendary creative mind and not elsewhere.

19. However, it may be recalled that prior to the introduction of the doctrine into English law, it was evolved in German administrative law(The German Concept of 'Vertrauenschutz' sought to protect the confidence that subjects had placed in government), which was subsequently borrowed and developed by the European Court. (M Schroeder, "Administrative Law in Germany" in Seerden and Stroink (eds) Administrative Law of the European Union (London 2005) p. 119.)

20. The judicial maturity of the doctrine of 'legitimate expectation' can be traced to the opinion of the Judicial Committee delivered by Lord Fraser in Attorney-General of Hong Kong vs Ng Tuen Shiu (1983) 2 AC 629, (1983) 3 All ER 346. Ng was an illegal immigrant from Macau. The government announced a policy of repatriating such persons and stated that each would be interviewed and each case treated on its merits. Ng was interviewed and his removal ordered. His complaint was that at the interview he had not been allowed to explain the humanitarian grounds on which he might be allowed to stay, but only to answer the questions put to him; that he was given a hearing, but not the hearing in effect promised, as the promise was to give one at which 'mercy' could be argued. The judicial Committee agreed that an that narrow point, the government's promise had not been implemented; his case had not been considered on its merits, and the removal order was quashed. Ng succeeded on the basis that he had a legitimate expectation that he wouldbe allowed to put his case, arising out of the government promise that everyone affected would be allowed to do so.

21. The model elucidation of legitimate expectation appears from the speech of Lord Fraser in Council of Civil Service Unions vs Minister for the Civil Service Unions vs Minister for the Civil Services ("GCHQ '') reported in 3 All ER 935 wherein held that:-

"Legitimate, or reasonable, expectation may arise either from an express promise given on behalf of a public authority or from the existence of a regular practice which the claimant can reasonably expect to continue."

22. The Prime Minister issued an instruction that civil servants engaged on certain work would no longer be permitted to be members of trade unions. The House of Lords held that those civil servants had a legitimate expectation that they would be consulted before such action was taken, as it was. a well-established practice for government to consult civil servants before making significant changes to their terms and conditions of service. In this case, if may be noted, legitimate expectation arose not (as in Ng) out of a promise, but out of the existence of a regular practice which could reasonably be expected to continue.

23. In R vs Brent London Borough Council, exp Gunning (1986) 84 LGR 168, the legality of a decision to close schools was challenged by a group of parents, ratepayers and parent governors, who alleged, inter alia, inadequate consultation. Hodgson J said:-

"The parents had no statutory right to be consulted, but that they had a legitimate expectation that they would be consulted seems to me to be beyond question. The interest of parents in the educational arrangements in the area in which they live is self- evident ..... .local education authorities habitually do consult on these matters. In 1980 and 1983 this local authority itself had comprehensive consultations, which had led to the decision in 1983 to retain all school sites. Local education authorities are exhorted by the Secretary of State to consult and results of the consultations are something which takes into account (in deciding whether to agree to closures). On any test of legitimate expectation, it seems to me that these parents quality".

24. In a subsequent case, the Court of Appeal used this as an opportunity to reconsider the complete development in Britain' in the area of legitimate expectation.

25. The government principles are to be found in the decision of the Court of Appeal in R vs North and East Devon Health Authority exp Coughlan [2001] QB 213. As the Court of Appeal stated (at paragraph 56 of their judgment) the starting point is to determine what the legitimate expectation of the applicant was. This involves looking at the precise terms of the promise, the circumstances in which it was made and the nature of the discretion that was involved.

26. At paragraph 57 of Coughlan three categories of case were identified:-

a. Those where the public authority was only required to bear in mind its previous policy given weight, but no more, if it thinks right to the promise before deciding to change course.

b. Those where the promise is of consultation before a particularcourse is adopted.

c. Those where the promise has induced a legitimate expectation of a benefit which is substantive.

27. In the first category of case the Court of Appeal held that it could only intervene on traditional Wednesbury [1948] 1 KB 223 grounds. In the second category of case the consultation has to be given unless there is an overriding reason to resile from the promise. Here the Court Judge what fairness requires. In the third category of case the Court will require the promise to be performed it to frustrate the promise is so unfair as to amount to an. abuse of power. The Court weighs up the requirements of fairness against any overriding interest relied upon for the charge of policy.

28. In R (on the application of Nadarajah and Abdi vs Secretary of State for the Home Department [2005] EWCA Civ 2363, the Court of Appeal after reviewing the authorities suggested that the applicable test was as follows:-

"The principle that good administration requires public authorities to be held to their promises would be undermined if the law did not insist that any failure or refusal to comply is objectively justified as a proportionate measure in the circumstances."

29. The Court of Appeal went on to state, at paragraph 69:-

"Proportionality will be judged, as it is generally to be judged, by the respective force of the competing interests arising in this case. Thus where the representation relied on amounts to an unambiguous promise; where there is detrimental reliance, where the promise is made to an individual or a specific group; these are instances where denial of the expectation is likely to be harder to justify as a proportionate factor."

30. Those observations were, as the Court of Appeal recognised at paragraph 67, obiter. They are not consistent with the decision in Coughlan by which the Court of Appeal was bound. Subsequent authority has applied Coughlan rather then Nadarajah: R (on the application of Bancoult) vs Secretary of State for Foreign and Commonwealth Affairs [2007] EWCA Civ 498.

31. There is a recent and significant decision of the Court of Appeal in R (Bhatt Murphy) and Others vs Secretary for the Home Department [2008] EWCA Civ 755. In this case the Court of Appeal was called upon to consider, as if now has on at least twelve occasions since the beginning of the decade, the principles which underpin the notion of legitimate expectation.

32. In Bhatt Murphy. Lord Justice Laws began by stating that:-

"Legitimate expectation is now well known public law headline. But it reach in practice is still being explored. In one of leading case, ex P Coughlan [2001] QB 213, Lord wolf Mr as he then was, giving the judgment of the court, described it as "still a devolved field of law" (paragraph 59). This case show that put broadly (there are refinements) it encompasses two kinds. There is procedural legitimate expectation, and there is substantive legitimate expectation. But in certain types of cases these terms are more exclusive than they appear. These appeals therefore call for some account of material principles, however well trodden in ground. I acknowledge that much of the ground is at the foothills. But the path falters a little further up." Again, in the same judgment Lord Justice Laws has further observed that;

"A very broad summary of the place of legitimate expectations in public law might be expressed as follows. The power of public authorities to charge policy is constrained by the legal duty to be fair (and other constraints which the law imposes). A charge of policy, which would otherwise be legally unexceptionable, may be held unfair by reason of prior action, or inaction, by the authority. If it has distinctly promised to consult those affected or potentially affected, then ordinarily it must consult (the paradigm case or procedural expectation). If it has distinctly promised to preserve existing promised to preserve existing policy for a specific person or group who would be substantially affected by the charge, then ordinarily it must keep its promise (substantive expectation). If, without any promise, it has established or policy distinctly and substantially affecting a specific person or group who in the circumstances was in reason entitled to rely on its continuance and did so, then ordinarily it must consult before effecting any change (the secondary case of procedural expectation) To do otherwise, in any of these instances, would be to act so unfairly as to perpetrate on abuse of power."

33. Laws LJ then proceeded to give a detail impression of the subject from which it might be hoped that Courts subsequently might not need to visit the same ground to same degree. The outline given law LJ in Bhatt Murphy can be summarized as follows:-

Procedural legitimate expectation (i) The 'paradigm case'

There remains an important distinct between procedural legitimate expectation and substantive expectation.

Within procedural legitimate expectation, Laws LJ drew a further distinction between the "paradigm case" and "secondary case" of procedural legitimate expectation. The 'paradigm case' arises where a public authority has provided an unequivocal assurance, whether by means of express promise or an established practice, than will give notice or embark upon consultation before if changes an existing substantive policy.

34. In the paradigm case the court will not allow the decision maker to effect the proposed charge without notice or consultation, unless the want of notice or consultation is justified by the force of an overriding legal duty owed by the decision maker (as in CCUS). There may be questions such as whether the claimant for relief must himself have of the promise or practice, or relied on it.

35. It is however more difficult to impose such limitations in a procedural case; as "the unfairness or abuse of power which the court will check is not merely to do with how harshly the decision bears upon any individual. In exp Nadarajah [2005]. EWCA Civ 1363) generally requires that where a public authority has given a plain assurance, if should be held to it. Procedural legitimate expectation (ii) The secondary case.

36.	There is then what laws LJ referred to as there 'secondary' case of rocedural legitimate expectation. This is in circumstances where has been no previous promise or practice of notice or consultation. An example (given in Ex p Baker) is the case of Ex p Scheme [1993] 1 FCR 306 where the claimants were the parents of two children who went to a school outside the local authority's district. The local authority had paid for the elder child's travel costs, but then changed their policy. They stopped paying for the elder child's travel, and never paid for the younger's. There had been no promise or practice of notice or consultation. The Court nevertheless held that the claimants enjoyed a legitimate expectation that the benefit would continue in relation to the elder child until there had been communicated to them some rational ground for withdrawing it on which they had been given an opportunity to comment.

37.	The second example referred to in ex p Baker is the Ex p Unilever case [1996] STC 681). Unilever concerned the Inland Revenue's treatment of a taxpayer's claims for loss relief against corporation tax. A time limit for making such claims was stipulated in the legislation, but (as was common ground) the Revenue enjoyed a discretion to entertain late claims. On thirty occasions over a period of more than 20 years Unilever submitted late claims and Revenue accepted them. But them for the accounting years, 1986, 1987 and 1988, with no prior notice, warning or consultation, Unilever's claims were refused on the ground that they were not made within the statutory time limit. Sir Thomas Bingham MR as he then was said:-

"On the history here, I consider that to reject Unilever's claims in reliance on the time limit, without clear and general advance notice, is so unfair as to amount of an abuse of power."

38. It is plain both from Sir Thomas Bingham's judgment and that of Simon Brown LJ (Hutchison LJ added no reasoning of his own) that the court regarded the Revenue's conduct as outrageous.

39. Laws LJ's view was that this secondary, case of legitimate expectation will not often be established. Where there has been no assurance either of consultation (the paradigm case of procedural expectation) or as to the continuance of the policy (substantive expectation), there will generally be nothing in the case save a decision by the authority in question to effect a charge in its approach to one or more of its functions. And generally, there can be no objection to that, for it involves no abuse of power.

40. In identifying the circumstances in which this secondary case of procedural expectation will run, Laws LJ indicated that the key feature will be that the impact of the authority's past conduct on potentially affected persons must," be pressing and focused":-

"One would expect at least to find an individual or group who in reason have substantial grounds to expect that the substance of the relevant policy will continue to ensure for their particular benefit: not necessarily for ever, but at least for a reasonable period, to provide a cushiori against the change. In such , a case the change cannot lawfully be made, certainly not made abruptly, unless the authority notify and consult."

41. Laws LJ in Bhatt Murphy distinguished between substantial and procedural legitimate expectation by noting that in the procedural case we find a promise or practice or notice or consultation in the event of a contemplated charge. In the substantive case we have a promise or practice of present and future substantive policy. In such cases there will either be an authoritative representation of what the relevant policy is and will continue to be, or the simple fact of a policy being settled and established in practice.

42. Review of the authorities, as carried our Bhatt Murphy (above) shows that where a substantive expectation is to run, the promise of practice on which it is based must be more than a simple assumption that the policy with no terminal date will continue in effect until rational grounds for its cessation arise.

43. The legal position in India is more or less the same as in England. The precise content of this doctrine, which enables an aggrieved person to seek his remedy by judicial review, has also been the subject matter of evolution through judicial decisions.

44. In Navjyoti Coop. Group Housing Society v Union of India (1992) 4 SCC 477, the Supreme Court recognized that by reason of application of the said doctrine, an aggrieved party would be entitled to seek judicial review (ld. At 494).

"If he could show that a decision of the public authority affected him of some benefit or advantage which in the past he had been permitted to enjoy and which he legitimately expected to be permitted to continue to enjoy either until he was given reasons for withdrawal and the opportunity to comment such reasons."

45. In this case the seniority as per the existing list of cooperative housing society for allotment of land was altered by subsequent decision. The previous policy was that the seniority amongst housing societies in regard to allotment of land was to be based on the date of registration of the society with the Registrar. But on 20-1-1990, the policy was changed by reckoning seniority as based upon the date of approval of the final list by the Registrar. This altered the existing seniority of the society for allotment of land. The Supreme Court held that the societies were entitled to a legitimate expectation that the past consistent practice in-the matter of allotment be followed even if there was no right in private law for such allotment. The authority was not entitled to defeat the legitimate expectation of the societies as per the pervious seniority list without some overriding reason of public policy as to justify change in the criterion. No such overriding public interest was shown.

46. The next case in which the doctrine of legitimate expectation was considered is the case of Food Corporation of India vs Kamdhenu Cattle Feed Industries. (1993) 1 SCC 71. There the Food Corporation of India invited tenders for sale of stocks of damaged food grains and the respondent's bid was the highest. All tenderers were invited for negotiation, but the respondent did not raise his bid during negotiation while others did. The respondent filed a writ petition claiming that if had a legitimate expectation of acceptance of its bid, which was the highest. The High Court allowed the writ petition. Reversing the judgment, the Supreme Court referred to CCSU Case and to Preston, in re (1985 AC 835) and held that though the respondents bid was highest, still it had no right to have it accepted. No doubt, its render could not be arbitrarily rejected, but if the Corporation reasonably fell that the amount offered by the respondent was inadequate as per the factors operating in the commercial field, the non-acceptance of bid could not be faulted. The procedure of negotiation itself involved giving due weight to the legitimate expectation of the highest bidder and thus was sufficient.

47. In MP Oil Extraction vs State of MP (1997) 7 SCC 592 the Supreme Court ruled that:-

"the doctrine of legitimate expectation has its application-only in the realm of public law and that in an "appropriate case, constitutes a substantive and enforceable right".

48. On the facts of the instant case, it was held that the industries, with whom the State government had entered into agreements for supply of sal seeds, had a legitimate expectation that in accordance with the renewal clause and in accordance with the past practice, the agreements would be renewed in the usual manner. The Court also ruled that the selected industries, with which the state had entered into agreements for supply of sal seeds at concessional rates, needed the protection of continuing such agreements and hence, the renewal clause was provided in those agreements. The Court attached considerable importance to the need for protection of such selected industries by upholding the validity of the renewal clauses in those agreements, although it was apparent in the mind of the Court that to ensure fair play and transparency in the state's action, it was desirable that distribution of state largesse was effected by inviting open tenders or by public auction. The Court, however, felt that special agreements entered into with the selected industrial units by the state government were permissible. The decision reflects the mind of the court that it considered the doctrine of legitimate expectation as an equitable principle and that in order to give full effect to this principle, application of another principle in the realm of pubic law may, if need be, have to be restricted.

49. The Supreme Court: laid down a clear principle that claims on legitimate expectation required reliance on representation and resultant detriment in the same way as claims based on promissory estoppel. In National Buildings Construction Corporation vs Raghunathan (1998) see 66, the respondents were appointed in CPWD. They went on deputation to NBCC in Iraq and opted to draw, while on deputation, their grade pay in CPWD plus deputation allowance. Besides that, NBCC granted them foreign allowance at 125% of the basic pay. Meanwhile their basic pay in CWPD was revised w.e.f. 1-1-1986 on the recommendation of the Fourth Pay Commission. They contended that the aforesaid increase of 125% should be given by NBCC on their revised scales. This was not accepted by NBCC. The argument of the respondents based on legitimate expectation was rejected in view of the peculiar conditions and financial stringency (due to embargo put by UNO) under which NBCC was working in Iraq. On the facts of the case, the Court, found that since there was no promise or agreement or contract of service executed by NBCC for payment of foreign allowance to its employees, who were posted on overseas projects, they could not have any legitimate expectation of receiving such allowance. The Court further rule that the question, whether the expectations and the claims made thereupon were legitimate or not, was essentially a question of fact and therefore, the rules of pleading would strictly apply. A party which seeks a relief from the Court claiming expectation, ought to place such facts before the court as would enable it to satisfy itself that such claim is legitimate. It was observed by the Supreme Court that the doctrine of legitimate expectation had both substantive and procedural aspects.

50. Recently the Supreme Court of India has considered the scope and meaning of this principle in various decisions. In Ram Parvesh Singh vs State of Bihar (2006) 8 SCC 381, the Supreme Court discussed this principle by referring to its earlier decisions in the following words:-

"What is legitimate expectation" Obviously, it is not a legal right. It is an expectation of a benefit, relief or remedy that may ordinarily flow from a promise or established practice. The term 'established practice' refers to a regular, consistent predictable and certain conduct, process or activity of the decision-making authority. The expectation should be legitimate, that is, reasonable, logical and valid. Any expectation which is based on sporadic or casual or random acts, or which is unreasonable illogical or invalid cannot be a legitimate expectation. Nor being a right, it is not enforceable as such. It is a concept fashioned by courts, for judicial review of administrative action. It is procedural in character based on the requirement of a higher degree of fairness in administrative action, as a consequence of the promise made, or practice established. In short, a person can be said to have a 'legitimate expectation' of a particular treatment, if any representation or promise is made by an authority, either expressly or impliedly, or if the regular and consistent past practice of the authority gives room for such expectation in the normal course. As a ground for relief, the efficacy of the doctrine is rather weak as its slot is just above 'fairness in action' but far below 'promissory estoppel'. It may only entitle an expectant: (a) to an opportunity to show cause before the expectation is dashed; or (b) to an explanation as to the cause for denial. In appropriate cases, court may grant a direction requiring the Authority to follow the promised procedure or established practice. A legitimate expectation, even when made out, does not always entitle the expectant to a relief. Public interest, change in policy, conduct of the expectant or any other valid or bonafide reason given by the decision maker, may be sufficient to negative the 'legitimate expectation'. The doctrine of legitimate expectation based on established practice (as contrasted from legitimate expectation based on a promise), can be invoked only by someone who has dealings or transactions or negotiations or negotiations with an authority, on which such established practice has a bearing, or by someone who has a recognized legal relationship with the authority. A total stranger unconnected with the authority or a person who had no previous dealings with the authority and who has not entered into any transaction or negotiations with the authority, cannot invoke the doctrine of legitimate expectation, merely on the ground that the authority has a general obligation to act fairy."

51. The Supreme Court referred to its earlier decision in Union of India vs Hindustan Development Corporation (1993) 3 SCC 499, wherein the Court has, inter alia, held :-

"It is generally agreed that legitimate expectation gives the applicant sufficient locus standi for judicial review and that me doctrine of legitimate expectation is to be confined mostly to right of a fair hearing before a decision which results in negating a promise or withdrawing on undertaking is taken. The doctrine does not give scope to claim relief straightaway from the administrative authorities as no crystallized right as such is involved. The protection of such legitimate expectation does not require the fulfillment of the expectation where an overriding public interest requires otherwise. In other words whether a person's legitimate expectation is not fulfilled by taking a particular decision then decision-maker should justify the denial of such expectation by showing some overriding public interest. Therefore, even if substantive protection of such expectation is contemplated that does not grant an absolute right to a particular person. It simply ensures the circumstances in which that expectation may be denied or restricted. A case of legitimate expectation would arise when a body by representation or by past practice aroused expectation which it would within its powers to fulfill. The protection is limited to that extent and judicial review can be within those limits. But as discussed above a person who bases his claim on the doctrine of legitimate expectation, in the first instance, must satisfy that there is a foundation and thus has locus standi to make such a claim. In considering the same several factors, which give rise to such legitimate expectation must be present. The decision taken by the authority must be found to be arbitrary, unreasonable and not taken in public interest. If it is a question of policy, even by way of change of old policy, the courts cannot interfere with a decision. In a given case whether there are such facts and circumstances giving rise to a legitimate expectation, it would primarily be a question of fact. If these tests are satisfied and if the court is satisfied that a case of legitimate expectation is made out then the next question would be whether failure to give on opportunity of hearing before the decision affecting such legitimate expectation is taken, has resulted in failure of justice and whether on that ground the decision should be quashed. If that be so then what should be the relief is again a matter which depends on several factors."

52. The Supreme Court also took notice of its decision in Punjab Communications Ltd. vs Union of India (1994) SCC 727, wherein the Court had held :-

"The principle of 'legitimate expectation' is still at a stage of evolution. The principle is at the root of the rule of law and requires regularity, Page 4186 predictability and certainty in the Governments dealings, with the public. The procedural part of it relates to a representation that a hearing or other appropriate procedure will be afforded before the decision is made. However, the more important aspect is whether the decision maker can sustain the change in policy by resort to Wednesbury principles of rationality or whether the court can go into the question whether the decision-maker has properly balanced the legitimate expectation as against the need for a change. In sum, this means that the judgment whether public interest overrides the substantive legitimate expectation of individuals will be for the decision-maker who has made the change in the policy. The choice of the policy is for the decision-maker and not for the court. The legitimate substantive expectation merely permits the court to find out if the change in policy which is the cause for defeating the legitimate expectation is irrational or perverse or one which no reasonable person could have made."

53. Very recently in case of Sethi Auto Service Station vs Delhi Development Authority (2009) 1 see 180 it 'has been reiterated that:-

"32 that the golden thread running through all these decisions is that a case for applicability of the doctrine of legitimate expression, now accepted in the subjective sense as part of our legal jurisprudence, arises when an administrative body by reason of a representation or by past practice of conduct aroused an expectation which it would be within its powers to fulfill unless some overriding public interest comes in the way. However, a person who based his claim on the doctrine of legitimate expectation, in the first instance, has to satisfy that he has relied on the said representation and the denial of that expectation has worked to his detriment. The Court could interfere only if the decision taken by the authority was found to be arbitrary, unreasonable or in gross abuse of power or in violation of principles of natural justice and no taken in public interest. But a claim based on mere legitimate expectation, without anything more cannot ipso facto give a right to invoke these principles".

54. In our jurisdiction the principle of legitimate expectation has been developed by the decision of the Apex Court. In Soya-Protein Ltd. vs Secretary Ministry of Disaster Management and Relief 22 BLD 378 = 6 BLC681 it is held that:-

"54. There is no doubt that the Government can always change its policy and the Courts will not interfere with such change, if made for a better one or for public interest or for some overwhelming reason for which a change of policy had become unavoidable, provided of course, the Government acts fairly and reasonably. In this case, in discontinuing the School Feeding Program, the Government had failed to I) implement its own policy decision thwarting the legitimate expectation of the petitioner that Government would continue their said program which was solemnly accepted in their policy decision."

55. In Golam Mostafa vs Bangladesh 2007 (XV) BLT (HCD) 128, decision of Soya Protein was followed in applying the doctrine of legitimate expectation in the field governed by the Contract Act. It was observed that.

56. The upshot of the decisions noted above are that judicial review may be allowed on the plea of frustration of legitimate expectation in the following situations:-

i)	If there is a promise by the authority expressed either by their representations or by conducts.

ii) The decision of the authority was arbitrary or unreasonable within the Wednesbury principal.

iii) There was a failure on the part of the concerned authority to act fairly in taking the decision.

iv) The expectation to be crystallized into a legitimate one, it must be based on clear facts and circumstances leading to a definite expectation and not a mere anticipation or a wish or hope and also must re reasonable in the circumstances.

57. In BTMC vs Nasiruddin Chowdhury cited in 5 BLC (AD) 144 the Apex in a detailed discussion accepted the position that a legitimate expectation cannot be defeated by the executive action unless public interest clearly requires negation of such expectation but of the some time found that such an expectation can be given effect to by the Court only when the facts of the case clearly and unambiguously give rise to such on expectation.

58. In the case DG, BWDB vs BJ Geo Textile, 57 DLR (AD) 1 (the Appellate Division relied upon 51 DLR (AD) 56) wherein it was held that ;-

"45. but when a contract is concluded the contractor has a legitimate expectation that he will be dealt with fairly."

46. In such event, the cancellation of the contract unilaterally without regard to the subsequent development is a high feat of arbitrariness which rightly attracts the writ petition".

59. In Syed SM Hasan vs Bangladesh (2008) 60 DLR (AD) 76 where is a number of persons are selected for appointment or promotion and some of them are appointed or promoted, then without appointing the rest of the list, preparation for fresh expectation and cannot be sustained.

60. Recently the Hon'ble Appellate Division formulated the principle in Government of Bangladesh vs Md Jahangir Alam, reported in 1 (2012) LN] (AD) 49 = 17 BLC (AD) 115 wherein observed that;-

"38. An examination of the various decisions discussed and noted above would show that the principle of legitimate of expectation may arise or be applicable both in the subjective or procedural Sense in the following manner.

i)	although the concerned person may not have the legal right but because of well established prior practice, he would have an expectation which is crystallized into a legitimate one, based On the consistent conduct of the concerned authorities; unless there is overwhelming public interest to do otherwise;

ii)  mere indulgence may create an expectation in the mind of the incumbent but on its own, without more, would not render if a legitimate one;

iii)it is however, a legitimate expectation on the part of the incumbent that the concerned authorities; under the circumstances of the case, would act fairly;

iv) when an incumbent has an expectation, which is reasonable in the circumstances, capable of including expectations which may go beyond enforceable legal rights and render if legitimate;

v)	a public authority is bound to follow a certain procedure which is culminated into a promise or undertaking, because of its express or implied consistent practice unless of course, it does not contravene any statutory duty;

vi) if from the evidence it is apparent that contractual term, is frequently departed from to some thing beneficial to the incumbent, his expectation may be crystallized into a legitimate one,

vii) if the practice is well established that it would be unfair on the part of the Government to depart from the said practice legitimate expectation may rise that the incumbent can reasonably expect the said practice to continue to his benefit, even though he may not have strict legal right to the said benefit.

viii) if some benefit or advantage which a class of persons had in the past been allowed by the Government which they can legitimately expect to continue unless there is same rational grounds for the authority to withdraw it,

ix) not a mere anticipation or a wish or a hope it must be a definite expectation,

which is reasonable and fair in the circumstances based on clear facts and consistent practice so that a person or a class of persons may feel that there is no reason to discontinue the practice to his or their disadvantage, then the said expectation would be crystallized into a legitimate one and in such a case, the power of judicial review would be available to protect the said legitimate expectation unless there is overwhelming public interest against it. "

61. In the Chief Engineer vs People s Republic of Bangladesh (Rural Development) 32 BLD (AD) 177 = 17 BLC (AD) 91 wherein observed that;-

"19. The doctrine of legitimate expectation is a concept which 'is akin to that a promissory estoppel and· this concept has been developed in the European Community Law. According to the doctrine, where a person is the victim of an unfavourable decision taken by a public authority, this may amount to an infringement of that person's legitimate expectation, where for example, the decision contradicts an earlier promise or course of conduct on the part of the public authority concerned. Therefore, this doctrine is circum scribed by certain limitations and exceptions. The first and foremost consideration is that is that there must be a foundation in the petition claiming legitimate expectation and secondly, there must be a promise of a representation of the part of the public authority on the claim of the persons aggrieved by the decision."

62. In view of the above extracted principle of legitimate expectation the particular manifestation of the duty to act fairly is that part of the recent evolution of administrative law which may enable an aggrieve party to evoke judicial review if he can show that he had a reasonable expectation of some occurrence or action preceding the decision complained of and that reasonable expectation was not fulfilled in the event. The two phrases reasonable expectation and 'legitimate expectation' are treated as synonymous.

63. We now proceed to examine that the present case in light of the above extracted principle and relevant law.

64. After hearing the learned counsels for the parties it is emerged that the petitioners joined their respective post before amendment of Rules 1979. No doubt, amended Rules 1979 stipulated that the petitioners will get their promotion after completion of 10(ten) years service with a Bachelor Degree. But the settle law is that the condition of service cannot be altering to disadvantage employee. Every service requires promotion avenues. In absence of the same, the moral of the employee go down which amount to finish their initiative in the service.

65. In the case of the petitioners, when they were entered in service as per the old Rules, the lime bound promotion was there. The petitioners joined keeping in view of the future prospects. To the charge of Rules 1979 even the respondents have not given the retrospective effect, therefore, the petitioners cannot be put under amended Rules 1979 which change the conditions of service and alter advantage of the employee.

66. The doctrine of legitimate expectation provides that the statements of policy or intention of the Government or its Department in administering its affairs should be without abuse or discretion. The change of law and or/Rule could not be disregarded unfairly or applied selectively for the reason that unfairness in the form of unreasonableness is akin to violation of natural justice. It means that said actions have to be in conformity of Article 27 of the Constitution of the People's Republic of Bangladesh, of which non-arbitrariness is a second fact. Public Authority cannot claim to have unfettered discretion in public law as the authority is conferred with power only to use them for public good. Generally legitimate expectation is essentially procedural in character as it gives assurance of fair play in administrative action but it may in a given case be enforced as a substantive right. But a person claiming it has to satisfy the Court that his rights had been altered by enforcing a right in private law or he has been deprived of some benefit' or advantage which he was having in the past and which he could legitimately expect to be permitted to continue unless it is withdrawn on some rational ground or he has received assurance from the decision making Authority which is not fulfilled.

67. The potentially important point is that Change of policy should not violate the substantive legitimate expectation and if it does so it must be as the change of policy which is necessary and such a change is not irrational or perverse. The legitimate expectation must be based on legal ground and should stands on lawful root.

68. It is evident from service records of the petitioners that prior to the amended Rules 1979 coming into force, the petitioners' promotion was governed by the Rules 1979. This past practice had been in mode/trend for a numbers of years and it can be said that the expectation of the petitioners that they would be promoted as Sub-Registrar.

69. While we 'have closely scrutinized annexure, we found that there' was no prior notice or warning given to the petitioners in this regard. Even the respondents utterly failed to explain the necessity and/or public interest to change the terms and conditions of the petitioners promotion. The aforesaid expectation cannot be termed or being based on 'sporadic or casual or random acts of the respondents, or as an unreasonable or illogical or invalid expectation. This expectation can be said to have arisen in the mind of the petitioners in the normal course, in view of the consistent past practice of the respondent as reflected in Rule 1979. In our view this expectation was legitimately entertained by the petitioners and acquired vested right in the matter of promotion. It is for the decision maker to justify its decision to change the Rule 1979 in the manner it did, by showing overriding public interest. Therefore, we have no difficulty in concluding that the amended Rule 1979 seeks to serve a purpose which would help in achieving promotion those who were joined after enactment the same. However, by applying the same logic, we are unable to appreciate as to what is the' purpose sought to be achieved by the proviso to the amended Rule 1979 which unduly restricts the rights of the petitioners who have accepted terms and condition of the Rule 1979.

70. Pertinently the respondents have not disclosed, either by filling an affidavit-in-opposition or even by making submissions before us as to what is the justification for changing the terms and conditions of promotion to the petitioners. The provision of the Amended Rule 1979 contains restriction the petitioners promotion as a Sub-Registrar. We are in view that in terms of the petitioners legitimate expectation extracted from the above mentioned ratio of the decisions, the restriction introduced by SRO No. 156-Ain/96 dated 27-8-1996 (Annexure-A) is ultravires the Constitution and also discriminatory as it offend Articles 27 of the Constitution of the People's Republic of Bangladesh.

71. The next point of be a focus by the petitioners with regards to retrospective effect. While we have scrutinized the impugned Gazette (Annexure-A) we have not seen any word concerning retro respective effect on it. In this regard we must come across of the provision of Article 133 of Constitution of Bangladesh, Article 133 provides that:-

"133. Subject to the provisions of this constitution Parliament may be law regulate the appointment and conditions of service in service of Republic:

Provided that it shall be competent from the President to make rules regulation the appointment and condition of service of such persons until provision in that behalf is make by or under any law, and rules so made shall have effect subject to the provisions of any such law."

72. It is pertinent to mention here that the Article 133 starts with the expression "subject to the provisions of the conditions" which when properly construed, means that Article 133 will have application subject to any specific provisions made in the Constitution. In this respect we may seek did of Article 309 of the Indian Constitution. Article 309 of the Indian Constitution is substantially the same as Article 133 of our Constitution.

73. In BS Bhadera vs India AIR 169 (SC) 118 wherein Indian Supreme Court held that:-

"Any Rule made under Article 309 can be both prospective and retrospective, but the Rule must not be inconsistent with the fundamental rights guaranteed by the Constitution and if a Rule with retrospective operation purports to take away the vested rights and are arbitrarily and not reasonable". If has confirmed in PD Aggarwal vs UP AIR 1987 SC 1676 that it will be subject to scrutiny under Article 14 and 16. In our Constitution Article 136 provides that:-

"136. Provision may be made by law for the reorganization of the service of the Republic by the creation amalgamation or unification of service and such law may vary or revoke any condition of service of a person employed in the service of the Republic."

74. However, no such provision has been made in Article 133.

<u>75. The above provision Article 136 would be unnecessary if the law or Rule made under Article 133 could operate retrospectively to vary or revoke the condition of employees already employed, Properly Construed, variation or revocation of conditions of services of the existing employee is permissible only by made under Article 136 of the Constitution.</u>

<u>76. A Rule made under Article 133 can not be give retrospective effect to affect a vested right. In this gesture we can refer the citation of Matiur Rahman vs Chowdhury Md Mahfuzul Islam reported in 8 MLR (AD) 217 = 55 DLR (AD) 105 (briefly "BADC case") wherein it was held that-</u>

<u>"21. the general Rule of law being that unless mere is a clear indication from the wording of the statute it is not to receive a construction retrospective in effect. The cardinal principle of construction is that every statute is prima facie prospective unless it is expressly or by necessary implication given a retrospective effect. While interpreting a statute the Court is to look of the general scope and purview of the statute and at the remedy sought to be applied and consider what the former state of the law was and what is contemplated by the legislature. Keeping these in mind we have thoroughly scrutinized the BADC Service Regulations, 1990 but we dited to find from its language, an intention to give it a retrospective effect. Under the circumstances the respondents claim to be considered for promotion to the post of Superintending Engineer under the BADC Regulations, 1968".</u>

77. In view of the BADC case (above) Article 133 gives the authority power to regulate the appointment and service conditions of persons in the service of the Republic. But it does not give power to prohibit promotion beyond the provision of law.

78. In ratio of above mentioned case this Court already made a Rule absolute in a similar matter in Writ Petition being No. 1164 of 2011. In this case one Abdur Rahman Bhuiyan, who joined as TC Muharrir under registration Directorate on 26-2-199 and subsequently promoted to the post of Head Assistant on 4-4-2006, as a petitioner filed this writ petition before this Court impugning the amended provision of Schedule 1, (SL No. 6, Column 3) of the Rules 1979 debarring the petitioner from promotion against the aforesaid posts despite being eligible for the same, where-upon this Court vide the judgment and Order dated 15-11-2011 held that the impugned amended Rules, 1979 shall not operate as a bar in case of promotion of the petitioner to the post of Sub- Registrar.

<u>79. Further to that we can straighten out that in view of Section 6(C) of the General Clauses Act, 1897 the rights created under the provisions of the Rules 1979 shall not be adversely affected by the amendment made in 1996.</u>

80. Moreover, the Apex Court in our country has observed in the case of Tareque Rahman vs Bangladesh reported in 63 DLR (AD) (2011) that It is well established that the legislature has full power to make a law with retro respective effect so as to destroy a right or remedy all together but this must expressly laid down or by necessary implication in the repealing legislation."

81. It is plain from the Annexure-A by the amended Rule 1979 the promotion will be gave after putting 10 years of service in the feeder post with a Bachelor Degree Amendment to the Rules 1979, shall hamper the future prospect of the petitioners and thus adversely effect the working of the directorate of registration. The petitions cannot be denied to their due promotion as per old law i.e. under Rules 1979.

82. We do not agree with the oral submission of the learned DAG that the respondents have rightly changed the criteria of promotion of the petitioners.

83. We would like to add force to our views by the reference of Grid Corporation of Orissa vs Rasanada 2003, 10 SCC 297 wherein it is held that

"the condition of service cannot be altered to the disadvantage of the employees".

84. Having regards to the discussions made above in the fact and circumstances of this case, we have no option but to make the Rule absolute. The eligibility criteria for promotion against the post of Sub-Registrar from/amongst the posts of Head Assistant and Upper Division Assistants of registration Directorate and head clerk/Head Assistants of District Registration office under Schedule No. 1 (SL No.6, Column-5) of the Gazetted Officer (Registration Department) Recruitment Rules, 1979 as contained in SRO No. 156-Ain/96 dated 27-8-1996 (Annexure-A) to the Writ Petition is declared to be ultra vires of the Constitution of the People's Republic of Bangladesh so far as it relates to the petitioners.

85. The respondents are directed to apply the unamended/original Rules 1979 (Annexure-A-1)

for the promotion of the petitioners against the post of Sub-Registrar.

Accordingly the Rule is made absolute.

End.

Khalilur Rahman (Md) & others ------ Petitioners
Vs

full_judgment:
Md Iftikhar Rasool J: This Rule is directed against the judgment and order dated 13-4-1995 passed by the Additional District Judge, Chandpur in Miscellaneous Appeal No. 8 of 1992 affirming the judgment and order dated 9-3-1992 passed by the Subordinate Judge, Chandpur in Miscellaneous Case No. 60 of 1990 allowing the pre-emption Case under section 24 of the Non-Agricultural Tenancy Act, 1949.

2. Facts relevant for disposal of this Rule, in short, are that opposite party No. 1 filed Miscellaneous Case No. 60 of 1990 under section 24 of the Non-Agricultural Tenancy Act of 1949 against the petitioners and others in the Court of the Subordinate Judge, Chandpur for pre-emption of the disputed land transferred by opposite party Nos. 4-11 by four different kabalas, two of which were registered on 22-1-1981 and the rest two on 24-1-1981 for total consideration of Taka 1,11,000.00 without serving any notice upon the opposite party No. 1 as per section 23 of the said Act. In the pre-emption application opposite party No. 1 stated that he was the youngest son of his father having been born on 16-5-1969 and attaining majority on 16-5-1987. It is further stated by opposite party No. 1 in the pre-emption application that he was entitled to file the pre-emption case within three years from the date of attainment of majority as per the provisions of section 6 of the Limitation Act and that he came to know of the disputed kabalas from Md Salamatullah Khan and Habibur Rahman and thereafter taking certified copies of the disputed kabalas he definitely came to know of the transfer on 13-5-1990. It is further stated by opposite party No. 1 in the pre-emption application that on 24-3-1978 and 19-9-1978 some lands and share of the disputed building belonging to his deceased father were transferred by way of forgery and false personification and the said two deeds were registered with the District Registrar's Officer at Comilla for declaration of those two kabalas as collusive, fraudulent and forged, Title Suit No. 117 of 1986 was filed in the Court of the Assistant Judge, Chandpur. Opposite Party No. 1 coming to know of the disputed kabalas transferring the disputed land and the share of disputed building in favour of the present petitioners by opposite party Nos. 4-11, the opposite party No. 1 instituted the instant Miscellaneous case upon deposit of the amount of the consideration money of Taka 1,11,000.00 together with the statutory compensation at the rate of 5%.

3. The petitioners as opposite party Nos. 1-3 in the instant miscellaneous case contested the same by filing a joint written objection wherein they denied all material allegations made in the application and staying, inter alia, that the case is barred by limitation and that the actual name of opposite party No. 1 is Jinnat Ali Bhuiyan and using such name Title Suit No. 117 of 1986 was filed by him. The entire interest of opposite party No. 1 (i.e. the pre-emptor) in the land as well as in the building has been transferred by two registered kabalas dated 24-3-78 and 19-9-78 and that the interest of opposite party No.1 in the disputed holding having been transferred and he having no subsisting interest in the disputed holding, he cannot maintain the miscellaneous case for pre-emption and, as such, the pre-emption case instituted by opposite party No. 1 is liable to be dismissed.

4. During trial of the case the petitioner (i.e. opposite party No. 1) examined 5 PWs as against 4 OPWs and thereafter the trial Court allowed the miscellaneous case filed by opposite party No. 1 by his judgment and order dated 9-3-1992. Against said judgment and order the petitioners as appellants filed Miscellaneous Appeal No. 8 of 1992 before the District Judge, Chandpur and the said appeal was transferred to the Court of the Additional District Judge, Chandpur who after hearing dismissed the appeal and affirmed the judgment and order passed by the Subordinate Judge, Chandpur in Miscellaneous Case No. 60 of 1990.

5. Being aggrieved by the impugned judgment and order by the Additional District Judge, Chandpur on 13-4-1995 in Miscellaneous Appeal No. 8 of 1992 the petitioners moved this Court under section 115 of the Code of Civil Procedure and obtained the Rule. Opposite Party No. 1 has opposed the Rule.

<u>6. It is admitted that the present petitioners as appellants filed FMA No. 52 of 1992 against the judgment and order dated 9-3-1992 passed by the Subordinate Judge, Chandpur allowing the Miscellaneous Case No. 59 of 1990 under section 24 of the Non-Agricultural Tenancy Act. It is seen that the aforesaid Miscellaneous Case was instituted by the opposite party No. 1 for pre-emption of some lands of the disputed holding and share of building transferred to the present petitioners by co-sharer opposite party Nos. 4-11 on the basis of registered kabalas dated 22- 3-1979, 17-8-1979, 7-4-1979,11-4-1979 and 14-4-1979. It is noticed that in the Miscellaneous Case No. 59 of 1990 the present opposite party No. 1 as pre-emptor set up the case almost on identical lines as he set up in the instant Miscellaneous Case No. 60 of 1990. He claimed that he was a minor at the time of transfer of the disputed land and share in the building and he attained majority on 16-5-1987. It was his further case in the Miscellaneous Case No. 59 of 1990 that he came to know of the transfers made by opposite party Nos. 4-11 from Salamatullah Khan and Habibur Rahman for the first time on 10-5-1990. A Division Bench of this Court by judgment and order dated 23-2-1998 dismissed the appeal filed by the present petitioners and affirmed the judgment and order of the Subordinate Judge, Chandpur. Against the judgment and order of the Division Bench of this Court the present petitioners filed Civil Petition for Leave to Appeal No. 585 of 1998 before the Appellate Division. The Appellate Division by their judgment and order dated 9-12-1998 were pleased to dismiss the Civil Petition for Leave to Appeal. So, it appears that Appellate Division upheld the observations and findings of the High Court Division on all counts including the questions of limitation and minority of the opposite party No. 1 at the relevant time of the transfers made by opposite party Nos. 4 to 11 in favour of the petitioners. Paradoxically enough the petitioners while contesting Miscellaneous Case No. 59 of 1990 and the instant Miscellaneous Case No. 60 of 1990 did not make any attempt for staying the proceedings of these two miscellaneous cases, till disposal of Title Suit No. 117 of 1986 and there is no material before us to show that any attempt to this effect was ever made by the present petitioners before the trial Court. The petitioners as appellants in FMA No. 52 of 1992 also did not make any prayer for staying the proceedings of Miscellaneous Case No. 59 of 1990 till disposal of Title Suit No. 117 of 1986.</u>

<u>7. Mr Syed Mohammad Hossain, the learned Advocate appearing for the petitioners, argues that this Court in its revisional jurisdiction can stay proceedings of Miscellaneous Case No. 60 of 1990 till disposal of Title Suit No. 117 of 1986 after setting aside the judgments and orders passed by the lower appellate Court and the trial Court and this will meet the ends of justice.</u>

<u>8. Mr MA Wahab Mia, the learned Advocate appearing for the opposite party No. 1 contends that the above submission of the learned lawyer of the petitioners is not tenable and if such plea is accepted then this Court will have to by-pass the judgment and order of the Appellate Division passed in Civil Petition for leave to Appeal No. 585 of 1998 which arose out of Miscellaneous Case No. 59 of 1990. It is submitted by Mr MA Wahab Mia, the learned Counsel for opposite party No. 1 that factually and legally both the courts below concurred with each other and this Court in its revisional jurisdiction will not interfere with the concurred findings of both the Courts below unless there is gross and palpable illegality committed by those courts. He further contends that when the petitioners did not pray for stay of the proceedings of Miscellaneous Case No. 59 of 1990 and Miscellaneous Case No. 60 of 1990 till disposal of Title Suit No. 117 of 1986, the petitioners will be deemed to have given a go-by to this plea.</u>

<u>9. We have given our anxious consideration to this submissions made by the learned lawyers of both the parties. On the question of limitation which is mixed question of law as well as of fact, the petitioners have not been able to place any material before us to show that opposite party No. 1 had any knowledge of the disputed kabalas four in number before 13-5-1990. There is also no material before us that any notice of the disputed transfer as required under section 23 of the Non-Agricultural Tenancy Act was served upon the opposite party No. 1. Section 24 of the said Act provides that if no notice under section 23 is issued or served upon the petitioner (opposite party No. 1 in the instant case) he can file a case under section 24 of the Non-Agricultural Tenancy Act for pre-emption of the disputed land within four months from the date of knowledge of the transfer. In the instant case the opposite party No. 1 has specifically stated that he filed the case within four months from the date of his knowledge of the disputed transfer. This being the position, the present case appears to have been filed within four months from the date of knowledge of the disputed transfer. The plea of the petitioners is, that the proceedings of Miscellaneous Case No. 60 of 1990 may be stayed till disposal of Title Suit No. 117 of 1986 after setting aside the judgment and orders of both the Courts below. We have already held that the findings of both the Courts below being concurrent we find no cogent legal ground to set aside those two judgments and orders. The fate of this case is linked with the fate of Miscellaneous Case No. 59 of 1990. The petitioners having failed in FMA No. 52 of 1992 as well as in the Civil Petition for leave to Appeal No. 585 of 1998 there is no scope for staying the proceedings of Miscellaneous Case No. 60 of 1990 till disposal of Title Suit No. 117 of 1986 after setting aside the judgment and orders of the Courts below.</u>

10. In the background of the facts and circumstances of the case and for the reasons stated above we find no substance in this Rule. The Rule is accordingly discharged without any order as to costs. Stay granted earlier by this Court is hereby vacated.

Send down the LC Records at once to the Court concerned.

End.
