case_source: (From Judgment and order dated 17-7-2000 passed by the High Court Division in Writ Petition Nos. 3773, 4490 and 4491 of 1999)
full_judgment:
Md Tafazzul Islam J: These three appeals by leave filed by the writ respondents are against the Judgment and order dated 17-7-2000 passed by the High Court Division in Writ Petition Nos. 3773, 4490 and 4491 of 1999 by which the Rules were made absolute and the assessments of customs duties and other levies on the imported Hard Boards and MDF Boards on the basis of proportionate value were declared to have been made without lawful authority and of no legal effect and the writ respondents were also directed to return the bank guarantees furnished by the respondents.

2. The writ petitioner respondent in Civil Appeal No. 133 of 2002 filed Writ Petition No. 3773 of 1999 stating, inter alia, that they and other business firms previously imported Hard Boards of size 8' x 4' x 2.5 mm declaring invoice value of those @ US$ 2.10 per sheet and there being no fixed tariff value on Hard Boards of the above size, the customs authority assessed customs duty and other levies on the said imported Hard Boards on the basis of the declared invoice value that is @ US$ 2.10 per sheet and accordingly, on the assumption that customs duty will also be assessed on such size of Hard Board in similar manner, that is fixing the value @ US$ 2.10 per sheet, the writ petitioner respondent by opening Letter of Credit dated 13-7-1999, imported 5600 sheets of Hard Board of similar size that is 8' x 4' x 2.5 mm from Thailand and after the arrival of goods submitted bill of entry for assessment of customs duty and other levies but on the basis of a complaint made by some business rivals of the respondent to the effect that the respondent was trying to evade customs duty by making false declaration regarding the thickness of the imported Hard Boards, an inquiry was made by the customs authority and after detailed inquiry the allegation made in the above complaint was found to be baseless but even then the customs authority illegally and arbitrarily fixed value on the above imported Hard Boards @ US$ 3.40 per sheet by applying the principle of proportionate value on the basis that tariff value @ US$ 4.00 per sheet has been fixed on Hard Boards of size of 8' x 4' x 3 mm by the Gazette Notification dated 19-5-1999. Being aggrieved the respondent filed appeal before the appropriate Customs Authority but since there was no response the respondent had to invoke writ jurisdiction. The writ petitioner respondent in Civil Appeal No. 134 of 2002 filed Writ Petition No. 4490 of 1999 more or less on similar facts except that 8400 sheets of Hard Boards of similar size were imported by them from Thailand by opening Letter of Credit dated 14-10-1999 and though invoice value of those were @ US$ 2.05 per sheet, the customs authority, illegally fixed the value @ 3.34 per sheet applying the principle of proportionate value. The writ petitioner respondent in Civil Appeal No. 135 of 2002 filed Writ Petition No. 4491 of 1999 also on similar facts except that they imported 2880 sheets of MDF Board of size 8' x 4' x 2.25 mm from Singapore by opening Letter of Credit dated 6-10-1999 invoice value of which was @ US$ 2.00 per sheet and for such MDF Board there being no fixed tariff value, assessment has to be made on the basis of invoice value @ US$ 2.00 per sheet and even if MDF Board is regarded as Hard Board even then there being no fixed tariff value for the imported size of 8' x 4' x 2.25 mm, assessment has to be made on the basis of invoice value @ US$ 2.00 per sheet but the customs authority arbitrarily and illegally fixed value @ US$ 3.60 per sheet applying the principle of proportionate value.

3. The High Court Division heard the above writ petitions analogously and made the Rules absolute holding that in the Gazette Notification dated 19-5-1999 no tariff value being fixed on the sizes of Hard Boards and MDF Boards imported by the writ petitioners respondents and previously the customs authority having assessed customs duty and other levies on similar sizes of Hard Boards fixing the value thereon on the basis of declared invoice value, the respondents acquired legal right to be assessed at that rate and the imposition of the proportionate value on the same kind of goods, otherwise in the absence of any tariff value, is without any lawful authority.

<u>4. Leave was granted to consider as to whether the High Court Division in the respective writ petitions committed illegality in directing the customs authority to assess the customs duty, etc, on the basis of invoice value that was prevailing at the time of opening of letters of credit inasmuch as Customs Authority has the authority to determine normal value and realise duty thereon at the rate prevailing on the date of submission of the bill of entry and whether the High Court Division erred in holding that "the petitioner has acquired a legal right and equal protection of law and, as such, the respondents are estopped from claiming proportionate value and the same is against principle of natural justice" as there is no question of acquiring vested right in the Invoice value under the Customs Act.</u>

5. Mr AJ Mohammed Ali, the learned Additional Attorney-General appearing on behalf of the appellants, submits that the High Court Division was wrong in directing the customs authority to assess the customs duty on the basis of the invoice value because in case of disagreement with the invoice value, in terms of section 25(1) of the Customs Act the customs authority is to determine the normal value and realise customs duty and other levies thereon at the rate prevailing on the date of the submission of the bill of entry and further the High Court Division erred in holding that the petitioner has acquired a legal right since there is no question of acquiring of legal or vested right in the invoice value under the Customs Act.

6. Dr M Zahir, the learned Counsel appearing on behalf of the respondents, submits that the fixing of proportionate value on the goods, instead of declared invoice value, is illegal and without any lawful authority because there is no mention of proportionate value either in the Tariff Code or in the Customs Act and that earlier the customs authority released Hard Boards of similar sizes on the basis of declared invoice value without raising any objection whatsoever and accordingly, on the legitimate expectation that the Hard Boards would be assessed in the manner as assessed in the past, the respondents imported those and so the customs authority is now estopped from imposing proportionate value on the imported Hard Boards and further, there being no tariff value for MDF Boards assessment on the same will also be made on the basis of invoice value.

7. The first question raised is, whether the customs duty, etc., on the imported Hard Boards and MDF Boards should be assessed on the basis of Invoice value as ordered by the High Court Division irrespective of the provisions of section 25 of the Customs Act.

8. Section 25(1) of the Customs Act provides that the value of any imported good shall be taken to be the normal price which they would fetch on the date referred to in section 30, that is the date of submission of the bill of entry, on its sale in the open market between a buyer and a seller independent of each other. However, where in exercise of power under section 25(7) of the Customs Act, tariff value is fixed by notification published in the official Gazette the provision of fixing normal value under section 25(1) as above shall not be applicable.

9. Admittedly, the respondents in Civil Appeal Nos. 133 and 134 of 2002 imported from Thailand respectively 5600 and 8400 sheets of Hard Board, sizes being 8' x 4' x 2.5 mm and the respondent in Civil Appeal No. 135 of 2002 imported 2880 sheets of MDF Board from Singapore size being 8' x 4' x 2.5 mm and the invoice value of the above Hard Boards and MDF Boards are respectively US$ 2.10, 2.05 and 2.00 per sheet and by SRO No. 75 issued on 15-5-1999 issued under section 25(7) of the Customs Act, Government fixed tariff value on Hard Board size 8' x 4' x 3 mm, which comes under the Heading No. 4411.11.00 of HS Code, @ US$ 4.00 per sheet and as it appears in the HS Code, no tariff value has been fixed on other sizes of Hard Boards and in the HS Code there is also no mention of MDF Board. However, even if MDF Board, falls within the category of Hard Boards, the position is that there is also no fixed tariff value on Hard/MDF Boards of the sizes imported, that is 8' x 4' x 2.25 mm. It also appears that in the present case the customs authority fixed proportionate value @ US$ 3.40, 3.34 and 3.60 respectively per sheet instead of invoice value of US$ 2.10, 2.05 and 2.00 respectively taking into consideration the fact that for Hard Boards of size 8' x 4' x 3 mm, the tariff value has been fixed @ US$ 4.00 per sheet.

10. In the case of Mr Ayub and others vs Collector of Customs and others, Writ Petition No. 1495 of 1996, dispute arose when the customs authority fixed the indicative value on the imported goods and the High Court Division held that such methods of determining the normal value with various adjectives such as indicative value, enhanced valuation price, recorded value, loaded value and commissioners value, etc have no sanction in law and accordingly, the High Court Division directed the customs authority not to use such attributes or any other adjectives so far the normal value is concerned.

11. In the case of Rahmania Vanaspati Product Ltd vs Collector of Customs, 4 BLC 85 question arose as to whether the customs authority can make assessment of customs duty and other levies on the basis of indicative value. The High Court Division held as follows:

"From a reading of the provision of section 25(1),(2)(3) and section 30(1) of the Act it is very much seen that Customs Authority is authorised to assess customs duties on imported merchandise at the value prevalent on the date the bill of entry is presented for assessment of customs duties. The undefined position is that the customs authority fixed the indicative value for the purpose of assessment of customs duties of the imported CDSO and CPO, the kind of merchandises imported by the petitioners, much long before the presentation of the Bill of Entry. This being the factual position, the indicative value that has been fixed by the circular dated 3-6-1994 cannot be considered to have been fixed in the light of the provisions of section 25(1),(2)(3) and section 30(1) of the Act."

12. The High Court Division, in the case of Sew Bishar Prasad vs Collector of Customs 54 DLR 173, also took similar view.

13. Further in terms of section 30A of Customs Act, which was incorporated in the Customs Act wef 1-7-1995, that is before opening of letters of credit in the present cases in the year 1999, provides that for the purpose of section 30, the value and the rate of duty applicable to any goods shall respectively include the value as determined under section 25 of the Customs Act.

<u>14. Accordingly, in terms of the provisions of section 25(1) and 30A of the Customs Act there being no fixed tariff value on the Hard Boards and MDF Boards on the sizes imported, normal value has to be fixed on the basis of market value prevailing on the date when the bill of entry was submitted.</u>

15. The second question of the leave granting is, whether the respondents on the basis of previous assessment acquired a legal/vested right to be assessed on the basis of invoice value.

16. As it appears from the contents of the note sheets on the bills of entry annexed with the Writ Petition Nos. 3773 and 4990 of 1999, on earlier occasion the customs authority in case of similar size of Hard Boards fixed tariff value on the basis of invoice value and the case of the respondents is, that it is their legitimate expectation that they will be dealt with similarly regarding assessment of the imported Hard Boards in question acquiring a vested right.

17. This question of vested right regarding payment of customs duty and other levies, as distinguished from fixation of the value of imported goods, at first, came up for consideration in Hannan's Case, 40 DLR 273. As it appears in the above case in view of the acute shortage of sugar, notification was issued under section 19 of the Customs Act and section 4(1) of the Sales Tax Ordinance, 1982 declaring some exemption on imported sugar and relying on the same the petitioner opened letter of credit for import of sugar complying with all the terms and conditions as laid down in the above notification but after opening of the letter of credit, customs duty was enhanced by subsequent SRO. The High Court Division  considering the special situation under which the above notification was issued under section 19 declaring exemptions held that customs duty and other levies cannot be levied on the basis of subsequent SRO enhancing customs duty because the importers acquired vested right to get the consignment cleared at a lower rate which was in force on the date on which letter of credit was opened and exemption of customs duty having been provided under section 19 of Customs Act, the same has no bearing with the rate of duty as contemplated in sections 18 and 30 of the Customs Act and section 30 will operate only insofar as rate of duty levied under section 18 and has no reference to exemption under sections 19 of the Customs Act. On appeal, the Appellate Division (vide 42 DLR (AD) 167) apart from the question of vested right also considered the principle of promissory estoppel as the importer imported the goods on the assurance of the Government which was notified in the public notice. As it appears although it was argued before the Appellate Division that notification under section 19 of the Customs Act is always subject to provision of section 30 and section 30 will prevail over the notification under section 19 of the Customs Act, the Appellate Division decided the case only relying on the of principle of promissory estoppel.

18. In the case of Collector of Customs vs Ahmed Hossain, 48 DLR (AD) 199, the Appellate Division also considered similar question of vested right so far payment of customs duty and other levies are concerned. In the above case, the order of the Deputy Collector of Customs dated 7-12-1991 was impugned contending that section 19 of the Customs Act relates to exemption of customs duty and a notification (SRO) under that section is never subject to the provisions of section 30 of the Customs Act and the customs authority acted illegally in passing the impugned order taking a contrary view. The Appellate Division considering the very important distinction which was made in Hannan's case, held that notification under section 19 is independent of rate of duty as mentioned in section 30 and there is no connection between sections 19 and 30 of the Customs Act.

19. However, the claim of vested right, so far it relates to fixation of value of the imported goods, came up for consideration in the case of Khairul Bashar vs Collector of Customs, 50 DLR 225. As it appears in the above case, at the time of opening of the letter of credit, the rate of customs duty as well as the tariff, value of the imported goods was much lower and both customs duty as well as tariff value were increased by SRO issued after opening of the letter of credit and question arose as to whether an importer is entitled to pay customs duty etc. at the rate which was in operation on the date of opening of the letter of credit and on the basis of tariff value which was also in operation on the date of opening of the letter of credit. The High Court Division, considering the fact that tariff value is imposed to keep the value of imported goods in conformity with the price of similar goods in the international market so that importer cannot, in collusion with the exporter undervalue the goods to be imported to evade the payment of proper customs duty, declined to follow 42 DLR (AD) 167 and 48 DLR (AD) 199 for fixing value of the imported goods as in the aforesaid decisions the provisions of section 25 of the Customs Act were not interpreted and the High Court Division held that customs duty is payable by the importer on the basis of tariff value in force on the date of presentation of bill of entry and not on the basis of invoice or tariff value which was in existence at the time of opening of the letter of credit and further, there is no question of importer acquiring vested right in the invoice value or the tariff value prevailing at the time of opening of the letter of credit.

20. Then in Mustafizur Rahman’s Case, 51 DLR (AD) 40 the claim of vested right, so far it relates to fixation of tariff value on the imported goods, came up for consideration and question arose as to whether by a notification the tariff value could be enhanced giving retrospective effect, specially when the tariff value at the time of opening the respective letters of credit was much lower. The petitioner of the above case relied on 42 DLR (AD) 67 and 48 DLR (AD) 199. As it appears during argument of the above case, the learned Attorney-General could not make any distinction between the facts of the above case and facts involved in 42 DLR (AD) 167 and 48 DLR (AD) 199 and on that consideration the Appellate Division allowed the appeal holding that the petitioner acquired vested right to get the tariff value fixed at the rate which was prevalent at the date of opening of the letter of credit.

21. But subsequently in Mizanur Rahmin's case 52 DLR (AD) 149 this issue was finally settled. In this case, the importer imported galvanised plain sheets and at the time of opening of the letter of credit, the tariff value in respect of galvanised plain sheets as fixed by SRO was much lower but by the time bill of entry was submitted, the tariff value was raised by SRO and relying on 42 DLR (AD) 167, 48 DLR (AD) 199 and also Mostafizur Rahman case, that is 51 DLR (AD) 40, it was argued that the goods were imported taking into account the tariff value which existed at the time of opening of that letter of credit.

22. The Appellate Division explained under what circumstance's decision was given in 51 DLR (AD) 40, which was a case under section 25(7) of the Customs Act. The Appellate Division after discussing the implications of sections 18 and 19 as well as section 30 of the Customs Act held that no vested right has been acquired by the importer to pay customs duty etc., on the basis of tariff value declared by notification (SRO) in force on the date of opening of the letter of credit and the importer has to pay tax and duty on the basis of tariff value in force on the date of presentation of the bill of entry and the argument of acquiring vested right may be tenable in case of exemption case granted in special circumstance as in Hannan's case and thus the principle laid down in the cases reported in 42 DLR (AD) 167 and 48 DLR (AD) 199 were distinguished. The Appellate Division also found it difficult to understand as to how an importer could acquire vested right in the invoice value or the tariff value prevailing at the time of opening letter of credit.

<u>23. In the present cases, the writ petitioner respondents claim legal vested right on the ground that on earlier occasions on import of Hard Boards of similar size by the respondents the customs authority assessed customs duty, etc., on the basis of invoice value. In 52 DLR (AD) 49, the Appellate Division held that no vested right accrued even though at the time of opening of the letter of credit there was a notification (SRO) providing for lesser tariff value. In the present cases on previous occasion the customs authority made assessment on the basis of invoice value. So, there is no question of acquiring vested right by the respondents merely on the basis of earlier assessment.</u>

<u>24. Further, in view of adding of section 30A in the Customs Act wef 1-7-1995, which is long before the opening of the letter of credit in the present cases, the provisions of section 30 have been made applicable to section 25 also and so the position regarding acquiring vested right has also been completely changed.</u>

<u>25. So, in the present cases, in terms of the provisions of sections 25(1) and 30A of the Customs Act, normal value has to be fixed on the imported Hard Boards as well as MDF Boards. In the result the appeals are allowed without any order as to cost. The impugned judgment and order dated 17-7-2000 making the Rules absolute declaring the assessment of Customs duties and other levies on the imported Hard Board and MDF Boards to have been made without any lawful authority and of no legal effect and further directing the writ respondents to return the bank guarantees furnished by the writ petitioners are hereby set aside.</u>

End.

parties:
Maksuda Haque ------ Petitioner
Vs.
Firoz Ahmed Sharif and others ------ Opposite Parties
full_judgment:
This rule was issued calling upon the opposite party No. 1 to 3 to show cause as to why the impugned judgment and order dated 4-5-2010 passed by the learned Additional District Judge, 1st Court Barisal, in Miscellaneous Appeal No. 10 of 2008 reversing those of dated 27-3-2008 passed by the learned Joint District Judge, 1st Court Barisal in Miscellaneous Case No. 47 of 2005 dismissing the case should not be set aside and/or pass such other or further order or orders as to this Court may seem it and proper.

2. The short facts leading to the disposal of the rule is that the opposite party Nos. 1-3 as pre-emptor filed Miscellaneous Case No. 47 of 2005 in the court of learned Joint District. Judge, 1st Court, Barisal claiming pre-emption against document dated 11-5-1999 under section 24 of the Non-Agriculture Tenancy Act and the case was filed on 6-6-2005.

3. The case was filed on the allegation that the property in dispute originally belonged to Abdul Gani, who died leaving behind two sons named Kanchan Ali and Kashem Ali. Kanchan Ali died leaving behind 4 sons 3 daughters and one widow. The pre-emptors are 3 sons of Kanchan Ali and they have been in possession in their ancestral property of disputed SA khatian No. 580. The pre-emptors at first came to learn about kabala on 29-5-2005 from Alo Miah in presence of Kamrul and Somir that their uncle Kashem Ali sold 0.38 acre of land out of 0.60 acre to stranger opposite party No. 1 and got definite knowledge on 05-6-2005 after obtaining certified copy of the impugned document dated 11-5-1999. Pre-emptors had no knowledge of sale because no notice was served. The disputed land is necessary because it is adjacent to their homestead and they are co-sharers by inheritance. The disputed land is within the Barisal City Corporation hence the case was filed under section 24 of the Non-Agricultural Tenancy Act.

4. The petitioner as opposite party No. 1 appeared and contested the case by filing written objection contending inter alia that Kashem Ali sold 0.38 acre of land to this petitioner by kabala dated 11-5-1999 and delivered possession. The pre-emptors had earlier knowledge and opposite party No. 1 purchased the land when the pre-emptors refused to purchase the same due to financial inability. Opposite party No. 1 mutated Khatian No. 4409 on 9-4-2004 and has been in possession upon payment of rent and also opened separate holding in the corporation. The land under pre-emption was low and it was filed up with earth and erected structure and let out 15 cubit tin-shed room with latrine and planted many valuable trees within the knowledge of the pre-emptors. The disputed land was acquired in LA Case No. 1 of 2004-2005 for the purpose of Dapdapia Bridge and opposite party No. 1 applied for compensation. The brother of the pre-emptors named Bazlur Rahman also sold his share on 30-4-2002 to some local persons but no pre-emption was filed against this document because the consideration is higher than the earlier disputed document dated 11-5-2009 and it was disputed document dated 11-5-2009 and it was further stated that the price of the land has increased noticeably and the pre-emptors being extremely greedy are out to get this valuable land at a low price and has filed this case with false story of knowledge which is liable to be dismissed; it was alleged that price of land increased abnormally by lapse of time. Immediately after sale there was chance of possession and change of nature and character within the knowledge of the pre-emptor opposite party.

5. The case of the petitioner is that they had no knowledge of the sale by their uncle and the land is necessary because it is adjacent to their homestead and the case of opposite party No. 1 is that she has improved the land situated adjacent to the pre-emptors; homestead within their knowledge and also opened corporation holding and the instant case was filed after about 7 years.

6. Trial Judge framed as many as 6 issues as to maintainability, limitation, defect of party, whether pre-emptors are co-sharer, whether opposite party made any improvement in the case land and whether the pre-emptors are entitled to relief sought for.

7. During the course of trial pre-emptors examined 3 witnesses and opposite party No. 1 also examined 3 witnesses and adduced documentary evidence in her support.

8. Trial judge upon perusal of the pleading and hearing the parties and considering both oral and documentary evidence dismissed the case by judgment and order dated 27-3-2008 on the finding that the date of knowledge was not proved in evidence and no pre-emption was filed against other more valuable transfer.

9. The pre-emptors preferred Miscellaneous Appeal No. 10 of 2008 before the learned District Judge, Barisal which on transfer was heard by the learned Additional District Judge, 1st court, Barisal who was pleased to allow the appeal by judgment and order dated 4-5-2010.

10. Mr Abdul Quayum, the learned Senior Advocate appearing with Mr Md Ali Reza while Mr Md Afzal Hossain, the learned Advocate appearing with Mr ASM Khasru on behalf of the opposite party to oppose the rule.

11. Mr Abdul Quayum, the learned Senior Advocate appearing on behalf of the petitioner submits that the learned appellate court commit-ted error of law occasioning failure of justice in reversing the judgment of the learned trial court without complying with the provisions of Order 41 Rule 31 of the Code of Civil Procedure and the same being not a proper judgment of reversal is liable to be set aside.

12. He next submits that the learned appellate court upon misreading and non-consideration of material evidence failed to notice that the case land is next to homestead of the pre-emptor and opposite party has been in possession upon payment of rent Exhibit-Ga series according to Mutation Khatian Exhibit-ka and OPW-2 and OPW-3 are close neighbors of both the parties which was not denied at all by the pre-emptors and possession of opposite party for more than 6 years falsified the claim of knowledge thus the learned appellate court committed error of law occasioning failure of justice.

13. He further submits that the learned appellate court misread the evidence and wrongly found opposite party has not filed any document supporting mutation but Exhibit-ka itself is the mutation khatian and such misreading affecting the merit of the case shows that the learned court failed to apply judicial mind occasioning failure of justice.

14. Learned Advocate also submits that the learned appellate court upon misconception of law failed to appreciate that by lapse of time the claim of pre-emption has become barred by time and the learned appellate court did not assign any reason why the statement of PW 2 and PW 3 regarding knowledge could be believed and upon misreading of evidence failed to consider that pre-emptors definitely failed to discharge the heavy onus to prove knowledge thus committed error of law occasioning failure of justice.

15. He next submits that the learned appellate court did mat consider that PW 2 clearly admitted in evidence that the relation between pre-emptors and vendor-uncle was good till death of uncle and this statement makes alleged knowledge false and PW 2 also stated that he got the knowledge of the disputed purchase through one Azahar in front of Daroga Bari but this was not the case of pre-emptor and the learned appellate court committed error of law occasioning failure of justice.

16. He further submits that the pre-emption case is not maintainable because the compensation in the Land Acquisition Case which is admitted in evidence was withdrawn by petitioner thus the learned court below committed error of law occasioning failure of justice.

17. He also submits that the learned appellate court committed error of law occasioning failure of justice in reversing the judgment of the learned trial court without complying with the provisions of Order 41 Rule 31 of the Code of Civil Procedure and the same being not a proper judgment of reversal is liable to be set aside.

18. He lastly submits that the learned appellate court did not consider that PW 2 clearly admitted in evidence that the relation between pre-emptors and vendor uncle was good till death of uncle and 'this statement makes alleged knowledge and PW 2 also stated that he got the knowledge of the disputed purchase from one Azahar in front of Daroga Bari but this was not the case of pre-emptor in the application and the learned appellate court committed error of law occasioning failure of justice.

19. The learned Advocate also submits that the P.W. I made out true story about his knowledge in course as it stated filed instant case after being knowledge of the disputed document when he himself went to be withdrawal the compensation money of the statement of PW 1 the case of date of knowledge false true but the learned appellate court only reproduce the piece mill evidence of the parties. And erroneous he held that the, date of knowledge4 is proved in evidence without assigning any cogent reasons. Because he only reproduces the evidence but did not assign any reason to show that the date of knowledged is proved. In this connection the learned Counsel has referred the case of Abdul, Mazid Howlader and others vs Lahajuddin Howlader and others reported in 4 BLT (AD) 275.

20. Learned Advocate also submits that there is no enmity between the transfer of the disputed document and the pre-emptor and the compensation was admittedly given was pre-emptee considering his present possession. In this connection the learned advocate appearing on behalf of the petitioner has referred the case of Mohammad Akbar Chowdhury vs Khalilur Rahman reported in 18 BLT (AD) 314. He has referred the case of Satya Ranjan vs Surendra Nath reported in 13 DLR 338.

21. Learned Advocate also submits that the judgment of the appellate court has been passed in violation of the provisions of law as contain in Order 41 Rule 31 of the Code of Civil Procedure and also the settled principle of law as decided in the case Reliable Jute Traders and another vs Sonali Bank and others reported in 7 BLC High Court Division page 16. The learned Advocate has drawn my attention to the fact that from the cross of PW I it clearly proved that it is a got up story the date of knowledge is concocted and the appellate court did not at all consider this material evidence and this non consideration of material evidence affecting the merit of the case and touching the root of the case which has occasioning failure of justice.

22. Learned Advocate for the petitioner in support of his contention has referred the case of Habibur Rahman (Md) and others vs Gulman Begum reported in 64 DLR (AD) page 133 para 17.

23. Learned Advocate lastly submits that the claim of pre-emption is a predatory right that is while the legislature has imposed condition for claiming pre-emption.

24. As against this Mr Md Afzal Hossain, the learned Advocate appearing on behalf of the opposite party submits that no independent finding as to the issues framed by the trial judge and also no discussion of evidence adduced by the parties in the judgment of the trial judge. The judgment of the last court of fact is based on legal evidence.

25. Mr Afzal, has also pointed out that the trial judge is silent about his finding believe and disbelieve it is point for consideration of each case is to be decided in its own fact, circumstances and materials on record.

26. Mr Afzal also submits that the question of source of knowledge of the witnesses* is not relevant.

27. He further submits that in the instant case. OPW 1 is the constituted Attorney of the petitioner she resides in America. If any improvement is made that is done at their risk. He also submits that there is no mention about the cost incurred towards development they done it at their own risk. This also no description of the quantum of land of the khatian and also no proof as regard withdrawal of the compensation money and also did not mention any date of withdrawal of the money. So the impugned judgment of the last court of fact does not suffer from any legal infirmity material irregularity and illegality for which the appellate court judgment can be interfered with in support of his contention he has referred the case of Anowara Khatun vs Md Abdul Hye and others reported in 5 BLC (AD) 14.

28. I have heard the learned Advocate for both sides perused the impugned judgment and order of the last court of fact and also considered the submissions as advanced by the learned Advocates of both sides in support of their respective cases and also considered the citation as referred by both the learned Advocates in support of their respective contention.

29. On perusal of the impugned judgment and order of the last court of fact I find the impugned judgment and order of the last court of fact was not a proper judgment of reversal based on proper appreciation of both oral and documentary evidence on record and also in utter

violation of the settled principle of law as decided, in the case of Abdul Mazid Howlader and another vs Lahajuddin Howlader, reported in 4 BLT (AD) page 275 where our Apex Court held that:-

"In this case admittedly the application for pre-emption was filed after 7 years of transfer and a heavy burden lies on the pre-emptor to discharge the onus of proof that he filed the case within four months from the date of his knowledge. The pre-emptor having failed to discharge the initial onus by adducing cogent and reliable evidence the learned single judge ought to have held that the application for pre-emption is barred by limitation."

30. In another case of Md Akbar Chowdhury vs Khalilur Rahman reported in 18. BLT (AD) page 314 where our Apex Court held that:-

"Pre-emption petition was barred by limitation. It appears that the definite case of the pre-emptor is that he came to know about the transfer on 10-1-1997. The transfer in question is by sale deed dated 29-2-1992. Therefore after about five years the pre-emptor petitioners came to the court with the plea that they came to know about the sale on 10-1-1997 but in the petition there is no statement as when the purchaser demanded possession and whether anybody else was present at the time of such demand. The name of PW 2 was not mentioned in the pre-emption petition. Therefore the appellate court rightly disbelieved the story of knowledge of the petitioners from 10.01.1997 and the High Court Division affirmed the same.

Now let us see in rule 2 of order 6 of the Code of Civil Procedure provides that "Every pleading shall contain, and contain only, a statement in a concise form of the material facts on which the party pleading relies for his claim or defence, as the case may be, but not the evidence by which they are to be proved, and shall, when necessary, be divided into paragraphs, numbered consecutively, Dates, sums and numbers shall be expressed in figures".

31. In the case of Satya Ranjan Haldar and others vs Surendra Nath Das reported in 13 DLR 338 where it is held that:-"As to the point of limitation, on the face of the application for pre-emption, it is not of time, that is beyond four months from the date of the transfer. In order to bring his application within four months from the date of knowledge the petitioner respondent alleged that he was not aware of the transfer till he was informed by some persons mentioned in his petition. To counteract the evidence of those gentleman the purchasers asserted that soon after the purchase in the month of Falgun they went to cultivate the land. It was cultivating season. It is admitted that the petitioner respondent is holder of the land contiguous to the land transferred. There is no reason why he should not know about the fact of cultivation of the disputed land by the purchasers. The learned Sub-ordinate Judge is of the opinion that until and unless the registered kabala is taken back from the Registration office it is not possible for them to go to the land to cultivate it which is contrary to what generally happens. Generally after payment of the full consideration and execution of the kabala (where it is stated that the land has been given in possession of the transferees) the transferees take possession of the land and they never wait for getting back the registered kabala from the Registration office. In the kabala it is definitely stated: "From today you being the rightful owner of the property sold to you being fully armed with all our right, title and interest by right of purchase from us, do must happily own, possess and enjoy for time to come mutating your names in place of ours in the sherista of landlord."

32. This reasoning of the learned Sub-ordinate Judge is apparently faulty and he should not have relied on the evidence of P.W. 2 who happens to be the purohit (family Brahmin) of the petitioner respondent and admittedly who is interested in the case of the petitioner respondent.

<u>33. I find on perusal of the impugned judgment and order of the Appellate Court, the Appellate Court on total non-application and non-consideration of both oral and documentary evidence passed the impugned judgment which is based on legal perversity, material irregularity and illegality as well as such I am of the definite view that the appellate court as final court of fact can himself reassess the oral and documentary evidence under its appellate jurisdiction and both the parties are at liberty to adduce further evidence if any in support of their respective cases and the learned Appellate Court on perusal of the oral and documentary evidence and after due consideration of the same write out a fresh judgment and in that view of the matter the Miscellaneous Appeal No. 10 of 2008 is send back on remand to the appellate court for rehearing the appeal on merit and the learned Appellate Court is hereby directed to dispose of the Appeal expeditiously preferably within three months positively from the date of receipt of the copy of the judgment with this observation the rule is made absolute. The impugned judgment and order dated 4-5-2010 passed by the learned Additional District Judge 1st Court Barisal is hereby set aside.</u>

34. The order of stay as granted at the time of issuance of the rule is hereby recalled and vacated.

Send down the lower courts record along with a copy of this judgment to the concern court forthwith for information and necessary action.

End.

parties:

vs.

full_judgment:
Bijan Kumar Das, J: This First Miscellaneous Appeal is directed against the judgment and order dated 7-9-1987 passed by the District Judge, Dhaka in Miscellaneous Case No. 59 of 1986 under section 35(3) of the Wakfs Ordinance setting aside those dated 21-2-1986 passed by the Waqf Administrator in Enrolment Case No. 1579 directing the Waqf Administrator to dispose of the said EC No. 15719 after the disposal of Title Suit No. 27 of 1974 pending in the Court of the Subordinate Judge, Dhaka. One Alhaj Md Hossain Khan filed an application under section 50 of the Waqf Ordinance, 1962 being Diary No. 5184 dated 17-10-1984 praying for cancellation of the enrolment made in the said EC No. 15719 in respect of Alhaj Md Yusuf Sarder Waqf Estate on the allegation that the petitioner and another filed Title Suit No. 27 of 1974 for declaration of title and recovery of possession of the schedule properties including other properties against the aforesaid Alhaj Md Yusuf Sarder (now deceased) who was the sole defendant in the said suit. It is alleged that during tendency of the suit the defendant Alhaj Md Yusuf Sarder created waqf of the suit property by a declaration dated 1-7-1976 and constituted himself as the first mutwalli of Yusuf Sarder Waqf Estate. It is stated in the application for cancellation of the enrolment that the property mentioned therein appertaining to Mouza Dhanmondi, Khatian No. 26 and plot Nos. 692-694 and 696 measuring 0.24 katha 2 chhatak belonged to the petitioner and his co-sharers and their uncle Alhaj Md Yusuf Sarder had no interest in the said property but he fraudulently created a waqf in respect of the said property and got it enrolled in EC No. 15719. It is stated that no notice for enrolment of the suit property as waqf property was served on the co-sharers and they prayed for cancellation of the enrolment of the property as waqf property.

2. The Administrator of Waqf heard the matter and by order dated 21-2-1986 rejected the prayer for cancellation on the finding that there was no reasonable ground to declare the property as secular property.

<u>3. Being aggrieved thereby the said Md Hossain Khan submitted a petition under section 35(1) of the Waqf Ordinance, 1962 to the learned District Judge and that the learned District Judge by the impugned judgment and order noticed that Title Suit No. 27 of 1974 for declaration of title and recovery of possession was filed by the said Md Hossain Khan against the Wakif Alhaj Md Yusuf Sarder (since deceased) and during pendency of the suit the said wakif Alhaj Md Yusuf Sarder created the wakf-e-Lillah on 1-7-1976 and accordingly, the transfer in question was hit under section 52 of the Transfer of Property Act. The learned District Judge further found that the present mutwalli Md Tobarak Ali Sikder had instituted Title Suit No. 247 of 1984 in the 3rd Court of the Subordinate Judge against the petitioner Md Hossain Khan for a decree for declaration that the suit land was waqf property but subsequently, the said suit was dismissed for want of tadbir. The learned District Judge further noticed that on the basis of a direction of the learned District Judge, Dhaka in Miscellaneous Case No. 200 of 1979 the Administrator enrolled the property as waqf property and the Administration of Waqfs while deciding the application filed under section 50 of the Waqfs Ordinance considered irrelevant issues but did not consider the relevant issue as to whether the wakif had title in the property in question and the property was made waqf in accordance with law. In any view, the learned District Judge noticed that the Administrator of Waqf should decide the application filed under section 50 of the Waqfs Ordinance after the disposal of Title Suit No. 27 of 1974. Accordingly, by order dated 7-9-1987 the learned District Judge set aside the judgment and order of the Waqf Administrator dated 21-2-1986 in connection with EC No. 15719 and directed that the matter may be re-heard and disposed of after disposal of Title Suit No. 27 of 1974.</u>

4. Being aggrieved thereby Alhaj Md Tobarak Ali Sikder being the mutawali of the alleged Alhaj Md Yusuf Sarder Waqf Estate preferred the Miscellaneous Appeal before this court.

5. Mr Md Fazlul Karim, the learned Senior Advocate on behalf of the appellant, has taken me through the judgments of the courts below including the judgment of the Waqf Administrator and submits that under section 50 of Waqfs Ordinance only the Administrator of Waqfs may decide if the property in question is waqf property or not and the civil Court is excluded from deciding the said question. The learned Senior Advocate further submits that section 102 of the Waqfs Ordinance, 1962 is a bar in entertaining any suit inasmuch as it is provided therein that except as otherwise expressly provided in the said Ordinance, no decision or order of the Administrator shall be questioned in any suit or other proceeding in any court. In support of his submission the learned Advocate for the appellant relied on a decision in the case of Syed Shah Mohammad Osman Ghani vs Bangladesh, through Secy. Ministry of Public Works and Urban Dev and others reported in 39 DLR 451 and in the case of Syed Masud Ali and others vs Md Asmatullah and others reported in 32 DLR (AD) 39. Mr Karim also relied on a decision in the case of Afazuddin Mollah and others vs Mobarak Ali Munshi and others reported in 46 DLR 587.

6. Mr MA Samad, the learned Advocate appearing for the respondent, submits that the present respondent along with two others instituted Title Suit No. 57 of 1973 against the Wakif Alhaj Yusuf Sarder praying for declaration of title and recovery of possession. The said suit was transferred several times and it was re-numbered as Title Suit No. 27 of 1974, Title Suit No. 333 of 1992, thereafter Title Suit No. 1 of 1994 of the Court of the Subordinate Judge, 3rd Court, Dhaka and the alleged wakif created the alleged waqf property during pendency of the said suit on 1-7-1976 and thus the alleged transfer shall be subject to the decision to be passed in the Civil Suit. According to Mr MA Samad, the aforesaid Title Suit No. 57 of 1973 which was ultimately re-numbered as Title Suit No. 1 of 1994 in the Court of the Subordinate Judge and Artha Rin Adalat No. 3, Dhaka was decreed in favour of the plaintiffs and the said decree was set aside by the appellate Court but in revision the High Court Division made the Rule absolute and restored the judgment and decree of the trial Court whereupon a Civil Petition for leave to appeal was filed before the Appellate Division which was subsequently dismissed. A review application was then filed before the Appellate Division but the review was also dismissed. Mr Samad therefore submits that the civil Court has decided the question that the property dedicated by the wakif Alhaj Md Yusuf Sarder as wakf-e-Lillah was a secular property belonging to the plaintiffs of the suit and also directed recovery of possession of the suit property and accordingly, the property in question could not be treated as waqf property. Mr Samad therefore, submits that the impugned decision of the learned District Judge passed in Miscellaneous Case No. 59 of 1986 under section 35(3) of the Waqfs Ordinance is required to be modified inasmuch as civil Court has decided the Title Suit and it is no more necessary to re-hear the cancellation matter by the Waqf Administrator in connection with EC No. 15719 any more and this court may decide the matter finally.

7. I have considered the submissions of the learned Advocates for both the parties and perused the impugned orders and all other connected papers. It appears from the judgment of the learned District Judge and also from the order of the Waqf Administrator in EC No. 15719 that Title Suit No. 57 of 1973 was instituted by Md Hossain Khan and two others against the alleged wakif Alhaj Md Yusuf Sarder and that during pendency of the said suit the aforesaid Alhaj Md Yusuf Sarder created the waqf on 1-7-1976 in respect of the property in question. From additional paper book filed by the appellant it appears that Alhaj Md Yusuf Sarder filed a written statement in the said Title Suit No. 57 of 1973 on 21-12-1973 but did not claim the waqf nature of the property in question. In the written statement the wakif Alhaj Md Yusuf Sarder did not claim that he had created wakf-e-Lillah in respect of the property involved in the suit. There is therefor no hesitation in holding that the alleged waqf was created on 1-7-1976 during pendency of Title Suit No. 57 of 1973. Thus the Administrator of Waqfs illegally enrolled the property as wakif-e-Lillah on 21-2-1986 on the basis of an order passed by the learned District Judge in Miscellaneous Case No. 200 of 1979. In that view of the matter, when waqf property was created during of a civil suit in a competent civil Court for declaration of title, the waqf administrator was not permitted to invoke adjudicatory jurisdiction under section 50 of the Waqf Ordinance. In the present case also the wakf administrator had no jurisdiction to enroll the property as waqf property as wakif-e-Lillah on 21-2-1986 as the civil suit being Title Suit No. 27 of 1974 was not decided till then and the waqf administrator committed a gross error of law in allowing enrolment of the property in question as waqf-e-Lillah at a time when the suit for declaration of title in a competent civil Court was pending.

8. Mr MA Samad, the learned Advocate for the respondent, has submitted an additional affidavit enclosing certified copy of the judgments passed in the civil suit by the trial Court, by the lower appellate Court, by the High Court Division and by the Appellate Division. It is stated that Title Suit No. 27 of 1974 was ultimately re-numbered as Title Suit No. 1 of 1994 of the Court of the Subordinate Judge and Artha Rin Adalat No. 3, Dhaka and the trial Court by judgment and decree dated 26-6-1995 decreed the suit in favour of the plaintiff Md Hossain Khan and others declaring plaintiffs 16 annas title in the suit land and directing recovery of possession. It is also stated that in the said suit that the present appellant claiming himself to be Mutawalli impleaded himself as defendant No. 28 and contested the suit and the aforesaid decree was passed on contest against defendant No. 28 and ex parte against the rest. The defendant No. 28 then preferred Title Appeal No. 194 of 1995 before the learned District Judge, Dhaka and the learned Additional District Judge, 5th Court, Dhaka by judgment and decree dated 20-4-1996 allowed the appeal and set aside the judgment and decree dated 26-5-1995 and 5-7-1995 respectively of the, trial Court. The present respondent then moved the High Court Division and obtained a Rule in Civil Revision No. 1495 of 1996. A learned Single Judge of the High Court Division by judgment and order dated 17-11-1994 made the Rule absolute set aside the judgment and decree of the lower appellate Court and restored those of the trial Court. Against the said decision of the High Court Division the present appellant filed Civil Petition for Leave to Appeal No. 194 of 2000 before the Appellate Division and their Lordship dismissed the said Leave Petition on 21-11-2001 maintaining the order of the High Court Division who restored the judgment and decree of the trial Court which decreed the suit in favour of the plaintiff declaring plaintiffs sixteen annas title to the suit land and directing recovery of possession of the suit property. It is further stated that the present appellant then filed a Review. Petition No. 1 of 2002 before the Appellate Division for review of the judgment of the Appellate Division passed in Civil Petition for Leave to Appeal No. 194 of 2000 and their Lordship of the Appellate Division dismissed the said review petition on 26-10-2002. The certified copy of the judgments passed in the aforesaid matters have been enclosed with the additional affidavit filed by the respondent and marked Annexure A, B, C, D respectively. It thus appears that Title Suit No. 27 of 1974 which was finally re-numbered as Title Suit No. 1 of 1994 instituted by the present respondent and others against the wakif Alhaj Yusuf Sarder, who died during pendency of the suit was decreed declaring plaintiffs (present respondent) title to the suit property which was maintained up to the Appellate Division. Since the alleged waqf was created on 1-7-1976 during pendency of the title suit it cannot have any legal effect. The civil Court having decided the title in favour of the present respondent. Alhaj Md Yusuf Sarder had no title in the property to create the alleged waqf on 1-7-1976. The transfer of the property as waqf property during pendency of the suit is hit by the doctrine of listeners under section 52 of the Transfer of Property Act and the creation of the alleged waqf on 1-7-1976 is subject to the decision in Title Suit No. 27 of 1974 which was ultimately decided in favour of the present respondent, who was the plaintiff in the said suit and against Alhaj Md Yusuf Sarder (since deceased) who was the sole defendant in the said suit. The issue with respect to the nature and character of the property has been set at rest by the civil Court in a suit instituted before the creation of the alleged waqf declaring plaintiffs title and granting recovery of possession and thus the secular property could not be treated as waqf property. In the facts of the case the alleged wakf had no title in the property to create the waqf. After the decision of the civil Court in respect of the nature and character of the property in a suit instituted before the creation of the alleged Waqf the Waqf Administrator cannot invoke its adjudicatory jurisdiction to decide whether the property is waqf property or not as provided under section 50 of the Waqfs Ordinance.

<u>9. The decision cited by the learned Advocate for the appellant in 39 DLR 451 has no application in the facts of the present case. in the said decision a Division Bench held—"The sole question of law raised is as to whether a plaintiff has the option to file a civil suit for a declaration that a particular property is waqf property although section 50 of the Waqfs Ordinance, 1962 provides that any question whether a particular property is waqf property or not shall be decided by the Administrator of Waqfs. The plaintiff-petitioner filed such a suit and also obtained an ex-parte decree. On appeal, the suit was dismissed on the sole ground that the suit was not maintainable in view of the provisions of section 50 of the said Ordinance." In the said decision their Lordships further held "Under section 102 of the Waqfs Ordinance, 1962 no decision or order of the Administrator shall be questioned in any suit or other proceeding in any Court, except as otherwise expressly provided in the said Ordinance. The express ouster is attracted only after the Administrator has given a decision or order. In the entire Ordinance we do not find any express ouster forbidding the civil Courts to entertain any suit as to the waqf character of a suit property. It is only when the Administrator of Waqfs gives a decision or order in relation to the same that the bar of section 102 is attracted." In the present case the civil suit was instituted long before the creation of waqf and that the wakf in his written statement submitted in the said suit did not claim that he has created waqf in respect of the property in question. The waqf administrator allowed enrolment of the property on the basis of an order passed in Miscellaneous Case No. 200 of 1979 by the learned District Judge, Dhaka though there is no such provision in the Waqfs Ordinance empowering the District Judge to pass an order for enrolment of a property as waqf property. Chapter 4 of the Waqfs Ordinance, 1962 relates to enrolment of waqfs. Section 47 of the Waqfs Ordinance provides for enrolment of waqf and section 48 of the Waqfs Ordinance provides for register of waqfs. Section 49 of the Waqfs Ordinance provides power of the Administrator to cause enrolment of waqf and to amend the register and section 50 of Waqfs Ordinance provides that any question whether a particular property is waqf property or not shall be decided by the Administrator provided that the mutawalli or any person aggrieved by any decision or order of the Administrator in this behalf may, within three months from the date of such decision or order, submit a petition to the District Judge in accordance with the provision of sub-section (1) of section 35; and if such a petition is filed, the provisions of section 35 shall apply. In the present case an application for cancellation of the enrolment was filed before the Administrator of waqfs under section 50 of the Waqfs Ordinance on the ground that the property is not waqf property which was dismissed by the waqf administrator and the present respondent being aggrieved thereby filed a petition to the learned District Judge in accordance with sub-section 1 of section 35 and the learned District Judge passed the impugned order. The petition under section 35(1) of the Waqfs Ordinance filed before the learned District Judge empowers the learned District Judge to declare that the property is not a waqf property or that the property is waqf property within the limit stated in the petition. In view of my above finding that the property could not be a waqf property as decided in the civil suit and affirmed up to the Appellate Division it may be declared that the suit property is not a waqf property. The decision cited by the learned Advocate for the appellant, namely, 46 DLR 587 again has no manner of application in the facts of the present case. In the said decision a learned Single Judge considered sections 64(2), 35(3), 38 and 50 of the Waqfs Ordinance. I have already held that the waqf administrator, in the facts of the case, had no adjudicatory jurisdiction to invoke section 50 of the Waqfs Ordinance for the purpose of deciding whether the property in question is waqf property or not as the civil Court had decided the issue and has decreed the suit in favour of the plaintiff declaring plaintiffs sixteen annas title and directing recovery of possession of the suit property. The decision cited by the learned Advocate for the appellant reported in 32 DLR (AD) 39 again has no manner of application in the facts of the present case. In view of my above findings I do not find any substance in this appeal.</u>

10. In the result this appeal is dismissed with modification that the property in question is not waqf property and the Waqf Administrator is not required to decide the question as directed by the learned District Judge in the impugned Order dated 7-9-1987 in Miscellaneous Case No. 59 of 1986.

In the facts of the case, I do not make any order as to costs.

Send down the LCR at once.

End.

Tabarak Hussain with Md Abdus Shahid, ASM Nazmul Haque and Md Abdullah Mahmud Chowdhury, Advocates-For the Appellant. 
Enayet Hossain Khan with Md Ziaul Haque and Nazmul Islam, Advocates-For the Respondents.

Younusco K Textiles Ltd. ----- Defendant-Appellant

full_judgment:
Syed Amirul Islam J: As common questions of facts and law are involved in these two appeals they were heard together and are being disposed of by this judgment which will govern both the appeals.

2. Appeal No. 234 of 2004 is from judgment and decree dated 18-4-2004 passed in Title Suit No. 100 of 1997 passed by the learned Joint District Judge, First Court, Gazipur.

3. Similarly, Appeal No. 235 of 2004 arose out of Title Suit No. 101 of 1997 of the aforesaid Court and both the suits were heard analogously by the Court below and by common judgment dated 18-4-2004 both suits were disposed of by the impugned judgment. The trial Court by the impugned judgment decreed both the suits and allowed the prayer for pre-emption made by the plaintiffs in respect of 'A' Schedule property of the respective suits as Shafi-i-Jar under the Muslim Law and being aggrieved by the aforesaid judgment the defendant has preferred these appeals before this Court.

4. The crux of the plaintiffs' case is that they are the owner by purchase of the 'B' Schedule land and 'A' Schedule land has been transferred by the vendor i.e. defendant Nos. 2 and 3, to defendant No. 1 on 9-3-1997 and immediately after their knowledge about the transfer of the 'A' Schedule land to the defendant No. 1 they have performed Talab-i-Muwsibat and thereafter, taking certified copy on 18-3-1997 of the sale deeds the plaintiffs definitely came to know that the 'A' Schedule land has been sold to the defendant No. 1 by the other defendants and made Talab-i-Ishhad immediately on 19-3-1997. He performed Talab-i-Ishhad in presence of two witnesses to invoke his right of pre-emption under the Muslim Law.

5. The plaint case, in short, is that the plaintiffs have title to and possession in the 'B' Schedule property by purchase and plaintiffs No. 1 and 2 have title to and possession in 2.58 acres of land i.e. the 'B' Schedule land, which are contiguous to the suit land i.e. 'A' Schedule land in the southern side. The further case is that the plaintiffs have seen construction of wall in 'A' Schedule land in the later part of 1995 by the defendant No. 2 Company as owner. The positive case of the plaintiffs is that on 9-3-1997 the plaintiff No. 2 along with 2 other persons, namely, Messrs Ershad Hossain and Md Ismail Meah were passing through 'A' Schedule land when plaintiff No. 2 found one Abu Bakar Siddique living in a newly constructed CI sheet but and on his query as to who raised the but and how he was living there Abu Bakar Siddique disclosed that the defendant No. 2 Company had sold the 'A' Schedule property to defendant No. 1 Company and defendant No. 1 had raised the but for him as he is the caretaker of defendant No. 1 and upon hearing this the plaintiff No. 2 for self and on behalf of plaintiff No. 1 at once made Talab-i-Muwsibat and asserted their purported right to pre-empt the said land in presence of the said two persons and thereafter, he sent a man to make a query to the local registration office who obtained certified copy of the kabalas in question on 18-3-1997 when he definitely came to learn about the aforesaid transfer and made Talab-i-Ishhad in presence of witnesses telling that Talab-i-Muwsibat had already been made on 9-3-1997. This time Messrs Ershad Hossain and Aman Ali and some other employees of Plaintiff No. 1's company went upon the land of 'A' Schedule. The purchaser is stranger whereas the plaintiffs are neighbors and, as such, they have instituted the suit under the Muslim Law to pre-empt the 'A' Schedule land after due compliance with the formalities as are required under the Muslim Law.

6. Both the suits were contested by defendant No. 1 company purchaser by filing written statement. It is stated that the suits are malafide, fraudulent, misconceived and are not maintainable in their present form according to law and the 'A' Schedule land is not liable to be pre-empted under the Muslim Law as the suit land is neither houses nor gardens. A ground of limitation is also taken in the written statement and it is specifically asserted that Talab-i-Muwsibat and Talab-i-Ishhad has not been properly performed in accordance with Muslim Law and the plaintiffs have no locus standi to file and maintain the suits as Shafi-i-Jar inasmuch as the 'A' Sche-dule land is neither mansion house nor gardens nor small piece of land. All the mate-rial allegations made in the plaint have been denied. The positive case is that the lands alleged to have been purchased by the plaintiffs are well demarcated by boundary wall and the lands of 'A' Schedule are sepa-rated by another pucca boundary wall and boundary wall of 'A' Schedule land is 7.50 ft in height. It is further averred that both the lands of 'A' and 'B' Schedules have boundary walls on all sides having only one entrance gate on the eastern boundary wall by the side of the public road known as Kashimpur Road. It is further asserted that neither on 9-3-1997 nor on any other date the plaintiff No. 2 with Messrs Ershad Hossain and/or Md Ismail Meah passed through or could pass through the 'A' Schedule land as it is surrounded on all sides by a boundary wall and has a gate on the eastern side which leads to Kashimpur Road and therefore, it was not possible for the plaintiff No. 1 or anybody else to enter into or pass through the 'A' Schedule land except through the main entrance gate on the northern side of the eastern wall and the gate remains closed under the supervision of security guard and nobody can enter the 'A' Schedule land without permission and assistance of the employees and security guards of the defendant No. 1. The further positive case of defendant No. 1 is that Abu Bakar Siddique was not present in the 'A' Schedule land on 9-3-1997 as he was on leave

for one month from 25-2-1997. The plaintiffs and their men were aware of all the developments from the time of negotiation between defendant No. 2 and defendant No. 1 for sale and execution of the agreement, cons-truction of CI sheet but and semi-pucca toilets for employees, execution of tripartite agreement and registration of the sale deeds on 7-3-1996 and Messrs YK Ltd installed and fixed signboard on the eastern wall and installed electric and telephone connection in the 'A' Schedule land on their purchase on 7-3-1996. It is also asserted that the lands allegedly purchased by the plaintiffs are bounded on all sides by pucca boundary wall and the plaintiffs are carrying on their manufacturing works therein conveniently and without any inconvenience or difficulty. It further appears that the other side of the story of defendant No. 1 is that the 'A' Schedule land was purchased by defendant No. 2 from different owners with a view to set up an industry thereon and took loan by mortgaging the said land to the Sonali Bank and on their failure to repay the amount, the bank instituted a case in Artha Rin Adalat being Mortgage Suit No. 139 of 1990 and as defendant No. 2 had no other means to liquidate the liability of the bank entered into an agreement for sale with the defendant No. 1 to sell 8.43 acres of land inclu-ding the 'A' Schedule land and subsequently, a tripartite agreement was executed between the defendant No. 1, defendant No. 2 and Sonali Bank and ultimately the entire land was transferred to the defendant No. 1 through different sale deeds pursuant to the agreement and/or these things were within the know-ledge of the plaintiffs. It is also the case of the defendant No. 1 that after purchase of 'A' Schedule land defendant No. 1 sold 0.42 acres of land out of north-eastern part of 'A' Sche-dule land to one Md Serajul Islam through registered kabala dated 16-9-1996 and delive-red specific possession to the purchaser and thus they are in possession of 5.08 acres out of total 'A' Schedule lands. It is also contended in the written statement that neither 'A' Schedule nor 'B' Schedule land has been specified as required by Order VII, rule 3 of the Code of Civil Procedure and on that count also the suit is liable to be dismissed.

7. Mr Tabarak Hussain, the learned Advocate appearing for the defendant-appellants in both the appeals, argued extensively and also intensively both on point of law as well as facts. Mr Hussain at the very outset raised a question of law as to the maintainability of the suits under Muslim Law inasmuch as the defendant No. 1 is a company incorporated under the Companies Act and it bought 'A' Schedule land from another company i.e. defendant No. 2, of the suit and the plaintiff No. 1 of both the suits is also a company and in the background of these admitted facts he submitted that the instant suits are misconceived and not maintainable for pre-emption under the Muslim Law, inasmuch as a company being a jural person and not being a natural person is not capable of professing any faith. Therefore, neither the appellants nor the plaintiff-respondent No. 1 can be treated as Muslim within the meaning of Muslim Law and the concept of faith as revealed by the Holy Quran can only be followed by a natural person on his own volition. Mr Hussain further submits that a company exists independently of its share-holder and it is now well settled that share-holders of a company are not the owners of a company and they are simply beneficiary of a company. To fortify his submission on this point, Mr Hussain relying on the case reported in ILR 1 (Allahabad) 564 submitted that the settled proposition of law is that a suit filed under the Muslim Law for pre-emption is guided by the law of the vendor and in a case where both the pre-emptor and the vendor are Muslims and the vendee is a non-Muslim in that case also the Muslim Law is to be applied. Therefore, the suit, so far it relates to plaintiff No. 1, is misconceived and not maintainable in law. To fortify his submission he has also relied on the decision reported in 1983 CLC 1983 wherein it has been held that personal law of vendor governs the transaction and not that of vendee for the purpose of determining the right of pre-emption. Mr Tabarak Hussain then also raised another interesting question of law i.e. as to the constitutionality of the law of pre-emption under the Muslim Law. Mr Hussain submits that after the emergence of Bangladesh and coming into force of the Constitution of Bangladesh, certain fundamental rights are conferred upon all the persons irrespective of religious faith and caste or creed, etc. Article 42 of the Constitution ensures right to the property i.e. every citizen shall have the right to acquire, hold, transfer or otherwise dispose of property. Mr. Hussain, to elaborate his submission further submits that the provision of pre-emption under the Muslim Law imposes restriction upon a citizen in the matter of acquisition of property which is, therefore, hit by the provision of Article 42 of the Constitution, inasmuch as the unfettered right of a person either to transfer property or to acquire property is restricted to some extent by the law of pre-emption under the Muslim Law and therefore, it offends Article 42 of the Constitution. To fortify his submission he has relied on the decision reported in AIR 1962 (SC) 1476 wherein the Indian Supreme Court in determining the question of constitutionality of pre-emption law held that restriction imposed by that law in the matter of transfer and/or acquisition of property on the ground of contiguity of land is hit by Article 19(1)(f) of the Indian Constitution. Mr Hussain has also relied on the decision reported in AIR 1980 Allahabad. That was also a case under the Muslim Law wherein the Allahabad High Court took the view that the Muslim Law as to pre-emption in exercise of right as Shafi-i-Jar is void as it imposes an unreasonable restriction on a person in either transferring a property or in acquiring a property from fellow person. In this connection, he has further submitted that Bangladesh is a People's Republic having a secular Constitution although the vast majority of the population professes the faith of Islam and, in that view of the matter, if the Muslim Law of pre-emption is examined in the context of Article 7(2) read with Articles 26, 28 and Article 42 it would lead to the conclusion that the provision of Suffa is not only volatile of Article 42 of the Constitution but is also discriminatory, inasmuch as it confers an additional benefit to a Muslim and on that ground as well the law is liable to be declared void.

8. Mr Tabarak Hussain thereafter made his submission on the merits of the appeal. His first submission is that even if it is found by this court that Muslim Law of pre-emption is a valid law then also the instant suits are not maintainable under the Muslim Law because the plaintiffs are not entitled to get the relief as prayed for, inasmuch as on two. grounds the plaintiffs have instituted the suits, namely, as Shafi-i-Khalid and Shafi-i-Jar and from the impugned judgment it is found that the trial Court found that the plaintiffs were not entitled to get an order of pre-emption as Shafi-i-Khalid and decreed the suit in favour of the plaintiff-respondents as Shafi-i-Jar and the plaintiffs have not preferred any cross-appeal against that finding of the trial Court. Mr Hussain now submits that the suit land cannot be the subject matter of pre-emption under the Muslim Law and the plaintiffs cannot invoke the law as Shafi-i-jar, inasmuch as the subject matter is not 'Agar' or land nor the suit land is 'Ruba' or mansion or 'hait' or garden i.e. he contends that a person can invoke the Muslim Law of pre-emption as a Shafi-i-Jar only in respect of a homestead or mansion, garden or small piece of land and in the instant case admittedly, the 'A' Schedule land is not a homestead nor it is garden adjoining to any homestead nor it is a small piece of land, inasmuch as the plaintiffs have instituted the suits for pre-empting 8.69 acres of land. In this connection, he relied on Digest of Muslim Law by Bailee, Tybee’s Muslim Law, section 539 and 12 DLR 93. Mr Tabarak Hussain then submits that it is apparent from the materials and evidence on record that the suit lands have been purchased by the appellant company in order to set up industry and before that the vendor company also bought the land with an intention to set up industry and therefore, the Muslim Law of pre-emption has no manner of application to commercial plots and in decreeing the suit the trial Court lost sight of this important question of law that right of pre-emption cannot be enforced in case of commercial plots. For this proposition, Mr Hussain relies on the case reported in PLD 1990 (Karachi) 387. Mr Hussain made another plank of attack on the impugned judgment by submitting that in decreeing the suits, the trial Court has also committed another illegality in not giving any finding as to the necessity of the suit land by the plaintiffs. In elaborating his submission the learned Advocate further submits that the case of the plaintiffs is that they require the lands for their own purpose but what is the purpose has neither been explained in the plaint nor in the evidence. They simply made a vague statement that the land is required for them. To fortify his submission he contends that one of the stringent principles of law of pre-emption under the Muslim Law is that one cannot resort to pre-emption for his enrichment at the cost of the buyer. Therefore, the plaintiffs were under the legal obligation to explain the necessity of acquiring the 'A' Schedule land by them. But they have miserably failed to discharge their onus on that point. In support of this contention the learned Advocate relied on the decision reported in PLD 1991 (Lahore) 217. Mr Tabarak Hussain then submits, with much emphasis, that the plaintiffs filed the suits for pre-emption as contiguous land owners and thus, they are to prove their ownership of the contiguous land and also required to prove that the legal formalities for the purpose of the Talabs, namely Talab-i-Muwsibat and Talab-i-Ishhad, have been performed at the earliest opportune moment but the plaintiffs have failed to show or establish their ownership or 'Milk' to the 'B' Schedule land by producing cogent evidence both oral and documentary and until and unless the plaintiffs can establish their ownership to the 'B' Schedule land, the plaintiffs will have no locus standi to maintain the suit. In the instant case, the plaintiffs have examined 3 witnesses including plaintiff No. 2 in support of their case but surprisingly, the plaintiffs, for reasons best known to them, did not examine any impartial witness and thus have miserably failed to prove that they are the owners of the 'B' Schedule land and to establish the ownership no document of title has been produced or admitted into evidence by the plaintiffs before the trial Court to establish their title to 'B' Schedule land and it was incumbent upon the plaintiffs to prove their ownership to the 'B' Schedule land in view of the fact that it has been specifically stated by the defendants in their written statement that the plaintiffs are not the owner of contiguous 'B' Schedule land. Mr Tabarak Hussain further submits that the settled proposition of law is that only the owners of the contiguous land can maintain a suit for pre-emption under the Muslim Law as Shafi-i-jar but, in the instant suits, the plaintiffs miserably failed to prove their title to the contiguous land and, in that view of the matter, mere possession of the 'B' Schedule land will not give them any ladder to pre-empt the land. In support of his contention, he relies on the decisions reported in 12 DLR 93 and 1983 CLC 1883.

9. Mr Tabarak Hussain then comes up with another formidable submission and referring to the evidence on record, he submitted that the plaintiff No. 2 in his evidence stated that he does not know what are the requirements of Shafi-i-jar or Shafi-i-Khalid and what formalities are required to perform Talab-i-Muwsibat or Talab-i-Ishhad and this frank and open admission of the plaintiff No. 2 has demolished the entire case of the plaintiffs, inasmuch as a person who does not know what formalities are required to perform for valid performance of Talabs, it is impossible on his part to perform the same. This piece of evidence belies the story of performance of the said Talabs by the plaintiff’s No. 2. Therefore, the plaintiffs failed to prove the performance of the Talabs made by him as claimed in his evidence. Mr Tabarak Hussain further contends that to get a decree for pre-emption under the Muslim Law there must be stringent compliance with the formalities and performance of the formalities must be clearly proved which is absent in the present suits. Mr Tabarak Hussain further submits that the evidence of the PWs shows that the PW 1 did not utter any word to exercise the right of pre-emption whereas law requires that the pre-emptor must express his intention of exercising the right of pre-emption in some way. In this connection, he relies on the decision reported in 49 CWN 761. Thus, the testimony of PW 1 itself established that Talab-i-Muwsibat was not performed in the suit land. Mr Tabarak Hussain drawing our attention to the evidence of PWs 2 and 3 submitted that they do not support the plaintiffs on this point about the Talab-i-Muwsibat and failure on the part of the plaintiffs to prove the Talab-i-Muwsibat disentitled the plaintiffs to get any relief in the suits. Mr Hussain then submits that the trial Court on misreading and non-consideration of material portion of evidence erroneously held that Talab-i-Muwsibat was properly performed by the plaintiffs for the suit land and thereby the instant appeals are liable to be allowed in the light of the principle of law as laid down in 10 ILR Calcutta 383. Mr Hussain further submitted that the impugned judgment is liable to be set aside yet on another ground i.e. legal pro-position of law is that under the Muslim Law the pre-emptor is required to make Talab-i-Ishhad with the least delay but in the instant case according to the plaint, they came to know about the sale of the suit property on 9-3-1997 and after obtaining certified copy of the sale deeds on 18-3-1997 they made Talab-i-Ishad on 19-3-1997. In this connection, Mr Tabarak Hussain relies on the decision reported in ILR 17 Calcutta 544, 1991 CLC Karachi 209, 19 DLR 759 and ILR 28 Allahabad 24.
