vs.
Md Shohrab Hossain and ors ------ Opposite-Parties
full_judgment:
AK Badrul Huq J: It is wretchedness to record message that many litigants in order to steer clear of order /judgment/decree maintained by last ladder of hierarchy adopt dubious role and take recourse to ingenious methods including filing of fraudulent litigation to rout order/judgment and decree of Court. Seekers of justice in whose favour verdict had been passed are to wait and wait to receive fruit of verdict and justice and they become victims of justice in hands of unscrupulous litigants.

2. The present matter in hand is an apt illustration how judgment and decree awarded in favour of decree-holder here defendant-petitioner by Court of appeal which have been maintained by Appellate Division rendering final touch has been ventured to be thwarted by judgment-debtors and persons litigating under judgment-debtors.

3. Refusal to reject plaint of first-fifth-opposite parties on point of bar of law as embodied in Order VII, rule 11 of the Code of Civil Procedure (for short the Code) prompted defendant-petitioner to approach this Court in Civil revision petition under section 115 of the Code.

4. Portrayal of essential facts forming background of this revision petition as emerged from Revision Petition, annexures annexed in Petition, judgments of Courts awarded in earlier proceeding and papers produced before this Court will be instructive in resolving war of words and these are succinctly put down hereunder:

A. Petitioner of civil revision petition Sreemati Purabi Rani Barmani as plaintiff on 3-1-1984 laid a suit being Title Suit No. 5 of 1984 in Fourth Court of Subordinate Judge (now Joint District Judge), Dhaka for a decree of Partition in respect of Nine annas and Thirteen gondas share which came to 10.25 acres from total divisible 17.13 acres of property. Petitioner, also, sought other incidental and consequential reliefs in suit. Suit was, thereafter, renumbered as Title Suit No. 88 of 1985 and, again renumbered as, Title Suit No. 81 of 1992 in Fourth Court of Assistant Judge, Gazipur.

B. Hasen Ali was defendant No. 4 in Title Suit No. 5 of 1984. Summons had been duly served upon him. On his death his heir sons Insad Ali. Emdadul Huq, Dhukai Mia, Ead Ali, Naib Ali, Sohrab Hossain, Idris Ali. Bellaluddin, Alauddin, wives Billatunnessa and Rasatunnessa and daughters Rasheda Khatoon, Surja Banoo. Kanchan Bala, Laljan Bibi and Jobeda Khatoon had been substituted as defendant Nos. 4(ka)-4(Tha). Summons and registered notices upon substituted Defendant Nos. 4(ka)-4(Tha) had been issued and duly served upon them. defendant Nos. 1-3 Arfan Ali, Akbar Ali contested the suit in laying written statement.

C. Title Suit No. 81 of 1992 did not meet with success. Suit stood dismissed. Judgment and decree is dated 31-12-1996. Appeal being Title Appeal No. 22 of 1997 carried by petitioner as appellant was crowned with success. Appeal was allowed. Judgment and decree passed in Title Suit No. 81 of 1992 was set aside. Suit was decreed in preliminary form. In the appeal defendant Nos. 4(Ka-Tha) had been respondents.

D. Learned Assistant Judge, though, dismissed the suit found that some land in the name of Bhabuk Barman was recorded as vested property and defendant admitted the suit land to be under possession of plaintiff.

E. Learned Appellate Judge in awarding decree in favour of petitioner positively found:

i. Plaintiff-(petitioner) is daughter of Durgacharan.

ii. Bhabuk had 0.59 acres of property and that 0.59 acres of property had been claimed as vested property and Government failed to prove that the property was of Bhabuk and it was treated as vested property.

iii. Plaintiff (petitioner) as heir daughter of Durgacharan is the owner of entire 10.25 acres of property. Judgment and decree of the appellate Court is dated 30-7-1998.

F. Defendant Nos. 1 and 2 Erfan Ali and Akbar Ali having felt aggrieved of above adjudication approached the High Court Division in a revision petition under section 115 of the Code. Revision petition had been numbered as Civil Revision No. 4651 of 1998. Rule obtained stood discharged by a Single Bench of High Court Division. Judgment is dated 25-7-2001. High Court Division concurred with the finding reached by Court of appeal that Durgacharan succeeded 10.25 acres of property and after his death plaintiff (petitioner) inherited the said property. Finding of Court of appeal below was based upon proper appreciation of evidence on record. Judgment was followed by a decree drawn up on 14-8-2001.

G. Unsuccessful termination of Civil Revision case before the High Court Division could not deter defendants to make a halt. They went to Appellate Division in Civil Petition for Leave to Appeal No. 1562 of 2001. Appellate Division by judgment dated 20-5-2002 dismissed Leave Petition. In recording dismissal Appellate Division held that learned Counsel for petitioner (Defendant) could not improve the case of the defendant to show that plaintiff (petitioner) was not the daughter of Durgacharan and Mr Bhuiyan failed to assail finding of fact arrived by lower appellate Court and then of High Court Division which discharged Rule on merit by hearing parties.

H. Final decree of Partition had been drawn up on 21-11-2002.

I. Substituted defendant Nos. 4(cha) and 4(jaha) Sohrab Hossain and Alauddin as plaintiff Nos. 1 and 2 (first and second-opposite parties) and Md Quayyum Molla, Mohammadullah and Golam Kibria as plaintiffs (third-fifth opposite parties) filed a suit being Title Suit No. 76 of 2001 in Second Court of Joint District Judge, Gazipur. Reliefs sought are:

(1) A decree declaring ownership of plaintiffs in respect of 7.35 acres of land described in schedule 'A' to the plaint be passed in favour of plaintiffs and against defendants.

(2) A decree declaring that the decree passed in Title Suit No. 86 of 1995 of the Court of Senior Assistant Judge, Fourth Court, Gazipur on the basis of judgment and decree dated 30-7-1998 passed in Title Appeal No. 22 of 1997 in respect of 'A' schedule land is fraudulent, collusive, malafide, inoperative, null and void, illegal and not at all binding upon the plaintiffs.

(3) Other incidental reliefs had been, also, sought.

J. First-fifth-opposite parties by way of petition for amendment of plaint under Order VI, rule 17 of the Code sought insertion of the number of Title Suit as "81 of 1992" in place of "86 of 1995". The petition was allowed by Court and Title Suit No. "81 of 1992" stood substituted in place of "86 of 1995".

K. Case projected in plaint is that Durgacharan Barman died leaving behind two daughters namely, Sukhi Barmani and Bishika Rani Barmani alias Bishaka Barmani. Sukhi Barmani died unmarried and Bishika Rani Barmani became absolute owner and possessor of 10.25 acres of property left by Durgacharan Barman. Bishika Barmani died leaving behind only son Bhabuk Chandra Barman who became exclusive owner of 10.25 acres of property by way of inheritance. Bhabuk Chandra Barman by a registered deed of exchange dated 23-9-1999 transferred 4.00 acres of property in favour of plaintiff No. 1. Bhabuk Chandra Barman, thereafter, by registered deed dated 1-4-2001 sold 1.05 acres of property to plaintiff Nos. 2-4. Bhabuk Chandra again sold 1.00 acres of property in favour of plaintiff No. 5 by a registered sale deed dated 1-4-2001. Further case is that plaintiff No. 1 by way of Heba became owner of 0.22 acres of property and plaintiff Nos. 1 and 2 became owners in respect of 0.08 acres of property by way of inheritance. The plaintiffs, thus, become owners in possession over 7.35 acres of property.

L. In the suit decree-holder-petitioner Purabi Rani Barmani was made defendant No. 3.

M. Petitioner on presentation of a petition under Order VII, rule 11 of the Code sought rejection of plaint canvassing basic grounds which are:

1. In Title Suit No. 5 of 1984 which was renumbered as Title Suit No. 81 of 1992, Hasen Ali, father of plaintiff Nos. 1 and 2 (present first and second opposite parties) was defendant No. 4 and on his death plaintiffs Nos. 1 and 2 (first and second opposite parties) and other heirs of Hasen Ali were substituted and summons upon them had been duly served and in spite of due service of summons they did not appear in the suit. End Ali, the son of Hasen Ali, stood in the witness box as defendant's witness.

2. Property of Bhabuk was recorded in SA khatian No. 148 and his address having been shown in India, Deputy Custodian of Vested Property was made defendant No. 5 and defendant No. 5 contested suit on presentation of a written statement.

3. Preliminary decree had been passed on 30-7-1998 in Title Suit No. 81 of 1992 and the deeds dated 23-9-1999 and 1-4-2001 were created by plaintiff Nos. 1-5 (first-fifth opposite parties) after preliminary decree and on the basis of above deeds plaintiffs (opposite parties) got no right to file the suit and suit is barred under the principles of res judicator.

4. Suit land of Title Suit No. 81 of 1992 and suit land of present Title Suit No. 76 of 2000 are same and inseparable.

5. Bhabuk, transferor of deeds of plaintiffs (opposite parties) was represented by Deputy Custodian of vested Property.

6. Over the same subject matter in between the parties and their representatives further litigation is barred by law.

N. Learned Joint District Judge, Second Court, Gazipur by order dated 7-8-2002 rejected the petition laid under Order VII, rule 11 of the Code. Reasons which weighed with learned Joint District Judge in recording rejection are:

i. Preliminary decree passed in Title Suit No. 81 of 1992 was not disposed of finally.

ii. Suit was not only for partition but, also, for declaration and parties are not same and the suit did not appear to be barred by principles of resjudicata.

5. Feeling aggrieved, petitioner approached this Court in this Revision Petition.

6. First-fifth-opposite parties put up resistance to revision petition on laying affidavit-in-opposition controvert statements made in revision petition. Basic contentions tabled in affidavit-in-opposition is that suit is not hit by principles of res judicata under section 11 of the Code.

7. Contentions pressed into service from side of petitioner are catalogued hereunder:

i. Controversy in respect of heir ship of petitioner Sreemati Purabi Rani Barmani as daughter of Durga-charan and her right, title, interest and possession for an area of 10.25 acres which was the suit property in Title Suit No. 81 of 1992 was finally adjudicated and determined by highest Court of land and same matter cannot be reopened and reagitated by opposite party Nos. 1 and 2 and other opposite party Nos. 3-5 who claimed title from Bhabuk Barman and the suit is barred by law and plaint is liable to be rejected under inherent power of Court under section 115 of the Code if not under Order VII, rule 11 of the Code.

ii. Seeking declaration that decree passed in Title Suit No. 81 of 1992 of the Court of Senior Assistant Judge, Gazipur on the basis of judgment and decree dated 30-7-1998 passed in Title Appeal No. 22 of 1997 in respect of schedule land is fraudulent, collusive, malafide, inoperative, null, void and not binding upon plaintiffs is absolutely barred by law and plaint is liable to be rejected in exercise of inherent power under section 115 if not under Order VII, rule 11 of the Code.

Guiness Peat (Trading) Limited vs Md Fazlur Rahman, 44 DLR (AD) 242. Abdul Jalil and others vs Islamic Bank Bangladesh Ltd and others, 53 DLR (AD) 12 and T Arivandandam vs TV Satyapal and another, AIR 1977 SC 2421 have been relied upon in support of contentions pressed.

8. Contentions raised from side of petitioner have been given rejoinder in bringing home contention from side of first-opposite parties which are:

i. Plaint cannot be rejected on question of resjudicata and question of resjudicata can be decided only on production of evidences at the time of trial.

ii. Decree passed by appellate Court which was maintained by High Court Division and Appellate Division against opposite parties is an ex parte decree and not a contested decree and an ex parte decree even if maintained by Appellate Division can be very much challenged in a suit and plaint, thus, cannot be rejected as barred by law.

Sreemati Pushpa Rani Das and another vs AKM Habibur Rahman and others, 1993 BLD (AD) 217 had been pressed in aid of contention raised.

9. In the wake of contentions advanced from both parties, the kernel question that survives for determination is whether plaint can be rejected either on the strength of provision envisaged in Order VII, rule 11 or in inherent power of Court embodied in section 151 of the Code.

10. In approaching the question principles of law on res judicata embodied in section 11, Order VII, rule 11 and inherent power envisaged in section 151 of the Code can be explored.

11. Doctrine of res judicata has received a statutory sanction in the Code as a matter of prudence and to give due weightage to a finding or decision so as to reach finality in the matter of a dispute between the same parties or litigating under the same parties. The doctrine, thus, is to achieve finality of dispute between parties being a principle of prudence so as to give efficacy to a finding of Court rather than permit the parties to go to trial more or less on the same issues over again. Judicial verdict has its special sanctity and cannot be the subject matter of discussion at any future time involving identical or similar issues. The doctrine of res judicata or constructive res judicata predominantly is a principle of equity, good conscience and justice. In Cari-Zeiss Stiftung vs Rayner and Keeler Ltd and others (1967). The Law Reports: Appeal Cases 853 = (1966) 2 All ER it has been aptly stated by Lord Upjohn that the broader principle of res judicata is founded on twin principles so frequently expressed in Latin that there should be an end to litigation and justice demands that the same party shall not be harassed twice for the same cause.

12. Order VII, rule 11 of the Code deals with power of Court to reject a plaint. Rule contemplates that stillborn suit should be nipped in the bud at its inception so that no further time is consumed on a fruitless litigation. A suit which is on the face of it incompetent under law should not be allowed to further encumber legal proceedings. If the suit is barred by law it is the statutory duty of Court to reject plaint.

13. Section 151 of the Code does not formulate any new doctrine but only a Legislative recognition of well-known doctrine and principle that every Court has inherent power to act ex debitio justitiae to do that real justice for administration of which alone it exists. Under section 151 Court acts ex debitio justitiae according to equity, justice and good conscience of a case and in consonance with fundamental principles of judicial procedure. It has been ruled by Superior Courts of sub-continent that a plaint may be rejected under the provision of Order VII, rule 11 and if plaint cannot be rejected under Order VII, rule 11 same can be very well rejected in exercise of inherent power under section 151.

14. Law on the subject has been spelt out, discussed and considered in good number of cases of our jurisdiction as well as foreign jurisdiction. Of those Burma!! Eastern Ltd vs Burmah Eastern Employees Union and others, 18 DLR 709 may profitably be taken notice of. High Court considered the rejection of plaint matter under the provision of Order VII, rule 11 and in considering it laid down the principle that a plaint can be thrown in limini if not under Order VII, rule 11 then under Court's inherent power. Murshed CJ speaking for the Court observed at Paragraph No. 10:

Order 7, rule 11 of the Code as quoted above, enumerates certain categories under which the Court is called upon to reject a plaint, but, it is obvious that they are not exhaustive. It appears from the language of rule 11 of Order 7 that it requires that an incompetent suit should be laid at rest at the earliest moment so that no further time is wasted over what is bound to collapse as not being permitted by law.

It has been, also laid down in Paragraph No. 11:

A suit may be specifically barred by law and, in such an event, the matter would come under the express terms of clause (d) of rule 11 of Order VII of the Code. But, even in a case where a suit is not permitted by necessary implication of law in the sense that a positive prohibition can be spelt out of legal provisions, the Court has an inherent jurisdiction to reject the plaint. This really amounts to saying that Order 7, rule 11, is not exhaustive. Hardly any authority is needed for such a proposition. I may, however, refer to some decisions on this point.

Murshed CJ in the case, also considered other authorities notably, amongst others, are Thakur Haribar Bakhsh Singh vs Thakur Jagannath Singh, AIR 1924 Oudh 413 and Radhakishen vs Wali Md AIR 1956 Hyderabad 133.

15. In the yardstick of the above stated principles and enunciation of law by Superior Courts the question posed now shall be answered.

16. In Title Suit No. 5 of 984 then renumbered as Title Suit No. 81 of 1992 petitioner was plaintiff. Predecessor of first and second-opposite parties Hasen Ali had been defendant No. 4 and on his death his heirs sons, daughters and wives including first and second-opposite parties had been substituted and first and second opposite parties were substituted as defendant Nos. 4(cha) and 4(Jaha), From certified copy of service return which has been produced before this Court it stood exposed to view that summons upon substituted defendants including substituted defendant Nos. 4(cha) and 4(Jaha) (first and second opposite parties) had been duly served and there was a declaration made by serving officer as to the service of summons upon them. From certified copy of order dated 7-2-1996 it is brought to light that learned Assistant Judge made a note in the order sheet that summons upon substituted defendants had been duly served. Learned Judge further noted that registered notices were kept with the record. Service of summons upon substituted defendants including substituted defendant No. 4(cha) and 4(jaha) who are (first and second opposite parties) is an evidence as to the service of summons as contemplated in rule 19A of Order V of the Code. The noting as to the due service of summons upon substituted defendants including defendant Nos. 4 (cha) and 9(jaha) (first and second opposite parties) dated 7-2-1996, also, got a strong presumption as mandated in section 114(e) of The Evidence Act of 1872.

17. In Title Suit No. 81 of 1992 schedule property is as follows:

Out of 17.13 acres of property opposite parties claimed property is 7.35 acres of land. Schedule property in both the suits are exactly the same.

19. In Title Suit No. 81 of 1992 petitioner as plaintiff set up her claim over 10.25 acres of property as the daughter of Durgacharan. In Title Suit No. 76 of 2001. First-fifth opposite parties put up claim in respect 7.35 acres of property out of petitioner's decreed 10.25 acres of property of Title Suit No. 81 of 1992 raising contention that petitioner is not daughter of Durgacharan and Bhabuk Chandra Barman inherited 10.25 acres of property as daughter's son of Durgacharan and Bhabuk being owner and possessor of 10.25 acres of property transferred 4.00 acres of property by way of registered deed of exchange dated 23-9-1999 in favour of first-opposite party and then Bhabuk by way of registered deed dated 1-4-2001 sold 1.05 acres of property to second-fourth-opposite parties and, thereafter, Bhabuk transferred 1.00 acre of property by a registered sale deed dated 1-4-2001 in favour of fifth-opposite party. First and second opposite parties by way of Heba and inheritance claimed 1.22 acres of property from their father Hasen who was defendant No. 4 in Title Suit No. 82 of 1992.

20. Learned Senior Assistant Judge as Trial Judge in Title Suit No. 81 of 1992 in his Judgment positively found that some property in plot No. 205 had been recorded in the name of Bhabuk as vested property and lease taken by defendant No. 1 in respect of 0.59 acres of property was absolutely illegal. Learned Trial Judge dismissed suit not on the point that petitioner is not the daughter of Durgacharan but on the point that she got no possession on such property.

21. Learned Subordinate Judge, First Court, Gazipur as Appellate Judge taking into consideration evidences and materials on record positively rendered decision that Durgacharan having been dead his property was inherited by his two daughters Bishika Rani Barmani and Purabi Rani Barmani alias Prabhati Barmani and Bishaka Rani Barmani having been dead without any son Purabi Rani Barmani inherited the entire 10.25 acres of property left by Durgacharan and Purabi Rani Barmani became the owner and possessor of entire 10.25 acres of property. Appellate Judge, also, categorically found that Government who was defendant No. 5 in suit failed to prove that Bhabuk had been owner of 0.59 acres of property out of suit property that is 10.25 acres of property and Bhabuk left for India and said 0.59 acres of property had been vested property. The Appellate Judge rendered decision that government failed to prove that Bhabuk had been owner of 0.59 acres of property. Learned Appellate Judge in allowing the appeal granted a preliminary decree to the extent of nine annas and thirteen gondas which came to 10.25 acres of property. Finding reached by Appellate Judge that Durgacharan inherited 10.25 acres of property and on the death of Durgacharan petitioner inherited said property rested on proper appreciation of evidence and the finding had been maintained by High Court Division and as well as by Appellate Division.

22. Case projected by first-fifth-opposite parties in plaint is that Durgacharan died leaving behind two daughters namely, Sukhi Barmani and Bishika Rani Rarmani alias Bishaka Barmani and Sukhi Rani Barmani died unmarried that Bishika Rani Barmani alias Bishaka Barmani became absolute owner and possessor of 10.25 acres of property left by Durgacharan and Bhabuk Barman got entire 10.25 acres of property. In view of firm decision recorded by Appellate Judge as to inheritance, ownership and possession in respect of entire 10.25 acres of property of Durgacharan by petitioner Purabi Rani Barmani and, also, as to non-ownership of Bhabuk over 0.59 acres of property which had been maintained by Appellate Division the claim put forward by first-fifth-opposite parties that Bhabuk Barman inherited 10.25 acres of property from her mother Bishika Rani Barmani and that first-fifth opposite parties by way of exchange and sale deeds from Bhabuk Barman and, also, of Heba and inheritance from predecessor Hasen. defendant No. 4 of earlier suit acquired ownership and title over 7.35 acres of property out of petitioner's decreed 10.25 acres of property stand absolutely barred by law and first-fifth-opposite parties cannot be allowed to reopen the matter which reached to its finality by highest Court of land that is the Appellate Division.

23. Preliminary decree had been passed on 30-7-1998 by appellate Court which, also became a decree of Trial Court. Appellate judgment is dated 30-7-1998. Judgment passed by High Court Division in Civil Revision No. 4651 of 1998 is dated 25-7-2001. Judgment of Appellate Division is on 20-5-2002. Final decree had been drawn up on 21-11-2002. Deed of exchange and other deeds of first-fifth-opposite parties are dated 23-9-1999 and 1,4,2001 which are after a long period of preliminary decree and during pendency of Civil Revision case before High Court Division.

24. This drives us to a legal aspect of the matter of a great public importance which is relief sought by opposite parties. Relief sought in respect of decree passed by Appellate Court has been stated earlier.

25. Decree passed by Court of appeal stood merged in decree of High Court Division and that decree was maintained by Appellate Division. Can a decree which stood merged in decree of High Court Division and sustained by Appellate Division be challenged in a Court Subordinate to High Court Division and, also, Appellate Division? Answer is in firm negative. If suit in hand is allowed to be proceeded with and not buried at doorstep majesty of law and administration of justice shall break down and sanctity of judgment and decree of Superior Court shall be flung to the wind and dubious and unscrupulous litigants shall be encouraged to lay misconceived and fraudulent cases to challenge Judgments passed by the Apex Court. This tendency of dishonest litigants deserves to be taken serious note of and curbed by recording appropriate order and issuing necessary direction including imposing of exemplary costs in the interest of the majesty of law and administration of justice.

26. Coming now to contention advanced from side of first-fifth-opposite parties that decree passed was ex-prate and not contested against opposite parties and decree. though, maintained by Appellate Division can very much be challenged before Subordinate Court.

27. This contention does not hold water at all and can be ruled out without any hesitation. Decree is decree whether contested or ex parte and all decrees contested or ex parte got purity and carry force of law. Ex parte decree cannot be impaired on ground of its being ex parte. It has earlier been posited that summons upon first and second opposite parties who were substituted defendant Nos. 4 (cha) and 4(jaha) had been duly served and learned Judge made a note as to due service of summons upon all substituted defendants. First and second opposite parties allowed the suit to be directed ex parte against them.

28. The authorities relied upon from side of petitioner and first-fifth-opposite parties now may be taken heed of.

29. Authorities relied upon from side of petitioner shall be addressed now. In Guiness Peat (Trading) Limited vs Md Fazlur Rahman (Supra), plaintiff-respondent instituted a Money Suit before Third Court of Subordinate Judge, Dhaka asserting that defendant, a Trading company of London, offered to plaintiff by telexes to sell 150 metric tons of skimmed milk of Hungarian origin as per specification. On arrival at Chittagong Port plaintiff rejected the goods, but for mitigating loss sold away the same. In the plaint it had been averred that cause of action of suit arose on 12th March, 1982 when Letter of Credit was opened in favour of defendant. Appellate filed an application under Order VII, rule 11 of the Code for rejection of the plaint on the ground that Court had no jurisdiction since the defendant did not reside or carry on business within jurisdiction of this Court. Bar of suit contemplated under rule 11(d) was not pleaded and bar of cause of action postulated in rule 11(a) was pressed into service.

Appellate Division held:

"In considering an application for rejection of a plaint the specific provision under Order VII, rule 11 should ordinarily be followed. A resort to section 151 of the Code may be made in the interest of justice only in an exceptional case where the suit is foredoomed and if it is allowed to be proceeded with it will amount to an abuse of the process of the Court."

30. In Abdul Jalil and others vs Islamic Bank Bangladesh Ltd and others (Supra). petitioner as plaintiff earlier instituted a suit in Court of Subordinate Judge, Dhaka for declaration of title and partition of suit properties. The suit on contest was dismissed by trial Court which decree was affirmed up to the Appellate Division. Petitioner then instituted a suit in Fifth Court of Subordinate Judge, Dhaka praying for declaration that decree passed in earlier Title Suit was illegal and invalid and was not applicable in respect of 'Ga' schedule land of present suit. Before trial Court defendants filed an application under Order VII, rule 11 read with Order 14 rule 2 of the Code for rejection of plaint of Title Suit No. 92 of 1991. Learned Subordinate Judge as Trial judge rejected defendant's prayer for rejection of plaint. Against which defendants moved before High Court Division in Civil Revision No. 2757 of 1999 and a Division Bench by judgment dated 18th November, 1999 made the Rule absolute and rejected plaint under Order VII, rule II of the Code. Plaintiffs took a Civil Petition for Leave to Appeal before Appellate Division. Appellate Division laid down:

It is settled that where a plaint cannot be rejected under Order 7 rule 11 of the Code the Court may invoke its inherent jurisdiction and reject the plaint taking recourse to section 151 of the Code.

Appellate Division further held:

"The present suit cannot be allowed to be proceeded further. As the ultimate result of the suit is as clear as daylight such a suit should be properly buried at its inception so that no further time is consumed in a fruitless litigation. When the ultimate result is clear, the plaintiffs cannot be allowed to re-open the same matter afresh after losing up to the Appellate Division. This is merely a gambling in litigation which cannot be allowed."

31. In T Arivandandam vs TV Satyapal and another, (Supra) a sorry story of a long drawn out series of legal proceedings, revealing how father of the petitioner contested an eviction proceeding, lost it, appealed against it, lost it again, moved a Revision only to be rebuffed by summary rejection by High Court and, thereafter, Court's generosity in the matter of granting time to vacate the premises had been fully exploited by the father of the petitioner and the suit of the petitioner set upon a clever adventure in filing a suit before Fourth Additional First Munsif, Bangalore for a declaration that the order of eviction which had been confirmed right up to High Court was one obtained by "fraud" and collusive had been portrayed. Observation of eminent Judge VR Krishna lyer who spoke for Court is couched in the following terms:

The trial Court would insist imperatively on examining the party at the first hearing so that bogus litigation can be shot down at the earliest stage. The Penal Code is also resourceful enough to meet such men, and must be triggered against them. The trial Court in this case will remind itself of section 35A, CPC and take deterrent action if it is satisfied that the litigation was inspired by vexatious motives and altogether groundless.

Further observation framed in the following language:

The pathology of litigative addiction ruins the poor of this country and the Bar has a role to cure this deleterious tendency of parties to launch frivolous and vexatious cases.

The long arm of the law must throttle such limitative caricatures if the confidence and credibility of the community in the Judicature is to survive. The contempt power of the Court is meant for such persons as the present petitioner.

32. This brings us to the authority placed from the side of opposite parties. Before adverting to the authority it is always to be borne in mind that a decision is only an authority for what it actually decides, it cannot be quoted for a proposition that may seem to follow from it. Every judgment must be read applicable to the particular facts proved or assumed to be proved since the generality of expression which may be found therein are not intended to be exposition of whole law but governed or qualified by the particular facts of the case in which such expression occurs. What is of the essence in its decision is its ratio and not every observation found nor what logically followed from the very observation made in it. It is not a profitable task to extract a sentence or word from a judgment divorced from the context of the question under consideration.

33. In Sreemati Pushpa Rani Das and another vs AKM Habibur Rahman and others (Supra), defendants filed an application for rejection of plaint on ground that previously between parties, a suit being Title Suit No. 78 of 1977 was filed by respondent and the same was withdrawn and the cause of action of that suit is same and defendant brought Title Appeal No. 93 of 1990 in the same Court for permanent injunction and got decree on contest and against which respondent filed Title Appeal No. 100 of 1991 and, as such, present suit was not maintainable as barred by res judicata. The Appellate Division held that whether the suit was barred by res judicata or not was a matter to be decided at the time of trial and the same cannot be decided from a reading of plaint. The fact and circumstances of the case relied upon got no bearing in fact and circumstances of case in our hand. In cited case Title Suit No. 78 of 1979 was withdrawn and right and title of parties had not been finally adjudicated and Title Suit No. 93 of 1990 for permanent injunction was dismissed and Title Appeal had been filed. No finality had been attached by any decision by Superior Court but in case in hand judgment and decree reached to finality by highest Court of land i.e. Appellate Division.

<u>34. The judicial verdict awarded by Appellate Court which is final Court of fact as to inheritance of petitioner Purabi Rani Barmani from her father Durgacharan in respect of entire 10.25 acres of property and former's ownership and possession over that 10.25 acres of property and, also, as to Bhabuk Barman's non-ownership over 0.59 acres of property out of said 10.25 acres which was maintained by last ladder of hierarchy, that is Appellate Division cannot be allowed to be challenged in a suit laid by first-fifth-opposite parties. Plaint is to be nipped in the bud and it merits rejection. In equality, good conscience and administration of justice and, also, in interest of majesty of law and sanctity and finality of verdicts of superior Court inherent power under section 151 of the Code requires to be invoked and exercised to bury suit of first-fifth-opposite parties at the threshold if not under Order VII, rule 11 of the Code.</u>

35. Before parting we are inclined to record an observation that no litigant has a right to lay fraudulent, shady, ill-motivated and untenable proceeding in a Court of law when those cases are throttling the functioning of justice dispensation system which itself is groaning under unbearable arrears and backlogs. For blameworthy conduct of these types of unprincipled and dishonest litigants compensatory cost is to be awarded upon them.

36. Corollary thereof is, that Rule arising out of civil revision petition under section 115 of the Code got merit and it succeeds. Rule is made absolute. Order dated 7-8-2002 passed by learned Joint District Judge, Second Court, Gazipur in Title Suit No. 76 of 2001 refusing to reject plaint stands set aside. Plaint of Title Suit No. 76 of 2001 of said Court stands rejected.

Regard being had to the blameworthy conduct of first-fifth-opposite parties we award a compensatory cost of Taka 5,000 upon first-fifth-opposite parties. Cost shall be paid to petitioner who is being dragged to further malafide and fraudulent litigation.

End.

full_judgment:
Abdus Salam Mamun J: This Rule Nisi was issued under Article 102 of the Constitution of the People's Republic of Bangladesh calling upon the respondents to show cause as to why the impugned order dated 2-1-1997 vide Annexure-F and the impugned orders 15-11-1994 and 29-1-1996 vide Annexure-H and H(1) should not be declared to have been passed without lawful authority and are of no legal effect and as to why the respondent Nos.1-3 should not be directed to levy and collect customs duty, VAT and other taxes in respect of the said imported consignment on the basis of the C&F value.

2. Facts relevant for disposal of this Writ Petition are that the petitioner opened Letter of Credit being No.AGR/CASH/424/96 dated 24-11-1996 for import of 7 units of Used Vehicles as per C&F value, vide Annexure-C. The aforesaid LC goods arrived at the port of Chittagong on 30-12-1996 and the clearing agent of the petitioner submitted Bill of Entry on that date, vide Annexure-E. But respondent No.3 opened a file being number 4059/AP/ Group/10/96-97 stating in its para(2) that the C&F agent has applied for physical verification of the consignment for having no Model Code of these two units of reconditioned vehicle, vide Annexure-F.

3. On 2-1-1997 the petitioner by a letter addressed to the Commissioner of Customs, Customs House, Chittagong applied for assessment of customs duty and charges on the basis of C& F value of the imported goods stating also that the Yellow Book Value on those reconditioned vehicles were not applicable, vide Annexure-G. But by impugned Annexure-F, in paragraph Nos. 8-11 the respondent held that though the importer claimed that the C&F value was applicable in his consignment but failed to produce any documents in support thereof and that according to the order of the Board of Revenue the assessment of the reconditioned vehicles will be on the basis of Yellow Book Value excluding depreciations. The respondent thereafter has shown in "the said file the difference between the Yellow Book Value and the declared value of these two units showing that the Yellow Book Value of a TOYOTA CARINA Car ST-180 of 1838 CC manufactured in the year 1992 was US$ 4883.82 equivalent to Taka 2,34,738.11 but the importer has declared it to the customs authority at US$ 2200 equivalent to Taka 1,06,535.60 to be the Invoice or C&F value and there is a difference of Taka 1,28,202.51. In the case of TOYOTA LITEACE Micro bus KS 30G-QB 4486 CC and manufactured in the year 1991 the Yellow Book Value was US$ 2855.36 equivalent to Taka 88,182.19 and the importer has declared its invoice or C&F value to be US$ 1800 equivalent to Taka 55,886.24 having difference of Taka 32,215.91. Since there is a difference between the C&F Value and the Yellow Book Value, in the consignment the respondent has assessed duties on the basis of Yellow Book Value.

4. Thereafter, the petitioner invoked Writ Jurisdiction of this Court and obtained the instant Rule and an ad-interim order to the effect that "Pending hearing of the Rule, respondent Nos.1 and 2 are directed to allow the petitioner to release the goods covered under LC No.AGRA/CASH/424/96 dated 24-11-1996 on payment of duties and taxes thereon on the basis of C&F value declared by the petitioner within one week."

5. Mr Md Hasan Rajib Prodhan, learned Advocate appearing on behalf of the petitioner, submits that there is no provision in the Finance Act, 1995-96 and in the Customs Act, 1969 to assess customs duty on the basis of Yellow Book Value and that the impugned administrative Orders, SRO. have no legal sanction and are violative of the Customs Act, 1969. The impugned standing orders are Annexures-H and H(1) and I to this Writ Petition. He further argued that the impugned order of assessment is violative of section 25 of the Customs Act and in the consignment in question value means the normal value or C& F value alone and that the National Board of Revenue has no right to fix a value under section 25 as a whole and the impugned Standing Orders tantamount to denying the benefit of section 25 of the Customs Act and that the Yellow Book Value is much higher than the C&F value. Assessment on the Yellow Book Value is detrimental to the interest of the petitioner-importer and the invoice value declared by the petitioner was correct and he was entitled to release the imported reconditioned vehicles on the basis of C&F value.

6. The respondent No.1 has entered appearance by filing an Affidavit-in-Opposition stating that the SRO No.215 dated 12-12-1995 has provided mode of assessment of duty of certain imported items on the basis of Yellow Book Value and the same is enforceable in law. In view of this SRO the petitioner was not entitled to release his goods on the basis of C&F value and that the National Board of Revenue issued this SRO No.215 in the greater national interest.

7. Mrs Nusrat Jahan, learned Assistant Attorney-General appearing on behalf of the respondent, submits that the Bill of Entry of this consignment was submitted by the agent of the petitioner on 30-12-1996 and the impugned SRO No.215 came into force on 12-12-1995 and, as such, on the date of presentation of Bill of Entry and assessment of duties and taxes on 2-1-1997 this impugned SRO Annexure-I(1) was in force. The Standing Order No.1653/96 dated 29-1-1996 has provided depreciation for imported reconditioned vehicles on year wise slabs. The petitioner was being aware of this SRO and other Standing Orders opened his LC on 24-11-1996 and was thus bound to pay duties and taxes on the basis of law prevalent on the date of presentation of Bill of Entry. The Bill of Entry of this consignment was presented on 30-12-1996 and on that date the basis for assessment of duties and Taxes were the Yellow Book Value in the case of imported reconditioned vehicles and the petitioner is stopped from denying it.

8. The learned Assistant Attorney-General next argued that the dispute between the importer and the Customs Officials on the point of invoice or C&F value and the Yellow Book Value of the imported reconditioned vehicles as the basis of assessment of duties has already been resolved and decided by the Hon'ble Appellate Division of the Bangladesh Supreme Court in the case of Commissioner of Customs, Chittagong vs Giasuddin Chowdhury and others, reported in 50 DLR (AD) 129. In paragraph 22 of that case, their Lordships have been pleased to hold that "The writ-petitioner's claim of assessment on invoice value and not on Yellow Book Value is a matter of interpretation and not a question of jurisdiction to assess customs duties. So the Writ petitioner has to pay Yellow Book Value before his goods are released."

Imported goods in that reported case were also reconditioned vehicles.

9. Relying upon this decision the learned Assistant Attorney-General contended that there is no scope for the petitioner to argue on invoice value of the imported consignment.

<u>10. The petitioner, on the other hand, submits that the Yellow Book Value is a stranger to the Customs Act, 1969 and not recognised by the Customs Act as a method of assessing duties.</u>

<u>11. We find that these arguments have thoroughly been discussed and dealt with in the case of Nasiruddin Ahmed and another vs Commissioner of Customs, Chittagong and others reported in 50 DLR 232 holding that Yellow Book Value shall be the basis for assessment of duties in cases of reconditioned imported vehicles.</u>

<u>12. In the interpreting Article 152 of the Constitution of the People's Republic of Bangladesh "Law" means any Act, Ordinance, Order, rule, regulation, by-law, notification or other legal instrument, and any custom or usage having the force of law in Bangladesh." So, we find that the Standing Orders, SRO, have their forces of applicability and Yellow Book Value was applicable in the case of the petitioner as mode of assessment of duties.</u>

13. Yellow Book is the book issued by the manufactures along with the vehicle providing its description and specifications together with manufacturer's and retail prices and accepted in the International Market, whereas an invoice is 'a written account of the particulars of goods sent or shipped to a purchaser, factor, etc with the value, or prices, or charges annexed generally issued by the supplier or the dealer. In the commercial transactions the supplier's statements or written account about description, specifications and price of the commodities is less dependable, for more than one reason that it could be varied, inflated or manipulated for the purpose of evading duties which is unfortunately, a common phenomenon in the field of Trade and Commerce. The manufacturer's book, called the Yellow Book, is more dependable because the manufacturer usually manufactures more than one piece of similar product considering its demand in the market and having same identification number called the HS Code, Model number, Engine and Chassis number of the batch and of same design and this is a lot of the same nature and specifications and amenities and they fix prices in the factory considering manufacturing cost and profit in view of consumption in the international market maintaining one standard of the same lot.

14. We find that there are provisions for depreciations in the impugned Standing Order to the benefit of the importers of the reconditioned vehicles complacent to their usability.

15. The respondent has stated in his Affidavit-in-opposition that the mode of assessment of duty on the basis of Yellow Book Value was introduced in the greater national interest. Greater national interest is the interest of the people as a whole and it mainly depends upon the persons to whom responsibility is entrusted to secure the interest for and on behalf of the people. If they practice the same in their management, conduct and discharge of official duties, the businessmen concerned to our utmost trust, shall also secure greater national interest.

<u>16. In the case of Federation of Pakistan vs Md Saifullah Khan, PLD 1989 (SC) 166 their Lordships held that 'Courts always keep in view the higher interest of the country while resolving matters of national importance in accordance with the Constitution and law. National interest must take precedence over private interests and individual rights.'</u>

<u>17. Learned Assistant-Attorney-General has lastly, argued that the Writ Petition is not maintainable on the face of efficacious alternative remedy provided by the Customs Act under sections 193 and 196. She has relied upon the case of Bangladesh and others vs Mizanur Rahman, reported in 52 DLR (AD) 149 where their Lordships have held that forum provided by the Customs Act for appeal against any order of the customs officials including the assessment order is an efficacious alternative remedy and the petitioner only on point of his grievance of assessment of Customs duties cannot invoke the 'Writ Jurisdiction. "Ordinarily Writ Petition against an assessment of Customs duty or imposition of fine is not maintainable and remedy of appeal is to be availed of against the same."</u>

<u>In the instant writ petition, except the Order of impugned assessment of duty there is no other grievances of this petitioner and, as such, we find that the extraordinary jurisdiction of the High Court Division is not available to a person whose grievances arise out of the order of assessment of customs duties. He has to prefer an appeal in accordance with the Customs Act, 1969.</u>

18. This Court by the ad-interim order allowed the petitioner to clear his goods on the basis of invoice value. Since we held that Yellow Book Value was applicable to 'his consignment as basis of assessment of duties and charges, the petitioner is therefore, directed to pay the balance duty to the respondents within 30 (thirty) days from this date and the respondents are at liberty to realise the balance duties after expiry of 30 (thirty) days in accordance with law.

In the result, the Rule is discharged without any order as to costs.

End.

Abdul Jalil Miah and anr ----- Plaintiff-Petitioners
vs

full_judgment:
This Rule was issued calling upon the opposite party Nos.1 and 2 to show cause as to why the judgment and decree dated 23-11-96 and 31-12-96 respectively passed by the learned Additional District Judges, 6th Court, Dhaka, in Title Appeal No. 239 of 1995 affirming the judgment and decree dated 17-7-95 and 25-7-95 respectively passed by the learned Subordinate Judge, 4th Court, Dhaka, in Title Suit No. 244 of 1992 dismissing the suit should not be set aside.

2. That on 25-2-81 the petitioners as plaintiffs filed Title Suit No. 276 of 981 in the First Court of Subordinate Judge, Dhaka (transferred to 4th Court of Subordinate Judge and Artha Rin Adalat renumbered as Title Suit No. 244 of 1992) for declaration of title and recovery of khas possession of the following land of Schedule 'A' comprising of an area of 0.1256 acres of land out of the land of CS Plot Nos. 88 and 107 corresponding to SA Plot Nos. 62 and 12 corresponding to RS Plot No. 557 of Mouza Old Tejkunipara, JL No. 80 now Tejgaon, JL No. 3, PS Tejgaon, District Dhaka recorded in CS Khatian No. 175 corresponding to SA Khatian Nos. 43 and 13 corresponding to RS DP Khatian No. 301 butted and bounded by:

On the north, house of Noorjahan Begum, Abdul Momin and Siddique.

In the south, house of Abdul Huq & others.

On the east a road.

On the west house of Abdur Razzak.

Schedule-"B"

An area of more or less 2 kathas equivalent to 0.0330 acres of land being part of CS Plot No. 107 corresponding to SA Plot No.12 corresponding to RS Plot No. 557 now wrongly included in RS Plot No. 556 of Mouza Old Tejkunipara, JL No. 89, now Tejkunipara, JL No. 5, recorded in CS Khatian No.175 corresponding to SA Khatian No.13 corresponding to RS DP Khatian No. 301 marked 'X' in the hand sketch map and butted and bounded by:

On the north, house of Noorjahan Begum and Abdul Momin Siddique.

On the south, plaintiff's house.

On the east a road.

On the west, house of defendants."

3. The case of the plaintiffs, in short, is that the land of CS Khatian No. 175 of Mouza Tejkunipara, PS Tejgaon, District Dhaka originally belonged to 2 brothers, Fazar Ali Sheikh and Mabu Sheikh alias Nabu Sheikh. That for convenience of the possession, the said two brothers namely, Fazar Ali and Mabu, amicably partitioned their entire property before CS operation. By such amicable partition, the lands of CS Plot Nos. 87, 107 and 120 were given in the Saham of Mabu Sheikh and the lands of CS Plot Nos. 88, 106, 108, 118 and 416 were given in the Saham of Fazar Ali Sheikh. Accordingly, during CS operation the lands of CS Plot Nos. 87,107 and 120 were shown in the possession of Mabu Sheikh in the column provided for recording possession and the lands of CS Plot Nos. 88, 106, 108, 118 and 416 were shown in possession of said Fazar Ali Sheikh and the record was finally published accordingly. That the said Fazar Ali Sheikh while in exclusive possession of the land of CS Plot Nos.88 and other plots referred to above, died leaving one son Abdul Jabbar as his legal heir and successor. The said Abdul Jabbar sold different portions of CS Plot No. 88 to different people for valuable consideration and put the purchasers into possession within specific block. The said Abdul Jabbar sold an area of ten kathas equivalent to 0.1650 acres of land to one Sirajul Islam, son of Hajee Abdul Ghani Mal for valuable consideration by a registered Kabala No. 3017 dated 6-3-56 registered in the office of Sadar Sub-Registrar, Dhaka, and put the said Sirajul Islam into possession of the land sold to him within specific boundary. The said Sirajul Islam possessed his purchased land for some years and then sold to different people. The said Sirajul Islam sold an area of 4½ (four and half) khatas equivalent to 0.0750 acres of land out of his purchased ten khatas equivalent to 0.1650 acres of land out of the land of CS Plot No. 88 to the plaintiff No. 2 for valuable consideration by a registered kabala dated 14th Ashar, 1373 BS corresponding to 29-6-66 and put the plaintiff No. 2 into possession of the said 0.0750 acres of land within the following boundary:

On the north, land of Md Siddiqur Rahman.

On the south, land of Abdul Hoque.

On the east, land of Syed Ali.

On the west, land of Abdur Razzak Chowdhury.

That the said Mabu Sheikh, while owner of the exclusive possession of the land of CS Plot No. 107, died leaving one son Abdul Majid, as his legal heir and successor. After the death of the said Mabu Sheikh, his son said Abdul Majid sold different portions of the land of CS Plot No. 107 to different people. The said Abdul Majid sold an area of two kathas and two chataks equivalent to 0.0517 acres of land out of the land of CS Plot No. 107 to the plaintiff No. 1 for valuable consideration by a registered kabala dated 21st Chaitra, 1375 BS corresponding to 4-4-69 and put the plaintiff No.1 into possession within the following boundary:

On the north, land of Abdul Majid.

On the south, land of plaintiff No. 2.

On the east, 12 feet wide road.

On the west, land of Sharrifunnessa.

That during SA operation the land of CS Plot No. 88 was changed to SA Plot No. 62 and recorded as SA Plot No. 62 and SA Khatian No. 43 and the land of CS Plot No. 107 was changed to SA plot No. 12 for an area of 0.54 acres of land and recorded in SA Khatian No. 13 of Mouza Tejkunipara and the SA Khatians were finally published. The plaintiff No. 2 after her purchase of 4½ kathas of land out of the land of CS Plot No. 88 corresponding to SA Plot No. 62 got her name mutated and jama was separated from the Government acquired estate vide MS Case No.1114 (SG) 74-75 dated 12-9-75 from the office of CO (Rev), Tejgaon and paid rent separately. Similarly the plaintiff No.1 also after his purchase of 3 kathas 2 chataks of land out of the land of CS Plot No.107 corresponding to SA Plot No.12 got his name mutated and jama was separated from the Government acquired estate and paid the rent to the Government separately. That the plaintiff No.1 is the husband of the plaintiff No.2, they for the convenience of possession and enjoyment, amalgamated their purchased lands and surrounded the same by distinct boundary marks. The plaintiffs constructed three-storied building in the purchased portion of CS Plot No. 88 by obtaining plan approved by DIT and they kept the portion of CS Plot No.107 vacant within the same boundary, the same was duly recorded in the names of plaintiffs as against which the defendant filed an objection case under Rule 30 of the EBT Rules and managed to obtain a favourable order, against which the plaintiff filed an appeal No. 28471 of 1979 under Rule 31 of the said Rules. That during the pendency of the said appeal, the defendant trespassed into the suit land and thereby dispossessed the plaintiffs from the suit land on the 10th Poush, 1385 BS which compelled the plaintiffs to file the instant suit.

4. That the opposite party Nos.1 and 2 as defendant Nos.1 and 2 contested the suit by filing written statement denying the material allegations of the plaint contending, inter alia, that defendant Nos. 1 and 2 purchased 9-1/8 decimals of land in the south eastern part of CS Plot No.107 of CS Khatian No. 175 (contiguous to western part of CS Plot No. 106) from Abdul Jabbar Mia, son of Fazar Ali Sheikh, original CS recorded tenant by kabala dated 7-12-62 and 10-12-62 and has been in possession of the said purchased land by erecting boundary wall and constructing semi-pucca house thereon. That the plaintiff No.1 purchased in the name of plaintiff No. 2 some land from CS Plot No. 88 (which is contiguous to CS Plot No.106), that as there was no road to enter into the land purchased by the plaintiff, the plaintiff requested the defendant No.1 and local influential person for making arrangements of a road. According to the request of the plaintiff No.1, the Matabbars of the locality took initiative to construct 12 feet wide road. That the local members namely, Mahabubur Rahman Goraha, Md Ali Akbar, Md Abdul Majid, Md Omar Ali, Golam Mohiuddin, Abdur Rashid and Abdur Motaleb took decisions :

i. That the road will be constructed on the land of Abdur Razzaque Chowdhury and the plaintiff No.2 on the southern part of CS Plot No.88.

ii. That the defendant No.1 will give 9 x 70 square feet land from southern part of CS Plot No.106 to Abdur Razzaque and plaintiff No.2.

iii. That another 12 feet road will be constructed on CS Plot No.107 belonging to Abdul Majid.

iv. That Abdul Majid will give the said land for the construction of the road without receiving any consideration.

v. That after purchasing 3 kathas and 2 chataks of land in Plot No.107 from Abdul Majid, 1 katha land will be given to the plaintiff and 2 kathas 2 chataks land will be given to the defendant.

vi. A joint fund was raised to implement the decision to purchase the land, earth filling, shifting of pucca house and for the construction of the road.

That thereafter an arbitration was held on 6-6-68 consisting of about 11/12 prominent persons of the locality and accordingly, a Salishnama was prepared with the consent of plaintiff and defendant where they had put their respective signatures. Thereafter the Matabbars gave delivery of 9 x 70 square feet of land to Abdur Razzaque and plaintiff No.1 by demolishing the wall and the house demarcated the boundary of the plaintiff and the defendant respectively by erecting boundary wall and after payment of consideration money for 3 kathas and 2 chataks of land, a 12 feet road was constructed on the RS Plot No. 580. That in terms of the Salishnama dated 6-6-68, the plaintiff No.1 was supposed to get kabala from Abdul Majid in his name for 3 kathas and 2 chataks of land and out of that land to exchange 25 x 60, 2 kathas 2 chataks of land of the defendant No.1 which has already been transferred to the plaintiff earlier. That accordingly, the defendant No.1 has been possessing the suit land (i.e. 2 kathas and 2 chataks of land of Plot No.107) from 1968 along with his earlier purchased land of Plot No.106. On the other hand, the plaintiff also has been in possession of the remaining 1 katha of land in CS Plot No.107 along with his earlier purchased land of CS Plot No.88. That the defendant as well as the Matabbars of the locality requested the plaintiff to execute an exchange deed but the plaintiff avoided the proposal by this or that plea. That the defendant acquired the suit land in exchange of their 9 x 70 square feet of land from CS Plot No.106 to plaintiff and Abdur Raz Haque. That the plaintiffs have no right, title and interest in the suit land but, taking advantage of the name of the plaintiff No.1 appearing in the kabala, filed the suit with a malafide intention to grab the suit land and, as such, the suit is liable to be dismissed.

5. During the course of trial the learned Subordinate Judge, 4th Court, Dhaka on consideration of the evidence on record and after perusing the papers, documents and exhibits dismissed the suit of the plaintiff by his judgment and decree dated 17-7-95 and 25-7-95 respectively.

6. Being aggrieved by the judgment and decree passed by the learned Subordinate Judge, 4th Court, Dhaka, the plaintiff-appellant-petitioner preferred an appeal, being No. 239 of 1999 before the learned District Judge, Dhaka which was ultimately heard and disposed of by the learned Additional District Judge, 6th Court, Dhaka who was pleased to dismiss the appeal after hearing the appeal and affirmed the judgment and decree passed by the trial Court by his judgment and decree dated 23-11-96 and 31-12-96 respectively.

7. Being aggrieved by and dissatisfied with the judgment and decree passed by the learned Additional District Judge, 6th Court, Dhaka, the plaintiff-appellant-petitioner preferred the instant Revisional Application before the High Court Division under Section 115 of the Code of Civil Procedure and obtained the present Rule.

8. The learned Counsel Mr Khandker Mahbubuddin Ahmed with Mr Anwarul Azim Khair, appearing on behalf of the plaintiff-appellant-petitioner, submits that both the Courts below were absolutely wrong and erroneous in dismissing the case of the plaintiff. Both the Courts below, without applying their judicial mind and without proper assessment of the evidence on record, came to a wrong and erroneous finding in dismissing the suit of the plaintiff. The learned Counsel further submits that it is a suit for declaration with a prayer for recovery of khas possession. Admittedly, the plaintiff No. 2 purchased 4½ kathas of land on 29-6-66 in CS Plot No.88 and subsequently plaintiff No.1 purchased 3 kathas and 2 chataks of land by a registered kabala dated 4-4-1969 from Abdul Majid in CS Plot No.107. The plaintiff Nos.1 and 2 are husband and wife. On the other hand, the defendant purchased 5½ kathas of land in CS Plot No.106. The suit land is situated in CS Plot No.107 comprising 2 kathas and 1 chatak of land out of 3 kathas and 1 chatak of land purchased on the basis of sale deed dated 4-4-69. Admittedly, the title deed is in the name of the plaintiff. The defendant claimed the suit land comprising 2 kathas and 1 chatak which was decided to be transferred in the name of the defendant in a Salish in exchange of 9 x 70 square feet of land in CS Plot No. 106 which belonged to the defendant for constructing a 12 ft. road to go to the house of the plaintiff. The learned Counsel next submits that the basis of the claim of the defendants over the suit land was the so-called Salishnama of exchange executed on 6-6-68. When the defendants managed to record the suit land in CS Khatian No. 107 against which, an appeal under Rule 31 of EBT was pending, at that time their names and the defendants on 10th Poush, 1385 BS forcibly entered into the suit land and dispossessed the plaintiff from the suit land. Both the Courts below, ignoring the legal implication of exchange under section 118 of the Transfer of Property Act came to a wrong and fallacious decision in dismissing the suit of the plaintiff. The section provides that, a transfer of property in completion of an exchange can be made only in the manner provided for the transfer of such property by sale. The learned Counsel also submits that the plaintiff in his deposition, categorically denied that he did not put his signature in the so-called Salishnama to exchange the property of the plaintiff. Since transfer of property by exchange can be made only in the manner provided for transfer of property by sale in the eye of law, the Salishnama has got no legal bearing unless it is a registered instrument. Section 54 of the Transfer of Property Act defined sale as under: "Sale how made Such transfer, in the case of tangible immovable property of the value of one hundred (Taka) and upwards, or in the case of a reversion or other intangible thing, can be made only by a registered instrument." Now, in the absence of any registered deed of exchange in pursuance of the so-called Salishnama, it is absolutely an inoperative document which is denied by the plaintiff. The learned Counsel further submits that both the Courts below committed an error of law in not taking into consideration the legal implication of section 118 of the Transfer of Property Act and acted illegally in dismissing the suit of the plaintiff. The defendant did not acquire any right, title and interest in the suit property because in pursuance of the so-called Salishnama no deed of exchange was actually executed and registered. The observation made by the Courts below that the plaintiff has got no right, title and interest in the suit property is absolutely wrong and perverse, even the defendant did not challenged the title of the plaintiff and if the defendant challenged the title of the plaintiff, in that case there can be no execution of the exchange of deed because unless two persons mutually agree to transfer the ownership of one thing and ownership of another, there can be no exchange according to the definition of exchange under section 118 of the Transfer of Property Act. Rather, the defendant did not acquire any right, title and interest by the so-called Salishnama in the suit property. The learned Courts below did not arrive at any finding that the defendant actually handed over the possession of 9 x 70 square feet of land from CS Plot No. 106 in exchange of the suit land. Admittedly, the defendant purchased 5½ kathas of land in CS Plot No. 106 but an Advocate Commissioner was appointed by the Court at the instance of the plaintiff for measurement of the suit land and also the land of the defendant in CS Plot No. 106, who submitted a report that the defendant's land comprising of 5½ kathas remained intact. Therefore, the assertion made by the defendant and observed by the Courts below that the defendant handed over the possession of 9 x 70 square feet of land from CS Plot No. 106 in exchange of the suit land proved to be false. Finally, the learned Counsel submits that the Courts below did not at all discuss anything about the evidence of Advocate Commissioner and his report. The learned Courts below without consideration of the material evidence on record i.e the Advocate Commissioner's report affecting the merit of the case came to a wrong and fallacious finding in dismissing the suit of the plaintiff which is liable to be interfered by this Court and hence the Rule should be made absolute.

9. On the other hand, the learned Counsel Mr Abdul Quaiyum with Mr Sasti Sarker, appearing on behalf of the defendant-respondent-opposite parties, submits that the concurrent finding of the facts cannot be disturbed in revision under section 115 of the Code of Civil Procedure. The learned Counsel further submits that in furtherance of a Salish, a common fund was raised to purchase the suit land from Abdul Majid. But the plaintiff, taking advantage of the deed in his name, subsequently denied to execute the exchange deed. Next, he submits that both the Courts below concurrently found that the plaintiff was not dispossessed from the suit land. The learned Counsel finally submits that the judgment of affirmance is generally immune to be assailed unless it is vitiated by misreading and non-consideration of the material evidence on record. In the instant suit, there is no misreading and non-consideration, as such no interference is called for in revision by this Court hence, the Rule should be discharged.

<u>10. On a meticulous examination of the evidence on record, papers, documents and Exhibits, it transpires that both the Courts below did not take into consideration the vital legal implication under section 118 of the Transfer of Property Act. The learned Courts below by non-considering the legal aspect of the case has acted illegally in dismissing the suit of the plaintiff. In the eye of law, the so-called Salishnama cannot be treated as an instrument of exchange deed and a valid document and virtually no exchange deed in pursuance of the so-called Salishnama was executed. "Exchange" defined under section 118 of the Transfer of Property Act reads as follows:</u>

<u>"When two persons mutually transfer the ownership of one thing for the owner-ship of another, either thing or both things being money only, the transaction is called an "exchange."</u>

<u>A transfer of property in completion of an exchange can be made only in the manner provided for the transfer of such property by sale."</u>

<u>The defendant claimed the suit property solely on the basis of Salishnama, but in pursuance of the so-called Salishnama as a matter of fact, no deed of exchange was executed. The plaintiff in his evidence emphatically denied that plaintiff Nos. 1 and 2 did not put their signatures in the so-called Salishnama. It is a fictitious paper created by the defendants only to grab the property. The learned Courts below, without applying their judicial mind and without considering the legal bearing of the so-called Salishnama, came to a wrong and erroneous finding in dismissing the suit of the plaintiff which is liable to be interfered by this Court. In this connection, I like to refer the case of Hussain Ahmed Chowdhury alias Ahmed Hossain Chowdhury vs Md Nurul Amin reported. in 47 DLR (AD) 162 wherein it has been held:</u>

<u>"If there is misreading of evidence and non-consideration of some material evidence then it was incumbent on the revisional Court to consider the same and to arrive at a proper finding on the material evidence on record and to finally dispose of the case."</u>

11. Another decision can also be cited which is the case of Habibullah (Md) vs Sher Ali Khan reported in 57 DLR (AD) 55 wherein it is stated:

"The High Court Division while exercising its revisional jurisdiction is competent to reverse the judgment of the Courts below when the same has been made either upon misreading or non-consideration of the material evidence causing failure of justice."

12. In view of the facts and circumstances of the case and also the legal position, the findings of the Courts below are absolutely wrong and erroneous in dismissing the suit of the plaintiff, as such, the judgment and decree passed by the Courts below are liable to be set aside.

13. From the discussion made above and the facts and legal position of the case, the impugned judgment and decree dated 23-11-96 and 31-12-96 respectively passed by the learned Additional District Judge, 6th Court, Dhaka, in Title Appeal No. 239 of 1995 affirming the judgment and decree dated 17-7-95 and 25-7-95 respectively passed by the learned Subordinate Judge, 4th Court Dhaka, in Title Suit No. 244 of 1992 dismissing the suit is hereby set aside and the case of the plaintiff being Title Suit No. 244 of 1992 be decreed.

17. In the result, the Rule is made absolute without any order as to the costs.

Lower Courts records be sent down at once with a copy of the judgment.

End.

caseno: Contempt Petition No, 2 of   2014 with Suo Moto Rule No.2 of 2014.
lawyer:
Aneek R. Huq, Advocate -----For the Petitioner. 
Rais Uddin Ahmed, Advocate -----For the Respondents.
Tanveer Hossain Khan, Advocate -----For the respondent in Suomoto Rule No. 2 of 20 14.
Rafique-ul-Huq, Senior Advocate, Rokanuddin Mahmud, Senior Advocate Ajmalul Hossain QC, Senior Advocate Dr Kazi Akter Hamid and Manzill Murshid, Advocates-Learned -----Amicus Curiaes.
parties:
Oxinel Services Pte. Ltd ------ Petitioner
Vs.
SOM Kalimullah, MD, Bangladesh Telecommunication Company Limited 
(BTCL) and others ------ Respondents
full_judgment:
Md Rezaul Hasan J: This Rule has arisen out of the petition for drawing up contempt proceeding, filed by the petitioner, against the accused-contemner Mr SOM Kalimullah, Managing Director, Bangladesh Telecommunication Company Limited (BTCL) and 3 other officials of BTCL, alleging, amongst other that, this contempt petition is directed against the contemner-opposite parties, for committing contempt of this Court, by not obeying this Court's order dated 23nd of July, 2013 as regards admitting a new Bank Guarantee and adjust with the previous bank Guarantee and to return back the remaining amount to the petitioner; that the contemner-opposite party No. 1 Bangladesh Telecommunication Company Limited (hereinafter referred to as BTCL) is a company incorporated under the Companies Act, 1994 represented by (1) Mr SOM Kalimullah, Managing Director, BTCL, son of late Mohammad Dayem Mia, 28/2, Baily Road, Dhaka-1000, (2) Mr Md Bahadur Ali, Member (Finance) of BTCL, (3) Mr Md Moyez Mollah, Director (Finance & Accounts) of BTCL, and (4) Mr Shah Farid, son of late Saiful Islam, Deputy Director (Accounts-1), Bangladesh Telecommunications Company Limited of 37/E, Eskaton Garden, Telejogajog Bhaban, Dhaka; that the petitioner in the course of business furnished a Bank Guarantee being BG No. IFICI STOCK/ BG/07/2011 dated 4-5-2011 issued by IFIC Bank Limited for Taka 14,000,000 (One crore forty lakh) with BTCL; that during the continuance of the business, without having reasonable cause, BTCL has asked the IFIC Bank Limited to encash the said Bank Guarantee; that the amount (US $ 83,142.33 = BDT 68,17,617) claimed by BTCL was a disputed one and also much less than the amount of the said Bank Guarantee for Taka 1.40 crore; that this petitioner, having no other alternative, sought relief from this Court for justice; that upon hearing the grievance of the petitioner, this Court was pleased to pass order of injunction, on 30-10-2012, against the encashment of the Bank Guarantee by the BTCL; that as the disputed amount was much less than the amount of the Bank Guarantee, the petitioner filed a petition for reducing the said Bank Guarantee; that the petitioner in its petition applied for reducing the amount of the Bank Guarantee upto the disputed amount and to return the rest of the amount to the petitioner; that upon hearing the petition, this Court was pleased to pass an order on 23-7-2013. In the said order it is clearly stated that, "Accordingly the petition to reduce the amount of Bank Guarantee from Taka 14,000,000 is allowed and the petitioner is permitted to submit a fresh Bank Guarantee, containing similar terms and conditions, for Taka 68,17,617 in favour of the BTCL and then to withdraw the existing one and to renew the same from time to time, till the dispute is resolved finally."; that thereafter the said order passed by this Court was communicated to BTCL and IFIC Bank; that having knowledge of the said order, the IFIC Bank Limited issued a fresh Bank Guarantee being No. IFIC/STOCK/BG/05/20 13 dated 1-10-2013 for BDT 68,17,671 (Sixty Eight Lakh Seventeen Thousand Six Hundred and Seventy One Taka) only on A/C of the petitioner complying this Court order and sent the same to BTCL for acknowledgement vide letter No. IFICB/ADV/BG/2013/1973 dated 30-9-2013. But it is very unfortunate that the BTCL had neither cried out this Court's order, nor acknowledged the Bank Guarantee issued by the IFIC Bank Limited; that the conduct and attitude of the BTCL towards the order passed by this Court certainly falls under the offence of Contempt of the court. The said Bank Guarantee and letter for acknowledgement dated 30-9-2013 is annexed herewith this petition as "ANNEXURE: "B" and "B(1)"; that it is pertinent to mention here; that despite the fact that the contemners are very much aware of the concerned order, they have shown utmost disregard to the order passed by this Court and that this conduct amounts to gross Contempt of this Court; that the contemners-opposite parties are guilty of contempt of Court; that almost 6 (Six) months have already been elapsed but the said order by this Court has not been complied with as yet; that, instead of complying the said order, the contemner-opposite parties have sent a letter being No. IAS/8-6/2011/67 dated 30-9-2013 to IFIC Bank Limited by clearly stating that "We would like to inform you that BTCL has objection regarding reduce the amount of Bank Guarantee Taka 14,000,000 (One crore forty lakh) and we will inform you in this regard later on." that BTCL was given reasonable time, by this court, by an order dated 13-6-2014, to submit their objection, if any, within which they did neither appear nor show any cause, and, in the result, this Court was pleased to passed the said order dated 23-7-2013 for the petitioner; that abovementioned reply by BTCL certainly poses a serious challenge to the dignity, authority and majesty of this Court as well as to the rule of law; that the said letter dated 30-9-2013 is annexed herewith as "Annexure: "C"; 15. The leaned amicus curiae, Mr Manzil Murshid, with reference to the Rule, the affidavit offering unconditional apology and the queries made from the Bench, submits that, in the facts and circumstances of this case, the question is whether both the actions and the inactions of the respondents tantamount to contempt of court or not and if it does, whether acceptance of unconditional apology shall advance the cause of justice by ensuring compliance of this Court's Order, shall uphold the rule of law or maintain the dignity of this Court as the custodian of the Constitution and protector of the Rule of law. In the present legal jurisprudence, he submits, "Contempt of Court" is nowhere defined in any statutes of the land. However, in the case of Moazzem Hossain vs State, 35 DLR (AD) 290, 293, Fazle Munim, CJ (as his lordship then was) held that, Contempt may be constituted by any conduct that brings authority of the Court into disrespect or disregard or undermines its dignity and prestige   conduct or action causing obstructions or interfering with the course of justice is contempt. He next submits that, on the other hand, Oswald defined contempt of court as follows: "It may be said to be constituted by any conduct that tends to bring the authority and administration of law into disrespect or disregard or interfere with or prejudice parties, litigant or their witnesses during the litigation" [Contempt of Court, 1910, p.6]. He then adds that, contempt has been classified into three categories in the case of Abdul Halim vs Dr. Md Tareque, reported in 63 DLR 465 (para-13), such

i) Scandalization of court

ii) Disobedience to the orders of the court and

iii) Interference with the due course of justice. In the instant case, he points out, the actions of the contemnor-respondents falls within the mischief of the last two categories.

16. Mr Murshid has also cited the case of Mahbubur Rahman Sikder vs Mujibur Rahman Sikder 35 DLR (AD) 203, wherein it was held that willful disobedience to the order of the court or willful breach of the undertaking given to the court is contempt of Court.
