<u>18. Next, in the facts and circumstances of this case, the learned Amicus Curiae; Mr Murshid has placed series of decisions of Appellate Division in the matter of accepting of apology. In considering whether they apology should be accepted or not, the learned amicus curiae points out that, in the case of Abdul Karim Sarker vs State, 38 DLR (AD) 188, Fazle Munim CJ. (as his lordship then was) mentioned five facts to be considered. They are:</u>

<u>i) whether the appellant appreciated that his act was within the mischief of contempt;</u>

<u>ii) whether he regretted it ;</u>

<u>iii) whether his regret was sincere;</u>

<u>iv) whether it was accompanied with expression of the resolution never to repeat again and</u>

<u>v) Whether he made humble submission to the authority of the court.</u>

In view of the above noted five criteria vis-a-vis their conduct, he continues, the apology of the contemnor-respondents does not seem to be sincere. Rather their apology was a paper apology coming from the pen not from his heart as is observed in the case of LD Jaikwal vs State of UP: AIR 1984 SC 1374, relied upon in 38 DLR (AD) 188. Since, in spite of having full knowledge of the order dated 23-7-13, the respondents have repeatedly obstructed implementation of the said Order in the manner aforesaid, So the apology offered cannot be considered as sincere apology, he submits. Rather, the prayer for unconditional  apology has been made only, after issuance of the  Ride, he points out, to escape the consequences for committing contempt. No other coherent conclusion but this can be drawn in the facts and circumstances of the instant case. The learned amicus curiae, next submits, on this issue,, that in the case of State vs Nazrul Islam, Advocate, 37 DLR 200, (paragraph-7), it was held that a court of law will not be satisfied with a mechanical offer of an unconditional apology unless the contemnor purges himself of the offence of contempt of Court. In the case of AKM A Awal vs The State, 16 DLR (SC) 429 (para-20), it was held that in contempt cases courts have never accepted the apology of a person who does not admit that he has committed .any offence. What is called unconditional apology necessarily means that there should be an admission as to the commission of contempt.

19. Learned amicus curiae Mr Murshid elaborates, that, in spite of being unconditional apology, it was not accepted in the case of Vineet Kumar Mathur vs India: 7 SCC 714 (para-10). In that case it was held that where the violation of the court's order was deliberate and pre-planned indicating certain defiant attitude on the part of the contemnors, the court refused to accept the unconditional apology. In the similar way, he adds to the series, the case of Shanisur Rahman vs Tahera Nargis: 44 DLR (AD) 237 (para-12), per ATM Afzal, J (as his lordship then was), where the apex court has held that apology is an act of contrition and continued further that if the apology is qualified, hesitating and sought to be used as a device to escape the consequences of the contemnor's action, it must be rejected. Here, he submits, the apology has been used as a device to escape the consequence of the contemner's action.

However, in spite of having full knowledge of the  order dated 23-7-13 and received a legal notice  dated 19-11-2013 (Annexure-D), the respondent  Nos.1 and 2 have flatly refused implementation  of the said order, as if it was a matter of their sweet will, and having done so, the respondent  came before this Court with unconditional apology: the intent of which is obvious.. He went on to submit, that the contemnor-respondents did not comply with the order of this Court and have challenged the authority of this Court, and thereby attempted to frustrate the administration of justice and the rule of law. Besides, in this case, the contemnor-respondents, though did not justify their action at the time of seeking apology, however, before offering that apology they have raised  objection as to reduction of BG defying the written order of this court, dated 23-7-13 and paving no heed to the legal notice dated. 19-11-2013: (Annexure-D) demanding compliance., vet not corning up with any explanation as to why the BG  amount should not be reduced, pursuant to this  court's order dated 13-6-2013. Rather they should be punished for repeated disobedience and disregarding the order of this Court as well as for undermining the dignity and majesty of this court. He next adds, the  case of Elders Ltd vs Sunil Chandra Chowdhur  54 DLR 226, (para 5), Syed Amirul Islam (as his  lordship then was), emphasized on the action  rather than intention of the contemnors. His Lordship held that it is the effect of the contemnor's action which is to be taken into consideration in deciding whether contempt was committed  or not. In the instant case the actions and inactions of the contemnor-respondents will also have to be considered in assessing and .determination of the gravity of the offence and the punishment to be awarded. He has, referring to the leading case of Crown vs Moulvi Abdul Rashid Tarkabagish MLA  of Serajgonj 1 DLR (1949) 177, 181, submits  that, Ellis J. while refusing to accept the apology  observed that: "To accept it, would inevitably create the impression that contempt of this kind, however much they may be condemned in theory, can in practice be purged by an expression of regret. Such an impression would be indeed disastrous-and would do nothing to deter others in the position of the Moulvi Sahib from interfering with the course of justice. From our part, we are determined to see that such interference shall be visited with a prompt and deterrent punishment." In the facts and in view of the decisions cited, being clearly applicable to the case in hand, the apology offered by the contemners is liable to be rejected, he concludes.

21. I have heard the learned amicus curiae, perused the order dated 13-6-2013 and 23-7-2013 passed in Arbitration Application No. 27 of 20 12, the petition for drawing, contempt proceeding along with the documents annexed, the Rule, the affidavit filed by the contemners and have also consulted the decision cited above.

22. The facts leading to issuance of the Rule, registered as Contempt Petition No.2 00014 has been recorded herein above as well as the facts and arguments have also been noted, along with the case law referred to in the course of arguments.

23. In the instant case, as revealed from the materials on record, the contemnor-respondents had, full knowledge of both, orders dated 13-6-2013 and 23-7-2013, contents of which have been noted herein above. The contemnors Nos. 1 and 2 have (1) willfully and deliberately violated the orders of this Court; (2) they did not come up to show cause as to why the BG amount should not be reduced, as they were required to, vide order dated 13-6-2013 passed in the Arbitration Application No. 21 of 2012; (3) they have refused to comply with the-order dated 23-7-2013, passed in the said Arbitration Application, reducing the BG amount to the extent that covers the disputed claim, vide, their letter dated 30-9-2013 (Annexure-C) addressed to the Manager, IFIC Bank, Stock Exchange Branch; (4) they did not come up before this court to review or to modify or to set aside the order dated 23-7-2014; (5) they did not go to the Appellate Division against said order, though they could have taken any of these steps if they had minimum fear about the consequence of flouting this court's order; (6) They, were not hesitant to wield their muscle in that they even did not pay any heed to the legal notice dated, 19-11-2013 (Annexure-D), issued upon them (contemners Nos. 1 and 2) demanding that they should comply with the order dated 23-7-2013, passed by this court, quoting the very order in the legal notice, setting forth the facts and law in detail: (7) in doing so, in a repeated fashion, the contemners have flouted the aforesaid orders of the Court and the demand made in the legal notice shewing a degree of arrogance hitherto unknown and gave a damn to this Court's order of binding character and (8) thereby, they have deliberately defied to comply with same.

<u>24. In the facts and circumstances of this case, this Court does not consider their apology, as sincere one. Besides, the apology, in my considered view, has been offered only to escape the consequence of committing contempt of this court, showing utter disrespect and giving clear  damn to the authority and dignity of this court. It is not material in such a case at what stage the apology has been offered, though in the instant case the contemners had four occasions to comply with this court's order, before seeking apology after issuance of the Rule on 23-1-2014.</u>

<u>25. I have also considered the views expressed by the Supreme Court of Pakistan in Re: contempt of court proceedings against General (Reid) Mirza Aslam Beg. It has been held in that case (at paragraph No.8) that, "It is accepted as legal proposition that a Judge who stops summarily (brevimanu), any attempt (contempt) to interfere with the course of justice actually performs his Constitutional and public duty. The duty I of a Judge sitting to punish the Court's own contempt, therefore, means to prevent and stifle any damage to public confidence in an important organ of the State and not the protection of the individual Judges. No personal interest is therefore involved. These are accepted rules in the dispensation of justice in contempt cases. It may be emphasized here that in this context when the Judge takes up the proceedings or acts in response to direct contempt the proceedings are not to take the form of the trial and the same may be concluded brevimanu which means "summarily". It is not thus necessary that there be a written charge, framing of issues, or to hold regular trial or examination No other proof is necessary when it is a case of direct contempt."</u>

26. In the facts and circumstances of this case, I find all the decisions cited above apply to this case. The contemners No. 1 and 2 have, by their repeated defiance have aggravated the offence, gave an impression that they have unquestionable might and power to flout orders of this court giving a damn to it, that they are persons superior to this court and that they are untouchable or that the hands of the court are too short to reach them.

<u>27. Hence, in a case like this, as has been rightly pointed out by the learned amicus curiae, this court should not accept the apology offered as a routine job or without taking into consideration the conduct of the contemners and its effect in defeating the course of justice. In respectful allegiance to the ratio decided in the cases cited above, and being anxious that least it will disseminate an impression that this Court's orders can be flouted at one's sweet will, subject only to taking a bit discomfort in filing an affidavit seeking unconditional apology, will no doubt ridicule this Court and render its authority exists in theory only, resulting to the determination of an ordered society to exist and grow, based on the rule of law. To give way to such arrogant, audacious and repeated acts of defiance, as recorded hereinabove, would no doubt result in indulging many others, of any stratum. of the society, to flout this court's order of binding charter and to allow an era of lawlessness to begin, which this court is oath bound to prevent. This court's voice must be louder enough to be heard by those who are bound to comply with the same.</u>

<u>28. This Court should ensure effectiveness and workability of the administration of justice system and the rule of law to sustain in this country, by awarding appropriate punishment to the offenders, without discrimination as well as let- ting all concerned to hear the voice of this court and to understand that the age old proverb that the hands of this court is long enough to reach any offender. At the same time the admonition of Mr Ellis J (as his lordship then was) should be given weight to, albeit it is too late an stage to realize the truth and accuracy in his lordship's admonition, vide 1 DLR (1949) 177, quoted above,</u>

29. I have considered the conduct of contemner No.2, Mr Shah Farid Deputy Director, (Accounts-I) of BTCL, at the relevant time. He has, in my view, as a subordinate officer, complied with the instruction of the contemner No. I. in writing letter dated 30-9-2013 under ref No. IAS/8-6/2011 167. (Annexure-C).raising objection to the bank concerned and thereby defying to obey this court's order dated 23-7-2013. Similarly, I have also reviewed the conduct of Mr Helal Ahmed, Manager, IFIC Bank, Stock Exchange Branch, 16, Motijheel C/A, Dhaka-1000. In the petition for drawing contempt proceeding it has been stated that he has complied with this court's order. Besides, his explanation that, by his aforesaid letter he has only wanted to know from BTCL if they had taken any step to modify or review or set aside the order dated 23-7-2013, although the expression was not proper, it was candidly admitted. Considering this explanation, along with the statements made in the petition that he has complied with court's order, Urn inclined to give him benefit of doubt. Therefore the apology offered by Mr Shah Farid of BTCL, being a subordinate officer, and Mr Helal Ahmed of IFIC Bank are accepted and they are hereby discharged from the charges, with warning to be cautious in future in their dealings in court matters.

30. However, for the reasons as well as in the facts and circumstances recorded hereinbefore and having considered the degree of proof required to decide such a case along with the nature of this proceedings, I find, on the contrary, that Mr SOM Kalimullah, Managing Director, BTCL, (retired after the proceedings was initiated), is guilty of repeatedly committing the offence of contempt of court. Besides, I have considered the aggravating and extenuating circumstances. I find no extenuating circumstances in this case. The aggravating factors, has been noted herein- above. Moreover Contemner No. 1. instead of prohibiting defiance of this Court's order dated 23-7-2013, knowing lv gave approval to his subordinate Officer to write the letter dated 30-9-2013 (Annexure-C)  for which he alone should be saddled with the liability for committing Contempt of Court.

31. Before patting of, in view of the provisions laid down in Article 111 read with Article 108 of the Constitution, in the facts and circumstances of this case; I further declare, as law forming part of the contempt jurisprudence and jurisdiction, so far as the nature, duty of this court and procedure is concerned that,

(i) This Court should not act mechanically, to make it a routine job, in accepting the apology offered by the contemners, in each and every case. Rather, this Court has to ensure that the letters and spirit of Article 112 and Article 109 of the Constitution are respected and upheld by all quarters, government and, non-government;

(ii) Apology offered may be taken as a mitigating factor, but not to discharge the contemner from their liability, though it is within discretion of this court to decide whether the contemners will be discharged or not and, if not, to ascertain the quantum of the punishment.

(iii) Article 7 read with Articles 39(2), 108, 111 and 112 of the Constitution, considered together and with reference to the scheme of the Constitution, make it abundantly clear that the peoples power to punish the contemner has been invested in the Supreme Court to be exercised by the honorable Judges of this Court, so that the authority, dignity and majesty of this Court is upheld, an ordered society based on the rule of law can exist and the justice is even handedly secured to those who deserve. The people's will reflected in the Articles, referred to hereinabove, should be given effect to by this Court, without any discrimination.

(iv) Once this Courtpasses any binding order in any proceeding then it, in substance, becomes a public order and this Court is legally entrusted to implement the same in the public interest and the rule of law to prevail.

(v) Refusal to obey this Court's order is an explicit challenge to it's authority and is a breach of public order by an arrogant patty having no fear in undermining and in ridiculing the authority of this Court, rendering its judgment and order a nullity and such ,conduct cannot go unpunished with impunity, moreover, in such a caseit is immaterial at what stage the apology is offered.

(vi) That the power of the Supreme court, the Appellate Division and the High Court Division, being the court of records, as embodied under Article 108 of the Constitution of the People's Republic of Bangladesh, cannot be restricted and trammeled by any ordinary legislation including the, Contempt of Courts Act[even if enacted] and their inherent power is elastic, unfettered and not subjected to any time limit. [Following the ratio decided in the case of Pritam Pal v. High Court of Madhya Pradesh, Jabalpur, AIR 1992 SC 904,with reference to Articles 129 and 215 of the Constitution of India].

(vii) "It is accepted as legal proposition that a Judge who stops summarily, (brevimanu), any attempt (contempt) to interfere with the course of justice actually performs his Constitutional and public duty. The duty of a Judge sitting to punish the Court's own contempt, therefore, means to prevent and stifle any damage to public confidence in an important organ of the State and not the protection of the individual Judges. No personal interest is therefore involved. These are accepted rules in ,he dispensation of justice in contempt cases. It may be emphasized here that in this context when the Judge takes up the proceedings or acts in response to direct contempt the proceedings are not to take the form of the trial and the same may be concluded brevimanu which means "summarily". It is not thus necessary that there be a written charge framing of issues, or to hold regular trial or examination No other proof is necessary when it is a case of direct contempt.", as has been held by his lordship Mr Justice Muhammad Asfzal Zullah, the Chief Justice of Pakistan (as his lordship then was) in Re: Contempt of court proceedings against General (Retd) Mirza Aslam Beg.

(viii) Compliance of the Court's order cannot be treated as an extenuating circumstances in all cases, since it is duty of the person concerned to obey the same. However, if the Court is satisfied that non-compliance was not deliberate or international, or that the contemner was not at all aware of the order required to be complied with or if the order to be complied with was lacking clarity to such an extent that the duty to comply with the same was honestly not comprehensible to the person(s) obliged to comply the court's order, then the court should take lenient view.

(ix) Contempt by a person who is a party to the proceedings and contempt by a person who is not such a party, cannot be weighed on the same scale. However, gravity of the offence does not depend on the question as to whether the contemner was a party or act, but upon the nature of the offence.

In the result, the Rule issued in Contempt Petition No.2 of 2014 is made absolute-in-part. The Suo moto Rule No.2 of2014 is discharged.

Order

In view of the applicable law and the findings recorded herein above, Mr SOM Kalimullah, son of late Mohammad Dayem Mia, 28/2, Baily Road, Dhaka-1000, Managing Director, BTCL, at the time of drawing the proceeding, (now retired), is hereby held guilty of committing contempt of this court. His apology is rejected. Further, considering the aggravating factors, hereinbefore recorded at paragraph number 23, he is hereby sentenced to suffer simple imprisonment for a period of 4(four) months, with immediate effect and to pay a fine of Taka 1,00,000 (one lakh), to be deposited in Bangladesh Bank under the concerned head, within 1(one) month of drawing of up of this judgment and order and shall submit affidavit in compliance before this court, within 2(two) weeks thereafter, true copy of the affidavit of compliance shall be submitted to the jail authority. In default he shall suffer civil imprisonment for, further period of 1(one) month.

The execution of the sentence will be processed through the, learned Registrar of this Court and, for that purpose, he is directed to take the convict into his interim custody and to take such decision as he may deem fit, by ordering interim detention or custody through the law enforcing agenciesv.as the situation may require, till the convict is handed over to the concerned Officer-in-charge along with the order for committal.

Let, copy of this order be served upon the learned Registrar of the Supreme court of Bangladesh, along with 3(three) sets of order of committal, in Form No. II (contempt), Appendix- III of the Supreme Court of Bangladesh (High Court Division) Rules, 1973, one to be kept with him, two other copies to be handed over to the Officer-in-charge of the concerned Police Station, one for their record and another to be handed over to the Jail Authority, for execution of this court's order.

Another signed copy of the order of committal be kept with record, for ready reference, if so required.

End.

lawyer:
Md Fazlul Karim with A Wahab, Saifuddin Ahmed, Fawzia Karim Feroze and Khandaker Aminul Haque, Advocates-For Plaintiff-Petitioner.

full_judgment:
A.K. Badrul Huq, J: Seekers of Justice many a time are to take long circuitous routes both on account of hierarchy of Courts and Procedural law. Such seekers of Justice are and can be dragged to the last ladder of the said hierarchy and for receiving Justice they have to pass through a long arduous journey of procedural law. The present matter in hand can be depicted as one in this regard.

2. Redressal of grievance by granting restitution to defendants-opposite parties on allowing Review Miscellaneous Case No. 62 of 1995 laid under Order XLVII, rule 1 read with section 151 of The Code of Civil Procedure (for short The Code) by trial Court and sustained by Appellate Court in Miscellaneous Appeal No. 177 of 1997 prompted plaintiff-petitioner to invoke this Court's Revisional Jurisdiction envisaged under section 115 of The Code on laying Revision Petition.

3. Portrayal of essential facts forming background of this Revision Petition as emerged from Revision Petition, Annexures annexed in Petition, Counter Affidavit filed by defendants-opposite parties, Judgments of Courts below which are under challenge in Revision Petition and paper and documents produced before this Court will be instructive in resolving controversy and those are succinctly stated hereunder:

a. Petitioner as Plaintiff on 5-9-1968 instituted a suit being Title Suit No. 261 of 1968 in Third Court of Munsif (now Assistant Judge), Dhaka for decree of eviction of licensee Defendants Md. Sekander Ali and his son Monu from properties described in Schedule A, B and C. Schedule A, B and C properties will be described hereinafter as suit property.

b. Suit was decreed ex parte on 27-2-1975. Immediate after, Decree was put to execution in Decree Execution Case No. 14 of 1975.

c. Defendant Md. Sekander Ali on 4-3-1975 filed a Petition under Order IX, rule 13 of The Code for setting aside Decree passed ex parte in Title Suit No. 261 of 1968. The Petition had been numbered as Miscellaneous Case No. 54 of 1975.

d. Operation of ex parte decree was stayed by Court on 27-3-1975 on strength of a Petition laid by Defendant Md. Sekandar Ali in Miscellaneous Case No. 54 of 1975.

e. Petitioner in spite of order of stay dated 27-3-1975 on 23-8-1980 evicted Defendant Md. Sekander Ali from suit property. The eviction matter was brought to notice of Court and Court by order dated 30-8-1980 directed petitioner to hand over possession to Defendant Md. Sekander Ali within 24 hours.

f. Appeal being Miscellaneous Appeal No. 400 of 1980 filed by Petitioner against said order dated 30-8-1980 stood dismissed by Appellate Court by Judgment dated 29-9-1980.

g. Civil Revision Petition under section 115 of The Code was carried by Petitioner against the Appellate Judgment. Civil Revision Petition had been numbered as Civil Revision No. 1321 of 1980. Rule issued on Civil Revision Petition was made absolute by High Court Division by Judgment dated 26-2-1991 and Appellate Judgment was set aside. High Court Division recorded direction to dispose of Miscellaneous Case No. 54 of 1975 within one (1) month of receipt of record since said Miscellaneous Case was pending for 15 years.

h. Miscellaneous Case No. 54 of 1975 laid under Order IX, rule 13 of The Code was allowed by Judgment dated 9-9-1991 and ex parte Decree dated 27-2-1975 recorded in Title Suit No. 261 of 1968 was set aside.

i. Defendant Md. Sekander Ali on 28-10-1991 submitted a petition under section 144 read with section 151 of The Code for restitution of possession on suit property. The Petition had been numbered as Miscellaneous Case No. 69 of 1991. Miscellaneous Case was rejected on 19-11-1992 on ground that Petitioner of Miscellaneous case in support of his claim did not produce any document nor did prove his claim in accordance with law.

j. Review Petition under Order XLVII, rule 1 read with section 151 of The Code, thereafter, had been presented on 2-1-1993. Petition was numbered as Review Miscellaneous Case No. 62 of 1995.

k. Learned Senior Assistant Judge, Third Court, Dhaka by Judgment dated 9-7-1997 allowed Review Miscellaneous Case and recorded order for restitution of possession suit property. In recording restitution on allowing Review Miscellaneous Case learned Senior Assistant Judge considered respective case of parties, perused and examined record, pleadings of parties and rendered decision that Petition laid under section 144 of The Code and record of Decree Execution Case No. 14 of 1975 were placed and tagged with the record of the case and since ex parte decree passed in Title Suit No. 261 of 1968 stood set aside in Miscellaneous Case No. 54 of 1975 laid under Order IX, rule 13 of The Code and since suit was restored to its file and number, Petitioner of Miscellaneous Case (Md. Sekander Ali) was entitled to restitution of possession on suit property and predecessor Court through oversight rejected Petition laid under section 144 and section 151 of The Code and by that justice had been impaired seriously. In rendering decision learned Senior Assistant Judge took into account Judgment and orders passed in different proceedings between parties which went upto High Court Division. Learned Senior Assistant Judge, also, took into account Basaratullah being dead his heirs Fazle Karim and others vs Government of Bangladesh and others, 1996 BLD (AD) 9. Learned Senior Assistant Judge directed Opposite Party of Review Miscellaneous Case and Petitioner of this Revision Petition to hand over possession on suit property to petitioner, here Opposite Partyside in Revision Petition by way of restitution.

l. Petitioner felt aggrieved of above adjudication and sought setting aside through a Medium of appeal being Miscellaneous Appeal No. 177 of 1997 before learned District Judge, Dhaka. Learned District Judge, Dhaka by Judgment dated 24-7-2002 dismissed appeal and maintained decisions rendered by learned Senior Assistant Judge, Dhaka with partial modification. In dismissing appeal learned District Judge considered submissions brought home from both sides, examined record and Judgment under challenge in appeal and, also, took into account authorities such as Hamejuddin Howlader and another vs Mainuddin Shaikh and another, 10 DLR 645, Abdul Hamid vs Abdul Jabbar, 34 DLR (AD) 209, Alhaj Md. Ruhul Amin vs Dhaka Municipal Corporation and others, 36 DLR 1 and Keramat Ali Bhuiyan being dead his heirs Shahida Khanom and another vs Ramizuddin Ahmed Bhuiyan, 43 DLR (AD) 58. Learned Appellate Judge recorded following decisions:

(i) Miscellaneous Case No. 54 of 1975 laid under Order IX, rule 13 of The Code was allowed and ex parte decree passed in Title Suit No. 261 of 1968 was set aside and suit was restored to its file and number and all relevant papers and documents had been in record and court which passed order under Review did not take into consideration all those matters and on strength of section 144 of The Code Petitioner of Miscellaneous Case (Present Opposite Partyside) got entitlement to get possession by way of restitution. Learned Appellate Judge, also, rendered decision that Court committed wrong in rejecting Petition for restitution on 19-11-1992 and by that justice had been seriously jeopardised.

(ii) Opposite Party (present Petitioner) of Miscellaneous Case illegally dispossessed Md. Sekander Ali from his lawful possession and Sekander Ali was entitled to get restitution in accordance with law and learned Senior Assistant Judge correctly passed order dated 9-7-1997.

(iii) Review Miscellaneous Case was not barred by limitation. Learned Appellate Judge modified partially order of learned Senior Assistant Judge dated 9-7-1997 in the terms that Petitioner to Miscellaneous Case (present Opposite Partyside) would get restitution through Court.

4. Feeling still dissatisfied, Petitioner approached this Court in this Revision Petition.

5. Md. Sekander Ali having been dead, his heirs, sons, daughters and wife have been substituted in proceedings and heirs are Opposite Party Nos. 1-8 in this Revision Petition.

6. Statements contained in Revision Petition have been controverted from side of Opposite Parties on Presentation of a Counter Affidavit. Statements made in Counter Affidavit are that Defendants filed Miscellaneous Case No. 54 of 1975 under Order IX, rule 13 of The Code for setting aside ex parte decree dated 27-2-1975 passed in Title Suit No. 261 of 1968 and an application for stay of all further proceeding of Title Execution Case No. 14 of 1973 was filed in said Miscellaneous Case No. 54 of 1973 and Court allowed application and stayed all further proceeding of Title Execution Case No. 14 of 1975 by its order dated 27-3-1975. But Petitioner suppressing the said order of stay managed to evict Defendant side from properties of A, B and C schedule of plaint on 23-8-1980. Executing Court detected fraud practised upon Court by Petitioner and directed petitioner to hand over possession on properties described in A, B and C schedule of plaint within 24 hours by its order dated 30-8-1980. All those orders were in record but when judgment dated 19-11-1992 was passed in Miscellaneous Case No. 69 of 1991 Petitioner separated those orders from record and, as such, Court found that opposite parties did not file those orders and rejected said Miscellaneous Case and, thus, application for Review was allowed when those orders were located in record.

7. Mr Md. Fazlul Karim along with Mr A Wahab, Mr Saifuddin Ahmed, Ms Fawzia Karim Firoze and Mr Khandaker Aminul Haque, learned Counsels appeared for Petitioner. Opposite Parties are represented by Mr Khandaker Mahbubuddin Ahmed with Mr SM Munir, learned Counsels.

8. Sustainability of decisions recorded by courts below has been assailed raising five Branches of contentions and those contentions have been repelled from side of Opposite Parties.

9. First Branch of contention pressed into service is in respect of scope of section 144 of The Code. Restitution can be sought by any party entitled to any benefit by way of restitution before Court of first instance when a decree is varied or reversed and unless a decree is varied or reversed, question of restitution does not arise since decree had not been varied or reversed by superior Court, it is contended. In support of contention reliance has been put on U Maung Gyee vs U Ba Tin, AIR 1928 Rangoon 293, Gopal Paroi vs Swarna Bewa, AIR 1931 Calcutta 14, Kundan Kishanlal vs Board of Revenue Uttar Pradesh at Allahabad and others, AIR 1972 Allahabad 184, Ashutosh Nandi and another vs Kunda Kamini Dasi and others, 33 CWN 908 and Industrial Electric Corporation Ltd vs Kalimuddin Ahmed and others, 21 DLR 951.

10. Contentions so raised have been repelled from side of Opposite Parties in putting forward rival contentions that setting aside and reversal got similar meaning and even if section 144 of The Code is not attracted, restitution can be very much made in invoking inherent jurisdiction of Court under section 151 of The Code.

11. Rival contentions advanced from both sides may now be addressed.

12. The word "Restitution" has not been defined in The Code. The word "Restitution" stated in Wharton's Law Lexicon, Fourteenth Edition is hereunder:

"The restoring anything unjustly taken from another; also putting in possession of lands or tenements who had been unlawfully disseised of them."

13. In Black's Law Dictionary, Sixth Edition, Restitution has been stated thus:

"An equitable remedy under which a person is restored to his or her original position prior to loss or injury, or placed in the position he or she would have been, had the breach not occurred, Act of restoring; restoration; restoration of anything to its rightful owner; the act of making good or giving equivalent for any loss, damage or injury; and indemnification."

14. In Corpus Juris Secundum (CJS) 77 Restitution is defined in the following terms:

"as meaning the act of restoring; restoration; restoration of anything to its rightful owner; act of making good, or of giving an equivalent for any loss, damage, or injury; indemnification; the action of restoring or giving back something to its proper owner; that of making restoration to one for loss or injury previously inflicted

At common law the word "restitution" was employed to denote the return or restoration of a specific thing or condition, but in modern usage restitution may go beyond the act of returning the thing taken, and in its broad sense, is not confined to the return of something of which one has been deprived, but includes compensation for loss, damage, or injury done to another.

15. In Halsbury's Laws of England law of restitution has been couched in the following language:

Where a wrongful or irregular execution has been set aside or where a judgment or order has been reversed after execution thereon has taken place, restitution will be made to the successful party. The order setting aside the execution or reversing the judgment or order should provide for this; and if it does execution may issue upon it in the ordinary course. If the order does not so provide, another order may be made, or a writ called a writ of restitution be issued commanding the judgment-creditor to restore the property or pay over the proceeds of sale.

<u>16. Restitution is, thus, restoration of anything to a person from which it was taken away earlier, return of something of which one has been deprived, act of making good for loss, damage and injury.</u>

17. Section 144 of The Code postulates that where and insofar as a decree is varied or reversed, the Court of first instance shall, on the application of any party entitled to any benefit by way of restitution or otherwise, cause such restitution to be made as will, so far as may be, place the parties in the position which they would have occupied but for such decree or such part thereof as has been varied or reversed; and, for this purpose, the Court may make any orders, including orders for the refund of costs and for the payment of interest, damages, compensation and mesne profits, which are properly consequential on such variation or reversal.

18. The principle of restitution is that on the variance or reversal or setting aside of a judgment, order or decree when the person deprived of right to any property through an erroneous judgment he may be entitled to restitution of his right or property and that it is the duty and obligation of a Court to do justice to seekers of justice.

19. The judicial Committee of Privy Council while examining the question under section 144 of The Code in Jai Berham vs Kedar Nath Marwari, AIR 1922 (PC) 269=LR 491A 351 observed:

It is the duty of the Court to place parties in the position which they would have occupied but for the wrong decree.

The Judicial Committee then observed:

The duty of the Court to grant restitutk n arises even outside the provisions of section 144.

The Judicial Committee further observed:

"Nor indeed does this duty arise merely under the said section and it is inherent in the general jurisdiction of the Court to act rightly and fairly according to the circumstances towards all the parties involved."

20. The Supreme Court of India in Lal Bhagwant Singh vs Sri Kishen Das, AIR 1953 SC 136 in dealing on Doctrine of Restitution observed:

The Doctrine of restitution is that on the reversal of a judgment the law raises an obligation on the party to the record, who received the benefit of the erroneous judgment, to make restitution to the other party for what he had lost and it is the duty of the Court to enforce that obligation unless it is shown that restitution would be clearly contrary to the interests of justice.

21. Our Appellate Division, also, dealt with the scope and applicability of section 144 of The Code in Abdul Hamid vs Abdul Jabbar, 34 DLR (AD) 208. Appellate Division in the said case considered good number of authorities on section 144 as well as section 151 of The Code. Appellate Division, also, considered the decision of The Judicial Committee of Privy Council in Jai Berham vs Kader Nath Marwari (Supra). The observation of The Appellate Division is couched in following language:

'Restitution' simply means restoration of something to a person from which it was taken away earlier under an erroneous judgment of a court. Question of restitution arises when the erroneous judgment of the court is varied, reversed or set aside. Section 144 of The Code which provides for restitution says that restitution thereunder is available when a decree is varied or reversed.

22. Restitution, if not covered under section 144 of The Code, can be, also, made in exercise of inherent power under section 151 of The Code. Section 151 of The Code does not formulate any new doctrine but only gives a legislation recognition of the well known doctrine and principle that every court has inherent power to act ex debitio justitiae and to do that real Justice for the administration of which alone it exists. It is always to be remembered that under inherent power court acts ex debitio justitiae according to equity, justice and good conscience of a cause and in consonance with fundamental principles of Judicial procedure. Justice is the pursuit and end of all law. Justice is divine and all procedure and technicality must bend to the cause of justice.

23. The Calcutta High Court in Birendra Nath Basu Thakur and another vs Surendra Kumar Basu Thakur and others, 44 CWN 438 considered the power of Court to direct restitution in inherent Jurisdiction under section 151 of The Code. Calcutta High Court relying on the Privy Council case of Jai Berham vs Keder Nath Marwari (Supra) held:

The power of a court to direct restitution is inherent in the Court itself. It rests on the principle that a court of justice is under a duty to repair the injury done to a party by its acts.

24. In Abdul Hamid vs Abdul Jabbar (Supra) our Appellate Division, took into account various authorities of Indian Jurisdiction and held:

Section 144 is not exhaustive and it only defines the procedure for restitution in the case of a reversal of a decree. In the case of reversal of an order the same remedy should be given by the court in the exercise of its inherent power under section 151 of The Code. The inherent power of the Court should be exercised at its discretion, according to the merit of the case. This discretionary power cannot be exercised when restoration, if allowed, will run counter to the interest of justice.

In the case restitution was sought under section 144 of The Code and Appellate Division treated the said Petition under section 144 of The Code to be one under section 151 of The Code to meet the ends of justice.

25. In the interest of justice in the case of variance, reversal or setting aside an order /judgment/decree restitution can be very much made under inherent power as envisaged in section 151 of The Code. To put it differently, in the case of setting aside, variance and reversal of judgment remedy of restitution, if cannot be granted under section 144 of The Code, should be given by court in the exercise of inherent power under section 151 of The Code.

26. I shall now address myself to authorities relied upon from side of Petitioner. Before adverting to authorities it is to be kept in view that a decision is only an authority for what it actually decides. It cannot be quoted for a proposition that may seem to follow from it. Every judgment must be made applicable to particular fact and generality of expression that may be found cannot be regarded as proposition of whole law but must be regarded as governed and qualified by particular facts of case in which such expression occurs. It is neither desirable nor permissible to pick out a word or a sentence from the Judgment divorced from the context of the question under consideration and treat it to be complete law. Keeping in view this proposition of law authorities cited may now be approached and considered.

27. In U Mating Gyee vs U Ba Tin, AIR 1928 Rangoon 293, Principle enunciated is that section 144 of The Code gives no discretion to learned Judge and restitution should be ordered as a matter of course in order to bring about status-quo ante.

28. In Gopal Paroi vs Swarna Bewa, AIR 1931 Calcutta 14, Principle propounded is that section 144 of The Code only applies where a decree is "varied or reversed" and it is perfectly certain that a decree is only varied or reversed by a superior Court on appeal or on revision or it may be, on reference and if a decree is set aside either by a proceeding in suit itself or if it is set aside by a decree in another suit altogether or if, without being set aside by such a decree, is superseded those are matters which are not within the words of section 144.

29. In Kundan Kishanlal vs Board of Revenue, Uttar Pradesh at Allahabad and others, AIR 1972 Allahabad 184 principle settled is that where an ex parte decree is set aside, it cannot be said that decree has been varied or reversed. A decree can be varied or reversed on appeal or in some similar proceedings. When an ex parte decree is set aside, a new decree is passed, thereafter, and that decree cannot be said to be result of any variation or reversal of any prior decree. It is further stated that a restitution in such a case may be claimed under section 151 of The Code. In the case it is, also, settled that a decree can be varied or reversed in exercise of inherent power under section 151 of The Code.

30. In Ashutosh Nandi and another vs Kundal Kamini Dasi and others, 33 CWN 908 principle emerged is that provision in section 144 of The Code that Court which is to make restitution is Court of firs instance implies a Court decree of which is reversed by a Court of Appeal and section 144 only refers to cases where a decree of Court of first instance is reversed on appeal or revision.

31. In Industrial Electric Corporation Ltd vs Kalimuddin Ahmed and others, 21 DLR 951 principle that has been enunciated is that principle of restitution whether based on section 144 or section 151 of The Code is that when a Judgment is reversed, the law raises an obligation on the party who received benefit on erroneous judgment to make good to other party that very thug which he had obtained from him. Under such circumstances it is duty of Court to enforce that obligation unless it is shown that that would be contrary to real justice of case. It has been further stated that there are circumstances where restitution can be granted which is not strictly covered by provision of section 144 of The Code of Civil Procedure in exercise of inherent powers of Court. Lal Bhagwant Singh vs Sri Kishen Das AIR 1953 SC 136 had been referred to and relied upon in the case.

<u>32. From above authorities, principles emerged is that restitution can be sought and made when a decree obtained by a Decree-Holder stands varied, reversed and set aside and restitution can be very much granted on strength of section 144 of The Code and, also, on strength of inherent power envisaged under section 151 of The Code. I am in complete agreement with principles enunciated in above authorities. But I am afraid that petitioner cannot derive any benefit from the aforesaid authorities.</u>

<u>33. In case in hand ex parte decree recorded on 27-2-1975 in Title Suit No. 261 of 1968 stood set aside in Miscellaneous Case No. 54 of 1975 laid by defendant Md. Sekander Ali. Decree passed since stood set aside, possession of parties was required to be placed to that position before ex parte decree that is to bring about status-quo ante Md. Sekander Ali on presentation of petition under sections 144 and 151 of The Code sought restitution of possession on suit property. Learned Trial Judge on a consideration of proceedings between parties, different orders, fact and circumstances of case recorded order of restitution on allowing Review Miscellaneous Case and said decision recorded by learned Senior Assistant Judge was maintained by Appellate Judge canvassing reasons. No exception can be taken to the decisions rendered and conclusion reached by the Judges.</u>

34. Second Branch of contention brought home from side of Petitioner is that Review Miscellaneous Case was barred by limitation in as much as order under review was dated 19-11-1992 and Review Miscellaneous Case was registered as Miscellaneous Case No. 62 of 1995 and case stood barred on the face of record.

35. Countering the said contention it has been contended from side of Opposite Parties that Review Miscellaneous Case had been filed on 2-1-1993 and that was very much within time fixed by law and not barred by limitation.

<u>36. Annexure-C to Revision Petition is Petition under Order XLVII, rule 1 read with section 151 of The Code. On careful scrutiny it appears that Petition was filed on 2-1-1993 but it was registered as Miscellaneous Case No. 62 of 1995. It is not known what was reason for registering Miscellaneous Case in the year 1995. Mere registration of case in year 1995 cannot make Opposite Parties out of Court on point of limitation when Petition under Order XLVII, rule 1 and section 151 of The Code had been presented on 2-1-1993 within period of limitation fixed by law which is 90 days as provided in Article 173 of The Limitation Act.</u>

37. Third Branch of contention pressed is on Jurisdiction of Judge to review order under Review Miscellaneous Case. It has been emphatically submitted from side of Petitioner that Judge who passed order under review was not the same Judge who reviewed order. Order XLVII, rule 2 of The Code and Alhaj Md. Ruhul Amin vs Dhaka Municipal Corporation and others 36 DLR 1 had been referred to in support of contention.

38. Order XLVII, rule 2 of The Code is quoted hereunder:

"2. An application for review of a decree or order of a Court, not being High Court Division, upon some ground other than the discovery of such new and important matter or evidence as is referred to in rule 1 or the existence of a clerical or arithmetical mistake or error apparent on the face of the decree, shall be made only to the judge who passed the decree or made the order sought to be reviewed; but any such application may, if the Judge who passed the decree or made the order has ordered notice to issue under rule 4, sub-rule (2), proviso (a), be disposed of by his successor."

39. Reading of Order XLVII, rule 2 of The Code demonstrates that if ground for review is discovery of such new and important matter or evidence as is referred to in rule 1 or existence of a clerical or arithmetical mistake or error apparent on face of decree, then review will lie to Judge who passed decree or made order as well as to his successor in office. But if review is made on any other ground then it shall be made only to Judge who passed decree or order sought to be reviewed. It is, thus, grounds which are material for forum of presentation of Review Petition. The above view adopted has been, also, expressed in Paragraph No. 24 in Judgment delivered in Alhaj Md. Ruhul Amin vs Dhaka Municipal Corporation and others, 36 DLR 1 on which reliance has been put and great emphasis has been given from side of Petitioner, though, the same is of no assistance to Petitioner. Paragraph No. 24 is quoted hereunder:

"24. Rule 2 however has qualified the application of rule 1 as far as the ground and forum for review are concerned. If the ground for review is the discovery of such new and important matter or evidence as is referred to in rule 1 or the existence of a clerical or arithmetical mistake or error apparent on the face of the decree, then the review will lie to the Judge who passed the decree or made the order as well as to his successor in office. Review on these grounds are entertainable and disposable by the Court which passed the decree or made the order. The presence or absence of the original Judge who passed the decree or made the order is immaterial. But if an application for review of a decree or order is made on any other ground, then rule 2 provides that the said application "shall be made only to the Judge who passed the decree or made the order sought to be reviewed." So, it is the ground of review which makes all the differences in the forum for review. If, however, the Judge who passed the decree or made the order has ordered notice to issue under rule 1, sub-rule (2), proviso (a), the application for review may be disposed of by his successor."

40. Under Order XLVII, rule 1 of The Code a review can be made when there is error apparent on the face of the record.

<u>41. Review was sought canvassing ground that all papers were kept in record and order passed by Court directing restitution of suit property within 24 hours had been, also, in record and Court through oversight did not take into stock of above and there had been error apparent on face of record. Omission to advert to apply mind to papers already on record and failure to take into consideration those papers is an error which is very much apparent on face of record. Rule 2 of Order XLVII of The Code is not at all attracted in case of Opposite Parties. May be Petition had not been articulated properly but bad pleading cannot oust a litigant public seeking justice from Court. It is always to be kept in view that it is the substance and not the form which is to be looked at and considered. Moreover, Review Petition had been presented to Judge who passed order under Review and Judge having been transferred, successor Judge disposed of Review matter. There was, as such, no want of Jurisdiction on part of learned Senior Assistant Judge in disposing of Review Miscellaneous Case. Proposition of law propounded in Alhaj Md. Ruhul Amin vs Dhaka Municipal Corporation and others (Supra).</u>

42. Bar of Order XLVII, rule 8 of The Code in disposal of restitution matter along with Review Miscellaneous Case has been Fourth Branch of contention. Contention has been pressed that Review matter was required to be disposed of after making note in Register but Court at once heard original case ie restitution matter. Gour Krishna Sarkar and another vs Nilmadhab Saha and others, AIR 1923 Calcutta 113 has been relied upon on the above contention.

43. Repelling said contention it is contended from side of Opposite Parties that Order XLVII, rule 8 of The Code is no bar in hearing original matter ie restitution matter, while disposing Review matter.

<u>44. Review is allowed on reviewing Judgment/Order or Decree under review. Order passed by learned Senior Assistant Judge was sought to be reviewed and only point that survived for determination before Reviewing Court was whether the order dated 19-11-1992 rejecting Miscellaneous Case No. 69 of 1991 laid under sections 144 and 151 of The Code demanded review or not and that matter could be decided and disposed of in disposing of Review Miscellaneous Case. Rules, procedures and technicalities of law cannot stand in the way in administration of justice and seekers of Justice cannot be denied justice on the plea of breach of rules, procedural hurdles and technicalities. It is well settled that principal object behind all legal formalities is to safeguard paramount interest of justice and mere technicalities unless offering an insurmountable hurdle should not be allowed to defeat the ends of justice. No insurmountable hurdle transpired in deciding the restitution matter in disposing Review Miscellaneous Case. Authority placed got no manner of application in the facts and circumstances of the case and, as such, I do not like to make an idle parade of discussing the same.</u>

45. Fifth and Last Branch of contention advanced from side of Petitioner is that Decree of eviction had been passed only in respect of property of Schedule-C to plaint and not in respect of properties of Schedule-A and B but Opposite Parties sought restitution in respect of properties of all the three schedules ie Schedule A, B and C and restitution, thus, cannot be granted in respect of properties of Schedule A and B.

46. Said contention has been countered from side of Opposite, Parties pressing into service contention that Writ of Delivery of possession was in respect of Schedule-A, B and C properties and Petitioner got possession over Schedule-A, B and C properties and decree had been varied, reversed and set aside in respect of Schedule-A, B and C properties and, as such, Opposite Parties are entitled to restitution in respect of Schedule-A, B and C -properties. Challenge has been thrown by Opposite Parties to Petitioner to substantiate the plea on producing copy of Writ of Delivery of possession and copy of Execution Case showing that decree was put into execution only in respect of Schedule-C property and not in respect of Schedule A and B properties and Petitioner got possession only of 'C' schedule property.

47. In order to get myself satisfied from which property Opposite Parties were evicted and Petitioner got possession and what schedule property had been stated in Decree Execution Case. I wanted papers from the Petitioner side but those papers could not be produced before me.

48. In Revision Petition plaint of Title Suit No. 261 of 1968 has been annexed as Annexure-A. On examination of the Plaint it transpires that there are three (3) schedules, Schedule A, B and C and decree of eviction had been sought in properties described in Schedule 'A' 'B' and 'C' and there is no such averment that though Schedule-A and B had been given, actually eviction was sought only in respect of Schedule-C property. Reliefs sought are hereunder:

"a) a decree for eviction of the defendants in favour of the plaintiff and against the defendants;

b) delivery of vacant possession of the suit land and the suit but therein to the plaintiff after removing all obstacles and obstructions of the defendants there from;

c) all costs of the suit;

d) other ancillary relief or reliefs which the plaintiff is legally or equitably entitled to."

49. From certified copy of judgment of ex parte decree which has been produced before me from side of Petitioner it appears that decree was in respect of whole properties of Three Schedules. The ordering portion is quoted hereunder:

"Order

that the suit be decreed ex preterit cost.

The defendant be evicted from the suit premises after removing all obstructions there from.

<u>50. The judgment itself manifests that the Decree of eviction was in respect of suit premises and suit premises comprises of Schedule-A, B and C properties and Defendant Md. Sekander Ali, the predecessor of present Opposite Party Nos. 1-8 stood evicted from suit premises in execution of decree and since the decree recorded in Title Suit No. 261 of 1968 stood set aside, reversed and varied in respect of properties described in Schedule-A, B and C, Opposite Parties who are legal heirs of Md. Sekander Ali are entitled to have restitution of possession in respect of A, B and C schedule properties.</u>

51. All Five Branches of contentions pressed into service from the side of Petitioner could not impress me and those having been devoid of any substance stand ruled out.

52. Examination of decision, reason and conclusion reached by learned Senior Assistant Judge and maintained by learned Appellate Judge with modification it does not indicate that those suffer from any illegality, legal infirmity, perversity and error of law. The decisions rendered and reason assigned in leading to decision and conclusion reached appear to have been informed by tradition and methodised by analogy.

53. In exercising Revisional Jurisdiction under section 115 of The Code two conditions are to be satisfied:

i. There must be an error of law resulting in an error in the decision and

ii. By that error a failure of justice has been occasioned.

Mere error of law is not the only ground for interference in Revisional Jurisdiction under section 115 of The Code and along with error of law it is to be demonstrated that a failure of justice has been occasioned by that error of law and only then interference by this Court can be called for, otherwise not. It has already been posited that decisions rendered and conclusion reached by Courts below neither appear to have suffered from error of law nor a failure of justice seem to have been occasioned.

54. The inevitable conclusion that flows is that rule arising out of Civil Revision Petition under section 115 of The Code is without any merit and the same, thus, fails. Rule stands discharged.

55. Order staying operation of the Judgment/Order dated 24-7-2002 recorded by learned District Judge, Dhaka in Miscellaneous Appeal No. 177 of 1997 affirming Judgment and order dated 9-7-1997 passed by Senior Assistant Judge, Third Court, Dhaka in Miscellaneous Case No. 62 of 1995 stand vacated.

56. Regard being had to fact and circumstances of the case I direct the parties to bear their respective cost.

Copy of this Judgment be transmitted to courts below.

End.

caseno: Writ Petition Nos. 6433-39 of 2003 and 5950 of 2003
lawyer:
Mahbubur Rahman with Ashik Al Jalil, Advocates—For the Petitioner. 

Fida M Kamal, Additional Attorney-General with Syeda Afsar Jahan, Assistant Attorney-General—For the Respondents.
parties:
Cab Express (BD) Ltd ------- Petitioner
vs
Commissioner of Customs and others ------- Respondents
full_judgment:
Mirza Hussain Haider J: In all these Rules the question raised is whether assessment of customs duty on the basis of an SRO issued subsequent to the opening of the Letters of Credit is without lawful authority. Since common questions of law and fact are involved in all these Rules the same are taken up together for hearing and disposed of by this one judgment.

2. The case of the petitioners in all these writ petitions is that, they opened their respective Letters of Credit being inspired by SRO No. 56-Ain /99 /1780/Cus dated 16-3-1999 issued under section 19 of the Customs Act, 1969 and section 14(1) of the VAT Act, 1991 by the National Board of Revenue allowing import of Taxi Cabs upon fulfilment of certain conditions incorporated in the said SRO at an exemption of customs duty above 7.5%. The petitioners pursuant to the said SRO upon fulfilling all the conditions incorporated therein imported the vehicles as mentioned in their respective Writ Petitions vide their respective Letters of Credit from India. The petitioners on different dates from 19th March, 2003 to 3rd July, 2003 got their consignments inspected by the approved PSI agents. On arrival of all the consignment at Benapole land port the petitioners submitted their concerned Bills of Entry along with all necessary papers on different dates from 2-9-2003 to 13-10-2003 for assessment of customs duty and release of the goods on the basis of the aforesaid SRO No. 56 dated 16-3-1999.

3. The writ petitioners in their respective petitions stated that earlier the customs authority for unknown reasons refused to accept the Bills of Entry from the importers of taxicab and, as such, delay was caused in submitting the Bills of Entry for release of the vehicles. However, upon receipt of the said Bills of Entry the customs authority by their impugned orders, demanded customs duty and other charges on the basis of SRO No. 158- Ain /2003 /2010/Cus dated 12-6-2003 and refused to assess and release the vehicles on the basis of SRO No. 56 dated 16-3-1999.

4. Being aggrieved by and dissatisfied with the orders of the customs authority the petitioners obtained these Rules in all these writ petitions.

5. The respondent No. 1 i.e. the Commissioner of Customs, Customs House, Benapole. Jessore entered appearance and contested these Rules by filing affidavit-in-opposition through the learned Assistant Attorney-General, The contention of the respondents are that the writ petitioner's goods arrived at Benapole land port between 8-5-2003, to 12-5-2003 i.e. 1 (one) month and 4 (four) days before the relevant SRO No. 56 of 1999 was amended by SRO No. 158 dated 12-6-2003. Although the petitioners had ample time to present the Bills of Entry before SRO No.158 was issued but the petitioners submitted their respective Bills of Entry subsequent to issuance of SRO No. 158 of 2003, as such, the petitioners' goods are liable to be assessed on the basis of the said SRO which was prevalent on the date of submission of their Bills of Entry as contemplated in section 30 of the Customs Act 1969. In the present cases since the rate of duty was subsequently amended by SRO No. 158 of 2003 issued on 12-6-2003 and the Bills of Entry were presented on 21-6-2003 i.e. after the said SRO came into force, duty should be assessed on the basis of the subsequent SRO No. 158. Further contention of the said respondent is that the importers were probably waiting for a favourable change in the budget but when they found the budget unfavourable they took the plea that they are entitled to get benefit of the previous SRO since the Letters of Credit have been opened under the said SRO by which a vested right has already been created in their favour. The petitioners have not submitted their Bills of Entry prior to the amendment of SRO No. 56 by SRO No. 158 dated 12-6-2003 though the goods arrived much earlier and, as such, they cannot claim any vested right. The contention of the respondent is that to claim a vested right the petitioners have a vested duty of submitting the Bills of Entry at the earlier possible date subsequent to arrival of the goods in Bangladesh. It is contended that the petitioners had sufficient time prior to issuance of the amended SRO No.158 dated 12-6-2003 but they did not avail the opportunity of submitting their respective Bills of Entry and, as such, they cannot take the plea of vested right now.

6. Mr Mahbubur Rahman, the learned Senior Advocate appearing with Mr Ashik Al Jalil, the learned Advocate for the petitioners in all these writ petitions, submits that the impugned orders passed by the customs authority are illegal and without lawful authority as the import was made pursuant to the special benefit granted by SRO No. 56 of 1999 to the importers of taxicab for the purpose of meeting the urgent cry of the public in the public transport sector in the Metropolitan area because of the vacuum created by banning two strokes 3-wheeler auto rickshaws plying in the Metropolis and because of the rapid growth of the population in those areas. Such facilities were given to the importers by the said SRO to meet the growing public demand in the transport sector. He further submits that in the said SRO the authority has incorporated certain terms and conditions which were required to be fulfilled for availing the facilities for exemption of customs duty granted in the said SRO. According to him, upon completion of all the terms and conditions of the SRO No. 56 dated 16-3-1999 and the goods having been inspected by the approved PSI agents, who found the same to be in accordance with the requirements and the goods having reached Bangladesh prior to issuance of the subsequent SRO No. 158 of 2003 but the petitioner being unable to present their respective Bills of Entry because of the refusal to accept the same by the customs authority for the reasons best known to them and because the customs authority having received the Bills of Entry in accordance with section 79(2) of the Act, now they cannot deny the benefit of SRO No. 56 dated 16-3-1999 to the petitioners. According to him the subsequent SRO having reduced the rate of exemption and putting a bottom line in the CC of the taxicab the same is not at all applicable for the consignments which reached Bangladesh much earlier than the issuance of the subsequent SRO. In this respect he relied on the decisions in Hannan case, reported 42 DLR (AD) 167. Ahmed Hossain's case reported in 48 DLR (AD) 199 and Khairul Bashar's case reported in 50 DLR 225. Accordingly, he submits that the importers upon fulfilling all the requirements of SRO No. 56 of 1999 having opened the Letters of Credit and having brought the goods in the Benapole Land Port prior to issuance of SRO No. 158 of 2003 a vested right has been created to get their goods assessed under the earlier SRO. He submits that the authority having promised by SRO No. 56 dated 16-3-1999 to give certain facilities to the importers upon fulfilling the terms and conditions incorporated therein, now they cannot go back upon it i.e. on their promise, as the same is binding upon them and such binding is termed as promissory estopped. Mr Rahman submits that his view is fully supported by the decision given in the case of Commissioner of Customs and others vs Monohor Ali and others reported in 2003 BLD (AD) 59 = 8 BLC (AD) 87. While making his submission Mr Rahman drew our attention to a judgment delivered by one of the Benches of this Court, in Writ Petition No. 4603 of 2003 (wherein one of us is a party) and submits that upon accepting the view taken in Monohor Ali's case their Lordships made the Rule absolute. Accordingly, he submits that the petitioners in all these Rules being on the same footing are entitled to get the same result.

7. Mr Rahman in addition to his above submissions emphatically submitted on section 19 of the Customs Act. According to him, in all these Rules the questions raised relate to exemption of duty granted under section 19 of the Customs Act. In this regard he further submits that under no circumstances the date of submission of Bills of Entry will be the relevant factor for assessment of customs duty because SRO No. 56 dated 16-3-1999 was issued in special circumstances for special purpose on public interest and gave some special terms and conditions to be fulfilled to get benefit of the said SRO. The actions of the importers upon fulfilling all the terms and conditions under such special circumstances entitles them to get the facilities and incentives given in the said SRO. Lastly, Mr Rahman submits that upon fulfilment of all the terms and conditions incorporated in the concerned SRO No. 56 of 1999 the taxicabs imported by the petitioners now cannot be used for any other purpose other than the purpose for which those were manufactured and imported. Accordingly, he submits that at least for ends of justice the petitioners should be allowed to avail the facilities of exemption granted in the said SRO No. 56 of 1999.

8. On the other hand, Mr Fida M Kamal, the learned Additional Attorney-General appearing for respondent No. 1, submits that since all the Bills of Entry in all the writ petitions were submitted after the amended SRO No. 158 dated 12-6-2003 came into force the customs authority, according to section 30 of the Act, rightly passed the impugned orders refusing to assess customs duty on the basis of earlier SRO No. 56 dated 16-3-1999. He next submits that the Assistant Commissioner issued all the impugned orders, which are under challenge in all the writ petitions, so the alternative remedy in the form of appeal was the appropriate forum available for all the writ petitioners and having not availed the forum of appeal all these writ petitions are not maintainable. Thirdly, he submits that the price certified by the approved PSI agents are not binding upon the customs authority because the PSI facilities are given under section 25A of the Customs Act and in all these cases the matters relate to exemption of duty under section 19 of the Act. So, the question of availing CRF facilities provided under section 25A does not attract these cases. According to him, the CRF certificate is not in dispute in these cases rather, the question of exemption and the rate of duty are in dispute in all these rules so under no circumstances the Monohor Ali case will be applicable. According to him, since Monohor Ali case is not applicable, the question of vested right is also not a matter to be decided in these cases, mere opening of Letters of Credit during the subsistence of the previous SRO, will not create any vested right so far the applicability of the rate of duty is concerned. According to him, so long section 30 read with section 30A of the Customs Act with a non-obstante clause subsists, passing of the impugned orders are justified and, as such, the rate of duty applicable on the basis of the rate prevailing on the date of submissions of the Bills of Entry, regardless of the date of opening of the Letters of Credit, should be applicable in the present cases and, as such, the impugned orders have been rightly passed. Referring to Monohor Ali's case reported in 2003 BLD (AD) 59 = 8 BLC (AD) 87,the learned Additional Attorney-General submits that it is clearly distinguishable on the facts as determined in Para 17 of the said decision. Both sections 30A and 25A came into operation of 1-7-1995, but in section 30A there is nothing to suggest that it excluded the operation of section 25A of the Customs Act. At the present moment section 25A stands amended and does not contain the non-obstante clause and, as such, Monohor Ali's case is not applicable in the fact and circumstances of the present rules. Under such circumstances he submits that since section 30A contains non-obstante clause it obviously overrides all other sections of the Customs Act including sections 19, 25 and 30. Thus the petitioners under all circumstances are liable to pay customs duty at the rate prevalent on the date of submission of the Bills of Entry.

9. Replying to petitioners' submissions on Hannan's case reported in 42 DLR the learned Additional Attorney-General submits that the said case was decided for limited purpose giving special emphasis on special circumstances for importing sugar. According to him, in 1984 when there was scarcity of sugar in the country the Government decided and issued Gazette Notification for import of sugar giving incentive to the importer by a concessional rate and specifying the time limit for import of the same with condition to make the shipment within 15 days, but the view taken therein is clearly distinguishable from the facts and circumstances of the instant cases. Thus the importers in the present cases are liable to pay the customs duty prevalent on the date of submission of their Bills of Entry. According to him, the exemption granted by SRO No. 56 of 1999 was in force till the subsequent SRO No.158 was issued, whereby the exemption previously granted was withdrawn in certain aspect. Accordingly, the rate of duty will be as per subsequent SRO No. 158 of 2003 which was prevailing when the Bills of Entry were submitted. On elaborating this point, the learned Additional Attorney-General submits that the government has the power to exempt the rate of duty under section 19 of the Customs Act, but proviso to that section says that the same cannot be done more than once in the year so as to increase the rate of duty. Thus by exercising the power under section 19 the rate of duty as fixed by SRO No. 56 of 1999 being amended by subsequent SRO No. 158 of 2002 is a lawful exercise of power. He submits that SRO No. 56 came into force in 1999 and SRO No. 158 came into force in 2003. So the proviso to section 19 is also not violated as the change was made nearly after 4 years. According to him, the Government vis-a-vis the customs authority, can fix the customs duty within the ceiling and also the exemption can be varied to any extent within that ceiling but once a year. Thus he submits, section 19 empowers the authority to exempt the customs duties and sections 30 and 30A empowers the authority to realise the same on the basis of the rate prevalent on the date of presentation of the Bills of Entry. In support of his contentions, he relied on the case of Selim (Md) vs Collector of Customs and others reported in 54 DLR 287 and Mizanur Rahman case in 52 DLR (AD) 149.

10. Lastly, the learned Additional Attorney-General submits that the unreported 'decision of this Court in Writ Petition No. 4603 of 2003, judgment delivered on 27-8-2003, wherein one of us is a party, their Lordships wrongly relied on Monohor Ali's case and made the Rule absolute which, according to him is not applicable to any of these cases. His contention is that the pleadings and submissions made in these Rules were neither placed nor considered in the said writ petition. The said judgment is per in curium and, as such, has no binding effect. He relied on the decision reported in 10 BLT 104 = 5 BLC 528 (Abul Kalam Khan vs Reaz Morshed and others). In consolidating his submissions, the learned Additional Attorney-General pointed out that the impugned orders, challenged in these writ petitions, not being the final order all these petitions are pre-mature. Without any final decision being passed shelter of law cannot be sought under Article 102 of the Constitution. The petitioners rather had alternative remedy in appeal under section 193 of the Act. Without exhausting the statutory alternative remedy the instant writ petitions are not maintainable.

11. We have heard the learned Advocates at length and perused all the writ petitions along with the papers annexed thereto, the supplementary affidavits, affidavits-in-opposition and also the affidavits-in-reply. It appears to us that the questions raised in all these Rules are whether exemption under section 19 of the Customs Act and section 14 of the VAT Act as granted by SRO No. 56 of 1999, will be applicable in the cases where the Letters of Credit were opened and inspections were held prior to amendment of the said exemption or at the amended rate provided by subsequent SRO No. 158 of 2003 which was prevalent on the date of presentation of Bill of Entry. It appears that both section 19 of the Customs Act and section 14 of the VAT Act deal with the power of the government to exempt customs duty, tax and supplementary duties on certain goods imported by the importers. Now the question is, whether such exemption granted by SRO No. 56 of 1999 will be applicable in the present case. To resolve the point raised in these rules, let us see the relevant provisions of law and the concerned SRO. Section 19 of the Customs Act reads as follow:

"19. General power to exempt from customs duties:—(1) If the Government is satisfied after consultation with the Board, that it is necessary in the public interest to do so, it may, subject to such conditions, limitations or restrictions, if any, as it thinks fit to impose by notification in the official Gazette, exempt any goods imported into or exported from, (Bangladesh) or into, or from any specified port or station or area therein, from the whole or any part of the customs duties chargeable thereon.

Provided that if, in a financial year, exemption under this sub-section is given in respect of any goods the rate of duty cannot be changed more than once in that year so as to increase that rate.

(2) An exemption granted under sub-section (1) shall be effective from the date mentioned in the notification issued under that sub-section."

SRO No. 56 of 1999 under which the Letters of Credit were opened and the goods imported, reads as follows:

“প্ৰজ্ঞাপন

ঢাকা, ২-১২-১৪০৫ বাংলা/১৬ই মার্চ ১৯৯৯ ইংরেজি ৷
