12. Section 30 of the Customs Act dealing with determination of the rate of duty and tariff value on imported goods, as amended in 2001, reads as follows:

"30. Date for determination of rate of duty and tariff value of imported goods—The rate of duty and tariff value applicable to any imported goods shall be the rate in force on the date a bill of entry is delivered under section 79."

Section 30A of the Customs Act which was inserted by Act 12 of 1995 deals with value and effective rate of duty and reads as follows:

"30(A) Value and effective rate of duty—Notwithstanding anything contained in any other law for the time being in force or any decision of any court, for the purpose of section 30, the value and the rate of duty applicable to any goods shall respectively include the value as determined under section 25 and any amount of duty imposed under section 18. 18A or 18B and the amount of duty that may have become payable in consequence of the withdrawal of the whole or any part of the exemption or concession from duty whether before or after the conclusion of a contract or agreement for the sale of such goods or opening of a letter of credit in respect thereof."

13. So far sections 30 and 30A are concerned it appears that the rate of duty will be applicable to any importer on the basis of rate in force on the date of submissions of Bill of Entry.

<u>14. Now coming to the question whether the date of submission of Bills of Entry will be the basis for assessment of the rate of customs duty in these cases or not. We are to see how and when the Bills of Entry were submitted. The petitioners have taken a plea that on arrival of the goods at Benapole Port in the month of April to May 2003 the petitioners tried to submit their Bills of Entry. But for reasons best known to them the authority did not receive the same nor the authority took any step under section 82 of the Customs Act for not presenting the bills of entry within time rather by receiving the same in September/ October 2003 the respondents now cannot take the plea that since the bills of entry were presented subsequent to issuance of SRO No. 158 the duty should be assessed under the said SRO nor it could be said that since the budget was unfavourable they took the plea of vested right. Rather, upon allowing the petitioners to submit their bills of entry and receiving the same after more than four months the customs authority, it appears, allowed the extended period as provided under section 79(2) of the Act, as such, now they cannot pass any order taking advantage of SRO No. 158. Again, to see the applicability of section 30A in these cases, we are to see the scope of applicability of section 19 of Customs Act and section 14 of the VAT Act. As per the said sections, the Government has general power of exemption of customs duty and VAT under some special circumstances in public interest. To do so the Government Authority may exempt any customs duty or VAT party or wholly on any goods. As a matter of fact, the rate of customs duty enumerated by the authority under section 18 remains the same until and unless a part of it or whole of it is exempted under section 19. Actually, sections 18 and 19 are completely independent sections and one does not control the other. In these cases by incorporating the word "subject to the conditions mentioned below" in SRO No. 56 it clearly meant fulfilment of some special conditions incorporated therein to avail the exemption facilities granted under section 19 which shows that the exemption was granted to meet the immediate public demand for public transport when two stroke auto-rickshaws were decided to be withdrawn from the street of the metropolis for public interest, similar is the case under section 14 of the VAT Act.</u>

15. In Mizanur Rahman's case their Lordships found a distinction between Hannan's case and Ahamed Hossain's case on one hand and the case of Mustafizur Rahman on the other hand, although the Bills of Entry in all these cases were submitted after the subsequent SRO was issued but the Letters of Credit were opened prior to the issuance of the subsequent SRO, as in the present cases. The question arose in those cases whether the petitioners should pay duty at the rate prevalent on the date of opening of the Letter of Credit or at the rate prevalent on the date of presentation of the Bills of Entry. Their Lordships while deciding Hannan's case and Ahmed Hassain's case observed that "the importers by opening Letters of Credit earlier to withdrawal of exemption obtained a vested right which cannot be taken away by issuing a subsequent SRO. On the other hand, in the case of Mostafizur Rahman vs Government of Bangladesh and 6 others, reported in 51 DLR (AD) 40, their Lordships held that the notification issued under section 19 of the Act was without any condition, limitation or restrictions and, as such, the subsequent notifications cannot have any effect when a right had vested in the importers and he had acted upon the assurance provided by that right that he would have to pay duties at the rate mentioned in the previous notification SRO". The said view was reviewed in Mizanur Rahman's case, reported in 52 DLR (AD) 149, therein their Lordships held "we therefore review our opinion expressed in that decision in 51 DLR (AD) 40 and hold that no vested right is acquired by the importer to pay sales tax and customs duty on the basis of tariff value declared by notification imposed on the date of opening of the Letter of Credit. The importer has to pay tax and duty on the basis of tariff value in-force on the date of submission of the bill of entry." But however, the view taken in Hanna's case and Ahmed Hossain's case still remains unchanged. In Mizanur Rahman's case the matter in issue was tariff value and the other 3(three) cases i.e. Hannan's case, Ahmed Hossain's case and Mostafizur Rahman's case the matter in issue was exemption of duty. In the case of Khairul Bashar (Md) and 8 others vs Collector of Customs and others reported in 50 DLR 225 the distinction between exemption under section 19 and declaration of tariff value under section 25(7) of the Customs Act was recognised. Upon noting such distinctions it has been held that the importers acquired no vested right in the invoice value or the tariff value existing at the time of opening of the Letter of Credit. So, it appears that Hannan's case and Ahmed Hossain's case are on exemption of customs duty granted under section 19 of the Customs Act which is also the subject matter of the present cases.

16. In Hannan's case it has been held that the subsequent SRO cannot destroy or take away or curtail or extinguish the vested right created on the petitioner by the earlier SRO. It was further held that the importer having already fulfilled the terms and conditions of the earlier notification he could not be deprived of the right of a concessional rate customs duty by a subsequent notification. In that case the petitioner's point was that the Government is estopped from denying the right by a subsequent notification with retrospective effect which has already been granted upon announcement of the concessional rate of duty and taxes by an earlier notification. This was nothing but the government was estopped by its own promise to do anything beyond the promise made earlier. This contention of promissory estoppel was accepted by their Lordships and accordingly, it was held that the Government cannot destroy or take away or curtail or extinguish the right created to the importers by the earlier notification. In other decision referred above the arguments of vested right was also considered. It appears from Monohar Ali's case that their Lordships observed "this Division in Mizanur Rahman's case has accepted that the submissions on vested right may be tenable in specific circumstances under section 19 of the Customs Act as to the customs duty."

<u>17. It is recognised by the superior courts that specific assurance may give some right to exist promissory estoppel. The doctrine of promissory estoppel has been called in various judgments and it has been described in various terms such as equitable estoppel, quasi estoppel or new estoppel. Justice Bhagwati in one of the judgments observed "it is not really based on the principle of estoppel but it is a doctrine involved by equity in order to prevent injustice where a promise is made by a person knowing that it would be acted on by the person to whom it is made and, in fact, it is so acted on and it is inequitable to allow the party making the promise to go back upon it". His Lordships further observed "they are really promises and promises intended to be binding intended to be acted upon and in fact, acted upon. It is an equitable principle evolved by the courts for doing justice and there is no reason why it should be given only a limited application by way of defence." Similarly, in the present cases, it appears that by SRO No. 56 the Government intended to allow a class of people having public limited company or a Private Limited Company with minimum 10 lac Taka as the paid up capital and having tax payers identification number can import taxicabs for using the same as public transport upon fulfilling certain conditions e.g. the vehicles must be black in colour, installed with catalytic converters, meter, roof sign showing the word "Taxi", etc. Further conditions were that the importers would execute undertaking that the same would be used only as taxicabs not for any other purposes. Upon fulfilling such terms and conditions if the cabs are imported then the duty above 7.5% would be exempted. So, it appears that by the said SRO, the Government has made a promise that upon fulfilment of such conditions if the importers import taxicabs they will be given the benefit as mentioned therein. The petitioners having acted upon accordingly, the Government now cannot go back upon it. If they go back it will be inequitable. So it appears that the doctrine of promissory estoppel operates when one of the parties in reliance of the promise made by the other party acts to his detriment and in such case the other party should not be allowed to go back from his promise as the same would cause injustice on the party relying upon the said promise.</u>

<u>18. Lord Denning in the "High Trees" case observed "that a promise intended to be binding, intended to be acted on and in fact, acted on, is binding so far as its terms properly apply". The contention of Lord Justice Denning in the aforesaid case and the contention of Justice Bhagwati as referred above are found to be fully applicable in the present cases. It has been observed by Lord Denning in Robertson vs Minister of Pensions (1949-1 KB 227) "the Crown cannot escape by saying that estoppels do not bind the Crown for that doctrine has long been exploded. Nor can the Crown escape by praying in aid the doctrine of executive necessity, that is, the doctrine that the Crown cannot bind itself so as to letter its future executive action". It is still held general that "the Crown is not immune from liability under the doctrine of promissory estoppel." Thus the promise made by the Government through the National Board of Revenue, the supreme authority of collecting Revenue of the country, by issuing SRO No. 56 dated 16-3-1999 cannot now come back from the said promise because of the subsequent amendment incorporated by SRO No. 158, of 2003. It may be noted here that by the subsequent SRO No. 158 the amendment as regards exemption of duty has been reduced and a bottom limit has been fixed by incorporating taxi cabs being not less than 1301 CC meaning any person importing Motor car or taxicab below 1300 CC and above 2000 CC would be liable to pay customs duty on the regular rate i.e. import of taxicabs from 1301 CC to 2000 CC upon fulfilling the conditions contained in the SRO No. 56 may get the benefit of exemption of duty above 15%. This amendment appears to be shifting from the promise already made in the earlier SRO. The petitioners having opened the Letters of Credit, and shipment having been made prior to issuance of the subsequent SRO upon fulfilling all the terms and conditions including the inspections of the vehicles under sections 25A and 25B by the approved PSI agents they have acted in accordance with the conditions of the SRO and, as such, the promisor, i.e. the Government, now cannot fall back and ask for payment of customs duty on any other basis other than SRO No. 56. Under such circumstances it appears that the position of the petitioners in the present cases are as such that the situation has taken place, arising out of promise made under section 19 of the Act, to exempt the imported taxicab from assessing or paying taxes and duties under special circumstances. Thus the importers having acted on the promise made by the government under section 19 of the Act to avail the facilities granted in SRO No. 56 on compliance of all the terms and conditions incorporated therein, the government, rather the respondents, are estopped from going back from that promise rather the same is binding on them. The principle of promissory estoppel and fair action are applicable to the facts of the case and the respondent are debarred having no justification in law to supersede earlier notification which has to remain in force without limitation to time. Thus subsequent notification to the extent it superseded the earlier one will have no binding effect in such special cases concerning public interests, this view finds support in the case of Collector of Customs vs Abul Hossain reported in 42 DLR (AD) 167 and in the case of Collector of Customs and others vs Ahmed Hossain and others 48 DLR (AD) 199.</u>

19. The view taken in Mustafizur Rahman's case thought reviewed and set aside in Mizanur Rahman's case but the view taken in Hannan's case has not been set aside or reviewed in any other decision. Though it is submitted from some quarter that the principle enunciated in Hannan's case if especiality and exception of its own but we find that the principle annunciated therein is related to exemption of duty under section 19 in some special circumstances which we find similarity with present cases. In the said case the government allowed some incentive to the genuine importers to import sugar within a specific time to meet the urgent need in the market as there were scarcities of the same in 1984. Similarly, in the present case the Government by SRO No. 56 asked a class of people to import taxicabs upon fulfilment of certain conditions enunciated therein, to meet the urgent need of filling up the vacuum in public transport created when two strokes 3(three) wheeler auto-rickshaws were withdrawn from the street of the Metropolitan area for environmental degradation by a Government order. To meet such vacuum and urgent need of meeting the cry of the public transportation, SRO No. 56 was issued. So if it is submitted that the decision in Hannan's case is an exception of its own the same principle also applies in these cases. Strictly speaking, when it appears that the concerned SRO was issued for a particular purpose and for public interest and the importers having fulfilled all the terms and conditions incorporated in the said SRO upon obtaining loans from the commercial banks and upon opening the Letters of Credit through the concerned banks, the Government or the customs authority cannot be allowed to work inconsistently, whimsically and capriciously to the prejudice of the importer who acted accordingly and fulfilled the conditions of the said SRO issued at an earlier point of time. The view finds support in the case of Chairman, Board of Investment and others vs Bay Trawling Limited and others, reported in 51 DLR (AD) 79 Moreover, a person is entitled to claim benefit under a SRO wherein the authority has promised such exemption if he suffers loss for no fault of his own. But he is not entitled to claim such benefit in a situation where the person would not suffer any loss by such payment as a result of his being able to realise the same from a third party or third person wherefrom such loss could be realised by him. Reason being that the person who has suffered no loss by making an unauthorised payment to another person cannot get refund of the same from that person as he was able to make good the loss by shifting the burden of the same on the shoulders of another person. The petitioners in these writ petitions being Private Limited Companies upon importing taxicabs, undertook to use the same as taxicabs for the purpose of public transportation they cannot shift the burden of payment of extra duty on a subsequent purchaser and, as such, the loss incurred would be completely of their own. Under such situation it is discouraged that the extra duty should be realised from them. This view finds support in the case of Tamanna Steel Galvanizing Industry Ltd vs Bangladesh and others, reported in 50 DLR 8.

<u>20. Now coming to the question of maintainability of the writ petitions when the statutory relief is available by way of appeal under section 193 of the Customs Act not being availed of by the petitioners instead the petitioners have come before this Court under the writ jurisdiction without availing the said forum. In all these Rules it appears that the petitioner have challenged the impugned order passed by the authority directing to assess the customs duty on the consignments at a rate fixed by SRO No. 158 dated 12-6-2003 instead of exempted rate under SRO No. 56 dated 16-3-1999. Here the question arises as to the applicability of SRO No. 158 dated 12-6-2003 which is a Statutory Regulatory Order passed under the authority of section 19 of the Act and section 14 of the VAT Act that means here the question of interpretation of law as well as the applicability and the authority of the SRO arises. It is the settled principle that where the vires of Statute of statutory provision is under question the remedy can be availed of under the Writ Jurisdiction as provided in Article 102 of the Constitution though alternative remedy having not been availed. In such a case the alternative remedy is neither efficacious nor adequate and where the wrong complained is so inextricably mixed up the High Court Division may, for the prevention of public injury and vindication of public justice, examine such complaint. This view has been taken by our Appellate Division in the case of Dhaka Warehouse Ltd vs Assistant Collector of Customs and others, reported in 1991 BLD (AD) 327 which has also been noticed in Mizanur Rahman 's case. In the present cases the question relates to interpretation of sections 19 and 30 of the Act. Thus, in our opinion, availing the writ jurisdiction under Article 102 of the Constitution under such situation is permissible. Ordinarily writ petition against an order of assessment of customs duty or imposition of fine is not maintainable and remedy of appeal is to be availed against the same. But in the present cases the assessment having not been made and no question of imposition of any fine being there rather the only question for determination in these rules is whether SRO No. 158 is applicable under the facts and circumstances of the cases. Our opinion is that the present writ petitions are maintainable because the remedy provided in the Act would not be equally efficacious to bar the jurisdiction under Article 102 of the Constitution. Thus, in not availing the alternative remedy there is no bar under facts and circumstances of these writ petitions to vindicate the grievances under the writ jurisdiction.</u>

<u>21. So far the contention of the learned Additional Attorney-General as to maturity of the Writ Petitions is concerned it is found that by refusing to assess customs duty on the basis of SRO No. 56 and directing to assess duties on the basis of SRO No. 158 the Customs Authority has taken the final decision for assessment and, as such, the Writ Petitions are not prematured.</u>

<u>22. Under the facts and circumstances stated above and the decision referred to above, only question left out to see is, whether section 30A is applicable in these cases in such a situation. The language of section 30A clearly shows that for the purpose of imposition of duty and exemption of duty section 30 will be applicable under any circumstances generally. But in a case where the situation of present nature arises and the government having amended the benefit given under SRO No. 56 restricting the same to certain limit without any prior notice in general to the public even after continuation of the previous SRO for more than 4 years the action taken by the government appears to be inconsistent and capricious prejudicing the persons who had already acted upon on the basis of the previous SRO. Under such situation, in our view, section 30A will not be applicable. In fact, upon reading the language of section 30A it appears that the rate of duty is to be ascertained by taking into account any duty imposed under section 18 or any exemption or concession of duty granted under the Act. Thus, in the present cases considering the speciality of the facts and circumstances sections 30 or 30A should be read independent of section 19 and accordingly, any exemption granted under section 19 should not be affected by section 30 or 30A of the Act or the date of submission of Bills of Entry. The above issues were not placed and argued in writ petition No. 4603 of 2003 and, as such, these rules being decided in favour of the petitioners as per reasoning stated above, we do not want to make any comment on the said judgment.</u>

23. Considering the facts and circumstances of the cases and the decisions stated above, we are of the view that all the rules succeed and accordingly, the impugned orders in each of the writ petitions are hereby declared to have been passed without lawful authority and of no legal effect.

24. In the result, the Rules in all the 8 (eight) writ petitions being Writ Petition Nos. 6433-6439 of 2003 and 5950 of 2003 are made absolute.

25. The respondents are hereby directed to assess the customs duty and other charges for the petitioner's imported consignments as per SRO No. 56 dated 16-3-1999 which was in force at the time of opening of the Letters of Credit and release the Taxicabs within 1(one) month from the date of receipt of this order.

26. The Bank Guarantee furnished by the writ petitioner in Writ Petition No. 5950 of 2003 is liable to be released and the respondents are accordingly, directed to do the needful in this regard within 1(one) month from the date of receipt of this order.

Considering the circumstances, there will be no order as to cost.

End.

caseno:
First Miscellaneous Appeal No. 193 of 1994
with
Civil Rule No.264 (FM)of 1994
lawyer:
Sasanka Sekhar Sarker. Advocate for SS Haider, Senior Advocate— For the Appellants
Miah Abdul Gafur with Ataur Rahman Khan, Advocates — For the Respondents
parties:
Tara Miah and another ------ Appellants
Vs.
Shahjada Sarder and others ------ Respondents
full_judgment:
Gour Gopal Saha J: This appeal is directed against the order dated 17-7-94 passed by the 1st Court of Subordinate Judge, Narayangonj in Title Suit No.41 of 1993 (Partition) rejecting the plaintiff''s prayer for temporary injunction under Order 39 rules 1 and 2 CPC.

2. The appellants as plaintiffs filed the aforesaid suit for partition claiming 10 decimals of land in their share out of 2.37 1/2 acres of land consisting of a tank, a dwelling house and naal land. After filing the suit the plaintiffs filed the application for temporary injunction praying for restraining the defendants from making any construction in suit plot No 86 only and from changing the nature and character of suit land.

3. Defendant Nos. 8 and 9, 11-15 opposed the application for injunction contending, inter anti, that the plaintiffs have no title and possession in the suit land. It has been further contended in the written objection that defendant Nos. 9-15 have title and possession over 3 decimals of land in suit plot No. 86 in which their homestead stands and the said land has also been duly recorded in their names in the RS Khatian and they have been paying rent regularly to the appropriate authority. It has been further contended that defendant No. 9 has already constructed a pucca building in suit plot No. 86 and there are other structures standing thereon and the said land is well fenced by walls on all four sides and under such circumstances there is absolutely no ground for granting temporary injunction on vague and indefinite assertions of the plaintiffs.

<u>4. The learned Subordinate Judge by the impugned order dated 17-7-94 found that the plaintiffs have failed to make out a prima facie case in support of their claim for temporary injunction. The learned Subordinate Judge on consideration of the materials on record also found that there is nothing on record to prima facie prove that the plaintiffs have possession in suit plot No. 86. On the other hand, the constesting defendants have produced the certified copies of the finally published RS Khatian in which 26 decimals of land has been recorded in their names. From the DCR and the rent receipts produced by the contesting defendant if is found that they have been paying rent to the appropriate authority for the said land. RAJUK has already approved their plan for construction of buildings in the said land. It has been clearly asserted in the written objection that the construction of the building has already been finished. Suit plot No. 86 admittedly measures 32 decimals of land in which the contesting defendants appear to have possession over 20 decimals of land. The plaintiffs alleged claim of 10 decimals of land in this particular part is totally vague and indefinite. In such circumstances, the learned Subordinate Judge found that the plaintiffs have failed to make out a prima facie case for injunction. From the facts and circumstances of the case and materials on record we find that the learned Subordinate Judge was perfectly justified in refusing the plaintiffs'' prayer for temporary injunction. We find no illegality in the impugned order calling for our interference.</u>

<u>5. The principle of relating to the grant of temporary injunction against co-sharers is well-settled by now. Ordinarily a co-sharer is entitled to possess every inch of the joint property but when a co-sharer is found to be in exclusive possession over a specific portion of the joint property he is entitled under the law to protect his possession against the inroads of his co-sharers by way of injunction until the joint property is partitioned by metes and bounds. But in this case we find nothing on record to show that the plaintiffs have possession in suit plot No. 86 not to speak of exclusive possession. In that view of the matter the appeal is found to be without any substance and, as such, it is liable to be dismissed.</u>

6. In the result, the appeal is dismissed and the connected Rule being Civil Rule No. 264 (FM) of 1994 is discharged. There shall be no order as to costs.

The order of maintaining status quo is hereby vacated.

End.

caseno: Civil Revision No. 524 of 1990 with Civil Revision No.525 of 1990.
lawyer:
Syed Ziaul Karim, Advocate — For the Petitioner. 

Md Nurul Haque with AKM Shahidul Haque and Chamon Akhtar, Advocates — For the Opposite Parties.
parties:
Siddique Ali Mia  ------ Petitioner
Vs.
Atahar Ali Fakir, being dead one of his heirs 1 (a) Abul Fakir &ors ------ Opposite Parties
full_judgment:
These two Rules arise out of Title Suit No. 539 of 1980 of the court of the then Munsif, Jhalakati and Title Suit No. 421 of 1977 of the same court. The petitioner is the plaintiff of Title Suit No. 539 of 1980 and the opposite party No. 1 is the plaintiff of Title Suit No. 421 of 1977 and the opposite party No. 1 is defendant No. 1 in Title Suit No. 539 of 1980 and the present petitioner is defendant No. 1 in Title Suit No. 421 of 1977. Both the suits were analogously heard by the learned Munsif and disposed of by him by one judgment. Similarly the appellate Court also heard the appeals analogously and disposed of the same by one judgment. Hence both the Rules were heard together and being disposed of by this judgment.

2. The petitioner as plaintiff filed Title Suit No. 539 of 1980 before the court of .Munsif now Assistant Judge, Jhalakati for declaration that the certificate sale dated 15-1-63 in Certificate Sale case No. 1832-JK /1961-62 of the Sadar South Certificate Court of Barisal and Certificate Sale Case No. 1832-JK /1961-62 of the Sadar south at Barisal and certificate sale dated 30-11-63 in Certificate Sale Case No. 313 (JK) of Certificate Court at Jhalakati and the Certificate Sale dated 30-11-63 in Certificate Sale Case No. 6166 (JK) of Certificate Court at Jhalakati described in the schedule ''Ka'' of the plaint in respect or schedule "Kha" is illegal, fraudulent, collusive, inoperative without jurisdiction and not binding upon the plaintiff.

3. The case of the plaintiff, in short, is that "Kha" schedule land originally belonged to opposite party Nos.9-16 Sudhangshu Kumar and opposite party Nos.9-16 made a settlement of the above described land in favour of the plaintiff and opposite party Nos.17 and 18 on 20th Baisakh, 1358 BS. The plaintiff and opposite party Nos.17 and 18 after settlement created dwelling huts, planted fruit trees, constructed graveyard, cultivated the null land and paid rent on receipt of dakhilas and thus they had been continuing in the peaceful possession over the suit land. The settlement was made after RS operation and the State acquisition operation was not held in the locality and the record of SA Khatian was wrongly prepared as per RS khatian in the name of Shudhangshu Kumar and opposite party Nos.9-16. Thereafter the plaintiff petitioner and opposite party Nos.17 and 18 as plaintiffs filed a suit being numbered 339 of 1976 for declaration of their title over the suit land against Sudhangshu Kumar and opposite party Nos.9-16 before the court of Munsif at Jhalakati. The suit was decreed on compromise on 18-9-1976. The plaintiff petitioner and the opposite party Nos.17 and 18 on the basis of the decree dated 18-9-1976 filed Mutation Case No. 5-JK/ 1977-78 under section 54 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act before the Circle Officer (Revenue) Jhalakati and obtained an order of mutation and accordingly a new khatian being No. 801 was opened in their names and paid Government rent and obtained dakhilas for years together. It is stated in the plaint that the opposite party No. 1 is a greedy man of the locality and the opposite party Nos. 2-8 are his associates.

4. The opposite parties Nos. 1-8 knowing fully well about the right, title and interest of the petitioner and opposite party Nos.17 and 18 illegally and for wrongful gain managed to create the "ka" schedule certificate sale cases in respect of "Kha" schedule land of the plaint. It is further stated in the plaint that the certificate debtors of the "ka" schedule certificate cases were disinterested at the time of certificate sale, notices upon the opposite party Nos.9-16 were not served and the same was fraudulently shown to have been served, the certificate sale was illegal, without jurisdiction, fraudulent and were null and void. The petitioner and opposite parties Nos.17 and 18 being the legal owner of the land of the "Ka" schedule certificate cases were not made parties, the notices under sections 7 and 46 of the Public Demand Recovery Act were not at all served upon the certificate debtors, the "ka" schedule certificate sales remained confined in papers and it was not at all acted upon and therefore the physical possession was not delivered.

5. The opposite. party Nos. 1, 5, and 6 appeared in the said title suit on 10-6-1981, filed a joint written statement on the allegation, inter alia, that the suit was not maintainable and that suit was bad for defect of parties and the suit was barred by res judicata and the suit property was under-valued, the plaint was insufficiently stamped and the suit was barred by limitation and was not maintainable for want of cause of action. The opposite party Nos.9-16 were the legal owners and accordingly, for non-payment of Government rent the "ka" scheduled certificate cases were started and the same were legally and lawfully purchased by opposite party Nos.1-8. The story of the settlement of the petitioner was false. The petitioner at the time of alleged settlement was not a citizen of Pakistan and the father of the petitioner on 3-2-53 for the first time entered into Pakistan and that at the time of the alleged pattan the plaintiff was a boy of 2/3 years only and therefore the suit of the plaintiff-petitioner was liable to be dismissed.

6. The opposite party No. 1 as plaintiff earlier filed the Title Suit No. 421 of 1977 for setting aside the sole decree obtained by the petitioner and opposite party Nos.17-18. In that case present petitioner being defendant No. l contested the suit by filing written statement. The learned Munsif now Assistant Judge heard both the suits analogously and delivered one judgment for both the suits.

7. Being aggrieved by and dissatisfied with the aforesaid judgment, the plaintiff preferred an appeal before the learned District Judge, Jhalakati and the appeal was registered as Title Appeal No. 86 of 1986. Similarly, being aggrieved by the judgment of the trial Court the opposite party No. I preferred 2 appeals before the learned District Judge, Jhalakati which were registered as Title Appeal No. 87 of 1986 and 88 of 1986, The learned appellate Court below heard these 3 appeals analogously and disposed of by the impugned judgment whereby he dismissed Title Appeal No. 86 of 1986 and allowed Title Appeal No. 87 of 1986 by reversing the judgment of the trial Court and decreed Title Suit No. 421 of 1977. The present petitioner being aggrieved by the aforesaid judgment and decree passed by the learned appellate Court below preferred Civil Revision No. 524 of 1990 calling in question the legality and propriety of the judgment and decree passed by the appellate Court below in Title Appeal No. 86 of 1986 and preferred Civil Revision No. 525 of 1990 against the judgment and decree passed by the appellate Court below in Title Appeal No. 87 of 1986.

8. Mr Syed Ziaul Karim, the learned Advocate appearing for the plaintiff appellant petitioner, submits that the trial Court found the petitioners in possession of the suit property but the learned appellate Court without reversing the finding of possession illegally dismissed the appeal and the impugned judgment is liable to be set aside. The learned Advocate submits that the trial Court observed that the claim of the contesting defendants was barred under section 66 of the Code of Civil Procedure, and found that the "ka" schedule certificate cases were fradulently created but the appellate Court below without reversing the finding of the trial Court illegally accepted the "ka" schedule certificate cases and thereby committed an error of law resulting in an error in the decision occasioning failure of justice. The learned Advocate further submits that both the courts below misdirected themselves in not considering the rent receipts filed by the plaintiff-petitioner as a genuine document of his possession and of his title and the learned Advocate submits that the courts below have committed an error of law in accepting the death certificate of Sudhangshu Kumar in evidence without calling the Death Register or without examining the authority concerned who granted the same. The learned Advocate further submits that in allowing the appeal No. 87 of 1988 the appellate Court lost sight of the fact that witnesses of the defendant opposite parties are highly interested and inter-related. The learned Advocate finally submits that in any view the impugned judgment is not tenable in law and the appellate Court below on misreading of evidence has dismissed Title Appeal No. 86 of 1988 and allowed title Appeal No. 87 of 1986.

9. Mrs Chamon Akhter, the learned Advocate appearing for the opposite party No. 1, submits that the appellate Court below on proper scrutiny of materials on record rightly dismissed Title Appeal No. 86 of 1986 and allowed Title Appeal No. 87 of 1986. The learned Advocate further submits that the appellate Court below after considering the documentary evidence adduced by the defendant-opposite party No.  1 in their Title Suit No. 421 of 1977 rightly arrived at a finding that the defendant opposite party No. I has been able to prove his case and thereby rightly decreed the suit and allowed the appeal. The learned Advocate further submits that although the appellate Court below did not make any observation as to the interestedness and relationships of the witnesses of the defendant opposite party Nod nevertheless in view of the facts and circumstances of the case they are found to be most competent witnesses and their testimony cannot be thrown away on this ground alone. The learned Advocate further submits that since the defendant opposite party No. 1 is the real owner, section 66 of the Code of Civil Procedure has no manner of application in the instant suit.

<u>10. On a perusal of the impugned judgment it appears that the appellate Court below on scrutiny of the materials on record found that the plaintiff-petitioner has failed to prove his case in respect of his title to the suit land and also found that he fraudulently, obtained decree in Title Suit No. 339 of 1976. It appears on persusal of the judgments of both the courts below that both the courts arrived at a concurrent findings of fact that the plaintiff petitioner could not prove his case. Although there is no elaborate discussion by the appellate Court with reference to the evidence adduced by the PWs in Title Suit No. 539 of 1980, nevertheless it appears that the findings arrived at by the appellate Court are based on material and evidence on record and the trial Court made elaborate discussions with reference to the materials on record and arrived at a positive findings that the defendant No. 1 of Title Suit No. 339 of 1976 died before the decree was passed in that suit. It is also found by the learned trial Court that the summons of Title Suit No. 339 of 1976 was not duly served on the defendant of that suit. The trial Court on a scrutiny of the evidence adduced by the plaintiff petitioner however, arrived at a finding that the plaintiff petitioner has failed to prove his title but he has found plaintiff petitioner in possession of the suit land. With this finding that trial Court dismissed the suit. Ziaul Karim, the learned Advocate appearing for the plaintiff petitioner, submitted that the trial Court committed an illegality in taking into evidence the death certificate without calling for witnesses to prove the same. Besides, by oral evidence it has been proved that the defendant No. I of Title Suit No. 339 of 1976 died on 26-10-76. It further appears from the evidence of DW 4 that the plaintiff petitioner filed the aforesaid suit, after the death of Sudhangshu Kumar or after he left for India and taking into consideration all the evidence the trial Court arrived at a finding that the decree obtained by the plaintiff petitioner in Title Suit No. 339 of 1976 was fraudulent, void and inoperative. The learned appellate Court also found that the plaintiff petitioner has miserably failed to substantiate his contention that he took settlement from the original owner Sudhangshu Kumar, and others. Since both the courts have arrived at a concurrent finding based on the materials on record it is very difficult to interfere with such findings sitting under the revisional jurisdiction.</u>

11. Therefore, I do not find any substance in the submissions made by the learned Advocate for the plaintiff petitioner in respect of title Appeal No. 86 of 1986 and it appears to me that the appellate Court rightly dismissed the appeal and thereby he has not committed any illegality whatsoever. In that view of the matter the Rule in Civil Revision, No. 524 of 1990 is discharged without cost.

<u>12. On a perusal of the impugned judgment it appears that the learned appellate Court below on consideration of the materials on record and documentary evidence produced by the plaintiff in TS No. 421 of 1977 has arrived at a finding that the plaintiff has been able to prove his case and proved that they are in possession of the suit land in pursuance of the auction sale of the land held earlier. It may be mentioned that the trial Court considered this evidence and observed that although they filed these papers but there is not an iota of evidence adduced by the plaintiff to show that the auction sale was acted upon and that the possession was given to the plaintiff of Title Suit No. 421 of 1977. It further appears that the appellate Court below did not take into consideration the khatian, rent receipts and exhibits filed by the plaintiff petitioner in Title Suit No. 421 of 1977 in support of their contention. Here it may be mentioned that the trial Court below on proper scrutiny and analysis of evidence adduced by the witnesses of both the parties arrive at a finding that the plaintiff petitioner, was able to prove his possession in the suit land although he has miserably failed to substantiate his contention as to the title to the suit land, but the appellate Court below did not controvert that point nor reversed the findings of the Trial Court on that point. In dismissing, Title Suit No. 421 of 1977, the trial Court discussed the evidence adduced by the witnesses of the defendant opposite party No. I of the present Rule and observed that they are highly interested and partisan witnesses and, as such, the oral testimony of the witnesses were discarded by the trial Court on that account. The appellate Court overlooked this aspect of this case and without adverting to that point only considered the documentary evidence adduced by the opposite party No. I and arrived at a finding that the opposite party No. I has been able to prove his case. It thus appears that the impugned judgment of Title Appeal No. 87 of 1986 suffers from gross illegality and infirmity and that in view of the matter I am of the view that the impugned judgment so far it relates to Title Appeal No. 87 of 1986 cannot be maintained.</u>

13. In the result, the Rule in Civil Revision No. 524 of 1990 is discharged and the Rule in Civil Revision 525 of 1990 is made absolute. The judgment and decree passed by the appellate Court in Title Appeal No. 87 of 1986 are set aside and those of the trial Court are restored and Title Suit No. 421 of 1977 is disposed.

14. In view of the circumstances of the case there will be no order as to costs in respect of both the Rules.

Send down the LCR at once.

End.

lawyer:
BM Elias. Advocate with Jyotirmoy Barua, Advocate -----For the Petitioner. 
Md Abdul Haque Advocate -----For the Opposite Party.
parties:
Masud Haider (Md) ------ Petitioner 
Vs.
Md Golam Ambia (Harun) ------ Opposite Party
full_judgment:
Leave was granted and Rule was issued in this Civil Revision under section 115(4) of the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908 about sustainability of the judgment and order dated 20-2-2014 by which the learned District Judge, Mymensingh summarily rejected Civil Revision No.6 of 2014 and thereby affirmed the order dated 29-1-2014 passed by the learned Senior Assistant Judge, Mymensingh Sadar, in Other Class Suit No.396 of 2012 rejecting an application for obtaining expert opinion on certain signatures of the plaintiff.

Plaintiff's Case:

2. In the above noted suit opposite party Md Golam Ambia (Harun), as plaintiff, prayed for eviction of the defendant (petitioner) as a tenant of two shops. Plaintiff claims that the shops were leased out to the defendant No.1 as a monthly tenant under a written agreement dated 1-4-2005. The monthly rent was fixed at Taka 1,400 for the previous tenure of 3 years. Thereafter they verbally agreed to increase the monthly rent to Taka 4,500 for the next tenure. Accordingly the defendant paid the rent for May, 2012, but defaulted in paying the rent for the subsequent months. Apart from such default, defendant No.1 has sub-let one of the shops to defendant No.2 without the consent of the plaintiff. So the plaintiff issued a legal notice to the defendant under section 106 of the Transfer of Property Act, 1882 for termination of the tenancy and finally instituted the suit.

Case of Defendant No. 1:

3. Defendant No. 1, in his written statement, admits that under a written agreement he has been a tenant under the plaintiff. However he claims that, after expiry of the second tenure of 3 years, they verbally agreed to fix the monthly rent at Taka 2,800 effective from May, 2012 and that, on 2-6-2012, he paid in cash Taka 2,800 for that month. But without delivering any receipt on that date, the plaintiff, after 2/3 days, sent a receipt of Taka 9000. Upon defendant's query, the plaintiff told that the figure 9,000 had been written through mistake and it would not be repeated in future. So on 3-7-2012 he paid Taka 2,800 for June 2012. But plaintiff did not deliver any receipt on the plea that he had no printed form. On the following day plaintiff demanded Taka 9,000 for June 2012 on the plea that defendant had already paid Taka 9,000 for May, 2012.

4. So the defendant sent the monthly rent by postal money order for the period of June to November, 2012. The plaintiff duly received the money so sent. Lastly the defendant has filed Rent Case No. 42 of 2013 in the Court of Rent controller wherein he has been regularly depositing the rent.

Deliberation in Revision:

5. At the hearing of this Revision, Mr Jyotirmoy Roy, the learned Advocate for the petitioner-defendant, submits that both the Courts below committed an error of law in rejecting the application of the defendant for expert examination, because the principal ground of the eviction prayed for by the plaintiff is the alleged default of the defendant in paying of the rent for the period of June to November 2012 and therefore plaintiff's signatures on the receipts of the money order are vital evidence for proper adjudication of the dispute.

6. In support of his submission the learned Advocate refers to the case of Tarak Chandra Majhi vs Atahar Ali Howlader (13 BLT) (AD) (2005) page-3 = 8 BLC (AD) 67.

7. In reply Mr Md Abdul Haque, the learned Advocate for the opposite party plaintiff, submits that according to section 73 of the Evidence Act, the Court is competent to compare the disputed signatures and handwriting of the plaintiff and thereby to arrive at a proper decision.

8. Mr Haque, the learned Advocate next submits that, apart from the default of the defendant in paying the monthly rent, the plaintiff has taken other grounds for eviction, namely violation of the agreement by way of sub-leasing the shops to another person and non-payment of electricity bills and service charge and therefore adjudication of the dispute is possible without obtaining opinion of the expert on the disputed signature.

Findings and Decision in Revision.

9. The issue raised in this Revision is whether expert opinion should be obtained for ascertaining the alleged receipt of the monthly rent of June to November, 2012 allegedly sent by the defendant by postal money order.

10. Courts below rejected the application of the defendant for expert examination on the reasoning that the court can compare any disputed handwriting or signature under section 73 of the Evidence. The trial court relied on this case of Abdul Matin Chowdhury vs Chapala Rani (37 DLR (AD) 2005).

11. But, as pointed out by Mr Jyotirmoy Barua, the learned Advocate for the defendant petitioner, the view taken by the Appellate Division, in the Case of Tarak Chandra Majhi vs Atahar Ali Howlader (13 BLT) (AD) (2005) page- 3=8 BLC (AD) 67, has also observed that in case of a contentious handwriting or signature, it is risky to rely on the observation of the presiding Judge and that the safe course is to obtain expert opinion.

12. In consideration of the facts and circumstances of the case and the above views of the apex court, I hold that expert opinion will assist the court in the proper adjudication of the dispute between the parties.

13. The submission of Mr Md Abdul Haque, the learned Advocate for the plaintiff (opposite party) with regard to certain other grounds as pleaded by the plaintiff, I hold that those other grounds are to be decided by the trial court in consideration of the evidence led by the parties, but those grounds should not deprive the defendant from obtaining the expert opinion on the alleged signatures relating to the principal ground.

<u>14. The defendant has produced the original of the admitted agreement in this Court. So the disputed signatures of the plaintiff on the receipts of the money order (in original) should be compared with those in said admitted agreement.</u>

<u>15. It is noted that expert opinion is one piece of evidence and should be considered with other evidence on record.</u>

16. In view of the above, I hold that the impugned judgment is not sustainable.

17. In the result, the Rule is made absolute. The judgment and order dated 20-2-2014 passed by the learned District Judge, Mymensingh in Civil Revision No.6 of 2014 and the order dated 29-1-2014 passed by the learned Senior Assistant Judge, Sadar, Mymensingh in Other Class Suit No. 396 of 2012, so far it relates to rejection of the application for obtaining expert opinion, are hereby set aside.

18. The learned Senior Assistant Judge, Sadar, Mymensingh is directed to pass necessary orders for obtaining expert opinion on the signature of the plaintiff as appearing on the admitted agreement and those appearing in the original postal receipts of the money order.

19. For the above purpose, the learned Senior Assistant Judge shall, within 10 days after receipt of the copy of this judgment and order, direct the defendant No. 1 to produce the said original agreement and the said original money receipts, failing which he shall proceed with the case without the expert opinion.

20. The learned Senior Assistant Judge shall expeditiously dispose of the suit in accordance with law, preferably within 6 (six) months from the receipt of the copy of this judgment.

21. The learned Advocate for the defendant petitioner may take back all the annexure, except the impugned judgment by substituting photocopies thereof.

22. No order as to cost.

Send at once a copy of the judgment and order to the Courts below.

End.

caseno: Civil Revision No. 1461 of 2003 with Civil Revision No. 1462 of 2003.
lawyer:
Hasan Foez Siddique with Md Habibullah, Advocates—For the Petitioners. (in both the Rules). 
Md Lutfor Rahman Mondal with KM Zahid Sarwar, Advocates—For the Opposite Parties. (In both the Rules).
parties:
Tara Bibi alias Tahera Begum & ors ----- Defendants-Petitioners 
vs. 
Salma Rani & ors  ----- Plaintiffs-Opposite
full_judgment:
The Rule in Civil Revision No. 1461 of 2003 is directed against the judgment and decree dated 30-11-2002 passed by the learned Additional District Judge-in-charge, 5th Court, Dhaka, in Title Appeal No. 181 of 1999 (heard analogous with Title Appeal No. 182 of 1999) dismissing the appeal and affirming the judgment and decree dated 25.2.1999 passed by the learned Subordinate Judge and Commercial Court No. 1, Dhaka in Title Suit No. 23 of 1992 (heard analogous with Title Suit No. 22 of 1992) decreeing the suit.

2. The Rule in Civil Revision No. 1462 of 2003 is directed against the judgment and decree dated 30.11.2002 passed by the learned Additional District Judge-in-charge, 5th Court, Dhaka, in Title Appeal No. 182 of 1999 (heard analogous with Title Appeal No. 181 of 1999) dismissing the appeal and affirming the judgment and decree dated 25.2.1999 passed by the learned Subordinate Judge and Commercial Court No. 1, Dhaka in Title Suit No. 22 of 1992 (heard analogous with Title Suit No. 23 of 1992) dismissing the suit.

3. Short facts necessary for disposal of the Rule are, that the predecessor-in-interest of the Opposite Party Nos. 1-14 named Emdaduddin, as plaintiff instituted Title Suit No. 480 of 1978, subsequently renumbered as Title Suit No. 23 of 1992 in the 1" Court of learned Subordinate Judge, Dhaka impleading Md Soleman, the predecessor-in-interest of petitioner No. 1 of this Rule seeking for the following relief:

"10. The plaintiff, therefore, prays:

a) that a decree may be passed in favour of the plaintiff and against the defendant by declaring that the plaintiff is the sole sixteen annas owner of the entire suit property;

b) that a decree for recovery of khas possession of "B" Schedule land by removing all obstructions there from may be passed in favour of the plaintiff and against the defendant;

c) that a decree for confirmation of possession of the "A" Schedule land may be passed in favour of the plaintiff and against the defendant

17. Mr Mohammad Habibullah, the learned Advocate for the petitioner, on appearing before this Court, submitted that the defendant of Title Suit No. 23 of 1992 having specifically pleaded that the Exhibit 1 was not executed by Soleman, that deed was created by false personification, and that no payment of consideration was made as against the said deed and Soleman did not execute the said deed it was the duty of the trial Court to decide specifically as to whether the said deed was executed by Soleman and any consideration was passed against the said deed. He further submitted that the plaintiff of Title Suit No. 23 of 1992 also failed to prove that any possession was handed over in his favour on the strength of Exhibit 1. He further submitted that the plaintiff of Title Suit No. 23 of 1992 has sought for recovery of khas possession in the 'B' schedule land in the plaint against Soleman alleging him to be a licensee under him. But the Courts below neither gave any finding upon the said relief nor discussion and considered any evidence in support of the said positive case of the plaintiff.
