He submitted that onus heavily lay upon the plaintiff of Title Suit No. 23 of 1992 to prove due execution of Exhibit 1. by Soleman, payment of consideration made by PW 1 and acceptance of said consideration by Soleman and handing over possession of the suit property by Soleman in favour of the PW 1 but the PW 1 having failed to do so by adducing evidence and the DW 17 by adducing oral and documentary evidence having been able to prove that the Exhibit 1 was a forged deed out and out, the judgment and decree impugned in the Rule are although concurrent is liable to be interfered by this Court in revision. He relied upon the case law upon onus of proving due execution of Exhibit 1 as reported in 1987 BLD (AD) 306.

18. Mr Md Lutfor Rahman Mondal, the learned Advocate for the opposite party on appearing before this Court, on the other hand, submitted that in view of section 101 of the Evidence Act, the burden of proof of the pleadings case cannot be shifted. He further submitted that the plaintiff of Title Suit No. 22 of 1992 came up before the Court with a specific pleadings but they failed to discharge their onus as per law. He further submitted that the Title Suit No. 23 of 1992 was filed during life time of Soleman and he died long after four years of filing of the suit but said Soleman did not make any attempt to compare the LTI as contained in the back of page No 1 of Exhibit 1 with his admitted LTI. He further submitted that no prayer was made by Soleman for making a comparison of the signature of LTI as contained in Exhibit 1 with his admitted signature and LTI to prove that the Exhibit 1 was not executed by Soleman. He further submitted that the Exhibit 1 was admitted into evidence and was marked as Exhibit 1 without having any objection from the defendant side. He further submitted that the Exhibit 1 being a registered instrument that carries a presumption of correctness and validity. In support of his contention he relied upon the case law reported in 1993 BLD (AD) 150 and the case of Abdullah and 3 others vs Abdul Hakim and others, reported in 20 DLR (SC) 205. He further submitted that the execution of Soleman has been proved beyond doubt by the plaintiff by adducing the evidence of PW 1 and PW 2 who corroborated each other. Mr Mondal submitted that the impugned judgment and decree being the judgment of affirmance there is nothing to interfere by this Court unless a strong case of no consideration of any evidence or no reading of any evidence or misreading of any evidence on record is made out. He relied upon the case law of Azifannessa vs Sakur Miah and others, reported in 30 DLR (AD) 41. He lastly submitted that the Exhibit 1 being a registered document and having been exhibited without any objection, the same shall be presumed to be correct and valid. In support of his contention he relied upon the decision reported in 1993 BLD (AD) 114.

<u>19. On perusal of the case law reported in 1993 BLD (AD) 114 it appears that our Appellate Division has held that the presumption of correctness of a Registered Document is a rebut table presumption and after giving due opportunity to the parties concerned the same can be rebutted. So, that decision goes against Mr Mondal. The presumption of correctness is not conclusive. On perusal of the Case law reported in 20 DLR (SC) 205 it appears that objection as to formal proof of document to be taken at earliest point of time. Here in the instant case the document Exhibit 1 itself is the questioned document. Its formal proof although was not objected initially but the very deed having classified to be a forged one, the defendant will not be debarred from questioning the validity of that deed. That decision does not apply in the instant suit.</u>

20. In reply Mr Mohammad Habibullah, the learned Advocate for the petitioner, submitted that the presumption of correctness of a registered documents does not carry any evidentiary value of correctness. He submitted that the presumption is always rebut table and he relied upon the decision reported in 7 BLR (AD) 306.

21. I have heard the learned Advocates of both the parties and considered their respective submissions.

22. On perusal of the judgment of the courts below it appears that neither the learned Joint District Judge and Commercial Court No. 1, Dhaka, being the trial Court, discussed and considered any evidence of the defendants of Title Suit No. 23 of 1992 nor the learned Additional District Judge being the last Court of facts made any discussion and consideration of any evidence of the plaintiffs of Title Suit No. 22 of 1992. So it appears that the judgments and decrees impugned in the Rule are based upon total no consideration of the evidence, both oral and documentary as adduced by the plaintiffs of Title Suit No. 22 of 1992 and the defendants of Title Suit No. 23 of 1992. It further appears that both the Courts below decreed the Title Suit No. 23 of 1992 upon assumption on saying অনুমতি হয় Mr Lutfor Rahman Mondal, the learned Advocate for the opposite parties in both the Rules, submitted that the judgment and decree impugned in the Rules being concurrent, there is no scope to interfere with those judgment and decree in revision. Mr Lutfor Rahman Mondal further submitted that this Court in exercise of its power under section 115(1) of the Code of Civil Procedure is not entitled to enter into the evidence. Mr Mondal in support of his argument cited the case law reported in 5 DLR (FC) 147 and the case law of Ajufannessa vs Safar Mia and others reported in 30 DLR (AD) 41.

23. On perusal of the case law reported in 5 DLR 147 it appears that the fact of that case is distinguishable from the fact of the instant case. That case law is not at all applicable in the instant case.

24. On perusal of the case law of Ajufannessa vs Safar Miah and others reported in 30 DLR (SC) 41 it appears that the said suit was a suit for declaration of title. The trial Court disbelieved the plaintiff's Dakhilas, which were marked as Exhibit 4 series and that finding was affirmed by the learned Additional District Judge in appeal. That concurrent finding were disturbed by the High Court Division in 2nd appeal and upon those disturbance of concurrent findings the Appellate Division held. "concurrent finding of file s as to the genuineness of the rent-receipts found by the two lower courts in 2nd appeal to the High Court, unless such finding is vitiated by error of law or procedure such finding is binding on the High Court." The above finding of the Appellate Division is by now the established principle of law. But in the instant case, the trial Court decreed the suit keeping totally out of consideration of the entire evidence of the plaintiffs of Title Suit No. 22 of 92 and the evidence of defendants of Title Suit No. 23 of 1992. So I am of the view that the above case law cited by Mr Mondal is not applicable in the instant case.

25. To meet the objection as raised by Mr Lutfor Rahman Mondal that concurrent finding of facts cannot be interfered by this Court, I felt necessity of extending my hands towards the judicial pronouncements of our Appellate Division giving authority to the High Court Division to interfere with the concurrent finding of facts based upon no consideration of material evidence on record, misreading of material evidence of record and also on total non-consideration of evidence on record.

<u>26. In the case of Sakhina Khatun and others vs Mansur Alam and others reported in 48 DLR (AD) 160 it has been settled that "there being a total non consideration of all the witnesses of the preempted, the learned Single Judge acted wrongly in refusing to exercise his revisional jurisdiction in a case where due to total non-consideration of the material evidence on record an erroneous decision has been arrived at occasioning a failure of justice. In that decision the concurrent findings of the trial Court, Appellate Court and of the High Court was set aside by our Appellate Division. The above authority, authorizes this Court to enter into the entire evidence of both the parties in view of the facts that admittedly the Courts below have given their findings upon no considering the entire evidence of the defendant of Title Suit No. 23 of 92 and the evidence of plaintiffs of Title Suit No. 22 of 1992.</u>

27. Before entering into the evidence for discussion and consideration let us decide as to whether the trial Court and as well as the lower appellate Court were justified in shifting the burden of proving the forged nature of Exhibit 1 upon the defendant of Title Suit No. 23 of 1992 and upon the plaintiff of Title Suit No. 22 of 1992 and was justified in decreeing the Title Suit No. 23 of 1992 for granting a decree for eviction of the defendant of Title Suit No. 23 of 1992 holding him to be a licensee under the plaintiff.

28. Mr Lutfor Rahman Mondal submitted that the burden of proof of pleadings case does not shift and submitted that the burden of proving that the Exhibit 1 is a forged deed was upon the defendant of Title Suit No. 23 of 1992 and upon the plaintiff of Title Suit No. 22 of 1992. Mr Mondal in support of his contention relied upon section 102 of the Evidence Act and upon the case-law of Kambhu Lakshmana vs Tangirala Venkateshwala reported in 2 DLR 82. On perusal of the said case law it appears that the fact of that case is quite distinguishable from the fact of the instant case and the cited case law has got no manner of application in the instant case.

29. The plaintiff in Title Suit No. 23 of 1992 filed the suit for declaration of title, confirmation of possession in schedule 'A' land and recovery of Khas possession in the 'B' Schedule land of the plaint against defendant Md Soleman alleging, inter alia, that Soleman sold the suit property to him by a Kabala deed dated 31-11-73 at a consideration of Taka 7000.00. Md Soleman by filing a written statement totally denied the said sale and denied his execution as contained in Exhibit 1. Md Soleman denied to have receipt of any consideration money as against the Exhibit 1. Md Solaiman categorically asserted the Exhibit 1 to be a forged deed and made out a case that the said Exhibit 1 was created by false personification. The defendant Nos. 5-8 being the subsequent purchasers from the heirs and legal representatives of defendant Soleman have stated categorically in their written statement that Soleman was a no Bengali and could not know how to write Bengali. Those defendants also brought a specific case that the plaintiff of Title Suit No. 23 of 1992 had created the Exhibit 1 by false personification with the help of scribe and witnesses of the deed. The plaintiffs of Title Suit No. 22 of 1992 also established a specific and distinct case that Soleman did not execute the Exhibit 1 and did not receive any single farthing towards consideration from the plaintiff of Title Suit No. 23 of 1992 as against the Exhibit 1. It is their case that the Exhibit 1 was created by Emdad, the plaintiff of Title Suit No. 23 of 1992 by false personification with help of the deed writer of Exhibit 1 and also with the help of witnesses as mentioned in the deed.

30. This is by now settled that whenever the execution of a deed is totally denied and a clear case of creation of a forged document is made out by false personification, in that case, the onus of proving due execution, payment of consideration and delivery of possession in the suit land entirely rests upon the alleged purchaser who claims title upon that deed. This view finds support from the case law reported in 47 DLR 248 and the case law reported in 44 DLR 79.

<u>31. In view of the above it is my considered view that the onus of proving of due execution of Exhibit 1 by Soleman and payment of consideration was rested upon the plaintiff of Title Suit No. 23 of 1992. The onus of proving of granting license to Soleman in 'B' schedule land was also rested upon the plaintiff of Title Suit No. 23 of 1992.</u>

32. Now let us consider as to whether the plaintiff of Title Suit No. 23 of 1992 by adducing PW 1, PW 3 could be able to prove due execution of Exhibit 1, payment of consideration as against that document and the fact of granting licence to Soleman by adducing legal evidence.

33. Mr Md Lutfor Rahman Mondal, the learned Advocate for the opposite party, took me to the judgments of the Courts below and Mr. Mohammad Habibullah, the learned Advocate for the petitioner, took me to the material evidence on record which is available.

34. On perusal of the decree passed by the trial Court, it appears that the learned Subordinate Judge and Commercial Court No. 1, Dhaka, without discussing and considering a single documentary evidence of the defendant and without discussing and considering the specific case of both the parties as to granting of licensee have passed the judgment and decree in a slipshod manner. From the judgment of the appellate Court it also appears that he being the last Court of fact has affirmed the judgment of the trial Court blindly in a very slipshod manner and without discussing and considering any evidence on record. On perusal of the Written Statement of the defendant Nos. 5-8, it appears that they taken a very positive case that Md Soleman did not know how to write in Bengali, he used to put his signature in English. The DWs adduced evidence in support of the said contention. The plaintiff of Title Suit No. 22 of 1992 has exhibited the passport of Md Soleman and that was marked as Exhibit B. It appears from Exhibit B that his name was written in English just at the bottom of his photograph as contained in the passport. It further appears that Soleman had sworn affidavit before the Magistrate, 1st Class on 6-11-1979 wherein he put his signature in English and that was marked as Exhibit 8. Another affidavit was sworn by Soleman on 3-2-1973 before the Magistrate, 1st Class, Dhaka and that was marked as Exhibit K(1), the signature as contained in the said affidavit was written in English. From the Exhibit M and M 1, it appears that Soleman was a merchant, and he entered into import trade contract under the Government of Pakistan by putting his signature in English in the year 1961. From the Exhibit 0 it appears that he made a correspondence to the Controller of Import and Export of the Government of East Pakistan and he put his signature in English and other documents the Exhibits 1, 2, 3, 4 were also signed in English by Soleman. The Exhibit K2 is another affidavit sworn by Soleman before the Magistrate, 1st Class on 20-5-1972 and that was also signed in English. On the other hand, there is not a single document produced by the plaintiff of Title Suit No. 23 of 1992 to prove that Soleman used to put his signature in Bengali. It is true, that the plaintiff of Title Suit No. 22 of 1992 ought to have taken positive step for comparing the LTI as contained in the back of the first page of Exhibit 1 with the admitted LTI of Md Soleman but from the record it appears that the suit came up for peremptory hearing after the death of Soleman.

35. In the instant case, the defendant of Title Suit No. 23 of 1992 having totally denied the execution of Exhibit 1 and having specifically asserted that the instrument was a forged one. The PW 1 had to prove due execution, payment of consideration. On perusal of the evidence of the PW 1 it appears that to prove the fact of execution of Md Soleman he has simply adduced in his examination-in-chief “নালিশী সম্পত্তি আমি ১৯৭৩ সনে ৭০০০ (সাত হাজার টাকা)দিয়া মোঃ সোলেমানের নিকট হইতে খরিদ করিয়াছি। দলিল নং ২৭২৬৫ তাং ৭-১১-৭৩ (প্রদঃ নং ১)এই সেই সাফ কবলা দলিল। নালিশী সম্পত্তি খরিদ করিবার পর আমাকে দখল বুঝাইয়া দেন।” Save and except this evidence there is no other evidence available on record to show that the PW 1 adduced any positive evidence to prove due execution made by Soleman. The PW 2 being another witness has adduced “বাদী মৃত সোলেমানের নিকট হইতে ক্রয় করিয়াছিলাম। ক্রয়/বিক্রয়ের সময় আমি উপস্থিত ছিলাম। বিক্রয়ের পর অর্ধেক অংশের দখল বুঝাইয়া দেয় এবং অবশিষ্ট অংশের দখল হস্তান্তরের জন্য সময় নেয়।” Save and except this evidence there is no other evidence to prove that Soleman put his signature upon Exhibit 1. The PW 3 also stated in his examination-in-chief that “বাদী ক্রয় করিয়া নালিশী সম্পত্তি প্রাপ্ত হইয়াছে।” This PW 2 and PW 3 are neither witness to the deed nor are scribes of the deed. Due execution can be proved by the following modes : (1) by calling as a witness a person who wrote the document; (2) by citing a witness who saw the writing down of the deed and saw to put signature by the executants upon the deed; (3) who is qualified to express an opinion as to the writing by virtue of section 47 of the Evidence Act; (4) by comparison of the handwriting as specified under section 73 of the Evidence Act; (5) by the admission of the person against whom the documents is tendered and (6) by expert evidence.

36. In the instant case the mode of proving as stated above in (3), (4), (5) and 6 are absent. From the Exhibit 1 it appears that the writer of the deed was Bachchu Miah and two other witnesses named Rafiqul Islam and A Kiron Shaheen put signatures as witness but those persons were not brought before the Court to prove due execution.

37. So far the writing of the Exhibit 1 and execution is concerned PW 1 was put a question:

“দলিলটা কোন জায়গায় বসিয়া লিখিয়াছে?” and he replied “দলিলটা সোলেমান মিয়া লিখাইয়াছে। তাহা কোথায় লিখাইয়াছে তাহা আমি বলিতে পারি না।” Thereafter, PW 1 was asked “দলিল লিখার সময় হইতে আজ পর্যন্ত কি আপনি খোঁজ নিয়াছেন যে, উহা কোথায় লিখা হইয়াছিল? at this he replied “কোর্টে লিখা হইয়াছে" Thereafter he was asked" খোঁজটা কবে নিলেন?" at this stage he replied "কথা হবার পর সপ্তাহ খানেক পরে শুনলাম তাহার বন্ধুর কাছে লিখতে দেওয়া হইয়াছে।" at one stage he was asked a question in the following form “সোলেমান কবে প্রথম কোন তারিখে জায়গা বিক্রির কথা বলিয়াছে?” at this he replied "১৯৭৩ সালের তারিখ মনে নািই জানুয়ারি বা ফেব্রুয়ারির মধ্যে হইতে পারে" Thereafter he admitted "৩/৪ মাস কথাবার্তার পর ফাইনাল হইল" Thereafter he admitted ফাইনাল হইবার ২ মাস পরে লেনদেন হয়। বিক্রির টাকা-পয়সার লেনদেন একদিনেই হইয়াছিল। "From this evidence it appears that the execution and payment of consideration was made in August 1973. Thereafter PW 1 was asked a question দলিল লিখার কয় দিন পরে টাকা পয়সা লেনদেন হইল? Thereafter he replied "রেজিষ্ট্রি যেদিন হয় সেদিন লেনদেন হয়।” From this evidence it is very much clear that actually Exhibit 1 was not executed in the usual course of normal business in view of the fact that the Exhibit 1 shows its date of execution on 6-11-73 and the date of registration on 13-11-73.

<u>38. On perusal of Exhibit 1, it further appears that the stamps used for the purpose of writing of the deed were purchased on 30-10-1973 and the fourth page was a demy paper. The date of execution mentioning "6-11-1973" was written in a different ink and by a different person as it appears from the said deed. The stamps used for the purpose of writing of affidavit in support of the transfer were purchased on 13-11-1973. From this it is very much incredible to believe that after purchase of stamps on 13-11-1973, how could a deed be executed on 6-11-1973. Moreover, the PW 2 did not adduce a single evidence that he saw execution by Md Soleman. From this evidence it is proved beyond doubt that the plaintiff of Title Suit No. 23 of 1992 hopelessly failed to prove due execution by Md Soleman. Moreover the DW 1 could not produce any document at the trial to prove Soleman used to put his signature in Bengali. Soleman entered his appearance in the suit through an Advocate and executed Vokalatnama in English. There is no evidence on record to believe that Exhibit 1 was executed by Soleman. So, it is my considered view that the plaintiff of Title Suit No. 23 of 1992 has hopelessly failed to prove due execution of Exhibit 1 by Soleman.</u>

<u>39. So far as payment of consideration is concerned the PW 1 was put a question in the following form দলিল লিখার কয় দিন পরে টাকা পয়সা লেনদেন হইল? he replied "রেজিষ্ট্রি যেদিন হয় সেদিন লেনদেন হয়।” Thereafter, he was asked the following question দলিল লিখার কয় দিন পরে টাকা পয়সা লেনদেন হইল? at this he replied "একমাস/দেড়মাস পরে লেনদেন হয়" It is the case of plaintiff of Title Suit No. 23 of 1992 that the deed was written some times before 6-11-1973 and thereafter the payment was made. So as per the PW 1, the payment was made in December 73 or January 1974. The PW 2 in his cross-examination has said "বাদী সোলায়মানকে সদর সাব রেজিষ্ট্রি অফিসের নীচের তলায় টাকা দিয়াছিল। সকাল ১০-৩০ মিনিটের সময় টাকা দিয়াছিল। ঐ দিন রেজিষ্ট্রি হয়।" This evidence is quite contradictory with PW 1. There is no other evidence available on record to show that any consideration was made. From the discussions made above it is crystal clear that no execution was made by Soleman and no payment of consideration was made as against the Exhibit 1. The Courts below having failed to discuss and consider this evidence have caused a serious miscarriage of justice by the impugned judgment and decree and the same is liable to be interfered by this Court in view of the case law of Sakhina Khatoon versus Mansur Alam, reported in 48 DLR (AD) 160.</u>

40. Let us decide the other issue that is, whether the plaintiff of Title Suit No. 23 of 1992 was accorded licence to be part of the suit land by Soleman or Soleman was accorded permission to reside in "B" schedule land to the plaint by PW 1. The evidences on record are sufficient to decide this question. The Courts below although did not decide this question specifically but the evidence having been found sufficient as adduced by the DW 17, I find that this issue should be decided by this Court to meet the ends of justice in view of the case of Kabir Ahmed versus Md Nurul Islam, reported in 4 MLR (AD) 1.

41. To decide the issue, let us discuss the evidence on record. Soleman's wife was examined as DW 2 who in her evidence adduced

“এমদাদ উদ্দিন পিয়নের চাকুরী করিতেন। আমার স্বামীর জানা শোনা লোক ছিলেন। মাঝে মাঝে আমাদের বাসায় আসিতেন সাহায্য নেওয়ার জন্য। তিনি পাকিস্তান সময় হইতেই আমাদের বাসায় আসা যাওয়া করিতেন। বাংলাদেশ হওয়ার পর উক্ত এমদাদ আমার স্বামীর নিকট হইতে কিছুদিন নালিশী সম্পত্তিতে থাকিবার জন্য অনুমতি চাহিয়াছিলেন এবং কিছুদিন পর চলিয়া যাইবে বলিয়া অঙ্গীকার করিয়াছিলেন। সেই মর্মে আমার স্বামী উক্ত এমদাদ উদ্দিনকে নালিশী সম্পত্তির সামান্য কিছু অংশে অর্থাৎ ৩ টি রুমে থাকিবার জন্য অনুমতি দেন। আমার স্বামীর সহিত তাহার কথা ছিল যে, আমার স্বামী যখন তাহাকে চলিয়া যাইতে বলিবেন তখন সে বাড়ী ছাড়িয়া চলিয়া যাইবে। এইরুপে কিছুদিন বাড়ীতে অবস্থান করা অবস্থায় উক্ত এমদাদ উদ্দিন আমার স্বামীর বিরুদ্ধে বর্তমান নং ২৩/১৯৯২ নং মোকদ্দমা ১৯৭৮ সালে করেছিলেন।”

From the cross-examination it appears that no damage was caused and those evidence remained unshaken.

42. DW 6 Abdul Hamid, in his examination-in-chief, adduced the following evidence "এমদাদ উদ্দিন পাকিস্তান আমলে সোলেমানের নিকট আসা যাওয়া করিত। এমদাদ উদ্দিন সেটেলমেন্ট অফিসের পিয়ন ছিল। এমদাদ উদ্দিন গরীব ছিল এবং সাহায্য এর জন্য সোলেমানের নিকট আসিত। এমদাদ উদ্দিন ১৯৭২ সনে মার্চ/এপ্রিল মাসে সোলায়মান সাহেবকে বলে যে, ছেলেমেয়ে অসুবিধায় আছি এবং তাহাকে কয়েক মাস থাকার অনুমতি দেওয়ার জন্য অনুরোধ করে এবং আরো বলে যে কয়েকমাস পরে চলিয়া যাইবে। উক্ত কথার উপর ভিত্তি করে সোলেমান তাহার বাড়ীতে এমদাদকে থাকতে দিয়াছে। বাড়ীটার উত্তর দিকে ২টা রুমে এমদাদ উদ্দিনকে থাকতে দেয়। প্রথম একটা রুম নিয়া পরবর্তীতে অসুবিধার জন্য আরো একটা রুম নেয়। থাকতে দেওয়ার ঘটনা ১৯৭২ সনের প্রথম দিকের ঘটনা। নালিশী বাড়ীর বাকী অংশতে সোলেমান সাহেব তাহার ফ্যামিলি নিয়া ছিল।”

<u>43. On the other hand, the plaintiff of Title Suit No. 23 of 1992 could not adduce any positive evidence to prove that Soleman was granted licence to stay in the "B" schedule land to the plaint. Upon consideration of the above evidence it is very much clear that in fact, no transfer was made by Soleman in favour of the PW 1 and the PW 1 was granted permission by Soleman to stay in a part out of the suit homestead. Both the Courts below did not discuss and consider the, above evidence. From the facts and circumstances and discussions made, I have no hesitation but to hold that the Exhibit 1 was not executed by Soleman, no payment in consideration was made against the said deed and no delivery of possession was made in favour of PW 1 on the strength of that Exhibit. The Exhibit 1 is nothing but a forged deed. The judgment and decree impugned in the Rule are not sustainable in law and are liable to be set aside. There is merit in the Rules.</u>

44. In the result, both the Rules are made absolute, however, without any order as to costs. The judgment and decree dated 30-11-2002 passed by the learned Additional District Judge-in-charge, 5th Court, Dhaka, in Title Appeal No. 181 of 1999 (heard analogous with Title Appeal No. 182 of 1999) dismissing the appeal and affirming the judgment and decree dated 25-2-1999 passed by the learned Subordinate Judge and Commercial Court No. 1, Dhaka in Title Suit No. 23 of 1992 (heard analogous with Title Suit No. 22 of 1992) decreeing the suit is hereby set aside. The judgment and decree dated 30-11-2002 passed by the learned Additional District Judge-in-charge, 5th Court, Dhaka, in Title Appeal No. 182 of 1999 (heard analogous with Title Appeal No. 181 of 1999) dismissing the appeal and affirming the judgment and decree dated 25-2-1999 passed by the learned Subordinate Judge and Commercial Court No. 1, Dhaka in Title Suit No. 22 of 1992 (heard analogous with Title Suit No. 23 of 1992) dismissing the suit is also hereby set aside. Title Suit No. 22 of 1992 is hereby decreed with cost and Title Suit No. 23 of 1993 is dismissed with cost. The kabala deed alleged to have been executed by Md. Soleman on 6-11-1973 and registered on 13-11-1973 in favour of PW 1, Emdaduddin is hereby declared void and the same is cancelled. The title of plaintiff of Title Suit No. 22 of 1992 is hereby declared and the possession of the opposite party plaintiffs of Title Suit No. 23 of 1992 in part of the suit land are nothing but permissive possession granted by Soleman. The plaintiff of Title Suit No. 22 of 1992 is entitled to get recovery of khas possession after evicting the plaintiff of Title Suit No. 23 of 1992, on execution of the decree. All further proceedings of Title Execution Case No. 1 of 1999 now pending in the Court of Subordinate Judge and Commercial Court No. 1, Dhaka appear to be not maintainable as being infructuous one. The defendant Nos. 5-8 being a purchaser during tendency of the suit, their title will be governed according to section 52 of the Transfer of Property Act.

Send down lower Court's record at once.

End.

full_judgment:
Sheikh Hassan Arif J: Rule Nisi was issued calling upon the respondents to show cause as to why the impugned order being No. 59 dated 24-11-2011 (Annexure-D-2) passed by the Joint District Judge and Artha Rin Adalat, 1st Court, Jessore in Artha Rin Execution Case No. 11 of 2007 should not be declared to have been passed without lawful authority and is of no legal effect.

2. Short back ground facts, relevant for the disposal of the Rule, are that Islami Bank Bangladesh Limited, Benapole Branch, Police Station-Benapole, District-Jessore-(respondentNo.3), as plaintiff, filed Artha Rin Suit No. 31 of 2006 before the First Court of Artha Rin Adalat, Jessore against the petitioner and others for realization of loan of Taka 1,24,84,730. The defendants having not contested, the said suit was decreed ex-parte on 22-2-2007 (decree drawn up on 1-3-2007). Accordingly, the respondent-bank put the said decree into execution through Artha Execution Case No. 11 of 2007 filed before the same Adalat. In the said execution process, the mortgaged properties of the petitioner and others were put on auction-sale through news papers in view of the provisions under section 33(1) of the Artha Rin Adalat Ain, 2003 ("the said Ain"). However, the said auction did not succeed due to the absence of bidders. The executing Adalat then proceeded for the 2nd auction in view of the provisions under sub-section (4) of section 33 of the said Ain and fixed 5-11-2007 for the same. The 2nd auction also ended up in failure as no bidder participated therein. In such situation, the decree holder bank, on 7-3-2011, filed an application before the executing Adalat praying for title of the mortgaged property in view of the provisions under sub-section (7) of section 33, whereupon the petitioner filed objection against' the same. After hearing the parties, the Adalat, vide impugned order dated 24-11-2011, allowed the application filed by the bank conferring title of the mortgaged properties upon it and fixed 28-11-2011 for presentation and preparation of certificate of sale. At this stage, the petitioner moved this Court and obtained the aforesaid Rule. At the time of issuance of the Rule, this Court, by order dated 15-12-2011, stayed operation of the impugned order dated 24-11-2011.

3. The Rule is contested by the respondent No. 3 bank through learned advocates, who also filed affidavit-in-opposition.

4. Mr Shah Mohd Monir Sharif, learned advocate, along with Mr Mohammad Imran Jahangir, learned advocate, appearing for the petitioner, mainly submits that since the Adalat proceeded for the 2nd auction under sub-section (4) of section 33 and completed the same unsuccessfully, the Adalat acted without jurisdiction in conferring title on the' decree-holder-bank under subsection (7) of section 33 of the said Ain. According to him, since 2nd auction took place, the decree holder batik as Well as the Adalat had no option but to proceed' for conferring the right of possession and enjoyment of the mortgaged property on the decree-holder-bank in view of sub-section (5) of section 33. In short, Mr Sharif wants to convince this Court that once the 2ndauction is taken place in view of sub-section (4) of section 33, there is no scope either for the Adalat or for the decree holder to go for the conferment of title of the mortgaged property in view of sub-section (7) of section 33 of the said Ain.

5. Mr Sharnim Khaled Ahmed, learned senior counsel, along with Mr Mohammed Abdul Baset, learned advocate, appearing for the respondent No. 3-bank, on the other hand, submits that the provisions under section 33 have given free leverages to the decree holder either to go for the 2nd auction or to seek conferment of title upon it under sub-section(7) of section 33 of the said Ain. According to him, even if the 2nd auction is taken place, the decree holder will at any stage be at liberty to ask for conferment of title in view of the provisions under sub-section (7) of section 33. Mr Ahmed further argues that since sub-section (7) of section 33 commences with the words "notwithstanding anything contained in sub-sections (4) and (5)", the provisions under sub-sections (4) and (5) have been made subjugated to the provisions under sub-section (7). In other words, according to him, the provisions under, sub-section (7), in clear terms, have ruled out the applicability of the provisions under sub-section (4) and (5) and, as such, even if the proceedings under sub-sections (4) and (5) are adopted or initiated, the decree holder can exercise its option to apply for title under sub-section (7) even in the middle stage of the proceedings under sub-sections (4) and (5). 6. The main question to be determined in this writ petition is whether once the 2 auction sale in view of sub-section (4) of section 33 is adopted, in other words, if the 2nd auction is taken place unsuccessfully, whether or not the bank can apply for the conferment of title of the mortgaged property in view of the provisions under sub-section (7) of section 33, and, upon such application, whether the Adalat can confer such tile under the said provisions.

7. It appears that, in view of sub-sections (1),( 2), (2Ka), (2Kha), (2Ga) and (3) of section 33 of the said Ain, the Adalat is obliged to go for an auction sale of the mortgaged property, and the holding of such 11 auction of the mortgaged property is mandatory. The said 11 auction has to be taken place in accordance with the provisions and procedures mentioned in the above mentioned sub-sections of section 33. Sub-section (4) of section 33 speaks about the 2nd auction after the 11 auction as taken place under the said sub-sections fails either for absence of bidders or for any other reasons. In going for the 2nd auction, the procedures mentioned as regards the 11 auction have to be followed. Sub-section (5) further provides that if the 2nd auction, as taken place in view of sub-section (4), fails for any reason, the right to possession and enjoyment of the mortgaged property will be conferred on the decree holder and, in such case, the decree holder will be at liberty to realize the decreetal amount through sale of the mortgaged property, again in accordance with the pro-visions mentioned in sub-sections (1),( 2), (2Ka), (2Kha), (2Ga), (3) and (4) of section 33. Sub-section (6), however, provides that if excess money is realized through such auction sale, the decree-holder will refund the same to the judgment debtor, and if the sale proceeds do not cover the decreetal amount, the decree-holder will be at liberty to go for the 2nd or further execution cases in view of section 28 of the said Ain. Sub-section (6Ka) further provides that if the decree holder fails to sell the mortgaged property after such con-ferment of right to possession and enjoyment, it will be at liberty to go for further execution cases.

8. The above provisions under section 33 describe the chronology of actions to be taken by the decree-holder as well as the Adalat for realization of the decreetal amount through sale of the mortgaged property. However, sub-sections 6 (Kha) and (7) of section 33 have made a leap-frog approach in the said chronology of actions. According to sub-section 6(Kha), even after con-ferment of right to possession and enjoyment of the mortgaged property, the decree-holder would be at liberty to apply for conferment of title of the mortgaged property on it under sub-section (7) for a period of 6(six) years, and this sub-section 6(Kha) even stars with a strong non-obstante pro-vision with the words (“"এই ধারার ভিন্নতর যাহা কিছুই থাকুক না কেন"”)(notwithstanding anything contained in this section). This means, the Legislature has given this sub-section, namely sub-section 6(Kha), a special overriding status which is that whatever is contained in the entire section 33 of the said Ain, after conferment of the right to enjoyment and possession of the mortgaged property under sub-section (5), the decree holder would be at liberty to apply for the conferment of title during a period of 6(six) years and that the title of the said property would automatically vest in the decree holder and a certificate to that effect would be issued by the Adalat upon expiry of the said six years' period. It further appears that, the Legislature has given another powerful leverage on the decree holder under sub-section (7), which also starts with the words [“উপ-ধারা (৪) ও (৫) এর বিধান সত্ত্বেও”] [notwithstanding the provisions in sub-sections (4) and (5)1 According to the provisions under this sub-section (7), notwithstanding the provisions under sub-sections (4) and (5), the decree holder will be at liberty to apply for conferment of title of the mortgaged property on it, and once such application is made, the Adalat will refrain from following the proceedings under sub- sections (4) and (5) [উপ ধারা (৪) ও (৫) এর কার্যক্রম অনুসরণ করা হইতে বিরত থাকিবে], and, accordingly, issue a certificate declaring that the title of the said property has been vested as such. Again, once such certificate is issued, the same will be regarded as a title deed and will be registered accordingly by the local sub-registrar.

<u>9. As indicated above, the Legislature has deliberately given sub-sections 6(Kha) and (7) a separate status. Thus, the provisions under sub-section 6(kha) are such that they can be followed even notwithstanding whatever contained in the entire section 33. This means, once the right to enjoyment and possession of the mortgaged property is conferred on the decree holder, it will be at liberty to even immediately apply for conferment of title under sub-section (7). In which case, it will not be obligatory on it to try to sell the property through 2nd, 3rd or 4th auctions. To obtain that special status under sub-section 6(kha), the precondition is that the right to possession and enjoyment of the property is conferred on the decree holder in view of sub-section (5).</u>

<u>10. Similarly, sub-section (7) has also given a special leverage on the decree holder; According to the said provisions, not-withstanding the provisions under sub-sections (4) and (5), the decree holder will be at liberty to file an application for conferment of title on it by the Adalat, and once such application is made, the Adalat will even refrain from following the proceedings under sub-sections (4) and (5) and will confer such title on the decree holder through a certificate of title issued by it declaring such title. The only hurdle in the said provisions under sub-section (7) is that the provisions under sub-sections (1), (2), 2(Ka), 2(Kha), 2(Ga) and (3) of section 33 cannot be jeopardized. In other words, it recognizes the mandatory nature of the 1st auction in view of sub-sections (1), (2), 2(Ka), 2(Kha), 2(Ga) and (3). Thus, once the 1st auction is done and it fails for any reason, the decree-holder bank will be at liberty to either proceed for the 2nd auction and then for conferment of right to possession and enjoyment under sub-section (5) or it can ask for conferment of tile under sub-section (7). This option of conferment of title can be exercised by the decree holder either immediately after the 1st auction or after conferment of right to possession and enjoyment of the mortgaged property or even after conclusion of the 2 auction, though unsuccessfully. This intention of the Legislature to give almost a free leverage to the decree holder is clear from the provisions mentioned under sub-section 6(Kha) and section (7) of section 33. While sub-section 6(Kha) has given the decree holder a free leverage to apply for title once the right to enjoyment and possession of the mortgaged property is conferred on it under sub-section (5), sub-section (7) gives it another leverage by providing that notwithstanding the provisions under sub-section (4) and(5), the decree holder will be at liberty to apply for conferment of title. The only precondition is to satisfy the Court that the 1st auction has taken place. In. the course of hearing, we have examined the earlier decisions of this Court in Setara Begum vs Al-Arafa Islami Bank, 14 MLR 480 = 61 DLR 791 and Atiqullah vs Artha Rin Adalat, 16 BLC 486, as referred to by the parties. However, since those decisions did not address the issues as raised in this writ petition directly, we do not need to discuss them with elaboration.</u>

<u>11. In the case before us, the admitted position is that the 200 auction has taken place, though not successfully as no bidder participated. This means, in the meantime, the mandatory precondition of holding the 1st auction has already been fulfilled. Thus, the decree holder bank is now at liberty to wait for the conferment of right to possession and enjoyment of the mortgaged property under sub-section (5) and then apply for the conferment of title or wait for 6(six) years for such conferment of title automatically. At the same time, it has in the meantime acquired the other leverage to apply for the conferment of title directly even without waiting for the conferment of right-to enjoyment and possession of the mortgaged property under sub-section (5). This free leverage of decree holder bank is clear from the provisions under sub-section (7), which at first has overruled the effect of the provisions under sub-sections (4)  and (5) and then provides that once an application is made by the decree holder for, conferment of title, the Adalat will even refrain from following the proceedings under sub-sections (4) and (5). This means at any stage of the proceedings under sub-sections (4) and (5), the decree-holder-bank is entitled to apply for such conferment of title. Therefore, though argued by Mr Sharif, we do not find any indication in the clear provisions under section 33 that once the 2nd auction is taken place-the decree holder can only ask for conferment of right to possession and enjoyment of the mortgaged property. We rather find that the provisions under sub-section (7) have made it clear that the Legislature wanted to give a free leverage to the decree holder bank or financial-institution to apply for the conferment of title at any stage after the 1st auction is done and failed. Therefore, just holding of the in auction will not be a bar against the decree-holder bank preventing it from applying to get the title of the mortgaged property under sub-section (7).</u>

12. Regard being had to the above discussions of law and facts, we have no option but to hold that the Rule has no merit and, as such, the same should be discharged.

13. Accordingly, the Rule is discharged without any order as to costs. The order of stay granted at the time of issuance of the, Rule, thus, stands vacated. The Adalat below is directed to proceed with the execution of the decree in accordance with law.

Communicate this at once.

End.

lawyer:
Md Khalilur Rahman, Advocate ----- For the Petitioners. 
SRM Lutfor Rahman Akand, Advocate ----- For the Respondent No.4
parties:
Zahirul Islam & others ----- Petitioners
Vs.
Government of Bangladesh and others ----- Respondents
full_judgment:
Md Ashfaqul Islam J: At the instance of the petitioners, this Rule Nisi was issued calling upon the respondent to show cause as to why the impinged 8 (eight) notices dated 1-2-2003 issued under the signature of respondent No.3 for rehearing of Settlement Appeal Case Nos. 2846, 2847, 2849, 2850, 2857, 2858, 2859 and 3025 of 1999 with a reference to Miscellaneous Case No. 760 of 2002 (Annexure-E, E (1), E(2), E(3), E(4), E(5), E(6) and E(7) should not be declared to have been passed illegally and without lawful authority and why direction should not be issued to send the draft publication of Khatian Nos. 237, 155, 125 and 245 of Mouza Shantinagar, Police Station Motijheel, Dhaka prepared in the name of the petitioners to the Settlement Press for final publication.

2. Facts leading to the issuance of the present Rule, in short, are that after completing all the stages of proceeding for survey and settlement of recent Mohanagari settlement under relevant Rules of Stale Acquisition and Tenancy Rules, 1955 (herein after referred to as SA and T Rules, 1955) (i.e. proceeding known as khanapuri, Bujaral, Attestation, objection and Appeal) 1.20 acres of land covered by DP Khatian No. 237 of Mouza Shantinagar, under Police Station Motijheel, District-Dhaka were recorded in the names of Hazi Zahirul Islam, Jainal Abedin, Hazi Mahbubul Islam, Mojibul Islam (the petitioner Nos. 1, 2, 3, 5) and 8 others, 0.4050 acre of land covered by DP khatian No. 155 were recorded in the name of Hazi Zahirul Islam (The Petitioner No. 1),0.0730 acre land covered by DP Khatian No. 125 were recorded in the name of Kamal Uddin (the petitioner No.4) and 0.0078 acre land covered by DP Khatian No. 245 were recorded in the name of Mojibul Islam (the petitioner No.5).

3. The petitioners and their other co-sharers have been owning and possessing a total 1.837 acres of land covered by the aforesaid 4 khatians No. 237, 155, 125 and 245 and some other lands total being 3.21 acres from the time of their predecessors namely Hazi Hafizuddin, Afsaruddin and Md Taher who purchased the 3.21 acres of land including the lands covered by the aforesaid four DP khatian from its lawful owners Bamacharan Pal, Boloram Pal, Hororam Pal and Gupal Chandra Pal by registered sale deed No. 4911 dated 26-8-1952 and have been owning and possessing the same by constructing residential-cum-commercial building.

4. While the predecessors of the petitioners were owning and possessing the aforesaid 3.21 acres of land along with the building thereon, including the land covered by aforesaid four I) DP Khatians, the then Dhaka Improvement Trust (DIT) issued notice for requisition of 2.19 acre of land including the land covered by 4 khatians for the purpose of acquisition for constructing North-South Road by starting LA Case Nos. 8/65-66 through the ADC (LA) Dhaka. Subsequently the aforesaid 2.19 acre of land was de-requisitioned by notice dated 24th April 1968.

5. The land covered by the order of derequisition as well as of 4 DP Khatians as mentioned above were wrongly recorded in the name of Collector, Dhaka as khas land but at the time of preparation of RS record the land in question' was duly and correctly ordered to be recorded in the name of petitioner No.5 and the predecessors of other petitioners and other co-sharers in Settlement Appeal Case No.1 53 and accordingly RS and DP khatian No. 53 was prepared though the respondent No.4 did not participate in any proceeding under Rules 28 to 31 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act Rules 1955 at the time of operation of RS record of right before the survey and settlement authority but fraudulently entered his name in the said RS Khatian at the time of final publication in collusion with the staffs of the Settlement Press and on the basis of the said fraudulent RS khatian managed to have recorded his name in the recent Mohanagari Record of Right against which the petitioners and others filed Objection Case Nos. 10, 12,61,40,41,43,57,24, 0,46,44,47,48,42,28,25,22 and 69 under Rule 30 of SA and T Rules, 1955. The objection officer heard both the parties and allowed the objection Case Nos. 10 and 12 by analogous judgment dated 23-6-1999.

6. Against the said judgment passed by the, objection officer respondent Nos. 4 and 5 preferred Settlement Appeal Case Nos. 284/99, 2847/90, 2849/99, 2850/99, 2857/99, 2954/99, 2859/99 and 3025/99 under Rule 31 of SA and T Rules, 1955 and being refused by the Appeal Officer preferred writ petition No. 1103 of 1999 before this Court without impleading the petitioners and their co-sharers and obtained Rule. The present petitioner Nos. 1-3 and 5 other co-sharers on being added as party in that writ petition contested the Rule, which was discharged on 25-7-2001 by this Court. After that the Appeal Officer heard both the parties and dismissed the said appeal cases by analogous judgment dated 9th April 2002 (annexure-D and D-1).

7. It is further stated that after the judgment given in the appeal cases under, Rule 31 there is no provision other than to send the DP khatian to the settlement Press for final publication .under Rule 32 of SA and T Rules, 1995 and the petitioners were waiting for such finally published khatian but all on a sudden on 3rd February 2003 the petitioners obtained separated 8 notices issued under the signature of Settlement Officer, Dhaka, the respondent No.3 dated 1-2-2003 for re-hearing of the self name appeal Case Nos. 2846/99, 2847/99, 2849/99, 2850/99, 2857/99, 2858/99, 2859/99 and 3025/99 under Rule 31 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Rules, 1955 by giving a reference of Miscellaneous case No. 760 of 2002. It is at this state the petitioner moved this Division under Article 102 of the constitution and obtained the present Rule.

8. Mr Md Khalilur Rahman, the learned counsel appearing on behalf of the petitioners after taking us with the petition, the impugned notices and other annexure with the petition, mainly pressed that the impugned notices dated 1-2-2003 for re-hearing of the appeal Case Nos. 2846/99, 2847/99, 2849/99, 2850/99, 2857/99, 2858/99, 2859/99 and 3025/99 afresh has been issued. Without any lawful authority and without jurisdiction which should be declared unconstitutional. In elaborating his argument the learned Advocate submits that the notices for re-hearing of the appeal cases is absolutely in violation of State Acquisition and Tenancy Rules; 1955. He submits that once the appeal has been disposed on contest under Rule 31 no review or other, application lies and settlement authority has no jurisdiction to re-open the mailer other than to send the draft application khatian for final publication in the settlement press under Rule 32 of the SA and T Rules, 1955. This is well settled as he submits. In support of his contentions he placed reliance on the decision of Romisa Khanam vs Bangladesh 61 DLR 18, (where one of us was a party), Md Abtab Ali Sheikh vs Director of Land Records 11 MLR 226 and Capital Co-operative Housing Society Ltd vs Bangladesh 45 DLR 289.

9. Mr SRM Lutfor Rahman Akand, the learned Advocate appearing on behalf of the respondent No.4 and 5 by filing affidavit-in-opposition, on the other hand, opposes the Rule and submits that this writ petition should be discharged in that the impugned notices in respect of filing of the Miscellaneous Case No. 760 of 2002 for re-hearing, of Appeal Cases Nos. 2846/99, 2847/99, 2849/99, 2850/99,2857/99,2858/99,2859/99 and 3025/99 is absolutely in accordance with law since the same has been permitted under Rule 42 of the Tenancy Rules, 1955. He submits that Rule 42 clearly provides the settlement authority has jurisdiction to re- hear the appeal before publication of the record of right and hence the instant writ petition filed against those notices regarding re-hearing of the appeals is not maintainable under Article 102 of the constitution.

10. We have heard the learned advocate for both sides at length and considered their submissions. We have also perused the petition, impugned notices, other annexure appended to the petition and the affidavit-in-opposition carefully. The matter is well settled by this Court as well as the Appellate Division of the Supreme Court.

11. In the case of Romisa Khanam vs Bangladesh in which one of us was a party, Justice MA Rashid (as he then was) while dealing with the same point observed as follows: -

"In the scheme of revision of a record-of- rights under section 144 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, 1950 there are various stages laid down in the Rules, 1955. After completion of attestation the Revenue Officer shall under Rule 29 published the draft record-of-rights for public inspection. Under Rule 30, the Revenue Officer shall decide summarily in presence of the interested parties any objection regarding ownership or possession of land or of any interest in land. Any person aggrieved by such an order on any objection made under Rule 30 may appeal to the Revenue Officer appointed with additional designation of Settlement Officer or of Assistant Settlement Officer commonly known as Appellate Officer within 30 days from the date of order appealed against. Any order passed on such appeal appears to be final as no further appeal or revision is provided there from.

After disposal of the objections under Rule 30 and appeals under 31 and correction of the draft record-of-rights in accordance with the original and appellate orders on all objections, the Revenue Officer shall proceed to frame final record of rights under Rule 31 and then, publish record of rights under Rule 33. Under Rule 34, the Revenue Officer shall within sixty days of the final publication make a certificate stating the fact of such final publication and the date thereof, etc. And the Government by a notification in the official gazette may declare with regard to any specified area that the record-of-rights has been finally published for every village included in such area and such notification shall be conclusive proof of such publication.

Chapter VIII of said Rules, 1955 deals with general power of Revenue Officer in revising record-of-rights under section 144 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, 1950 Rule 42 gives special power to a Revenue Officer appointed with additional designation of Settlement Officer to direct at any time before the publication of the final record of rights that any portion of the proceedings referred to in Rule 28 to 32 in respect of any district, part of a district or local area shall be cancelled and the proceedings shall be taken up fresh from such stage as he may direct. Similarly, such Settlement Officer is empowered under Rule 42A upon an application or receipt of an Official Report to correct any entry that has been procured by fraud in record-of-right before final publication, and after consulting the relevant records and making such other enquiries as he deems necessary, to direct excision of the fraudulent entry and his act in doing so shall not be open to an appeal. At the same time, the Revenue Officer shall make the correct entry after hearing the parties and record his finding in a formal proceeding for the purpose of future reference. But none of such powers under Rule 42 or 42A of the Rules, 1955 appears to empower such Settlement Officer to sit and or act as an appellate authority over an appellate order passed under Rule 31 and set-aside such, appellate order or direct the Appellate Officer to hear an appeal afresh in respect of a particular holding. Nor the Appellate Officer is empowered to rehear an appeal which was finally disposed by him. The Settlement Officer therefore most illegally cancelled the appellate orders and compelled the Appellate Officer to hear the appeals afresh."

<u>12. Against this decision Bhawal Raj Court of Wards Estate who was the respondent in the said case unsuccessfully moved the Appellate Division in Civil Petition for Leave to Appeal Nos. 1447-52 of 2008. The Appellate Division finally set at rest of the same once for all. All other decisions as referred to above are on the same point and all these decisions settled the proposition of law that once appeal has been disposed of on contest under Rule 31 of Sate Acquisition and Tenancy Rules, 1955 no review or other application lies and the settlement authority have got no jurisdiction to re-open the mater other than to send the draft publication khatian for final publication under Rule 32 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Rules, 1955. Even Rule 42 does not empower the Settlement Officer to sit and act as an appellate authority over an appellate order passed under Rule 31 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Rules 1955. In that view of the matter, this Rule is made absolute without any order as to cost. The impugned 8 (eight) notices dated 1-2-2003 issued under the signature of respondent No.3, the Settlement Officer is hereby declared to have been passed without any lawful authority and, as such, no legal effect and it is also directed to send the draft publication khatian Nos. 237, 155, 125 and 245 of Mouza Shantinagar, Police Station Motijheel, Dhaka prepared in the name of the petitioners to the settlement press for final publication.</u>

End.

case_source: (From the judgment and order dated 20-5-2008 passed by the High Court Division in Writ Petition Nos. 6262 of 2005, 6671 of 2004, 2678 of 2005, 1512 and 1513 of 2006 and 3797 of 2003).
full_judgment:
Shah Abu Nayeem Mominur Rahman J: These leave petitions filed under Article 103 of the Constitution arise out of a common judgment and order dated 20-5-2008 passed in Writ Petition No. 6262 of 2005 heard and disposed of along with Writ Petition Nos. 2678 of 2005, 3797 of 2003, 6671 of 2004, 1512 and 1513 of 2006, making the Rules absolute. 
2. The facts and circumstances giving rise to the filing of the writ petitions are similar and the contesting respondents, the grounds as well as the issue involved in the writ petitions are same. Accordingly, the Rules issued in the writ petitions were heard and disposed of by a common judgment. The petitioners in the writ petitions are however, different. The common case in the writ petitions is that the respective case lands originally belonged to Bhawal Raj Court of Wards Estate and the petitioners are the successors-in-interest of the tenants under the Bhawal Raj Court of Wards Estate and accordingly, in the CS Khatian the respective case lands stand in the name of Bhawal Raj Court of Wards Estate and thereafter after the acquisition of the land of the Zaminders on cessation of the Seminary system the rent receiving interest of the Mouza under which the case lands belonged was acquired by the Government under section 3(1) of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, 1950 vide notification No.2773 LR dated 26-2-1952 and the said notification of acquisition was published in the Dhaka Gazette on 24-3-1952, whereby it was notified that all interest of rent receiving vested in the Government with effect from 14-4-1952 and the schedule given in the said Gazette notification includes the Mouza under which the case lands are situated and that thereafter by a notification No.3126 LR dated 27-2-1956 published in the Dhaka Gazette on 29-2-1956; the Government acquired the lands of the Bhawal Raj Courts of Wards Estate, in respect of which the rent receiving interest was acquired earlier, on declaration of the compensation assessment rolls under section 43(2) read with sections 46C and 46E(3) of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, 1950 and thereby the respective case lands of the writ petitioners vested in the Government with effect from the date of publication of the said notifications and thus, since then the tenants under the Bhawal Raj Court of Wards Estate became tenants under the Government in respect of such vested lands. Accordingly, during SA Survey Operation the names of the writ petitioners and or their-predecessors-in-interest were correctly recorded in the SA Khatian without any objection from any quarter and thereafter during the Revisional Survey Operation, the names of the writ petitioners and or their predecessors-in-interest were duly recorded in the RS Khatian correctly and without objection. Thus the petitioners directly or through their predecessors-in-interest have been owning and possessing their respective case land as tenants on payment of rates and rents initially to the Bhawal Raj Court of Wards Estate and subsequently, after cessation of Zamindary system, to the Revenue Authority of the Government openly and publicly without any objection. During the recent Mahanagor Survey Operation the Revenue Authority found the writ-petitioners in possession of their respective case lands and accordingly, the draft records of right was prepared in their respective names in accordance with law i.e. under Rule 29 of the State Acquisition Rules, 1955, (hereinafter referred to as the said Rules, 1955). The leave petitioner Bhawal Raj Court of Wards Estate filed objection under Rule 30 of the said Rules for removing the names of the writ petitioners as appearing against their respective possession in their respective case lands in the draft records of right challenging their tenancy and that the revenue authority after full-fledged hearing rejected the objection of the leave petitioner and being aggrieved there against the leave petitioner preferred appeals under Rule 31 of said Rules, 1955 unsuccessfully and thereby draft record of right was published in respective names of the writ petitioners under Rule 33 of the said Rules, 1955 but it appears that the leave petitioner Bhawal Raj Court of Wards Estate filed an application mentioning Rule 42A of the State Acquisition Rules for correction of the published draft record of right and on the basis of said application fresh hearing was taken and the names of the writ petitioners were substituted by the name Bhawal Raj Court of Wards Estate as tenants in respect of the case lands in the respective Khatians on the basis of the CS Khatian, disbelieving the intermediary transfers made during the period till the promulgation of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act and disregarding the acquisition of the rent receiving interest and vesting of the case lands in the Government through gazette notifications dated 26-2-1952 and 27-2-1976 referred to above, and the fact of payment of Rates and Taxes to the Government by the writ petitioners in respect of their respective case lands as tenants and that though the names of the writ petitioners were ordered to be substituted by the name of the leave petitioner but the writ petitioners were ordered to be shown as "illegal possessors though force" and thus the possession of the writ petitioners in the case lands is admitted. Being aggrieved as such the writ petitioners moved the High Court Division and obtained the Rules and the High Court Division after hearing the parties made the Rules absolute observing, amongst others: 
"We requested Mr. Khondaker Mahbubuddin Ahmed to assist us in finding where said respondent No.2 stands in the scheme of the Act. He was very responsive and submitted a written submission. 
He submitted that by the Bangladesh Laws (Amendment) Ordinance, 1976 (Ordinance No. IX of 1976) under new section 2A the power of the Court of Wards vested in the Divisional Commissioner of respective areas. By the Bangladesh Laws Board of Land Administration in place of the Government is the Court of Wards, which reverted to pre-President's Order 12 of 1973. 
He submitted that after acquisition of rent receiving interest of the concerned estates, the tenants of the Bhawal Raj Estate were no more tenants under them and they became "Malik" directly under the Government. Article 143(c) of the Constitution is not applicable in the case of present record of rights and the circular dated 10-11-2002 is illegal and any action taken thereupon must be set aside. 
Lastly, he submitted that management of the properties of disqualified owners by the Court of Wards is a matter of long past. Either they have overcome their disqualification in the meantime or have died leaving heirs to inherit the estates. A relevant question therefore, arises if there is at all any necessity or scope for such Court of Wards to function in Bangladesh. That is a matter which is best to be left to be considered and decided by the legislature. But the country has suffered the "Enemy Property" and "abandoned property" and the litigations enough to take lesson. He however, cautioned against any strong observation from this Division in respect of the two Courts of Wards, which are still functioning in the country and the, attention of proper quarters might be drawn. 
But one cannot prevent the law to take its own course. After the publication of general notification No. 2773 dated 26-2-52 under section 3 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, 1950 and the notification No. 3126 dated 27-2-56 declaring the Compensation Assessment-rolls under section 43(2) read with section 46 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, all rent receiving interests stood acquired and the tenants of any such rent receivers became "Malik" directly under the Government and all non-retainable khas land vested in the Government". 
In the case of Bangladesh vs. Madan Gopal Jew 33 DLR (AD) 13, the Appellate Division set at rest all controversy regarding the impact of such wholesale acquisition as under: 
"it is to be further observed that it is now well settled on the authority of Jalil Ahmed vs. Province of East Pakistan 19 DLR 106 decided by a Special Bench and affirmed by the Supreme Court of Pakistan in Tanvir Ahmed Siddiky vs. Province of East Pakistan 20 DLR (SC) 144 = PLD 1968 SC 185 that on the publication of the notification under section 3 of the Act, all rent receiving interests including that of Debater and Waqf Estate stood acquired and all non-retainable khas land also stood vested in the Government." 
3. Section 8A of the Court of Wards Act, 1879 provides that if the rent-receiving interests of a ward in any estate under the charge of the Court are acquired under the provisions of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, 1950, then notwithstanding anything contained elsewhere in this Act, the remaining properties of such ward including khas lands under the charge of the Court shall continue to remain under its charge and shall be managed in accordance with the provision of this Act, as if such Ward was a disqualified proprietor of an estate. Section A was inserted by section 2 of the East Bengal Court of Wards (Amendment) Act, 1952 (Act X of 1952). Then, under section 2A of the Bangladesh Laws (Amendment) Ordinance, 1976 (Ordinance IX of 1976) the Commissioners shall, until otherwise specifically provided for by law, possess and exercise within the powers and authority now vested in the Courts of Wards, subject to the control and direction of the Government and to such restrictions and provisions as the Government may prescribe, and that, on the technical ground on maintainability of the writ petition, when confronted, Mr. TH Khan failed to produce any gazette notification of final publication of the recent record of rights. He said due to the pendency of the Rules, the record of rights could not be finally published. Under section 145A of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, 1950, when the Government would establish the Land Survey Tribunal only after final publication of last revised record of rights prepared under section 144 and after establishment of such Tribunals, any suit challenging correctness of the last revised record of rights shall lie in such Tribunal. 
Mr. Nurul Amin and Abul Quashem adopted the arguments of Mr. TH Khan, Mr. Qashem however, insisted for decision on title. We can only say if any person on behalf of so-called Bhawal Raj Court of Wards Estate or Bhawal Raj Estate is still aggrieved he can go to a Civil Court of competent jurisdiction for vindication. He does not have any remedy under the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, 1950. They have already exercised their choice by institution of Title Suit No. 188 of 2006 in the 4th Court of Joint District Judge at Dhaka for declaration of title in certain lands and they may pursue the cause there. 
4. We have perused the leave petitions impugned judgment and order, the writ petitions, affidavit-in-opposition and the annexures thereto. We have considered the submissions made by the learned Advocate appearing for the leave petitioner and also the learned Advocates of the respondents, who filed caveat. The learned Additional Attorney-General appeared for the Government. The learned Advocate for the leave petitioner submitted that admittedly the case land belonged to Bhawal Raj Court of Wards Estate and that while passing impugned order allowing the application filed under Rule 42A of the State Acquisition Rules, 1955 in disposing of the appeals, the appellate officer disbelieved the transfers of the case lands made as claimed by the respective writ petitioners; and ordered for substitution of the name of the Bhawal Raj Court of Wards Estate in place of the names of the respective writ petitioners appearing against the respective case lands in the draft record of rights, but possession of the writ petitioners have been maintained. The learned' Advocate for the leave petitioner submitted that the alleged transfer of the case lands in the names of "the writ petitioners and or their predecessors-in-interest" have been shown fraudulently on the basis of forged documents and that in the meantime the record of right in respect of the case lands on the basis of Mohanagar Survey have been published in accordance with law in the name of the leave petitioner Bhawal Raj Court of Wards Estate and therefore the writ petitioners cannot get any relief in the present forum and they are to move the Civil Court for relief, if any. The learned Additional Attorney-General while making his submission in favour of the leave petitioner found it difficult to support the leave petitioner, since confronted with the gazette notifications dated 25-3-1952 showing acquisition of rent receiving interest under section 3(1) of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act in respect of the lands covered by Mouza 262 under JL No.2 and the gazetee notification dated 29-2-1956 showing acquisition and vesting of the lands, in respect of which the rent receiving interest have been acquired, under section 43(2), 46C and 46E(3) of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act 1950 in favour of the government and the ground rent payment receipts given by the revenue office in favour of the writ petitioners in respect of the case lands admitting their tenancy under the Government, copy of which has been annexed by the writ-petitioner of WP No. 1449 of 2008. 
5. The learned Advocate appearing for the aviators i.e. writ-petitioners, submitted that the leave petitioner Bhawal Raj Court of Wards Estate has challenged their ownership i.e. tenancy under the Government, malafide and for illegal gains. It has been submitted that the application filed under Rule 42A of the State Acquisition Rules is a misconceived application and not entertain able, inasmuch as the said application did not contain any ingredient of any fraud and that it is the established principle of law that a mere allegation of fraud is not sufficient and unless the ingredients of fraud is disclosed in the petition, no cognizance thereof is to be taken. The aviators produced copy of the application of the leave petitioner filed allegedly under Rule 42A of the State Acquisition Rules, which runs as under:

6. The learned Advocate placed before us the Rule 42A of the State Acquisition Rules, 1555, which runs as under: 
"42A. Correction of fraudulent entry before final publication of record-of-rights.—The Revenue-officer, with the additional designation of Settlement Officer shall, on receipt of an application or on receipt of an official report for the correction of an entry that has been procured by fraud in record-of-rights before final publication thereof, after consulting relevant records and making such other enquiries as he deems necessary, direct excision of the fraudulent entry and his act in doing so shall not be open to appeal. At the same time, the Revenue-officer shall make the correct entry after giving the parties concerned a hearing and recording his finding in a formal proceeding for the purpose of future reference." 
and submitted that there being no correction made in the records of right in the recent khatian prepared during Mahanagar Survey and the names of the tenants and their respective possession in respect of the case lands as appearing being in accordance with records made during previous Survey Operations i.e. in the SA Khatian and RS Khatian, the question of commission of any fraud does not arise and therefore Rule 42A under reference cannot have any application in the instant case. Further, there being no mention of any act of fraud in the body of the application of the leave petitioner dated 14-7-2002, as filed, the application as framed and filed was liable to be rejected in limini and the entertainment of the application, as filed, mentioning Rule 42A of the State Acquisition Rules, 1955, was illegal and without lawful authority and the impugned order passed on the basis of such illegal application cannot have any legal effect and liable to be set aside. 
7. Considering the facts and circumstances of the case and the submissions of the learned Advocates of the respective parties and on perusal of the Rule 42A of the State Acquisition Rules, 1955 as well as the application filed by the leave petitioner Bhawal Raj Court of Wards Estate dated 14-7-2002, quoted above, and the gazette notifications dated 24-3-1952 and 29-2-1956 as well as ground rent payment receipts issued by the Government revenue office and earlier by the Bhawal Raj Court of Wards Estate and also the transfer made through registered deed of gift and having regard to the fact that the SA record of right and RS record of right were correctly prepared in the names of the writ petitioners and or their predecessors-in-interest in respect of their respective lands and also the fact of admission, as to the possession of the writ petitioners in their respective case lands in the draft Mahanagar record of right, we do not find any reason to interfere with the judgment and order passed by the High Court Division. The learned Advocate appearing for the leave petitioner, when confronted with the aforesaid gazette notifications dated 24-3-1952 and 29-2-1956, as to acquisition of rent receiving interest and the vesting of lands of the leave petitioners, including the case lands, found it difficult to substantiate the locus standi of the leave petitioner in challenging the draft records of right prepared in the names of the respective writ petitioners in respect of their respective case lands prepared during the Mohanagar Survey. Further, with the publication of the gazette notifications dated 24-3-1952 and 29-2-1956 the leave petitioner ceased to have any right, title and interest and possession in the case lands, because of acquisition, and vesting of said lands in the Government. The learned Additional Attorney- General could not deny the granting of the ground rent payment receipts, copy of which have been annexed to the affidavit-in-opposition, admitting the writ petitioners as tenants under the Government. 
8. On plain reading of the Rule 42A, quoted above, it appears that Settlement Officer is empowered to pass order only on receipt of an application or on receipt of an official report, for correction of an entry in the record of right, procured by fraud, before final publication thereof. Thus the said Rule cannot be applicable in the instant case, inasmuch as the record of right as prepared is in accordance with the past records of right prepared during SA Operation and RS Operation and there being no change as to the names as appearing in the said records of right the question of fraud in recording the entry of names in the recent record of right prepared after the Mahanagar Survey does not arise. Apart from that after final publication of the record of right, after the SA Survey the only mode for correction of the same was through Civil Court and thus subsequent to preparation of SA record of right, the RS record of right was prepared and after final publication thereof the mode for correction of any wrong entry appearing in the RS record was through Civil Court and without moving the Civil Court no correction in recent records of right is lawful or permissible and as such the draft record of right in the instant case having been prepared following the preparation of the SA and RS records in accordance with law, the attempts of the leave petitioner for correction under Rules 30 and 31 of the State Acquisition Rules, 1955 have failed. The plain reading of the application dated 14-7-2002, quoted above, allegedly filed under Rule 42A of the State Acquisition Rules, 1955, ex-facie appears to be a vague application, inasmuch as the said appellation contains no specific allegation of any act of fraud and it is the settled principle of law that an application, not having disclosed any act of fraud in its body, is not entertain able and liable to be rejected. Without correcting the SA Khatian and RS Khatian as prepared in respect of the case lands in accordance with law earlier, the leave petitioner cannot get its name entered in the recent record of right prepared during Mohanagar Survey allegedly only on the basis of CS Khatian. 
9. Thus we are of the view that the leave petitioner had no locus standi to challenge the draft Mahanagar Survey Khatian as prepared in the names of the respective writ petitioners, at least after publication of the gazette notifications dated 24-3-1952 and 29-2-1956. 
10. It has been submitted that in the body of the impugned judgment the High Court Division made certain observations as to the locus standi of the Manager of the Bhawal Raj Court of Wards Estate in representing the Estate and the very existence of Bhawal Raj Court of Wards Estate itself in the eye of law, and hence the learned Advocate for the leave petitioner submitted that the such observations as appearing in the body of the impugned judgment need be corrected by expunging the same. On perusal of the Court of Wards Act, 1879, it appears that the Bhawal Raj Court of Wards Estate was created under the said Act and the Management and Guardianship of said Wards is to be managed by the manager appointed under section 20 of the said Act and section 39 of the Court of Wards Act, 1879 provides that every manager appointed by the Court shall have power to manage all property which may be committed to his charge, to collect the rents of the land entrusted to him, as well as all other money due to the ward, and to grant receipts, therefore; and may, under the orders of the Court, grant or reduce such leases and farm as may be necessary for the good management of the property. The "Manager' under the said Act is also responsible to look after the interest of wards as if the property is his own and is also a counter. The manager of Bhawal Raj Court of Wards Estate, appointed under section 20 of the Court of Wards Act, is to look after the retained properties till those are released in accordance with the provision of the Court of Wards Act. The Bhawal Raj Court of Wards Estate shall remain in existence and is to be managed by such manager until released in accordance with the Act. The Estate of the Bhawal Raj Court of Wards Estate is being managed under the Court of Wards Act and directly managed and looked after by the manager appointed and the Bhawal Raj Court of Wards Estate, at present, is functioning in accordance with law. Thus the observations made regarding existence of the Bhawal Raj Court of Wards Estate and as to its functioning and locus standi, in the body of impugned judgment passed by the High Court Division are expunged and will be of no effect in the eye of law. 
Accordingly, with the above observations the leave petitions are dismissed. 
End.
