case_source: (From the Judgment and Order dated March 29, 2001 passed by the High Court Division in First Miscellaneous Appeal No. 315 of 1981).
full_judgment:
Md. Ruhul Amin J: The appeal, by leave, is against the judgment dated March 29, 2001 of a Single Bench of the High Court Division in First Miscellaneous Appeal No. 315 of 1981 allowing the same upon setting aside the judgment and order dated September 23, 1980 of the 1st Court of Subordinate Judge (now Joint District Judge), Barisal in Miscellaneous Case No. 36 of 1979 dismissing the same. The Miscellaneous Case was registered upon an application filed under Order IX, rule 13 of the Code of Civil Procedure. The same was filed seeking getting aside of the ex parte decree dated December 19, 1978 passed in Title Suit No. 77 of 1965.

2. The appellants filed Title Suit No. 77 of 1965 seeking setting aside of the decree dated September 26, 1962 passed in Title Suit No. 468 of 1962.

3. The respondent No.1 was the defendant No. 2 in Title Suit No. 77 of 1965. He upon service of summons entered appearance and filed written statement. While the suit was awaiting for disposal before the trial Court, as seen from the materials on record in connection with the civil revision the record of the Title Suit No. 77 of 1965 was called for by the High Court Division and after disposal of the civil revision the records were sent down. After receiving the records by the trial Court fresh summons was issued to the defendants and after receiving the service return date was fixed for taking steps and the order so passed by the Court was shown to the defendant's (herein respondent No. 1) Advocate on May 26, 1978. The suit was fixed for peremptory hearing on December 19, 1978 and on that date the suit was decreed ex parte. The respondent No.1 who was defendant No.2 in the suit filed application under Order IX, rule 13 of the Code of Civil Procedure on April 19, 1979 seeking setting aside of the ex parte decree dated December 19, 1978 alleging that he was not aware of the receiving of the record from the High Court Division by the trial Court and that summons was not served on him after receiving back of the record from the High Court Division and that his Advocate engaged prior to calling for the records by the High Court Division in connection with civil revision did not inform him about the receiving of the record from the High Court Division by the trial Court and that also about the date for taking steps after receiving of the record from the High Court Division and finally about the date of peremptory hearing of the suit and, as such, he was not aware of the ex parte decree and that for the first time he came to know about the ex parte decree from Shamsher Ali Sheikh (PW 2) on 2nd of Baishakh, 1386 BS.

4. The Miscellaneous case was opposed by filing written objection stating, inter alia, that after receiving the record from the High Court Division the date was communicated to the petitioner through his learned Advocate and that summons was duly served on the petitioner and the petitioner was fully aware of the date of peremptory hearing of the suit and intentionally allowed the suit to be disposed of ex parte with the object of harassing the plaintiff-opposite party. It was also contended that the Miscellaneous Case was barred by limitation and, as such, liable to be dismissed.

5. The petitioner in the Miscellaneous Case, i.e. respondent No.1 herein, in support of his case of initial knowledge about the ex parte decree examined himself as PW 1 and his cultivator, PW 2 and also examined another witness in support of his contention that summons was not served on him. The opposite party in the Miscellaneous Case examined the process server and the person in whose presence the summons was served as well as himself.

6. The trial Court, on the findings that petitioner i.e. respondent No.1, failed to adduce any tangible evidence either oral or documentary to substantiate his case of knowing about the ex parte decree for the first time on 2nd of Baishakh, 1386 BS., that the petitioner to substantiate his contention that his learned Advocate did not inform him the date of peremptory hearing of the suit, has not examined his Advocate, that although petitioner in his deposition stated that he came to know about the arrival of the record from the High Court Division on April 26, 1976 but he has not stated how he came to know about the arrival of the record and, as such, his said contention cannot be accepted, that his contention that he did not know anything about the suit after receiving of the record from the High Court Division and consequent thereupon the suit was decreed ex parte has not been established, that summons was served on the petitioner, i.e. respondent No.1, on May 8, 1978, that in the background of the facts and circumstances of the case and the evidence on record it can be said that the petitioner was aware of the position of the suit after arrival of the record from the High Court Division, that the petitioner failed to prove his contention that he for the first time came to know about the ex parte decree on 2nd of Baishakh, 1386 BS dismissed the Miscellaneous case on the ground of limitation. The trial Court also held "that there was no sufficient cause for non appearance of the petitioner when the suit was called on for hearing". As against the judgment of the trial Court the respondent No.1 filed First Miscellaneous Appeal before the High Court Division.

7. The High Court Division, in the background of the contention of the appellant that his learned Advocate did not inform him about the receiving of the record by the trial Court from the High Court Division and also about the date of peremptory hearing of the suit, observed that the suit was decreed ex parte due to fault or laches of the Advocate of the appellant and, as such, he should not suffer for the laches and negligence of his Advocate. The High Court Division also observed that as the summons was served by hanging on the fencing of the 'ghor' (sic) and, as such, "it is unsafe to infer that defendant No.2 had knowledge about the date of hearing of the Title Suit No.77 of 1965" and that "Learned court below was not legally justified in holding that the said service vide Exhibit A was a good service according to law and that defendant No. 2 had knowledge about the date of the said suit. The High Court Division was of the view that even if the engaged lawyer was informed vide order No. 47 dated 2-5-78 that will be the knowledge of the lawyer not of the party unless sufficiently proved by facts and circumstances, that if due to laches or fault of the lawyer the suit was decreed ex parte, the party (defendant No. 2) should not be made liable for that", that from the evidence of the witness examined by the opposite party (in the Miscellaneous Case) and upon perusal of the Exhibit A (service return) it is seen that the service of summons "was not personal but the substituted service by hanging on the fencing of the ghor (sic)", that the witness No. 1 and witness No. 2 of the opposite party (in the Miscellaneous Case) are not uniform on vital point and, as such, on the basis of their evidence it cannot be said that the summons was duly served on the petitioner (in the Miscellaneous Case). The High Court Division finally held "that there were sufficient causes for defendant No.2 (appellant) A. Malek Meah preventing him from attending the court on the date fixed for hearing and due to default of any step by him Title Suit No. 77 of 1965 was decreed ex parte setting aside the decree dated 26-9-62 of Title Suit No. 468 of 1962 which the defendant No.2 had interest to protect and for which he filed written statement in Title Suit No.77 of 1965 long ago to contest, if the ex parte decree of Title Suit No. 77 of 1965 stands due to dismissal of Miscellaneous Case No. 36 of 1979 under Order IX, rule 13 of the Code of Civil Procedure vide impugned judgment the appellant (defendant No. 2) A. Malek will be seriously prejudiced sustaining loss and will be deprived finally of the chance to contest for disposal of the suit on merit". On the aforesaid findings and observations the High Court Division upon allowing the appeal set aside the judgment of the trial Court.

8. Leave was obtained for consideration of the contention that ex parte decree was passes: on December 19, 1978 and the Miscellaneous case was filed on April 19, 1979 alleging date of knowledge on 2nd of Baishakh, 1386 BS which was not proved and consequent thereupon the Court of first instance having had held that the Miscellaneous Case was barred by limitation and that the said finding having not been reversed by the High Court Division and thereby finding of the Court of first instance as to limitation as remains unreversed, the judgment of the High Court Division is not sustainable in law and that without reversing the finding of fact as to service of summons the High Court Division having had come to a wrong finding that the defendant No. 2 was prevented by sufficient cause, the judgment of the High Court Division is not sustainable in law.

9. Point for consideration in the appeal whether after receiving the record from the High Court Division summons issued to the respondent No. 1, i.e. defendant No. 2, was served on him and the service of summons in the manner was a good service and the contention of the respondent No.1 that his engaged Advocate did not inform him about the arrival of the record as well as about the date of peremptory hearing of the suit in spite of informing the learned Advocate about arrival of record was established by the respondent No. 2 and whether the respondent No.1 i.e. defendant No. 2, the petitioner in the Miscellaneous Case established the date of his initial knowledge about the ex parte decree dated December 19, 1978. It may be mentioned the Miscellaneous case was filed on April 19, 1979 stating that the respondent No.1 came to know about the ex parte decree on 2nd of Baishakh, 1386 BS from PW 2 who was told about the ex parte decree by certain Kala Sarker.

10. The trial Court on consideration of the evidence of PW 1 i.e. petitioner in the Miscellaneous Case and the PW 2, held that plaintiff miserably failed to establish that he for the first time came to know about the ex parte decree on 2nd of Baishakh, 1386 BS. The trial Court discarded the evidence of PW 2 not being a disinterested witness since PW 1 stated that PW 2 is his cultivator. The trial Court also noticed in the evidence of PW 2 that Kala Sarker was present in Court while PW 2 was deposing but said Kala Sarker was not examined without offering any explanation from the side of the petitioner in the Miscellaneous case. The trial Court in the background of the evidence on record held that the petitioner i.e. respondent No.1 herein, did not establish the date of initial knowledge by tangible evidence. The trial Court rejected the contention of the respondent No.1 that his learned Advocate did not inform him about the arrival of the record from the High Court Division as well as about the date of peremptory hearing of the suit since the learned Advocate was not examined and no explanation was offered for not examining him.

<u>11. In the afore state of the matter we are of the view that respondent No.1 having not been corroborated as to his contention that his learned Advocate did not inform him about the arrival of the record at the trial Court from the High Court Division and the date of peremptory hearing, the trial Court rightly rejected the said contention. The High Court Division was of the view that knowledge of the Advocate of the respondent No. 1 as to arrival of record at the trial Court from High Court Division as well as about the date of peremptory hearing was not in the knowledge of the respondent No.1 and that for the aches of the Advocate of the respondent No.1 he should not suffer. We like to observe that High Court Division was quite unmindful of the fact that the contention of the respondent No.1 of not having any information from his engaged Advocate about the receiving of the record by the trial Court and of fixation of the suit for peremptory hearing was not established by any reliable evidence. Now the question is, whether summons was served on the respondent No.1 who was petitioner in the Miscellaneous Case. The respondent No.1 as PW 1 deposed that summons was not served on him and he tried to establish that fact by the evidence of PW 3 who deposed that in his presence no summons was served on the respondent No.1. It may be mentioned on scrutiny of the service return the trial Court noticed that name of PW 3 did not appear in the service return as Mokabela witness and, as such, the trial Court discarded his evidence. It may also be mentioned that this PW has stated that he did not receive any summons from Court for deposing in the case. PW 1 has also not said that he took out summons in the name of the PW 3. In that state of the matter, it appears that the said witness was procured to depose something about which he had no idea. The trial Court, on consideration of the evidence of OPW 3, the process server and OPW 1 person whose name appeared in the service return as Mokabela witness and also on consideration of the evidence of OPW 2 who was opposite party No. 4 in the Miscellaneous Case, held that summons was duly served on the respondent No.1 i.e. the petitioner in the Miscellaneous Case. Since the Miscellaneous case was filed beyond the period of limitation and that as the petitioner in the Miscellaneous Case failed to establish his initial date of knowledge about the ea- parte decree, the trial Court dismissed the Miscellaneous Case on the finding of limitation. The respondent No.1 tried to establish the date of knowledge of the ex parte decree by the evidence of PW 2, who being cultivator of the respondent No.1 trial Court considered him not disinterested witness, in our view, quite legally, but High Court Division without reversing the finding of the trial Court on limitation set aside the judgment of the trial Court.</u>

<u>12. The High Court Division set aside the judgment and order of the trial Court on the ground that the manner in which the summons was served, i.e. by hanging, being not personal service the same was not a good service since the service of summons "was a substitutory service by hanging on the fencing of the ghor and not personal service on defendant No. 2 A. Malek Meah" i.e. petitioner in the Miscellaneous case. It is in the evidence of OPW 1, whose name appeared in the service return, Exhibit A, that process server offered the summons to the petitioner in the Miscellaneous case i.e. respondent No.1 and he having had refused to accept the summons, process server served the summons by hanging on the fencing of the hut. Considering the evidence of OPW 1 along with the evidence of OPW 3 we are of the view service of summons on the respondent No.1, was quite good service and the High Court Division was in serious error in holding that the summons served in the manner was not a good service. It is seen from the judgment of the High Court Division that the said Division discarded the evidence of OPW 1 and OPW 3 upon observing that they differed with each other on some vital points. The High Court Division while making the said observation did not specify on which vital point the said witnesses differed with each other. The High Court Division while disposing of the appeal did not discuss the evidence of the said witnesses. We are of the view that High Court Division was in error in discarding the evidence of OPW 1 and OPW 3 without discussing and considering the evidence of the said witnesses and specifying in what particular point they differed. The High Court Division was of the view that respondent No.1 should not suffer for the laches and negligence of his learned Advocate and thereupon was of the view that Miscellaneous Case was required to be allowed to give a chance to the respondent No.1 to contest the suit since relief sought in the suit was for setting aside a decree obtained by the respondent No.1 in an earlier suit. With due respect to the learned Judge of the High Court Division we like to mention that the learned Judge was quite unmindful of the fact whether the petitioner in the Miscellaneous Case established the laches and negligence of his learned Advocate in not informing about arrival of record from the High Court Division and also date of peremptory hearing or, in other words, whether the petitioner's contention that his engaged Advocate did not inform him about the receiving of the record from the High Court Division and fixing the case for peremptory hearing was at all established. From the judgment of the High Court Division it is not seen that the High Court Division arrived at any such finding that petitioner i.e. respondent No.1, established his contention that his engaged Advocate did not inform him about the arrival of the record from the High Court Division and the fixation of the case for peremptory hearing. The trial Court on consideration of the materials on record held that petitioner, i.e. respondent No.1, failed to establish his contention that his engaged Advocate did not inform him about the receiving of the record by the trial Court and fixing the case for peremptory hearing. This vital finding of the trial Court was not reversed by the High Court Division. The High Court Division while setting aside the judgment of the trial Court also did not reverse the finding of the trial Court that the petitioner i.e. respondent No.1 failed to establish his initial date of knowledge about the ex parte decree. The High Court Division in setting aside the judgment of the trial Court did not advert itself to the question of limitation as considered by the trial Court. The first Court of appeal being the last Court of fact while reversing the judgment appealed is required to dispose of the appeal on independent discussion of the evidence relied upon by the Court of first instance and to assign reason for reversing or rejecting the finding and reasoning given by the trial Court while setting aside or reversing the judgment of the said Court. The appellate Court is also required to arrive at independent finding in support of its disagreement with the finding and decision of the trial Court or, in other words, while considering the finding and decision of the trial Court erroneous. In the instant case the High Court Division as the last Court of fact was required to discuss the evidence and to record reason for not placing reliance on the evidence which was considered reliable by the trial Court in making its decision, but the said established procedure was not complied with by the High Court Division while reversing the judgment and decision of the trial Court.</u>

13. In the background of the discussions made herein-above we find merit in the appeal.

14. Accordingly, the appeal is allowed. There is no order as to costs.

End.

full_judgment:
Mr. Md. Emdadul Haque Azad J:- This Rule, was issued at the instance of the defendant-respondent-petitioners calling upon the plaintiff appellant-opposite party Nos.1 and 2 to show cause as to why the judgment and decree dated 08.02.2011 (decree signed on 14.02.2011) passed by the learned Joint District Judge, First Court, Rajbari in Title Appeal No.24 of 2007 allowing the appeal and reversing/setting aside the judgment and decree dated 29.01.2007 (decree signed on 05.02.2007) passed by the learned Senior Assistant Judge, Rajbari Sardar, Rajbari in Title Suit No.55 of 2000 dismissing the suit should not be set aside. 

2. The fact relevant to the disposal of the instant Rule are that on 09.04.2000, the Opposite party Nos.1-2 as plaintiffs instituted Title Suit No.55 of 2000 in the Court of the learned Assistant Judge, Sadar, Rajbari against the petitioners and the other opposite parties praying for a declaration that a registered kabuliyat being No.8264 dated 07.12.1999 executed in their name vide Settlement Case No. (XII-30/98-99)/(XII-151/95-96) for the period ranging from 29.09.1999 to 28.08.2000 is valid, effective and of legal force. 

3. The facts of the plaint of the aforesaid suit, in brief, are that the suit land belongs to the Government as khas land; that the plaintiffs took settlement of the same for 99 years from the Government vide Settlement Case No. (XII-30/98-99)/(XII-151/95-96) and as such a kabuliyat was registered in their name on 07.12.1999; that since settlement the plaintiffs have been enjoying and possessing the suit land by having the same mutated in their name and also by paying rent to the Government exchequer; that the plaintiffs have their homestead in the suit land and they have been possessing the same since the flood in 1988 by planting different trees; that they did not violate any of the terms of the kabuliyat dated 07.12.1999; that the Assistant Commissioner (Land), Rajbari Sader, Rajbari (defendant No.4) vide his letter dated 12.03.2000 asked the plaintiffs to appear before him for the purpose of hearing in respect of the Kabuliyat and that on his appearance the said defendant threatened to cancel their kabuliyat and hence, the suit. 

4. The Government as defendant Nos.1-4 contested the suit by filling a written statement denying the material facts of the plaint and contending, inter alia, that the suit land belongs to the Government as khas land and the same was settled/leased out in favour of the plaintiffs upon execution and registration of a bi-lateral deed of kabuliyat; that the suit land was also mutated in the name of the plaintiffs; that subsequently due to violation of the terms of the kabuliyat the Assistant Commissioner (Land) issued a notice upon the plaintiffs on 22.03.2000 and as such the said kabuliyat was cancelled later on; that the plaintiffs have no right, title, interest and possession in the suit land and therefore, the suit is liable to be dismissed. 

5. The petitioner No.1 as added defendant No.6 contested the suit by filling a separate written statement denying the material facts of the plaint and contending, inter alia, that the suit land originally belonged to Satish Chandra Das, who granted settlement of the same along with other lands in favour of Mohammad Mozahar Ali Miah and Azhar Ali Miah; that in order to recover arrear k rents for 1360-1362 BS from the said tenants Azhar and Mozahar, Satish Chandra filed Rent Suit No.60 of 1957 in the Court of the then Munsif, Goalando and that suit was compromised between the parties on 26.02.1957; that while the said Azhar and 
Mozahar were enjoying and possessing the land, rent roll record was prepared in their name; that the said Mozahar Hossain transferred his share i.e. 181/2 decimals of land in favour of one Solemannesa by a registered sale deed dated 22.02.1961; that in order to sell the suit land Solemannesa entered into a contract for sale with the defendant-petitioner No.1 on 25.11.1988 fixing the consideration money at Tk.12,000/-; that following the death of Solemannesa her sons, Pran Sheikh and Ramzan Sheikh executed and registered a sale deed in his favour on 16.07.2000; that thereafter on 20.08.2000 the defendant-petitioner No.1 went to the local Tahshil Office to pay rent/land development tax and came to learn that the suit land has been recorded in the name of the Government instead of Solemannesa; that the Government has no right, title, interest and possession in the suit land; that the kabuliyat of the plaintiff's is collusive and ineffective; that the defendant-petitioner No.1 has right, title, interest and possession in the suit land and therefore, the suit is liable to be dismissed with cost. 

6. The predecessor of the petitioner Nos.2-6 as added defendant No.7 also contested the suit by filling another written statement denying the material facts of the plaint and contending, inter alia, that the suit land originally belonged to Satish Chandra Das, who granted settlement of the same along with other lands in favour of Azhar Ali Miah and Mozahar Ali Miah; that in order to recover arrear rents for 1360-1362 BS from the said tenants Azhar and Mozahar, Satish Chandra filed Rent Suit No.60 of 1957 in the Court of the then Munsif, Goalando and that suit was compromised between the parties on 26.02.1957; that pursuant to the said compromise decree, Azhar and Mozahar were admitted as tenants and they remained in possession of the suit land as owner thereof; that Azhar Miah died leaving behind widow Khodeja, 2 sons-Abdul Latif and Golam Sarwar and one daughter Jahanara Begum as his heirs; that the said heirs of Azhar Ali transferred the suit land in favour of the added defendant No.7 by a registered sale deed being No.4239 dated 15.06.1982 and delivered possession in his favour; that the suit land became uncultivable because of situation by the flood of 1988; that the ancestral/paternal residence of the plaintiff's was in Sujanagar, Pabna  and because of destruction of their house in Pabna by a flood in 1988, they stared looking for a piece of land for residential purposes; that the plaintiffs are the distant relatives of the said defendant No.7 and therefore, the latter allowed the former to live in the suit land on a temporary basis given the uncultivable nature of the suit land and accordingly, the plaintiffs erected homestead in the suit land in the first part of 1989 and started living therein and planted various trees; that at that time the plaintiffs undertook to vacate the suit land soon after they get another piece of suitable land; that in the middle of November, 2000 they claimed title to the suit land on the basis of a kabuliyat from the Government and that even being requested to vacate the suit land the plaintiffs refused to do so and as such the said defendant filed Title Suit No.214 of 2000 against the plaintiffs in the Court of the learned Assistant Judge, Rajbari Sader, Rajbari praying for a decree for declaration of title and recovery of khas possession; that the suit land is not at all the khas land of the Government and therefore, the suit is liable to be dismissed with cost. 

7. The suit was tried by the learned Senior Assistant Judge, Sader, Rajbari. During trail the plaintiffs examined 2 P.W.s and the defendant examined 6 D.W.s in support of their respective cases. 

8. The learned Senior Assistant Judge, Sader Rajbari by his judgment and decree dated 29.01.2006 (decree signed on 05.02.2006) dismissed the suit on contest holding that the suit is not maintainable and also that plaintiffs have no right, title, interest and possession in the suit land.

9. I have meticulously gone through the revisional application, the impugned judgment and decree, the pleadings of the respective parties, evidence led by them and other materials on record and also heard the learned Advocates for both the sides at length and perused the decisions relied upon by both the parties with utmost circumspection and the relevant provisions of law wherefrom it transpires that the preparation and publication of S.A. record of rights, if any, in the khas khatians of the Government as well as the maintainability of Rent Suit No.60 of 1957 are the predominant issues in this case apart from other connected issues and I will endeavor to address all the issues in proportion to their respective weight and importance. 

26. It is the case of the plaintiff-opposite party Nos.1-2 and the Government (defendant Nos.1-4) that the suit land vested in the Government as khas land during the S.A. operation, but neither the plaintiffs nor the Government adduced any evidence including the khas khatian itself before the Courts below in support of their contention. Again, although the Government filed a written statement, they did not adduce any evidence, oral or documentary, to show as to when, why and how the suit land became khas in their name and as such the written statement of the Government will not ipso facto be admissible in evidence unless and until the same is supported by competent witness of convincing nature, and as such Section 92 of the SAT Act as well as the decisions referred to by the defendant: petitioners will stand in the way of the claim of plaintiff-opposite party Nos.1-2 as well as the Government. At this juncture I think it is necessary to quote Section 92 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, 1950, which runs as follow: 
"92(1) The interest of a raiyat in a holding shall be extinguished —
(a) when he dies intestate leaving no heir entitled to inherit under the law of inheritance to which he is subject; 
(b) when he surrenders his holding at the end of any agricultural year by giving notice in the prescribed form and in the prescribed manner and within the prescribed period to the Revenue-officer; 
(c) when he voluntarily abandons his residence without making any arrangement for payment of the rent as it falls due and cesses to cultivate his holding either by himself or by members of his family or by, or with the aid of, servants or laborers or with the aid of, partners or bargadars for a period of three successive years; Or - 
(d) when such interest has devolved by inheritance, under the law of inheritance to which such raiyat is subject, on a person who is not a bona fide cultivator and such person has not cultivated the land comprised in the holding either by himself or by members of his family or by, or with the aid of, servants or laborers or with the aid of, partners or bargadars during the period of five years from the date on which such interest has so devolved on him and there is no sufficient cause why he has not so cultivated the land. 

(2) When the interest of a raiyat in a holding is extinguished under sub-section (1), the Revenue-officer may enter on the holding; and the holding shall, with effect from the date on which the Revenue-officer so enters on it, vest absolutely in the Government free from all encumbrances except the encumbrances on the holding which is extinguished under clause (a) of the said sub-section, but the persons whose interests in the holdings are extinguished under clauses (b), (c) and (d) of that sub-section shall continue to be personally liable for the money secured by the encumbrances on such holdings. 
(3) Before entering on a holding under sub-section (2), the Revenue-officer shall cause a notice to be published in the prescribed manner declaring his intention to so enter on the holding and specifying the reasons thereof and also inviting objections from all persons interested in the holding and shall consider any objections that may be submitted to him within the period specified in that behalf in the notice and shall record a decision.

27. In the case of Bangladesh and others vs. Mallick Ali Ahmed and others, 3 CLR (AD) 345, it has been held: 
"The treating of the suit land as escheat property by the government and thereby declaring the same as khas land of the government without making it clear in any manner as to how and why the suit property can be treated as escheat property has been illegal." 
It is pertinent to mention here that the Government did not turn up before the Courts below as well as this Court in the course of the Rule hearing to establish its claim to the suit land and therefore, the plaintiffs as well as the Government signally failed to prove that the suit land ever vested in the Government as khas land in view of the Government's failure to adduce evidence in support of its written statement. This view finds support from the case of Md. Serajul Islam vs. Mrs, Hosne Ara Begum and others 34 BLD 55, wherein it has been held that: 

"The filing of the written statement without giving any oral testimony in support of the same before the Court below and without facing cross-examination the same will not be considered ipso facto as evidence, rather, either of the pleadings must be proved by giving oral evidence." 

28. It appears from Ext.2 of Title Suit No.214 of 2000 (from which Civil Revision No.2748 of 2014 arose and which has been heard and disposed of in simultaneous with the present Rule) that Rent Suit No.60 of 1957 was filed by the then Zaminder Satish Chandra Das against his tenants Mozahar Ali Miah and Azahar Ali Miah for realizing the arrear rent in respect of the suit land for 1360-1362 BS (corresponding to 1953-1955) and the said Rent Suit was filed within 3(three) years for realizing the arrear rents for the period prior to Section 3 of the SAT Act came into force as on 14th April, 1956 and hence, the said Rent Suit is maintainable within the meaning of Article 110 of the First Schedule to the Limitation Act, 1908 and therefore, the compromise decree dated 26.02.1957 (Ext.2 of Title Suit No. 214 of 2000) drawn up in that rent suit is also legal. In this connection I think it would be profitable to quote Article 110 of the First Schedule to the Limitation Act, 1908, which runs as follows: 
Description of suit	Period of limitation	Time from which period begins to run
110. For arrears of rent.	Part VI-Three years (cntd) Three years	When the arrears become due


It also appears from the abovementioned compromise decree dated 26.02.1957 that landlord Satish Chandra Das admitted Mozahar Ali and Azahar Ali as his tenants for the period prior to Section 3 of the SAT Act came into force and following the acquisition of the rent receiving interest by the Government, the said tenants Mozahar Ali and Azahar Ali became direct tenants under the Government and the petitioners having acquired their title to the suit land by successive transfers by dint of 3(three) separate registered sale deeds dated 01.03.1961 (Ext.2 of Title Suit No.154 of 2000), 15.06.1982 (Ext.5 of Title Suit No.214 of 2000) and 16.07.2000 (Ext.3 of Title Suit No.154 of 2000) from them and their transferees, are the lawful title holders of the suit land. 

29. It is a settled principle of law that the plaintiff has to prove his case on the balance of probabilities and he/she cannot bank or capitalize on the weakness of the defendant. But the Court of appeal below turned down this century-old settled proposition and wrongly shifted the plaintiffs' burden of proof on the defendants by holding that "---কিন্তু নথি পর্যালোচন দেখা যায়  যে বিজ্ঞ নিম্ন আদালত সাক্ষ্য আইনের প্রচলিত বিধি লংঘন করে ৬-৭নং পক্ষভূক্ত বিবাদীর Barden of Proof বাদী ও ১-৪ নং বিবাদীর উপর ন্যস্ত করেছেন। ৬-৭নং পক্ষভূ্ক্ত বিবাদী তাদের জবাবে নালিশী জমিতে স্বত্বের দাবীর সর্মথনে যে সব দলিলপত্র দাখিল করেছেন তা পর্যালোচনা দেখা যায় যে আর এস ২৫৯ খতিয়ারেন ১৮৫ দাগের জমি উল্লেখ নাই। আর এস ২৫৯ খতিয়ানে ১৮৫ দাগই নাই। অথচ বিজ্ঞ নিম্ন আদালত ৬-৭ নং বিবাদীর কাগজপত্র সঠিকভাবে পর্যালোচনা ও অনুধোবন না করেই ৬-৭ বিবাদীর কাগজপত্র বিশ্বাস করেছে। এস এ খতিয়ান কিভাবে সরকারের নামে হয়েছে বিজ্ঞ নিম্ন আদালত তা প্রমানের ভার বাদী ও ১-৪ নং বিবাদী সরকারের উপর অর্পন করে গুরুতর ভূল সিদ্ধান্তে উপনীত হয়েছেন কেননা Record of Rights এ অবশ্যই একটি Legal Presumption আছে।-----------

30. The above findings of the lower appellate Court is erroneous and perverse on two counts, firstly since the plaintiff-opposite party Nos.1-2 and the Government claim the suit land to be the khas land of the Government, it is their bounden duty of proof their contention: There exists a large body of case law on this point. For instance, in the case of Md. Naimuddin Sarder @ Naimuddin Sarder vs. Md. Abdul Kalam Biswas @ Md. Abul Kalam Basiruddin @ Abul Kalam Azad and another, 39 DLR (AD) 237, it has been held that: 

"Plaintiff in order to succeed must establish his own case to obtain a decree and weakness of the defendant's case is no ground for passing a decree in favour of the plaintiff." 

Secondly, it is as clear as broad daylight from R.S. Khatian No.259 (Ext.l of Title Suit No.154 of 2000) that R.S. Plot No.185 is present in the .said khatian showing 37 decimals of land in sixteen annas share. On this point the learned Advocate for the opposite party Nos.1-2 submits that the said finding is merely a slip of pen on the part of the lower appellate Court and in fact the appellate Court below meant R.S. Khatian No.148 (Ext. 1/Ka of Title Suit No.154 of 2000). On scrutiny of R.S. Khatian No.148, it is found that Plot No.285 appears therein, but the quantum of land in the said plot is completely different, namely 15 decimals in eight annas share. Moreover, lands of both the R.S. Khatian being Nos.259 and 148 belonged to Zaminder Satish Chandra Das and as such I find it difficult to accept the submissions advanced from the plaintiffs on this point. Rather, I subscribe to the view that the Court of appeal below wrongly recorded the said finding as to R.S. Khatian No.259 and Plot No.185 upon his total non-application of judicial mind to the materials on record, which is very unbecoming and deplorable on the part of a judicial officer. 

31. It appears from paragraph 3 of the plaint that the plaintiffs entered into the suit land after the flood of 1988 whereas they allegedly took settlement of the same in 1999 and they did not at all clarify in their pleadings submitted and evidences adduced in any of the suits in what capacity they possessed and enjoyed the suit land for the intervening period between 1988 and 1999 and as such I am constrained to hold the view that the plaintiffs entered into the suit land as -mere trespassers. Moreover, I think that if the suit land had ever been recorded in the khas khatian of the Government, it would have settled the same in favour of anyone one else, and in the absence of any such lease, government's title to the suit land is not proved at all and therefore, the claim of the plaintiffs also fails since they are claiming interest in the suit land through the Government. 

Furthermore, the plaintiffs stated in paragraph 7 of the plaint that the Assistant Commissioner (Land), Rajbari Sadar, Rajbari (defendant No.4 to the suit) by his letter dated 12.03.2000 merely threatened to cancel their kabuliyat, but at no point of time their lease was actually cancelled, and the threat of cancellation as opposed to any actual cancellation is merely an apprehension which cannot substitute the cause of action of the suit as framed and therefore, the suit is premature and liable to be dismissed as being not maintainable in law as per the decision given in the case of Kamaluddin (Md.) and another vs. Secretary, Ministry of Land, Bangladesh and others 56 DLR (AD) 212, wherein it has been held that: 
"unless final order is passed in a matter, person interested in the matter or persons apprehensive of being affected by the act of the functionaries -- performing functions in connection with the affairs of the Republic or of a local authority is not entitled to invoke the writ jurisdiction." 

It is worth to mention here that although the above decision has been made on a writ petition, the same extends to civil jurisdiction as well given the fact that writ jurisdiction forms part of civil jurisdiction. 

32. As I have already found that the plaintiffs are mere trespassers into the suit land, they have neither got any locus standi to institute the present suit nor to question the accuracy or genuineness of the title deeds of the defendant-petitioners, however, defective title the letters might have to the suit land. On the 'balance of probabilities' which is the standard of proof in civil jurisdiction as opposed to 'beyond reasonable doubt' in criminal jurisdiction and also on the weight of evidence and preponderance of documents available in the records of the case, it appears to me that the defendant-petitioners have lawful title to the suit land, which can be questioned only by a person having a better title thereto. That not being so, the case of the plaintiffs totally fails. 

33. On perusal of the pleadings, evidence and other materials on record, I am of the considered view that the judgment of the trial Court is very much sound, proper and in accordance with law for the reasons stated above and it does not suffer from any Misreading or non-reading of evidence or non-consideration or misconstruction of any document affecting the merit of the case and as such I find no reason to interfere with the same. On the other hand, the Court of appeal below misread and mis-appreciated the provisions of law, the evidence and materials on record and came to an erroneous decision by failing to apply its judicial mind to the given set of facts and as such it failed to independently assesses the evidence and other materials on record in violation of its mandatory obligation under Order 41 Rule 31 and 33 of the Code of Civil Procedure since it turned down the decision of the trial Court on some perverse, unfounded and untenable findings without assigning any reason and also without reversing the findings of the trial Court and thus, the impugned judgment and decree being not a proper judgment of reversal, is illegal and liable to be set aside. 

34. Accordingly, I find merit in the Rule for which it succeeds. In the result, the Rule is made absolute and the judgment and decree dated 08.02.2011 (decree signed on 14.02.2011) passed by the Joint District Judge, First Court, Rajbari in Title Appeal No.24 of 2007 allowing the appeal is hereby set aside and the judgment and decree dated 29.01.2007 (decree signed on 05.02.2007) passed by the Senior Assistant Judge, Rajbari Sadar, Rajbari in Title Suit No.55 of 2000 dismissing the suit is hereby affirmed. 

35. No order as to cost. The interim order of stay granted earlier at the time of issuance of the Rule is hereby vacated. 

36. Send down the Lower Court Record along with a copy of this judgment to the Court concerned at once. 

End.

case_source: (From the judgment and order dated the 8th and 9th day of December, 1997 passed by the High Court Division in Writ Petition No. 1377 of 1995).
full_judgment:
Md Fazlul Karim J: The appeal by leave is directed against the judgment and order dated the 8th and 9th day of December, 1997 passed by the High Court Division in Writ Petition No. 1377 of 1995 discharging the Rule.

2. The appellant filed Case No. 1007 of 1988 before the Chairman, Court of Settlement, Dhaka under Section 7(1) of the Abandoned Buildings (Supplementary Provisions) Ordinance, 1985 (Ordinance No. 54 of 1985) stating, inter-alia, that the case property belonged to Rafi Ahmed Fidai who got the same by way of allotment from the then Government of East Pakistan. Rafi Ahmed Fidai sold the suit land to Mrs. Zakia Khatoon at Taka 8,000 on 6-6-1963 and Zakia Khatoon sold the suit property again in favour of the appellant, Mrs. Ambia Khatun for Taka 12,000 by executing a deed of sale on 21-3-1974 and registered the same on 18-4-1974. Zakia Khatoon paid municipal taxes and the appellant which living in the suit property after purchase used to pay electricity bills and WASA bills and the draft RS record in respect of the suit property has been prepared in the name of the appellant and as such, the provisions of the Ordinance No. 54 of 1985 have no manner of application as the appellant was in possession and no notice was served upon the appellant. So, the inclusion of the case property under Section 5(1)(b) was illegal. The Court of Settlement by its judgment and order dated 20-12-1994 dismissed the case of the appellant for deleting the property from the list of abandoned buildings whereupon the appellant moved the High Court Division against the said judgment and order but the Rule was discharged by the impugned order.

3. Leave was granted to consider that submissions of the learned Counsel for the appellants that—

"the question of 'jurisdictional fact' with regard to non-issuance of statutory notice prior to enlistment of the property in 'Kha' list was specifically raised before the Court of settlement, thereby raising in fact the question of absence of jurisdiction of the Court of settlement over the matter but this question was not considered at all, and without resolving this issue the Court assumed jurisdiction over the matter inasmuch as the respondent Government failed to place any notice even before the High Court Division to justify the jurisdiction of the Court of Settlement over the matter and thus, the High Court Division failed to consider the absence of jurisdiction of the Court of Settlement over the matter. the learned Advocate next submitted that the appellant produced all original title deeds including the deed of sale dated 6-6-1963 executed and registered by the original lessee Rafi Ahmed Fidai in favour of the appellant's vendor Zakia Khatoon, and the said deed was testified to have been recorded by the official of the record room in the relevant volume before the Court of Settlement, but the Court of Settlement having been influenced by extraneous consideration did not consider this vital evidence including the assessment roll for the year 1967-68 and other documents and found erroneously the document of 1963 to be forged and created fraudulently and thus, the High Court Division committed an error of law in discharging the Rule."

4. Mr. MI Farooqui, learned Counsel, appearing for the appellant submitted that the question of 'jurisdictional fact' with regard to non-issuance of statutory notice prior to enlistment of the property in 'Kha' list was specifically raised before the Court of Settlement thereby raising in fact the question of absence of jurisdiction of the Court of Settlement over the matter, but this question was not considered at all and without resolving this issue, the Court of settlement assumed jurisdiction over the matter and the learned Judges of the High Court Division also failed to consider the absence of jurisdiction of the Court of Settlement over the matter inasmuch as the respondent Government failed to place any statutory notice even before the High Court Division to justify the jurisdiction of the Court of Settlement over the matter, and in that view of the matter, the High Court Division committed error of law. The learned Counsel further submitted that appellant produced all original title deeds including original deed of sale dated 06-06-1963 executed and registered by the original lessee Rafi Ahmed Fidai in favour of the appellant's Vendor Zakia Khatoon and the said deed was testified to have been recorded by the official of the record room in the relevant volume before the Court of Settlement but the Court of Settlement having been influenced by extraneous consideration, did not consider this vital evidence on record including the assessment roll for the year 1967-68 and other documents and found erroneously the document of 1963 to be forged and fabricated and the High Court Division also failed to consider this aspect of the case and committed an error of law. The learned Counsel finally submitted that in view of the relevant original title deeds on record and possession lying with the appellant, the 'legitimate inference' would be that the appellant and her vendor had always been in control, management and enjoyment of the property in question, and the finding, contrary by the Court of Settlement, must be held to be an act without jurisdiction, and the High Court Division have committed an error of law by not interfering under Article 102 of the constitution.

5. Mr. MI Farooqui referring to Section 4 of the Ordinance No. 54 of 1985 argued that it has been stated therein that in pursuance of a notice in any form issued thereunder at any time before 30th October, 1988 the Government may take over possession of any abandoned property or building. This power of issuing this type of notice in any form gave arbitrary power to the Government and hence is void ability, He further referring to Section 4 (b) (ii) of Ordinance No. 54 of 1985 and contends that no building shall be taken possession of as abandoned property under President Order No. 16 of 1972 except in pursuance of a notice in any from issued under PO No. 16 of 1972 and no such notice is issued in respect of a building, in execution of a decree or order passed by a Court in a suit filed by the Government. He submitted that this is clear discrimination in equality and is hit by equality clause under Article 27 and 31 of the Constitution.

6. Mr. MK Rahman, learned Additional Attorney-General appearing for the respondents submitted that the document in favour of Zakia Khatoon alleged to have been executed by Rafi Ahamed Fidai on 6-6-1963 were forged, null and void and mere paper transaction and has been created by false personation inasmuch as the signature of Rafi Ahmed Fidai appearing on his deed does not tally with the signature of Rafi Ahmed Fidai in the alleged sale deed. The sale deed alleged to have been executed by Zakia Khatoon in favour of the petitioner on 21-3-1974 is also void, inoperative, without consideration and a paper transaction and the same is hit by Article 6 of PO No. 16 of 1972. Furthermore, the LTI is quite different from the alleged LTI of Zakia Khatoon inasmuch as said Zakia Khatoon had no existence and her name was never mutated with the Housing and Settlement Department. It was found by the Court of Settlement on consideration of the alleged transfer deed and evidence on record that Rafi Ahmed Fidai never transferred the property to Zakia Khatoon or anybody else. Rafi Ahmed Fidai was a non-local and during liberation war his whereabouts were not known and he ceased to manage, occupy and supervise the case property in person, hence the property was rightly vested in the Government as abandoned under PO No. 16 of 1972; that Zakia Khatoon, the vendor of the writ petitioner was a fake person who did not purchase the land from original owner Rafi Ahmed Fidai. Zakia Khatoon was not examined in this case before the Court of Settlement and no evidence came before the Court about the existence of alleged Zakia Khatoon inasmuch as her signature in the first page of the kabala executed in favour of Ambia Khatun does not tally with LTI in the rest of the pages of the deed and the expert opined in the similar way. The Court of settlement also came to a finding about the fakeness of Zakia Khatoon and that she was a fictitious person. So, the question of purchase of the case property by Zakia Khatoon on 6th June, 1963 does not at all arise. Accordingly, the purchase of the case property by the present writ petitioner from her does not arise. Her Kabala and the kabala in the name of Zakia are products of false personation. All these are findings of facts in a petition, so the High Court Division cannot look into it. The findings of the Court of Settlement are based on facts and materials produced before it. The High Court Division could interfere with the findings of facts under its jurisdiction under Article 102 of the Constitution only if it could be shown that the tribunal had acted without jurisdiction or made any finding upon no evidence or without considering any materials evidence and facts causing prejudice to the complaining party or that it had acted malafide or in violation of any principle or natural justice.

7. The learned Additional Attorney-General, appearing for the respondents further submitted that Article 25 of President's Order No. 16 of 1972 clearly provides that the Government may make rules for carrying out the purposes of the order and in exercise of such power Government has framed the notice in the form in exercise of the power vested under Bangladesh Abandoned Property (Taking over Possession) Rules, 1972 and in rule 6 residential and other buildings in the urban area have been classified as one category of abandoned property. For taking over possession of abandoned property, notice in Form I, II, III and IV as the case may be issued. The learned Counsel urged that notice in any form means depending on the category of abandoned property and notice in any form of the specimen given as per rule 3 should be issued before taking over of the abandoned property. So, there is no violation of any law and it was not arbitrary. Mr. Rahman submitted that the Appellate Division held that once the property is listed as abandoned property it must be presumed that Government has formed opinion regarding abandoned character of the property as defined in Article 2 of the PO No. 16 of 1972.

8. The learned Counsel for the appellant though strenuously argued regarding the jurisdiction issue of the Court having no initial jurisdiction in the matter to enquire into the question regarding the assumption of jurisdiction on the plea of absence of any notice require under the Abandoned Property Order, 1972 has lost sight of the fact that the property automatically vested as Abandoned Property upon commencement of the said order inasmuch as the impugned notice dated 17-3-1986 was not a notice treating the property as abandoned one. Accordingly the question of 'jurisdictional fact' regarding non-issuance of statutory notice prior to enlistment of the property as abandoned property was of no substance.

9. Mr. MI Farooqui, learned Counsel, has cited a decision in support of the above contention in the case of Baldwin and Francis Ltd as Parents Appeal Tribunal reported in (1959) AC 663 which arose to consider the effect of Sections 9(3), 14(4), 85 and 87 of the Patents Act, 1949, that no appeal lay to the Court of Appeal from the decision of the Parents Appeal Tribunal in the said proceedings, that it was an inferior tribunal and that the only remedy of persons aggrieved by its decision was by way of an order of certiorari.

10. The fact leading to the case that was a company made an application for a patent, whereupon, on the publication of its specification, the owners of a prior dated patent holder opposed the application on the ground, inter-alia, that its specification could not fairly describe the invention or method by which it was to be performed without referring to their prior dated patent, and that such a reference should be directed under Section 9 of the Act. Both the patents applied for and the prior dated patent concerned improvements designed to prevent the re-closing of an electric circuit in which an earth fault had developed, until that fault was repaired. In opposition proceedings under Section 14, the superintending examiner, on behalf of the comptroller, decided that the later invention could not be performed without substantial risk of infringement of the prior dated patent, and, accordingly, there being no proposals for amending its specification, the superintending examiner, by a final decision, ordered that the patent applied for should be sealed with a reference to the prior dated patent. On appeal, the Patents Appeal Tribunal reversed this decision. The owners of the prior dated patent applied for an order of certiorari on the ground that there was error of law appearing on the face of the record in that the tribunal had misconstrued the rival specifications or one of them.

11. In the said decision it was held, inter alia, that—

"In some of those cases it has been said that the tribunal, in falling into an error of this particular kind, has exceeded its jurisdiction. No tribunal, it is said, has any jurisdiction to be influenced by extraneous considerations or to disregard vital matters. This is good sense and enables the Court of Queen's Bench to receive evidence to prove the error. But an excess of jurisdiction in this sense is very different from want of jurisdiction altogether which is, of course, determinable at the commencement, not at the conclusion of the inquiry, whereas an excess of jurisdiction is determinable in the course of or at the end of inquiry. But allowing that a tribunal which falls into an error of this particular kind does exceed its jurisdiction, as I am prepared to do, nevertheless I am quite clear that at the same time it falls into an error of law too; for the simple reason that it has not determined according to law.' That it indeed, how Blackburn J put it in Reg vs De Reuzen And the decision in the Northumberland case itself shows that, even though no evidence is given, nevertheless if such an error appears from the documents properly before the Court, or by legitimate inference therefrom, then certiorari may be granted to quash the decision; and the certiorari can properly be said to be for error of law on the face of the proceedings. It may be excess of jurisdiction as well, but it is certainly error of law."

12. The cited decision has also no application in the facts and circumstances of the instant case because the starting point of possession and alleged ownership of Zakia was on and from 18-04-1974 when the property has already vested as an abandoned property by operation of Section 4 of the Abandoned Property (Control, Management and Disposed of) Order, 1972, PO No. 16 of 1972 effective from 28-2-1972. Thus, it is too late in the day to allege they want of jurisdiction of the Tribunal to allege that there was no notice treating the property as an abandoned one when the property has already vested before the alleged pure phase on 18-4-1974 by the writ-petitioner and ignoring the very fact that the writ-petitioner herself resorted to the jurisdiction of the Court of Settlement challenging the alleged notice dated 17-3-1986 in order to raise the question of issuance to jurisdictional fact or want of jurisdiction before the High Court Division in writ jurisdiction, although the same is not at all relevant in the matter inasmuch as there is no error occurring was alleged effecting the alleged jurisdiction and accordingly there is no such illegality for assuming jurisdiction in certiorari as there is also no error of law on the face of the proceeding. It is to be borne in mind that the writ petitioner herself filed the case before the Tribunal thereby surrendering to the jurisdiction of the Tribunal. In any view of the matter on the given fact the writ petition is not maintainable challenging treating of the property as an abandoned one.

13. Section 2(1) of the Bangladesh Abandoned Property Order, 1972 defined Abandoned Property as under:

(1) "abandoned property" means any property owned by any person who is not present in Bangladesh or whose whereabouts are not known or who has ceased to occupy supervise or manage in person his property, including—

Inclusion clauses

(i) any property owned by any person who is a citizen of a State which at any time after the 25th day of March, 1971, was at war with or engaged in military operation against the People's Republic of Bangladesh;

(ii) any property taken over under the Bangladesh (Taking over of Control and Management of Industrial and Commercial Concerns) Order, 1972(Acting President's Order No. 1 of 1972), but does not include-

Exclusion clauses

(a) any property the owner of which is residing outside Bangladesh for any purpose which, in the opinion of the Government, is not prejudicial to the interest of Bangladesh;

(b) any property which is in the possession or under the control of the Government under any law for the time being in force.

Explanation —"Person who is not present in Bangladesh" includes anybody of persons or company constituted or incorporated in the territory or under the laws of a State which at any time after the 25th day of March, 1971, was at war with or engaged in military operations against the People's Republic of Bangladesh.

14. Article 4 thereof provides that "On commencement of this Order, all abandoned properties in Bangladesh shall vest in the Government and shall be administered, controlled, managed and disposed of, by the transfer or otherwise, in accordance with the provisions of this Order.

15. Thus, since the whereabouts or otherwise of the original allotted Rafi Ahmed Fidai was not known or that there was nobody found to control, manage or otherwise, the property became an abandoned property by operation of law.

16. The appellant was alleged to have been inducted in the building pursuant to the sale deed dated 18-4-1974 although the said property became abandoned property pursuant to the provision of PO No. 16 of 1972 on and from 28th February, 1972 and vested in the Government as under Article 4 the vesting was automatic. Moreover, the appellant did not allege any instances of illegality or irregularity either of law and on fact regarding the abandoned character of the property prior to her alleged purchase on 18-4-1974 but has simply impugned the issuance of alleged or notice contained in Memo No. 9/619 dated 17-3-1986 in favour of Ambia Khatoon stating that;

"এই বাড়ীতে বসবাসের স্বপক্ষে আপনার নিকট যে কাগজপত্র আছে তাহা আগামী ১০(দশ) দিনের মধ্যে এই অফিসে দেখাইবার জন্য অনুরোধ করা যাইতেছে। উল্লেখ্য যে, বাড়ীটি অত্র মন্ত্রণালয়ের পরিত্যক্ত তালিকায় অর্ন্তগত আছে বলিয়া দেখা যায়। সরকারী এই কাজে আপনার সহযোগিতা আমাদের কাম্য। "

17. From the aforesaid impugned notice in the writ petition it is apparent that it has simply asked the alleged occupant to produce any paper in support of her alleged possession within 10 days from the date stating further that the house in question has already been enlisted in the list of abandoned property. So apparently the said property has already been vested in the Government and treated as abandoned property and the purport of the notice, as it appears, was only to ascertain the alleged nature possession of the said Mosammat Ambia Khatoon in the abandoned property and to show the basis for such possession in the house which is an abandoned property.

18. In that view of the matter no question of any alleged jurisdictional fact with regard to the non-issuance of any statutory notice prior to the declaration of the building as abandoned one or enlistment of the property in 'K' list under the provision of supplementary provision of 1985 was involved. Moreso, the present alleged occupant, Ambia Khatoon was allegedly inducted in the property only on 18-4-1974 upon her alleged purchase of the date and as such, the question of absence of jurisdiction of the Court of Settlement in the matter on the alleged issuance of impugned notice giving rise to jurisdictional fat do not arise and hence the ultimate resolution of the issue before the Settlement Court regarding ascertainment of the alleged possession of Ambia Khatoon by the Court of Settlement was with jurisdiction.

19. It appears that the original allotment of the building from Housing and Settlement Department was in favour of Rafi Ahmed Fidai, the admitted original lessee pursuant to a deed of lease dated 1-1-1960 but the alleged transfer either in favour of Zakia Khatoon on 6-6-1963 or in favour of Ambia Khatoon on 18-4-1974 was neither through a legal document i.e. a deed of lease of deed of sale with no intimation whatsoever to the Housing and Settlement Department as to the transfer by the alleged deeds and that Ambia Khatoon has also failed to produce Zakia before the authority or Court of Settlement and the alleged identity of said Zakia Khatoon has not been proved. Furthermore, the alleged deeds of Zakia Khatoon and Ambia Khatoon dated 18-4-1974 were found to be forged by the Court of Settlement.

20. Be it mentioned here that Ambia Khatoon filed the Case No. 1007 of 1998 for alleged release of the instant house No. 8/15, block-D, Salimullah Road, Mohammadpur, Dhaka and the Court of Settlement on perusal of the materials on record and the deposition of the parties found that the alleged transfer from original allottee, Rafi Ahmed Fidai in favour of alleged Zakia Khatoon is not backed by the evidence on record. Exhibit 5 is Form 'A' showing application for certificate under Section 3 of the Transfer of Properties (Pakistan) Ordinance, 1947. This Exhibit 5 dated 15-5-1963. Its serial No. 9 shows consideration for which the property is intended to transfer. In this serial no Rs 9000 only is written. If it was intended to sell at Rs. 9000 the sale deed would have contained the same consideration. On enquiry of the sale deed in favour of Zakia Khatoon by Rafi Ahmed Fidai shows that Rafi Ahmed Fidai allegedly sold the case property at Taka 8,000. Thus, either kabala is false or the said Form 'A' is false.

21. The Court of Settlement further proceeded to hold that PW 1 Rahman Jahangir produced papers relating to payment of taxes to Dhaka Municipality in Exhibit 12 series; this document do not relate to the case property of 8/15 Salimullah Road, Mohammadpur, Dhaka. Instead it relates to 105 of Quaid-e-Azam Road. Moreover, one Zakia Khatoon is related to a property in 8/15 Razia Sultana Road but the case property is of 8/15, block-D, Salimullah Road. The Court of Settlement upon considering the relevant material on record has doubted about the existence of any woman named Zakir Khatoon from whom the appellant allegedly purchased on 21-3-1974. The Court of Settlement also held that no voter's list or any of this sort was produced to show that Zakia Khatoon was a voter at the elections including that on Paurashava election and has held that the appellant's alleged purchase was a fake purchase and the reason being fake purchase based on some forged and invalid document also for the reason that Rafi Ahmed Fidai got the allotment for the house at Taka 3000 in the year of 1960 and the alleged purchase in favour of Zakia Khatoon in the year, 1963 was for Taka 8000 within the lapse of 3 years. But the alleged purchase in favour of Ambia Khatoon on 1974 was only for 12,000 for the house which was abnormally low price. The Tribunal also held that the alleged transfer by the alleged Zakia Khatoon in favour of Ambia Khatoon was on the basis of a false and fake document as the appellant could not produce Zakia Khatoon in the Court and that her alleged LTI in first page of kabala in favour of Ambia Khatoon does not tally with LTI in rest of the pages of the document which was affirmed by the report of the expert. It is in evidence of PW1 Noor Jahan Begum, wife of Rafi Ahmed Fidai, the original allotte that it found one Rahman Jahangir, PW 1 as the occupant of the house just after independence of Bangladesh and who as well could not recognize Zakia Khatoon or Ambia Khatoon. So, admittedly one Rahman Jahangir PW 1 was in illegal possession of the case property on 28-2-1972 in absence of Rafi Ahmed Fidai, the original allotted and considering all the aspects of the case the Tribunal held that Zakia Khatoon was fictitious a person and that the alleged transfer by Rafi Ahmed Fidai in favour of Zakia Khatoon was denied by his wife, Noor Jahan Begum and that the alleged kabalas are the products of false personation. As regard the possession of the document and papers by Ambia Khatoon PW 1 Noor Jahan Begum deposed that after liberation her articles and papers were stolen from her case house has substance and that taking the advantage of the possession of the said papers of the same house Ambia Khatoon has raised the plea of purchase by way of a forged document obtained through false personation and accordingly the Tribunal as well found that the appellant. Ambia Khatoon an impostor through improper means at least by means as stated by PW 1 Noor Jahan Begum, the wife of original lessee, Rafi Ahmed Fidai and accordingly the Tribunal held that "since the appellant Ambia Khatoon in Case No. 1007 of 1998 has not furnished facts about possession of the case property on or before commencement of PO No. 16 of 1972 and since we have held that entire transaction of sale as false and fake the case property as absolutely abandoned property," and accordingly held that from the evidence Noor Jahan Begum the admitted wife of Rafi Ahmed Fidai and on her son of Safi Ahmed Fidai that the property was abandoned by them during the liberation war in 1971 and it has been rightly held to be abandoned property within the meaning of Section 2(1) of the PO No. 16 of 1972 and accordingly vested in the Government. The Tribunal has further held that the sale deed in the name of Zakia Khatoon and Ambia Khatoon having been forged and fabricated such deeds do not confer any title and ownership in the case property inasmuch as under Article 6 of PO No. 16 of 1972 such sale is null and void. The Tribunal has held that the inclusion of the case property in the 'Kha' list of the abandoned building was rightly done and thus held that there is no scope for exclusion of the case property from such list.

22. As against the said finding of Court of Settlement the High Court Division as well observed that the findings of the fact arrived at by the Tribunal cannot be looked into in this petition or in writ certiorari as because the finding of the Court of Settlement are based on facts and materials produced before it and the Court is not to interfere with the said findings of facts under its jurisdiction under Article 102 of the Constitution. The Tribunal in its view, has not acted without jurisdiction or made any finding without any basis or without considering any material evidence and facts cause prejudice to the writ-petitioner or that it has acted malafide or in violation of principle of natural justice.

23. In the case of Mostafa Kamal vs. First Court of Settlement reported in 48 DLR (AD) 61 wherein it has been held that;

"Court of Settlement on consideration of materials on record arrived at a finding that Nasima Khatun is not the daughter and heir of original lessee Mohina Khatun and that the said lessee has not been in possession of the house in question at the relevant time. The learned Judges of the High Court Division upon taking into consideration of such clear finding of facts of the Court of settlement refused rightly to interfere with the judgment of that Court upon a correct appreciation of the legal principle that the High Court Division in exercise of its writ jurisdiction cannot sit as a Court of Appeal over the judgment of the Court of Settlement for resetting questions of fact. Thus, we find no illegality in the impugned judgment and order of the High Court Division."

24. In the case of Government of Bangladesh vs. Md Jalil reported in 48 DLR (AD) 10 = 15 BLD (AD) 175 = 49 DLR (AD) 26 wherein it has been held that;

"It must be said that the High Court Division failed to appreciate the purport of the judgment of the Court of Settlement as a whole. The Court of Settlement not only disbelieved the testimony as to the alleged death of Alimannessa and burial in Mohammadpur on 10-3-1975, but also disbelieved that evidence adduced by the respondents in its entirety, the inconsistencies in the evidence as to their possession of the disputed house till June 1974 were pointed out and it was observed that by resorting to tricks to falsely prove their mother's death on 10-3-1975 in Bangladesh they not only be-fooled themselves but also exhibited a conduct which compelled the Court "to take an adverse view against the petitioners case". It was clearly found that the respondents failed to disprove the stand taken by the Government that Alimannessa was not present in Bangladesh on 28-2-1972 which means that their evidence as to alleged possession of the disputed house till June 1974 was also disbelieved. That being the position the High Court Division was not at all justified in holding that the Court of settlement filed to taken notice of the evidence of the respondents as to their possession of the disputed house. The High Court Division having no other reason did not at all act legally and property in interfering with the findings of fact made by the Court of Settlement. The High Court Division was not a Court of Appeal required to make determination of facts on its own. It could interfere with the findings of a tribunal of fact under its extraordinary jurisdiction under Article 102 only if it could be shown that the tribunal had acted without jurisdiction or made any finding upon no evidence or without considering any material evidence and facts causing prejudice to the complaining party or that it has acted malafide or in violation of any principle of natural justice. In the absence of any of these conditions the interference by the High Court Division will itself be an act of without jurisdiction. This precisely has happened in the present case and therefore, this appeal must succeed."

<u>25. It appears that admittedly the property has been listed as an abandoned property. Thus, the onus lies upon the appellant to rebut the presumption provided in subsection (2) of Section 5 that the same was not an abandoned property No oral evidence has been adduced before the settlement Court of prove that on 28-2-1972 when President's Order No. 16 of 1972 was promulgated the original lessee, Rafi Ahmed Fidai had been present in Bangladesh or his whereabouts were known or that he did not cease to occupy, supervise or manage in person the house in question and the said position was admitted by PW 1 Nurjahan Begum, the wife of Rafi Ahmed Fidai. The Court of Settlement upon assigning cogent reasons held that the kabala of the appellant's vendor is forged and fabricated document and the original lessee, Rafi Ahmed Fidai did never appear physically before any authority for any purpose after the liberation war in Bangladesh. The High Court Division has thus, rightly, maintained the order of the Court of Settlement by the impugned judgment and order. It also appears that the High Court Division upon examining the different provisions of the Ordinance of 1985 including section 7 came to the finding that the said section can give the appellant exactly the same remedy which she was praying for in the petition, that the Court of Settlement has been given the specific power to exclude the disputed property from the impugned list. The appellant has urged before the Court of Settlement that the building is not an abandoned property or that it has not vested in the Government and that her right or interest in the building has not been affected by the provisions of PO No. 16 of 1972. But in the facts and circumstances of the case when the State has devised an alternative forum for giving complete relief to the appellant, the learned Judges observed, she could not invoke the writ jurisdiction without exhausting the remedy provided for in the Ordinance.</u>

<u>26. In the instant case the broad fact alleged by the writ-petitioner, Ambia Khatoon is that she is the transferee from one Zakia Khatoon vide a deed of sale executed and registered on 18-4-1974. Zakir Khatoon allegedly purchased the property from the original allottee, Rafi Ahmed Fidai executed on 6-6-1963 in her favour and the said deed of Zakia Khatoon has highly been disputed and the same was neither produced in the case nor any material was placed before the Court to substantiate the sale of Rafi Ahmed Fidai in favour of Zakia Khatoon so as to devolve the interest of Zakia Khatoon in favour of the writ-petitioner Ambia Khatoon pursuant to her alleged purchase dated 18-4-1974.</u>

<u>27. Be that as it may, we are concerned with the property which has been vested as abandoned property pursuant to the PO No. 16 of 1972 as admittedly neither Rafi Ahmed Fidai nor the alleged Zakia Khatoon could be found in possession or control to manage the property on 28-2-1972 when the PO No. 16 of 1972 came of effective.</u>

28. In view of the above, we find no substance in the submissions of the learned Counsel for the appellant.

29. Accordingly, the appeal is dismissed without any order as to costs.

End.
