full_judgment:
Md. Ruhul Amin J : This appeal, by leave, is by the heirs of defendant No. 1 against the judgment dated May 9, 2001 of a Single Bench of the High Court Division in Civil Revision No. 3560 of 1993 making absolute the Rule obtained against the Judgment and decree dated November 17, 1993 of the 1st Court of Subordinate Judge (now Joint District Judge), Barisal in Title Appeal No. 67 of 1985 allowing the same and thereby dismissing the suit upon reversing the judgment and decree dated April 28, 1985 of the Court of Munsif (now Assistant Judge) Upazila Babuganj, Barisal in Title Suit No. 285 of 1984 decreeing the same in part and thereby declaring title of the plaintiff Nos. 2-4 acquired by the kabala dated September 30, 1975 and also declaring title of the defendant Nos. 1 and 2 to have been acquired by adverse possession in respect of the part of the land in suit and that further declaring the judgment and decree in Title Suit No. 206 of 1976 void and not binding upon the plaintiffs.

2. The suit was filed seeking primarily the reliefs which are:

(ক) বিরোধীয় (খ)তফছিল বর্ণিত ডিক্রি ভাক্ত, ফেরবী ও nul and void  সাব্যস্থে তাহা রহিত ও বাদীয়গণ প্রতি বাধ্যকর না থাকা মর্মে ঘোষনা মূলক ডিক্রি দিবার।

(খ)বিরোধীয় (গ)তফছিল বর্ণিত ভূমিতে বাদীগণের রায়তি স্বত্ব থাকা মর্মে ঘোষনা মূলক ডিক্রি দিবার। Schedule 'Kha' to the plaint is as follows :

(খ) তপছিল বিরোধীয় ডিক্রি মোঃ বরিশালের ২য় মুন্সেফি আদালত দেং মোঃ ২০৬/৭৬ এরশেদ আলী হাওলাদার গং-বনাম-আশ্বিনী কুমার গং-বাদী। -বিবাদী।

রুজুঃ-১১-৩-৭৬

তায়দাদঃ- ৩০০০/০০

ছোলে সুত্রে ডিক্রির তাং ২০/৬/৭৬

And Schedule 'Ga' to the plaint is as follows:

(গ) তপছিল

জিঃ বাখরগঞ্জ ষ্টেশন বাবুগঞ্জ অধীন জে, এল, ৩৫ নং তেহেরগতি মৌজায় এস, এ ৬০ নং খতিয়ানের ৫১১৯/৫৯২০/৫৯২৭/৫৯২৮/৫৯২৯/৫৯৩০/৫৯৫৮/ দাগে জমি ২.২৩ শঃ।

ষ্টেশন মৌজা ঐ এস, এ, ১২৮২ নং খতিয়ানের ৫৯৪২ দাগের হিং। এস, এ, ১২৮৩ নং খতিয়ানের ৫৯৫১ দাগের হিং। আনী এস, এ, ১২৮৪ নং খতিয়ানের ৫৯৩৯ দাগের। ।০ এস, এ, ১২৮৫ নং খতিয়ানের ৫৯৫৩ দাগের হিং। ।০ আনী, এস, এ, ১২৮৬ নং খতিয়ানের ৫৯৩৭ দাগের হিং। /৬।।// মোট জমি ২.২৩+.৩৮= ২.৬১ শতাংশ।

3. It may be mentioned the land as in schedule 'Ga' is part of the land described in schedule 'Ka' which is as follows:

জিলা বাখরগঞ্জ অধীন ষ্টেশন বাবুগঞ্জ অন্তর্গত ৩৫ নং জে, এল, দেহেরগতি মৌজায় হাল ৫৯২০ দাগের হিং।। আনা এবং হাল ৫৯১৯/৫৯২৯/৫৯৩০ নং দাগের হিং ১ আনী এবং হাল ৫৯১৯/৫৯২৯/৫৯৩০ নং দাগের হিং ১ আনী এবং হাল ৫৯৫৮ নং দাগের হিং//০ আনী এবং হাল ৫৯৪৫/৫৯৪৬/৫৯৪৭ নং দাগের হিং।। ১৩ ক্রান্তি অংশে ২.৮১ শতাংশ ভূমির তৎকালীন মালিক পত্তন দাতা ১-৯ নং বিবাদীগণের নিকট হইতে বিগত ১৩৫১ সনের মাঘ মাসের ১৫ তারিখে পত্তন মুলে বার্ষিক মং ১০ টাকা জমায় আপোষ মতে মালিক দাখিলকার ২নং বাদী যাহা রিভিশনাল জরিপের ১৮২৬/১/২৪৩৯ তথা এস, এ, ৬০/৭২ নং খতিয়ানে পরিমিত হইয়াছে।

২। জিলা ষ্টেঃ মৌজা জে, এল, ঐ মধ্যে হাল ৫৯৪২/৫৯৫১/৫৯৩৯/৫৯৫৩ নং দাগের //০ আনী এবং হাল ৫৯৩৭ নং দাগের হিং ।/৬।// ক্রান্তি অংশে যথাক্রমে ৩৮ শতাংশে ভূমির তৎকালীন পত্তন দাতা ১৩/১১ নং বিবাদীগনের নিকট হইতে বিগত ১৩৫১ সনের মাঘ মাসের ১৫ তারিখে বার্ষিক ২ ।।০ আনা জমায় আপোষ মতে মালিক দাখিলকার ২ নং বাদী যাহা রিভিশনাল জরিপে ১৮১৬/২,২৯৮৯/২৬৬/২৪৬/২৭৪৫ তথা এস, এ, ১২৮২/১২৮৩/১২৮৫/১২৮৬ নং খতিয়ানের পরিমিত হইয়াছে।

4. It was the case of the plaintiffs that defendant Nos. 1-6 and defendant Nos. 8-11 of Title Suit No. 206 of 1976 died long before the institution of the said suit, that plaintiff No. 1 and the defendant Nos. 4-6 of the instant suit i.e. Title Suit No. 285 of 1984, are the heirs of defendant Nos.1-6 of Title Suit No. 206 of 1976, that plaintiff No. 1 and the defendant Nos. 4-6 got their names mutated on March 10, 1969 and that plaintiff No. 1 and defendant Nos. 4-6 each having 8 annas share, that defendant Nos. 4-6 sold their share to the plaintiff Nos. 2-4 on September 30, 1975, that defendant Nos.1 and 2 of the instant suit i.e. Title Suit No. 285 of 1984, although had no title but they instituted Title Suit No. 206 of 1976 seeking declaration of their title impleading the plaintiff No. 1 and the predecessor of the defendant Nos. 4-6 of the instant suit upon giving wrong address and thereupon, suppressing summonses obtained degree fraudulently in respect of the land of the plaintiff No.1 and defendant Nos. 4-6 of the instant suit, that the plaintiffs or their predecessors did not settle the land in suit to the defendants, that the plaintiffs came to know about the fraudulent decree obtained by the defendant Nos.1 and 2 in Title Suit No. 206 of 1976 on 15-10-1976 and that upon obtaining the information supplied by the Court on 12-11-1976 became certain about the fraudulent decree obtained by the defendant Nos.1 and 2 in Title Suit No. 206 of 1976. Hence the suit.

5. The suit was contested by defendant No. 1 by filing written statement denying the material averments made in the plaint and also contending that the suit was barred by limitation. The definite case of the defendant No. 1 is that the plaintiff case that defendant Nos. 1-6 and 8-11 of Title Suit No. 206 of 1976 died before filing of the same is not correct, that plaintiff No. 1 and the defendant Nos. 4-6 of the instant suit are not the heirs of the defendant Nos. 1-6 and 8-11 of Title Suit No. 206 of 1976, that defendant Nos. 4-6 had no interest in the land described in schedule 'Ga' and that defendant Nos.1 and 2 got the land by settlement and are in possession thereof, that summonses of Title Suit No. 206 of 1976 were duly served on the defendants, that defendant Nos.1 and 2 of the instant suit got the land by settlement from the defendants of the Title Suit No. 206 of 1976 on 15th March, 1351 BS and since then the defendants are enjoying the land so got by settlement, that defendants of the Title Suit No. 206 of 1976 and the plaintiff No. 1 of the instant suit entered appearance in Title Suit No. 206 of 1976 upon engaging an Advocate and they filed solenama, and on the basis of the said solenama the suit was decreed, that the solenama so filed was quite genuine, that the plaintiffs have filed the suit making untrue statements.

6. The trial Court decreed the suit on the finding that the suit is not had for defect of party and that summonses of Title Suit No. 206 of 1976 were suppressed and thereupon decree was obtained, that defendants failed to dislodge the contention of the plaintiffs that defendant Nos.1-6 and 8-11 of Title Suit No. 206 of 1976 died before the institution thereof, that the defendant Nos.1 and 2 in the instant suit obtained decree in Title Suit No. 206 of 1976 against dead persons, that the document of the .plaintiff Nos. 2-4 by which they have purchased the land claimed by them as in schedule 'Ga' from defendant Nos. 4-6 of the instant suit is genuine and the said plaintiffs are in possession, that defendants failed to establish their case of taking oral settlement of the land in suit and that their story of taking settlement orally is a get-up story, that defendant No. 2 is in possession of part of the land in suit, that defendants have acquired title by adverse possession as regard the land of plaintiff No. 1.

7. On appeal by the defendant No. 1 the appellate Court reversed the judgment and decree of the trial Court on the finding that the suit as framed was not maintainable since the evidence on record shows that the defendants are in possession of the land in suit and, as such, plaintiffs were required to seek declaration of title and recovery of khas possession. The appellate Court also observed that trial Court was in error in decreeing the suit in part i.e. decreeing the suit in favour of the plaintiff Nos. 2-4. The appellate Court further held that the document on the basis of which plaintiff Nos. 2-4 were claiming the land in suit is not genuine since the signature of the executants of the kabala and the signature of the identifier of the said kabala is of the same hand. It was also noticed by the appellate Court that the PWs 2 and 3 admitted possession of the land in suit by the defendants. It may be mentioned it was the contention of the appellant that the suit framed is not maintainable since the land in suit is unspecified and description of the land claimed by the plaintiffs is vague, in that there is no statement that plaintiffs are in possession of which part of the land of the suit plots as mentioned in schedule 'Ga'. The appellate Court upon allowing the appeal set aside the judgment and decree of the trial Court and thereupon dismissed the suit.

8. As against the judgment and decree of the appellate Court the plaintiff No. 3 alone moved the High Court, Division in revisional jurisdiction and obtained the Rule. The High Court Division made the Rule absolute on the finding that the decree passed in Title Suit No. 206 of 1976 was obtained without serving summonses on the defendants, that the judgment of the appellate Court has been passed without adverting to the Exhibits 2-4 and that the finding of the appellate Court as to genuineness of the Exhibit, i.e. the kabala, on the basis of which plaintiff Nos. 2-4 were claiming the land in suit which they are said to have purchased from defendant Nos. 4-6 of the instant suit is not correct since land claimed by the plaintiff Nos. 2-4 was transferred by the elder brother on behalf of his minor brothers, that the trial Court was in error in passing a decree in respect of the land claimed by plaintiffs in favour of defendant Nos.1 and 2 who said to have acquired title thereof by adverse possession, that the trial Court in the background of which materials declared the title of the defendant Nos.1 and 2 in part of the land in suit said to have acquired said title by adverse possession was under the law required to dismiss the suit, that appellate Court while setting aside the judgment and decree of the trial Court did not advert itself to the evidence on record and that did not reverse the finding and decision of the trial Court. It has also been held by the High Court Division that the appellate Court while setting aside the judgment and decree of the trial Court did not reverse the finding of the trial Court as regard the decree i.e. the compromise decree, obtained in Title Suit No. 206 of 1976 and that the appellate Court was in error by discarding the Exhibit 1 i.e. kabala, on the basis of which plaintiff Nos. 2-4 claimed half of the land of 'Ga' schedule comprising the entire land in suit and as to which declaration of title has been sought.

9. Leave was granted to consider the contention that the plaintiff Nos.1-4 filed the suit seeking declaration of title in respect of 2.61 acres of land and the Courts below found that the plaintiff Nos. 2-4 are in possession of 8 annas share of the land in suit and the defendant Nos. 1 and 2 are in possession of the rest 8 annas share of the plaintiff No. 1 and that the plaintiff No. 1 is out of possession of the land in suit and thereupon decreed the suit in part, but the land in suit as claimed by the plaintiff No. 1 as well as by the plaintiff Nos. 2-4 are not specified or, in other words, was not shown separately in the schedule of the plaint, and without specification of the share of the plaintiff Nos. 2-4 as the mere declaratory decree cannot be sustainable in law which was passed by the trial Court and restored by the High Court Division and that the High Court Division was in serious error in not noticing the fact that the plaintiffs are out of possession of the land in suit and, as such, without the prayer for consequential relief the suit seeking simple declaration of title was not maintainable.

10. The learned Advocate-on-Record in support of the appeal reiterated the contention making which leave was obtained.

<u>11. The respondent No. 1 i.e. petitioner, before the High Court Division in the revisional application entered appearance through the learned Advocate-on-Record but did not file concise statement. The learned Advocate-on-Record appearing for the respondent No. 1 submitted that the learned Senior Counsel would make submission in the appeal for the respondent No. 1 and the learned Counsel who would make submission on behalf of the respondent No. 1 at the moment is not available and, in that state of the matter, the learned Advocate-on-Record when called upon to make submission he did not make any submission on behalf of the respondent No. 1. It may be mentioned since no concise statement was filed under the Rules of the Appellate Division, the Advocate-on-Record for the respondent No. 1 or the learned Counsel, who as submitted by the learned Advocate on Record, would have made submission for the respondent had no right of making submission on behalf of the respondent No. 1.</u>

12. It is seen from the judgment of the High Court Division that the said Division while setting aside the judgment and decree of the lower appellate Court did not address itself to the question of maintainability of the suit, particularly because of the fact that the trial Court decreed the suit in part in respect of unspecified land and that the relief sought as regard the land described in schedule 'Ga' to the plaint being declaration simpliciter although because of the evidence of PWs 2 and 3 it was found by the primary Court of fact as well as by the last Court of fact that the plaintiff No. 1 is not in possession of the land of 'Ga' Schedule part of which, not specified, claimed by him along with plaintiff Nos. 2-4.

13. In the afore state of the matter the High Court Division was in error in reversing the judgment and decree of the appellate Court and thereupon restoring the judgment and decree of the trial Court when one of the plaintiffs is out of the possession of the land in suit and that there is no specification in which particular part of the plots in suit which particular plaintiff or plaintiffs are in possession.

14. The suit was filed seeking declaration in respect of 2 matters, one of which is, that the decree obtained in Title Suit No. 206 of 1976 was null and void and the other, relief was for declaration of title of the plaintiffs in respect of the land described in schedule 'Ga' attached to the plaint. It may be mentioned land of schedule 'Ga' is part of the land described in schedule 'Ka' attached to the plaint. The plaintiffs, in all 4, sought for declaration of title in respect of the land measuring 2.61 acres described in schedule 'Ga' attached to the plaint. It was averred in the plaint that plaintiff No. 1 is the owner of the half of the land in suit and the plaintiff Nos. 2-4 are the owners of the half of the land in suit. There is nothing in the plaint to show which particular half of the land of the plots mentioned in schedule 'Ga' is possessed by the plaintiff No. 1 and which other part of the land of the said plots are being possessed by the plaintiff Nos. 2-4. As stated hereinbefore, that trial Court on due consideration of the evidence on record arrived at the finding that of the plaintiffs, the plaintiff No. 1 is not in possession of the land claimed by him and that land claimed by the plaintiff No. 1 is being possessed by the defendant No. 2 from the schedule 'Ka' and 'Ga' (as mentioned hereinbefore) where land in suit claimed by the plaintiffs have been described it is seen that the plaintiffs are not claiming the entire land of the plots mentioned in schedule 'Ga' to the plaint and on the top of that, as has already been mentioned PWs 2 and 3 have admitted that defendant Nos.1 and 2 are in possession of the land in suit claimed by the plaintiff No. 1. The suit, being a simple declaratory one, on the face of the materials on record was not maintainable since plaintiffs being out of possession were required to seek for consequential relief i.e. recovery of possession along with the prayer for declaration of title, but the plaintiffs have prayed for mere declaration of title. The appellate Court while setting aside the judgment and decree of the trial Court noticed this particular material fact that plaintiff No. 1 is out of possession of the land in suit and that there is no specification of the land claimed by the plaintiffs, particularly by plaintiff Nos. 2-4 and thus the trial Court in passing the part decree in favour of the plaintiff Nos. 2-4 was in error or, in other words, the decree passed by the trial Court was not a legal one and thereupon set aside the judgment and decree of the trial Court. The High Court Division while interfering with the judgment and decree of the lower appellate Court was quite unmindful of the fact that of the 4 plaintiffs, who are claiming the land of schedule 'Ga' jointly, since there was no specification which particular half is being possessed by which plaintiff or plaintiffs, sought for declaration of title and that in the background of the evidence on record it was found by the Court i.e. the Court of first instance, that part of the land in suit claimed by the plaintiff No. 1 is in possession of the defendant Nos.1 and 2 and thereupon, decreed the suit in part in favour of the plaintiff Nos. 2-4 but being unmindful of the fact there is no specification of the land claimed by the plaintiff No. 1 and the plaintiff Nos. 2-4 and it appears from the averments made in the plaint that the plaintiffs, in all 4, are in joint possession of the land of the plots as mentioned in schedule 'Ga' to the plaint. It also appears from the schedule 'Ka' and 'Ga' that plaintiffs are not claiming the entire land of the plots mentioned in the second part of the schedule 'Ga'.

<u>15. Plaintiff for the purpose of success in his suit and thereupon to have the relief sought in the suit is required first, to establish that the suit as framed is maintainable and that when the Court finds that the suit is maintainable then goes for consideration of the claim of the plaintiff(s) in respect of the subject matter of the suit and that while the claim made in the suit is being established by legal evidence, the Court passes a decree in favour of the plaintiff and if it is otherwise then dismisses the suit. Thus, the plaintiff is to establish first for having the relief in the suit instituted by him that his suit as framed is maintainable and if same is not established then generally the Court is not required to go for adjudication of other contentions making which relief has been sought in the suit. Law as in Order VII, rule 3 of the Code of Civil Procedure requires the plaintiff to give clear description of the land in suit so that the land in suit is identifiable. In the instant case, it is seen that the particulars of the land as in schedule 'Ga' to the plaint is vague and unspecified. In that state of the matter it is clear that the plaintiffs have sought for declaration of title in respect of unspecified, vague and undivided land. If the land in suit is vague, unspecified and that relief sought is in respect of undivided portion of land of particular plot(s), in that case suit seeking mere declaration of title is not maintainable. In this regard, reference may be made to the case of Tayeb Ali vs. Abdul Khaleque and others reported in 43 DLR (AD) 87. Since plaintiffs' suit was not maintainable as they filed a mere declaratory suit in respect of unspecified as well as undivided portion of the land and, as such, even if any adjudication is made as regard the relief sought as to the decree obtained in Title Suit No. 206 of 1976 would be of no purpose since in the absence of seeking consequential relief of recovery of possession mere declaration of title as regard the land described in the schedule 'Ga' cannot be allowed, as because the land as regard which declaration of title has been sought is vague and unspecified as well as relief has been sought as to land of undivided part of the plots mentioned in schedule 'Ga'</u>

16. In the background of the discussions made herein-above we find merit in the appeal.

Accordingly, the appeal is allowed without any order as to costs.

End.

case_source: (From the Judgment and Order dated 26-11-1996 passed by the High Court Division in First Miscellaneous Appeal No. 9 of 1982)
full_judgment:
Md Ruhul Amin CJ: This appeal, by leave, is directed against the judgment dated November 26, 1996 of a Single Bench of the High Court Division in First Miscellaneous Appeal No. 9 of 1982 dismissing the same.

<u>2. The appeal was filed against the judgment and order dated June 29, 1982 of the 1st Court of Additional District Judge, Bakerganj in Miscellaneous Case No. 5 of 1980 allowing the same. The aforesaid miscellaneous case was registered upon an application filed under Order XLVII, rule 1 of the Code of Civil Procedure by the respondent herein in Title Appeal No. 166 of 1973 seeking review of the judgment and decree dated 31-12-79 affirming the judgment and decree dated August 22, 1973 passed in Title Suit No. 634 of 1970 decreeing the same. The suit was filed seeking decree for permanent injunction and for declaration that the property in suit is not enemy property i.e. vested property.</u>

3. The appellant filed Title Suit No. 634 of 1970 seeking the relief as stated hereinbefore stating, inter alia, that he obtained decree in Title Suit No. 198 of 1970 of the 1st Court of Subordinate Judge (now Joint District Judge, Bakerganj) and on the basis of the said decree got his name recorded in the revenue record, that the defendant No. 2 illegally declared the property in suit as enemy property and he having had come to know about the said fact filed objection on November 5, 1970 and that the defendant No. 2 rejected the said objection and thereupon, treating the land in suit vested property, threatened the appellants to evict them from the land in suit.

4. The suit was contested by the defendant No. 2 alleging that the decree obtained in Title Suit No. 198 of 1970 was fraudulent one and that the same was filed impleading dead persons and that the appellant obtained the compromise decree therein showing dead persons as parties to the compromise. It was also the case of the defendant No. 2 that part of the property in suit along with building and tin shed was requisitioned and the same is possessed by the defendants. The defendant also denied the possession of the plaintiff in the land in suit. The definite case of the defendant No. 2 is that the property in suit was treated as enemy property on February 18, 1967 since the owners of the property migrated to India, that recorded owner Sreenath Chatterjee died on July 24, 1947 and, as such, decree obtained in Title Suit No. 198 of 1970 showing said Sreenath Chatterjee as party to the compromise was illegal.

5. The trial Court on consideration of the materials on record held that plaintiff acquired title in the land in suit on the basis of the decree in Title Suit No. 198 of 1970 and thereupon got his name mutated in the revenue record and paid rent, that the defendant failed to establish his contention that the decree in Title Suit No. 198 of 1970 was obtained against the dead persons. The trial Court also found possession of the plaintiff in the land in suit and thereupon decreed the suit with the finding that the order of treating the property in suit as enemy property is illegal. The trial Court restrained the defendant No. 2 permanently from interfering with the possession of the plaintiff.

6. The defendant No. 2 went on appeal, Title Appeal No. 166 of 1973. The appellate Court by the judgment and decree dated December 31, 1979 dismissed the appeal and thereby affirmed the judgment and decree of the trial Court passed in Title Suit No. 634 of 1970 of the 2nd Court of Munsif (now Assistant Judge) Barisal on August 22, 1973.

7. As against the judgment and decree in Title Appeal No. 166 of 1973 the respondent herein i.e. the appellant in the aforementioned appeal, filed an application under Order XLVII, rule 1 of the Code of Civil Procedure seeking review of the appellate judgment contending that at the time of hearing of the suit and the appeal the appellant i.e. the respondent herein, could not place material documents i.e. death certificate of Sreenath Chatterjee and the record of the Requisition Case No. 55 of 1959.

8. In the petition for review it was stated that the plaintiff of Title Suit No. 634 of 1970 is claiming the property on the basis of the decree obtained in Title Suit No. 198 of 1970, which was filed averring that the land in suit orally was settled to him by the recorded tenants, that the suit i.e. Title Suit No. 634 of 1970, was contested by the defendant No. 2, i.e. petitioner in the review petition, whereupon Miscellaneous Case No. 5 of 1980 was registered, primarily contending that the recorded tenants of the property left for West Bengal, India and thereupon the property in question was treated as enemy property and that some of the recorded tenants died long before obtaining decree in Title Suit No. 198 of 1970, that the solenama on the basis of which Title Suit No. 198 of 1970 was decreed was a fraudulent one and that the said solenama was said to have been signed by persons who died long before filing of the Title Suit No. 198 of 1970, that the government is in possession of the property on the basis of Requisition Case No. 55 of 1959, that during the trial as well as at the time of hearing of the appeal in spite of exercising due diligence could not bring on record the vital papers, i.e. the record of the Requisition Case No. 55 of 1959 and the death certificate of Sreenath Chatterjee, who died on July 24, 1947.

9. The application for review was opposed by the plaintiff in Title Suit No. 634 of 1970 i.e. plaintiff-respondent in Title Appeal No. 166 of 1973, contending that the death certificate of Sreenath Chatterjee sought to be produced before the Court by the petitioner is forged and that the petitioner had all the opportunities to produce the death certificate and the record of the requisition case before the trial Court as well as before the appellate Court but he did not do so and that the petitioner is guilty of serious laches and negligence and, as such, the review application filed seeking production of the papers for the consideration of the Court, which he could have produced earlier, should not be allowed as the petitioner is guilty of laches and negligence.

<u>10. The appellate Court by the order dated June 29, 1982 allowed the review application on the finding "Thus I am convinced that the date of death of Sreenath Chatterjee is 24-7-47. When a man died in July, 1947 he cannot be made defendant in a suit filed in 1970 or he cannot appear or effect a compromise. If the death certificate could have been procured at the time of the appeal, this would have in all probability negatived the OPs claim. The requisition record also shows that a portion of the property was under requisition at the time when the decree was obtained. In such circumstances, it cannot but he said that the petitioner could not produce the death certificate and the record of the requisition case at the time when the decree was passed and the petitioner has been aggrieved because of this by such a decree. Therefore, the application under Order XLVII, rule 1 of the Code of Civil Procedure for review of the judgment should be granted and the appeal should be reheard. The point is accordingly, disposed of".</u>

11. As against the order of the 1st Court of Additional District Judge Bakerganj allowing the Miscellaneous Case No. 5 of 1980 the plaintiff of Title Suit No. 634 of 1970 moved the High Court Division in appellate jurisdiction, First Miscellaneous Appeal No. 9 of 1982. The High Court Division dismissed the appeal upon observing " The learned Court Of appeal below in the circumstances of the case held that the petitioners could not produce the death certificate and the record of the Requisition Case No. 55 of 1959 at the time when the decree was passed in spite of exercise of due diligence and the petitioners have been aggrieved and accordingly, allowed the application for review under Order XLVII, rule 1 of the Code of Civil Procedure and passed order for re-hearing of the appeal. I have already pointed out that the application under Order XLVII, rule 1 of the Code of Civil Procedure was simply allowed and an order was passed for re-hearing of the appeal i.e. Title Appeal No. 166 of 1973. So that appellant's claim that the judgment and decree dated 31-12-1979 passed in Title Appeal No. 166 of 1973 affirming the judgment and decree dated 22-8-1973 passed in Title Suit No. 634 of 1970 of the 2nd Court of Munsif, Barisal were set aside is not correct. The appeal being Title Appeal No. 166 of 1973 as per order of the Court of appeal below be re-heard".

<u>12. Leave was granted to consider the contentions that the High Court Division failed to consider the scope of the review petition in the light of the provision of review provided in the Code of Civil Procedure and thereupon, the High Court Division while allowing the review directed the re-hearing of the appeal, that the High Court Division failed to take into consideration that the defendant has attempted to avoid the provision of Order XLI, rule 27 of the Code of Civil Procedure taking recourse to provision of review under Order XLVII, rule 1 of the Code of Civil Procedure and neither the lower appellate Court which passed the impugned order of review nor the High Court Division decided the rigors of proof lying on the defendant in producing additional evidence while getting an appeal disposed of on consideration of the evidence and that the High Court Division has not given direction as to how the alleged death certificate will be considered without allowing the plaintiffs a chance of disproving the same, that the High-Court Division failed to consider that decree obtained by the plaintiffs in the previous suit being based on prior compromise between them and the original owner of the property the present plea of the defendant in the instant suit to the effect that the compromise decree was a fraudulent one is not maintainable unless a separate suit is instituted by the defendant for the said purpose.</u>

13. The learned Counsel in support of the appeal submitted that respondent was required to seek remedy against the decree in Title Suit No. 198 of 1970 and unless the said decree is set aside plaintiff's right, title and interest in the land in suit remains fortified and the genuineness of the decree in Title Suit No. 198 of 1970 can no way be the subject matter of the appeal re-hearing whereof has been ordered by the appellate Court and affirmed by the High Court Division, that the respondent has chosen wrong forum to agitate the question of obtaining the decree in Title Suit No. 198 of 1970 against the dead persons, that there is no scope to consider the review application in view of the provision of Order XLVII, rule 1 of the Code of Civil Procedure, as the facts alleged for review were very much within the knowledge of the respondent, particularly the record of the Requisition case and, as such the same having not been produced before the  Court or step having not been taken for production thereof before the Court, it cannot be said that after due diligence the said record could not be produced before the Court, that facts pleading which the review application was filed were pleaded in detail in the written statement and that as the same demonstrate that the facts sought to be placed before the Court through the review application were very much within the knowledge of the respondent and he having had not taken step for production thereof, either before the trial Court or the appellate Court, the High Court Division as well as the lower appellate Court were in error in allowing the review application in total disregard of the provision of Order XLVII, rule 1 of the Code of Civil Procedure, that the issue raised as to matter of death of Sreenath Chatterjee could have been brought before the Court by leading oral evidence but having had not done so in spite of the fact that in the written statement in detail the said issue was raised and, as such, the High Court Division as well as the appellate Court were in error in allowing the review application and thereby in allowing the respondent to bring on record the fact which could have been brought on record at the time of trial as well as at the time of hearing of the appeal and thus, the action of the High Court Division as well as of the appellate Court in the name of the re-hearing of the appeal is nothing but given premium of the laches or negligence to the respondent.

14. Let us see how far the application for review allowed by the trial Court and affirmed by the High Court Division was legally competent and sustainable.

15. The provision for review in Order XLVII, rule 1 reads as follow :

"1.-(1) Any person considering himself aggrieved—

(a) by a decree or order from which an appeal is allowed, but from which no appeal has been preferred,

(b) by a decree or order from which no appeal is allowed, Or

(c) by a decision on a reference from a Court of Small Causes, and who, from the discovery of new and important matter or evidence which, after the exercise of due diligence, was not within his knowledge or could not be produced by him at the time when the decree was passed or order made, or on account of some mistake or error apparent on the face of the record, or for any other sufficient reason, desires to obtain a review of the decree passed or order made against him, may apply for a review of judgment to the Court which passed the decree or made the order".(rest of the provisions are not necessary for the disposal of the appeal)

<u>16. It is seen from the aforesaid provision of the law relating to review, that an application for review is entertainable from the discovery of new and important matter or evidence which, after the exercise of due diligence, was not within the knowledge or could not be produced by a party at the time when the decree was passed or order made, or on account of some mistake or error apparent on the face of the record, or for any other sufficient reason.</u>

<u>17. In the instant case as it appears from the judgment of the High Court Division and the appellate Court that the review was sought to be brought before the Court for the certified copy of the death register relating to the fact of death of Sreenath Chatterjee said to have died on July 24, 1947, one of the owners and the recorded tenant of the land in suit and who was a signatory to the compromise petition on the basis of which Title Suit No. 198 of 1970 of the 1st Court of Subordinate Judge, Barisal was decreed and thereby title of the appellant herein in respect of the land in suit was declared and further, the record of Requisition Case No. 55 of 1959 was not within the knowledge of the respondent herein.</u>

<u>18. The law relating to the review as in Order XLVII, rule 1 is that a review of a decree or order may be sought on the discovery of an important matter or evidence which after exercise of due diligence was not within the knowledge of the person seeking review or could not be produced by the person who is seeking review at the time of hearing of the case and the decree was passed. In the instant case as is seen from the written statement of the defendant No. 2 (herein respondent) that the facts on the basis of which review of the judgment and decree passed in Title Appeal No. 166 of 1973, which was preferred against the judgment and decree passed in Title Suit No. 634 of 1970 decreeing the suit, which was a suit for permanent injunction and for a further declaration that the property in suit is not enemy property (now vested property) was sought were categorically stated therein. In the written statement it was categorically asserted by the respondent herein that Sreenath Chatterjee one of the recorded tenants of the land in suit died on July 24, 1947. The fact of requisition of part of the property was also stated in the written statement.</u>

19. In the afore state of the matter in our opinion the facts i.e. record of the Requisition Case No. 55 of 1959 and the fact of alleged death of Sreenath Chatterjee on July 24, 1947 were very much within the knowledge of the respondent herein who sought for review of the decree passed in Title Appeal No. 166 of 1973. We are of the view as the facts averred in the written statement i.e. requisitioning of the property in suit, by initialing Requisition Case No. 55 of 1959 and the alleged death of Sreenath Chatterjee were within the knowledge of the respondent herein and, as such it can reasonably be held that the respondent being in possession of the facts and in possession of the materials made the statements in the written statement about requisition of property and death of Sreenath Chatterjee. In that view of the matter, it cannot be said that the respondent at the time of passing the decree in Title Appeal No. 166 of 1973 was not aware of the said materials and was not in possession of the papers on the basis of which review has been sought, since the respondent having had not been in possession of the materials relating to requisition of the property in Requisition Case No. 55 of 1959 and the materials relating to death of Sreenath Chatterjee, he would not have asserted the fact of death and the date as July 24, 1947 and, as such, there is no reason-able ground for the respondent to produce the said papers at the time of hearing of the appeal, review of the judgment and decree whereof was sought by filing the application for review alleging the facts i.e. record of the Requisition Case No. 55 of 1959 and the certified copy of the death register relating to the death of Sreenath Chatterjee which were very much within the knowledge of the respondent and, as such, it cannot be said that the said facts could not be discovered at the time of hearing of the appeal "after the exercise of due diligence", since in the background of the facts averred in the written statement it can reasonably be said that the respondent was very much in possession of the materials for the production whereof review application has been filed seeking review of the decree passed in Title Appeal No. 166 of 1973 and there being no explanation why those materials could not be produced before the Court at the time of passing the decree sought to be reviewed, we are of the view the appellate Court ought not to have entertained the review application and thereupon passed the order allowing the review for rehearing of the appeal.

20. On perusal of the judgment of the High Court Division it is seen that the said Division affirmed the order allowing the review application upon observing "the learned Court of appeal below in the circumstances of the case held that the petitioners could not produce the death certificate and the record of the Requisition Case No. 55 of 1959 at the time when the decree was passed in spite of exercise of due diligence and the petitioners have been aggrieved and accordingly, allowed the application for review under Order XLVII, rule 1 of the Code of Civil Procedure and passed order for re-hearing of the appeal. I have already pointed out that the application under Order XLVII, rule 1 of the Code of Civil Procedure was simply allowed and an order was passed for re-hearing of the appeal i.e. Title Appeal No. 166 of 1973, so that appellant's claim that the judgment and decree dated 31-12-79 passed in Title Appeal No. 166 of 1973 affirming the judgment and decree dated 22-8-1973 passed in Title Suit No. 634 of 1970 of the 2nd Court of Munsif, Barisal were set aside is not correct. The appeal being Title Appeal No. 166 of 1973 as per order of the Court of appeal below be re-heard". On perusal of the aforesaid observation of the High Court Division and the view expressed by the said Division it appears that the said Division has misconstrued, in the background of the facts on record, the provision of review as in Order XLVII, rule 1 of the Code of Civil Procedure. In that view of the matter, in our view, the High Court Division was in error in maintaining the order of the appellate Court allowing the prayer for review for re-hearing of the appeal. The law relating to review and the time tested ground(s) entitling one of the parties in the judgment has been re-stated in the case of Basharatullah, being dead his heirs: Fazle Karim and others vs Government of Bangladesh and others reported in 1996 BLD (AD) 9 = 48 DLR (AD) 178 wherein it has been held :

"Consistently with the principle that there is to be end to the litigation, it is well recognised that review is not an appeal nor re-hearing merely on the ground that one party or another conceives himself to be dissatisfied with the decision sought to be reviewed. Unless a prayer for review is based on the grounds mentioned above the Court will not sit on the matter again for a re-hearing or further hearing which is already concluded by decision even if that be erroneous".

<u>21. It may be mentioned in the instant, case review was sought said to be on discovery of new and important matter or evidence which was not known or could not be produced before the Court. The High Court Division as well as the appellate court while considering the propriety and legality of the prayer for review were of the view that respondent was not aware of the materials on discovery whereof prayed for review and as such said materials could not be produced before the Court. As mentioned hereinbefore the contention of the respondent as to discovery of the materials only after disposal of the appeal is being negatived by the definite averments about the laid materials in the written statement. Because of the nature and kind of the statements made about the materials on the basis whereof review has been sought it can reasonably be said that unless those materials were being in the possession of the respondent the said statement could not have been made.</u>

<u>22. It is seen from the judgment of the High Court Division as well as from the order passed by the trial Court allowing the application for review that the respondent, who was the petitioner in Miscellaneous Case No. 5 of 1980, sought review for consideration of the genuineness of the decree passed in Title Suit No. 198 of 1970 on the ground that the said decree was obtained without impleading the respondent and further, for bringing the fact before the Court that the decree in the said suit was obtained upon impleading the dead person, particularly Sreenath Chatterjee who is said to have died on July 24, 1947 and as such the compromise decree obtained in the aforementioned title suit was not a genuine one. The matter of death of Sreenath Chatterjee on July 24, 1947 has been sought to be brought before the Court by producing death certificate. Suffice it to say the genuineness of the decree obtained in Title Suit No. 198 of 1970 was not an issue in Title Suit No. 634 of 1970 of the 2nd Court of Munsif (now Assistant Judge, Barisal) as against whereof Title Appeal No. 166 of 1973 was filed and dismissed. Title Suit No. 634 of 1970 was filed seeking the decree for permanent injunction and for a declaration that the property in suit is not an enemy property (now vested property). The said declaration was sought on the basis of the decree obtained in Title Suit No. 198 of 1970. The respondent under the law was required to seek relief against the decree passed in Title Suit No. 198 of 1970 for establishing its contention that the decree was not genuine since the same allegedly to have been obtained impleading a dead person as defendant and consequently, obtaining of compromise decree on the basis of the compromise entered into between the plaintiff herein appellant and the defendant. Since the subject matter of the Tile Suit No. 634 of 1970 out of which Title Appeal No. 166 of 1973 arose was quite different and distinct from the relief sought through review of decree in Title Appeal No. 166 of 1973, i.e. seeking of relief against the decree passed in Title Suit No. 198 of 1970, the respondent was required to file separate suit seeking setting aside of the decree earlier obtained by the appellant in Title Suit No. 198 of 1970. The High Court Division and the appellate Court lost sight of the matter that respondent's endeavour to have the relief against the decree passed in Title Suit No. 198 of 1970 upon resorting to review of the decree passed in Title Suit No. 166 of 1973 was misconceived one and also was not legally well founded.</u>

23. In view of the aforestate of the matter we find merit in the submission of the learned Advocate for the appellant that respondent was required to seek remedy against the decree passed in Title Suit No. 198 of 1970 by instituting a separate suit and that the respondent by resorting to review had chosen a wrong forum for ascertaining the question of genuineness of the decree obtained in Title Suit No. 19-8 of 1970.

24. It has already been mentioned herein-before that the application for review was not legally well conceived one since the facts alleging which review was sought were very much, in the background of the averments made about those facts in the written statement of the respondent filed in Title Suit No. 634 of 1970, within the knowledge of the respondent. It also may be mentioned that there was specific plea in the written statement Sreenath Chatterjee died on July 24, 1947 but the respondent did not take any step to establish the said fact. From the averments made in the written statement is seen that the respondent was in possession of the materials in support of alleged death of Sreenath Chatterjee on July 24, 1947 and in that view of the matter for re-agitating the said fact upon resorting to review was not legally competent. The contention, as stated hereinbefore, upon making which leave was obtained, in our view, in the background of the materials on record, appears to be of merit, primarily question of genuineness of the decree obtained in Title Suit No. 198 of 1970 was not an issue in Title Suit No. 634 of 1970 out of which Title Appeal No. 166 of 1973 arose, second issue as to genuineness of the decree in Title Suit No. 198 of 1970 could only be the subject matter of a suit seeking declaration about the said decree i.e. decree in Title Suit No. 198 of 1970 and in no way can be the matter for adjudication within the scope of Title Suit No. 634 of 1970 as framed and the review as sought. We have already mentioned hereinbefore that, the ground upon which review was sought does in no way conform to the requirement of the provision of law as in Order XLVII, rule 1 of the Code of Civil Procedure for maintaining an application for review or entitling a person to seek review against a decree, the order of the High Court Division affirming the order of the appellate Court passed in Miscellaneous Case No. 5 of 1980 allowing the application filed seeking review for re-hearing of the appeal was not maintainable.

25. In the background of the discussion made hereinabove we find merit in the appeal.

Accordingly, the appeal is allowed without any order as to costs.

End.

full_judgment:
<u>Md Abdur Rashid J: In the above writ petitioners, assessment of duties and other charges on the basis of tariff value on the imported goods of the petitioner was challenged.</u>

2. Upon further applications on the behalf of the petitioner, on 1-8-06 in the above three Writ Petitions and on 3-7-06 in Writ Petition No. 108 of 1998 supplementary Rule Nisi was issued against constitutionality of SRO No. 215 dated 12-12-95.

3. First two writ petitions arise out of assessment of customs duty and other charges on imported goods, namely, 'Caustic Soda' while in the latter two petitions, imported goods was Soda Ash'. As the petitioner is the same in all the writ petitions and the issues involved are also common, we heard the writ petitions together and now, dispose of them by this order.

4. The petitioner is an importer. In Writ Petition No. 107 of 1998, he on 18-12-97 opened a letter of credit for import of Caustic Soda. After arrival of the goods at Chittagong two bills of entry being No. C-32211 and C-32215 were submitted on 8-1-98 for release of the goods on the basis of C&F value at the rate of US$ 190 per metric ton.

5. Some date the concerned customs authority ordered for assessment for the imported goods on the basis of tariff value at the rate of US$ 375 per metric ton by way of adjustment at the rate of 1.9348% on the basis of tariff value. In the supplementary affidavit, in support of C&F value, the petitioner annexed number of documents under 'H' series to show CRF certified value of said 'Caustic Soda', which never exceeded US$ 260 per metric ton in the immediate past.

6. It is also stated that the National Board of Revenue by a circular dated 12-11-97 recorded price of Caustic Soda of origin of China classified under HS Code No. 2815.11.00 at the rate of US$ 260 per metric ton (Annexure-1) and by further notification dated 4-6-98 the Finance Ministry further clarified that such value would override the tariff value.

7. In Writ Petition No. 1443 of 1998, letter of credit was established on 16-4-98 for import of Caustic Soda and after arrival of the goods at Chittagong two bills of entry being C-60496 and C-60499 were submitted on 26-5-98 for release of the goods on the basis of C&F value at the rate of US $ 189 per metric ton.

8. The concerned Customs Authority however ordered to impose tariff value at the rate of US$ 375 per metric ton by way of adjustment at the rate of 1.9451. In the application for supplementary rule the petitioner also annexed same documents as in the earlier supplementary affidavit as Annexure-H series and T and I(1) in support of C&F values.

9. In the Writ Petition No. 108 of 1998, letter of credit was established on 18-12-97 for import of Soda Ash and after arrival of the goods, three bills of entry were submitted on 8-1-98 for release of the goods on the basis of C&F value at the rate of US$ 131 per metric ton but the concerned customs authority imposed tariff value at the rate of US$ 220 per metric ton by way of adjustment at the rate of 1.6463 by SRO notification No. 26 dated 11-10-97.

10. In the application for supplementary rule, the petitioner annexed amongst other decision of the valuation committee dated 11-10-99, which after consideration of various prices found US$ 138 per metric ton highest recorded value of such Soda Ash at the contemporary period would be more reasonable (Annexure-1) and CRF certificate issued by an approved PSI agent certifying the price of 'Soda Ashes' never exceeded US$ 160 per metric ton within last decade and those values were accepted by the customs authority as Annexure-J, K, and L series. The petitioner also annexed copy of a unreported judgment dated 8-8-05 passed in Writ Petition No. 6687 of 1997 by this Division, which fixed US$ 160 per metric ton as price of 'Soda Ash' during the period.

11. In Writ Petition No. 1349 of 1998, letter of credit was established 16-4-98 for import of Soda Ash and after arrival of said goods six bills of entry were on 21-5-98 submitted for release of the goods at the rate of C&F value of US$ 128 per metric ton. But the concerned customs authority ordered for assessment at the rate of US$ 220 per metric ton on the basis of tariff value by notification No. 30 dated 1-12-97 by way of adjustment at the rate of adjustment 01.6849. In the application for supplementary rule, the petitioner annexed aforesaid documents annexed to writ petition No. 108 in support of the price of Soda Ash as Annexure-I series, K and L series. The petitioner also annexed aforesaid judgment dated 8-8-05 passed in Writ Petition No. 6687 of 1997.

12. Mr. Rafique-ul-Haq, the learned senior Advocate appearing for the petitioner took us through the record and several SROs and submitted that SRO No. 215 dated 12-12-98 was already declared to be without any lawful authority and of no legal effect by a Division Bench of this Division in Writ Petition No. 2017 of 1997 dated 26-11-06 with the result that the assessment of customs duty and other charges on the imported goods namely Caustic Soda and Soda Ash by the customs authority at the rate of tariff value, which was far higher than that of recorded CRF value at the relevant time was unauthorized and arbitrary.

13. He submitted that the petitioner produced numbers of documents in support of the C&F value which was backed even by a decision of the customs authority and also a decision of this Division but the customs authority loaded tariff value which was higher than the recorded value and beyond international market price and, as such, the assessment was arbitrary and illegal.

14. In support, he cited aforesaid judgments passed in Writ Petition Na. 2017 of 1997 (Caustic Soda) and Writ Petition No. 6687 of 1997 (Soda Ash) and Salim vs Commissioner of Customs 56 DLR 228 of which one of us is the author.

15. On behalf of the customs authority no affidavit-in-opposition could be filed. Mr. Md Rezaul Islam, learned Assistant Attorney-General however, tried to defend the assessment orders on the basis of tariff value, which would prevail C&F value.

16. Only issue, in the facts and circumstances of the cases, that is facing as is whether or not the decision of the customs authority assessing the value of the imported goods on the basis of tariff value as per relevant notification was well founded and lawful.

17. In the first two writ petitions as stated hereinbefore imported goods were Caustic Soda while in the last two ones Soda Ash. After arrival of the goods, bills of entry were submitted on behalf of the petitioner for release of the goods on the basis of C&F value. In support of said value, number of documents was produced including decision of the customs authority, the government and this Division on the price of the imported goods at the relevant period.

18. In the first two writ petitioners we find that the National Board of Revenue on 12-11-97 circulated a direction to the effect that the price of Caustic Soda of origin of China was recorded at the rate of US$ 260 per metric ton and to be classified under HS Code No. 2815.11.00, (Annexure-I). It further directed that if the said value was in force on 30-6-98 then said goods ought to be assessed upon such value. If tariff value was fixed upon the goods and higher than the recorded value, then the duty would to be assessed on tariff value. When recorded value was higher than the tariff value, then duty would be assessed on such recorded value.

19. The Finance Ministry however, by its notification SRO No. 50 dated 4-6-98 notified that the tariff value would not apply in case of goods recorded in the schedule, (Annexure-1(1). The legal effect of two Annexure-I and I(1) was clearly intended to override the tariff value as notified by notification No. 33 dated 30-12-97 vis-a-vis recorded value. It also appears from the copies of PSI certificates for the period from 10-5-02 to 3-11-05 (Annexure-H series) submitted by the petitioner in support of its value the price of Caustic Soda never crossed US$ 257 per metric ton.

20. In view of such materials, we are unable to accept the valuation of Caustic Soda at the rate of tariff value at US$ 375 per metric ton as nearest ascertainable international market price. Consequently, the valuation of the customs authority of Caustic Soda must be held to be inflated and arbitrary.

21. In respect of valuation of imported Soda Ash, we find in the unreported case of Ms. Kemal Trading Co Ltd, writ petition No. 6677 of 1997 dated 8-8-05 that the value of Soda Ash at the time of submission of bills of entry for clearance of Soda Ash on 15-10-97 was considered. In the case, the customs authority also valued Soda Ash on the basis of tariff value at the rate of US$ 220 per metric ton. A Division Bench of this Division found that the fixation of tariff value at the rate of US$ 220 per metric ton was inflated and that there was no justification in the increase of tariff value from US$ 160 to 220 and accordingly, held that the importer was entitled to get imported consignment assessed at the rate of tariff value of US$ 160. We are told that the decision has not been challenged. If so, we do not find any reason to take a view different from said decision on the valuation of Soda Ash.

22. Originally section 25 of the Customs Act amongst other provided that value of imported goods liable to customs duty should be the actual price that is the price actually paid or payable, or the nearest ascertainable equivalent of such price. Sub-section (2) of said section also provided for determination of the price in respect of imported goods in accordance with the rules that may be made in this behalf. In the absence of the rules, sometime, the government fixed tariff value for the purpose of assessment. Then, section 25A was introduced.

<u>23. Original scheme of section 25 has undergone change by amendment number of times. But the intention remained the same that the imported goods should be assessed on the actual price or nearest equivalent of the international market price. The device for determination of the value was discovered and older ones updated time to time primarily to prevent the unscrupulous importers from evading and/or cheating the government revenue.</u>

24. In the case of Md Salim, one of us was the author the view taken on determination of the value of imported goods for assessment on the basis of invoice value vis-a-vis tariff value was as follows:

“It is clear from the above provision that customs duty is to be levied on the actual price or the nearest equivalent of such price the imported goods would fetch on a sale in the international market between a buyer and seller independent of each other. Sub-section (7) of section 25 of the Customs Act no doubt, empowers the Government to fix by notification in the official gazette tariff value for the goods imported or exported for the purpose of levying customs duty. But such price is not conclusive and an importer or exporter, as the case may be, is always entitled to prove the actual price of such goods.

In the case before us, the importer produced duly endorsed and attested invoices quoting the price of the imported goods. In the absence of any document whatsoever to the contrary, such invoice value cannot be ignored."

25. We are told that the decision was not challenged. Tariff value as notified by the Government time to time cannot be said to be infallible. The importer is always entitled to have his goods assessed on the basis of the price he paid or ascertainable equivalent of such price in the international market under sub-section (1) if section 25 and prove such price at the time of assessment.

26. Mr. Rafique-ul-Huq strenuously challenged the constitutionality of SRO No. 215 dated 12-12-95. He wanted to impress upon us saying that the value of Caustic Soda or Soda Ash at the relevant time of import could not be higher than the CRF certified value as well. He also submitted that the government most illegally took away Caustic Soda and Soda Ash from the schedule of SRO No. 316 dated 3-11-94. He submitted that in view of section 25A of the Customs Act and said SRO No.316, the petitioner had vested right to have his imported goods assessed not higher than the CRF certified value even when he imported the goods after the exclusion of said goods by SRO No. 215 dated 12-12-95. In support, he relied upon the unreported decision dated 26-11-06 of a Division Bench of this Division in the case of Mohammad Zakir vs the Commissioner of Customs in Writ Petition No.2017, wherein said SRO No. 215 dated 12-12-95 was declared to have been made without any lawful authority and of no legal effect.

27. Section 25A of the Customs Act appears to be first introduced by the Finance Act, 1994 with effect from 1st day of July, 1994. Said section empowers the Government by notification in the official gazette of declare the quality, quantity, price, description and customs classification of any goods verified and certified in the prescribed manner by an approved pre-shipment agency shall be accepted as the basis for assessment notwithstanding any other provisions in the Customs Act. Result ensued that such certified value would override all other value including the tariff value.

28. The Government also issued SRO No.316 dated 3-11-94 to carry out the purpose of said section 25A. It appears certain goods were time to time taken out of the purview of said SRO No. 316 dated 3-11-94 for PSI certification.

29. In the case of the Commissioner of Customs vs Monhar Ali, the Appellate Division noticed that by SRO No.244 dated 31-12-96 12 certain goods were taken out of said SRO No. 316 dated 3-11-94 of the scheme of CRF certification by a pre-shipment agency. The importer in the case conscious of such change imported various goods, which were not included in said SRO No.244, and the goods arrived with certification by approved PSI agency. Long after the opening of the letter of credits, SRO No. 113 dated 11-5-97 was issued, which fixed tariff value on the goods, described in schedule-1 including those of the petitioner. The Appellate Division affirmed the decision of this Division that the importer had vested right to have his goods assessed on the value that was prevalent at the time of opening of the letter of credit.

<u>30. In the case in our hands, SRO No. 215 was issued on 12-12-95 taking Caustic Soda and Soda Ash out of the purview of SRO No. 316 dated 3-11-94. Knowing fully well of such change, the importer opened letter of credit on 18-12-97; 16-4-98; 18-12-97 and 16-4-98 respectively in the aforesaid writ petitions.</u>

<u>31. Mr. Rafique-ul-Huq challenged SRO No. 215 taking out of the vested rights of the importer on two counts, first, the authority of the Government in issuing such notification and then, constitutionality of the notification. His submissions on the authority of the Government and vested right of the importer did not appeal us at all. But in view of the decision of another Division Bench in above case of Mohammad Zakir and the merit of the case on the valuation, we did not find any need to dwell such upon the question of constitutionality of SRO No. 215 dated 12-12-95.</u>

32. Immediate after dictation of this judgment, an unreported decision dated 6-8-05 of the Appellate Division in the case of Nasiruddin Ahmed vs. the Commissioner of Customs in Civil Appeal No. 102 of 1998 came to our notice. In the case, this Division found SRO No. 215 dated 12-12-95 constitutional in the following terms,

"So, the authority which issued the SRO (316) dated 3-11-94 also amended the aforesaid SRO vide issuing another SRO No. 215 dated 12-12-95 under section 25A of the said Act. As such we do not find any reason as to why this amended Notification dated 12-12-95 should be called ultra-vires section 25A of the Customs Act or the previous SRO No.316 dated 3-11-94. Since the self-same authority, which issued the SRO No.316 dated 316, had also issued this amended SRO on 12-12-95. We are of the view that there is no illegality on the part of the authority to issue the above amended SRO does not in any way infringe the provision of section 25A of the Customs Act or the previous SRO dated 3-11-94."

33. In disposing of the appeal, the Appellate Division approved the above view of this Division regarding SRO No. 215 dated 12-12-95 in the above case and other writ petitions. The Appellate Division however, dismissed the appeal of the importer holding that the assessment of duties on the basis of Yellow Book value for the imported reconditioned cars and vehicles from abroad could not be said to be illegal and without jurisdiction.

<u>34. Earlier decision of this Division in WP No.201 of 1996 approved by the Appellate Division declaring the SRO No.215 dated 12-12-95 constitutional was not brought to the notice of the Division Bench neither in the case of Md Zakir nor to us. In view of endorsement by the Appellate Division to the earlier decision in Nasiruddin Ahmed, decision of this Division in Md Zakir was not the correct statement of law. Now, none else but the Bar should take the responsibility for this Division to be trapped in to find the wrong end of law in the latter case of Md Zakir. We could not help but to take the pain to make the record straight in the light of the decision of the Appellate Division on the constitutionality of SRO No.215 dated 12-12-95.</u>

<u>35. For the aforesaid reasons, there is however, no escape from the conclusion that the assessments on the basis of the tariff value by the customs authority of duty and other charges of the imported goods, namely, Caustic Soda and Soda Ash must be held to be arbitrary and cannot be sustained in law.</u>

<u>36. In the result, all the writ petitions are made absolute without however any order as to cost. Assessment made of Caustic Soda and Soda Ash on the basis of tariff value are hereby declared to have been made without any lawful authority and as such, of no legal effect.</u>

37. The concerned customs authority is hereby directed to assess said imported goods in the light of our above observations and as per the valuation of imported goods rule, 1997 and shall refund the Bank Guarantee received, after receipt of the balance, due if any, in cash on final assessment within a period of thirty days of receipt of this order, positively.

Communicate at once.

End.
