case_source: (From the judgment and order dated 17-6-2003 passed by the High Court Division in Civil Revision No.6541 of 2001).
full_judgment:
Syed Mahmud Hossain J: This appeal by leave by the preemptee-appellant arises out of the judgment and order dated 17-6-2003 passed by the High Court Division in Civil Revision No. 6541 of 2001 making the Rule absolute and setting aside the order dated 6-9-2001 passed by the learned Senior Assistant Judge, Kanaighat, Sylhet in Miscellaneous Case No. 18 of 2001 dismissing the miscellaneous case for restoration of Pre-emption Case No. 58 of 1984 of the d Court.

2. The facts, leading to this appeal, in brief, are as follows:

The respondent filed Pre-emption Case No. 82 of 1980 in the then Second Court of Munsif (now Assistant Judge), Sadar, Sylhet under section 96 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, 1950 for pre-emption. The case of the pre-emptor, in short, is that the case holding originally belonged to Hason Miah, the predecessor-in-interest of the pre-emptors and some of the respondents of the pre-emption case and the khatian was accordingly prepared and finally published. On the death of Hason Miah, the preemptor's predecessor, Barkatullah and others became owners and subsequently, on the death of Barkatullah, the pre-emptor and others became co-sharers in the case holding. Respondent Nos. 2- 7 of the original miscellaneous case transferred the case land behind the back of the pre-emptor to the preemptee-appellant who is a stranger to the case holding.

3. The preemptee in the original miscellaneous case took no step in spite of service of notice and also did not appear in the case. As a result, the pre-emption case was allowed ex-parte on 14-3-1985. After that, the pre-emptor got delivery of possession through Court. The pre-emptee then filed Miscellaneous Case No.15 of 1985 for setting aside the ex parte judgment and order dated 14-3-1985. On getting notice of the case, the pre-emptors submitted a written objection denying the allegations raised in the application for hearing and upon hearing the Court dismissed the case by its judgment and order dated 19-11-1985. The pre-emptee preferred a revisional application before the High Court Division and upon hearing, the Rule was made absolute by setting aside the ex parte judgment and order dated 14-3-1985.

4. The pre-emptor engaged an Advocate to represent him before the High Court Division but because of his financial constraint he could not keep contact with his engaged Advocate and as such, he could not know about the disposal of the case. The pre-emptee expressed in the locality on 10-8-2001 that he had got the judgment in his favour in the original pre-emption case from the High Court Division. Subsequently, after enquiry, the pre-emptor came to know about the restoration of the original pre-emption case and subsequent disposal of the same. The pre-emptor then filed Miscellaneous Case No.18 of 2001 under Order IX, rule 9 read with section 151 of the Code of Civil Procedure for restoration of the original pre-emption case upon setting aside the default order, stating that, pre-emptor No.1 is a woman and other pre-emptors are minors and they could not keep contact with the engaged Advocate in the High Court Division and as such, they were in the dark about the result of the revisional application.

5. The learned Senior Assistant Judge, Kanaighat, Sylhet by his judgment and order dated 6-9-2001 dismissed the case on the ground that the engaged lawyers of both the parties were informed with due notice to the parties and as such, the application for restoration of the pre-emption case was not within time and the pre-emptor also failed to file any application for condonation of delay and as such, the application for restoration was barred by limitation.

6. Being aggrieved by and dissatisfied with the judgment and order dated 6-9-2001, the pre-emptor filed a revisional application before the High Court Division and obtained Rule in Civil Revision No. 6541 of 2001. The learned Single Judge of the High Court Division, after hearing the parties, by his judgment and order dated 17-6-2003 made the Rule absolute restoring the miscellaneous case for pre-emption to its original file and number.

7. Feeling aggrieved by and dissatisfied with the judgment and order dated 17-6-2003 passed by the High Court Division, the preemptee-appellant moved this Division by filing Civil Petition for Leave to Appeal No. 1608 of 2003, in which, leave was granted on 27-7-2005, resulting in Civil Appeal No. 189 of 2005.

<u>8. Mr Md Nawab Ali, learned Advocate-on-Record, appearing on behalf of the appellant, submits that the learned Single Judge of the High Court Division failed to appreciate that the pre-emptor never asserted in Miscellaneous Case No. 18 of 2001 filed under Order IX, rule 9 of the Code of Civil Procedure that Mr Monwar Hossain Khan and Mr Abdul Munim, learned Advocates were no longer the Advocates of the pre-emptor and that no material was placed to show that the vokalatnama of the said Advocates was revoked after disposal of Miscellaneous case under Order IX, rule 13 of the Code of Procedure and the learned Single Judge of the High Court Division misdirected himself in holding that showing the order of the Court to the said learned Advocates was not proper communication of the order to the pre-emptor and in that view of the matter, the impugned judgment is bad in law.</u>

9. We have considered the submissions of the learned Advocate for the appellant, perused the impugned judgment and the materials on record.

10. At the very outset, it is necessary to go through the grounds, on which, leave was granted, which are quoted as under:

"The learned Single Judge of the High Court Division failed to appreciate that the pre-emptor never asserted in his application under Order IX, rule 9 of the Code of Civil Procedure in Miscellaneous Case No. 18 of 2001 that Mr. Monwar Hossain Khan and Mr Abdul Munim, learned Advocates were no longer the Advocates of the pre-emptor and that no materials was placed to show that the vokalathnama of the said Advocates were revoked after disposal of Miscellaneous Case under Order IX, rule 13 of the Code of Procedure and the learned Single Judge of the High Court Division misdirected himself in holding that showing the order of the Court to the said learned Advocates was no proper communication of the order of the Court to the pre-emptor and in that view of the matter, the impugned judgment is bad in law. The learned Single Judge of the High Court Division failed to appreciate correctly the principle of law enunciated in the case of Mokbul Ahmed and others vs Md Ullah and others reported in 54 DLR 399 and the same has no manner of application in the instant case. In the facts and circumstances of the present case, the principle enunciated in the case of MA Wahab and others vs Abul Kalam and others reported in 44 DLR (AD) 13 also has no manner of application in the present case. Hence the learned Judges of the High Court Division was not justified in placing reliance on the said decisions. The High Court Division erred in failing to appreciate that the pre-emptor-respondent did not allege before the trial Court that appointment of the lawyers who had endorsed the order of the Court on behalf of the pre-emptor-respondent was terminated but for the first time in the revisional application the preemptors stated that their relationship with the lawyer ceased after disposal of the miscellaneous case under Order IX, rule 13 of the Code of Civil Procedure which is an afterthought and in that view of the matter, the impugned order is bad law.

<u>11. The pre-emption case was allowed ex-parte and the pre-emptee filed an application for setting aside the ex parte judgment and order allowing pre-emption. The miscellaneous case filed under Order IX, rule 13 of the Code of Civil Procedure was dismissed on 19-11-1985. After that, the pre-emptee filed Civil Revision No. 204 of 1985 renumbered as Civil Revision No. 9227 of 1991 before the High Court Division and obtained Rule, which was made absolute on 8-8-1999 and as a result, the ex parte order allowing the miscellaneous case was set-aside.</u>

12. While making the Rule absolute, the High Court Division stated as follows:

"As the case is a very old one, the trial Court is directed to dispose of the pre-emption case within a period of 1 (one) year from the date of receipt of the record from this Court after giving due notice to the concerned parties."

13. But the Court concerned notified Mr Monwar Hossain and Mr MA Matin, who were the learned Advocates of the pre-emptor and they also signed the order-sheet. Therefore, it appears that no notice was served upon the pre-emptor after receipt of the case record from the High Court Division.

<u>14. There is no gainsaying the fact that all the proceedings relating to the pre-emption case ended after disposal of the miscellaneous case filed under Order IX, rule 13 of the Code of Civil Procedure. It is alleged that the learned Advocates who were intimated about the receipt of the record did not inform the pre-emptor. In this connection, it is pertinent to quote sub-rules (1) and (2) of rule 4 of Order III of the Code of Civil Procedure:</u>

<u>"4. (1) No pleader shall act for any person in any Court, unless he has been appointed for the purpose by such person by a document in writing signed by such person or by his recognized agent or by some other person duly authorized by or under a power-of-attorney to make such appointment.</u>

<u>(2) Every such appointment shall be filed in Court and shall be deemed to be in force until determined with the leave of the Court by a writing signed by the client or the pleader, as the case may be, and filed in Court, or until the client or the pleader dies, or until all proceedings in the suit are ended so far as regards the client."</u>

<u>15. Having gone through the sub-rule (2) of rule 4 of Order III, we find that the vokalatnama remains valid unless cancelled with the leave of the Court by the client or Advocate or until the client or the Advocate dies or until all proceedings in the suit are ended so far as regards the client. As soon as the all proceedings under Order IX, rule 13 came to an end, all proceedings in relation to the pre-emption case shall be deemed to have come to an end and the vokalatnama executed by the pre-emptor shall be deemed to have been terminated or lost its efficacy according to sub-rule (2) of rule 4 of Order III of the Code of Civil Procedure.</u>

16. Therefore, the arrival of the case record in the Courts below must be intimated by issuing notice upon the parties and not their learned Advocates.

17. The High Court Division rightly relied upon the case of Mokbul Ahmed vs Md Ullah and others reported in 54 DLR 399 wherein it has been held that it was incumbent upon the learned Judge to communicate the order to the parties about the arrival of the record from the High Court Division.

18. We approve of the principle laid down in the above case.

19. In this connection, reliance may be placed on paragraphs 4, 5 and 6 of the case of Md Wahab vs Abul Kalam, (1992) 44 DLR (AD)13 which are quoted below:

"4. Rule 466(2) of the erstwhile High Court Civil Rules and Orders were the same as present Rule 388(2) of the Civil Rules and Orders. On Rule 466(2) CJ Choudhury observed in the case reported in 15 DLR 99 as follows:

"This Rule contemplates that if on the date fixed any important order is passed this order is to be signed by the Pleader and endeavour should be made to get the signature of the Pleader. But if an order is passed on an off date, in a case not appearing in the cause list or on a date not fixed for a case, it is still more incumbent on the Court to see that the order is communicated."

5. The above interpretation of former Rule 466(2) (now Rule 388(2)) is being consistently followed by the High Court Division (see Md Wasiq Khan vs Md Sabiq Khan, 33 DLR 35 and Jaharunnessa vs Safed Ali Bepary and others, 36 DLR 253).

6. The suit in question was transferred from one Court to another by virtue of a Gazette notification. The transfer was given effect to on an off-date. It was incumbent upon the Court to inform the parties or their Advocates of the transfer. Proceedings continued (sic) in the new Court to the prejudice of one of the parties and in his ignorance of the order of transfer are not valid (see Rahela Khatun vs Seraj Sarker, 35 DLR 345). An order of the Court affecting one of the pillars of the suit, namely, place of trial, cannot be meant for communication to the Pleader Commissioner only. It was meant for communication to all the parties involved. Since the Court's order was not communicated and the course of the suit took an adverse turn to the prejudice of the defendant behind his back and without his knowledge, the suit was rightly restored by the High Court Division on terms and we find no ground for interference."

20. In the above case, the case was transferred from one Court to another in the same Judgeship pursuant to a Gazette notification and this Division held that non-communication of the Court's order took an adverse turn to the prejudice of one of the parties.

<u>21. Admittedly before placing the miscellaneous .case for pre-emption for hearing the provision, the learned Advocates of the pre-emptor were notified about the receipt of the case record from the High Court Division. On the facts and in the circumstances of the present case such a notice is not a compliance with Rule 388(2) of the Civil Rules and Orders. We are of the view that the communication of arrival of the case record from the High Court Division to the learned Advocates of the pre-emptor was not a sufficient compliance with the direction of the High Court Division. What's more, in the absence of pendency of any proceeding in the Court below, fresh initiation thereof in the Court below must be intimated to the parties to the proceeding and not their learned Advocates.</u>

22. In the light of the findings made before, we do not find any ground in this appeal for our interference.

Accordingly, the appeal is dismissed and the trial Court is directed to dispose of the case after notifying the parties and not their learned Advocates as expeditiously as possible.

End.

full_judgment:
Md Muzammel Hossain CJ: This petition for leave to appeal under Article 103 of the Constitution of the People's Republic of Bangladesh is directed against the judgment and order dated 13-1-2011 passed by the High Court Division in Writ Petition No. 2252 of 2010 making the Rule absolute with a direction upon the writ respondents to transfer the writ petitioners service as computer operators to the revenue budget of the Bangladesh Technical Education Board with effect from 1-7-2005 within 2(two) months from the date of receipt of the judgment provided that the writ petitioners would not get any further salary for the period they had served on contract basis for which they had already been paid. 
2. The present respondent Nos. 1-3 as petitioners filed Writ Petition No. 2252 of 2010 before the High Court Division stating, inter alia, that the writ petitioner No. 1 passed BA Examination in the year 1996 from Gouranadi Government College, Barisal and that the writ petitioner No. 2 passed BSc Examination in the year 1998 from Sardah College, Rajshahi and the writ petitioner No. 3 passed MSc Examination in the year 2000 from Jagannath University College, Dhaka. They were appointed on 9-6-2004 as Computer Operators in the scale of Taka 4,125 (250-5505) in the Project for Computerization of Examination Activities of Bangladesh Technical Education Board (BTEB) pursuant to Notification No. বাকাশিবো/এম.আই.এস/২০০৪/১৫৩(৬) dated 9-6-2004 issued by the Bangladesh Technical Education Board. The writ petitioner Nos. 1, 2 and 3 joined on 14-6-2004, 24-6-2004 and 12-6-2004 respectively in their service. The writ petitioners continued their job till June, 2005 on the basis of the above mentioned appointment and at the end of the Project the petitioners were allowed to retain their posts as Computer Operators on contractual basis for a period of 6(six) months each time till June, 2009 vide letters dated 30-6-2005, 22-1-2006, 24-7-2006, 28-12-2006, 25-7-2007, 31-12-2008 and 22-1-2009 issued by the writ respondent No. 1 petitioner with commitment that they would be appointed to their posts on regular basis on the revenue head of the Government as soon as sanctions for the said posts is obtained from the government. The service of the writ petitioner No. 2 on contractual basis was discontinued since 25-7-2007 but he was verbally allowed to work on daily basis till June, 2009. 
3. The Ministry of Education vide Memo No. শিম/শাঃ১৬(প্রজেক্ট)৬-২-/২০০৫/(অংশ-১)/৩২ dated 30-1-2008 (Annexure-C) sanctioned 9(nine) posts of the Project for computerization of examination activities of the Board and out of the 9(nine) posts 4(four) posts were Computer Operators. The writ petitioners stated that clause 49 of the Project Profile (Annexure-D) contemplates that after the life time of the project the manpower (ten persons) of the Computerization of the project would be transferred to the revenue budget of the Board for the public interest and for continuing the computerization of examination activities in BTEB. But out of 4 sanctioned revenue posts of Computer Operators, only in one post a Computer Operator of the Project was appointed and in three other posts, persons from outside were appointed on the basis of Memo No. বাকাশিবো/প্রাঃ/০৮/২০১/২০১০/১৫২২ dated 23-2-2010 (Annexure-E) and by Memo No. বাকাশিবো/প্রাঃ/০৮/২০১/২০১০/১৫২২ dated 23-2-2010 (Annexure-G) only one post of Despatch Rider of the Board who was in service on contract basis was absorbed and appointed in the revenue posts. Thus, to the great mental shock and dismay, the writ petitioners were  illegally left out of the appointment denying them the equal treatment and frustrating their legitimate expectation for appointment to the sanctioned revenue posts pursuant to clause 49 of the Project Profile. The writ petitioners further asserted that the Notification vide SRO No. 182 /Ain/2005 Shama/Bidhi-1 /S-9/2000 dated 20-6-2005 published in Extra-ordinary Gazette dated 20-6-2005 concerning regularization and fixing seniority of the persons who have been transferred to the revenue set up from development project is not applicable in the case of the writ petitioners' service since they were appointed in the Project on 9-6-2004 prior to the publication of the said Notification and as per Rule 2(ka) of the Rules of 2005 contained by the aforesaid Notification "development project" means any project approved by the government under development budget started between 9th April, 1972 to 30th June, 1997. 
4. On 23-7-2007, 27-7-2008 and 29-7-2008 the writ respondents issued certificates of good performance [Annexure-F, F(1) and F(2)] respectively in favour of the writ petitioners and under such circumstances, having requisite qualifications, the writ petitioners rendered commendable service to the Board for a long period and that they have got legitimate expectation that they would be appointed to the vacant regular posts of Computer Operators with grade and scale as mentioned in Memo No. শিম/শাঃ১৬/বোর্ড (প্রজেক্ট)৬-২/২০০৫/(অংশ-১)/৩২ dated 30-1-2008 (Annexure-C) creating 9(nine) posts under the revenue set up of the Board. There are instances and age old practice for the Board's employees to be absorbed and appointed in permanent posts from contractual service and recently also one Md Faruque, son of Md Moinuddin Sardar, a Despatch Rider of the Board on contractual basis was absorbed and appointed to the revenue post vide Memo No. বাকাশিবো/প্রাঃ/০৮/২০১/২০১০/১৫২২ dated 23-2- 2010. The writ respondent No. 2 on 6-7-2003 issued public advertisement vide Memo No. বাকাশিবো/প্রাঃ/২০০৮/৮১২ dated 6-7-2008 inviting applications for appointment to  various permanent posts including 3(three) Computer Operators under the Board, but still now, no appointment to the permanent vacant posts of Computer Operators has been made by the Board and these posts are lying vacant with the Board. 
5. A Division Bench of the High Court Division after hearing both parties by the impugned judgment and order dated 13-1-2011 made the Rule absolute with direction. 
6. The present petitioner being aggrieved by the impugned judgment and order dated 13-1-2011 passed by the High Court Division preferred the instant Civil Petition for Leave to Appeal before this Division. 
7. Mr AFM Mesbahuddin, the learned Advocate appearing on behalf of the respondents- petitioners submits that the High Court Division did not consider the facts that the Bangladesh Technical Education Board sent the proposal to the Ministry of Education for transfer of the writ petitioners' service to the revenue setup, but the Ministry of Establishment rejected the proposal and as such they have no authority to transfer the petitioner's service to the revenue setup. He submits that the High Court Division ignored the facts that the respondent Nos. 1-3-Writ petitioners applied for and appeared in the competency tests for direct appointment and thus they waived their right if any and, as such, the judgment and order of the High Court Division with direction is liable to be set-aside. He further submits that the High Court Division on misconception of law relying upon clause 49 of the project profile held that the petitioners were promise bound to transfer the service of the respondent Nos. 1-3 to the revenue budget of the Board in public interest at the end of the project. He finally submits that the High Court Division overlooked that the project namely computerization of Examination Activities of Bangladesh Technical Education Board started for the period of 2(two) years from July, 2002 to June, 2004 and after completion of the project the petitioners sent proposal to the Ministry to absorb the respondent Nos. 1-3 but the Ministry refused and, as such, the impugned judgment and order passed by the High Court Division is liable to be set-aside. 
8. On the contrary the respondent Nos. 1-3 appearing in persons contended that there is no illegality in the impugned judgment and order passed by the High Court Division because the writ-respondent-petitioner appointed the respondent Nos. 1 to 3 with the condition that after the life time of the project their service will be transferred to the revenue setup. Clause 49 of the Project Profile contemplates that after the life time of the project the man-power of the computerization of the project will be transferred to revenue setup of the Board for the public interest and for continuing the computerization of examination activities in the Board. 
9. We have heard the learned Advocate for both the parties and perused the civil petition for leave to appeal, impugned judgment and order of the High Court Division and other materials on record. 
10. It appears that pursuant to notification dated 9-6-2004 (Annexure-A) upon recommendation of the Selection Committee (second) of the Bangladesh Technical Education Board-petitioner, the respondent Nos.1-3 were appointed as computer operators in the Project for Computerization of Examination Activities of Bangladesh Technical Education Board and the respondent No. 1 joined on 14-6-2004, the respondent No. 2 joined on 24-6-2004 and the respondent No. 3 joined on 12-6-2004 in their respective service for the period of the project. The terms and conditions of the appointment as per Memo dated 9-6-2004 reads as under:

11. On perusal of Annexure-B series it appears that at the end of the Project the respondent Nos. 1-3 were retained in their respective posts as Computer Operators on contractual basis for a period of 6(six) months in each time till June, 2009 vide letters dated 30-6-2005, 22-1-2006, 24-7-2006, 28-12-2006, 25-7-2007, 31-12-2007, 15-7-2008 and 22-1-2009 issued by the petitioner. Though the service of the respondent No. 2 on contractual basis was discontinued on 25-7-2007 yet he was verbally allowed to work on daily basis till June, 2009. Earlier Ministry of Establishment by its Memo dated 27-4-2005 (Annexure-1) rejected the proposal of the Ministry of Education vide Memo dated 29-3-2005 to transfer the 10 posts of the Computerization of the Project to the revenue budget. 
12. Considering the necessity of the service of the Computer Operators, the Bangladesh Inter-Education Boards Coordinating Sub-Committee in their 377th meeting dated 30-11-2006 (Annexure-K) discussed about regularization of the service of the Computer Operators in the created and existing vacant technical posts and the Chairman of the concerned Boards on principle agreed to the proposal. In the said meeting of the Bangladesh Inter-Education Boards Coordinating Sub-Committee adopted amongst others the following resolution: 
উল্লিখিত জাতীয় গুরুত্বপূর্ন ও সংবেদনশীল কাজের গুরুত্ব অনুধাবন করে কম্পিউটার কেন্দ্রের কার্যক্রম সুষ্ঠুভাবে পরিচালনার জন্য সংস্থাপন মন্ত্রণালয় ও অর্থ মন্ত্রণালয়ের অনুমোদনক্রমে শিক্ষা মন্ত্রণালয় পত্র নং-শিম/শাঃ১০/পদ সৃষ্টি কম্পিঃকেন্দ্র-১/২০০০/৫৯৬, তারিখঃ ১-৯-২০০৫ইং এর মাধ্যমে শিক্ষা বোর্ড কম্পিউটার কেন্দ্রের ঢাকা, রাজশাহী, কুমিল্লা, যশোর, চট্টগ্রাম, বরিশাল, সিলেট ও বাংলাদেশ মাদরাসা বোর্ডের জন্য ১০২টি স্থায়ী পদ সৃজন করে। সৃজনকৃত ও পূর্বের শূন্য টেকনিক্যাল পদসমূহে শিক্ষা বোর্ড কম্পিউটার কেন্দ্রের সকল বোর্ডে বর্তমানে কর্মরত চুক্তিভিত্তিক ও মাস্টার রোল ভিত্তিক কর্মকর্তা ও কর্মচারীদের স্থায়ীভাবে নিয়োগদানের ব্যাপারে এ কমিটির বিভিন্ন সভায় ব্যাপক আলোচনা হয়েছে। চুক্তিভিত্তিক ও মাস্টাররোল ভিত্তিক নিয়োজিত জনবলের কম্পিউটার কেন্দ্রের ফলাফল প্রক্রিয়াকরণ এবং কম্পিউটার ও এম.আর.মেশিন, প্রিন্টার ইত্যাদি সংক্রান্ত কাজে বিশেষভাবে দক্ষতা অর্জন করেছে ও বর্তমানে কর্মরত জনবল এ সমস্ত কাজে পারদর্শী। কাজেই শিক্ষা বোর্ড কম্পিউটার কেন্দ্রে বর্তমানে কর্মরত কর্মকর্তা ও কর্মচারীদের উক্ত সৃজনকৃত শূন্য পদে নিয়োগ পাওয়ার অগ্রাধিকার রয়েছে এবং সে মোতাবেক বিভিন্ন সময়ে স্ব-স্ব বোর্ডের চেয়ারম্যান তাদের প্রতিশ্রুতিও প্রদান করেছেন।  
13. In the meeting of the Bangladesh Technical Education Board dated 8-1-2008 in respect of appointment of employees on contractual basis it has been acknowledged that against the 10 posts created in the Project for Computerization of Examination Activities of the Board 10 persons were appointed to the said posts in the Project after following required formalities and after the completion of the Project for smooth functioning of the Computerization of Examination Activities the employees appointed under the Project Profile were subsequently appointed on contractual basis. The Ministry of Establishment and the Ministry of Finance already approved the posts created by the Board under the development budget for the Computer Cell and it was expected that the final order by the Government would be issued immediately in this regard and in the circumstances it was decided to further appoint the employees on contractual basis in the Computer Cell who were earlier appointed on contractual basis. The relevant abstract from the minutes of the meeting of the aforesaid meeting dated 8-1-2008 is reproduced below: 
সিদ্ধান্তসমূহঃ
১।বোর্ডের পরীক্ষা পদ্ধতি কম্পিটারাইজেশন প্রকল্পের মাধ্যমে সৃষ্টিকৃত ১০টি পদের জনবল যথাযথ প্রক্রিয়ার মাধ্যমে প্রকল্পের আওতায় সৃষ্ট পদে নিয়োগ প্রদান করা হয়েছিল। প্রকল্পের মেয়াদ শেষ হওয়ার পর বোর্ডের পরীক্ষা পদ্ধতি কম্পিউটারাইজেশনের কাজ সচল রাখার জন্য প্রকল্পের মাধ্যমে নিয়োগকৃত জনবলকে চুক্তিভিত্তিক নিয়োগ প্রদান করে কার্যক্রম অব্যাহত রাখা হয়। 
বোর্ড কর্তৃক কম্পিউটার সেলের জন্য উন্নয়ন খাতে সৃষ্ট পদগুলো রাজস্ব বাজেটে স্থানান্তরের লক্ষ্যে ইতোমধ্যে সংস্থাপন মন্ত্রণালয় ও অর্থ মন্ত্রণালয়ের অনুমোদন পাওয়া গিয়াছে। আশা করা যায় উক্ত পদগুলো রাজস্ব খাতে অচিরেই চূড়ান্ত জিও জারী হবে। এমতাবস্থায়, কম্পিউটার সেলের জন্য পূর্বে চুক্তিভিত্তিক নিয়োগকৃত কর্মকর্তা/কর্মচারীদের চুক্তিভিত্তিক নিয়োগ প্রদান করা যেতে পারে।
14. From the above discussions, we find that apart from the stipulations made in clause 49 of the Project Profile to the effect that after the completion of the Project the manpower of the Computer Cell of the Project will be transferred to revenue budget of the Bangladesh Technical Education Board for the public interest, the petitioners in the meeting of the Board on 8-1-2008 decided to re-appoint the employees who were earlier appointed on contractual basis for smooth functioning of the Computerization of Examination Activities of the Board vide Memo dated 8-1-2008. In this context it is pertinent to quote clause 49 of the Project Profile which reads as under: 
"After the life time of the project the manpower (ten persons) of the computer cell of the project will be transferred to revenue budget of Bangladesh Technical Education Board for the public interest and for continuing of the computerization of examination activities in BTEB." 
15. Sanction for 9 posts of the Project for Computerization of Examination Activities of Bangladesh Technical Education Board was awarded on temporary basis by the Ministry of Education vide Memo dated 30-1-2008 (Annexure-C) with the approval of the Ministry of Establishment and the Ministry of Finance and out of 9 posts there were 4 (four) posts of Computer Operators along with 5(five) other posts and it was decided that the payment of the aforesaid posts will be made from revenue budget. 
16. It appears that the petitioner published recruitment notice vide Memo dated 6-7-2008 (Annexure-H) inviting applications amongst others for 3(three) posts of Computer Operators. Thereafter upon interview and recommendation of the Selection Committee one Md. Shahadat Hossain a computer operator of the Project was appointed in one out of 4(four) sanctioned posts and in other three posts, persons from outside the Project were appointed vide Memo dated 23-2-2010 (Annexure-E) but the respondents were left out of the appointment to the regular sanctioned revenue posts of Computer Operators. 
17. It appears that the notification issued vide SRO No. 182/Ain/2005/Shama/Bidhi-1 /S-9 /2000 dated 20-6-2005 published in Extraordinary Gazette concerning regularization and fixing seniority of the persons who have been transferred to the revenue setup from development project is not applicable to the writ petitioners because as per Rule 2(ka) these Rules are meant only for those development projects which started between 9th April, 1972 to 30th June, 1997. 
18. In the instant case before us the respondent Nos. 1-3 were appointed as Computer Operators under the Project for computerization of examination activities of the Bangladesh Technical Education Board pursuant to notification dated 9-6-2004. We have noticed that clause 49 of the Project Profile unequivocally provided that after the conclusion of the Project the manpower of the computer cell of the project will be transferred to the revenue budget of the Board. It is true that there is no provision for re-appointment of the manpower of the computer cell when a project is completed. But clause 49 provides for transfer of them to the revenue budget after the completion of the Project. It has been asserted on behalf of the petitioner that the Ministry of Establishment rejected the proposal of the Ministry of Education for transfer of the respondents' service to the revenue setup. But this does not improve the case of the petitioner in any way. Because the petitioner made representation to the respondent Nos. 1 to 3 that their service would be transferred to the revenue budget after completion of the project. 
19. The writ petitioners acted upon this representation to their detriment by not seeking other employment after completion of the project. Issuance of certificate of good performance in favour of the writ petitioners by the writ respondents [Annexures-F, F(1) and F(2)] together with their continuous appointment on contractual basis for a period of 6 months each time till June, 2009 gave high hope and created legitimate expectation among them that their job would be absorbed in the revenue setup. We have also seen that after completion of the Project the respondent Nos.1-3 were appointed as Computer Operators on contractual basis for smooth functioning of the Computerization of Examination Activities of Bangladesh Technical Education Board till June, 2009. We have seen that service of the respondent No. 2 though discontinued on 25-7-2007 yet he was verbally allowed to work on daily basis till June 2009. It also appears that the Ministry of Education vide Memo dated 30-1-2008 (Annexure-C) sanctioned 9(nine) posts of the Project for computerization of Examination Activities of Bangladesh Technical Education Board including 4(four) posts of Computer Operators of the Board on temporary basis with the approval of the Ministry of Establishment and the Ministry of Finance. But out of 4(four) sanctioned revenue posts of Computer Operators, only one person, Md Shahadat Hossain, a computer operator of the Project was appointed in the revenue budget and the respondent Nos. 1-3 were left out on the alleged ground that they failed to qualify themselves to be appointed under the revenue budget and, as such, they could not be appointed. 
20. From the facts of the case it appears that 3(three) posts are lying vacant but the service of the respondent Nos. 1-3 were not transferred under the revenue budget. As per clause 49 of the Project Profile respondent Nos. 1-3 made representation to the petitioner that after the completion of the Project their service should be transferred under the revenue budget without any examination for selection to those posts. The respondent Nos. 1-3 having relied on clause 49 joined in the service under the Project and had worked there till the completion of the Project and after completion of the Project the petitioner was obliged to appoint the respondent Nos. 1-3 under the revenue budget and, as such, the petitioners are estopped by the doctrine of promissory estoppel to appoint anyone other than the respondent Nos. 1 to 3 under the revenue budget. When a person makes a representation to any other person to do something and in reliance of which representation, the represent or changed his position to his detriment, the represent or cannot go back from his representation. This Court in a number of cases held that represented will be estopped by the doctrine of promissory estoppel to retract from going back from his commitment. 
21. The position of law is well settled that the Government shall be estopped from refusing any representation made by it on the basis of which any person has acted to his detriment, except that there is no estoppel against statute or there is no application of estoppel to prevent the performance any constitutional or statutory duty.
22. The doctrine of promissory estoppel was invoked by this Division in the case of Collector of Customs, Custom House, Chittagong vs A. Hannan reported in 42 DLR (AD) 167. In this case to avoid scarcity of sugar in the country the Government decided to import sugar under Wage Earners' Scheme and waived certain formalities. The Government issued notification reducing the existing customs duty and sales tax on the importation of sugar on fulfillment of certain conditions. The respondent availed this opportunity for importing sugar at the concessional rate of duty and sales tax fulfilling the conditions but before the arrival of the cargo and submission of the bill of entry the concessional rate was withdrawn by the Government. The Collector of Customs took view that the respondent was not entitled to concessional rate of customs duty and taxes because the bill of entry was delivered to the customs authority after the withdrawal of the concessional rate. This Division held that the importer having acted upon the assurance given, the Government cannot retrace its steps and ask for duty at the rate mentioned in the subsequent notification. 
23. The Supreme Court of India in the case of M/s. Motilal Padampat Sugar Mills Co. Ltd. vs State of Uttar Pradesh, AIR 1979 (SC) 621 at page 644 observed as under: 
"But it is necessary to point out that since the doctrine of promissory estoppel is an equitable doctrine, it must yield when the equity so requires. If it can be shown by the Government that having regard to the facts as they have subsequently transpired, it would be inequitable to hold the Government to the promise made by it, the Court would not raise equity in favour of the promise and enforce the promise against the Government." 
24. In the instant case, by not appointing the respondents Nos.1-3 to the sanctioned posts of the computer operators, the petitioner has not served any public interest for which their action can be justified rather, as it is admitted fact that these respondents were appointed Computer Operators and gained technical knowledge and expertise from the service they rendered for a long time even after the life time of the project period, their non-appointment has caused much detriment to the public interest. 
25. Apart from the doctrine of promissory estoppels, doctrine of legitimate expectation is also applicable in the instant case. The doctrine of legitimate expectation contributed to the expansion of the duty to observe the requirements of natural justice by extending the duty beyond the relatively narrow range of rights and interests to which principles of natural justice had traditionally been applied. 
26. The legitimate expectation doctrine is invoked in a range of cases, the common theme of which was the principle that when administrative officials had created or induced a belief in a person about the possible exercise of their powers, any change affecting this belief should be conditioned by the rules of natural justice. The legitimate expectation doctrine provided important procedural benefits, namely, the right to be notified of, and to be heard in opposition to, the revocation of an existing benefit. The doctrine of legitimate expectation can be invoked broadly into four categories of cases. 
27. In the first category of cases a person acts upon relying on a generally applicable policy but the policy is subsequently changed to his disadvantage. The second category included cases in which a policy or norm of general application exists and continues but is not applied to the case of the person affecting him seriously. Third category arises when an individual is given a promise or a representation is made to him but which is not honoured due to a subsequent change to the policy. The fourth category of cases arise when an individual is given a promise or a representation is made to him which is subsequently dishonoured not for any change of policy but for the decision taken by the authority not to keep the promise. 
28. A substantive legitimate expectation is based on a promise or representation about an actual advantage or benefit. The Hong Kong Court of Appeal defined the substantive legitimate expectation doctrine in the following terms: 
"The doctrine recognizes that, in the absence of any overriding reason of law or policy excluding its operation, situations may arise in which persons may have a legitimate expectation of a substantive out-come or benefit, in which event failing to honour the expectation may, in particular circumstances, result in such unfairness to individuals as to amount to an abuse of power justifying intervention by the court." [Tung vs Director of Immigration (2002) 1 HKLRD 561, 600] 
29. The substantive legitimate expectation doctrine arises in two scenarios. The first is when a person who enjoys a benefit or a advantage argues that he expects that the benefit or advantage will continue. The other scenario is when a person has not yet enjoyed a benefit or advantage but argues that rightfully he expects that it will be granted. 
30. The protection of legitimate expectation is at the root of the principle of rule of law that requires that the government's dealings with public will be in a regular manner, predictable, certain, fair and not opposed to natural justice. In the case of Council of Civil Service Unions vs Minister for the Civil Service (1984) 3 All ER 935 House of Lords observed that for a legitimate expectation to arise in favour of a person the decision of the administrative authority must affect such person either (a) by altering rights or obligations of that person which are enforceable by or against him in private law or (b) by depriving him of some benefit or advantage which he has in the past been permitted by the decision maker to enjoy and which he can legitimately expect to be permitted to continue to do until some rational ground for withdrawing it has been communicated to him and he has been given an opportunity to comment thereon or he has received assurance from the decision-maker that they will not be withdrawn without first giving him an opportunity of advancing reasons for contending that they should not be withdrawn. 
31. This Division in the case of SSA Bangladesh Limited vs Engineer Mahmud-ul-Islam reported in 24 BLD (AD) 92 = 9 BLC (AD) 84 held as under: 
"60. The principle of legitimate expectation as enunciated in Schmidt vs Secretary of State of Home Affairs reported in (1969) I Ch. 140 imposed upon the Government or the concerned Authorities a duty to act fairly and reasonably in dealing with the rights and/or interest of the people and in case of any breach thereof the Court should act upon in striking down any order in exercise of judicial review of executive action and in case of any unreasonableness or inertness or even latches in its part for which some or part of which benefit is lost causing prejudice to the people at large, the Court may direct the concerned to exercise its functions fairly, reasonably and in accordance with law and established principles." 
32. The Supreme Court of India while explaining the nature and scope of the doctrine of legitimate expectation in the case of Food Corporation of India vs M/s Kamdhenu Cattle Feed Industries (1993) 1 SCC 71 at page 76, paragraph 8 observed as under: 
"The mere reasonable or legitimate expectation of a citizen, in such a situation, may not by itself be a distinct enforceable right, but failure to consider and give due weight to it may render the decision arbitrary, and this is how the requirement of due consideration of a legitimate expectation forms part of the principle of non-arbitrariness, a necessary concomitant of the rule of law. Every legitimate expectation is a relevant factor requiring due consideration in a fair decision making process. Whether the expectation of the claimant is reasonable or legitimate in the context is a question of fact in each case. Whenever the question arises, it is to be determined not according to the claimant's perception but in larger public interest wherein other more important considerations may outweigh what would otherwise have been the legitimate expectation of the claimant. A bonafide decision of the public authority reached in this manner would satisfy the requirement of non-arbitrariness and withstand judicial scrutiny. The doctrine of legitimate expectation gets assimilated in the rule of law and operates in our legal system in this manner and to this extent." 
33. In the case of Sethi Auto Service Station vs Delhi Development Authority, 2009 (1) SCC 180 DK Jain, J observed: 
"32 A case for applicability of the doctrine of legitimate expectation, now accepted in the subjective sense as part of our legal jurisprudence, arises when an administrative body by reason of a representation or by past practice or conduct aroused an expectation which it would be within its powers to fulfill unless some overriding public interest comes in the way. However, a person who bases his claim on the doctrine of legitimate expectation, in the first instance, has to satisfy that he has relied on the said representation and the denial of that expectation has worked to his detriment. The Court could interfere only if the decision taken by the authority was found to be arbitrary, unreasonable or in gross abuse of power or in violation of principles of natural justice and not taken in public interest. But a claim based on mere legitimate expectation without anything more cannot ipso facto give a right to invoke these principles." 
34. The present respondent as writ petitioners laid a foundation in the petition that they were appointed in the Project with an understanding that after the life time of the Project their service will be transferred to the revenue budget of Bangladesh Technical Education Board for the public interest and continuing of the Computerization of Examination Activities of Bangladesh Technical Education Board pursuant to clause 49 of the Project Profile. Thereby the writ petitioners successfully made out a case of their service to be transferred to the revenue setup on the doctrine of legitimate expectation. From a plain reading of clause 49 of the Project Profile it is evident that Bangladesh Technical Education Board made a representation to the writ petitioners that after the completion of Project their service would be transferred to revenue budget of Bangladesh Technical Education Board. Thus the writ petitioners were assured that they would be regularized in the revenue setup after the completion of the Project. In the instant case the writ petitioners having requisite qualifications appeared before the competent Selection Committee who after proper examination through a competitive examination among the prospective candidates found the writ petitioners to be competent and qualified and appointed them in the Project. After the life time of the Project the writ petitioners were not transferred to the revenue setup pursuant to clause 49 of the Project Profile. For the reason best known to the writ respondent No. 1 petitioner at the end of the Project the writ petitioners were allowed to retain in their respective posts as Computer Operators on contractual basis till June 2009 after completion of the project. It has been noticed that the writ respondent No. 1-petitioner made representation/commitment that they will be appointed to their posts on regular basis in the revenue setup of the Government as soon as sanction for the said posts is obtained from the Government. On perusal of the Annexure B series it appears that the writ petitioners-respondent Nos. 1 to 3 were appointed on temporary basis for a period of six months and their services were renewed after the expiry of every six months till 22-1-2009. It is true that the writ petitioners after completion of the Project continued their service on contractual basis and they also faced interview for direct appointment in those posts but failed to succeed in the interview. Since the writ petitioners were assured that pursuant to clause 49 of the Project Profile after life time of the Project their service would be transferred to the revenue budget rather their service were continued on contractual basis till 2009. The writ petitioners-respondent Nos. 1 to 3 in a compelling circumstance having no other alternative continued their service on contractual basis after completion of their Project and thereby they cannot be termed to have waved their right of being absorbed in the revenue setup under the Government. 
35. It also appears that the respondent Nos. 1-3 successfully completed 5(five) years of their service to the Board with dedication and sincerity. It is their legitimate expectation that after the completion of the Project their service will be transferred to the revenue setup pursuant to clause 49 of the Project Profile. We find that the High Court Division rightly found that the respondent Nos. 1 to 3 having appeared before the Interview Board for direct appointment to the post of Computer Operators of the Board have not waved their right to be transferred to the revenue setup of the Board. From Annexure-B series of the writ petition we find that the respondent Nos. 1 to 3 continued in their service till June, 2005 on the basis of their earlier appointment and that the Project ended on 30-6-2005. Therefore, the respondent Nos. 1-3 were legally entitled to have their service transferred to the revenue budget of the Board on and from 1-7-2005. We do not find any merit in the submission of the learned Advocate appearing for the petitioner. 
36. In the above facts and circumstances, we are of the view that the High Court Division having considered all the materials on record and the submissions advanced on behalf of both the parties arrived at a correct decision in making the Rule absolute with a direction upon the petitioner-Board to transfer the respondents' service as Computer Operators to the revenue budget with effect from 1-7-2005 within 2(two) months from the date of receipt of the judgment. However, the writ-petitioners-respondents would not get any extra salary for the period they served on contractual basis which does not require any interference by this Division. 
Accordingly, the leave petition is dismissed. 
End.

Qumrul Haque Siddique, Advocate instructed by Md. Nawab Ali, Advocate-on-Record—For Respondent Nos.1-4 and 6. 
None Represented—For Respondent Nos. 5, 7-21.

Vs

full_judgment:
Nazmun Ara Sultana J: This appeal, by leave at the instance of the defendants, is directed against the judgment and order dated 6-4-2006 passed by the High Court Division in Civil Revision No. 3757 of 2002 making the rule absolute.

2. The respondent Nos. 1 to 6 herein, as plaintiffs, instituted Title Suit No. 68 of 1999 in the court of the Senior Assistant Judge, Dacope, Khulna against the government of Bangladesh represented by the Deputy Commissioner, Khulna and others praying for declaration that the order passed in Miscellaneous Case No. 1/1998-99 by the defendant No. 4 declaring the suit land as government khas land is illegal, null and void, without jurisdiction and not binding upon the plaintiffs and also for permanent injunction. The case of the plaintiffs, in short, was that Rameshwar and others were the owners of 20.26 acres of land of SA Khatian No. 330 which was sold in Certificate Case No. 358/61-62 of the office of the Certificate Officer, Khulna and the plaintiff No. 1 auction purchased the 15 annas share of the said land and the defendant Nos. 7 and 8 purchased 10 gondas share each in open auction held on 30-5-1962 and the sale was confirmed on 30-7-1962 and auction purchasers got sale certificate on 22-9-1962 and they got delivery of possession of the suit land through process of law and then mutated their names in the SA Khatian vide Mutation Case No. 9 of 1965 and they are in possession on payment of rent to the government. That the plaintiff No. 1 transferred some lands out of his auction purchased land to the plaintiff Nos. 2 to 6 and thus the plaintiff Nos. 1 to 6 are in possession of 18.99 acres of land.

3. That Kesta Majhee, son of Gour Gopal Majhee, instituted Title Suit No. 380 of 1963 in the court of the then 2nd Munsif, Khulna for setting aside the above auction sale which was ultimately dismissed on compromise. Thereafter Durlov Chandra Roy and others instituted Title Suit No. 259 of 1966 in the same very court against the plaintiff No. 1 and defendant Nos. 7 and 8 and others claiming right, title and interest in respect of 1.65 acres of land out of the above auction purchased land and obtained ex-parte decree on 14-2-1967. Challenging that decree the plaintiff No. 1 and the defendant Nos. 7 and 8 instituted Title Suit No. 314 of 1969 and obtained decree against which Durlov Chandra and others filed Title Appeal No.124 of 1973 which was ultimately dismissed after hearing. That Nilkanta Mandal-son of Madar Chandra Mandal also instituted Title Suit No. 770 of 1980 in the court of the then 1st Munsif, Khulna against the plaintiff No. 1, defendant Nos. 7 and 8 and others for declaration of their title in respect of 5.96 acres of land out of that auction purchased land which was ultimately dismissed on 7-1-1990. Thereafter Naren Majhee, son of Kesta Majhee, filed Miscellaneous Case No. 43 of 1990 before the defendant No. 3 against the plaintiff No. 1 and defendant Nos. 7 and 8 and others which was ultimately dismissed for default and then Naren Majhee instituted Title Suit No. 94 of 1996, which on transfer, was renumbered as Title Suit No.25 of 1998, for partition in respect of 4.6250 acres of land out of the auction purchased land but ultimately the said suit also was dismissed on 7-6-1998 for-non prosecution. That the defendant No. 2 by order dated 25-8-1996 passed in Miscellaneous Case No. 3 of 1996, made the entire auction purchased land as Government khas land and as against that order the plaintiff No. 1 and the defendant Nos. 7 and 8 filed Appeal No. 334 of 1996 before the Additional Divisional Commissioner (Revenue), Khulna Division who allowed that appeal and directed the defendant No. 2 to dispose of the matter according to law and also directed the parties to maintain status quo in respect of the auction purchased land. The defendant No. 2 by order dated 25-8-1996, again made the entire auction purchased land as government khas land. As against that order several appeals were filed and ultimately in Appeal No. 27 of 1997-98, Land Appeal Board, after hearing, by order dated 28-8-1997 sent the case back on remand to the defendant No. 2 who in turn sent the same to the defendant No. 4 with direction to dispose of the case upon starting a miscellaneous case. The defendant No. 4 then, without any notice to the plaintiff No. 1 and defendant Nos. 7 and 8, started Miscellaneous Case No. 1 of 1998-99 under section 92 (2) of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act and by order dated 1-4-1999 made 15.6350 acres of land of SA Khatian No. 330 as government khas land leaving 4.6250 acres of land in favour of Naren Majhee. The plaintiffs alleged that the initiation of the proceeding of Miscellaneous case No. 1/1988-89 and all other subsequent actions were wholly illegal, void and of no legal effect and are not binding upon the plaintiffs. It is also alleged by the plaintiffs that they never abandoned their residence on the suit land and that they are in possession of the entire auction purchased land along with the defendant Nos. 7 and 8 and that the suit land cannot vest in the government as khas land.

4. The defendant No. 1 and the added defendant Nos. 9 to 19 contested the suit by filing two separate sets of written statements.

5. The defendant No. 1 in its written statement stated that the suit property was found without any owner. That 37.00 acres of land appertaining to CS Khatian No. 98 of Mouza Sutar Khali under Police Station-Dacope belonged to Tarak Chandra Majhi, Gaur Chandra Majhi and Rakhal Majhi to the extent of 4 annas share each and to Shanyashi Mondol, Shibnath Mondal, Puma Charan Mondal, Haran Chandra Mondal and Ratikanta to the extent of 16 gondas shares each and the same was recorded in the RS Khatian No. 285 in the names of the descendants of those recorded owners including some of the aforesaid persons and that the said property was recorded in the finally published SA Khatian No. 330 in the name of the Rameswar, Gour Chandra, Rakhal, Shannyashi, Puma Charan, Ratikanta and others and that one Jiban Krishna Majhee and others, one set of the recorded tenants got 16.74 acres of land separated and recorded in SA Khatian Nos. 330(1), 330(2) and 330(3) and the remaining 20.26 acres of land remained in the original SA Khatian No. 330 in the names of Rameswar and others; that the recorded tenant Gaur Chandra Majhee while owning and possessing 4.6250 acres of land, died leaving behind his only son Kesto Majhee who has been possessing his property inherited from his father and that 15.63 acres of land is ownerless which was made government khas land in terms of report of the tahsildar under section 92(2) of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act on 6-9-1994 against which appeal was filed and ultimately the matter was sent to the Additional Deputy Commissioner for final disposal and accordingly the Additional Deputy Commissioner sent the matter to the Assistant Commissioner (Land), Dacope who started Miscellaneous Case No. 1 of 1998-99 under section 92(2) of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act and served notice upon both the parties and by order dated 1-4-1999 made 15.63 acres of land as government khas land and granted lease of the said property to the lessees in the year 1405 BS in Miscellaneous Case No. 37/98-99, 38/98-99, 31/98-99, 32/98-99 and 40/98-99 and that the lesees are in possession of the suit land within the knowledge of the plaintiffs. That the added defendant Nos. 9 to 19, the lesees are in actual possession of the suit land and that the story of auction purchase of the case land by the plaintiff No. 1 and the defendant Nos. 7 and 8 is false and baseless.

6. The contesting defendant Nos. 9 to 19, in their written statements reiterated the statements made by the defendant No. 1 in its written statement and further stated that they, being landless cultivators, got lease of the suit property for the year 1403 BS and then again for the year 1405 BS and they are in possession of the same.

7. The trial court, on consideration of evidence adduced by both the parties dismissed the suit by the judgment and decree dated 27-9-2000 on the finding that the plaintiffs failed to prove their exclusive possession in the suit land and also their case of auction purchase. The plaintiffs then preferred Title Appeal No. 394 of 2000 before the learned District Judge, Khulna who ultimately transferred the said appeal to the learned Additional District Judge, 1st Court, Khulna. This appellate court also found that the plaintiffs could not prove their case of auction purchase of the suit land and their exclusive possession therein and, therefore, by the judgment and decree dated 18-4-2002 dismissed the appeal affirming the judgment and decree of the trail court.

8. Being aggrieved by that judgment and decree of the appellate court below the plaintiffs filed the Civil Revision 3757 of 2002 before the High Court Division and obtained rule. A Single Bench of the High Court Division, after hearing both the parties, made that rule absolute by the impugned judgment and order. The High Court Division set aside the judgment and decree of both the trial court and the appellate court below and decreed the suit in part declaring the order passed in Miscellaneous Case No. 1/1998-99 by the defendant No. 4 declaring the suit land as government khas land as malafide, illegal, null and void and not binding upon the plaintiffs and directing the defendant-opposite party Nos. 1 to 4 to restore possession of the suit land in favour of the plaintiffs upon evicting the lesees therefrom without delay. The High Court Division dismissed the plaintiffs' prayer for perpetual injunction.

9. The High Court Division found that the contesting defendants could not produce any evidence or material before court to prove that the auction sale of the suit land in Certificate Case No. 358 of 1961-62 was fraudulent, collusive etc. The High Court Division observed that the original copy of the sale certificate-the Exhibit-4 was granted under the signature of the Certificate Officer, Chalna, Khulna on 27-9-1962 and that this Exhibit-4 proved that the suit land was sold in auction in Certificate Case No. 358 of 1961-62 and that this Exhibit-4 showed also that the possession of the auction sold land was delivered to the auction purchasers on 5-10-1962 by one Dhirendra Nath, a process server of the RCO Office, Chalna. The High Court Division pointed out also that after auction purchase the plaintiffs mutated their auction purchased land in their names in SA Khatian in Mutation Case No. 9 of 1965 and also paid rent regularly and were granted rent receipts. The High Court Division made observation to the effect also that the suit land could not be treated as escheat property on the face of Exhibit-3 the mutated khatian of the suit land in the name of the plaintiffs and that the government also could not produce any iota of evidence to prove the suit land became escheat property. The High Court Division took into consideration the previous suits (as mentioned by the plaintiffs in their plaint) filed by different persons in respect of the suit land against the plaintiffs and the defendant Nos. 7 and 8 and noted that all those suits were ultimately dismissed by competent courts of law. The High Court Division pointed out also that the Government though filed written statement in this suit on 24-3-2000 but did not take any step to set aside the auction sale as yet. The High Court Division made observation to the effect also that in Miscellaneous Case No. 1 of 1998-99 the suit and though was declared as government khas land under section 92 (1) (a) of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, but there was nothing to show that any of the owners of the suit land died intestate leaving no heir rendering the suit land as escheat property. The High Court Division further found that before declaring the suit land as the khas land of the government treating the same as escheat property no notice was served upon the plaintiffs as per provision of law. The High Court Division made observation to the effect also that there was no evidence at all to prove that after declaring the suit land as khas land of the government as per section 92 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, the government took possession of the suit land. The High Court Division opined that the alleged 'eksona' lease of the suit land in favour of the defendant Nos. 9 to 19 and also few others is illegal and without jurisdiction and the government is now under legal obligation to restore possession of the suit land from its lessess to the SA recorded owners, the plaintiffs.

10. Being aggrieved by this judgment and order of the High Court Division the contesting defendants filed Civil Petition for Leave to Appeal No. 1342 of 2006 before this Division and leave was granted to consider the submissions of the learned Counsel for the leave-petitioners to the effect that both the trial court as well as the appellate court below, upon proper consideration of evidence on record, dismissed the suit and there is nothing on record to show that the findings of the courts below are shockingly perverse or are vitiated by non-reading of the material evidence or misconstruction of any important documents affecting the merit of the suit and that the High Court Division upon mere surmise and conjecture held that since the lessees are in unauthorized possession the government is under legal obligation to restore possession of the suit land to the plaintiff Nos. 1 to 6 after evicting the lessees therefrom; that the High Court Division committed error of law in holding that no notice was served upon the plaintiff No. 1 and the defendant Nos. 7 and 8 under the provision of section 92 (3) of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, 1950 in Miscellaneous Case No. 1 of 1998-99 overlooking the Exhibit-ঞ, the record of the proceeding of said Miscellaneous Case No. 1 of 1998-99 and that the High Court Division, without controverting the findings of the courts below to the effect that notice of the said Miscellaneous case was duly served upon the plaintiff No. 1 and that there is no evidence to prove that the co-sharers of SA Khatian No. 330 resides in this country, erroneously held that the suit land was illegally declared as government khas land under section 92 (2) of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, 1950 in Miscellaneous Case No 1 of 1998-99.

11. We have heard Mr Biswajit Deb Nath, the learned Deputy Attorney-General for the defendant-appellants and Mr Qumrul Haque Siddique, the learned Advocate for the plaintiff-respondents.

12. Mr Biswajit Deb Nath has made submissions mainly to the effect that in this suit the plaintiffs though have produced an alleged sale certificate but they could not produce writ of delivery of possession in support of the genuineness of the alleged auction sale, that the failure of the plaintiffs not to produce the writ of delivery of possession reasonably tells against the claim of the plaintiffs that the suit land was sold in auction. The learned Deputy Attorney-General has argued that both the trial court and the appellate court below, on consideration of this fact, rightly came to the findings that the plaintiffs' alleged auction sale of the suit land in Certificate Case No. 358 of 1961-62 has not been proved at all. The learned Deputy Attorney-General has argued that the High Court Division, in setting aside the concurrent findings and decision of the courts below, did not state anything to the effect that the findings and decision of the courts below were shockingly perverse or vitiated by non-reading or misconstruction of the material evidence on record. The learned Deputy Attorney-General has argued to the effect also that in Miscellaneous Case No. 1 of 1998-99 notice was duly served upon the plaintiff No. 1 and he also appeared in that case and in the circumstances the plaintiffs now cannot challenge the order passed in that Miscellaneous Case No. 1 of 1998-99 on the ground that they were not served notices of that miscellaneous case. The learned Deputy Attorney-General has argued also that in that Miscellaneous Case No. 1 of 1998-99 the suit land was declared as khas land of the government on consideration of the report of the local tahshilder to the effect that the suit land was escheat property as there was no owner of the suit land and, as such, the declaration of the suit land as khas land of the government treating the same escheat property has not been illegal or unauthorized at all.

13. Mr Qumrul Haque Siddique, the learned Advocate for the plaintiff-respondents, on the other hand, has made submission to the effect that the original copy of the sale certificate, the Exhibit-4, proves that the suit land was sold in auction in the year 1962 and the possession of this land also was delivered in favour of the auction purchasers, that the contesting defendants though has claimed that this auction sale of the suit land in Certificate Case No. 358 of 1961-62 is collusive, fraudulent, but they could not produce any iota of evidence before court to substantiate this claim that the suit land was sold in auction by the government and the government mutated also the name of the auction purchasers in SA Khatian of the suit land and also received rents from the auction purchasers and granted rent receipts in favour of them regularly upto 1981 and in the circumstances the government now cannot say that the suit land, being escheat property, has vested in the government under section 92 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act. The learned Advocate has argued that in this suit the contesting defendants did not state anything as to who were owners of the suit land and which of the owners of the suit land died leaving no heir and as to how the suit land became escheat property; that the government did not say anything as to what happened and when did it happen which authorized the government to invoke the powers of section 92 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, 1950 to declare the suit land as khas land of the government. The learned Advocate has argued that the government itself allowed the plaintiffs to purchase the suit land in auction in the year 1962 and thereafter mutated the name of the plaintiffs in respect of the suit land in SA Khatian and accepted rent from the plaintiffs for the suit land for a long time since 1962 and also granted rent receipts to the plaintiffs and in the circumstances the government cannot say now that the suit land became escheat property and, as such, it was made khas land of the government rightly. The learned Advocate for the plaintiff-respondents has argued that the High Court Division, on meticulous examination of the evidence and other materials on record and on consideration of all aspects rightly set-aside the findings and decision of the courts below and rightly decreed the suit in part.

14. We have considered the submissions of the learned Advocates of both the sides and gone through the impugned judgment and order of the High Court Division and also those of the courts below.

15. Admittedly, the suit land originally belonged to Rameshwar and others and it was recorded in SA Khatian No. 330 in the name of said owners. The plaintiffs' case is that for arrears of rent the suit land was sold in auction in Certificate Case No. 358 of 1961-62 of the office of the Certificate Officer, Khulna and the plaintiff No. 1 purchased 15 annas share and the defendant Nos. 7 and 8 purchased the remaining anna share of the suit land in open auction held on 30-5-1962 and this sale was confirmed on 30-7-1962. To prove this case the plaintiffs have filed the original copy of the sale certificate which has been marked as Exhibit-4. It appears that the High Court division, on examination of this sale certificate and on consideration of all other facts and circumstances held that there was no reason to doubt the genuineness of this Exhibit-4. The High Court Division, on examination of this Exhibit-4 found also that this Exhibit-4 includes papers showing delivery of possession also which showed that the auction purchasers were duly deliverer possession of their auction purchased land on 5-10-1962 by one process server of the RCO Office, Chalna named Dhirendra Nath. We have also examined this Exhibit-4 which is the original copy of sale certificate. There is no reason to doubt the genuineness of this Exhibit-4. The contesting defendants though have alleged that the auction sale of the suit land was collusive and fraudulent, but did not plead any case to the effect that there was actually no such certificate case at all and the suit land was never sold in auction or that the Exhibit-4 is forged and manufactured by the plaintiffs. The Government-defendant did not bring the relevant register of certificate cases to show that there was actually no such certificate case in respect of the suit land and the suit land was never sold in auction in any such certificate case. In this circumstance the High Court Division rightly accepted this Exhibit-4 as genuine one and rightly held that this Exhibit-4 proves that this suit land was sold in auction. On scrutiny of this Exhibit-4 we also find that this Exhibit-4 includes some papers which show that the auction purchasers were given delivery of possession of their auction purchased land by a process server of RCO office, the learned Counsel for the Government-appellant did not raise any question as to these papers of Exhibit-4 showing delivery of possession either before us or at the time of seeking leave to appeal, though in the impugned judgment these papers were given importance by the High Court Division. The contesting defendants though have alleged that this allege auction sale of the suit land was fraudulent and collusive but could not adduce any evidence or materials before court to substantiate this claim. Rather, it appears that after this auction sale the government duly mutated the name of the auction purchasers in SA Khatian of the suit land the Exhibit-3 by starting Mutation Case No. 9 of 1965 and also accepted rent from the auction purchasers for a long period and granted rent receipts to them. The High Court Division, on consideration of all these facts and circumstances and evidence on record rightly opined that the government now, by saying only that the auction sale was fraudulent, cannot be absolved from discharging their onus to prove by sufficient cogent evidence that the auction sale was not held at the instance of the government or that there was illegality or irregularity in the conduct of the auction sale and that it was not a proper transaction. The High Court Division, upon consideration of the entire evidence and also pleadings of the parties, rightly found that no attempt at all was made from the side of the government-defendant to prove that the auction sale of the suit property was fraudulent one and was not initiated at the instance or the government as the certificate holder. The High Court Division rightly held also that according to section 20 of the public demand recovery act the auction purchaser's right, title and interest in the suit land became absolute from the date of auction held on 30-5-1962 and in the circumstance the suit property could not be treated as escheat property.

16. Evidently, the trial court and the appellate court below without examining and appreciating the Exhibit-4 properly and without taking into consideration the facts that the Government mutated the names of the auction purchasers in the SA Khatian of the suit land and also accepted rents from them and granted rent receipts to them came to the wrong findings and decision. The findings and decision of the courts of facts vitiated by misconstruction, misreading and non-consideration of material evidence and facts and circumstances on record.

17. In this suit the government though has claimed the suit property as escheat property but it appears that neither in their pleadings nor in the evidence has the contesting defendants made it clear at all as to how could the suit property be treated as escheat property. The contesting defendants have stated only that on a report of local tahshil office the defendant No. 4 declared the suit land as khas land of the government treating the same as escheat property in Miscellaneous Case No. 1 of 1998-99. But where in this suit it has been proved sufficiently that at the instance of the government the suit land was sold in auction in favour the plaintiff No. 1 and the defendant Nos. 7 and 8 in the year 1962 and the government also accepted this auction-purchasers as owners of the suit land by mutating their names in the SA Khatian of the suit land and also by accepting rents from them and granting rent receipts for a long period the treating of the suit land as escheat property by the government and there-by declaring the same as khas land of the government without making it clear in any manner as to how and why the suit property can be rebated as escheat property has been illegal. It should be mentioned here that before declaring the suit property as khas land of the government there were so many litigations in respect of the suit land. Several persons filed several suits against the auction purchaser’s plaintiff Nos. 1 and defendant Nos. 7 and 8 claiming the suit land but all those suits were ultimately dismissed. In this present suit the government-defendant, of course, has, contended that in none of those previous suits the government was made a party and, as such, the result of those suits are not binding upon the government. But the government, admittedly, could know about the auction sale in question in the year 2000 at least, when it filed written statement in this present suit but the government did not file any suit for declaring that auction sale of the suit land collusive, fraudulent etc as yet. It has been contended from the side of the contesting defendants that in Miscellaneous Case No. 1 of 1998-99 notices were duly served upon the plaintiffs. But in this present suit filed within the statutory period of limitation this question-whether notices of impugned Miscellaneous Case No. 1 of 1998-99 were served upon the plaintiff or not is not at all important to be discussed and considered. The plaintiffs have right to challenge the impugned order passed in this Miscellaneous Case No. 1 of 1998-99 before a civil suit within the statutory period of limitation even if they got notice of that miscellaneous case and appeared in that case and contested.

<u>18. However, in this suit it has been proved sufficiently that the plaintiff No. 1 and the defendant Nos. 7 and 8 purchased the suit land in auction held at the instance of the government in the year 1962 and they also got delivery of possession of the suit land. The mutated khatian of the suit land in the name of the plaintiffs, series of rent receipts showing acceptance of the rents by the government from the plaintiffs for the suit land and also the oral evidence adduced by the plaintiffs prove sufficiently that the plaintiffs got possession of the suit land after their auction purchase and were also in possession of the same, at least till the suit land was leased out to different lessees by the government on the basis of the impugned order passed in Miscellaneous Case No. 1 of 1998-99. The plaintiffs have filed this suit in the year 1999. In the circumstances the High Court Division rightly directed the defendant-opposite party Nos. 1 to 4 to restore possession of the suit land in favour of the plaintiffs upon evicting the lessees therefrom without delay making observation to the effect that the government granted 'eksona' lease of the suit land to the defendant Nos. 9 to 19 and few others illegally and without jurisdiction and, as such, the government is under legal obligation to restore possession of the suit land from its lessees to the SA recorded owners, the plaintiffs.</u>

19. So, from the above discussion, it is evident that there is nothing wrong or illegality in the impugned judgment and order of the High Court Division. The High Court Division rightly set aside the judgments and decrees of the courts below and rightly decreed the suit in part.

In the circumstances this appeal is liable to be dismissed.

Hence this appeal be dismissed on contest without any order as to cost.

End.

Harendra Nath Nandy with Md Sarafatullah, Advocates—For Opposite Party No. 1.
