full_judgment:
These three Rules were issued in Civil Revision Nos. 2525 of 2005, 2526 of 2005 and 2527 of 2005 arising out of Title Appeal No. 145 of 1996 against the Title Suit No. 60 of 1994 (original Title Suit No. 180 of 1990), Civil Revision No. 2526 of 2005 arising out of Title Appeal No. 144 of 1996 against the Title Suit No. 16 of 1995 (original Title Suit No. 137 of 1994) and Civil Revision No. 2527 of 2005 arising out of Title Appeal No. 143 of 1996 against the Title Suit No. 72 of 1994 (original Title Suit No. 194 of 1990) calling upon the opposite party No. 1 to show cause as to why the judgment and decree dated 15-2-2005 and 22-2-2005 passed by the learned Additional District Judge, 1st Court, Jhenidah, in Title Appeal Nos. 143 of 1996, 144 of 1996 and 145 of 1996 allowing the appeal and reversing the judgment and decree dated 30-6-1996 and 7796 respectively passed by the learned Senior Assistant Judge, Additional Court, Jhenidah, in Title Suit Nos. 60 of 1994, 16 of 1995 and 72 of 1994 decreeing the suit should not be set aside.

2. Since the three appeals were heard and disposed of by one judgment so the three Rules were also disposed of by this single judgment.

3. The short fact of the case is that the plaintiffs-petitioners brought the Title Suit No. 180 of 1990 in the Court of learned Senior Assistant Judge, Additional Court, Jhenidah for a declaration that the ex parte decree passed in Title Suit No. 283 of 1988 on 3-6-1990 in favour of the respondent-opposite party in respect of 14 decimals of land under suit Plot No. 1057 of SA Khatian No. 90 of Mouza Teordah No. 254 was collusive, inoperative, illegal, void and not binding upon the plaintiff-petitioners who claimed themselves to be necessary parties was not in pleading in Title Suit No. 283 of 1988. Title Suit No. 283 of 1988 was brought by defendant-opposite party for declaration of his title in 14 decimals of said land. The said suit was transferred to the Court of learned Senior Assistant Judge, Additional Court, Jhenidah for trial and the Title Suit No. 180 of 1990 was renumbered as 60 of 1994.

4. The plaintiff-petitioners case, in brief, is that 25 decimals of land under SA Khatian No. 90, Mouza Teordah No. 254 was taken on lease by one Mubarak Mridha from CS recorded tenant Ratikanta and others. While he was possessing thereof he sold the same to Abdur Rashid Miah by a registered kabala dated 2-3-1965. While Abdur Rashid was in possession thereof by mutating his name and by payment of rent thereof he sold the same to the plaintiff petitioner Nos. 13 by three separate kabalas dated 12-11-86. The plaintiff-petitioner No. 4, the father of plaintiff-petitioner, possessed the suit land on their behalf along with other lands of the suit plot by paying rent and, by mutating their name and amalgamating the same with his other adjoining nonsuited lands under his own Plot Nos. 1058 and 1059 by establishing a paddy crushing mill and Chatal thereon. On 8-7-91 respondent-opposite party secretly managed to obtain the ex parte decree in Title Suit No. 283 of 1988 and thereafter threatened to dispossess the plaintiff-petitioners from the 14 decimals of said land by virtue of the said ex parte decree dated 3690. So the plaintiff-petitioners brought the Title Suit No. 180 of 1990 and thereafter the said suit was renumbered as Title Suit No. 60 of 1994 which was filed for declaration that the ex parte decree passed in Title Suit No. 283 of 1988 is not binding on them. The suit was dismissed by his judgment and decree dated 21-11-1991. The plaintiff-petitioners filed the Title Appeal No. 216 of 1991 against the dismissal order. The appeal was heard by the learned Additional District Judge, 1st Court, Jhenidah who was pleased to allow the appeal and set aside the judgment and decree passed by the trial Court and by the said judgment the Title Suit No. 60 of 1994 was sent on remand to the Trial Court for fresh trial analogously with Title Suit No. 72 of 1994 (a suit brought by respondent-petitioner Lutfur Rahman for declaration of his title in 14 decimals of land and for partition by metes and bounds) by taking into consideration the evidence, documents already filed by either party and by giving an opportunity to the parties to adduce further oral evidence, if necessary. Accordingly, the Title Suit No. 60 of 1994 was analogously tried with Title Suit No. 72 of 1994 brought by the plaintiff-petitioners for their declaration of title in 14 decimals of land, all these three suits between the same parties over the same suit land.

5. The case of the defendant (respondent-opposite party) Lutfur Rahman is that the suit land along with other lands originally belonged to TC Tude under whom Rati Kanta and Makhan Sundari Dasya were the tenants. They defaulted in payment of rent, TC Tudi obtained a rent decree against them. Subsequently, he sold 14 decimals of said land to Didar Baksh and Chan Khan, Ratikanta and Makhan Sundari again defaulted in payment of rent and again the land was put to auction for sale on obtaining rent decree. Didar Baksh and Monaim purchased the same in auction and went into possession thereof. Thereafter, they sold 14 decimals of land to Abdul Gani on 20-6-60. While in possession thereof Abdul Gani sold the same to respondent-opposite party Lutfar Rahman who went into possession of the land and constructed building thereon. Plaintiff-petitioners threatened to dispossess Lutfar Rahman from the said building on 6th Sravan, 1397 BS so he brought the Title Suit No. 72 of 1994 and prayed for injunction, but show cause notices were served upon the plaintiff-petitioners but they constructed building on the said land in spite of serving of such notice. Plaintiff-petitioners were never in possession of the said 14 decimals of land before hand. The defendant-opposite party in their additional written statement also stated that the record of right in respect of the said land in the name of Mobarak Mridha was wrongly recorded. He also denied the allegation that Abdur Rashid was in possession of the said land. But the plaintiff-petitioners are in possession of the said land and by constructing godown and Chatal thereon. So, according to him, plaintiff-petitioner's false Title Suit No. 60 of 1994 and Title Suit No. 16 of 1995 are liable to be dismissed and the case brought by him as plaintiff being 'Title Suit No. 72 of 1994 needs to be decreed.

6. During the trial the Title Suit No. 60 of 1994 was dismissed by the learned Senior Assistant Judge, Jhenidah by his judgment and order dated 21-11-91.

7. Being aggrieved by the judgment and order of dismissal the plaintiff-petitioners filed an appeal being No. 45 of 1996 before the learned Additional District Judge, 1st Court, Jhenidah, who after hearing the appeal was pleased to allow the appeal and set aside the judgment and order passed by the trial Court and sent the case on remand for fresh trial analogously with other two suits directing the trial Court to take further evidence and to hear the parties, if necessary.

8. The learned Senior Assistant Judge, Additional Court, Jhenidah tried the Title Suit No. 60 of 1994, Title Suit No. 72 of 1994 and 16 of 1995 analogously and by taking into consideration all the documents already filed and examining the evidence on record decreed the Title Suit No. 60 of 1994 and Title Suit No. 16 of 1995 brought by the plaintiff-petitioners and dismissed the Title Suit No. 72 of 1994. He also declared title of the plaintiff-petitioners to the said land and further declared that the ex parte decree passed in Title Suit No. 283 of 1988 is inoperative and not binding upon the plaintiff-petitioners by his judgment dated 30-6-96, in other words, the plaintiff-petitioners obtained the judgment and decree of both the cases in his favour and the case of the defendant-opposite parties were dismissed.

9. Being aggrieved by the judgment and decree the defendant-opposite party preferred the Title Appeal Nos. 143 of 1996, 144 of 1996 and 145 of 1996 against the judgment and decree of the learned Senior Assistant Judge. Additional Court, Jhenidah dated 30-6-96 in respect of Title Suit No.72 of 1994, Title Suit No. 16 of 1995 and Title Suit No. 60 of 1994 respectively. This revisional application is related to Title Appeal No; 145 of 1996 arising out of Title Suit No. 60 of 1994 which is in respect of plaintiff-petitioner's prayer for declaration that the ex parte decree obtained by the defendant-opposite party in Title Suit No. 283 of 1988 is not binding upon the plaintiff-petitioners. Thereafter, the lower Appellate Court heard all the three appeals analogously being Title Appeal Nos. 143 of 1996, arising out of Title Suit No. 72 of 1994, Title Appeal No. 144 of 1996 arising out of Title Suit No. 16 of 1995, Title Appeal No. 145 of 1996 arising out of Title Suit No. 60 of 1994. The learned lower appellate Court allowed all the appeals and set aside the judgment and decree passed by the trial Court and in Title Appeal No. 143 of 1996 on the prayer of the appellants lawyer before the Appellate Court who submitted that as a matter of fact the lawyer who conducted the Title Suit No. 72 of 1994 before the trial Court could not produce some important documents and the plaint also needs to be amended, therefore, if the appeal is sent on remand to the trial Court for proper adjudication of the eases justice would be met. On the prayer of the lawyer of the appellants of Title Appeal No. 143 of 1996 the lower appellate Court sent all the appeals on remand to the trial Court for fresh trial directing the trial Court by giving an opportunity to both the parties to adduce evidence and produce documents and amend the plaint, if necessary.

10. Being aggrieved by the judgment and decree dated 15-2-2005 and 22-2-2005 passed by the learned Additional District Judge, 1st Court, Jhenidah, in Title Appeal Nos. 143 of 1996, 144 of 1996 and 145 of 1996 allowing the appeal and reversing the judgment and decree dated 30-6-96 and 7-7-96 respectively passed by the learned Senior Assistant Judge, Additional Court Jhenidah, in Title Suit Nos. 60 of 1994, 16 of 1995 and 72 of 1994 the respondent-petitioner preferred the instant revisional application before the High Court Division under section 115 of the Code of Civil Procedure and obtained the present Rule.

11. Mr Muhammad Nazrul Islam with Mr Syed Al-Asafur Ali, appearing on behalf of the respondent-petitioners, submits that the learned lower appellate Court is absolutely wrong and erroneous in sending the case back on remand unnecessarily for fresh trial which will take a long time to dispose of the suit causing hardship to parties. Next, he submits that the appellate Court committed an error of law by passing further order of allowing fresh evidence when fresh evidence has already been adduced by the plaintiff-petitioners and also examined more witnesses by the plaintiff-petitioners and the defendants also. He further submits that the lower appellate Court committed an error of law by giving an opportunity to the defendant-opposite party to fill up the lacuna by taking fresh evidence who miserably failed to prove his case even at the time of fresh trial earlier when the case was remanded for retrial in Title Appeal No. 216 of 1991. The learned Counsel finally, submits that the lower appellate Court only to shirk his responsibility sent the case on remand for fresh trial to the trial Court where there is a Provision under section 117 of the Code of Civil Procedure that the appellate Court is absolutely empowered to examine and take evidence, if necessary, for proper adjudication instead of sending the case back to the trial Court for causing unnecessary delay.

12. On the other hand, the learned Counsel Mr Harendra Nath Nandy with Mr Md Sarafatullah, appearing on behalf of the appellant-opposite party, submits that if the suits are sent on remand to the lower appellate Court without sending these to trial Court for fresh trial this will be more expedient. He conceded to the submission of the learned lawyer of the petitioner that a direction may kindly be given to the lower appellate Court to dispose of the appeals in accordance with law, if necessary, by taking the evidence or examining the witnesses by the appellate Court itself, without sending the suits to the trial Court.

<u>13. On a meticulous examination of the evidence on record, documents and other connected papers and after hearing the submission of both the parties it appears to me that if the case is sent to lower appellate Court for expeditious hearing of the appeals instead of sending the cases to the trial Court for fresh trial and for proper adjudication justice would be met. In this connection, I like to refer the decision in the case of AR Abul Bashar Chowdhury vs Upazila Nirbahi Officer reported in 1992 BLD 662 ref 1986 BLD (AD) 135 wherein it has been held:</u>

<u>"Appellate Court being the final Court of facts the entire evidence, both oral and documentary, are sufficiently before him and there is no necessity for sending the case for fresh trial on flimsy ground".</u>

14. In view of the discussion made above and the facts and circumstances of the case and also the legal position, the judgment and decree dated 15-2-2005 and 22-2-2005 passed by the learned Additional District Judge, 1st Court, Jhenidah, in Title Appeal No. 145 of 1996 heard analogously with Title Appeal Nos. 143 of 1996 and 144 of 1996 allowing the appeal and reversing the judgment and decree dated 30696 and 7796 passed by the learned Senior Assistant Judge, Additional Court, Jhenidah, in Title Suit Nos. 60 of 1994 heard analogously with Title Suit No. 16 of 1995 and 72 of 1994 decreeing the suit and the order of remand for sending the suits to the trial. Court for fresh trial is hereby set aside and the lower appellate Court is directed to rehear the appeals as expeditiously as possible preferably within 3(three) months and dispose of the appeals in accordance with law, if necessary, by examining witnesses and taking additional evidence, without sending the suits to the trial Court for fresh trial.

15. In the result, all the three Rules are disposed of in the light of the above observations.

16. The order of stay granted earlier by this Court at the time of issuance of the Rule is hereby vacated.

Lower Court's records be sent down at once with a copy of the judgment.

End.

full_judgment:
Mahmudul Hoque J: On an application under Article 102 of the Constitution of Bangladesh this Rule Nisi has been issued on 5-11-2012 at the instance of the petitioner calling upon the respondents to show cause as to why they should not be directed to receive entire decretal amount with interest, if any, from the petitioner by 12 equal installments of one month each starting from January, 2013 and/or such other or further order or orders passed as this Court may seem fit and proper.

2. Subsequently, this Court has issued another Supplementary Rule on 12-5-2014 calling upon the respondents to show cause as to why the proceedings of Artha Jari Case No. 142/2009 arising out of the Judgment and Decree dated 25-2-2009 passed by the Respondent No.3 in Artha Rin Suit No. 145/2007 so far as relates to sale or disposal otherwise of the mortgaged property situated out- side the territorial jurisdiction of the Executing Court should not be declared void, illegal and without jurisdiction and as to why the Order No. 12 dated 23-6-2010 allowing an application of the Decree Holder Bank filed under provision of section 33(7) of the Artha Rin Adalat Ain, 2003 for issuance of a Certificate of Title connected to the mortgaged property and Order No. 24 dated 26-5-2011 sending the said Certificate for registration passed by the Respondent No.3 in Artha Jari Case No. 142/2009 (Annexure-'E') should not be declared to have been passed without lawful authority and are of no legal effect, and/or such other or further order or orders passed as this Court may seem fit and proper.

3. Facts relevant for the disposal of this Rule in brief, are that the Respondent No. 2 Jamuna Bank Ltd. as Plaintiff' filed Artha Rin Suit No. 145 of 2007 in the Artha Rin Adalat No.2, Dhaka against the petitioner and Others as defendants for recovery of Taka 27,37,944 contending inter alia that at the request of one Mr. Shahabuddin Talukder, the defendant No.1 in Suit, the Plaintiff Bank granted a Cash Credit facility of Taka 20, 00,000 to him who enjoyed the same upon renewal from time to time. The defendant No.1 having failed to pay the said outstanding dues to the Bank as per terms and conditions of the sanction letter, the Bank filed the Suit for recovery of the same. The defendant No.1 contested the suit by filing written statement. The Artha Rin Adalat after hearing decreed the suit against the Defendant No. 1 on contest and ex parte against the rest on 25-2- 2009. In the suit the petitioner has been made defendant No. 3 as being 3rd party mortgagor.

4. The Decree-Holder Bank put the decree in execution by filing Artha Execution Case No. 142 of 2009. In the Execution Case the mortgaged property was placed on auction under Section 33(1) of the Artha Rin Adalat Ain, 2003 ("Ain") but no bidder participated in the auction. Thereafter, the Adalat directed the Decree Holder Bank to take step under section 33 (4) of the Ain fixing 22-4-2010 and then 23-6-2010 for holding auction. The Bank though took step under section 33 (4) of the Ain for holding auction of the mortgaged property for the second time but did not publish notice in the dailies, as directed by the Adalat. Subsequently, the Bank instead of taking step for publication of the auction notice in the dailies filed an application under section 33(7) of the Ain on 23-6-2010 praying for issuance of a certificate vesting the title of the mortgaged property in the Decree Holder Bank. The Adalat allowed the application and issued a certificate under section 33(7) of the Ain as prayed for and sent the same to the concerned Sub-Registration office for registration. After obtaining certificate under section 33(7) of the Ain, the petitioner came to know that the Bank is trying to sell the property at a shockingly low price to any person. Thereafter, the petitioner hurriedly rushed to the Bank and placed a positive proposal on 22-10- 2012 agreeing to pay the decretal amount with a view to save her property from auction and requested the Bank to allow her installments to pay the amount within 6(Six) months, but the Bank refused the proposal of the petitioner. At this stage the petitioner moved this Court by filing this Writ Petition for a direction upon the Bank to receive decretal amount with interest and to redeem the mortgage and obtained the present Rule and Stay.

5. Subsequently, the petitioner obtained a Supplementary Rule on 12-5-2014 on the ground of territorial jurisdiction of the Executing Court as the property in question is situated in the District Rajbari.

6. The Respondent No.2 Bank contested the Rule by filing affidavit-in opposition and Counter Affidavit denying the material facts made in the petition contending, inter alia, that the petitioner filed an application before the Executing Court on 13-1-2010 praying two months time to pay the decretal amount by four instalments. The Court allowed the prayer by its order dated 10-2-2010, but the petitioner did not pay any of the instalments. However, after registration of the certificate in favour of the Bank the petitioner filed the instant Writ Petition only to obstruct disposal of the property and to delay the recovery of the Bank's dues and as such the Rule is liable to be discharged. It is also stated that the petitioner never approached the Bank with any proposal to pay the decretal amount before filing of the instant writ petition. During pendency of this Rule the petitioner by two identical applications dated 10-2-2013 and 2-7-2013 respectively approached the Bank. In reply to the said letters the Bank on 16-7-2013 sent a letter with registered A/D wherein the Bank invited the petitioner to sit with them to resolve the dispute amicably fixing 27-7-2013 at 10.00 A.M. However, said letter was returned unserved as the recipient was not found at the address. In such a situation the Bank sent two of its officials at the address wherein they were informed by the landlord of the building that the petitioner had moved away from the address five years back. Further case of the Respondent No. 2 is that the title of the property in question has already been vested in the Bank by a certificate issued by the executing Court on 26-5-2011 under section 33(7) of the Ain before issuance of this Rule and partial possession of the land has already been delivered to the Bank. Since the title of the property in question vested in the Decree Holder Bank long before the filing of this petition, at this belated stage there is no scope for the petitioner to get her property back.

7. Mr. Aminul Islam, learned Advocate appearing for the petitioner firstly, submits that admittedly the mortgaged property is situated in District Rajbari. Given that the decree in the Artha Rin Suit was passed by the Artha Rin Adalat in Dhaka, it has no jurisdiction to deal with the property situated beyond its territorial jurisdiction either by auction or by issuing a certificate of title. It is indeed the duty of the Executing Court as well as the Decree Holder to send/transfer the Execution Case to the Court having territorial jurisdiction to deal with the property in execution proceedings under section 27(1) of the Ain read with sections. 38 and 39 of the Code of Civil Procedure ("Code"). And as such issuance of a certificate of title under section 33(7) of the Ain by the Executing Court having no territorial jurisdiction over the property is illegal and without lawful authority. Secondly, Mr. Islam submits that the Decree Holder having taken steps under Section 33(4) of the Ain for auction of the mortgaged property for the second time it cannot apply for granting certificate of title under section 33(7) of the Ain jumping over the provisions as contained in Section 33(5) & (6) of the Ain and as such, issuance of the certificate of title in favour of the Decree Holder without taking recourse to section 33(5) and (6) of the A in is palpably illegal and without lawful authority. It is also argued that the Decree Holder can ask for a certificate of title of the property only after taking recourse to section 33(1) of the Ain without taking any step under section 33(4) as provided in Section 33(7) of the Ain. But in the present case the Decree Holder in total violation of the provision of section 33(7) obtained the certificate of title of the mortgaged property and as such the certificate of title is not sustainable in law and liable to be declared to have been issued by the Court without lawful authority and in violation of law. Thirdly, Mr. Aminul Islam, submits, that, intention of the legislature is to recover the money from the loanee, but not to acquire the property of the mortgagor, borrower or guarantor by the bank. Therefore, whenever the Judgment-debtor approaches a bank to pay the decretal amount, it is incumbent upon the Decree Holder to receive the money and to redeem the mortgage in favour, of the mortgagor. He also submits that redemption of mortgage is a legal right of the mortgagor. Mere acquisition of title by a certificate issued by the Court under section 33(7) of the Ain does not ipso facto dis-entitle the mortgagor to have the mortgage redeemed upon payment of the decretal amount to the Bank. Since it is a legal right, the, right of redemption subsists. until a third party's interest gets involved in the property. In the present case no third party interest is involved and as such the Bank is under an obligation to release the property in favour of the petitioner upon receipt of the decretal amount. In support of his submissions he has referred to the cases of Smt. Uma Kanoria vs Pradip Kumar Daga reported in AIR 2003 Cal 162, Shaba Yeshwant Naik vsVinod Kumar Gosalin reported in AIR 1985 Bombay 79, Hari Das Basu vs. National Insurance Company Ltd. reported in AIR 1932 Calcutta 213, Prem Chand Dey vs Mokhoda Debi reported in 17 ILR (1990) 699 and a judgment of this Court passed in World Resources Ltd. Vs Artha Rin Adalat No.3, Dhaka reported in 66 DLR 637, and section 27(1) of the Ain along with Sections 38 and 39 of the Code.

8. Mr Ariful Islam, learned Advocate appearing for the Respondent No.2 Decree Holder Bank firstly submits that the provisions of Section 27(1) of the Ain and sections 38 and 39 of the Code are applicable in the case of Money Decree only and not in a case of Mortgage Decree. Because, in a Mortgage Decree the property in question is not required to be attached before auction sale as the property being a part of the decree is under the custody and control of the Court which passed the decree and can be put into execution for auction sale. But in a Money Decree if any property is required to be attached which is situated outside the territorial jurisdiction of the court, the court is under an obligation to transfer the Decree to a competent court having territorial jurisdiction over the property as it cannot attach the property outside its territorial jurisdiction. Therefore, since the decree in question is a Mortgage Decree the executing court is not required to transfer the decree to the court where the property is situated and as such in the instant case the certificate issued by the Dhaka Court, vesting title of the property in the Decree Holder Bank is valid and lawful and cannot be questioned. Moreover, putting emphasis on the word "may" occurring in section 39(1) of the Code he submits, that it is the discretion of the Executing Court to decide whether it will send the case to another court for execution.

9. Secondly, Mr Ariful Islam states that the Suit was decreed in 2009, the certificate under section 33(7) of the Ain vesting the title of the mortgaged property in the Decree Holder Bank was issued on 26-5-2011, and pursuant to the said certificate partial possession of the property has already been delivered to the Decree Holder. Bank. In this situation the Petitioner-Judgment-debtor raised the question that the property was not within the jurisdiction of the Court at Dhaka for the first time. This objection to jurisdiction was not raised until the execution proceedings ended with the issuance of Certificate and therefore, it comes too late. Mr Islam submits that the petitioner cannot raise questions as to jurisdiction at a belated stage of the proceedings when the execution case has already been disposed of. In support of his submissions he has referred to a catenae of cases namely, Jagernath Sahai vs Dip Rani Koer reported in 22 ILR (1895) 871, Messrs, HN Dutta and Co. vs Smt. Tarubala Dassireported in AIR 1937 Cal 570, Tarach and vs. Misrimal reported in AIR 1970 Rajasthan, 58, Laxmi Narain vs Firm Ram Kumar Suraj Box reported in AIR 1971 Rajasthan 30, Sakil Nath Roy Chowdhury Vs Jessore United Bank Ltd. reported in AIR 1939 Calcutta 403, Begg, Dunlop and. Co. vs Jagannath Marwari reported in 16 CWN 402, Maseyk vs Steel and Co. and another reported in 14 ILR (1887) 662, Gopi Mohan Roy vs Doybaki Nundun Sen reported in 19 ILR (1891) 13 and Shaikh Abdul Hadi. vsMst. Kabultunnissa reported in 80 IC (1924) 901.

10. Heard the learned Advocates for the par- ties, perused the Application, Supplementary Affidavits, Affidavit-in-Opposition, Counter Affidavit and the Annexures annexed thereto.

11. In the instant Rule the first question raised is whether the Artha Rin Adalat, Dhaka can issue a certificate declaring the title of the property vested in the Decree Holder under Section 33(7) of the Ain where the property is situated outside the territorial jurisdiction of the said Court. To meet the question raised, Section 27(1) of the Ain along with Sections 38 and 39 of the Code of Civil Procedure may be looked into which run thus:-

২৭। (১) অর্থ ঋণ আদালত কর্তৃক প্রদত্ত কোন আদেশ বা ডিক্রি উক্ত আদালত কর্তৃক, অথবা উক্ত আদালত জারীরজন্য অন্য যে আদালতে প্রেরণ করে, সেই আদালত কর্তৃক জারী হইবে।

Sections 38 and 39 CPC:

S 38. Court by which decrees may be executed-A decree may be executed either by the Court which passed it or by the court to which it is sent for execution.

S 39. Transfer of decree-The Court which passed a decree may, on the application of the decree-holder, send it for execution to another Court,-

(a) if the person against whom the decree is passed actually and voluntarily resides or carries on business, or personally works for gain, within the local limits of the jurisdiction of such other Court, or

(b) if such person has no property within the local limits of the jurisdiction of the Court which passed the decree sufficient to satisfy such decree and has property within the local limits of the jurisdiction of such other Court, or

(c) if the decree directs the sale or delivery of immovable property situated outside the local limits of the jurisdiction of the Court which passed it, or

12. It appears from the language as used in the above quoted section 27(1) that should the mortgaged property be situated beyond the jurisdiction of the Executing Court, it is incumbent upon the court to send the case to the court having local jurisdiction for execution of the same. In the present case, admittedly, the property is situated in Rajbari District, but the Artha Rin Adalat at Dhaka initiated the process of auction and issued the certificate under section 33(7) of the Ain which is absolutely beyond its territorial jurisdiction as per provisions contained in section 27(1) of the Ain and sections 38 and 39 of the Code.

13. It is evident from section 27(1) of the Ain, that this section provides for an execution case to be instituted in the court which passed the decree, and that for the convenience of execution, that court may send the execution case to another court and the said power is vested with the Adalat in which the case is filed and the Adalat may on its own motion send the execution case or upon an application filed by any of the parties or the Decree Holder requesting to exercise its power.

14. The above provisions of the Ain are basically similar to that of Sections 38 and 39 of the Code which provides the provisions for institution and transfer of an Execution Case.

15. Now the question is whether the Artha Rin Adalat is under a legal obligation to transfer the Execution Case to another Adalat of the District where the property in question situates. To answer the question the provisions in Section 33(1) of the Ain may be looked into which runs thus:

৩৩(১) অর্থ ঋণ আদালত ডিক্রি বা আদেশ জারীর সময় কোন সম্পত্তি বিক্রয় ক্ষেত্রে বাদীর খরচে বিজ্ঞপ্তি প্রচারের তারিখ হইতে অন্যূন ১৫(পনের) দিবসের সময় দিয়া সীলমোহরকৃত টেন্ডার আহবান করিবে, উক্ত বিজ্ঞপ্তিকমপক্ষে বহুল প্রচারিত একটি বাংলা জাতীয় দৈনিক পত্রিকায়, তদুপরি ন্যায় বিচারের স্বার্থে প্রয়োজন মনে করিলে স্থানীয় একটি  পত্রিকায়, যদি থাকে, প্রকাশ করিবে; এবং আদালতের নোটিশ বোর্ডে লটকইয়া ও স্থানীয়ভাবে ঢোল সহরত যোগও উক্ত বিজ্ঞপ্তি প্রচার করিবে।

16. This section as quoted, above provides provisions for fixing of the auction notice in the notice board of the Executing Court and beating of drum in the locality. The action of beating of drum in the locality invariably requires to take place where the property is situated or in its immediate vicinity. The purpose of beating the drum in the locality is that the people of that locality must be made aware that the property in question is in the process of auction sale.

17. In view of such requirement of Section 3.3(1) of the Ain, it is not possible for the Adalat in Dhaka to send its process server or "Dhuli" to the territorial jurisdiction of another Adalat of a different district. The reason is simple, namely, the order of the Executing Court cannot be executed beyond its territorial limit for publicity by the Dhuli, without the assistance of the process server or "Dhuli" of another Court in whose jurisdiction the order is to be carried out. Moreover, without compliance of such requirement the auction sale cannot be legally held.

18. It is not disputed, that when a decree is passed by the competent Artha Rin Adalat the execution case has to be filed in that Court under section 27 of the Ain, but if the decree has to be satisfied by way of auction or otherwise the Execution Case needs to be transferred to the court where the property is situated. However, the word "may" occurring in section 39(1) of the Code or in section 27(1) of the Ain might give an impression about the discretion of the court where the Execution Case is filed. Almost in all the cases referred to by the learned counsels of both the parties the intent and purport of the word "may" has been exhaustively discussed unanimously in the Apex Courts of Indian Jurisdiction came to a common finding that the provisions of section 39 plainly indicate the acceptance by the legislature of the general principle that no court can execute a decree in which the subject matter of the suit or of the application for execution property is situated entirely outside the local limits of its jurisdiction.

19. In the unreported case of S. Co. Cement Limited represented by its Managing Director vs Artha Rin Ada/at No.4, Dhaka (Writ Petition No. 5360 of 2010) a Division Bench of this Court held that:

"The mortgaged property in relation to an auction sale situated in another District the Artha Rin Adalat is under a legal obligation to send the execution case to the concerned Artha Rin Adalat of the other District where the property is situated. This is unavoidably necessary for proper execution and satisfaction of the decree" (Per Md. Emdadul Huq, J).

20. Therefore, the certificate issued by the Court indeed, had no jurisdiction and as such the issuance of certificate by the Artha Rin Adalat in Dhaka is illegal and without jurisdiction.

21. The second question raised is whether the Artha Rin Adalat can issue a certificate on an application filed by the Decree Holder under section 33(7) of the Ain when it took steps under section 33(4) of the Ain for holding further auction of the mortgaged property and, thereby obviating the necessity of following the provisions contained under section 33(5) and (6) of the Ain. To meet the question as raised in the instant case the provisions of Section 33(5) and (7) of the Ain may be looked. into which runs thus:-

৩৩। (৫) কোন সম্পত্তি [উপ-ধারা] (১),(২),(২ক),(২খ),(২গ),(৩) ও (৪) এর বিধান অনুয়ারে] বিক্রয় করা সম্ভব না হইলে, উক্ত সম্পত্তি, ডিক্রীকৃত দাবী পরিপূর্ণভাবে পরিশোধিতত না হওয়া পর্যন্ত, দখল ও ভোগের অধিকারসহ ডিক্রিদারের অনুকূলে ন্যস্ত করা হইবে, এবং ডিক্রিদার [উপ-ধারা] (১),(২),(২ক),(২খ),(২গ),(৩) ও (৪) এর বিধান অনুয়ারে]

উক্ত সম্পত্তি বিক্রয় করিয়া অপরিশোধিত ডিক্রির দাবী আদায় করিতে পারিবে, এবং আদালত ঐ মর্মে একটি সার্টিফিকেট ইস্যু করিবে।

(৭) উপ-ধারা (৪) ও (৫) এর বিধান সত্ত্বেও, ডিক্রিদার উল্লেখিত সম্পত্তি মালিকানা সত্ত্বে পাইতে আগ্রহী মর্মে আদালতের নিকট লিখিতভাবে আবেদন করিলে, আদালত,উপ-ধারা  (১),(২),(২ক),(২খ),(২গ),(৩) ও (৪) এর বিধানাবলীর কোনরূপ হানি না ঘটাইয়া। উপ-ধারা (৪) ও (৫) এর কার্যক্রম অনুসরণ করা হইতে বিরত থাকিবে; এবং ডিক্রিদারের পার্থিমতে  উল্লেখিত সম্পত্তির স্বত্ব ডিক্রিদারের অনুকূলে ন্যস্ত হইয়াছে মর্মে ঘোষণা প্রদানপূর্বক তৎমর্মে একটি সনদপত্র জারী করিবে এবং জারীকৃত এইরুপ সনদপত্র স্বত্বের দলিল, হিসাব গণ্য হইবে; এবং আদালত উহার অনুলিপি সংশ্লিষ্ট  স্থানীয় সার-রেজিস্ট্রারের অফিসে নিবন্ধনের জন্য প্রেরণ করিবে।

22. From a plain reading of the aforesaid provisions of law it appears that in the event of having a certificate of title under section 33(7) of the Ain the Decree Holder Bank is required to follow the provisions of section 33(1) to (3) and shall refrain from taking any steps under sub-sections (4) and (5). But in the present case the Decree Holder took steps under Section 33(4) for holding further auction of the mortgaged property. It is noted that for the purpose of getting a certificate of title under section 33(7) of the Ain the law does not enjoin upon a Decree Holder Bank to take steps under section 33(4) of the Ain. However, as in the present case, when the Bank takes steps under section 33(4) there is no escape route to sidetrack or jump over the provisions of section 3(5) and (6). The Decree Holder Bank in this situation ought to have invoked the process under section 33(5) of the Ain upon the failure of the auction and thereafter to follow other' provisions as contained in Section 33(6) of the Ain. Evidently the Decree Holder Bank deviating from that sequential process instead of taking resort to the aforesaid provisions of law straightway applied under section 33(7) of the Ain praying for issuance of the certificate declaring title of the mortgaged property vested in the Bank. This Court finds such invocation of the law to be contrary to the provisions contained in Section 33(7) of the Ain. As per provisions of law once the Decree Holder takes step under Section 33(4) for holding further auction there remains no option but to follow the said provision to its statutorily intended and prescribed conclusion and progressing in stages through the express provisions of section 33(5) (6) and (7) of the Ain.

23. Since the Artha Rin Adalat issued a certificate directly under section 33(7) of the Ain without allowing prior necessary recourse to the provisions of section 33(5) and (6), the impugned order passed by the court is, accordingly, found to be illegal.

24. Apart from these, if we consider the Certificate of Title issued under section 33(7) to be a valid one, in that case, there is yet another aspect to the case before us, that is, whether the petitioner's right of redemption of the mortgage remains alive and extant as on the date of issuance of the Rule notwithstanding the issuance of Certificate of Title under section 33(7) of the A in when the petitioner before us, i.e. Mrs. Rokaiya Amin made overtures to meet the entire claim of the Bank. To meet this question the provision contained in section 5(4) of the Ain may be looked into which runs thus;

৫। (৪) The Transfer of Property Act, 1982 অথবা বর্তমান প্রচলিত অন্য কোন আইনে বিপরীত যাহা কিছুই থাকুক না কেন, উপ-ধারা (৩) এর অধীনে বন্ধকী যাহা কিছুই থাকুক না কেন, উপ-ধারা (৩) এর অধীন বন্ধকী মামলা ব্যাতিরেকে, এই আইনের অধীন দায়েরকৃত কোন মামলায়,আদালত কর্তৃক প্রদত্ত ডিক্রি বাদী প্রতিষ্ঠানের পক্ষে নিষ্ক্রিয় সমাপ্তির (Force clouser) প্রাথমিক ডিক্রি হিসাবে গণ্য হইবে;এবং ঋণের বিপরীতে বাদীর অনুকূলে বন্ধকী স্থারব সম্পত্তি ডিক্রির ধারাবাহিকতায় নিলাম বিক্রয় মাত্রই উক্ত প্রাথমিক ডিক্রি চুড়ান্ত ও ক্রয় বৈধ গণ্য হইবে এবং অতঃপর উক্ত সম্পত্তি পুনরুদ্ধার করিবার কোন রুপ অধিকার (Right to redeem) বিবাদী দায়িকের থাকিবে না।

25. It is evident that under section 5(4) in the case of suit for sale on the basis of a mortgage, as is the case in the present instance, preliminary decree shall become final upon an auction sale taking place and concomitantly the right to redemption shall be deemed to come to an end at that point in time. It is clear from the law that until such auction sale and final decree, the right to redeem remains intact. Applied in conjunction with section 33(7), however, that deeming provision of section 5(4) may very well be argued to meet its limitation in the circumstances envisaged in section 33(7) given that the fact or concept of an. auction sale does not arise in section 33(7) scenario. In that scenario the very issuance of Certificate of Title and its registration thereof may be construed by many as a finality of the Execution process, thereby, extinguishing a right of redemption at the point of such issuance. The petitioner's respond to that line of thinking by stressing that the right to redeem is in fact a legal and substantive right to property which ought not to be extinguished by mere implication given that section 33(7) remains silent on the extinguishments of the capacity to redeem existing in any mortgagor. It is pointed out that this question of redemption could also have been better understood, should section 5(4) have borne express reference to the status of a right of redemption in the context of section 33(7), But clearly section 5(4) bears no such reference to section 33(7). It is, accordingly, argued that such absence of specific declaration of the law extinguishing the right of redemption on the issuance of a section 33(7) Certificate of Title, it would be misconceived to expressly find on such extinguishments to the detriment of a mortgagor and this would go beyond the rules of either statutory interpretation or construction. This Court finds merit in these submissions as the petitioner is willing to redeem the mortgage upon satisfaction of the Bank's outstanding claims in its totality.

<u>26. This Court is of the view that the transfer of title under section 33(7) does not indeed envisage the right of foreclosure. In the scheme of the Act, foreclosure in the sense of a Imitation on the right of redemption can only arise when associated with an auction sale contemplated in section 5(4), Beyond that, section 33(7) appears to this Court to operate independently of section 5(4) and the provisions in section 33(7) in not contemplating a transfer, by sale must be found also not to envisage the existence, of the corresponding right of foreclosure. Therefore, the right of redemption under section 33(7) is always found to be alive and extant.</u>

<u>27. It is also relevant to note that section 33(9) of the Act speaks of a final disposal of an execution case on, inter alia, issuance of a section 33(7) Certificate of Title. That provision, however, remains qualified by certain amendments introduced into the Act in 2010 adding Sections 33(7ক) and (7খ) facilitating delivery of possession to the property as coursed by the Certificate of Title. These latter provisions, as are to be read as independent and self-contained provisions in section 33, are declaratory of the legislative intent to revive an execution case on certain specified grounds, if need be, even after court's declaration of conclusion of an execution process under section 33(9).</u>

<u>28. Indeed, sections 33(7ক) and (7খ) have no bearing on the question of the right of redemption but these go to establish the fact that even upon a Section 33(7) Certificate of Title being issued the executing court does not necessarily become functus officio immediately thereafter. That view facilitates a better understanding, therefore, of the effect of declaring the Execution Case No. 142 of 2009 to be finally disposed of under Section 33(9) upon registration of the Certificate of Title granted. Indeed in the present instance the Court assumed jurisdiction under section 33(7ক) notwithstanding, it is this Court's view that the right of redemption of mortgage has never stood extinguished at any material time. Accordingly, it was always open to the petitioner in particular in the facts and circumstances to seek redemption of her mortgage upon a settlement arrived at with the bank or financial institution concerned, So, once the loan repayment is forthcoming, the Adalat will correspondingly find it within its power to permit such repayment and recovery of loan, thereby, doing that which is right and just as contemplated in section 57.</u>

29. This understanding of the law and considering the rights and responsibilities of the parties in the context of section 33(7) leads this Court to hold that the petitioner before us is still entitled to redeem the mortgage upon making payment of the bank's outstanding.

30. Taking into consideration, the above, this Court finds the Impugned Orders to be seriously wanting in legal sufficiency and contrary to the relevant provisions of flaws and principles and, thereby, to be shorn of all. validity and legal effect.

31. In the result, the Rule is made absolute. Accordingly this Court hereby declares the Impugned Orders dated 23-6-2010 and 26-5-2011 passed by the Artha Rin Adalat issuing Certificate of Title and thereby sending the same for registration respectively to be illegal and without lawful authority. The petitioner is directed to meet the outstanding claim of the Bank within a period of 2 (two) months from the date of receipt of a certified copy of this Judgment and Order.

32. The petitioner is put on notice that such liability shall have to be met in conformity with the Artha Rin Decree subject to the express provision of the law. Similarly, it shall be incumbent upon the Respondent No.2 Bank to facilitate and ensure the due redemption of the mortgage by the petitioner in accordance, with law upon receipt of full payment of all its outstanding claim. Any failure by the petitioner to comply with the directions above shall automatically entitle the respondent No.2 Bank to proceed and deal in and with the property in question in accordance with law after transferring the case to the Artha Rin Adalat Rajbari as per provision of section 27(1) of the Ain.

33. The ad interim Order of restraint as initially granted is, hereby, recalled and vacated.

There is no order as to costs.

Communicate this order at once.

End.

case_source: (From the judgment and order dated the 18th day of October, 2011 passed by the High Court Division in Civil Revision No.2571 of 1998 with Civil Revision No.2572 of 1998)
full_judgment:
Md Muzzammel Hossain CJ: I have gone through the judgments proposed to be delivered by my brothers, Surendra Kumar Sinha, J. and Md Abdul Wahhab Miah, J. I agree with the reasoning and findings given by, Md Abdul Wahhab Miah, J.

Surendra Kumar Sinha J: I have had the advantage of reading the draft copy of the judgment prepared by my learned brother Md Abdul Wahhab Miah, J. While agreeing with the conclusion arrived at by my learned brother that the appeal and the connected petition be dismissed, as some vital questions of law are involved in these matters, it is desirable that I should add something of my own.

<u>3. The pivotal question which arises for consideration in these matters is whether the Administrator of Waqfs can accord sanction for transferring any part of the Waqf property by way of lease exceeding 5(five) years in exercise of its power under section 56 of the Waqfs Ordinance, 1962 or in the alternative, a mutawalli of a waqf estate can transfer by lease in perpetuity any part of the waqf property with prior approval of the Administrator. An opinion on the point requires consideration of the facts which are succinctly narrated below:</u>

Appellant is a mutawalli of a Waqf Estate who instituted Title Suit No. 26 of 1992 (the plaintiff) against the respondent Nos.1-3 seeking nullity of lease deed dated 18th May, 1965 executed by his father Ahidulla as mutawalli of the waqf eatate in favour of respondent Nos. 1 (the defendant) on the ground that his father though executed the lease deed in respect of the suit land measuring an area of 0.92 acre, he did not pay the salami and rent and also did not take over possession of the suit land and thus, the defendant violated the terms of the lease deed, and that the lease was not acted upon. Defendant also instituted Title Suit No. 38 of 1992 seeking declaration of title in respect of 1st schedule land and for recovery of khas possession in respect of 2nd schedule land measuring an area of 0.04 (0.03) acre. His case is that the plaintiff's father Ashidulla, the mutawalli, with prior sanction of the Administrator of Waqfs leased out 0.92 acre of land of plot No.932 at a premium of Taka 300 and handed over possession on the same day. He developed the land and constructed houses in a portion of the land. He also purchased 0.04 acre of land of plot No. 933 situated contiguous to the suit plot for path way and mutated his name, paid rent and taxes to the authorities and thereafter, he was dispossessed from the 2nd schedule of land taking advantage of his temporary absence from the suit land. Appellant's defence case in the latter suit is similar to that of his plaint case and vice versa.

4. The trial Court heard both the suits analogously and held that the plaintiff-appellant had no title and possession in the suit land; that the suit without seeking consequential relief is not maintainable under section 42 of the Specific Relief Act; that the defendant acquired title in pursuance of lease deed dated 18th May, 1965; that he is in possession of a portion of the suit land but, he failed to prove the portion in which he is in specific possession and that the defendant's claim of dispossession in respect of the second schedule land by the plaintiff by raising 4(four) thatched huts is inconsistent with his pleadings. With these findings the trial Court dismissed both the suits. Two appeals were filed, one by the plaintiff and the other by the defendant being Title Appeal Nos. 57 of 1995 and 182 of 1995 respectively. The Court of Appeal below allowed Title Appeal No. 57 of 1995, decreed Title Suit No.26 of 1992 and declared the impugned deed void and not binding upon the plaintiff, dismissed Title Appeal No.182 of 1990 and thereby affirmed the judgment of the trial Court dismissing Title Suit No. 38 of 1992. Feeling aggrieved by the said judgments, the defendant moved the High Court Division in Civil Revision Nos. 2571 and 2572 of 1998. A Single Bench of the High Court Division heard both the rules analogously and by the impugned judgment made both the rules absolute, set aside the judgment and decree passed in Title Suit Nos. 26 of 1992 and sent back the Title Suit No. 38 of 1992 to the trial Court for writing out a fresh judgment for deciding the defendant's claim of possession and dispossession in respect of e schedule land on the basis of the evidence available with the record. The learned Judge noticed that there are conflicting findings as regards the finding of possession followed by dispossession as claimed by the defendant in respect of the 2nd schedule land.

5. After remand, the trial Court dismissed the suit, but the Court of Appeal below believed the defendant's case of possession followed by dispossession and decreed the suit declaring the defendant's title in the suit land and allowing the prayer for recovery of khas possession in respect of 0.03 acre of land. Plaintiff moved a revision petition in the High Court Division which affirmed the judgment of the Court of Appeal below observing that the Court of Appeal below rightly found on the basis of the evidence that the plaintiff dispossessed the defendant in respect of 0.03 acre of land and that the plaintiff could not point out any misreading or non-consideration of the evidence on record. The High Court Division rightly found that the defendant has been able to prove his title in the suit land and that the plaintiff has dispossessed the defendant in respect of 0.03 acre of land without due process of law and thereby, it has committed no illegality in maintaining the judgment of the Court of Appeal below. More so, the leave petition is also barred by 242 days and the explanation offered for the delay is not satisfactory. Mr Abdul Wadud Bhuiyan appearing for the plain-tiff also finds it difficult to assail the judgment of the High Court Division.

6. It was urged on behalf of the appellant that the High Court Division misconstrued section 56 of the Waqfs Ordinance, 1962 and illegally held that a mutawalli of a waqf estate can transfer a portion of the waqf property by lease exceeding five years in failing to notice that such lease tantamount to absolute transfer which is not intended by the legislature. It was further urged that the Administrator has power to accord sanction of grant of lease for a limited period, inasmuch as, the use of coma (,) after the word 'exchange' in sub-section (1) of section 56, and the use of words 'or by way of lease for a term exceeding 5 years' thereafter manifestly suggest that a mutawalli has no power even, with prior sanction of the Administrator to grant lease of any part of the waqf property in perpetuity.

7. Points raised require analytical consideration of certain provisions of the Waqfs Ordinance and other laws relevant for the disposal of the in matters. Sections 27 to 46 have been placed in Chapter III of the Ordinance under the heading "Powers and Functions of the Administrator and the Committee" like saplings in a row. Section 27 relates to the general powers and functions of the Administrator which include investigation and determination of the nature and extent of waqfs and waqf properties, inspection of accounts, returns for ensuring that the waqf properties and income arising there from are applied to the objects and for the benefit of any class of persons for which such waqfs are created and to give direction for proper administration of the Waqfs, etc. Section 28 deals with general powers and functions of the Committee, which consists as per section 20, the Administrator as chairman and ten members to be appointed by the Government, of whom, one shall be a mutawalli of the Shia Sect, three from the mutawallis of Sunnis sect and the remaining six shall be from among the prominent, respectable and benevolent citizens of Muslim community. Section 32 authorizes the Administrator of Waqfs to remove the mutawalli in cases covered by clauses I-IV of sub-section (1). Sub-section (4) of section 32 authorizes the Administrator to appoint a new mutawalli under the circumstances mentioned therein. Section 33 empowers the Administrator of Waqfs to transfer any part of a waqf i property with previous sanction of the Government for the improvement and benefit of the waqf, and section 34 empowers to take administration, control, management and maintenance of any waqf property.

8. According to Mr Bhuiyan, the power of sanction for transfer of a portion of the waqf Property has exclusively been given to the Government and section 33 shall override the other provisions of the Ordinance, in view of the non-obstante clause "notwithstanding anything contained elsewhere in this Ordinance", used in it. This section, it is contended, shall prevail despite anything contrary contained in any other provision, i.e. section 56 of the Ordinance, which authorizes a mutawalli of any immovable property of a waqf to transfer by sale, gift, mortgage or exchange, or by way of lease for a term exceeding 5 years with previous sanction of the Administrator. True, this clause is used in contradiction to the expression 'subject to' any other provision of the Ordinance, but when the non-obstante clause refers to the provision of a statute in general, the intention of the legislature must be determined and the clause has to be construed accordingly. It is often used by way of abundant caution, but mainly used as a legislative device, in case of conflict to give the provision containing non-obstante clause an overriding effect over any other provision of the statute. But, when the two provisions are apparently inconsistent, it is the duty of the Court to harmoniously interpret those provisions so that both the provisions may be operative. Reference in this connection is the case of Dominion of India vs Shribai A. Arabinda Bose, AIR 1955 SC 296 in which, it has been observed:

"Although ordinarily there should be a close approximation between the non-obstante clause and the operative part of the section, the non-obstante clause need not necessarily and always be coextensive with the operative part, so as to have the effect of cutting down the clear terms of an enactment. If the words of the enactment are clear and are capable of only one interpretation on a plain and grammatical construction of the words thereof a non-obstante clause cannot cut down the construction and restrict the scope of its operation. In such cases the non-obstante clause has to be read as clarifying the whole position and must be understood to have been incorporated in the enactment by the legislature by way of abundant caution and not by way of limiting the ambit and scope of the operative part of the enactment."

<u>9. What's more, I find no inconsistency between the two provisions. Section 33 deals with the power of the Administrator to transfer waqf property when he is in charge of such property in the absence of the mutawalli. This section is found in chapter III, whereas, section 56 is found in Chapter VI under the heading 'Transfer of Waqfs Property.' These two chapters provide for two distinct purposes. It is established principle that the duty of the Court is to effectuate the purpose of an enactment and not to defeat it. In Bates, (1965)1 WLR 1133 (1147), Lord Denning, MR stated the object is to ascertain the intention of the legislature. This intention must be discovered, of course, from the words which they have used but the words must be sensibly interpreted. We are not here to make nonsense of them. If we look at the history, the practice of grouping sections of an Act under different headings was first introduced in UK in 1845 in the Clauses Consolidation Acts (Thring, Practical legislation, Ed.1902). According to Maxwell on the Interpretation of Statutes, 12th Edn. page 11, the headings pre-fixed to sections or sets of sections in some modern statutes are regarded as preambles of those sections. They cannot control the plain words of the statute but they may explain ambiguous words'. Head notes may, in some cases, be looked upon in the light of preambles if there is any ambiguity in the meaning of the sections on which they throw light. The arrangement of sections into parts and their headings are substantive parts of the Act and as is pointed out by Craies on Statute Law, 5th Edn, page 165, 'they are gradually winning recognition as a kind of preamble to the enactments which they precede limiting or explaining their operations'. The above views make no hesitation in arriving at the conclusion that sections 33 and 56 deal with different subjects showing operation in separate fields and are not intended to overlap so as to restrict each other.</u>

10. We have the privilege of hearing Mr Mahmudul Islam as amicus curiae. Learned amicus curiae argued that sections 33 and 56 do not conflict with each other for, the sections are found in two chapters for different objects. Section 56 does not restrict permanent lease by a mutawalli provided that the mutawalli has obtained previous sanction of the Administrator. In this connection he has referred to the proviso to sub-section (1) of section 56 which, according to him, manifests that the bar is qualified by the words in contravention of any other law. Mr Islam contended that if such transfer by way of sale, gift, mortgage, exchange or lease for a period exceeding 5 years is barred by any existing law in force then notwithstanding the previous sanction of the Administrator, the transfer would be invalid. He has referred the cases of State of Rajasthan vs Sripal Jain, AIR 1963 SC 1323 and Rohit Pulp and Paper Mills Ltd. vs Collector of Central Excise, Baroda, (1990) 3 SCC 447 in support of his contention. According to Mr Islam, the words used in both sections are clear enough to come to the conclusion that there is no scope to give any statutory interpretation by restricting the power of the Waqfs Administrator. Mr Islam finally contended that the generic words used in section 33 should receive a limited interpretation by reason of its context by legitimately drawing upon the noscitur a sociis principle. In the other words, it is submitted that the restricted words used in the section should be interpreted by applying the principle of 'noscitur a sociis' or on the analogy of the 'ejusdem generis' principle

11. In the case of Rohit Pulp and Paper Mills Ltd., the assessee has a factory in which different variety of paper and paper boards are being manufactured. Paper and paper board' are goods falling under Item 17(1) of the Central Excise and Salt Act, 1944. Two notifications were issued one on March, 1984 in respect of the above Item providing 10% ad valorem paper plus Rs 1005 per metric tonne. Second notification provides for a concession in respect of paper and paper boards falling under Item 17(1) of the schedule manufactured out of pulp containing not less than 50% by weight of pulp made from materials other than bamboo and cleared on or after April 1st, 1944, at the rate of Rs 450 per metric tonne. The above concessional rates were subject to certain conditions set up in the proviso to the notification stating that the exemption contained in the notification shall not apply to cigarette tissue, glassine paper, coated paper (including waxed paper) and so on. The assessee initially paid excise duty as per previous notification but later on it claimed confessional rate prescribed by the latter notification. The Excise Department refused to permit the assessee to avail this concession in respect of his manufactured goods. It claimed concessional rates on the ground that the word 'coated paper' has been set out in the proviso along with other 4 items and used in wider sense and includes coated papers of all varities, it should be interpreted by applying the principle of 'noscitur a sociis' or on the analogy of 'ejusdem generis' principle.

12. The Supreme Court accepted the claim holding that there is no reason why rationally logical restriction should not be placed in the proviso based on the classification and that coated paper in the second proviso refers only to coated paper used for industrial purposes and not to coated varieties of printing and writing paper" and in the context with which we can legimately draw upon the noscitur a sociis principle.

13. In State of Bombay vs Hospital Mazdoor  Savha, AIR 1960 SC 610, the question involved was that two employees of a chain of hospitals were removed and in their place two state servants were appointed. The retrenched employees filed a writ of mandamus directing to rein-statement in their posts on the ground that the retrenchment was void as it did not comply the provisions of sections 25F and 25H of the Industrial Disputes Act, 1947. The petition was resisted on the ground that the writ petition was not maintainable, inasmuch as, the hospitals did not constitute an 'industry' and so, the relevant provisions of law were not applicable. The question involved in the appeal for consideration is whether group of hospitals constitutes an 'industry'. The writ petition was ultimately allowed on the reasoning that the orders had not complied the mandatory provisions of law. On appeal from the said judgment it was raised that the definition of 'industry' defined in section 2(j) of the said Act is so wide denotation, 'hospitals' can be excluded from the definition. It was urged that in construing the definition, the Court must adopt the rule of construction 'noscuntur a sociis'.

14. Gajendragadkar, J. upon consideration of the opinions expressed by different authors on Interpretation of Statutes came to the conclusion that the maxim 'noscuntur a sociis' is merely a rule of construction and it cannot prevail in cases where it is clear that the wider words have been deliberately used in order to make the scope of the defined word correspondingly wider. It is only where the intention of the Legislature in associating wider words with words of narrower significance is doubtful, or otherwise not clear that the present rule of construction can be usefully applied. It can also be applied where the meaning of the words of wider import is doubtful; but where the object of the Legislature, in using wider words, is clear and free of ambiguity, the rule of construction in question cannot be pressed into service".

15. 'Noscitur a sociis' is a Latin maxim which means that it is known by its associates. To say more clearly, the meaning of a word is to be judged by the company it keeps. It is a rule laid down by Lord Bacon that the coupling of words together shows that they are to be under-stood in the same sense. Where the meaning of a particular word is doubtful or obscure, or where a particular expression taken singly is inoperative, the intention of the Legislature may be ascertained by looking at adjoining words, or at expressions occurring in other parts of the same statute. One provision of the statute must be construed by the bearing it will have upon another (Latin for Lawyers, 31C Edn. page 195). 16. In this connection the Judicial Committee of the Privy Council in Attorney-General for Ortario vs Mercer, (J.yy3) AC 767 (778) said It is a sound, maxim of law that every word in a statute ought prima-facie to be construed in its primary and natural sense, unless a secondary or more limited sense is required by the subject or the context. Whether there is a particular description of objects, sufficient to identify what was intended, followed by general or omnibus description, the latter description will be confined to the objects of the same class or kind of the former. This rule is not applicable in this case, inasmuch as, the philosophy of this rule is applied in cases when the meaning of a doubtful word may be ascertained by reference to the meaning of words associated with it. When two or more words which are susceptible of analogous meaning, the more general is restricted to a sense analogous to a less general.

17. The efusdern generis rule is a particular application of the broader maxim 'noscitur a sociis' principle. The difference between these two rules as explained in Words and Phrases Vol. XIV, page 207, is thus: Associated words take their meaning from one another under the doctrine of noscitur a sociis, the philosophy of which is that the meaning of a doubtful word may be ascertained by reference to the meaning of words associated with it; such doctrine is broader than the maxim ejusdem generis. The ejusdem generis rule has been clearly explained in a New Zealand case in Cooney, (1901) 21 NZLR 106 (108) by William, J. thus:

"There is a very well known rule of construction that if a general word follows a particular and specific word of the same nature as itself, it takes its meaning from that word, and is presumed to be restricted to the same genus as that word. No doubt that rule is one which has to be followed with care; but if not to follow it leads to absurd results, then it ought to be followed",

18. This doctrine, according to Maxwell on the Interpretation of Statutes, 12th Edn. P. 289 means that, where two or more words which are susceptible of analogous meaning are coupled together they are understood to be used in their cognate sense. They take as it were their colour from each other, i.e. the more general is restricted to a sense analogous to a less general. Lord Campbell in RV. Edmundson (1859) 28 WC 213 explained this rule by saying accede to the principle laid down in all the cases which have been cited, that, where there are general words following particular and specific words, the general words must be confirmed to things of the same kind as those specified.

19. In dealing with wider words in the con-text of the ejusdem generis rule, Lord Bramwell in Great Western RY. vs Sarindon Ry, (1884) 9 AC 786 said "As a matter of ordinary construction where several words are followed by a general expression which is as much applicable to the first and other words as to the last, that expression is not limited to the last applies to all. For instance, horses, oxen, pigs, and sheep, from whatever country they may come the latter words would apply to horses as much as to sheep. The ejusdem generis rule according to Craies on Statute Law, Seventh Edition, is one to be applied with caution and not pushed too far, as in the case of many discussions, which treat it as automatically applicable, not as being, what it is, a mere presumption, in the absence of other indications of the intention of the Legislature. In NAIGOV Bolton Corporation, (1943) AC 166, Lord Wright said, The ejusdem generis nile is often useful or convenient, but it is merely a rule of construction, not a rule of law.

20. The position has been summed up in Halsbury's Laws of England, 3rd Edn, page 397 thus: "As a rule, where a statute there are general words following particular and specific words, the general words must be confined to things of the same kind as those specified, although this, as a rule of construction, must be applied with caution, and subject to the primary rule that statutes are to be constructed in accordance with the intention of the parliament. For the ejusdem rule to apply, the specific words must constitute a category, class or genus; if they constitute such a category, class or genus; then only things which belong to that category, class or genus fall within the general words".

21. According to the established principle of interpretation of statutes, the specific words must apply not to different objects of a widely differing character but to something which can be called a class or kind of object. Where this is lacking the rule cannot apply. Where the words are clearly wide in their meaning they ought not to be qualified on the ground of their association with other words. So, general words following particular words will not include anything of a class superior to that to which the particular words belong. In cases where there is no doubt that the wider words have been deliberately used in order to make the scope of the defined words correspondingly wider, where the intention of the legislature in associating wider words with words of narrower significance is used is doubtful, the above rule of construction can be used. It is the established rule of construction that the statutes are to be construed in accordance with the intention of the Legislature.

22. On a plain reading of section 56 we find no ambiguity in the language used therein with the language used in section 33 of the Ordinance. There is no doubt on reading section 33 as a whole about the meaning of the words used therein which can be ascertained by reference to the meaning of words associated with it. Therefore, we need not draw upon the noscitur a sociis is or ejusdem generis principles. Section 33 restricts the Administrator in transferring any part of a waqf property while he is in charge of the said property. He can transfer the property for the welfare of the estate with prior permission of the Government. Whereas, the substance of sub-section (1) of section 56 is that a mutawalli can transfer any part of a waqf property in any manner as provided therein but the only restriction is in respect of lease for a period exceeding five years. In such case previous permission of the Waqfs Administrator is necessary. Even if any transfer by way of lease is made for a period exceeding five years with-out sanction of the Administrator, such transfer can be declared void by the Civil Court only on the prayer of the Administrator. Sub-section (4) makes the thing more clear, which provides that even if a mutawalli transfers any property in contravention of sub-section (1) and afterwards he becomes the owner of the property, he may re-convey the property on the direction of the Administrator. It is also provided in sub-section (5) that if any transfer is made in contravention of sub-section (1), such transfer shall be deemed to be an act of malfeasance.

23. If the object and purpose of section 56 are considered together, there would be no difficulty in holding that the words of wide import have been deliberately used by the Legislature in the exercise of powers by the mutawalli to transfer any part of the waqf property by way of lease exceeding 5 years with the sanction of the Administrator. Section 33 empowers the Administrator any sort of transfer of any portion of the Waqf Property with previous sanction of the Government, whereas, in case of transfer by mutawalli other than lease not exceeding 5 years previous sanction of the Administrator is not necessary. There is no ambiguity in the words used in those provisions. There cannot be any doubt of using wider words in section 56(1) and the intention of the Legislature in using wider words is clear and free from any ambiguity. These two provisions would be realized if we bear in mind the scheme of Chapters III and VI. The intention of the Legislature in providing these two provisions in different chapters is clear. On a plain reading of section 56 it suggests that it would be inappropriate to put a restrictive interpretation.

24. In the proviso to sub-section (1) of section 56, it is stated that even if there is previous sanction such transfer shall not be validated if it is in contravention of any other law, that is, if any other law prohibits such transfer, any lease exceeding five years even with the previous sanction of the Administrator shall be invalid. Now it is to be looked into whether the lease in question has been granted in violation of any existing law, that is, the Non-Agricultural Tenancy Act, 1949 (Act, 1949) and the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, 1950 (Act, 1950). The answer to this point depends upon the determination of the nature of the land transferred and the application of those laws in the context of the execution of the deed in question. Admittedly, the suit land is situated within Sylhet City Corporation area and the nature of the suit land has been mentioned as (Bangla) (vegetable garden). Thus the suit land is non-agricultural land. 'Non-agricultural land' within section 2(4) of the Act, 1949 means "land which is used for purposes not connected with agriculture or horticulture and includes any land which is held on lease for the purposes not connected with agriculture or horticulture irrespective of whether it is used for any such purpose......

25. A land which was originally leased for agricultural or horticultural purposes but is being used for purposes not connected with agriculture or horticulture without the consent of the landlord and if the period for which the land has been so used is less than twelve years will not be included in the category of 'non-agricultural land' in view of section 2(4)(b). This exception is not applicable to this case in view of the admitted fact that the lease was granted not for a period less than twelve years. So the primary test in determining a particular land is non-agricultural or not, rests firstly as to whether the land is a 'non-agricultural land' as defined in the Act of 1949, and secondly, the purpose for which the tenancy was created.

<u>26. This definition excludes agricultural and horticultural lands including the lands held in lease for purposes not connected with agriculture and horticulture. The land is in the nature of horticulture but the lease deed does not show that the lease was granted for horticulture purposes. It means that the land which is used for purposes not connected with agriculture or horticulture and includes any land which is held on lease for purposes not connected with agriculture or horticulture irrespective of whether it is used for any such purposes or not is non-agricultural land. There are two classes of non-agricultural tenants under the said Act, namely (a) tenants, and (b) under-tenants. 'Non-agricultural tenant' within the meaning of section 2(5) of Act, 1949 is a person who holds non-agricultural land under another person with consent of that person and is, or but for a special contract would be, liable to pay rent to such person for that land. In the Act of 1950, almost similar definition has been given in section 2(17). Under this Act, a tenant who holds land for purposes not connected with agriculture or horticulture, but does not include a person holding land together with any building standing thereon and necessary adjuncts thereto under a lease other than a lease in perpetuity.</u>

27. The difference under these two enactments is that if any person holds any premises on such land under a contract to pay rent for such occupation such person shall riot become a 'non-agricultural tenant' under the Act of 1949 and secondly, a lease in perpetuity has been excluded from the category in the latter Act. According to section 1(2) of the Act of 1949 the word 'tenant' means a person who has acquired from the proprietor or a tenure holder a right to hold non-agricultural land for any of the purposes provided in the said Act, and includes also the successors-in-interest of persons who have acquired such a right. Under the latter Act, tenant means a person who holds land under another person and is, or but for a special contract would be, liable to pay for that land to that person. Under the definition a 'borga cultivator' is excluded from the category of tenant. Under-tenant as per sub-section (3) of section 3 of Act;, 1949 means a person who has acquired a right to hold non-agricultural land for any of the purposes provided in the Act either immediately or under a tenant and includes also the successors-in-interest of per-sons who have acquired such a right.

28. The defendant's tenancy was created after the Act of 1949 came into force in 1965, and therefore, he was an under-tenant within the meaning of Act, 1949 during the relevant times. Section 4 provided the purpose for which a non-agricultural tenant may hold non-agricultural land i.e. for (a) homestead or residential purposes; (b) manufacturing or business purposes; or (c) religious or other purposes. The word 'homestead' includes gardens, tanks and land necessary for enjoyment as home-stead. Under section 2(14) of the Act, 1950, the word 'homestead' means a dwelling house with the land under it, together with any court-yard, garden, tank, place of worship and private burial or cremation ground attached and appertaining to such dwelling house, and includes any out-buildings used for the purpose of enjoying the dwelling house or for purposes connected with agricultural or horticulture and such lands within well-defined limits, whether vacant or not, as are treated to be appertaining thereto.

29. The expression 'other purposes' used in clause (c) of section 4 of Act, 1949 means purposes other than non-agricultural and horticulture. The courts below on construction of the lease deed came to a definite finding that the lease was granted in perpetuity. Provisions have been made for the protection of under-tenants in Chapter IV of Act, 1949. Section 20 provides that an under-tenant shall be liable to ejectment on two grounds namely (a) if he has used the land in a manner which renders it unfit for use for any of the purposes specified in section 4, and (b) the term of the lease has expired when he holds the non-agricultural under a written lease. There is no allegation that the defendant has been using the land in contravention of section 4. Since the lease is in perpetuity, clause (b) of section 20 is not also applicable in this case.

30. Other protections given to an under-tenant are those provided in sections 21 and 22. Section 21 recognizes the succession by the heirs of 'under-tenant' in case of his death subject to the provisions of sections 90 and 91 of the Act, 1950. These provisions are also not applicable in this case. Section 22 recognizes all rights and liabilities of a tenant as set forth in sections 7, 8 and 10. If the term is not less than twelve years specified in the lease deed and in that case, section 6 shall apply and also section 20 in so far as they are inconsistent with the provisions of section 22 shall not apply. Section 6 provides the manner of use of non-agricultural land by a tenant.
