If these Account Assistants are upgraded to Administrative Officer, then 5 senior posts such as Account Officers, Reporter, Head Assistant, Typist and Librarian will be affected. In Crime Detection Department, the Administrative Officer is at serial No. 5 and Office Superintendent/Head Assistant is at serial No. 6 and Upper Division Assistant is at serial No. 8. If Upper Division Assistant is upgraded to Administrative Officer, two senior officers to them will be prejudiced. In the office of Divisional Deputy Inspector General, (Inspection), it has separate service Rules. In this Department there is no post of Administrative Officer. Now if a Upper Division Assistant or Account officer or Accountant, who ranks at serial No. 3 is promoted to the post of Administrative Officer in the similar rank to the Special Department, there will create anomaly in this Department.

155. Similarly in the District Superintendent of Police Department, there is no post like Administrative Officer. If the Head Assistant is upgraded to the post of Administrative Officer, there is no clarification whether such Head Assistant will be upgraded above Medical Officer who is at serial No.1. Similarly the Upper Assistant/Head mohorar, a Reader are at serial No. 6. If this Upper Assistant is upgraded to Administrative Officer, there will create more anarchy in the administration.

156. In the Dhaka Metropolitan Police, the post of Administrative Officer is at serial No. 1, the Upper Assistant is at serial No. 2 and the Head Assistant/head mohora/CA are at serial No. 4. If the Head Assistant is upgraded to Administrative Officer, certainly the other two employees who are above their rank and status will be prejudiced. There are criteria for promotion to the higher posts of Administrative Officer. If these criteria are not fulfilled and the Upper Division Assistants are upgraded to the rank of Administrative Officer, the service Rules will be violated. In respect of Chittagong Metropolitan Police also similar provisions for the posts and status. In Khulna Metropolitan Police, the post of Upper Assistant/Head mohora /accountant/reader/CA are in the same rank at serial No. 5 and above them is the post of Head Assistant and the Administrative Officer is two step higher than Head Assistant.

So, the Khulna Metropolitan Police Service Rules are completely different from Chittagong Metropolitan Police.

157. In respect of Rajshahi Metropolitan Police, the post Head Assistant is one step lower than the Khulna Metropolitan Police. If Head Assistant post is upgraded to Administrative Officer, then the Accounts Officer will be prejudiced and then if the Upper Division Assistant is upgraded to Administrative Officer, the other Upper Employees holding the higher posts will be prejudiced. In the Transmission Department, there is no post like Administrative Officer and Head Assistant are at serial No. 1. The post-Upper Assistant/ Accountant and Casher are at serial No. 3. The post of Head Assistant must have three years experience in the feeder post and Upper Assistant must have five years experience in the feeder post. So, there will create anomaly if this Upper Assistant is upgraded with the Administrative Department. In Railway Police, there is no post like Administrative Officer and Head Assistant is at serial No. 1. Their rank and status is similar to Communication Department. In the Armed Police Battalion, there is no post like Administrative Officer and the post of typist is at serial No. 1 and Head Assistant is two step lower than typist. There will also create anomaly if this Upper Assistant is upgraded above typist.

158. In respect of Police Academy, Sarada, there is no post of Administrative Officer and Senior Medical Officer is heading the seniority. A Senior Head Assistant is at serial No.7. If he is upgraded in the rank of Administrative Officer, how he will be accommodated is not clear because if he is accommodated then he will be senior to Medical Officer. The Head Assistant/Upper Assistant and Accountant are at serial No. 9. If they are upgraded then they have to supersede eight senior posts. In Local Police Training School, Head Assistant is at serial No. 3 and Upper Assistant/Accountant is at serial No. 4. If these two groups are upgraded they will be put above the Medical Officer. There is no post of Administrative Officer in this department. In the police hospital, the Superintendent (Medical Officer) is heading the post and Head Assistant-cum-Accountant is at serial No. 4 and Office Assistant-cum Typist is at serial No. 6. There is no post like Administrative Officer. If these posts are upgraded as Special Officer, then they must be placed above Superintendents.

159. In the Food Department, there is separate service Rules under the name the Non-Cadre Gazetted Officers and Non-gazetted Employees (Director General of Food) Recruitment Rules, 1983. In these Rules, the provisions for recruitment, promotions, scales, everything have been clearly mentioned in the schedule. Head Assistant/Head Assistant-cum-Accountant/Superintendent are at serial No. 9. UDA/ LDA-cum-typist/stenographer/steno typist are at serial No. 11. If these two groups are upgraded, since there is no post of Administrative Officer, they must have to be placed at 8 or 9 grade Certainly they will be placed above the Chemist, which post is senior most and the post has been year marked for promotion from Assistant Chemist with five years experience.

160. In the Public administration, there is a service Rules under the name বাংলাদেশ সচিবালয় (ক্যাডার বহির্ভূত কর্মকর্তা এবং নন গেজেটে কর্মচারী নিয়োগ বিধিমালা), ২০১৪. Under these Rules, different grades have been amalgamated in Rule 6(Gha) and the post of Administrative Officer has been abolished. According to this Rules, the Deputy Secretary (Non-cadre) is at serial No.1, Senior Assistant Secretary (Non-cadre) is at serial No. 2, Assistant Secretary (non-cadre) is at serial No. 3 and there are different criteria for promotion of those posts from the lower post. These Rules have been promulgated by repealing the previous Rules namely বাংলাদেশ সচিবালয় (ক্যাডার বহির্ভূত গেজেটেড এবং নন গেজেটেড কর্মকর্তা কর্মচারী নিয়োগ বিধিমালা), ২০০৬.

161. Similarly in the Supreme Court, there is a service Rules under the name বাংলাদেশ সুপ্রীমকোর্ট হাইকোর্ট বিভাগ (কর্মচারী নিয়োগ বিধিমালা)১৯৮৭. Except one department there are separate service Rules in respect of the writ petitioners regulating the procedure for recruitment, promotion and other related matters. The recruitment, promotion, status and other benefits are being regulated by the respective service Rules of the Departments. Thus it will not be fair to equate the Senior Assistants of the Secretariate with those working in the Supreme Court of Bangladesh, Police Department, Local Government and Engineering Department, Customs Department, various Tribunals, Appellate Tribunals etc. In some departments there are posts of Administrative Officers and alike posts, the post of Administrative Officers has been abolished in the Department and new Rules have been framed deleting those posts. Under such circumstances, if Senior Assistants or Upper Division Clerks or Stenographers or typists are equated with those posts giving them similar status and rank, there is no use of framing Rules by different Departments. These Rules have been framed by the concerned Departments for the purpose of recruitment, promotion and administration of their employees. One service Rules can not regulate the employees of other Department. Similarly the criteria for appointment of each Department and pro-motion are completely different.

162. The expression equal protection of law or equality before law has to be interpreted in its absolute sense. All persons are equal in all respect disregarding different conditions and circumstances in which they are placed. Equal protection of law means all persons are equal in all cases. It means the persons similarly situated should be treated equally. The term equality is a dynamic concept with many aspect and diminution and it cannot be confined within traditional and doctrinaire limits. Indian Supreme Court taking into consideration article 14 of the Constitution held that article 14 does not forbid reasonable classification for the purposes of legislation. There can be permissible classification provided two conditions are satisfied namely; (a) the classification must be founded on an intelligible differentia which distinguishes persons or things that are grouped together for other left out of the group; (b) differentia must have a rational relation to the object sought to be achieved by the statute in question. The classification may be founded on different basis. There cannot be any question of discrimination on the ground of some acts providing for different set up and each must be taken to be a class by itself. The legislature has a right to make such provision for its Constitution as it thinks fit subject always to the provisions of the Constitution. References in this connection are EP Royappa vs TN, AIR 1974 SC 555, Maleka Gandhi vs India, AIR 1970 SC 597, Romana Shetly vs International Airport Authority, AIR 1979 SC 1628, Ajay Hashia vs Khalid Mujud, AIR 1983 SC 130, A L Kalra vs P & N Corporation of India, AIR 1984 SC 1361, Shree Ram Krishna Dal Mia vs Shree SR Tendulkar, AIR 1958 SC 538, S. Azeez Brother vs Union of India, AIR 1968 SC 662, Jibendra Kishore Achary vs Province of East Pakistan, 9 DLR (SC) 21 and Kazi Mohammad Akhtaruzzman vs Bangladesh, Writ Petition No. 2252 of 2009 disposed of along with three other writ petitions. Sheikh Abdus Sabur vs Returning Officer, 41 DLR (AD) 30 and Bangladesh vs Md Azizur Rahman, 46 DLR (AD) 19.

163. In Jibendra Kishore (supra), it has been observed, "It is not possible to formulate a comprehensive definition of the clause 'equal protection of law'; nevertheless some broad propositions as to its meaning have been enunciated. One of these propositions is that equal protection of the laws means that no person or class of persons shall be denied the same protection of the laws which is enjoyed by other persons or other classes, in like circumstances, in their lives, liberty and property and in pursuit of happiness. Another generalization more frequently stated is that the guarantee of equal protection of the laws requires that all persons shall be treated alike, under like circumstances and conditions, both in the privileges conferred and in the liabilities imposed. In the application of these principles, however, it has always been recognized that classification is not arbitrary or capricious, is natural and reasonable and bears a fair and substantial relation to the object of the legislation. It is not for the Courts, in such cases, it is said, to demand from the legislature a scientific accuracy in the classification adopted. If the classification is relevant to the object of the Act, it must be upheld unless the relevancy is too remote or fanciful. A classification that proceeds on irrelevant consideration, such as differences in race, colour or religion will certainly be rejected by the Courts. Applying these tests to the present case, it cannot but be held that if, in consequence of abolishing the system of private rent for agricultural land, it also became necessary to make some provision for the outgoing landlords, the classification of the land-lords in the basis of their net incomes at the time of their expropriation was a necessary, and not an unreasonable, classification."

<u>164. In Sheikh Abdus Sabur (supra), this court held: "Equality before law" is not to be interpreted in its absolute sense to hold that all persons are equal in all respects disregarding different conditions and circumstances in which they are placed or special qualities and characteristics which some of them may possess but which are lacking in others. The term 'protection of equal law' is used to mean that all persons or things are not equal in all cases and that persons similarly situated should be treated alike. Equal protection is the guarantee that similar people will be dealt with in a similar way and that people of different circumstances will not be treated as if they were the same. A single law therefore cannot be applied uniformly to all persons disregarding their basic differences with others; and if these differences are identified, then the persons or things may be classified into different categories according to those distinctions; this is what is called 'permissible criteria' or "intelligible differentia",. The Legislature while proceeding to make law with certain object in view, which is either to remove some evil or to confer some benefit, has power to make classification on reasonable basis. Classification of persons for the purpose of legislation is different from class legislation, which is forbidden. To stand the test of 'equality' a classification, besides being based on intelligent differentia, must have reasonable nexus with the object the legislature intends to achieve by making the classification. A classification is reasonable if it aims at giving special treatment to a backward section of the population; it is also permissible to deal out distributive justice by taxing the privileged class and subsiding the poor section of the people. The above views have been approved in Azizur Rahman (supra).</u>

165. On the above conspectus, we hold the view that almost all the writ petitions except writ petition Nos. 6263 of 2014 and 6264 of 2014 are not maintainable. All judgments except those in writ petition Nos. 6263 of 2014 and 6264 of 2014 are set aside. The appeals are, therefore, allowed without any order as to costs with the above observations. CP Nos. 1445, 1768, 2133, 2134.and 2320 of 2015 are dismissed. CP Nos.1415, 1416, 1417, 1418, 1419, 1420, 1421 of 2015, 703 of 2014, 2026 of 2015, 2295 of 2010, 955 of 2011, 1854 of 2011, 2539 of 2012 and 1782 of 2015 are disposed of with the above observations. Civil Petition for Leave to Appeal Nos. 644 and 645 of 2015 are dismissed.

This judgment will have prospective operation so as not to disturb the procedure in relation to decisions already rendered.

End.

full_judgment:
Sharif Uddin Chaklader J : This appeal by the plaintiffs directed against judgment and decree dated 30-9-2009 passed by the learned Joint Directed Judge, 1st Court, Dhaka dismissing Title Suit No. 136 of 2006.

2. In the suit plaintiff prayed for a decree for declaration of 16 annas ownership in the suit property with further prayer of confirmation of possession.

3. It is plaint case that suit land originally belongs to Amol Sing Bahadur, Sib Krishana Sing Bahadur, sons of la t Maharaj Pran Krishna Sing Bahadur, Maharaj Kumod Krishna, Nirod Chandra Sing, Nogendra Chandra Sing and Dijendra Chandra Sing sons of late Maharaj Krishana Singh Bahadur who were the CS recorded owners and possessor of the suit property and their names have been recorded in CS khatian 16842/13, CS dag No. 211 area of lands measuring 9342 Ajautangsha, in CS dag No. 212 area of land measuring 3480 Ajutangsh, CS dag No. 213 area of land 5900 Aujutangsh, CS dag No. 223/369 the area of land measuring 7080 Ajutangsha, CS dag No. 329 area of land measuring 2328 Ajutangsha. But in the suit claim was made for the land of CS dag No. 223/369 of area of land 7080 Ajutangsha. Out of this area of land, plaintiff's claim is for 473 Ajutangsha of land. The CS recorded owners paid rents and taxes of land in question to the concerned authority in time and enjoyed the same peacefully to the knowledge of all. Predecessor of plaintiff Sreemati Sarnalata Dey wife of, Srejukta Dinehs Chandra Dey became owner and possessor of the suit land from Sree Sudhindar Chandra Sing Sharma, Sree Shurid Chandra Sing Sharma, sons of late Promod Chandra Sing Sharma, Sreemati Surama Devi, wife of, late Promon Chandra Sing Sarnia, Sree Debesh Kumar Sing Sharma, Sree Somesh Kumar Sing Sharma, Sreemati Sibani Debi, wife of late Shudir Chandra Sing Sarma, Sree Surath Chandra Sing Sharma, Sere Suresh Chandra Sing Sharma sons of late Girindra Chandra Singh Sharma by registered deed of sale being No. 1495 dated 15-5-1941. Syed Ali Habib, son of late, Syed Abdul Latif become owner and possessor of the suit land from Sreemati Sarnalata Dey, wife of Sree Dinesh Chandra Dey by registered deed of perpetual lease being No. 4593 dated 30-9-1950 followed by registered deed of sale being No. 4594 dated 30-9-1950. The predecessor of the vendor and the vendor paid rents and taxes to the concerned authorities for the suit land. Before being alienated they possessed the land in question peacefully and after they divested themselves of the suit land, the vendees stepped into their shares and being bonafide owners in possession paid rents and taxes in time of the concerned authorities. Name of Syed Ali Habib, son of, Syed Abdul Latif was duly recorded in SA khatian No. Sabek 1328 Hal 804, SA dag No. 1800, area of land measuring 0473 Ajutangsha. Being bonafide owner in possession he paid Government rents, taxes of the suit land to the concerned authorities in time. Syed Ali Habib died leaving Syed Ali Azhar, Syed Ali Mazhar, Syed Ali Asgar and Syeda Khatun sons and wife respectively of the deceased who stepped into the shoes of Syed Ali Habib in the suit land by dint of inheritance. They being bonafide owners in possession of the suit land, sold the same by an indenture of sale to Abdul Majid, son of late, Nur Muhammad being registered deed No. 12222 dated 29-9-1960. Abdul Majid died on 20-10-1983 leaving Abdur Aziz, Abdur Rashid, Nazma Begum, and Panchi Bibi as his sons, daughters and wife respectively. Plaintiff field succession case NO. 947 of 1983 in the Court of district delegate 3rd Sub-ordinate Judge, Dhaka and got succession certificate on 2-4-1984 for drawing money deposited in different Banks in the name of deceased Abdul Majid. After the death of Abdul Majid, his aforesaid sons, daughters and wife became owner and possessor of the property as successor as per Muslim law of inheritance. Plaintiff No. 1 is the husband of the plaintiff No. 2. Plaintiff No. 1 purchased 0074 Ajutangsha from Mrs Panchi Bibi by registered deed of sale being No. 1064 dated 12-3-1992, at a valuable consideration and got possession thereof. Plaintiff further purchased 0086 Ajutangsha of land from Mrs Amena Begum by registered deed of sale being No. 1241 dated 30-3-1992 at a valuable consideration and got possession thereof. Plaintiff also purchased an area of land measuring 0086 Ajutangsha of land from Mrs Nazma Begum by registered deed of sale being No. 1242 dated 30-3-1992. Plaintiff No. 1 against purchased 0090 Ajutangsha of land from Abdul Aziz by registered deed No. 2084 dated 21-5-1992. Plaintiff No. 1 again purchased 0061 Ajutangsha of land from A.bdur Rashid by registered deed No. 2.312 dated 8-6-1992. Plaintiff No. 1 again purchased 0051 Ajutangsha of land from Abdul Aziz by registered deed No. 1901 dated 14-5-1998 at a valuable consideration and got possession thereof. Plaintiff No. 2 purchased 0061 Ajutangsha and 0051 Ajutangsha of land from Abdur Rashid and Abdur Aziz by registered deeds of sale being No. 2318 dated 8-6-1992 and No. 2005 dated 21-5-1992.

4. IN this way by 8 registered sale deeds plaintiffs became owner and possessor of three Katha nine chataks of land with structures standing thereon to the knowledge of all including the defendants. Plaintiffs mutuated their names and got mutated Parcha, rent receipt, DCR and where/are paying government land revenue and taxes in their names. But due to reason not known they realized rents from the plaintiffs for 0473 Ajutangsha of land. When objection raised to this, they were said that when Tasdik Parcha will be published finally they will realize rents from the plaintiffs accordingly. Their names were recorded in Tasdik Parcha for 0586 Ajutangsha of land, in Khatian No. 5257 DP 3432, Dag No. 5344, Mouia Wari, Police Station-Sutrapur, Dhaka. In the opinion column it is remarked that there is a 4(four) storied pucca building in possession of the plaintiffs. The names of the plaintiffs were duly recorded and mutated in Dhaka City Corporation and the plaintiffs have been allotted holding No. 16/1/A, Rankin Street, Dhaka and the plaintiffs have been paying holding taxes to the Dhaka City Corporation in time and they have enjoyed the suit property peacefully without any objection from anybody of are quarter whatsoever.

5. It is further case of plaintiffs that without notifying and hearing the plaintiffs defendant No. 5 arbitrarily cancelled the mutation in separation Case No. 2177/94-95 and given 0473 Ajutangsha of land in the Miscellaneous case No. 20/97-98 by stating in his office on the application of the defendant No. 1. The Miscellaneous Case was filed on 25-6-1997, that is, after lapse of 7 years, which is hopelessly barred by law of limitation. Defen-dant No. 1 on 25-6-1997 applied for correction of the quantum of area of land and accordingly defendant N. 5 corrected on 25-5-2004 the same without giving any notice required as provided under law and without giving any opportunity for hearing in the matter by the plaintiffs. The plaintiffs came to know about the said illegal action when they went to the Tashsil Office for payment of government land revenue there. Thereafter, plaintiffs filed a review case in the office of the defendant No. 5 which was not considered by the defendant No. 5 showing reason as time barred. The plaintiffs being aggrieved and dissatisfied with the impugned order preferred Miscellaneous Appeal No. 18 of 2005 before the Additional Deputy Commiss-ioner (Revenue), Dhaka who dismissed the appeal. Thereafter, plaintiffs preferred appeal No. 112 of 2005 on 25-8-2005 before the additional Divisional Commissioner, Dhaka but instead of getting order in favour of the plaintiffs the order of additional Divisional Commissioner went against the plaintiffs on 26-12-2005 dismissing the appeal.

6. Thereafter, plaintiffs filed the suit showing cause of action as :—

"The cause of action for the suit arose on 25-5-2004, 13-7-2005 and 26-12-2005 as the plaintiffs did not get justified order in their favour before ADC (Rev) land Kotwali, ADC (Rev) Dhaka and Additional Divisional Commissioner, Dhaka respectively which still exists in Mouza Wari under Police Station Sutrapur, District Dhaka, which is the jurisdiction of this learned Court."

7. Defendant No. 1 contested the suit by filing written statement and in the written statement the plaint case was denied line by line and it is his specific case that predecessor of the plaintiffs purchased land from Sree Sarnalata Dey when Title Suit No. 141 of 1945 was pending and this purchase is hit by lis pendency, Plaintiffs filed Title Suit No. 171 of 1985 impleading Kaniz Fatema, predecessor of the defendant No. 1 Suit was dismissed. Plaintiffs filed Title Appeal No. 120 of 1957 and thereafter plaintiffs filed Appeal from Appellate Decree No. 195 of 1958 and these appeals were dismissed thereby title of Sarnalata, predecessor of the plaintiffs and also of the plaintiffs totally lost and extinguished. It is further case of this defendant that suit land originally belongs to Maharaj of Durgapur, Mymensingh and CS Khatian was prepared in the name of heirs of Maharaj Durgapur, Mymensingh who filed Partition Suit No. 145 of 1927 in the Court of Sub-ordinate Judge, 4th Court, Mymensingh and in that suit, sham for an area of 1475 Ajutangsha was allowed to Raja Shibkrishna Sing. For the remaining land of the aforesaid dag the other heirs who got saham, from them, Charulata Paul by registered deed No. 2369 dated 19-9-1938 purchased 4 kathas and 1 chha tak 6½ gandas of land and got possession and from Charulata Paul, Kaniz Fatema by registered deed No. 4113 in 1950 purchased the said land ands got possession. Direndra Chandra Sing and other 3 sons of raja Shibkrishna Sing also got 4/7 shares and for title and recovery of possession against Charulata Paul, Sarnalata Paul and others as plaintiffs filed Title Suit No. 141 of 1945 in the court of Sub-ordinate Judge, 1st Court, Dhaka renumbered before the court of additional Sub-ordinate Judge, Dhaka as Title Suit No. 40 of 1951. The suit was dismissed on 25-5-1951 and while the said suit was pending Sarnalata Paul sold some land to Syed Ali Habib. Sarnalata Dey did not get any land in the suit and by purchase from Sarnalata Dey, Syed Ali Habib also did not get any land as his purchase was hit by lis pendency. Kaniz Fatema, the predecessor of defendant purchased the decree of that suit on 22-4-1952 and replaced his name as decree holder and by executing decree through Title Execution case No. 66 of 1952 of Court of 5th Sub-ordinate Judge, Dhaka wherein Advocate Commissioners were appointed, got 0488 Ajutangsha of land and got possession by court on 25/8/1953 and demarcated by opening khatian No. 16842/13. The heirs of Syed Ai Habib filed Title Suit No. 171 of 1955 before the Munsif, 6th Court, Dhaka for declaration of title and for khash possession against the mother of this defendant, Kaniz Fatema as defendant. The suit was dismissed on 28-6-1957, against which Title Appeal No. 120 of 1957 was filed. Appeal was dismissed on 5-11-1957. Against which decision plaintiffs of that suit filed Appeal from Appellate Decree No. 195 of 1958 before the High Court Division. This appeal also dismissed by the High Court Division by judgment dated 25-8-1959. Against that decision, plaintiffs of that suit did not take any step as such, plaintiffs have no title over the suit property as they purchased the land from a person who had no title and possession over the suit land. In this way Kaniz Fatema by purchase became owner of 4 khathas 1 Chhatak = .0608 Ajutangsha of land and by decree got .1158 Ajutangsha of land. Later on, Kaniz Fatema sold .856 Ajutangsha of land to Lutfar Rahman and retain. 0302 Ajutangsha of land was is in her possession till her death. In the recent survey, the name of Kaniz Fatema was first recorded for 1022 Ajutangsha of land, later on, by deducting 0.056, Ajutangsha of land which was sold and recorded in the name of Lutfor Rahman, 0240 Ajutangsha of land was recorded in the name of Kaniz Fatema in khatian No. 5523 and 5520. It is further case of this defendant that in schedule dag of Kaniz Fatema, plaintiffs surreptitiously in Mutation Case No. 2177/1994-95 mutated their names of which defendant after came to know filed Miscellaneous Case No. 20/1997-98 which was allowed and recording of the name of the plaintiffs in Mutation Case No. 2177/1994-95 was cancelled on contested hearing. Against the decision of Miscellaneous Case No. 20/1997-98, Miscellaneous Appeal No. 112 of 2005 was filed before the Assistant Commis-sioner (Revenue), Dhaka which was also dismissed. Against that, Miscellaneous Appeal 18 of 2005 was filed before Additional Divisional Commissioner which was also dismissed.

8. Defendant No. 2-6 also contested the suit by filing written statement in which they have denied the case of plaintiff and it is their specific case that the suit land originally belonged to Hemendra Mohon Bashak and Copal Bashak and others; the suit land was enlisted in sensuous list leased out of Nirmal Chandra Bashak in EP Case 228 of 1967 and EP Case No. 11 of 1971. The original owner having left this country before 1947 without any maintenance of the suit land and without any person for looking the property to India, as such, SA khatian No. 1800 has been prepared accordingly and included the property in VP sensuous list and the suit land have been recorded in its 16 annas title and recorded in the Government correctly and RS and SA khatian also prepared in the name of Government as vested property as original owner left for India before 1947, as such, the suit property has been rightly declared as enemy property as vested property and Government having possession and its management, plaintiff can not claim title of vested property and the suit is liable to be dismissed with cost.

9. In the suit plaintiff examined 4 witnesses and defendant examined 3 witnesses. Learned Judge by the impugned judgment dismissed the suit holding that plaintiffs by purchase from Hemendra Chandra Bashak did not acquire any title in the suit land. Learned Judge further held that Sarnalata Debi from whom plaintiffs claim their title her title having been extinguished by decree passed in title Suit No. 40 of 1951 and in title Execution Case No. 66 of 1952, and this decision having been upheld upto the High Court Judicature at Dhaka, plaintiff acquired no title over the suit property. Learned Judge found that mutation in the name of plaintiffs having been cancelled and affirmed upto the appellate forum, plaintiffs title to the suit land is a myth.

10. Mr Md Mafizur Rahman with Mr AQM Shafiullah, the learned Advocates, appearing for the appellants, submits that, learned Judge committed gross illegality in not holding that plaintiffs purchased the suit land from one Abdul Majid by registered deed which has presumptive value and plaintiffs are in possession of the suit land by constructing 4 storied building which, as per Section 40 of.the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act has presumptive value and registered the kabala legally and plaintiff after purchase mutated their names, paying taxes to the Government as such acquired title over the suit property. Learned Advocates further submits that plaintiff filed rent receipt, dakhilas and also enquiry report wherein plaintiff's possession has been found and further submit that land of defendant No. 1 and plaintiff are totally different as such, plaintiff's suit ought to be decreed.

11. Mr Aminul Islam, the learned Advocate, appearing for the defiant No. 1, submits that, it is admitted position that defendant purchased the land from Sarnalata Dey while Title Suit No. 141 of 1951 and later on Misc. Case No. 40 of 1951 was pending and in that suit it was declared Sarnalata dey has no title over the suit property as such, purchase from Saranalata Dey Syed Ali Habib and Hemendra Mohon and from then plaintiffs acquired no title over the suit property. Learned Advocate further submits that on the facts of the given case cause of action as given is not sustainable in law.

12. We have considered the submissions of the learned Advocates of both the parties, Exhibits filed by the parties and depositions of the witnesses.

13. On the submissions of the learned Advocates and materials on record two questions calls for determinations, i) whether plaintiffs' acquired title in the suit property by purchase from Majid and ii) whether the suit on the cause of action as given by the plaintiffs is maintainable.

14. To answered the first question, we have gone through the depositions of the witnesses and Exhibits filed by the parties. It appears that plaintiffs Exhibited Exhibit 1, certified copy CS khatian, produced the deed of acquiring title from Sarnalata dey by which Syed Ali Habib in certified copy as exhibt 7, plaintiffs also produced Exhibit 8 which is the deed of 30-9-1952. Plaintiff produced Exhibit 8 and 9 by which Syed Ali Habib at first got pattan, lease and thereafter, purchased the land from Sarnalata Dey in certified copy, Plaintiff also produced Exhibit 9 to 18 i.e. deed of purchase of the plaintiffs in certified copy, plaintiffs did not produce any original deed. We do not find any explanation as to whereabouts of the originals of these deeds as such, an averse presumption may be drawn against the plaintiffs.

15. It is case of plaintiffs that from Sarnalata Dey they have derived title. It is the case of defendant that Sarnalata Dey has no title. Title Suit No. 141 of 1945 was field by Dhirendra and 3 others, sons of Roy a Shib Krishna Sing for declaration of title and recovery of possession against Sarnalata, Swarna Lata and others. This suit was re-numbered as Title Suit No. 40 of 1951 when transferred to the Court of Additional Sub-ordinate Judge, Dhaka. Suit was decreed on 25-5-1951. Decree was passed against Sarnalata Dey. As such, Sarnalata Dey had no title, Syed Ali Habib while the suit was pending purchased the suit land from Sarnalata Dey as such, by successive purchase from titleless Sarnalata plaintiffs acquired no title over the suit property. Titleless person can not confer title but can give birth to litigation as possession of the plaintiffs as claimed is totally unauthorized and illegal.

16. Purchase of Syed Ali Habib is hit by section 53 of Transfer of Property Act. The position of plaintiffs become more worser when Syed Ali Habib filed Title Suit No. 171 of 1955 against Kaniz Fatema, the predecessor of defendant No. 1 in the court of Munsif, 6th court, Dhaka for declaration of title and for khas possession. The suit was dismissed on 28-6-1957. Title Appeal No. 120 of 1957 and Appeal from Appellate Decree No. 195 of 1958 were taken by Syed Ali Habib and was dismissed on 25-8-1959. As such plaintiffs have no title in the suit property.

17. In the question mutation. It appears in Mutation Case No. 2177/1994-95 mutation was done in faovur of plaintiffs but when defendant No. 1 came to know of such wrong recording, he filed Miscellaneous Case No. 20/1994-98 and got the mutation in favour of plaintiffs set-aside. Plaintiffs against the said order of canceling mutation, filed Miscellaneous Appeal No. 112 of 2005 before the Additional Deputy Commissioner (Revenue) Dhaka and there-after, filed Miscellaneous Appeal No. 18 of 2005 before the Additional Divisional Commissioner Dhaka and all the appeals were dismissed.

18. Next we have seen that Exhibit filed by the parties. It appears from Exhibit 'Uma' khatian No. 870/1 the suit land recorded in the name of defendant and from Exhibit `Cha' enquiry report shows that the defendants are in possession. From Exhibit `Cha' Fazlur Rahman plaintiff claimed he got mutation of .0473 Ajutangsha of land but he has found in possession of 0.0006 Ajutangsha of land. From Exhibit `Chha' it appears that plaintiffs appeal being time barred was rejected and also Assistant Commissioner found that mutation in favour of plaintiff was done contradictory to the decision of the High Court Division passed in Second Appeal No. 195 of 1998. Exhibit 'Ja' is decision of Additional Deputy Commissioner (Revenue) dismissing Miscellaneous Appeal No. 18 of 2005 filed by the plaintiff. Exhibit 'Ja-1' is Miscellaneous Appeal No. 18 of 2005 filed by the plaintiff and exhibt 'Jha' is the power of attorney.

19. The case of action as shown for filing that suit shown against the decision of revenue authority. Defendant raised objection that the suit is not maintainable as the plaintiffs did not exhaust the procedure laid down in Section 147 and 149 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, 1951. Section 147 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act speaks as:—

"Appeals-Subject to any special provisions for appeal made in this Part or in any rules made under this Act, as appeal shall lie from every original or appellate order made under any of the provisions of this Part by a Revenue officer as follows, namely :—

(a) to the Collector, when the order is made by a Revenue officer sub-ordinate to the Collector;

(b) to the Commissioner of the division, when the order is made by the Collector of a district within the division, and (c) to the Board of Land Administration when the order is made by the Commissioner of a division.

<u>20. It appears that suit was filed without exhausting the procedure as laid down in section 147(c), as such, the suit is not maintainable.</u>

21. Since in the plaint the cause of action has been shown as the order passed by the revenue authority setting-aside the mutation of the plaintiff and mutated the name of the defendant plaintiff has other hurdle too to maintain the suit i.e. Section 143B of the State Acquisition and tenancy Act which runs as :—

"144 B Bar to Jurisdiction of Civil Court-(1) When an order has been made under sub-section 1 of section 144 directing the preparation of revision of record of rights in respect of any area, then, subject to the provisions of section 111, a civil Court shall not entertain any suit or application for the alternation of any rent or determination of the status of any tenant of the incidents of any tenancy in such area and if any such suit or application relating to such area is pending before a civil Court on or after the date of such order, it shall not be further proceeded with and shall abate and if any judgment, decree or order has been passed in any such suit for any order has been passed on any such application, after the said date, it shall be inoperative and of no legal effect.

(2) No suit or application shall be brought in a civil Court in respect of any order directing the preparation or revision of record-of-rights under this Chapter or in respect of framing, publication, signing or attesting of such a record or any part of it, and if any such suit or application is pending before a civil Court, it shall not be further proceeded with and shall abate and if any judgment, decree or order has been passed in any such suit or any order has been passed on any such application, it shall be inoperative and of no legal effect."

22. It is settled by two suits that plaintiffs acquired no title over the suit land and the suit is not maintainable, learned Judge has committed no illegality in dismissing the suit. We find no merit in the appeal.

23. In the result, the appeal is dismissed without any order as to cost.

Send down the lower court records.

Communicate this judgment at once.

End.

full_judgment:
Refusal to grant reliefs to plaintiff Sreemati Hari Rani Basak by Courts below prompted her to knock at the door of this Court as petitioner on bestowing a Civil Revision Petition under section 115 of the Code of Civil Procedure (for short the Code). Civil Revision Petition has been numbered as Civil Revision No. 380 of 1991.

2. Portrayal of intrinsic datum forming backdrop of Civil Revision Petition may succinctly be stated.

3. Sreemati Hari Rani Basak as plaintiff on 19-1-1979 instituted a Suit being Title Suit No. 48 of 1979 in the First Court of Subordinate Judge, Dhaka seeking following reliefs:

a. A decree may be passed in favour of plaintiff and against defendants by confirming possession of plaintiff on "A" schedule property.

b. A decree for recovery of khas possession may be passed in favour of plaintiff and against defendants Nos. 4-12 in respect of "B" schedule property.

c. A decree may be passed in favour of plaintiff and against defendants by declaring that suit property cannot be treated as Vested and Non-resident Property.

d. A decree may be passed restraining defendants permanently not to disturb in any way plaintiff's possession in suit property.

4. Core contentions contended in plaint are:

a. Ramchandra Basak, Radhika Mohan Basak and Krishna Chandra Basak were rightful owners of suit property and their names had been correctly recorded in Cadastral Survey Khatian to the extent of 2 annas 13 gondas 1 kara 1 krantee share; 8 annas share and 5 annas, 6 gondas 2 karas and 2 krantes share respectively. Ramchandra Basak died leaving behind only son Madan Mohan Basak as his heir and Madan Mohan Basak became owner of 1/6 share of the property Radhika Mohan Basak, also, drew his last leaving behind only one son Gokul Chandra Basak as his only heir and Gokul Chandra Basak became owner of 1/2 share of property. Krishna Chandra Basak breathed his last leaving behind only son Kala Chand Basak as his only heir and Kala Chand Basak became rightful owner of 1/3 share of the property. Kala Chand Basak died leaving behind daughter Hari Rani Basak, the plaintiff, and Hari Rani Basak became owner to the extent of 1/3 share of property.

b. Suit property was put to auction in respect of property of Gokul Chandra Basak and Madan Mohan Basak and plaintiff purchased auction on 21-3-1939 through Court and got into possession of the auction purchased property. Plaintiff Hari Rani Basak by way of inheritance as well as auction purchase became 16 annas owner of suit property. Plaintiff Hari Rani Basak has been exercising acts of ownership and possession on suit property and her name had been correctly recorded in last Revisional Settlement Khatian as 16 annas owner and possessor of suit property. Plaintiff has been paying rent and got rent receipts.

c. Fourth-twelfth defendants were inducted as monthly tenants in a portion of Suit property by plaintiff and tenants defendants paid rents up to month of November, 1971, During War of Liberation of 1971, plaintiffs as well as tenants fourth-twelfth defendants left suit holding and took shelter on the other side of the border for safety of their lives. During the liberation movement plaintiff lost all counterfoils signed by tenants defendants and, also, some relevant title deeds and papers in respect of suit property. At the end of Liberation War plaintiff and fourth-twelfth defendants returned back to Bangladesh. Fourth-twelfth defendants took possession on portion of property as ejectable monthly tenants. Plaintiff demanded rent from tenants defendants defendants expressed their financial difficulty and requested plaintiff with folded hands to wait for some time. Fourth-twelfth defendants mounted endeavour to get lease of "B" schedule property from Assistant Custodian, Vested and Non-Resident Property disclosing that suit property is Vested and Non-Resident Property.

d. Cause of action of the suit arose on 17th September, 1978 when fourth-twelfth defendants refused to pay rent to plaintiff. Plaintiff, thus, had been constrained to present suit in Court on payment of ad valorem court fee on the valuation of suit which is Taka 50,000.

5. Third-defendant, Assistant Custodian of Vested Property contested the suit on presentation of a written statement pressing into service basic contentions:

a. Madan Mohan Basak, Gokul Chandra Basak and Kala Chand Basak had been exercising and enjoying case holding and they left Bangladesh with their family members in 1964 leaving the holding under care and custody of Dulal Chandra Basak, husband of plaintiff and cunning Dulal Chandra Basak taking advantage of long absence of original owners and their heirs adopted various devices to grab suit property which is purely an Enemy and Vested Property.

b. In Title Suit No. 195 of 1967 before Sixth Court of Munsif, Dhaka plaintiff took the stand that by amicable partition among other co-sharers she got 16 annas share of the holding but in the present suit she stated that she became the sole 16 annas owner and possessor of suit property by virtue of inheritance from her father Kala Chand Basal and, also, by way of auction purchase. Suit property is Enemy Property under Defence of Pakistan Rules of 1965. Plaintiff got no right, title and interest on the holding.

6. Fourth-twelfth defendants, also, laid a separate written statement, with similar averments as averred in written statement filed by third defendants except the stand not adopted by Third defendants but assumed by them that plaintiff is not the daughter of Kala Chand Basak and she is the daughter of one Krishna Chandra Basak who died leaving behind 3 sons who left for India in the year 1950. Defendants are in possession of suit property long before 1960. Under threat and coercion plaintiff's husband realised some money from some of defendants posing himself to be the owner of suit property without issuing any Rent Receipts and some of defendants paid money under mistaken belief that plaintiff's husband Dulal Chandra Basak was owner of suit property. Defendants became aware that suit property vested in Government as vested property and they applied for lease of suit property. Defendants became aware of a fraudulent suit and ex parte decree obtained by plaintiff and they laid Title Suit No. 306 of 1978 in the Sixth Court of Munsif, Dhaka for cancellation of decree.

7. Over pleadings learned Subordinate Judge framed following issues:

i. Is the suit maintainable in its present form?

ii. Is the suit barred by limitation and hit by principles of waiver, estoppel and acquiescence.

iii. Is the suit bad for defect of parties?

iv. Is the plaintiff entitled to get a decree for confirmation of possession on "A" schedule property, recovery of khas possession on "B" schedule property, permanent injunction and for declaration as prayed for?

8. Over pleadings and issues plaintiff and third-defendants fought out the suit. Fourth-twelfth defendants, though laid written statement, did not put up contest at the time of trial of suit. Evidence, both oral and documentary, had been led in support of respective contentions of plaintiff and third-defendant. Plaintiff examined two witnesses including herself as PW 1. Third-defendant placed on witness box one witness, DW 1 Tahshilder of Vested Property Cell in support of the case tabled by him. Fourth-twelfth defendants did not examine any witness in lending assurance to case put forth by them.

9. Learned Subordinate Judge as Trial Judge decided first, second and third issues in favour of plaintiff but decided fourth and fifth issues against plaintiff. In deciding fourth and fifth issues against plaintiff learned Trial Judge dismissed the suit Judgment and decree is dated 21-12-1986.

10. Plaintiff could not reconcile to above Judgment and decree and sought setting aside those through a medium of an appeal being Title Appeal No. 27 of 1987 in the Court of District Judge, Dhaka. Learned Additional District Judge, First Court Dhaka heard the appeal and by Judgment and Decree dated 14-10-1990 dismissed the appeal and maintained Judgment and Decree awarded by learned Trial Judge.

11. Feeling dissatisfied with appellate Judgment and Decree plaintiff Sreemati Hari Rani Basak as petitioner approached this Court in Civil Revision petition.

12. Sreemati Hari Rani Basak having breathed her last during pendency of Civil Revision her legal heirs had been substituted as petitioner Nos. 1(1)-1(10). Sreemati Hari Rani Basak shall be referred to hereinafter as plaintiff-petitioner. Substituted petitioners shall be described as petitioners. Third-defendant shall be known as third-defendant-opposite party. Fourth-twelfth defendants shall be described as fourth-twelfth defendants-opposite parties.

13. Petitioners submitted three Supplementary Affidavits incorporating some material facts and annexing some documents and papers as Annexures.

14. Second-defendant-Second opposite party Additional Deputy Commissioner (Revenue), though did not lay any written statement, and, also, did not put up contest in the suit along with contesting third-defendant-opposite party filed Counter-Affidavit controverting statements made in Revision Petition.

15. Eleventh-defendant-eleventh-opposite party, also, though did not put up contest in the suit in spite of filing written statement along with other defendants- opposite parties, brought into existence Affidavit-in-opposition traversing statements embodied in Revision Petition.

16. Grounds pressed into service and contentions advanced from side of petitioners are catalogued hereunder:

i. Plaintiff-petitioner on oath having stated that she is the daughter of Kala Chand Basak, a co-sharer having 5 annas interest in suit property and contesting defendant having adduced no evidence contrary to that of plaintiff, Courts below committed an error of law in failing to hold that plaintiff is the daughter of Kala Chand Basak, and, plaintiff, as such, is entitled to a decree prayed for in the suit and by decisions of Courts below a failure of justice has been occasioned.

ii. Plaintiff-petitioner having asserted her source of title on inheritance as well as auction purchase of shares of other two co-sharers in the suit property, Courts below committed an error of law in failing to dispose of claim of plaintiff with reference to legal evidence on record and decisions of Courts below in dismissing the suit of plaintiff suffers from a gross illegality and legal infirmity and a failure of justice has been occasioned to plaintiffs-petitioners.

iii. Rule 3 of Order VIII enshrines: It shall not be sufficient for a defendant in his written statement to deny generally the grounds alleged by the plaintiff, but the defendant must deal specifically with each allegation of fact of which he does not admit the truth, except damages. Rule 5 of Order VIII postulates: Every allegation of fact in the plaint, if not denied specifically or by necessary implication, or stated to be not admitted in the pleading of the defendant, shall be taken to be admitted except as against a person under disability: Provided that the Court may, in its discretion, require any fact so admitted to be proved otherwise than by such admission. Mandate of rule 5 of Order VIII is that unless allegation of fact contained in the plaint is not specifically denied, that allegation of fact shall be taken to be admitted. Since third-defendant opposite-party did not put forward any specific denial in respect of statement of fact in the plaint that she is the grand-daughter of Krishna Chandra Basak and daughter of Kala Chand Basak that statement shall stand treated as admitted by third-defendant-opposite party.

Evidence provided by plaintiff as PW 1 in respect of her heirship from her father Kala Chand Basak could be endeavoured to be flung to the winds by way of cross-examination from side of fourth-twelfth defendants but plaintiff PW 1 was not at all cross-examined from side of fourth-twelfth defendants. Cross-examination of a witness is the greatest legal engine for discovery of the truth. Cross-examination is directed to bring to light truth by clarifying matters which a witness may deserve to keep concealed. Failure on the part of fourth-twelfth defendants-opposite parties to cross-examine plaintiff PW 1 definitely raises presumption and legal inference that evidence provided by plaintiff PW 1 in examination-in-chief has been accepted by fourth-twelfth defendants. Support for the proposition of law is sought to be drawn from authoritative observation of  Lord Chancellor Herschell in the case of Browne vs Dunn (1983)6, R 67, AEG Carapiet vs AY Derderain, 1961 Calcutta 359 DB and Nur Mohammad and another vs Sultan Ahmed and another, 40 DLR 369.

23. Authoritative observation of Lord Chancellor Hershell in the case of Browne vs Dunn (Supra) has been couched in the following language:

"Now my Lords, I cannot help saying that it seems to me to be absolutely essential to the proper conduct of a cause where it is intended to suggest that a witness is not speaking the truth on a particular point, to direct his attention to the fact, by some questions put in cross-examination showing that imputation is intended to be made, and not to take his evidence and pass it by as a matter altogether unchallenged and then, when it is possible for him to explain, as perhaps he might have been able to do if such questions had been put to him, the circumstances which it is suggested indicate that the story he tells ought not to be believed, to argue that he is a witness unworthy of credit Mr Lords, I have always understood that if you intend to impeach a witness give are bound, whilst he is in the box, to give him an opportunity of making any explanation which is open to him, and as it seems to me, that is not only a rule of professional practice in the conduct of a case, but is essential to fair play and fair dealing with witness."

24. In AEG Carapiet vs AY Derderain (Supra) it has been laid down

"Wherever the opponent has declined to avail himself of the opportunity to put his essential and material case in cross-examination, it must follow that he believed that the testimony given could not be disputed at all. It is wrong to think that this is merely a technical rule of evidence. It is a rule of essential justice."

25. In Nur Mohammad and another vs Sultan Ahmed and another (Supra) it has been held:

"It is a well settled principle of law regarding cross examination that on failure of a party to cross-examine the witness of his adversary appearing against him on material evidence it will be presumed by Court that testimony given by that witness-in-chief has been accepted as it cannot be suggested that his statement on a particular fact is untrue unless he is cross-examined drawing his attention to that fact and thereby giving him an opportunity to explain the same. This rule of cross-examination is not merely "a technical rule of evidence" but it is as well "a rule of essential justice" because it is essential to fair play and fair dealing with witnesses."

38. In Naigar Timapa vs Bhaskar Parnzaya and another (Supra) it has been held:

Under section 316 of the Civil Procedure Code (Act X of 1877) the title of a purchaser at a Court sale becomes complete upon his payment of the purchase-money and confirmation of the sale by the Court. When the sale is admitted, production of a certificate is not necessary to prove that fact.

39. In Jagannath (Plaintiff) vs Baldeo (Defendant) (Supra) it was held:

It was not incumbent on a purchaser at an execution-sale under Act VIII of 1859, which was confirmed in his favour under that Act, when suing for possession of the property, to produce a sale-certificate, but it was competent for him to prove his purchase aliunde. The confirmation of the sale in his favour was prima facie evidence of his title to the property, and was sufficient to pass such title to him, of which a certificate, if afterwards obtained by him, would merely be evidence that the property had so passed.

40. The order affirming the sale will be sufficient to pass a title to the purchaser, and the certificate which might afterwards be obtained by him would merely evidence that the property so passed.

44. Point No. 3: The term "Enemy" is derived from the word "Enemigo" The literal meaning of "Enemigo" is "An Enemy". In Public Law, the term "Enemy" signifies either  the state which is at war with another or a  citizen or subject of such state, or a person,  partnership, or Corporation doing business  within the territory of an enemy state or an ally thereof.

The concept of "Enemy" and "Enemy Property" were offspring of Defence of Pakistan Ordinance, 1965 (XXIII of 1965) and Rules framed thereunder. Defence of Pakistan Ordinance and Rules framed thereunder made by Central Government of Pakistan in exercise of powers conferred by section 3 of The Ordinance are reproduction of Defence of India Act and Rules of 1939 made under the Act. On 6-9-1965 Emergency was proclaimed by the then President of the then Pakistan who declared that grave emergency existed and Pakistan was in eminent danger of being threatened by war. Further declaration was that Pakistan was at war with India. In pursuance of Declaration of Emergency the then President of Pakistan promulgated Defence of Pakistan Ordinance, 1965 (XXIII of 1965). In exercise of powers conferred by section 3 of the Ordinance, Central Government framed Rules, which are called The Defence of Pakistan Rules. In exercise of power conferred by Rule 182 of Defence of Pakistan Rules, which is contained in Part XVI of aforesaid Rules dealing with Enemy Property, empowers the Government to promulgate order and prescribe thereby the doing of certain acts by custodian as stipulated in clauses (a) and (f).

45. In exercise of the power conferred by sub-rule 1 of Rule 182 of the Defence of Pakistan Rules, the then Governor of East Pakistan promulgated East Pakistan Enemy Property (Land and Buildings) Administration and Disposal Order, 1966 and this Order was promulgated for administration and management of Enemy Property in erstwhile East Pakistan.

46. In sub-rule 2 of Rule 2 of The Defence of Pakistan Rules the expression "Enemy" has been defined as hereunder:

"Enemy" means any person or State at war with Pakistan.

In sub-rule 3 of Rule 2 "Enemy Territory" has been coined as follows:

Any area which is under the sovereignty of or administered by or for the time being in the occupation of a State at war with Pakistan.

In Rule 161 of The Defence of Pakistan Rules the expression "Enemy" had been stated in the following way:

(a)	any State or sovereign of State at war with Pakistan or

(b) any individual resident in any enemy territory.

Sub-rule 1 of Rule 169 defines any Enemy subject as hereunder:

(a) any individual who possesses the Nationality of State at War with Pakistan or having possessed such Nationality at any time has lost it without acquiring another Nationality.

Sub-rule 4 of Rule 169 defines "Enemy property" as follows:

"Enemy Property" means any property for the time being belonging to or held or managed on behalf of an enemy as defined in rule 161, an enemy subject or an enemy firm, but does not include property which is "evacuee property" under the Pakistan "Administration of Evacuee Property Act."

47. In the backdrop of definition of "Enemy" and "Enemy Property" defined and coined in The Defence of Pakistan Rules, the pivotal points now emerge are: Whether plaintiff-petitioner or her predecessor father Kala Chand Basak had been resident in enemy territory, that is India, during the period of Proclamation of Emergency and whether they were enemies as defined under sub-rule 2 of Rule 2 of Defence of Pakistan Rules and whether the property can be treated as Enemy property now Vested property.

58. The word "Domicile" is derived from Latin word "Domus" meaning home or dwelling house. "Domicile" is the legal conception of Home and the term "Home" is frequently used in defining or describing the legal concept of Domicile. In Corpus Juris Secundum 28 page 3 it is stated:

Domicile is the relation which the law creates between an individual and a particular locality or country. What has been said to be the most comprehensive and correct definition which could be given is that in a strict legal sense the domicile of a person is the place where he has true, fixed, permanent home and principal establishment and to which, whenever he is absent, he has the intention of returning.

59. In Bell vs Kennedy (1868) LR 1 HL 307 it has been laid down:

A domicile of origin though intended to be abandoned will continue until a new domicile is acquired and the new domicile is not acquired until there is not only a fixed intention of establishing a permanent residence in some other country but this intention is carried out by actual residence there.

60. In Winans and another vs Attorney-General (1904) AC 287 the question of loss of domicile of origin of a citizen came up for consideration. It has been held:

The onus of proving that a domicile has been chosen in substitution for the domicile of origin lies upon those who assert that the domicile of origin has been lost. The domicile of origin continues unless a fixed and settled intention of abandoning the first domicile and acquiring another as the sole domicile is clearly shown.

Observation of Lord Halsbury, in the case, has been couched in the following terms:

The law is plain, that where a domicile of origin is proved, lies upon the person who asserts a change of domicile to establish it.

61. The question of loss of domicile came up before the Allahabad High Court in Abida Khatoon and another vs State of UP and others, AIR 1963 Allahabad 260. Observation of Dhawan, J. has been coined in the following language:

Citizenship does not evaporate with the passing of time; it clings to a person wherever he may roam. It cannot be taken away from him, unless he voluntarily renounces it or is guilty of some conduct involving loss of citizenship. The onus of proving that a citizen of India has lost his citizenship is on the party seeking to deprive him of his rights as a citizen.

Further observation is in the following terms:

To every adult person the law assigns a domicile which is called the domicile of origin and which remains attached to him until a new and different domicile takes its place. The domicile of origin must prevail until the party has not only manifested but carried into execution an intention of abandoning his former domicile and acquiring another as his sole domicile.

62. The proposition of law enunciated in Winans and another vs Attorney-General (Supra) and Abida Khatoon and another vs State of UP and others (Supra) was quoted with approval in Superintendent and Remembrancer of Legal Affairs, Government of East Pakistan vs Kiron Chandra Dutta, 17 DLR 60 = 15 PLR Dhaka 436 and, also, in Remembrancer of Legal Affairs, Government of Bangladesh vs Adyaita Chandra Adhikary 33 DLR 314.

66. Former Enemy Property now Vested Property personnel i.e. Assistant Custodian, cannot take possession of the alleged leased out property without having the property partitioned by metes and bounds on institution of a regular and proper suit for partition. The legal debate came up for consideration in Anil Kumar Dutta Chowdhury vs Province of East Pakistan and others, 23 DLR 108. fourth-twelfth-respondents in Writ Petition had been granted lease/settlement of the suit land by Third-Respondent Assistant Custodian of Enemy Property and lessee had been authorised by Enemy Property Authority to go to possession on suit land. Petitioner of Writ Petition is a co-sharer to the extent of one (1) anna share in some khatians and two (2) annas share in some other khatians. Question arose whether lessee could get into possession of suit property without a partition of the leased out property on a properly instituted civil suit. It has been held:

Even if the co-sharers made amicable arrangement for separate possession of their lands for convenience that would not amount to partition of the lands in question by metes and bounds in accordance with law.

It has been further laid down:

A co-sharer is presumed to have right, title, interest and possession in every inch of the disputed land. In the present case the petitioner's right and possession in the lands in question have been admitted by the respondents who cannot now interfere with the same without bringing a suit for partition in a civil Court in accordance with law.

The dictum laid down by Judicial verdict is that a co-sharer in possession of a property could not be said to be in unlawful possession within the meaning of Enemy Property laws and was not liable to be ousted from the property without bringing a partition suit in Civil Court.

In that case we have clearly held that a person who is in possession of a property of an enemy by virtue of an agreement either of tenancy or of purchase cannot be termed as an illegal or unauthorised occupier and, as such, cannot be asked to quit the property and hand over possession thereof to the custodian of enemy property.

71. In Messrs MM Ispahani Ltd vs Deputy Custodian of Enemy Property (Lands and Buildings) and Director of Land Records & Surveys, East Pakistan, Eden Buildings, Dhaka and another 26 DLR 493 which was a case of a person in possession of an enemy property by holding over on the expiry of lease agreement and, also, on the basis of an agreement for purchase, Siddiky CJ once again considered the legal debate and laid down :

Any person in occupation of a property which is declared to be an enemy property cannot, in general, be said to be in unlawful possession thereof only because the property has been declared to be an enemy property.

72. In Ananda Mohan Kundu and others vs Province of East Pakistan, Chief Secretary, Government of East Pakistan, Eden Buildings and others 20 DLR 976 which was a case of two person in possession of an enemy property on the strength of an agreement for purchase. Siddiky, CJ over again observed:

What the legislature intended is that all enemy property should vest in the Custodian for the purpose mentioned in rule 182 of the Defence of Pakistan Rules with a view to protecting the enemy properties being utilized in any manner for the benefit of the enemy or in the interest of the enemy State and to the prejudice of Pakistan. Therefore, it amounts to only a control over the enemy property by the Custodian. If after vesting of the enemy property in the Custodian it is found on enquiry that a person who is occupying the said property is holding some sort of a document of title, though imperfect, from the real owner of the property who happens to be the enemy, then, if the occupier is a citizen of Pakistan he cannot be ousted from the property because of mere vesting order of the Government.

In the said case it has been further stated:

There is considerable force in the argument of Mr Ahmed that mere vesting of the enemy property in the Custodian does not transgress on the title or the ultimate right of the real owner and a person in possession of the enemy property by virtue of a document of however limited or imperfect nature it may be cannot be said to be a trespasser and he cannot be ousted from it by the Custodian.

73. Shah Ghulam Nabi and others vs Vice-Chairman, East Pakistan Enemy Property Management Board, Dacca and others 22 DLR 48 was a case of three persons in possession of premises where a Rice and Oil Mill were situated on the footing of an agreement for partnership. AS Chowdhury J (as his Lordship then was) took into stock Mamtazuddin Ahmed Chowdhury vs Deputy Commissioner & Assistant Custodian of Enemy Property, Comilla (Supra), Messrs MM Ispahani Ltd vs Deputy Custodian of Enemy Property (Lands and Buildings) and Director of Land Records and Surveys, East Pakistan, Eden Buildings, Dacca and another (Supra) and Ananda Mohan Kundu and others vs Province of East Pakistan, Chief Secretary, Government of East Pakistan, Eden Buildings and others (Supra) and held:

The respondents can oust the petitioners only by obtaining an order of eviction in a properly/property constituted suit.

Even testimony of plaintiff PWs 1 and PW 2 on factum of possession could not be, also, blown away by way of any cross-examination from the side of contesting third defendant-opposite party.

88. On a careful assessment of pleadings, evidences, materials on record and fact and circumstances of the case the irresistible conclusion that can be drawn is that plaintiff-petitioner could successfully prove her right, title and possession on suit property and plaintiffs petitioner is entitled to get decree of confirmation of possession on 'A' Schedule property and, also, for a decree of recovery of khas possession against fourth-twelfth-defendants in respect of 'B' Schedule property.

89. Point No. 4 stands ruled out in the terms that plaintiff-petitioner is entitled to a decree of confirmation of possession in respect of property described in schedule 'A' and recovery of khas possession in schedule 'B' property to the plaint.

90. Point No. 5: Plaintiff-petitioner had already been armed with a decree of Permanent Injunction in respect of suit property against the Government of Bangladesh, Deputy Custodian of Enemy Property (Land and Buildings) and Assistant Custodian (Land and Buildings) and Additional Deputy Commissioner, Dhaka in Title Suit No. 195 of 1967, Decree of Permanent Injunction, though passed ex parte, had neither been challenged by Government nor by Enemy Property Authority till today in spite of their clear and definite knowledge of ex parte decree from date of its passing, and, especially from the day when summons of present Title Suit No. 48 of 1979 had been served upon First-Third Defendant i.e. Government of Bangladesh, Deputy Custodian of Enemy Property and Assistant Custodian of Enemy Property (Land and Building) and Additional Deputy Commissioner (Revenue), Dhaka and they contested suit on laying written statement and producing DW 1 as witness. It had been positively found that fourth-twelfth-defendants-opposite parties are ejectable tenants under plaintiff-petitioner and fourth-twelfth-defendants-opposite parties are now restrained by a decree of Permanent Injunction from disturbing in any way plaintiff's petitioner's possession on suit property.

91. Point No. 5 is resolved in epithet that plaintiff-petitioner is entitled to a decree of Permanent Injunction against fourth-twelfth-defendants-opposite parties and fourth-twelfth-defendants-opposite party are restrained by a decree of Permanent Injunction from disturbing in any way plaintiff's petitioner's possession over suit property.

92. Point No. 6: In view of discourse made in foregoing paragraphs the insurmountable verdict that can be proclaimed is that decisions reached by Learned Trial Judge and Appellate Judge do not at all claim any justification as those are not backed by legal evidence, materials on record and fact and circumstances of the case. There had been misconstruction and misreading of material documents and total misdirection in the approach on the part of Learned Trial Judge and Appellate Judge in resolving legal controversies. Decisions suffer from sheer waywardness, gross illegality, legal infirmity and grave error of law. Decisions, though concurrent, having been vitiated by error of law, cannot claim any immunity from being censured in exercise of Revisional Jurisdiction envisaged in section 115 of The Code Interference is, therefore, called for.

93. Point No. 6 stands answered in the language that Judgments under challenge in Civil Revision case cannot be sustained on evidences, materials on record, fact and circumstances of the case and, also, in safe dispensation of Civil Justice.

94. Having bestowed my anxious and dis-passionate consideration on pleadings, evidences, materials on record, facts, circumstances and pros and cons of the case, also, ruminating laws and principles of Enemy Property and other legal aspects, I am of the considered view that Rule springing out of a Civil Revision Petition under section 115 of The Code carries substance. It survives. Rule is made absolute. Judgments and Decrees recorded by Courts below stand set aside/ quashed. Plaintiff-petitioner's suit is decreed in following terms:

A. Possession of plaintiff-petitioner in 'A' Schedule Property is confirmed.

B. Recovery of khas possession on B Schedule property is granted in favour of plaintiff-petitioner and against defendants-opposite parties. Decree-Holder-plaintiff-petitioner shall get possession of B Schedule property within four (4) months from date of receipt of this Judgment.

C. Suit property could and can neither be treated nor be declared as former Enemy Property now Vested Property and treating suit property as Vested Property is illegal, void, ultra vires and without jurisdiction.

D. Fourth-twelfth-defendants-opposite parties are restrained by way of Permanent Injunction from disturbing in any way plaintiff-petitioner's possession on suit property.

95. Status quo granted by this Court at the time of issuance of Rule stands vacated.

96. Civil Rule No. 11(R) of 2000 arising out of a Petition for Contempt of Court is not at all pressed, and, as such, it stands discharged for non-prosecution.

97. No cost.

Lower Courts Records are sent down.

End.
