full_judgment:
Mir Hashmat Ali J: This Rule Nisi was issued calling upon the respondents to show cause as to why Order dated 17-5-2006 passed by the First Court of Settlement, Dhaka in Case No. 362 of 1989 dismissing the case for non-prosecution should not be declared to have been made without lawful authority and is of no legal effect.

2. Thirteen petitioners in the instant Writ Petition challenged the Order dated 17-5-2006 passed by the First Court of Settlement, Dhaka passed in Settlement Case No. 362 of 1989 dismissing the case for non-prosecution at the instance of respondent No.5 without discussing the matter on merit.

3. Short facts of the petitioners case are that the case property originally belonged to one Janaki Ballav Dutt, who made a registered will in favour of his wife Sreemati Mallika Sundari Dutt and son Kalipada butt. After his death they obtained probate from the Court of District Judge, Dhaka andsold out the cte property to (i) Md. Faiz Hossain Miah, (ii) Abdul Latif Mia, (iii) Joynal Abedin Mia and (iv) Serajul Islam by registered deed No. 432 dated 28-11-1945.

4. After purchase they went into possession and enjoying the case property and mutated their names in the records of Dhaka Municipal Corporation. The SA record the name of the previous owner Janaki Ballav Dutt was maintained. During the enjoyment of the case property the said Md Faiz Hossain Mia died leaving behind his six sons, namely (i) Moazzem Hossain (ii) Nur Hossain, (iii) Ahmed Hossain, (iv) Mosharraf Hossain, (v) Mobarak Hossain and (vi) Muzammel Hossain as his legal heirs. Abdul Latif Mia died leaving behind two sons namely, (i) Aminul Islam and (ii) Mominul Islam who were enjoying the property. After death of Joynal Abedin has three sons (i) Azizul Huq, (ii) Zahirul Huq and (iii) Mezbaul Huq were in possession of the case property. Serajul Islam also died leaving behind his only daughter Selina Khatun as his legal heir and all of them became the owners in possession of the case property in ejmali.

5. Immediately after liberation of Bangladesh, the aforesaid owner and successors of late Md Faiz Hossain Mia, late Abdul Latif Mia, late Joynal Abedin and late Serajul Islam were at their village home at Keranigonj and the case property was under their lock and key; taking advantage of absence of the owners from the house some miscreants illegally entered into the case property, occupied the same and they made an application to the Sub-Divisional Office (South), Dhaka on 3-12-1973 to release the same and paid Municipal Taxes up to 1973. Subsequently, the case property was enlisted in 'Ka' list of the abandoned property, which was published in Bangladesh Gazette on 23-9-1086. Consequently, the petitioners and other co-sharer filed an application under section 7 of the Abandoned Building (Supplementary Provision) Ordinance, 1985 and it was registered as Settlement Case No. 362 of 1989. Further case of the petitioners are that the aforesaid co-sharer made amicable partition of their joint property along with the case property and the heirs of late Md Faiz Hossain Mia named as Moazzem Hossain, Noor Hossain, Ahmed Hossain, Mosharraf Hossain, Mobarak Hossain and Mozammel Hossain got the case holdingin their share and all the said heirs of late Md Faiz Hossain died except Mobarak Hossain, the petitioner No. 1-3 are the heirs of the said Noor Hossain, the petitioners No. 4-7-are the heirs of late Md Mosharraf Hossain, petitioners No. 8-10 are the heirs of late Md Mozammel Hossain, petitioner No. 11 is the heir of late Ahmed Hossain, and petitioners No. 12-13 are the heirs of late Md Moazzam Hossain.

6. The respondent No.4 Md Shahidul Islam is the DN holder of the property in question. The petitioners while in their village home in Keranigonj, in their absence the Court of Settlement dismissed the case for default on 13-11-1991. Against the said Order co-sharers including present petitioner Nos. 4-7,12-13 and respondent No.5 as petitioners filed Writ Petition No. 2129 of 1999 before the High Court Division of the Supreme Court and obtained Rule. After hearing the learned Advocate of the par- ties, the said Rule was made absolute vide judgment and Order dated 29-6-2004 and directed the Court of Settlement to dispose of the case within one month from the date of receipt of the judgment after serving notice to all petitioners.

7. The record of the Court of Settlement was sent back to the Court of Settlement, which was received by the Court of Settlement on 13-10-2004. The Court of Settlement was not constituted; the case was fixed for hearing on 9-11-2004 without notifying the parties. The matter was adjourned till 21-3-2006. But the Court of Settlement did not notify the same to all the parties. In the meantime, the respondent No. 5 filed an application before the Court of Settlement on 30-4-2006 without serving copies for all the parties. The said application was heard on 30-4-2006 without notifying all the parties which was subsequently, re-fixed on 17-5-2006 and, after hearing the same, the Court of Settlement, 1st Court of Dhaka vide Order dated 17-5-2006 allowed the application for dismissal the case for non-prosecution.

8. The petitioners on 10-4-2007 through one Haji Md Musa came to know for the 1st time that the Court of Settlement dismissed the case for non-prosecution. Then and there the petitioner rushed to the Court of Settlement and after perusal the case record came to know about the dismissal of the case for non-prosecution.

9. Thereafter, the petitioner filed an application before the Court of Settlement, 1st Court, Dhaka for restoration of the case stating that after the remand Order of the High Court the respondent No.5, Mobarak Hossain filed an application for withdrawal of the case without their consent. The Court of Settlement served no notice to the parties whatsoever or upon any of the co-applicants.

10. The petitioners before this Court as applicants filed an application to the Court of settlement for restoration the case.

11. The Court of Settlement heard the said application on 15-4-2007 and after hearing the petitioners, the Court of Settlement rejected the application for restoration vide Order dated 15-4-2007 on the ground that the Court of Settlement has no jurisdiction to restore the case.

12. Being aggrieved, the petitioners filed instant Writ Petition and obtained Rule.

13. Mr MI Faruqui, Senior Advocate appearing with Mr Md Ruhul Quddus and Mr Mohammad Zahid Imam, the learned Advocates for the petitioners submits that under section 10 of the Law of Abandoned Property Ordinance, 1985 (Ordinance No. LIV of 1985) the Court of Settlement has no power to pass any Order for non-prosecution even if prayed for. He further submits that the Code of Civil Procedure 1908 shall not apply to the Court of Settlement and, as such, the Order XXIII of the Code of Civil Procedure is not applicable, wherein the Court has empowered to withdraw the suit or proceeding. He further submits that our apex Court in their various decisions has decided that after filing of a case before the Court of Settlement, the Court of Settlement has nothing to do but to give decision of the matter. He further submits that Section 10 of the Ordinance No. LIV if 1985 has given procedure for disposal of cases of the Court of Settlement, beyond the said procedure the court of Settlement has no power to dispose of cases even if prayed for. He further submits that in the instant case one of the power holders Mr Mobarak Hossain, who was the applicant before the Court of Settlement filed an application for non-prosecution against the interest of Power of Attorney giver. But the said application was filed beyond the knowledge of the petitioners. The Court of Settlement served no notice to the petitioners as directed by the High Court Division in Writ Petition No. 2129 of 1999 and thus the Court of Settlement violated the direction of the High Court Division and committed illegality. He further submits that the Order of non- prosecution or withdrawal of the case, the Court of Settlement has no jurisdiction and thus the Court of Settlement acted beyond its jurisdiction. In support of his contention, he cited the case of Sukurjan Bibi vs Chairman, Court of Settlement, Dhaka reported in 54 DLR 215, the case of Government of the People s Republic of Bangladesh vs Md Shamsul Haque, reported in 56 DLR (AD) 101.

14. Mr Md Khalilur Rahman appearing with Md TH Shakil Hossain and Mr Md Khalilur Rahman (Helal) the learned Advocate for the respondent No.4 by submitting affidavit-in-opposition submits that the respondent No.4 purchased the property from one Shibli and entered into the possession of the property. He further submits that though the property in question originally belong to Haji Faiz Hossain, Miah Abdul Latif, Joynal Abedin Miah and Serajul Islam, the predecessors of the petitioners transferred the same to three non-Bengali namely (i) Shamim Ahammed, (ii) Haji Mohammad Omar and (iii) Nafis Ahammed. Lastly in the year 1969 and during liberation war or thereafter said three non-Bengalis left the country for Pakistan deserting their all properties including the case property. Accordingly, the property was devolved upon the Government by operation of PO 16 of 1972. Thereafter; Government sold out the property to five allottees namely Md Nazrul Islam, Haji Emran Hossain, Md Mobarak Hossain, Md Shahidul Islam and Hafiz Akanda by registered deed of trans- fer No. 1920 dated 11-3-1986, 1921 dated 11-3- 1986, 1922 dated 11-3-1986 and 1923 dated 11-3- 1986 respectively. Thereafter the suit property was ultimately devolved upon Md Shafat Imtiaz who transferred 0.0108 acres of land to Haji Shamsul Huque on 18-5-2003 and said Haji Shamsul Huque got approval of the plan from RAJUK for constructing a nine storied building in the said land and also completed the construction of nine storied building. The respondent No.5 for himself and as attorney of others who collusively filed Settlement Case No. 362 of 1989 before the Court of Settlement and ultimately he withdrawn the case by filing application and the Court of Settlement withdrawn the case for non-prosecution. He further submits that since the respondent No. 5 acted for himself and on behalf of other petitioners as power of attorney holder of the petitioners all act done by the respondent No. 5 in respect of the case-property is binding upon all others petitioners. He further submits that who has filed the case, he has power to withdraw the case and the Court of Settlement passed the Order in accordance with law and thereby committed no illegality. He further submits that the petitioners claim that they have inherited the case property but fact remains that the predecessor of the petitioners already transferred their share in favour of three non-Bengali namely Haji Mohammad Omar, Shamim Ahmed and  Nafiz Ahmed and, as such, the petitioners have no interest in the case property. He further submits that the casebefore the Court of settlement is a fruitless litigation and Court should not allow continuing to a fruitless litigation. In support of his contention, he cited the case of Sanatannessa Bewa vs Haipatullah Sarkar reported in 41 DLR (AD) 105.

15. He further submits that since the petitioners have no interest over the case property, they are not aggrieved person according to Article 102 of the Constitution and, as such, they cannot file an application for enforcement of any fundamental right. In support of his contention, he cited the case Mian Ahmed Kibria vs Government of Bangladesh, reported in 18 BLD 459.

16. We have heard the learned Advocates of both the parties at length and perused the Writ Petition, supplementary affidavit, affidavit in opposition and the annexures thereof.

17. We have also perused the impugned Order dated 17-5-2006 Annexures-'B' series. We find that the settlement case was dismissed forenoon-prosecution against which the petitioner obtained this Rule. To consider the matter let us see the sequence of the case. It appears that the petitioners filed Settlement Case No. 362 of 1989 before the Court of Settlement under section 7 of the Abandoned Building (Supplementary Provision) Ordinance, 1985 (Ordinance No. 54 of 1985). The said case was dismissed for default due to the absence of the petitioners. Being aggrieved the petitioners filed Writ Petition No. 2129 of 1999 before this Court and the said, Rule was made absolute and the said Order of dismissal for default dated 13-11-1991 was declared illegal and the Court of Settlement directed to dispose of the case within one month from the date of receipt of the judgment after notifying the parties. The said direction was received by the Court of Settlement on 13-10-2004. But the petitioners were not notified by the Court of Settlement and several dates were adjourned due to non-availability of appointment of member and appointment of lawyer for conducting the case of the Government.

18. Subsequently, on 27-12-2005 one Mobarak Hossain claiming himself as power of attorney holder filed an application for non-prosecution of the case.

19. In paragraph No. 16 of the Writ Petition, the petitioners claimed that there is no consent of the petitioners for filing an application for non-prosecution of the settlement case.

20. It further appears that no notice was served upon the petitioners for the same. But the Court of Settlement dismissed the case for non-prosecution.

21. Let us see, whether Court of Settlement is authorised to dismiss a case for non-prosecution. Section 10 of Law of Abandoned Property Ordinance (Ordinance No. 54 of 1985) has been enacted for the purpose of Power and Procedure of Court of Settlement for disposal of a case.

22. Section 10 runs thus:

Power and procedure of Court of Settlement-

10. Power and procedure of Court of Settlement:

(1) Except as otherwise provided in this Ordinance, the provisions of the Code of Civil Procedure, 1903 (Act V of 1908), shall not apply to a Court of Settlement.

(2) For the purpose of hearing an application, a Court of Settlement shall have all the powers of a Civil Court, while trying a suit under the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908 (Act V of 1908), in respect of the following matters, namely:-

(a) Summoning and enforcing the attendance of any person and examining him on oath;

(b) Requiring the discovery and production of any document;

(c) Requiring evidence on affidavit;

(d) Requisitioning any public record or copy thereof from any office; and

(e) Issuing commissions for the examination of witnesses or documents.

(3) Any proceeding before a Court of Settlement shall be deemed to be a judicial proceeding within the meaning of section 193 of the Penal Code (Act XLV of 1860).

(4) A Court of Settlement shall hold its sit- tings at such place or places as the Government may fix.

(5) A Court of Settlement shall, after such enquiry as it may deem necessary and after giving reasonable opportunity to the parties concerned of being heard and also adducing evidence, both oral and documentary, if any, make such decision on the prayer of the applicant as it deems fit.

(6) The decision on [of] the Court of Settlement shall be final and shall be binding on all parties concerned and shall not be called in question in any other Court.

(7) No appeal shall lie from any Order of decision of the Court of Settlement to any other Court of authority.

23. From the above, we find that the Court of Settlement has no power to use the provisions of Civil Procedure Code. Since the Civil Procedure Code is not applicable in the cases pending before Court of Settlement. In this regard Order XXIII of the Civil Procedure Code wherein the provisions of withdrawal of cases has been enacted is not applicable for the Court of Settlement. It further appears from sub section 5 of section 10 of the said Ordinance, which has made mandatory upon the Court of Settlement to make decision as it deems fit and, as such, it is clear that the Court of Settlement is to dispose of the case on the basis of the materials before it notwithstanding the fact that the petitioner is absent or took no steps. This view has already been supported in various decisions of this Court. In the case of Government of the People's Republic of Bangladesh and another reported in 56 DLR (AD) 101, which has been held that; "It appears from the .impugned Order that the Court of Settlement dismissed the case for default and that although the law requires decision is to be given as to whether the enlistment of the abandoned building have been done legally or not and accordingly, the High Court Division rightly sent the case back on remand for deciding the issue in the light of the observation made therein".

24. Whether the property in question is abandoned or not is to be decided by the Court of Settlement not by any other Court. Similar view was taken in the case of Sukurjan Bibi vs Chairman, Court of Settlement, Dhaka reported in 54 DLR 215. Wherein it has been held that:

"There is no scope for the Court of Settlement to pass an ex-parte Order of dismissal for default as the Court of Settlement is required to give a decision on the issues raised by the parties ."

25. Similar view was also taken in the case of Shamima Begum vs Chairman, Court of Settlement reported in 52 DLR 456, the case of Chand Miah Talukder vs Chairman, Court of Settlement, Bangladesh Abandoned Building reported in 45 DLR 304, the case of Bangladesh vs Feroz Ahmed reported in I BLC (AD) 149.

26. Mr Md Khalilur Rahman, the learned Advocate appearing for the respondent No.4 took the floor of the respondent No.5 and submitted that the petitioners have got no interest in the case property and that the Court should not entertain a suit or case for fruitless litigation.

27. Whether the petitioners have got no interest and title over the case property or they are fighting for a fruitless litigation is the matter of evidence which is to be decided by the Court of Settlement itself after recording of evidences adduce by the respective parties at the time of trial of the case, not by this Court and, as such, we do not find any sub- stance in the submission of the learned Advocate for the respondent No.4 and thus the decisions cited by him are not applicable in the facts and circumstances of the instant case.

<u>28. In the earlier judgment passed in Writ Petition No. 2129 of 1999, the Court of Settlement was directed to dispose of the case within one month from the date of receipt of the judgment after notifying the parties concerned. But the Court of Settlement without notifying all the concerned parties passed an Order of dismissal for non-prosecution and that all the parties were not aware of any application for non-prosecution. Since the Court of Settlement is not empowered to apply Order XXIII of the Code of Civil Procedure and since in several decisions it has been settled that the Court of Settlement is to give decision to its cases, there is no provision for dismissal for non-prosecution or dismissal for default and, as such, the impugned Order of dismissal for non-prosecution is liable to be declared to have been made without lawful authority and is of no legal effect.</u>

29. The learned Advocate for the petitioners submitted that it is not possible for the Court of Settlement to dispose of the case within one month after notifying all the parties concern and prayed for a direction to dispose of the case after notifying all the parties preferably within 3 (three) months from the date of receipt of this judgment and Order of this Court.

30. Considering the submissions, we feel that the justice will be met if we direct the Court of Settlement to dispose of the case after notifying all the parties concern preferably within 3(three) months from the date of receipt of this judgment and Order.

31. In the result, the Rule is made absolute, however, without any Order as to the cost. The Court of Settlement is directed to give decision of the case after notifying all the parties concerned preferably within 3 (three) months from the date of receipt of this Judgment and Order.

Communicate the Order at once.

End.

full_judgment:
Syed Md. Ziaul Karim J: This Rule, at the instance of defendant-petitioner calls in question the legality and propriety of the order dated 13-6-2013 passed by learned Joint District Judge, first Court, Dhaka, rejecting an application for rejection of the plaint under Order VII, rule 11(d) and section 151 of the Code of Civil Procedure (briefly as the Code) in Title Suit No. 462 of 2011.

2. Materials facts leading to this Rule are that on 25-5-2011 opposite party No. 1 as plaintiff instituted Title Suit No. 462 of 2011 in the first Court of Joint District Judge, Dhaka, impleading the petitioner and opposite party Nos. 2-20 and others as defendants for the following relieves:

(ক) নালিশী ৩৩ শতাংশের কাতে ১৬১-১/২ শতাংশ ভূমির মালিক বাদিনী মর্মে স্বত্ব ঘোষণার ডিক্রি দিতে,

(খ) বাদিনীর বরাবর উক্ত ১৬১-১/২ শতাংশ ভূমির সাহাম বন্টনের নিমিত্তে ৰিবাদীগণের বিরুদ্ধে প্রাথমিক ডিক্রি দিতে

(গ) বিবাদীদের বিরুদ্ধে নালিশী ভূমির খাস দখল পুনরুদ্ধার সহ সার্ভে জানা এ্যাডভোকেট কমিশনার নিয়োগের মাধ্যমে সার্ভে করিয়া প্রদত্ত প্রতিবেদন অনুযায়ী নালিশী ১৬১-১/২ শতাংশ ভূমি চূড়ান্ত ডিক্রি দিতে,

(ঘ) ১নং বিবাদীর নামীয় জাল দলিল নং ১৩৫৯০ তাং ২৩-১২-৫৯ বাতিলের ডিক্রি দিতে,

(ঙ) মোকদ্দমার খরচ বাদিনীর অনুকূলে বিবাদীদের প্রতিকুলে ডিক্রি দিতে এবং

(চ) বাদিনী আইন ও ইক্যূইটি মতে আর যে যে প্রতিকার পাইতে তাহার ডিক্রি দিতে মর্জি হয় ৷

তপসিল

ঢাকা জেলার সাবেক কেরানীগঞ্জ হালে রমনা থানাধীন, ২৮০ এস, এ, ৬নং বড় মগবাজার মৌজান্থিত সি,এস, ৬২৮ পরে ১৮৭ এস, এ, ৫৮৬ নং খতিয়ানভুক্ত সি,এস, দাগ নং ৩৬৯ মোট ভূমি ১.১৮ ও ইহার কাতে ৮৩ শতাত্শ এবং এস, এ, ১০১ ৭ দাগের ৩২ শতাংশ ইহার কাতে ১৬-১/২ শতংশ ভূমি নালিশী ভূমি বটে ৷ ইহার আর, এস, খতিয়ান নং ১ ৭১ ৭, দাগ নং ৩৫৭৩ জমির পরিমাণ ২০৬৪ অযুতাংশ এবং আর, এস, খতিয়ান নং ১৫২২, দাগ নং ৩৬২০ জমির পরিমাণ, ১৩৮৮ মোট দুই দাগের কাতে, বাদিনীর, ১৬-১/২ শতাংশ নালিশী ভূমি বটে I যাহার চৌহদ্দি-উত্তরে রমজান আলি খান মজলিশ দক্ষিণে খোদা বক্স, পূর্বে আবদুল করিম, পশ্চিমে হামিদ হোসেন ৷

3. The petitioner as defendant No. 1 appeared in the suit by filing written statement denying all the materials allegations made in the plaint.

4. In suit, the defendant No. 1 by an application dated 10-1-2013 sought to reject the plaint of the suit under Order VII, rule 11(d) of the Code stating that suit is not maintainable in the present form; the suit is barred by res-judicata and by limitation inasmuch as identical relieves were sought by the plaintiff in previously instituted suit which was decided against him. So the instant suit is barred under law.

5. After hearing the learned Judge rejected the application by the impugned order holding that the question of res-judicata and limitation cannot be decided before trial.

6. Feeling aggrieved the petitioner preferred the instant Revision and obtained the present Rule.

7. The learned Advocate appearing for the petitioner seeks to impeach the impugned order on three fold arguments:

Firstly: That the instant suit the plaintiff claimed for declaration of title, recovery of possession partition and cancellation of the deed but those issues were earlier decided in Title Suit No. 164 of 1976 (re-number 239 of 1987 lastly renumbered as Title Suit No. 164 of 1997). So the instant suit is not at all maintainable.

Secondly: The instant suit is absolutely barred by limitation and res-judicata inasmiuchas the matter in issue directly and substantially in issue of the instant suit has been directly and substantially issue of the former suit, between the same parties.

Third and lastly: The learned Judge of the Court below failed to appreciate such question of law, thereby rejected the application for rejection of the plaint which is an error of law resulting in an error in the decision occasioning failure of justice.

8. In support of his contentions the learned Counsel refers the following cases:

(a) In the case of Abdul Jalil vs Islamic Bank Bangladesh Ltd. 53 DLR (AD) 12 held:

"Code of Civil Procedure : (V of 1908) Sections 11, 151 and Order VII, rule 11 It is well settled that where a plaint cannot be rejected under Order VII, rule 11 of the Code of Civil Procedure the court may invoke its inherent jurisdiction and reject the plaint taking recourse to section 151 of the Code of Civil Procedure.

Sections 11, 151 and Order VII, rule 11

As the ultimate result of the suit is as clear as day light such a suit should be buried at its inception so that no further time is consumed in a fruitless litigation."

9. The learned Advocate appearing for the opposite party No. 1 opposes the Rule and submits that the relieves claimed in the instant suit are completely different from that of the former suit. So the plaint of the instant suit can-not be rejected before trial. He adds that the question of res-judicata is mixed question of fact and law which can be decided only at the trial on taking evidence. Moreso the plaintiff has an ample opportunity to amend her plaint at any time before trial. So the plaint cannot be rejected at this stage.

10. In support of his contentions he refers the following cases:

a) In the case of Sreemati Pushpa Rani Das vs AKM Habibur Rahman 13 BLD (AD) 217 held:

"Code of Civil Procedure, 1908

Order VII, rule 11.

The plea of res-judicata is not available in rejecting a plaint under Order VII, rule 11 CPC.-This matter can only be decided on the trial and it cannot be decided from a reading of the plaint res-judicata can be made an issue in the suit."

(b) In the case of Mahbubul Haque (Md.) vs Md. A Kader Munshi 52 DLR (AD) 49 = 20 BLD (AD) 82 held:

"Code of Civil Procedure (V of 1908)

Section-11

Rejection Order VII, rule 11(d)

Res-judicata of plaint—

Question res-judicata cannot be decided from a reading of the plaint and should be decided at the time of trial. Sreemati Pushpa Rani Das vs AKM Habibur Rahman, 13 BLD (AD) 217 relied.

Limitation

Question of limitation is a mixed question of law and fact which can be decided at the time of trial on taking evidence."

(c) In the case of Md. Shahabuddin vs Habibur Rahman 16 BLD (AD) 279 = 50 DLR (AD) 99 held: "Order VII, rule 11 Rejection of plaint on ground of limitation.

The question of limitation in a suit is a mixed question of law and fact which can be decided only in the trial on taking evidence. In view of the relieves prayed in the suit, the plaint cannot be rejected under Order VII, rule 11 of the Code."

11. In order to appreciate their submissions we have gone through the records and given our anxious considerations to their sub-missions.

12. The point for consideration whether the impugned order calls for interference by this Court.

13. For the convenience of understanding the provisions of Order VII, rule 11 of the Code of Civil Procedure reads hereunder:

"11—The plaint shall be rejected in the following issues: (a) Where it does not disclose a cause of action. (b) Where the relief claimed is under-valued, and the plaintiff, on being required by the Court to correct the valuation within a time to be fixed by the Court fails to do so; (c) Where the relief claimed is properly valued, but the plaint is written upon paper insufficiently stamped and the plaintiff, on being required by the Court to supply the requisite stamp-paper within a time to be fixed by the Court, fails do so.(d) Where the suit appears from the statement in the plaint to be barred by any law."

14. Provided that the time fixed by the Court for the correction of the valuation or sup-plying of the requisite stamp-paper shall not exceed twenty one days.

15. On going to the materials on record it transpires that earlier same plaintiff instituted Title Suit No. 164 of 1976 (re-numbered as Title Suit No. 164 of 1997) for declaration of title in 0.161/2 acres of land appertaining to SA plot No. 1017, recovery of Khas possession in the suit property and for declaration that registered deed No. 13590 dated 23-12-1959 is fraud, fraudulent, inoperative and not binding upon him. The trial Court by its judgment and decree dated 28-2-2001 dismissed the suit holding:

“যেহেতু ১নং বিৰাদী ডি, ডব্লিউ-১ নিজেই স্বীকার করিয়াছেন যে, নালিশী এস, এ, ১০১৭ দাগের অর্ধেকাংশে বাদিনীয় স্বত্ব রহিয়াছে সেহেতু বাদিনীর স্বত্বের দাবীটি অবিশ্বাস করিৰার কোন কারণ নাই । তাহাছাড়া দালিলিক ভাবেও প্রমাণিত হইয়াছে যে, বাদিনী তাহার পূর্ববর্তী হামিদ হোসেনের নিকট হইতে খারিজ সূত্রে নালিশী দাগে l স্বত্ববান হইয়াছে ৷ বাদিনীর স্বত্বের আরো মজবুত ভিত্তি হইল তাহার বায়া হামিদ হোসেন নালিশী দাগে বাড়ী নির্মাণ করিয়া বসবাস করিতেছেন ৷ কিন্তু দুঃখজনকভাবে বাস্তবতা হইল বাদিনীর মোকদ্দমাটি যথাযথ আকারে দায়ের করা হয় নাই ৷ উভয় পক্ষের স্বীকৃত মতে এবং স্বীকৃত সি, এস, ১৮৭ খতিয়ান দৃষ্টে দেখা যায় সি,এস, ৩৬৯ দাগের মোট সম্পত্তি ১.১৮ একর ৷ কিন্তু আরজীর তপসিলে উক্ত দাগের ১৬-১/২ শতাংশ ভূমি বাবদ স্বত্ব সাব্যস্থ ক্রমে খাস দখলের প্রার্থনা করা হইঁয়াছে এবং উহাতে এস, এ, ১০১৭ দাগটি উল্লেখ করা হইয়াছে ৷ এস, এ, ১০১৭ দাগ সংক্রান্ত এস, এ, খতিয়ান ৫৮৬ পর্যালোচনা করিয়া দেখা যায় উহাতে ৩২ শতাংশ ভূমি হামিদ হোসেন এবং মোছাম্মৎ সৈয়দা সামসুজ্জাহান বেগমের নামে রেকর্ড হইয়াছে । অর্থাৎ না���িশী সম্পত্তি ভোগ, অনির্দিষ্ট এবং অচিহ্নিত ৷ যেহেতু সি,এস, খতিয়ান এবং দাগের ভূমি সম্পর্কে অদ্যাবধি বাই মিটস এন্ড রাউন্ড বিভাগ বন্টন হয় নাই সেহেতু বন্টনের মোকদ্দমা ব্যতীত বাদিনী কোন প্রকার প্রতিকার লাভ করিতে অধিকারী নহেন ৷ বণ্টনের মোকদ্দমা বাদিনী অবশ্যই প্রতিকার পাইতে অধিকারী হইবেন ৷ তবে স্বত্ব সাব্যস্ত ক্রমে খাস দখলের প্রার্থনায় আনীত মোকদ্দমাটিতে বাদিনী নালিশী সম্পত্তি তাহার দখল এবং বেদখলের ঘটনাটি প্রমাণ করিতে না পারার এবং নালিশী সম্পত্তি ভোগ, অনির্দিষ্ট ও অচিহ্নিত হওয়ায় বর্তমান আকারে ও প্ৰকারে মোকদ্দমাটি পরিচালনাযোগ্য নহে বর্তমান আকারে আনীত মোকদ্দমাটি তামাদিতে ও বারিত ৷ বাদীপক্ষ তাহার প্রার্থীত ক্রমে ডিক্রি কিংবা অন্য কোন প্রতিকার লাভ করিতে পারে না ৷ ১নং বিবাদিনীর নামীয় নালিশী ২৩-১ ২-৫৯ ইং তারিখের দলিলটি সম্পর্কে কোন প্রকার ঘোষণা লাভ করিতেও বাদীপক্ষ অধিকারী নহে ৷ মোকদ্দমাটি খারিজযোগ্য ৷”

16. Against the aforesaid judgment and decree the plaintiff preferred First Appeal No. 688 of 2001 before the High Court Division. After hearing the first appeal was dismissed by the judgment and decree dated 18-8-2009 holding:

"We are of the considered view that as the plaintiff appellant has got right, title in half portion of disputed SA plot No. 1017, she can get her share of land by filing a partition suit impleading all the co-sharers including defendant No. 1. From the evidence on record it appears that the plaintiff-appellant failed to prove her case of dispossession from the suit land and the present suit is not maintainable for non-specification of suit land and, as such, the learned Sub-ordinate Judge rightly dismissed the suit. We find no merit in the appeal.

In the result the appeal is dismissed without any order as to cost and the impugned order dated 28-2-2001 and decree dated 1-3-2001 are affirmed. The plaintiff-appellant is at liberty to file a fresh partition suit if she is so advised."

17. From the plain reading of the former suit it appears that the schedule given in that suit was unspecified. So in an unspecified land plaintiff is not entitled to get a decree. It is pertinent to point out that the High Court Division in its judgment held: that the plaintiff have got right, title in half portion of the disputed SA plot No. 1017, she got her share of land by filing a partition suit impleading all the co-sharers as defendants. Thereafter the plaintiff instituted the instant suit praying for the aforesaid relieves.

<u>18. The only point urged by the learned Counsel for the petitioner is that the instant suit is barred by res-judicata and also barred by limitation and the relieves claimed in the instant suit is substantially in issue in the former suit between the same parties. It has been well settled that the question of res-judicata and limitation raised in the application for rejecting the plaint are mixed question of law and fact which can only be decided at trial on taking evidence.</u>

19. In the case of Mahbubul Haque (Md.) vs Md. A Kader Munshi 52 DLR (AD) 49 held:

"Code of Civil Procedure (V of 1908)

Order VII, rule 11(d).

Question of limitation and res-judicata raised in the application for rejecting the plaint are mixed questions of law and fact which need thorough investigation on adequate evidence for arriving at a correct decision on framing specific issues by the trial Court."

20. The aforesaid views receives support in the case of Sreemati Pushpa Rani Das vs AKM Habibur Rahman 13 BLD (AD) 217 held:

"The plea of res-judicata is not available in rejecting a plaint under Order VII, rule 11 CPC.- This matter can only be decided on the trial and it cannot be decided from a reading of the plaint res-judicata can be made an issue in the suit."

21. And in the case of Shahabuddin vs Habibur Rahman 50 DLR (AD) 99=16 BLD (AD) 279, it was held that question of limitation is a mixed question of law and fact which can be decided at the time of trial on taking evidence.

<u>22. It further appears to us that in the former suit the trial Court as well as the Court of appeal categorically observed that the schedule of the plaint do not disclose any specification of the land in which the plaintiff sought for declaration of title. It is true that in an unspecified land no Court can grant any relief to the plaintiff. On careful scrutiny of the instant suit we find that the specification of the land has been clearly given in the instant suit. Moreso the plaintiff has an ample opportunity to amend the plaint in a justification form of relief, during pendency of the suit.</u>

23. In the case of Sk. Md. Junaid vs Turner Morrison and Co. Ltd. 26 DLR 111 held;

"Order VII, rule 11 (d) CPC.

Suit barred by limitation— It must prima facie appeared to be so-Court without rejecting the plaint, should allow it for amendment.

Clause (d) of rule 11, Order VII applies when it appears from the statements in the plaint that the suit is barred but it has no application when there is no clear or specific admission in the plaint suggesting that the suit is barred. This clause is attracted only when on the admitted facts as appearing from the plaint itself the suit is prima-facie barred. As for instance when from the statements made in the plaint it appears that the cause of action arose beyond the period of limitation fixed under the statute and no indication is given that limitation has been saved, the plaint may be rejected. In a proper case, when it appears to be barred by limitation, the plaint may be allowed to be amended without rejecting it. It is not mandatory for the Court to reject the plaint.

In the instant suit, it appears that the plaint was initially checked and sealed by the ministerial staff and then presented before the learned Sub-ordinate Judge. The Court then passed an order to register the plaint and issue notice upon the defendant, presumably on satisfaction that the plaint suffered from no latches with the meaning of Order VII, rule 11 CPC. In pursuance of the notices, the defendant-petitioner appeared and filed a petition praying for rejecting the plaint. The learned Judge in exercise of his discretion rejected the same without reasons recorded in the judgment. The original Court having disallowed the prayer for rejecting of the plaint by a judicial order, in exercise his discretion, we think, we should not interfere with the same under section 115 CPC and the lower Court passes a judicial order in exercise of its discretion, the High Court shall be reluctant to interfere with such order and there has been an absolute failure of justice of the case."

<u>24. Now coming to clause (d) of rule 11, it appears that clause (d) of the rule authorise the rejection of a plaint when the suit appears from the statements in the plaint to be barred by any law. This Clause applies when it appear from the statements in the plaint that the suit is barred but it has no application where there is no clear or specific admission in the plaint suggesting that the suit is barred. This clause is attracted only when on the admitted facts as appearing from the plaint itself the suit is prima facie barred. As for instance when from the statements made in the plaint it appears that the cause of action arose beyond the period of limitation fixed under the statute and no indication is given that limitation has been saved, the plaint may be rejected. In a proper case, when it appears to be barred by limitation, the plaint may be allowed to be amended without rejection. It is not mandatory for the Court to reject the pliant. It may ask the plaintiff to amend it so as to make suit maintainable. Where the plaintiff does not comply with such an order the Court may reject the plaint. Reference may be made to the cases reported in 18 CWN 1340. AIR 1928 Oudh 495 and AIR 1953 Cal 222.</u>

25. In the case of Ratan Chand Dharam Chand vs The Secretary of State for India in Council, reported in 18 CWN 1340, a Division Bench of Calcutta High Court while considering the scope of Order VII, rule 11(d) observed as follows :—

"That rule obviously has no application, for there was no statement in the plaint which suggested that the suit was barred. On the contrary it was specifically stated that notice under section 80 had been served on the "Collector" without specifying the district. The defect was not discovered till after the defendants had entered appearance and it was then too late to reject the plaint".

Similarly in the case of Maqsood Ali vs Deputy Commissioner, Bara Banki, reported in AIR 1928, Oudh, 495, a Division Bench of Oudh held that if the suit was not on the face of it barred by any law, Order VII, rule 11 (d) had no application. The relevant portion of the judgment ran as follows:

"We do not consider that the suit appeared from the statement in the plaint to be barred by law and we do not think that rule had any application. He has pointed out to us that in a suit which was filed in a similar manner a Bench of the Allahabad High Court stated in Nachhu vs Secy, of State that the plaint ought to have been rejected under the proviso of section 54(c) of the old Code of Civil Procedure, that clause was exactly the same as Order VII, rule 11 (d). The learned Judge composing the Bench gave no reasons for this conclusion and did not give any effect to it for we find that the suit with which they were concerned had been dismissed but the Sub-ordinate Judge and as their order was an order dismissing the appeal, the plaint was apparently not rejected. Their Lordships said: "It ought to have been rejected" but gave no effect to that view. We have only to note in respect of this point that exactly the same question could have been raised in Bhagchand Dagadusa vs Secy, of State. There the suit had been dismissed by the District Judge. The appeal had been dismissed by the High Court and the appeal was again dismissed by their Lordships of the Judicial Committee. It was not there suggested that the proper procedure was to reject the plaint. In a case such as this we are of opinion that the suit is not on the face of it barred by law. The very arguments which have been advanced in appeal show that the suit on the face of it is not barred by law, as the suit has been found to be a suit that has to be dismissed after consideration of the legal arguments. Therefore we are unable to accept this view of the learned Counsel.

26. The Calcata High Court in the case of Sreedam Chandra Bhur vs Tencori Mukherjee Reported in AIR 1959 Cal. 222 also held that Order VII, rule 11(d) was attracted only when on the admitted facts as papering from the plaint itself the suit was prima facie barred. The Division Bench in this connection observed as follows:-

"This clause is attracted only when on the admitted facts as appearing from the plaint itself the suit is prima facie barred. As for instance when from the statements made in the plaint it appears that the cause of action arose beyond period of limitation fixed under the statute and no indication is given that limitation has been saved, the plaint may be rejected. Even in such a case, an opportunity is to be given to the plaintiff to amend the plaint by setting out an acknowledgement in writing signed by the defendant within the period of limitation if it is so prayed, and that without passing an order for rejection of the plaint. 'Gunnaji Bhavaji vs Makanji Khoosal Chand', 34 Bom. 250. As was observed in 'Ratan Chand vs Secy, of State 18 Cal. WN 1340, action is to be taken under Order VII, rule 11 of the Code of civil Procedure only if there is a clear and specific admission in the plaint from which it follows that the suit is barred. Reference may also be made to the observations of this Court.' Prankrishna vs Kripannath' 21 Cal WN 209 held:

"Let us now consider whether on the plaint as filed the Court will be justified in rejecting in limine the plaint under clause(d), rule 11, Order VII, Civil PC. In the body of the pliant there is no admission for the Council of the Assembly is the Government under section 80, Civil PC. On the other hand, it is seriously contested on behalf of the plaintiff that neither of the two bodies can even be deemed to be the government. The learned Sub-ordinate Judge refers to his order vaguely to the Trend of French Statutes conferring greater and  greater powers on the French Settlement in India and creating a 'Council du Government' there and later a cutting out Chandernagore from the Federation and conferring on Chandemagore all those powers with a separate delegate of the 'Commissionaire de la re-oblique, it is evident that the Chandernagore administration is a government in the grammatical and ordinary sense of the word though its functions may fall short of the those of the Governments existing in India.

We do not think it necessary to refer to other points urged before us by the con-tending parties. Suffice it to say that the question whether even if the Code of Civil Procedure applies, whether section 80 would be attracted or not cannot be decided merely on the plaint as it stands. The Court should have registered the plaint, issued notices on the defendants and allowed them to file their written statements. After issues were raised it would have been open to the Court to take up one or more of the issues as preliminary ones and decide the same. Objection that had been raised by the Court 'suo-motu' and such other objection as may be raised by the defendants would have to be tried on the merits, and only after all the necessary facts and materials are brought before the Court."

27. There is no reason to differ from the above principles of law. In the instant case, there is nothing on record to show that on the admitted facts as appearing from the plaint itself the suit is prima facie barred. So the rule 11 (d) is not at all attracted here and the plaint cannot be rejected on that score.

28. We find that both the parties are claiming their right, title, interest and possession in the suit land. So from the plain reading of the plaint of two suits we find that genealogy of acquiring title by the parties have been categorically described. Therefore we find that the grounds urged for rejection of the plaint are absolutely the subject-matter of evidence which cannot be decided before taking the evidence. On plain reading of the statements of the plaint it is evident that the same clearly discloses the cause of action the relieves claimed is not under valued, the plaint was not written upon paper insufficiently stamped and not barred by any other law.

29. In the case of Sundar Ali being dead his heirs: Mannan vs Md. Serajul Islam Sarker 56 DLR (AD) 210 held:

"For the ascertainment of the cause of action the Court is required to read the plaint in its entirety.

30. In the case of Abdul Malek Sawdagar vs Md. Mahbubey Alam 57 DLR (AD) 18 held:

"The question whether the plaint is liable to be rejected being barred by law must be apparent from the statement made in the plaint itself and not from the written statement or any other material other than that has been put in the plaint.

31. In the case of Md. Abul Khair vs Pubali Bank Ltd. 21 BLD (AD) 32 = 53 DLR (AD) 62 held:

Where in a suit an application under Order VII, rule 11 of the Code is filed for rejecting the plaint on the ground that the averments made in the plaint do no disclose a cause of action for the suit, the Court is not called upon to decide the suit on merit on taking evidence. It is only the averment made in the plaint which are to be considered to come to a finding as to whether those disclose a cause of action. The Court while deciding such application is not permitted in law to travel beyond the averments made in the plaint."

32. Therefore, the Court below after considering the materials on record and aforesaid principles of law, by rejecting the application committed no error of law. Moreso, it appears that findings arrived at by the Court below having been rested upon consideration and discussions of materials on record and also on a correct and proper analysis of legal aspects involved in suit. Moreover, we do not find any misreading or misappreciation of the materials on record. Therefore, the findings of the Court below are not liable to be disturbed by the High Court Division in exercise of power under section 115(1) of the Code of Civil Procedure.

33. Moreover the impugned order in its entirety is well founded in the facts and circumstances of the case. So, the submissions advanced by the learned Counsel for the petitioner are not the correct exposition of law and facts. However we have gone through the decisions as referred by him. We are in respectful agreement with the principles enunciated therein but the facts leading to those cases are quite distinguishable to that of the instant case. Therefore we are unable to accept his submissions. On the contrary the submissions advanced by the learned Counsel for the opposite party No. 1 prevail and appear to have a deal of force.

34. In the light of discussions made above and the preponderant judicial views emerging out of the authorities referred to above, we are of the view that the impugned order suffers from no legal infirmity which calls for no interference by this. Court. Thus the Rule having no merit fails.

35. In the result, the Rule is discharged without any order as to cost. The order of stay granted earlier stands vacated.

The office is directed to communicate the order at once.

End.

full_judgment:
JN Deb Choudhury J: This first miscellaneous appeal was filed against the judgment and order dated 2-11-2015 passed by the learned Joint District Judge, First Court, Dhaka in Title Suit No. 984 of 2014, rejecting an application for temporary injunction.

2. The appellant as plaintiff filed Title Suit No. 984 of 2014 on 28-10-2014 before the learned Joint District Judge, First Court, Dhaka, for declaration of title and declaration that the present revisional record of rights are wrong and for staying the proceeding of Miscellaneous Case Nos. 97 of 2014 and 115 of 2014, pending before the Assistant Commissioner (Land) Gulshan Circle, Dhaka, the defendant-respondent No. 10.

3. Plaintiff's case as stated in the plaint in short, is that, 164 decimals land of CS Plot No. 130 under CS Khatian No. 13 originally belonged to Jamir Bhuiyan, Kadam Bhuiyan and Jabu in 4 annas share each and Sayed Bhuiyan and Hayed Bhuiyan in 2 annas share each and CS, SA and RS record of rights were duly prepared. Sayed Bhuiyan while in possession of his 21.05 decimals of land also purchased 20.5 decimals from Abu Bhuiyan, son of CS tenant Jamir Bhuiyan and 5 decimals from another co-sharer Hayed Bhuiyan by registered kabala dated 16-3-1944 and thus became owner of total 47 decimals. Sayed Bhuiyan sold 17.5 decimals and 24.75 decimals by two registered kabalas dated 26-2-1964 and 27-1-1967 respectively and 4.75 decimals remained with him. Sayed Bhuiyan died leaving behind 3 sons namely Asan Uddin, Basir Uddin alias Kerali and Rustom Ali and a daughter Saleman Nessa. Rustom Ali sold his entire share to his brother Asan Uddin by registered kabala dated 26-10-1978. Asan Uddin also purchased 16 decimals, 20 decimals and 17 decimals from his co-sharers by three separate registered deeds dated 7-2-1973, 5-7-1986 and 25-7-1996 respectively. By that way Asan Uddin became the owner of total 63.10 decimals of land by way of inheritance and purchase. Asan Uddin died leaving behind 6 sons namely Miaz Uddin, Yar Uddin, Saiz Uddin, Taiz Uddin, Azim Udin and Laiz Uddin. Thereafter they sold the suit land to Saidur Rahman Dipu and Mafizul Islam by registered Kabala dated 8-11-2009 who subsequently sold the suit land to the plaintiff through their constituted attorney by registered kabala dated 25-7-2010.

4. The further case of the plaintiff is that, after purchase, the plaintiff constructed a boundary wall and possessing the same by mutating his name vide Mutation Case No. 3821 of 2010-2011 and on payment of rent to the Government. The vendors of the plaintiff also paid rent to the Government by mutating their names. The defendant No. 1 filed Miscellaneous Case No. 97 of 2014 and the defendant Nos. 1-9 jointly filed Miscellaneous Case No. 115 of 2014 before the Assistant Commissioner (Land), Gulshan Circle, Dhaka for cancellation of the mutation of the plaintiff.

5. After filing of the suit, the plaintiff filed an application under Order 39 rule 1 and 2 read with section 151 of the Code of Civil Procedure and prayed for an order of temporary injunction against the defendants to restrain them from entering into the suit land forcefully and from destroying the boundary wall of the petitioner along with an order of stay of further proceeding of Miscellaneous Case No. 97 of 2014 and 115 of 2014. On 28-10-2014 the Trial Court issued show cause notice along with an ad-interim order of injunction in the following terms:

“ইতিমধ্যে আগামী ধার্য্য তারিখ পর্য্ন্ত বিবাদীগণ যাহাতে জোর পূর্বক নালিশ সস্পত্তিতে প্রবেশ করিতে না পারে বা দখল করিতে না পারে তা তপসিল বর্ণিত সম্পত্তির কোন রকম পিরিবর্ত্ন করিতে না পারে  এবং সহকারী কমিশনার ভূমি, গু���শান সার্কেল এ চলমান মিস কেস নং-৯৭/১৪ এবং ১১৫/১৪  এর কার্য্ক্রম গ্রহণ করিতে না পারে তৎমর্মে বিবাদীগণকে অন্তবর্তীকালীন আদেশ দ্বারা বারিত করা হইল।”

6. Which remains in force till 21-5-2015, while the application for extension of the same filed under section 151 of the Code of Civil Procedure was rejected on the ground that, there is no scope for any extension, if the party, whose favour ad-interim order was passed, prays for any adjournment.

7. The defendant Nos. 1-9 filed written statement on 9-6-2015 and also filed written objection against the prayer for temporary injunction on the same date on stating that the plaintiff on creating false documents trying to grab the suit land and also got the mutation of the record of rights beyond the knowledge of the defendants. The present City Khatian also stood in the name of the defendant Nos. 1-9 concerning 1864 decimals of land against which the plaintiff's vendors filed Land Survey Case No. 1111 of 2008 before the Land Survey Tribunal, Dhaka against the defendants, which is still pending.

8. By the impugned order dated 2-11-2015 the Trial Court rejected the application for temporary injunction mainly on the reasoning that without taking evidence the question of possession cannot be decided.

9. Being aggrieved the plaintiff-appellant preferred the instant First Miscellaneous Appeal and the same was admitted on 24-11-2015. After admission filed an application for stay of further proceeding of Miscellaneous Case No. 97 of 2014 and 115 of 2014, pending before the defendant-respondent No. 10 and also prays for an order of status-quo in respect of possession and position of the suit property and after hearing a Division Bench passed an ad-interim order, which is as follows:

"Heard the learned Advocate and perused the application, considering the facts and circumstances the application is allowed. Let all further proceeding of Miscellaneous Case Nos. 97 of 2014 and 115 of 2014, now pending before the defendant opposite party No. 10 be stayed and the parties are directed to maintain status-quo in respect of possession and position of the suit property till disposal of the appeal."

10. Mr. Ali Imam Khaled Rahim, the learned advocate appearing for the plaintiff-appellant submits that the Trial Court while rejecting the application for temporary injunction failed to consider that the plaintiff is in possession of the suit land by constructing boundary wall and the defendant Nos. 1-9 trying to enter into the suit land forcefully and unless an order of temporary injunction is passed, the defendants will dispossess the plaintiff, which will render multiplicity of proceedings. He next submits that in the proceedings before the defendant-respondent No. 10 being Miscellaneous Case No. 97 of 2014 and 115 of 2014 are related to selfsame property and the fate of the said proceedings depends upon the result of the present suit and accordingly, the proceedings of Miscellaneous Case Nos. 97 of 2014 and 115 of 2014 are liable to be stayed till disposal of the suit. In support of his contention he relied upon two decisions, reported in 47 DLR (AD) 38 and 14 BLD (AD) 1 and accordingly, prays for allowing the appeal on allowing the application for temporary injunction as prayed for.

11. On the other hand, Mr. Md. Khalilur Rahman, the learned advocate appearing with Mr. Mohammad Babrul Amin, the learned advocate for the respondent Nos. 1-9 submits that so far the order of status-quo as passed by this Court on 24-11-2015, is concern, they have no objection, if the same is continued till disposal of the suit; but, so far the stay of further proceeding of Miscellaneous Case No. 97 of 2014 and 115 of 2014 pending before the defendant-respondent No. 10, submits that the said proceedings cannot be stayed by a civil court in view of section 4 of the Code of Civil Procedure and in view of the provisions of section 143 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, 1950. He next submits that the mutation proceeding being an independent proceeding and after disposal of the same there are independent forum for the aggrieved parties and, as such, the civil court has no jurisdiction to stay the further proceeding of the said miscellaneous cases. In support of his contention he relied upon some decisions, reported in 18 BLC 46, 6 BLC 241, 60 DLR (AD) 38 and 12 MLR (AD) 137 = 59 DLR (AD) 126.

12. We have heard the learned advocates for both the parties and perused the impugned judgment and order along with other annex-tires which were annexed with the applications.

13. We have earlier mentioned that so far the order of status-quo is concern both the learned advocates for appellant and respondent Nos. 1-9 have no objection, if the same is continued till disposal of the suit.

14. Now the only consideration before this Court, whether the further proceedings of Miscellaneous Case Nos. 97 of 2014 and 115 of 2014, now pending before the defendant-respondent No. 10, Assistant Commissioner (Land) Gulshan Circle, Dhaka can be stayed by a civil Court.

15. It appears from the prayer of the plaint that the plaintiff not only prayed for declaration of title; but, also prayed for further declaration regarding the revisional record of rights and proceedings of Miscellaneous Case Nos. 97 of 2014 and 115 of 2014.

<u>16. It appears that the contesting defendants filed an application before the Trial Court for rejection of plaint and the said application has been rejected by the Trial Court on 15-9-2015 and the defendants till today did not challenge the said order. It is settled principle of law that the record of rights are not a document of title and it is always subject to the result of a civil suit, where title is disputed. The revenue authority is bound to give effect of the ultimate decision of the civil court concerning any record of rights. In our view proceeding of a mutation case or a case concerning correction or cancellation of a record of rights will be a futile exercise, while a civil suit is pending concerning the land of that record of rights in between the parties thereto.</u>

17. In appreciating the respective arguments we have considered the decisions referred by the learned advocate for the appellant.

18. It appears that in the case of Syed Mohammad Salem Azam vs The Secretary, Ministry of Works, Government of Bangladesh, reported in 47 DLR (AD) 38 our Hon'ble Appellate Division held that,

"We are not impressed by this argument. Respondent No. 1 had every jurisdiction to review its own order if the earlier order dated 8-8-1984 was obtained by the appellants by fraud and misrepresentation, but the impugned order on review must reveal what fraud and misrepresentation the appellants made or committed while obtaining the order dated 8-8-1984. The impugned order dated 8-11-1993 does not contain any indication to that effect. It simply says that the previous order dated 8-8-84 is cancelled. Furthermore, no indication has been given as to why criminal proceeding shall be instituted against the appellants for misappropriating Government property. What materials prompted respondent No. 1 to review its earlier order and what facts weighed upon him are simply absent in the impugned order. The impugned order is therefore not a speaking order and cannot be sustained.

There is however a more fundamental objection to the impugned order. Respondent No. 4 has filed Title Suit No. 106 of 1984 for a declaration that the order dated 8-8-1984 passed by respondent No. 1 is collusive and void and has amended the plaint for a further declaration that the appellants are not the son and daughter of the said Syed Mohammad Azam. The suit is still pending and respondent No. 1 is very much a party to the suit. Any decision taken by respondent No. 1 concerning the order dated 8.8.84 or any conclusion drawn by him regarding the death or otherwise of Syed Mohammad Azam during the pendency of the said title suit is an affront to a judicial proceeding and is an attempt to pre-empt a judgment. Respondent No. 4 being dissatisfied with the order dated 8.8.84 lodged a three-pronged attack on it by filing a case in the Court of Settlement, by filing a title suit and by making a representation to respondent No. 1. He lost the Settlement Court case, the title suit is pending and during the pendency of the title suit he obtained an order in his favour on those very matters which are the subject matter for trial in the title suit. His conduct too is not free from censure because it was at his instance that the impugned order dated 8-11-93 was passed. It was an unwarranted inroad into a judicial proceeding and cannot be condoned in any way."

19. And in the case of Basarat Howlader, Secretary, Gutapara Matslzajibi Samabay Samity Ltd. vs Mummara Matshajibi Samabay Samity Ltd., reported in 14 BLD (AD) 1, their Lordships held that,

"Whether the order for enquiry was made before the issuance of the Rule Nisi or thereafter, it was absolutely improper on the part of the learned Advocate for the Writ petitioner-Respondents to pray for postponement of hearing "in order to afford the Government an opportunity of settling the dispute", nor do we think it was proper for the Court to allow the Government "to decide the matter according to law" when the Court itself was in scission of the matter to do exactly the same. The Government is within its rights to conduct any number of internal inquiries into the disputed question of settlement, but as long as the legality or illegality of settlement is before the Court, the Government has no power to decide the issue this way or that way. It is for the Court to decide the matter. The Court cannot simply abandon its judicial responsibility in favour of the Government. It was open to the Writ-Petitioners to withdraw the writ petition and submit themselves to the jurisdiction of the Government, but it was not open to them to keep the writ petition pending and allow the Government to "decide the matter according to law". In other words, the Writ petitioners cannot pursue two remedies at the same time, one at the Governmental level and the other in a Court of law, more so in the constitutional jurisdiction. The High Court Division also misjudge the submission of the learned Advocate for the Writ Petitioners and should not have acceded to his prayers."

20. Now let us examine the law and decisions as cited by the learned advocate for the respondents.

21. We have gone through the section 4 of the Code of Civil Procedure. The revenue authority cannot decide the title of the respective parties and it is only the civil court which can decide so and from that point of view section 4 of the Code of Civil Procedure is not restricting power of a civil court in deciding title which will be reflected in the record of rights. Similarly section 143 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, 1950 is also subject to decision of title by a civil Court.

22. In a case of Golden Re-Rolling Industries Ltd. vs Subordinate Judge, Artha Rin Adalat No. 1, Dhaka, reported in 60 DLR (AD) 38, our Apex Court held that,

"The High Court Division held that it is an established principle of law that where an alternative remedy exists a party cannot have recourse to the inherent jurisdiction of the Court under section 151 of the Code of Civil Procedure. In this connection, the High Court Division relied on the case of Shahidur Rahman Majumder (Md.) Shahidullah Majumder vs Sahirunnesa reported in 1 BLC (AD) 43."

23. In the case of Fatema Khatun vs Fazil Mia, reported in 6 BLC 241, a single Bench of the High Court Division held that,

"the recent record of right would prevail inasmuch as presumption attached to the State Acquisition record of right."

24. In the case of Faizur Rahman (Md.) vs Md. Mokarram Hossain, reported in 18 BLC 46, a Division Bench of the High Court Division held that,

"the suit was filed without exhausting the procedure as laid down in section 147(c), as such the suit is not maintainable."

25. And in the case of Mr. Bazlur Rahman Sarker vs Kamala Kanto Barman, reported in 12 MLR (AD) 137 = 59 DLR (AD) 126, our Hon'ble Appellate Division held that,

"On reading provision of section 143 of the Act and the Rule 23(4) of the Tenancy Rule, 1955 we are of the view that the Revenue Officer in the facts and circumstances of the instant case in cancelling the mutation obtained by the plaintiff in respect of the land in suit was quite legal. It may be mentioned plaintiff got his name mutated upon sticking out name of Bipin Chandra who said to have acquired the land in suit by settlement from landlords, but in support of claim of settlement no evidence was brought on record. As stated hereinbefore the appellate Court set aside the judgment of the trial Court which dismissed the suit, primarily on the ground that revenue authority had no jurisdiction to correct the record of rights by cancelling the mutation earlier made in the name of the plaintiff on the view that the correction so made affected the right, title and interest of the person whose name was entered in the record of right upon mutation. In view of the provision of section 143 of the Act and the Rule 23(4) of the Tenancy Rule, 1955 in our opinion the appellate Court was in serious error in setting aside the judgment of the trial Court on the view that the revenue officer had no jurisdiction to correct the record of rights prepared upon mutation in the name of the plaintiff."

<u>26. On going through the decisions cited by both the learned advocates for both sides it appears that none of the decision directly related with the issue before us. In the present case the only question before this Court is whether a civil court can stay the proceeding concerning record of rights pending before the revenue authority i.e. the Assistant Commissioner (Land) Gulshan Circle, Dhaka by way of temporary injunction. In a suit for declaration of title the civil court can decide both title and possession while the revenue authority only authorized to deal with the record of rights regarding amalgamation subdivision and consolidation of holdings as provided in Chapter XV of Part V of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, 1950. All the record of rights concerning which any dispute arise shall subject to decision regarding title by a civil Court apart from amalgamation, subdivision and consolidation of holdings as provided in Chapter XV of Part V of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, 1950. In view of section 54 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act the revenue officer is bound to carry on the final order or decree as passed by a civil court. This proposition has been settled in the case of Abdul Moin vs Bangladesh represented by the Secretary, Ministry of Land, Secretariat Building, reported in 53 DLR 506, wherein a Division Bench of the High Court Division held that,</u>

<u>"When the matter was subsequently brought before the Additional Deputy Commissioner (Revenue) he was required in law to decide the matter either giving a decision instead of forwarding the same to the Ministry of Land by giving unwarranted and illegal observations. Since the question of title and possession have been settled by the highest Court of the country the Additional Deputy Commissioner (Revenue) had, in fact, no option in law but to mutate the name of the petitioner by correcting the record of right. The Additional Deputy Commissioner (Revenue) not only acted without jurisdiction in sending the matter to the Ministry of Land without deciding the matter himself with untenable observations but also did so in colourable exercise of his official power. The impugned order dated 3-6-1998 passed by the Additional Deputy Commissioner (Revenue) Sylhet is therefore declared to have been passed without any lawful authority."</u>

27. Though the learned advocates for both the parties failed  to cite any decision on the point, of this Court or our Hon'ble Appellate Division; we considered an unreported decision passed in the case of Durgawati vs Nan Bai, passed in Writ Petition No. 4933 of 2005 by the Chattisgarh High Court of India (collected from internet), wherein his Lordship held that,

"By this petition filed under Article 227 of the Constitution of India, the petitioners challenge the legality and validity of the order dated 29-7-2005 (Annexure P/7), passed by the IInd Additional District Judge, Ambikapur Distt. Surguja, in Misc. Civil Appeal No. 07/05 (Nan Bai vs Durgawati) whereby, the learned Additional District Judge directed the parties to maintain status quo in mutation proceedings with regard to plaint schedule 'A' land as obtained on 27-9-2004.

I have heard the learned counsel appearing for the parties, perused the pleadings and documents appended there-to. It is evident that the mutation does not confer any right of the title or ownership. However, when admittedly there is a dispute with regard to title ownership of the land, it is proper that the proceedings before the Revenue Authorities must await the decision of the Civil Court in respect of the ownership right of the land in dispute. The judgment and order dated 15-2-2005 (Annexure P/5) passed by the Civil Judge, Class I, is without any basis and, as such, if the mutation proceedings is permitted to go on, there would be unnecessary multiplication of the disputes. Therefore, it is well settled that the civil court proceedings with regard to the same land must be given precedent. The appellate Court has rightly considered the dispute in its proper perspective and granted interim relief of status quo with regard to the mutation proceedings by the impugned order. There is no irregularity, illegality or perversity in the impugned order dated 29-7-2005 (Annexure P/7), passed by the IInd Additional District Judge, Ambikapur Distt. Surguja, in Miscs. Civil Appeal No. 07/05."

<u>28. Upon considering the respective cases and the laws and decisions as stated above we are of the view that the civil court can restrain parties from proceeding with any case pending before a revenue authority. The mutation of record of rights does not confer any right title and interest over the concerned land, mores, where there is dispute regarding title, Revenue authority should await till the result of the same by the civil Court. The proceeding before the Revenue authority if not maintain status-quo, then multiplicity of proceedings and conflicting decisions may arise and the proceedings of civil Court should be given precedent then the Revenue proceedings. In the present case though the application filed by the plaintiff-appellant for temporary injunction and stay is to some extend defective inasmuch as they could pray for restraining the defendant No. 10 from proceedings with the mutation proceedings instead of praying an order of stay. However, this is mere a technical defect which cannot disentitle the plaintiff from getting a substantial order.</u>

29. Accordingly, we find merit in the miscellaneous appeal.

30. In the result, the first miscellaneous appeal is allowed.

31. The application for temporary injunction is allowed in the form of status-quo, directing the plaintiff and the defendant-respondent Nos. 1-9 to maintain status-quo in respect of possession and position of the suit land and directing the defendant-respondent No .10 also to maintain status-quo with regard to proceedings of Miscellaneous Case Nos. 97 of 2014 and 115 of 2014 pending before him, till disposal of the suit.

32. The Trial Court is hereby directed to dispose of the suit expeditiously preferably within 6(six) months from the date of receipt of this order.

Send a copy of this judgment to the court concern.

End.

parties:
Sultan (Md.) and another ----- Petitioners
Vs.
Attar Ali and others ----- Opposite-Parties
full_judgment:
On an application under section 115(4) of the Code of Civil Procedure, the petitioners obtained leave challenging legality and propriety of the judgment and order dated 28-3-2011 passed by the learned District Judge, Moulvi bazar, in Civil Revision No. 16 of 2009. Point of law involves herein whether present suit i.e. Title Suit No. 108 of 2008 for declaration of title, confirmation of possession and permanent injunction is barred by res-judicata and limitation in view of the judgment passed in Title Suit No. 59 of 1999 for permanent injunction filed by the plaintiff-opposite party impleading petitioners herein as defendants for the self-same property. Both the courts below arrived at a negative finding.

2. Brief fact is that opposite party No. 1 herein as plaintiff filed Title Suit No. 108 of 2008 in the court of learned Assistant Judge, Rajnagar, Moulvibazar, impleading the petitioners and others as defendants seeking declaration of title, confirmation of possession and permanent injunction contending inter alia that the plaintiff and proforma defendant No. 3 purchased the suit land from SA recorded tenant by registered deeds dated 23-3-1981, 11-8-1981 and 25-6-1985 respectively and are in possession of the same; lands of the schedule No. 3 are purchased by the plaintiff and proforma defendant No. 3 without executing any deed but still they are in possession of the land; Record of right stands in their name; On 15-11-1999 defendant Nos. 1 and 2 threatened the plaintiff to dispossess from the land, consequently the plaintiff filed Title Suit No. 59 of 1999 for permanent injunction which was dismissed vide judgment and decree dated 30-8-2000; Then the plaintiff as appellant filed Title Appeal No. 152 of 2000 in the, court of learned District Judge, Moulvi bazar; Learned District Judge allowed the appeal and send the suit back on remand for retrial but the plaintiff could not pursue his cause in the trial court for his personal difficulties resulting which the suit was again dismissed on merit vide judgment and decree dated 19-4-2005; plaintiff and proforma defendant No. 3 are still in possession of the suit land on payment of rents and taxes to the Government exchequer; From 19-7-2008, defendant Nos. 1 and 2 along with pro-forma defendant Nos. 4-12 claiming title over the suit land and on 15-8-2008 defendant Nos. 1 and 2 threatened the plaintiff to dispossess from the suit land; Hence the suit.

3. On 16-6-2009, defendants-petitioners filed an application under Order VII, rule 11 of the Code of Civil Procedure for rejection of plaint on the ground that the suit is barred by res-judicata as because regarding the selfsame property, plaintiff filed Title Suit No. 59 of 1999 against the same set of defendants for permanent injunction which was dismissed vide judgment and decree dated 19-4-2005.

4. After hearing the parties and perusing relevant papers/documents learned Assistant Judge rejected the application and directed the parties to maintain status-quo.

5. Being aggrieved, defendants as petitioners filed Civil Revision No. 16 of 2009 under section 115(2) of the Code of Civil Procedure in the Court of learned District Judge, Moulvi bazar. After hearing the parties and perusing relevant papers/documents, learned District Judge dismissed the civil revision and thereby affirm findings of the trial court.

6. Having aggrieved by and dissatisfied with the judgment and order, defendants as petitioners preferred this revisional application under-section 115(4) of the Code of Civil Procedure and obtained leave along with an order of stay.

7. Mr. Tabarak Hossain, learned advocate appearing for the petitioners submits that the former suit for permanent injunction between the same parties over the selfsame property was finally decided by a competent court vide judgment and decree dated 19-4-2005 and, as such, present suit i.e. Title Suit No. 108 of 2008 is barred by res-judicata. He also submits that the court below committed an illegality in not holding that the cause of action as stated in the former suit was 15-11-1999 as such, present suit for declaration after 9(nine) years from the date of cause of action is clearly barred by limitation. In support of his submissions, learned advocate referred to the case of Abdul Malek Sawdagar vs Md. Mahbubey Alam, reported in 57 DLR (AD) 19 and the case of Hafizuddin Sarker and Lakjan Bewa being dead their heirs: Nur Hossain vs Bangladesh, reported in 42 DLR (AD) 57.

8. On the other hand Mr. Sudipta Arjun, learned advocate for the opposite party No. 1 by filing a counter affidavit submits that the issue of the formar suit and present suit are distinct and separate as such, court below rightly and justly passed the impugned judgment and order. He also submits that the plea of res-judicata can be resolved at the trial after framing an issue and cannot be decided from a reading of the plaint. He further submits that the question of limitation is a mixed question of law and fact which can be decided only after taking evidence as such, there is nothing to interfere with the impugned judgment and order. In support of his submissions, learned advocate referred to the case of Md. Danesh vs Md. Kala Meah, reported in 1985 BLD (AD) 275, the case of Rawshan Jamil vs Md. Adiluzzaman, reported in 19 BLC (AD) 129 and the case of Shahabuddin (Md.) vs Habibur Rahman, reported in 50 DLR (AD) 99.

9. Heard the learned advocates. Perused the revisional application, counter affidavit, annexures appended thereof, judgment and order of the courts below and citations referred by the learned advocates.

<u>10. Admittedly, opposite party No. 1 here-in as plaintiff instituted Title Suit No. 59 of 1999 for permanent injunction impleading the petitioners herein along with others as defendants over the selfsame suit land. The suit was dismissed vide judgment and decree dated 30-8-2000 against which plaintiff as appellant preferred appeal in the court of learned District Judge who after hearing the parties allowed the appeal and send back the suit on remand for retrial. It is also admitted that after remand, plaintiff failed to pursue his cause in the trial court which is admitted by the plaintiff in paragraph No. 5 of the plaint of present suit i.e. Title Suit No. 108 of 2008 but question remains whether present suit i.e. Title Suit No. 108 of 2008 for declaration of title, confirmation of possession and permanent injunction is barred by res-judicata in view of the judgment arid decree passed in Title Suit No. 59 of 1999 filed by the same plaintiff for dispute over the self same property against same set of defendants seeking permanent injunction. It is already settled by our apex court that Order VII, rule 11 clause (d) is not available for rejection of plaint under section 11 of the Code of Civil Procedure inasmuch as the plea of res-judicata as contained in section 11 of the Code can be resolved at the trial after framing an issue and cannot be decided from a mere reading of the plaint. It is also settled that the question of limitation being a mixed question of law and fact should be decided only at the trial after taking evidence. Formar suit i.e. Title Suit No. 59 of 1999 filed by the opposite party No. 1 as plaintiff for permanent injunction and the present suit filed by the self-same plaintiff for declaration of title, confirmation of possession and permanent injunction. So, it cannot be said that the issues decided in the former suit are same in the present suit. It appears from the averments of the plaint that the plaintiff failed to pursue his cause in the former suit when the same was send back on remand for retrial for his personal difficulties. Whether there was willful negligency of the plaintiff in pursuing his cause in the former suit after sent back on remand or the plea taken in the plaint is genuine is also matter of evidence. In such view of the matter, I do not find any reason to interfere with the findings of the appellate court below.</u>

11. Facts and circumstances of the cases cited by the learned advocate for the petitioners are quite distinguishable from the facts and circumstances of the case in hand.

12. Accordingly, leave is dismissed without any order as to cost.

13. Impugned judgment and order dated 28-3-2011 passed by the learned District Judge, Moulvi bazar in Civil Revision No. 16 of 2009 affirming those of dated 5-7-2009 passed by the learned Assistant Judge in Title Suit No. 108 of 2008 is maintained.

14. Order of stay granted at the time of granting leave is hereby vacated.

15. Learned Assistant Judge, Rajnagar, Moulvi bazar, is directed to dispose of the Title Suit No. 108 of 2008 within a period of 6(six) months from the date of receipt of this order.

Communicate a copy of this judgment to the court concern at once.

End.
