In the above background of the cases, let us consider the first question i.e. on maintainability of the writ petitions. 32. To decide the question, it is necessary to study the relevant provisions of section 193 of the Act and rules 5(4) and 13 of the Rules. 33. For better understanding, the aforesaid provisions are quoted below:- "Section 193. Appeals to Commissioner (Appeal)-(1) Any person aggrieved by any decision or order passed under this Act, not being a decision or order passed under section 82 or section 98, by an officer of customs lower in rank than a Commissioner of Customs, may appeal to the Commissioner (Appeal) within three months from the date of communication to him of such decision or order: Provided that the Commissioner (Appeal) may, if he is satisfied that the appellant was prevented by sufficient causes from presenting the appeal within the aforesaid period of three months, allow it to be presented within a further period of two months. (2) Every appeal under this section, shall be in such form and shall be verified in such manner as may be specified by rules made in this behalf." “অভিন্ন পণ্যের (identical goods) বিনিময় মূল্য।– ৪) এই বিধির অধীন অভিন্ন পণ্যের একাধিক বিনিময় মূল্য পাওয়া গেলে উহাদের মধ্যে সর্বাপেক্ষা কম বিনিময় মূল্যের ভিত্তিতে আমদানিকৃত পণ্যের মূল্য্ নির্ধারন করিতে হইবে।” ১৩। আপীল।– আমদানিকৃত পণ্যের মূল্য নির্ধারনের ক্ষেত্রে আমদানিকারকের ঘোষিত মূল্য ব্যতীত এই বিধিমালায় বর্ণিত কোন পদ্ধতিতে ভিন্নতর মূল্য নির্ধারণ করা হইলে আমদানিকারককে সেই সম্পর্কে উক্ত মূল্য নির্ধারনের তারিখেই লিখিতভাবে অবহিত করিতে হইবে এবং কোন সংক্ষুব্ধ আমদানিকারক আইনের section 193 অথবা, ক্ষেত্রমত, section 196 এর অধীন উক্ত মূল্য নির্ধারনের বিরুদ্ধে আপীল দায়ের করিতে পারিবেন।” 34. It is true that under rule 5(4) of the Rules, the Customs Authority has to assess goods on the minimum value available for identical goods, but, under rule 13 of the Rules, if the goods are assessed in any other procedure under the Rules except the value declared by the importer, in such case, the aggrieved importer has to file an appeal under section 193 or section 196, as the case may be, of the Act against the valuation of the goods. 35. Now, let us study the decisions as referred to by the contending parties. 36. In the case reported in 54 DLR 72, as referred to by Mr Ariff, it was decided by the High Court Division that,- "it is borne out from record that the impugned order was corum non judice having been passed by the Chairman of the Board alone without the presence and participation of other members who also did not sign the impugned order. As a Result the impugned order was wholly without jurisdiction and hence void. It is needless to mention here that section 5 of the Limitation Act was not applicable in the instant case. Moreover, the impugned order as we have found is illegal and without jurisdiction. Therefore, the petitioner, in our opinion, is not debarred from invoking writ jurisdiction of this Court under Article 102 of the Constitution without availing of the alternative remedy by way of appeal before the Revenue Authority." 37. In this referred case, the constitution of the Debt Settlement Board itself was not proper, as there was absence of two other members and the Chairman alone passed the impugned order. So, the order was corum non-judice. This is not the scenario of the instant cases. 38. In the case reported in 31 DLR 184, it was decided by the High Court Division as under:- "It is true that an alternative remedy was available but it was not availed of. Ordinarily writ jurisdiction is not available to a person who does not seek alternative remedy provided by law but this provision may be waived if an impugned order is, on the face of it, without jurisdiction or is violative of any provision of the Constitution." 39. In this case, the High Court Division decided that writ jurisdiction may be availed of on the ground that the notice served was not a notice as contemplated in Article 177 of the late Constitution. This is not also relevant to the present cases. 40. However, we are in agreement with the view taken by their lordships in the above two cases as referred by Mr Arif that if an order is corum non-judice/without jurisdiction, a person may invoke writ jurisdiction in such case. 41. The 3rd case referred by Mr AFM Hasan Arif is the unreported judgment date 19-1-2015 passed by the High Court Division in Writ Petition No. 2777 of 2006. This case is relating to declaration that assessment of duty @ 25% is violative of Article 27 of the Constitution being discriminatory. So, the facts and circumstances of this case is quite distinguishable from the instant cases and, as such, this decision is not also applicable here. 42. The latest decision of the Appellate Division as placed before us by the learned Deputy Attorney-General is the decision reported in 20 BLC (AD) 64. The judgment of this case was delivered on July 22, 2014. In this case, their lordships decided as under:- "Admittedly, the respondent has filed the writ-petition challenging the order dated 31-1-1995 (Annexure-E to the writ-petition), that is, the assessment made by the Customs Authority on the imported goods. Such assessment made by the Customs Authority can only be challenged by filing an appeal as proved under section 193 of the Customs Act. Section 193 of the Customs Act as quoted below: '193. Appeals to Commissioner (Appeal)-(1) Any person aggrieved by any decision or order passed under the Act, not being a decision or order passed under section 82 or section 98, by an officer of customs lower in rank than a Commissioner of Customs, may appeal to the Commissioner (Appeal) within three months from the date of recommendation to him of such decision or order. Provided that the Commissioner (Appeal) may, if he is satisfied that the appellant was prevented by sufficient causes from presenting the appeal within the aforesaid period of three months, allow it to be presented within a further period of two months. (2) Every appeal under this section, shall be in such form and shall be verified in such manner as may be specified by rules made in this behalf.' Having considered the above section, we find that a person aggrieved by a decision or order passed, under this Act may appeal to the Commissioner (Appeal) within 3 (three) months from the date of communication to him of such decision or order. The assessments order dated 31-1-1995 comes within the purview of section 193 of the Customs Act and, as such, the writ petition filed by the respondent before the High Court Division was not at all maintainable. 43. In this connection, reliance may be placed on the case of Bangladesh vs Mizanur Rahman, 52 DLR 149, in which, it has been held as under: 'In the instant case, the writ-petitioner released the imported goods on payment of the assessed duty and he neither preferred an appeal against the order of assessment under section 193 of the Act nor filed any application for refund of the alleged excess duty under section 33 of the Act nor gave any explanation for non-filing of any appeal or application for refund. In the face of provisions for appeals under sections 193 and 196 of the Act and also provision for refund of any excess duty under section 33 of the Act within six months of such payment his writ petition is not maintainable. Having considered the case referred to the above, we are of the view that the principle expounded in the above case applies to the facts and circumstances of the present case and therefore, they very writ petition filed by the respondent was not maintainable. Classification of the imported goods and assessment thereon by the Customs Authority are disputed questions of fact which could not be resolved in the writ jurisdiction. The High Court Division exercised writ jurisdiction without considering this aspect of the case at all and on this score alone the writ petition was not maintainable." 44. From this decision, it is evident that in this case the Appellate Division held that the writ petition is not maintainable on two counts-the first one was that the assessment order comes within the purview of section 193 of the Customs Act and, as such, the writ petition filed by respondent before the High Court Division was not at all maintainable. The second was that disputed question of fact was involved in the case. So, writ petition was not maintainable. Thus, by this decision, the Appellate Division clearly set out the principle that assessment made by the Customs Authority can only be challenged by filing an appeal as provided under section 193 of the Customs Act, 1969. The said decision of the Appellate Division is binding upon us. 45. Similar decision was taken in the unreported judgment dated 23-7-2014 passed in Writ Petitions No. 4406 of 2012, 5466 of 2012 and 5789 of 2012 wherein their lordships decided as under:- "Even after knowing the fact of final assessment made on 4-4-2012 and the same order of final assessment was informed to the Bank Manager by the impugned letters. These Writ Petitions were filed even after knowing about the final assessment. The petitioners did not undertake the appropriate forum as per the provision of the Customs Act. 1969 including section 193 and/or 196 filing of appeal/review before the Appellate Tribunal constituted under the Customs Act as the appropriate forum including. the Commissioner of Customs and/or Customs Appellate Tribunal, instead, the petitioners filed this Writ Petitions, without exhausting the above forum challenging the final assessment even after knowing through the impugned orders as to the final assessment made by the Customs. Authority of the imported goods. In such circumstances we are of the view that these Writ Petitions do not merit any further discussion as these Writ Petitions have been filed challenging the encashment of the bank guarantees furnished by the petitioners in order to get the imported goods released which are merely consequences final assessment made by the Customs Authority as per provisions of the Customs Act 1969 the Valuation Rules. 200 and also pursuant to the judgments and orders passed by this court on the Writ Petitions in the year of 2005, thus, these writ petitions are premature. Accordingly, we do not find merit in the Rules." 46. Now, let us study whether the final assessments made by the customs authority are corum non-judice/without jurisdiction. 47. It is not the case of the petitioners that the assessments were made by a person not legally empowered/competent to make assessment. Rather, it is the case of the petitioners that the relevant customs authority made assessments violating the provision of rule 5(4) of the Rules. Thus, it appears that the assessment was made by person/persons having legal jurisdiction to make assessment, but assessments were made wrongly, not following rule 5(4) of the Rules. 48. In this matter, our considered view is that there is a difference between an order passed by a competent person/authority having legal jurisdiction to entertain and decide the matter but which suffers from some irregularity error (wrong) and an order passed by a person who has no competency or jurisdiction to entertain and decide the matter at all. An order may also be without jurisdiction if it is passed by a person not being lawfully appointed as an authority to pass such order. In the former case, a person's remedy lies before the appellate forum, if such forum is available under a law and in the later cases, a person may avail writ jurisdiction. 49. In the light of our above observations, we are of the view that if an assessment order is passed by a person, who has no legal competency/authority to make assessment, in such case 'a person aggrieved' may invoke writ jurisdiction. A person may also avail writ jurisdiction if on the face of assessment order, it is apparent that those are malafide or fraudulent. In other cases a person aggrieved by an assessment order has to file an appeal under sections 193/196 of the Act read with rule 13 of the Rules. 50. In these cases, admittedly, final assessments were made by person/persons who had legal authority/competency to make final assessments. The case of the petitioners, as it transpires from the materials on record, that the assessments were made wrongly and not following the provision of rule 5(4) of the Rules. 51. In the above admitted scenario, our considered view is that the petitioners' remedy lies in the appellate forum. 52. In the facts and circumstances as discussed in the foregoing paragraphs, vis-a-vis the law, we are of the view is that the instant writ petitions are not maintainable and the petitioners appropriate remedy is by way of preferring appeals before the appropriate Customs Authority in accordance with the provisions of rule 13 of the Rules read with sections 193/196 of the Act. 53. Further, we would like to mention that in the affidavit-in-reply, respondent No. 7 Mr AHM Shahabuddin Nagari himself admitted that he did not get any information regarding price anywhere by different searches of sugar price, raw sugar price and price of sugar from Brazil and so, wrote "Not available." He further admitted that the Customs House, Chittagong had full authority to ignore the price supplied the office of respondent No. 7. He also admitted that he supplied the highest and lowest values to the Chittagong Customs House on the basis of 100 bills of entry of sugar imported from Brazil, India, Guatemala and some bills of entry from Thailand. Therefore, it is evident from the affidavit-in-reply of respondent No. 7 that he has not supplied the value at which the sugar of different origins had been assessed by the Customs Authorities at the relevant time. Rather, he supplied the values mentioned in the bills of entry by the importers. In the affidavit-in-reply, respondent No. 2 also clearly stated that respondent No. 7 has not discharged his function duly and whimsically supplied data relating to values of sugar (Annexures-C and D) prepared on the basis of disputed invoices sup-plied by the petitioners. Therefore, the fruitless data base supplied by respondent No. 7 was ignored by the committee lawfully and the committee following the provisions of the Rules and the Act lawfully assessed the goods to duties. 54. The aforesaid disputed facts cannot be decided in exercising jurisdiction under article 102 of the Constitution and this question may only be decided in appellate forum. On this count also the instant writ petitions are not maintainable. 55. In view of the discussions made in the foregoing paragraphs, vis-a-vis the law, we find no merit in the arguments of Mr Arif and we find merit and force in the arguments of Mr Maniruzzaman. 56. Since it has been decided that the instant writ petitions are not maintainable, we do not like to embark upon the other question raised in these writ petitions. 57. In the result, the Rules are discharged without any order as to costs. 58. The orders of stay stand vacated. 59. The petitioners are at liberty to avail the forum of appeal in accordance with law, if not otherwise barred by limitation. 60. This judgment of ours do govern Writ Petitions No. 9567 of 2011, 9568 of 2011, 9569 of 2011, 9608 of 2011, 9653 of 2011, 9654 of 2011, 9655 of 2011, 9657 of 2011, 9659 of 2011, 9660 of 2011, 9661 of 2011, 9662 of 2011, 2993 of 2011, 9664 of 2011 and 9665 of 2011. Communicate the judgment to respondent No. 1 at once. End.

case_source: (From the Judgment and Order dated July 19, 1992 passed by the High Court Division in Writ Petition No. 336 of 1987)
full_judgment:
Md Ruhul Amin J: The appeal, by leave, is against the judgment dated July 19, 1992 of the High Court Division in Writ Petition No. 336 of 1987 making the Rule absolute and thereupon declaring inclusion of the building in holding No. 6/5, Block F, Lalmatia, Mohammadpur, Dhaka in the list of abandoned buildings unlawful and without lawful authority.

2. Facts, in short, are that the property in question was owned by one Mr SM Hasan who got the same by lease deed dated May 31, 1966 from the Government of the then East Pakistan. It is the case of the respondent that while said Mr SM Hasan was owning and possessing the property in question he, on August 1, 1973, entered into a written agreement to sell the property for a consideration of Taka 28,000 and that upon receiving Taka 27,000 executed a deed of agreement on 1-8-1973, that Mr SM Hasan delivered possession to the respondent and since then he is owning and possessing the property in question, that as Mr SM Hasan did not execute and register the deed in favour of the respondent he was constrained to file Title Suit No. 528 of 1978 on 2-10-1978 for the specific performance of contract for sale of land, that the summons of the said suit was served on the defendants including the Government of Bangladesh, that the suit ultimately was decreed ex parte on 15-6-1979 and the respondent through the Court got the kabala executed and registered on September 20, 1979. Thereafter, the respondent got his name recorded in the Revenue record and that also got his name recorded in the offices providing utility services and paid the rates and taxes.

3. It is the contention of the respondent that while he was in peaceful enjoyment of the property in question the same was listed as abandoned property in the list of abandoned buildings and the list was published in the Gazette on September 23, 1986.

4. The respondent filed case, being No. 17 of 1987 (Kha 14, Lalmatia, Mohammadpur) seeking release of the property before the Court of Settlement as per provision of section 7 of the Ordinance No. 54 of 1985 averring the facts as stated hereinabove.

5. The appellant No. 1 contested the case before the Court of Settlement contending, amongst others, that listing of the property in the Kha list is guide legal. It was the specific case of the appellant No. 1 that after liberation of the country whereabouts of Mr SM Hasan, the owner of the property were not known and that he was not in Bangladesh and thereupon the property having had assumed the character of the abandoned property the same has legally been listed in the list of abandoned buildings. It was also the contention of the appellant No. 1 before the Court of Settlement that the agreement for sale claimed to have been executed by Mr SM Hasan is not genuine and that the agreement for sale is a fabricated one and that the same has been brought into existence only to grab the property.

6. It may be mentioned section 7 of the Ordinance No. 54 of 1985 requires the claimant of the property, who has filed petition before the Court of Settlement seeking exclusion of the property from the list of abandoned buildings, or to return the same to him or contending that the building is not an abandoned property and has not vested in the Government and that his right and interest in the building has not been affected by the provision of the Ordinance No. 54 of 1985, is to establish that the building in question is not an abandoned property. So, it is seen from the provision of section 7 of the Ordinance that onus of establishing that the inclusion of the building, i.e. exclusion whereof from the list of abandoned properties has been sought for by a claimant of the building, in the list of abandoned building is not legal is on the claimant and he is to establish that the building in question is not an abandoned property.

7. It is seen from the judgment of the Court of Settlement that the respondent herein before the said Court based his claim in the property in question on the basis of the ex parte decree obtained in the suit filed seeking specific performance of contract for sale of land said to have been entered into between the respondent and Mr SM Hasan, the owner of the property on the basis of lease from the Government of the then East Pakistan. It is also seen from the judgment of the Court of Settlement that the said Court directed the respondent to file the deed of agreement said to have been executed by Mr SM Hasan and the lease deed on the basis whereof Mr SM Hasan got the property in question. Although the respondent took time to produce the said documents but ultimately did not produce the said documents before the Court of Settlement. It seems the Court of Settlement in the background of the contentions of the appellant No. 1 who was opposite party before the Court of Settlement, that the agreement for sale said to have been executed by Mr SM Hasan was not genuine and that Mr SM Hasan after emergence of Bangladesh was not in Bangladesh and that when PO 16 of 1972 came into force whereabouts of Mr SM Hasan, prior to that and after that, were not known, directed the respondent to produce the said documents to ascertain the genuineness of the agreement for sale claimed to have been executed by Mr SM Hasan on August 1, 1973.

8. It may be mentioned the Court of Settlement when it finally took up the case for hearing on the date fixed neither the respondent nor his lawyer was present. The Court of Settlement dismissed the case on the finding "From the papers submitted before us by the parties and in the absence of original agreement for sale and that other evidence on the point it is difficult for us to appreciate the case of the petitioner."

9. In the fact and circumstances mentioned above we find that the petitioner has not been able to establish his case as asked for.

10. As against the judgment of the Court of Settlement the respondent moved the High Court Division in writ jurisdiction and obtained the Rule. The High Court Division on the findings and observations that the Court of Settlement disregarded the ex parte decree and also the kabala in favour of the petitioner (herein respondent) on the ground that he was not able to furnish the deed of agreement which was the basis of the ex parte decree and the kabala, and that the Court of Settlement did not refer to any other aspect of the case, that no notice was issued upon the petitioner before enlisting the property in the Kha list as required by section 4 of the Ordinance No. 54 of 1985, that as per provision of Article 7(3) of PO 16 of 1972 the Government is required to serve a notice if it intends to take possession of the building which has been considered as abandoned building or abandoned property, that in case of noncompliance with the notice served under Article 7(3) of PO 16 of 1972 the Government is required to proceed as per provision of Article 7(4) of PO 16 of 1972, that as no notice under section 7(3) of PO 16 of 1972 was served thereby the petitioner was deprived of valuable right to approach the appropriate authority as per provision of the said PO 16 of 1972 for the redress of his grievance as regard treating the property as abandoned and, as such, non service of notice under Article 7(3) of PO 16 of 1972 "has itself rendered the inclusion of the property in question in the Kha list illegal", that the Court of Settlement went beyond its jurisdiction in dismissing the case upon ignoring the ex parte decree and later on the kabala executed through the Court in favour of the petitioner and that in ignoring the said decree and kabala the Court of fact, in fact, made those nugatory, that as per provision of section 7 of the Ordinance of 1985 the Court of Settlement is limited to the consideration of right or interest of the claimant of the property and examination of title or questioning the same is not within the jurisdiction of the said Court, that the Court of Settlement is not authorised to adjudicate the title of the claimant, particularly when there is a decree of the civil Court, that jurisdiction of the Court of Settlement is primarily limited to the inquiry whether the property is an abandoned property and that in the presence of a decree of the civil Court the Court of Settlement which has been established for a specific purpose is not authorized to give a contrary finding as to the title of the party, that the Court of Settlement was in error in not giving any finding whether the notice under Article 7(3) of PO 16 of 1972 was served upon the petitioner and that the Court of Settlement only because of the absence of the deed of agreement and the original lease deed was in error in holding that the ex parte decree and the kabala were fraudulent, that no notice was served on the petitioner before listing the property. The High Court Division finally observing "thus we are in a position to say that the Court of Settlement was not authorised to nullify the decree obtained from the Civil Court and the kabala in favour of the petitioner only on the ground that the petitioner was not able to file the original deed of agreement" made the Rule absolute upon setting aside the order of the Court of Settlement and thereupon declared that the property in question is not an abandoned property.

11. Leave was granted to consider the contentions that the High Court Division was wrong in holding that the Court of Settlement was wrong in not excluding the property in question from the list of abandoned property in view of the decree of specific performance obtained by the writ petitioner-respondent and that the High Court Division was wrong in assuming that non-service of notice in treating the property as abandoned property is an admitted fact and holding that in the absence of service of notice the property cannot be treated as an abandoned property.

12. It may be mentioned the High Court Division while making the Rule absolute has observed "in the instant case it is not disputed that no notice was issued upon the petitioner before enlisting the property in the `Kha' list, and therefore want of notice from the Government to the petitioner under Article 7(3) of PO 16 of 1972 has itself rendered the inclusion of the property in question in the 'Kha' list illegal. Therefore, we hold that the Settlement Court erred in not giving any finding whether the notice upon the petitioner under Article 7(3) of PO 16 of 1972 was served upon the petitioner. We find that no notice was actually served".

13. The writ respondent i.e. the appellant No. 1 contested the Rule by filing affidavit-in-opposition. The said respondent denied the contention of the writ petitioner as to non-service of notice prior to the listing of the property as abandoned property and publication of the list in the Gazette and thereupon, it was asserted that notice was issued and served on the occupant of the property as per provision of Ordinance No. 54 of 1985 prior to the listing of the property as abandoned property and publication of the list in the official Gazette.

<u>14. In our view in the background of the aforesaid assertion of the respondent i.e. appellant No. 1, the High Court Division was in serious error in holding that non service of notice prior to the listing of the property is an undisputed one. We are of the view that the High Court Division was in error in holding that no notice was served prior to the listing of the property since the writ petitioner did not place any material before the Court of Settlement in support of his contention that in listing the property as abandoned property no notice was served. The petitioner did not lead any evidence to substantiate his contention as to non service of notice since it is not seen from the judgment of the Court of Settlement that any such contention was raised and the respondent made attempt to establish his claim of non-service of notice in listing the property as abandoned property. It may be mentioned because of the provision of sections 5(2) and 7(1) of the Ordinance No. 54 of 1985 whatever facts are asserted by the petitioner before the Court of Settlement in support of his claim to the property listed as abandoned, it is he who is to establish the same and thereupon onus to rebut the said fact is on the authority that listed the property as abandoned property.</u>

<u>15. It is seen from the judgment of the High Court Division that it has taken serious exception as regard the judgment of the Court of Settlement in dismissing the petition filed by the respondent under section 7 of the Ordinance No. 54 of 1985 for not taking into consideration the ex parte decree in a suit for specific performance of contract for sale of land and the kabala obtained in execution of the said decree as regard the property in question. In the case of CQMH Md Ayub Ali vs Bangladesh and others reported in 47 DLR (AD) 71 it has been held that a decree in suit for specific performance of contract for sale of land is not a bar for listing a building as abandoned building. This being the position the listing of the building in question as abandoned property was quite legal. Provision of section 7 of the Ordinance No. 54 of 1985 enjoins upon the claimant of the property, which has been listed as abandoned property, in view of the provision of section 5(2) of the Ordinance, to establish that the building listed as abandoned is not an abandoned property. From the judgment of the Court of Settlement it is seen that the respondent miserably failed to establish before the said Court that the building in question is not an abandoned property.</u>

<u>16. The High Court Division while making the Rule absolute and thereupon declaring that property in question is not an abandoned property held that the Court of Settlement was in error in not taking into notice the ex parte decree in the suit for specific performance of the contract for sale of building in question and the kabala obtained on the basis of the said ex parte decree and thereupon dismissing the case filed under section 7(1) of the Ordinance 54 of 1985. Suffice it to say that as per provision of section 5 of the Ordinance the decree of the kind obtained by the writ petitioner was not a bar in listing the property in question as abandoned building as has been held by this Division in the case reported in 47 DLR (AD) 71. On going through the judgment of the High Court Division it is seen that the said Division proceeded on the premise that the Court of Settlement was in error in ignoring the decree passed in the suit for specific performance of contract and the kabala obtained on the basis thereof but the same was not a legally well founded premises because of the proposition of law laid down in the case reported in 47 DLR (AD) 71. It is seen from the judgment of the Court of Settlement that the said Court in disposing of the case did not enter into the question of title of the respondent, rather proceeded to ascertain the fact whether at the relevant time, in the background of the contention of the appellant before the Court of Settlement that after emergence of Bangladesh whereabouts of Mr SM Hasan were not known and that he was not in Bangladesh either before or after the promulgation of PO 16 of 1972 the owner of the property was in Bangladesh when PO 16 of 1972 was promulgated. To ascertain the genuineness of the agreement for sale, since presence of the owner of the property in Bangladesh at the relevant time was assertively challenged by the abandoned property authority, the respondent was directed by the Court of Settlement to produce the same but the respondent did not produce the said agreement for sale. Undoubtedly, the Court of Settlement was within its jurisdiction in directing the respondent to produce the agreement and the lease deed before the said Court for the purpose of making decision on the question as to whether at the relevant time whereabouts of Mr SM Hasan were known and that he was in Bangladesh. Since those facts are in the negative i.e. Mr SM Hasan's whereabouts were not known and that he was not in Bangladesh after emergence of Bangladesh, and, as such, undoubtedly the property in question on the promulgation of PO 16 of 1972 assumed the character of abandoned building and in that background of the fact the property was legally listed in the list of abandoned buildings.</u>

17. The learned Counsel for the respondent has submitted that the Court of Settlement in disposing of the case did not give adequate opportunity to the respondent to place his case. It has also been submitted by the learned Counsel for the respondent that the Court of Settlement in not allowing the respondent to place evidence and thus having had shut out the opportunity of producing evidence for proper adjudication of the case, as such, the High Court Division was quite correct in setting aside the judgment of the Court of Settlement. It is seen from the judgment of the Court of Settlement that opportunity was given to the respondent to produce the materials required by the Court but he failed to do that and in that background of the fact of the case the Court of Settlement dismissed the case against him. From the judgment of the Court of Settlement it is seen that the evidence which was required to be produced by the respondent for adjudication of the case, he having had not produced the same the Court dismissed the case upon observing that in the absence of the said material and oral evidence "it is difficult for us to appreciate the case of the petitioner" and further observing "the petitioner has not been able to establish his case as asked for". This being the position the submission of the learned Counsel for the respondent that the Court of Settlement decided the case on shutting out the evidence by way of depriving the respondent from producing evidence is not well conceived one. It has also been submitted by the learned Counsel that in view of the provision of section 10(5) of the Ordinance the Court of Settlement was required to decide the case on merit on the basis of evidence on record but the said Court having had not done so the judgment of the said Court has rightly been set aside by the High Court Division. This submission is not correct. Since it is seen from the judgment of the Court of Settlement that the said Court on consideration of the materials brought on record from the side of the respondent and default made by him in not producing the material directed by the Court, the Court dismissed the case on the finding that the respondent failed to prove his case and the Court had observed in the background of the materials on record "it is difficult for us to appreciate the case of the petitioner".

18. In the background of the proposition of law laid down by this Division a decree in a suit for specific conformance of contract and a kabala obtained on the basis thereof is no bar in listing a property in the list of abandoned building. Because of the provisions of section 5(2) and section 7(1) of the Ordinance No. 54 of 1985 it was incumbent upon the respondent to establish that the building in question is not an abandoned property and that the said onus having not been discharged by the respondent or in other words, it having not been established by the respondent that the property in question is not an abandoned property and that it having not been established by the respondent that at the relevant time whereabouts of the owner of the property were very much known as he was very much present in Bangladesh and was managing the property in question the High Court Division was in error in setting aside the judgment of the Court of Settlement. The respondent had also not established his contention that no notice was served in listing the abandoned building. The High Court Division as already mentioned proceeded on the premises that "it is not disputed that no notice was issued upon the petitioner before enlisting the property in the Kha list" although it was the definite assertion of the writ respondent i.e. the appellant, that notice under the provision of Ordinance No. 54 of 1985 was duly issued and served before listing the property in question in the list of abandoned buildings.

<u>19. The law is now settled as to the extent of power of the High Court Division while exercising jurisdiction in certiorari in respect of the judgment of the Tribunal or a subordinate Court and that while the High Court Division exercising the jurisdiction in certiorari the same is not competent to act as a Court of appeal i.e. to reassess the evidence and the other materials on record and then to arrive at a decision which it feels ought to have arrived at by the Tribunal or the subordinate Court in making the judgment although while making the judgment the Tribunal or the subordinate Court did not leave the evidence out of consideration or that misread the evidence or misconstrued the document or misinterpreted the law and that had any one of those errors been not committed the judgment would have been otherwise. In the instant case there is no situation i.e. there is total absence of any of the aforesaid situations i.e. non consideration of the evidence, misreading of the evidence, misconstruction of the document or misinterpretation of the law relating to abandoned property. There is also no error of procedure. This being the position, the High Court Division was in error in making the Rule absolute on the view that the Tribunal was in error in not considering the ex parte decree obtained in a suit for specific performance of contract and the kabala obtained pursuant to that decree. The law is settled now that a decree obtained in a suit for specific performance of contract for sale of the abandoned property is no bar in treating a property as abandoned property and listing the same in the list of abandoned buildings. In the case of Government of Bangladesh vs Md Jalil and others reported in 49 DLR (AD) 26 as to the extent of power of the High Court Division in certiorari it has been held—"It could interfere with the findings of a tribunal of fact under its extraordinary jurisdiction under Article 102 only if it could be shown that the tribunal had acted without jurisdiction or made any finding upon no evidence or without considering any material evidence/facts causing prejudice to the complaining party or that it had acted malafide or in violation of any principle of natural justice. In the absence of any of these conditions the interference by the High Court Division will itself be an act without jurisdiction".</u>

20. In the case of Ayesha Salahuddin vs Chairman, Second Labour Court and another reported in 32 DLR (AD) 68 it has been held—"The jurisdiction in the nature of certiorari is exercised by the High Court Division to issue such writs where the subordinate Tribunals act wholly without jurisdiction or in the excess of it or in violation of the principles of natural justice or refuse to exercise jurisdiction vested in them or where there is an error apparent on the face of the record. The jurisdiction in the nature of certiorari is not so wide or large as to enable the High Court Division to convert itself into a Court of appeal and examine for itself materials to come to a new finding and substitute it with findings of the tribunal whose judgment is under challenge".

<u>21. In the instant case the High Court Division, in fact, in spite of the absence of any one of situations stated hereinbefore on fresh assessment of the materials and placing reliance on the materials which under the law could only have been the materials for consideration by the Court of Settlement, but in spite of having the opportunity respondent withheld the said materials, had the same been filed before it in deciding the question whether the property is an abandoned property and the respondent is entitled to get the property released from the list of abandoned buildings came to a different finding and thereupon substituted the said finding for the finding of the Court of Settlement and then made the Rule absolute.</u>

22. In the background of the findings arrived at and the decision made hereinbefore we find merit in the appeal.

23. Accordingly, the appeal is allowed.

There is no order as to costs.

End.

parties:
Province Of East Pakistan (Now Bangladesh)
Vs.
Syeduddin Ahmed
full_judgment:
Badrul Haider Chowdhury, J:—This appeal by special leave is directed against the judgment and order of the High Court Division in F.A. No.70 of 1964.

2. Bangladesh is the appellant. The respondent as plaintiff instituted the suit for declaration of his title to the suit land alleging, inter alia, that he was alloted 5 acres of Govt. Khas land from mouza Telikhali in 1958. The Settlement was made in Settlement case No.3 of 1958-59. It was duly approved by the Additional Collector and since then the plaintiff has been in possession of the said land. In 1962 the Board of Revenue, it is alleged, by an order dated 3-10-61 cancelled the settlement. Hence the suit.

3. The appellant contested the suit by filing written statement contending, inter alia, that the respondent or the members of his family were not cultivators and he was therefore, not entitled to settlement of Government khas lands under the rules. The Board of Revenue was justified in cancelling the settlement.

4. Plaintiff examined three witnesses and the defendant did not examine any witness at the trial. The trial Court dismissed the suit mainly on the ground that the very basis of the settlement in favour of the plaintiff was lacking namely, the plaintiff was not a bonafide cultivator and since he did not come within the category of person to whom settlement could be given, such settlement was inoperative illegal, without jurisdiction and void abinitio and the same could not be binding against the Government. In this view of the matter the suit was dismissed.

5. On appeal the High Court Division in a carefully considered judgment noticed the kabuliyat Ext.3 and considered the contention whether the plaintiff respondent could validly claim settlement and the Board of Revenue had any authority for cancelling this settlement. Reliance was placed on two unreported decision of the High Court Division in F.A. No.33 of 1964 and F.A. No.226 of 1963. The learned Judges took the view that the Board of Revenue exercises administrative control but such power and control do not extend to cancellation of lease granted by a valid settlement. Ext.3 the Kabuliyat was considered and the view was, if the lessee had violated any of the terms of the lease, the Government could proceed against him for cancellation of the lease and his eviction from the land. In this view of the matter it was held that the Board of Revenue had no authority to cancel the lease granted by the Revenue Deputy Collector, Bakerganj which was approved by the Additional Collector. The Judgment and decree passed by the trial court are set aside and the suit was decreed.

6. Leave was granted to consider the question of correctness of decision given bb the High Court Division and whether the High Court Division erred in decreeing the suit on erroneous interpretation of the expression "bonafide cultivator".

7. Mr. A.W. Bhuiya, Additional Attorney General appearing for the appellant submitted mainly on the ground that the respondent plaintiff did not answer the description of bonafide cultivator and settlement was given by the District Authorities contrary to the direction given in the Government Estate Manual. The Board of Revenue cancelled the settlement in exercise of its power. The decree that has been passed by the High Court Division, therefore, requires to be reversed.

8. The plaintiff was an employee of the Bakerganj Collectorate. He stated in the plaint that he was granted settlement of 12'80 acres of agricultural lands under Mouza Char Acharya in 1952 but as the Char land was the subject matter of litigation he could not be given possession though he paid Salami and rent. He mentioned that in Misc. Case No. 699-R.A. dated 19-8-58, the then Commissioner Mr. W.B. Kadri, C.S.P. gave direction for settlement of some lands to the affected tenants of Char Acharya. He also prayed for settlement as he was affected tenant of Char Acharya. The Revenue Deputy Collector by his order dated 7.3.59 accepted the proposal for settlement of 5 acres of land with the plaintiff and accordingly direction was given to open a new Khatian in Register 1.

9. Ext.3 kabuliyat was executed by the plaintiff in favour of the Collector, Bakerganj. One of the condition of the kabuliat runs thus:

"Within three years from this date I shall stay in the land with my family by constructing suitable dwelling house within the boundary of this land of Kabuliyat. I shall not live in any other house. If I do so or I do not construct a good house or if I do not live on this land, then the Government shall eject me under section 44(B) of the Bengal Tenancy Act. To that I shall not be entitled to raise any objection or I shall not be entitled to claim compensation or mesne profits".

Then again plaintiff stipulated:

"I shall cultivate land my-self or with the members of my family and I shall make the whole land cultivable within the period of this settlement If I do not cultivate the land then the Government shall eject me from this land after expiry of the period of this settlement in accordance with the provisions of the said Act."

10. In the written statement the Government took the stand that kabuliyat had not been signed either by the executor or by the recipient or by anybody, it does not bear any date of execution and the gaps in the 1st paragraph have not yet been filled up. Notwithstanding such assertion, it appears that the name of tenant was entered in Register II as a tenant and the plaintiff was given the possession of the land. The plaintiff paid salami as required and paid rent upto 1962. By Memo No.3191 AI dated 3-10-61 it seems the Board of Revenue cancelled the settlement of the plaintiff on the ground that the candidates of these cases were Collectorate staff and other staff who were serving in strategic positions which enabled them to get settlement for themselves by "exercising undue-influence" (Ext. E/2).

11. An appeal was preferred and it was disposed of by the Secretary, Revenue Department by its order dated 7-7-62. It was considered that the appellants were not entitled to settlement of the Government khas land and as such the settlement with them were not legal "though some of the petitioners claim that kabuliyats for the lands executed by them have been accepted by the Government thereby establishing a relationship of landlord and tenant between them and the Government, that stand is not correct because the Kabuliyats were not accepted by the Collector or an authorised agent of the case" and the order was passed. "The appeals are therefore failed on merit". Then the last paragraph mentioned: "Again, the orders for settlement of lands by the Collector in these were cancelled under Orders of the Governor and not under any order of the Board of Revenue and as such, no appeal is actually maintainable. The result is that the appeal petitions fail."

12. When the order of cancellation was passed the plaintiff was not given a show cause notice as to why his settlement shall not be cancelled. The cancellation order is dated 3-10-61 and by that time the plaintiff went into possession upon payment of salami and rent. The impression that was created was that the order was passed by the Board of Revenue and an appeal was preferred by the aggrieved settlement holders including the plaintiff but this appeal was also disposed of without giving any hearing to the plaintiff. In other words, at no stage the plaintiff was heard as to why his settlement shall be cancelled. This position has led him to file the suit. The learned trial court considered the evidence and came to the conclusion that plaintiff did not answer the description of a bonafide cultivator as mentioned in the Government Estate Manual. According to Government Memo No.12965- L.R. dated the 12-8-1957 certain principles regarding settlement of land have been laid down. Clause (3) reads as follows:

"Lands shall be settled only with a bonafide cultivator or a member of a family of a bonafide Cultivator who will cultivate the lands himself or get them cultivated by the members of his family".

13. It lays down the rule of priority as to who will get preference to get Government khas land: In this case the main objection of the Government is that the plaintiff was not a bonafide, cultivator. It was alleged in the order of cancellation that the plaintiff got the settlement by exercising "undue influence". Neither he was heard nor his appeal was disposed of after giving him any hearing. So the question of undue influence has not been substantiated. In the suit the plaintiff examined witnesses but the Government did not. Therefore the very basis that the plaintiff obtained settlement by .exercising undue influence appears to be lacking.

14. Leave was not granted to consider the question whether the Board of Revenue had authority to cancel the settlement. In passing it may be noticed that the Secretary, Revenue Department mentioned in his order that these settlements were cancelled "under orders of the Governor and not under any order o!' the Board of Revenue and, as such, no appeal is actually maintainable," (Ext.8/a). The learned Additional Attorney General mainly argued on the point that initially the settlement was bad because the plaintiff respondent was not a bonafide cultivator. He relied on clause (iii) of Rule 63 of the Manual which is quoted above.

15. Mr. Bhuiyan contended that the finding of the trial Court was that the plaintiff respondent was an employee of the Government and he was "by no means a bonafide cultivator" and concluded "the Board of Revenue was perfectly justified in cancelling the same which is definitely binding against the plaintiff". Section 76 of the East Bengal State Acquisition and Tenancy Act provides for settlement and use of land vested in the Government and its assets: and says- "the Government shall be competent to make settlement of such land in accordance with such rules as it may make in this behalf or to use or otherwise deal with such land in such manner as it thinks fit."

Provided that no land shall be settled with a person unless he is a person to whom transfer of land can be made under section 90."

"Provided further that in making settlement of any cultivable land preference shall be given to an applicant for settlement who cultivates land by himself or by the members of his family". Section 78 of the East Bengal State Acquisition and Tenancy Act gives the rule making power and clause(zt) provides for the rules for settlement of lands referred to in section 76. In section 82 'bonafide cultivator' is defined for the purpose of part V means "a person who cultivates lands by himself or by members of his family or by, or with the aid of servants or labourers or with the aid of partners or bargadars, and also includes on agricultural labourer;". The learned Additional Attorney General is correct in contending that this definition in section 82 in only for the purpose of that part and this definition is wider then the persons meant by the bonafide cultivator in rule 63(3). That rule is to be taken as principle to be followed in the matter of settlement of the Government khas land and it mentioned 'bonafide cultivator' and includes the "members of the family of such cultivator who will cultivate the land himself or get them cultivated by members of his own family". In other words, it excludes the servants or labourers or partners or bargadars or cultivator labourer. The idea is plain, namely, Government land should be settled with the bonafide cultivator or a member of the family of bonafide cultivator. The emphasis is on "who will cultivate the land himself or get them cultivated by the members of his own family". Ext.3 the kabuliat exactly speaks in the same terms: "I shall cultivate land myself or with the members of my family ". When in the kabuliyat members of the family are included, it is difficult to appreciate the judgment of the trial court when the evidence of P.W.3 Fazlul Hoque was brushed aside by observing: "I decide that Fazlul Huq simply looks after and manages the suit property under the plaintiff" and concluded that "Fazlul Huq the nephew of the plaintiff though allegedly resides with his maternal uncle the plaintiff cannot be member of his family". To say the least, those who are conversant with the family condition of our villages would not consider the assertion of P.W.3 Fazlul Hoque as something improbable when he says that he resides in the plaintiff's house and manages his property and also ploughs land.

16. "Member of family" is often defined: in some enactments as to who are/who are not members of the family. Those enactments specify the conditions of conferring certain privilege or liability with which they are to be saddled. For example: The alienation of Law (Distressed Circumstances) (Restoration) Ordinance, 1976 (XXVIII of 1976) provides for restoration of alienated land under certain circumstances and transfer of agricultural land with in the specified period shall be deemed to have been made for economic distress if the transferor and the members of his family do not own in the aggregate after transfer more than three acres of land. Section (3) says "for the purpose of this section 'family' in relation to a transferor, includes wife, son unmarried daughter" and excludes a class of people expressly.

17. In the land Development Tax Ordinance, 1976 (XLII of 1976) rate of tax is specified at 90 paisa for standard bigha if the land held by a family does not exceed 25 standard bighas and sub-section (5) of section 3 provides: "for the purpose of this section family is in relation to a person, includes such persons and his wife, son unmarried daughter, son's wife, son's son and son's unmarried daughters" and excludes an adult and married son who have been living in a separate mess.

<u>18. Thus it is clear that the expression `family' is to be understood in the light of the given enactment. In so far settlement of the khas land is concerned the expression 'Family' has not been used in definitive sense; the emphasis is only on the point that the land should be cultivated by himself or by member of the family. Evidence was led by the plaintiff that his nephew ploughed the land who resided with him. This evidence was not rebutted. Since this condition is satisfied it cannot be said that the plaintiff respondent did not answer the description of the person to whom settlement could be made.</u>

19. Next it is to be remembered that the settlement was made in 1959 and the kabuliyat was executed, rent and Salami have been paid, the kabuliyat was therefore acted upon. When the kabuliyat is acted upon, it created a jural relationship between the parties and one of the condition in the kabuliat is that "within 3 years he shall construct a dwelling house and shall not live in any other house". Then it says "if I do so or I do not construct a good house or if I do not live on this land, then the Government shall eject me under section 44(B) of the Bengal Tenancy Act". Section 44(B) of the Bengal Tenancy Act is in the following terms:

"A non-occupancy raiyat shall subject to the provisions of this Act, be liable to ejectment on one or more of the following grounds, and not otherwise (namely):

(b) on the ground that he has used the land in a manner which renders it unfit for the purpose of the tenancy, or that he has broken a condition consistent with this Act and on breach of which he is under the terms of a contract between himself and his landlord, liable to be ejected.

But the lease was not cancelled on the aforesaid grounds. It was apparently cancelled because the plaintiff was not "a bonafide cultivator". The cancellation order was passed by the Governor and not by the Board of Revenue. This cancellation was done without following the principles of natural justice and the plaintiff was constrained to institute the suit wherein he led evidence on all factual aspects namely (a) upon the proposal by the Revenue Deputy Collector the Additional Collector approved the settlement whereupon kabuliat was executed (b) before the expiry of 3 years the settlement was cancelled without observing the principle of natural justice; (c) positive evidence was led that the nephew of the plaintiff ploughed the land who lived with him as member of his family; (d) Government defendant did not adduce any evidence to rebut the claim of the plaintiff; (e) Jural relationship had been created by the execution of the kabuliat, (f) No proceeding was taken under section 44(B) for violation of the settlement condition; (g) payment of Salami and rent had been made and no complaint had been made of any default; (h) that the Governor cancelled the settlement whereas consistent stand was taken that it was a Board of Revenue who did it and the finding was recorded by the trial Court that the Board of Revenue had ample power so to do.

20. We have not heard on the point of power of the Board of Revenue in such matters especially in the matter of cancellation of settlement. It is clear from Ext.8(a) the order was passed by the Governor and not by the Board of Revenue. The observations of the High Court Division on this point need not be taken to have been approved by this judgment. The ratio of the decision rests on the point that at no stage, any investigation was made on the point that the plaintiff respondent was not a bonafide cultivator nor land was being cultivated by a member of his family. If such investigation is not done, as has not been done, the opinion is that the appeal preferred by the Government against the decision of the High Court Division decreeing the suit must be dismissed.

21. In the result therefore this appeal is dismissed. No costs.

End.
